kbs.etymology: Initialism of the English corporate name Korean Broadcasting System, the official title of South Korea's national public broadcaster 한국방송공사 (韓國放送公社). Founded as a public corporation in 1973, its institutional lineage traces back to colonial-era radio station JODK (1927) and the post-liberation Seoul Central Broadcasting Station (1947).

history.meaning: Gyeongseong Broadcasting Station, the first radio station on the Korean peninsula
state-run Seoul Central Broadcasting Station using the international call-sign acronym KBS
Korean Broadcasting System, restructured as South Korea's flagship public broadcasting corporation

kbs.notes: In Korean broadcasting jargon, KBS is also referred to as 공영방송 (public broadcaster) or K본부 (K-Headquarters), and its headquarters in Yeouido is the primary setting of the drama The Producers (프로듀사).

rootFamily.gloss: Korea Broadcasting System (full Korean corporate name)

m.etymology: Single-letter Latin initialism abbreviating MBC (Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation, 문화방송 / 文化放送), where Munhwa (문화 / 文化) means 'culture'. In South Korean television production and journalism, networks routinely refer to rival broadcasters by their initial letter (M, S, K) to avoid naming competitors directly on air.

history.meaning: Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation founded as a commercial radio and television broadcaster
industry shorthand referring to MBC in cross-network dialogue and press reporting

morphemes.meaning: abbreviated initial of Munhwa (문화 / 文化, 'culture') in MBC

m.notes: In television scripts and variety shows on KBS or SBS, staff often say M사 (Company M) or 엠본부 (M-Headquarters) when mentioning MBC programs or personnel.

s.etymology: Single-letter Latin initialism abbreviating SBS (originally Seoul Broadcasting System, 서울방송 / 서울放送, launched in 1990). Used in Korean broadcasting industry parlance as a veiled one-letter designation (often paired with -사 'company' or -본부 'headquarters') to reference the commercial network SBS from rival stations.

history.meaning: Seoul Broadcasting System established as a private commercial television and radio network
national commercial broadcaster referred to by its single initial S in rival network discourse

morphemes.meaning: abbreviated initial of Seoul (서울) in SBS

s.notes: Together with K (KBS) and M (MBC), S (SBS) forms the traditional 'Big Three' terrestrial networks (지상파 3사) of South Korean television.

x파일.etymology: Hybrid loanword compound combining the Latin letter X (signifying an unknown, secret, or classified variable, popularized globally by the 1990s American television drama The X-Files) with 파일, borrowed from English file (ultimately from French file and Latin filum 'thread' used to string documents together). In South Korean media slang, it specifically denotes a leaked confidential dossier of celebrity rumors after the notorious 2005 advertising agency 'Entertainment X-File' scandal.

history.meaning: title of the American sci-fi series about unclassified FBI investigations
leaked corporate research dossier profiling South Korean celebrities' private lives and rumors
any secret dossier, exposé compilation, or unverified gossip sheet in politics or entertainment

x파일.notes: In Korean entertainment contexts, X파일 overlaps with 찌라시 (chirashi, private rumor sheets), but X파일 implies a more systematic corporate or agency dossier.

가.etymology: Native Korean nominative (subject) case particle attached to vowel-final nouns, first attested in early Modern Korean (16th–17th centuries) as a phonological complement to older 이.

history.meaning: nominative marker after vowels
subject particle (post-vocalic)

가.notes: Pairs allomorphically with 이 after consonant-final nouns.

가게.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가게 ('temporary market stall or awning added onto a building').

history.meaning: market stall, lean-to shop
shop, store

가게.notes: Everyday native word for a small retail shop, alongside Sino-Korean 상점 (商店).

가격.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 가격 (價格), joining 가 (價, 'price, value') and 격 (格, 'standard, level').
가격.notes: Coexists with native Korean 값 ('price, worth', as in 반값 'half price').

가구.etymology: Sino-Korean 가구 (家具), compounding 가 (家, 'house, home') and 구 (具, 'utensil, implement, furnishing').

history.meaning: household implements and furnishings
furniture

가구용.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (家具用) formed from 가구 (家具, 'furniture, household fittings', composed of 家 'house, household' + 具 'tool, implement, utensil') and the Sino-Korean attributive suffix -용 (用, 'for the use or purpose of'). Literally 'for household-implement use'.

history.meaning: household utensils, tools, and domestic furnishings in Classical and Sino-Korean usage
designated or manufactured specifically for use on furniture

morphemes.meaning: for the use or purpose of (用)

가구용.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -용 (用) attaches productively to nouns to indicate intended purpose, as in 가정용 (for home use), 업무용 (for business use), and 방송용 (for broadcast use).

가까이.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb and noun formed from the stem 가깝- of 가깝다 ('to be near, close', Middle Korean 갓갑다) + adverbial/nominalizing suffix -이.

history.meaning: near, closely
near, close by

가깝다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) p-irregular descriptive verb (adjective) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 갓갑다 (kaskapta, 'to be near, close'). Internally derived from an older spatial noun root related to ᄀᆞᆺ (kos, 'edge, border, verge') or 갗 (kach, 'near side, surface') combined with the deadjectival/deverbal suffix -갑다, followed by assimilation of the cluster -sk- to tense -kk- (깝).

history.meaning: to be spatially near or closely related (attested in Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447)
to be close in distance, time, or interpersonal intimacy (via cluster tensification sk > kk)

가깝다.notes: 가깝다 is a ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) adjective: before vowel-initial suffixes, the final ㅂ vocalizes to 우, producing 가까워요 (polite present) and 가까운 (attributive 'close/near').

rootFamily.gloss: edge, rim, border (from Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ)

가끔.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'sometimes, from time to time', attested in Early Modern Korean as 갓금 / 가끔, likely related to 갈다 ('to alternate') or 금 ('dividing line, interval').

history.meaning: at intervals, occasionally
sometimes, occasionally

가난.etymology: Nativized Sino-Korean word derived from 간난 (艱難, 'hardship, distress, privation'), composed of 간 (艱, 'difficult, hard, distressing') and 난 (難, 'trouble, difficulty, adversity'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 간난 (kannan), the medial geminate -nn- simplified phonologically to -n- (가난), and its meaning narrowed from general life tribulations to economic poverty.

history.meaning: hardship, distress, severe difficulty in Classical Chinese and 15th-century Middle Korean
material poverty, destitution (after phonological degemination of -nn- > -n-)

가난.notes: Because 가난 underwent phonetic reduction from 간난 (艱難) centuries ago, most native speakers perceive it as a pure Korean (고유어) word rather than a Sino-Korean compound.

rootFamily.gloss: hardship and adversity (literary doublet 艱難)

가느다랗다.etymology: Native Korean adjective built from the stem 가늘- of 가늘다 ('to be thin, slender', Middle Korean 가늘다) + expressive intensive suffix -다랗다.

history.meaning: to be thin, fine
quite thin, slender, fine

가늠하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from the noun 가늠 ('aim, sight line, estimate, standard of judgment') plus the light verb -하다 ('to do'). The noun 가늠 derives from an older Korean verbal root connected to sighting along a line or groove (compare 갈다 / 가르다 'to divide, align') used by archers and carpenters to line up a target before being extended metaphorically to gauging or sizing up a situation.

history.meaning: sighting mark on a bow or tool used to align aim or measurements
to take aim at a target; by extension, to gauge, estimate, or judge a situation

morphemes.meaning: aim, sight, estimate, standard of judgment
light verb deriving active verbs ('to do')

가늠하다.notes: Frequently used with indirect questions such as 승패를 가늠하다 (to gauge victory or defeat) or 깊이를 가늠하기 어렵다 (hard to fathom the depth), and is the root of the gun-sight term 가늠자 (rear sight).

rootFamily.gloss: rear sight on a firearm; benchmark (가늠 + 자 'ruler')

가능성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (可能性) formed from 가능 (可能, 'possibility, capability', from 可 'permissible, able' + 能 'ability, competence') and the abstract quality suffix -성 (性, 'nature, property, -ity'). Coined in Meiji-era Japan (kanosei 可能性) as a philosophical and scientific translation of German Möglichkeit and English possibility, then adopted into Korean in the late 19th to early 20th century.

history.meaning: being able or permissible in Classical Chinese prose
Meiji Japanese philosophical neologism translating European 'possibility / potentiality'
possibility, likelihood, or latent potential in Korean

가능성.notes: In Korean, 가능성 covers both 'likelihood/chance' (성공할 가능성 'chance of succeeding') and 'latent talent/potential' (발전 가능성 'potential for growth').

가능하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun 가능 (可能, 'possibility, feasibility') with the native Korean adjective-deriving light verb -하다 ('to be'). 가능 consists of 가 (可, 'permissible, fitting, can') and 능 (能, 'capable, able, skilled'), reinforcing ability and permissibility together.

history.meaning: can, able to, permissible in Classical and Literary Chinese
to be possible, feasible, or practicable in Korean

가능하다.notes: Grammatically, 가능하다 is an adjective (형용사) rather than an action verb in Korean, so its present-tense declarative form is 가능하다 (not 가능한다), and its attributive modifier form is 가능한 ('possible').

가다.etymology: Core native Korean verb of motion descending directly from Middle Korean 가다 ('to go, move away, pass').

history.meaning: to go, proceed
to go

가다.notes: Also serves as a productive directional and aspectual auxiliary verb (-어 가다).

가닿다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound (합성동사) uniting 가- (stem of 가다 'to go', Middle Korean 가다 kata) and 닿다 ('to touch, reach, arrive at', Middle Korean 닿다 tahta). The compound preserves the literal trajectory of 'going and making contact with a destination', used both for physical arrival and for words, feelings, or signals reaching a recipient.

history.meaning: independent Middle Korean verbs meaning 'to go' and 'to touch/reach'
to go and reach a destination; for a message or emotion to reach someone

가닿다.notes: Whereas 닿다 alone simply means 'to touch or reach', 가닿다 highlights the distance or effort traversed before finally reaching the target (e.g., 진심이 시청자에게 가닿다 'for sincerity to reach the viewers').

rootFamily.gloss: to come and reach hither (오- + 닿다)
to go, move away from speaker

가득.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 가득 ('full to the brim, abundantly').

history.meaning: full, plentifully
full, to the brim

가득.notes: Combines with 하다 to form 가득하다 ('to be full') and pairs with 차다 ('to fill up').

가득하다.etymology: Derived from the native Korean adverb 가득 ('full to the brim, abundantly') combined with the productive adjective-forming suffix -하다. Middle Korean attestations show ᄀᆞᄃᆞᆨᄒᆞ다 (gádòk-hòdà), reflecting the older vowel ㆍ (arae-a) in both syllables of the root before regular vowel shift to ㅏ and ㅡ. Across modern Korean, 가득 pairs with both -하다 as a descriptive adjective and 채우다/차다 in spatial expressions of fullness.
가득하다.notes: Commonly modifies nouns in the adnominal form 가득한 ('filled with'), as in 햇살 가득한 방 ('a room filled with sunshine').

가디건.etymology: Borrowed from English cardigan (named after James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan), referring to an open-front knitted sweater.

history.meaning: buttoned knitted sweater
cardigan

가디건.notes: Prescriptive orthography lists 카디건, while 가디건 is widespread in everyday usage.

가로등.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (街路燈) composed of 가로 (街路, 'street, urban thoroughfare', from 가 街 'street, crossroads, town avenue' + 로 路 'road, path') and 등 (燈, 'lamp, lantern, light'). Introduced during modern urban electrification via Sino-Japanese 街路灯 (gairoto) to designate public lamps lining city streets.

history.meaning: Classical Chinese components meaning 'town thoroughfare' and 'oil lamp/lantern'
gas or electric streetlamp illuminating urban roads and sidewalks

가로등.notes: A classic false friend within Korean: learners often mistake 가로 in 가로등 for the native Korean word 가로 ('horizontally, widthwise'), when it is actually Sino-Korean 街路 ('city street'), the same root found in 가로수 (街路樹, 'street tree').

가로지르다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 가로 ('across, crosswise, horizontally', Middle Korean ᄀᆞᄅᆞ) with 지르다 ('to thrust, take a shortcut, cut straight through'). Because the stem 지르- follows the Korean 르-irregular conjugation, adding -어 doubles the liquid ㄹ to produce 가로질러 ('cutting right across'). In everyday Korean it describes walking diagonally across a courtyard, square, or field instead of going around the edge.
가로지르다.notes: Takes the object particle -을/-를 on the space being crossed (마당을 가로지르다, 공원을 가로지르다).

가루.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean ᄀᆞᄅᆞ ('flour, powder'), which belonged to the alternating ᄀᆞᆯㅇ- stem class before vowel-initial particles. Through the regular loss of ㆍ (arae-a) and vowel rounding in the second syllable, ᄀᆞᄅᆞ developed into modern 가루. It serves as the productive head of many culinary compounds such as 밀가루 ('wheat flour'), 콩가루 ('soybean powder'), and 계핏가루 ('cinnamon powder').
가루.notes: Often triggers sai-siot (ㅅ) in culinary compounds such as 고춧가루 ('chili powder') and 계핏가루 ('cinnamon powder').

가르쳐주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb formed from 가르치- (stem of 가르치다 'to teach, instruct, point out', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄀᆞᄅᆞ치다 kolochita, derived from the root of 가르다 'to divide, sort, discern' plus causative/intensive suffix -치-), connective suffix -어 (contracted to 가르쳐), and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give', Middle Korean 주다 cwuta). Literally 'to teach/inform for someone's benefit'.

history.meaning: to point out, distinguish, and instruct (attested in Hunminjeongeum Eonhae, 1459)
to teach, tell, or show someone something for their benefit (with vowel loss ㆍ > ㅏ)

morphemes.meaning: to teach, point out, inform (from Middle Korean ᄀᆞᄅᆞ치-)
infinitive connective suffix (contracts with 이 to 여)

가르쳐주다.notes: In everyday Korean, 가르쳐주다 often translates simply as 'to tell' or 'to let someone know' (e.g., 전화번호 좀 가르쳐주세요 'Please tell me your phone number'), not just formal classroom teaching.

가르치다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 가르치다 ('to teach, instruct; to point out'), historically derived from the root of 가르다 ('to divide, discern').

history.meaning: to teach, point out
to teach, instruct

가르치다.notes: In Modern Korean, the older single verb split into 가르치다 ('to teach') and 가리키다 ('to point at').

가리다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to cover, shield, screen, obscure'. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄀᆞ리다 (kolita, 'to hide, block from view, screen'). Following the 18th-century loss of the Middle Korean vowel ㆍ (arae-a), ᄀᆞ리다 ('to cover/obscure') merged phonologically with the originally distinct Middle Korean verb 가리다 (kalita, 'to divide, choose, discriminate', from 갈다/가르다), making modern 가리다 a homophonous pair.

history.meaning: to conceal, screen, or block from sight (attested in Yongbieocheonga, 1447)
to cover, shield, or obscure from view (after regular vowel shift ㆍ > ㅏ)

morphemes.meaning: to cover, shield, screen (from Middle Korean ᄀᆞ리-)

가리다.notes: Modern Korean has two homophonous verbs spelled 가리다: one meaning 'to cover/block' (햇빛을 가리다 'to block the sunlight', from Middle Korean ᄀᆞ리다) and another meaning 'to sort out/be picky' (낯을 가리다 'to be shy with strangers', from Middle Korean 가리다).

가리키다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to point at, indicate', diverging in Early Modern Korean from Middle Korean 가르치다 ('to point out; to teach').

history.meaning: to point out, instruct
to point at, indicate

가만히.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 가만 (Middle Korean 가만, 'quietly, still') + adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: quietly, without moving
still, quietly, motionlessly

가방.etymology: Entered Korean in the late 19th–early 20th century via Japanese 鞄 (kaban, 'bag, satchel'), itself widely traced to Dutch kabas ('handbag, basket') or Chinese 夾板.
가방.notes: Functions like a core everyday noun covering backpacks, briefcases, and travel suitcases.

가볍다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 가챦다 (> 가볍다, 'light in weight, not heavy').

history.meaning: light in weight
light, gentle, minor

가보다.etymology: Native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction formed from 가- (stem of 가다 'to go', Middle Korean 가다 kata) + connective suffix -아 (which coalesces into the stem vowel ㅏ) + the experiential auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing', Middle Korean 보다 pwota). Literally 'to go and see', grammaticalized to express trying out a trip or having the experience of visiting a place.

history.meaning: to go and see; early serial verb construction in Middle Korean
to visit a place, go check something out, or have the experience of going

morphemes.meaning: to go, move toward a destination
infinitive connective suffix (coalesced with stem vowel ㅏ)
experiential auxiliary verb ('to see; to try')

가보다.notes: In the past tense (가 봤다 'have been to'), it expresses life experience of visiting a place, whereas in the future/volitional (이만 가 볼게요 'I should get going now'), it softens the announcement of one's departure.

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look at; auxiliary 'to try doing'
to come and see / try coming (오- + -아 보다)

가서.etymology: Inflected sequential connective form of the native Korean verb 가다 ('to go', Middle Korean 가다 kata), consisting of the verb stem 가- and the connective suffix -아서 (where the initial vowel -아- merges with the identical stem vowel -ㅏ-). Historically, -아서 developed from the infinitive suffix -아 plus 서 (originally the stem of 서다 / 셔다 'to stand, exist in a state'), meaning 'having gone and remaining in that destination, (one then does X)'.

history.meaning: having gone and being there (stem 가- + infinitive -아 + 셔 from 셔다 'to stand/be')
go and (then); after going to a place (with vowel coalescence 가아 > 가 and 셔 > 서)

morphemes.meaning: to go, move away from the speaker
sequential and causal connective suffix ('and then, after, because')

가서.notes: Unlike 가고 ('goes and...'), which links two independent events, 가서 requires the second action to take place at the destination reached by going (e.g., 방송국에 가서 만나자 'Let's go to the station and meet there').

가세요.etymology: Polite subject-honorific inflected form of the native Korean verb 가다 ('to go', Middle Korean 가다 kata). Composed of the verb stem 가-, the subject-honorific suffix -시- (Middle Korean -시-), and the polite informal sentence-final ending -어요, which contracts phonologically with -시- into -세요 (-시- + -어요 > -셔요 > -세요). Used for polite commands ('please go'), questions ('are you going?'), statements, and standard farewells.

history.meaning: honorific verb 'to go' in 15th-century Middle Korean
polite honorific present/imperative 'please go; you go' (via monophthongization 셔 > 세)

가세요.notes: Forms the core of the standard Korean farewell 안녕히 가세요 ('Go in peace / Goodbye', said to someone who is leaving, in contrast to 안녕히 계세요 'Stay in peace', said to someone remaining behind).

rootFamily.gloss: to pass away; to return (honorific 돌아가시다)

가수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (歌手) composed of 가 (歌, 'song, chant, to sing') and the agentive suffix -수 (手, literally 'hand', used productively in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean compounds to denote a skilled practitioner or specialist in a craft or activity). Attested in Classical Chinese poetry (e.g., Tang dynasty verse) and standardized across modern East Asia to mean a professional singer or recording artist.

history.meaning: skilled singer or court vocalist in Tang and Song dynasty Chinese literature
professional singer or pop/classical vocalist in modern Korean

morphemes.meaning: hand; person skilled in a craft or profession (手)

가수.notes: The character 수 (手, 'hand') forms numerous occupational and role nouns in Korean, such as 선수 (選手, athlete/player), 운전수 (運轉手, driver), and 기수 (騎手, jockey).

가스레인지.etymology: Loanword compound from English gas range, combining gas ('fuel gas') and range ('cooking stove').

history.meaning: gas-fueled kitchen stove
gas stove, cooktop

cognates.meaning: fuel gas (source of the loanword 가스)

가스비.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining the loanword 가스 ('gas', borrowed from English gas / Dutch gas, originally coined in the early 17th century by Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont as a phonetic spelling of Ancient Greek khaos 'chaos, primordial void, atmosphere') with the Sino-Korean bound morpheme -비 (費, 'expense, fee, cost, charges'). Literally 'gas utility fee'.

history.meaning: aeriform fluid or fuel vapor (coined by J. B. van Helmont from Greek khaos)
household utility bill for heating and cooking gas in South Korea

morphemes.meaning: heating or cooking gas (loanword from English/Dutch 'gas')

가스비.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -비 (費) attaches productively to both Sino-Korean and English loanword stems to name everyday bills and expenses, such as 전기세/전기비 (electricity bill), 식비 (food expenses), and 교통비 (transportation costs).

rootFamily.gloss: living expenses, cost of living (生活費)

가슴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가숌 ('chest, breast, heart').

history.meaning: chest, breast, heart
chest, heart (emotional seat)

가시다.etymology: Subject-honorific verb derived from the native Korean verb 가다 ('to go', Middle Korean 가다 kata) through the insertion of the productive subject-honorific prefinal suffix -시- (Middle Korean -시- before consonant-initial endings, -샤- before vowel-initial endings) plus the citation ending -다. Used to show deference toward the person performing the act of going or departing.

history.meaning: honorific verb 'to go, proceed' in 15th-century Middle Korean texts
to go, leave, or pass away (subject-honorific form of 가다)

morphemes.meaning: to go, move away from speaker

가시다.notes: In addition to honoring someone's physical movement, 가시다 (especially as 돌아가시다 'to go back') is the standard respectful Korean euphemism for dying or passing away.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass away, die (honorific 돌아- + 가시다)

가식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (假飾) meaning 'pretense, affectation, hypocrisy, fakery', composed of 가 (假, 'false, fake, feigned, borrowed') and 식 (飾, 'adorn, decorate, embellish, disguise'). Literally 'false adornment'—the act of dressing up one's outward demeanor to conceal one's true feelings or motives.

history.meaning: superficial embellishment or disguised appearance in Literary Chinese
pretense, insincerity, putting on airs in interpersonal behavior

가식.notes: Commonly paired with the suffix -적 (가식적인 미소 'a fake/affected smile') or negated as 가식 없다 ('to be genuine, unpretentious, down-to-earth').

가옥.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound noun (家屋) formed from two near-synonymous roots: 가 (家, 'house, home, household') and 옥 (屋, 'roof, room, building, dwelling structure'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese and used in modern Korean to denote physical residential structures in legal, architectural, and historical contexts.

history.meaning: dwelling house and roofed structure in Classical Chinese
residential buildings or houses (especially in legal, architectural, or traditional contexts)

가옥.notes: While everyday speech uses the native Korean word 집 ('house, home'), 가옥 belongs to formal, legal, or cultural registers (e.g., 전통 가옥 'traditional houses', 가옥 침입 'housebreaking').

rootFamily.gloss: traditional Korean house (韓屋, clipped from 한국 가옥)

가운데.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가온대, a compound of 가온 ('middle, center') and 대 ('place, spot').

history.meaning: center place, middle
middle, center, among

가위.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'scissors, shears'. Attested as early as the 12th-century Song dynasty Chinese glossary Jilin leishi (계림유사 / 鷄林類事, 1103) transcribed phonetically as 割子蓋 (Early Middle Korean *kăi), and recorded in 15th-century Hangul texts as ᄀᆞ애 (koay) and ᄀᆞ외 (kooy). Through labiovelar glide insertion after the loss of ㆍ (ᄀᆞ애 > 가왜 > 가외 > 가위), it reached its modern form 가위.

history.meaning: scissors (transcribed in the 1103 Song dynasty glossary Jilin leishi)
scissors, shears (attested in 15th-century Hunminjeongeum Eonhae and杜詩諺解)
scissors (via vowel shift ㆍ > ㅏ and diphthongal labialization 가외 > 가위)

가위.notes: Do not confuse 가위 ('scissors') with its etymologically unrelated homophone 가위 in 가위눌리다 ('to experience sleep paralysis / have a nightmare').

rootFamily.gloss: the act of cutting with scissors (가위 + -질)
X-shaped scissor cross or mark (가위 + 표 標)

가위바위보.etymology: Three-part compound noun naming the hand game 'rock-paper-scissors' (literally 'scissors-rock-cloth'), composed of native Korean 가위 ('scissors', Middle Korean ᄀᆞ애), native Korean 바위 ('rock, boulder', Middle Korean 바회 pahwoy), and 보 (clipped from 보자기 'wrapping cloth', attested in Early Modern Korean as 보 / 보션, representing the flat cloth/paper that wraps the rock). Coined in the 20th century as a Koreanized chant replacing Japanese jan-ken-pon.

history.meaning: the three individual Middle and Early Modern Korean nouns for scissors, boulder, and cloth wrapper
both the name of the game 'rock-paper-scissors' and the rhythmic chant shouted by players

morphemes.meaning: wrapping cloth, equivalent to 'paper' (clipped from 보자기)

가위바위보.notes: Notice that the Korean order is 'scissors-rock-cloth' (가위-바위-보) rather than English 'rock-paper-scissors', and in casual games players often chant 안내면 진 거, 가위바위보! ('If you don't throw, you lose—scissors, rock, paper!').

가을.etymology: Native Korean season noun descending from Middle Korean 가싦 ('autumn, harvest season').

history.meaning: autumn, fall
autumn, fall

가이드북.etymology: Borrowed from English guidebook (guide + book), referring to a printed handbook for travellers or visitors.

history.meaning: handbook of information for travellers
guidebook

가장.etymology: Native Korean superlative adverb descending from Middle Korean 가장 ('to the utmost limit; most').

history.meaning: utmost, extreme; most
most, best (superlative)

가장자리.etymology: Native Korean compound historically traced to Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ (modern 갓, 'outer edge, brink, border', preserved in 바닷가 and 창가) combined with an old velar-nasal linking element and 자리 ('place, spot, area'). Literally denoting 'the area along the outer rim', 가장자리 refers to the border or margin of a stone slab, dish, page, or courtyard. It contrasts directly with 한가운데 ('the very center').
가장자리.notes: Used for flat surfaces, cloths, dishes, and yards; compare 모서리 ('sharp corner/edge where two sides meet').

가정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (家庭) composed of 가 (家, 'house, family, household') and 정 (庭, 'courtyard, domestic hall, yard inside a family compound'). In Classical Chinese, 家庭 referred literally to the physical house and courtyard where family instruction took place; in the late 19th century, it was semanticized across East Asia (influenced by Japanese katei translating English 'home') to mean the domestic family unit and home life.

history.meaning: the house and inner courtyard of a family residence in Classical Chinese literature
home, household, and the domestic family unit in modern Korean

가정.notes: Whereas 가족 (家族) refers to the people who are family members, 가정 (家庭) refers to the 'home' or 'household' as a social and domestic environment (e.g., 가정을 꾸리다 'to start a home/family'). Also homophonous with 가정 (假定, 'assumption/hypothesis').

rootFamily.gloss: for home or household use (家庭用)

가져가다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 가지다 ('to have, hold, take') + connective -어 + 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to take and go
to take away, carry with one

가져다드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble compound verb formed from 가져다 (contracted from 가지어다가, 'take and shift location') + 드리다 (humble verb 'to give').

history.meaning: to bring and present to an elder/superior

가져다주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 가져다 (contracted from 가지어다가, 'take and transfer') + 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to bring and give to someone

가져오다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 가지다 ('to hold, take') + connective -어 + 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to take and come
to bring here, fetch

가족.etymology: Sino-Korean 가족 (家族), compounding 가 (家, 'house, household') and 족 (族, 'clan, kin, lineage').

history.meaning: household clan, family members
family

가족분.etymology: Hybrid honorific compound combining Sino-Korean 가족 (家族, 'family') with the native Korean honorific person suffix/classifier -분 ('esteemed person').

history.meaning: family member (honorific)

가족사진.etymology: Sino-Korean four-morpheme compound noun (家族寫眞) joining 가족 (家族, 'family', from 가 家 'house, household' + 족 族 'clan, kin, lineage') and 사진 (寫眞, 'photograph', from 사 寫 'sketch, copy, depict' + 진 眞 'true, reality'). In premodern China and Korea, 사진 (寫眞) meant a painted lifelike portrait; in the 19th century, it was repurposed in Japan (shashin 写真) and Korea to designate camera photography.

history.meaning: lifelike portrait painting ('copying true likeness') in Classical Chinese and Joseon Korean
family photograph or studio portrait of a household's members

가족사진.notes: In Korean family culture, taking a formal studio 가족사진 is a major milestone event marking anniversaries, sixty-first birthdays (환갑), or multi-generational gatherings.

가죽.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가짗 ('skin, hide, leather'), derived from 갗 ('skin') + suffix -욱.

history.meaning: animal hide, leather, bark
leather, hide, pelt

가지.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 가지 ('tree branch; kind, sort, variety').

history.meaning: branch, bough; kind, sort
branch; kind/variety (bound noun)

가지.notes: The sense 'kind, category' developed metaphorically from branches ramifying from a single trunk.

가지다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 가지다 ('to hold in hand, possess, keep').

history.meaning: to hold, possess
to have, hold, possess

가지다.notes: Frequently contracted in speech and writing to 갖다.

cognates.meaning: pardon, allowance; phonetic loan character (仮借)
cognates.word: かしゃ / かしゃく (kasha / kashaku)

가차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (假借) composed of 가 (假, 'borrow, lend, grant temporarily, pardon') and 차 (借, 'borrow, lend, make allowance for'). Originally a Classical Chinese term meaning 'to lend/borrow' (and one of Xu Shen's Six Principles of Chinese characters, 육서 六書, denoting 'phonetic loan characters'), it developed the extended sense of 'granting leniency, pardon, or leeway'. In modern Korean it survives almost exclusively in negative expressions meaning 'relentless, without mercy or hesitation'.

history.meaning: to lend or borrow; phonetic loan character; to grant indulgence or pardon in Classical Chinese

history.form: 가차 (假借) — 가차 없다 / 가차 없이
history.meaning: allowance, mercy, or hesitation (bound largely to negative predicates: 'mercilessly, without hesitation')

가차.notes: Almost a fossilized cranberry word in modern everyday Korean: you will virtually always encounter it in 가차 없다 ('to be merciless/unforgiving') or 가차 없이 ('without hesitation, ruthlessly').

rootFamily.gloss: to be merciless, relentless, unforgiving (假借 없다)
release on parole, provisional release (假釋放)

가치.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound noun (價値) formed from 가 (價, 'price, value, appraisal') and 치 (値, 'price, worth, cost, to be worth'). While attested in Literary Chinese for commercial price, the compound was standardized in Meiji-era Japan (kachi 価値) to translate European philosophical, ethical, and economic concepts of 'value' (German Wert, English value) as distinct from monetary price (가격 價格).

history.meaning: monetary price or commercial worth of goods in Literary Chinese
abstract worth, merit, significance, or economic value in modern Korean

가치.notes: Compare 가치 (價値, abstract 'worth, value, merit', as in 읽을 가치가 있다 'worth reading') with 가격 (價格, concrete 'monetary price tag'). Also forms 가치관 (價値觀, 'one's system of values').

rootFamily.gloss: value system, outlook on values (價値觀)

가판대.etymology: Sino-Korean 가판대 (街販臺), from 가 (街, 'street') + 판 (販, 'sell, trade') + 대 (臺, 'platform, stand').

history.meaning: street-selling stand
street stall, newsstand, display table

가편하다.etymology: Broadcasting production jargon verb clipped from 가편집하다 (假編輯하다, 'to perform a rough cut or preliminary edit'). Combines the Sino-Korean prefix 가- (假, 'provisional, temporary, rough') + 편 (編, 'weave, compile, edit', clipped from 편집 編輯 'editing') + the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). In Korean television production, 가편 refers to assembling raw footage into a draft narrative sequence prior to final editing (종편 終編).

history.meaning: to perform provisional/rough editing of film or television footage
industry clipping used by television PDs and editors for assembling a rough cut

morphemes.meaning: compile, edit (編, clipped from 편집 編輯)
light verb deriving active verbs ('to do')

가편하다.notes: In Korean TV production rooms (like those in The Producers), editing progresses from 가편 (假編, rough cut by junior PDs) to 본편 (本編, main edit) and finally 종편 (終編, final post-production with subtitles, CG, and audio mixing).

rootFamily.gloss: final post-production editing (終編, clipped from 종합편집)

각.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun (角, Middle Chinese *kæwk) originally depicting an animal's horn, from which it extended in Classical Chinese to mean a sharp corner, geometric angle, or edge. In modern Korean military, workplace, and colloquial usage, 각 (角) further evolved to mean crisp, squared-off folded edges (as on laundry or uniforms) and, in slang, a favorable 'angle' or situation (e.g., 각이 나오다).

history.meaning: animal horn; sharp corner, projection, or geometric angle in Classical Chinese and Middle Korean
angle, corner; crisp folded creases (각을 잡다) or a promising situational angle in modern Korean

각.notes: The idiom 각을 잡다 ('to set the angles') comes from Korean military barracks culture of folding blankets and uniforms with razor-sharp creases, and by extension means 'to snap to strict discipline or posture'. Homophonous with 각 (各, 'each').

rootFamily.gloss: angle, degree of inclination, perspective (角度)

cognates.word: 各々 (おのおの / かくかく, onoono / kakukaku)

cognates.meaning: each, respectively (rare reduplication of 各 gè)

각각.etymology: Sino-Korean reduplicated compound 各各 (각각), formed by doubling the Hanja 各 (각, 'each, every, individual'). In Old Chinese, 各 (*kˤak) combined the semantic component 口 ('mouth, call') and 夂 ('foot arriving'), originally meaning 'to arrive independently' before shifting to 'each, separate'. Reduplication in Sino-Korean expresses distributive plurality ('each and every one, respectively').

history.meaning: to arrive separately; each, individual
each and every one; respectively
each, apiece, respectively (adverb and noun)

각각.notes: Can function both as an adverb ('respectively, separately') and as a noun ('each one'), often paired with 다르다 (각각 다르다, 'each is different').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 각각

각도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 角度 (각도), composed of 角 (각, 'horn, corner, angle') and 度 (도, 'measure, degree, standard'). Originally a geometric term adopted across the East Asian Sinosphere during the Meiji/modern scientific translation era to render Euclidean 'angle (in degrees)', it broadened metaphorically to mean 'perspective, viewpoint, or approach' in broadcasting and everyday discourse.

history.meaning: horn/corner + measure/degree
geometric angle; degree of inclination
history.stage: Early Modern Sinitic / Meiji Scientific Coinage

history.meaning: geometric angle; camera angle; analytical perspective

각도.notes: In television production (*프로듀사*) and photography, 각도 refers both literally to camera angles (카메라 각도) and figuratively to the 'angle' or framing of a story (다른 각도에서 보다).

rootFamily.gloss: vision, point of view, perspective (視角)

각서.etymology: Sino-Korean orthographical borrowing 覺書 (각서), adapted from Japanese 覚書 (おぼえがき, *oboegaki*, 'memorandum, note to remember, diplomatic note'), where the native Japanese verb 覚える (*oboeru*, 'to remember') and 書く (*kaku*, 'to write') were read in Korean using the Sino-Korean readings of their underlying characters: 覺 (각, 'to awaken, perceive, remember') and 書 (서, 'writing, document'). In Korean, the sense narrowed from a general memo to a formal or binding written pledge/promissory Undertaking.

history.meaning: aide-mémoire, memorandum, diplomatic note
memorandum of understanding (MOU); binding written pledge of accountability

각서.notes: In everyday Korean drama tropes, 각서를 쓰다 ('to write a 각서') means signing a solemn personal pledge promising never to repeat a mistake, whereas in diplomacy/business 양해각서 (諒解覺書) means a 'Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 각서

각설이.etymology: Hybrid Korean derivative built from the Sino-Korean narrative transition word 각설 (却說, 'setting aside the previous topic; returning to the main story', from 却 'step back, set aside' + 說 'speech, story') plus the native Korean agentive nominal suffix -이 (-i, 'person who does'). Traditional itinerant folk performers and beggars opened their rhythmic chants (*각설이타령*) with the stock storytelling formula '각설하고...' ('Setting that aside...'), causing listeners to nickname the singers themselves 각설이.

history.meaning: setting aside digressions; returning to the main narrative (classical storytelling transition)
itinerant folk performer who sings the Gakseori-taryeong; ragtag street beggar

각설이.notes: Famous in Korean folklore for the upbeat satirical chant *각설이타령* ('얼씨구 씨구 들어간다, 절씨구 씨구 들어간다, 작년에 왔던 각설이 죽지도 않고 또 왔네' — 'The beggar who came last year didn't die and came back again!').

rootFamily.gloss: to change the subject, return to the main point (却說하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 각설이

각오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 覺悟 (각오), composed of 覺 (각, 'to awaken, perceive') and 悟 (오, 'to comprehend, realize spiritually'). Originating in Chinese Buddhist translations as a rendering of Sanskrit *bodhi* or *pratibodha* ('awakening from delusion into ultimate truth'), the word underwent a secular semantic shift (reinforced by Japanese 覚悟 *kakugo*) toward 'mental readiness to face hardship, firm resolve, or bracing oneself for consequences'.

history.meaning: spiritual awakening, realization of Buddhist truth
realization of inevitable fate; mental preparedness for danger or death
resolve, determination, bracing oneself for difficulty

각오.notes: Frequently used in the warning phrase 각오해! ('Brace yourself!' / 'Be prepared for what's coming!') or 각오를 다지다 ('to firm up one's resolve').

각자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 各自 (각자), formed from 各 (각, 'each, individual') and 自 (자, 'self, oneself, nose'). Attested since Classical Chinese texts (such as the *Shiji* and *Zhan Guo Ce*), it literally means 'each person by oneself' and functions in Korean as both a noun ('each individual') and an adverb ('individually, separately').

history.meaning: each person for oneself; individually
each individual, each person's own; separately

각자.notes: While 각각 (各各) applies broadly to objects, cases, or people ('each item'), 각자 (各自) specifically refers to human agents acting independently ('each person on their own', e.g., 각자 계산하다 'to pay separately / go Dutch').

cognates.meaning: each seeks a way to survive
cognates.word: 各自圖生 / 各自图生 (gèzì túshēng)

각자도생하다.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean idiom (사자성어) 各自圖生 (각자도생) combined with the native Korean verbalizer -하다 (-hada, 'to do'). The idiom breaks down into 各 (각, 'each') + 自 (자, 'oneself') + 圖 (도, 'to plan, scheme, seek') + 生 (생, 'life, survival'), literally 'each person devises their own means of survival'. Widely recorded in the *Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty* (*Joseon Wangjo Sillok*), notably during the Imjin War and severe famines when central relief collapsed and subjects had to fend for themselves.

history.meaning: scattering during war or famine so each person may seek survival independently (Joseon Sillok)
to each fend for oneself in a competitive or unsupported environment

각자도생하다.notes: Revived as a major sociopolitical buzzword in 2010s–2020s South Korea to describe hyper-competitive workplaces (like broadcasting stations) or economic crises where institutional safety nets fail and individuals must survive alone.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 각자도생하다

cognates.word: 間 (かん / あいだ, kan / aida)

간.etymology: Sino-Korean bound and relational noun 間 (간, 'interval, space between, relationship'). The Hanja 間 (originally written 閒) is an ideogrammatic compound showing the moon (月) or sun (日) glimpsed through the crack of a double door (門), hence 'crevice, gap, interval in space or time'. In Korean, it frequently acts as a postnominal bound noun expressing mutual relationship between parties (e.g., 부부 간 'between husband and wife').

history.meaning: chink in a doorway through which moonlight shines; gap, interval
space between, interval of time, among
between, among, relationship (bound noun)

간.notes: Do not confuse this relational bound noun 간 (間, 'between') with homophones like 간 (肝, 'liver; boldness') or native/suffixal 간 ('saltiness of food'). Placed after two nouns or a plural noun, it marks mutual relations: 선후배 간 ('between seniors and juniors').

간단하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 간단 (簡單, 간 'bamboo slip, brief, simple' + 단 'single, uncomplicated') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

history.meaning: concise and simple
to be simple, brief, straightforward

간당간당하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic (의태어, mimetic) adjective formed from the reduplicated root 간당간당 (*gandang-gandang*, depicting a small object dangling precariously on the very edge of falling, or a state/supply on the verge of running out) plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Korean vowel-harmony sound symbolism pairs the bright-vowel (양성모음) form 간당간당 (lighter, more acute precarity) with the dark-vowel (음성모음) counterpart 건둥건둥 / 근동근동 (heavier swaying).

history.meaning: swaying lightly at the tip; dangling precariously
to dangle precariously; to be hanging by a thread (of ratings, deadlines, or survival)

morphemes.meaning: be in the state of / adjectivalizer (-하다)

간당간당하다.notes: Used both physically (a loose tooth or a cup on a table edge) and figuratively in workplace/TV drama contexts for a show on the brink of cancellation, a battery at 1%, or someone barely passing a cutoff.

rootFamily.gloss: thrillingly close to danger, hair-raisingly precarious

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 간당간당하다

간만.etymology: Apheretic (clipped) form of the hybrid Korean noun 오래간만 (*oraeganman*, 'after a long interval of time'), which dropped the initial element 오래- ('for a long time', derived from the Middle Korean verb 오라다 *orada*, 'to be long in time'). The remaining stem combines Sino-Korean 間 (간, 'interval, space of time') with the native Korean delimiter/bound noun 만 ('to the extent of, after the passage of a period').

history.meaning: to be long in time + interval + after the lapse of
an interval after a long time has passed
after quite a while, for the first time in a long time (colloquial clipped form)

morphemes.meaning: after the passage of a duration (-만)

간만.notes: Almost always appears with the locative particle -에 as 간만에 ('for the first time in a while; for once') or with the copula as 간만이다 ('Long time no see!'), registering as slightly more casual and punchy than 오랜만에 / 오래간만에.

rootFamily.gloss: after a long time (full standard form)
after a long while (contracted standard form)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 간만

간섭하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound verb 干涉 (간섭) + native Korean verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Hanja 干 (간, originally depicting a forked weapon or pestle, hence 'to strike against, encroach upon, offend, concern') combines with 涉 (섭, showing two feet 步 crossing water 水, 'to wade across a stream, traverse, become involved in'). Together, 'encroaching and wading into another's affairs' yielded the Classical Chinese and modern East Asian sense 'to meddle, interfere, or intervene'.

history.meaning: to encroach upon and wade into; to have a bearing on or become entangled in
to meddle in, interfere with another's autonomy or affairs

간섭하다.notes: Carries a strongly negative connotation of unwelcome nosiness or micromanagement (e.g., 사생활에 간섭하다 'to meddle in someone's private life'), unlike 개입하다 (介入하다, 'to intervene'), which is more neutral.

rootFamily.gloss: constructive/destructive wave interference in physics (干涉現象)

cognates.meaning: to guard, watch over, keep in custody

간수해두다.etymology: Compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 看守 (간수, 'watching over, guarding, keeping safe', from 看 'to look at, watch with hand 目+手' + 守 'to guard, protect under a roof 宀+寸') + verbalizer -하- (inflected in the infinitive/connective form 해 < 하여) + the native Korean auxiliary verb 두다 (*duda*, Middle Korean 두다 *tuda*, 'to place, keep in reserve for future benefit'). Literally 'to guard/look after something and put it away safely'.

history.meaning: to watch over and guard
to take care of / preserve + to put away for safekeeping
to keep safely tucked away, preserve carefully for later

morphemes.meaning: put, keep in place for later (두다)

간수해두다.notes: Adding the auxiliary -어/아 두다 (-해 두다) emphasizes storing something securely so that its safe state is maintained over time (e.g., tucking away a receipt, valuable, or secret document). Also famously used in 몸 간수 잘하다 ('to take good care of oneself').

rootFamily.gloss: to look after, keep safe (看守하다)
nursing, caring for a patient (看護)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 간수하다

간지럽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective from Middle Korean 간지랍다, built on the sensory root 간질- ('tickling sensation') + adjective-forming suffix -업다.

history.meaning: ticklish
ticklish, itchy

간판.etymology: Sino-Korean 간판 (看板), combining 간 (看, 'look at, view') and 판 (板, 'wooden board, plank').

history.meaning: viewing board, shop sign
signboard, storefront sign

갈구다.etymology: Colloquial native Korean verb popularized in late 20th-century South Korean military barracks and hierarchical workplace slang meaning 'to hound, ride, pick on, or mentally wear down a subordinate'. Philologists trace it to an expressive phonological reshaping or dialectal transitive derivation of 갉다 (*gakda*, Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆯ다 / 갉다, 'to scratch, scrape, gnaw away at') or 갈다 (*galda*, 'to grind, sharpen, abrade'), metaphorically 'grinding or gnawing away at someone's nerves'.

history.meaning: to grind, rub, scrape, gnaw at
to hound, rag on, pick on a junior in military or workplace hierarchy (slang)

갈구다.notes: Note the homonymy: in standard literary Korean, 갈구다 can also be a contraction of 갈구하다 (渴求하다, 'to thirst for, crave earnestly'), so context (e.g., 후임을 갈구다 'to haze/pick on a junior' vs. 사랑을 갈구다 'to crave love') immediately distinguishes the two.

rootFamily.gloss: the act of hounding or picking on someone (nominalized form)
to scratch, scrape, gnaw at (probable base verb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 갈구다

갈굼당하다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb combining 갈굼 (*galgum*, the substantive/gerundive noun formed from the slang verb stem 갈구- 'to hound, pick on' + native nominalizing suffix -ㅁ) with the Sino-Korean adversative passive auxiliary verb 당하다 (當하다, from Hanja 當 'to face, undergo, bear' + native verbalizer -하다). Literally 'to undergo hounding; to be on the receiving end of workplace/military ragging'.

history.meaning: hounding, picking on a subordinate (nominalized slang)
to suffer being hounded, ragged on, or picked on by a superior

갈굼당하다.notes: In Korean morphology, attaching 당하다 (當하다) to a verbal noun creates an adversative passive emphasizing that the subject suffered an unpleasant experience against their will (compare 무시당하다 'to get ignored', 배신당하다 'to get betrayed').

rootFamily.gloss: to hound, pick on, rag on someone

갈다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 갈다 ('to grind, whet, sharpen; to plow; to replace/change').

history.meaning: to grind, sharpen; to replace
to grind/sharpen; to change/replace

갈라지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 갈라- (infinitive stem of 가르다, 'to divide, split') + inchoative auxiliary -지다 ('to become').

history.meaning: to become divided or split
to split, crack, fork

갈래.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun derived from the verb 가르다 (*gareuda*, 'to split, divide, part'; stem alternating as 갈르- / 갈-) plus the native Korean deverbal nominalizing suffix -애 (-ae, which turns action verbs into concrete nouns, as in 마개 'stopper' < 막다 'to block', 날개 'wing' < 날다 'to fly'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean from the verb ᄀᆞᄅᆞ다 (*koroda*, 'to divide, branch off'), yielding 갈래 ('a branch, fork, division, or literary/musical genre').

history.meaning: to divide, split, branch off + nominalizer
fork in a road/river, branch, braid/pigtail, or taxonomic/artistic genre

갈래.notes: Highly versatile native word: used for forks in a road (세 갈래 길 'three-way road'), braids of hair (두 갈래 머리 'twin pigtails'), confused states of mind (갈래갈래 찢어지다 'torn into shreds'), and literary genres (문학의 갈래).

rootFamily.gloss: crossroads, fork in the road (갈림 + 길)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 갈래

갈색.etymology: Sino-Korean 갈색 (褐色), compounding 갈 (褐, 'coarse undyed hempen/woollen cloth, brown') and 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: color of coarse brown cloth
brown

갈수록.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean adverb formed from the stem 가- of 가다 ('to go, progress') + correlative ending -ㄹ수록 ('the more ... the more').

history.meaning: as time goes on, increasingly

갈아입다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 갈아- (from 갈다, 'to change, replace') and 입다 ('to put on, wear clothes').

history.meaning: to change one's clothes

갈지자.etymology: Graphic-metaphorical compound built from the traditional Korean *hun-eum* (훈음, 'native gloss + Sino-Korean reading') of the Chinese character 之 (지): 갈 (*gal*, prospective adnominal form of native 가다 'to go', citing the classical verb sense of 之 'to go') + 지 (之, the character's Sino-Korean sound) + 자 (字, 'letter, character'). Because the cursive and printed strokes of 之 switch directions back and forth like a Z, 'the character 갈 지 (之)' became the standard Korean idiom for a zigzag path or a drunken, staggering walk (갈지자걸음).

history.meaning: the Chinese character 之 ('to go' + reading ji)
history.stage: Middle and Early Modern Korean Hanja Pedagogy

history.meaning: a zigzag shape or staggering trajectory resembling the strokes of 之

morphemes.meaning: to go (prospective gloss of 之, from 가다 + -ㄹ)

갈지자.notes: Korean often describes shapes using the *hun-eum* (gloss + sound) of visually evocative Hanja: e.g., 갈지자 (之字, 'zigzag'), 한일자 (一字, 'straight horizontal line'), and 열십자 (十字, 'cross shape'). In dramas, 갈지자로 걷다 vividly depicts someone staggering home drunk.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 갈지자

감.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun 感 (감, 'feeling, sensation, intuition, knack'). The Hanja 感 is a phono-semantic compound combining 心 (심, 'heart, mind') with 咸 (함, Old Chinese *gˤrom, 'all, together; to touch/move'). In Modern Korean (paralleling Japanese 感 *kan*, as in 感がいい 'having good intuition'), 감 is used as a standalone noun meaning 'sixth sense, gut feeling, creative flair, or touch' (часто related to 감각 感覺 'sense' and 직감 直感 'intuition').

history.meaning: to touch or stir the heart; to be emotionally moved
feeling, sensation; gut instinct, creative knack or flair

감.notes: Extremely common in entertainment and broadcasting slang: 감이 좋다 ('to have great intuition / creative flair'), 감을 잡다 ('to get the hang of it / catch the vibe'), and 감이 떨어지다 ('to lose one's touch'). Do not confuse with native Korean 감 ('persimmon') or the suffix -감 ('material fit for, candidate for', e.g., 신랑감 'husband material').

감각.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 感覺, combining 感 (느낄 감, 'to feel, be moved, respond', containing the heart radical 心) and 覺 (깨달을 각, 'to awaken, perceive, notice', built with 見 'to see'). Together they express both bodily perception through the five senses and an intuitive knack or aesthetic flair. In everyday Korean it appears frequently in collocations such as 방향 감각 ('sense of direction') and 색채 감각 ('sense of color').
감각.notes: Pairs with 있다/좋다/뛰어나다 when praising someone's aesthetic flair or intuitive knack.

감귤.etymology: Sino-Korean botanical compound 柑橘, pairing 柑 (감자나무 감, 'sweet mandarin tree') with 橘 (귤나무 귤, 'tangerine, citrus'), both written with the wood radical 木. Cultivated for centuries on Jeju Island and prized as royal winter tribute during the Joseon dynasty, 감귤 functions in modern Korean both as an umbrella term for citrus fruits and specifically for Jeju mandarins. In casual speech, the single syllable 귤 is also used on its own.
감귤.notes: Used as a collective citrus term (감귤류) and for fresh Jeju tangerines (제주 감귤).

cognates.meaning: catching a cold (archaic medical term, kanki; modern 風邪 kaze)

감기.etymology: Sino-Korean medical compound 感氣 (감기), composed of 感 (감, 'to be touched, affected, or afflicted by') and 氣 (기, 'air, breath, vital energy, atmospheric influence'). Rooted in traditional East Asian medicine (attested in Joseon medical treatises such as the *Dongui Bogam* and *Joseon Wangjo Sillok*), it originally meant 'having one's vital energy (氣) afflicted (感) by external pathogenic wind and cold (風寒)', equivalent to Chinese 感冒 (감모). In Modern Korean, it is the everyday word for the common cold.

history.meaning: affliction of bodily qi by external pathogenic wind-cold (traditional medicine)
the common cold (viral upper respiratory infection)

morphemes.meaning: breath, air, vital energy, pathogenic influence (氣)

감기.notes: Korean idioms treat a cold as something that 'catches hold of' you rather than something you catch: 감기에 걸리다 (literally 'to get caught/snagged in a cold'). For influenza, Korean uses 독감 (毒感, literally 'poisonous/severe cold').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 감기

감기다.etymology: Native Korean morphological passive formed from the verb stem 감- (감다, 'to wind, coil, wrap around; to close one's eyes') plus the native passive suffix -기-, which attaches regularly after nasal-final stems ending in ㅁ or ㄴ. When describing objects, 감기다 depicts string, ribbon, or cloth tape tightly coiled around a surface (테이프가 감겨 있다). With 눈 ('eyes'), it expresses eyelids growing heavy and closing involuntarily.
감기다.notes: Often appears in the resultant-state pattern -어 있다 (감겨 있다, 'to be wrapped around').

rootFamily.gloss: to wind, wrap; to close eyes

감다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 감다, representing homophonous roots meaning 'to close (one's eyes)', 'to wind/coil around', and 'to wash (hair)/bathe'.

history.meaning: to close (eyes); to wind/wrap; to bathe
to close (eyes); to wind/coil; to wash (hair)

감독하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 감독 (監督, 감 'inspect, watch over' + 독 'oversee, direct') + verbalizer -하다.
감독하다.notes: Used for overseeing a workplace, directing a film, or coaching a team.

cognates.meaning: being deeply moved, emotional excitement, inspiration
to move emotionally, touch the heart

감동.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 感動 (감동), formed from 感 (감, 'to feel, touch the heart') and 動 (동, 'to move, stir, set in motion'). Attested in Classical Chinese (such as the *Book of Changes* / *Yijing* and *Zhuangzi*, where Heaven and Earth touch and set all things in motion), it literally describes an external stimulus touching (感) the inner mind and stirring (動) deep emotion.

history.meaning: to touch and stir into motion (cosmic resonance or human emotion)
deep emotional movement, inspiration, being touched to the heart

감동.notes: A watch-out for learners: 감동 (感動, 'emotional movement / being touched') differs by just one final consonant from 감독 (監督, 'director, PD/filmmaker')—a frequent pun in Korean variety shows and *프로듀사*! To say 'I was touched', use 감동받다 or 감동하다.

감방.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 監房 (감방), composed of 監 (감, 'to oversee, inspect from above, confine in prison', abbreviated from 감옥 監獄 'prison') and 房 (방, 'room, chamber, cell'). The character 監 originally depicted a person (人 + 臣 'eye looking down') gazing into a basin of water (皿) as a mirror to inspect, evolving to mean 'supervise, detain, prison'.

history.meaning: supervision/prison + room
prison cell within a modern penitentiary or police lockup
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian Penal Terminology

history.meaning: prison cell, jail cell

감방.notes: Specifically denotes an individual cell or shared cell room inside a prison, whereas 감옥 (監獄) or 교도소 (矯導所) refers to the prison facility as a whole, and 독방 (獨房) is a solitary confinement cell.

rootFamily.gloss: solitary confinement cell / single room (獨房)

감사하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 감사 (感謝, 감 'feel, be moved' + 사 'thank, express gratitude') + native verb/adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: felt gratitude, appreciation
to be thankful, to thank

감사합니다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 감사 (感謝, 'gratitude, heartfelt appreciation', combining 感 'to feel, be moved' + 謝 'to thank, acknowledge a kindness') plus 합니다, the formal polite (하십시오체) present indicative of 하다 ('to do, express').

history.meaning: to feel and express gratitude
to be grateful -> thank you (polite formal)

감사합니다.notes: Written -ㅂ니다 is pronounced [함니다] ([kamsahamnida]) by regular nasal assimilation of ㅂ before ㄴ; pairs with native Korean 고맙습니다 / 고마워요.

감상적.etymology: Sino-Korean 감상적 (感傷的), from 감상 (感傷, 감 'feel' + 상 'grieve, wound', 'sentimentality') + determiner suffix -적 (的).

history.meaning: sentimental, easily moved
sentimental

감상하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound joining 鑑賞 with the light verb -하다, built from 鑑 (거울 감, 'bronze mirror, inspect closely, discern quality') and 賞 (상줄 상 / 맛볼 상, 'to prize, savor, take delight in'). In traditional East Asian aesthetics, 鑑賞 described examining calligraphy, paintings, or antiques with clear discernment. In modern Korean, 감상하다 is the standard polite verb for enjoying music, visual art, literature, or natural scenery.
감상하다.notes: Takes artworks, music, films, or scenery as its direct object (그림을 감상하다, 음악을 감상하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to view an exhibition or show

감싸다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 감- (from 감다, 'to wind around, coil') and 싸다 ('to wrap, cover').

history.meaning: to wrap up, envelop, protect

cognates.meaning: taking into consideration, making allowances for

감안하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound verb 勘案 (감안, 'weighing various factors, taking into account') + native Korean verbalizer -하다 (-hada). Composed of 勘 (감, 'to investigate, collate, verify by comparing, deliberate', combining 甚 'intense' + 力 'effort') and 案 (안, originally 'wooden legal/official desk', hence 'case record, proposal, thought, examination'). Literally 'to examine and weigh official records/circumstances before deciding'.

history.form: 勘 (khamH, 'verify, investigate') + 案 ('anH, 'desk, legal case, plan')
history.meaning: to collate and examine official cases/matters
to take into consideration, factor in, make allowance for circumstances

감안하다.notes: Belongs to formal and analytical register; frequently appears in conditional or concessive clauses like ...점/상황을 감안하면 ('Taking the situation/fact into account...') or ...을 감안하더라도 ('Even making allowances for...').

rootFamily.gloss: to endure, bear patiently (堪耐/勘耐하다)

감정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 感情 (감정), formed from 感 (감, 'perception, emotional response to external stimuli') and 情 (정, 'inner feeling, disposition, passion, genuine state', composed of 心 'heart' + phonetic 青). While both characters appeared in classical Chinese philosophy (where 性 is innate nature and 情 is its stirred emotional manifestation), 感情 was standardized in late 19th-century East Asian psychology translations as the equivalent of English 'emotion' or 'sentiment'.

history.form: 感 (komX, 'be stirred by stimuli') + 情 (dzjeng, 'inner passion/feeling')
history.meaning: emotional stirring of the heart in response to things
psychological emotion, sentiment, personal feelings
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian / Modern Korean

감정.notes: Watch out for the common homophone 감정 (鑑定, 'appraisal, evaluation, forensic analysis'). Also, in colloquial Korean, 감정이 있다 ('to have [bad] feelings') or 감정 상하다 ('to have one's feelings hurt') often implies lingering resentment or hurt pride.

cognates.meaning: to dare, have the boldness to (classical/modern auxiliary)

감히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adverb combining the single Hanja root 敢 (감, 'to dare, venture, have the audacity, presume') with the native Korean adverb-forming suffix -히 (-hi, Middle Korean -히). In Classical Chinese epistolary and courtly etiquette, 敢 was used both for bold action and in humble self-deprecating formulas (e.g., 敢問 'I humbly dare to ask'); in Korean, 감히 preserves both the sense of 'how dare [someone]!' and 'if I may boldly venture to...'.

history.meaning: to dare, venture, presume
daringly, presumptuously, boldly (hybrid Sino-Korean adverb)

감히.notes: Has two distinct pragmatic uses depending on person: in 2nd/3rd-person questions (네가 감히! 'How dare you!'), it expresses outrage at someone overstepping hierarchy; in 1st-person polite statements (제가 감히 말씀드리자면... 'If I may boldly venture to say...'), it signals humble deference.

rootFamily.gloss: boldly, daringly (敢行하다, 'to dare to carry out')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 감히

갑자기.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the bound ideophonic/descriptive root 갑작- (*gapjak-*, expressing an abrupt, unexpected, or startling occurrence, preserved in 갑작스럽다 'sudden, abrupt') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -이 (-i). Attested in Early Modern Korean texts (18th–19th centuries) as 갑쟉이 / 갑작이, which underwent morphophonemic resyllabification in standard 20th-century Korean orthography to reflect its surface pronunciation 갑자기. It gradually overtook the older Middle Korean adverbs 믄득 (*meundeuk* > 문득) and ᄀᆞ업시.

history.meaning: abruptly, all of a sudden (from root 갑작- + adverbial -이)
suddenly, unexpectedly, out of nowhere (phonemicized spelling)

갑자기.notes: Compare 갑자기 ('suddenly', for any external event or action happening without warning) with 문득 ('suddenly, all at once', restricted to a fleeting thought, memory, or realization crossing one's mind).

rootFamily.gloss: all of a sudden, abruptly (intensified variant)
with a sudden start, startled (ideophonic cognate root)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 갑자기

갓.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'just now, freshly, newly', attested in Early Modern Korean as 갓 and historically related to Middle Korean 갓/가장 ('just, barely').

history.meaning: just now, newly
freshly, just (e.g. 갓 구운 빵 'freshly baked bread')

강.etymology: Sino-Korean 강 (江, 'river'), from Middle Chinese *kæwng (originally the proper name of the Yangtze River, generalized to large rivers).

history.meaning: large river
river

강.notes: Replaced older native Korean 가람 ('river') in everyday vocabulary.

cognates.word: 強力 (きょうりょく, kyōryoku)

강력하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound adjective 強力 (강력, 'powerful strength, mighty force') + native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Built from two near-synonymous Hanja roots: 強 (강, 'strong, powerful, unyielding', originally depicting a strong bow 弓 and phonetic/beetle 弘+虫) and 力 (력, 'muscle strength, sinew, force', originally a pictograph of a plow or muscular tendon). Combining both roots intensifies the sense to 'high-powered, potent, or forceful'.

history.meaning: mighty strength, powerful force
to be powerful, potent, forceful (of policies, candidates, or adhesives)

morphemes.meaning: be in the state of / adjectivalizer (-하다)

강력하다.notes: Stronger and more formal than simple 강하다; often used as a prenominal modifier or adverbial in news and workplace Korean: 강력한 후보 ('a strong/front-running candidate'), 강력 추천 ('strong recommendation', often abbreviated in slang as 강추), and 강력 범죄 ('violent crime').

강렬하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound adjective 強烈 (강렬, 'intense, fierce, blazingly vivid') + native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Composed of 強 (강, 'strong, powerful') and 烈 (렬, 'fierce, ardent, blazing', showing fire 灬/火 beneath 列 'to split/arrange', originally meaning 'raging fire'). While 강력하다 (強力하다) emphasizes sheer force or efficacy, 강렬하다 draws on the 'blazing fire' metaphor of 烈 to describe sensory, emotional, or visual intensity.

history.form: 強 (gjang, 'strong') + 烈 (ljet, 'raging fire, fierce, ardent')
history.meaning: fiercely strong, blazingly intense
to be intense, vivid, fierce (of impressions, sunlight, colors, or desires)

morphemes.meaning: be in the state of / adjectivalizer (-하다)

강렬하다.notes: Key distinction for learners: use 강력하다 (強力) for power, authority, or effectiveness (강력한 무기 'powerful weapon'), but use 강렬하다 (強烈) for sensory or emotional impact (강렬한 인상 'a striking/vivid impression', 강렬한 눈빛 'a piercing/intense gaze', 강렬한 햇빛 'blazing sunlight').

강물.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 강 (江, 'river') with native Korean 물 ('water').

history.meaning: river water

cognates.meaning: to force, compel, demand by coercion

강요하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound verb 強要 (강요, 'coercion, compulsion, forcing') + native Korean verbalizer -하다 (-hada). Composed of 強 (강, here used in its verbal/adverbial sense 'by force, against someone's will, to compel', Middle Chinese rising tone *gjangX*) and 要 (요, 'to demand, request, require'). Literally 'to demand something by force against another person's free will'.

history.form: 強 (gjangX, 'by force, compel') + 要 ('jiew, 'demand, seek')
history.meaning: to demand coercively, compel against one's will
history.stage: Middle Chinese roots / Modern Sino-Japanese legal coinage

history.meaning: to force, coerce, impose one's will or demands on someone

강요하다.notes: Commonly used for psychological or social pressure as well as legal coercion: 희생을 강요하다 ('to force someone to make sacrifices') or 대답을 강요하다 ('to press/force someone for an answer'). In the prompt's drama line, 강요하시는 mixes an honorific suffix (-시-) with 'forcing' for polite irony toward a superior.

강철.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 강철 (鋼鐵), from 강 (鋼, 'tempered steel') and 철 (鐵, 'iron').
강철.notes: Literally 'hardened iron', used for high-tension piano wire and hardware.

cognates.word: 強 (きょう / つよい, kyō / tsuyoi)

강하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the single Hanja root 強 (강, 'strong, powerful, tough, vigorous') plus the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada, Middle Korean -ᄒᆞ다). In Old Chinese, 強 (*N-k양) combined 弓 ('bow', signifying tension and power) with 畺/弘+虫 (a beetle known for strength and hard carapace). Attested in Middle Korean texts as 強ᄒᆞ다 (*kang-hoda*), competing with and complementing native Korean 세다 (*seda*, 'strong, forceful').

history.meaning: strong bow; powerful, vigorous, unyielding
to be strong, powerful, resilient
to be strong, mighty, resistant (physically, mentally, or institutionally)

morphemes.meaning: be in the state of / adjectivalizer (-하다)

강하다.notes: Takes the locative/dative particle -에 to mean 'strong at / resilient against': 스트레칭에 강하다 ('good at stretching'), 위기에 강하다 ('strong in a crisis'), or 약자에게 약하고 강자에게 강하다 ('gentle to the weak and tough against the strong'). Its direct antonym is 약하다 (弱하다, 'weak').

갖다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed by syncopation (vowel deletion) of 가지다 (*gajida*, 'to hold in hand, possess, have, take'), where the stem 가지- (*gaji-*) drops -이- before consonant-initial endings to become 갖- (*gat-*). Interestingly, in 15th-century Middle Korean, 가지다 (*kajida*, 'to hold, possess') and 갖다 (spelled 갗다 *kachta*, intransitive 'to be complete, ready, fully equipped', the base of transitive 갖추다 'to equip, prepare') were distinct verbs; in Modern Korean, syncopated 가지다 merged phonologically into 갖다.

history.form: 가지다 (kajida, 'to hold/possess') vs. 갗다 (kachta, 'to be complete')
history.meaning: to hold, take, possess (distinct from 갗다 'to be equipped')
to have, possess, hold, or take (syncopated stem before consonant endings)

morphemes.meaning: have, hold, possess (갖-, contracted from 가지-)

갖다.notes: Morphological rule for learners: 갖- is a defective/contracted stem that ONLY appears before consonant-initial endings (갖고, 갖지, 갖는다) or as the colloquial connective 가져 > 갖다 (as in 갖다 주다 'to bring and give'). Before vowel-initial endings (-어/아, -으니, -으려고), you must use the full stem 가지- (가져, 가지니, 가지려고 — never *갖아!).

rootFamily.gloss: to have, hold, possess (full uncontracted verb)
to equip, prepare, possess all requisites (causative of archaic 갗다)
all sorts of, every kind of (adnominal from archaic 갗다 'complete')

같다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 갋다 ('to be like, be the same as').

history.meaning: to be the same, resemble
to be the same, like, similar

같은.etymology: Adnominal (관형사형) inflected form of the native Korean descriptive verb 같다 (*gatda*, 'to be the same, identical, like'), composed of stem 같- (*gat-*) + adnominal modifier suffix -은 (-eun). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean (*Hunminjeongeum Eonhae*, 1446; *Seokbo Sangjeol*, 1447) as ᄀᆞᇀ다 (*kotda*, adnominal form ᄀᆞᄐᆞᆫ *koton*). With the loss of the vowel ㆍ (*arae-a*, which shifted to ㅏ in initial syllables) and orthographic morphophonemicization, ᄀᆞᄐᆞᆫ regularly developed into modern 같은.

history.meaning: to be the same, equal, like (stem ᄀᆞᇀ- + adnominal -ᄋᆞᆫ)
same, identical; like, such as (adnominal modifier)

morphemes.meaning: be the same, like, equal (같- < Middle Korean ᄀᆞᇀ-)

같은.notes: Spacing changes the meaning: when spaced after a noun with a particle or used to mean 'identical' (나와 같은 생각 'the same thought as mine', 같은 팀 'the same team'), it means 'same'; when attached directly after a noun without a particle (너 같은 사람 'a person like you', 가족 같은 분위기 'a family-like atmosphere'), it means 'like, such as, typical of'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be the same, equal, like (base adjective)
together; like, as (adverb derived from 같- + -이)
identical, exactly the same (intensified with 똑-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 같다

같이.etymology: Native Korean adverb and postposition from Middle Korean 가티, derived from the stem 갋- of 같다 ('to be the same') + adverbial suffix -이.

history.meaning: like, in the same way
together; like, as

같이.notes: Pronounced [가치] via regular palatalization of ㅌ before ㅣ.

갚다.etymology: Native Korean verb (고유어) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as the Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447) as 갚다 (Yale: kaphta), from the verbal root 갚- (to return an obligation, repay, avenge). It is etymologically related to the native noun 값 (price, value; Middle Korean 값 kaps), reflecting an ancient Old/Middle Korean root *kap- denoting reciprocal exchange and worth.

history.meaning: to repay a debt, return a favor, or exact vengeance
to pay back (money or debt), repay (a favor), or retaliate (a grudge)

갚다.notes: Used for paying back borrowed money (돈을 갚다), returning a favor (은혜를 갚다), and taking revenge (원수를 갚다).

rootFamily.gloss: to pay back in kind, retaliate

개.etymology: Represents both the Sino-Korean bound counter 개 (個, 'individual item, piece') and the native Korean noun 개 ('dog', from Middle Korean 가히).

history.meaning: unit counter / dog
piece/item (counter); dog

개꿈.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성어) formed from the pejorative prefix 개- (literally 'dog', from Middle Korean 가히 kahi > 개 kay, used productively as a derogatory prefix meaning 'wild, vain, useless, or absurd') and 꿈 ('dream', Middle Korean 꿈 skwum, a nominalization in -ㅁ of the verb 꾸다 skwuta 'to dream'). Contrasts directly with 길몽 (吉夢, 'auspicious dream') or 용꿈 ('dragon dream').

history.meaning: dog + dream (uncompounded roots in Middle Korean)
a silly, meaningless, or chaotic dream with no prophetic value

개꿈.notes: In Korean folk culture, vivid dreams of pigs or dragons foretell wealth, whereas a worthless or jumbled dream is dismissed with '개꿈 꾸었네' ('Just had a nonsense dream').

개떡같이.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb composed of 개떡 ('coarse bran cake', from derogatory prefix 개- 'inferior, rough' + 떡 'steamed rice cake', Middle Korean ᄯᅥᆨ stek), the adjectival stem -같- ('to be like', Middle Korean 같다 kathta), and the adverbializer -이. Originally referring to poor-quality cakes steamed from leftover bran during lean times, 개떡같이 came to mean 'in a sloppy, crude, or half-baked manner'.

history.meaning: rice cake + to be like/similar
like a coarse bran-cake; sloppily, roughly, poorly

개떡같이.notes: Most famously paired with 찰떡같이 ('like glutinous rice cake') in the proverb 개떡같이 말해도 찰떡같이 알아듣다 ('Even if someone explains it sloppily, you understand it perfectly').

rootFamily.gloss: coarse bran cake; something poorly made
perfectly, seamlessly (lit. like sticky rice cake)

개방.etymology: Sino-Korean 개방 (開放), compounding 개 (開, 'open') and 방 (放, 'release, let out').

history.meaning: opening up, throwing open
opening (to the public), openness

개방하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 개방 (開放, 'opening up') + native light verb -하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to open (doors, facilities, or access)

개성.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 個性, combining 個 (개, 'individual, single item, piece') and 性 (성, 'innate nature, character, quality', composed of heart 忄 and birth 生). Popularized across East Asia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries via Meiji Japanese 個性 (kosei) as a philosophical and psychological translation of Western 'individuality' and 'distinctive personality'.

history.meaning: single tally/unit + innate human nature or disposition
distinctive individual character, individuality, uniqueness

개성.notes: In Korean, 개성 있다 ('to have individuality/character') is a common compliment for someone with unique style or charm, often used instead of calling someone merely 'pretty'.

개수.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 個數 (also written 箇數), formed from 個 (개, 'single item, piece, general counter for objects') and 數 (수, 'number, count, figure'). Although compounded of two Sino-Korean roots, South Korean orthography prescribes writing 개수 without a sai-siot (사이시옷), while preserving the traditional tensified pronunciation [개쑤] (gaessu).

history.meaning: count of individual bamboo tallies or items
the exact number of individual items or pieces

개수.notes: Under the 1988 South Korean spelling reform, only six two-syllable Sino-Korean words keep the sai-siot ㅅ (곳간, 셋방, 숫자, 찻간, 툇간, 횟수); 개수 is spelled without ㅅ even though it is pronounced [개쑤].

rootFamily.gloss: a separate item, a different matter (別個)

개싸움.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성어) combining 개 ('dog', Middle Korean 가히 kahi > 개 kay, used both literally and as a pejorative modifier for unruly, undignified behavior) and 싸움 ('fight, quarrel', Middle Korean 싸홈 ssahom, nominalized from the verb 싸호다 ssahota 'to fight' + -ㅁ). From a literal pack of dogs snarling and biting, it shifted to mean an unrestrained, mud-slinging human brawl.

history.meaning: dog + fighting/combat
a literal dogfight; a chaotic, undignified all-out brawl or mud-slinging match

개싸움.notes: Frequently used in media and politics (e.g., 진흙탕 개싸움, 'a mud-pit dogfight') to criticize bitter, undignified feuds where both sides lose face.

rootFamily.gloss: to fight tooth and nail, engage in a dogfight

개싸움하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed by verbalizing the native compound noun 개싸움 ('dogfight, unruly brawl', from 개 'dog' + 싸움 'fight', Middle Korean 가히 + 싸홈) with the productive light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota). Literally 'to engage in a dogfight', it denotes fighting fiercely and messily without rules or decorum.

history.meaning: to fight + to do
to brawl fiercely, fight tooth and nail without dignity

개싸움하다.notes: Can be written either as a single compound verb (개싸움하다) or analytically with the object particle (개싸움을 하다) for extra emphasis.

rootFamily.gloss: to fight in gangs or factions

개업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 개업 (開業), from 개 (開, 'open, begin') and 업 (業, 'business, trade').
개업.notes: Refers to launching a new shop, café, or practice.

개월.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) bound classifier noun from 個月 (or 箇月), combining the generic counter 個 (개, 'individual unit, piece', originally a bamboo tally 箇) with 月 (월, 'moon, month'). Originally a Chinese classifier construction (Number + 個 + 月), it was borrowed into Korean as a single bound noun 개월 used after Sino-Korean numbers to count elapsed months.

history.meaning: (so many) individual months
months (bound counter used with Sino-Korean numerals for duration)

개월.notes: Pair Sino-Korean numbers with 개월 (예: 삼 개월 'three months') and native Korean numbers with 달 (예: 세 달 'three months'); mixing them (*세 개월) is ungrammatical.

개인.etymology: Sino-Korean 개인 (個人), compounding 개 (個, 'single, individual') and 인 (人, 'person').

history.meaning: single person, individual
individual, private person

개인적.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) derived noun/determiner from 個人的, formed by suffixing -的 (-적, 'relating to, having the character of, -ic/-al') to 個人 (개인, 'individual, private person', from 個 'single' + 人 'person'). Adopted during the late 19th-century modernization period alongside Meiji Japanese 個人的 (kojinteki) to render Western concepts of 'personal' and 'individual'.

history.meaning: individual, personal (Meiji philosophical/legal coinage)
personal, private, individual (used attributively or with -으로 as 'personally')

개인적.notes: As a -적 word, it cannot stand alone before a noun without 이다 unless it is a fixed compound; in speech, use 개인적인 생각 ('personal thought') or adverbially 개인적으로 ('personally').

개입하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verbal compound combining 개입 (介入, 'intervention, stepping in') with the native light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). The Sino-Korean root joins 介 (개, 'to lie between, interpose, mediate; boundary') and 入 (입, 'to enter, step into'), literally 'to enter between two parties or into an ongoing affair'.

history.meaning: to lie between/mediate + to enter into
to intervene, step in, interpose oneself in a situation or dispute

개입하다.notes: Takes the locative particle -에 (예: 문제에 개입하다, 'to step into/intervene in a problem') and is neutral-to-formal compared to 참견하다 ('to meddle/butt in').

개장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 開場, combining 開 (열 개, 'to open, unbolt') with 場 (마당 장, 'grounds, venue, market place'). Borrowed into administrative and commercial Korean during the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries for the public opening of theatres, markets, parks, and cafés. It contrasts with 개점 (開店, opening a retail shop) by emphasizing a shared venue or hall.
개장.notes: Frequently paired with 정식 ('official') as 정식 개장 ('grand opening') or combined with -하다 to form the verb 개장하다.

개짜리.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Korean unit counter 개 (個, 'piece, item') with the native suffix -짜리 ('worth of, consisting of that number of units').
