history.meaning: item consisting of N pieces/units

개콘표.etymology: Modern South Korean broadcasting compound formed from 개콘, the standard two-syllable acronym (두음절 줄임말) of KBS's flagship sketch-comedy show 개그 콘서트 (from English loanwords 'gag' + 'concert', aired 1999–2020 and revived in 2023), plus the Sino-Korean noun 표 (票, 'ticket, voucher; brand label, mark'). In KBS variety-department parlance (as in The Producers), it denotes an admission ticket to Gag Concert (or a Gag Concert-branded style).

history.meaning: Gag Concert (English loanwords) + ticket/label (Sino-Korean)
admission ticket to KBS Gag Concert; Gag Concert-style brand/trademark

개콘표.notes: In Korean pop culture, suffixing -표 (票) to a person or show name can mean either a literal ticket ('Gag Concert ticket') or 'made in the signature style of X' (예: 엄마표 도시락, 'Mom's homemade lunchbox').

개판.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native Korean 개 ('dog', Middle Korean 가히, used as a derogatory prefix meaning 'wretched, disorderly, wild') with 판 ('board, scene, arena, situation', from Sino-Korean 板 'plank, board' extended to a stage of action or round of a game). While popular folk lore links it to wartime dog-meat/food distribution boards (개밥판), philologists analyze it directly as pejorative 개- + 판 ('a dog's arena/scene', i.e., a lawless shambles).

history.meaning: dog + wooden board / stage of action
total chaos, utter shambles, a disorderly mess

개판.notes: Extremely common in casual speech and in the idiom 개판 오분 전 ('five minutes before total chaos'), though rough in register—avoid in formal writing.

rootFamily.gloss: scene, situation, round of a game (板)
the final round, the very end (막판)

걔.etymology: Native Korean colloquial third-person singular pronoun formed by the phonological contraction of the medial demonstrative determiner 그 ('that [near the listener or already mentioned in discourse]', Middle Korean 그 ku) and the noun 아이 / 애 ('child, kid, young person', Middle Korean 아히 ahi > Early Modern 아희 > 아이 > colloquial 애): 그 아이 > 그 애 > 걔.

history.meaning: that child (uncontracted demonstrative phrase)
that kid; casual third-person pronoun ('he, she') among peers or for younger people

morphemes.meaning: child, kid, young person (contracted from 아이)

걔.notes: Part of the symmetrical colloquial pronoun triad 얘 (이 애, 'this kid'), 걔 (그 애, 'that kid / he / she'), and 쟤 (저 애, 'that kid over there'); use only for friends, peers, or younger people.

rootFamily.gloss: that kid over there; he/she (저 아이)

걔네.etymology: Native Korean colloquial plural pronoun formed by attaching the collective/associative plural suffix -네 ('the group of, and company, household of', from Middle Korean collective/honorific plural marker -내 -nay) to 걔 ('that kid, he/she', contracted from 그 아이, Middle Korean 그 아히). It denotes either 'those kids / they' or 'that person's family/place'.

history.meaning: that child + collective group suffix
those kids, they (casual); that person's family or house

걔네.notes: Can optionally take the redundant plural marker -들 (걔네들) in conversation, and before a noun like 집 (걔네 집) it means 'his/her family's house'.

거.etymology: Colloquial native Korean bound noun contracted from 것 ('thing, object, fact', Middle Korean 것) by dropping final -ㅅ.

history.meaning: thing, object
thing, one (colloquial bound noun)

거기.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 그어긔, contracted from 그 ('that, near listener') + 어긔 ('place').

history.meaning: that place
there (near listener or mentioned place)

거두다.etymology: Native Korean verb (고유어) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean (such as the Yongbieocheonga, 1447, and Worin Seokbo, 1459) as 걷우다 / 거두다 (Yale: ketwuta), morphologically derived from the verbal root 걷- (걷다, 'to gather, fold up, collect') + transitive/intensive suffix -우- + -다. From the core agrarian meaning 'to gather in or harvest crops', it broadened to 'to take in and care for a person, achieve results, or wrap up'.

history.meaning: to gather up, harvest crops, fold away, or take into custody/care
to harvest, achieve (success), collect, or take in and look after someone

거두다.notes: A versatile literary and everyday verb: 곡식을 거두다 ('harvest grain'), 성과를 거두다 ('reap success'), and 사람을 거두다 ('take someone under one's wing').

rootFamily.gloss: to collect, gather up, roll up sleeves/hem
to gather in, take back, withdraw
harvesting, gathering in, taking care of

거듭나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (고유어 합성어) combining the adverb 거듭 ('again, repeatedly, anew', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 거듭 ketup, derived from the root 걷- 'to fold in layers' + adverbial suffix -읍) and the verb 나다 ('to be born, sprout, come forth', Middle Korean 나다 nata). Originally coined in early Korean Protestant Bible translations to render 'born again' (John 3:3), it entered general secular Korean to mean 'to reinvent oneself or be reborn as'.

history.meaning: repeatedly / in layers + to be born or emerge
to be born again (spiritually); to be reborn or transformed into something new and better

morphemes.meaning: to be born, emerge, come forth

거듭나다.notes: Typically used with the particle -(으)로 (예: 진정한 프로듀서로 거듭나다, 'to be reborn as a true producer') to describe personal growth or a dramatic turnaround.

rootFamily.gloss: to be repeated over and over

거르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular verb (르 불규칙 동사, conjugating as 걸러, 걸렀다). Attested in Middle Korean as 걸우다 / 거르다 (Yale: kelwuta / keluta), it encompasses two closely linked senses in Korean lexicography: (1) to strain, filter, or sift liquids or powders through a mesh, and (2) to skip, pass over, or omit a step, meal, or turn in a sequence.

history.meaning: to strain liquid through a sieve; to pass over or skip an interval
to filter, strain, screen out; to skip (a meal, day, or turn)

morphemes.meaning: filter, strain; skip, pass over (르-irregular stem)

거르다.notes: Watch the 르-irregular conjugation (거르다 → 걸러, 걸러서) and don't confuse it with 가르다 ('to split/divide', 갈라) or 고르다 ('to choose', 골라).

rootFamily.gloss: to filter out, screen out, weed out

거름.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어) attested in Early Modern Korean (17th-century glossaries such as the Yeogeo Yuhae, 1690) as 거름, derived by adding the deverbal nominalizing suffix -음 (-um) to the native adjective stem 걸- (걸다, 'to be rich, fertile, thick [of soil or broth]', Middle Korean 걸다 kelta). Literally 'that which makes soil rich and fertile', hence compost, manure, or fertilizer.

history.meaning: to be rich, fertile, or thick (of soil or liquid)
manure, compost, fertilizer applied to enrich soil

거름.notes: Do not confuse with 걸음 ('step, pace, walk', from 걷다 'to walk'), which is pronounced identically [거름] in standard Korean!

rootFamily.gloss: to be fertile, rich (of soil or liquid)
base manure; foundation or stepping stone for future success

거리.etymology: Represents both native Korean 거리 ('street, road, thoroughfare'; also 'material/stuff for', from Middle Korean 거리) and Sino-Korean 거리 (距離, 거 'distance' + 리 'separate', 'distance').

history.meaning: street, road / distance between points
street, avenue; distance; material

거보다.etymology: Colloquial lexicalized contraction of the native Korean phrase 그것 보다 ('to look at that'), represented in subtitle lemmatization as 거보다 for spoken interjections like 거 봐! or 거 봐라! ('See that! Look! I told you so!'). It combines 거 (colloquial truncation of 그것 'that thing', from medial demonstrative 그 + bound noun 것) with the verb 보다 ('to see, look at', Middle Korean 보다 pwota).

history.meaning: to look at that thing
See! Look at that! Told you so! (interjection confirming a prior prediction)

거보다.notes: In real conversation, you will hear this as 거 봐! (intimate), 거 봐요! (polite), or 내 말 맞지? 거 봐! ('I was right, wasn't I? See, told you so!').

rootFamily.gloss: hey, look here (lit. look at this)
to wait and see (how things turn out)

거세다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb combining the intensive prefixal element 거- (expressing raw, untamed force, compare 거칠다 'rough, turbulent') with 세다 ('to be strong, forceful', Middle Korean 세다). Because the stem 거세- ends in the vowel ㅔ, the polite suffix -어요 merges directly without vowel insertion to yield 거세요 and past 거셌어요. It characteristically modifies moving natural forces such as blustery wind (거센 바람), driving rain, or river currents.
거세다.notes: Adnominal modifier form is 거센 (거센 바람 'gusty wind', 거센 파도 'rough waves').

거스름돈.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 거스름 (deverbal noun from 거스르다, 'to go counter to, return change') and 돈 ('money').

history.meaning: change returned after payment

거야.etymology: Native Korean colloquial grammatical phrase contracted from 것이야 (것 + -이야). It consists of 거, the spoken form of the bound/defective noun 것 ('thing, fact, act', Middle Korean 것 kes), fused with the intimate (해체) copula -야 (post-vocalic allomorph of -이야, from copula root 이- 'to be' + sentence-final ending -아/야). After prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ, -(으)ㄹ 거야 expresses future intention or probability; after -는/-ㄴ, it forms an explanatory cleft ('it is that...').

history.meaning: it is a thing/fact that... (bound noun + copula)
will / probably (with -(으)ㄹ); it is the case that... (intimate speech level)

morphemes.meaning: thing, fact (colloquial form of bound noun 것)

거야.notes: Always leave a space before 거야 after a verb modifier (예: 갈 거야 'I will go', 한 거야 'it's that I did it'), because 거 (것) is a bound noun, not a verb suffix!

rootFamily.gloss: polite form: will; it is that (것이에요)
confirmative form: it is that, of course (것이지)

거울.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 거우로 ('mirror, looking glass').

history.meaning: mirror
mirror

거의.etymology: Native Korean adverb (고유어) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as the Yongbieocheonga, 1447, and Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447) as 거의 or 거위 (Yale: keuy / kewuy), alongside the variant 거싀 (kesuy, with the archaic consonant ㅿ z). Derived from an Old/Middle Korean root expressing close proximity to a limit or boundary, it has meant 'almost, nearly, for the most part' for over five centuries.

history.meaning: almost, nearly, close to completion
almost, nearly, practically (often paired with totalizers like 다 or 없다)

morphemes.meaning: almost, nearly (monomorphemic adverb in modern Korean)

거의.notes: Frequently pairs with 다 ('all') in positive sentences (거의 다 왔어, 'Almost there!') and with 없다 ('none') in negative sentences (거의 없어, 'There is hardly any').

cognates.meaning: to be rejected (sharing Sino-root 拒絶)
to be rejected (sharing Sino-root 拒絕)

거절당하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) passive/adversative compound verb formed by combining 거절 (拒絶, 'refusal, rejection', from 拒 'to ward off, resist' + 絶 'to cut off, sever') with the Sino-Korean passive auxiliary stem -당하다 (當하다, from 當 'to face, undergo, suffer' + native light verb 하다 'to do'). Literally 'to undergo/suffer a cutting-off refusal'.

history.meaning: refusal/severance + to undergo/face + to do
to be rejected, be turned down, suffer a refusal

거절당하다.notes: Replacing -하다 with -당하다 (當하다) instead of neutral -되다 highlights that the subject experienced the rejection as an unwelcome or painful blow.

rootFamily.gloss: to refuse, reject, turn down (拒絶하다)
to be denied, vetoed, rejected (拒否當하다)

거절하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verbal compound formed from 거절 (拒絶, 'refusal, rejection') + native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). The classical Sino-Korean compound pairs 拒 (거, 'to ward off with the hand 扌, resist, oppose') and 絶 (절, 'to sever silk threads 糸, cut off completely'), literally 'to ward off and cut off (a request, offer, or confession)'.

history.meaning: to ward off and sever relations or requests
to refuse, decline, turn down (an offer, request, or romantic confession)

거절하다.notes: The standard everyday verb for turning down a request, invitation, or confession of love (고백을 거절하다), whereas 거부하다 (拒否하다) sounds more institutional ('veto, boycott, reject authority').

rootFamily.gloss: to be rejected, turned down (拒絶當하다)

거제도.etymology: Sino-Korean geographical proper name (巨濟島) for Korea's second-largest island, located off the coast of South Gyeongsang Province. The name 巨濟 (거제, from 巨 'great, vast' + 濟 'to cross water, ferry across, aid') was enacted in 757 CE (Year 16 of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla) during the nationwide sinicization of native place names (replacing earlier Silla 裳郡 *Songak-gun), signifying a 'great maritime crossing', followed by 島 (도, 'island').

history.meaning: Great Crossing County (Unified Silla administrative renaming in Samguk Sagi, 757 CE)
Geoje Island (major island and shipbuilding hub off southeastern Korea)

거제도.notes: Historically famous as the naval base headquarters of Admiral Yi Sun-sin (near Hansando) and site of the Korean War Geoje POW camp; today renowned for shipbuilding and coastal scenery.

rootFamily.gloss: Jeju Island, sharing 濟 'water crossing' and 島 'island' (濟州島)

거주하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verbal compound combining 거주 (居住, 'residence, dwelling') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). The Sino-Korean root is a classical coordinate compound of two synonymous verbs: 居 (거, 'to dwell, sit, occupy a place') and 住 (주, 'to halt, stay, reside permanently').

history.meaning: to dwell and stay in a place
to reside, live, be domiciled (in a region or building)

거주하다.notes: A formal/administrative counterpart to native 살다 ('to live'): forms and news broadcasts ask for where you 거주하다 (예: 서울에 거주하고 있습니다), while friends ask 어디 살아?.

거지.etymology: Homographic Korean form representing two distinct etymologies: (1) In conversational syntax ('it is, of course'), the contraction of bound noun 것 ('thing, fact', Middle Korean 것 kes) + copula 이- ('to be') + epistemic confirmative ending -지 ('of course / isn't it'); (2) As a lexical noun ('beggar'), attested in Early Modern Korean as 거유지 / 거러지 (from verb 걸- 'to beg/filter through' + person suffix -어지, influenced by Sino-Korean 丐 개 'to beg').

history.meaning: (1) it is a fact that, of course; (2) one who goes around begging (beggar)
(1) colloquial ending 'it is (obviously)'; (2) noun 'beggar, panhandler'

morphemes.meaning: thing, fact (contracted from 것 in grammatical phrase 거지; or root 걸- in noun 'beggar')
copula 'to be' (fused in grammatical phrase 거지)
confirmative sentence-final ending (or nominal suffix -지 in 'beggar')

거지.notes: Context makes the two homographs unmistakable: preceded by a modifier with a space (그런 거지, 'That's how it is, right?') vs. standalone noun 거지 ('beggar', often used in slang like 거지 같다, 'to be awful/trashy').

거짓말.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성어) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean (such as the Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447, and Worin Seokbo, 1459) as 거즛말 (Yale: kecus-mal). Composed of 거짓 ('falsehood, fake, untruth', from Middle Korean 거즛 kecus, which underwent palatal vowel fronting ㅡ > ㅣ after ㅈ in the 18th–19th centuries) and 말 ('word, speech, language', Middle Korean 말 mal).

history.meaning: false speech, untruth, lie
a lie, falsehood, fib

morphemes.meaning: falsehood, fake, untruth (from Middle Korean 거즛)

거짓말.notes: Pronounced [거진말] (geojinmal) because final ㅅ assimilates to [n] before the nasal ㅁ; contrasts with 참말 ('true words, truth').

거짓말하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed by combining the native compound noun 거짓말 ('lie, untruth', Middle Korean 거즛말 kecus-mal, from 거즛 'falsehood' + 말 'speech') with the productive light verb 하다 ('to do, say, make', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota). Attested from the 15th century as 거즛말ᄒᆞ다 ('to utter false speech').

history.meaning: to speak falsehoods, tell a lie
to lie, tell a lie, fib

거짓말하다.notes: In casual speech, people also say 뻥치다 ('to bluff/lie') or 구라치다 (slang), while 거짓말하다 is standard across all registers.

거창하다.etymology: Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the bound root 거창- ('grand, massive, imposing in scale', historically linked in Joseon-era Sino-Korean usage to 巨創 / 巨敞, from 巨 'huge, vast' + 創 'to establish on a grand scale' or 敞 'spacious, grand, open', though treated as a native/unmarked root in modern Korean dictionaries) + the adjectival formative 하다 ('to be', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: to be vast, spacious, and grandly built in scale
to be grand, massive, grandiose, or overblown (of plans, titles, or events)

morphemes.meaning: grand, massive, grandiose in scale (巨敞/巨創)

거창하다.notes: Often used with a slightly self-deprecating or ironic nuance: 거창한 계획은 아니고요 ('It's not some grandiose plan or anything') or 이름만 거창하다 ('Only the name is high-sounding/overblown').

rootFamily.gloss: grandly, on a massive or pretentious scale
to be long-winded, pompous, elaborate (張皇하다)

cognates.word: 据置 / 据え置き (sueoki / kyochi)

거치.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun from 據置 (in Japanese Shinjitai 据置), combining 據/据 (거, 'to fix in place, hold fast, rest upon, occupy') and 置 (치, 'to place, set up, install, leave in position'). Adopted in modern technical and financial terminology, it denotes either fixing equipment onto a mount/stand (as in broadcasting cameras or phones) or leaving a loan principal untouched during a grace period.

history.meaning: fixing firmly in place; leaving an asset or principal untouched in position
mounting or fixing a device (camera, phone) on a stand; loan grace/deferment period

morphemes.meaning: fix in place, rest on, hold fast (據/据)

거치.notes: In everyday life and TV production, you will encounter 거치 most often in 거치대 (據置臺, 'mount, tripod, phone/camera holder') or 거치 카메라 ('mounted/fixed camera').

rootFamily.gloss: to mount/fix in place; to defer loan principal (據置하다)

거칠다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adjective attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 거츨다 (kechulta, "to be overgrown with weeds, uncultivated, coarse"). In Early Modern and Modern Korean, the second-syllable vowel ᅳ (eu) fronted and raised to ᅵ (i) via palatal assimilation after the affricate ᄎ (ch), yielding 거칠다, while the sense broadened from overgrown land to rough textures, harsh weather, and unruly behavior.

history.meaning: to be overgrown with weeds, uncultivated, coarse
rough, coarse, harsh, wild

거칠다.notes: Applies equally to physical surfaces (거친 피부, "rough skin"), turbulent nature (거친 파도, "rough waves"), and abrasive speech or manners (거친 말투, "coarse tone").

거품기.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed from the native Korean noun 거품 ('foam, froth, bubbles', attested in Middle Korean as 거품) and the Sino-Korean instrument suffix -기 (器, 'vessel, implement, tool'). Rather than naming the wire loops by shape, Korean names the kitchen whisk functionally as a 'foam-maker'. This pattern parallels other everyday kitchen tools built with -기.
거품기.notes: With the instrumental particle -로 (거품기로), it expresses 'with a whisk'.

걱정.etymology: Korean noun first attested in Early Modern Korean (17th century) as 걱졍 ('worry, anxiety, concern'), of native or obscured origin.

history.meaning: worry, anxiety
worry, concern

걱정하다.etymology: Formed from 걱정 ('worry, concern') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to feel anxious, worry
to worry, be concerned

걱정해주다.etymology: Native Korean compound benefactive verb formed from the noun 걱정 ("worry, anxious concern", attested from Early Modern Korean as 걱정), the light verb 하다 ("to do", Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, conjugated in its infinitive/connective form 해-), and the auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 cwuta, "to give; to perform an action for someone's benefit"). Literally "to do worrying and give [that care] to someone".

history.meaning: anxious concern + to do + to give
to worry about someone for their sake, show caring concern

morphemes.meaning: to give; to do for someone's benefit

걱정해주다.notes: Adding -어/해 주다 transforms simple "worrying" (걱정하다) into an expression of warm gratitude ("thank you for caring/worrying about me": 걱정해줘서 고마워요). In polite speech toward elders, 주다 is replaced by 드리다.

cognates.meaning: item, matter, measure word for affairs or clothing

건.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) bound noun and counter from Hanja 件 (사건 건, geon, "item, matter, case, document"). In Chinese characters, 件 is an ideogrammic compound of 人 ("person") and 牛 ("ox"), originally signifying the division or sorting of cattle and goods into distinct enumerable units, which evolved into a classifier for legal cases, official matters, and incidents.

history.meaning: to divide; distinct item, article, or matter
case, matter, incident; counter for cases or documents

건.notes: Look out for a major homograph in spoken Korean: as a Sino-Korean counter/bound noun (件), 건 means "case" or "matter" (열 건, "ten cases"; 이 건에 대해서, "regarding this matter"), whereas in casual grammar 건 is the contraction of 것은 ("the thing is").

rootFamily.gloss: agenda item, matter for discussion (案件)

건강.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from Hanja 健康 (건강, geon-gang), combining 健 (굳셀 건, geon, "strong, robust, vigorous, unflagging") and 康 (편안 강, gang, "peaceful, hale, prosperous, unobstructed"). In Classical Chinese the two characters occurred separately for physical vigor (健) and tranquil well-being (康), later coalescing in East Asian medical and everyday vocabulary to denote holistic physical and mental health.

history.meaning: robust strength + peaceful well-being
health, physical and mental soundness

건강.notes: In Korean, 건강 is a noun ("health"); to say "healthy" as a modifier, use the descriptive verb 건강하다 (e.g., 건강한 모습, "a healthy appearance").

rootFamily.gloss: to be sturdy, hale and hearty (強健-)

건너.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb derived from the stem of 건너다 (Middle Korean 건너다, 'to cross over to the other side').

history.meaning: across, the opposite side
the other side, across

건너가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 건너- (from 건너다, 'to cross') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to cross over and go
to cross over, go across

건너다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 건너다 ('to cross a river, road, or boundary').

history.meaning: to cross over
to cross, go across

건너편.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native 건너 ('across, opposite') with Sino-Korean 편 (便, 'side, direction').

history.meaning: the opposite side, across the way

건네받다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 건네다 ('to pass across, hand over', causative of 건너다 'to cross') with 받다 ('to receive, accept'). Because 건네다 encodes movement across the space between two people and 받다 encodes reception by the recipient, 건네받다 vividly captures an object passing directly from hand to hand. It forms a natural converse pair with 건네주다 ('to hand over to someone').
건네받다.notes: Often appears in the past adnominal form 건네받은 ('that was handed to one').

건네주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 건네- (from 건네다, causative of 건너다, 'to pass across, hand over') and 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to hand over, pass to someone

건드리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb attested in Early Modern Korean alongside 건딜다, built on the tactile root 건드- ('lightly tipping or brushing') plus the transitive formative -리-. Unlike 만지다 ('to touch or feel intentionally with the hand'), 건드리다 implies nudging, disturbing, or accidentally grazing something fragile or best left alone. Figuratively, it also describes poking at a sensitive topic or ruffling someone's pride.
건드리다.notes: Frequently used in warnings or negative imperatives (건드리지 마세요, 'please do not touch/disturb it').

건물.etymology: Sino-Korean 건물 (建物), compounding 건 (建, 'build, erect') and 물 (物, 'thing, structure').

history.meaning: erected structure
building, structure

건물주.etymology: Sino-Korean 건물주 (建物主), formed from 건물 (建物, 'building') + 주 (主, 'owner, proprietor').

history.meaning: proprietor of a building
building owner, landlord

건반.etymology: Sino-Korean 鍵盤 'keyboard': the board of keys on a piano or similar instrument.
건반.notes: A piano key is never 열쇠, the word for a door key.

건반투성이.etymology: Hybrid compound joining Sino-Korean 건반 (鍵盤, 건 'key' + 반 'board', 'musical keyboard') and native suffix -투성이 ('covered with, full of').

history.meaning: full of keys / covered in keyboard keys

건방지다.etymology: Derived from the Early Modern Korean noun 건방 ("pretentiousness, putting on airs, unwarranted conceit" — traditionally associated in folk and lexical etymology with Sino-Korean 乾放, from 乾 마를 건 "dry, empty, ungrounded" + 放 놓을 방 "unrestrained, loose, insolent") combined with the native Korean adjective-deriving suffix -지다 (-jida, "to be characterized by, full of"). Literally "full of ungrounded arrogance".

history.meaning: unfounded airs/insolence + to bear the quality of
presumptuous, cheeky, cocky, conceited

건방지다.notes: Strongly criticizing in tone, typically used when someone younger, junior in rank, or inexperienced acts above their station (e.g., 건방지게 굴다, "to act cheekily/arrogantly").

rootFamily.gloss: to act cocky, put on airs

건축.etymology: Sino-Korean 건축 (建築), compounding 건 (建, 'establish, erect') and 축 (築, 'build, construct').

history.meaning: building and construction
architecture, construction

건축가.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character noun 건축가 (建築家): 건축 ('architecture, building') + specialist suffix -가 (家, 'expert, professional').
건축가.notes: The same suffix -가 appears in 작가 (作家, 'writer, author').

건축법.etymology: Sino-Korean 건축법 (建築法), combining 건축 (建築, 'architecture, building construction') and 법 (法, 'law, act, code').

history.meaning: building construction law
building code, architecture law

걷다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 걷다 ('to walk', ㄷ-irregular: 걸어) or homophonous 걷다 ('to roll up sleeves, fold back, gather', regular: 걷어).

history.meaning: to walk; to roll up, gather
to walk; to roll up / collect

걸다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 걸다 ('to hang, hook, fasten, stake').

history.meaning: to hang, hook, fasten
to hang, latch, dial/speak to (말을 걸다)

걸리다.etymology: Native Korean passive and intransitive verb derived from 걸다 ('to hang, hook') + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be hung, be caught
to be hung, get caught, take (time)

걸쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the verb stem 걸- of 걸다 ('to hook, fasten') and 쇠 ('iron, metal').

history.meaning: metal latch, hook, hasp

걸어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound from 걸어- (infinitive of 걷다, 'to walk') + 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to walk and go
to walk (to a place), go on foot

걸어보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 걸다 (Middle Korean 걸다 kelta, "to hang, hook, fasten; by extension, to engage a mechanism, start an engine, dial a phone, or stake a bet"), linked via the infinitive suffix -어 (-eo) to the auxiliary verb 보다 (Middle Korean 보다 pwota, "to see; as an auxiliary, to try doing and see the outcome"). In phrases like 시동을 걸어보다, it means "to try firing up [an engine or project]".

history.meaning: to hang, hook, fasten + to see, test
to try hanging, dialing, starting up, or staking

걸어보다.notes: Note the two homophonous stems: 걸어보다 from 걸다 ("to hang / start up / dial / bet") vs. 걸어보다 from 걷다 (ㄷ-irregular verb meaning "to walk", i.e., "to try walking"). Context (such as 시동을 걸어보다, "let's fire it up!") immediately disambiguates them.

rootFamily.gloss: to hang, dial, start an engine, bet
to be hung, caught, or take time

걸어오다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound from 걸어- (infinitive of 걷다, 'to walk') + 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to walk and come
to walk here, come on foot

걸음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 거름, formed from 걷-/걸- ('to walk') + nominalizing suffix -음.

history.meaning: step, pace, walking
step, pace, gait

걸쭉하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built on the root 걸- ('thick, rich, fertile', seen in 걸다 'to be thick of liquid or rich of soil') extended with the intensive suffix -쭉 and the adjective formative -하다. Korean sound symbolism pairs the dark vowel ㅓ with a heavy, substantial texture, contrasting with 묽다 ('thin, watery'). It is restricted to liquids, sauces, porridges, and batters rather than solid objects.
걸쭉하다.notes: Do not confuse with 두껍다 ('thick' of flat solid objects like books, walls, or coats).

검다.etymology: Native Korean basic color adjective descending from Middle Korean 검다 ('to be black, dark').

history.meaning: to be black, dark
to be black

검사.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun from Hanja 檢事 (검사, geomsa, "public prosecutor"), composed of 檢 (조사할 검, geom, "to examine, investigate, verify") and 事 (일 사, sa, "official affair, duty, service"). Adopted during late 19th-century Korean judicial modernization (alongside Meiji Japanese 検事 kenji) to denote the state legal officer who investigates crimes and prosecutes indictments; completely homophonous in Hangul with 검사 (檢査, "inspection, examination").

history.meaning: to examine/verify + official affair or duty
public prosecutor, state attorney

검사.notes: Korean has two major everyday words spelled 검사: 檢事 ("public prosecutor", a prestigious legal profession frequently featured in K-dramas) and 檢査 ("inspection, medical test"). Both share the first Hanja 檢 ("to examine").

검사하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 검사 (檢査, geomsa, "inspection, examination, test") — composed of 檢 (조사할 검, geom, "to check, verify, examine") and 査 (조사할 사, sa, "to investigate, scrutinize, inspect") — plus the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, "to do").

history.meaning: to check and scrutinize officially
history.stage: Literary Chinese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: to examine, inspect, test, audit

검사하다.notes: Used across medical contexts (혈액 검사하다, "to do a blood test"), quality control (제품을 검사하다, "to inspect products"), and school/office checks (소지품을 검사하다, "to check belongings").

cognates.word: 検索語 (けんさくご, kensakugo)

검색어.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) three-character compound 檢索語 (검색어, geomsaegeo), formed from 검색 (檢索, "search, index lookup, information retrieval" — from 檢 조사할 검 "to examine, check" + 索 찾을 색 "to seek, search, rope for pulling out") and the Sino-Korean suffixoid 어 (語, 말씀 어, "word, term, language"). Originally a library-science and lexicographical term for an index entry, it became central to modern Korean media culture as the term for internet search engine queries.

history.meaning: index lookup / retrieval + word or term
search term, search engine query keyword

검색어.notes: In Korean entertainment and broadcasting (such as *The Producers*), 실시간 검색어 (often abbreviated 실검, "real-time trending search terms" on portals like Naver) was the ultimate barometer of celebrity buzz and public controversy.

rootFamily.gloss: to search, look up online (檢索-)

cognates.meaning: cowardice, timidity (as in 卑怯 hikyō)

겁.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun from Hanja 怯 (겁낼 겁, geop, "fear, fright, timidity, cowardice"). In Chinese character formation, 怯 (Middle Chinese *khyap) combines the semantic heart radical 忄 (心, "heart, mind") with the phonetic-semantic component 去 ("to leave, shrink away"), vividly portraying a heart shrinking back in dread or timidity. Completely integrated into everyday Korean as if it were a native word.

history.meaning: timid, shrinking back in fear, cowardly
fear, fright, timidity

겁.notes: Forms numerous idiomatic expressions in Korean: 겁이 많다 ("to be easily scared / timid"), 겁이 없다 ("to be fearless"), and 겁을 먹다 (literally "to eat fear", meaning "to get cold feet or be intimidated").

겁나다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 겁 (怯, geop, "fear, fright") and the native Korean intransitive verb 나다 (Middle Korean 나다 nata, "to come out, sprout, arise, occur"). Literally "fear arises [in one]", following a productive Korean psychological-verb template where an emotion noun pairs with 나다 (cf. 화나다 "anger arises", 탐나다 "desire arises"). Phonologically realized as [검나다] due to nasal assimilation of ㅂ before ㄴ.

history.meaning: fear + to come forth, arise
to be scared, feel fear; (slang, as 겁나) terribly, super

겁나다.notes: Notice the agency distinction between 겁나다 ("fear arises spontaneously in me" — takes the subject particle 이/가) and 겁내다 ("to show fear toward / be afraid of something" — takes the object particle 을/를). In casual slang, the infinitive 겁나 is also used as an intensifier meaning "crazy/super" (e.g., 겁나 맛있다, "crazy delicious").

겁쟁이.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 겁 (怯, 'fear, timidity') with the native characterizing person suffix -쟁이.

history.meaning: coward, timid person

것.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested in Middle Korean as 것 ('thing, object, fact'). In everyday spoken Korean it regularly contracts to 거, with subject 게, topic 건, and object 걸.
것.notes: Essential building block in grammar patterns such as -(으)ㄹ 거예요 ('will') and -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 ('seems like').

history.meaning: thing, fact
spoken contracted forms

겉.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun meaning "outside, exterior, outer surface". Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 겉 (keth) and 긧 (kuyth, "outer surface, husk, exterior"). Its underlying final aspirated stop ㅌ (th) neutralizes to [t] at the end of a syllable ([걷]), but resurfaces via resyllabification before vowel-initial particles (such as 겉에 [거테] "on the outside" and 겉으로 [거트로] "outwardly").

history.meaning: outer surface, husk, exterior
outside, exterior, surface appearance

겉.notes: Constantly paired with its native antonym 속 ("inside, interior, inner mind"): e.g., 겉과 속이 다르다 ("to be two-faced; literally, one's outside and inside are different"). Also inspires the popular food-texture slang 겉바속촉 ("crispy on the outside, moist on the inside").

rootFamily.gloss: to spin on the surface, fail to fit in

겉면.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 겉 ('outer surface, exterior', Middle Korean 것) with Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface').

history.meaning: outer surface, exterior side

겉면.notes: Pronounced [건면] by nasal assimilation of 겉 [걷] before ㅁ.

겉보기.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun formed from 겉 (Middle Korean 겉 keth, "outside, exterior, surface") + 보- (stem of 보다, Middle Korean 보다 pwota, "to see, look at") + the deverbal nominalizing suffix -기 (-gi). Literally "looking at the exterior", denoting how something or someone appears on the surface at first glance, often contrasted with hidden reality or actual substance.

history.meaning: exterior + to look at + nominalizer
outward appearance, superficial look, at first glance

겉보기.notes: Most frequently encountered in the contrast phrase 겉보기에는 ("at first glance / on the outside, [it looks X, but in reality...]"), and in astronomy as 겉보기 등급 ("apparent magnitude" of a star).

rootFamily.gloss: model, exemplar to look up to

게.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) contracted phrase formed from the bound noun 것 (Middle Korean 것 kes, "thing, fact, one") plus the nominative subject particle -이 (-i). In Early Modern and Modern Korean, intervocalic ㅅ lenited and dropped in casual speech (거시 > 것이 > 거이), and the resulting hiatus ᅥ + ᅵ coalesced into the front mid vowel ᅦ, producing 게 (ge).

history.meaning: the thing (as grammatical subject)
the thing [subject]; what is (colloquial contraction)

게.notes: Essential in spoken Korean after adnominal verb endings (-는/-은/-을 게): e.g., 먹는 게 남는 거다 ("what you eat is what remains"), or in the idiom 게 눈 감추듯 ("like a crab hiding its eyes" — where 게 is the homophonous native noun meaning "crab"!).

게다가.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 거기에다가 (거기 'there' + locative-additive -에다가 'in addition to').

history.meaning: on top of that, thereunto
moreover, besides, in addition

게스트.etymology: Modern Korean loanword (외래어) borrowed from English guest (/ɡɛst/), adapted to Korean syllable structure by inserting epenthetic ᅳ (eu) after both the sibilant and final stop of the coda cluster -st (게스트, geseuteu). The English word derives via Middle English gest from Old Norse gestr ("guest, stranger"), from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis ("stranger, guest, host"). In Korean broadcasting, it specifically denotes an invited celebrity or participant appearing on a program.

history.meaning: stranger, invited visitor under hospitality
special guest on a TV/radio show; guest at a venue or lodging

morphemes.meaning: guest, invited broadcast participant (from English guest)

게스트.notes: While native 손님 covers everyday guests and customers (at home, restaurants, or shops), 게스트 is the standard industry term in TV/radio production (*The Producers*) for a celebrity guest booked for a variety show, talk show, or concert.

rootFamily.gloss: regular/recurring guest on a show (固定 guest)

게스트하우스.etymology: Borrowed from English guesthouse (guest + house), denoting a small lodging house or traveller's inn.

history.meaning: lodging house for visitors
guesthouse

게임.etymology: Modern Korean loanword (외래어) borrowed from English game (/ɡeɪm/), adapted into Korean phonology by rendering the English diphthong /eɪ/ as two syllables, 게-임 (ge-im). English game descends from Middle English game, from Old English gamen ("joy, glee, sport, pastime"), from Proto-Germanic *gamaną ("fellowship, merriment, amusement"). In Korean, it covers video/computer games, sports matches, and variety-show mini-games.

history.form: Old English gamen > Modern English game
history.meaning: merriment, pastime; structured contest or play
video game, variety-show game, sports match or set

morphemes.meaning: game, contest, structured play (from English game)

게임.notes: In Korean variety shows (예능), 복불복 게임 ("luck-of-the-draw penalty games") and 기상 미션 게임 ("wake-up mission games") are staple segments; colloquially, 게임이 안 되다 means "to be no match for someone / out of someone's league".

rootFamily.gloss: game console or arcade machine (game + 機)

겨우.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adverb meaning "barely, narrowly, with difficulty; only, merely". Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 계우 (kyeywu, "barely, with great difficulty"), derived by adding the archaic adverb-forming suffix -우 (-wu) to the verb stem 계- (Middle Korean 계다 kyeyta, "to be unable to bear, to be overwhelmed by one's load", preserved today in compounds like 힘겹다 "to be arduous" and 눈물겹다 "to be moved to tears"). Later monophthongization/reanalysis shifted 계우 to 겨우.

history.meaning: to be overwhelmed by -> with great difficulty, barely
barely, narrowly, with difficulty; only, merely

morphemes.meaning: to be taxed or overwhelmed (from Middle Korean 계-)

겨우.notes: Has two distinct nuances depending on context: before an action verb it means "barely / after great struggle" (겨우 끝냈다, "I barely finished it"), whereas before a quantity or number it means "only / a mere" (겨우 백 원, "a mere 100 won").

rootFamily.gloss: to be arduous, beyond one's strength (힘 + 겹다)

겨울.etymology: Native Korean season noun descending from Middle Korean 겨싦 ('winter').

history.meaning: winter
winter

cognates.meaning: grid, standard, style, status, grammatical case

격.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun from Hanja 格 (격식 격, gyeok, "standard, class, status, stature, grammatical case"). In Old and Classical Chinese, 格 (from 木 "tree" and phonetic 各) originally meant "tall, straight branches of a tree" or "wooden lattice frame", evolving semantically to "measuring frame, standard, rule", and thence to "social rank, dignity, or intrinsic caliber". Also used as a bound noun meaning "in the manner or capacity of".

history.meaning: tree branch, wooden lattice; standard, rule, pattern
status, stature, class, dignity; grammatical case; in the capacity of

격.notes: Very common in everyday praise or critique of someone's class and stature: 격이 다르다 ("to be in a different league / of a higher class") and 격이 떨어지다 ("to lose dignity / lower one's standards").

rootFamily.gloss: dignity, class, nobility of character (品格)
formality, established rule or decorum (格式)

격자틀.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 격자 (格子, 격 'grid, lattice' + 자 'object') with native 틀 ('frame, framework').

history.meaning: lattice frame, grid frame

겪다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb meaning "to experience, undergo, go through (especially difficulties or major events)". Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 겪다 (kyekkta, also written 겯다 in early texts), where its primary sense was "to host or entertain a guest, to see a major household affair or ceremony through to completion". From the effort of seeing a demanding affair through, the meaning generalized to undergoing life experiences, trials, and hardships. Pronounced [경따] before consonants due to coda cluster simplification of ㄲ to [k].

history.meaning: to host a guest, conduct an affair, pass through an event
to experience, undergo, go through (events or hardships)

겪다.notes: Unlike the Sino-Korean verb 경험하다 (經驗-, "to experience" neutrally, such as a hobby or travel), native 겪다 carries a deeper, more visceral weight and frequently collocates with trials, turmoil, or emotional milestones (어려움을 겪다, "to go through hardship"; 실패를 겪다, "to suffer failure").

cognates.word: 見積もり (みつもり, mitsumori)

견적.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 見積 (견적, gyeonjeok, "estimate, price quotation"), adapted by applying Sino-Korean character readings to the Japanese commercial compound 見積 (みつもり, mitsumori, nominalized from the native Japanese verb 見積もる mitsumoru, "to estimate by eye", composed of 見 볼 견 "to see, view" + 積 쌓을 적 "to pile up, calculate volume or sum"). Adopted during the modern commercial and industrial era as the standard term for cost estimates.

history.meaning: visual assessment and calculation of quantity or cost
cost estimate, price quotation, assessment

견적.notes: Used formally in business (견적을 내다, "to draw up a price quote") and humorously in Korean slang (견적이 안 나온다, literally "an estimate doesn't even come out", meaning a situation or mess is so hopeless you can't even begin to fix it).

결.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 결 (kyel), originally denoting a wave, ripple, or directional flow on the surface of water before extending to the parallel lines of wood grain and woven texture. In culinary and craft contexts, it refers to the stratified, flaky layers of laminated pastry or the natural fiber alignment of timber. Across centuries of Korean usage, it also grammaticalized into a bound temporal noun meaning 'in the course of' or 'while' (as in 잠결에, 'in one's sleep').

history.meaning: wave, surface ripple, natural grain or texture
grain of wood or stone; texture of fabric or skin
grain, texture, flaky pastry layers, or passing wave

morphemes.meaning: wave, grain, fiber alignment, or layered texture

결.notes: When praising baked goods such as tarts, croissants, or pies in Korean, 결이 살아 있다 ('the layers are alive/distinct') is the classic compliment for a flaky crust.

결과.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 結果 (결과, gyeolgwa, "result, outcome"), composed of 結 (맺을 결, gyeol, "to tie a knot, form, bear fruit") and 果 (열매 과, gwa, "tree fruit; outcome"). Originally a literal botanical phrase in Classical Chinese meaning "to form and bear fruit" (paired with 開花 개화, "to blossom"), which evolved through Chinese Buddhist discourse on karmic fruition into the general abstract noun for the outcome or consequence of any action.

history.meaning: to bear fruit on a plant; karmic fruition in Buddhism
result, outcome, consequence, effect

결과.notes: Remember its botanical metaphor: 원인 (原因, "cause") is the seed/source, and 결과 (結果, "result") is the fruit it bears. Can also be used adverbially at the end of a clause (그 결과, "as a result of that").

rootFamily.gloss: hindsight analysis, judging by the outcome (結果論)

결국.etymology: Sino-Korean 결국 (結局), compounding 결 (結, 'tie up, conclude') and 국 (局, 'board game match, situation'); originally referred to finishing a game of Go (바둑).

history.meaning: conclusion of a game or affair
in the end, ultimately, after all

결근하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 결근 (缺勤, gyeolgeun, "absence from work") — composed of 缺 (이지러질 결, gyeol, "to lack, be deficient, be missing", simplified in Japanese shinjitai as 欠) and 勤 (부지런할 근, geun, "diligence, official duty, work attendance") — plus the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, "to do"). Coined in modern workplace administration to contrast with 출근 (出勤, "going to work").

history.meaning: lacking attendance at work + to do
to be absent from work, miss a workday

결근하다.notes: Distinguish 결근하다 (缺勤-, "to be absent from work/office") from 결석하다 (缺席-, "to be absent from school, class, or a formal meeting"). Unexcused absence from work is 무단결근 (無斷缺勤).

rootFamily.gloss: to go to work, report for duty (出勤-)
to be absent from school or a meeting (缺席-)

cognates.word: 決断力 (けつだんりょく, ketsudanryoku)

결단력.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) three-character compound 決斷力 (결단력, gyeoldannyeok, pronounced [결딴녁] with post-liquid tensification of ㄷ and liquid-nasal assimilation of ㄹ+ㄹ/ㄴ), formed from 결단 (決斷, "firm decision, resolute judgment" — from 決 결단할 결 "to breach a dike, decide, resolve" + 斷 끊을 단 "to cut off, sever hesitation, judge") and the suffixoid 력 (力, 힘 력, "power, capacity, strength"). Literally "the power to sever doubt and decide".

history.meaning: to sever doubt and decide + strength/capacity
history.stage: Classical Chinese to Modern East Asian

history.meaning: decisiveness, resolve, ability to make tough decisions

결단력.notes: Watch the pronunciation: 결단력 is pronounced [결딴녁] — the ㄷ tenses to [ㄸ] after the Sino-Korean coda ㄹ, and the suffix 력 (underlyingly /ljʌk/) assimilates after ㄴ to [녁]. Idiomatically paired with 있다/없다 (결단력이 있다, "to be decisive").

결론.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 結論 (결론, gyeollon), composed of 結 (맺을 결, gyeol, "to tie a knot, bind together, conclude") and 論 (논할 론, ron/lon, "to discuss, argue, discourse, thesis"). Literally "tying up a discourse", standardized across modern East Asian rhetoric and logic (alongside Meiji Japanese 結論 ketsuron) as the term for both a formal logical conclusion and the final outcome of a discussion.

history.meaning: to tie up / conclude + discussion or argument
conclusion, final outcome of a discussion or story

결론.notes: In traditional three-part Korean essay structure, a text progresses through 서론 (序論, "introduction"), 본론 (本論, "main body"), and 결론 (結論, "conclusion"). In conversation, 결론부터 말하면 ("to start with the bottom line / long story short") is a high-frequency discourse marker.

rootFamily.gloss: to draw a conclusion, wrap up (結論-)
main body of an argument (本論)

결방.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) broadcasting compound 缺放 (결방, gyeolbang, "broadcast preemption or cancellation"), formed by combining 缺 (이지러질 결, gyeol, "to lack, omit, be absent") with 방 (放, 놓을 방, clipped from 방송 放送, "broadcasting"). Coined in 20th-century Korean radio and television industry jargon by analogy with 결근 (缺勤, "absence from work") and 결강 (缺講, "cancellation of a lecture") to denote skipping a regularly scheduled episode.

history.meaning: omission of a scheduled broadcast
preemption or cancellation of a scheduled TV/radio program

결방.notes: A signature television-industry term central to *The Producers* (프로듀사): when a regular drama or variety show episode is preempted for breaking news, election coverage, or a baseball game, networks announce 금주 결방 ("preempted this week"). Do not confuse with 종영 (終映, permanent end of a series).

rootFamily.gloss: for a broadcast to be preempted/canceled (缺放-)

cognates.meaning: settlement of accounts, closing the books

결산.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 決算 (결산, gyeolsan, pronounced [결싼]), composed of 決 (결단할 결, gyeol, "to decide, settle, finalize") and 算 (셈 산, san, "to calculate, count, reckon"). Originally a fiscal and accounting term meaning the final settlement of revenues and expenditures at the close of an accounting period (paired with 예산 豫算, "budget/preliminary estimate"), it broadened in Korean media and culture to mean a comprehensive "wrap-up" or year-end review.

history.meaning: finalizing and closing financial accounts for a fiscal period
settlement of accounts; comprehensive wrap-up or year-end summary

결산.notes: In television and pop culture, 연말 결산 (年末決算) or 총결산 (總決算) means a "year-end wrap-up / grand retrospective" summarizing the biggest hits, ratings, or events of the year. In finance, it remains the strict term for closing the books.

rootFamily.gloss: to settle accounts, do a final wrap-up (決算-)
exact settlement or splitting of accounts (精算)

결정.etymology: Sino-Korean 결정 (決定), compounding 결 (決, 'decide, breach a dike') and 정 (定, 'settle, fix').
결정.notes: Combines with 하다 ('decide') or 내리다 ('make/hand down a decision').

cognates.meaning: to be decided, determined (決定される)

결정되다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean passive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 결정 (決定, gyeoljeong, "decision, determination" — from 決 결단할 결 "to breach a dike to channel water; to resolve, decide" + 定 정할 정 "to fix, establish firmly") and the native Korean inchoative/passive verb 되다 (Middle Korean 도외다 twoyta, "to become, to be done"). Serves as the regular passive counterpart to 결정하다 ("to decide").

history.meaning: firm resolution/decision + to become
history.stage: Classical Chinese and Middle Korean components

history.meaning: to be decided, to be determined or settled

결정되다.notes: In Korean workplace and production meetings, passive 결정되다 (or 결정나다) is often preferred over active 결정하다 when announcing schedules or casting choices, as it presents the decision as an objective consensus ("it has been decided": 결정되었습니다).

rootFamily.gloss: for a decision to be reached (決定 + 나다)

cognates.word: 決定的 (けっていてき, ketteiteki)

결정적.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) three-character noun and determiner 決定的 (결정적, gyeoljeongjeok, pronounced [결쩡적]), formed from 결정 (決定, "decision, determination" — from 決 결단할 결 "to decide" + 定 정할 정 "to fix, settle") and the Sino-Korean suffix 적 (的, 과녁 적, originally "target, bullseye", repurposed in modern Sino-Japanese and Sino-Korean to translate European adjectival suffixes such as -ive and -ic). Literally "having a decisive or clinching character".

history.meaning: having the quality of determining an outcome
decisive, crucial, definitive, clinching

결정적.notes: Grammatically, words ending in -적 (的) cannot take -다 directly; instead, place 결정적 directly before a noun (결정적 순간, "the decisive moment"), add the copula 이다 (결정적인 단서, "a decisive clue"), or add 으로 for the adverb (결정적으로, "decisively / most importantly").

cognates.word: 結晶体 (けっしょうたい, kesshōtai)

결정체.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) three-character compound 結晶體 (결정체, gyeoljeongche, pronounced [결쩡체]), composed of 결정 (結晶, "crystal, crystallization" — from 結 맺을 결 "to tie, form, coalesce, solidify" + 晶 맑을 정 "crystal, clear brilliance", a character formed from three suns 日 depicting sparkling light) and the suffixoid 체 (體, 몸 체, "body, substance, solid form"). Literally "a solid body formed by crystallization", used both scientifically for mineral crystals and figuratively for the "pure essence" or culmination of a quality.

history.meaning: solid body formed by chemical crystallization
crystalline solid; figurative crystallization, pure essence, or epitome

결정체.notes: Beware of the Hanja false friend: the 결정 in 결정체 is 結晶 ("crystal", 맺을 결 + 맑을 정), NOT 決定 ("decision", 결단할 결 + 정할 정)! Figuratively, Koreans say 노력의 결정체 ("the crystallization/fruits of hard work") or 귀여움의 결정체 ("the pure essence of cuteness").

결정하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 결정 (決定, gyeoljeong, "decision, determination") — composed of 決 (결단할 결, gyeol, originally depicting a hand opening a breach in a dike to let pent-up water flow out, hence "to resolve a dilemma, decide") and 定 (정할 정, jeong, "to fix, settle firmly in place") — combined with the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, "to do").

history.meaning: to resolve and settle firmly + to do
history.stage: Classical Chinese and Middle Korean components

history.meaning: to decide, determine, resolve upon

결정하다.notes: When joining a subordinate clause meaning "to decide to [do X]", Korean attaches the purposive nominalizer -기로 before 결정하다 (e.g., 출연하기로 결정했다, "decided to appear on the show"). Pronounced [결쩡하다] with tensification after ㄹ.

결제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 決濟, combining 決 (결, 'to decide, settle, breach a dike') and 濟 (제, 'to cross a river, relieve, complete'). Literally 'settling and completing an obligation', adopted into modern commercial Korean (alongside Japanese 決済 kessai) to denote financial settlement and payment of accounts or bills.

history.meaning: to settle/decide + to cross over, complete, relieve
financial settlement, payment of bills or transactions

결제.notes: Carefully distinguish 결제 (決濟, financial payment with ㅐ/ㅔ) from its near-homophone 결재 (決裁, executive approval/sign-off of documents with ㅐ).

cognates.meaning: to settle an account, pay off

결제하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from the Sino-Korean noun 결제 (決濟, 'financial settlement, payment', from 決 'decide, settle' + 濟 'complete, relieve') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, make'). Literally 'to perform a financial settlement'.

history.meaning: settling and completing a transaction
to pay off, settle a bill or account

morphemes.meaning: to do (light verb deriving verbs from nouns)

결제하다.notes: Used across retail and banking (e.g., 카드로 결제하다 'to pay by card'); do not confuse with 결재하다 (決裁하다, 'to approve/sign off on a proposal').

rootFamily.gloss: repayment, paying back a debt (辨濟)

결혼.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 結婚, composed of 結 (결, 'to tie a knot, bind, unite') and 婚 (혼, 'marriage, take a wife', originally dusk 昏 when bridal processions took place plus 女 'woman'). Literally 'tying the matrimonial bond'.

history.meaning: to tie/bind + marriage ceremony at dusk
marriage, matrimony

결혼.notes: The standard modern term for marriage; traditional or formal contexts also use 혼인 (婚姻), which pairs the groom's family (姻) and bride's family (婚).

결혼하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative combining 결혼 (結婚, 'marriage', from 結 'tie, bind' + 婚 'wedlock') with the productive native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). It displaced older native expressions such as 시집가다 (for a woman) and 장가가다 (for a man) as the gender-neutral verb 'to marry'.

history.meaning: binding in matrimony
to get married, wed

결혼하다.notes: Takes the comitative particle -과/-와 or -하고 for the partner (e.g., 그 사람과 결혼하다 'to marry that person'), never the object marker -을/-를.

결혼해주다.etymology: Compound benefactive verb formed from 결혼하다 (結婚하다, 'to marry', from 結 'tie' + 婚 'marriage' + 하다 'do'), conjugated into the infinitive/connective stem 결혼해 (via 해 contraction of 하여), plus the auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, do as a favor for someone'). Literally 'to do someone the favor of marrying them'.

history.meaning: to perform marriage for the benefit of another
to marry (someone, framed as a favor or gracious act)

결혼해주다.notes: Adding the benefactive auxiliary -아/어 주다 frames marriage as a gift or favor bestowed by the partner, making it standard in marriage proposals (나랑 결혼해 줘 'Marry me').

결혼해줄래.etymology: Inflected phrase built on 결혼해주다 ('to do the favor of marrying', from 結婚 'marriage' + 해 'do and' + 주다 'give/favor') plus the intimate interrogative-volitional ending -(으)ㄹ래 ('will you / would you like to', historically from prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ + bound noun 터/거 + copula or desiderative construction). Famous in Korean pop culture as the title of Lee Seung-gi's 2009 hit song 'Will You Marry Me?'.

history.meaning: will you do me the favor of marrying me?

morphemes.meaning: will you? / want to? (intimate prospective question ending)

결혼해줄래.notes: In *The Producers* (*프로듀사*) and broader Korean variety culture, 결혼해줄래 immediately evokes Lee Seung-gi's classic proposal anthem as well as the literal intimate proposal 'Will you marry me?'.

겸.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and particle from 兼 (겸, 'to combine, unite, hold two things simultaneously'). The character 兼 is an ideogram showing a single hand (又) grasping two stalks of grain (秝, doubled 禾) at once, whence the meaning 'doing or serving two functions together, cum, combined with'.

history.meaning: a hand holding two stalks of grain; to combine, do concurrently
combined with, serving dual purposes, cum

겸.notes: Used both between nouns (아침 겸 점심 'breakfast cum lunch / brunch') and after prospective verb forms -(으)ㄹ 겸 (산책도 할 겸 'partly to take a walk as well').

rootFamily.gloss: combining two errands at once (兼事兼事)
holding concurrent posts or side job (兼職)

겸사겸사.etymology: Reduplicated Sino-Korean adverb derived from 兼事兼事 (겸사겸사), combining 兼 (겸, 'to combine, do concurrently') and 事 (사, 'matter, affair, errand'). By repeating 兼事 ('concurrent affair'), Korean formed an expressive four-syllable adverb meaning 'while one is at it, combining multiple errands or purposes at the same time'.

history.meaning: concurrent business or secondary purpose
combining two or more errands/purposes at once, while at it

겸사겸사.notes: Often used modestly in conversation to downplay a visit or favor so the listener does not feel burdened ('I had other errands nearby anyway, so I came by 겸사겸사').

겹치다.etymology: Native Korean verb derived from 겹 (Middle Korean 겹, 'layer, fold, ply') + verbalizing/intensive suffix -치다.

history.meaning: layer, fold
to overlap, pile up, coincide

경마장.etymology: Sino-Korean three-morpheme compound from 競馬場, consisting of 競 (경, 'to compete, race, vie'), 馬 (마, 'horse'), and 場 (장, 'open ground, venue, arena'). Literally 'venue for racing horses', coined in modern East Asian usage to translate Western 'racecourse / horse-racing track'.

history.meaning: horse racing + venue/grounds
horse racetrack, racecourse

경마장.notes: The suffix -장 (場) productively forms venues and facilities across Korean: 운동장 (sports field), 주차장 (parking lot), 수영장 (swimming pool).

경사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 慶事, combining 慶 (경, 'to congratulate, celebrate, felicity, blessing') and 事 (사, 'affair, event, matter'). Literally 'an auspicious or felicitous event'. Note that Korean 경사 has a homograph 傾斜 ('slope, incline'), which is unrelated.

history.meaning: auspicious affair, celebratory occasion in a household or state
joyous occasion, happy event, cause for celebration

경사.notes: Frequently paired with its antonym 조사 (弔事, 'condolence event / funeral') in the compound 경조사 (慶弔事, 'weddings and funerals; family milestones') and used in the exclamation 경사 났네! ('What a happy occasion!').

rootFamily.gloss: congratulations and condolences; family milestones (慶弔事)

경우.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 境遇, composed of 境 (경, 'boundary, territory, environment, state') and 遇 (우, 'to meet, encounter, befall'). Originally denoting 'the circumstances or lot one encounters in life', in Korean it broadened grammatically into the standard noun for 'case, instance, or supposition' (e.g., ~하는 경우 'in the case that...').

history.meaning: boundaries and encounters; the circumstances one meets in life
situation, case, instance; logical/moral reasonableness (as in 경우가 바르다)

경우.notes: Besides meaning 'case/situation' (~할 경우 'in case of...'), 경우 also means 'proper social sense or decorum' in idioms like 경우가 없다 ('to be unreasonable/rude, lacking sense of propriety').

cognates.meaning: details, circumstances, how things came about

경위서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 經緯書, combining 經 (경, 'warp threads running lengthwise on a loom'), 緯 (위, 'weft/woof threads running crosswise'), and 書 (서, 'writing, document'). In Classical Chinese, 'warp and woof' (經緯) metaphorically meant the full, interwoven sequence of how an event unfolded from beginning to end; adding 書 yields 'a formal written statement detailing the circumstances of an incident'.

history.meaning: warp and weft threads of a loom; longitude and latitude; full details of an affair
written incident report explaining how an error or event occurred

경위서.notes: In Korean office and broadcasting workplace culture, having to write a 경위서 is a dreaded disciplinary step after a broadcast accident or workplace mistake—slightly more factual than a 시말서 (始末書, formal written apology/confession of fault).

rootFamily.gloss: details, circumstances of an event (經緯)

경찰.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 警察, consisting of 警 (경, 'to warn, guard against, keep vigil') and 察 (찰, 'to inspect, examine closely, observe'). Although attested in Tang Chinese in the literal sense of 'exercising vigilance and close inspection', it was repurposed in Meiji Japan (警察 keisatsu) to translate the modern Western institution of the 'police' and adopted into Korean during the late Joseon enlightenment reforms (1894 Gabo Reform).

history.meaning: to guard vigilantly and inspect closely
modern state police force; police officer

경찰.notes: Refers both to the police institution as a whole and to an individual police officer (more formally 경찰관, 警察官).

경찰서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 警察署, formed by adding 署 (서, 'public office, government bureau, administrative station') to 경찰 (警察, 'police', from 警 'guard, warn' + 察 'inspect, observe'). Literally 'police administrative office'.

history.meaning: police + government bureau/station
district police station, precinct headquarters

경찰서.notes: The bound Sino-Korean suffix -서 (署) specifically designates public safety or administrative offices, such as 경찰서 (police station), 소방서 (消防署, fire station), and 세무서 (稅務署, tax office).

경첩.etymology: Korean hardware noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 경쳡, referring to the two folding metal leaves that join a door or lid to its frame.

history.meaning: metal door hinge
hinge

경합.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 競合, combining 競 (경, 'to contend, vie, race') and 合 (합, 'to join, meet together, clash'). Literally 'coming together in contention', denoting a close contest, neck-and-neck rivalry, or competing bids for a role, award, or broadcast slot.

history.meaning: to vie/compete + to come together, clash
close competition, vying against rivals, contention

경합.notes: More formal than 경쟁 (競爭, general competition); 경합 emphasizes head-to-head contention for a specific prize, election, or casting spot (e.g., 치열한 경합을 벌이다 'to wage fierce contention').

경향.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 傾向, composed of 傾 (경, 'to lean, incline, tilt to one side') and 向 (향, 'to face toward, direction'). Literally 'leaning toward a particular direction', developing the abstract sense of 'tendency, inclination, predisposition, or ideological trend'.

history.meaning: to lean/tilt + to face toward a direction
tendency, trend, inclination, disposition

경향.notes: Very common in the grammatical pattern -(으)ㄴ/는 경향이 있다 ('there is a tendency to... / tends to...').

경험.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 經驗, combining 經 (경, 'to pass through, undergo, warp thread') and 驗 (험, 'to test, examine, verify by proof'). Literally 'passing through and verifying firsthand', popularized across East Asia in the late 19th century (via Japanese 経験 keiken) as the philosophical and everyday translation of English 'experience' and German 'Erfahrung'.

history.meaning: to pass through and verify by practical proof
personal or practical experience, lived knowledge

경험.notes: Contrast 경험 (經驗, general personal/professional experience) with 경력 (經歷, formal career history/work experience on a resume) and 체험 (體驗, bodily/hands-on field experience).

경험하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining the noun 경험 (經驗, 'experience', from 經 'pass through, undergo' + 驗 'verify, test') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to undergo and verify firsthand; to experience'.

history.meaning: undergoing and verifying firsthand
to experience, go through, undergo

경험하다.notes: Often used alongside the native Korean verb 겪다 ('to undergo, suffer through'), though 겪다 leans toward hardships whereas 경험하다 is neutral or positive.

곁.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) spatial noun, directly inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 곁 (kyet, 'side, flank, immediate vicinity'). Attested in early Hangul texts such as *Seokbo Sangjeol* (1447), it preserves its final aspirated dental stop ㅌ intact and is morphologically related to 겨드랑이 ('armpit', historically from 곁 'side' + 으랑 + 이).

history.meaning: side, flank, space immediately beside someone
one's side, beside, emotional or physical proximity to a person

곁.notes: Unlike 옆 (general physical 'side/next to' for objects or people), 곁 carries warm, intimate, or poetic nuance and is used almost exclusively for staying by a person's side (내 곁에 있어 줘 'Stay by my side').

rootFamily.gloss: sidelong glance, looking askance (곁 + 눈 + 질)
side dish or accompaniment; bystander role (곁 + 들이다)
armpit (historically derived from 곁 'side of torso')

계기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 契機, combining 契 (계, 'tally, notch, agreement, crucial bond') and 機 (기, 'trigger of a crossbow, loom mechanism, pivotal moment, opportunity'). Literally 'the interlocking trigger mechanism', used in modern East Asian philosophy (translating German *Moment* in Hegel) and everyday prose for a decisive 'turning point, catalyst, or occasion'.

history.meaning: notched tally/join + crossbow trigger or pivotal mechanism
decisive occasion, catalyst, turning point, motive

계기.notes: Whereas 기회 (機會) is a future 'chance/opportunity' to seize, 계기 (契機) usually looks back at the 'catalyst/turning point' that prompted an action (e.g., 이번 일을 계기로 'taking this event as a turning point').

계단.etymology: Sino-Korean 계단 (階段), compounding 계 (階, 'steps, stairs, rank') and 단 (段, 'step, stage, tier').

history.meaning: flight of steps, tiers
stairs, staircase

계단참.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 계단 (階段, 'stairs') with native 참 ('resting station, stage along a route').

history.meaning: staircase landing

계란.etymology: Sino-Korean 계란 (鷄卵), compounding 계 (鷄, 'chicken, domestic fowl') and 란 (卵, 'egg').

history.meaning: chicken egg
egg (chicken egg)

계란.notes: Used interchangeably in everyday Korean with native 달걀.

계란말이.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound combining 계란 (鷄卵, 'chicken egg', from 鷄 'chicken, fowl' + 卵 'egg, ovum') with 말이 ('something rolled up'), a nominalization of the native Korean verb 말다 ('to roll up, curl') via the deverbal noun suffix -이. Literally 'egg roll / rolled omelet'.

history.meaning: chicken egg + to roll up + nominalizer
savory Korean rolled omelet sliced into bite-sized pieces

morphemes.meaning: to roll up, wrap (native verb stem 말다)

계란말이.notes: A staple Korean banchan (side dish), lunchbox item, and pojangmacha bar snack; its native Korean synonym using 달걀 ('egg') is 달걀말이.

계량스푼.etymology: Modern Korean culinary hybrid combining Sino-Korean 계량 (計量, from 計 셈할 계 'calculate, reckon' + 量 헤아릴 량 'measure volume or weight') with 스푼, borrowed from English spoon (ultimately Old English spōn, 'sliver of wood, spoon'). In Korean home cooking and café baking, 계량스푼 refers to standardized sets of tablespoons (큰술, 15 ml) and teaspoons (작은술, 5 ml), pairing naturally with 계량컵 ('measuring cup').
계량스푼.notes: Pairs with 큰술 ('tablespoon') and 작은술 ('teaspoon') in Korean recipes.

계량하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal noun 計量 joined with the native light verb -하다, combining 計 (셈할 계, 'to count, calculate, gauge') and 量 (헤아릴 량, 'to measure capacity or weight'). While everyday lengths or heights take the native verb 재다, 계량하다 is the precise culinary and laboratory verb for measuring exact weights or volumes of flour, sugar, butter, or coffee beans.
계량하다.notes: Commonly modified by 정확히 ('accurately') or 그램 단위로 ('in grams').

계산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 계산 (計算), from 계 (計, 'measure, plan, sum up') and 산 (算, 'reckon, count').
계산.notes: In shops and cafés, 계산하다 is the everyday verb for settling the bill at the register.

계산하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 계산 (計算, 계 'count, reckon' + 산 'calculate with counting rods') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: reckoning and calculation
to calculate; to settle/pay a bill

계세요.etymology: Polite conjugated form of the native Korean suppletive honorific existential verb 계시다 ('to be, stay, exist [of an esteemed person]'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 겨시다 (kyesita, from root 겨- + honorific suffix -시- + -다), combined with the polite informal sentence-final ending -어요 (realized as -세요 after the honorific stem 계시-).

history.meaning: to be, exist, dwell (honorific)
is here / stays (polite statement or question); please stay (polite imperative)

morphemes.meaning: be, stay, exist (honorific verb stem 계시-, from MK 겨시다)

계세요.notes: Forms the core of the farewell 안녕히 계세요 ('Stay in peace' — said to the person remaining behind, whereas 안녕히 가세요 'Go in peace' is said to the person leaving).

rootFamily.gloss: to be, stay, exist (honorific dictionary form)
while someone is present / alive (계실 때)

계속.etymology: Sino-Korean 계속 (繼續), compounding 계 (繼, 'succeed, carry on') and 속 (續, 'connect, continue').

history.meaning: uninterrupted continuation
continuously, keep on; continuation

계시다.etymology: Native Korean subject-honorific existential verb descending from Middle Korean 겨시다 ('to be, stay, dwell [honorific]').

history.meaning: to be, reside (honorific)
to be, stay (honorific of 있다)

계약.etymology: Sino-Korean 계약 (契約), compounding 계 (契, 'engraved tally, deed, covenant') and 약 (約, 'bind, promise, agreement').

history.meaning: binding covenant or contract
contract, agreement

계약과.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 계약 (契約, 'contract') + either Sino-Korean suffix -과 (課, 'department, division') or native comitative particle -과 ('and/with').

history.meaning: contracts division (契約課) / with the contract (계약+과)

계약서.etymology: Sino-Korean 계약서 (契約書), combining 계약 (契約, 'contract, agreement') and 서 (書, 'written document').

history.meaning: written contract document
contract form, written agreement

계약하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound from 계약 (契約, 'contract, covenant', composed of 契 'notched tally, deed, agreement' and 約 'bind with cord, promise, covenant') plus the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, make'). In ancient China, 契 referred to carving notches on two halves of wood or bamboo held by contracting parties as proof of obligation.

history.meaning: notched tally and bound promise; covenant, legal agreement
to sign or enter into a contract, make an agreement

계약하다.notes: Essential in Korean entertainment, broadcasting, and real estate (전세/월세 계약하다 'to sign a housing lease'; 재계약하다 'to renew a contract').

cognates.meaning: bank account (source model for Korean 計座)

계좌.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 計座, composed of 計 (계, 'to calculate, count, reckon, accounting') and 座 (좌, 'seat, position, ledger slot'). Coined in Korean banking as a nativized adaptation replacing the Japanese colonial-era banking term 구좌 (口座, from Japanese kōza) with 計 ('calculation/account') + 座 ('account slot').

history.meaning: account slot in a ledger; bank account
bank account, financial account

계좌.notes: Older speakers occasionally still say 구좌 (口座), a calque from Japanese kōza, but 계좌 (計座) is now the sole standard term in banking (e.g., 계좌 번호 'bank account number', 계좌 이체 'wire transfer').

계주.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 契主, combining 契 (계, 'traditional Korean mutual-aid and rotating savings association, covenant') and 主 (주, 'master, host, organizer, head'). While 契 is a Chinese character ('covenant'), the institution of the 계 (契) is a distinctly Korean communal rotating credit association dating back to the Silla and Goryeo dynasties, and the 계주 is the organizer who collects dues and manages payouts.

history.meaning: communal mutual-aid association + head/organizer
leader/organizer of a rotating savings club (gye)

계주.notes: In Korean dramas and daily life, a 계주 holds everyone's pooled savings (계돈); a common trope is a dishonest 계주 absconding with the fund (계가 깨지다). Note also the homonym 계주 (繼走, 'relay race').

rootFamily.gloss: member of a savings club (契員)

계집애.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun formed from 계집 ('woman, female', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 겨집 kyecip, then the standard neutral word for 'woman, wife') plus 애, the contracted colloquial form of 아이 ('child', Middle Korean 아ᄒᆡ ahoy). Literally 'female child, girl', though both 계집 and 계집애 underwent pejoration or colloquialization as Sino-Korean 여자 (女子) and 소녀 (少女) took over polite registers.

history.meaning: woman/female + child
girl, young female (colloquial, rough, or affectionately blunt)

morphemes.meaning: female, woman (native root 계집, from MK 겨집)

계집애.notes: Sounds rough, earthy, or demeaning if used by strangers, though parents, grandmothers, or close female friends often use 계집애 (or dialectal 기집애/지지배) with teasing affection; its male counterpart is 사내아이 / 머스마.

계통.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 系統, combining 系 (계, 'silk thread connecting things in succession, lineage, series') and 統 (통, 'main silk thread gathering smaller threads together, govern, interconnect'). Literally 'connected threads and their governing main line', hence 'an interconnected system, network, genealogical/professional lineage, or field of work'.

history.meaning: connecting thread/lineage + main governing thread/continuity
system, network, lineage, professional sector or field

계통.notes: Besides technical systems (신경 계통 'nervous system'), in everyday conversation 이쪽 계통 ('this line of work / this industry sector') is very common when discussing careers like broadcasting or entertainment.

계피.etymology: Sino-Korean 계피 (桂皮), compounding 계 (桂, 'cassia / cinnamon tree') and 피 (皮, 'bark, skin').

history.meaning: dried bark of the cassia tree
cinnamon, cassia bark

계획.etymology: Sino-Korean 계획 (計劃), compounding 계 (計, 'reckon, calculate') and 획 (劃, 'draw lines, lay out, devise').

history.meaning: calculated design or scheme
plan, project

계획하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 계획 (計劃, 'plan, project') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: to plan, arrange

고개.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 고개 ('mountain ridge or pass; nape of the neck, head').

history.meaning: mountain pass; back of the neck, head
head (in nodding/turning); hill pass

고개.notes: The anatomical sense ('head/neck' in 고개를 끄덕이다 'nod one's head') and topographical sense ('hill crest') share the image of a curved crest.

고급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 高級, composed of 高 (고, 'high, tall, lofty') and 級 (급, 'grade, rank, step, order of threads'). Originally designating a high official rank or advanced level, in modern Korean it also functions pre-nominally for 'high-end, luxury, upscale, or gourmet' (e.g., 고급 식당 'upscale restaurant', 고급 정보 'insider/high-level tip').

history.meaning: high + rank, grade, or step
high grade, advanced level; upscale, luxury, high-end

고급.notes: Forms the top tier of the three-level proficiency and quality scale: 초급 (初級, elementary/entry-level), 중급 (中級, intermediate/mid-grade), 고급 (高級, advanced/high-end).

고급스럽다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed by attaching the native Korean adjectival suffix -스럽다 ('having the quality or appearance of, -some, -ly', from Middle Korean -스ᄅᆞᆸ다) to the Sino-Korean noun 고급 (高級, 'high grade, luxury', from 高 'high' + 級 'grade, class'). Literally 'having a high-class or luxurious air'.

history.meaning: high-grade + having the quality/air of
upscale, classy, refined, luxurious-looking

morphemes.meaning: having the quality/feel of (native adjectival suffix, ㅂ-irregular)

고급스럽다.notes: Conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular adjective (고급스러워요, 고급스러운); in casual slang, speakers also use the punchier coined verb 고급지다 ('to be swanky/fancy').

고기.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) noun directly inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 고기 (kwoki, 'flesh, meat of animals, birds, or fish'). In Middle Korean and traditional compounds, 고기 covered both terrestrial meat and fish (hence 물고기 'water-flesh = live fish' and 불고기 'fire-meat'); in modern standalone usage, 고기 defaults to mammal/poultry meat and, at Korean barbecue restaurants, specifically pork or beef.

history.meaning: flesh or meat of animals, birds, or fish
meat (especially beef or pork in dining contexts); fish (in angling or 물고기)

고기.notes: While 고기 means 'meat' (and often implies pork belly 삼겹살 or beef when Koreans say 고기 먹으러 가자 'Let's go eat meat'), fishers still call fish 고기 (고기 잡다 'to catch fish') alongside 물고기 ('live fish') and 생선 (生鮮, 'fish as food').

cognates.word: 高等學校 / 高等学校 (gāoděng xuéxiào)
cognates.meaning: institution of higher learning; high school

고등학교.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 高等學校, combining 고등 (高等, 'high grade, advanced level', from 高 'high' + 等 'rank, grade') and 학교 (學校, 'school', from 學 'study, learn' + 校 'schoolhouse, enclosure'). Adopted into modern Korean educational terminology in the mid-20th century (modeled alongside Japanese 高等学校) to denote the three-year upper secondary school preceding university.

history.meaning: higher-level academy or upper secondary educational institution
three-year senior high school (grades 10–12)

고등학교.notes: Often abbreviated in colloquial speech and compounds to 고교 (高敎/高校, gogyo) or simply -고 (-高) at the end of school names, while a high school student is 고등학생 (고딩 in slang).

고르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 고르다 ('to make even or uniform; to sort out, select').

history.meaning: to level, tune, choose
to choose, pick; to level/smooth

고리.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 고리 (kwoli), denoting a curved metal ring, loop, or hook used to fasten doors, hang utensils, or link chains. In traditional Korean architecture and furniture, iron and brass 고리 served both as pull-rings on double doors and as wall hooks for keys and lanterns. In Modern Korean it also extends metaphorically to a connecting link between people or events (연결 고리).

history.meaning: metal ring, loop, or hook for fastening and hanging
hook, ring, loop, or connecting link

고리.notes: Often compounded with the object it holds or attaches to, such as 옷고리 (coat hook) or 열쇠고리 (key ring).

고맙다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 고맙다 ('worthy of reverence, grateful'), related to an older root associated with respect.
고맙다.notes: Conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 고마워요 in polite speech and 고맙습니다 in formal speech.

history.meaning: revered; grateful
thankful, grateful

고모.etymology: Sino-Korean 고모 (姑母), compounding 고 (姑, 'father's sister') and 모 (母, 'mother, older female relative').

history.meaning: father's sister
paternal aunt

고모.notes: Distinguished in Korean kinship from 이모 (姨母, mother's sister) and 숙모 (叔母, father's brother's wife).

고모님.etymology: Hybrid honorific kinship term combining Sino-Korean 고모 (姑母, 'paternal aunt') with the native honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: paternal aunt (honorific)

고민.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 苦悶, formed from 고 (苦, 'bitter, painful, suffering') and 민 (悶, 'stifled, oppressed in heart, agonized', depicting a heart 心 shut inside a doorway 門). Whereas Chinese 苦闷 and Japanese 苦悶 retain a literary sense of heavy anguish, modern Korean 고민 softened into the everyday word for 'worry, concern, mulling over a personal or practical dilemma.'

history.meaning: bitter distress and mental anguish
inward torment, agonizing over a problem
worry, trouble, deliberation over a choice or concern

고민.notes: Used constantly in daily conversation even for light choices (점심 뭐 먹을지 고민이다, 'I'm debating/torn over what to eat for lunch') as well as serious life worries.

고백.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 告白, combining 고 (告, 'to tell, announce, declare') and 백 (白, 'white, clear; to speak plainly and openly').
