Literally 'to declare openly and without concealment.' Used both for confessing a secret or wrongdoing (and translating religious/literary 'confession') and, very prominently in modern Korean pop culture, for confessing romantic feelings to someone.

history.meaning: to explain or state plainly to superiors or the public
confession of truth, conscience, or love
confession of romantic feelings; candid admission

고백.notes: Without further context, 고백받다 ('to receive a confession') and 고백하다 in Korean drama dialogue almost always refer to confessing romantic feelings.

cognates.meaning: to confess (romantic feelings or a secret)

고백하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative formed from the noun 고백 (告白, 'open declaration, confession', from 告 'announce' + 白 'speak plainly') and the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 (-hada, 'to do, make'). Literally 'to make an open confession,' whether of hidden romantic love or of an untold truth.

history.meaning: to declare openly, confess
to confess one's love; to admit or own up to

고백하다.notes: Marks the person confessed to with the dative particle -에게 / -한테 (e.g., 선배한테 고백하다, 'to confess one's feelings to a senior').

cognates.meaning: a life of hardship (literary Buddhist term)

고생.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 苦生, formed from 고 (苦, 'bitter, painful, hard') and 생 (生, 'life, living'). Originating in Buddhist and classical usage for 'a bitter, toilsome life,' it broadened in Korean to denote any physical or emotional hardship, toil, or trouble endured while accomplishing a task.

history.meaning: hard, bitter living; suffering and toil
hardship, trouble, hard work, ordeal

고생.notes: Central to Korean workplace etiquette: 고생하셨습니다 / 고생 많았어 ('You worked so hard / Thank you for your trouble') is the warmest everyday expression of appreciation after a shoot or project.

고생하다.etymology: Verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 고생 (苦生, 'hardship, bitter toil', from 苦 'bitter' + 生 'living') + the native Korean verb-forming suffix -하다 ('to do, undergo'). Literally 'to undergo hardship or toil,' used both for enduring adversity and as a polite formula acknowledging someone's effort.

history.meaning: to live in hardship, suffer privation
to suffer, have a hard time, work hard through difficulties

고생하다.notes: In Korean broadcasting sets (like *The Producers*), 고생하셨습니다! ('Thank you all for your hard work!') is shouted by the PD and cast at the wrap of every filming session.

cognates.meaning: to file a criminal complaint, press charges
to tell, inform; (legal) to file a lawsuit

고소하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) legal verb formed from 고소 (告訴, from 告 'report, accuse' + 訴 'sue, appeal, complain to an authority') + -하다 ('to do'). In Classical Chinese and East Asian legal codes, 告訴 meant petitioning a magistrate against a wrongdoer; in modern Korean law, it specifically denotes filing a formal criminal complaint or pressing charges (distinct from its native Korean homonym 고소하다 'nutty, savory; satisfyinglyServes-them-right').

history.meaning: to lodge an accusation before a magistrate
to sue, press criminal charges against someone

고소하다.notes: Has a famous native Korean homonym 고소하다 (adjective: 'nutty and savory like roasted sesame oil; secretly gratifying when a rival gets their comeuppance'), often punned on in Korean variety and drama scripts.

rootFamily.gloss: indictment, accusation by a third party

고시원.etymology: South Korean Sino-Korean coinage written 考試院, combining 고시 (考試, 'state civil-service, bar, or diplomatic examination', from 考 'examine, test' + 試 'test, try') and 원 (院, 'building, hall, residence'). Originally emerging in the 1970s–1980s around Seoul university districts (such as Sillim-dong and Noryangjin) as ultra-compact boarding rooms where students isolated themselves to study for national exams (고시), 고시원 evolved into low-cost, deposit-free micro-studio housing for students and young urban workers.

history.meaning: cubicle study-dormitory for civil service and bar exam candidates
tiny, low-cost single-room dormitory for students or budget renters

고시원.notes: A quintessential symbol of struggling youth or rookie life in Seoul dramas; upgraded modern versions with private bathrooms are often marketed as 고시텔 (gositel, a blend of 고시원 + 호텔).

고위층.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 高位層, formed from 고위 (高位, 'high rank, senior position', from 高 'high' + 位 'rank, seat, position') and the collective stratum suffix -층 (層, 'layer, story, social class'). Literally 'the high-ranking stratum,' referring to top executives, senior government officials, or upper management.

history.meaning: the upper social or institutional stratum holding senior positions
upper management, top brass, high-ranking officials

고위층.notes: In broadcasting and corporate dramas, 방송국 고위층 ('the network's upper management / top brass') refers to the division directors and executives above the PDs.

cognates.word: 固有名詞 / 固有名词 (gùyǒu míngcí)

고유명사.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) grammatical compound written 固有名詞, combining 고유 (固有, 'inherent, peculiar to one entity', from 固 'firm, fixed' + 有 'possess') and 명사 (名詞, 'noun', from 名 'name' + 詞 'word, part of speech'). Adopted in modern East Asian linguistics to translate European grammatical 'proper noun' (Latin nomen proprium), and frequently used figuratively in Korean for a person or brand that has become synonymous with a quality ('the very byword for...').

history.stage: Late 19th–Early 20th c. East Asian grammatical coinage
history.meaning: proper noun naming a specific individual person, place, or institution
proper noun; figuratively a household byword or synonymous icon

고유명사.notes: Often used metaphorically in entertainment commentary: 예능의 고유명사 ('a household name / synonymous icon of variety shows').

고의성.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 故意性, formed from 고의 (故意, 'deliberate intent, on purpose', from 故 'reason, deliberate' + 意 'mind, intention') and the abstract quality suffix -성 (性, 'nature, quality, -ness'). Used in legal, disciplinary, and everyday contexts to assess whether an action or broadcast incident had 'deliberate intent' (고의성이 있다/없다).

history.meaning: deliberate purpose or premeditated thought
the quality of being intentional; willfulness

고의성.notes: Common in regulatory or dispute contexts (such as KCSC放送審議 hearings in *The Producers*): 고의성이 다분하다 ('it is blatantly intentional').

고이다.etymology: Native Korean verb representing two historically distinct stems that share the modern spelling 고이다: transitive 고이다 (the uncontracted standard doublet of 괴다, 'to prop up, wedge a support beneath a heavy stone, table leg, or beam so it sits steady') and intransitive 고이다 ('for rainwater, puddle water, or tears to gather in a depression'). Both stems conjugate identically as 고여요, 고입니다, and 고였어요, with transitivity distinguishing propping an object (돌을 고이다) from pooling liquid (물이 고이다).
고이다.notes: In the transitive 'prop up' sense, 고이다 alternates freely with its contracted vowel form 괴다 (받침대를 고이다/괴다).

morphemes.meaning: prop up beneath; collect in a pool

고장.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 고장 (故障, 고 'incident' + 장 'obstruction', meaning 'mechanical breakdown, malfunction') and native Korean 고장 (Middle Korean 곳양, 'region, locality, hometown').

history.meaning: region, locality / obstacle, malfunction
breakdown, out of order; region/district

고정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 고정 (固定, 고 'firm, solid' + 정 'fix in place') + -하다.
고정하다.notes: Standard carpentry and mechanical verb for fastening panels, screws, or hinges.

고집.etymology: Sino-Korean 고집 (固執), compounding 고 (固, 'firm, solid, obstinate') and 집 (執, 'grasp, hold fast').

history.meaning: holding firmly to one's view
stubbornness, obstinacy, insistence

고쳐놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 고쳐 (gochyeo, the infinitive/connective form of 고치다 gochida, 'to fix, repair, reform, correct', from Middle Korean 고티다 gotida) and the completive/preparatory auxiliary verb 놓다 (nota, literally 'to put down, leave in a resulting state'). Expresses fixing, repairing, or straightening something out so that the corrected state stays in place.

history.meaning: to repair/alter + to set in place
to fix up, get something repaired, or straighten out a habit/problem for good

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb denoting completion with a lasting result

고쳐놓다.notes: Often used both for physical repairs (고장 난 걸 고쳐놓다 'have the broken item fixed') and colloquially for reforming someone's bad attitude (버릇을 고쳐놓다 'straighten out someone's bad habits').

rootFamily.gloss: to get something done in advance

고쳐지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 고쳐 (connective stem of 고치다 gochida, 'to fix, repair, cure, reform', from Middle Korean 고티다 gotida) + the passive/inchoative auxiliary suffix -지다 (-jida, 'to become, come to be'). Means 'to get repaired, be corrected, or be cured.'

history.meaning: to renew, mend, correct
to be repaired, get fixed, be reformed (of a habit or illness)

morphemes.meaning: passive/inchoative verbal auxiliary ('to become, get V-ed')

고쳐지다.notes: Frequently used in the negative when lamenting stubborn habits: 성격이 쉽게 안 고쳐진다 ('One's personality/habit isn't easily changed').

rootFamily.gloss: to fix and leave in working order

고치다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 고티다 ('to mend, repair, alter, cure'), with regular palatalization of 티 > 치.

history.meaning: to change, repair, correct
to fix, repair, mend, cure

고통.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) coordinate compound written 苦痛, uniting 고 (苦, 'bitter, affliction, hardship') and 통 (痛, 'ache, physical or mental pain'). Attested in Classical Chinese and Buddhist scriptures for physical and existential suffering, and standard in modern Korean for severe physical pain or emotional agony.

history.meaning: bitter pain and bodily or mental suffering
pain, agony, torment
pain, suffering, distress

고통.notes: More formal and intense than native 아픔 (apeum); pairs with 받다 (고통을 받다 'to suffer pain') and 스럽다 (고통스럽다 'to be painful, agonizing').

고프다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adjective inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 골ᄑᆞ다 (golpoda, 'to be hungry, be depleted or sunken inside'). Originally used more broadly for physical exhaustion or emptiness, in modern Korean it is bound almost exclusively to 배 ('stomach, belly') in the expression 배(가) 고프다 ('to be hungry') and figurative expressions of emotional craving (사랑에 배고프다 'hungry for love').

history.meaning: to be empty inside, famished, exhausted
to be hungry (with 배 'belly')
to be hungry, crave

고프다.notes: Conjugates with ㅡ-irregular drop before -아/어: 고프- + -아 -> 고파 (배고파요 'I'm hungry').

고향.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 故鄕, formed from 고 (故, 'old, former, ancestral') and 향 (鄕, 'village, countryside, native district'). Borrowed from Classical Chinese poetry and prose (famous from Han and Tang verse such as Li Bai's 靜夜思) for one's ancestral village or birthplace, and extended figuratively to a spiritual home or origin point (마음의 고향).

history.meaning: one's old village or ancestral homeland
native place, birthplace
hometown; spiritual home or place of origin

고향.notes: Carries strong nostalgic warmth in Korean culture, especially around Chuseok and Lunar New Year (귀향 'returning to one's hometown').

곡.etymology: Sino-Korean 곡 (曲, 'melody, tune, musical piece; bend'), from Middle Chinese *khjowk.

history.meaning: bent; musical tune or song
piece of music, song, tune (also counter for songs)

곤란하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) descriptive verb formed from 곤란 (困難, from 困 'distressed, hemmed in, exhausted'—depicting a tree 木 confined inside an enclosure 囗—and 難 'difficult, hard') + -하다. In conversational Korean, 곤란하다 often means not merely 'technically difficult' but 'socially awkward, puts me in a tight spot, cannot be accommodated.'

history.meaning: hardship, distress, obstacle
to be difficult, troublesome, or socially awkward/inconvenient

morphemes.meaning: difficult, hard (pronounced 란 by lateralization after ㄴ)

곤란하다.notes: Notice the phonological assimilation /n/ + /n/ -> [ll] ([골란하다]). Saying 그건 좀 곤란한데요 ('That puts me in a bit of a difficult spot') is a classic polite Korean refusal.

rootFamily.gloss: to be in an awkward predicament

곤란해지다.etymology: Inchoative verb formed from 곤란해- (infinitive stem of 곤란하다 困難-, 'to be difficult, awkward, in a bind') + the native Korean auxiliary verb -지다 ('to become, turn into'). Means 'to become awkward, turn into a sticky predicament, or put someone in a tight spot.'

history.meaning: to come to be in a difficult or awkward position

곤란해지다.notes: Frequently used in workplace negotiations: 이러시면 제가 참 곤란해집니다 ('If you do this, it puts me in a really awkward position').

rootFamily.gloss: to become embarrassed/put on the spot

곧.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 곧 ('on the spot, immediately, soon, namely').

history.meaning: immediately, directly, namely
soon, right away; namely

곧장.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 곧- (seen in the adjective 곧다 'to be straight, upright' and the adverb 곧 'immediately, right away', Middle Korean 곧) plus the intensifying adverbial suffix -장. Uniting spatial straightness with temporal immediacy, 곧장 describes heading directly to a place without stopping along the way (곧장 가다) or moving to the next step without hesitation.
곧장.notes: Modifies motion and action verbs directly (곧장 가다, 곧장 들어오다, 곧장 향하다).

cognates.meaning: scoring target or point in sports (donor word)

골.etymology: Borrowed from English goal ('boundary marker, scoring target, point scored in ball games') in the early 20th century with the introduction of association football and modern athletics to Korea. Note that Korean also has a native homonym 골 ('valley, furrow; brain/head', from Middle Korean 골 gol), which appears in idioms like 골치 아프다 ('headache-inducing').

history.meaning: boundary, limit, marker
scoring posts or point scored in football/sports; objective
goal in sports (also native homonym: furrow, valley; brain/temper)

골.notes: Pronounced with tense [꼴] in casual sports exclamation (골 넣다 'to score a goal', 골대 'goalpost').

rootFamily.gloss: reaching the finish line; getting married

골고루.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated/emphatic adverb derived from the stem 고르- of 고르다 (goreuda, 'to be even, uniform, level, well-balanced', from Middle Korean 고ᄅᆞ다 goroda). Through intensive prefixal reduplication (*골-고르-오 > 골고루), it came to mean 'evenly, equally across all parts, without leaving anything out.'

history.meaning: to be even, equal; evenly
evenly distributed across every person or variety
evenly, equally, a bit of everything

골고루.notes: Familiar from both dining advice (반찬을 골고루 먹다 'eat a balanced variety of side dishes') and ensemble show direction (분량을 골고루 챙기다 'give everyone even screen time').

골목.etymology: Native Korean compound noun joining 골 (Middle Korean 골, 'valley, narrow lane between houses') and 목 ('neck, narrow passage').

history.meaning: narrow passage or lane
alley, narrow side street

골목길.etymology: Native Korean compound joining 골목 ('narrow lane between buildings', itself from 골 'narrow valley, trough, neighborhood quarter' + 목 'neck, narrow passage') with 길 ('road, path', Middle Korean 길ㅎ). Korean regularly uses 목 ('neck') metaphorically for narrow connecting passages (길목, 손목, 발목), so 골목길 vividly evokes intimate residential lanes branching off a main thoroughfare.
골목길.notes: Pronounced [골목낄] with tensification of ㄱ after the final ㄱ of 골목.

골백번.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Korean emphatic compound formed from the native Korean intensifying prefix 골- (gol-, 'full to the brim, a full hundredfold/ten-thousandfold', seen in 골백번 and 골만번) + Sino-Korean 백 (百, 'hundred') + 번 (番, 'time, occurrence'). Literally 'a full hundred times over,' used hyperbolically in speech for 'hundreds of times, countless times.'

history.meaning: a full hundred times; countless times over
hundreds of times, over and over again

morphemes.meaning: native intensifying prefix ('full, thorough, many times over')

골백번.notes: Used in exasperated or emphatic hyperbole: 골백번도 더 말했다 ('I've told you a hundred times already!') or 내가 골백번 생각해도 ('even if I think it over a hundred times').

cognates.meaning: player who defends the goal in football/hockey (donor word)

골키퍼.etymology: Direct loanword (외래어) from English goalkeeper (goal + keeper). Adopted in Korean football (soccer) terminology for the player positioned to guard the goal, and occasionally used metaphorically for a gatekeeper or last line of defense.

history.meaning: player defending the goal in team sports
goalkeeper, goalie

골키퍼.notes: Often shortened colloquially in Korean sports commentary to 키퍼 (kipeo) or paired with the Sino-Korean synonym 수문장 (守門將, 'gate-guarding general').

곱다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 곱다 ('to be fine, lovely, delicate, smooth').

history.meaning: beautiful, fine, delicate
fine-grained, lovely, gentle

곱다.notes: Conjugates as 고와 / 고운; describes both refined beauty and finely ground powder or sand.

곳.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 곳 ('place, spot, locality').

history.meaning: place, location
place, spot

공.etymology: Represents three major etymological strands in Korean: (1) Sino-Korean 공 (功, from Middle Chinese kuwng, 'merit, achievement, painstaking effort'), as in 공을 들이다 ('to put great effort into') and 공을 세우다 ('to achieve credit/merit'); (2) Sino-Korean 공 (公, 'public, official, impartial'), as in 공과 사 ('public duty and private affairs'); and (3) native Korean 공 (gong, 'ball', from Middle Korean 공디 gongdi). In workplace drama dialogue, 공 usually refers to credit/effort (功), public affairs (公), or a ball.

history.form: 功 (kuwng > 공) / 公 (kuwng > 공) / 공디 (gongdi)
history.meaning: merit, labor (功); public, official (公); ball (공디)
effort, credit, merit (功); public affairs (公); ball; zero (空)

morphemes.meaning: merit, effort (功); public duty (公); ball

공.notes: Key idioms include 공을 들이다 ('invest painstaking effort'), 공을 가로채다 ('steal the credit'), and 공과 사를 구분하다 ('keep public/work and private matters separate').

공간.etymology: Sino-Korean 공간 (空間), compounding 공 (空, 'empty, sky, void') and 간 (間, 'interval, room, space between').

history.meaning: open interval, physical space
space, room

공갈.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 恐喝, combining 공 (恐, 'to fear, terrify, frighten') and 갈 (喝, 'to shout angrily, berate, threaten'). In criminal law, 공갈 denotes extortion or blackmail by intimidation; in everyday colloquial Korean, 공갈 (and 공갈치다) also means 'bluffing, empty threats, or hollow fibs' (as in the pastry 공갈빵 'hollow puffed bread').

history.meaning: frightening and shouting down a victim to extort property
blackmail, extortion (legal); empty bluff or lie (colloquial)

공갈.notes: Appears both in legal compounds like 공갈협박 ('blackmail and intimidation') and playful everyday words like 공갈젖꼭지 ('pacifier / dummy nipple') and 공갈빵 ('hollow Chinese balloon bread').

공감하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb formed from 공감 (共感, from 共 'together, shared' + 感 'feel, emotion, response') + the native verbalizer -하다. Literally 'to feel together,' expressing emotional resonance, empathy, or relating deeply to someone else's experience or story.

history.meaning: shared feeling, emotional resonance (rendering German Einfühlung / English empathy)
to empathize, relate to, identify with

공감하다.notes: A core buzzword in Korean television writing and social media: 시청자들이 공감할 수 있는 이야기 ('a story viewers can relate to') and 폭풍 공감 ('relating 100% / intense empathy').

공공.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 公共, pairing 公 (공변될 공, 'public, official, impartial') with 共 (한가지 공, 'together, shared in common'). Adopted across East Asian civic vocabulary in the late nineteenth century to translate 'public' in contrast to 사 (私, 'private'). In contemporary Korean it stands directly before nouns as a modifier in compounds such as 공공 도서관 ('public library') and 공공 장소 ('public place').
공공.notes: Used prenominally without 의 before institutional nouns.

공구함.etymology: Sino-Korean 공구함 (工具函), combining 공구 (工具, 공 'work, craft' + 구 'tool') and 함 (函, 'box, case').

history.meaning: box for work tools
toolbox

공기.etymology: Sino-Korean 공기 (空氣), compounding 공 (空, 'sky, empty space') and 기 (氣, 'vapor, breath, atmosphere').

history.meaning: atmosphere, air
air, atmosphere

공동.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) coordinate compound written 共同, combining 공 (共, 'together, shared by all') and 동 (同, 'same, united, together'). Attested since Classical Chinese for acting or holding something in common, and used productively in Korean as a noun and pre-nominal modifier meaning 'joint, shared, collaborative, co-.'

history.meaning: together in unison, shared in common
joint, communal, shared, co-

공동.notes: Functions like the English prefix 'co-' or 'joint' in compounds such as 공동연출 ('co-direction'), 공동구매 ('group buying'), and 공동체 ('community').

공동구매.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) four-character compound written 共同購買, formed from 공동 (共同, 'joint, collective', from 共 'together' + 同 'same') and 구매 (購買, 'purchasing, buying', from 購 'buy, procure' + 買 'buy'). Denotes consumers pooling orders together to obtain wholesale or discounted prices.

history.meaning: collective purchasing by a consumer cooperative or workplace union
online or group buying (often shortened to 공구)

공동구매.notes: Frequently abbreviated in everyday speech and online communities to 공구 (gonggu, a homonym of 工具 'tool').

공동연출.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) broadcasting and theater compound written 共同演出, combining 공동 (共同, 'joint, collaborative') and 연출 (演出, 'direction, staging, production', from 演 'perform, develop' + 出 'bring forth'). Refers either to joint stage/television direction or to a co-director (co-PD) sharing directing duties on a program.

history.meaning: joint direction of a play, film, or television program; co-director

공동연출.notes: A central plot concept in *The Producers* (*프로듀사*), where variety programs are helmed by a 메인 연출 (main PD) or paired in a 공동연출 (co-PD) system.

cognates.meaning: time and effort devoted to a skill; workmanship; kung fu
devising a scheme, ingenuity; (Zen) spiritual practice

공부.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun written 工夫, from 공 (工, 'work, craft, skill') and 부 (夫, 'man, laborer'). In Classical and Vernacular Chinese, 工夫 meant 'the labor and time a craftsman devotes to a task,' which Neo-Confucian scholars (such as Zhu Xi) specialized to mean 'devoted moral and academic self-cultivation.' Korean adopted this Neo-Confucian scholarly sense as the standard everyday word for 'study, academic learning.'

history.meaning: corvée laborers; time and effort expended on work
scholarly and moral self-cultivation, diligent study of texts
study, academic learning, learning about life

공부.notes: A fascinating false friend across East Asia: the same characters 工夫 mean 'study' in Korean (공부), 'cleverness/devising a method' in Japanese (kufū), and 'time/effort/martial skill' in Mandarin (gōngfu).

cognates.meaning: to devise, figure out a method (false friend from same Hanzi 工夫)

공부하다.etymology: Verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 공부 (工夫, 'academic study, scholarly effort', originally 'craftsman's time and labor' -> Neo-Confucian 'scholarly cultivation') + the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Serves as the universal Korean verb for 'to study.'

history.meaning: to devote oneself to Confucian learning and scholarship
to study (a subject, for exams, or at school)

공부하다.notes: Takes an object with -을/를 (한국어를 공부하다 'study Korean') or functions intransitively (열심히 공부하다 'study hard').

공사하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from 공사 (工事, "construction work"), combining 공 (工, "work, craft, labor") and 사 (事, "affair, matter, task"), suffixed with the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: craftsmanship, labor, or public works project
construction work or engineering project
to carry out construction or repair work

공사하다.notes: Frequently used both for civil engineering projects and metaphorically in slang for cosmetic surgery ("remodeling").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공손하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 공손 (恭遜, 공 'reverent, respectful' + 손 'humble, deferential') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

history.meaning: respectful and modest
to be polite, courteous, respectful

공식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 공식 (公式), from 공 (公, 'public, official') and 식 (式, 'form, ceremony, formula').

공업사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 공업사 (工業社), composed of 공업 (工業, "manufacturing industry", from 工 "craft, work" + 業 "business, trade, profession") and 사 (社, "company, association, firm"). In South Korean usage, it became specialized as a clip of 자동차공업사 (自動車工業社, "automobile industrial workshop").

history.meaning: manufacturing trade and commercial association
industrial workshop; specifically an auto body and repair shop

공업사.notes: In everyday Korean, 공업사 almost always refers to a full-service auto repair and body shop (1급 공업사) rather than a general factory.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공연.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 공연 (公演), formed from 공 (公, "public, open, official") and 연 (演, "to perform, practice, act out, expound"). Adopted in the modern era alongside Meiji Japanese theatrical vocabulary to denote a live show or concert presented before an audience.

history.meaning: public; to flow out, practice, or perform
public theatrical or musical performance
concert, stage show, public performance

공연.notes: Covers concerts, theater, musicals, and dance shows alike; compare 콘서트, which is narrower and used mainly for music concerts.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공연장.etymology: Sino-Korean 공연장 (公演場), from 공연 (公演, 공 'public' + 연 'perform') + 장 (場, 'place, hall, venue').

history.meaning: public performance venue
concert hall, theater, performance venue

공연하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative combining the noun 공연 (公演, "public performance", from 公 "public" + 演 "perform, act") with the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do, to make").

history.meaning: public performance or stage presentation
to stage a concert, play, or public performance

공연하다.notes: Note the homograph 공연하다 (空然하다, "to be pointless, uncalled-for"), which is an adjective and triggers contraction to 괜히/괜찮다.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.word: 公營放送 / 公營廣播 (gōngyíng guǎngbō)

공영방송.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 공영방송 (公營放送), uniting 공영 (公營, "public operation/management", from 公 "public" + 營 "manage, operate, camp") and 방송 (放送, "broadcasting", from 放 "release, emit" + 送 "send, transmit").

history.meaning: public management + transmission of radio waves
public broadcasting network or system (such as KBS or EBS)

공영방송.notes: In South Korea, KBS (Korean Broadcasting System) and EBS are the flagship 공영방송 networks, contrasted with 민영방송 (민방, commercial networks like SBS).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.word: 空五二空 / 零五二零

공오이공.etymology: Sino-Korean digit-by-digit numerical sequence 공오이공 (空五二空), reading out the four digits 0-5-2-0 using 공 (空, "empty, void, zero", colloquial telephone/code reading for 0 alongside 영 零), 오 (五, "five"), 이 (二, "two"), and 공 (空, "zero").

history.form: 空 + 五 + 二 + 空
history.meaning: void/emptiness, five, two, void/emptiness
spoken digit string 0-5-2-0 (used for passcodes, room numbers, or phone numbers)

공오이공.notes: When reading phone numbers, door-lock passcodes, or extension numbers aloud in Korean, 0 is routinely pronounced 공 (空) rather than 영 (零) for crisp phonetic distinction.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 公園, combining 公 (공변될 공, 'public, communal, open to all') and 園 (동산 원, 'walled garden, orchard, parkland'). Adopted across East Asia in the late nineteenth century to render civic 'public parks' open to every citizen—contrasting with private gardens (정원 庭園)—공원 is the universal modern Korean noun for neighborhood, riverside, and national parks.
공원.notes: Combines into specific park types such as 동네 공원 ('neighborhood park'), 국립공원 ('national park'), and 수변 공원 ('waterside park').

공유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 공유 (共有), composed of 공 (共, "together, in common, shared") and 유 (有, "to have, possess, exist"). Originally a legal term for joint ownership of property, it broadened to general sharing of information, files, and experiences.

history.meaning: to possess together or hold in common
joint property ownership; common possession
sharing (of data, resources, feelings) or joint ownership

공유.notes: Used both for digital/informational sharing ("Share button", schedule sharing) and as a pun in pop culture on the actor Gong Yoo (공유, 孔劉).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: to hold in common, to share

공유하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from the noun 공유 (共有, "joint possession, sharing", from 共 "together, common" + 有 "possess, have") and the native Korean verbal suffix 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: joint ownership or common possession
to own jointly; to share information, files, or feelings

공유하다.notes: Unlike 나누다 (native Korean "to divide/share food or feelings"), 공유하다 emphasizes simultaneous access or mutual possession without splitting the object into smaller pieces.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner 공적 (公的), derived from 공 (公, "public, official, impartial, state") and the adjectival/attributive suffix 적 (的, "pertaining to, -ic, -al"). Contrasts directly with 사적 (私的, "private, personal").

history.meaning: public/impartial + target/attributive marker
of a public or official nature
official, public, institutional

공적.notes: Frequently paired with 사적 (私的, "personal/private") in workplace dramas when drawing the line between professional duty and private feelings. Has a common homophone 공적 (功績, "merit, achievement").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공제하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb 공제하다 (控除하다), combining 공제 (控除, "deduction, subtraction", from 控 "pull back, hold back, control" + 除 "remove, exclude, divide") with the native light verb 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: to hold back and remove
to deduct or withhold (taxes, fees, expenses) from a total

공제하다.notes: Standard accounting and payroll term encountered on paystubs and tax returns (e.g., 소득공제 "income tax deduction", 세액공제 "tax credit/deduction").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공중파.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 공중파 (空中波), formed from 공중 (空中, "in the air, sky, midair", from 空 "sky, air" + 中 "middle, within") and 파 (波, "wave"). Originally referring to unguided radio waves transmitted through the atmosphere, it came to designate major terrestrial television networks (KBS, MBC, SBS) in contrast to cable TV.

history.meaning: midair + wave (electromagnetic wave propagated through the air)
terrestrial broadcast waves; major over-the-air television networks

공중파.notes: In broadcasting jargon, 지상파 (地上波, "terrestrial waves", as opposed to satellite) is the technically precise term preferred by regulators, while 공중파 remains widespread in everyday speech.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공짜.etymology: Sino-Korean 공 (空) 'empty' with the native suffix -짜: something that costs nothing.
공짜.notes: Casual; 공짜로 means 'for free'. The same suffix appears in 진짜 'the real thing' and 가짜 'a fake'.

공천.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 공천 (公薦), an abbreviation of 공개추천 (公開推薦, "open/official recommendation") or 공적추천 (公的推薦), combining 공 (公, "public, official") and 천 (薦, "to recommend, present, offer").

history.meaning: official/public + to recommend a candidate for office
official nomination of an election candidate by a political party

공천.notes: A central term in South Korean election politics, often used metaphorically in office comedy for being "anointed" or officially backed by upper management.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

공항.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 공항 (空港), combining 공 (空, "sky, air", short for 항공 航空 "aviation") and 항 (港, "harbor, port"). Coined in East Asia as a calque of English "airport" (literally "harbor of the sky").

history.meaning: sky/air + harbor/port (calque of English "airport")
airport, aerodrome for commercial aviation

공항.notes: In Korean celebrity and entertainment culture, 공항패션 ("airport fashion") is a major media beat where stars showcase outfits to photographers before departing overseas.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

곶간.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean compound spelled 곳간 in contemporary standard orthography (frequently written 곶간 in older or colloquial texts), derived from 고 (庫, "storehouse, treasury, granary") + the native Korean genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 간 (間, "room, space, bay"). Middle Korean attests 고〯간 (庫間), where the rising tone and tensing of the following consonant produced 곳간/곶간.

history.meaning: storehouse room, treasury chamber
household granary, pantry, or storage shed for grain and provisions

곶간.notes: Standard South Korean orthography prescribes 곳간 (with ㅅ), though 곶간 appears in subtitles and older literature; famous from the proverb 곳간에서 인심 난다 ("Generosity comes from a full granary").

과연.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb 과연 (果然), formed from 과 (果, "fruit, result, outcome, in fact, resolutely") and the adverbial suffix 연 (然, "to be so, thus, in that manner"). Literally meaning "turning out in accordance with the expected result."

history.meaning: truly so, turning out as expected; in actual outcome
history.stage: Classical Chinese (attested in Zuozhuan and Mengzi)

history.meaning: indeed, sure enough, just as expected; or "really?" in suspenseful questions

과연.notes: Used in two distinct ways on Korean variety shows: affirmatively ("Sure enough, just as we thought!") and as a cliffhanger caption ("Will they really succeed?!").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

과음하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb 과음하다 (過飮하다), formed from 과음 (過飮, "excessive drinking", from 過 "pass beyond, exceed, excess" + 飮 "drink, swallow") and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: to exceed proper measure + to drink
to drink alcohol excessively, to overindulge in drink

과음하다.notes: Even though 飮 (음) simply means "to drink" in Classical Chinese, 과음하다 and 음주 (飮酒) in Korean specifically refer to drinking alcoholic beverages.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

과일.etymology: Historically derived from the Sino-Korean compound 果實 (果 실과 과, 'tree fruit' + 實 열매 실, 'seed, fruit, fullness'). During the transition from Middle to Early Modern Korean, intervocalic ㅅ weakened and dropped between vowels (과실 > 과일), thoroughly nativizing the word in everyday speech. Modern Korean uses 과일 as the ordinary culinary word for edible fruit while retaining 과실 (果實) in orchard, botanical, or legal registers.
과일.notes: Often paired with 제철 ('in season', 제철 과일 'seasonal fruit') or 깎다 ('to peel/slice fruit').

과잉.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 과잉 (過剩), composed of 과 (過, "pass beyond, exceed, excess") and 잉 (剩, "leftover, surplus, remainder"). Denotes an amount or degree that surpasses what is necessary or appropriate.

history.meaning: to exceed + surplus or remainder
excess, oversupply, overabundance (of production, emotion, or reaction)

과잉.notes: Often used as a modifier before abstract nouns, such as 과잉보호 ("overprotection"), 의욕과잉 ("excessive zeal"), or 자의식 과잉 ("excessive self-consciousness").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

과자.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 과자 (菓子 / 果子), combining 과 (菓/果, "fruit, berry, confection") and the nominal diminutive suffix 자 (子, "child, seed, small object"). Originally denoting tree fruits and nuts served as refreshments, the term shifted in Korea and Japan to grain- and sugar-based confections, biscuits, and packaged snacks.

history.meaning: fruits and nuts served as dessert or tea accompaniment
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Goryeo and Joseon Sino-Korean

history.meaning: confections, cookies, crackers, and packaged snacks

과자.notes: In modern Korean, 과자 covers both sweet cookies/biscuits and savory bagged chips/crackers (like potato chips or shrimp crackers), unlike English "cookies" or "candy".

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

과장님.etymology: Hybrid honorific title combining Sino-Korean 과장 (課長, 과 'section, department' + 장 'head, chief') with the native honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: section chief, department manager (honorific)

관계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 관계 (關係), formed from 관 (關, "wooden crossbar of a gate, frontier pass, to close, to implicate or involve") and 계 (係, "to tie, bind, connect, pertain to"). Literally "to interlock and bind together."

history.meaning: to interlock, implicate, or have bearing upon
history.stage: Literary Chinese (Song–Ming vernacular and administrative prose)

history.meaning: relationship, interpersonal connection, relevance, or involvement

관계.notes: Historically gave rise to the ubiquitous native-feeling adjective 괜찮다 via phonological contraction of 관계하지 아니하다 ("it does not matter / has no bearing").

rootFamily.gloss: to have nothing to do with, unrelated

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

관련.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 관련 (關聯 / 關連), composed of 관 (關, "gate bar, to involve, connect") and 련/연 (聯, "to join in a continuous thread, link, unite"). According to South Korean initial-sound rules (두음법칙), 聯 is read 련 after the alveolar nasal ㄴ of 관.

history.meaning: to link together or be mutually connected
connection, relevance, reference to a topic

관련.notes: While 관계 often refers to interpersonal or structural relationships between entities, 관련 focuses on topical relevance ("related to X", e.g., 방송 관련 일 "work related to broadcasting").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: to relate to, be connected with

관련하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb 관련하다 (關聯하다), derived from the compound noun 관련 (關聯, "connection, relevance", from 關 "involve, connect" + 聯 "link, join") plus the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: mutual linkage or connection
to relate to, pertain to, or have a connection with

morphemes.meaning: to do, to be in a state of

관련하다.notes: Most frequently encountered in the connective forms ~와/과 관련하여 ("regarding ~, in connection with ~") or passive/adnominal 관련된 ("related to ~").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

관리.etymology: Sino-Korean 관리 (管理), compounding 관 (管, 'pipe, key, oversee, control') and 리 (理, 'put in order, administer').

history.meaning: supervision and maintenance
management, maintenance, care

관리비.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 관리비 (管理費), combining 관리 (管理, "management, administration, maintenance", from 管 "bamboo tube, key, to govern/control" + 理 "veins in jade, to put in order, manage") and the suffixal noun 비 (費, "expense, fee, cost").

history.meaning: administration/upkeep + expenditure
monthly building or apartment maintenance fee; administrative expenses

관리비.notes: In South Korean apartment living (where the majority of urban residents live), 아파트 관리비 is a monthly itemized bill covering security, elevator upkeep, cleaning, and shared utilities.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

관리소장.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 관리소장 (管理所長), contracted from 관리사무소장 (管理事務所長), combining 관리 (管理, "management, maintenance", from 管 "control" + 理 "manage"), 소 (所, "place, office, bureau"), and 장 (長, "chief, head, director").

history.meaning: management office + chief/director
superintendent or chief manager of an apartment complex or building

관리소장.notes: In large Korean apartment complexes, the 관리소장 heads the on-site 관리사무소 (management office) and works closely with the residents' representative council (입주자대표회의).

rootFamily.gloss: director of an office or institute

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: to care about, show solicitude for

관심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 관심 (關心), formed from 관 (關, "to bolt a gate, involve, connect, hold within") and 심 (心, "heart, mind"). Literally "holding something upon one's mind or heart."

history.meaning: to involve one's heart/mind; to be solicitous or concerned about
interest, attention, curiosity, or regard toward someone or something

관심.notes: Beware the false friend with Mandarin 關心 (guānxīn), which means "to care for / show warm concern for someone's well-being"; Korean 관심 means intellectual curiosity or romantic/personal interest ("having interest in").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

관찰.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 관찰 (觀察), composed of 관 (觀, "to look at carefully, view, contemplate") and 찰 (察, "to examine closely, inspect, discern"). Combines two near-synonyms of attentive visual and mental scrutiny.

history.meaning: to watch closely and examine; also an imperial circuit inspector (觀察使)
history.stage: Classical Chinese and Joseon Administrative Sino-Korean

history.meaning: scientific, clinical, or attentive observation; reality-TV "observation" format

관찰.notes: In Joseon history, a 관찰사 (觀察使) was a provincial governor; in modern Korean TV (*The Producers*), 관찰 예능 ("observation variety show") is a major genre filming celebrities' unscripted daily lives.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

관하다.etymology: Sino-Korean relational verb formed from 關 (관계할 관 / 빗장 관, originally 'wooden gate-bolt' and by extension 'to interlock, connect, bear upon') plus the native verbalizer -하다. In modern Korean syntax, 관하다 is a defective relational verb used almost exclusively after the dative particle -에 in connective and adnominal frames: -에 관해(서) ('concerning, about') and -에 관한 ('on, regarding', modifying a following noun).
관하다.notes: Slightly more formal than ~에 대해(서) / ~에 대한 ('about'); very common in book titles, clues, and explanations.

광고.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 광고 (廣告), formed from 광 (廣, "wide, broad, extensive") and 고 (告, "to tell, announce, inform, proclaim"). Literally "to announce widely to the public." Adopted in the late 19th century (first modern Korean newspaper ad appeared in the *Hanseong Jubo* in 1886) for commercial advertising.

history.meaning: to proclaim or notify widely
public notice; commercial advertisement in print, radio, TV, or digital media

광고.notes: In Korean broadcasting, TV commercials are called either 광고 or CF (from Konglish/Japanese "Commercial Film"), while product placement inside a drama is called PPL (간접광고).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

광고하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb 광고하다 (廣告하다), formed by attaching the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do") to the Sino-Korean noun 광고 (廣告, "advertisement, wide announcement", from 廣 "wide, broad" + 告 "inform, announce").

history.meaning: wide announcement; commercial advertisement
to advertise a product or service; colloquially, to broadcast a secret to everyone

광고하다.notes: In everyday conversation (as in *The Producers*), "광고하다" is often used sarcastically when someone blabs or makes a scene: 동네방네 광고하다 ("to advertise it to the whole neighborhood!").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

광장.etymology: Sino-Korean 광장 (廣場), compounding 광 (廣, 'wide, broad, spacious') and 장 (場, 'open ground, place').

history.meaning: broad open ground
plaza, public square

괘씸하다.etymology: Early Modern Korean adjective 괘씸하다 ("insolent, detestable, ungrateful, offensive"), attested in 18th–19th century texts in variants such as 패심ᄒᆞ다 (悖心ᄒᆞ다, from 悖 "perverse, rebellious, contrary to propriety" + 心 "heart, mind") and 괘심ᄒᆞ다 (掛心ᄒᆞ다 or labialized shift 패심 > 괘심 > 괘씸), combined with the native adjective-forming suffix -하다. Tensing of ㅅ to ㅆ (괘심 > 괘씸) expresses heightened emotional displeasure.

history.meaning: perverse-minded, insolent, contrary to propriety and gratitude
detestable, impudent, shameless, offensive (especially of a junior or ingrate)

morphemes.meaning: insolent, offensive, ungrateful (historically from 悖心/괘심)
to be in a state of (adjectiveizer)

괘씸하다.notes: Typically used by a superior, elder, or benefactor who feels a subordinate or younger person has violated etiquette or shown brazen ingratitude (hence the tongue-in-cheek "괘씸죄" — the "crime of rubbing a boss the wrong way").

rootFamily.gloss: insolence, audacity (unofficial "offense of annoying a superior")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

괜찮다.etymology: Contracted in Early Modern Korean from 관계하지 아니하다 (Sino-Korean 관계 關係 'relation, concern' + negated -하지 아니하다 'does not matter'), via 괜치 않다 > 괜찮다.

history.meaning: to not matter, be of no concern
to be okay, fine, all right, decent

괜찮아지다.etymology: Inchoative verbal derivative 괜찮아지다, formed from the adjective stem 괜찮- ("to be okay, fine, acceptable", itself a historical phonological contraction of 關係하지 아니하다 > 관계치 않다 > 관치 않다 > 괜치 않다 > 괜찮다, "to not matter / have no problematic bearing") + the connective suffix -아 + the auxiliary inchoative verb 지다 ("to become, come to be").

history.meaning: to have no bearing upon; to not matter
to be all right, fine, acceptable, or decent
to become okay, get better, recover, or improve

morphemes.meaning: be okay, acceptable (from 關係치 아니하-)

괜찮아지다.notes: The standard, warm expression for recovery from illness, emotional distress, or an awkward situation ("It'll get better" / "I'm feeling better now").

rootFamily.gloss: to be okay, fine, all right
in vain, pointlessly, for no reason

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

괜찮은.etymology: Adnominal (attributive) form of the adjective 괜찮다 ("to be okay, fine, decent"), attaching the descriptive adnominal suffix -은 to the stem 괜찮-. The stem 괜찮- arose in Early Modern Korean via progressive contraction of Sino-Korean 관계(關係) + -하지 아니하다 (관계치 않다 > 관치 않다 > 괜치 않다 > 괜찮다, influence also reinforced by 공연히 아니하다 "not in vain"). Literally "not posing any problem," which underwent semantic amelioration to "good, decent, quite nice."

history.meaning: unrelated, posing no issue or hindrance
acceptable, permissible; positively good, decent, attractive, or worthwhile

morphemes.meaning: be okay, fine, decent (from 關係치 않-)

괜찮은.notes: By understatement (litotes), calling a person or restaurant 괜찮은 사람 / 괜찮은 곳 in Korean is genuine praise meaning "a really good/attractive person" or "a great spot," not merely "mediocre."

괜하다.etymology: Syncopated native-Sino hybrid adjective contracted from 공연하다 (空然하다), composed of Sino-Korean 공연 (空然, from 空 gong 'empty, vain' + 然 yeon 'so, thus, state of being') and the native adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Through phonological erosion in colloquial speech (공연하다 > 고연하다 > 괴연하다 > 괜하다), the word lexicalized as an independent everyday adjective meaning 'needless, pointless, or uncalled-for'.

history.meaning: to be empty, groundless, or without reason
to be uncalled-for or pointless
needless, pointless, gratuitous

괜하다.notes: Frequently used in its adnominal form 괜한 (e.g., 괜한 걱정 'needless worry' or 괜한 소리 'uncalled-for remark') to express regret or mild annoyance at unnecessary trouble.

괜히.etymology: Contracted form of 공연히 (空然히), derived from the Sino-Korean root 공연 (空然, from 空 gong 'empty, in vain' + 然 yeon 'so, thus') combined with the native Korean adverb-forming suffix -히 (-hi). Phonetic reduction across generations (공연히 > 고연히 > 괴연히 > 괜히) obscured its Sino-Korean origin in everyday speaker intuition.

history.meaning: in vain, groundlessly
without good reason, pointlessly
for nothing, needlessly, for no reason

morphemes.meaning: contracted from 공연 (空然), in vain/empty

괜히.notes: Often precedes a past-tense verb (e.g., 괜히 왔다 'I came for nothing / I shouldn't have come') to express mild regret over doing something unnecessary.

굉장하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean root 굉장 (宏壯, composed of 宏 goeng 'wide, spacious, grand' + 壯 jang 'robust, magnificent, imposing') combined with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Originally describing the imposing scale of palatial architecture or literary style, it broadened in modern Korean to mean 'remarkable, tremendous, or awesome'.

history.meaning: spacious and magnificent; grand and imposing
to be grand, vast, and imposing
remarkable, tremendous, grand

굉장하다.notes: Despite its classical Hanja origins, 굉장하다 is ubiquitous in everyday spoken Korean to praise anything impressive, equivalent to 'amazing' or 'tremendous'.

굉장히.etymology: Derived from the Sino-Korean stem 굉장 (宏壯, from 宏 goeng 'wide, grand' + 壯 jang 'robust, magnificent') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -히 (-hi). Through semantic bleaching from 'magnificently, grandly', it developed into a high-frequency degree intensifier meaning 'extremely, very'.

history.meaning: grandly, imposingly
extremely, very, tremendously

굉장히.notes: Sounds slightly more articulate and mature than 너무 or 진짜, making it a favorite intensifier in broadcast interviews and workplace conversation.

교과서.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 敎科書, formed from 敎 (가르칠 교, 'teach'), 科 (과정 과, 'subject, course of study'), and 書 (글 서, 'book, writing'). Coined during the modernization of East Asian school systems in the late nineteenth century, it replaced traditional primer titles for standard classroom books. Figuratively, 교과서처럼 ('like a textbook') describes speech or behaviour that is technically by-the-book or overly stiff.
교과서.notes: Often used metaphorically in 교과서처럼 ('by the book; stiffly').

교수.etymology: Sino-Korean 교수 (敎授), composed of 敎 gyo ('teach, instruct') + 授 su ('confer, transmit, hand down'). Attested in Chinese since the Han and Song dynasties as an official academic title for instructors in imperial academies, and used in Korea during the Goryeo and Joseon periods before becoming the modern university rank 'professor'.

history.meaning: to instruct and transmit knowledge; instructor at an imperial school
state-appointed Confucian academy instructor
university professor; instruction

교수.notes: When addressing or referring to a professor politely, always attach the honorific suffix -님 (교수님); bare 교수 is reserved for objective status or news reports.

교육비.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 교육비 (敎育費), formed from 교육 (敎育, 'education', from 敎 gyo 'teach, instruct' + 育 yuk 'rear, nurture, bring up') + the bound Sino-Korean suffix -비 (費 bi, 'expense, cost, expenditure').

history.meaning: expenditure for schooling and instruction
education costs, tuition and schooling expenses

교육비.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -비 (費) productively attaches to activity nouns to denote expenses, as in 교통비 (transportation costs), 식비 (food expenses), and 사교육비 (private tutoring expenses).

교직.etymology: Sino-Korean 교직 (敎職), composed of 敎 gyo ('teach, instruct') + 職 jik ('office, duty, post, profession'). Denotes the teaching profession as an institutional vocation or career path.

history.meaning: office or duty of teaching
teaching profession, faculty position

교직.notes: Frequently encountered in university settings in the phrase 교직 이수 ('completing a teaching certification track alongside one's university major').

cognates.meaning: to alternate, to supersede, to replace

교체하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 교체 (交替, composed of 交 gyo 'exchange, intersect, alternate' + 替 che 'replace, substitute') combined with the native Korean light verb -하다 (-hada, 'to do'). Originally referring to alternating shifts or successions, it now broadly means replacing or swapping out personnel or parts.

history.meaning: to alternate in turns, to succeed one another
to replace, to substitute, to swap out

교체하다.notes: Used across mechanical contexts (replacing parts), sports (substituting players), and television broadcasting (replacing cast members or producers on a program).

교체해야.etymology: Inflected conditional/obligatory form of 교체하다 ('to replace'), composed of Sino-Korean 교체 (交替, from 交 gyo 'exchange' + 替 che 'replace'), the native verb-deriving stem -하- (-ha-), and the conjunctive ending -아야/-어야 (-aya/-eoya, which contracts with 하- to 해야 haeya, 'only if one does'), expressing either a necessary condition ('only if replaced') or obligation when followed by an explicit or elided 하다/되다 ('must replace').

history.meaning: to alternate, to replace in turn
only by replacing
must replace; only if replaced

morphemes.meaning: necessary-condition conjunctive ending (contracting with 하- to 해야)

교체해야.notes: In colloquial Korean, the auxiliary 하다 or 되다 is frequently dropped after -어야/아야/해야, leaving 교체해야 at the end of an utterance to mean 'we have to replace [them]'.

교회.etymology: Sino-Korean 교회 (敎會), compounding 교 (敎, 'teaching, religion') and 회 (會, 'assembly, gathering').

history.meaning: religious congregation
church (especially Protestant church in contemporary South Korea)

구.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 구 (九, 'nine'), from Middle Chinese *kjuwX; also used for Sino-Korean 구 (區, 'district, ward').

history.meaning: nine / administrative district
nine; district/borough

구간.etymology: Sino-Korean 구간 (區間), composed of 區 gu ('area, district, divide, boundary') + 間 gan ('interval, space between'). Coined in modern East Asian transport, administrative, and mathematical terminology to denote a bounded segment or stretch between two points.

history.meaning: bounded interval or stretch between two points
section, segment, interval (of a road, broadcast, or domain)

구간.notes: Common in traffic and transit reports (정체 구간 'congested stretch') as well as television ratings analysis (시청률 상승 구간 'ratings spike segment').

구경하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 구경 (traditionally analyzed as 求景, literally 'seeking a view/scenery', from 求 gu 'seek, look for' + 景 gyeong 'scenery, view, spectacle'; also historically attested with folk-etymological Hanja 口景 or Buddhist 究竟) combined with the native verb-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 구경ᄒᆞ다, meaning to watch a spectacle or go sightseeing.

history.meaning: to observe, to look at a sight or spectacle
to look around, to sightsee, to browse, to watch as a spectator

구경하다.notes: Covers everything from window-shopping and touring model-home showrooms (구경하는 집) to standing by idly watching a commotion (싸움 구경).

구내식당.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 구내식당 (構內食堂), formed from 구내 (構內, 'inside the premises/compound', from 構 gu 'construct, enclosure, premises' + 內 nae 'inside') + 식당 (食堂, 'dining hall, restaurant', from 食 sik 'eat, food, meal' + 堂 dang 'hall').

history.meaning: dining hall located within institutional grounds
in-house cafeteria, company canteen

구내식당.notes: In major Korean broadcasting stations (such as KBS in The Producers) and corporate headquarters, the 구내식당 is a central social hub where staff and celebrities cross paths.

rootFamily.gloss: in-house snack bar / commissary (構內賣店)

구도심.etymology: Sino-Korean 구도심 (舊都心), combining prefix 구- (舊, 'old, former') with 도심 (都心, 도 'capital, metropolis' + 심 'heart, center').

history.meaning: former city center
old town, historic downtown

구두.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from Japanese kutsu (靴, 'shoes'; voiced to -gutsu in compounds), referring in Korean specifically to Western-style or dress shoes.

history.meaning: shoes, boots
dress shoes, leather shoes

구두.notes: Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 구두 (口頭, 'oral, verbal', as in 구두 계약 'verbal agreement').

구리.etymology: Native Korean metal noun descending from Middle Korean 구리 ('copper, bronze').

history.meaning: copper, bronze
copper

구매하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 구매 (購買, composed of 購 gu 'buy, procure' + 買 mae 'buy, purchase') combined with the native Korean light verb -하다 (-hada, 'to do').

history.meaning: to buy, to purchase
to purchase, to procure

구매하다.notes: More formal and commercial than the native Korean verb 사다 ('to buy'); standard in retail, e-commerce (구매 확정 'confirming purchase'), and corporate procurement.

구멍.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 구무 / 구멍 ('hole, opening, cavity').

history.meaning: hole, cavity
hole, opening, gap

구면.etymology: Sino-Korean 구면 (舊面), composed of 舊 gu ('old, former, previous') + 面 myeon ('face, meeting, acquaintance'). Literally 'an old face', denoting the relationship of having met someone previously or being already acquainted.

history.meaning: a familiar face; someone known from before
prior acquaintance, having met before

구면.notes: Directly contrasts with 초면 (初面, 'first time meeting'); typically used with the copula 이다 as in 우리 구면이죠? ('We've met before, haven't we?').

구별하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 구별 (區別, combining 區 'divide into areas, classify' and 別 'separate, distinguish') plus the native light verb -하다. Both characters originally denoted dividing plots or sorting items by kind. In modern Korean, 구별하다 means recognizing the difference between two things so they are not confused.
구별하다.notes: Frequently pairs with 수 있다/없다 ('can/cannot tell apart').

구분.etymology: Sino-Korean 구분 (區分), composed of 區 gu ('divide, area, category') + 分 bun ('divide, separate, part'). Originally meaning to partition into sections, it denotes a clear distinction, demarcation, or classification.

history.meaning: to divide and separate; to demarcate
distinction, division, classification

구분.notes: While often used interchangeably with 구별 (區別), 구분 emphasizes partitioning a whole into categories (e.g., 공과 사의 구분 'separating public duty and private life'), whereas 구별 emphasizes telling two things apart by their traits.

cognates.meaning: to divide, to classify, to demarcate

구분하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 구분 (區分, from 區 gu 'divide, category' + 分 bun 'divide, separate') combined with the native Korean verb-deriving suffix -하다 (-hada, 'to do').

history.meaning: to partition, to divide into categories
to distinguish, to classify, to tell apart

구분하다.notes: In everyday conversation, 구분하다 is frequently used alongside 구별하다 in the sense of 'telling two similar things apart'.

rootFamily.gloss: to tell apart, to differentiate (區別하다)

구석.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 구석 ('inner corner, nook, recessed spot').

history.meaning: corner, nook
corner, nook, secluded spot

구성.etymology: Sino-Korean 구성 (構成), composed of 構 gu ('construct, frame, put together') + 成 seong ('complete, form, become'). Denotes the structural organization, lineup, or makeup of a whole from its constituent elements.

history.meaning: to put together and form; to compose
composition, makeup, structure, program lineup

구성.notes: In Korean television production, 구성 specifically refers to the structural formatting and segment planning of a variety show, crafted by a 구성작가 (format/continuity writer).

구절.etymology: Sino-Korean 구절 (句節), composed of 句 gu ('phrase, clause, verse line') + 節 jeol ('joint of bamboo, section, stanza, paragraph'). Originally a classical philological term for clauses and sections in texts, now referring to any memorable phrase, passage, or verse.

history.meaning: phrases and clauses; textual divisions
phrase, passage, verse, expression

구절.notes: Commonly used when quoting a memorable line from a book, poem, scripture, or song lyric (e.g., 유명한 구절 'a famous passage').

구조.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 構造, joining 構 (얽을 구, 'to interlock wooden beams, frame a building', written with the tree radical 木) and 造 (지을 조, 'to build, fashion, construct'). Rooted in traditional East Asian timber architecture where pillars and crossbeams interlock into a load-bearing frame, 구조 in modern Korean denotes both the physical layout of a building or object and the abstract structure of a text or system.
구조.notes: Common in architectural and analytical phrases like 건물 구조 ('building layout') and 내부 구조 ('internal structure'). Note homograph 구조 (救助, 'rescue').

구질구질하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated ideophonic root 구질구질- (gujilgujil-), evoking something damp, dingy, slovenly, or unpleasantly clingy, combined with the adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Related by Korean vowel harmony ablaut to the yang-vowel counterpart 고질고질하다.

history.meaning: wet and muddy; untidy, squalid, or tiresomely petty
pathetic, messy, shabby, clingy and undignified

morphemes.meaning: ideophone of messy, squalid, or clingy behavior

구질구질하다.notes: In modern relationship and K-drama dialogue, 구질구질하게 굴다 vividly describes acting pathetic or clingy, such as begging an ex-partner or making lame excuses.

구체적.etymology: Sino-Korean 구체적 (具體的), formed from 구체 (具體, literally 'having a complete body/form', from 具 gu 'possess, equip, complete' + 體 che 'body, substance, form', a classical phrase from Mencius 구체이미 具體而微) + the determiner-forming suffix -적 (的 jeok, '-ic, -al'). Repurposed in Meiji Japan (具体的) to translate European philosophical terms for 'concrete' (contrasting with 추상적 抽象的 'abstract') and borrowed into Korean.

history.meaning: possessing all parts of the body/whole
having tangible form; concrete, specific
concrete, specific, detailed

구체적.notes: Grammatically a noun/determiner that takes 이다 (구체적인 계획 'a specific plan') or the instrumental particle 으로 (구체적으로 'specifically, in detail').

구하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 구 (求, 'seek, request, obtain', or 救, 'save, rescue') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to seek/obtain; to rescue/save
to look for, get, find; to save/rescue

구호실.etymology: Sino-Korean 구호실 (救護室), combining 구호 (救護, 구 'rescue, relieve' + 호 'protect, care for') and 실 (室, 'room').

history.meaning: relief and first-aid room
first-aid room, medical aid station

국물.etymology: Compound noun composed of 국 (guk, 'soup', attested in Middle Korean as 국 and widely considered either native or a very early nativized borrowing from Old/Middle Chinese 羹 kæng 'broth, soup') + native Korean 물 (mul, 'water, liquid', Middle Korean 믈 meul). Denotes the liquid broth of a soup, stew, or dish as distinct from its solid ingredients (건더기).

history.meaning: soup liquid, broth
broth of soup or stew (with labial vowel rounding 믈 > 물)
soup broth; (idiomatically) fringe benefit or cut of profits

국물.notes: Pronounced [궁물] (gungmul) due to nasal assimilation of /k/ before /m/; idiomatically, 국물도 없다 ('there isn't even broth left for you') means 'you get zero sympathy or share of the reward'.

국자.etymology: Hybrid Korean kitchen noun combining native Korean 국 ('soup, broth', Middle Korean 국) with the Sino-Korean nominal suffix -자 (子, 아들 자, productively used in household implement names such as 의자 'chair' and 탁자 'table'). Literally 'soup-implement', 국자 denotes a deep-bowled spoon with a long handle for stirring and serving soup, broth, punch, or liquid batter. Pronounced [국짜] with regular tensification.
국자.notes: Also functions as an informal kitchen measure: 한 국자 ('one ladleful').

국장.etymology: Sino-Korean 국장 (局長), composed of 局 guk ('bureau, department, office, board') + 長 jang ('chief, head, leader, elder'). Denotes the executive head of a government bureau or a major division (such as the Variety Bureau 예능국 or Drama Bureau 드라마국) at a broadcasting network.

history.meaning: chief of an administrative bureau or department
bureau chief, department director

국장.notes: In Korean television networks, the 국장 (such as 예능국장 'Director of the Variety Department') is a high executive rank above chief producers (CP) and main producers (PD).

국장님.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native compound combining Sino-Korean 국장 (局長, from 局 guk 'bureau, department' + 長 jang 'chief, director') with the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (-nim, from Middle Korean 님 nim 'lord, master, esteemed person').

history.meaning: master, lord; honorific suffix for respected persons
Director, Bureau Chief (polite title of address and reference)

국장님.notes: In Korean workplace culture, superiors are never addressed by given name or bare title; 국장님 functions as both 'Director' and the polite second-person pronoun 'you' when speaking to them.

국장실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 국장실 (局長室), composed of 국장 (局長, 'bureau chief, director', from 局 guk 'bureau' + 長 jang 'chief') + the bound Sino-Korean suffix -실 (室 sil, 'room, office, chamber').

history.meaning: private office of a bureau chief
director's office

국장실.notes: Being summoned to the 국장실 at a broadcasting station is a classic K-drama trope signaling either a major reprimand over broadcast incidents or a high-stakes assignment.

cognates.meaning: Mr. (familiar suffix for males or juniors)

군.etymology: Sino-Korean bound title noun 군 (君 gun, 'lord, ruler, gentleman'). In Classical Chinese and Joseon Korea, 君 was an elevated royal title for princes and meritorious lords; in the modern era (reinforced by Meiji Japanese usage of 君 -kun), its register shifted in everyday speech to a familiar or affectionate title attached to the names of younger or unmarried males.

history.meaning: sovereign, lord, gentleman of noble character
feudal title for princes and ennobled officials
Mr., Master (title for a boy, younger man, or junior male colleague)

morphemes.meaning: lord, gentleman; title for a junior male

군.notes: Paired with 양 (孃 yang, 'Miss') for young women; often used by older bosses or elders (e.g., 백승찬 군 'young Mr. Baek Seung-chan') to sound formally affectionate or slightly old-fashioned.

rootFamily.gloss: Grand Prince, son of a Joseon king and queen (大君)

군데.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun and counter for places, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 군ᄃᆡ (gundoe). Etymologically analyzed as a fossilized compound incorporating the Middle Korean bound noun ᄃᆡ (doe > modern 데 de, 'place, spot').

history.meaning: place, spot, location
place, location (with monophthongization ㆎ > ㅔ)
place, spot (chiefly after numerals or determiners like 한 군데, 몇 군데)

군데.notes: Always preceded by native Korean numerals or determiners (한 군데 'one place', 두 군데 'two places', 몇 군데 'several places') when counting discrete locations or spots.

군만두.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound consisting of 군 (gun, contracted adnominal past participle from 구운 guun, of the native p-irregular verb 굽다 gupda 'to roast, bake, pan-fry') + Sino-Korean 만두 (饅頭 mandu, 'dumpling', borrowed from Middle/Mandarin Chinese 饅頭 mántou).

history.meaning: stuffed wheat dumpling; roasted/fried dumpling
pan-fried or deep-fried dumplings

morphemes.meaning: to roast, bake, pan-fry (p-irregular verb stem)

군만두.notes: The contracted modifier 군- ('roasted/fried', from 구운) also appears in beloved Korean winter snacks like 군밤 (roasted chestnuts), 군고구마 (roasted sweet potato), and 군옥수수 (grilled corn).

군청.etymology: Sino-Korean 군청 (郡廳), composed of 郡 gun ('county, administrative district') + 廳 cheong ('government office, hall, agency'). Refers to the local government headquarters administering a rural county (군).

history.meaning: administrative office of a county (gun)
county office, county hall

군청.notes: In South Korea's local government hierarchy, rural counties have a 군청 (郡廳), cities have a 시청 (市廳), and urban districts within large cities have a 구청 (區廳).

굳이.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adverb derived from the adjective stem 굳- (gut-, from 굳다 gutda 'to be hard, firm, resolute', Middle Korean 굳다) + the adverb-deriving suffix -이 (-i). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean phonemic spelling as 구디 (gudi, 'firmly, obstinately'), which underwent regular palatalization (/ti/ > /tɕi/) in Early Modern Korean while retaining morphophonemic spelling 굳이 in modern orthography.

history.meaning: firmly, resolutely, obstinately
stubbornly, insistently (after palatalization /t/ > /tɕ/ before /i/)
going out of one's way, intentionally, insists on (when unnecessary)

굳이.notes: Pronounced [구지] (guji) due to palatalization of ㄷ before ㅣ; often used alone as a skeptical rhetorical question (굳이? 'Do we really need to go out of our way to do that?').

rootFamily.gloss: to harden, to solidify, to lock in

굴다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) l-irregular verb 굴다 (gulda), attested in Middle Korean as 굴다 ('to behave, to act toward someone, to conduct oneself'). Syntactically requires a preceding manner adverb or adverbial clause specifying the nature of the behavior.

history.meaning: to act, to behave, to conduct oneself
to behave, to act (in a specified, often negative or conspicuous manner)

굴다.notes: Almost always paired with evaluative adverbs describing annoying or striking behavior, such as 못되게 굴다 ('to act mean'), 구질구질하게 굴다 ('to act pathetic/clingy'), or 까칠하게 굴다 ('to act prickly').

rootFamily.gloss: behaves, acts (present declarative with l-deletion before -ㄴ-)

굴리다.etymology: Native Korean morphological causative verb derived from the intransitive stem 구르- / 굴- (구르다, Middle Korean 굴다 / 구울다, 'to roll, tumble, turn over') combined with the causative suffix -리- (-li-) and dictionary ending -다. From the physical sense of making a round object roll, it developed vivid colloquial metaphors in Modern Korean: 'to work or drill a subordinate relentlessly' (making them run or roll around nonstop) and 'to circulate capital or rack one's brain' (머리를 굴리다).

history.meaning: to roll, turn over (intransitive)
to cause to roll, to turn something over
to roll (something); to work someone hard; to circulate (funds)

굴리다.notes: In workplace dramas like *The Producers*, 신입을 굴리다 ('to roll a rookie') is prime office slang for putting a new hire through grueling, nonstop tasks.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 굴리다

굴욕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 屈辱, composed of 屈 (굴, 'to bend, stoop, crouch, submit') and 辱 (욕, 'disgrace, shame, insult, humiliation'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese 屈辱, where it originally described the physical posture of bowing or yielding under duress alongside the social dishonor of submission.

history.meaning: bending in submission and suffering disgrace
humiliation, mortification, disgrace

굴욕.notes: Frequently paired with عکس/media slang as 굴욕 사진 ('humiliating/unflattering photo' of a celebrity caught off guard).

굵다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 굵다 ('to be thick in girth or diameter, coarse').

history.meaning: thick around, stout
thick (of cylinders, lines, raindrops, or voice)

굵다.notes: Contrasts with 두껍다, which measures flat thickness (books, walls, fabric).

굶기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb formed from the verb stem 굶- (굶다, Middle Korean 굼다 / 굶다, 'to go without a meal, go hungry, starve') plus the productive causative suffix -기- (-ki-) and citation ending -다. It shifts the valence from experiencing hunger oneself to inflicting hunger on another by withholding food or failing to provide meals.

history.meaning: to go without food, to fast or starve (intransitive)
to make someone go hungry, to starve someone

morphemes.meaning: to go hungry, skip a meal

굶기다.notes: Don't confuse intransitive 굶다 ('to skip a meal / starve oneself') with causative 굶기다 ('to starve someone else / make someone skip meals').

rootFamily.gloss: to go hungry, skip a meal

굽다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 굽다 ('to roast, bake, grill over heat' [ㅂ-irregular: 구워]; or homophonous 'to be bent, curved' [regular: 굽어]).

history.meaning: to roast, bake; to bend
to bake, roast, grill; to be curved

궁금하다.etymology: Adjective attested from Early Modern Korean as 궁검하다 and 궁금하다, combined with the native adjective-forming suffix -하다. Korean philologists frequently link the root 궁금- to Sino-Korean 窮禁 (from 窮 'exhausted, cornered, distressed' + 禁 'restrained, suppressed, pent-up'), originally denoting a stifled, anxious frustration in one's chest when cut off from news of someone, which subsequently broadened in Modern Korean to mean 'curious, wondering, eager to know'.

history.meaning: to feel anxious, stifled, or worried due to lack of news
to be curious, to wonder; to feel anxious about someone's news

궁금하다.notes: Unlike English 'curious' (which can mean 'strange/peculiar'), 궁금하다 only describes a person's mental state of wanting to know something.

rootFamily.gloss: curiosity, a question on one's mind

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 궁금하다

궁금해하다.etymology: Derived verb formed from 궁금하다 ('to be curious, wonder anxiously') + auxiliary -어하다, which converts an internal psychological adjective into a transitive/observable verb.

history.meaning: to wonder about, be curious about

권리.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 權利, composed of 權 (권, 'steelyard weight, authority, power') and 利 (리, 'sharp, benefit, profit, advantage'). Although 權利 appeared in Classical Chinese (such as Xunzi) meaning 'political power and material self-interest', it was repurposed in 1864 by W. A. P. Martin in his Chinese translation of Wheaton's *Elements of International Law* (萬國公法) to translate Western legal 'right' (jus), spreading via Meiji Japanese 権利 (kenri) into Modern Korean.

history.meaning: power and wealth; authority and profit
legal or moral right (translation of Western 'right')
right, entitlement, privilege

권리.notes: Be careful with pronunciation: 權利 (권리, [귈리] 'right, entitlement') vs. 權力 (권력, [귈력] 'political power, authority').

cognates.meaning: key money, non-refundable premium paid to a landlord

권리금도.etymology: Polymorphemic form consisting of the Sino-Korean compound noun 권리금 (權利金, 'key money, commercial goodwill fee', composed of 權 권 'authority, right' + 利 리 'benefit, interest' + 金 금 'metal, money') followed by the native Korean inclusive/concessive postpositional particle -도 ('also, too, even'). In South Korean real estate law and commerce, 권리금 denotes the lump-sum payment a new tenant pays to the outgoing tenant or landlord for intangible business value, clientele, and location rights.

history.meaning: fee paid for the transfer of commercial rights or lease privileges
even key money; goodwill fee as well

권리금도.notes: In Korean commercial leases, 권리금 ('key money / goodwill fee') is paid to the previous shop owner for fixtures and regular customers, distinct from 보증금 ('refundable security deposit').

귀.etymology: Native Korean body-part noun descending from Middle Korean 귀 ('ear').

history.meaning: ear
ear; corner/edge

귀띔.etymology: Native Korean compound noun derived from 귀 (Middle Korean 귀, 'ear') + 띄- (causative stem of 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다, 'to open [one's eyes or ears], to rise/awake', contracted from 띄우- in 귀를 띄우다 'to open someone's ears to something') + the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ. Literally 'an ear-opening', it came to mean dropping a quiet hint or giving someone an advance heads-up so they can catch on.

history.meaning: to open or awaken the ear (to information)
an indirect hint, a quiet tip or heads-up

귀띔.notes: One of the most frequently misspelled Korean words: the standard spelling is 귀띔 (with 띄 from 띄우다 'to open/float'), never *귀뜸.

rootFamily.gloss: to give a hint, tip off

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 귀띔

귀빈.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 貴賓, composed of 貴 (귀, 'noble, precious, high-ranking, honored') and 賓 (빈, 'guest, visitor', a character containing 貝 'cowrie shell/valuables' indicating ceremonial gifts presented to a guest). Used since Classical Chinese for an honored or aristocratic visitor, and in modern Korean for VIPs at state, corporate, or broadcasting events.

history.meaning: noble or honored guest
distinguished guest, VIP

귀빈.notes: Commonly seen in airports, hotels, and broadcasting halls as 귀빈실 (貴賓室, 'VIP lounge / reception room').

cognates.meaning: spirits of heaven and earth,鬼神; fierce god

귀신.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 鬼神, composed of 鬼 (귀, 'spirit of a deceased person, ghost, demon') and 神 (신, 'heavenly spirit, deity, supernatural power'). In Classical Chinese cosmology and Confucian ritual, 鬼神 denoted the dual forces of yin spirits (鬼, returning to earth) and yang spirits (神, expanding in heaven); in Korean vernacular usage it narrowed primarily to mean a ghost, apparition, or folk spirit.

history.meaning: ancestral spirits and heavenly deities; yin and yang spiritual forces
ghost, spirit of the dead, supernatural entity

귀신.notes: In Korean idioms, 귀신 doesn't just mean a spooky ghost—it also describes someone with uncanny skill or obsession (e.g., 일 귀신 'a workaholic/pro at work').

귀신같이.etymology: Derived hybrid adverb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 귀신 (鬼神, 'ghost, supernatural spirit') + the native Korean similative adjective stem 같- (같다, Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆮ다, 'to be like, to be the same as') + the productive adverbial suffix -이. Literally meaning 'in a manner like a ghost', it describes actions performed with uncanny intuition, startling speed, or inexplicable accuracy.

history.meaning: like a spirit or ghost
like a ghost; uncannily, with supernatural accuracy or speed

귀신같이.notes: Often paired with verbs of knowing or sensing—귀신같이 알아채다 means 'to figure something out with uncanny, sexto-sense accuracy'.

귀엽다.etymology: Hybrid Korean adjective attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 그위엽다 and 귀엽다, formed from the Sino-Korean root 貴 (귀, Middle Korean 그위 / 귀, 'noble, precious, esteemed') plus the native Korean deadjectival suffix -엽다 / -업다 (which derives adjectives of emotional evaluation) and -다. The meaning evolved from 'noble, respectable, and worthy of high esteem' in Middle Korean to 'endearing, darling, cute' in Modern Korean, initially applied to cherished children and later to anything adorable.

history.meaning: noble, precious, worthy of esteem and affection
endearing, lovable, darling
cute, adorable, charming

morphemes.meaning: native Korean adjective-forming suffix (cf. 노엽다, 두렵다)

귀엽다.notes: irregular ㅂ-stem adjective: the ㅂ turns into 우 before vowels (귀엽다 → 귀여워요, 귀여운). Its shared root with 귀하다 (貴 'precious') explains why calling someone 'precious' became calling them 'cute'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 귀엽다

귀찮다.etymology: Contracted lexicalized adjective derived from the phrase 귀하지 아니하다 (via intermediate 귀치 않다), consisting of Sino-Korean 貴 (귀, 'precious, noble, valued') + -하- ('to be') + negative nominalizer -지 + negative auxiliary 않다 (contracted from 아니하다, 'to not be'). In Early Modern Korean, 귀치 않다 meant 'ignoble, beneath one's station, or unworthy of value'; by semantic shift, what is unwelcome and beneath one's concern came to mean 'tiresome, bothersome, annoying, a hassle'.

history.meaning: to not be noble, precious, or worthy of regard
unwelcome, unpleasant, bothersome
to be bothersome, tiresome, annoying, a hassle

귀찮다.notes: Remarkably, 귀엽다 ('cute') and 귀찮다 ('bothersome') come from the exact same Hanja 貴 (귀, 'precious')—귀찮다 literally started out meaning 'not precious (귀하지 않다)'!

rootFamily.gloss: chronic laziness / finding everything a hassle (slang blend with -ism)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 귀찮다

귀찮아하다.etymology: Psychological process verb formed from the adjective stem 귀찮- (귀찮다, 'to be bothersome, tiresome', historically contracted from 귀하지 아니하다 'not precious/worthy') + the infinitive connective -아 + the auxiliary verb 하다 ('to do, feel, treat as').
