In Korean morphosyntax, attaching -아/어하다 converts subjective internal-state adjectives into active verbs that can take a third-person subject and an accusative object, expressing outward behavior of finding something annoying.

history.meaning: to be unworthy of regard > to be bothersome
to find (something) bothersome, to show annoyance or reluctance toward

morphemes.meaning: to be bothersome, tiresome (from 貴하지 않다)
auxiliary verb turning subjective adjectives into active psychological verbs

귀찮아하다.notes: Use 귀찮다 for your own feeling ('귀찮아' = 'It's a hassle for me'), but use 귀찮아하다 when describing someone else's visible annoyance ('피디님이 귀찮아해요' = 'The PD finds it bothersome').

귀척.etymology: Early 21st-century South Korean colloquial acronymic slang (줄임말) clipped from the two-word phrase 귀여운 척 ('pretending to be cute, putting on a cute act'). It combines the initial syllable 귀 of 귀여운 (the adnominal modifier form of 귀엽다 'to be cute', ultimately from Sino-Korean 貴) with the native Korean bound noun 척 (also 체, 'pretense, feigned air, act').

history.meaning: pretending to be cute, putting on a cute front
acting-cute slang; feigned cuteness

귀척.notes: Follows a productive Korean slang pattern of clipping '[Adjective] + 척' into two syllables: 예쁜 척 → 예척 ('acting pretty'), 멋진 척 → 멋척 ('acting cool'), 잘난 척 → 잘척 ('showing off').

귀티.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from the Sino-Korean morpheme 貴 (귀, 'noble, aristocratic, high-born, precious') + the native Korean noun 티 ('outward sign, air, look, trace, vibe'). Literally 'a trace or air of nobility', it denotes an innate look of refined upbringing, elegance, or wealth that radiates from a person's appearance or demeanor.

history.meaning: sign or air of nobility/high birth
history.stage: Early Modern / Modern Korean hybrid compound

history.meaning: noble refinement, aristocratic or affluent air

morphemes.meaning: outward sign, air, look, trace (native Korean)

귀티.notes: Almost always used with the verb 나다 or 흐르다: 귀티가 나다 / 귀티가 흐르다 ('to radiate class / look effortlessly upper-class'), contrasting with 촌티 ('country-bumpkin vibe').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 귀티

cognates.meaning: precious, noble, exalted (rendered onto native root)

귀하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adjective composed of the single-character Sino-Korean root 貴 (귀, Middle Chinese *kjwijH*, 'noble, of high rank, precious, rare, costly') and the native Korean adjective-deriving suffix -하다 (Middle Korean -ᄒᆞ다, 'to be'). Attested continuously since 15th-century Middle Korean (귀ᄒᆞ다) for both social nobility and rare material or emotional value.

history.meaning: to be noble, exalted, rare, or precious
to be precious, valuable, rare, or noble

귀하다.notes: 귀하다 is the foundational root behind a surprising family of everyday Korean words: 귀엽다 ('cute'), 귀찮다 ('bothersome', lit. 'not precious'), 귀티 ('classy air'), and 귀빈 ('VIP').

규정.etymology: Sino-Korean 규정 (規定), compounding 규 (規, 'compass, standard, rule') and 정 (定, 'fix, establish, settle').

history.meaning: established rule or stipulation
regulation, rule, provision

규정되다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean passive verb composed of the Sino-Korean noun 규정 (規定, 'regulation, stipulation, definition', from 規 규 'carpenter's compasses, rule, standard' + 定 정 'to settle, fix, determine') and the native Korean passive/inchoative verb 되다 (Middle Korean 도외다, 'to become, be made into'). Literally 'to become fixed by a standard or rule', hence 'to be defined, prescribed, or regulated'.

history.meaning: to fix by a standard + to become
history.stage: Classical Chinese root + Middle Korean verb

history.meaning: to be defined, stipulated, or regulated

규정되다.notes: In formal broadcast, legal, and academic Korean, replacing -하다 ('to define', 규정하다) with -되다 ('to be defined', 규정되다) creates an objective, impersonal tone.

규칙.etymology: Sino-Korean 규칙 (規則), compounding 규 (規, 'compass, circle-standard') and 칙 (則, 'rule, law, norm').

history.meaning: standards and rules
rule, regulation

균일하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 균일 (均一, 균 'equal, even' + 일 'one, uniform') + -하다.
균일하다.notes: Adverbial 균일하게 ('evenly, uniformly') is common in painting and baking instructions.

귤.etymology: Sino-Korean monosyllabic noun from 橘 (귤, Middle Chinese *kjwit*, Old Chinese *kʷrɯd*, 'mandarin orange, tangerine, Citrus reticulata'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as *Hunmong Jahoe* and medical compendia) as 귤, referring to the prized citrus fruit cultivated in the warm southern climate of Jeju Island and presented as royal tribute during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties.

history.meaning: mandarin orange tree and its fruit (native to southern China/East Asia)
tangerine, mandarin orange (valuable Jeju tribute fruit)
tangerine, mandarin orange (Citrus unshiu / reticulata)

귤.notes: Often called 감귤 (柑橘) in formal or agricultural contexts (especially 제주 감귤, Jeju tangerines), while 귤 is the everyday word for the winter snack.

rootFamily.gloss: dried tangerine peel used in traditional tea/medicine (橘皮)

그.etymology: Native Korean medial demonstrative determiner and third-person pronoun descending from Middle Korean 그 ('that [near listener or already mentioned]; he/she').

history.meaning: that (medial); the aforementioned
that, the; he/she

그.notes: Forms the medial member of the Korean three-way demonstrative system 이 ('this') — 그 ('that near you / known') — 저 ('that over there').

그거.etymology: Colloquial contraction of the native Korean demonstrative pronoun 그것 (그 'that' + 거 < 것 'thing').

history.meaning: that thing, it (colloquial)

그것.etymology: Native Korean compound pronoun formed from medial demonstrative 그 ('that') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object'), attested since Middle Korean.

history.meaning: that thing
that thing, it

그나마.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized adverb formed from the medial demonstrative pronoun 그 (Middle Korean 그, 'that') and the concessive postpositional particle -(이)나마 ('even if only, at least that much', itself a compound of the disjunctive/approximative particle -(이)나 and the particle -마). Literally meaning 'even if it is only that', it expresses partial relief that a suboptimal situation is at least better than the worst-case alternative.

history.meaning: even if it is only that; at least that much
at least, even so, thankfully (under poor circumstances)

morphemes.meaning: even if only, at least (concessive particle)

그나마.notes: 그나마 always implies that the overall situation is unsatisfactory, but there is one silver lining (e.g., 그나마 다행이다 = 'At least that much is fortunate [given how bad things are]').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 그나마

그나저나.etymology: Native Korean discourse-marking adverbial compound formed from the medial demonstrative pronoun 그 ('that [near listener or already mentioned]') + disjunctive particle -나 ('or, whether') + the distal demonstrative pronoun 저 ('that over there') + disjunctive particle -나 ('or, whether'). Contracted from expressions like 그거나 저거나 or 그리하나 저리하나 ('whether it is that or the other'), it sets aside preceding details to pivot the conversation to a new or more pressing topic ('anyway, by the way').

history.meaning: whether it be that way or that other way; regardless of that and the other
anyway, be that as it may, by the way

그나저나.notes: Notice the built-in Korean demonstrative contrast between 그 ('that, just mentioned') and 저 ('that over there'): 그나저나 literally sweeps aside 'that or the other' to ask a fresh question.

rootFamily.gloss: like this or like that; somehow or other
that thing or that other thing; anyway

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 그나저나

그날.etymology: Univerbated native Korean compound combining the medial/anaphoric determiner 그 ('that, the aforementioned', from Middle Korean 그) with 날 ('day', from Middle Korean 날), lexicalised as a single word when pointing back to a specific day known in context.

history.meaning: that day
that particular day

그날.notes: Standard Korean spacing joins high-frequency demonstrative + time nouns into one word: 그날 ('that day'), 그때 ('that time'), 그해 ('that year').

그냥.etymology: Contracted from 그 모양 (native 그 'that' + Sino-Korean 모양 模樣 'form, state, appearance'), literally 'in that state as it is'.

history.meaning: in that same state
just, as it is, without any special reason

그늘.etymology: Native Korean noun continuing Middle Korean 그늘 (an old ㅎ-final stem 그늘ㅎ-, cognate at a deeper root level with 그림자 'cast silhouette, shadow'). Whereas 그림자 refers to the dark outline projected onto a surface, 그늘 denotes the cool, sun-sheltered space beneath leafy branches, deep eaves, or a garden wall (나무 그늘, 처마 그늘). Figuratively, it can also signify protective shelter or a quiet trace of sadness on someone's face.
그늘.notes: Pairs with 지다 to form 그늘지다 ('to be shaded, cast in shade').

그니까.etymology: Colloquial phonological contraction of the native Korean conjunctive adverb 그러니까 ('so, therefore, because it is so'), formed by dropping the medial liquid syllable -러- via rapid-speech syncope (그러니까 > 그니까; compare 그런데 > 근데 and 그러지 > 그지). The underlying form 그러니까 derives from the demonstrative verb/adjective stem 그러- (from 그 'that' + -러-) plus the causal/sequential connective suffix -(으)니까 ('because, since, when').

history.meaning: because it is like that; therefore, so
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean standard form

history.meaning: so, therefore; I know right, that's what I'm saying (colloquial contraction)

morphemes.meaning: contracted stem of 그러- ('to be/do like that', from demonstrative 그)

그니까.notes: In everyday speech, 그니까 (along with its even further reduced cousins 긍까 and 그니까 말이야) often means 'Exactly! That's what I'm saying!' rather than just 'therefore'.

rootFamily.gloss: but, by the way (colloquial contraction of 그런데)
right?, isn't it? (colloquial contraction of 그렇지)

그다음.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') and 다음 ('next, following').

history.meaning: the next one, after that

그대로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb combining demonstrative 그 ('that') and particle/bound noun 대로 ('in accordance with, just as').

history.meaning: just like that
just as it is, intact, without change

그동안.etymology: Native Korean compound noun lexicalized from the phrase 그 동안, combining the medial demonstrative determiner 그 (Middle Korean 그, 'that') with the noun 동안 ('interval of time or space, span, while'). Originally denoting a specific preceding interval ('that span of time'), it fused into a single compound meaning 'in the meantime, during that time, up to now'.

history.meaning: that interval of time or space (phrasal combination)
during that time, in the meantime, for a while up to now

그동안.notes: Essential in Korean greetings after a separation: 그동안 잘 지냈어요? ('Have you been well during that time / all this while?').

그때.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of the medial demonstrative determiner 그 (Middle Korean 그, 'that') and the native noun 때 (Middle Korean ᄠᅢ, 'time, moment, occasion, season'). Originally a two-word noun phrase meaning 'that time', it became univerbated in Modern Korean orthography as 그때 ('at that time, back then, at that moment').

history.meaning: that time, that season or moment
at that time, back then, then

morphemes.meaning: time, moment, occasion (from Middle Korean ᄠᅢ)

그때.notes: Reduplicating it as 그때그때 means 'from time to time, on each occasion as it arises, case by case'.

rootFamily.gloss: at this time, right now (이 + 때)
on each occasion, case by case

그래.etymology: Native Korean interjection and intimate-level (해체) conjugated form derived from the demonstrative verb 그러다 ('to do so') or adjective 그렇다 (both contracted from 그러하다, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'to be/do like that', from demonstrative 그 'that' + -러- + 하다) plus the infinitive/intimate sentence-final ending -어/-아. Phonological coalescence of 그러- + -어 (or 그러하- + -여 > 그러해) yielded 그래, which grammaticalized from 'it is so / do so!' into the everyday affirmative interjection 'okay, sure, yes, alright'.

history.meaning: being so, doing like that (infinitive form of 그러ᄒᆞ다)
it is so; do like that; yes, okay, sure (intimate style)

morphemes.meaning: to be/do like that (from 그러하- / 그렇-)
intimate sentence-final / infinitive ending (coalescing into 애)

그래.notes: Intonation changes everything: falling 그래. means 'Okay / Sure / I see', rising 그래? means 'Really? / Is that so?', and reduplicated 그래, 그래 softens reassurance ('There, there / Okay, okay').

rootFamily.gloss: to do so, act like that

그래도.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러하여도 / 그리하여도 (from 그러하다 'to be so' + concessive ending -어도).

history.meaning: even if it is so
even so, still, nevertheless

그래서.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그리하여서 / 그러하여서 (그러하다 'to be so, do so' + causal connective -어서).

history.meaning: because it was so
so, therefore, for that reason

그램.etymology: Loanword from English gram and French gramme, introduced during the French metric system standardization of 1795 from Late Latin gramma and Ancient Greek grámma (γράμμα, 'written character, small weight', from gráphō 'to write'). Korean adapts the initial consonant cluster gr- by inserting the epenthetic vowel 으 to yield 그램. In Korean kitchens, markets, and cafés, it functions primarily as a bound or post-numeral measure noun (백 그램, 'one hundred grams').
그램.notes: Follows Sino-Korean numerals (오십 그램 '50 grams', 이백 그램 '200 grams') and is abbreviated g in print.

그러게.etymology: Native Korean conversational interjection and adverbial form derived from the demonstrative stem 그러- (contracted from 그러하-, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'to be/do like that', from medial demonstrative 그 'that') + the adverbative/resultative suffix -게 ('in such a manner, so that'). As an interjection, it arose via ellipsis of the clause 그러게 말이다 ('that is indeed how the matter stands / that's just what I'm saying'), expressing sympathetic agreement ('indeed, tell me about it, I know right').

history.meaning: in that manner, so as to be like that (adverbial form)
indeed, tell me about it, I know right (conversational interjection)

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix ('in that way, so that')

그러게.notes: Adding -요 creates the polite interjection 그러게요 ('Tell me about it / I know, right?'), one of the most natural ways to validate someone's complaint or observation in Korean.

rootFamily.gloss: to be like that, to be so
to do like that, to say so

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 그러게

그러니까.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러하니까 (그러하다 'to be so' + causal/explanatory ending -으니까).

history.meaning: therefore, so; I mean, that is to say

그러다.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative pro-verb contracted from 그러하다 / 그리하다 ('to do so, say so, be like that').

history.meaning: to do so, be so
to do so, say so

그러다가.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb formed from 그러다 ('to do so') + transfer/interruptive ending -다가.

history.meaning: while doing so, and then

그런.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative determiner contracted from 그러한, the adnominal form of 그러하다 ('to be like that, be such').

history.meaning: such, of that sort
such, like that

그런다고.etymology: Inflected quotative/concessive form of the native Korean demonstrative verb 그러다 (contracted from 그러하다, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'to do like that, act or say so', based on medial demonstrative 그 'that'). It consists of the verb stem 그러- + the present-tense active declarative suffix -ㄴ다 + the quotative/complementizer particle -고. In spoken Korean, 그런다고 frequently functions as an elliptical concessive connector (short for 그런다고 해서, 'even if one does/says that; just because things happen like that').

history.meaning: saying that one does so; (short for 그런다고 해서) even if one acts/says like that

morphemes.meaning: to do or say like that (from 그러하-)

그런다고.notes: Often introduces a pushback or rhetorical question: 네가 그런다고 뭐가 달라져? ('Just because you act/say like that, what changes?').

rootFamily.gloss: to do like that, to say so
even if it is so (from 그렇다 + -다고)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 그러다

그런데.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb contracted from 그러한데 (그러하다 'to be so' + circumstantial/contrastive ending -ㄴ데).

history.meaning: given that situation; however
however, but, by the way

그럼.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb and interjection contracted from 그러면 ('if so, then') or from the substantive form 그러함 ('being so; of course').

history.meaning: then, in that case; of course

그럼요.etymology: Polite native Korean affirmative interjection formed from 그럼 ('of course, certainly; if so') + the polite addressee particle -요. The base interjection 그럼 arose via phonological contraction of 그러함 (the substantive nominalization in -ㅁ of 그러하다, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'being so, it is indeed so', or overlapping with the conditional adverb 그러면 'if that is so [then naturally]'). Adding -요 elevates the intimate affirmation 그럼 into polite conversational register.

history.meaning: being so; if it is so > naturally, of course
of course, certainly, by all means (polite interjection)

morphemes.meaning: of course, naturally (contracted from 그러함 'being so')

그럼요.notes: Note the tonal/functional split in plain 그럼: as an interjection it means 'Of course!' (polite: 그럼요), whereas as a conjunction (short for 그러면) it means 'Then / In that case'.

rootFamily.gloss: of course; then, in that case
if so, then, in that case

그렇게.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative adverb contracted from 그러하게 (그러하다 'to be like that' + adverbial ending -게).

history.meaning: in that way
like that, so, in that manner

그렇다.etymology: Native Korean ㅎ-irregular demonstrative adjective contracted from 그러하다 (Middle Korean 그러하다, from demonstrative 그 + -러- + 하다).

history.meaning: to be like that, be so
to be so, be like that

그렇지.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean demonstrative adjective 그렇다 (contracted from 그러하다, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'to be like that, to be so', from medial demonstrative 그 'that' + -러- + 하다) combined with the committal/confirmative sentence-final suffix -지 (which grammaticalized from the Middle Korean nominalizer -디). Because -지 presupposes shared knowledge between speaker and listener, 그렇지 means either 'That's right! / Bingo!' (falling intonation) or 'Right? / Isn't that so?' (rising intonation).

history.meaning: to be like that + committal/confirmative ending -지 (< -디)

morphemes.meaning: to be like that, to be so (from 그러하-)

그렇지.notes: In fast casual speech, 그렇지 frequently drops its ㅎ and contracts to 그치 or 그지 ('Right? / Ain't it?').

rootFamily.gloss: to be like that, to be so

그렇지만.etymology: Native Korean conjunctive adverb lexicalized from the demonstrative adjective stem 그렇- (contracted from 그러하-, Middle Korean 그러ᄒᆞ다, 'to be like that, to be so', from medial demonstrative 그 'that') + the adversative/concessive connective ending -지만 (from Middle Korean -디만ᆞᆫ, composed of nominalizer -디 + restrictive particle 만 'only' + topic particle ᆞᆫ). Literally meaning 'it is so, only [on the other hand]...', it serves as the standard adversative conjunction 'however, but, nevertheless'.

history.meaning: although it is so, granted that it is like that, but
however, but, nevertheless

morphemes.meaning: to be like that, to be so (from 그러하-)

그렇지만.notes: Compared to 그러나 (formal/written 'however') and 근데 (casual spoken 'but'), 그렇지만 sits comfortably in polite spoken conversation and everyday writing.

rootFamily.gloss: to be like that, to be so

그릇.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 그릇 ('vessel, bowl, dish, container').

history.meaning: vessel, dish, receptacle
bowl, dish, vessel (also counter for servings)

그리.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 그리, formed from the medial demonstrative root 그 ('that [near listener or known in discourse]') + the directional and manner adverbial suffix -리 (part of the systematic Korean deictic triad 이리 'this way/so', 그리 'that way/so', 저리 'that way over there/so'). From its spatial sense ('toward that place') and manner sense ('in that way, like that'), it developed a degree sense ('all that much, so very'), especially before negative or evaluative predicates.

history.meaning: toward that place; in that manner, like that
like that, so; all that (much), particularly (often with negation)

morphemes.meaning: directional/manner adverbial suffix ('way, manner, to that degree')

그리.notes: Part of the symmetrical Korean deictic set 이리 ('this way'), 그리 ('that way / so'), 저리 ('that way over there'); in degree usage, 그리 좋지 않다 means 'not all that good'.

rootFamily.gloss: that way over there, like that (저 + -리)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 그리

그리고.etymology: Native Korean conjunction lexicalized from 그리하고 (그리하다 'to do so' + connective ending -고 'and').

history.meaning: doing so, and
and, furthermore

그리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 그리다 ('to draw lines, paint a picture'; also homophonous with 그리다 'to yearn for, miss').

history.meaning: to draw, paint; to long for
to draw, paint, depict

그리워하다.etymology: Native Korean psychological transitive verb formed from the descriptive adjective 그립다 ("to be missed, longed for", from Middle Korean 그리다 "to yearn for" + adjectival suffix -브-) combined with the auxiliary construction -어하다 ("to feel or show outwardly"). Because Korean adjectives like 그립다 cannot take a third-person subject in plain declaratives or an accusative object (-을/를), adding -어하다 converts the internal state into an active, observable transitive verb.

history.meaning: to yearn for, long for someone absent
to be missed, to evoke longing (adjective)
to miss fondly, to actively long for

morphemes.meaning: to do; to feel or manifest outwardly

그리워하다.notes: Use 그립다 ("X가 그립다") for first-person feelings ("I miss X"), but use 그리워하다 ("X를 그리워하다") when describing someone else missing X or when using the object marker -을/를.

그릴.etymology: Borrowed from English grill, which came through French gril and grille ('gridiron, metal grating') from Latin crāticula, diminutive of crātis ('wickerwork lattice, hurdle'). Because Korean syllable structure does not allow initial consonant clusters, gr- is adapted with epenthetic 으 and final -ll is realized as liquid ㄹ in 그릴. In modern Korean cooking it denotes both an outdoor barbecue grate and the top-heat broiler element inside an oven.
그릴.notes: Used with 에 굽다 ('to grill/broil on a grill').

그림.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 그림, derived from 그리다 ('to draw, paint') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: drawing, painting, picture
picture, drawing, painting

그림자.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 그리메 ('shadow, reflection'), formed from the root of 그리다 ('to outline, trace') + suffix -자.

history.meaning: shadow, reflection, image
shadow, silhouette

그만.etymology: Native Korean adverb and noun lexicalized from the medial demonstrative determiner 그 ("that, near the listener or already mentioned in discourse", Middle Korean 그) plus the bound noun and delimiter particle 만 ("extent, degree, just that much", Middle Korean 만). Literally meaning "up to that extent and no further", it shifted from indicating a measured limit to commanding or describing the cessation of an action ("no more, stop").

history.meaning: to that extent, that much
stopping at that point; no more, enough

그만.notes: Standing alone as an exclamation ("그만!"), it is a direct command meaning "Stop!" or "Enough!"; before a verb, it means "no longer" or "unintentionally / ended up doing".

rootFamily.gloss: only to that extent; passable, stop doing

그만두다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb formed from the adverb/noun 그만 ("up to that point, no more", from demonstrative 그 "that" + bound noun 만 "extent") and the transitive verb 두다 ("to put, place, leave behind", Middle Korean 두다). Literally meaning "to leave something at that point without going further", it developed the standard senses of "to quit (a job), stop (an activity), or drop (a matter)".

history.meaning: to leave a matter at that extent
to quit, discontinue, resign from, stop doing

그만두다.notes: Commonly contracted in casual spoken Korean to 관두다 ("회사를 관두다" = to quit the company; "관둬!" = drop it / forget it!).

그만하다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adjective derived from 그만 ("that extent, that much; no more", from medial demonstrative 그 "that" + bound noun 만 "extent/degree") combined with the light verb and adjectivalizer 하다 ("to do; to be"). Originally an adjective meaning "to be of that size or degree", it split functionally into an adjective ("to be about that much; to be tolerable/not worse") and an active verb ("to stop doing, call it a day").

history.meaning: to be of that extent or degree
to stop doing, quit; (adj.) to be about that size or passably well

morphemes.meaning: to do; to be of such a quality

그만하다.notes: Watch the part-of-speech split: as an action verb ("이제 그만하자" = let's stop now) it conjugates with processive endings, whereas as an adjective ("병세가 그만하다" = the illness is no worse/tolerable; "그만하면 잘했다" = if it's to that extent, you did well) it describes degree.

rootFamily.gloss: to be of this extent; to stop here

그분.etymology: Compound third-person honorific pronoun formed from the native Korean medial demonstrative determiner 그 ("that, near the listener or previously mentioned", Middle Korean 그) and the honorific bound noun 분 ("esteemed person"). The classifier/noun 분 is attested from Early Modern Korean and is generally traced to a semantic specialization of Sino-Korean 分 (분, "portion, social station, status"), shifting from "one's distinguished status" to an honorific counter and pronoun root for people.

history.meaning: that person of status / that esteemed individual
that person (honorific); he, she (polite)

그분.notes: Korean lacks native gender-specific polite pronouns for "he" or "she" in spoken conversation; 그분 is the standard respectful way to refer to a third person of either gender.

그어야지.etymology: Inflected deontic/volitional form of the native Korean ㅅ-irregular (ㅅ 불규칙) verb 긋다 ("to draw a line, mark off, strike", Middle Korean 긋다). Before the vowel-initial infinitive suffix -어, the stem-final consonant -ㅅ deletes (긋- + -어 -> 그어), which reflects the loss of an intervocalic voiced fricative (ㅿ) in Middle Korean. The modal ending -야지 (contracted from -어야 하지) adds the sense of personal resolution or obligation ("should draw, must draw").

history.meaning: having drawn a line (infinitive of 긋다)
should draw (a line); I ought to mark it off

morphemes.meaning: to draw (a line), strike (ㅅ-irregular stem 긋-)
deontic/volitional modal ending (should, must, intend to)

그어야지.notes: Frequently used in the idiom "선을 그어야지" ("You have to draw the line / set clear boundaries!"), where 긋다 drops its ㅅ before -어.

rootFamily.gloss: to draw a line; to set a boundary figuratively
to make a mark in Korean history, be epoch-making

그전.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun (혼종어) combining the native Korean medial demonstrative determiner 그 ("that, the aforementioned", Middle Korean 그) with the Sino-Korean temporal/spatial noun 전 (前, "front, before, prior"). Originally a two-word phrase meaning "before that (time)", it fused into a single lexicalized temporal noun referring to a time prior to a previously mentioned reference point.

history.meaning: before that time, prior to that occasion
before then, formerly, the time prior to that

그전.notes: Written as one word without a space (그전) when meaning "before that time / formerly", contrasting with 이젠 ("now") or 그 후 ("after that", which is written with a space).

그중.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun (혼종어) composed of the native Korean medial demonstrative determiner 그 ("that, those", Middle Korean 그) and the Sino-Korean noun 중 (中, "middle, center, inside, among"). Literally denoting "the interior or midst of those things", it lexicalized as a single compound word meaning "among them, out of those".

history.meaning: in the midst of those
among them, out of those; to some extent (as an adverb)

그중.notes: According to Korean orthography, 그중 ("among them") is fused into a single word without a space, whereas other nouns before 중 (e.g., 회의 중 "in the middle of a meeting") require a space.

rootFamily.gloss: meanwhile, in the midst of that (그 와중에)

그쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun and pronoun joining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') and 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: that side, that direction; you/your side

그치.etymology: Colloquial spoken Korean interjection and tag question contracted from 그렇지 ("that is so, right?"), which is the native Korean demonstrative adjective 그렇다 ("to be so, to be like that", itself a contraction of 그리하다) inflected with the confirmative sentence-final suffix -지. In rapid speech, the stem-final ㅎ of 그렇- drops and the vowel sequence -어러- reduces, yielding 글치 or 그치.

history.meaning: it is indeed so (confirmative)
that's right; isn't it so?
right?, isn't that so?, exactly! (colloquial contraction)

morphemes.meaning: to be so, to be like that (contracted from 그렇-)

그치.notes: Add -요 at the end (그치요 / 그쵸) to keep the casual, conversational warmth while remaining polite to listeners.

rootFamily.gloss: that is so; right? (standard uncontracted form)
to be so, to be like that
right? (polite contracted form of 그렇지 않아요)

그해.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining medial demonstrative 그 ('that') with 해 ('year, sun').

history.meaning: that year
that year

cognates.word: 極 (きょく / ごく, kyoku / goku)

극.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Hanja 極 (극, "ridgepole, utmost limit, extreme, pole"). In Classical Chinese, 極 originally referred to the highest central ridgepole beam (棟極) supporting the peak of a timber roof; because nothing in a building stands higher than the ridgepole, its meaning extended metaphorically to the ultimate limit, extremity, or zenith of any state, as well as geographical and magnetic poles.

history.meaning: ridgepole at the highest peak of a roof; supreme point
the utmost limit, zenith, pole
extreme, culmination, pole (e.g., 극에 달하다 "to reach an extreme")

극.notes: Often appears in the set phrase "극에 달하다" ("to reach an extreme / peak") or "극과 극은 통한다" ("opposites attract / extremes meet"); note that homophonous 극 (劇) means "drama/theater".

rootFamily.gloss: to overcome, surmount a hardship (克服, distinct Hanja 克; compare 極度 극도 "extreme degree")

cognates.word: 極端的 (きょくたんてき, kyokutanteki)

극단적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner from 極端的 (극단적), composed of 극단 (極端, "extreme, extremity, farthest edge") plus the adnominal/abstract suffix -적 (的, "characteristic of, -ic/-al"). 極 ("ridgepole, utmost limit") and 端 ("tip, end, extremity of a thread or cloth") reinforce each other as a synonym compound meaning "the very farthest end", while -적 adapts the word into a modifier or predicate noun ("extreme, radical").

history.meaning: the farthest end or utmost limit
extreme, radical, drastic (in nature)

극단적.notes: Nouns ending in -적 (的) take 이다 ("극단적이다" = is extreme), -인 before a noun ("극단적인 선택" = an extreme choice), or -으로 as an adverb ("극단적으로" = extremely).

근거.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 根據 (근거), a compound of 근 (根, "root of a tree, base, origin") and 거 (據, "to lean on, grasp, occupy, rely upon as support"). Attested in Classical Chinese historical texts (such as the *Book of Han*) for having a firm root and foothold, it evolved from physical "roots and support" to logical or empirical "grounds, basis, or evidence" for an argument or belief.

history.meaning: deep roots and firm foothold; base of operations
foundation, basis, authority, evidence for a claim

morphemes.meaning: 據 (to rely on, occupy, evidence, basis)

근거.notes: Frequently paired with 있다/없다: "근거 없는 소문" means an "unfounded/baseless rumor", while "무슨 근거로?" asks "On what basis / grounds?".

근데.etymology: Native Korean colloquial conjunction formed by phonological contraction of 그런데 ("but, however, by the way"), where the medial liquid-vowel sequence -러- drops between ㄱ and ㄴ (그런데 > 근데). 그런데 itself is a grammaticalization of the demonstrative adjective stem 그러하- / 그러- ("to be so, to be like that") + the adnominal modifier -ㄴ + the bound noun 데 ("place, circumstance, situation", Middle Korean 뎨/데), literally meaning "in that circumstance".

history.meaning: in a situation that is like that
however, but, by the way (standard conjunction)
but, by the way, anyway (colloquial contracted conjunction)

morphemes.meaning: to be so, to be like that (contracted from 그러-)

근데.notes: One of the most frequent discourse markers in spoken Korean; it smoothly pivots the topic ("by the way...") or introduces a mild counterpoint ("but wait..."), though in formal writing you should spell out 그런데.

rootFamily.gloss: but, however, by the way (uncontracted standard form)
then, in that case (contracted from 그러면)

cognates.word: 肌肉 (jīròu; cf. 筋肉 jīnròu)

근육.etymology: Sino-Korean anatomical noun from 筋肉 (근육), composed of 근 (筋, "sinew, tendon, muscle fiber", written with Bamboo 竹, Flesh 月/肉, and Strength 力 to evoke tough, fibrous cords of strength) and 육 (肉, "flesh, meat"). Used in premodern East Asian medical texts for "sinews and flesh" collectively, the compound was standardized in late 19th-century Meiji Japan (筋肉) and adopted into Korean as the technical anatomical translation for Western "muscle".

history.meaning: sinews/tendons and flesh of the body
history.stage: Classical Chinese & Traditional East Asian Medicine

history.meaning: anatomical muscle, musculature

근육.notes: In pronunciation, nasal-liquid epenthesis (ㄴ 첨가) applies at the morpheme boundary, so 근육 is pronounced [근뉵] (geun-nyuk), not [그뉵].

근처.etymology: Sino-Korean 근처 (近處), compounding 근 (近, 'near, close') and 처 (處, 'place, locality').

history.meaning: nearby place
vicinity, neighborhood, nearby

글.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 글 ('writing, text, script, composition'), historically linked to the root of 그리다 ('to draw, inscribe').

history.meaning: writing, characters, literature
writing, text, piece of writing

글귀.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native Korean 글 ('writing, text, prose or verse', Middle Korean 글) with 귀, the older nativized Sino-Korean pronunciation of 句 (글귀 구, 'phrase, clause, poetic line'). Although modern Sino-Korean standardizes 句 as 구 in compounds like 문구 (文句) and 구절 (句節), the traditional reading 귀 remains preserved in standard 글귀. It typically refers to a memorable motto, inscription, clue rhyme, or literary quote.
글귀.notes: Pronounced [글뀌] with tensification after ㄹ; collocates with 적다 ('write down') and 새기다 ('inscribe, take to heart').

글쎄.etymology: Native Korean discourse interjection derived by contraction and tensification from a phrase built on the demonstrative adverb 그리 ("like that, so") and the verb 하다 ("to do, say, be"), historically reconstructed from 그리하세 or 글세 ("let's say so / well, if you put it like that"). Expressive word-internal tensification (ㅅ > ㅆ) yielded 글쎄, which signals hesitation, reluctance to agree, or exasperated pushback.

history.meaning: well, let us say so; speaking of that
well..., I'm not sure; I mean, seriously! (interjection)

글쎄.notes: Intonation changes the meaning completely: with a drawn-out falling-rising tone ("글쎄요..."), it means "Well, I'm not really sure"; with a sharp, clipped tone ("글쎄, 아니라니까!"), it means "I'm telling you / Seriously, listen to me!".

rootFamily.gloss: well, I'm not sure (polite form of 글쎄)

글쎄요.etymology: Polite interjection formed from native discourse marker 글쎄 (contracted from 그러할세 / 그리할까, expressing hesitation) + polite particle -요.

history.meaning: well..., let me see, I am not sure (polite)

글씨.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 글시, from 글 ('writing') + 시 ('seed, form, style').

history.meaning: written characters, handwriting
handwriting, written letters

글씨체.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 글씨 ('handwriting, script') with Sino-Korean 체 (體, 'body, style, form').

history.meaning: handwriting style, script style, font

글자.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound descending from Middle Korean 글짜, combining native 글 ('writing') with Sino-Korean 자 (字, 'letter, character').

history.meaning: written character
letter, character

글자.notes: Pronounced [글짜] with tensification reflecting the traditional compound link.

긁히다.etymology: Native Korean morphological passive formed from the verb stem 긁- (긁다, 'to scratch, scrape, rake', carrying the complex coda ㄺ) plus the passive suffix -히-. In spoken Korean, the velar stop ㄱ of ㄺ merges with the following ㅎ to produce aspirated [글키다] ([글켜요], [글킵니다]). It describes polished wood, metal, glass, or skin sustaining a scrape or scratch from a sharp edge.
긁히다.notes: Pronounced [글키다]; contrasts with active transitive 긁다 ('to scratch, scrape').

금.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 금 (金, 'gold, metal', from Middle Chinese *kim) and native Korean 금 (Middle Korean 금, 'drawn line, crease, crack, limit').

history.meaning: gold, metal / line, crack, limit
gold; line, crack, crease

금고.etymology: Sino-Korean 금고 (金庫), compounding 금 (金, 'gold, money, valuables') and 고 (庫, 'storehouse, treasury, vault').

history.meaning: strongbox or vault for valuables
safe, vault, strongbox

금메달.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 금 (金, 쇠 금 / 황금 금, 'gold') with the loanword 메달, borrowed from English medal (via French médaille and Italian medaglia, ultimately tracing back to Vulgar Latin medālia 'small coin'). Together with 은메달 ('silver medal') and 동메달 ('bronze medal'), 금메달 designates first-place championship honors and is used playfully in conversation for top-marks praise.
금메달.notes: Takes the verb 따다 ('to win/clinch a medal') or 받다 ('to receive a medal').

금박.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 金箔, joining 金 (황금 금, 'gold') with 箔 (발 박 / 금박 박, 'bamboo screen, paper-thin metal leaf'). In traditional Korean decorative arts—especially Joseon royal silk stamping (금박장), lacquerware, and book illumination—artisans beat gold into gossamer sheets thinner than paper. Modern Korean uses 금박 for gilt lettering on books and frames, decorative foil, and edible gold leaf on pastries.
금박.notes: Pairs with 입히다 ('to gild, apply gold leaf') or 찍다 ('to stamp in gold foil').

금방.etymology: Sino-Korean 금방 (今方), compounding 금 (今, 'now, this moment') and 방 (方, 'just now, right then').

history.meaning: this very instant
just now; right away, very soon

금붕어.etymology: Compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 금 (金, "gold, golden") and the Korean noun 붕어 ("crucian carp, *Carassius auratus*"). The word 붕어 itself is a phonological nativization of Sino-Korean 부어 (鮒魚, "crucian carp", attested in Middle Korean as 부어 and developing an epenthetic velar nasal -ㅇ- in Early Modern Korean). Because ornamental goldfish were selectively bred from golden-mutated crucian carp in China, Korean specifies the fish as a "golden crucian carp".

history.meaning: golden crucian carp, goldfish
history.stage: Late Middle / Early Modern Korean (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: goldfish (*Carassius auratus*)

morphemes.meaning: crucian carp (from 鮒魚 부어 via nasal epenthesis)

금붕어.notes: In Korean pop culture and slang, "금붕어 기억력" ("goldfish memory") is a playful idiom for someone who forgets things after three seconds, and 붕어빵 is the beloved winter pastry shaped like a carp.

금빛.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 금 (金, 'gold') with native 빛 ('light, color, gleam').

history.meaning: golden color, golden gleam

금색.etymology: Sino-Korean 금색 (金色), compounding 금 (金, 'gold') and 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: color of gold
gold color, golden

금속.etymology: Sino-Korean 금속 (金屬), compounding 금 (金, 'metal, gold') and 속 (屬, 'category, class').

history.meaning: the class of metals
metal

금액.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 金額 (금액), composed of 금 (金, "gold, metal, money, currency") and 액 (額, "forehead, inscribed wooden plaque, fixed quota or sum"). In Classical Chinese administration, 額 shifted from "forehead" to the "header plaque" over a gate and then to a "stipulated numerical quota or total written at the head of a ledger", giving 金額 the precise meaning of "total monetary sum or charge".

history.meaning: forehead; inscribed plaque; fixed quota or total number
amount of money, monetary sum, price, charges

금액.notes: More formal than 돈 ("money") or 값 ("price"); you will see 금액 constantly on receipts, bank apps, contracts, and billing statements (e.g., 결제 금액 = payment amount).

금요일.etymology: Sino-Korean 금요일 (金曜日), from 금 (金, 'metal/gold, Venus') + 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary') + 일 (日, 'day').
금요일.notes: All seven days of the week in Korean end in 요일: 월요일 (Moon), 화요일 (Fire/Mars), 수요일 (Water/Mercury), 목요일 (Wood/Jupiter), 금요일 (Metal/Venus), 토요일 (Earth/Saturn), 일요일 (Sun).

cognates.meaning: prohibition of alcohol; to abstain from liquor

금주.etymology: Sino-Korean verb-object compound noun from 禁酒 (금주), composed of 금 (禁, "to forbid, prohibit, restrain, abstain", showing trees 林 over an altar/omen 示 to mark taboo sacred ground) and 주 (酒, "alcohol, fermented liquor", showing water 氵 and a fermenting jar 酉). Literally "prohibiting or abstaining from liquor", it refers both to personal sobriety and to institutional alcohol bans.

history.meaning: state ban on brewing or drinking liquor; ritual abstinence
abstaining from alcohol, sobriety, alcohol prohibition

금주.notes: Pair it with 금연 (禁煙, "quitting/no smoking"): Koreans often declare "오늘부터 금주·금연!" ("No drinking and no smoking starting today!") after a rough hangover; also note the homophone 금주 (今, "this week").

금지.etymology: Sino-Korean 금지 (禁止), compounding 금 (禁, 'forbid, restrict') and 지 (止, 'stop, halt').

history.meaning: forbidding and stopping
prohibition, ban

금화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 金貨, combining 金 (황금 금, 'gold') and 貨 (재화 화, 'coin, currency, valuable goods', written with the cowrie-shell radical 貝 reflecting ancient shell money). Paralleling 은화 (銀貨, 'silver coin') and 동화 (銅貨, 'copper coin'), 금화 denotes minted gold coinage in historical and economic contexts while also serving as the classic emblem of buried treasure in stories.
금화.notes: Contrasts with 지폐 ('paper banknote') and 일반 동전 ('everyday coin').

급.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and suffix from Hanja 級 (급, "rank, grade, class, step, tier"). In Classical Chinese, 級 (composed of Silk 糸 and Reach 及) originally denoted the graded order of silk threads; under Qin dynasty military law, soldiers were promoted one rank for each enemy head severed in battle, causing 級 to mean both "severed head", "step of a staircase", and "hierarchical rank or class".

history.meaning: order of silk threads; step of promotion in military rank; stair step
official grade, tier, or step in hierarchy
rank, class, league, tier (e.g., 급이 다르다 "to be in a different league")

급.notes: In everyday Korean slang and TV banter, "급이 다르다" means "to be on a whole different level / in another league", and "A급 / 특A급" means "A-list / top-tier".

rootFamily.gloss: level, standard (水準; compare 동급 同級 "same rank/peer")

cognates.word: 急上昇 (きゅうじょうしょう, kyūjōshō)

급상승하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound verb formed from 급상승 (急上昇, "sharp rise, sudden surge") and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do"). The Sino-Korean stem combines 급 (急, "sudden, rapid, steep, urgent") with 상승 (上昇, "rising, ascending", from 上 "up, above" + 昇 "to rise, ascend like the sun [日] over a measure [升]"). Together they describe a steep, rapid upward climb.

history.meaning: ascending, rising upward
to spike sharply, skyrocket, surge rapidly (in ratings, prices, or rankings)

급상승하다.notes: A staple of Korean broadcasting and internet media: "시청률이 급상승하다" means "viewership ratings skyrocket", and "급상승 검색어" (often shortened to 실검) refers to trending/surging search terms.

rootFamily.gloss: to rise, ascend, go up (上昇-)

급하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 급 (急, 'urgent, pressing, hasty, steep') + native adjective-forming verb -하다.

history.meaning: to be urgent, pressing
to be urgent, hasty, in a hurry

급히.etymology: Derived adverb combining Sino-Korean 급 (急, 'urgent, hasty') with the native adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: urgently, hastily
hurriedly, urgently, in haste

긋는다는.etymology: Inflected adnominal quotative form of the native Korean ㅅ-irregular transitive verb 긋다 ("to draw a line, mark off, strike", Middle Korean 긋다). Because the present-tense processive indicative marker -는다 begins with a consonant (ㄴ), the verb stem 긋- retains its final coda consonant ㅅ (pronounced [근는다] via nasal assimilation of ㄷ/ㅅ before ㄴ). The suffix -는 at the end is a contraction of the quotative adnominal construction -고 하는 ("that [someone] draws / the act of drawing").

history.meaning: to draw a line, mark off, sever
(the act/claim) that one draws a line or marks off

긋는다는.notes: Because ㅅ is pronounced as [ㄷ] in syllable coda and assimilates to the following nasal ㄴ, 긋는다는 is pronounced [근는다는] (geun-neun-da-neun).

rootFamily.gloss: should draw (a line) (inflected vowel-initial form where ㅅ drops)

긋다.etymology: Native Korean ㅅ-irregular (ㅅ 불규칙) transitive verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 긋다 (alternating between stem 긋- before consonants and 그ᅀ- with the voiced spirant ㅿ before vowels, meaning "to draw a line, mark a boundary, sever"). When Middle Korean ㅿ was lost in the 16th century, vowel-initial forms lost the consonant entirely (그어, 그으니), creating the modern ㅅ-irregular paradigm while preserving 긋- before consonants.

history.meaning: to draw a line, mark off a limit, cut across
to draw (a line), strike (a match),划 (a boundary), charge on credit (외상을 긋다)

morphemes.meaning: to draw a line, mark, strike (ㅅ-irregular stem)

긋다.notes: A classic ㅅ-irregular verb: drop the ㅅ before vowel endings (긋다 -> 그어요, 그어서, 그은), and note that its nominalized derivative 금 ("drawn line / crease") is completely native Korean, unrelated to 금 (金, "gold").

rootFamily.gloss: a drawn line, crease, boundary mark (deverbal noun from 긋- + -ㅁ)
to draw a line; to set a clear boundary with someone

cognates.word: 肯定的 (こうていてき, kōteiteki)

긍정적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner from 肯定的 (긍정적), composed of 긍정 (肯定, "affirmation, acknowledgment") and the suffix -적 (的, "characteristic of, -ive"). In Classical Chinese, 肯 originally depicted flesh (月/肉) attached to bone (冎), meaning "the tender meat at the joint" (as in *Zhuangzi*'s 肯綮), before shifting to "to be willing, consent, approve"; combined with 定 ("to settle, fix, decide"), 肯定 came to mean "to affirm or acknowledge positively".

history.meaning: willing consent; logical affirmation (contrasting with 否定 부정 "negation")
affirmative, positive, optimistic in outlook

긍정적.notes: Its direct antonym is 부정적 (否定的, "negative"); in everyday Korean, "긍정적으로 생각하다" means "to think positively / look on the bright side".

rootFamily.gloss: negative, pessimistic (否定的, antonym sharing -定的)

cognates.meaning: spirit, mind, vital energy, breath, mood
breath, air, vital energy, qi, spirit

기.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Hanja 氣 (기, "breath, vapor, vital energy, spirit, aura"). In early Chinese script, 氣 combined curling cloud/vapor lines (气) with Rice (米), depicting steam rising from hot cooked grain given to guests, and symbolizing the invisible vital breath or life-force (*qì*) nourished by food and respiration. In Korean, it became deeply embedded in everyday idioms describing personal confidence, stamina, and emotional spirit.

history.meaning: rising steam/vapor; vital breath, cosmic life-energy, pneuma
vital energy, breath, spirit, disposition
spirit, vitality, aura, confidence, energy

기.notes: Essential for natural Korean idioms: "기가 막히다" ("breath is blocked" = to be dumbfounded, or amazingly good), "기가 죽다" ("spirit dies" = to feel intimidated/crestfallen), and "기운" (氣運, "energy/strength").

rootFamily.gloss: mood, feeling, state of spirits (氣分)

기간.etymology: Sino-Korean 기간 (期間), compounding 기 (期, 'appointed time, term') and 간 (間, 'interval, span').

history.meaning: interval of time
period, duration, term

기계.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 機械 (기계), composed of 기 (機, "loom, trigger mechanism, pivot, contrivance", with Wood 木 and subtle threads 幾) and 계 (械, "wooden fetters, instrument, appliance, tool"). In Classical Chinese (notably *Zhuangzi*, where an old gardener rejects a well-sweep lever as a 機械 that breeds a "mechanical heart" 機心), the compound meant an ingenious mechanical contrivance; in modern East Asia it became the standard word for "machine".

history.meaning: clever wooden lever or mechanical contrivance (e.g., in Zhuangzi)
machine, machinery, mechanical apparatus; automaton-like person

기계.notes: Pronounced [기계] or [기게] in standard Korean; someone who is hopeless with technology or gadgets is humorously called a "기계치" (機械癡, "machine-idiot / technophobe").

rootFamily.gloss: precision instrument, apparatus, device (器機/機器)
airplane, aircraft (飛行機, sharing 機)

기관차.etymology: Sino-Korean 기관차 (機關車), from 기관 (機關, 'engine, mechanism') + 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, train car').

history.meaning: engine-powered rail car
locomotive

기꺼이.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the stem of 기껍다 (Middle Korean 깃겁다, 'to be glad, joyful') + adverbial suffix -이.

history.meaning: joyfully, gladly
gladly, willingly, with pleasure

기념.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 紀念 (or 記念, 기념), composed of 기 (紀, "to arrange threads, chronicle, record", or 記, "to write down, remember") and 념 (念, "to keep in mind, ponder, recall", composed of Now 今 over Heart 心, literally "holding present in the mind"). Combining "to record/chronicle" and "to hold in mind", the compound means "commemoration, celebration, or keeping a memory alive".

history.meaning: recording and holding in memory; keeping in mind
history.stage: Literary Sinitic & Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: commemoration, celebration of a milestone or occasion

morphemes.meaning: 紀 / 記 (to record, chronicle, remember)
念 (to keep in mind, think of, remember)

기념.notes: Very productive in compounds: 기념일 (紀念日) is an "anniversary / memorial day", 기념품 (紀念品) is a "souvenir / memento", and in casual speech Koreans say "퇴사 기념으로 한잔하자" ("Let's grab a drink to celebrate quitting!").

rootFamily.gloss: anniversary, memorial day, commemorative day (紀念日)

기념일.etymology: Sino-Korean three-morpheme compound 紀念日, composed of 紀 (기록할 기 / 벼리 기, 'to chronicle, thread together'), 念 (생각 념, 'to hold in mind, remember', combining 今 'now' over 心 'heart'), and 日 (날 일, 'day'). Joined together, 기념 ('commemoration, keeping a memory alive') plus 일 ('day') designates an annual personal milestone or civic remembrance day.
기념일.notes: Productively forms compounds like 결혼기념일 ('wedding anniversary') and 개교기념일 ('school founding day').

기다려주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb composed of 기다리다 ("to wait for", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 기드리다 and 기들우다) linked via the infinitive suffix -어 (기다리- + -어 -> 기다려) to the auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give; to perform an action for someone's benefit", Middle Korean 주다). The auxiliary -어 주다 adds warm interpersonal nuance, framing the act of waiting as a patient favor or kindness toward the other person.

history.meaning: to wait + to give/bestow
to wait for someone (as a kindness or favor)

morphemes.meaning: to wait, await (from Middle Korean 기드리-)
to give; to do for someone's benefit

기다려주다.notes: In Korean, simply saying "기다리다" states the neutral fact of waiting, whereas "기다려주다" ("기다려 줘서 고마워" = "Thank you for waiting for me") acknowledges that the other person generously gave their time for your sake.

rootFamily.gloss: to wait for an esteemed person (humble benefactive)

기다리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 기드리다 ('to wait for, await').

history.meaning: to wait for, await
to wait, await

cognates.meaning: to look forward to, expectation, anticipation
to expect, look forward to, anticipation

기대.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 期待 (기대), a synonym-reinforcing compound of 기 (期, "appointed time, cycle of the moon 月, to hope for, expect") and 대 (待, "to wait for, await, stand by on the road 彳"). Originally meaning "to set an appointed time and wait in hope", it became the standard East Asian noun for "expectation, anticipation, or looking forward to something".

history.meaning: to hope for an appointed time and await someone or something
expectation, anticipation, hope placed in someone or something

morphemes.meaning: 期 (appointed time, period, to hope for, expect)

기대.notes: Notice the active vs. passive verbs: 기대하다 means "to expect / look forward to", while 기대되다 ("내일이 기대돼요!") is the idiomatic way to say "I'm excited for / looking forward to tomorrow!". Also do not confuse with native Korean 기대다 ("to lean on").

rootFamily.gloss: to expect, anticipate, look forward to (期待-)
expected value, level of expectation (期待値)

기대다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Early Modern Korean 기대다 ('to lean one's body or an object against a support').

history.meaning: to lean against
to lean on, rest against, rely on

기대다.notes: Distinct from Sino-Korean 기대하다 (期待하다, 'to expect, look forward to').

기대하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 기대 (期待, 기 'expect, await a set time' + 대 'wait for') + -하다.
기대하다.notes: Conveys warm anticipation rather than mere neutral waiting.

기도하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 기도 (祈禱, "prayer, supplication") plus the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do"). Both Hanja characters carry the semantic altar/spirit radical 示 (礻): 기 (祈, with phonetic 斤) means "to beseech the spirits for good fortune", and 도 (禱, with phonetic 壽 "longevity") means "to offer ritual prayers for long life or aid in distress". Together with 하다, it is the universal Korean verb "to pray".

history.meaning: ritual supplication to heaven, spirits, or Buddha for blessings and relief
to pray (in religious worship or earnest personal wish)

기도하다.notes: Used across all religions as well as figuratively in everyday life; Note the humorous modern slang "기도 메타" ("prayer meta" from gaming/broadcasting), meaning crossing your fingers and just praying something works out when it's out of your control.

rootFamily.gloss: to wish earnestly for, pray for (祈願, sharing 祈)

기둥.etymology: Native Korean architectural noun descending from Middle Korean 기동 ('pillar, wooden column, post').

history.meaning: pillar, column
pillar, column, post

기록.etymology: Sino-Korean 기록 (記錄), compounding 기 (記, 'write down, note') and 록 (錄, 'inscribe, copy, register').

history.meaning: written account or register
record, documentation

기록하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 기록 (記錄, 'written record or chronicle') and the native verbalizer -하다 (-hada, 'to do'). The Sino-Korean stem combines 기 (記, 'to write down, remember') and 록 (錄, 'to copy, inscribe, register on metallic or bamboo tablets'). It has been standard across Korean administrative annals, including the Joseon Veritable Records (실록), and remains the everyday verb for logging events or setting a record.

history.meaning: to inscribe and preserve a written account
to record, document, or log in writing

morphemes.meaning: light verb suffix forming active verbs

기록하다.notes: Frequently paired with the auxiliary 두다 (기록해 두다, 'to write down for safekeeping/future reference').

기름.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 기름 ('oil, fat, grease').

history.meaning: oil, grease, fat
oil (cooking oil, lamp oil, or fuel)

기름칠.etymology: Native-hybrid compound combining the native Korean noun 기름 ('oil, fat, grease', Middle Korean 기름) with the suffix -칠 (漆, originally 'lacquer, varnish', generalized to any act of coating, brushing, or smearing a surface). Just as 페인트칠 means 'applying paint', 기름칠 means brushing or rubbing oil onto metal hinges or dry wood.
기름칠.notes: Combines with -하다 to form the verb 기름칠하다 ('to oil, lubricate').

기본.etymology: Sino-Korean 기본 (基本), compounding 기 (基, 'foundation, base') and 본 (本, 'root, origin, basis').

history.meaning: foundation and root
basics, foundation, default

cognates.word: 基本的 (きほんてき, kihonteki)

기본적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner from 基本的 (기본적), composed of 기본 (基本, "foundation, basis, fundamentals") and the adnominal/abstract suffix -적 (的, "characteristic of, -ic/-al"). 基 (containing Earth 土 and phonetic 其) denotes the rammed-earth foundation of a building, while 本 (a stroke at the bottom of a Tree 木) denotes the root and trunk of a tree; together with -적, they mean "foundational, basic, or underlying".

history.meaning: the earthen foundation of a structure and root of a tree; basis
basic, fundamental, elementary in nature

morphemes.meaning: 基 (foundation of a building, base, groundwork)
本 (root of a tree, origin, fundamental)

기본적.notes: Most frequently heard in the adverbial form 기본적으로 ("basically, fundamentally, by default") or the modifier 기본적인 ("기본적인 예의" = basic manners/etiquette).

rootFamily.gloss: foundation, groundwork, basics (基礎, sharing 基)
root, essence, fundamental nature (根本, sharing 本)

기분.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기분 (氣分), combining 氣 (기, "breath, vital energy, spirit, atmosphere") and 分 (분, "portion, allotment, state, disposition"). While attested in Classical Chinese for one's innate temperament or vital constitution, its everyday modern Korean usage denoting subjective mood or emotional state was heavily shaped by Meiji-era and modern Japanese 気分 (kibun).

history.meaning: vital allotment, innate temperament, atmospheric state
personal mood, emotional state, physical feeling
mood, feeling, frame of mind

기분.notes: Frequently paired with verbs like 좋다 (to be good) or 나쁘다 (to be bad) to describe transient emotional states (e.g., 기분이 좋다, "to feel good / be in a good mood").

기뻐하다.etymology: Derived from the native Korean adjective 기쁘다 (gippeuda, Middle Korean 기쁘다 kippeuta, 'to be joyful, pleased') by attaching the psychological verbalizer construction -어하다 (-eohada). In Korean grammar, subjective internal-state adjectives like 기쁘다 cannot directly take a third-person subject in declarative statements without converting into an observable behavioral verb via -어하다. Thus 기뻐하다 literally means 'to show or feel joy outwardly' and is the standard way to say that someone else is glad or thrilled.

history.meaning: to be glad, joyful (adjective)
to rejoice, be delighted (third-person/active verb)

기뻐하다.notes: When speaking respectfully about an elder or guest, the honorific infix -(으)시- attaches to form 기뻐하시다 ('to be delighted').

기쁘다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 깃브다, formed from the verb stem 깃- ('to rejoice') + adjective-forming suffix -브다.

history.meaning: to be glad, joyful
to be happy, glad, pleased

기쁨.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verbal noun derived from the adjective stem 기쁘- (기쁘다, "to be joyful, glad, delighted") plus the productive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ. In 15th-century Middle Korean texts such as the Seokbo Sangjeol (1447), the verb appears as 기브다 (kìpùtá) and its nominalization as 기븜 (kìpúm), before the medial bilabial stop underwent glottal tensioning (ㅂ > ㅃ) in Early Modern Korean.

history.meaning: joy, gladness, delight
joy, delight, happiness

기쁨.notes: Follows the productive native Korean pattern of turning descriptive verbs into abstract nouns via -ㅁ/-음 (compare 슬프다 "sad" -> 슬픔 "sadness", 아프다 "painful" -> 아픔 "pain").

기사.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기사 (記事), composed of 記 (기, "to record, write down, chronicle") and 事 (사, "matter, affair, event"). In Classical Chinese and traditional Korean historiography, 記事 denoted recording historical facts or an annalistic account; during the late 19th-century modernization of the press (reinforced by Japanese 記事 kiji), it specialized into a newspaper or broadcast news article.

history.meaning: to record events; written historical account
newspaper report, journalistic article
news article, journalistic report, written item

기사.notes: A prominent Korean homophone: 기사 can mean "news article" (記事), "driver/chauffeur or engineer" (技士), or "knight" (騎士) depending on the underlying Hanja.

기사님.etymology: Hybrid honorific title combining Sino-Korean 기사 (技士, 기 'skill, craft' + 사 'specialist', meaning 'technician, engineer, professional driver') with native honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: driver, technician, engineer (polite address)

cognates.meaning: in an article, on the page of a report

기사상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 기사상 (記事上), formed from 기사 (記事, "news article, report", from 記 기 "to record" + 事 사 "matter, event") and the productive Sino-Korean bound relational suffix -상 (上, originally "top, above, surface", used abstractly to mean "from the standpoint of, in the text of, on the surface of").

history.meaning: written account + on the surface of / with respect to
in the literal text of the article, as stated in the report

morphemes.meaning: in terms of, on the surface of, according to (上)

기사상.notes: The bound suffix -상 (上) attaches to Sino-Korean nouns to frame a perspective or domain (e.g., 사실상 "in fact", 이론상 "in theory", 기사상 "as written in the article, as opposed to behind-the-scenes reality").

기색.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기색 (氣色), borrowed from Classical Chinese 氣色, combining 氣 (기, "vital breath, spirit, inner energy") and 色 (색, "color, facial countenance, visible look"). Originally a traditional East Asian medical and physiognomic term referring to how inner vital energy manifests in one's facial complexion, it broadened in Korean to mean any subtle facial expression, demeanor, or outward sign of emotion.

history.meaning: facial complexion reflecting internal vital energy; countenance
facial expression, look, outward sign or hint of feeling

기색.notes: Often used in negative or observant contexts such as 지친 기색이 없다 ("showing no sign of fatigue") or 당황한 기색 ("a flustered look").

기세.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기세 (氣勢), from Classical Chinese 氣勢, composed of 氣 (기, "vital breath, spirit, morale") and 勢 (세, "force, power, momentum, strategic posture"). In classical military treatises, it described the surging morale and strategic momentum of an army; in modern Korean, it denotes a person's fierce momentum, intimidating confidence, or unstoppable drive.

history.meaning: military morale and strategic momentum; surging force
momentum, spirited vigor, forceful attitude

기세.notes: Commonly appears in the four-character idiom 기세등등 (氣勢騰騰, "riding high with triumphant momentum") and constructions like ~할 기세다 ("looking ready/determined to do X at any second").

기술.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 技術, pairing 技 (재주 기, 'deft manual skill, artistry', written with the hand radical 扌) and 術 (재주 술 / 길 술, 'method, practiced art, technique'). Originally referring to mastered artisanal methods and practical arts, 기술 in modern Korean spans everything from culinary, carpentry, and masonry craftsmanship to advanced industrial engineering and digital technology.
기술.notes: Covers personal craft/technique (요리 기술 'cooking skill') as well as science and engineering (과학 기술).

기싸움.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun (기싸움, 氣싸움), combining Sino-Korean 기 (氣, "vital energy, spirit, willpower, aura") with native Korean 싸움 ("fight, struggle, contest"), which is the deverbal noun of 싸우다 ("to fight", from 15th-century Middle Korean 싸호다 ssàhòtá + nominalizer -옴/-움). Literally a "clash of vital energies", it refers to a psychological battle of wills or unspoken dominance contest.

history.meaning: vital spirit + fighting, combat
battle of wills, psychological standoff, clash of egos

기싸움.notes: A quintessential Korean drama and variety-show trope: when two rivals or senior colleagues lock eyes and refuse to back down without raising their voices, Koreans call it 팽팽한 기싸움 ("a tense battle of wills").

rootFamily.gloss: to be intimidated, have one's spirit crushed (氣죽다)

기어들어가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial compound verb 기어들어가다, built from three native verbal roots linked by the infinitive/connective suffix -어/-아: 기다 ("to crawl, creep on hands and knees", Middle Korean 기다 kìtá) + -어 + 들다 ("to enter, go in", Middle Korean 들다 tùltá) + -어 + 가다 ("to go, move away from the speaker", Middle Korean 가다 kàtá). Together they trace manner ("crawling"), path ("entering"), and deictic direction ("going in").

history.meaning: to crawl + to enter + to go
to crawl inside, to slink or creep back in

기어들어가다.notes: Beyond physical crawling, it is used figuratively for slinking away in humiliation or speaking in a tiny, intimidated voice (목소리가 기어들어가다, "one's voice trails off timidly").

rootFamily.gloss: to crawl out, creep out toward the speaker

기어코.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb 기어코 (期於코), grammaticalized via phonological contraction of 기어하고 (期於하고, "aiming at / determinedly doing"). The Sino-Korean base 기어 (期於) combines 期 (기, "to expect, stipulate, resolve upon") and the classical prepositional particle 於 (어, "at, toward, in"), while -코 is the aspirated contraction of the light verb stem 하- ("to do", formerly ᄒᆞ-) plus the connective suffix -고 (*hako > *hko > kho).

history.meaning: resolving upon and doing; aiming at without fail
in the end, at all costs, insistently, without fail

기어코.notes: Closely synonymous with 기어이 (期於이), which derives from the same Sino-Korean root 期於 plus the native adverbial suffix -이; 기어코 often carries a slightly stronger nuance of stubborn persistence or "going ahead and doing it anyway".

rootFamily.gloss: by all means, without fail, in the end (期於이)

기억.etymology: Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶), compounding 기 (記, 'remember, record') and 억 (憶, 'recall, keep in mind').

history.meaning: retention and recollection in mind
memory, recollection

기억나다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb combining Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶, 'memory') with native 나다 ('to arise, surface, come out').

history.meaning: to come to mind, be remembered

기억하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 기억 (記憶, 'memory, recollection') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: to remember, recall

기업.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기업 (企業), composed of 企 (기, originally picturing a person standing on tiptoe to look ahead; hence "to plan, initiate, undertake") and 業 (업, "work, trade, undertaking, profession"). Re-popularized across East Asia in the Meiji period via Japanese 企業 (kigyō) to translate Western concepts of commercial "enterprise" and "business corporation".

history.meaning: to initiate an undertaking; planned work
commercial enterprise, business firm
enterprise, corporation, business company

morphemes.meaning: to stand on tiptoe, plan, undertake (企)

기업.notes: Forms the base of major economic terms in Korean, such as 대기업 (大企業, "major conglomerate / chaebol") and 중소기업 (中小企業, "small and medium-sized enterprises, SMEs").

기울어지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 기울다 (Middle Korean 기울다, 'to tilt, incline') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to tilt, lean, slant
to become tilted, lean over, slant

기울이다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 기우리다, formed from 기울다 ('to tilt, lean') + causative suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to tilt or incline
to tilt, tip; to devote (attention or effort, e.g. 귀를 기울이다)

기원하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb 기원하다 (祈願하다), combining the Sino-Korean noun 기원 (祈願, "prayer, earnest wish", from 祈 기 "to pray to deities, beseech" + 願 원 "to wish, desire, vow") with the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do"). Originally a Buddhist and ritual term for offering prayers for a specific vow, it is now widely used in formal greetings and broadcast slogans for wishing success, victory, or recovery.

history.meaning: ritual prayer and vow to deities or Buddhas
to pray earnestly for, to wish for (success, health, peace)

morphemes.meaning: to do (native light verb forming verbs from nouns)

기원하다.notes: Do not confuse with the homophonous verb 기원하다 (起源하다, "to originate from, trace one's origin to"), which uses 起源 (起 "to rise" + 源 "source/spring").

rootFamily.gloss: wish, cherished desire ( 소원 / 所願)

기자.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기자 (記者), composed of 記 (기, "to record, write down, chronicle") and the agentive suffix 者 (자, "person who does"). While 記者 appeared in Classical Chinese to mean "one who records events, scribe, chronicler", it was revitalized in Meiji Japan as 記者 (kisha) to translate English "newspaper reporter / journalist" and quickly entered late 19th-century Korean journalism.

history.meaning: scribe, chronicler, author of a record
newspaper reporter, press journalist
reporter, journalist, correspondent

기자.notes: In Korean broadcasting and print media, reporters commonly sign off their segments or bylines with their full name followed by 기자 (e.g., KBS 뉴스 홍길동 기자입니다).

기자님.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean honorific noun 기자님 (記者님), combining Sino-Korean 기자 (記者, "reporter, journalist", from 記 기 "to record" + 者 자 "person") with the native Korean honorific title suffix -님. The suffix -님 derives from 15th-century Middle Korean 님 (ním, "lord, master, esteemed person", which as an independent noun later gained an initial consonant via palatalization/prosthesis to become 현대어 임, "beloved/lord").

history.meaning: recorder/journalist + lord, esteemed person
reporter (honorific title of address or reference)

기자님.notes: In the entertainment industry depicted in *The Producers*, publicists, managers, and PDs routinely address entertainment reporters as 기자님 to maintain cordial media relations and favorable coverage.

기적.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 기적 (奇蹟 / 奇跡), composed of 기 (奇, 'extraordinary, rare, marvellous') and 적 (蹟/跡, 'footprint, trace, vestige, accomplished deed'). Literally meaning 'an extraordinary trace or wondrous deed', the term entered East Asian literary prose to denote supernatural wonders and later translated Latin miraculum in Christian and modern secular contexts. In everyday spoken Korean, 기적이에요 ('it's a miracle!') is used hyperbolically for unexpectedly rapid recoveries or strokes of luck.

history.meaning: extraordinary trace or wondrous deed
miracle, marvel, remarkable turn of events

기적.notes: Pronounced [기적] without tensification; 기적처럼 ('like a miracle, miraculously') is a common adverbial phrase.

기절초풍하다.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character idiomatic verb 기절초풍하다 (氣絕焦風하다), compounded from 기절 (氣絕, "fainting, losing consciousness", literally 氣 기 "breath/vital energy" + 絕 절 "to cut off, cease"), 초풍 (焦風, a traditional Korean medical term for an acute convulsive fit or stroke-like shock, from 焦 초 "scorched, anxious, acute" + 風 풍 "wind disorder, palsy, seizure"), and the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do"). Literally "to have one's breath cut off and suffer an acute wind-fit", it evolved into a vivid hyperbole for fainting dead away from shock or astonishment.

history.meaning: cessation of breath/consciousness + acute convulsive wind-fit
to faint dead away from shock; to be scared or astonished out of one's wits

기절초풍하다.notes: Almost always used hyperbolically in everyday speech (e.g., 엄마가 알면 기절초풍할 일, "something that would make Mom faint dead away if she found out") rather than for an actual medical emergency.

sources.title: Naver Korean Dictionary — 기절초풍하다 (氣絕焦風하다)

cognates.word: 既定事實 / 既定事实 (jìdìng shìshí)

기정사실.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound noun 기정사실 (既定事實), composed of 기정 (既定, "already decided or settled", from 既 기 "already, completed" + 定 정 "to fix, settle, determine") and 사실 (事實, "fact, reality", from 事 사 "matter, affair" + 實 실 "fruit, substance, reality"). Coined and popularized in modern East Asian legal, political, and journalistic prose (alongside Japanese 既定事実 kitei jijitsu) as an exact rendering of French/diplomatic *fait accompli*.

history.meaning: already settled + actual matter/reality
established fact, fait accompli
an established fact, fait accompli, foregone conclusion

기정사실.notes: Frequently extended with the suffix -화하다 (化하다, "to make into") as 기정사실화하다 ("to treat or spin something as a fait accompli"), a classic media tactic when leaking casting or dating rumors.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn into a fait accompli (既定事實化하다)

sources.title: Naver Korean Dictionary — 기정사실 (既定事實)

기지개.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 기지게 ('stretching one's body and limbs').

history.meaning: stretching the limbs
body stretch (idiomatic with 켜다: 기지개를 켜다)

기차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 기차 (汽車), literally 'steam vehicle', from 기 (汽, 'steam') + 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle').
기차.notes: Remains the everyday Korean word for intercity trains even in the era of electric high-speed rail.

기차역.etymology: Sino-Korean 기차역 (汽車驛), combining 기차 (汽車, 기 'steam' + 차 'vehicle', 'train') and 역 (驛, 'post station, railway station').

history.meaning: railway train station
train station

기차표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 기차표 (汽車票), joining 기차 (汽車, 'steam/rail train') with 표 (票, 'ticket, slip').
기차표.notes: Parallel to 입장표 ('admission ticket') and 차표 ('transit ticket').

기특해.etymology: Intimate/informal conjugated form (기특해) of the Sino-Korean descriptive verb 기특하다 (奇特하다), composed of 기특 (奇特, from 奇 기 "rare, wondrous, unusual" + 特 특 "special, outstanding, distinctive") and the native Korean light verb 하다 (conjugated with -어/아 as 해). In Classical Chinese and Buddhist texts, 奇特 meant "wondrous and extraordinary"; in both Korean and Japanese (奇特 kitoku), its meaning shifted amelioratively toward "commendable, admirable, touchingly praiseworthy".

history.meaning: rare and extraordinary, wondrous, marvelous
to be wondrously admirable, commendable, praiseworthy
admirable, praiseworthy, sweet (intimate/informal conjugation)

morphemes.meaning: intimate/informal connective or sentence-final ending (-어/아 -> 해)

기특해.notes: Social register warning: 기특하다 / 기특해 is used strictly downward (by elders, seniors, or superiors toward children, juniors, or pets) to praise thoughtful or mature behavior; using it toward a boss or elder sounds patronizing and rude! Also watch out for the Mandarin false friend 奇特 (qítè), which still means "weird/peculiar" rather than "praiseworthy".

rootFamily.gloss: to be admirable, praiseworthy, sweet (奇特하다)

기회.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 기회 (機會), from Classical Chinese 機會, combining 機 (기, originally a "loom" or "crossbow trigger mechanism", metaphorically "pivotal spring of action, critical juncture") and 會 (회, "coming together, meeting, convergence"). Literally the "convergence of a pivotal trigger-moment", it came to mean "favorable juncture, opportunity, chance".

history.meaning: critical juncture, convergence of timing and circumstance
opportunity, chance, occasion

기회.notes: Notice how the character 機 (기, "loom / trigger mechanism") links concrete machines like 기계 (機械, "machine") and 비행기 (飛行機, "airplane") with abstract turning-points like 기회 (機會, "opportunity") and 위기 (危機, "crisis").

기획사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 기획사 (企劃社), formed from 기획 (企劃, "planning, project design", composed of 企 기 "to stand on tiptoe, anticipate, undertake" + 劃 획 "to draw lines, delineate, devise a plan") and the Sino-Korean suffix -사 (社, "company, society, firm"). While literally any "planning agency", in contemporary South Korean usage it almost always refers to an entertainment talent and music production agency (연예 기획사).

history.meaning: project planning + commercial company/firm
entertainment management agency; planning firm

기획사.notes: In K-pop and Korean broadcasting (such as *The Producers*), 기획사 is the standard industry word for talent agencies that scout, train, and manage idols and actors (short for 연예 기획사).

긴장하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 긴장 (緊張, 긴 'tight, taut' + 장 'stretch a bowstring') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: stretching taut; mental tension
to be nervous, tense up, stay on alert

길.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 길 (stem 길ㅎ, 'road, path, way, journey').

history.meaning: road, path, course
road, street, path, way

길가.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 길 (gil, Middle Korean 길 kil, 'road, way, street') and 가 (ga, Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ kos, 'edge, border, margin'). Because the second element historically began with a genitive-locative boundary marker (saisiot), the initial consonant of 가 undergoes obligatory tensification in standard pronunciation, yielding [길까] (gilkka). It forms part of a productive spatial series with 창가 ('windowside'), 문가 ('doorway edge'), and 강가 ('riverside').

history.meaning: edge or margin of a road
roadside, pavement edge, street outside a gate

길가.notes: Always pronounced [길까] with a tense ㄲ on the second syllable, just like 창가 [창까] and 강가 [강까].

길거리.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) synonymic compound noun 길거리, combining 길 ("road, path, way", from 15th-century Middle Korean 길ㅎ kìlh, an h-final noun) and 거리 ("street, thoroughfare, crossroads district", attested in Early Modern Korean as 거리). The pairing of two near-synonyms ("road" + "street") creates a concrete collective noun referring to public streets and busy urban thoroughfares.

history.meaning: road, path + street, thoroughfare district
history.stage: Middle and Early Modern Korean components

history.meaning: street, public thoroughfare, roadside

길거리.notes: While 길 can refer to any path, route, or abstract way, 길거리 specifically evokes a bustling public street with pedestrians, shops, and street vendors (e.g., 길거리 음식, "street food"; 길거리 캐스팅, "street scouting by an agency").

길다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem adjective descending from Middle Korean 길다 ('to be long in length or duration').

history.meaning: to be long
to be long

길바닥.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun 길바닥, composed of 길 ("road, street", from Middle Korean 길ㅎ kìlh) and 바닥 ("bottom, floor, flat ground surface", from Middle Korean 바닿 pàtàh / 바닥). Note that because Middle Korean 길ㅎ ended in a latent glottal fricative ㅎ, some compounds show aspiration (like 길가), whereas 길바닥 is leveled in modern standard pronunciation to [길빠닥] with tensification. Literally "the floor/bottom of the road", it emphasizes the hard, bare pavement or being cast out onto the streets.

history.meaning: road, way + bottom, ground surface
bare street surface, pavement; out on the streets

길바닥.notes: Carries a gritty, earthy, or desperate connotation compared to neutral 길거리: sitting on the pavement is 길바닥에 앉다, and going broke/homeless is 길바닥에 나앉다 ("to end up sitting out on the bare street").

rootFamily.gloss: palm of the hand (hand + flat surface)

길이.etymology: Native Korean derived measure noun descending from Middle Korean 기리, formed from 길- (길다, 'to be long') + nominalizing suffix -이.

history.meaning: length; for a long time
length

김.etymology: Sino-Korean family name 김 (金), written with the Hanja 金 ("gold, metal", from Old Chinese *kəm > Middle Chinese *kim). In Korean, this character has two distinct Sino-Korean readings reflecting vocalic divergence: 금 (keum) when used in common nouns meaning "gold, metal, money, Friday", and the conservative palatalized/fronted reading 김 (kim) when used as a Korean surname and in related historical toponyms (such as 김해 金海, seat of the Gaya royal clan, and 김포 金浦). In royal foundation legends of Silla (김알지, Kim Alji) and Geumgwan Gaya (김수로, Kim Suro), the surname was mythologically associated with golden boxes or golden eggs.

history.meaning: metal, bronze, gold; royal clan surname in Silla and Gaya
history.stage: Middle Chinese / Old Korean (Three Kingdoms period)

history.meaning: Kim (most common Korean family name)

김.notes: Kim (김, 金) is the most common surname in Korea, borne by roughly 21% of the population; remember that the exact same Hanja 金 is read 김 for surnames and certain place names (김해, 김포) but 금 for "gold" (금메달, "gold medal") or "Friday" (금요일).

rootFamily.gloss: Gimhae, historic city and origin of the Gimhae Kim clan (金海)
