김밥.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun 김밥, formed from 김 ("edible laver, dried seaweed sheets of the genera *Pyropia*/*Porphyra*") and 밥 ("cooked rice, meal", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 밥 pàp). While wrapping seasoned rice in roasted laver (김쌈 / 복쌈) has deep roots in Joseon-era cuisine, the cylindrical rolled form sliced into bite-sized rounds was also influenced during the 20th century by Japanese *norimaki* (海苔巻き), before evolving distinctly Korean seasoning (sesame oil and salt rather than sushi vinegar) and varied cooked fillings.

history.meaning: dried laver seaweed + cooked grain/rice
history.stage: Middle and Early Modern Korean components

history.meaning: gimbap (cooked rice and fillings rolled in dried laver seaweed)

김밥.notes: Unlike Japanese sushi rolls (*makizushi*), Korean 김밥 seasons the rice with toasted sesame oil (참기름) and salt rather than rice vinegar, and typically uses cooked or pickled fillings like ham, egg, spinach, burdock root, and yellow pickled radish (단무지).

김밥집.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) three-part compound noun 김밥집, composed of 김밥 ("seaweed rice roll", from 김 "dried laver" + 밥 "cooked rice") and 집 ("house, building, shop", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 집 cìp). In Korean compound formation, appending 집 to a food or beverage noun productively designates a restaurant or specialty shop serving that item.

history.meaning: seaweed rice roll + house/shop
history.stage: Modern Korean compound from native roots

history.meaning: gimbap shop, casual snack-food diner (bunsikjip) specializing in gimbap

김밥집.notes: A Korean 김밥집 (often bearing names like 김밥천국, "Gimbap Heaven") is much more than a gimbap stand: it is an affordable 24-hour comfort-food diner serving ramyeon, tteokbokki, donkatsu, and stews to busy production crews and office workers.

김치찌개.etymology: Compound culinary noun 김치찌개, combining 김치 ("fermented seasoned vegetables") and native Korean 찌개 ("thick, bubbling stew"). The word 김치 originates from Sino-Korean 沈菜 ("submerged/brined vegetables", from 沈 침/담 "to submerge, soak" + 菜 채 "vegetables"), attested in 16th-century Middle Korean as 딤채 (tìmcháy), which underwent palatalization (딤채 > 짐채) followed by velar dissimilation/hypercorrection and vowel raising (짐채 > 김채 > 김치). The second element 찌개 derives from the native verb 찌다 ("to steam, stew, boil down thickly") plus the deverbal instrument/product suffix -개.

history.meaning: salted vegetables submerged in brine
fermented kimchi + thick boiled stew
kimchi stew (spicy stew boiled with aged kimchi, pork or tuna, and tofu)

morphemes.meaning: fermented seasoned vegetables (from 沈菜 딤채 > 김치)
to steam, boil down thickly (from 찌다)

김치찌개.notes: Along with 된장찌개 (soybean paste stew), 김치찌개 is the quintessential everyday Korean meal; it is best made with 묵은지 or 잘 익은 김치 (well-fermented, sour kimchi) rather than freshly made kimchi.

cognates.meaning: gypsum, plaster of Paris, orthopedic cast

깁스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) 깁스, borrowed via Japanese ギプス (gipusu) from German Gips or Dutch gips ("gypsum, plaster of Paris, orthopedic plaster cast"), which entered Japanese and subsequently Korean medical terminology during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Germanic word derives from Latin gypsum ("plaster, gypsum"), borrowed from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos, "chalk, gypsum, plaster"), ultimately of Semitic origin (compare Arabic جِبْس jibs and Akkadian gaṣṣu, "gypsum, whitewash").

history.meaning: gypsum mineral, lime plaster, whitewash
plaster of Paris; medical plaster cast for fractures
orthopedic cast, splint, or brace (plaster or fiberglass)

morphemes.meaning: orthopedic cast (from German Gips / Dutch gips via Japanese ギプス)

깁스.notes: Even though modern hospitals usually use synthetic fiberglass or removable splints (반깁스, "half-cast/splint") rather than actual gypsum plaster, Koreans still call any orthopedic limb cast 깁스.

rootFamily.gloss: to wear or be put in a cast

cognates.meaning: to put on a plaster cast (gipusu o suru)

깁스하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword and native Korean verb 깁스하다, formed by combining the medical loanword 깁스 ("orthopedic cast", from German Gips / Dutch gips via Japanese ギプス gipusu, ultimately from Ancient Greek γύψος gúpsos "gypsum, plaster") with the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do"). In Korean usage, it means both to have an injured limb immobilized in a cast and to wear a cast.

history.meaning: plaster of Paris, orthopedic cast
to wear a cast, to have a limb put in an orthopedic cast

morphemes.meaning: orthopedic cast (from German Gips via Japanese ギプス)

깁스하다.notes: Can be used either as a single compound verb (팔에 깁스하다) or split with the accusative particle as 깁스를 하다 ("to wear/get a cast") and 깁스를 풀다 ("to have a cast removed").

깊다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 깊다 ('to be deep, profound').

history.meaning: to be deep
to be deep, profound

까나리.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) ichthyological noun 까나리, designating the Pacific sand lance (*Ammodytes personatus*, a small, slender schooling fish that burrows into sandy seabeds along Korean coasts) and, by common metonymy, 까나리액젓 (fermented sand-lance fish sauce). In early Korean dialects and regional fishery records, the young fish is also known as 양미리 in eastern provinces, while 까나리 became the standard name along the West Sea (Yellow Sea) coast, notably in Baengnyeongdo and Chungcheong, famous for producing pungent fermented sand-lance sauce.

history.meaning: Pacific sand lance (*Ammodytes personatus*)
sand lance; pungent fermented sand-lance fish sauce used in kimchi and variety-show penalty games

morphemes.meaning: Pacific sand lance (*Ammodytes personatus*); sand-lance fish sauce

까나리.notes: In Korean pop culture—especially KBS's *2 Days & 1 Night* (*1박 2일*, directed in real life by the staff portrayed in *The Producers*)—까나리 is synonymous with 까나리액젓 (fermented sand-lance fish sauce), the notorious dark-brown penalty liquid disguised as iced coffee!

rootFamily.gloss: fish-sauce iced coffee penalty drink (까나리 + 아메리카노)

까나리카노.etymology: Contemporary Korean variety-show portmanteau 까나리카노, blending native Korean 까나리 (short for 까나리액젓, "fermented sand-lance fish sauce") with the clipped loanword -(아메리)카노 (from English/Italian *Americano*, "espresso diluted with water"). Coined on the flagship KBS reality-variety program *2 Days & 1 Night* (*1박 2일*), the word exploits the visual similarity between dark amber sand-lance fish sauce on ice and an iced Americano in a game of luck (*bokbulbok*, 복불복).

history.meaning: fermented sand-lance fish sauce + iced Americano coffee
fish-sauce iced coffee (infamous variety-show penalty drink)

morphemes.meaning: sand lance / fermented sand-lance fish sauce (까나리액젓)

까나리카노.notes: A quintessential piece of KBS variety-show lore featured in *The Producers* (*프로듀사*): because clear fermented sand-lance sauce (까나리액젓) over ice looks identical to an iced Americano, cast members play Russian roulette by picking a cup at random.

까놓다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb 까놓다, formed from the main verb 까다 ("to peel, shuck, crack open, uncover", Early Modern Korean ᄭᅡ다) linked via the elided infinitive suffix -아 to the auxiliary/resultative verb 놓다 ("to put down, leave in an open or completed state", 15th-century Middle Korean 놓다 nòhtá). Literally "to peel/uncover and leave open", it developed the idiomatic colloquial sense "to lay all one's cards on the table, disclose candidly without hiding anything".

history.meaning: to peel/uncover and leave in that state
to peel beforehand; (figuratively) to lay one's cards on the table, speak candidly and openly

morphemes.meaning: to put, leave in a resulting state (auxiliary verb)

까놓다.notes: Most frequently encountered in the conversational discourse marker 솔직히 까놓고 말해서 (or 탁 까놓고 말해서), meaning "speaking frankly with all cards on the table / to be brutally honest".

rootFamily.gloss: to peel, shuck, expose; to bash/criticize
to put down, let go, leave in a state
to turn inside out, expose completely (까 + 뒤집다)

까다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb 까다, attested in Early Modern Korean with the initial obstruent cluster ᄭᅡ다 (skata > tense kkada). Its primary physical sense is "to peel, hull, shuck, or crack open an outer shell or skin" (such as peeling fruit, garlic, or cracking an egg). A secondary colloquial sense, "to strike, kick, or beat" (possibly influenced by or converged with native impact verbs), combined with the metaphor of "stripping away someone's facade/skin" to yield the ubiquitous modern slang meaning "to bash, roast, disparage, or criticize harshly".

history.meaning: to peel, hull, shuck, crack open a shell or husk
to peel, shell, uncover; to kick/hit; (colloquial slang) to bash, roast, criticize harshly

morphemes.meaning: to peel, uncover; to strike; (slang) to bash, criticize harshly

까다.notes: Extremely versatile in colloquial Korean: peeling an apple is 사과를 까다, opening a bottle of beer is 맥주병을 까다, revealing one's cards is 패를 까다, and roasting someone online or in an article is 남을 까다 (passive 까이다, "to get roasted/bashed").

rootFamily.gloss: to be peeled; (slang) to get bashed, roasted, or rejected (passive of 까다)
to lay cards on the table, uncover openly (까다 + 놓다)
to peel off, strip away (까다 + 벗기다)

까다롭다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Early Modern Korean as 가ᄃᆞᆯ압다 (gadolapda) and ᄭᅡᄃᆞ롭다 (kkadoropda), formed from a base related to 가닥 (gadak, 'strand, branch, complexity') or 가ᄃᆞᆯ (gadol, 'fork, branching condition') plus the adjectival suffix -압다/-롭다 (-apda/-ropda, 'characterized by'), evolving with word-initial fortition from 'intricate and tangled' to 'fussy, fastidious, or hard to please'.

history.meaning: to be intricate, complicated, or difficult to deal with
to be fussy, complicated, or demanding
to be picky, fastidious, demanding, or complicated

까다롭다.notes: Used both for people who have fussy, hard-to-please tastes and for rules, procedures, or conditions that are intricate and strict.

까딱.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic (mimetic) adverb depicting a quick, slight nodding or tilting motion of the head or finger, or figuratively a momentary slip or misstep. It features tense initial consonant ㄲ (kk) and yang vowel ㅏ (a) to convey a small, sharp, sudden movement, contrasting with its yin-vowel counterpart 꺼떡 (kkeotteok, 'a larger, heavier nod') and lenis 가뜩 (gatteuk).

history.meaning: with a slight nod or sudden tilt
with a slight bob; by one slight slip or miscalculation

morphemes.meaning: mimetic root for a slight bob, tilt, or slip

까딱.notes: In condicional phrases like 까딱 잘못하면 ('if one makes even a slight slip'), it emphasizes how easily a precarious situation can go wrong.

rootFamily.gloss: to nod slightly; to budge or flinch (usually in negative)
to keep bobbing or nodding one's head up and down

까먹다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 까다 (kkada, 'to peel, shell, or hull', from Middle Korean ᄢᅡ다, skada) + linking suffix -아 (-a) + 먹다 (meokda, 'to eat, consume', from Middle Korean 먹다, mekda). From the literal sense 'to peel and eat (fruit, nuts, or eggs)', it developed two vivid colloquial metaphors: 'to squander or eat into (capital, savings, or time)' and 'to completely forget'.

history.meaning: to peel or shell and eat
to peel and eat; to use up or squander; to forget colloquially

morphemes.meaning: to peel, shell, or strip off
to eat, consume; auxiliary of completive consumption

까먹다.notes: Informal and colloquial whether meaning 'to forget' (비밀번호를 까먹다) or 'to eat into/squander' money or time; avoid in formal writing where 잊어버리다 or 소모하다 is preferred.

까불다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ᄭᅡᄇᆞᆯ다 (kkabolda) and ᄢᅡᄇᆞᆯ다 (skabolda, 'to winnow grain by tossing it up and down in a flat basket'). Because winnowing makes light chaff dance and flutter restlessly in the air, the verb underwent semantic extension to mean 'to move around frivolously', 'to act cheeky or flippant', and 'to squander money recklessly'.

history.meaning: to winnow grain by tossing it up and down
to winnow; to bob up and down; to act frivolously or cheeky
to act cheeky, flippant, or boisterous; to squander

morphemes.meaning: to toss up and down, winnow; to act flippantly or cheeky

까불다.notes: 까불지 마! ('Don't get smart with me!' / 'Stop messing around!') is one of the most common colloquial reprimands in Korean dramas and everyday speech.

rootFamily.gloss: to winnow grain (causative/intensive derivative preserving the literal agricultural sense)
a cheeky, playful, or mischievous person
to keep acting cheeky or bobbing about

까이다.etymology: Native Korean morphological passive formed from 까다 (kkada, 'to peel, shell, kick, or disparage/reject', from Middle Korean ᄢᅡ다, skada) + the passive suffix -이- (-i-) + citation ending -다 (-da). Alongside literal senses ('to be peeled, scraped, or hatched'), modern colloquial Korean uses 까다 for 'to dump/reject someone' or 'to bash/criticize', giving 까이다 the vivid slang senses 'to get dumped/turned down' and 'to get chewed out'.

history.meaning: to be peeled, shelled, or hatched
to be peeled or scraped; (colloquial) to be rejected, dumped, or criticized

morphemes.meaning: to peel, kick, criticize, or turn down

까이다.notes: Extremely common in workplace and dating slang: 고백했다가 까이다 means 'to confess one's feelings and get turned down', while 부장님한테 까이다 means 'to get chewed out by the department head'.

rootFamily.gloss: to peel; (slang) to bash, criticize, or turn down
to peel and eat; to forget
to pass the buck or shift blame onto someone else

깍듯하다.etymology: Native Korean deadjectival formation built on the bound root 깍듯- (kkakdeut-, 'clear-cut, square, and scrupulously observant of etiquette', related by consonant symbolism to 깎다, kkakda, 'to pare, trim neatly') + the adjectivalizer -하다 (-hada). It originally evokes edges trimmed cleanly and precisely, metaphorically describing manners that are impeccably courteous and observant of hierarchy.

history.meaning: to be clear-cut, proper, and strictly courteous
to be strictly polite, deferential, and unfailingly courteous

morphemes.meaning: strictly courteous, clear-cut in manners (bound root)

깍듯하다.notes: Typically describes bowing, greeting, or treating seniors with textbook, formal deference (e.g., 깍듯하게 인사하다, 'to bow/greet with impeccable politeness').

rootFamily.gloss: in a strictly polite and deferential manner (adverb)
cubed radish kimchi (named from cutting radish into neat, sharp cubes)

깎다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 깍다 ('to pare, whittle, peel, trim, lower a price').

history.meaning: to whittle, shave, pare
to peel, carve, trim, discount

깔개.etymology: Native Korean derived noun formed from the verb stem 깔- (깔다, 'to spread out, lay underneath', Middle Korean ᄭᆞᆯ다) plus the productive native nominalizing suffix -개, which creates names for everyday household implements (compare 덮개 'cover', 베개 'pillow', 지우개 'eraser'). Literally 'a thing spread underneath', 깔개 denotes any mat, rug, desk blotter, or trivet pad laid over a surface.
깔개.notes: Often specifies its place or use in compounds like 책상 깔개 ('desk blotter'), 컵 깔개 ('coaster'), and 바닥 깔개 ('floor mat').

깔끔하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive adjective formed from expressive root 깔끔- ('neat, clean-cut, sharp') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be neat, tidy, clean and streamlined

깔다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 깔다 ('to spread out a mat, rug, or bedding underneath').

history.meaning: to spread out, lay down underneath
to spread, lay (a rug, sheet, floor), install

깔리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 깔다 (kkalda, 'to spread out, lay down, or pave', attested in Middle Korean as ᄭᆞᆯ다, kkolda / ᄠᆞᆯ다, skolda) + the passive suffix -리- (-ri-) + ending -다 (-da). From the physical sense 'to be spread out on the floor or ground', it extends to background music or atmosphere 'settling in', assumptions 'underlying' a statement, or goods/people 'being distributed everywhere'.

history.meaning: to be spread out or laid down underneath
to be spread, paved, pinned underneath, or underlying

morphemes.meaning: to spread out, lay down on a surface

깔리다.notes: In broadcasting and media contexts, 배경음악이 깔리다 means 'background music plays softly underneath', while 기본 전제가 깔려 있다 means 'an underlying premise is built in'.

rootFamily.gloss: to spread out, lay down (a mat, bedding, or foundation)
to look down on or belittle someone (literally 'lay down and sit on')

깔아주다.etymology: Native Korean compound benefactive verb composed of 깔다 (kkalda, 'to spread out, lay down, or install', from Middle Korean ᄭᆞᆯ다, kkolda) + connective suffix -아 (-a) + auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, 'to give, do for someone's benefit', from Middle Korean 주다, cuda). Literally 'to spread out (bedding or a mat) for someone', it is widely used for 'installing software/apps for someone' or 'setting the stage / rolling out the mat so someone can shine'.

history.meaning: to spread out a mat or bedding for someone
to lay out for someone; to set the stage for; to install (software) for someone

morphemes.meaning: to spread out, lay down, install
benefactive auxiliary verb ('to do for someone')

깔아주다.notes: The idiom 멍석을 깔아주다 ('to roll out the straw mat for someone') means to set up the perfect opportunity or stage for someone to perform or show off.

rootFamily.gloss: to spread out, lay down, install
to be spread out or laid underneath
straw mat laid on the courtyard floor

깜깜하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated ideophonic adjective formed from 깜깜 (kkamkkam, intensive reduplication of the color/light root 감-/깜-, expressing pitch blackness or complete darkness) + the adjectival suffix -하다 (-hada). By Korean vowel harmony and consonant fortition, tense ㄲ (kk) and yang vowel ㅏ (a) produce a concentrated, stark sense of total darkness or total ignorance, contrasting with 껌껌하다 (kkeomkkeomhada, 'gloomy, deeply dark').

history.meaning: to be pitch-dark or far out of sight and news
to be pitch-dark, jet-black; to be completely ignorant or clueless about something

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated ideophonic root for pitch darkness or total blankness

깜깜하다.notes: Used both literally for a pitch-black night or room (밖이 깜깜하다) and figuratively when someone is completely in the dark about a topic or memory (앞날이 깜깜하다, 'the future looks bleak/uncertain').

rootFamily.gloss: to be gloomy and deeply dark (yin-vowel counterpart)
to be distant, dim, or completely without news (lenis counterpart)
to be jet-black (color adjective from the same root family)

깜놀하다.etymology: Modern Korean colloquial clipped blend (신조어, neologism originating in 2000s internet and variety-show slang) formed by taking the first syllables of 깜짝 (kkamjjak, ideophone for a sudden startle or jump) and 놀라다 (nollada, 'to be surprised or startled', from Middle Korean 놀라다) to create the noun 깜놀 (kkamnol), followed by the light verb suffix -하다 (-hada).

history.meaning: to be suddenly startled or taken aback (full phrase)
to get totally startled or shocked (syllabic clipping)

morphemes.meaning: clipped initial syllable of 깜짝 ('with a startle')
clipped initial syllable of 놀라다 ('to be surprised')

깜놀하다.notes: A quintessential Korean syllabic acronym (줄임말) ubiquitous in TV variety show captions (자막), text messages, and casual speech; use 깜짝 놀라다 in formal contexts.

rootFamily.gloss: with a sudden startle or jump (ideophonic adverb)
to be surprised, startled, or astonished

깜빡이다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 깜빡 ('momentary blink or flicker') + verbalizing suffix -이다.

history.meaning: to blink (eyes), flicker or flash (light)

깜빡하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 깜빡 ('blinking shut; momentary lapse of awareness') + -하다.

history.meaning: to slip one's mind, momentarily forget; to blink/flicker

깜짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb descending from Middle Korean 감짝 ('with a sudden startle or flinch').

history.meaning: startled, with a sudden jolt
with a start, suddenly surprised (깜짝 놀라다)

깨끗이.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 깨끗- of 깨끗하다 ('to be clean') + adverbial suffix -이.

history.meaning: cleanly, purely
cleanly, neatly, completely

깨끗이.notes: Takes -이 rather than -히 because the root ends in -ㅅ.

깨끗하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested from Early Modern Korean as 깨끝하다 / 깨끗하다 ('to be clean, unsoiled, tidy').

history.meaning: to be clean, pure
to be clean, neat, clear

깨다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in Middle Korean as ᄭᆡ다 (kkoyda, intransitive 'to wake up from sleep or drunkenness') and ᄢᆡ다 (skoyda, transitive 'to smash, shatter, or break'). In Modern Korean both historical roots converged phonologically into 깨다 (kkaeda), linking the sense of breaking through a shell or state of stupor with waking up to consciousness or sobriety.

history.meaning: to wake from sleep or intoxication / to shatter or break open
to wake up, sober up; to break or shatter
to wake up, sober up, become enlightened; to smash or break; (slang) to ruin the mood or shock expectations

morphemes.meaning: to wake up, sober up; to break or shatter

깨다.notes: In casual conversation, 분위기 깨다 means 'to ruin the mood', and someone described as 좀 깬다 means their behavior unexpectedly shatters a good impression ('is a turn-off').

rootFamily.gloss: to wake someone up; to be shattered or broken (passive/causative)
to realize, come to understand, awaken to a truth
to be awake; to be progressive or open-minded (깨어 있다)

깨닫다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄭᆡᄃᆞᆺ다 (kkoydotda, stem ᄭᆡᄃᆞᆯ- before vowels, exhibiting ㄷ/ㄹ-irregular alternation), formed from ᄭᆡ다 (kkoyda, 'to wake up, become conscious') + ᄃᆞᆺ다 (dotda, an archaic verb meaning 'to reach, grasp, or love/attend to'). Literally 'to awaken and grasp mentally', hence 'to realize, perceive, or attain enlightenment'.

history.meaning: to awaken to a truth, perceive, or attain Buddhist enlightenment
to realize, comprehend, or become aware of
to realize, perceive, or come to understand deeply

morphemes.meaning: to wake up, awaken from ignorance (from Middle Korean ᄭᆡ다)
to reach, grasp mentally (ㄷ-irregular stem 깨달- before vowels)

깨닫다.notes: Follows ㄷ-irregular (ㄷ 불규칙) conjugation: the final ㄷ of the stem 깨닫- changes to ㄹ before a vowel suffix (깨달아, 깨달으니, 깨달음).

rootFamily.gloss: to enlighten or make someone realize (causative)

깨뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed from 깨다 (Middle Korean 깨다, 'to break, shatter') + intensive transitive suffix -뜨리다.

history.meaning: to break, smash
to smash, shatter, break apart

깨우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb formed from 깨다 ('to wake from sleep, sober up') + causative suffix -우-.

history.meaning: to awaken someone
to wake (someone) up

깨지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb formed from 깨다 ('to break, smash') + auxiliary suffix -지다.

history.meaning: to become broken
to break, shatter, be chipped, fall through

꺼내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 끌어내다 (Middle Korean 끄어내다, from 끌다/끄다 'to pull, draw' + 내다 'to put out').

history.meaning: to draw or pull out
to take out, pull out, bring up (a topic)

꺼놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 끄다 (kkeuda, 'to extinguish a fire or light; to switch off an appliance', from Middle Korean ᄢᅳ다, skeuda, infinitive 꺼, kkeo) + the resultative auxiliary verb 놓다 (nota, 'to put, set, or leave in a state', from Middle Korean 놓다, nohta). It means 'to turn off (a phone, light, or engine) and leave it switched off'.

history.meaning: to extinguish a fire or lamp and leave it out
to switch off (a light, phone, or device) and leave it off

morphemes.meaning: infinitive stem of 끄다 ('to extinguish, turn off') with ㅡ-deletion before -어
auxiliary verb denoting maintenance of a completed state ('to leave as is')

꺼놓다.notes: Adding -놓다 (or -두다) emphasizes that the speaker deliberately switched the device off and kept it in that state (e.g., 휴대폰을 꺼놓다, 'to keep one's cell phone turned off').

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, be extinguished, be switched off (intransitive)
to turn on and leave on (antonym compound)

꺼지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb formed from 끄다 (Middle Korean 끄다, 'to extinguish, put out fire') + inchoative -어지다; also from 꺼지다 ('to sink in, cave in').

history.meaning: to be extinguished; to sink or collapse
to go out (of fire/light/power); to sink in, hollow out

꺾어놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 꺾다 (kkeokda, 'to snap, break off, bend back, or subdue', attested in Middle Korean as ᄭᅥᆨ다, kkeokda) + connective suffix -어 (-eo) + resultative auxiliary verb 놓다 (nota, 'to put or leave in a resulting state', from Middle Korean 놓다, nohta). It denotes bending, folding back, or subduing something (or someone's pride/momentum) and leaving it in that bent or defeated state.

history.meaning: to snap or bend back and leave in place
to bend back, fold over, or break someone's momentum and leave it so

morphemes.meaning: to snap, bend back, fold, or subdue
auxiliary verb indicating a maintained resultant state

꺾어놓다.notes: Used both physically (e.g., folding back a collar, joint, or branch) and figuratively (기를 꺾어놓다, 'to crush/take the wind out of someone's sails').

rootFamily.gloss: to snap, break off, bend, or subdue
to be snapped, bent, or broken in spirit (passive)

꺾이다.etymology: Native Korean passive and intransitive verb derived from 꺾다 ('to snap off, bend at an angle, fold', Middle Korean 꺽다) plus the passive suffix -이-. Literally describing a stem, branch, or sheet of paper getting bent or snapped, 꺾이다 extends spatially to roads, hallways, or pipes making an angular turn (길이 꺾이다) and metaphorically to intense heat, wind, or stubbornness subsiding (더위가 한풀 꺾이다).
꺾이다.notes: Pronounced [꺼끼다]; used both for physical creasing/snapping and for streets or stairs turning a corner.

껄끄럽다.etymology: Native Korean sensory and psychological adjective formed from the ideophonic root 껄끌- (kkeolkkeul-, describing a rough, prickly, grainy, or scratchy surface texture, the yin-vowel counterpart of 깔깔-) + the adjectival derivational suffix -업다 (-eopda, 'inducing the sensation of'). From tactile roughness that catches in the throat or against the skin, it evolved metaphorically to mean 'interpersonally awkward, prickly, or uncomfortable'.

history.meaning: to be rough to the touch, scratchy, or unpleasant
to be rough, grainy; to be awkward, uncomfortable, or strained (of a relationship or topic)

morphemes.meaning: mimetic root for rough, prickly, or scratchy friction
adjectival suffix (ㅂ-irregular) meaning 'evoking the feeling of'

껄끄럽다.notes: Follows ㅂ-irregular conjugation (껄끄러워, 껄끄러운); very frequently used for strained relationships or delicate subjects that make people uneasy (사이가 껄끄럽다).

rootFamily.gloss: to be rough, prickly, or scratchy in texture
to be dry and rough to the touch (yang-vowel counterpart)

껌.etymology: Modern Korean loanword (외래어) borrowed from English gum (specifically chewing gum), which ultimately derives via Old French gomme and Latin cummi / gummi from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), itself a borrowing from Ancient Egyptian qmyt ('acacia resin'). In Korean, the initial voiced velar stop /g/ of English gum was adapted with the tense unaspirated velar stop ㄲ (kk) as 껌 (kkeom), a regular phonetic pattern in early 20th-century English borrowings (compare 깡패, 게임 pronounced [께임]).

history.meaning: plant resin, gum exudate
sweetened chicle or synthetic resin for chewing
chewing gum; (colloquial) something trivially easy ('a piece of cake')

껌.notes: In colloquial Korean slang, 이 정도는 껌이지! ('This much is just gum!') means 'This is a piece of cake / super easy!', popularized by the expression 껌값 ('the price of a pack of gum', i.e., dirt cheap).

rootFamily.gloss: pocket change, dirt-cheap price (literally 'price of gum')
person who sticks inseparably to someone (literally 'gum-stuck')

껍질.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 겁질 ('outer skin, bark, rind, shell').

history.meaning: bark, husk, outer skin
peel, skin, bark, shell

꼬다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ᄭᅩ다 (kkoda) and ᄢᅩ다 (skoda, 'to twist strands together into rope or thread'). From the core physical action of twisting hemp or straw fibers together between the palms, it broadened to mean crossing or twisting one's legs or body, and figuratively viewing or interpreting things in a perverse, sarcastic, or cynical way.

history.meaning: to twist fibers or strands into cord or rope
to twist (rope); to cross (legs); to distort or view sarcastically

morphemes.meaning: to twist strands together, cross, or distort

꼬다.notes: 다리 꼬지 마 mirrors both the literal instruction 'Don't cross your legs' (traditionally considered impolite in front of elders) and the famous AKMU song title playing on 'Don't act pretentious/twisted'.

rootFamily.gloss: to become twisted, tangled, or go awry (passive/intransitive)
to twist slightly or make sarcastic remarks (비- + 꼬다)
twine, string, cord twisted from paper or fiber

꼬마.etymology: Native Korean noun referring to a small child or miniature object, related to older Korean 고마 ('small or subordinate figure').

history.meaning: little child, small thing
kid, little child, miniature item

꼬이다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 꼬다 (kkoda, 'to twist strands together', from Middle Korean ᄭᅩ다/ᄢᅩ다) + the passive suffix -이- (-i-) + ending -다 (-da). From 'to be twisted or tangled (of thread or wires)', it developed rich metaphorical meanings: plans or affairs 'going awry / getting complicated', traffic 'getting snarled', or a person's disposition 'becoming warped or cynical'. (A homonymous verb 꼬이다, 'to be lured/enticed or to swarm', derives from 꾀다.)

history.meaning: to be twisted into cord; to become tangled
to be twisted or tangled; for matters, schedules, or relationships to go awry or sour

morphemes.meaning: to twist strands together, cross, or distort

꼬이다.notes: 일이 꼬이다 ('things get tangled/go wrong') and 스텝이 꼬이다 ('one's steps get tangled', i.e., a project starts off on the wrong foot) are staple expressions in Korean workplace dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to twist sarcastically, make snide remarks
to twist and wriggle; to be tangled up

꼬집.etymology: Native Korean stem noun from 꼬집다 (Middle Korean 고집다, 'to pinch with thumb and fingertips'), used as a measure noun (한 꼬집 'a pinch').

history.meaning: to pinch
pinch (unit of salt, spice, or powder)

꼬투리.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 고토리 (gotori) and ᄭᅩ토리 (kkotori), designating the pod of beans or peas, or the stub/butt end of a stalk or cigarette. Morphologically related to 고투리/꼬투리 ('protruding tip, pod, or stalk-end', compare 꼭지, kkokji, 'stem/knob' and 끝, kkeut, 'end/tip'), it shifted metaphorically to mean 'the starting clue of an event' and 'a small pretext or flaw seized upon to nitpick or find fault'.

history.meaning: bean pod; stub end of a stalk or cord
bean pod; cigarette butt; a pretext, cause, or minor flaw used for fault-finding

morphemes.meaning: pod, stub end; pretext or flaw for nitpicking

꼬투리.notes: Almost always encountered in the collocation 꼬투리를 잡다 ('to seize on a minor detail to nitpick or find fault with someone').

rootFamily.gloss: stem, stalk knob, nipple, or handle tip
unopened flower bud; rounded tip or peak

꼭.etymology: Native Korean emphatic and mimetic adverb (light-vowel tensed form) meaning 'tightly, firmly; without fail, surely, exactly'.

history.meaning: firmly, precisely, without fail
tightly; surely, be sure to; exactly

꼭대기.etymology: Native Korean noun built from root 꼭- ('vertex, tip, crown', cf. 꼭지) + noun suffix -대기.

history.meaning: topmost point, summit
top, peak, summit, top floor

꼴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 골 (gol) and ᄭᅩᆯ (kkol, 'outward form, shape, figure, or appearance'). Initially a neutral word for 'form, shape, or mold' (still preserved in neutral compounds like 세모꼴, 'triangle shape', and 꼴찌, 'last place'), as an independent noun 꼴 underwent pejoration in Modern Korean to mean 'unsightly appearance, pathetic state, or spectacle'.

history.meaning: shape, outward form, figure, or appearance
shape (in compounds); unsightly state, spectacle, or plight (standalone)

morphemes.meaning: shape, form; unsightly appearance or spectacle

꼴.notes: Standalone 꼴 carries a strong derogatory or self-deprecating nuance (내 꼴이 말이 아니다, 'I look like a total mess'; 꼴도 보기 싫다, 'I can't even stand the sight of them'), whereas in geometry/grammar compounds (사다리꼴, 'trapezoid') it remains completely neutral.

rootFamily.gloss: last place, dead last in a ranking

꼼꼼하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated ideophonic adjective formed from 꼼꼼 (kkomkkom, describing close, dense, gapless attention to detail) + the adjectival suffix -하다 (-hada). Built with the tense bilabial stop ㄲ (kk) and rounded yang vowel ㅗ (o), it evokes examining every tiny nook without leaving a single gap, contrasting with 끔찍하다 or 느슨하다.

history.meaning: to be closely packed, meticulous, and attentive to every detail
to be meticulous, thorough, observant, and scrupulous

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated root denoting close, thorough, gapless care

꼼꼼하다.notes: Unlike 까다롭다 ('picky/hard to please', which can sound critical), 꼼꼼하다 ('meticulous, thorough') is a prized positive trait in Korean workplaces and character descriptions.

rootFamily.gloss: meticulously, thoroughly, with close attention to detail (adverb)

꼼장어.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun (originally Gyeongsang/Busan dialect, now universally recognized in culinary Korean alongside standard 꼼치/먹장어) combining the native Korean mimetic root 꼼지락-/꼼짝- (kkomjirak-, 'wriggling, squirming') + the Sino-Korean word 장어 (長魚, jang-eo, 'eel', literally 'long fish'). It refers to the inshore hagfish (Eptatretus burgeri), famous in Korean cuisine for still wriggling vigorously on the grill even after being skinned and sliced.

history.meaning: wriggling eel-like fish; inshore hagfish (originally southeastern dialect)
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean (20th c.)

history.meaning: hagfish (especially grilled or stir-fried as a popular late-night dish with soju)

morphemes.meaning: wriggling, squirming (clipped from native ideophone 꼼지락거리다)

꼼장어.notes: While biological dictionaries prescribe 먹장어 ('blind/ink eel') as the formal standard name, virtually all restaurants, menus, and TV shows call the grilled dish 꼼장어 (or 짚불 꼼장어).

rootFamily.gloss: inshore hagfish (formal biological standard name: 먹 'ink/dark' + 장어 長魚)
freshwater eel (민물장어) or conger eel (붕장어); literally 'long fish' (長魚)
to wriggle, squirm slowly (native ideophonic verb)

sources.title: 표준국어대사전 (Standard Korean Language Dictionary): 먹장어 / 꼼장어

꽂다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 곶다 ('to stick in, insert upright, plant').

history.meaning: to insert, stick in
to stick in, slot in (books, flowers, plug)

꽂히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 꽂다 (kkotda, 'to stick in, plant, pin, or thrust into', attested in Middle Korean as 곶다, gotda, with later initial fortition to ᄭᅩᆺ다) + the passive suffix -히- (-hi-) + ending -다 (-da). From 'to be stuck or pierced into a target (like an arrow or pin)', modern colloquial Korean extended it metaphorically to mean 'to become fixated on, smitten with, or hooked on' a person, song, or idea.

history.meaning: to be stuck, planted, or pierced into something
to be stuck or pinned into place
to be stuck or plugged in; (colloquial) to be smitten with, obsessed with, or hooked on

morphemes.meaning: to stick into, pin, insert, or plant

꽂히다.notes: Pronounced [꼬치다] (kkochida) because ㅈ + ㅎ coalesces into aspirated [ㅊ]; takes the dative particle -에 for the object of infatuation (그 노래에 완전 꽂혔어, 'I got totally hooked on that song').

rootFamily.gloss: to stick in, insert, plug in, or arrange (flowers)
skewer or pin used to pierce food (from Middle Korean 곶)

꽃.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Old Korean 叱 (attested phonogrammatically in Hyangga) and 15th-century Middle Korean 곶 (got, spelled 곶 in Yongbieocheonga stanza 2: 곶 됴코 여름 하ᄂᆞ니, 'its flowers are good and its fruit abundant'). In the Early Modern period, the initial lenis velar ㄱ underwent expressive fortition (경음화) to tense ㄲ, yielding ᄭᅩᆺ and modern 꽃 (kkot).

history.meaning: flower, blossom
flower, blossom
flower, blossom; the finest essence or highlight of something

꽃.notes: Remember the difference between final ㅊ in 꽃 ('flower', pronounced [꼳] in isolation, [꼬치] before subject marker -이) and final ㅈ in 꽂- ('to stick in'); both appear together in 꽃꽂이 [꼳꼬지] ('flower arrangement').

rootFamily.gloss: handsome young man ('flower boy': 꽃 + 미남 美男)

꽃꿀.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 꽃 ('flower, blossom') and 꿀 ('honey, nectar').
꽃꿀.notes: Pronounced [꼳꿀] as final ㅊ neutralizes to [ㄷ] and tensifies the following ㄱ.

꽃병.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the native Korean noun 꽃 ('flower, blossom', Middle Korean 곶) with the Sino-Korean noun 병 (甁, 'bottle, vase, pitcher'). While formal Sino-Korean also has 화병 (花甁), everyday spoken Korean strongly prefers the transparent hybrid 꽃병 ('flower-bottle').
꽃병.notes: Pronounced [꼳뼝] with neutralization of ㅊ to [ㄷ] and tensification of ㅂ to [ㅃ].

꽃집.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 꽃 (Middle Korean 곶, 'flower, blossom') and 집 ('house, shop').

history.meaning: flower shop, florist's

꽉.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'tightly, firmly, packed full to capacity'.

history.meaning: tightly, firmly
tightly, fast, chock-full

꽐라.etymology: Contemporary Korean drinking slang noun (attested from the late 20th / early 21st century in campus and workplace drinking culture) meaning 'a blackout-drunk state or a person who is dead drunk'. Two main etymological explanations exist in Korean philological commentary: (1) a humorous metaphor from 코알라 (koalla, 'koala', contracted with fortition to 꽐라), because a dead-drunk person clings limp and asleep to others or a table like a koala sleeping twenty hours a day; or (2) an ideophonic coinage mimicking slurred, babbling drunken speech (꽐라꽐라).

history.meaning: person clinging asleep or dead-drunk; slurred drunken stupor
wasted wreck; state of being blackout drunk

morphemes.meaning: state of being dead drunk or a wasted person (slang root)

꽐라.notes: Almost always used with 되다: 어제 술 마시고 완전 꽐라 됐어 ('I drank yesterday and got completely wasted/blackout drunk'). Strictly informal slang!

rootFamily.gloss: to get completely wasted / blackout drunk (slang phrase)
being dead drunk, blind drunk (Sino-Korean standard equivalent: 泥醉, 'mud-drunk')

꽤.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb meaning 'quite, fairly, considerably more than expected'.

history.meaning: considerably, quite
quite, fairly, pretty

꾸다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 꾸다 ('to dream a dream'; also homophonous 'to borrow money or grain').

history.meaning: to dream; to borrow
to dream (꿈을 꾸다); to borrow

꾸러미.etymology: Native Korean derived noun from 꾸리다 ('to wrap up, pack, bundle') + nominal suffix -어미.

history.meaning: wrapped bundle or string of items
bundle, packet, parcel

꾹.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic (mimetic) adverb expressing firm, steady downward pressure or tight closure (of lips, eyes, or hands). It belongs to a productive sound-symbolic paradigm in Korean: yang-vowel 꼭 (kkok, 'pinpoint, tightly, without fail') vs. yin-vowel 꾹 (kkuk, 'pressing down heavily, firmly, or suppressing an urge with deep force'), alongside lenis 국 and aspirated 푹.

history.meaning: pressing down firmly or holding back tightly
firmly, tightly (pressing down, shutting one's mouth, or enduring patiently)

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic root for firm, heavy pressure or patient suppression

꾹.notes: Compare 꾹 and 꼭: use 꾹 for heavy physical pressure or holding back emotions/tears (눈물을 꾹 참다, 버튼을 꾹 누르다), and 꼭 for pinpoint accuracy or certainty ('be sure to', 꼭 와야 해).

rootFamily.gloss: repeatedly pressing down or poking firmly (reduplicated adverb)
hiccup (mimetic noun formed from the sudden spasmodic sound 딸꾹)

꿀.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 꿀 ('honey').

history.meaning: honey
honey

꿇다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄢᅮᆯ다 (skulda) / ᄭᅮᆯ다 (kkulda, 'to kneel down, bend the knees to the ground'). The modern spelling 꿇다 (kkulta, with final cluster ㅀ) reflects historical aspiration merger from the causative/intensive suffix or phonological reanalysis in Early Modern Korean (compare 뚫다 from 뚤다).

history.meaning: to kneel down on the ground
to kneel down; to yield or submit
to kneel down; (figuratively) to bow down, yield, or be inferior to

morphemes.meaning: to kneel, bend the knees; to yield or be outclassed

꿇다.notes: Pronounced [꿀타] before consonants with ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ (which aspirate to ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅊ) and [꿇어 -> 꾸러] before vowels because ㅎ in the ㅀ cluster is silent intervocalically; 무릎을 꿇다 means both literally 'to kneel' and figuratively 'to surrender/submit'.

rootFamily.gloss: to make someone kneel down (causative verb)
to sit on one's knees (꿇어 + 앉다)
knee (the body part almost always paired with 꿇다)

꿈.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun descending from Middle Korean 꿈, formed from 꾸다 ('to dream') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: dream
dream, aspiration

꿈꾸다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb uniting the cognate object 꿈 ('dream') with its parent verb 꾸다 ('to dream').

history.meaning: to dream a dream
to dream, aspire to

꿈쩍.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb depicting a heavy or deliberate slight movement (most often in negative expressions like 꿈쩍도 안 하다 'not budge an inch').

history.meaning: with a slight budge or stir

cognates.meaning: green pheasant (Phasianus versicolor), historically compared with Old Korean *kijöŋ / Middle Korean 꿩

꿩.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 12th-century Early Middle Korean (Jilin leishi / 계림유사) as 雉曰蹇音 and in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄭᅯᆼ (kkwong, alongside dialectal/archaic ᄭᅯᆨ, kkwok), likely originating as an onomatopoeic formation imitating the male ring-necked pheasant's sharp, resonant call (꿩꿩, kkwong-kkwong).

history.meaning: pheasant (Phasianus colchicus)
pheasant (and a central figure in Korean proverbs and folk games)

꿩.notes: Appears in two of the most famous Korean proverbs: 꿩 대신 닭 ('a chicken instead of a pheasant', i.e., 'making do with the next best thing') and 꿩 먹고 알 먹기 ('eating the pheasant and its egg too', i.e., 'killing two birds with one stone').

rootFamily.gloss: male pheasant (수- 'male' + 꿩, with aspirated ㅋ preserving archaic ㅎ-prefix)

꿰뚫다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 꿰다 (kkweda, 'to thread a needle, string beads, or run a skewer through', from Middle Korean ᄭ다, kkweda) + 뚫다 (ttulta, 'to bore, drill, or pierce a hole through', from Middle Korean 뚫다/뚤다). Combining 'to thread through' and 'to bore through' creates an intensive verb meaning both physically 'to pierce/penetrate right through' and mentally 'to see right through someone's intentions or master a subject thoroughly'.

history.meaning: to thread through + to bore or pierce a hole
to pierce right through; to penetrate or have thorough insight into

morphemes.meaning: to thread, string, or run through (from 꿰다)
to bore, drill, or pierce through (from 뚫다)

꿰뚫다.notes: Frequently paired with 보다 as 꿰뚫어 보다 ('to see right through someone's mind, scheme, or the essence of a problem').

rootFamily.gloss: to thread (a needle), string together, or wear
to pierce, bore, drill through, or break through an obstacle
to see right through, penetrate mentally (꿰뚫어 + 보다)

끄다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄢᅳ다 (skeuda, 'to extinguish a fire, put out a flame'). With the regular change of the Middle Korean initial consonant cluster ㅺ (sk-) to tense ㄲ (kk-), it became Modern Korean 끄다 (kkeuda), expanding in the 20th century from extinguishing fires and lamps to switching off electrical appliances, engines, and broadcast equipment. (A homonymous verb 끄다, 'to pull/drag', is a variant of 끌다.)

history.meaning: to extinguish a fire or put out a lamp
to put out a fire or light
to extinguish (a fire); to turn off or switch off (lights, power, electronics)

morphemes.meaning: to extinguish, put out, turn off (ㅡ-drop stem before -어: 꺼)

끄다.notes: Conjugates with regular vowel-ㅡ deletion before -아/-어 suffixes (끄- + -어 -> 꺼, 껐다); its intransitive/passive counterpart 꺼지다 ('to go out / turn off') is also used in rude slang (꺼져!, 'Get lost!').

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, be extinguished, be switched off (intransitive)
to switch off and leave off (끄다 + 놓다)
to deal with an urgent crisis (idiom: 급한 불을 끄다, 'to put out an urgent fire')

끄덕이다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from mimetic root 끄덕 ('nodding up and down') + verbalizer -이다.

history.meaning: to nod (one's head)

끈.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어) attested in Early Modern Korean as 근 (geun) and ᄭᅳᆫ (skeun, 18th century), referring to a twisted cord, string, or strap; the initial consonant underwent tensification from *k- to kk- (ㄲ) in Modern Korean, likely reinforced by expressive sound symbolism for tightness and tension.

history.meaning: cord, string, strap
string, lace, strap, tether

끈.notes: Used both literally (신발끈 'shoelace') and figuratively in idioms like 끈을 놓지 않다 ('to not let go of the string', meaning to persevere or keep up hope/connection).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 끈

끈적거리다.etymology: Native Korean sensory verb formed from root 끈적 ('sticky, viscous, tacky') + iterative verbalizing suffix -거리다.

history.meaning: to be sticky, feel tacky or clammy

끊기다.etymology: Native Korean morphological passive verb (고유어) formed from the transitive verb stem 끊- (kkeunh-, 'to cut, to sever, to interrupt', Middle Korean 그츠다 / 근타) plus the native passive derivational suffix -기- (-gi-) and dictionary ending -다 (-da), meaning to be severed, cut off, or interrupted.

history.meaning: to sever, to cut off
to be severed, to be cut off, to lose connection

끊기다.notes: Frequently used in broadcasting and telecommunications when a call, signal, stream, or train of thought abruptly cuts out (연락이 끊기다, 방송이 끊기다).

rootFamily.gloss: to snap, come apart, get disconnected

끊다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 끊다 / 그츠다 ('to sever, cut off, interrupt, stop').

history.meaning: to cut off, sever, cease
to cut, sever, hang up, quit, buy (a ticket)

끊어지다.etymology: Native Korean compound inchoative-passive verb (고유어) combining the transitive verb stem 끊- (kkeunh-, 'to cut, to sever'), the infinitive connective vowel -어 (-eo), and the auxiliary verb 지다 (jida, Middle Korean 디다 dida, 'to fall, to become'), expressing a spontaneous state of snapping, breaking apart, or losing continuity.

history.meaning: to cut + to fall/become (analytic passive construction)
to get cut off, to snap, to black out (of memory/film)

끊어지다.notes: While 끊기다 often implies an external interruption or blockage, 끊어지다 emphasizes the state of coming apart on its own—famous in the drinking idiom 필름이 끊어지다 ('one's film snaps', i.e., to black out from alcohol).

끓다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb 끓다 ('to boil, seethe, bubble'), attested in Middle Korean as 끓다 with the ㅀ cluster. The final ㅎ triggers aspiration when followed by plain stops (so 끓고 is pronounced [끌코] and 끓지 is [끌치]), while dropping silently before vowels (끓어요 [끄러요]). Its causative-transitive counterpart 끓이다 ('to boil or cook soup/tea') was formed by adding the native causative suffix -이-.
끓다.notes: Intransitive: the liquid itself is the subject (물이 끓어요, 수프가 끓어요).

끓여주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb (고유어) formed from 끓이다 (kkeurhida, causative of 끓다 'to boil', Middle Korean 글히다 geulhida), conjugated with the infinitive suffix -여 (-yeo, contracted from -이어), plus the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, Middle Korean 주다, 'to give'), literally 'to boil and give (for someone's benefit)'.

history.meaning: to make boil + to give
to boil/cook (soup, ramen, tea) for someone

끓여주다.notes: In Korean culture, boiling ramen or soup for someone (라면 끓여주다, 미역국 끓여주다) is a classic everyday expression of care and domestic affection.

끓이다.etymology: Native Korean morphological causative verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 글히다 (geulhida) and ᄭᅳᆯ히다 (skeulhida), derived from the intransitive verb stem 끓- (kkeurh-, Middle Korean 글타 geulta, 'to boil, seethe') plus the native causative suffix -이- (-i-) and ending -다 (-da).

history.meaning: to boil, bubble (intransitive)
to bring to a boil, to heat liquid (transitive)
to boil, to cook (soup, stew, noodles, decoction)

끓이다.notes: Crucial transitivity pair for learners: 물이 끓다 ('the water boils' — intransitive) vs. 물을 끓이다 ('to boil water / cook soup or ramen' — transitive). Pronounced [끄리다] as ㅎ becomes silent before a vowel.

끔찍하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Early Modern Korean as 끔찍하다 ('startlingly intense, dreadful, terrible').

history.meaning: startling, overwhelming, dreadful
to be terrible, awful, ghastly; devoted (끔찍이)

끙.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic interjection and adverb imitating a suppressed groan of physical effort, strain, or ache.

history.meaning: groan, grunt (of effort or pain)

끙끙.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated ideophone/mimetic adverb (의성어·의태어, 고유어) imitating the guttural, strained sound of groaning under physical pain, heavy labor, or mental anguish; built on the tense velar onset ㄲ (kk-) and closed velar nasal coda -ㅇ (-ng) to evoke Pent-up effort or distress.

history.meaning: groaningly, moaningly, fretfully struggling

morphemes.meaning: sound of a strained groan or moan

끙끙.notes: Often pairs with 앓다 ('to be sick/suffer', 끙끙 앓다) or 대다/거리다 (끙끙대다 'to groan/fret repeatedly') when someone agonizes over a problem alone without speaking up.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 끙끙

끝.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 끝 / 귿 ('end, tip, extremity, conclusion').

history.meaning: tip, extremity, end
end, tip, finish

끝나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 끝 ('end, finish') and 나다 ('to come out, come about').

history.meaning: to come to an end
to end, finish, be over

끝내다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb (고유어) formed by incorporating the noun 끝 (kkeut, Middle Korean 귿 geut, 'end, tip, extremity') with the transitive verb 내다 (naeda, Middle Korean 내다, 'to put forth, to bring about, to produce'), literally 'to bring out the end' and thus 'to finish, complete, or conclude'.

history.meaning: end/tip + to bring forth
to finish, to complete, to put an end to

morphemes.meaning: to bring forth, produce, make happen

끝내다.notes: Pronounced [끈내다] due to nasal assimilation of ㅌ (reduced to ㄷ) before ㄴ. Contrast transitive 끝내다 ('to finish something') with intransitive 끝나다 ('something finishes/ends').

끝내주다.etymology: Native Korean colloquial compound verb/adjective (고유어) derived from 끝내다 (kkeunnaeda, 'to finish off, to bring to an ultimate end') plus the benefactive auxiliary 주다 (juda, 'to give'); originally a slang expression meaning 'to finish (someone) off completely / to blow one away', which underwent ameliorative semantic shift to mean 'to be phenomenal, awesome, or killer'.

history.meaning: to finish off for someone (literal benefactive)
to be awesome, thrilling, top-notch (colloquial)

끝내주다.notes: Exactly parallels English slang 'it slays' or 'it kills it'—most commonly heard in the adnominal form 끝내주는 (e.g., 끝내주는 맛 'killer taste') or adverbial 끝내주게 ('awesomely, brilliantly').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 끝내주다

끝부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 끝 ('end, tip') with Sino-Korean 부분 (部分, 'part, section').

history.meaning: end part, tip section

끼다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 끼다 ('to become wedged between; to wear on hands/fingers/eyes; to gather [of mist/smoke/dust]').

history.meaning: to insert/wedge; to form (cloud/mist)
to get stuck between; to put on (gloves/ring/glasses); to gather (fog/grime)

끼어들다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb (고유어) combining 끼다 (kkida, Middle Korean ᄢᅵ다 skida, 'to be wedged between, to squeeze in') in its infinitive form 끼어 (kkieo) with 들다 (deulda, Middle Korean 들다, 'to enter, go in'), literally 'to wedge oneself in and enter', hence 'to cut in, intrude, or step in'.

history.meaning: to wedge between + to enter into
to cut in line/traffic, to butt into a conversation, to intervene

끼어들다.notes: Used across physical and social contexts: cutting into traffic (끼어들기 금지 'no cutting in'), interrupting someone's speech (대화에 끼어들다), or a network/producer stepping into a project.

끼우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 끼다 ('to fit or wedge between') + causative suffix -우-.

history.meaning: to insert between, fit in
to insert, slot in, fit into place

끼워팔기.etymology: Native Korean compound verbal noun (고유어) formed from 끼우다 (kkiuda, causative of 끼다 'to insert, wedge in'), conjugated as 끼워- (kkiwo-), plus 팔다 (palda, Middle Korean ᄑᆞᆯ다 polda, 'to sell') and the nominalizer suffix -기 (-gi); literally 'inserting-and-selling', referring to commercial tying or package-deal bundling.

history.meaning: to insert/fit in + to sell
tie-in sale, package-deal bundling (especially in entertainment/commerce)

끼워팔기.notes: In K-drama and K-pop broadcasting (like in *The Producers*), 끼워팔기 specifically refers to talent agencies forcing a TV show to cast an unpopular rookie alongside their A-list star as a package deal.

rootFamily.gloss: to insert, slot in, put on

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 끼워팔기

끼치다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in Middle Korean as ᄢᅵ치다 (skichida, 'to leave behind, to bequeath, to extend influence to'), derived from the stem ᄢᅵ- (ski-) plus the intensive/causative suffix -치- (-chi-) and ending -다 (-da); evolved to mean 'to cause, exert (influence/harm/trouble), or give (chills)'.

history.meaning: to leave behind to posterity, to extend an effect upon
to cause (trouble/harm), to exert (influence), to give (goosebumps/shivers)

끼치다.notes: Almost always occurs in high-frequency collocations: 영향을 끼치다 ('to exert influence'), 폐를 끼치다 / 민폐를 끼치다 ('to cause trouble/inconvenience'), and 소름이 끼치다 ('to get goosebumps').

rootFamily.gloss: to get goosebumps, feel a chill

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 끼치다

나.etymology: Native Korean first-person singular pronoun descending from Middle Korean 나 ('I, me').

history.meaning: I, me
I, me (plain/intimate; humble counterpart is 저)

나가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 나- (from 나다, 'to emerge, come out') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go out, exit
to go out, leave, attend, advance

나가라고.etymology: Inflected indirect imperative quotative form of the native Korean compound verb 나가다 (nagada, Middle Korean 나가다, 'to go out, exit', from 나- 'emerge' + 가- 'go'), combined with the plain imperative suffix -(으)라 (-ra) and the quotative complementizer -고 (-go), used to report or issue a command to leave.

history.meaning: to go out, to exit
(telling/ordering someone) to go out or leave

나가라고.notes: Used both to relay a third-party order (나가라고 했다 'told me to leave') and as a standalone emphatic repetition when someone didn't hear or obey the first time ('I said get out!').

rootFamily.gloss: to step out for someone's sake

나가주다.etymology: Native Korean compound benefactive verb (고유어) formed from 나가다 (nagada, 'to go out, exit, step out', from 나- 'emerge' + 가- 'go') and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, 'to give, to do as a favor for someone'), literally 'to do someone the favor of stepping out or participating'.

history.meaning: to go out + to give/grant
to step out (of a room) or appear (on a show/event) as a favor to someone

나가주다.notes: Depending on context, 나가주다 can be a polite request to leave a room for privacy (잠시만 나가주시겠어요? 'Would you step out for a moment?') or a request for a guest to appear on a broadcast program as a favor.

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, exit, appear on TV

나누다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 나노다 ('to divide, split, share').

history.meaning: to divide, distribute, share
to divide, split, share (food, conversation, feelings)

나눔.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 나누다 ('to divide, share') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: division, sharing
sharing, distribution

나뉘다.etymology: Native Korean morphological passive of 나누다 ('to divide, split, share', Middle Korean ᄂᆞᆫ호다), formed by attaching the passive suffix -이- to the stem 나누- so 나누이다 contracts into standard 나뉘다. Because its stem ends in the vowel ㅟ, standard Korean orthography writes -어 without further contraction in 나뉘어요 and 나뉘었어요, while -ㅂ니다 attaches directly as 나뉩니다. It describes objects, spaces, teams, or opinions parting into distinct sections.
나뉘다.notes: Takes the particle -(으)로 to mark the resulting parts or number of divisions (두 쪽으로 나뉘다, 세 팀으로 나뉘다).

나다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 나다 ('to emerge, be born, sprout, happen, break out').

history.meaning: to come out, be born, arise
to come out, occur, sprout, break out

나들이.etymology: Native Korean compound deverbal noun (고유어), attested in Middle Korean as 나드리 (nadeuri), formed from the verb stems 나- (na-, from 나다 'to go out, emerge') and 들- (deul-, from 들다 'to enter, come in') plus the nominalizing suffix -이 (-i); originally meant 'going out and coming in', later specialized to 'a short outing, excursion, or stroll away from home'.

history.meaning: going out and coming back in; visiting outside the home
outing, excursion, picnic, stepping out for leisure

나들이.notes: Evokes a pleasant, lighthearted excursion (봄나들이 'spring outing', 가족 나들이 'family picnic')—more casual and warm than Sino-Korean 외출 (外出, 'going out') or 소풍 (逍風, 'picnic/field trip').

rootFamily.gloss: to go in and out frequently, frequent

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나들이

나란히.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the descriptive stem 나란- (나란하다, 'to be aligned evenly side by side', Middle Korean ᄂᆞᄅᆞᆫᄒᆞ다) plus the productive adverbial suffix -히. Built with bright vowel harmony (ㅏ–ㅏ), 나란히 evokes an orderly, companionable image of people walking or sitting shoulder to shoulder, or paired objects arranged evenly in a line.
나란히.notes: Commonly modifies 놓다 ('place'), 서다 ('stand'), 앉다 ('sit'), and 걷다 ('walk').

rootFamily.gloss: to be side by side, even

나름대로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverbial expression (고유어) formed from the bound noun 나름 (nareum, 'depending on, one's own way or capacity', historically a nominalization in -ㅁ of the verb 나르다 or 날다 'to measure out/apportion') plus the particle 대로 (daero, 'in accordance with, as'), meaning 'in one's own way' or 'by one's own standards'.

history.meaning: depending on how something is done; one's own manner or capacity
in one's own way, after a fashion, by one's own standards

morphemes.meaning: bound noun: depending on, one's own way/measure
in accordance with, as, after the manner of

나름대로.notes: In casual contemporary speech, 나름대로 is very often shortened to standalone adverbial 나름 (e.g., 나름 괜찮네 'It's pretty good in its own way / considering').

rootFamily.gloss: depending on; in one's own way (shortened)
depending on how one thinks about it
as it is, in its own state

나머지.etymology: Native Korean derived noun formed from the stem 남- of 남다 ('to remain, be left over') + nominal suffix -어지.

history.meaning: what is left over, surplus
remainder, the rest

나무.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 나모 (alternating stem 나모 / 남ㄱ, 'tree, wood, firewood').

history.meaning: tree, wood
tree, wood, timber

나무라다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 나모라다 (namorada) and 나모ᄅᆞ다 (namoroda), meaning 'to scold, reprove, or chide someone for a fault'; likely derived from an older verbal root *나모- (*namo-) with the verbalizing suffix -라-/-ᄅᆞ-.

history.meaning: to reprove, to censure, to scold for a fault
to scold, to chide, to rebuke gently or firmly

나무라다.notes: Unlike the noun 나무 ('tree', also Middle Korean 나모), 나무라다 is etymologically unrelated to wood; it implies correcting or chiding someone's mistake rather than explosive anger (혼내다).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나무라다

나무살.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 나무 ('wood') and 살 ('spoke, lattice bar, strip').

history.meaning: wooden slat, lattice bar, wooden spoke

나무젓가락.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining native 나무 (namu, Middle Korean 나모 namo, 'tree, wood') with 젓가락 (jeotgarak, 'chopsticks'), which itself combines Sino-Korean 저 (箸, jeo, 'chopsticks') + genitive 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + native 가락 (garak, Middle Korean 가락, 'slender stick, spindle, strand').

history.meaning: wood + chopsticks (箸) + slender stick
wooden chopsticks (especially disposable split wooden chopsticks)

나무젓가락.notes: In everyday Korean dining and delivery culture, 나무젓가락 usually refers specifically to disposable split wooden chopsticks (일회용 나무젓가락), as opposed to reusable metal chopsticks (쇠젓가락) used at home.

나무판.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native Korean 나무 ('tree, wood, timber', descending from Middle Korean 나모 / 남ㄱ-) with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 널빤지 판, 'sawn plank, flat board', written with the wood radical 木). While native 널빤지 emphasizes raw lumber planks, 나무판 broadly covers smooth wooden serving boards, sign plaques, slats, and carpentry panels.
나무판.notes: Compare 도마 ('kitchen chopping board') and 널빤지 ('thick wooden plank').

나뭇결.etymology: Native Korean compound of 나무 ('tree, wood') + genitive interfix 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 결 ('wave, grain, texture').
나뭇결.notes: Parallel to 물결 ('water wave') and 숨결 ('breathing rhythm').

나뭇잎.etymology: Native Korean compound noun from 나무 ('tree') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + 잎 (Middle Korean 닢, 'leaf').

history.meaning: tree leaf
tree leaf, foliage

나뭇잎.notes: Pronounced [나문닙] via ㄴ-insertion of historical initial 닢.

나불대다.etymology: Native Korean mimetic verb (고유어) formed from the ideophonic root 나불 (nabul, depicting something thin and light fluttering, or lips moving rapidly and frivolously) plus the verbalizing suffix -대다 (-daeda, indicating repetitive or annoying action), meaning 'to flap repeatedly' or 'to prattle, blabber, or run one's mouth'.

history.meaning: to flutter lightly; to chatter or wag one's tongue incessantly

morphemes.meaning: mimetic root: fluttering lightly; wagging lips/tongue

나불대다.notes: When applied to speech (입을 나불대다, 주둥이를 나불대다), it carries a strong pejorative nuance of someone running their mouth, blabbing secrets, or talking flippantly out of turn.

rootFamily.gloss: heavy/sluggish version: to flap or boast clumsily

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나불대다

나빠.etymology: Inflected intimate/infinitive form (해체 / 어간+아) of the native Korean adjective 나쁘다 (nappeuda, 'to be bad'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 낟브다 (natbeuda), a compound of 낟- (nat-, 'to be low, inferior, lacking') and 브다 (beuda, adjective-forming suffix); originally meant 'insufficient, lacking, inferior' before shifting to general 'bad, wicked, poor' in Modern Korean.

history.meaning: to be insufficient, lacking, inferior in quality or quantity
to be bad, mean, poor, harmful (infinitive/intimate form 나빠)

morphemes.meaning: to be bad, poor, mean (ㅡ-irregular stem)
infinitive / intimate speech level ending (ㅡ drops before -아)

나빠.notes: In Middle Korean, 'bad/wicked' was 머다/사오납다, while 낟브다 meant 'short of, lacking'; by the 19th century, 나쁘다 took over as the primary antonym of 좋다 ('good').

rootFamily.gloss: to be bad, poor, mean (dictionary form)
to dislike, feel offended by, consider bad

나빠하다.etymology: Native Korean psychological-behavioral verb (고유어) derived from the adjective 나쁘다 (nappeuda, Middle Korean 낟브다 natbeuda, 'to be bad, unpleasant') in its infinitive form 나빠- (nappa-) plus the auxiliary-derived verbalizer -하다 (-hada), which converts subjective internal states into observable third-person verbs ('to feel offended, to take something badly, to resent').

history.meaning: to be lacking, inferior, unpleasant
to regard as bad, to feel offended or displeased (in 기분 나빠하다)

나빠하다.notes: Most frequently appears in the phrase 기분 나빠하다 ('to feel offended / take offense'); Korean grammar requires -아/어하다 when describing another person's emotional reaction (그 사람이 기분 나빠해요).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel offended, be in a bad mood

나쁘다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 낟브다 ('to be insufficient, inferior, low in quality', from 낟- 'low/short' + -브다), which broadened in Modern Korean to mean 'bad'.

history.meaning: insufficient, inferior
to be bad, poor, harmful

나사.etymology: Sino-Korean 나사 (螺絲), compounding 나 (螺, 'spiral shell, conch') and 사 (絲, 'thread, wire').

history.meaning: spiral-threaded metal fastener
screw

나사선.etymology: Sino-Korean 나사선 (螺絲線), combining 나사 (螺絲, 'screw') and 선 (線, 'line, ridge').

history.meaning: helical line on a screw
screw thread, spiral groove

나서다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 나서다 (naseoda), formed by combining the verb stems 나- (na-, from 나다 'to emerge, come out') and 서- (seo-, from 서다, Middle Korean 셔다 syeoda, 'to stand'), literally 'to come out and stand in front', hence 'to step forward, volunteer, or intervene'.

history.meaning: to come out and stand forth; to leave a place
to step forward, to take the lead, to meddle or intervene, to set out

나서다.notes: Can be positive (발벗고 나서다 'to roll up one's sleeves and step forward to help') or critical when someone oversteps their bounds (네가 나설 자리가 아니야 'It's not your place to step in').

rootFamily.gloss: to stand ahead, take the lead

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나서다

나약하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb (한자어) formed from 나약 (懦弱, nayak, 'weak-willed, spineless, feeble')—comprising 懦 (나, originally 란/누, 'timid, cowardly, weak of heart') and 弱 (약, 'weak, fragile, young')—plus the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). By South Korean Initial Sound Rule (두음법칙), initial 난-/누- is realized as 나-.

history.meaning: timid and weak; lacking courage or resolve
to be weak-willed, feeble, spineless, frail

나약하다.notes: Unlike 약하다 (which describes physical weakness in general), 나약하다 specifically criticizes mental, moral, or emotional feebleness and lack of backbone (나약한 태도 'spineless attitude').

나오고.etymology: Conjugated connective form of the native Korean compound verb 나오다 (naoda, Middle Korean 나오다, 'to come out, emerge'), formed from 나- (na-, 'to emerge, be produced') + 오- (o-, 'to come') + the coordinative/sequential connective suffix -고 (-go, 'and'); in broadcasting and everyday Korean, 나오다 also means for results, ratings, food, or paychecks to be issued or turn out.

history.meaning: to come out, to emerge toward the speaker
come out and; appear (on screen) and; reach/yield (ratings or results) and

나오고.notes: In TV production (*The Producers*), 나오다 is the go-to verb for viewership ratings coming out (시청률이 잘 나오다 'ratings turn out well'), a scene/shot coming out well (그림이 나오다), or a celebrity appearing on screen (방송에 나오다).

rootFamily.gloss: to come out, appear, be produced (dictionary form)
to go out, exit, participate in a show

나오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 나- (from 나다, 'to emerge, come out') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come out, emerge
to come out, appear, be served

나이.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 나 (stem 나ㅎ, 'age, years of life') + incorporated nominative/noun suffix -이.

history.meaning: age, years of life
age

나중.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) that underwent heavy phonological attrition and nativization: attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 내죵 (乃終, naejyong, 'the very end, finally'), from Classical Chinese 乃 ('then, thereupon, only at') + 終 ('end, conclusion'), shifting via 나죵 (najyong, 16th c.) to modern 나중 (najung, 'later, the latter part').

history.meaning: thereupon at the end; ultimate conclusion
the end, finality, afterward
later, afterwards, the latter part

morphemes.meaning: then, thereupon (historical Sino-Korean 乃, nativized from 내 to 나)

나중.notes: Most native speakers today perceive 나중 as a pure native Korean word because 내 (乃) mutated to 나, obscuring its Hanja origin (乃終); most commonly used with the particle -에 as 나중에 ('later').

rootFamily.gloss: conclusion, end of a broadcast/event (終了)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나중

나침반.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 羅針盤, combining 羅 (벌일 라 / 그물 라, 'arranged in a ring, netted'), 針 (바늘 침, 'metal needle'), and 盤 (소반 반, 'circular plate, dial'). By the Korean initial-sound rule (두음법칙), historical 라- becomes word-initial 나-. Originally naming the traditional East Asian geomantic and maritime compass whose directional markings encircle a magnetized needle on a flat disc, 나침반 denotes any magnetic compass as well as a figurative guiding principle.
나침반.notes: Used literally for navigation tools (회중 나침반 'pocket compass') and figuratively (인생의 나침반 'compass in life').

나타내다.etymology: Native Korean transitive compound verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 나타내다 (natanaeda), formed from the bound stem 나타- (nata-, related to 낱- 'to appear, surface') plus the transitive verb 내다 (naeda, 'to bring forth, put out', causative of 나다), meaning 'to make appear, to reveal, to indicate, or to express'.

history.meaning: to make visible, to reveal outwardly, to manifest
to indicate, to represent, to express, to show

morphemes.meaning: bound root: to surface, become visible or manifest
to bring forth, put out (causative of 나다)

나타내다.notes: Forms a classic transitivity pair with intransitive 나타나다 ('to appear, show up'): 감정을 나타내다 ('to express/show emotion' — transitive) vs. 귀신이 나타나다 ('a ghost appears' — intransitive).

rootFamily.gloss: to be revealed, exposed, become apparent
to bring forth, produce, put out

cognates.word: 懶惰 (らんだ, randa) / 惰眠 (damin)

나태하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb (한자어) formed from 나태 (懶怠, natae, 'laziness, indolence, sloth')—composed of 懶 (나, originally 란, 'lazy, sluggish, disinclined') and 怠 (태, 'idle, negligent, remiss')—plus the native adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). Initial 란 (懶) becomes 나 by the South Korean Initial Sound Rule (두음법칙).

history.meaning: sluggish and negligent; remiss in duty
to be indolent, slothful, complacent, remiss

나태하다.notes: More formal and moralizing than native 게으르다 ('lazy'); 나태하다 implies becoming complacent, slacking off in one's discipline or duties, and letting one's standards slip.

rootFamily.gloss: negligence of duty, work-to-rule strike (怠業)

나트륨.etymology: Scientific loanword (외래어) borrowed via Japanese ナトリウム (natoriumu) from German Natrium, coined in 1807/1814 by chemists Humphry Davy and Jöns Jacob Berzelius in New Latin from natron ('naturally occurring sodium carbonate'), traced through Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn) and Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron) to Ancient Egyptian nṯrj ('divine salt / natron').

history.meaning: natural soda ash / natron salt used in mummification and cleansing
chemical element sodium (symbol Na)
sodium (chemical element and dietary nutrient)
history.stage: Modern Korean (via Japanese ナトリウム)

나트륨.notes: While the Korean Chemical Society officially recommends 소듐 (sodyum, from English 'sodium') in academic chemistry, 나트륨 remains universal on Korean nutrition labels and in health discussions (e.g., 나트륨 섭취 줄이기 'reducing sodium intake' from salty soups and ramen).

나흘.etymology: Native Korean day-counter noun (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 나ᄒᆞᆯ (nahol, 'four days'), formed from the native Korean numeral root *나- / *너- (cf. 네/넷 'four') plus the archaic native Korean day-counting suffix -ᄒᆞᆯ (-hol, surviving as -흘 in 사흘 '3 days', 나흘 '4 days', 열흘 '10 days').

history.meaning: a period of four days; the fourth day of the month
four days; the fourth day of a lunar/solar month

morphemes.meaning: native Korean suffix for counting days

나흘.notes: Famous native-speaker & learner trap: 사흘 ('three days', from 세/석 '3') and 나흘 ('four days', from 네/넉 '4') are frequently confused with Sino-Korean 사 (四, '4'); remember 사흘 = 3일 and 나흘 = 4일!

rootFamily.gloss: the fourth day; four days' time

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 나흘

낙.etymology: Single-morpheme Sino-Korean noun (한자어) from 樂 (락/낙, nak, 'joy, pleasure, delight, enjoyment', distinct from its reading 악 ak 'music' and 요 yo 'to delight in'); originally pronounced 락 (rak), initial ㄹ shifts to ㄴ (낙) in word-initial position under the South Korean Initial Sound Rule (두음법칙).

history.meaning: joy, pleasure, happiness, enjoyment
pleasure, small joy in life, source of enjoyment or comfort

낙.notes: Used especially for the simple pleasures that make daily life worth living: 무슨 낙으로 사니? ('What joy do you live for?') or 퇴근 후 맥주 마시는 게 유일한 낙이다 ('Drinking beer after work is my only joy'). In non-initial position, 락 is preserved (오락 娛樂, 쾌락 快樂).

cognates.meaning: scribbling, doodling, graffiti; originally an anonymous satirical drop-letter
omitted character in copying; (modern via Japanese) scribbling

낙서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (한자어) written 落書 (낙서, nakseo), combining 落 (락/낙, 'to fall, drop, omit') and 書 (서, 'writing, letter, document'). In traditional East Asian usage, 落書 meant either 'accidentally omitted characters in a manuscript' or 'an anonymous satirical note dropped in a public place'; in modern Korean (influenced by Japanese 落書き rakugaki), it came to mean 'doodling, scribbling, or graffiti'.

history.meaning: omitted writing; anonymous dropped letter criticizing authorities
scribbling, doodling (on desks/margins), wall graffiti

낙서.notes: Covers everything from innocent textbook margin doodles (책상 낙서) to street wall graffiti (벽면 낙서); combines with 하다 to form the verb 낙서하다 ('to scribble/doodle').

cognates.meaning: falling behind the ranks, straggling, dropping out
to fall behind the ranks; to become outdated or backward

낙오되다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean passive verb composed of the Sino-Korean noun 낙오 (落伍, from 落 'to fall, drop' + 伍 'five-man military squad, ranks, file') and the native Korean passive/inchoative verbalizer -되다 ('to become, be made into'). Originally a military term meaning to be dropped from a marching column, it gained iconic pop-culture currency in Korean variety shows (such as 2 Days & 1 Night) for being stranded behind by the cast and crew.

history.meaning: to fall out of a five-man military unit or marching formation
to be left behind the group; (variety TV slang) to be stranded on location

morphemes.meaning: passive verbalizer: to become, be subjected to

낙오되다.notes: In Korean variety shows like 1박 2일 (featured in The Producers), 낙오되다 specifically refers to the dreaded penalty of losing a game or missing the bus and getting left behind to find one's own way back.

rootFamily.gloss: straggler, person who falls behind (落伍者)
spot where someone was left behind (落伍地)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낙오되다

낙오지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 낙오 (落伍, 'falling out of the military ranks', from 落 'to fall, drop' + 伍 'five-man squad, file of troops') and the locative Sino-Korean suffix -지 (地, 'land, ground, place, spot'). Coined by productive Sino-Korean compounding to designate the exact location where a straggler or variety-show cast member is left behind.

history.meaning: falling behind the military ranks + place/ground
the spot where a straggler or cast member is left behind

낙오지.notes: The suffix -지 (地) productively turns event or action nouns into locations, just like 촬영지 ('filming location') or 목적지 ('destination').

cognates.meaning: to fall behind the ranks, drop out
to fall behind the ranks; to lag behind the times

낙오하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 낙오 (落伍, from 落 'to fall, drop' + 伍 'five-man military squad, ranks', with word-initial 락 becoming 낙 via the South Korean initial-sound law 두음법칙) and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). Originally denoted a soldier dropping out of a marching formation due to exhaustion, later generalized to lagging behind in studies, social progress, or travel games.

history.meaning: to drop out of a military squad or marching line
to fall behind, drop out of a group, or get left behind

낙오하다.notes: While 낙오하다 is the active intransitive verb ('to fall behind / straggle'), 낙오되다 emphasizes being passively left behind by circumstances or a departing vehicle.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낙오하다

난간.etymology: Sino-Korean architectural compound 欄干, pairing 欄 (난간 란, 'wooden balustrade, railing', formed with the wood radical 木) and 干 (줄기 간 / 방패 간, 'horizontal bar, protective rail'). Under Korean word-initial phonology (두음법칙), initial 란- (欄) is realized as 난- in 난간. Attested in classical Korean poetry and palace architecture for pavilion balustrades, it now refers to railings on balconies, staircases, bridges, and decks.
난간.notes: Collocates with 에 기대다 ('lean on a railing') and 을 잡다 ('hold onto a handrail').

cognates.meaning: separated by the chaos of war; scattered refugees
scattering and separation caused by war or turmoil

난리.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 亂離 (historical reading 란리, shifting to 난리 via initial-sound law 두음법칙 on 亂 and liquid assimilation /nalli/), composed of 亂 (란/난, 'rebellion, war, chaos, disorder') and 離 (리, 'separation, scattering, leaving'). Originally referred to the catastrophic upheaval of war that scatters families and populace, before undergoing colloquial semantic bleaching to mean any chaotic uproar, fuss, or sensation.

history.meaning: dispersal of the people amid the chaos of war or rebellion
wartime upheaval; (colloquial) huge uproar, commotion, or sensation

난리.notes: Colloquially paired with 나다 in 난리 나다 ('all hell breaks loose' or positively 'to be a massive hit/sensation') and 피우다/치다 in 난리 치다 ('to make a huge scene').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 난리

난방.etymology: Sino-Korean 난방 (煖房), compounding 난 (煖, 'warm, heat') and 방 (房, 'room').

history.meaning: warming a room
heating (indoor heating)

cognates.meaning: difficult problem, thorny question, hard subject

난제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 難題, composed of 難 (난, 'difficult, hard, arduous, troublesome') and 題 (제, 'topic, subject, heading, examination question; originally forehead'). In classical East Asian literary culture, 難題 denoted an unusually difficult poetic topic or civil-service examination prompt; in modern Korean it denotes any intractable problem, riddle, or dilemma.

history.meaning: a difficult poetic theme or examination question
hard problem, conundrum, dilemma, toughest riddle

난제.notes: Often used for grand unsolved problems (e.g., 수학의 난제 'unsolved problems in mathematics') or ironical everyday dilemmas in drama dialogue.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 난제

날.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 날 ('day, sky/weather; cutting blade edge; warp thread').

history.meaning: day; blade edge
day, weather; blade edge

날씨.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 날 ('day, sky condition') + -씨 ('state, condition, manner').
