history.meaning: state of the day/sky
weather

날아가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 날- (stem of 날다 'to fly', from Middle Korean ᄂᆞᆯ다 nol-ta) + infinitive linker -아 + directional auxiliary verb 가다 ('to go', from Middle Korean 가다 ka-ta). Literally meaning 'to fly off and go away', it developed a vivid colloquial and workplace slang sense meaning to vanish into thin air, get wiped out (like unsaved computer files), or be axed/fired from a program or position.

history.meaning: to fly away through the air
to fly away; (colloquial/slang) to be lost, wiped out, canceled, or fired

날아가다.notes: In TV production and office slang, 프로그램이 날아가다 means a show gets canceled/axed, and 목이 날아가다 ('one's neck flies away') means to get fired.

rootFamily.gloss: to send flying, blow away, lose (causative)
to come flying toward the speaker

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 날아가다

날아오르다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 날다 (nalda, Middle Korean ᄂᆞᆯ다 nolta, 'to fly') via the linking vowel -아 (-a) with 오르다 (oreuda, Middle Korean 오ᄅᆞ다 wolota, 'to rise, ascend, climb'). The compound literally means 'to ascend by flying' and is used both for birds or aircraft rising into the sky and figuratively for musical notes, spirits, or prices soaring upward. Because 오르다 is a 르-irregular verb, its infinitive stem doubles the liquid to 날아올라- before vowel-initial endings.

history.meaning: to fly upward, soar into the air
to soar, fly up, rise high (of birds, sound, or spirits)

날아오르다.notes: In musical descriptions, 소리가 높이 날아오르다 vividly captures a melody soaring into the upper register.

날이다.etymology: Native Korean predicate phrase composed of the native noun 날 ('day, date, weather', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 날 nal and in Old Korean hyangga phonograms as 日) followed directly by the copula 이다 ('to be', Middle Korean 이다 i-ta). Used to identify a specific calendar occasion or idiomatically to declare that a fateful or long-awaited day has arrived.

history.meaning: is the day / is a day
is the day (of an event or occasion)

날이다.notes: Be careful not to confuse native Korean 날 ('day; raw; blade') with the colloquial contracted object pronoun 날 (from 나를, 'me').

날짜.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 날 ('day') with Sino-Korean 자 (字, 'character, numeral'), with tensification of ㅈ > ㅉ.

history.meaning: calendar date, count of days
date, number of days

낡다.etymology: Native Korean adjective/verb descending from Middle Korean 낣다 ('to grow old and worn out, be dilapidated [of inanimate things]').

history.meaning: to be old, worn out
to be old, worn, weathered, outdated

낡다.notes: Used for objects, clothes, and buildings (contrasting with 늙다 for living beings).

남.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 남 ('other people, stranger, someone else'); also homophonous with Sino-Korean 남 (南 'south' or 男 'man, male').

history.meaning: others, unrelated person
others, stranger; south (南); male (男)

남기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 남기다, formed from 남다 ('to remain, be left over') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to leave behind, cause to remain
to leave behind, save, keep

cognates.meaning: men and women, male and female
men and women, male and female

남녀.etymology: Sino-Korean dvandva (coordinate) compound from 男女, combining 男 (남, 'man, male', ideogrammic compound of 田 'field' + 力 'strength/plow', representing labor in the fields) and 女 (녀, 'woman, female', originally a pictograph of a kneeling figure). Because 女 appears in word-medial position here, it preserves its historical nasal initial 녀 (/njʌ/) rather than undergoing the word-initial sound law (두음법칙) to 여.

history.meaning: men and women; males and females
men and women, both genders

남녀.notes: Notice the spelling and pronunciation difference between word-initial 여자 (女子, 'woman') and word-medial 남녀 (男女, 'men and women'): South Korean orthography keeps 녀 inside compounds.

rootFamily.gloss: everyone of all ages and both sexes (男女老少)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남녀

남다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 남다 ('to remain, be left over, exceed').

history.meaning: to remain, be left over
to remain, be left over

남미.etymology: Sino-Korean geographical proper noun from 南美, an abbreviation of 남아메리카 (南아메리카, 'South America'). It combines 南 (남, 'south') with 美 (미, 'beauty; America'), where 美 is clipped from 아미리가 (亞美利加), the 19th-century Chinese phonetic-semantic transliteration of 'America' (which also produced 미국 美國 for the United States).

history.meaning: South America (abbreviated Sino-Xenic geographical compound)
South America

morphemes.meaning: America (clipped from 亞美利加; literally 'beautiful' 美)

남미.notes: While Japanese uses 米 (rice, *bei*) to abbreviate America (hence 南米 *Nanbei*), Korean follows the Chinese convention of using 美 (beauty, *mi*), giving 남미 (南美), 북미 (北美, North America), and 미국 (美國, USA).

rootFamily.gloss: Central and South America, Latin America (中南美)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남미

남색.etymology: Sino-Korean 남색 (藍色), compounding 남 (藍, 'indigo plant and dye') and 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: color of indigo dye
indigo, navy blue

남아돌다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 남- (stem of 남다 'to remain, be left over', from Middle Korean 남다 nam-ta) + infinitive connective -아 + 돌다 ('to turn, revolve, circulate', from Middle Korean 돌다 tol-ta). Literally 'to be left over and keep circulating around', vividly describing resources, money, energy, or time that are in such surplus that there is more than enough to burn.

history.meaning: to remain over + to go around / circulate
to be in excess, have plenty to spare, have time or money to burn

남아돌다.notes: Frequently used with a teasing or exasperated tone—e.g., 시간이 남아도냐? ('Do you have time to burn?' / 'Do you have nothing better to do?').

rootFamily.gloss: to leave behind, save, make a profit (causative)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남아돌다

남자.etymology: Sino-Korean 남자 (男子), compounding 남 (男, 'male, man') and 자 (子, 'person, son').

history.meaning: male person, man
man, male

남자분.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean polite compound noun combining Sino-Korean 남자 (男子, 'man, male person', from 男 'male' + 子 'person, son') with the honorific bound noun/suffix -분 ('esteemed person'). The honorific classifier 분 was grammaticalized in Middle Korean from Sino-Korean 分 (분, 'portion, allotted status, social standing'), shifting from 'person of high station' to the standard polite counter and suffix for people.

history.meaning: male person + person of social standing/rank
gentleman, man (polite honorific reference)

남자분.notes: Adding -분 to gender or role nouns (남자분 'gentleman', 여자분 'lady', 손님분 'guest') is the standard polite way to refer to strangers or guests in broadcasting and service settings.

남쪽.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 남 (南, 'south') with native 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: south, southern side

남친.etymology: Modern Korean syllabic acronym/clipping (준말) of 남자친구 (男子親舊, 'boyfriend'), formed by extracting the initial syllable 남 from 남자 (男子, 'man, male': 男 'male' + 子 'person') and the initial syllable 친 from 친구 (親舊, 'friend': 親 'intimate, close' + 舊 'old, long-standing acquaintance'). Emerged in late 20th-century youth, PC-communication, and mobile-messaging slang as a symmetrical pair with 여친 ('girlfriend').

history.meaning: male friend; romantic boyfriend
boyfriend (colloquial clipped compound)

morphemes.meaning: man, male (clipped from 남자 男子)
friend, intimate companion (clipped from 친구 親舊)

남친.notes: To distinguish a platonic male friend from a romantic boyfriend (남친), modern Korean speakers insert 사 ('person' 사람) to say 남사친 (남자 사람 친구, 'guy friend').

rootFamily.gloss: girlfriend (clipped from 여자친구 女子親舊)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남친

남편.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 男便, composed of 男 (남, 'man, male') and 便 (편, 'side, direction, party', as as in 내 편 'my side' or 맞은편 'opposite side'). Coined inside Korean (a native Sino-Korean formation attested from Middle Korean 남편) as an indirect, respectful spatial expression literally meaning 'the male side (of the household or marriage)', which then lexicalized as the standard noun for 'husband'.

history.meaning: the male side of a couple; husband
husband

남편.notes: Its historical female counterpart 여편 (女便, 'the female side') attached the suffix -네 to become 여편네, which underwent pejoration into a rough/derogatory word for 'wife/woman', whereas 남편 remained neutral and polite.

rootFamily.gloss: the opposite side, across the street (맞은便)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남편

남한테.etymology: Native Korean noun-plus-postposition sequence composed of the pronoun/noun 남 ('other person, stranger, someone else', from Middle Korean 남 nam) and the colloquial animate dative/locative particle -한테 ('to, at, from a person'). The particle -한테 grammaticalized from Early Modern Korean 한데 ('in one place, together', from 한 'one, same' + 데 'place'), evolving from 'at the same place as [someone]' into an animate dative marker.

history.meaning: other person + in one place / together with
to others, to strangers, from other people

morphemes.meaning: colloquial animate dative particle: to, from (a person)

남한테.notes: Use -한테 primarily in spoken Korean for animate beings (people and animals); in formal writing or broadcasts, speakers often replace 남한테 with 남에게.

rootFamily.gloss: others' affairs, someone else's business (남의 일)

cognates.meaning: facing south, southern exposure (using native reading -muki)
cognates.word: 南向き (みなみむき, minamimuki)

남향.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 南向, composed of 南 (남, 'south') and 向 (향, 'to face toward, direction, orientation'). Rooted in classical East Asian geomancy (풍수지리 風水地理) and traditional Korean architecture (배산임수 背山臨水, backing a mountain and facing south toward water), a south-facing exposure maximizes low winter sunlight while keeping out summer heat, making it a prized feature in Korean housing.

history.meaning: facing toward the south (auspicious architectural orientation)
south-facing orientation, southern exposure (in real estate and architecture)

남향.notes: In Korean apartment hunting (as seen when characters discuss housing in K-dramas), 남향집 ('a south-facing home') commands a premium price because of natural daylight and lower heating bills.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 남향

납작하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from mimetic root 납작 ('flat, low and pressed down') + adjective-forming -하다.

history.meaning: to be flat and low
to be flat, flattened

cognates.meaning: to drag or pull away by force (literary)

납치.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 拉致 (historical reading 랍치, becoming 납치 in South Korean standard language via the initial-sound law 두음법칙), composed of 拉 (랍/납, 'to pull, drag, seize, break by force') and 致 (치, 'to cause to arrive, bring, deliver, convey'). Literally 'to seize by force and bring to a place', it became the standard legal and journalistic term for kidnapping or abduction across modern Korean and Japanese.

history.meaning: to drag along by force and bring to a place
kidnapping, abduction, hijacking

morphemes.meaning: to pull, drag, seize by force (拉)
to bring, cause to arrive, deliver (致)

납치.notes: In variety shows like 1박 2일 and The Producers, cast members jokingly call surprise cast pick-ups by the production crew 납치 ('abduction/kidnapping').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 납치

낫다.etymology: Native Korean irregular ㅅ-stem (ㅅ 불규칙) adjective 낫다 ('to be better, superior, preferable'), descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 낫다 (nas-ta, inflected 나ᄉᆞ니 nas-oni, 나아 na-a), where the intervocalic stem-final sibilant ㅿ (z) weakened and disappeared before vowel-initial suffixes. Historically shares its root with the verb 낫다 ('to get better, recover from illness'), diverging syntactically into an adjective ('better than') and an intransitive verb ('to heal').

history.meaning: to surpass, excel, be better than; to recover from illness
to be better, superior, preferable

morphemes.meaning: to be better, superior (irregular ㅅ-stem 나ㅅ-)

낫다.notes: Because 낫다 is a ㅅ-irregular adjective, the ㅅ drops before vowel endings (나아 'is better', 나은 'better [modifier]', 나을 'will be better'), distinguishing it in conjugation from 낮다 ('to be low' -> 낮아) and 낳다 ('to give birth' -> 낳아).

rootFamily.gloss: to recover from an illness, get well (homophonous sister verb)
to advance, move forward, improve (historical derivative)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낫다

낭만적이다.etymology: Built from 낭만 (浪漫, combining 浪 물결 랑 'rolling wave, unrestrained' and 漫 질펀할 만 'overflowing, lyrical'), coined phonetically and poetically in Meiji-era East Asia to render Western romantic and adapted into Korean with initial 랑- > 낭- by 두음법칙, followed by the Sino-Korean adjectival suffix -적 (的) and copula -이다. Before nouns it takes the modifier form 낭만적인 ('romantic', as in 낭만적인 분위기), while predicatively it conjugates via the copula.
낭만적이다.notes: Prenominal modifier form is 낭만적인 (낭만적인 밤 'a romantic evening'); adverbial form is 낭만적으로.

낮.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 낮 ('daytime, daylight hours, noon').

history.meaning: daytime, midday
daytime, day (as opposed to 밤 'night')

낮다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 낟다 / 낮다 ('to be low in height, level, or rank').

history.meaning: to be low
to be low (height, pitch, temperature, rank)

낮잠.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 낮 ('daytime, midday, noon', from Middle Korean 낮 nac) and 잠 ('sleep, slumber', from Middle Korean 잠 cam, itself the substantive nominalization in -ㅁ of the verb 자다 'to sleep'). Literally 'daytime sleep', denoting a short nap or siesta taken during daylight hours.

history.meaning: daytime/midday + sleep
daytime nap, afternoon siesta

낮잠.notes: Like 잠 ('sleep') and 꿈 ('dream'), 낮잠 pairs with the cognate verb 자다: 낮잠을 자다 ('to take a nap', literally 'to sleep a daytime sleep').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낮잠

낯가림.etymology: Native Korean compound noun derived from the phrase 낯을 가리다 ('to be shy around strangers', literally 'to distinguish or screen faces'), combining 낯 ('face, countenance', from Middle Korean 낯 nach) with 가림, the verbal noun (-ㅁ) of 가리다 ('to tell apart, discriminate, choose selectively; to screen/hide', from Middle Korean ᄀᆞ리다 koli-ta). Originally described an infant's developmental stage of recognizing and shying away from unfamiliar faces, and broadened to adult social shyness with strangers.

history.meaning: face + to distinguish, tell apart, or screen
shyness or wariness around strangers (in babies or shy adults)

morphemes.meaning: to distinguish, be selective about, screen (가리다)

낯가림.notes: To say 'I am shy around strangers' as a verb phrase, Koreans say 낯을 많이 가리다 (or 낯가림이 심하다, 'my stranger-shyness is severe').

rootFamily.gloss: unfamiliar, strange (lit. 'the face is unfamiliar', 낯 + 설다)
familiar (lit. 'the face is ripe/accustomed', 낯 + 익다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낯가림

낯설다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective formed from 낯 ('face, countenance', Middle Korean 낱/낯) and 설다 ('to be unripe, half-cooked, unaccustomed'). Literally meaning 'one's face is unaccustomed to it', 낯설다 originally described a face one had never met before, then broadened to unfamiliar places, sounds, and surroundings. Its exact antonym is 낯익다 ('familiar', literally 'face-ripened').
낯설다.notes: As a ㄹ-irregular stem, the adnominal modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ to become 낯선 ('unfamiliar, stranger').

낳다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb 낳다 ('to give birth to, bear offspring, lay eggs; to produce results'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 낳다 (nah-ta), a verb with a stable stem-final glottal/velar fricative ㅎ (/h/) that causes aspiration of following plain stops (e.g., 낳고 [나코], 낳다 [나타]) and drops phonetically between vowels (낳아 [나아]). Probably related internally to the root 나- ('to come out, be born, sprout').

history.meaning: to give birth to, bear offspring, bring forth
to give birth to, lay (eggs); (figurative) to produce or yield results

morphemes.meaning: to give birth, bear, bring forth

낳다.notes: One of Korean's most famous spelling traps is confusing 낳다 ('to give birth', 낳아 [나아]) with 낫다 ('to be better / recover', 나아 [나아])—remember that 낳다 keeps its ㅎ in spelling just like the aspirated breath of childbirth!

rootFamily.gloss: to be born, sprout, come out (intransitive counterpart)
to put forth, produce, bring out (causative)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 낳다

내.etymology: Native Korean first-person singular form descending from Middle Korean 내, representing either the contraction of 나의 ('my') or 나 + historical nominative -이 ('I' before 가).

history.meaning: I (nominative); my (genitive)
my; I (in 내가)

내기.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 내다 ('to put out stakes, produce') + nominalizing suffix -기.

history.meaning: wagering stakes, bet
bet, wager

내내.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb descending from Middle Korean 내내 ('all along, continuously from beginning to end').

history.meaning: constantly, all along
throughout, the whole time, all along

내년.etymology: Sino-Korean 내년 (來年), compounding 내 (來, 'come, coming, next', via initial law from 래) and 년 (年, 'year').

history.meaning: the coming year
next year

내놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내- (from 내다, 'to put out, bring forth') and 놓다 ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to put out and set down
to put out, set out, offer, put up for sale/rent

내다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 내다, originally the causative of 나다 ('to come out, arise') formed with -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to come out, produce, emit
to put out, make, pay, submit

내려가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go down, descend
to go down, step down, drop

내려놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to lower') and 놓다 ('to put down, release').

history.meaning: to lower and set down
to put down, set down, let go of

내려다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 내려다- (내리다 'to go down' + directional transfer suffix -어다) + 보다 ('to look at').

history.meaning: to look downward at
to look down on, overlook

내려다보이다.etymology: Native Korean passive/potential verb derived from 내려다보다 ('to look down at') + passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be visible below, be overlooked (of a view)

내려앉다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend, sink') and 앉다 ('to sit, settle').

history.meaning: to sink down, sag, collapse, alight

내려오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 내려- (from 내리다, 'to descend') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come down, descend
to come down, be handed down

내리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 나리다 ('to come down, fall from the sky, get off, lower').

history.meaning: to descend, fall, lower
to fall (rain/snow), get off, lower, brew (tea/coffee)

내밀다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 내- (stem of 내다 'to put out, bring forth', from Middle Korean 내다 nay-ta) and 밀다 ('to push, thrust, shove', from Middle Korean 밀다 mil-ta). Literally 'to push outward', used for sticking out a body part (hand, head, lips, chest), holding out an object or card toward someone, or pushing forward an opinion or demand.

history.meaning: to put out + to push/thrust
to push out, stick out, extend, hold out (a hand or object)

내밀다.notes: Because the root is the ㄹ-stem verb 밀다, the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, and ㅅ endings (e.g., 손을 내미는 사람 'a person holding out a hand', 내밉니다).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내밀다

내밀어주다.etymology: Native Korean polymorphemic benefactive verb construction formed from the compound verb 내밀- ('to push out, extend, lean forward', from 내다 'put out' + 밀다 'push') + infinitive linker -어 + benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's benefit', from Middle Korean 주다 cwu-ta). Expresses extending a hand, leaning one's face or shoulder forward, or offering an item toward someone as a helpful or affectionate gesture.

history.meaning: to push out / extend + to give (as a benefactive auxiliary)
to hold out, extend, or lean forward for someone's benefit

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary: to give, do for someone

내밀어주다.notes: In romantic K-drama scenes, 어깨를 내밀어 주다 ('to offer/lean a shoulder for someone to rest on') or 손을 내밀어 주다 ('to reach out a helping hand') highlights the warmth of the benefactive -어 주다.

rootFamily.gloss: to hold out, stick out, extend
to hand over, put out for someone (내다 + 주다)

내버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 내- (contracted from 내어, infinitive of 내다 'to put out, expel', Middle Korean 내다 nay-ta) and 버리다 ('to throw away, discard, abandon', from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다 poli-ta). Literally 'to cast out and abandon', it means both to throw something out completely and (especially in the serial construction 내버려 두다 or colloquial dialogue) to leave someone or something alone without interfering.

history.meaning: to put out/expel + to throw away/abandon
to throw out, cast aside, abandon, leave completely alone

내버리다.notes: Most frequently encountered in the phrase 내버려 두다 ('to leave alone / let it be'), which contracts in casual speech to 냅두다.

rootFamily.gloss: to leave alone (colloquial contraction of 내버려 두다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내버리다

내보다.etymology: Native Korean compound/serial verb construction formed from 내- (infinitive 내어 contracted to 내, from 내다 'to put out, submit, present, publish, pitch', Middle Korean 내다 nay-ta) + experiential auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing', from Middle Korean 보다 po-ta). Literally 'to put forth and see how it goes', used when trying to submit an application, pitch a program proposal, or muster up courage.

history.meaning: to put forth and see / to try putting out
to try submitting, pitching, or putting forth; to look out ahead

morphemes.meaning: to put out, submit, pitch (내다, infinitive 내어 -> 내)
experiential auxiliary: to try doing (literally 'to see')

내보다.notes: In broadcasting and office contexts, 기획안을 내보다 means 'to try pitching a proposal' and 사표를 내보다 means 'to try turning in a resignation letter'.

rootFamily.gloss: to put out, submit, produce, pay
to put out on the market or table (내놓다)

cognates.meaning: guest, visitor, honored guest at an event

내빈.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 來賓 (historical reading 래빈, shifting to 내빈 in South Korean standard orthography via the initial-sound law 두음법칙 on 來), composed of 來 (래/내, 'to come, arrive') and 賓 (빈, 'guest, visitor', a character containing 貝 'cowrie shell/valuables' indicating a guest honored with gifts). Literally 'guests who have arrived', used in formal events, weddings, and broadcasts for VIPs and honored guests.

history.meaning: a guest who comes to visit; an honored visitor
honored guests, visiting dignitaries at an event or ceremony

내빈.notes: A staple of formal Korean MC announcements: 내빈 여러분 ('Distinguished guests!'), often paired with 귀빈 (貴賓, 'VIP / honored guest').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내빈

내빼다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the directional/intensive prefix 내- (from 내다 'to put out, burst forth') and 빼다 ('to pull out, extract, withdraw', historically a causative formation related to 빠지다 'to fall out, slip away'). Literally 'to pull oneself right out', it evolved idiomatic colloquial usage meaning to bolt, slip away, or run off hastily from a sticky situation (originally ellipses of 발을 내빼다 or 꽁무니를 내빼다).

history.meaning: to pull right out / extract outward
to bolt, run away, slip off hastily

내빼다.notes: Colloquial and vivid—used when someone makes a quick getaway (걸음아 날 살려라 하고 내빼다, 'to bolt for dear life') or ducks out of responsibility.

rootFamily.gloss: to pull out, lure out, extract (빼내다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내빼다

내용.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 內容, composed of 內 (내, 'inside, interior, within') and 容 (용, 'to contain, hold, accommodate; vessel, appearance'). Literally 'what is contained inside', it was popularized across modern East Asian intellectual and media vocabulary (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 内容 *naiyō* translating German *Inhalt* / English *content*) to denote the substance or subject matter of a text, speech, broadcast, or vessel.

history.meaning: what is held within; inner capacity or appearance
contents, substance, details, subject matter (of a text, show, or talk)

내용.notes: Whereas 내용 (內容) refers to abstract substance, story, or information, 내용물 (內容物, adding 物 'thing') refers to the physical contents inside a package or box.

rootFamily.gloss: physical contents of a container (內容物)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내용

내일.etymology: Sino-Korean 내일 (來日), compounding 내 (來, 'coming, next') and 일 (日, 'day').

history.meaning: the coming day
tomorrow

내일모레.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining Sino-Korean 내일 (來日, 'tomorrow', from 來 'to come' [initial 래 -> 내 via 두음법칙] + 日 'day', literally 'the coming day') and native Korean 모레 ('the day after tomorrow', from 15th-century Middle Korean 모뢰 moloy). Although 모레 by itself already means 'the day after tomorrow', speakers juxtapose 내일 and 모레 either to mean 'the day right after tomorrow' or idiomatically 'in a day or two / very soon'.

history.meaning: tomorrow (the coming day) + the day after tomorrow
the day after tomorrow; in a day or two, right around the corner

morphemes.meaning: the day after tomorrow (native Korean, from Middle Korean 모뢰)

내일모레.notes: Often used hyperbolically for an imminent milestone: 내일모레면 마흔이다 ('I'm turning forty any day now!'). Note that Middle Korean originally had a native word for tomorrow too (하리/올제), which was replaced by Sino-Korean 내일 (來日), while native 모레 ('day after tomorrow') and 글피 ('two days after tomorrow') survived.

rootFamily.gloss: the day after tomorrow (native simplex form)
two days after tomorrow (three days from today)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내일모레

내주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 내- (contracted from 내어, infinitive of 내다 'to put out, bring forth, vacate, pay', Middle Korean 내다 nay-ta) and 주다 ('to give, grant, hand over', from Middle Korean 주다 cwu-ta). Literally 'to bring out and give', covering a wide range of senses from serving food or tea to a guest, vacating a room or seat for someone, to surrendering a lead or position in a competition.

history.meaning: to bring forth and give to someone
to bring out and serve, hand over, vacate (a room/seat), or yield (a lead)

morphemes.meaning: to put out, bring forth, vacate (내다, infinitive 내어 -> 내)

내주다.notes: In broadcasting ratings battles (a central theme of The Producers), 1위 자리를 내주다 means 'to surrender/yield the #1 ratings spot to a rival show'.

rootFamily.gloss: to put out, bring forth, produce
to put out, set out on the table or market (내놓다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 내주다

냄비.etymology: Recorded in Early Modern Korean as 남비 and standardized to 냄비 via umlaut (ㅏ > ㅐ before the high front vowel ㅣ in the following syllable). Most Korean etymologists trace 남비 to a borrowing from Japanese なべ (nabe, 'cooking pot, pan') during the late Joseon era, designating a shallower metal pot distinct from the deep traditional cast-iron cauldron (솥).
냄비.notes: Used for everyday stove-top pots for soup, stew, or boiling noodles.

냄새.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 내 ('smoke, vapor, odor') via extended Early Modern Korean 내암새 > 냄새.

history.meaning: vapor, smoke, smell
smell, scent, odor, aroma

냅두다.etymology: Colloquial and dialectal Korean contracted verb derived from the serial construction 내버려 두다 ('to leave alone, let be, leave untouched'). Through rapid-speech syncope and assimilation—passing through intermediate spoken variants 내버두다 and 내비두다—the три-syllable first component 내버려 (infinitive of 내버리다, from 내다 'put out' + 버리다 'throw away/abandon') compressed into the single closed syllable 냅-, preserving the bilabial stop /p/ (ㅂ) of 버리다 as a coda before the auxiliary verb 두다 ('to put, keep in a state').

history.meaning: to cast aside and leave in that state; to leave alone
history.stage: Early Modern to Standard Modern Korean

history.meaning: to leave alone, let it be (colloquial phonologically reduced compound)

morphemes.meaning: contracted from 내버려 ('abandoning/casting aside', from 내- + 버리다)
auxiliary verb: to leave in a state, keep, put (두다)

냅두다.notes: Extremely common in everyday spoken Korean—그냥 냅둬! ('Just leave it/them alone!')—whereas formal writing and news broadcasts use the full standard form 내버려 두다.

rootFamily.gloss: to throw out, abandon, leave alone (source verb)
to put, place, keep in a state (auxiliary verb)
to leave behind, leave as is (놔두다, from 놓아 두다)

냅킨.etymology: Borrowed from English napkin, referring to a cloth or paper serviette used at the table.

history.meaning: table serviette
napkin

냉동고.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 냉동고 (冷凍庫), formed from 냉동 (冷凍, 'freezing, refrigeration', from 冷 'cold, chill' + 凍 'to freeze, congeal') and the bound suffixal noun -고 (庫, 'storehouse, chamber, repository'). In South Korean orthography, the historical Sino-Korean initial 랭 (läng) underwent the initial sound law (두음법칙) to become 냉 (naeng). Coined in modern East Asian industrial and domestic appliance terminology on the model of Japanese 冷凍庫 (reitōko).

history.meaning: freezing + storehouse or chamber (Sino-Korean morphemic components)
refrigerated storage room; domestic freezer compartment or unit

냉동고.notes: While 냉장고 (冷藏庫, 'refrigerator') means a unit that 'stores cold' above freezing, 냉동고 (冷凍庫) specifically denotes the sub-zero 'freezing chamber' or standalone deep freezer.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

냉장고.etymology: Sino-Korean 냉장고 (冷藏庫), from 냉장 (冷藏, 냉 'cold' + 장 'store, preserve') + 고 (庫, 'storehouse, cabinet').

history.meaning: cold-storage cabinet
refrigerator, fridge

cognates.meaning: cold-heartedness, apathy; composure (as 冷静 reisei)
unfeeling, cold; calm and objective (as 冷靜)

냉정하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adjectival verb combining Sino-Korean 냉정 (冷情, 'cold emotion, unfeeling detachment', composed of 冷 'cold, frosty' + 情 'feeling, emotion, affection') with the native Korean adjective-forming light verb -하다 ('to be, to do'). Initial 冷 shifted from historical 랭 (laeng) to 냉 (naeng) under the South Korean initial sound law (두음법칙). Semantically, it spans both 'cold-hearted, callous' and 'cool-headed, dispassionate, objective' (overlapping in sense with Sinospheric 冷靜).

history.meaning: coldness of heart, lack of warm sentiment
to be cold-hearted; to be cool-headed, calm, and objective in judgment

냉정하다.notes: Depending on context, 냉정하다 can criticize someone as 'heartless/cold' or praise their ability to make a 'cool-headed, objective' assessment (냉정한 판단).

rootFamily.gloss: cold and indifferent, chilly in manner

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

너.etymology: Native Korean second-person singular plain pronoun descending from Middle Korean 너 ('thou, you').

history.meaning: you (singular)
you (intimate/plain)

너네.etymology: Native Korean colloquial second-person plural and associative pronoun formed from the second-person singular pronoun 너 (Middle Korean 너, 'thou, you') plus the associative group suffix -네 (Middle Korean -네, originally an honorific plural marker that grammaticalized into an associative plural meaning 'one's household, side, or group'). Thus 너네 literally means 'your side, your household, or you guys'.

history.meaning: second-person singular pronoun + associative/plural group suffix
you guys; your family or group (informal/colloquial)

너네.notes: In everyday speech, 너네 functions both as 'you guys' (plural subject/object) and as a possessive before group nouns, such as 너네 집 ('your family's house') or 너네 팀 ('your team').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

너는.etymology: Inflected topic-marked form of the native Korean second-person singular pronoun 너 (attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 너, 'thou, you') combined with the post-vocalic topic and contrastive particle -는 (Middle Korean -ᄂᆞᆫ / -는, 'as for, speaking of'). In colloquial speech, 너는 frequently contracts to 넌 (nen).

history.meaning: as for thee (second-person singular pronoun + topic marker)
as for you; you (topic or contrastive focus)

너는.notes: Because -는 marks either the sentence topic or contrast, 너는 often carries a pointed contrastive nuance ('What about *you*?' or '*You*, on the other hand...'), and usually contracts to 넌 in casual dialogue.

너도밤나무.etymology: Native Korean compound tree name formed from 너 ('you') + -도 ('also, too') + 밤나무 ('chestnut tree'), literally 'you-too-chestnut-tree' from its chestnut-like nuts and foliage.

history.meaning: beech tree, beechwood

너머.etymology: Native Korean noun lexicalized from the infinitive 넘어 of 넘다 ('to cross over, pass beyond'), spelled phonemically to denote the space beyond a height or barrier.

history.meaning: crossing over, beyond
beyond, the other side (of a mountain, wall, window, orshoulder)

너무.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb descending from Middle Korean 너모, derived from the verb stem 넘- of 넘다 ('to exceed, go over') + adverbial suffix -오.

history.meaning: excessively, over the limit
too, excessively; very, so much

너무하다.etymology: Native Korean verb/adjective derived from the adverb 너무 ('excessively, too much') + the light verb -하다 ('to do, to be'). The adverb 너무 is attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 너모 (nemo, 'in excess, beyond measure'), itself a deverbal derivation from the verb stem 넘- (넘다, 'to cross over, exceed, pass a boundary') + the adverbial/nominalizing suffix -오/-우. Combined with -하다, 너무하다 literally means 'to act in a way that crosses the boundary of moderation; to go too far or be harsh'.

history.meaning: crossing beyond a limit; excessively, overly
to go too far, to be excessive, unreasonable, or harsh

너무하다.notes: Exclaiming '진짜 너무하다!' ('You are really being too much!' / 'That is so unfair!') is a classic Korean conversational reproach when someone feels treated harshly or inconsiderately.

너비.etymology: Native Korean measure noun descending from Middle Korean 너비, derived from the older stem 너브- of 넓다 ('to be wide') + nominalizing suffix -이.

history.meaning: width, breadth; widely
width, breadth

너한테.etymology: Inflected dative/oblique pronoun formed from the native Korean second-person singular pronoun 너 (Middle Korean 너, 'you') + the colloquial animate dative particle -한테 ('to, at, from a person'). Philologically, -한테 grammaticalized from Early Modern Korean 한티 / 한듸 ('at the same place, together', composed of 한 'one, same' + 듸/데 'place'), which evolved from a comitative/locative noun phrase into the standard spoken dative marker for people and animals.

history.meaning: in one place, together with (source of the dative particle -한테)
to you, for you, from you (informal spoken dative)

너한테.notes: -한테 is strictly used for animate beings (people and animals) in spoken Korean; its slightly more formal written/spoken counterpart is -에게 (as in 너에게), while inanimate targets take -에.

너희.etymology: Native Korean second-person plural pronoun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 너희 (nehuy, 'ye, you all'). Morphologically analyzed as the second-person singular base 너 (ne, 'thou, you') + the archaic pronominal plural/collective suffix -희 (-huy, which also survives in the humble first-person plural pronoun 저희 cehuy 'we' and Middle Korean 누희 'who [plural]'). In casual speech, 너희 is frequently pronounced [너이] or contracted to 너네.

history.meaning: ye, you (plural addressed to equals or inferiors)
you guys, you all (intimate/non-honorific second-person plural)

너희.notes: Like singular 너, 너희 can only be used toward children, close childhood friends, or social subordinates; addressing a group of adults politely requires 여러분 ('everyone').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

너희들.etymology: Doubly pluralized native Korean second-person pronoun formed by attaching the general plural marker -들 (Middle Korean -ᄃᆞᆯ, -tol) to the already plural pronoun 너희 (Middle Korean 너희, nehuy, from 너 'you' + pronominal plural suffix -희). Because 너희 alone is often used as a collective or possessive modifier (e.g., 너희 집 'your family's house'), adding -들 reinforces distributive plurality ('you all individually as a group').

history.meaning: all of you, ye (plural pronoun + distributive plural suffix)
you guys, you all (distributive plural)

너희들.notes: Adding -들 makes it unambiguously clear that the speaker is addressing multiple listeners right in front of them ('all of you guys'), rather than using 너희 as a collective possessive ('your family/group').

넉.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral descending from Middle Korean 넉 ('four'), preserved before specific classifiers such as 달 ('month'), 장 ('sheet'), 잔 ('cup'), and 줄 ('row').

history.meaning: four (adnominal)
four (before select classifiers, e.g. 넉 달 'four months')

넉넉히.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the root 넉넉- of 넉넉하다 ('to be ample, plenty, more than enough') + adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: amply, sufficiently
generously, amply, with plenty to spare

넓다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 너브다 / 넓다 ('to be wide, broad, spacious').

history.meaning: to be wide, broad
to be wide, spacious, broad

넘겨주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 넘기다 ('to pass over, hand over, transfer', the lexical causative of Middle Korean 넘다 nem-ta 'to cross over, pass beyond' formed with the causative suffix -기-) + the infinitive/conjunctive linker -어 + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 cwu-ta, 'to give, do for someone'). Literally 'to cause something to cross over and give it to someone', hence 'to hand over, pass down, or transfer ownership/responsibility'.

history.meaning: to cause to cross over + to give
to hand over, pass down, turn over control or possession to someone

넘겨주다.notes: Frequently used in workplace and broadcasting contexts for handing over a project, slot, or baton to a successor, or passing the microphone/turn to the next speaker.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass over, hand over, flip (a page)
to take over, inherit from someone

넘기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 넘기다, formed from 넘다 ('to cross over, pass') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to pass over, cause to cross
to turn (a page), hand over, pass (a deadline or crisis)

넘다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 넘다 ('to cross over a height or boundary, exceed, overflow').

history.meaning: to cross over, exceed
to cross over, exceed, pass beyond

넘어가다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb attested in Middle Korean as 넘어가다 (nem-e ka-ta), composed of 넘다 (Middle Korean 넘다 nem-ta, 'to cross over a peak, ridge, or boundary') + the conjunctive suffix -어 + 가다 (Middle Korean 가다 ka-ta, 'to go'). From the concrete spatial sense 'to go over a mountain pass or threshold', it developed extensive metaphorical senses: 'to move on to the next topic', 'to let a mistake slide without punishment', and 'to fall for deception'.

history.meaning: to go across a ridge or boundary; to pass over
to cross over; to move on to the next item; to let something pass; to be tricked

넘어가다.notes: In conversation, '그냥 넘어가다' means 'to let it slide / overlook a fault without making an issue of it', whereas '속아 넘어가다' means 'to fall for a trick'.

rootFamily.gloss: to come across toward the speaker
to pass over, flip, hand over

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

넘어뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean intensive causative compound verb built from 넘어- (the conjunctive stem of 넘어지다 'to fall down, topple over', rooted in Middle Korean 넘다 nem-ta 'to tilt or cross over') + the transitivizing/causative suffix -뜨리다 (also realized as -트리다, evolving from Early Modern Korean -드리다 / -트리다 with fortition into tense ㄸ to express forceful or sudden causation). Literally 'to forcefully cause someone or something to topple over; to knock down or overthrow'.

history.meaning: to cause to topple or fall over
to knock down, trip up, throw down, or overthrow

넘어뜨리다.notes: Korean preserves a neat transitive/intransitive pair: 넘어지다 is intransitive ('to trip and fall by oneself'), while 넘어뜨리다 (or 넘어트리다, both standard) is transitive ('to knock someone/something down').

rootFamily.gloss: to drop, cause to fall from a height (sharing -뜨리다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

넘어지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive compound verb attested in Middle Korean as 넘어디다 (nem-e ti-ta), composed of 넘다 (nem-ta, 'to cross over, tilt past an upright threshold') + conjunctive suffix -어 + the inchoative/falling verb 디다 (ti-ta, 'to fall down, to become', which underwent early modern palatalization d > j before i to yield modern 지다). Originally describing something tilting past its balance point and falling, it became the standard verb for tripping or falling over on a surface.

history.meaning: to tilt over and fall down
to trip and fall, tumble, lose one's footing and fall down

넘어지다.notes: Distinguish 넘어지다 ('to fall over on the ground, trip, or slip' from a standing/walking posture) from 떨어지다 ('to fall or drop down from a height').

rootFamily.gloss: to knock down, cause to fall over
to collapse, cave in, fall down (of a standing body or structure)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

넣다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 녀타 (녛다, 'to put inside, insert').

history.meaning: to put in, insert
to put in, insert, include

넣어두다.etymology: Native Korean aspectual compound verb composed of 넣다 (Middle Korean 넣다 neh-ta, 'to put in, insert, place inside') + the conjunctive suffix -어 + the resultative/preparatory auxiliary verb 두다 (Middle Korean 두다 twu-ta, 'to put, keep, leave in a state for later'). Together, 넣어두다 expresses putting something inside a container or space and leaving it safely stored there for future contingencies ('to tuck away, stow away, keep in reserve').

history.meaning: to insert/put inside + to keep/leave in place
to put in and keep for later; to tuck away, stow, or file away

morphemes.meaning: keep, leave in a state for future use

넣어두다.notes: Used both literally ('tuck it away in your pocket/bag') and idiomatically, as in '그 말씀은 마음속에 넣어두세요' ('Keep that remark to yourself / tuck that thought away').

rootFamily.gloss: to leave behind, keep in reserve (sharing auxiliary 두다)

넣어드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble-benefactive compound verb combining 넣다 (Middle Korean 넣다 neh-ta, 'to put in, insert, send in, include') + conjunctive suffix -어 + the humble benefactive auxiliary 드리다 ('to give or offer to an esteemed person', derived from Early Modern Korean 드리다 'to cause to enter, offer up to a superior', historically the causative of 들다 'to enter'). Expresses performing the action of putting in, depositing, submitting, or delivering something inside on behalf of a respected recipient.

history.meaning: to put inside + to offer/present to a superior
to put in, deposit, include, or deliver inside for an esteemed person (humble)

morphemes.meaning: give/do for a respected recipient (humble counterpart of 주다)

넣어드리다.notes: Because 넣다 covers putting money into an account, submitting an application, or delivering food/mail into a room or office, 넣어드리다 is ubiquitous in polite Korean service and workplace speech.

rootFamily.gloss: to put in for someone (plain/equal benefactive)
to give/offer to a superior (humble verb/auxiliary)

넣어주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb formed from 넣다 (Middle Korean 넣다 neh-ta, 'to put in, insert, include') + the conjunctive linker -어 + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 cwu-ta, 'to give, do for someone's benefit'). Literally 'to put inside for someone', used when adding, inserting, depositing, or including something as a favor or service to an equal or subordinate.

history.meaning: to put inside + to give/do for someone
to put in, insert, add, or include for someone's benefit

넣어주다.notes: When asking a peer or staff member to include an item, add a scene in editing, or put something in a bag, '넣어주세요' ('Please put it in for me') is the natural everyday phrasing.

rootFamily.gloss: to put in for an esteemed person (humble counterpart)
to put in and keep for later

네.etymology: Polite Korean response interjection meaning 'yes, I see' (variant of 예); also homophonous with the adnominal numeral 네 ('four', from 넷) and pronoun 네 ('your' or 'you' < 너의 / 너+이).

history.meaning: yes (polite); four; your/you
yes (polite); four (before counters); your/you

네가.etymology: Nominative (subject) form of the native Korean second-person singular pronoun 너 ('you'). Historically doubly marked: in 15th-century Middle Korean, adding the vocalic nominative case marker -ㅣ (-i) to 너 (ne) produced the fused nominative form 네 (ney, 'thou [subject]'). From the 16th–17th centuries onward, the newly emerging post-vocalic nominative particle -가 (-ka) was pleonastically attached to 네, yielding 네가 ('you [subject]'). In modern spoken Korean, the phonological merger of ㅐ (ae) and ㅔ (e) made 네가 ('you') homophonous with 내가 ('I'), prompting speakers to disambiguate 'you' phonetically as 니가 [niga].

history.meaning: thou (second-person singular nominative)
you (singular intimate subject form, doubly marked for nominative case)
history.stage: 17th Century Early Modern to Contemporary Korean

morphemes.kind: native pronoun root (fused with archaic nominative -ㅣ)

네가.notes: Although standard orthography requires writing 네가, almost all speakers pronounce it [니가] in conversation so it is never confused with 내가 ('I').

rootFamily.gloss: I (first-person nominative, formed by parallel 나 + -ㅣ + -가)

네모나다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective formed from 네모 ('four-cornered figure, square or rectangle', itself composed of 네 'four' + 모 'corner, angle') plus -나다 ('to come forth with or exhibit a shape'). Although built with -나다, standard Korean grammar classifies 네모나다 as a descriptive adjective (형용사) rather than an action verb, so its present adnominal modifier is 네모난 ('square', 네모난 상자) rather than *네모나는.
네모나다.notes: Covers both squares (정사각형) and rectangles (직사각형) in everyday speech; compare 세모나다 ('triangular') and 동그랗다 ('round').

네시.etymology: Hybrid native-Sino-Korean clock-time expression meaning 'four o'clock', composed of the native Korean prenominal numeral 네 ('four', the determiner allomorph of 넷 before classifier nouns, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 네 / 넿 neyh) + the Sino-Korean bound classifier noun 시 (時, 'time, hour, o'clock'). Korean time-telling systematically pairs native Korean numerals (한, 두, 세, 네...) with Sino-Korean 시 (時) for hours, while using Sino-Korean numerals for minutes (분 分) and seconds (초 秒).

history.meaning: native numeral 'four' (prenominal form) + Sino-Korean 'hour/time'
four o'clock

네시.notes: In standard Korean spacing rules, numerals and bound unit nouns are spaced (네 시), though they are frequently written solid as 네시 in subtitles and casual text; remember that 'four hours' (duration) is 네 시간 (네 時間).

cognates.meaning: luminous sign made of glass tubes filled with neon gas

네온사인.etymology: Modern loanword (외래어) borrowed in the 1920s–1930s (initially via Japanese ネオンサイン neonsain) from English neon sign. The first element, neon, was coined in 1898 by British chemists Sir William Ramsay and Morris Travers from Ancient Greek νέον (néon, 'new Thing', neuter singular of νέος néos 'new') upon discovering the noble gas; the second element, sign, derives via Old French signe from Latin signum ('mark, token, indicator').

history.meaning: luminous gas-discharge sign using neon tubing (patented by Georges Claude in 1910)
neon sign; bright illuminated nightlife or commercial signage

네온사인.notes: In Korean pop culture and drama imagery, 네온사인 evokes bustling urban nightlife, entertainment districts, and late-night cityscapes after broadcasting shifts end.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

넥타이.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth / early twentieth century from English necktie (compound of neck + tie), entering Korean alongside Western suits and reinforced by Japanese ネクタイ.

history.meaning: band of fabric knotted around a shirt collar
necktie, tie

넥타이.notes: Whereas English speakers usually shorten necktie to tie, Korean keeps the full three-syllable 넥타이 in everyday conversation (넥타이를 매다, 'to put on a tie').

넷.etymology: Native Korean cardinal numeral descending from Middle Korean 넿 / 넷 ('four').

history.meaning: four
four

녀석.etymology: Native Korean colloquial noun attested from the 18th–19th centuries (Early Modern Korean) as 녀석 / 여석, used to refer familiarly, gruffly, or affectionately to a fellow, boy, or chap. Although its deeper pre-modern etymology remains debated among Korean historical linguists (with proposals linking it to an expressive derivative of 녘 'side/direction' or vernacular pejorative compounds), it notably resists the South Korean initial sound law (두음법칙, which normally turns initial ny- into y-) in standard orthography to preserve its distinctive expressive and gruff register.

history.meaning: fellow, rascal, chap (colloquial/familiar noun for a male or subordinate)
chap, fellow, guy, rascal (affectionate or mildly disparaging)

녀석.notes: Depending on tone of voice, 이 녀석 ('this fellow/kid') can express warm, gruff affection from a senior/parent or mild exasperation ('this little rascal!'). It is one of the very few native words spelled with initial 녀- in South Korea.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

년.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and counter 년 (年, 'year'), from Middle Chinese *nen.

history.meaning: year, harvest cycle
year (counter used with Sino-Korean numerals)

노끈.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 노 ('thin cord twisted from mulberry paper, hemp, or plant fiber', Middle Korean 노ㅎ) with 끈 ('string, lace, strap'). In traditional Korean households, 노 was hand-twisted from oiled hanji paper or hemp strands for binding books, parcels, and bundles, and compounding it with 끈 reinforced its everyday meaning as sturdy packing twine or kitchen string.
노끈.notes: Takes 묶다 ('tie with twine') and 풀다 ('untie twine').

노닥거리다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic/frequentative verb formed from the expressive mimetic root 노닥- (evoking unhurried, idle, repetitive chattering or trifling, phonesthemically linked to 놀다 'to play, idle away' and reduplicated in the adverb 노닥노닥) + the frequentative verbal suffix -거리다 ('to do repeatedly or continuously'). Conveys dawdling, chatting away idly, or whiling away time in light, unhurried banter.

history.meaning: to repeatedly chat idly or dawdle about without urgency
to dawdle, chat idly, lounge around bantering instead of working

노닥거리다.notes: Like most Korean mimetic verbs in -거리다, 노닥거리다 can swap its suffix to -대다 (노닥대다) with virtually identical meaning, often used when scolding coworkers or friends for lounging around chatting instead of working.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

노랗다.etymology: Native Korean ㅎ-irregular color adjective descending from Middle Korean 노라하다 ('to be bright yellow').

history.meaning: to be yellow
to be yellow, golden

노래.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 노래 ('song'), historically derived from the root 놀- of 놀다 ('to play, sing, enjoy oneself').

history.meaning: song
song, singing

cognates.meaning: karaoke box (private singing room, functional model)
cognates.word: カラオケボックス (karaoke bokkusu)

노래방.etymology: Hybrid native-Sino-Korean compound noun coined in South Korea around 1991 (first popularized in Busan with coin-operated private singing booths), combining native Korean 노래 ('song', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 노래 nwolay, historically derived from the verb stem 놀- nwol- 'to play, sing and dance' + nominalizing suffix -애) + Sino-Korean 방 (房, 'room, chamber'). Literally 'song room', serving as the native Koreanized counterpart to Japanese カラオケボックス (karaoke bokkusu).

history.meaning: native Korean 'song' + Sino-Korean 'chamber/room'
private karaoke singing room; noraebang establishment

노래방.notes: Unlike Western karaoke bars where patrons sing in front of strangers, a Korean 노래방 rents private soundproofed rooms to groups of friends or coworkers—a staple of Korean company dinners (회식). The -방 (房) pattern subsequently spawned PC방, 찜질방, and 만화방.

rootFamily.gloss: PC bang (internet gaming cafe, sharing suffix -방 房)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

노래하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from 노래 ('song') + light verb -하다.

history.meaning: to sing a song
to sing

노랫소리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of 노래 (Middle Korean 노래 nwolay, 'song', derived from 놀- 'to play, make merry' + nominalizer -애) + the epenthetic genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷 saisiot, direct descendant of the 15th-century Middle Korean genitive particle ㅅ -s) + 소리 (Middle Korean 소리 swoli, 'sound, voice'). Under standard Korean orthography, when two native nouns form a compound and the second initial consonant undergoes tensification ([소리] > [쏘리]), the interfix ㅅ is written on the preceding open syllable: 노래 + ㅅ + 소리 > 노랫소리.

history.meaning: song + genitive marker + sound/voice
the sound of singing; the sound of a song

노랫소리.notes: Notice the 사이시옷 ('s' interfix) in 노랫소리 and 노랫말 ('song lyrics'): because both compounds combine two native Korean words and tense the following consonant ([노래쏘리], [노랜말]), Korean spelling inserts ㅅ under 노래.

rootFamily.gloss: song lyrics (sharing 노래 + 사이시옷 ㅅ + 말)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: to make an effort, strive hard

노력하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from Sino-Korean 노력 (努力, 'strenuous effort, endeavor', composed of 努 'to exert oneself, strive with all one's might' + 力 'strength, power, force') + the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do'). Attested in Classical Chinese since the Han dynasty (famously in the Yuefu poem 長歌行: 少壯不努力，老大徒傷悲 'If in youth one does not exert oneself, in old age one grieves in vain').

history.meaning: to exert one's strength, strive diligently
to make an effort, endeavor, work hard toward a goal

노력하다.notes: Note the Hanja distinction between 노력 (努力, 'effort/striving', with 努 'strive', historically nasal initial n-) and 노동 (勞動, 'labor/work', with 勞 'toil', historically liquid initial l- > n-).

rootFamily.gloss: hard worker, person of great effort and perseverance

노릇노릇하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective built on 노릇- (related to 노랗다, 'yellowish, golden') + -하다, describing pleasantly browned or toasted surfaces.

history.meaning: to be nicely golden-brown (of baked or grilled food)

노릇해지다.etymology: Native Korean culinary change-of-state verb built from the bright-vowel color root 노릇- (related to 노르다 and 노랗다 'yellow, golden', and reduplicated in 노릇노릇하다 'evenly golden brown') plus -하- and the inchoative auxiliary -아/어지다 ('to become'). Within Korean sound symbolism, the bright vowel ㅗ evokes a warm, light, appetizing golden crust on bread, pastry, or grilled food, contrasting with dark-vowel 누렇다 ('dull or heavy yellow').
노릇해지다.notes: Signature baking and roasting verb paired with 굽다 ('bake, roast').

노마크.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed into Korean sports and colloquial usage from Japanese Wasei-eigo (Japanese-coined English) ノーマーク (nōmāku), which combines English no + mark ('to guard an opposing player in team sports'). Originally describing an offensive player in basketball or soccer left completely unguarded ('unmarked') with a clear shot at the goal, it broadened metaphorically in Korean media and everyday speech to mean 'a wide-open, uncontested opportunity' or 'someone left completely unattended'.

history.form: Japanese ノーマーク (nōmāku, from English no + mark)
history.meaning: unguarded offensive player in basketball/soccer; unmonitored target
unmarked/wide-open position in sports; an uncontested golden opportunity or unguarded person

노마크.notes: Because 노마크 is a Japanese-coined pseudo-anglicism (콩글리시/와세이에이고), native English speakers say 'wide open' or 'unmarked' (and 'open shot' rather than 노마크 찬스). In Korean dramas, calling a romantic interest '노마크' humorously frames them as an unguarded free agent!

rootFamily.gloss: to guard closely, mark an opponent or target person-to-person

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 노마크

cognates.meaning: to rack one's brains, worry anxiously
cognates.word: 勞心焦思 / 劳心焦思 (láoxīn jiāosī)

노심초사하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the four-character Sino-Korean idiom (사자성어, 四字成語) 노심초사 (勞心焦思) + the native light verb -하다 ('to do, to be'). The idiom pairs two parallel verb-object compounds: 勞心 (노심, historically 로심 before the initial sound law 두음법칙, 'to weary or toil one's mind/heart', from 勞 'toil, exhaust' + 心 'heart, mind') and 焦思 (초사, 'to scorch or burn one's thoughts', from 焦 'scorch, char, anxious' + 思 'thought, reflection'). Literally 'to exhaust one's heart and scorch one's thoughts', i.e., to fret and agonize anxiously.

history.form: 勞心 (로심, 'weary the mind') + 焦思 (초사, 'scorch one's thoughts')
history.meaning: classical parallel four-character idiom for extreme mental anguish and anxious fretting
history.stage: Classical Chinese & Literary Sino-Korean (勞心焦思)

history.meaning: to fret anxiously, agonize, worry oneself sick over an outcome

노심초사하다.notes: A high-frequency four-character idiom (사자성어) in Korean news and dramas, vividly picturing worry as something that 'tires the heart (勞心) and chars one's thoughts (焦思)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be impatient, anxious, fretful (sharing 焦)
mental and physical toil, labor (sharing 勞)

cognates.meaning: labor union (syllabic abbreviation of 労働組合 rōdō kumiai)

노조.etymology: Sino-Korean syllabic abbreviation (두음절 줄임말) of 노동조합 (勞動組合, 'labor union, trade union'), formed by extracting the first syllable 노 (勞, 'labor, toil', historically 로 ro before the South Korean initial sound law 두음법칙, from 노동 勞動 'labor') and the first syllable 조 (組, 'weave, organize, association', from 조합 組合 'union, association'). Directly parallels the Japanese abbreviation 労組 (rōso < 労働組合 rōdō kumiai).

history.meaning: labor union, trade union (full four-character Sino-Korean compound)
labor union (standard two-syllable journalistic and everyday abbreviation)

morphemes.meaning: labor, toil (勞, from 노동 勞動)
association, union, organize (組, from 조합 組合)

노조.notes: Korean news and workplace speech heavily favor two-syllable Sino-Korean abbreviations: 노동조합 ('labor union') becomes 노조 (勞組), and 노사 (勞使) abbreviates 노동자 ('workers') + 사용자 ('employers', i.e. labor and management).

cognates.meaning: laptop computer (clipped from ノートブックパソコン)

노트북.etymology: Modern loanword (외래어) clipped from 노트북 컴퓨터 (notebook computer), borrowed in the late 1980s and 1990s from English notebook (computer). The English compound joins note (via Old French from Latin nota, 'mark, written sign or memorandum') and book (from Old English bōc). Through semantic specialization via ellipsis in Korean, 노트북 came to mean exclusively a portable laptop computer, while a paper notebook is referred to as 공책 (空冊) or simply 노트 (note).

history.form: English notebook computer > Korean 노트북 컴퓨터
history.meaning: lightweight, portable personal computer roughly the size of a paper notebook
laptop computer

노트북.notes: Classic Korean false friend for English speakers: in Korean, 노트북 always means a 'laptop computer'. If you want a paper notebook for writing, ask for a 공책 (空冊) or 노트!

rootFamily.gloss: paper notebook; musical or written note

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

녹음하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb composed of Sino-Korean 녹음 (錄音, 'audio recording', formed from 錄 'to record, copy down, inscribe, register' + 音 'sound, voice, tone') + the native Korean verbalizing light verb -하다 ('to do, to make'). Historically, initial 錄 was read 록 (lok), shifting to 녹 (nok) in word-initial position under the South Korean initial sound law (두음법칙; compare non-initial 기록 記錄 'record'). Coined in modern Sinospheric technical terminology (cf. Japanese 録音 rokuon) with the rise of phonograph and broadcast audio technology.

history.meaning: inscribing or registering sound onto a physical or magnetic medium
history.stage: Early 20th Century Sino-Korean & Sinospheric Technical Coinage

history.meaning: to record audio, voice, or music

morphemes.meaning: record, register, copy down (錄, initial allomorph of 록)

녹음하다.notes: Korean broadcasting strictly distinguishes 녹음하다 (錄音하다, 'to record audio/sound', e.g., radio, voiceover, music) from 녹화하다 (錄畫하다, 'to record video/film', e.g., a TV show shoot). Also note the homophone 녹음 (綠陰, 'green shade of summer trees').

rootFamily.gloss: record, documentation (sharing 錄 in non-initial position as -록)

녹이다.etymology: Native Korean morphological causative built from the intransitive verb stem 녹- (녹다, 'to melt, thaw, dissolve', Middle Korean 녹다) plus the native causative suffix -이-. Literally used in kitchens and workshops for melting butter, chocolate, sugar, or beeswax (버터를 녹이다), it also extends idiomatically to warming chilled hands (언 손을 녹이다) and softening a guarded heart (마음을 녹이다).
녹이다.notes: Transitive counterpart of intransitive 녹다 ('something melts on its own').

녹차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 녹차 (綠茶, 'green tea'), composed of 綠 (녹, 'green', historically 록 lok, undergoing the South Korean initial sound law 두음법칙 l- > n- in word-initial position; compare non-initial 초록 草綠 'grass green') + 茶 (차, 'tea'). Notably, the character 茶 has two Sino-Korean readings reflecting different historical layers of Chinese borrowing: 다 (da, from earlier Tang-era Middle Chinese dæ, preserved in literary compounds like 다도 茶道 'tea ceremony') and 차 (cha, from later Northern Chinese chā, used for everyday tea terms like 차 茶 and 녹차 綠茶).

history.meaning: unfermented green tea leaves and the infusion brewed from them
green tea (applying initial sound law 록 > 녹)

morphemes.meaning: tea (茶, also read 다 in literary compounds)

녹차.notes: The character 茶 is uniquely read both 차 and 다 in Korean: when drinking tea it is 차 (녹차 'green tea', 홍차 'black tea'), but in traditional or botanical compounds it is read 다 (다도 茶道 'tea ceremony', 다과 茶菓 'tea and refreshments').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

녹화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 녹화 (錄畫, 'video recording, television taping, filming'), composed of 錄 (녹, 'to record, register, copy down', historically 록 lok before the South Korean initial sound law 두음법칙; compare North Korean 록화 and non-initial 기록 記錄) + 畫 (화, 'picture, image, painting'). Coined in modern Sinospheric broadcasting vocabulary (alongside Japanese 録画 rokuga) as the visual counterpart to 녹음 (錄音, 'audio recording'), literally meaning 'recording pictures/images'.

history.meaning: recording visual images onto film or magnetic tape (coined by analogy with 錄音 'recording sound')
video recording; television studio taping or location shoot

morphemes.meaning: record, register, copy (錄, initial allomorph of 록)

녹화.notes: In Korean television production (such as in *The Producers*), 녹화 refers specifically to the studio taping or filming session of a pre-recorded broadcast (녹화 방송), in contrast to a live broadcast (생방송 生放送). Do not confuse with the homophone 녹화 (綠化, 'greening/reforestation').

rootFamily.gloss: to record video, tape a broadcast, film
pre-recorded television broadcast (vs. 생방송 live broadcast)
audio recording (parallel formation with 錄 'record' + 音 'sound')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

녹화하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 녹화 (錄畫, 'video recording', from 錄 'to record, copy, inscribe' + 畫 'picture, drawing, image', coined in modern East Asian broadcasting alongside Japanese 録画 rokuga) combined with the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to copy or inscribe records + picture or drawing
recording moving images onto film or magnetic tape
to record video or pre-record a television broadcast

녹화하다.notes: Specifically refers to recording video or television programs (pre-recording vs. 생방송 'live broadcast'), whereas recording audio alone is 녹음하다 (錄音-).

논문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 논문 (論文), composed of 논 (論, 'to discuss, argue, debate, reason') and 문 (文, 'writing, text, literary composition'). Classically used in Chinese literary criticism for discursive essays or critiques of writing, and standardized across modern East Asia for an academic thesis, dissertation, or research paper.

history.meaning: discursive essay or critical discourse on literature
academic thesis, dissertation, or scholarly research paper

논문.notes: Covers everything from a university graduation thesis (졸업 논문) and master's/doctoral dissertation (석사/박사 학위 논문) to a peer-reviewed journal article.

놀다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 놀다 (nōl-da, with a long/rising tone on the stem 놀-). Historically denoted frolicking, playing music or games, enjoying leisure, and being unoccupied or idle; the long vowel of the stem shortened in most environments outside the initial syllable in contemporary speech, though the ㄹ-stem alternation remains intact.

history.meaning: to frolic, play music, amuse oneself, or remain idle
to play, hang out, party, or be unemployed/off work

놀다.notes: For teenagers and adults, 놀다 usually translates as 'to hang out' or 'to party' rather than childish play, and can also mean 'to be unemployed or off duty' (요즘 놀고 있어).

rootFamily.gloss: to tease, mock, or let sit idle

놀라다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 놀라다 ('to be startled, surprised, frightened').

history.meaning: to be startled, amazed
to be surprised, startled

놀랍다.etymology: Native Korean derived adjective formed from the verb stem 놀라- (놀라다, 'to be startled, surprised', Middle Korean 놀라다) plus the adjective-deriving suffix -ㅂ다 (from Middle Korean -브-). As a regular ㅂ-irregular adjective, stem-final ㅂ vocalizes to ㅜ before vowel-initial endings, yielding polite 놀라워요, past 놀라웠어요, and adnominal 놀라운 ('amazing') and 놀라울 만큼 ('surprisingly').
놀랍다.notes: Often appears in 놀라울 정도로 or 놀라울 만큼 ('to a surprising degree, remarkably').

놀아주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the stem 놀- (놀다, 'to play, hang out', Middle Korean 놀다) joined by the infinitive connective suffix -아 (-a) to the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, do for someone', Middle Korean 주다 twu-da/cwu-da). Literally means 'to bestow the favor of playing or spending time with someone'.

history.meaning: to play + to give (analytic benefactive construction)
to play with someone (especially a child or pet) or keep someone company

놀아주다.notes: Because -아 주다 implies doing a favor for the other person, saying 놀아주다 to friends can playfully imply you are doing them the favor of gracing them with your company (or begging them to humor you).

rootFamily.gloss: to listen to or grant a request

놀이공원.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the native Korean deverbal noun 놀이 ('play, game, recreation', from 놀다 'to play' + nominalizing suffix -이, Middle Korean 노리 noli) with the Sino-Korean noun 공원 (公園, 'public park', from 公 'public, shared' + 園 'garden, park'). Coined in modern Korean to denote a commercial theme or amusement park.

history.meaning: recreation/pastime + public garden or park
amusement park, theme park

놀이공원.notes: A classic hybrid word (혼종어) pairing native Korean 놀이 with Sino-Korean 공원; often used interchangeably with the Sino-Korean 유원지 (遊園地, 'pleasure grounds') or loanword 테마파크 ('theme park').

놀이터.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of 놀이 ('play, game', from 놀- 'to play' + nominalizer -이, Middle Korean 노리 noli) and 터 ('site, ground, lot, foundation', from Middle Korean 터ㅎ theh, a ㅎ-final noun meaning 'ground, site'). Literally 'a ground or site for playing'.

history.meaning: play/recreation + site or piece of ground
children's playground or figurative arena for enjoyment

놀이터.notes: Besides a physical neighborhood playground with swings and slides, 놀이터 is frequently used figuratively for any space where enthusiasts or professionals freely enjoy themselves.

놈.etymology: Native Korean noun 놈 ('guy, fellow, jerk'), descending from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 놈 (nòm, low pitch). In Middle Korean, 놈 was the ordinary, socially neutral word for 'person, human being' (contrasting with 남 nàm 'other person'); during the Joseon dynasty it underwent semantic pejoration, narrowing first to 'lowborn male / servant' and then to a derogatory or rough colloquial term for a male ('guy, bastard, jerk').

history.meaning: person, human being (neutral unmarked noun)
commoner or lowborn man; male servant
guy, fellow, rascal, jerk (familiar or derogatory)

놈.notes: While vulgar or insulting when aimed at strangers or superiors, 놈 is also used affectionately by older generations toward young boys or children (e.g., 이놈 'this little rascal') and casually applied to objects or animals.

놈이.etymology: Inflected nominative form composed of the native Korean noun 놈 ('guy, fellow, jerk', from Middle Korean 놈 nòm 'person, human being', which underwent pejoration to 'lowly male, rascal') followed by the native Korean nominative case particle -이 (-i, Middle Korean -이), marking the noun as the grammatical subject of a clause.

history.meaning: a person [subject] (phonemic spelling of 놈 + -이)
the guy / that jerk [subject] (morphophonemic spelling)

놈이.notes: Commonly appears after demonstrative or adjectival modifiers in emotional speech, such as 이 놈이 ('this guy/jerk!') or 어떤 놈이 ('which bastard/guy?').

농구하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean compound noun 농구 (籠球, 'basketball', literally 'basket-ball' from 籠 'bamboo basket, cage' + 球 'ball, sphere', coined in early twentieth-century East Asia as a calque of English basketball) plus the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do, play').

history.meaning: basket-ball (calque of English basketball)
to play basketball

농구하다.notes: Korean sports vocabulary systematically pairs 구 (球, 'ball') with descriptive Hanja: 농구 (籠球, basketball), 야구 (野球, baseball), 축구 (足球, soccer), 배구 (排球, volleyball), and 탁구 (卓球, table tennis).

농담.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 농담 (弄談), composed of 농 (弄, 'to play with, toy with, jest, mock') and 담 (談, 'talk, speech, conversation, chat'). Literally meaning 'playful or teasing speech', it has long been the standard Korean term for a verbal joke, jest, or playful banter.

history.meaning: playful or teasing talk, jesting conversation
joke, jest, kidding remark

농담.notes: Often shortened to 농 in casual expressions like 농담 반 진담 반 ('half joking, half serious', matching 진담 眞談 'serious talk').

높다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 높다 ('to be high, tall, elevated').

history.meaning: to be high, lofty
to be high, tall

높이.etymology: Formed in Middle Korean as 노피 (nwophi) by adding the productive deadjectival suffix -이 (-i) to the adjective stem 높- (nwoph-, 'high, lofty'). Remarkably, the identical morphological derivation produced both the adverb 높이 ('high up, aloft') and the noun 높이 ('height, altitude'), which were distinguished in 15th-century Middle Korean by pitch-accent tone patterns before merging segmentally in Modern Korean. In contemporary speech it modifies verbs of rising, flying, hanging, or praising.

history.meaning: high up, aloft (adverb); height (noun)
high, high up; height, elevation

높이.notes: Pronounced [노피] via regular liaison of the aspirated stop ㅍ before the vowel-initial suffix -이.

놓다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 노타 (놓다, 'to put down, set, release, let go').

history.meaning: to put, place, release
to put, place, let go; auxiliary (-어 놓다) 'do and keep in state'

놓이다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 노히다, formed from 놓다 ('to place, release') + passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be placed, be released
to be placed, lie on; to feel relieved (마음이 놓이다)

놓치다.etymology: Native Korean verb derived from the verb stem 놓- (놓다, 'to let go, release, put down', Middle Korean 놓다 noh-ta) combined with the intensive/derivational verbal suffix -치- (-chi-, which adds force, completeness, or inadvertence to an action). Literally 'to let slip completely out of one's grasp', extending to missing a vehicle, opportunity, or detail.

history.meaning: to let go, release + intensive suffix
to let slip, miss (a train, chance, or clue), fail to catch

놓치다.notes: Used equally for physical objects slipping from your hand, missing public transit (버스를 놓치다), missing a broadcast or cue, and letting a golden opportunity pass by (기회를 놓치다).

rootFamily.gloss: to leave as is, leave alone
to let slip out of one's grip

놔두다.etymology: Contracted native Korean compound verb from 놓아두다 (noh-a-twu-da), formed from 놓- (놓다, 'to put down, release', Middle Korean 놓다 noh-ta) + infinitive connective -아 (-a, which fuses with 놓- to form 놔- nwa- after deletion of intervocalic ㅎ) + auxiliary/main verb 두다 ('to place, keep, leave in a state', Middle Korean 두다 twu-ta).

history.meaning: to put down and keep in place
to leave behind, leave untouched, or let someone be

morphemes.meaning: place, keep, leave in a state

놔두다.notes: In colloquial speech, the contracted form 놔두다 (e.g., 그냥 놔둬! 'Just leave it alone!') is far more common than the uncontracted literary form 놓아두다.

rootFamily.gloss: to place, keep, leave for later

누가.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite subject pronoun formed from the older root 누 ('who', Middle Korean 누) + nominative particle 가.

history.meaning: who (subject)
who; someone (as subject)

누구.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite pronoun descending from Middle Korean 누고, formed from pronoun root 누 ('who') + interrogative ending -고.

history.meaning: who
who; someone, anyone

누구누구.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated pronoun formed by doubling 누구 ('who'), which itself arose from the fifteenth-century Middle Korean interrogative pronoun 누 (nwu, 'who') fused with the interrogative/focus postposition -구 (-kwu, variant of -고). Full reduplication (누구누구) expresses distributive plurality ('who all', 'which specific people') or indefinite enumeration ('so-and-so and so-and-so').

history.meaning: who (fusion of interrogative root and interrogative particle)
who all (interrogative plural) or so-and-so (indefinite placeholder)

누구누구.notes: When asking a question (오늘 누구누구 와? 'Who all is coming today?'), it asks for a list of names; in declarative sentences, it acts as a placeholder ('so-and-so') to avoid naming someone directly.

누군가.etymology: Native Korean indefinite pronoun contracted from 누구인가 (누구 'who' + copula -이- + interrogative/indefinite ending -ㄴ가).

history.meaning: someone, somebody

누나.etymology: Native Korean sex-relative kinship noun 누나 ('older sister of a male'), descending from the Middle Korean kinship root 누의 (nwuuy, 'sister of a male') through hypocoristic/vocative nasal suffixation (*nwuuy-na > 누나) in Early Modern Korean. Parallels the polite form 누님 (nwunim) and the general literary form 누이 (nwui, 'sister').

history.meaning: sister of a male (older or younger)
older sister of a male; close older female friend or partner of a male

누나.notes: Used exclusively by males to address or refer to an older blood sister, older female cousin, or close older female friend/romantic partner; females use 언니 instead.

누려보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the stem 누리- (누리다, 'to enjoy, be blessed with', from Middle Korean 누리다 nwulita 'to enjoy a long or prosperous life, rule/possess across generations', related to 누리 'world, age') connected via the infinitive suffix -어 (-eo, contracting to 누려-) to the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing'). Literally 'to try enjoying or experiencing (a privilege, luxury, or right)'.

history.meaning: to enjoy prosperity or longevity + to see/try
to try enjoying or get a taste of (luxury, freedom, or privilege)

morphemes.meaning: enjoy, possess blessings or rights (누리- + -어 > 누려-)

누려보다.notes: 누리다 takes abstract or elevated objects like 호사 ('luxury'), 특권 ('privilege'), 자유 ('freedom'), or 행복 ('happiness'), so 누려보다 means 'to get a taste of enjoying' such privileges.

누르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 누르다 ('to press down, push, suppress').

history.meaning: to press down, hold down
to press (a button or key), push down

눈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from two Middle Korean words distinguished by pitch/vowel length: 눈 ('eye; bud, sprout') and 눈ː ('snow').

history.meaning: eye, bud / snow
eye; snow

눈금.etymology: Native Korean compound joining 눈 ('eye; small inlaid calibration dot on a traditional balance beam', preserved in 저울눈) with 금 ('line, score, mark', nominalized from 긋다 'to draw a line' with -ㅁ). Combining the older 'scale-eye' sense with 'line', 눈금 denotes the evenly spaced measurement ticks on rulers, measuring jugs, scales, thermometers, and compass dials. Pronounced [눈끔] with tensification.
눈금.notes: Collocates with 눈금을 읽다 ('read the scale') and 눈금에 맞추다 ('align to the mark').

눈금자.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 눈금 (눈 'notch, mark' + 금 'line', 'scale division') and 자 (Middle Korean 자ㅎ, 'measuring stick, ruler').

history.meaning: graduated ruler, scale ruler

눈높이.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 눈 ('eye') with 높이 ('height, elevation', derived from the adjective 높다 'to be high' plus the nominalizing suffix -이). Used literally in architecture, galleries, and kitchens for positioning objects right at horizontal line of sight (눈높이에 맞추다), it also developed a widespread figurative sense of meeting children, learners, or guests at their own viewpoint.
눈높이.notes: Very common in 눈높이에 맞추다 ('adjust to eye level / tailor to someone's perspective').

눈물.etymology: Native Korean transparent compound noun 눈물 ('tears, teardrop'), attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 눈믈 (nwun-mul), compounded from 눈 ('eye', Middle Korean 눈 nwun) and 물 ('water', Middle Korean 믈 mul, whose vowel rounded from ㅡ *u* to ㅜ *wu* after the bilabial nasal ㅁ *m* in Early Modern Korean). Literally 'eye-water'.

history.meaning: eye-water, tears
tears, weeping, sympathy

눈물.notes: Part of a productive native Korean body-fluid compounding pattern with 물 ('water'): 눈물 ('eye-water' = tears), 콧물 ('nose-water' = snot), and 침/군침 (saliva).

rootFamily.gloss: tearfully, with tears in one's eyes
