In Classical Chinese (Middle Chinese dwojH top), 對答 denoted answering an interlocutor or sovereign face-to-face; in Korean it became the everyday core word for any spoken reply to a question or call.

history.meaning: to respond face-to-face to a question or address
spoken answer, reply, or response to a call or question

대답.notes: Used primarily for a spoken or interpersonal response to someone calling or asking a question (대답을 하다), whereas 답 or 정답 is preferred for the solution to a test problem, and 답변 for a formal or official reply.

대답하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 대답 (對答, 'answer, reply') and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean base combines 對 (대, 'to face, respond to') and 答 (답, 'to answer, reply'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 대답ᄒᆞ다 (對答ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: to face an interlocutor or superior and reply
to answer, to reply to a question or call
to answer, to reply, to respond

대답하다.notes: Primarily used for spoken, immediate responses to a call or question, whereas 답변하다 (答辯하다) sounds more formal and official, and 응답하다 (應答하다) emphasizes responding to a signal or appeal.

rootFamily.gloss: formal answer, written or official response
response, reply to a call or signal

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대답하다

대들다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 대- (the infinitive stem of 대다, from Middle Korean 다히다 'to touch, bring into contact, set against') and 들다 ('to enter, rush in, charge forward'). It originally denoted physically rushing head-on against an opponent, later shifting to mean defying or talking back to an authority figure.

history.meaning: to bring into contact + to enter or rush in
to rush at an opponent, to charge head-on
to defy, to talk back, to stand up aggressively against someone

대들다.notes: Carries a strong connotation of insubordination or rebellion against someone older or higher in rank (such as a boss, senior PD, or parent).

rootFamily.gloss: to touch, put against, bring into contact
to lunge at, pounce on, defy

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대들다

대로.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) bound noun and postpositional particle grammaticalized from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄃᆡ로, which was formed from the bound noun ᄃᆡ ('place, way, circumstance', the ancestor of modern 데) plus the instrumental/directional particle -로 ('by way of, as'). Subsequent vowel changes and loss of arae-a (ㆍ) yielded modern 대로 ('in accordance with, just as').

history.meaning: by way of the place or circumstance; according to
in the manner of, just as, separately by category
just as, in accordance with, as soon as

morphemes.meaning: place, way, state (from Middle Korean ᄃᆡ, modern 데)
instrumental particle: by way of, according to

대로.notes: Notice the spacing rule: after a noun it attaches directly as a particle (마음대로 'as one pleases', 법대로 'according to the law'), but after a verb/adjective modifier it is written with a space as a bound noun (말한 대로 'just as said', 보는 대로 'as soon as one sees').

rootFamily.gloss: properly, in its right way (제 + 대로)
as one wishes, at will (마음 + 대로)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대로

대리석.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大理石, literally meaning 'stone of Dali (大理)'. It derives from the Dali region (大理) in Yunnan Province, China, which has been celebrated across East Asia since the Tang and Song dynasties for quarrying fine white and dark-veined metamorphic limestone (marble).

history.meaning: veined metamorphic stone quarried in Dali, Yunnan
Dali stone, decorative marble
marble (architectural and sculptural stone)

morphemes.meaning: great (first character of the toponym Dali 大理)
vein in jade, pattern, order (second character of Dali 大理)

대리석.notes: Do not confuse the 대리 (大理, the city of Dali in Yunnan) inside 대리석 with the homophonous Sino-Korean word 대리 (代理, 'proxy, substitute, or assistant manager').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대리석

대문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 대문 (大門), literally 'great gate', from 대 (大, 'big, main') + 문 (門, 'gate').
대문.notes: Refers to the main outer gate leading from the street into a house's courtyard.

대박.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound combining the Sino-Korean prefix 대- (大, 'great, huge') with native Korean 박 ('gourd'). It draws on the traditional Korean folktale Heungbu-jeon (흥부전), in which sawing open a giant gourd (박) yields a windfall of gold and treasure, popularized in the 1990s via the idiom 대박이 터지다 ('a giant gourd bursts open').

history.meaning: a gourd bursts open revealing treasure (from Heungbu-jeon folklore)
commercial jackpot, windfall, smash success
big hit, jackpot; exclamation meaning 'awesome!' or 'no way!'

morphemes.meaning: gourd (traditional folk symbol of sudden fortune)

대박.notes: Its direct opposite in Korean slang is 쪽박 ('small gourd dipper used by beggars', meaning a total flop or going broke, as in 대박 아니면 쪽박, 'boom or bust').

rootFamily.gloss: small gourd bowl; total flop or bankruptcy
to hit the jackpot, become a smash hit

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대박

대보다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) compound verb (also written analytically as 대 보다) formed from 대- (the contracted infinitive 대어 of 대다, from Middle Korean 다히다 'to touch, bring into contact, compare') and the auxiliary/main verb 보다 ('to see, to try doing'). It means either 'to try touching' (often in warnings like 손만 대 봐라 'just dare touch it!') or 'to compare by placing side by side'.

history.meaning: to cause to touch + to see or test
to try touching; to place together to check or compare
to try touching; to compare directly side by side

morphemes.meaning: to touch, place against (contracted from 대어)
to see, to try doing (auxiliary verb)

대보다.notes: In dramatic dialogue, 손(만) 대 봐! ('Just try laying a finger on it!') is a classic idiomatic threat using the -아/어 보다 'try doing (and see what happens)' construction.

rootFamily.gloss: to touch, put in contact, supply
to lay a hand on, touch, start meddling with

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대보다

대본.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 臺本, borrowed in the modern era via Japanese theatrical terminology 台本 (daihon, where 台 serves as the simplified/shinjitai form of 臺). It combines 臺 (대, 'stage, raised platform, stand') and 本 (본, 'book, text, foundation'), literally denoting the foundational text used for a stage or broadcast performance.

history.meaning: playbook or script for theatrical performance on stage
script for theater, radio, or film production
TV/drama/variety show script; pre-arranged scenario

대본.notes: In Korean TV broadcasting (like *The Producers*), 대본 is the general term used for both drama scripts and variety show cue/script books, whereas 각본 (脚本) refers more specifically to a dramatic screenplay.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대본

대세.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大勢, composed of 大 (대, 'great, macro, overarching') and 勢 (세, 'force, momentum, trend, configuration of power'). In Classical Chinese historiography and strategy, it denoted the overarching momentum of events; in contemporary Korean media, it also refers to the hottest trend or most popular celebrity of the moment.

history.meaning: the overarching balance of power or inevitable tide of events
general state of affairs, prevailing social trend
mainstream trend; 'it' person or hottest rising star in pop culture

대세.notes: In K-pop and entertainment slang, calling a celebrity or group 대세 (or 대세 배우 / 대세 아이돌) means they are currently the undisputed hottest trend everyone is talking about.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대세

대신.etymology: Sino-Korean 대신 (代身), compounding 대 (代, 'replace, substitute') and 신 (身, 'body, person').

history.meaning: substituting for a person or thing
instead of, in place of, substitute

대안.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 代案, composed of 代 (대, 'to substitute, replace, act in place of') and 案 (안, 'desk, official document, plan, proposal'). Coined in modern East Asian legal and administrative discourse (alongside Japanese 代案 daian), it literally means a 'substitute proposal' or 'alternative plan'.

history.meaning: substitute bill or counterproposal in parliamentary/administrative procedure
alternative plan, counter-proposal
alternative, viable option or solution

대안.notes: Often used in the set phrase 대안이 없다 ('there is no alternative') or 대안을 제시하다 ('to present an alternative') when criticizing a plan without offering a backup solution.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대안

대장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 大將, combining 大 (클 대, 'great, supreme, chief') and 將 (장수 장, 'military commander, general'). Originally designating the top commanding general of an army in traditional Korean and East Asian ranks, 대장 passed warmly into everyday colloquial Korean—often with honorific -님 as 대장님—for the spirited leader of a crew, kitchen, neighborhood group, or adventure.
대장.notes: Frequently takes honorific -님 (대장님, 'Captain! / Boss!') in friendly banter. Note homographs 대장 (臺帳 'ledger') and 대장간 ('smithy').

대저택.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大邸宅, formed by prefixing 大 (대, 'great, grand, large-scale') to 邸宅 (저택, 'mansion, residence of a dignitary'). In Classical Chinese, 邸 (저) denoted the capital residence maintained for a feudal lord or high official, while 宅 (택) denoted a dwelling or estate.

history.meaning: official residence of a feudal lord or high dignitary
stately residence, noble mansion
grand mansion, sprawling luxury estate

대저택.notes: Whereas 주택 (住宅) is any ordinary residential house and 저택 (邸宅) is a mansion, 대저택 (大邸宅) specifically evokes a palatial estate with gardens and gates, typical of chaebol families in K-dramas.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대저택

대중.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大衆, composed of 大 (대, 'great, large') and 衆 (중, 'multitude, crowd of people'). Originally a Classical Chinese and Buddhist term translating Sanskrit mahāsaṅgha ('the great assembly of monks'), it was repurposed in modern East Asia to render the sociological concept of 'the general public' or 'the masses'.

history.meaning: a great multitude of people; the monastic assembly in Buddhism
the monastic community; a large crowd
the general public, the masses; popular (in compounds)

대중.notes: Functions as a key prefixal modifier in modern Korean for 'mass/popular/public': 대중문화 ('pop culture'), 대중교통 ('public transportation'), and 대중음악 ('popular music').

rootFamily.gloss: popular, appealing to the general public

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대중

대책.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 對策, composed of 對 (대, 'to face, respond to, counter') and 策 (책, 'bamboo slip, imperial examination question, stratagem, policy'). In Han-dynasty China, 對策 referred to a candidate's written policy essay responding to the emperor's political questions inscribed on bamboo slips (策); in modern Korean it means a countermeasure or strategy to handle a problem.

history.meaning: written policy response to imperial examination questions on bamboo slips
civil-service examination policy essay; political stratagem
countermeasure, response strategy, way of dealing with a crisis

대책.notes: The colloquial expression 대책 없다 ('to have no countermeasure') is widely used to describe a person or situation that is utterly hopeless, reckless, or impossible to handle.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대책

cognates.word: 代替 (だいたい / だいがえ)

대체.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) coordinate compound 代替, composed of two near-synonymous characters: 代 (대, 'to take the place of, substitute') and 替 (체, 'to change, replace, supersede'). Together they denote the act of substituting or replacing one thing or person with another.

history.meaning: to replace, to supersede one another
substitution, replacement of a role, item, or obligation
replacement, substitution (e.g., alternative energy or substitute holiday)

morphemes.meaning: to substitute, act in place of

대체.notes: Beware of the exact homophone 대체 (大體): as a noun/modifer (대체휴일 'substitute holiday', 대체 에너지 'alternative energy') it is 代替 ('replacement'), whereas as an emphatic adverb in questions (대체 왜 그래? 'Why on earth are you like that?', short for 도대체) it is 大體 ('in the main / on earth').

rootFamily.gloss: replacement, shift, change of players or parts

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대체

대출.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 貸出, composed of 貸 (대, 'to lend, loan at interest') and 出 (출, 'to put out, issue, go forth'). Standardized in modern East Asian banking and library administration (compare Japanese 貸出 kashidashi), it denotes issuing a financial loan or checking out books from a library.

history.meaning: to lend + to issue out
lending out bank funds or library materials
bank loan, credit loan; library book checkout

morphemes.meaning: to issue, send out, go out

대출.notes: Covers both taking out a bank mortgage/loan (은행 대출을 받다) and borrowing a book from a library (도서 대출), whereas borrowing money casually between friends uses native 빌리다.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대출

대충.etymology: An adverb evolved from Early Modern Sino-Korean 대총 (大總), composed of 大 (대, 'great, general, broad') and 總 (총, 'to gather, sum up, overall whole'). Originally a noun meaning 'the general outline or rough totality' (parallel to 대강 大綱 and 대략 大略), it underwent vowel raising of 오 to 우 in the second syllable (대총 > 대충) and shifted into an adverb meaning 'roughly, cursorily, or half-heartedly'.

history.meaning: the general whole, broad outline of a matter
in rough outline, approximately, without fine detail
roughly, cursorily, half-heartedly, loosely

morphemes.meaning: overall, sum, whole (from 總 총 via vowel raising)

대충.notes: While 대략 (大略) is neutral and objective ('approximately, roughly'), 대충 often carries a critical or casual nuance of cutting corners or doing something half-heartedly (e.g., 대충 해 'just do a quick/rough job of it').

rootFamily.gloss: roughly, in outline (from 大綱 'main cord of a net')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대충

cognates.meaning: pinch hitter; to stand in for someone

대타.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 代打, clipped from 대타자 (代打者, 'substitute batter') and borrowed from Japanese baseball terminology 代打 (daida). It combines 代 (대, 'to substitute, act in place of') and 打 (타, 'to strike, hit, bat'). From its literal baseball sense of a 'pinch hitter', it generalized in everyday Korean to mean any last-minute stand-in or substitute worker.

history.meaning: pinch hitter sent in to bat for another player in baseball
pinch hitter in Korean baseball
pinch hitter; last-minute replacement or stand-in (for a shift, broadcast, or blind date)

대타.notes: Extremely common in part-time jobs (알바 대타 'covering someone's part-time shift'), broadcasting (a guest or DJ filling in), and even blind dates (소개팅 대타).

rootFamily.gloss: base hit, safe hit; commercial hit

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대타

대표.etymology: Sino-Korean 대표 (代表), compounding 대 (代, 'act in place of, represent') and 표 (表, 'surface, display, model').

history.meaning: standing as the visible representative
representative, head, director

대표님.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean honorific title formed from Sino-Korean 대표 (代表, 'representative, head', often short for 대표이사 代表理事 'representative director / CEO') plus the native Korean honorific suffix -님 ('esteemed person', from Middle Korean 님 'lord, master'). 代表 combines 代 (대, 'to act on behalf of') and 表 (표, 'outer surface, manifest symbol, stand out').

history.meaning: representative (Sino-Japanese coinage) + native honorific suffix
esteemed representative director of a corporation
CEO, company head, entertainment agency boss (polite address/reference)

morphemes.meaning: to act on behalf of, represent
to manifest, display, stand as a symbol

대표님.notes: In Korean entertainment agencies, startups, and modern firms, 대표님 ('CEO') has largely replaced 사장님 (社長님, 'company president') as the preferred, sleeker title of address for the top boss.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대표

cognates.meaning: to face, to be toward, regarding
to face, toward, regarding, to treat

대하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the single Hanja root 대 (對, 'to face, confront, respond to, treat') and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 대ᄒᆞ다 (對ᄒᆞ다), it functions both as a main verb meaning 'to face or treat (someone)' and in grammaticalized postpositional phrases (-에 대해, -에 대한) meaning 'regarding, concerning'.

history.meaning: to stand opposite, to face, to answer or correspond to
to face, confront, stand opposite to
to treat a person; to face; (in -에 대해/대한) regarding, about

morphemes.meaning: to face, be opposite, treat, regard

대하다.notes: Most frequently encountered in its grammaticalized forms: N에 대해(서) (adverbial: 'about/regarding N', modifying a verb) and N에 대한 (adnominal: 'regarding/toward N', modifying a following noun).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대하다

대학.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大學, composed of 大 (대, 'great, higher, adult') and 學 (학, 'learning, study, school'). Originally the title of the Confucian classic Dàxué (大學, 'The Great Learning') and the name of the highest imperial academy in pre-modern China and Korea, it was repurposed in late 19th-century East Asia to translate the Western 'university' or 'college'.

history.meaning: The Great Learning (Confucian classic); highest imperial academy for adult scholars
modern Western-style university or college
university, college, higher education institution

대학.notes: In everyday speech, 대학 and 대학교 (大學校) are interchangeable for 'university/college', though strictly speaking a 대학교 ('university') comprises multiple constituent 단과대학 ('colleges', such as 법과대학 'College of Law').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대학

대학교.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 大學校, built from 大 (클 대, 'great, higher'), 學 (배울 학, 'learning, scholarship'), and 校 (학교 교, 'school, academy'). While 대학 (大學) traces back to the classical Confucian text Great Learning and Joseon's royal academy, modern Korean 대학교 denotes a degree-granting institution of higher education within the sequence 초등학교, 중학교, 고등학교, and 대학교.
대학교.notes: Often shortened to 대학 in compounds like 대학생 ('university student') and 대학원 ('graduate school').

cognates.word: 大型 (おおがた / たいけい)

대형.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 大型, composed of 大 (대, 'large, great, big') and 型 (형, 'earthen casting mold, model, type, size'). Literally meaning 'large model or size', it is used both for physical dimensions (such as large buses or appliances) and figuratively in media and commerce for 'large-scale, blockbuster, or major'.

history.meaning: clay mold for casting bronze; standard model or pattern
large-sized model or format
large-sized; large-scale, major, blockbuster (agency, project, or accident)

대형.notes: Forms a clean three-tier size system in Korean: 소형 (小型, 'small/compact'), 중형 (中型, 'medium/mid-sized'), and 대형 (大型, 'large/full-sized or major', as in 대형 기획사 'major entertainment agency').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 대형

대화.etymology: Sino-Korean 대화 (對話), compounding 대 (對, 'face each other') and 화 (話, 'speech, talk').

history.meaning: speaking face to face
conversation, dialogue

댁.etymology: A Sino-Korean (한자어) word written with the Hanja 宅 ('house, residence'), representing a historical phonological doublet of standard 택 (宅). The archaic reading 댁 preserves the unaspirated initial reflecting Middle Chinese voiced *ɖˠæk, specialized since Middle Korean (attested as 댁 宅) as an honorific noun for 'another person's esteemed home' and, by metonymy, a polite second-person pronoun ('you') among adults.

history.meaning: chosen dwelling place, residence, estate
noble residence, another person's esteemed home
residence, home (honorific of 집); polite 'you' between unfamiliar adults; wife's title by hometown

morphemes.meaning: esteemed residence, home; honorific second-person pronoun (doublet of 택 宅)

댁.notes: One of the most important honorific nouns in Korean: your own home is 집, while a respected interlocutor's home is 댁; similarly, in dramatic banter between strangers, 댁이 뭔데? means 'Who do you think you are?' (using 댁 as a stiff/distant 'you').

rootFamily.gloss: husband's family home (honorific, 시 媤 + 댁 宅)
one's own residence (formal, using the standard reading 택)
residential house, housing (using the standard reading 택)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 댁

더.etymology: Native Korean comparative degree adverb descending from Middle Korean 더 ('more, further').

history.meaning: more, further
more, further

더더욱.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) emphatic adverb formed by reduplicating the comparative adverb 더 ('more') onto 더욱 ('even more, all the more', which itself derives from Middle Korean 더옥 = 더 + intensifying suffix -옥). The double layering of 더 (더 + 더 + -욱) creates a strong emphatic sense of 'all the more so, still more'.

history.meaning: even more, still more
even more, all the more
all the more so, much more, especially so

더더욱.notes: Often paired with conditional or causal clauses (그럴수록 더더욱 'the more that is the case, all the more so...') to emphasize that a reason makes something doubly true or necessary.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더더욱

더듬다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) verb attested in Early Modern Korean as 더듬다, closely linked to the mimetic/ideophonic root 더듬더듬 ('gropingly, hesitantly, falteringly'). Its core image of feeling around repeatedly and uncertainly in the dark unified three senses: physical groping with the hands, stammering in speech (말을 더듬다), and mentally retracing faint memories (기억을 더듬다).

history.meaning: to feel about with the hands, to grope or falter
to grope for; to stammer; to retrace memories or footsteps

morphemes.meaning: to grope, feel about, falter, trace back

더듬다.notes: Learn its three classic collocations together: 벽을 더듬다 ('to grope along a wall'), 말을 더듬다 ('to stutter/stammer'), and 기억을 더듬다 ('to trace back/search one's memory').

rootFamily.gloss: to keep stammering or groping hesitantly

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더듬다

더럽다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) adjective attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 더럽다, with the prevocalic stem 더러ㅸ- (e.g., 더러ㅸᅥ 'being dirty'). The Middle Korean voiced bilabial fricative ㅸ (/β/) regularly lenited to /w/ before vowels in Early Modern Korean, explaining why modern 더럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective (더러워, 더러운).

history.meaning: impure, defiled, filthy, base
dirty, filthy, ignoble, foul
dirty, filthy; gross, disgusting; unfair or stingy (of temper/luck)

morphemes.meaning: dirty, filthy, gross (ㅂ-irregular stem < Middle Korean 더러ㅸ-)

더럽다.notes: In casual speech, the first vowel is often raised to 드럽다 ('super gross/nasty'), and its adverbial form 더럽게 (or 드럽게) is used as a slang intensifier meaning 'awfully, ridiculously' (e.g., 더럽게 비싸다 'ridiculously expensive').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더럽다

더부룩하다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the dark-vowel ideophonic/mimetic root 더부룩- ('thickly clustered, shaggy, uncomfortably stuffed or bloated', the vowel-harmonic counterpart to light-vowel 다보록-) and the adjectivalizer -하다. From describing grass or hair growing in thick, heavy tufts, it extended to the sensation of a stomach feeling heavy, gassy, and bloated from indigestion.

history.meaning: thickly overgrown, tufted, piled up heavily
bushy and unkempt (of hair/weeds); bloated and heavy (of the stomach)

morphemes.meaning: thickly clustered, shaggy; uncomfortably stuffed or bloated
to be in the state of (native adjectivalizer)

더부룩하다.notes: The go-to Korean expression for post-meal indigestion or bloating is 속이 더부룩하다 ('my stomach feels bloated and heavy').

rootFamily.gloss: nicely thick, lush, plentifully piled (light-vowel harmonic counterpart)
bushy, shaggy, unkempt (of hair or beard)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더부룩하다

더블.etymology: A 20th-century loanword (외래어) borrowed from English double, which came via Old French doble from Latin duplus ('twofold, twice as much', compounded from PIE *dwo- 'two' and *-plo- 'fold'). In Korean, it is widely used in broadcasting, fashion, and hospitality for double casting, double-breasted suits, double rooms, or double portions.

history.meaning: twofold, twice as large
twice as much in size, amount, or number; a pair or stand-in
double (portion, room, casting, or overlapping schedule)

더블.notes: Frequently appears in Konglish/media compounds like 더블캐스팅 ('double casting', two actors alternating one role) or with instrumental -로 (더블로 주다 'to give a double portion / twice as much').

rootFamily.gloss: double casting (two actors sharing one role)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더블

더욱.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 더옥 ('still more, even more'), formed from the comparative adverb 더 ('more') and the intensifying adverbial suffix -옥. Regular Early Modern Korean vowel raising of non-initial 오 to 우 transformed 더옥 into modern 더욱.

history.meaning: still more, even more, increasingly
even more, all the more
even more, all the more (slightly more formal/emphatic than 더)

더욱.notes: Compared to plain 더 ('more'), 더욱 sounds more emphatic and literary ('even more, all the more'), and adding -이 creates the sentence connector 더욱이 ('moreover, furthermore').

rootFamily.gloss: all the more, much more (emphatic reduplication)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 더욱

더하다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adjective formed from comparative adverb 더 ('more') + -하다 (replacing Middle Korean 더으다).

history.meaning: to add, increase
to add, increase; to grow more intense

덕분.etymology: Sino-Korean 덕분 (德分), compounding 덕 (德, 'virtue, kindness, favor') and 분 (分, 'allotted share, portion').

history.meaning: share of grace or favor received
thanks to, owing to (positive cause, especially in 덕분에)

던지다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) transitive verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as Seokbo Sangjeol and Worin Seokbo) as 던디다 ('to throw, cast, fling'). During the 17th and 18th centuries, regular Korean palatalization shifted dental 디 (di) before /i/ into postalveolar 지 (ji), yielding modern 던지다. Beyond physical throwing, it metaphorically denotes tossing out a question, remark, glance, or vote.

history.meaning: to throw, cast, hurl physically
to throw, fling (after 17th–18th c. palatalization 디 > 지)
to throw, pitch; to toss out (a question, joke, remark, or vote)

morphemes.meaning: to throw, cast, hurl (from Middle Korean 던디-)

던지다.notes: Very productive in figurative collocations where English uses 'ask', 'make', or 'cast': 질문을 던지다 ('to pose/toss out a question'), 농담을 던지다 ('to crack a joke'), and 표를 던지다 ('to cast a vote').

rootFamily.gloss: to fling away, throw down, abandon one's job or task
to toss or throw something to someone

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 던지다

덜.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) adverb meaning 'less, incompletely, not yet fully', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 덜 alongside the transitive verb 덜다 ('to subtract, lessen, take away from'). Like its antonym 더 ('more', alongside 더하다), 덜 originated as a bare verbal root used adverbially via zero-derivation to indicate a state falling short of completion.

history.meaning: less, short of a full amount; to deduct or lessen
less; not fully, incompletely, not yet

morphemes.meaning: less, incompletely (bare adverbial root of 덜다 'to lessen, deduct')

덜.notes: Before process verbs, 덜 often translates naturally into English as 'under-' or 'not fully yet': 덜 익다 ('to be undercooked or unripe'), 덜 마르다 ('to be not fully dry yet'), and 덜 자다 ('to not have gotten enough sleep').

rootFamily.gloss: to deduct, lessen, take off a portion, ease a burden
to be half-baked, incomplete, or immature as a person

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 덜

덜거덕거리다.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic verb formed from root 덜거덕 ('rattling or clattering sound of loose hard objects') + iterative suffix -거리다.

history.meaning: to rattle, clatter repeatedly

덥다.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) adjective attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 덥다, with the prevocalic stem 더ㅸ- (as in 더ㅸㅓ 'being hot' and the derived noun 더ㅸㅣ > 더위 'heat'). The loss of the Middle Korean voiced bilabial fricative ㅸ (/β/ > /w/) before vowels produced the modern ㅂ-irregular conjugation (덥다, 더워, 더운). It specifically denotes ambient atmospheric heat or how warm/hot a living body feels.

history.meaning: warm or hot (of weather, air, or bodily sensation)
hot, warm (after lenition of ㅸ > w)
hot, warm (specifically of weather, room temperature, or personal sensation)

morphemes.meaning: hot of weather or bodily sensation (ㅂ-irregular stem < Middle Korean 더ㅸ-)

덥다.notes: Crucial distinction for learners: 덥다 is only for weather, room temperature, or how your body feels ('I am hot' = 나 더워), whereas 뜨겁다 is for objects, food, or surfaces that are hot to the touch (뜨거운 커피 'hot coffee').

rootFamily.gloss: heat, hot weather (from Middle Korean 더ㅸㅣ)
to warm up, heat up food or liquid (historical causative of 덥다)
muggy, sultry, humid and hot (물 'water' + 덥다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 덥다

덧나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the prefix 덧- (deot-, 'in addition, on top of, repeatedly', from Middle Korean 덛- deot-) and the verb 나다 (nada, 'to arise, break out, sprout', from Middle Korean 나다 nada). Originally describing a secondary growth or outbreak occurring on top of an existing condition, it specialized to refer to a wound, sore, or illness becoming aggravated or infected again, and figuratively to an old grievance or problem flaring up worse.

history.meaning: to grow on top of; to break out again
to become aggravated (of a wound or illness); to flare up worse

덧나다.notes: Assimilates phonetically to [던나다] (deonnada) in standard pronunciation; used both medically for infected wounds and figuratively when meddling makes a situation worse.

rootFamily.gloss: to put on top of, add to, aggravate
snaggletooth, double tooth growing over another

덧문.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native prefix 덧- ('added over, outer layer') with Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door').

history.meaning: outer shutter door, storm door

덧문.notes: Pronounced [던문] by nasal assimilation of ㅅ [ㄷ] before ㅁ.

덧붙이다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining the derivational prefix 덧- ('additionally, on top of what is already there', historically from 더 'more' + sai-siot, seen in 덧신 'overshoes' and 덧칠 'extra coat of paint') with 붙이다 ('to attach, stick', causative of 붙다). Used concretely for affixing a reinforcing layer or patch, and very widely in speech and writing for appending a postscript, tip, or follow-up remark (말을 덧붙이다).
덧붙이다.notes: Very common in conversation as 한마디 덧붙이다 ('add a word') or 설명을 덧붙이다 ('add an explanation').

덧창.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native prefix 덧- ('added over, secondary') with Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window').

history.meaning: window shutter, storm window

덩굴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 덩굴 ('creeping or climbing plant stem, vine').

history.meaning: vine, creeper
vine, creeper, tendril

덩이.etymology: Native Korean noun and classifier 덩이 ('lump, clod, rounded mass'), attested in Early Modern Korean and expanded in everyday speech as 덩어리. When preceded by a native Korean numeral (such as 한 덩이, 두 덩이, 여덟 덩이), it acts as the natural measure word for whole round loaves of country bread, balls of kneaded dough, or blocks of tofu.
덩이.notes: Used with native Korean numerals (한 덩이, 두 덩이, 여덟 덩이).

덩치.etymology: Native Korean noun sharing the bound root 덩- (deong-, 'lump, mass, bulk', also seen in 덩어리 deong-eori and 덩이 deong-i, from Middle Korean 덩이 deong-i 'clod, lump') combined with the nominalizing suffix -치 (-chi, denoting a mass, figure, or entity). It originally denoted the physical bulk or volume of a mass and came to refer specifically to the overall frame, stature, or bodily build of a person or animal.

history.meaning: lump, clod, solid mass
physical bulk, bodily frame, build, or stature

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix indicating mass or figure

덩치.notes: Commonly collocated in phrases like 덩치가 크다 ('to have a large build') or the idiom 덩치 값을 못 하다 ('to not act one's size', i.e., to be timid despite a big frame).

덮개.etymology: Native Korean derived noun built from the verb stem 덮- (덮다, 'to cover, close over', Middle Korean 덥다) plus the productive native nominalizer -개 for household tools and parts (compare 깔개 'mat', 마개 'stopper', 지우개 'eraser'). Whereas 뚜껑 typically names a removable rigid lid on a pot or jar, 덮개 broadly covers hinged watch or compass covers, fabric flaps, keyboard covers, and protective casings.
덮개.notes: Pronounced [덥깨] with coda neutralization of ㅍ > ㅂ and tensification of ㄱ.

덮다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 덥다 / 덮다 ('to cover over, put a lid on, close').

history.meaning: to cover
to cover, close (a book or lid)

데.etymology: Native Korean bound noun descending from Middle Korean 대 ('place, spot, point, case').

history.meaning: place, spot, circumstance
place, spot, aspect (bound noun)

데려가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 데려- (from 데리다, Middle Korean 다리다, 'to have someone accompany one') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to take a person along
to take (someone) along

데려다.etymology: Native Korean contracted connective form of 데려다가 (deoryeodaga), itself derived from the verb stem 데리- (deori-, 'to accompany, bring along a person or animal', from Middle Korean 다리다 darida) plus the infinitive suffix -어 (-eo) and the transferential suffix -다가 (-daga, shortened to -다 -da, indicating an action performed and transitioned into another action at a destination). It expresses bringing someone to a place in order to do something next.

history.meaning: to accompany or lead a person along
bringing someone along and then (at the destination)
bringing someone in/along and; taking someone to

morphemes.meaning: to bring or take along (an animate being)
infinitive connective suffix (contracted with stem to 데려-)
shortened transferential suffix (-다가) indicating sequential action

데려다.notes: Frequently used either before another action verb (e.g., 데려다 쓰다 'bring someone in and use/hire them') or fused with 주다 as 데려다주다 ('to escort/drop someone off').

rootFamily.gloss: to bring someone along (toward the speaker)
to take someone along (away from the speaker)

데려다주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 데려다- (데리다 'to accompany' + transfer suffix -어다) + 주다 ('to give / do for someone').

history.meaning: to escort, walk or drive someone to a destination

데려오다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 데려- (from 데리다, 'to have someone accompany one') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to bring a person along
to bring (someone) here, fetch (a person)

데리다.etymology: Native Korean verb inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 다리다 (darida, 'to take or lead someone with oneself'), which underwent umlaut (regressive vowel assimilation triggered by the high front vowel /i/ in the second syllable) during the Early Modern Korean period to become 데리다 (deorida). It denotes causing an animate being (a person or animal of equal or lower status) to accompany oneself.

history.meaning: to have someone accompany one; to lead along
to bring or take along (a person or animal)

morphemes.meaning: to accompany, lead along (an animate being)

데리다.notes: In modern Korean, 데리다 never occurs as a bare finite predicate (*데린다 is ungrammatical); it is always used in connective or compound forms like 데리고, 데려오다, or 데려가다, and contrasts with the honorific 모시다 (used for elders/superiors) and 가지고 (used for inanimate objects).

rootFamily.gloss: to escort or drop someone off

cognates.meaning: first stroke in a game; first appearance on stage or in society
a person's first appearance or performance in a role

데뷔.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from French début ('first stroke at billiards or bowls; first appearance on the stage or in public'), derived by back-formation from the verb débuter ('to make the first stroke, play first'), itself composed of dé- (from Latin dis-) + but ('goal, mark, target', of Frankish origin). Its Korean orthography 데뷔 (debwi) directly reflects the French front rounded vowel /y/ in [de.by].

history.meaning: to play first at the mark; first stroke in a game, then first stage appearance
first public appearance of an entertainer, artist, or athlete

데뷔.notes: Unlike English speakers who often pronounce 'debut' as /deɪˈbjuː/, Korean preserves an approximation of the French pronunciation /de.by/ as 데뷔 [debwi] (often pronounced [debi] in casual speech).

rootFamily.gloss: debut stage or first broadcast performance

cognates.meaning: to play first; to make one's first appearance

데뷔하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword-native verb compound formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hada) to the French-derived loanword 데뷔 (debwi, from French début 'first public appearance', from débuter 'to play first toward the target'). It functions as an intransitive verb meaning to make one's official first appearance in the entertainment, literary, or sports world.

history.meaning: to make the first stroke; first appearance on stage
to make one's debut in entertainment, arts, or sports

morphemes.meaning: debut, first public appearance (from French début)

데뷔하다.notes: Central to Korean broadcasting and K-pop industry terminology, where trainees (연습생) work toward the milestone of 데뷔하다 on a music program or drama.

데서.etymology: Native Korean fused grammatical form combining the bound (dependent) noun 데 (de, 'place, spot, case, circumstance', inherited from Middle Korean ᄃᆡ doy 'place', originally grammaticalized from the locative noun 딯 dih) with the locative-ablative case particle 에서 (eseo, shortened to 서 seo after a vowel, meaning 'at, in, from'). In broadcasting and everyday speech, it follows an adnominal modifier (such as 그런 데서 or 다른 데서) to mean 'at such a place, outlet, or program'.

history.meaning: at or from a place or circumstance
at/from a place, institution, or media outlet (bound noun + particle)

데서.notes: Orthographically, when 데 functions as a bound noun meaning 'place' (requiring a space after the preceding modifier, e.g., 좋은 데서 'at a good place/outlet'), it is distinct from the clausal connective ending -데서 (contracted from -다고 해서 'because they say that...').

rootFamily.gloss: to a place, onto a spot (데 + 에다가)
whereas, while, in the circumstance that (-는 + 데)

데스크.etymology: Borrowed from English desk, used in Korean especially for a reception desk, front desk, or editorial desk.

history.meaning: table or counter for reception/office work
front desk, reception counter

데시벨.etymology: Borrowed from English decibel (from Latin deci- 'one-tenth' + bel, named after Alexander Graham Bell).

history.meaning: logarithmic unit of sound intensity
decibel (dB)

데워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 데우다 ('to warm up, heat liquids or food', causative of 데다) + -어지다.

history.meaning: to warm up, become heated

cognates.meaning: period of twenty-four hours; special commemorative day

데이.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English day, which descends from Old English dæg ('day, lifetime'), from Proto-Germanic *dagaz ('day'), and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- ('to burn, be hot', referring to the daylight hours when the sun burns). In Korean, unlike the everyday native word 날 (nal) or Sino-Korean 일 (日, il), 데이 is used specifically for named commercial, romantic, or commemorative occasions and event days.

history.meaning: daylight hours; period of twenty-four hours
twenty-four hour period; designated commemorative day
special event day or themed anniversary day

데이.notes: Korea has a vibrant culture of monthly 'Day' celebrations on the 14th of each month and beyond—such as 화이트데이 (White Day), 빼빼로데이 (Pepero Day), and 삼겹살데이 (Pork Belly Day)—making 데이 synonymous with a special themed occasion.

rootFamily.gloss: birthday (English loanword used in casual/event contexts)
D-Day, target date for an important event or broadcast

cognates.meaning: calendar date; romantic appointment or outing

데이트.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from American English date in its late 19th-century colloquial sense of 'a social or romantic appointment at a set time', which evolved from Middle English date ('point in time, calendar date'), borrowed via Old French date from Medieval Latin data, the feminine/neuter plural past participle of Latin dare ('to give, hand over'), originating in the Roman epistolary formula data Romae ('given [i.e. dispatched] at Rome on [such a day]').

history.meaning: given / handed over (used to mark the time and place a letter was dispatched)
specific calendar day; later (c. 1896 US slang) a romantic appointment
romantic outing or appointment between lovers or prospective partners

데이트.notes: Unlike English 'date', which means both a calendar date and a romantic outing, Korean 데이트 is restricted exclusively to romantic or social outings; calendar dates are expressed with 날짜 (naljja) or 일자 (日字, ilja).

rootFamily.gloss: to go on a romantic date
update (sharing the Latin root dare -> data -> date)

도.etymology: Represents the musical solfège loanword 도 (from Italian do, first note of the scale / C), Sino-Korean 도 (度 'degree of temperature/angle'; 道 'province, way'), and the native additive particle -도 ('also, too, even').

history.meaning: musical note C / degree / also, even
note C (do); degree (℃); also/too

도달하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb composed of the Sino-Korean noun 도달 (到達, dodal, 'reaching, attainment') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 (hada, 'to do'). The Sino-Korean root combines 도 (到, do, 'to arrive, reach, go to') and 달 (達, dal, 'to penetrate, reach through, attain, accomplish'), denoting the act of arriving at a physical destination or attaining a quantitative goal, standard, or conclusion.

history.meaning: to arrive at and reach through to a destination
to reach a destination; to attain a goal, level, or agreement

도달하다.notes: More formal and abstract than 도착하다 (到着하다, which is used for physical travel arrival); 도달하다 is preferred when reaching a target viewer rating, a philosophical conclusion, or a legal agreement.

rootFamily.gloss: arrival at a physical destination (到着)
to achieve, accomplish a goal (達成하다)
delivery, transmission, reaching the recipient (傳達)

도대체.etymology: Sino-Korean 도대체 (都大體), from 도 (都, 'all, wholly') + 대체 (大體, 'main body, gist'), used adverbially to intensify a question.

history.meaning: in the main, all in all
on earth, in the world, what/why ever

도려내버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb built from three verbal elements: 도리다 (dorida, 'to gouge, scoop, or cut out in a circle', attested in Early Modern Korean as 도리다), combined via its infinitive 도려- (doryeo-) with 내다 (naeda, 'to take out, extract', from Middle Korean 내다 naeda), and further compounded with the completive auxiliary verb 버리다 (beorida, originally 'to throw away, discard', from Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다 borida, grammaticalized to express complete, irreversible, or emphatic action). Together it means to ruthlessly gouge or carve something out completely.

history.meaning: to cut round + to extract + to cast away completely
to carve or gouge out completely and decisively

morphemes.meaning: to gouge out, carve out in a circle (도리다 + -어)
auxiliary verb indicating complete or irreversible action (버리다)

도려내버리다.notes: In television production (like in *The Producers*), this vivid physical verb ('gouge right out') is often used hyperbolically for ruthlessly editing or cutting someone's scenes completely out of a broadcast.

rootFamily.gloss: to gouge out, scoop out, excise
to carve or cut out in a circle
to throw away; (auxiliary) to do completely/regrettably

도마.etymology: Native Korean noun 도마 ('chopping block, cutting board'), attested in Middle Korean as 도마 (dòmà). Historically it denoted both a heavy wooden kitchen block for slicing vegetables and meat and a low wooden workbench. Because every traditional Korean kitchen relied on a seasoned wooden 도마 and kitchen knife (식칼), the word appears in numerous culinary expressions.
도마.notes: Also appears in the idiom 도마 위에 오르다 ('to come under public scrutiny', literally 'go onto the chopping board').

도망가다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb combining Sino-Korean 도망 (逃亡, 도 'flee' + 망 'run away, escape') with native 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to run away, flee, escape

도맡다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from the prefix 도- (都, do, 'all, entirely, altogether, in bulk', from Literary Chinese 都 dōu/dū 'capital city; to gather all together') attached to the native Korean verb 맡다 (matda, 'to take charge of, undertake, be entrusted with', from Middle Korean 맡다 matda). It literally means to undertake all of something in bulk, hence taking exclusive responsibility or monopolizing a role.

history.meaning: to receive in trust, take charge of
to take sole or full charge of; to undertake exclusively

morphemes.meaning: to take charge of, undertake, handle

도맡다.notes: Frequently used in the construction 도맡아 하다 ('to handle single-handedly / do all the work oneself'), especially when one person or team is burdened with every chore or role.

rootFamily.gloss: to take charge of, be responsible for
to entrust, leave in someone's care (causative)
wholesale selling in bulk (都賣, sharing the prefix 都-)

도매급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 도매 (都賣, domae, 'wholesale trade', composed of 都 do 'all together, in bulk' + 賣 mae 'to sell') and the suffix -급 (級, geup, 'class, grade, rank, level'). With an inserted genitive sai-siot sound in speech ([도매끕] domaekkeup, also standardized as 도매금 domaegum in dictionaries from 都賣金 'wholesale price'), it denotes being treated at a 'wholesale grade'—that is, having distinct individuals lumped together indiscriminately as a single batch.

history.meaning: selling in bulk (wholesale) + grade/price level

history.form: 도매급 / 도매금 (都賣級 / 都賣金)
history.meaning: wholesale level; being lumped together indiscriminately with others

도매급.notes: Almost always appears in the set idiomatic phrase 도매급으로 넘어가다 / 넘기다 ('to be lumped together and dismissed/blamed wholesale'), Note that while 도매금 (都賣金) is the prescriptive standard in South Korean dictionaries, 도매급 (都賣級) is overwhelmingly common in spoken and broadcast Korean.

도면.etymology: Sino-Korean 도면 (圖面), compounding 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, plan') and 면 (面, 'surface, sheet').

history.meaning: sheet with an architectural or engineering plan
blueprint, floor plan, technical drawing

도박.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 도박 (賭博, dobak), compounded from 도 (賭, do, 'to wager, bet, stake money or valuables', containing the semantic radical 貝 'cowrie shell, money' and phonetic 者) and 박 (博, bak, originally meaning 'broad, extensive' and also referring to an ancient Chinese board game, 六博 liùbó, played for stakes). Together they denote wagering money or valuables on games of chance, and figuratively any high-stakes, risky venture.

history.meaning: wagering valuables on games of chance or board games
gambling; a high-risk gamble or speculative venture

morphemes.meaning: ancient board game; to play for stakes, extensive (博)

도박.notes: Used both literally for illegal or casino gambling (도박장 'gambling den') and figuratively in media/business when a producer or executive takes a huge risk on an unproven cast or format (모험이나 도박 'an adventure or a gamble').

rootFamily.gloss: to gamble, take a high-stakes risk (賭博하다)

도서관.etymology: Sino-Korean 도서관 (圖書館), from 도서 (圖書, 도 'chart, map' + 서 'book', 'books and documents') + 관 (館, 'public building, hall').

history.meaning: hall for books and documents
library

도심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 都心, joining 都 (도읍 도, 'capital, metropolis') and 心 (마음 심, 'heart, core, centre'). Modeled on modern urban-planning terminology for the central business district ('heart of the city'), it contrasts the busy commercial core (도심) with quieter residential neighbourhoods and outskirts (외곽).
도심.notes: Often contrasted with 골목 ('quiet side lane') or 교외 ('suburbs').

도와달다.etymology: Native Korean compound auxiliary construction formed from 도와- (dowa-, the infinitive stem of the p-irregular verb 돕다 dopda, 'to help, assist', from Middle Korean 돕다 dopda with stem 도우-/도와-) and the defective quotative-request auxiliary verb 달다 (dalda, 'to give to me [the speaker/quoter]'), which occurs exclusively in indirect imperative quotations (such as 도와달라고 하다 'to ask someone to help me').

history.meaning: to help, aid, assist
to ask/beg (the addressee) to give help to the requester (in indirect quotation)

morphemes.meaning: to help, assist (p-irregular stem 돕- + -아 -> 도와-)
suppletive quotative verb meaning 'to give (to the speaker/subject)'
verbal citation ending (realized as -라 in quotative -달라고)

도와달다.notes: When quoting someone asking for help for themselves, Korean requires 도와달라고 하다 (using 달다) rather than 도와주라고 하다 (using 주다, which means 'help a third party').

도와드리다.etymology: Native Korean honorific compound verb composed of 도와- (dowa-, the infinitive form of 돕다 dopda, 'to help', from Middle Korean 돕다 dopda) and the humble/object-exalting auxiliary verb 드리다 (deurida, 'to offer, give to a superior or respected person', from Middle Korean 드리다 deurida, originally 'to cause to enter, present to the court or an elder'). It serves as the humble-polite equivalent of 도와주다 ('to help someone').

history.meaning: helping + to present/offer humbly to a superior
to humbly assist or do a favor of helping a respected person

morphemes.meaning: to help, assist (p-irregular stem 돕- + -아 -> 도와-)
humble benefactive auxiliary 'to offer/give to a respected recipient'

도와드리다.notes: Essential in workplace and customer-service registers (e.g., 무엇을 도와드릴까요? 'How may I assist you?'); it exalts the recipient of the help rather than the subject performing the action.

rootFamily.gloss: to humbly speak/tell to a superior (말씀 + 드리다)

도와주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 도와- (infinitive of ㅂ-irregular 돕다, 'to help') and benefactive auxiliary 주다 ('to give, do for someone').

history.meaning: to help someone
to help, assist

cognates.meaning: moral, ethical (as opposed to strictly legal)

도의적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun 도의적 (道義的, do-uijeok), formed from the classical ethical compound 도의 (道義, do-ui, 'the Way and righteousness; moral duty') plus the adjectival/determiner suffix -적 (的, -jeok, 'pertaining to, -ic, -al'). The root combines 도 (道, do, 'path, way, cosmic or moral principle') and 의 (義, ui, 'righteousness, justice, duty'), referring to obligations grounded in conscience and human decency rather than enforceable law.

history.meaning: the proper Way and righteousness; moral principles of human conduct
moral, ethical (especially regarding non-legal responsibility)

도의적.notes: Most frequently used in public apologies, politics, and workplace disputes in the collocation 도의적 책임 (道義的 責任, 'moral responsibility'), contrasting with 법적 책임 ('legal liability').

도입부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 도입부 (導入部), combining 도입 (導入, 'leading in, introduction') with suffix -부 (部, 'part, section').
도입부.notes: Refers to the opening passage of a musical work, essay, or novel.

도자기.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 도자기 (陶磁器), uniting 도기 (陶器, 'earthenware/stoneware') and 자기 (磁器, 'porcelain') under 기 (器, 'vessel, ware').
도자기.notes: Covers everything from rustic stoneware teacups to glazed porcelain electrical insulators.

도장.etymology: Sino-Korean 도장 (圖章), compounding 도 (圖, 'emblem, seal') and 장 (章, 'stamp, badge'); also homophonous with 도장 (塗裝, 'paint/varnish coating').

history.meaning: engraved name seal or stamp
personal seal, stamp; coating/finishing (塗裝)

도주로.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 도주로 (逃走路, dojuro), formed from 도주 (逃走, doju, 'flight, escape, running away') and the suffix/root 로 (路, ro, 'road, path, route'). The base 도주 combines 도 (逃, do, 'to flee, escape, evade') and 주 (走, ju, 'to run, dash'), so 도주로 literally denotes a 'fleeing-and-running road'—an escape route or getaway path.

history.meaning: to flee and run away + road or path
escape route, getaway path, line of retreat

도주로.notes: Common in police/crime dramas (e.g., 도주로를 차단하다 'to block off the escape route') and used humorously in everyday or variety-show contexts when someone looks for a way to slip out of an awkward meeting or room.

rootFamily.gloss: flight path, course, career path (進路)

도착.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 도착 (到着, dochak), composed of 도 (到, do, 'to arrive, reach, go to a place') and 착 (着, chak, 'to attach, touch, land, settle upon', variant of 著). Literally meaning 'to reach and touch down at a destination', it is the standard noun for the physical arrival of a person, vehicle, or parcel. (A homophonous Sino-Korean word 도착 倒錯 means psychological 'perversion/inversion', from 倒 'upside down' + 錯 'mixed up'.)

history.meaning: to reach and touch/settle at a place
arrival at a destination (of people, transport, or deliveries)

도착.notes: Pairs with 출발 (出發, chulbal 'departure') on schedules and transport boards; combines with 하다 as 도착하다 ('to arrive') and takes the locative particle 에 (e.g., 방송국에 도착하다 'to arrive at the broadcasting station').

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive at a destination (到着하다)
to reach, attain a goal or level (到達하다)

도착하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 도착 (到着, 도 'reach, arrive' + 착 'touch, land at') + native light verb -하다.

history.meaning: reaching a destination
to arrive

도출되다.etymology: Sino-Korean passive verb composed of the Sino-Korean noun 도출 (導出, dochul, 'derivation, drawing out, deduction') and the native Korean passive/inchoative verbalizer 되다 (doeda, 'to become, be done', from Middle Korean 되다 doyda). The Sino-Korean stem combines 도 (導, do, 'to lead, guide, conduct', composed of 道 'way' + 寸 'hand/inch') and 출 (出, chul, 'to come out, emerge'), literally meaning 'to be led or drawn out'.

history.meaning: leading/drawing out + to become (passive verbalizer)
to be derived, deduced, or drawn out (of a result, conclusion, or consensus)

도출되다.notes: A formal analytical verb frequently used in meetings, academic writing, and planning sessions with nouns like 결론 ('conclusion'), 결과 ('result'), or 합의 ('agreement')—e.g., 결론이 도출되다 ('a conclusion is reached/derived').

rootFamily.gloss: to derive, draw out, deduce (導出하다, active counterpart)
to induce, guide, lead to (誘導하다)

독.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun 독 (毒, dok, 'poison, venom, toxin, malice'), borrowed from Middle Chinese *dowk (毒), which originally depicted a noxious plant growing thickly (related to 艸 'grass' + 毋 'do not / harmful'). Beyond literal biological venom or chemical poison, it developed strong figurative senses in Korean of emotional bitterness, spite, or fierce, relentless grit. (A homophonous native Korean noun 독 dok means 'large earthenware jar/crock'.)

history.meaning: noxious herb, poison, venom; harmful, virulent
poison, venom, toxin; figurative spite or fierce resolve

독.notes: Appears in vivid Korean idioms such as 독이 오르다 ('for venom to rise', meaning either a seasonal creature becoming potent or a person becoming fiercely determined and sharp after a setback) and 독을 품다 ('to harbor venom/grudge').

rootFamily.gloss: fierce grit, venomous aura, malice (毒氣)

cognates.meaning: poisonous gas; fierce or malicious aura

독기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 독기 (毒氣, dokgi, pronounced [독끼] dokkki), composed of 독 (毒, dok, 'poison, venom, virulence') and 기 (氣, gi, 'breath, vapor, vital energy, spirit, aura'). Originally referring in traditional medicine and cosmology to noxious or pestilential vapors, it shifted metaphorically in everyday Korean to denote a fierce, venomous glint in one's eyes, ruthless determination, or biting spite.

history.meaning: poisonous vapor, noxious miasma, venomous breath
poisonous aura; fierce grit, venomous determination, or spite

독기.notes: In modern Korean drama and competitive contexts, 독기 is not always negative: 독기를 품다 ('to harbor fierce grit') or 눈에 독기가 서리다 ('to have a fierce glint in one's eyes') often describes an underdog's relentless drive to succeed.

독박.etymology: Hybrid Korean noun combining the Sino-Korean prefixoid 독- (獨, dok, 'alone, single, sole, exclusive') with 박 (bak, widely analyzed by Korean lexicographers as either the native noun 박 'gourd bowl'—from the image of having a gourd overturned onto one's head alone, cf. 바가지를 쓰다 'to be ripped off or saddled with an unfair burden'—or a vernacular truncation of 박다/박치기 'to be struck/saddled with', popularized via Korean Go-Stop card-game jargon where one player alone pays the entire penalty for all others). It means bearing the sole blame, cost, or penalty alone.

history.form: 獨 (dok, 'alone') + 박 (bak, 'gourd penalty / sole penalty in card games')
history.meaning: paying the entire penalty alone in a game of Hwatu (Go-Stop)
bearing the sole blame, financial loss, or exhausting burden all by oneself

morphemes.meaning: gourd / penalty burden borne by a loser

독박.notes: Used constantly in the idiom 독박을 쓰다 ('to take the fall alone / get stuck with the whole bill or blame') and in modern social compounds like 독박육아 ('solo parenting burden where one spouse does all the childcare').

독방.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 독방 (獨房, dokbang, pronounced [독빵] dokppang), composed of 독 (獨, dok, 'alone, single, solitary') and 방 (房, bang, 'room, chamber, cell'). It denotes a room occupied by a single person—either a private single room in a hospital, inn, or study center, or a solitary confinement cell in a prison.

history.meaning: single/solitary + chamber or room
single room; solitary confinement cell in a prison

독방.notes: Depending on context, 독방 can mean a coveted private room (e.g., 독방을 쓰다 on a business trip or at a hospital) or a punitive solitary cell in prison dramas (감옥 독방).

rootFamily.gloss: Cold-water or heated sleeping room; shared room (合房)

독서.etymology: Sino-Korean 독서 (讀書), literally 독 (讀, 'read aloud/study') + 서 (書, 'book, writing').
독서.notes: Classical East Asian compound used in modern Korean for reading books for pleasure or study.

독서등.etymology: Sino-Korean 독서등 (讀書燈), combining 독서 (讀書, 독 'read' + 서 'book') and 등 (燈, 'lamp, light').

history.meaning: lamp for reading books
reading lamp

독하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the Sino-Korean noun 독 (毒, dok, 'poison, venom, potency, virulence') and the native Korean adjectival suffix -하다 (-hada, 'to be characterized by', from Middle Korean -ᄒᆞ다). From its literal sense of 'poisonous, venomous', it broadened to describe strong alcohol or harsh chemicals ('potent, pungent') and human temperament ('ruthless, cold-blooded, fiercely tenacous').

history.meaning: to be poisonous, venomous, virulent, or fierce
to be poisonous; strong (of liquor); ruthless, harsh, or fiercely determined (of character)

독하다.notes: Pronounced [도카다] (dokada) due to aspiration of ㄱ + ㅎ; applied to a person (성격이 독하다 or 마음이 독하다), it can mean either 'ruthless/stone-hearted' or 'having iron-willed grit' (e.g., sticking to a grueling diet or study regimen).

rootFamily.gloss: poisonous snake, viper; a ruthless person (毒蛇)

돈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 돈 ('money, coin; traditional unit of weight equal to 3.75 grams').

history.meaning: coin, money; weight unit
money

돋보기안경.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 돋보기 (돋- 'amplify/raise' + 보- 'see' + -기, 'magnifying glass') with Sino-Korean 안경 (眼鏡, 'eyeglasses').

history.meaning: reading glasses, magnifying spectacles

돌.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 돌 (stem 돌ㅎ, 'stone, rock'); also homophonous with 돌 ('full year cycle, first birthday').

history.meaning: stone, rock
stone, rock, pebble

돌계단.etymology: Hybrid compound joining native Korean 돌 ('stone') with Sino-Korean 계단 (階段, 'stairs, steps').
돌계단.notes: Common in hillside lanes and courtyard entrances across older Seoul neighbourhoods.

돌고래.etymology: Compound noun formed from 돌- (dol-, attested in Early Modern Korean texts as 돗고래 dotgorae from 돝 dot 'pig' + 고래 gorae 'whale', Calquing or paralleling Classical Sino-Korean 해돈 海豚 'sea-pig' and 돈어 豚魚 'pig-fish' because of the porpoise/dolphin's plump snout and layer of blubber, later folk-etymologized or reshaped via 돌다 'to spin/turn' or 돌 'small') and the native Korean noun 고래 (gorae, 'whale', from Middle Korean 고래 goray). It denotes any dolphin or porpoise.

history.meaning: whale / 'pig-whale' (porpoise, dolphin, cf. 海豚 'sea pig')
dolphin, porpoise

morphemes.meaning: porpoise/dolphin specifier (historically from 돝 'pig', cf. 海豚 'sea-pig')

돌고래.notes: In Korean pop culture and variety shows, 돌고래 소리 ('dolphin sound') or 돌고래 고음 ('dolphin high note') is the standard slang for an ultra-high-pitched scream of excitement or vocal falsetto.

rootFamily.gloss: killer whale, orca (虎鯨 / 범 + 고래 'tiger whale')

돌길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 길 ('road, path').

history.meaning: stone path, cobblestone road

돌다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 돌다 ('to turn, revolve, spin, go around').

history.meaning: to turn, revolve, circle
to turn, spin, go around, circulate

돌다리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 다리 ('bridge').

history.meaning: stone bridge
stone bridge, stepping-stone bridge

돌다리.notes: Famous in the proverb 돌다리도 두들겨 보고 건너라 ('Even a stone bridge, tap it before crossing' — look before you leap).

돌담.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 돌 ('stone') and 담 ('wall, enclosure fence').

history.meaning: stone wall
stone wall

돌려드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble compound verb joining 돌려- (from 돌리다, 'to turn/give back') and humble 드리다 ('to give to a respected person').

history.meaning: to return, give back (humble)

돌려보내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 돌려- (from 돌리다, 'to turn back') and 보내다 ('to send').

history.meaning: to send back, turn away

돌리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 돌리다, formed from 돌다 ('to turn, spin') + causative suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to cause to turn or revolve
to turn, spin, run (an appliance), pass around

돌마당.etymology: Native Korean compound joining 돌 ('stone, rock', Middle Korean 돌ㅎ) with 마당 ('open courtyard, yard of a house', Middle Korean 마당). In traditional and restored Korean courtyard homes, a 돌마당 paved with flat granite flagstones keeps walking paths mud-free after rain, stores gentle warmth in the afternoon sun, and frames central garden beds.
돌마당.notes: Contrasts with 흙마당 ('earthen courtyard') and 잔디 마당 ('lawn yard'); compare 안마당 ('inner courtyard').

돌멩이.etymology: Native Korean compound/suffixed noun formed from 돌 (dol, 'stone, rock', inherited from Middle Korean 돌 dól with an underlying final aspirate, realized as 돌ㅎ dolh before vowels) and -멩이 (-meng-i, a variant of 망이/맹이 mang-i/maeng-i, meaning 'a small, hard, round lump or kernel', also seen in 알맹이 almaeng-i 'kernel, core'). Together they denote a small, hand-sized stone or pebble.

history.meaning: stone, rock
small round stone, pebble, cobble

morphemes.meaning: small round lump or discrete piece

돌멩이.notes: Be careful with Korean spelling: 돌멩이 (with ㅔ) is the sole standard orthographic form, whereas *돌맹이 (with ㅐ, influenced by 알맹이) is a very common spelling mistake.

돌바닥.etymology: Native Korean compound of 돌 ('stone') and 바닥 ('floor, ground surface').
돌바닥.notes: Parallel to 돌계단 ('stone steps') and 마룻바닥 ('wooden floor').

돌발.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 돌발 (突發, dolbal), compounded from 돌 (突, dol, 'to rush out suddenly, dash forward, protrude abruptly', originally depicting a dog 犬 rushing suddenly out of a cave/hole 穴) and 발 (發, bal, 'to shoot forth, issue, break out, occur'). It denotes an event, action, or emergency breaking out suddenly and unexpectedly.

history.meaning: to rush forth and break out abruptly
unexpected outbreak; sudden, spontaneous occurrence or action

돌발.notes: A staple term in live broadcasting and variety television for unscripted moments: 돌발 상황 ('unexpected situation/emergency'), 돌발 행동 ('spontaneous/unscripted action'), and 돌발 질문 ('surprise question').

돌벽.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining native 돌 ('stone') with Sino-Korean 벽 (壁, 'wall').
돌벽.notes: Pronounced [돌벽]; synonymous with pure-native 돌담 ('stone garden wall') when outdoors.

돌보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 돌아보다 (돌다 'to turn toward' + 보다 'to look after').

history.meaning: to look back at, look after
to take care of, look after, tend

돌아가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn, circle') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to turn and go back
to go back, return; to detour; to spin/operate

돌아가시다.etymology: Native Korean honorific compound verb derived from 돌아가다 (doragada, 'to go back, return; to pass away', from Middle Korean 도라가다 doragada, composed of 돌- dol- 'to turn, circle' + -아 -a + 가- ga- 'to go') inflected with the subject-honorific suffix -시- (-si-, from Middle Korean -시-) and citation ending -다 (-da). As an idiom for death, it reflects the traditional Korean and East Asian worldview that dying is 'returning' to one's original cosmic home or nature (cf. Sino-Korean 돌아갈 귀 歸 in 귀천 歸天 'returning to heaven').

history.meaning: (honorific) to go back, return; euphemistically, to pass away
(honorific) to return; to pass away, die (of an elder or respected person)

돌아가시다.notes: While literally meaning 'to go back / return' for an honored subject, when used without a destination locative it is the standard respectful Korean verb for 'to pass away / die' (replacing 죽다, which is blunt or disrespectful for elders).

rootFamily.gloss: to go back, return; (euphemistic) to pass away

돌아다니다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 돌아- (dora-, the infinitive of 돌다 dolda, 'to turn, circle, go around', from Middle Korean 돌다 dolda) and 다니다 (danida, 'to go back and forth, walk about, frequent', from Middle Korean 녀다 nyeoda / 다니다 danida). Literally meaning 'to go about in circles or from place to place', it describes moving or wandering around various places, or a rumor/story circulating widely.

history.meaning: to walk around from place to place, roam about
to go around, wander about, circulate (of people or rumors)

morphemes.meaning: to go about, move back and forth, frequent

돌아다니다.notes: Used both for people physically walking or traveling around (어디를 그렇게 돌아다니니? 'Where are you wandering around like that?') and for gossip or memes circulating among people (소문이 돌아다니다 'a rumor is going around').

rootFamily.gloss: to go about, commute, attend regularly
to look back, reflect on, inspect around (돌아 + 보다)

돌아보다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from 돌다 (dolda, 'to turn, rotate', from Middle Korean 돌다) connected via the infinitive linker -아 (-a) to 보다 (boda, 'to see, look at', from Middle Korean 보다). Literally 'to turn and look', it evolved to express both physically looking back and figuratively reflecting on past events or looking after someone.

history.meaning: to turn around and look
to look back; to reflect upon; to take care of

돌아보다.notes: Used both physically ('look back over one's shoulder') and introspectively ('look back on one's life/actions').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

돌아서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn around') and 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to turn around and stand
to turn around, turn one's back, pivot

돌아오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 돌아- (from 돌다, 'to turn around') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to turn and come back
to come back, return here

돌잔치.etymology: A native Korean compound noun combining 돌 (dol, 'full year cycle, first anniversary of a baby's birth', derived from the verb stem 돌- 'to turn/come full circle', Middle Korean 돓) and 잔치 (janchi, 'feast, banquet', attested in Middle Korean as 잔츼). Historically, high infant mortality made surviving the first full annual cycle a milestone celebrated with a banquet and fortune-telling ritual.

history.meaning: annual cycle + banquet/feast
first-birthday banquet and celebration

돌잔치.notes: The highlight of a 돌잔치 is the 돌잡이 (doljabi), where the baby picks an object (thread, money, brush) said to foretell their future career or longevity.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

돕다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 돕다 (stem 돕- > 도오- / 도와-, 'to help, assist').

history.meaning: to help, aid
to help, assist (conjugates 도와 / 도우니)

돗자리.etymology: A native Korean compound noun formed from 돗 (dot, an archaic bound root for rush or sedge mat, attested in Middle Korean as 돜, dok, 'woven reed mat') and 자리 (jari, 'mat, seat, place, spot', Middle Korean 자리). As 돜 lost its independent use, it compounded tautologically with 자리 via sai-siot (ㅅ) to specify a woven sedge or rush floor mat.

history.meaning: woven rush or sedge mat
woven straw/rush mat; picnic or vendor mat

morphemes.meaning: woven rush/reed mat (from Middle Korean 돜)

돗자리.notes: Wait or street fortune-tellers traditionally spread out a 돗자리 to set up shop; hence the idiom '돗자리를 깔다' ('spread out a mat') jokingly means someone's guesses are so uncanny they should become a fortune-teller.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

동감하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 동감 (同感, donggam, 'same feeling, shared sentiment'), composed of 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, together') and 感 (느낄 감, gam, 'to feel, emotion'), combined with the native light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do/feel'). Literally 'to have the same feeling', it denotes complete agreement or empathy with another's view.

history.meaning: shared feeling, identical sentiment
to feel the same way; to agree wholeheartedly

동감하다.notes: Often used as the crisp noun predicate '동감입니다' ('I feel the same way / I completely agree') in conversation.

동거.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun derived from Literary Chinese 同居 (동거, donggeo), composed of 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, together') and 居 (살 거, geo, 'to reside, dwell, live'). Originally referring broadly to extended family generations living under one roof in Confucian society, in contemporary Korean it specifically denotes unmarried romantic partners living together or shared housing.

history.meaning: dwelling together in the same household (often multi-generational kin)
living together; cohabitation (especially of an unmarried couple)

동거.notes: Without context, 동거 in modern Korean strongly implies romantic cohabitation before marriage, whereas living with a roommate is usually called 룸메이트生活 or 자취/합숙.

동거하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean verbalizer 하다 (hada, 'to do') to the Sino-Korean noun 동거 (同居, donggeo, 'living together, cohabitation'), from 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'together, same') and 居 (살 거, geo, 'to dwell, reside'). It expresses the act of residing under the same roof, particularly as an unmarried couple.

history.meaning: to dwell together in one household
to cohabit, to live together (especially romantically)

동거하다.notes: In Korean dramas like *The Producers*, discovering two characters are 동거하다 ('living under the same roof') is a classic comedic and romantic trope.

동경하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 동경 (憧憬, donggyeong, 'yearning, longing, admiration') plus the native light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do'). Both Hanja characters carry the heart radical (忄): 憧 (동경할 동 / 어리둥절할 동, dong, 'unsettled heart, yearning') and 憬 (깨달을 경 / 그리워할 경, gyeong, 'to awaken to, yearn for from afar').

history.meaning: restless, unsettled longing of the heart
to yearn for, admire from afar, idolize

morphemes.meaning: to long for from afar, awaken (憬)

동경하다.notes: Implies a romanticized, wistful admiration from a distance (such as idolizing a senior colleague or a glamorous lifestyle), rather than mere respect (존경하다).

rootFamily.gloss: object of admiration (憧憬의 對象)

동그라미.etymology: Native Korean noun derived from the descriptive stem 동그랗- ('to be round, circular') plus noun-forming suffix -미.
동그라미.notes: Contrasts bright-vowel 동그라미 ('neat small circle') with dark-vowel 둥근 ('broadly round').

동그랗다.etymology: A native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the sound-symbolic root 동글- (donggeul-, 'round, circular', the bright-vowel Ablaut counterpart of 둥글-, dunggeul-) and the adjectival suffix -앟다 (-ahda, which triggers ㅎ-irregular conjugation). In Korean vowel harmony, the bright vowel ㅗ (o) in 동그랗다 conveys a smaller, neater, or cuter roundness than the dark vowel ㅜ (u) in 둥그렇다/둥글다.

history.meaning: to be spherical or circular (dark vs. bright vowel harmony)
to be distinctly, neatly round or wide-eyed

동그랗다.notes: Frequently used in the idiom '눈이 동그래지다' ('for one's eyes to go wide and round in surprise'), showcasing Korean vowel harmony where 동그랗다 feels brighter and sharper than 둥그렇다.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

동글동글하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from light-vowel root 동글- (counterpart of 둥글다, 'round') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be nicely round, plump, or small and spherical

동기.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun written 同氣 or 同期 depending on sense, here 同期 (동기, donggi, 'same period/cohort'), composed of 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, together') and 期 (기약할 기, gi, 'period, term, appointed time'). Adopted via modern Japanese institutional usage (同期, dōki), it denotes people who entered a school, military unit, or company recruitment batch in the same intake period.

history.meaning: the same time period or cycle
peers of the same entering class or company recruitment batch

동기.notes: Crucial in Korean workplace and campus culture (like KBS rookie PDs in *The Producers*): 동기 are the rare workplace peers with whom you can drop strict age/rank hierarchy and speak comfortably. (Homophone: 動機 'motive').

동네.etymology: Nativized Korean spelling of Sino-Korean 동내 (洞內, 동 'village, ward' + 내 'inside, within').

history.meaning: inside the village or ward
neighborhood, town, local district

동네방네.etymology: A rhyming Sino-native compound adverb formed by reduplicating the pattern of 동네 (洞네, dongne, 'neighborhood, village', from Hanja 洞 'village/district' + native suffix -네) with 방네 (坊네, bangne, from Hanja 坊 'ward, urban quarter, neighborhood' + -네). Pairing the two synonymous administrative division roots 洞 and 坊 with the symmetrical suffix -네 creates an emphatic four-syllable expression meaning 'every single neighborhood, all over town'.

history.meaning: villages and urban wards alike
all over the neighborhood; far and wide across town

morphemes.meaning: every ward and quarter (坊 + -네, rhyming echo)

동네방네.notes: Almost always paired with verbs of gossiping or broadcasting, such as '동네방네 소문을 내다' ('to spread rumors all over town').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

동료.etymology: Sino-Korean 동료 (同僚), compounding 동 (同, 'same, together') and 료 (僚, 'official, companion in office').

history.meaning: fellow official or coworker
colleague, coworker, peer

동료애.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound noun (同僚愛, dongnyoae) built from 동료 (同僚, dongnyo, 'colleague, coworker' — composed of 同 'same, together' and 僚 'official, companion, bureaucrat') and the suffix 애 (愛, 사랑 애, ae, 'love, affection'). By phonological assimilation (비음화), underlying /동료애/ is pronounced [동뇨애]. It denotes solidarity and warm affection among coworkers.

history.meaning: fellow officials serving in the same court office
camaraderie; fraternal affection among coworkers

동료애.notes: In rom-coms, characters in denial about falling in love with a coworker often insist their feelings are 'just 동료애' (purely professional camaraderie).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

동사무소.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound noun (洞事務所, dongsamuso) combining 동 (洞, 고을 동, dong, 'neighborhood, municipal sub-district', originally 'mountain stream/valley village') and 사무소 (事務所, samuso, 'administrative office' — from 事 'affair/business', 務 'duty/work', and 所 'place/office'). It designates the local municipal office serving a neighborhood (동).

history.meaning: neighborhood administrative office in South Korean municipalities
local neighborhood district office (colloquially retained alongside 주민센터)

동사무소.notes: Although South Korea officially renamed 동사무소 to 주민센터 ('Community Service Center') in 2007 and later 행정복지센터, Koreans still overwhelmingly call it 동사무소 in daily speech.

동생.etymology: Sino-Korean 동생 (同生), compounding 동 (同, 'same') and 생 (生, 'birth, born of the same parents'), which specialized in Korean from 'sibling' to 'younger sibling'.

history.meaning: sibling born of the same parents
younger sibling (brother or sister)

cognates.meaning: flow line, movement trajectory in architecture/staging

동선.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun (動線, dongseon) composed of 動 (움직일 동, dong, 'to move, motion') and 線 (줄 선, seon, 'line, trajectory'). Coined in modern East Asian architecture, urban planning, and stage/broadcast production, it refers to the plotted trajectory or path along which people, actors, or cameras move through a space.

history.meaning: architectural circulation line or traffic flow diagram
movement path, stage/camera blocking route, daily travel trajectory

동선.notes: Originally technical jargon among TV producers, directors, and architects ('동선을 맞추다' = coordinate stage/camera blocking), it is now widely used in everyday Korean to mean one's daily route or whether two people's paths overlap ('동선이 겹치다').

rootFamily.gloss: gaze line, line of sight (視線)

동시.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun (同時, dongsi) composed of 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, together') and 時 (때 시, si, 'time, hour, moment'). Attested in Classical Chinese to denote events occurring in the same era or moment, in modern Korean it primarily functions with the locative particle -에 (동시에) or as a prenominal modifier meaning 'simultaneous'.

history.meaning: in the same era or at the exact same time
the same time; simultaneity (usually in 동시에, 'simultaneously')

동시.notes: Most frequently encountered with the particle -에 as '동시에' ('at the same time / simultaneously'), or as a prefix in broadcasting terms like 동시통역 ('simultaneous interpretation') and 동시녹음 ('sync sound recording'). (Homophone: 童詩 'children's poem').

rootFamily.gloss: the same era, contemporary age (同時代)

동안.etymology: Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 동안 ('interval of time or space, while').

history.meaning: interval, space or time between
during, for the duration of, while
