동전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 동전 (銅錢), from 동 (銅, 'copper, bronze') and 전 (錢, 'coin, money').
동전.notes: Originally referred to cast copper coins; now denotes small metal change of any alloy.

cognates.meaning: to sympathize, pity, feel sorry for

동정하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 동정 (同情, dongjeong, 'sympathy, compassion, pity') — composed of 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, shared') and 情 (뜻 정, jeong, 'feeling, emotion, sentiment') — and the native verbalizer 하다 (hada, 'to do'). While its literal root means 'sharing the same feeling', its modern sense narrowed to feeling pity or sorry for someone's plight.

history.meaning: having the same nature, disposition, or shared sentiment
to pity, feel sorry for, sympathize with someone's misfortune

동정하다.notes: Be careful with nuance: unlike 공감하다 ('to empathize as an equal'), 동정하다 often carries a slightly patronizing nuance of 'pitying' someone from a superior position—hence proud characters often snap '날 동정하지 마!' ('Don't pity me!').

동쪽.etymology: Hybrid directional compound combining Sino-Korean 동 (東, 동녘 동, 'east', traditionally analyzed as the sun 日 rising through the branches of a tree 木) with the native Korean bound/directional noun 쪽 ('side, direction'). Together with 서쪽 ('west'), 남쪽 ('south'), and 북쪽 ('north'), 동쪽 forms the standard everyday cardinal-direction set in modern Korean, largely superseding literary 동녘 in speech.
동쪽.notes: Pronounced [동쪽] with tensification; takes -(으)로 for 'eastward' (동쪽으로 향하다 'face/head east').

동창이.etymology: The Sino-Korean noun 동창 (同窓, dongchang, 'schoolmate, fellow alumnus') inflected with the native Korean nominative/subject case particle -이 (-i). 同窓 combines 同 (한가지 동, dong, 'same, together') and 窓 (창문 창, chang, 'window'), originating from the Classical Chinese scholarly metaphor of students studying side by side beneath the same study window (형설지공, 螢雪之功).

history.meaning: fellow scholars studying together by the same window
schoolmate / fellow alumnus (as grammatical subject)

morphemes.meaning: nominative (subject) case marker after a consonant

동창이.notes: In Korea, 동창 refers broadly to anyone who graduated from the same school (especially the same graduating year), and 동창회 (alumni reunion) is a major social network throughout adulthood.

돼.etymology: The contracted intimate/informal conjugated form (해체) or infinitive stem of the native Korean verb 되다 (doeda, 'to become; to work properly; to be permissible'), formed by fusing the stem 되- (doe-, from Middle Korean 도외다, do.oeda, 'to become, be formed') with the infinitive/intimate ending -어 (-eo) into 돼 (dwae).

history.meaning: becomes; is formed or completed
becomes; works out; is okay/permitted (contracted intimate/infinitive form)

morphemes.meaning: infinitive / intimate sentence-final ending (-어 contracted with ㅚ to ㅙ)

돼.notes: One of the most common spelling pitfalls for native Koreans is confusing 되 (stem only, valid before consonants like 되고, 되니) with 돼 (= 되어, required at the end of a sentence '안 돼!' or before -요 '돼요' and past tense '됐어').

rootFamily.gloss: to become, be okay, function properly

되게.etymology: A native Korean adverb grammaticalized from the adverbial (-게) form of the adjective 되다 (doeda, 'to be thick, hard, severe, intense', attested in Middle Korean as 되다, 'harsh, severe, stiff', homophonous with but distinct in sense from 되다 'to become'). Originally meaning 'severely, harshly, thickly', it bleached in colloquial speech into a general intensifier meaning 'really, super, very'.

history.meaning: harshly, severely, intensely
really, very, super (colloquial intensifier)

morphemes.meaning: to be severe, intense, thick (adjective stem)

되게.notes: Very common in casual, everyday conversation ('되게 좋다' = 'it's really great', '되게 웃기다' = 'super funny'), though avoided in formal writing where 매우 or 아주 is preferred.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

되다.etymology: Core native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 다외다 (> 되다, 'to become, turn into, be completed').

history.meaning: to become, be formed
to become, be done, work/function, reach

되도록.etymology: A lexicalized native Korean adverb formed from the stem of the verb 되다 (doeda, 'to become, be possible, be realized', Middle Korean 도외다) and the projective/purposive conjunctive suffix -도록 (-dorok, 'to the point that, so that', Middle Korean -도록). Literally meaning 'to the extent that it becomes possible/workable', it crystallized as an adverb meaning 'as much as possible, preferably'.

history.meaning: to the point that it comes to be / becomes possible
as much as possible, if at all possible, preferably

morphemes.meaning: to become, be possible, work out

되도록.notes: Often reinforced with -이면 as '되도록이면' ('if at all possible / preferably'), e.g., '되도록 빨리 오세요' ('Please come as soon as possible').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

되어버리다.etymology: A native Korean auxiliary verb construction combining 되어 (doeeo, the infinitive form of 되다, 'to become', Middle Korean 도외다) with the completive auxiliary verb 버리다 (beolida, originally 'to throw away, discard', Middle Korean 버리다). Through grammaticalization, 버리다 lost its literal sense of discarding and came to mark an action or change of state as completely, irreversibly, and often regrettably or unexpectedly finished ('ended up becoming').

history.meaning: to become + to cast away / finish off completely
to end up becoming; to turn into completely (often unexpectedly or irreversibly)

되어버리다.notes: Adding -어 버리다 expresses emotional involvement—either relief that something is finally over, or regret/surprise that things turned out that way ('바보가 되어버렸다' = 'ended up looking like a complete fool').

rootFamily.gloss: to throw away; (aux.) to do completely/regrettably

되어주다.etymology: A native Korean benefactive compound verb formed from 되어 (doeeo, infinitive of 되다, 'to become', Middle Korean 도외다) and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, 'to give; to do for someone's benefit', Middle Korean 주다). By combining 'become' with 'give', it expresses willingly taking on a role or becoming something for another person's sake ('to become [a friend/support] for someone').

history.meaning: to become + to give/bestow
to become (something) for someone's benefit; to act as support for someone

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary ('to do for someone', literally 'give')

되어주다.notes: A staple of emotional K-drama confessions andOST lyrics: '내 편이 되어주다' ('to become on my side / stand by me') or '힘이 되어주다' ('to become a source of strength for me').

rootFamily.gloss: to give; (aux.) to do for someone's sake
to do something for someone (polite benefactive)

되찾다.etymology: Native Korean prefix 되- ('back again, reverse') + 찾다 ('to find, seek, retrieve').
되찾다.notes: Used both literally for recovering lost items and figuratively for regaining health or voice.

되풀이하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from prefix 되- ('again, back') + 풀이 (deverbal noun from 풀다, 'unfolding, performance') + -하다.

history.meaning: to repeat over and over, iterate

된장찌개.etymology: A hybrid Sino-native Korean culinary compound combining 된장 (doenjang, 'fermented soybean paste') and 찌개 (jjigae, 'thick Korean stew'). 된장 itself is a hybrid of native 된 (doen, adnominal form of 되다, 'to be thick, stiff, hard, low-moisture' — contrasting with liquid soy sauce, 간장) and Sino-Korean 장 (醬, 장 장, jang, 'fermented paste/sauce'). 찌개 derives from the native verb 찌다 (jjida, 'to steam, simmer') plus the nominalizing suffix -개 (attested in early modern Korean as 지개).

history.meaning: thick fermented bean paste + simmered pot dish
savory Korean fermented soybean-paste stew

morphemes.meaning: thick, stiff, hard (adnominal 된 of 되다)

된장찌개.notes: Along with 김치찌개, 된장찌개 is the quintessential everyday Korean comfort food; asking someone what 찌개 to order at lunch is an iconic slice-of-life workplace ritual.

rootFamily.gloss: fermented soybean soup (lighter broth than stew)

두.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral descending from Middle Korean 두 ('two' before nouns and classifiers, apocopated from 둘).

history.meaning: two (modifier)
two (before counters/nouns, e.g. 두 개, 두 번)

두근거리다.etymology: Native Korean mimetic verb formed from root 두근 ('thumping of a beating heart') + iterative verbalizing suffix -거리다.

history.meaning: for the heart to thump repeatedly
to throb, palpitate, pound (of the heart)

두근대다.etymology: A native Korean verb formed from the mimetic/ideophonic root 두근 (dugeun, representing the thumping or pounding sound and sensation of a beating heart, attested in Early Modern Korean as 두군두군) and the verbal suffix -대다 (-daeda, 'to repeatedly make a sound or motion', interchangeable with -거리다). It depicts a heart pounding repeatedly from excitement, romance, or anxiety.

history.meaning: to thump or palpitate repeatedly in the chest
to throb, pound, flutter (of the heart with excitement or nerves)

morphemes.meaning: frequentative verbalizer ('to keep doing/making the sound of')

두근대다.notes: Interchangeable with 두근거리다 (slightly more standard/literary than -대다). In Korean pop culture, '가슴이 두근대다' is the signature physical cue that a character is falling in love.

두근두근하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic verb/adjective from 두근두근 ('pit-a-pat, thump-thump') + -하다.

history.meaning: for one's heart to pound with anticipation or nerves

두껍다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 둗겁다 ('to be thick in layer or flat depth').

history.meaning: to be thick
to be thick (of walls, boards, books, fabric)

두다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 두다 ('to put, place, keep, leave in place').

history.meaning: to put, keep, leave
to put, keep; resultative auxiliary (-어 두다) 'do in advance and keep'

두드리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 두드리다 ('to knock, tap, beat, hammer').

history.meaning: to beat, knock, rap
to knock on (a door), tap, drum

두려움.etymology: A native Korean abstract noun derived from the ㅂ-irregular adjective 두렵다 (duryeopda, 'to be fearful, afraid', from Middle Korean 두렵다 / 두리다, 'to fear, dread') by vocalizing the stem-final ㅂ to ㅜ (두려우-) and attaching the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ (-m). It names the emotional state of fear, dread, or reverent awe.

history.meaning: the state of fearing or dreading
fear, dread, apprehension, awe

morphemes.meaning: to fear, be afraid (stem 두렵- → 두려우- before vowel)

두려움.notes: Shows the productive Korean pattern for turning ㅂ-irregular adjectives into nouns: 두렵다 → 두려움 ('fear'), 어렵다 → 어려움 ('difficulty'), 아름답다 → 아름다움 ('beauty').

rootFamily.gloss: to fear, be afraid of (transitive verb)

두렵다.etymology: A native Korean ㅂ-irregular descriptive verb (adjective) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 두렵다 (duryeopda), derived from the Middle Korean transitive verb 두리다 (durida, 'to fear, be afraid of') plus the deverbal adjectival suffix -업다/-브다 (-eopda/-beuda). As 두리다 became obsolete on its own, 두렵다 survived as the standard adjective for feeling fear or apprehension.

history.meaning: to be fearsome, dreadful, afraid
to be afraid (of), fearful, apprehensive

두렵다.notes: Like other Korean emotion adjectives, 두렵다 directly describes a first-person subject's feeling ('나는 실패가 두렵다' = 'I am afraid of failure'), whereas third-person subjects usually require the verbal form 두려워하다.

rootFamily.gloss: to fear, dread (transitive verb for 3rd person/action)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

두르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular verb continuing Middle Korean 두르다 ('to encircle, wrap around'). Before -어, the stem 두르- doubles ㄹ to form 둘러 (둘러요, 둘렀어요). Remarkably versatile in everyday Korean, 두르다 describes tying an apron or scarf around the body (앞치마를 두르다), enclosing a space with bricks or a fence (담을 두르다), and swirling oil or butter around a hot pan (팬에 버터를 두르다).
두르다.notes: Forms compounds such as 둘러보다 ('look around') and 둘러싸다 ('surround').

두성.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun (頭聲, duseong) formed from 頭 (머리 두, du, 'head') and 聲 (소리 성, seong, 'voice, sound'). Adopted in modern East Asian musicology as a calque of Western vocal pedagogy terms (Italian *voce di testa*, German *Kopfstimme*, English *head voice*), it refers to high-register vocal production resonating in the cranial cavities.

history.meaning: cranial sound / voice resonating in the head (calque of Italian voce di testa)
head voice (high vocal register resonating in the head)

두성.notes: Frequently contrasted in Korean singing shows and karaoke banter with 흉성 (胸聲, 'chest voice'), 진성 (眞聲, 'natural/full voice'), and 가성 (假聲, 'falsetto').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

둘.etymology: Native Korean cardinal numeral descending from Middle Korean 둘 (stem 돓, 'two').

history.meaning: two
two

둘둘.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb built with the dark vowel ㅜ to depict winding, coiling, or rolling cloth, paper, string, or a scarf around and around in full turns. Within Korean sound-symbolic vowel harmony, dark-vowel 둘둘 suggests thicker, looser, or larger-scale wrapping (목도리를 둘둘 감다, 지도를 둘둘 말다) than its bright-vowel counterpart 돌돌, which evokes tighter, smaller, neater rolling.
둘둘.notes: Pairs most frequently with 감다/감기다 ('wind/be wound') and 말다/말리다 ('roll up/be rolled up').

둘러보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 둘러- (from 두르다, 'to turn around, encircle') and 보다 ('to look, see').

history.meaning: to look all around
to look around, browse, tour/inspect

둘러싸다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb combining 둘러 (dulleo, the 르-irregular infinitive form of 두르다, dureuda, 'to wrap around, encircle, put around the circumference', Middle Korean 두르다) and 싸다 (ssada, 'to wrap, pack, enclose', Middle Korean 싸다). Joining 'encircle' and 'wrap' yields an intensive verb meaning to completely surround, besiege, or envelop something from all sides.

history.meaning: to wrap around and enclose completely
to surround, encircle, besiege; to center around (an issue)

둘러싸다.notes: Used both spatially ('기자들이 방송국을 둘러쌌다' = 'Reporters surrounded the broadcasting station') and abstractly in news prose ('그 사건을 둘러싼 논란' = 'the controversy surrounding that incident').

rootFamily.gloss: to wrap around, encircle; to make excuses

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

둘레.etymology: Native Korean noun derived from the verbal root 두르- (dureu-, Middle Korean 두르다 twuleuta, 'to encircle, enclose, wrap around') plus a nominalizing suffix. Attested in Early Modern Korean as 둘레 (dulle), it denotes both the measurable circumference of a circle or tree trunk and the spatial perimeter immediately surrounding an object. Followed by the locative particle -에 (둘레에), it functions as a postpositional phrase meaning 'all around' or 'in a ring around'.

history.meaning: to surround, encircle, wrap around (verbal base)
circumference, perimeter, area around an object

둘레.notes: Familiar across Korea today in 둘레길 ('perimeter walking trail'), the scenic footpaths that circle mountains and old city walls.

둘째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral formed from 둘 ('two') + ordinal suffix -째.

history.meaning: second
second

둥.etymology: A native Korean bound (dependent) noun 둥 (dung), attested from Early Modern Korean in paired adnominal constructions (-는/-은/-을 둥). Likely related to the archaic noun 듯/듯하다 ('seeming, appearance'), it grammaticalized after adnominal verb clauses to indicate vague alternation, uncertainty, or hearsay—either between doing and not doing ('할 둥 말 둥', 'barely/half-heartedly doing') or listing rumored claims ('~라는 둥 ~라는 둥', 'saying things like X and Y').

history.meaning: appearance or uncertain state between two possibilities
bound noun expressing vague alternation ('whether/barely') or cited rumors ('saying things like...')

morphemes.meaning: bound noun indicating vague alternation, half-hearted action, or rumored examples

둥.notes: Appears in two classic patterns: (1) V-는 둥 마는 둥 ('barely doing V / doing V half-heartedly', like '보는 둥 마는 둥' = barely glancing), and (2) ~라는 둥 ('rumors/chatter saying things like...'). Always preceded by a space!

rootFamily.gloss: bound noun for 'seeming / appearing as if'
bound noun for 'pretending / acting as if'

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

둥글다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem adjective descending from Middle Korean 둥글다 ('to be round, circular, spherical').

history.meaning: to be round, spherical
to be round, circular; amiable

뒤.etymology: Native Korean spatial and temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 뒤 (stem 뒤ㅎ, 'back, rear, behind; after, later').

history.meaning: back, behind, after
back, behind, rear; after (in time)

뒤끝.etymology: A native Korean compound noun formed from 뒤 (dwi, 'back, rear, after, aftermath', from Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ, dwih, with final ㅎ) and 끝 (kkeut, 'end, tip, conclusion, outcome', from Middle Korean 귿, geut). Literally meaning 'the rear end' or 'the concluding aftermath of an affair', it evolved metaphorically to denote lingering resentment, pettiness, or holding a grudge after an argument is supposedly over.

history.meaning: the rear end; the final conclusion of a matter
aftermath; lingering grudge or petty resentment after a conflict

morphemes.meaning: back, rear, after, aftermath (Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ)

뒤끝.notes: In Korean social life, '뒤끝이 없다' ('to have no lingering grudge / let bygones be bygones cleanly') is high praise, whereas '뒤끝이 있다 / 작렬하다' means someone is petty and brings up old slights long afterward.

rootFamily.gloss: taking care of the aftermath, cleaning up after oneself
talking behind someone's back, gossiping afterward

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

뒤늦다.etymology: A native Korean compound adjective (descriptive verb) combining the noun/prefix 뒤- (dwi-, 'back, behind, after', Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ) and the adjective 늦다 (neutda, 'to be late, tardy', Middle Korean 늦다). Adding 뒤- ('afterward, in the rear') intensifies 늦다 to mean not merely running behind schedule, but realizing, regretting, or acting belatedly—after the crucial moment or opportunity has already passed.

history.meaning: to be late after the event has passed
to be belated, too late, after the fact (often as adverbial 뒤늦게, 'belatedly')

뒤늦다.notes: Unlike simple 늦다 ('to be late for an appointment'), 뒤늦다 (most often used as '뒤늦게 깨닫다/후회하다' or '뒤늦은 후회') specifically means 'belatedly / after the ship has sailed'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary)

뒤돌아서.etymology: Native Korean participial/adverbial form built from 뒤 ('back') + 돌아서다 ('to turn around and stand') + connective -어.

history.meaning: turning around, having turned one's back

뒤따르다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the spatial noun 뒤 (dwi, 'back, rear, behind'; Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ, twuyh) and the verb 따르다 (ttareuda, 'to follow, accompany'; Middle Korean ᄠᆞᄅᆞ다, ptolota). Literally meaning 'to follow behind', it describes coming right after someone in space or time, or succeeding an event as a consequence.

history.meaning: rear / behind + to follow after
to follow right behind; to accompany or ensue

뒤따르다.notes: Used both physically ('to follow behind someone') and abstractly ('fame is followed by responsibility').

뒤지다.etymology: A native Korean verb meaning 'to rummage through, search thoroughly, or turn inside out'. Derived from the spatial root 뒤- (dwi-, 'back, reverse, upside down'; Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ) combined with a verbalizing element related to turning over or disturbing (compare 뒤집다 'to flip over' and Middle Korean 뒤다 'to turn over, stir up'). Note that a homophonous verb 뒤지다 ('to fall behind' or vulgarly 'to die') derives from 뒤 + 지다 ('to fall').

history.meaning: to turn over, stir up, rummage through
to rummage through, comb through, search every corner

뒤지다.notes: Be careful of its two other homonyms: 뒤지다 meaning 'to lag behind' and the coarse slang 뒤지다 meaning 'to drop dead'.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn over, flip inside out

뒤집다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 드위집다 ('to turn upside down, flip over').

history.meaning: to overturn, invert
to turn over, flip, turn inside out

뒤집어쓰다.etymology: A native Korean serial verb compound built from 뒤집다 (dwijipda, 'to turn over, invert, flip inside out'; from 뒤- 'reverse' + 집다 'to pick up/turn'), the infinitive linker -어 (-eo), and 쓰다 (sseuda, 'to wear on the head, be covered with'; Middle Korean 스다, seuta). Literally 'to flip something over and pull it over one's own head', it developed the vivid figurative sense of being saddled with blame or taking the fall for a crime or mistake.

history.meaning: to turn over and put over one's head
to pull over one's head; to be covered in (dust/water); to take the blame/fall

morphemes.meaning: to wear on the head, take upon oneself

뒤집어쓰다.notes: Frequently collocated with 누명 (false accusation) or 죄 (blame/guilt), as in 누명을 뒤집어쓰다 ('to be framed / take the fall').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn over, flip inside out
to shift blame onto someone else (causative)
to wear on the head, be charged with

뒤쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 뒤 ('back, rear') and 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the back side, toward the rear

뒤처지다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb composed of 뒤 (dwi, 'behind, rear'; Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ) and 처지다 (cheojida, 'to sag, droop, lag behind, remain behind', the intransitive/passive derivative of 치다 or 처- 'to drop/hang down'). Literally 'to droop or lag in the rear', it denotes falling behind others in a race, competition, or societal progress.

history.meaning: behind + to droop, lag, stay behind
to fall behind, lag behind, be outpaced

뒤처지다.notes: A very common spelling trap for native speakers: it is spelled 뒤처지다 (with 처), NEVER *뒤쳐지다.

rootFamily.gloss: to lag behind, fall to the rear

뒤편.etymology: Hybrid Korean spatial compound joining the native noun 뒤 ('back, rear', Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ) with the Sino-Korean bound noun 편 (便, 'side, direction, quarter'). Because the second element begins with an aspirated stop ㅍ, Korean orthography writes 뒤편 without a linking ㅅ (unlike 뒷면 or 뒷골목). It forms a symmetrical directional series alongside 앞편 ('front side'), 왼편 ('left side'), and 오른편 ('right side').
뒤편.notes: Spelled 뒤편 without 사이시옷 before aspirated ㅍ; contrasts with 뒷면 ('reverse face of a flat object').

뒷골목.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 뒤 ('back, rear'), the genitive linking consonant -ㅅ- (사이시옷), and 골목 ('alley, narrow neighborhood lane', itself from 골 'narrow valley, groove' + 목 'neck, narrow passage'). The linking -ㅅ- triggers tensification of the following velar stop so the word is pronounced [뒫꼴목] / [뒤꼴목]. In everyday Korean, 뒷골목 evokes quiet residential side lanes tucked away behind a main thoroughfare.
뒷골목.notes: Pronounced [뒫꼴목] or [뒤꼴목] with tensification of ㄱ after 사이시옷.

뒷면.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 뒤 ('back') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface, page').

history.meaning: back side, reverse side, verso

뒷면.notes: Pronounced [뒨면] via nasal assimilation across the compound boundary.

뒷문.etymology: Hybrid compound joining native 뒤 ('back, rear') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door, gate').
뒷문.notes: Pronounced [뒨문] by nasalization before ㅁ; contrasts with 앞문 ('front door') and 대문 ('main gate').

뒷부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 뒤 ('back, rear') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + Sino-Korean 부분 (部分, 'part, section').

history.meaning: back part, rear section, latter part

cognates.meaning: getting a situation under control, settling a mess
to put in order, tidy up, clear away

뒷수습.etymology: A hybrid native-Sino-Korean compound noun formed from native Korean 뒤 (dwi, 'back, rear, aftermath'; Middle Korean 뒤ㅎ, whose final -ㅎ triggered fortition and is now represented by the interfix ㅅ as 뒷-, dwit-) and Sino-Korean 수습 (收拾, suseup, 'gathering up and putting in order'). 收拾 combines 收 (수, su, 'to gather, collect') and 拾 (습, seup, 'to pick up, tidy'). Together, 뒷수습 means cleaning up the mess or resolving the aftermath of an incident.

history.meaning: to gather up, collect, put in order
aftermath + gathering and settling
cleaning up the aftermath, damage control

morphemes.meaning: to gather, collect, bring under control (收)
to pick up, ten, tidy up (拾)

뒷수습.notes: Notice the 사이시옷 (saisiot, 'interfix ㅅ') in 뒷-: whenever native 뒤 attaches to a noun to mean 'aftermath' or 'rear', ㅅ is added if the pronunciation tenses (e.g., 뒷수습, 뒷감당, 뒷모습).

rootFamily.gloss: getting a crisis under control, settling (收拾)
cleaning up after an event or meal

드디어.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 드듸여, originally the infinitive form of 드듸다 ('to step on, tread upon'), grammaticalized into 'at last, finally'.

history.meaning: stepping forward; finally, at last
finally, at last

cognates.meaning: theatrical play or television drama series

드라마.etymology: An English loanword (*외래어*) borrowed in the 20th century from English drama, which came via Late Latin drama from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, 'an act, deed, theatrical play'), derived from the verb δράω (dráō, 'to do, act, perform'). In modern Korean broadcasting, 드라마 underwent semantic narrowing to refer specifically to scripted television serial dramas (especially K-dramas) rather than stage plays (연극).

history.meaning: deed, action, stage play
theatrical play or dramatic genre in radio/television
scripted television drama series

드라마.notes: In everyday Korean, 드라마 almost always means a TV series; stage plays are called 연극 (演劇, yeongeuk).

드라이버.etymology: Borrowed from English driver (in Korean hardware usage clipped from screwdriver via Japanese doraibā ドライバー).

history.meaning: tool for turning screws; vehicle driver
screwdriver; driver

드리고.etymology: An inflected conjunctive form of the native Korean humble verb 드리다 (deurida, 'to give/offer to a superior'), combining the stem 드리- with the coordinate connective ending -고 (-go, 'and, and then'). Historically, 드리다 evolved from Middle Korean 디리다 (tilita) / 드리다 (tulita), the causative of 들다 (tul-ta, 'to enter, go in'), originally meaning 'to cause to enter, to bring in / present before a palace or superior', before grammaticalizing into the standard humble suppletive counterpart of 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to cause to enter; to bring in and present to a superior
to give/offer (humble); to do an action for a respected person (-어 드리다)
give (humble) and; do for an elder/superior and

드리고.notes: Functions both as a standalone humble verb ('to give to an elder/superior') and as an auxiliary verb after -아/-어 (e.g., 도와드리고 'help them and...') to show respect to the recipient of the action.

rootFamily.gloss: to bring in, let in (etymological doublet from 들다 + -이-)

드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble verb descending from Middle Korean 드리다 (originally the causative of 들다 'to enter', meaning 'to cause an offering to enter a superior's presence').

history.meaning: to present or offer to a superior
to give, offer (humble counterpart of 주다)

cognates.meaning: to propel a ball with repeated light touches or bounces
dribbling a ball in soccer or basketball

드리블.etymology: An English sports loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English dribble ('to propel a ball by repeated short kicks or bounces'), itself a frequentative formation from Early Modern English drib ('to fall in drops, trickle'), related to drip and drop (from Old English dryppan). In Korean, 드리블 is used exclusively in sports contexts (soccer, basketball) for maneuvering the ball past defenders.

history.meaning: to fall in small drops; later (18th–19th c.) to kick or bounce a ball in short touches
dribble, dribbling the ball in soccer or basketball

드리블.notes: Unlike English 'dribble', which can also mean 'to drool saliva', Korean 드리블 only means dribbling a ball in sports (drooling is 침을 흘리다).

rootFamily.gloss: to dribble a ball (verbalized with 하다)
a player who dribbles the ball (dribbler)

드리우다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed from the Middle Korean stem 드리- ('to hang down, droop downward') and the causative suffix -우-. Originally used for letting a curtain, fishing line, or fringe hang vertically from above, it developed a classic poetic and everyday extension for trees, eaves, or clock towers casting long shadows across the ground. In vowel-initial endings, 우 contracts regularly with 어 to produce 드리워요 and 드리웠어요.
드리우다.notes: Most famously collocates with 그림자를 드리우다 ('to cast a shadow') and 커튼/발을 드리우다 ('to hang a curtain/blind').

드시다.etymology: Native Korean subject-honorific verb formed from 들다 ('to lift, take in hand, eat or drink') + honorific suffix -시-.

history.meaning: to eat, drink, have (honorific)

든든하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 든든- ('firm, reassuring, well-filled') + -하다.

history.meaning: solid, secure, reassuring
to feel reassured/secure; to feel satisfyingly full (of a meal)

듣다.etymology: Native Korean ㄷ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 듣다 (stem 듣- > 드러- before vowels, 'to hear, listen').

history.meaning: to hear, listen
to hear, listen to (conjugates 들어 / 들으니)

들다.etymology: Core native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from two Middle Korean verbs distinguished by tone: 들다 (low tone, 'to enter, go inside, cost, contain') and 들다 (high tone, 'to lift, hold in one's hand').

history.meaning: to enter, go in / to lift, hold
to enter, cost, set in; to hold, lift, carry

들려주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 들려- (from 들리다, causative of 듣다, 'to let someone hear') and benefactive 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to tell (a story), play (music or a sound) for someone

들르다.etymology: A native Korean 르-irregular verb meaning 'to stop by, drop in on the way'. It derives historically from the Middle Korean verb 들다 (tul-ta, 'to enter, go inside') extended with a suffixal or iterative element -르- (-lu-), shifting from 'to enter briefly' to 'to make a brief detour or visit while en route to another destination'.

history.meaning: to enter; to pass in by way of a place
to drop by, stop in at a place on one's way

morphemes.meaning: to stop by, drop in (historically from 들- 'enter')

들르다.notes: As a 르-irregular verb, its stem 들르- conjugates with doubled ㄹ before -어: 들러 (deulleo), 들렀다 (deulleotda)—never *들려 or *들렸다 (which come from 들리다 'to be heard').

들리다.etymology: Native Korean passive and causative verb descending from Middle Korean 들리다, formed from 듣다 ('to hear') + suffix -리- (or from 들다 'to lift' + -리-).

history.meaning: to be heard, let hear; to be lifted
to be heard, sound audible; to be lifted

들보.etymology: Native Korean architectural compound combining 들- (from 들다, 'to hold up, suspend across') and 보 (Middle Korean 보, 'crossbeam').

history.meaning: main overhead crossbeam
main ceiling beam, girder, tie beam

들어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 들어- (from 들다, 'to enter') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to go inside, enter
to go in, enter, fit inside, be required

들어가보다.etymology: A native Korean three-part serial verb construction formed from 들다 (deulda, 'to enter'; Middle Korean 들다, tulta) + -어 (-eo, connective) + 가다 (gada, 'to go'; Middle Korean 가다, kata), which together form 들어가다 ('to go in, enter'), followed by the connectivized auxiliary verb -아 보다 (-a boda, from 보다 'to see', Middle Korean 보다, pota, grammaticalized as an experiential or tentative auxiliary 'to try doing and see'). Literally 'to go inside and see how it is'.

history.meaning: to go inside + to see / try doing
to try going inside, to go in and check/see

morphemes.meaning: to go (deictic motion away from speaker)

들어가보다.notes: In standard Korean orthography, the main verb and auxiliary verb are spaced (들어가 보다), though in scripts and subtitles they are frequently written together as 들어가보다.

rootFamily.gloss: to come in, enter toward speaker

들어보다.etymology: A native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction combining 듣다 (deutda, ㄷ-irregular stem 듣-/들-, 'to hear, listen'; Middle Korean 듣다, tutta, stem 들-, tul- before vowels) with the infinitive suffix -어 (-eo) and the tentative/experiential auxiliary verb 보다 (boda, 'to see, to try doing'; Middle Korean 보다, pota). Literally 'to listen and see', it means 'to try listening to' or 'to hear someone out'. (In a secondary sense from 들다 'to lift', it can also mean 'to try lifting').

history.meaning: to hear / listen + to see / try
to listen to and see; to hear someone out; (also) to try lifting

morphemes.meaning: to try doing, test out (literally 'to see')

들어보다.notes: Because 듣다 ('to hear', ㄷ-irregular) and 들다 ('to lift' or 'to enter', ㄹ-stem) share the exact same conjugated form 들어, 들어보다 can mean 'to try listening' or 'to try lifting' depending on context.

들어서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb uniting 들다 ('to enter, move inward', connective 들어) with 서다 ('to stand, take up position'). Literally 'to enter and stand inside', it captures the moment a person crosses a threshold into a room, courtyard, or side street, rather than mere movement toward a place. By extension, Korean also uses 들어서다 when new shops or houses rise and take their place along a street.
들어서다.notes: Takes directional -(으)로 or locative -에 (골목으로 들어서다, 마당에 들어서다).

들어오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 들어- (from 들다, 'to enter') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to come inside, enter
to come in, enter (toward the speaker)

들어온다고.etymology: An inflected indirect quotative form of the native Korean compound verb 들어오다 (deureooda, 'to come in, enter, move in'), which combines 들다 (deulda, 'to enter'; Middle Korean 들다, tulta) + -어 (-eo) + 오다 (oda, 'to come'; Middle Korean 오다, wota). To this stem 들어오- are attached the present-tense processive adnominal/indicative marker -ㄴ- (-n-), the declarative ending -다 (-da), and the quotative particle -고 (-go), forming -ㄴ다고 ('[saying] that someone/something comes in or moves in').

history.meaning: to enter toward the speaker, to come inside
(saying/hearing) that someone comes in or moves in

morphemes.meaning: present indicative marker for action verbs

들어온다고.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes deictic direction: 들어오다 ('come in', toward where the speaker is) vs. 들어가다 ('go in', away from where the speaker is).

rootFamily.gloss: to come in, enter, move in

들여놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 들여- (from 들이다, causative of 들다, 'to bring inside') and 놓다 ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to bring inside and place (furniture, plants, or goods)

들여다보다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from 들이다 (deurida, 'to put in, direct inward', the causative of 들다 'to enter'; Middle Korean 드리다, tulita) + the infinitive linker -어 (-eo, contracting with 들리-/들이- to 들여-) + the directional particle/affix -다- (-da-, reinforcing direction toward a target, historically from 다가 'approaching') + 보다 (boda, 'to look, see'). Literally 'to direct one's gaze inward and look', hence 'to peer into, look closely inside, or examine'.

history.meaning: to direct inward + approaching + to look at
to peer into, look inside, examine closely

들여다보다.notes: Part of a symmetrical directional set of 'looking' verbs in Korean: 들여다보다 ('peer in'), 내다보다 ('look out'), 올려다보다 ('look up'), 내려다보다 ('look down'), 쳐다보다 ('stare up/at').

rootFamily.gloss: to look out (a window, into the future)
to bring in, let inside (causative of 들다)

들이다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 드리다, formed from 들다 ('to enter, go in') + causative suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to cause to enter, let in
to bring/let inside, spend (effort/time/money), dye

들이닥치다.etymology: A native Korean intensive compound verb formed from the verbal prefix 들이- (deuri-, derived from 들이다 'to drive inward, push in', causative of 들다 'to enter'; functioning as an intensive prefix meaning 'inward with sudden force or violence') and the verb 닥치다 (dakchida, 'to approach suddenly, surge upon, befall'; Middle Korean 닥티다, taktita). Together, it means 'to barge in suddenly, raid, or strike unexpectedly'.

history.meaning: inward forcefully + to surge upon or strike suddenly
to barge in, storm in, descend upon unexpectedly

morphemes.meaning: to approach suddenly, befall, surge upon

들이닥치다.notes: The prefix 들이- adds forceful, inward, or aggressive momentum to action verbs (compare 들이닥치다, 들이대다, 들이받다, 들이붓다).

rootFamily.gloss: to draw near, befall; (vulgar) to shut up
to push right up to, come on strong
to rush in, storm into a room

들이대다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb consisting of the intensive/directional prefix 들이- (deuri-, 'inward, forcefully toward a target', from 들이다 'to put in') and the verb 대다 (daeda, 'to touch, bring into contact, press against, supply'; Middle Korean 대다, tayta). Literally 'to thrust or press something right up against someone', it evolved the colloquial figurative sense of 'coming on strong, getting in someone's face, or aggressively making advances/arguments'.

history.meaning: inward forcefully + to put in contact with, press against
to thrust right in front of (e.g. a camera/mic); to come on strong, get pushy or flirt aggressively

morphemes.meaning: to touch, press against, bring into contact

들이대다.notes: In broadcasting and everyday slang, 카메라를 들이대다 means 'to shove a camera in someone's face', while 들이대다 alone often means 'to hit on someone aggressively' or 'to act pushy'.

rootFamily.gloss: to touch, put against, pull over (a car)
to barge in, storm in suddenly

들이마시다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed with the intensive inward prefix 들이- (derived from 들이다 'to bring/drive inward') attached to 마시다 ('to drink, draw in through the mouth or nose'). While 마시다 alone usually refers to drinking liquids, adding 들이- emphasizes drawing air, scent, or steam deep into the lungs. It pairs naturally with its antonym 내쉬다 ('to breathe out, exhale') in Korean descriptions of breathing.
들이마시다.notes: Pairs with 숨을 들이마시다 ('take a breath in') or 공기를 들이마시다 ('inhale air'); antonym is 내쉬다.

들이받다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the intensive/inward prefix 들이- (deuri-, 'forcefully inward/forward', from 들이다 'to drive in') and the verb 받다 (batda, 'to butt with the head, ram into, collide with'; Middle Korean 받다, patta, a distinct homonym of 받다 'to receive'). Literally 'to charge forward and ram head-on', it is used both for physical collisions (vehicles or horned animals) and figuratively for confronting authority head-on.

history.meaning: forcefully forward + to butt with the head or horns, ram into
to ram into, rear-end, butt head-on; to confront aggressively

morphemes.meaning: to butt, ram, strike with the head/front

들이받다.notes: Here 받다 is NOT 'to receive', but its native homonym meaning 'to headbutt / ram into' (as in 소가 뿔로 받다, 'a bull butts with its horns').

rootFamily.gloss: to butt with the head, ram into
to be rammed or hit by a vehicle (passive)
to thrust against, come on strong

들이붓다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb combining the intensive/inward prefix 들이- (deuri-, 'inward and forcefully', from 들이다 'to put in') with the ㅅ-irregular verb 붓다 (butda, stem 부어 before vowels; 'to pour liquid'; Middle Korean 븟다, pusta). Literally 'to pour right in heavily or non-stop', it describes dumping liquid (or torrential rain) into a space, as well as pouring massive money, time, or effort into an endeavor.

history.meaning: inward forcefully + to pour liquid, stream down
to pour right in heavily; to dump (water, alcohol, money, effort) into something

들이붓다.notes: Because 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb, the ㅅ drops before vowel-initial endings: 들이부어 (deuribueo), 들이부었다 (deuribueotda).

rootFamily.gloss: to pour liquid; (also homonym) to swell up
to pour out, dump out (antonymic prefix 퍼-)
to drink heavily, guzzle down liquid

들춰내다.etymology: A native Korean serial verb compound contracted from 들추어내다 (deulchueonaeda), which joins 들추다 (deulchuda, 'to lift up a cover, turn over, rummage'; derived from 들다 'to lift up' + intensive/transitive suffix -추-) with the connective -어 (-eo, contracting with -추- to -춰-) and 내다 (naeda, 'to put forth, bring out'; Middle Korean 내다, nayta). Literally 'to lift up a cover and bring out into the open', hence 'to dig up, unearth, or expose secrets, scandals, or the past'.

history.meaning: to lift up / turn over + to bring out into the open
to rummage and pull out; to dig up, expose, or unearth (secrets or past faults)

morphemes.meaning: to lift up, raise (들-) + intensive suffix (-추-) -> to turn up, rummage

들춰내다.notes: Often used when journalists or rivals dig up someone's buried past (과거를 들춰내다) or hidden weaknesses (약점을 들춰내다).

rootFamily.gloss: to lift up a edge/cover, rummage, expose
to lift up, hold; to enter

들켜지다.etymology: A colloquial double-passive native Korean verb formed by taking 들키다 (deulkida, 'to be caught in the act, be discovered, be found out'—already historically a passive/intransitive formation related to 들추다/들다 'to lift up/expose') and adding the auxiliary passive suffix -어지다 (-eojida, contracting with 들키- to 들켜지다). It emphasizes the spontaneous or involuntary state of a secret or hidden act becoming exposed or noticed.

history.meaning: to be caught in the act, be discovered
to get noticed, come to be discovered or exposed (colloquial double passive)

들켜지다.notes: Prescriptive Korean grammar considers 들켜지다 a redundant double passive (이중 피동) since 들키다 is already passive ('to be caught'), recommending 들키다 or 발각되다 in formal writing; however, 들켜지다 occurs in spoken dialogue to stress that something 'ends up getting noticed'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be caught, be found out (standard form)
to be revealed, come to light

들키다.etymology: A native Korean verb meaning 'to be caught in the act, be discovered, or have a secret found out'. Etymologically, it is an lexicalized passive formation (with the passive suffix -히- / -기- after an aspirated/velarized stem extension of 들-, 'to lift up, expose', akin to 들추다 'to lift up a cover and expose'). Because the hypothetical transitive base *들크다 no longer exists independently in Modern Korean, 들키다 functions as an independent verb taking an object marker (비밀을 들키다) or dative agent (남에게 들키다).

history.meaning: to have one's cover lifted, to be exposed/discovered
to be caught in the act, be found out, have one's secret discovered

morphemes.meaning: to lift up, uncover (historically related to 들다/들추다)

들키다.notes: Unusually for a passive verb, 들키다 can take a direct object with 을/를 specifying WHAT was discovered: 거짓말을 들키다 ('to get caught in a lie').

rootFamily.gloss: to lift up a cover, rummage, expose
to dig up, expose into the open

듯.etymology: A native Korean bound noun (의존 명사, uijon myeongsa) meaning 'appearance, manner, or likelihood, as if'. It descends directly from Middle Korean 듯 (tut) / ᄃᆞᆺ (tot), which functioned both as a bound noun meaning 'likeness, semblance' and as part of the similative endings -듯(이) and -듯 하다. It always requires a preceding adnominal modifier (-은/-는/-을 듯) to express conjecture ('appears to be') or comparison ('as if').

history.meaning: semblance, manner, as though, appearing to be
bound noun: appearance, likelihood ('as if, seems like')

듯.notes: Follows adnominal verb endings to show tense/aspect of the conjecture: 본 듯 (seems to have seen), 보는 듯 (seems to be seeing / as if seeing), 볼 듯 (seems likely to see).

rootFamily.gloss: to seem to be, appear as though
to seem, appear to be (auxiliary adjective)

듯하다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary adjective formed from the bound noun 듯 (Middle Korean 듯, 'seeming appearance, likelihood') + -하다.

history.meaning: to seem, appear as though
to seem like, appear to be

cognates.meaning: and so forth, et cetera; rank, class
et cetera, and so on; rank, grade, wait

등.etymology: A Sino-Korean bound noun derived from the Hanja 等 (등, deung), which in Classical Chinese originally denoted 'orderly rows of bamboo slips' (from 竹 'bamboo' + 寺 'government office/order') and hence 'rank, grade, class, equal', before grammaticalizing as a pluralizing and ejemplifying postnominal particle meaning 'and others of the same class, et cetera, and the like'. Note that Korean also has a native homonym 등 (Middle Korean 등, tung) meaning 'the back (of the body)'.

history.meaning: orderly bamboo slips; rank, class, grade; plural/exemplifying particle 'and the like, et cetera'
bound noun: and so on, et cetera, and the like; rank/tier

morphemes.meaning: rank, class, et cetera, and the like (等)

등.notes: Don't confuse Sino-Korean 등 (等, 'etc., and the like' or '1st/2nd place' as in 1등) with native Korean 등 ('back of the body', as in 등지다) or Sino-Korean 등 (燈, 'lamp/light').

rootFamily.gloss: et cetera, and so forth (reduplicated 等地/等等)
equality, being on the same rank (平等)

등기.etymology: Sino-Korean 등기 (登記), compounding 등 (登, 'ascend, enter in an official register') and 기 (記, 'record, write down').

history.meaning: official entry in a public register
property/title registration; registered mail (등기우편)

등불.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound descending from Middle Korean 등ㅅ불, combining Sino-Korean 등 (燈, 'lamp, lantern') with native 불 ('fire, light').

history.meaning: lamp flame, lantern light
lamp light, lantern light

등산.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun derived from 登山 (등산, deungsan), composed of the Hanja 登 (등, deung, 'to ascend, climb, mount up') and 山 (산, san, 'mountain, hill'). Attested in Classical Chinese since antiquity (e.g., Mencius and Tang poetry) in the literal Verb-Object structure 'to ascend a mountain', it denotes mountain hiking or mountaineering—one of South Korea's most popular recreational and social pastimes.

history.meaning: to ascend a mountain (verb-object construction)
mountain climbing, mountain hiking

등산.notes: In Korean corporate and social culture (especially among older generations and TV station bosses in *The Producers*), weekend 등산 is a classic mandatory-feeling team-building outing.

rootFamily.gloss: going to school (登校, ascending to school)

cognates.meaning: to appear on stage, make an entrance, enter the scene
to step onto the stage, make an appearance

등장하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 등장 (登場, deungjang, 'stepping onto the stage, making an entrance') and the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do'). 登場 is composed of 登 (등, deung, 'to ascend, mount, step up') and 場 (장, jang, 'stage, arena, site, open ground'). Originally a theatrical term for an actor stepping up onto the raised stage, it broadened to mean any person, character, or phenomenon appearing on the scene.

history.meaning: to step up onto a ceremonial/theatrical stage or threshing floor
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Meiji Japanese theatrical usage

history.meaning: to appear on stage; to make an entrance; to emerge on the scene

등장하다.notes: Used for dramatic or notable entrances of people, characters in a drama/show, or new products/trends entering society (antonym: 퇴장하다, 退場하다, 'to exit the stage').

rootFamily.gloss: characters in a play, novel, or drama (登場人物)
to exit the stage, leave the scene or field (退場하다)

cognates.meaning: to come on stage, appear on the scene

등장할지.etymology: An inflected interrogative/uncertain embedded form of 등장하다 (登場하다, deungjanghada, 'to appear on stage, make an entrance'), combining the Sino-Korean root 등장 (登 'ascend, step up' + 場 'stage, scene') + the verbalizer 하- (ha-) + the prospective/future adnominal suffix -ㄹ (-l) + the bound noun/ending 지 (ji, expressing an embedded question or uncertainty: 'whether/if [someone] will appear').

history.meaning: to step onto the stage + to do
whether (someone/something) will appear or make an entrance

morphemes.meaning: embedded question or uncertainty marker ('whether, if, who/what')

등장할지.notes: The ending -ㄹ지 is routinely paired with verbs of knowing or wondering, such as 누가 등장할지 궁금하다 ('I wonder who will make an appearance').

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on stage, make an entrance (登場하다)
characters in a story or show (登場人物)

등지다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the anatomical noun 등 (deung, 'the back of the body'; Middle Korean 등, tung) and the verb 지다 (jida, 'to carry on the back, bear, have at one's back'; Middle Korean 지다, cita). Originally meaning 'to have something at one's back' or 'to turn one's back toward someone', it developed the figurative meaning of 'to turn one's back on, alienate, become estranged from, or make an enemy of'.

history.form: 등 (tung, 'back') + 지다 (cita, 'to bear on the back')
history.meaning: to place at one's back; to turn one's back toward
to turn one's back on; to alienate, fall out with, or leave behind

morphemes.meaning: to bear on the back, face away from

등지다.notes: Can be used both as a single compound verb (세상을 등지다, 'to turn one's back on the world') and with the object particle (등을 지다, 'to alienate / become enemies with').

rootFamily.gloss: the back of the body, spine
to turn one's back on someone (idiomatic phrase)
to carry on one's back, bear a burden, or lose

cognates.meaning: the fourth letter of the Latin alphabet; abbreviation for Director/Day/Digital

디.etymology: A Korean loanword transcription (*외래어*) of the English letter name D (/diː/), the fourth letter of the Latin alphabet (which traces back through Latin D and Greek delta Δ to Phoenician daleth 'door'). In Korean broadcasting and television production (*프로듀사*), 디 (D) specifically represents the initialism for English Director, as found in 피디 (PD, 'Producer-Director' or 'Program Director') and 에프디 (FD, 'Floor Director').

history.meaning: fourth letter of the Latin alphabet; abbreviation for Director in broadcasting
the letter D; broadcasting abbreviation for Director (as in PD, FD)

morphemes.meaning: the Latin letter D; abbreviation for Director

디.notes: In Korean TV station jargon, PD (피디) combines P (Producer) and D (Director), and staff playfully break down or pun on the letters 피 (P) and 디 (D).

rootFamily.gloss: floor director on a TV set (FD)

디딤판.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native 디딤 (deverbal noun from 디디다, 'to step on, tread') with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 'board, plank, plate').

history.meaning: stepping board, stair tread, footboard

디저트.etymology: Borrowed from English dessert, which came from French dessert, a participial noun of desservir ('to clear the table', from des- 'un-, away' + servir 'to serve', ultimately Latin servire). Historically in European dining, dessert named the light sweet course brought out after the main dishes had been cleared away. Adapted into Korean phonology as 디저트, it coexists with Sino-Korean 후식 (後食, 'after-meal food'), often carrying a café or pastry nuance.
디저트.notes: Used especially for cakes, pastries, and café sweets; compare 후식 (後食) for traditional post-meal fruit or tea.

딛다.etymology: Native Korean verb contracted from 디디다 (Middle Korean 드듸다, 'to step on, tread on, set foot upon').

history.meaning: to step on, tread
to step on, set foot on

따다.etymology: A highly polysemous native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ᄠᆞ다 (ptota, 'to pluck, pick fruit/flowers, detach, scoop out') and ᄠᅡ다 (ptata). From the core physical action of 'plucking or detaching something from where it is fastened', its meaning expanded organically to 'popping open a sealed lid, bottle cap, or can', as well as 'winning points, prizes, or a license' and 'quoting an excerpt'.

history.meaning: to pluck, pick, detach, pull off
to pick (fruit); to pop open (a bottle/can/lock); to win/obtain (a prize, license, points); to quote

morphemes.meaning: to pluck, pick, pop open, win/obtain

따다.notes: When opening containers, Korean uses 열다 for doors/boxes, but 따다 specifically for popping off sealed caps, corks, or pull-tabs (맥주병을 따다, 캔을 따다).

rootFamily.gloss: bottle opener, corkscrew, can opener (literally 'thing that pops open')
to pick/pluck and bring, or to quote/borrow from (따오다)
to pick out, extract, win away

따뜻하다.etymology: Native Korean temperature adjective descending from Early Modern Korean 따듯하다 (tensed counterpart of Middle Korean 다슷하다, 'warm, genial').

history.meaning: to be warm
to be warm (of weather, objects, or heart)

따뜻해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 따뜻하다 ('to be warm') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to warm up, become warm

따라가다.etymology: A native Korean serial verb compound formed from 따르다 (ttareuda, 'to follow, go after, accompany'; Middle Korean ᄠᆞᄅᆞ다, ptolota, infinitive form ᄠᆞ라 -> 따라) + the infinitive linker -아 (-a) + 가다 (gada, 'to go, move away from the speaker'; Middle Korean 가다, kata). Literally 'to follow and go', it means 'to follow along after someone, accompany someone to a destination, or catch up with someone's level/pace'.

history.meaning: to follow and go after someone
to follow along to, go after, keep up with / match someone's skill

따라가다.notes: Used both for physically following someone to a place and figuratively for matching someone's skill or speed (그의 실력을 따라갈 수 없다, 'no one can match his skill').

rootFamily.gloss: to follow along toward the speaker (antonymic deictic center)
to follow around everywhere, tag along

따라다니다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb combining 따르다 (ttareuda, 'to follow, accompany'; Middle Korean ᄠᆞᄅᆞ다, ptolota) in its infinitive form 따라 (ttara) with 다니다 (danida, 'to go about, move around repeatedly, commute, frequent'; Middle Korean 녀다 / 다니다, tanita). Whereas 따라가다 describes a single directional movement following someone, 다니다 adds pluractional/iterative aspect, meaning 'to follow someone around everywhere, tag along, or shadow/pursue someone persistently'.

history.meaning: following + to go about repeatedly
to follow around everywhere, tag along, shadow, or court persistently

morphemes.meaning: to go around repeatedly, move about, attend

따라다니다.notes: Highlights repeated or continuous following—such as a rookie PD shadowing a senior producer all day, a fan following a celebrity, or rumors dogging someone everywhere.

rootFamily.gloss: to follow along to a destination (single direction)
to go around, commute, attend regularly

따라오다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 따라- (from 따르다, 'to follow') and 오다 ('to come').

history.meaning: to follow and come along
to follow (toward the speaker), come along with

따로.etymology: Native Korean adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᆞ로 (ttolo). It is analyzed as a lexicalized instrumental-directional adverb in -로 built on the fortis-reinforced root of 다르다 (Middle Korean 다ᄅᆞ다, "to be different, other"), literally meaning "by a different way" or "in a separate manner."

history.meaning: separately, apart from others
separately, individually, aside

morphemes.meaning: different, separate (fortis root related to 다르-)

따로.notes: Often reduplicated as 따로따로 ("each separately") or used in the dining phrase 따로 계산해 주세요 ("separate checks, please").

따르다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from two Middle Korean verbs that merged in form: 따르다 ('to follow, accompany, abide by') and 떠르다 ('to pour liquid into a cup or vessel').

history.meaning: to follow, accompany / to pour liquid
to follow, comply with; to pour (tea, water, wine)

따위.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅡ위, originally a neutral classifier meaning "sort, kind, class, or category" (compare the archaic compound 따위따위 "by category"). Over the 19th and 20th centuries, it underwent pejorative semantic shift to mean "the likes of" or "such trivial things."

history.meaning: kind, sort, category, class
and the like; the likes of (dismissive or derogatory)

따위.notes: In contemporary speech, attaching 따위 to a noun or pronoun (e.g., 나 따위가 "someone like me", 돈 따위 "mere money") strongly belittles the referent.

따지다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅡ지다, formed from the verb root 따- ("to pick apart, divide, distinguish") and the derivational suffix -지다. From the core sense of separating and telling things apart, it developed the meanings "to calculate precisely," "to look into closely," and "to argue over right and wrong."

history.meaning: to distinguish, tell apart, calculate
to examine closely, calculate, dispute or question

따지다.notes: In the fixed phrase 따지고 보면 ("if you look into it closely / strictly speaking"), it introduces a nuanced reassessment, whereas 따지다 alone often means "to talk back or argue."

딱.etymology: Native Korean mimetic and degree adverb meaning 'with a sharp snap/crack; right on the mark, exactly, firmly'.

history.meaning: sharply, abruptly, exactly
precisely, just, firmly; with a snap/thwack

딱딱하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 딱딱- ('hard, solid, stiff, unyielding') + -하다.

history.meaning: hard and rigid
to be hard, stiff, formal/rigid

딱딱해지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 딱딱하다 ('to be hard, stiff') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to harden, grow stiff or stale

딱지.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅡᆨ지 ("dried scab, stiff crust, paper patch"). It is derived from the ideophonic root 딱 (expressing something flat, hard, or adhering firmly to a surface) plus the nominalizing suffix -지. Its meaning expanded from scabs to folded paper game tiles and official penalty or disposal stickers.

history.meaning: scab, crust, stiff paper patch
scab; folded paper tile; official sticker or penalty ticket

morphemes.meaning: nominalizer for small objects or crusts

딱지.notes: Covers a vivid range of flat, stuck-on things: a wound scab, a folded paper slap-tile (딱지치기), a parking ticket, or a municipal bulky-waste disposal sticker (대형폐기물 스티커/딱지).

딱히.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from the ideophonic and descriptive root 딱 ("firmly, clear-cut, tightly," as in 딱하다 and 딱 잘라) combined with the deadjectival adverbial suffix -히. Originally meaning "firmly, definitely," it grammaticalized in Modern Korean primarily as a negative polarity adverb meaning "particularly" or "specifically (not)."

history.meaning: firmly, definitely, strictly
particularly, specifically (mainly with negative predicates)

딱히.notes: Almost always paired with a negative verb or standalone 아니요 (e.g., 딱히 없어요 "Nothing in particular"), functioning just like Japanese 別に (betsu ni).

딴.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᆞᆫ (tton). It represents a fossilized adnominal (-ㄴ) form of an old verb stem *ᄯᆞ- ("to be separate, different"), which is etymologically cognate with the root of 다르다 (Middle Korean 다ᄅᆞ다, "to be different") and 따로 (Middle Korean ᄯᆞ로, "separately").

history.meaning: other, different, separate
another, different, irrelevant, ulterior

딴.notes: Unlike 다른 ("other/different" in general), 딴 often carries a nuance of irrelevance, distraction, or straying from what one should be focusing on (e.g., 딴 사람, 딴생각).

딴생각.etymology: Compound noun formed from the native Korean determiner 딴 (Middle Korean ᄯᆞᆫ, "another, different") and 생각 (Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각, "thought, reflection," traditionally linked to Sino-Korean 生覺 or a lexicalized native noun). Literally "other thoughts," it denotes mental distraction, daydreaming, or harboring ulterior motives.

history.meaning: another thought, thinking of something else
daydreaming, distraction, ulterior motive, second thoughts

딴생각.notes: Depending on context, 딴생각 can be innocent ("daydreaming in class") or suspicious ("ulterior motives / cheating thoughts" in a relationship or contract).

딴생각하다.etymology: Compound verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다, "to do, think") to the compound noun 딴생각 (딴 "another, different" + 생각 "thought, idea"). Literally "to do other thoughts," it describes letting one's mind wander, daydreaming, or entertaining second or ulterior thoughts.

history.meaning: to think of something else
to daydream, be distracted, have second or ulterior thoughts

딴생각하다.notes: Often used as a warning—딴생각하지 마! ("Don't get any funny ideas!" or "Don't have second thoughts!").

rootFamily.gloss: to do something irrelevant, fool around

딴소리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining the determiner 딴 (Middle Korean ᄯᆞᆫ, "another, different") and the noun 소리 (Middle Korean 소리, "sound, voice, speech, remark"). Literally "a different sound or talk," it refers to an irrelevant remark, changing the subject, or backtracking on an earlier promise.

history.meaning: another sound, irrelevant talk
irrelevant remark, changing one's tune, going back on one's word

딴소리.notes: In conversation, 왜 또 딴소리야? ("Why are you changing your story now?") calls someone out for dodging the topic or contradicting a prior agreement.

rootFamily.gloss: to talk nonsense, change one's story

딸.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᆞᆯ (ttol) and earlier in the 12th-century Song-dynasty glossary Gyerim Yusa (鷄林類事) as 보달 (寶妲, *potal). The Middle Korean initial cluster ㅳ (pt-) arose when the first-syllable vowel of Old Korean *potal dropped via syncope.

history.meaning: daughter
daughter
daughter

딸.notes: Preserves one of Korean historical linguistics' clearest examples of vowel syncope turning a two-syllable word (*potal) into a tense-initial monosyllable (ᄯᆞᆯ > 딸).

딸기잼.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native Korean 딸기 (Middle Korean 떨기, 'berry, strawberry') with English loanword 잼 (jam).

history.meaning: strawberry jam

딸깍.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic adverb imitating the crisp metallic click of a latch, lock, or switch.

history.meaning: clicking or rattling sound of a small hard object
click, clack (of a latch, key, or switch)

딸리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᆞᆯ이다 (ttol.i.ta), derived by adding the passive suffix -이- (later assimilated to -리- after ㄹ) to the verb stem ᄯᆞᆯ- ("to follow, accompany, depend on," cognate with 따르다). It means "to be attached to, belong to, or have as dependents."

history.meaning: to be attached to, be accompanied by
to be attached/equipped with; to be burdened with dependents

딸리다.notes: Used both for physical amenities (가구가 딸린 방 "a furnished room") and family dependents (딸린 식구가 많다 "to have many mouths to feed").

땀.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᆞᆷ (ttom, with initial cluster ㅳ). Internal reconstruction links the root to the semantic field of heat and warmth (compare 따갑다 "burning hot," 따뜻하다 "warm") nominalized with the suffix -ㅁ, originally denoting moisture exuded from heat.

history.meaning: sweat, perspiration
sweat, perspiration; hard labor and effort

땀.notes: In Korean idioms, sweat is "poured" or "shed" (땀을 흘리다) rather than "broken," and pairs with 피 ("blood") in 피땀 ("blood and sweat / arduous toil").

땅.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄯᅡㅎ (ttah), a ㅎ-final noun (hence locative ᄯᅡ해 "on the ground"). During Early Modern Korean, the final -ㅎ dropped in citation form (leaving poetic/compound 따) while a velar nasal -ㅇ was generalized in ᄯᅡᆼ > 땅 to reinforce syllable weight.

history.meaning: earth, ground, land
ground, land, soil
ground, earth, territory, real estate

땅.notes: The older un-nasalized form 따 still survives in elevated expressions like 하늘과 따 차이 ("the difference between heaven and earth") and compounds like 따님/따지기.

땅속.etymology: Native Korean spatial compound combining 땅 ('earth, land, soil', from Middle Korean 딯/따ㅎ with initial cluster tensification) and 속 ('interior, inside'). Written as a single lexicalized noun in standard Korean orthography, it designates the subsurface layer of soil where roots, bulbs, and buried objects rest. It belongs to a productive native series with 물속 ('underwater') and 숲속 ('deep in the woods').
땅속.notes: Written as one word (땅속) without a space; pronounced [땅속] or [땅쏙].

때.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 때 ('time, moment, season, mealtime').

history.meaning: time, occasion, mealtime
time, moment, when (after -ㄹ/을)

때는.etymology: Topic-marked form of the native Korean noun 때 ("time, season, occasion") plus the topic/contrastive particle -는. The noun 때 is attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄢᅴ (pskuy), which evolved via monophthongization of ㅢ to ㅐ and reduction of the three-consonant cluster ㅲ to tense ㄸ in Early Modern Korean ᄯᅢ.

history.meaning: time, occasion, opportune moment
time, season, mealtime
as for the time; when, during the time of

때는.notes: As a narrative opener, 때는 바야흐로... ("The time was none other than...") sets the stage like "It was back in the days of..." in storytelling and variety captions.

때리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅢ리다 ("to strike, beat, slap"), developed via expressive initial fortition and vowel fronting from earlier 텨리다, an intensive/transitive derivative in -리- related to Middle Korean 티다 (Modern 치다, "to hit, strike").

history.meaning: to strike repeatedly, beat, slap
to hit, slap, beat, strike

때리다.notes: Beyond physical hitting, contemporary slang uses 때리다 for doing something boldly or abruptly, most famously in 멍때리다 ("to zone out / space out").

rootFamily.gloss: to quit abruptly, throw up a job
to beat down, catch by force

때마침.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb combining the noun 때 (Middle Korean ᄢᅴ, "time, moment, occasion") and the adverb 마침 ("just then, opportunely," derived from the verb root 맞- "to fit, hit the mark, meet" + nominal/adverbial suffix -ㅁ). Literally "fitting the moment," hence "just in time" or "opportunely."

history.meaning: fitting the moment, right on time
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (15th–18th c.)

history.meaning: just in time, opportunely, right at that moment

때마침.notes: More emphatic than 마침 alone, 때마침 highlights a fortunate coincidence in timing ("Right at that exact moment...").

rootFamily.gloss: right on time, at the proper time

때문.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested from Early Modern Korean as 때문 ('reason, cause, ground', almost always used with 에 or 이다).

history.meaning: reason, cause
because of, on account of (bound noun)

때우다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄠᆡ오다 (ptoy.wo.ta) and Early Modern Korean ᄯᅢ우다, originally meaning "to solder metal, plug a leak, or patch a hole in a pot." From plugging physical gaps (including dental cavities), it broadened to mean "to make do with (a quick meal)" or "to fill in for (a shift)."

history.meaning: to solder, patch a hole or crack in metal/pottery
to patch, mend, fill a gap
to solder, fill a tooth; to make do with; to fill in for someone

morphemes.meaning: to patch, solder, fill a gap, make do

때우다.notes: Used equally for dental work (충치를 때우다 "to get a cavity filled"), quick meals (점심을 라면으로 때우다 "to make do with ramyeon for lunch"), and covering a coworker's shift.

땡.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic noun and interjection imitating the sharp, resonant strike of a metal bell or gong (땡). In late 20th-century Korean broadcasting—most famously KBS's National Singing Contest (전국노래자랑)—a single bell strike (땡!) became the universal sound effect for disqualification, a wrong answer, or time running out.

history.meaning: clang or ring of a metal bell
clang of a bell; buzzer interjection for "wrong!" or "time's up!"

땡.notes: In Korean quiz and variety shows, 땡! ("Buzzer! Wrong!") is the universal opposite of 딩동댕! ("Ding-dong-dang! Correct!").

rootFamily.gloss: chime sound for a correct answer
to ring the closing bell, finish up

땡기다.etymology: Colloquial fortis and vowel-fronted variant of the native Korean verb 당기다 ("to pull, draw, attract, whet the appetite"), which is attested in Middle Korean as ᄃᆞᆫ기다 / 당기다. Through expressive initial tensification (ㄷ > ㄸ) and umlaut before -기- (ㅏ > ㅐ), 땡기다 came to express an intense pull or a strong craving for food or drink.

history.meaning: to pull, draw taut
to pull, attract, stimulate appetite (standard)
to pull tightly; to crave intensely (colloquial fortis variant)

morphemes.meaning: to pull, attract, crave (fortis variant of 당기-)

땡기다.notes: While prescriptive grammar prefers 당기다 (입맛이 당기다), in everyday speech 땡기다 (오늘 매운 게 땡긴다 "I'm really craving something spicy today") is far more natural and vivid.

rootFamily.gloss: to move up a date, advance in time

땡땡이.etymology: Native Korean colloquial noun derived from the reduplicated ideophonic root 땡땡 (expressing either small, taut, evenly spaced round dots or the clanging of a school bell) plus the nominalizing suffix -이. Consequently, 땡땡이 has two distinct colloquial senses: "polka-dot pattern" (standard 물방울무늬) and "playing hooky."

history.meaning: polka-dot pattern; truancy or playing hooky (from school-bell clang 땡땡)

morphemes.meaning: evenly spaced round spots / clanging bell (ideophonic)

땡땡이.notes: Watch the context: 땡땡이 셔츠 means a "polka-dot shirt," whereas 땡땡이 치다 means "to skip class/work and play hooky."

rootFamily.gloss: to play hooky, skip work or school
to be taut, firm, tightly swollen

떠나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 떠나다, formed from 뜨다 ('to rise, lift off from a spot') + 나다 ('to go out, emerge').

history.meaning: to rise and depart from a place
to leave, depart, set off

떠넘기고.etymology: Conjunctive form (-고 "and") of the native Korean compound verb 떠넘기다 ("to shift blame or work onto someone else"). It combines 떠- (infinitive of 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다, "to scoop up, lift") with 넘기다 ("to pass over, hand across," causative in -기- of 넘다 "to cross over"), literally "scooping up a burden and passing it over."

history.meaning: to scoop up and pass across
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: dumping (work/blame) on someone and; shifting responsibility and

떠넘기고.notes: Pairs naturally with 책임 ("responsibility"), 잘못 ("fault"), or 일 ("work") to describe palming off unwanted duties onto a junior colleague.

rootFamily.gloss: to shift blame or work onto others
to pass over, turn over, hand across
to take on, shoulder a burden oneself

떠돌다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb attested in Middle Korean as ᄠᅥ돌다, formed from 떠- (combining stem of 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다, "to float, rise from a surface") and 돌다 (Middle Korean 돌다, "to turn, go around, circulate"). Literally "to float and go around," it describes drifters wandering without roots or rumors circulating in public.

history.meaning: to float around, drift from place to place
to wander aimlessly, roam; to circulate (of rumors or stories)

떠돌다.notes: Frequently used in media and entertainment contexts for unverified rumors (떠도는 소문 "circulating rumors") as well as wandering drifters (떠돌이).

떠들다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄠᅥ들다 (pte.tul.ta), composed of 떠- (from ᄠᅳ다 "to float, rise, pry up") and 들다 ("to lift, raise"). Originally meaning "to lift or stir up together," it shifted in Early Modern Korean from "stirring up a commotion" to "making noise, chattering loudly, or clamoring."

history.meaning: to lift up together, stir up, agitate
to stir up a commotion, make a racket
to chatter loudly, make noise, clamor, spread talk

morphemes.meaning: to rise, pry or scoop up (from 뜨다)

떠들다.notes: Every Korean student knows the classroom command 떠들지 마! ("Stop talking / making noise!"), and the media phrase 세상이 떠들썩하다 ("the whole world is buzzing").

rootFamily.gloss: to be noisy, boisterous, in an uproar
to brag loudly, broadcast, make a fuss

떠들썩하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective derived from the stem of 떠들다 ('to make noise, chatter loudly') + expressive suffix -썩하다.

history.meaning: to be noisy, bustling, abuzz, uproarious

떠보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 떠- (combining form of 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다, "to scoop up, lift in the hand to heft") and the auxiliary/main verb 보다 (Middle Korean 보다, "to see, try, test"). Literally "to scoop/lift up and see how it weighs," it acquired the idiomatic sense "to sound someone out" or "probe someone's intentions."

history.meaning: to scoop or lift up to test; to probe
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: to sound someone out, test the waters, probe intentions

morphemes.meaning: to scoop, lift up to test (from 뜨다)

떠보다.notes: Often used with 마음 or 속마음 (속마음을 떠보다 "to sound out someone's true feelings") or by itself when someone asks a leading question to see how you react.

떠올리다.etymology: Native Korean compound causative verb composed of 떠- (from 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다, "to float, rise to the surface") and 올리다 (Middle Korean 올이다, "to raise, lift up," the causative of 오르다 "to ascend"). Literally "to make float up to the surface," it serves as the transitive partner of 떠오르다 ("to come to mind"), meaning "to recall, conjure up, or bring to mind."

history.meaning: to cause to float or rise upward
to float upward; to recall, recollect, bring to mind

morphemes.meaning: to raise, make ascend (causative of 오르다)

떠올리다.notes: Distinguish transitive 떠올리다 ("I recall a memory / bring an idea to mind") from intransitive 떠오르다 ("A memory/idea pops into my mind").

rootFamily.gloss: to rise to the surface, come to mind (intransitive)

떡.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄠᅥᆨ (ptek), with the initial ㅳ (pt-) cluster reflecting syncope of an earlier Old Korean first-syllable vowel. Philologists connect its root to Middle Korean ᄠᅵ다 (Modern 찌다, "to steam"), since traditional Korean rice cakes are made by steaming grain flour in an earthenware steamer (시루).

history.meaning: steamed or pounded grain cake
Korean steamed or pounded rice cake

떡.notes: Central to Korean idioms of unexpected luck or abundance: 누워서 떡 먹기 ("eating rice cake lying down" = a piece of cake) and 떡 본 김에 제사 지낸다 ("holding a ritual since you happened to see rice cake" = killing two birds with one stone).

떡볶이.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of 떡 (Middle Korean ᄠᅥᆨ, "rice cake"), 볶- (stem of 볶다, Middle Korean 복다, "to stir-fry, roast"), and the deverbal noun suffix -이. First recorded in the late 19th-century cookbook Siuijeonseo (시의전서) as ᄯᅥᆨ복기 for a savory soy-sauce court dish, it evolved in the 1950s in Sindang-dong, Seoul into the iconic spicy gochujang street dish.

history.meaning: cylindrical rice cakes stir-fried in soy sauce with beef and vegetables
braised or stir-fried spicy rice cakes (and royal soy-sauce varieties)

떡볶이.notes: Note the double ㄱ spelling in 떡볶이 (from 볶다 "to stir-fry"), pronounced [떡뽀끼]; its suffix -볶이 has spawned modern fusion names like 라볶이 (with ramyeon).

떡지다.etymology: Native Korean compound inchoative verb formed from the noun 떡 (Middle Korean ᄠᅥᆨ, "sticky pounded rice cake") and the verb 지다 (Middle Korean 디다, "to become, form into"). Literally "to turn into a sticky rice cake," it figuratively describes hair, fur, or fabric that clumps together and gets matted with oil, sweat, or dirt.

history.meaning: to clump into a sticky mass like pounded dough or rice cake
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (16th–19th c.)

history.meaning: to become clumped, matted, and greasy (especially of unwashed hair)

떡지다.notes: Most commonly heard in 머리가 떡졌다 ("My hair got all clumped and greasy") after pulling an all-nighter in an editing room without showering.

rootFamily.gloss: to become clumped, form a mass

떨다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄠᅥᆯ다 (ptel.ta), meaning "to shake, tremble, quiver, or knock off." In Modern Korean, besides physical shivering or trembling, it grammaticalized as an expressive transitive verb taking nouns of attitude or speech—literally "shaking out" or "displaying ostentatiously" (e.g., showing off, chattering, acting cute).

history.meaning: to shake, tremble, beat off dust
to tremble, shiver; to display or put on (airs, chatter, charm, fuss)

떨다.notes: When paired with attitude nouns—잘난 척을 떨다 / 유세를 떨다 ("to show off / flex"), 수다를 떨다 ("to chatter"), 애교를 떨다 ("to act cute")—it means "to put on a big display of."

떨리다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb descending from Middle Korean 떨리다, formed from 떨다 ('to shake, shiver') + suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be shaken, tremble
to tremble, quiver, feel nervous

떨어뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb formed from 떨어- (stem of 떨어지다, 'to fall') + intensive causative suffix -뜨리다.

history.meaning: to cause to fall, drop
to drop, let fall

떨어지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 떨어디다, from 떨다 ('to shake off, knock down') + auxiliary -어디다 (> -어지다).

history.meaning: to fall down, drop off
to fall, drop; to run out of; to be some distance away

떳떳하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅥᆺᄯᅥᆺᄒᆞ다, formed from the reduplicated ideophonic/descriptive root 떳떳- (expressing standing upright, open, and squarely in the open, related to 번듯하다 and 버젓하다) plus the adjective-forming light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). It means "honorable, aboveboard, and having a clear conscience."

history.meaning: to be upright, open, unashamed
to be honorable, aboveboard, have a clear conscience

떳떳하다.notes: Describes moral confidence when you have nothing to hide: 내가 떳떳하니까 ("Since my conscience is clear / Since I have nothing to be ashamed of").

rootFamily.gloss: honorably, squarely, with a clear conscience

떼다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 떼다 ('to detach, pull off, separate').

history.meaning: to detach, separate, unstick
to take off, peel off, remove (a label, seal, or gaze)

또.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 또 ('again, also, furthermore').

history.meaning: again, also, moreover
again, also, and then

또는.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) conjunctive adverb lexicalized from the adverb 또 (Middle Korean ᄯᅩ, 'again, also, furthermore') combined with the topic/contrastive particle -는 ('as for'). Through frequent use introducing an additional or alternative clause ('and as for another option...'), the sequence fused into a single coordinator meaning 'or, alternatively'.

history.meaning: again, also, moreover
furthermore, or else
or, alternatively

또는.notes: Unlike 공용/conversational 아니면 ('if not, or'), 또는 belongs to slightly more formal, written, or broadcast registers (e.g., contracts, news scripts, and narration).

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary (국립국어원 표준국어대사전) — 또는

또라이.etymology: Native Korean colloquial/slang noun (비속어) derived from 돌아이, a compound of the verb stem 돌- (from 돌다, 'to turn, spin; figuratively, to lose one's mind or go crazy') and the noun/suffix 아이 ('child, person'). Expressive initial tensification (경음화) shifted 돌- to 똘- (똘아이), which subsequently underwent resyllabification in casual speech to 또라이 ('person whose head has spun; nutcase').

history.meaning: to turn, revolve, spin around
person whose mind has turned; eccentric, nutcase
lunatic, nutcase, crazy person

morphemes.meaning: to turn, spin; to go crazy (from 돌다)

또라이.notes: While quite blunt and derogatory in serious contexts, friends and variety-show cast members frequently use 또라이 affectionately to mean an unpredictable 'madcap' or 'oddball'.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn, spin; to go crazy

또래.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᅩ래 ('group of the same age or class'). Philologists generally connect it to 돌 ('full cycle of a year, anniversary of birth', nominalized from 돌다 'to revolve, come full circle') with expressive initial tensification (ㄷ > ㄸ) and a collective/locative suffix -애, originally denoting children born within the same annual cycle.
