history.meaning: annual cycle, first-year birthday
group of equivalent age or category
peer group, people of the same age bracket

또래.notes: Because Korean social hierarchy and speech levels revolve tightly around age, 또래 refers not just to exact same-year peers (동갑) but to a comfortable 1-to-2-year age bracket of equals.

rootFamily.gloss: about the same age or size

또렷하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from expressive root 또렷- (light-vowel counterpart of 뚜렷-, 'clear, distinct, sharp') + -하다.

history.meaning: to be clear, distinct, vivid, sharp

똑같다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective combining emphatic adverb 똑 ('precisely, just') with 같다 ('to be the same').

history.meaning: to be exactly the same
to be identical, exactly alike

똑같이.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adverb formed from the ideophonic intensifier 똑 ('precisely, cleanly, with a sharp snap') + the adjective stem 같- (from 같다 'to be the same, identical', Middle Korean ᄀᆞᇀ다) + the deadjectival adverbial suffix -이. Literally 'in a manner that is snap-identical', hence 'in the exact same way, equally'.

history.meaning: equally, in the same manner
to be completely identical
in the exact same way, equally

똑같이.notes: Adding the prefix 똑- transforms 같아 ('like/similar') and 같이 ('together/alike') into an emphatic assertion of 100% identity or equal treatment ('without the slightest difference').

rootFamily.gloss: to be exactly the same, identical

똑똑이.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) deadjectival noun formed from the ideophonic root 똑똑 (representing crisp, distinct tapping sounds or clear-cut mental sharpness, as in 똑똑하다 'to be clear, articulate, clever') + the animate nominalizing suffix -이 ('person characterized by a trait'). Note that -이 is homophonous with the adverbial suffix in 똑똑히/똑같이, so context distinguishes the noun 'smart cookie' from the adverb 'clearly'.

history.meaning: to be distinct, clear-cut, unmistakable
to be smart, bright, articulate
a smart cookie, clever person (or adverb: clearly)

똑똑이.notes: The suffix -이 productively turns descriptive stems into affectionate or playful nicknames for people (e.g., 똑똑이 'smart cookie', 귀염둥이 'cutie', 겁쟁이/겁보 vs. 못난이 'ugly duckling').

rootFamily.gloss: sharp and capable reputation (as in 똑소리 나다)

똑똑하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated adjective formed from root 똑똑- ('clear, distinct, bright, sharp-witted') + -하다.

history.meaning: clear and distinct; intelligent
to be smart, clever, bright; clear/distinct

똑똑한.etymology: Adnominal (attributive) form of the native Korean adjective 똑똑하다 ('to be smart, clever; to be clear and distinct'), composed of the reduplicated ideophonic root 똑똑 (originally mimicking crisp, discrete knocking or dripping sounds, metaphorically extended to clear-cut speech and sharp intellect) + the adjective-forming suffix -하- + the adnominal modifier ending -ㄴ. Some 19th-century sources also associated it folk-etymologically with Sino-Korean 篤篤 ('earnest, thorough').

history.meaning: to be clear-cut, distinct, articulate
to be bright, intelligent, clear
smart, clever (attributive modifier)

똑똑한.notes: While 똑똑한 usually means 'smart/intelligent', its older sense of 'clear and distinct' survives in phrases like 똑똑한 발음 ('crisp pronunciation') and 똑똑히 봤다 ('I saw it clearly').

똑바로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb combining emphatic 똑 ('precisely, right') with 바로 ('straight, directly, upright').

history.meaning: straight, directly
straight, upright, properly, squarely

뚜껑.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 둿거우 / 뚜껑 (historically related to 덮다, 'to cover').

history.meaning: cover, lid
lid, cover, cap

뚫다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 둟다 / ᄠᅮᆶ다 (*twulhta* / *ptwulhta*, 'to bore a hole, pierce, penetrate'). It preserves the archaic root-final consonant cluster -ㅀ- (-lh-), which aspirates a following plain stop (e.g., 뚫다 [뚤타], 뚫고 [뚤코]) and drops its ㅎ before a vowel (뚫어 [뚜러]).

history.meaning: to bore a hole, pierce through
to pierce, penetrate, unclog
to pierce, drill, break through obstacles or traffic

뚫다.notes: Beyond physical piercing, 뚫다 is used metaphorically for breaking through heavy traffic (막히는 길을 뚫다), beating high competition odds (경쟁률을 뚫다), or securing a new business route.

rootFamily.gloss: to be pierced, unclogged, opened up
to develop a hole; (adverbially) staring intensely

뚫어주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound benefactive verb formed from the stem 뚫- (from 뚫다, Middle Korean 둟다 / ᄠᅮᆶ다 'to pierce, bore through, unblock') + the infinitive connective -어 + the auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다, 'to give; to perform an action for someone'). Literally 'to pierce or clear a blocked passage for someone's benefit'.

history.meaning: to pierce + to give
to pierce, unclog, or pry open for someone

뚫어주다.notes: In workplace and broadcasting slang, 뚫어주다 often means 'to open a door/connection for someone'—such as a veteran PD or manager securing a hard-to-get casting slot or sponsorship.

rootFamily.gloss: to be pierced, cleared, opened up

뛰다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 뛰다 ('to jump, leap, run; for the pulse/heart to beat').

history.meaning: to leap, jump, gallop
to run, jump, leap; to beat (of the heart)

뛰어가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb joining 뛰어- (from 뛰다, 'to run') and 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to run/leap and go
to run (toward a destination), go running

뛰어나다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adjective derived from the verb stem 뛰- (from 뛰다, Middle Korean ᄠᅱ다 'to jump, leap') + connective -어 + 나다 (Middle Korean 나다 'to come out, emerge'). Originally a spatial verb meaning 'to leap out ahead of the pack', it grammaticalized into a descriptive adjective meaning 'to stand out, be outstanding, excel'.

history.meaning: to leap + to emerge, come forth
to leap forth, surpass others
to be outstanding, exceptional, preeminent

뛰어나다.notes: Although built from two action verbs (뛰다 + 나다), 뛰어나다 conjugates as an adjective (descriptive verb) in Modern Korean: its attributive present form is 뛰어난 ('outstanding'), not *뛰어나는.

rootFamily.gloss: to stand out, be exquisite (synonymous native compound)

뛰어오다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) directional compound verb formed from 뛰- (from 뛰다, Middle Korean ᄠᅱ다 'to jump, leap, gallop, run') + the infinitive connective -어 + the deictic motion verb 오다 (Middle Korean 오다 'to come toward the speaker'). In Korean serial verb constructions, the first verb encodes manner of motion ('running') while the final verb encodes deictic path ('coming').

history.meaning: to leap, gallop + to come
to come leaping or running
to come running, rush over toward the speaker

뛰어오다.notes: Korean expresses English 'run here / run there / run in' by pairing the manner stem 뛰어- with directional verbs: 뛰어오다 ('come running'), 뛰어가다 ('go running'), 뛰어들다 ('rush in').

rootFamily.gloss: to go running, run away toward a destination

뛰어오르다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb combining 뛰다 ('to leap, bound, beat fast', Middle Korean  뛰다) in its infinitive form 뛰어 with 오르다 ('to rise, ascend', Middle Korean 오르다). Because 오르다 is ㄹ-irregular, its polite present and past forms double the liquid to 뛰어올라요 and 뛰어올랐어요. It is used both for physically leaping upward and for one's heart bounding in surprise.
뛰어오르다.notes: Conjugates as an ㄹ-irregular verb: 뛰어오르다 -> 뛰어올라요, 뛰어올랐어요, 뛰어오를.

뜨거워지다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 뜨겁다 ('to be hot') + inchoative auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to become hot, heat up

뜨겁다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 뜨겁다 ('to be hot to the touch, ardent').

history.meaning: to be hot
to be hot, scalding, passionate

뜨끈뜨끈하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) ideophonic adjective formed by full reduplication of the sensory root 뜨끈- (indicating deep, heavy, penetrating heat, etymologically sharing the initial thermal base *ptuk- of 뜨겁다 'to be hot', Middle Korean ᄠᅳ겁다) + the adjective-forming suffix -하다. Under Korean vowel-harmony symbolism, dark-vowel 뜨끈뜨끈하다 conveys heavier, more intense heat than its bright-vowel counterpart 따끈따끈하다 ('pleasantly warm, fresh-baked').

history.meaning: to be hot, burning
to feel deeply hot
to be piping hot, thoroughly heated

뜨끈뜨끈하다.notes: Koreans reach for 뜨끈뜨끈하다 specifically when praising soul-warming comfort foods like a steaming bowl of 국밥 (soup with rice) or a hot 온돌 floor on a freezing winter night after a shoot.

rootFamily.gloss: to be pleasantly warm, fresh out of the oven (bright vowel)

뜨다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb descending from Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다 (*ptuda*, 'to scoop up, ladle out, peel off a layer, take a pattern or rubbing'). From the traditional craft sense of lifting an impression or pattern off an original surface (본을 뜨다 'to take a mold/rubbing'), it extended in modern broadcasting and computing to 'copying, ripping, or capturing' a video/audio segment onto tape or disk.

history.meaning: to scoop up, peel off, lift a layer or impression
to trace a pattern, slice off, ladle out
to scoop; to take a mold/copy; to capture/rip media files

뜨다.notes: 뜨다 is one of Korean's most polysemous verbs: in a TV editing room, 가편집본을 뜨다 means 'to export/copy a rough cut', whereas 프로그램이 뜨다 (from homophonous 뜨다 'to rise/float') means 'the show becomes a hit'.

rootFamily.gloss: to model after, take a pattern or impression
to scoop out, slice or lift off a layer
to trace, copy by lifting an impression

뜬금없다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adjective formed from the noun 뜬금 + 없다 ('to lack, not exist', Middle Korean 없다). 뜬금 is composed of 뜬 (adnominal participle of 뜨다 'to float, be unanchored') + 금 (Middle Korean 금 'marked line, limit, or market price'), originally merchant jargon for a 'floating, fluctuating price' or an ungrounded measure; combined with 없다, it came to mean 'without any prior context, basis, or warning; out of the blue'.

history.meaning: to float + line/price + to lack
fluctuating market price; context or occasion
sudden, random, out of the blue, uncalled-for

morphemes.meaning: to lack, be without (stem of 없다)

뜬금없다.notes: Its adverbial form 뜬금없이 ('randomly, out of nowhere') is a staple of Korean conversation whenever someone changes the subject abruptly or makes an unexpected confession.

rootFamily.gloss: out of the blue, all of a sudden (adverb)
floating cloud; pipe dream (as in 뜬구름 잡다)

뜯어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 뜯다 ('to tear off, unseal, pluck apart') via connective -어 with 보다 ('to look at, inspect'). In concrete contexts such as sealed letters or parcels, it literally means breaking a seal or wrapper to see what is inside. Metaphorically, 'picking something apart with the eyes' developed the idiomatic sense of scrutinizing every fine detail of a face, drawing, or mechanism.
뜯어보다.notes: Has both the literal sense 'unseal/tear open to check' and the figurative sense 'inspect minutely' (찬찬히 뜯어보다).

뜻.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 뜻 ('mind, intention, will, meaning').

history.meaning: intention, will, meaning
meaning, sense; intention, will

띄다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb contracted from 뜨이다, the passive/causative derivative of 뜨다 (Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다 'to rise, float; to open the eyes') + suffix -이-. In the idiomatic collocation 눈에 띄다 ('to catch the eye, be noticeable, stand out'), the subject literally 'rises into or opens itself to the eye', hence 'to come into view, be spotted'.

history.meaning: to be seen, become visible, be raised into view
to be noticeable, catch the eye (uncontracted)
to catch sight of, stand out; to leave a space

띄다.notes: Be careful with Korean orthography: 눈에 띄다 ('to catch the eye') and 사이를 띄다 ('to leave a space') use 띄-, but when conjugated with -어 for word spacing, 뜨다/띄다 writes 띄어쓰기 ('word spacing').

rootFamily.gloss: to rise, float; to open one's eyes
to make float, launch, or space out

띄우다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) causative verb formed from the intransitive stem 뜨- (from 뜨다, Middle Korean ᄠᅳ다 'to float, rise into the air or water') + the composite causative suffix -이우- (-이- + -우-). Literally 'to cause to float or rise', it expanded from launching boats or kites to dispatching letters, leaving spaces between words, and colloquially 'lifting/hyping up' a mood or person.

history.meaning: to float, rise to the surface or sky
to cause to float, launch into water or air
to float, launch, send off, or hype up a mood/person

띄우다.notes: In social and entertainment settings, 분위기를 띄우다 means 'to liven up the mood/party', and 사람을 띄우다 means 'to flatter someone or hype them up as a star'.

rootFamily.gloss: to float, rise; to become popular/famous
to catch the eye; to space out
to flatter, boost, or hype someone up

띄워주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound benefactive verb combining 띄우- (from 띄우다 'to make float, launch; figuratively, to hype up or elevate someone', causative of 뜨다 'to float, rise') + connective -어 (contracting 띄우어 to 띄워) + auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's benefit'). In media and interpersonal contexts, it means 'to float something for someone' or 'to talk someone up, flatter them, and give them spotlight'.

history.meaning: to cause to float + to give
to float for someone; to boost, flatter, or promote someone

morphemes.meaning: to float, launch, hype up (stem of 띄우다)

띄워주다.notes: On Korean variety shows, hosts constantly practice 띄워주기—playfully exaggerating a guest's talent or status ('floating them up') to make them shine on camera.

rootFamily.gloss: to float, rise; to hit it big as a star
to back, support, or push someone forward

라고.etymology: Native Korean quotative particle used after vowel-final nouns (allomorph of 이라고) or in direct/indirect quotation (-라고 하다), combining declarative -라 and quotative -고.

history.meaning: quotative marker ('called..., saying...')
(said) that, called/named (quotative particle)

라디에이터.etymology: Borrowed from English radiator (from Latin radiāre, 'to emit rays/heat').

history.meaning: heating appliance or cooling heat exchanger
radiator (indoor heater)

라디오.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English radio (originally a clipping of radiotelegraphy), which derives from the Latin combining form radio- from radius ('spoke of a wheel, beam of light, ray'). The word entered Korean in the 1920s alongside the launch of Gyeongseong Broadcasting Station (JODK, 1927), the direct institutional ancestor of KBS.

history.meaning: wheel spoke, beam of light, ray
wireless audio transmission and receiver
radio broadcast or receiver

라디오.notes: Unlike native or Sino-Korean words where initial ㄹ shifts to ㄴ or ㅇ under the South Korean initial sound law (두음법칙), Western loanwords like 라디오 always keep their initial ㄹ.

라면.etymology: Sino-Korean / loanword (한자어·외래어) adapted in the early 1960s from Japanese ラーメン (rāmen, 拉麺), which itself was borrowed from Mandarin Chinese 拉麵 (lāmiàn, literally 'hand-pulled noodles': 拉 'to pull, stretch' [Korean Hanja reading 랍/라] + 麵 'wheat flour noodles' [Korean 면]). Following Samyang Foods' 1963 release of Korea's first instant fried noodles, Korean assimilated the word to the Sino-Korean reading 라면 (拉麵) and specialized its meaning to 'instant noodles'.

history.meaning: hand-pulled wheat flour noodles
broth noodle dish; instant noodles (1958+)
instant noodles (packaged or cup)

라면.notes: In Korean, 라면 always means packaged or cup instant noodles; if Koreans mean Japanese-style restaurant ramen with chashu and tonkotsu broth, they borrow the Japanese pronunciation directly as 라멘.

라벨.etymology: Borrowed from English label (influenced by continental European/Japanese pronunciation raberu), referring to an identifying tag or sticker.

history.meaning: identifying slip or sticker attached to an object
label, tag

라이벌.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English rival ('competitor vying for the same goal'), which entered English via Middle French from Classical Latin rivalis ('one who uses the same brook or stream as another; neighbor; competitor in love'), derived from rivus ('small stream, brook'). In Korean media and sports, 라이벌 denotes a peer competitor or ratings adversary.

history.meaning: person sharing the same irrigation stream; competitor in love
competitor striving for the same prize or status
rival, peer competitor

라이벌.notes: Korean pairs 라이벌 with Sino-Korean nouns like 라이벌 의식 ('sense of rivalry') or 라이벌전 ('rivalry match'), whereas its pure Sino-Korean synonym 경쟁자 (競爭者) sounds more formal and economic.

라이트.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English light (from Old English leoht 'brightness, luminous energy, lamp', from Proto-Germanic *liuhta, from Proto-Indo-European *leuk- 'bright, to shine'). While general 'light' is expressed by native Korean 빛 or 불, the loanword 라이트 narrowed in Korean to mean mechanical lighting equipment—specifically car headlights (clipped from 헤드라이트) or studio/stage lighting fixtures.

history.meaning: luminescence, daylight, lamp
electric lamp, vehicle headlight, stage illumination
automobile headlights; film/studio lighting rig

라이트.notes: When driving in Korea, 'Turn on your headlights' is 라이트 켜다 (short for 헤드라이트), whereas turning on a room light at home uses native 불을 켜다.

rootFamily.gloss: highlight, best scene of a broadcast

라인.etymology: Loanword (외래어) from English line, which derives via Old English line and Old French ligne from Latin linea ('linen thread, plumb-line, boundary stroke'), from linum ('flax, linen'). In Korean, 라인 underwent rich semantic expansion beyond physical lines to mean (1) facial or bodily silhouette ('profile line', e.g., V-라인, 턱선 라인), (2) an informal patronage clique or faction in politics and entertainment (라인을 타다), and (3) a narrative thread in broadcasting (러브라인).

history.meaning: linen string, plumb-line, drawn stroke
contour, boundary, queue, series
body/facial contour; patronage clique; narrative arc

라인.notes: In Korean entertainment and office culture, asking whose 라인 someone is on (누구 라인이야?) asks which senior star or executive's faction/inner circle backs them (e.g., 유재석 라인, 강호동 라인).

rootFamily.gloss: on-screen romantic storyline or couple arc

라임.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English lime ('tart green citrus fruit'), which entered English in the 17th century via French lime and Spanish lima from Arabic līma (ليمة), itself borrowed from Persian līmū (لیمو, 'citrus fruit, lemon/lime', cognitive with Sanskrit nimbū). (Note: in Korean hip-hop and poetry, homophonous 라임 separately transcribes English rhyme.)

history.meaning: citrus fruit, lemon or lime
small tart green citrus fruit
lime (citrus fruit); (homonym) poetic/rap rhyme

라임.notes: Because Korean lacks the English /r/ vs. /l/ distinction, 라임 is a double loanword: in cafés and kitchens it means 'lime' (citrus), while on music variety shows it means 'rhyme' (rap lyrics).

라준모.etymology: Sino-Korean personal name (인명 / 한자어) of the male lead character in the 2015 KBS drama The Producers (프로듀사), a veteran variety PD played by Cha Tae-hyun. The surname 라 (羅, Middle Chinese *la*, originally meaning 'bird-catching net' or 'fine silk gauze') is the historical and unassimilated variant of South Korean 나 (羅); the given name 준모 combines auspicious naming Hanja such as 준 (俊 'talented, eminent' or 準 'standard') and 모 (模 'model, pattern' or 謀 'counsel').

history.meaning: bird-net, silk gauze; ancient state and surname Luó/Ra
Korean clan surname Ra / Na (e.g., Naju Ra/Na clan)
Ra Joon-mo (fictional KBS 2 Days & 1 Night PD in The Producers)

라준모.notes: Although South Korea's initial sound law (두음법칙) normally converts surname 羅 from 라 to 나 (as in real-life star PD 나영석, on whom Ra Joon-mo is partly modeled), many families legally retain or restore the distinctive spelling 라.

rootFamily.gloss: to encompass, include comprehensively (網羅, literally 'net and bird-net')
Silla Kingdom (新羅, sharing the character 羅)

랜턴.etymology: Borrowed from English lantern (ultimately via Old French from Latin lanterna).

history.meaning: portable enclosed lamp
lantern, portable lamp

러그.etymology: Borrowed from English rug, denoting a thick woven floor mat or small carpet.

history.meaning: floor mat or small carpet
rug

러브라인.etymology: Korean-coined pseudo-Anglicism (외래어 합성어 / Konglish) compounded from English love (from Old English lufu 'affection, romantic attachment') + line (from Latin linea 'thread, connection'). Whereas English love line refers only to the heart crease in palmistry, Korean television writers and variety editors coined 러브라인 in the 1990s–2000s to describe an on-screen romantic subplot, coupling dynamic, or edited chemistry arc between cast members.

history.meaning: romantic affection + connecting thread or trajectory
scripted or edited romantic storyline/chemistry arc on TV

러브라인.notes: In Korean variety shows like Running Man or 2 Days & 1 Night (featured in The Producers), PDs and caption writers actively manufacture a 러브라인 ('love line') between two cast members through teasing subtitles and pink heart effects.

rootFamily.gloss: line, contour, faction, or narrative thread
love call, enthusiastic casting or recruitment offer (Konglish)

sources.title: Naver Korean Dictionary (Open Dictionary / 우리말샘) — 러브라인

러블리하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword-native adjective (외래어 + 고유어 파생어) formed from English lovely (from Old English luflic 'affectionate, lovable', from lufu 'love' + adjectival suffix -lic '-ly') + the productive Korean deadjectival suffix -하다 ('to be'). Borrowed in the 2000s via fashion magazines and entertainment media to describe an endearing, sweet, and effortlessly charming aesthetic or personality.

history.meaning: affectionate, lovable, amiable
delightfully charming, attractive
to be adorably charming, sweet, and lovely in style or persona

러블리하다.notes: In Korean pop culture, 러블리하다 is closely tied to actress Gong Hyo-jin (who plays Tak Ye-jin in The Producers), famously nicknamed '공블리' (Gong + Lovely) for her signature romantic-comedy charm.

cognates.meaning: setting a vessel afloat; debuting a new product or venture

런칭하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword-native verb (외래어 + 고유어 파생어) formed from English launching (gerund/verbal noun of launch, borrowed via Anglo-Norman launcher 'to hurl a lance, set a ship afloat', from Late Latin lanceare, from Latin lancea 'spear, lance') + the Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Following a systematic Korean borrowing pattern, the English verb is imported in its -ing nominalized form (런칭; prescribed standard spelling 론칭) before attaching -하다.

history.meaning: to hurl a lance; to slide a newly built vessel into the water
introducing a new enterprise, brand, or broadcast program
to launch a new TV program, brand, or product line

morphemes.meaning: launching, debuting a project or brand (from English launching)

런칭하다.notes: Korean almost always borrows English action verbs via their -ing gerund form + -하다 rather than the bare infinitive: 런칭하다 ('to launch'), 캐스팅하다 ('to cast'), 편집/에디팅하다 ('to edit'). Also note that while the National Institute of Korean Language prescribes 론칭하다, industry insiders overwhelmingly write and say 런칭하다.

rootFamily.gloss: launch, official debut of a show or brand

레.etymology: Borrowed from Italian musical solfège re, the second degree of the diatonic scale (or pitch D).

history.meaning: second solfège syllable (note D)
musical note D (re)

레몬.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English lemon, which traces back through Middle French limon and Medieval Italian limone to Arabic laymūn (لَيْمُون) and Persian līmū (لیمو, 'citrus fruit').

history.meaning: lemon, citrus fruit
yellow sour citrus fruit
lemon

레몬.notes: Word-initial English l- is written with ㄹ in Korean loanword orthography (레몬, 라디오, 램프).

레몬밤.etymology: Borrowed from English lemon balm, naming the perennial mint-family herb Melissa officinalis prized for its gentle lemon fragrance. In English, lemon entered via Old French limon and Arabic laymun from Persian, while balm comes via Old French basme from Latin balsamum and Greek balsamon ('fragrant resin, soothing aromatic'). Korean adapts the two-word botanical name as the single noun 레몬밤, widely used in gardening, herbal teas, and baking.
레몬밤.notes: Popular garden and herbal-tea plant in Korea alongside 박하 ('mint') and 로즈메리 ('rosemary').

레몬즙.etymology: Hybrid culinary compound combining the English loanword 레몬 ('lemon') with the Sino-Korean bound noun -즙 (汁, 진 즙, 'squeezed juice, sap, extract'). In Korean kitchen usage, 레몬즙 specifically denotes pure juice squeezed straight from a fresh lemon for baking, dressings, or curds, whereas 레몬 주스 refers to a sweetened beverage served in a glass.
레몬즙.notes: Distinguish culinary 레몬즙 ('squeezed lemon juice for cooking/baking') from beverage 레몬 주스.

레시피.etymology: Borrowed from English recipe, which derives directly from Latin recipe ('take!'), the second-person singular imperative of recipere ('to receive, take', from re- 'back' + capere 'to take'). In medieval and early modern Europe, physicians and cooks opened ingredient lists with the heading Recipe ('Take...'), which gradually became a noun for the formula itself. In modern Korean, 레시피 is standard in home cooking, bakeries, and cafés alongside native-Sino 조리법 (調理法).
레시피.notes: Often paired with 비밀 레시피 ('secret recipe') or 레시피를 적다/따라 하다 ('write down/follow a recipe').

레이스.etymology: Borrowed from English lace ('delicate openwork fabric', via Old French las from Latin laqueus 'noose, snare'); also homophonous with English race.

history.meaning: ornamental openwork fabric trimming
lace (fabric); race

렌즈.etymology: Borrowed from English lens (from Latin lēns, 'lentil', because a double-convex glass lens resembles the shape of a lentil seed).

history.meaning: lentil; curved optical glass
lens (optical lens, camera lens, contact lens)

렌치.etymology: Borrowed from English wrench, a hand tool used to grip and turn nuts or bolts.

history.meaning: tool for turning nuts and bolts
wrench, spanner

렌틸콩.etymology: Hybrid compound combining English loanword 렌틸 (lentil, from Old French lentille < Latin lēns) with native Korean 콩 ('bean, legume').

history.meaning: lentil legume
lentil, lentils

렌틸콩.notes: Shares its ultimate Latin root lēns ('lentil') with 렌즈 (lens), named for its biconvex lentil shape.

로드.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English road ('way, street, route'), which descends from Old English rad ('riding, horseback journey, expedition'), from Proto-Germanic *raido ('act of riding', nominal derivative of *ridana 'to ride'). In Korean entertainment and media, 로드 is especially productive in compound terms like 로드매니저 ('road manager' who drives and accompanies celebrities on field schedules) and 로드무비 ('road movie').

history.meaning: riding expedition, journey on horseback
public thoroughfare for vehicles and travelers
road, street route (especially in media, sports, and management compounds)

로드.notes: In the Korean entertainment industry (as seen throughout The Producers), a 로드매니저 (often shortened to 로드) is an entry-level manager responsible for driving the celebrity van and handling on-the-road logistics, distinct from a chief manager (실장/본부장) who negotiates contracts.

rootFamily.gloss: celebrity driver and field manager (road manager)
road movie, travel-format film or variety show

로비.etymology: Borrowed from English lobby, referring to the entrance hall or foyer of a hotel, theater, or large building.

history.meaning: entrance hall or foyer
lobby, foyer

롤.etymology: Borrowed from English roll, referring to a cylindrical roll of paper, fabric, or bread.

history.meaning: something rolled into a cylinder; bread roll
roll (of paper/fabric/bread)

룰.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English rule ('regulation, governing principle'), which entered Middle English via Old French reule from Classical Latin regula ('straight stick, measuring rod, pattern, standard'), derived from the verb regere ('to keep straight, guide, direct, rule'). In Korean, while formal laws use Sino-Korean 규칙 (規則) or 법칙 (法則), 룰 is the everyday word for game rules, sports regulations, and unspoken social codes (암묵적인 룰).

history.meaning: straight wooden bar, measuring ruler, standard pattern
code of conduct, governing principle, regulation
game rule, sports regulation, unspoken social rule

룰.notes: In Korean reality-variety shows like 2 Days & 1 Night, the PD's explanation of the 룰 (game rules for winning dinner or sleeping indoors) is the dramatic centerpiece of every episode.

rootFamily.gloss: game rules (especially in variety shows and sports)
local rule, house rule adapted to a specific setting
rule breaker, someone who defies conventions

를.etymology: Native Korean accusative (direct object) case particle used after vowel-final nouns, descending from Middle Korean 랄 / 를 (allomorph of 을).

history.meaning: accusative marker (post-vocalic)
direct object particle (after vowels)

리.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun (의존명사 / 한자어) derived from Hanja 理 (Middle Korean 리, 'veins in jade; natural order, principle, reason, logic'). In Old Chinese, 理 originally meant 'to carve jade following its natural grain' (combining the jade radical 王/玉 with the phonetic 里), evolving in Neo-Confucian philosophy into 'cosmic/rational principle'. In Modern South Korean, word-initial 理 dropped its ㄹ under the initial sound law (두음법칙) to become 이 (as in 이유 理由 'reason'), but as a post-adnominal dependent noun in -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 ('there is no reason/possibility that...'), it sits inside a phonological phrase and preserves its historical initial consonant 리.

history.meaning: to dress jade along its veins; natural order, governing principle
principle, reason, natural law
reason, logical possibility (bound noun in -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다/있다)

리.notes: Learners rarely realize that the 리 in 그럴 리가 없어! ('How could that possibly be! / There's no way!') is the exact same Hanja (理) as the 이 in 이유 (理由, 'reason') and 이치 (理致, 'logic')—preserved because bound nouns do not trigger the initial sound law!

리듬.etymology: Borrowed from English rhythm (ultimately from Ancient Greek rhythmós, 'measured motion, symmetry').

history.meaning: measured beat or recurring flow
rhythm

리본.etymology: Borrowed from English ribbon, referring to a narrow strip of fabric tied in a bow or used as trim.

history.meaning: narrow decorative band of fabric
ribbon, bow

cognates.meaning: exposure to danger, hazard, chance of loss

리스크.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English risk ('exposure to hazard or financial/reputational loss'), which entered English in the 17th century via French risque from early modern Italian risco / rischio ('peril, hazard', originally a Mediterranean maritime insurance term for danger encountered by cargo ships at sea). In Korean business and broadcasting, 리스크 is the standard term for project, ratings, or celebrity-scandal exposure.

history.meaning: maritime peril, hazard to insured cargo at sea
exposure to danger, chance of commercial or personal loss
business, financial, or reputational risk

리스크.notes: While native/Sino-Korean 위험 (危險) means immediate physical 'danger', 리스크 specifically denotes strategic, financial, or PR 'risk' (e.g., 출연자 리스크 'cast-member scandal risk' in TV production).

cognates.meaning: action or response triggered by a stimulus
expressive on-camera response in variety television

리액션.etymology: Borrowed from English reaction, from Medieval Latin reactionem ("a reciprocal action"), formed from Latin re- ("back, again") + actio ("a doing, performance"), from the verb agere ("to drive, do, act"). In South Korean broadcasting and variety television (예능), the loanword underwent semantic specialization to denote visible, camera-ready facial, vocal, or physical responses by cast members and studio audiences.

history.meaning: to drive, do, or perform an action
action performed in response to an event or stimulus
expressive on-camera or interpersonal response

morphemes.meaning: back, again, in response (from Latin re-)

리액션.notes: In Korean TV production, good 리액션 (expressive clapping, laughing, or gasping for the camera) is prized as a core skill for variety-show guests and audiences.

rootFamily.gloss: action; physical acting or stunt scene

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 리액션

리얼.etymology: Borrowed from English real, from Anglo-Norman real and Late Latin realis ("actual, relating to things themselves"), derived from Latin res ("thing, matter, fact"). In Korean television industry parlance, 리얼 functions both as a standalone clipping of 리얼 버라이어티 ("real variety", unscripted observational variety programs) and as a colloquial noun or modifier meaning "unscripted reality" or "for real".

history.meaning: thing, matter > relating to actual things
existing in fact, genuine, not artificial
unscripted reality television; genuineness

리얼.notes: In Korean variety production, calling a shoot 리얼 means the cast is filmed without a pre-written script or staged outcomes (as in 1박 2일 or Infinite Challenge).

rootFamily.gloss: to be realistic, vivid, or unscripted

cognates.meaning: creamy North Italian broth-cooked rice dish
Italian dish of rice cooked in stock

리조또.etymology: Borrowed from Italian risotto [riˈzɔtto], derived from riso ("rice") + the suffix -otto (originally a diminutive/augmentative suffix used in northern Italian dialects to designate specific culinary preparations). Italian riso traces back through Vulgar Latin risum and Classical Latin oryza to Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (oryza, "rice"), an ancient loanword from Indo-Iranian. While South Korea's National Institute of Korean Language prescribes 리소토, the popular spelling 리조또 captures Italian intervocalic [z] and geminate [tt] via Korean fortis ㄸ.

history.meaning: rice grain and plant
broth-simmered creamy northern Italian rice dish
Italian-style risotto dish in Korean dining

리조또.notes: Although official Korean loanword orthography writes 리소토 (avoiding tensed consonants like ㄸ in foreign borrowings), menus and speakers overwhelmingly use 리조또.

리프트.etymology: Borrowed from English lift, from Middle English liften ("to raise up"), borrowed from Old Norse lypta ("to raise, lift up"), a denominal verb derived from Proto-Germanic *luftuz ("air, sky, upper level", literally "to move into the air"). In Korean music-show and concert production (such as KBS Music Bank), 리프트 specifically denotes the high-speed hydraulic or mechanical stage lift (무대 리프트) that elevates K-pop performers through a trapdoor onto the stage deck.

history.meaning: air, sky > to raise into the air
act of raising; mechanical hoisting platform
hydraulic stage platform lift; ski chairlift

리프트.notes: Unlike British English where "lift" means a building's passenger elevator (Korean 엘리베이터), Korean 리프트 refers to hydraulic stage platforms, ski chairlifts, or automotive hoists.

rootFamily.gloss: hydraulic stage lift used in concerts and music shows

cognates.meaning: stage or broadcast rehearsal (often clipped to リハ)

리허설.etymology: Borrowed from English rehearsal, from Middle English rehersail ("repetition, recounting"), from Anglo-Norman rehercier ("to repeat, go over again"), formed from Old French re- ("again") + hercier ("to harrow a field, rake over"), from herce ("a harrow"), ultimately from Latin hirpex ("large rake"). Metaphorically, to rehearse was "to rake over the same ground again". In Korean broadcasting, it covers the sequence of dry rehearsal (드라이 리허설), camera rehearsal (카메라 리허설), and dress rehearsal before live air.

history.meaning: to harrow over again > repetition, recounting of words
practice session in preparation for a public performance
studio or stage run-through prior to broadcast or concert

리허설.notes: In Korean television studios, rehearsals are strictly tiered into 드라이 리허설 (blocking without cameras), 카메라 리허설 (camera/audio blocking), and 본방 (the live broadcast).

rootFamily.gloss: to rehearse a performance or broadcast
dry rehearsal without full camera or lighting setup
camera blocking rehearsal in a TV studio

링.etymology: Borrowed from English ring, denoting a circular metal band, hoop, or key ring.

history.meaning: circular band or hoop
ring, hoop, loop

마.etymology: Borrowed from Sino-Korean 麻 (삼 마, 'hemp, flax, bast fibre'), whose character depicts plant fibres hanging to dry under a shed roof. While native Korean 삼 refers specifically to hemp, Sino-Korean 마 serves as the general textile term covering crisp bast-fibre fabrics including hemp and linen, especially when modifying cloth items such as 마 식탁보 ('linen tablecloth').
마.notes: Placed directly before fabric or garment nouns (마 식탁보, 마 셔츠).

마감.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun (고유어) derived from the verb stem 막- (mak-, "to block, close off, stop, conclude") + the older vocalic nominalizing suffix -암 (-am, an archaic/lexicalized counterpart to productive -음), literally meaning "a closing off" or "shutting". Originally referring to closing commercial ledgers or shutting up shop at the end of a period, it specialized in modern publishing, journalism, and broadcasting into the standard word for a submission or production deadline.

history.meaning: blocking off, closing up, bringing to an end
closing of accounts or applications; submission deadline

마감.notes: While 데드라인 (deadline) is also used, 마감 is the everyday Korean term across newsrooms, editing bays, and application portals (e.g., 마감 시간 "closing/deadline time").

rootFamily.gloss: to close, finish up, or meet a deadline
to block, stop, close off (underlying verb root)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마감

마냥.etymology: Native Korean adverb (고유어) meaning "continuously, purely, unconditionally, simply to the full extent". Korean historical linguists connect it to Middle Korean 마장 (macang, "very much, to the utmost degree, all the way"), which underwent nasalization and palatalization of the final syllable in Early Modern Korean. A separate colloquial homophone 마냥 ("like, just as", attached to nouns) arose via dialectal phonological reduction of Sino-Korean 모양 (模樣, "shape, appearance, manner").

history.meaning: very much, to a great extent, all the way
purely, unconditionally, continually without reserve

마냥.notes: Distinguish standard adverb 마냥 before predicates (마냥 기쁘다 "to be purely/unconditionally happy") from colloquial noun-postposition 마냥 (아이마냥 "like a child", from 모양 模樣).

rootFamily.gloss: to be purely and innocently happy without worry
(archaic/dialectal) very much, to the fullest extent

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마냥

cognates.meaning: witch-hunt (sharing Sino-Japanese 魔女 + native hunting noun)

마녀사냥.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound (혼종어) formed as a modern loan translation (calque) of English witch-hunt: Sino-Korean 마녀 (魔女, "witch, female demon", from 魔 마 "demon, evil spirit, magic" + 女 녀 "woman") + native Korean 사냥 ("hunting, chase", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 사냥 sanyang, likely an early borrowing from a Jurchenic/Tungusic hunting term). In contemporary Korean media, it predominantly denotes collective public or internet persecution of a celebrity or public figure.

history.meaning: female demon/sorceress + game hunting in the field
historical European witch trials; figurative public/online persecution

마녀사냥.notes: In Korean journalism and entertainment shows, 마녀사냥 almost always refers to cyberbullying, trial by media, or netizens piling on a celebrity before facts are verified.

마누라냐.etymology: Inflected predicate form combining the native Korean noun 마누라 ("wife", blunt or familiar register) + the copula 이- (realized as zero after a vowel stem) + the plain interrogative sentence-final suffix -냐 ("is it / are you ...?"). Remarkably, in 15th–17th century Middle Korean, 마노라 (manwola) was a gender-neutral, supreme royal and aristocratic honorific meaning "Your Majesty / High Lord" (linked to 마루 "summit, ridge, head"). Over the late Joseon dynasty, the title underwent extreme semantic pejoration and narrowing: first to elderly noblewomen, then to "old woman", and finally to a man's blunt term for his wife.

history.meaning: Your Majesty, High Lord (supreme courtly title for royalty or masters)
elderly lady or mistress > familiar/blunt term for one's wife
are you (my) wife? (rhetorical rebuke to someone nagging)

마누라냐.notes: In Korean dramas, "너 내 마누라냐?" ("Are you my wife?") is a classic sarcastic retort when a colleague or friend nags excessively about one's personal habits.

rootFamily.gloss: noblewoman, madam (from the same honorific root 마루/마님)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마누라

마다하다.etymology: Native Korean verb lexicalized from 말다 ('to desist, decline') + declarative/quotative -다 + 하다 (literally 'to say no to, decline to do').

history.meaning: to refuse, decline
to refuse, turn down, shrink from (often in 마다하지 않다 'not hesitate/refuse')

마디.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 마대 ('joint or node of bamboo/bone; knot; musical measure; phrase of speech').

history.meaning: node of bamboo, joint, section
joint, node; musical bar/measure; word/phrase (한 마디)

마련.etymology: Originated in Joseon-era administrative Sino-Korean (이두/한자어) written 磨鍊 (마련), attested throughout the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty (朝鮮王朝實錄), from 磨 (마, "to grind, polish, hone") + 鍊 (련, "to smelt, refine metal, train"), literally "grinding and refining" and hence "working out a plan, preparing thoroughly". In modern Korean, alongside the full noun meaning "preparation, provision", it grammaticalized into a bound noun in -기 마련이다 / -(으)ㄹ 마련이다 meaning "it is pre-arranged by nature; bound to happen".

history.meaning: polishing and refining; formulating a state policy or preparation
preparation, arrangement; bound noun for natural inevitability (-기 마련이다)

마련.notes: Used in two distinct ways: as an action noun with 하다 (자금을 마련하다 "to secure/prepare funds") and as a grammatical pattern (-기 마련이다 "is bound to happen / only natural").

rootFamily.gloss: to be prepared, provided, or set up

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마련

마루.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 마루 / 마롤 (malo / malol, "ridge, summit, crest; raised wooden floor"), from a Proto-Koreanic root denoting the highest or central structural point. In traditional Korean architecture (한옥), 마루 referred to the elevated, ventilated wooden-plank hall (대청마루) connecting rooms; in modern urban housing and apartments, it shifted to mean either wooden flooring or the central family living room (거실).

history.meaning: mountain ridge, summit, roof ridge; raised wooden floor
wooden-floored central hall; living room in a modern home

morphemes.meaning: raised wooden floor, central living hall; ridge, crest

마루.notes: Older and colloquial speakers often say 마루 instead of Sino-Korean 거실 (居室) for the living room of an apartment, preserving the traditional hanok spatial term.

rootFamily.gloss: open wooden-floored central hall in a traditional hanok
mountain ridge or crest (preserving the original 'summit' sense)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마루

마루용.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Korean compound noun (혼종어) combining native Korean 마루 ("raised wooden floor, living room", from Middle Korean 마루 "ridge, wooden floor") + the productive Sino-Korean suffix -용 (用, "use, for the purpose of"). Literally "for living-room / wooden-floor use", designating household items (such as indoor slippers, cushions, or cleaning tools) meant strictly for the living-room floor as opposed to the bathroom (욕실용) or outdoors (실외용).

history.meaning: wooden floor / living hall + for the use of
designated for use on the living-room floor

morphemes.meaning: for the use or purpose of

마루용.notes: Korean homes strictly separate footwear and mats by zone: 마루용 슬리퍼 (living-room slippers) are never worn into the bathroom, which has its own 욕실용 슬리퍼.

마룻바닥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 마루 (Middle Korean 마루, 'raised wooden floor') + compound linker -ㅅ- (saisiot) + 바닥 ('floor, bottom surface').

history.meaning: wooden floor, floorboards

마르다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-irregular verb descending from Middle Korean 마르다 ('to become dry, dry up, grow thin').

history.meaning: to dry up, wither
to dry, run dry, become thin

마리.etymology: Native Korean bound classifier noun 마리, descending from Middle Korean 마리 ('head'), the older vowel-harmonic doublet of modern 머리 ('head'). Just as English counts livestock as 'twenty head of cattle', Korean grammaticalized the older form 마리 into the universal numeral classifier for animals, birds, fish, and insects while 머리 kept the anatomical meaning 'head'. It always combines with native Korean prenominal numerals such as 한 마리, 두 마리, and 세 마리.
마리.notes: Used only for non-human creatures; never used for people (use 명 or 분).

마무리되다.etymology: Native Korean compound passive/inchoative verb (고유어) formed from the noun 마무리 ("finishing touches, conclusion, wrap-up") + the passive/inchoative verbalizing suffix -되다 ("to become, be brought to"). The noun 마무리 derives from the verb 마무르다 ("to finish off, put in final order"), itself built on the older sartorial root 마르- (Middle Korean 마르- malo-, "to cut cloth to measure, tailor") — literally "to trim and hem a garment to completion".

history.meaning: to cut cloth to measure > to finish off neatly
to be wrapped up, brought to a conclusion

morphemes.meaning: passive/inchoative verbalizer: to become, be done

마무리되다.notes: Used when a project, broadcast shoot, or event naturally reaches its conclusion or is being wrapped up (e.g., 촬영이 잘 마무리되었다 "filming wrapped up well").

rootFamily.gloss: finishing touches, wrap-up; closer pitcher in baseball
to wrap up, finish off actively
to bring to a final close

마무리하다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb (고유어) combining the noun 마무리 ("finishing touches, wrap-up, completion", nominalized from 마무르다 "to finish off neatly, tidy up", ultimately from Middle Korean 마르- "to cut fabric to measure") + the active verbalizer -하다 ("to do, make"). In television and film production, 마무리하다 is the standard expression for wrapping up a day's shoot, a live broadcast segment, or post-production editing.

history.meaning: to finish off a piece of work > final touches, completion
to wrap up, conclude, put the finishing touches on

마무리하다.notes: Unlike 끝내다 ("to end/terminate", which focuses simply on stopping), 마무리하다 emphasizes tidying up loose ends and bringing something to a polished close.

rootFamily.gloss: to be wrapped up or concluded (passive)
to finish off, put in final order

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마무리하다

마법.etymology: Sino-Korean 마법 (魔法), compounding 마 (魔, 'demon, supernatural spirit') and 법 (法, 'art, method, law').

history.meaning: supernatural art or sorcery
magic, spell, wizardry

cognates.meaning: coarse yellow strawboard, cardboard (literal source of the Korean loan)

마분지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (한자어) written 馬糞紙 (마분지), borrowed from Meiji-era Japanese 馬糞紙 (babunshi), literally "horse-dung paper", composed of 馬 (마, "horse") + 糞 (분, "dung, manure, excrement") + 紙 (지, "paper"). Coined in late 19th-century Japan when cheap, unbleached paperboard manufactured from rice-straw pulp exhibited a coarse, fibrous, yellowish-brown texture strongly resembling dried horse manure. In modern Korean, the literal imagery has faded and it simply means thick, rough cardboard or chipboard.

history.meaning: coarse yellowish-brown strawboard resembling dried horse manure
thick coarse cardboard, chipboard, or paperboard

마분지.notes: Most Korean speakers use 마분지 for craft cardboard or stiff paperboard without realizing its Hanja (馬糞紙) literally translate to "horse-manure paper".

rootFamily.gloss: blank white sheet of paper (白紙)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마분지

마셔보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb construction (고유어) formed from 마시- (stem of 마시다 "to drink, swallow liquid", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 마시- masi-) + the infinitive/connective suffix -어 (contracting with 시 to 셔) + the experiential auxiliary verb 보다 ("to try doing, experience", grammaticalized from the lexical verb 보다 "to see, look at", Middle Korean 보- pwo-). Literally "to drink and see (how it is)", illustrating the cross-linguistically common grammaticalization of visual perception into an experiential or conative auxiliary.

history.meaning: to drink + and see / try experiencing
to try drinking, take a sip to taste or experience

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective linker (fused with 시 as 셔)
experiential auxiliary verb: to try doing (literally 'to see')

마셔보다.notes: In standard Korean spacing rules, main verb + auxiliary verb can be written spaced (마셔 보다) or fused (마셔보다); adding 보다 softens invitations (한번 마셔 봐 "give it a try/sip").

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look at; to try doing (auxiliary)

cognates.meaning: hygienic face mask; actor's facial features in showbiz slang

마스크.etymology: Borrowed from English mask (and French masque, partly via Japanese マスク masuku), from Middle French masque ("face covering"), from Old Italian maschera, derived from Medieval Latin masca ("mask, specter") and/or Arabic maskhara (مَسْخَرَة, "buffoon, mockery"). Alongside its literal meaning of a hygienic or protective face mask, Korean entertainment and casting terminology uses 마스크 (echoing French masque in theatrical arts) to mean an actor's or idol's facial bone structure, screen visage, or visual appeal.

history.meaning: theatrical disguise or face covering; facial visage
hygienic/protective face mask; an actor's facial features or look

morphemes.meaning: face mask; facial features/visage on screen

마스크.notes: When a Korean casting director or PD says "마스크가 좋다" or "마스크가 매력적이다", they mean the person has striking, camera-friendly facial features — not that they are wearing a mask!

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마스크

cognates.meaning: passkey designed to open multiple locks

마스터키.etymology: Borrowed from English master key, a compound of master (from Middle English maister, Old French maistre, from Latin magister "chief, director, teacher", built on the comparative root magis "more") + key (from Middle English keye, Old English cǣg "key, solution"). In Korean, it denotes both a physical or electronic passkey that unlocks every door in a building and, figuratively in television variety games, an all-purpose wildcard or solution.

history.meaning: chief/director + key > passkey opening all locks in a set
building passkey; figurative all-access wildcard in games/TV

마스터키.notes: Often contrasted with a standard 열쇠 (native Korean for key) or 카드키 (electronic keycard); in Korean dramas, a building's 마스터키 is a frequent plot device for unexpected room entries.

rootFamily.gloss: master, expert; master recording tape in broadcasting
to master a skill or subject completely

마시다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 마시다 ('to drink liquid, breathe in').

history.meaning: to drink
to drink; to inhale (fresh air)

마음.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 마음 ('heart, mind, inner spirit, intention').

history.meaning: heart, mind, disposition
heart, mind, feeling, inclination

마음가짐.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) composed of 마음 ("heart, mind, spirit", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄆᆞᄉᆞᆷ mosom) + 가짐 ("holding, keeping, bearing", the substantivized -ㅁ nominalization of the verb 가지다 "to have, hold, possess", Middle Korean 가지- kaci-). Literally "the way one holds or carries one's mind", forming a transparent parallel with 몸가짐 ("physical deportment, how one carries one's body").

history.meaning: heart/mind + holding/keeping + nominalizer
mental attitude, mindset, inner resolve

마음가짐.notes: Pairs naturally with 몸가짐 ("physical bearing/conduct"): 마음가짐 is one's internal mental posture or attitude toward a task, whereas 몸가짐 is one's external behavior.

rootFamily.gloss: physical deportment, how one carries oneself

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마음가짐

마음껏.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb built from 마음 ('heart, mind, spirit', Middle Korean ᄆᆞᅀᆞᆷ) and the productive degree suffix -껏 ('to the utmost extent of'). Literally meaning 'as much as one's heart holds', it follows the same morphological pattern as 힘껏 ('with all one's strength') and 정성껏 ('with all one's devotion').
마음껏.notes: Pronounced [마음껃] with automatic tensification of the suffix -껏.

마음대로.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb (고유어) formed from 마음 ("heart, mind, wish", from Middle Korean ᄆᆞᄉᆞᆷ mosom, which underwent regular lenition and loss of intervocalic 반치음 ㅿ /z/ and the shift of ㆍ arae-a to ㅏ in the first syllable and ㅡ in the second) + the particle 대로 ("in accordance with, just as", grammaticalized from the bound noun 대 + instrumental -로). Literally "according to one's heart", hence "as one pleases, freely, at will".

history.meaning: heart, mind, intention
according to one's wishes, as one pleases, freely

마음대로.notes: In spoken Korean, 마음대로 is very frequently contracted to 맘대로 (e.g., 네 맘대로 해! "Do whatever you want!"), which can sound either permissive or exasperated depending on tone.

rootFamily.gloss: heart, mind, inclination (often contracted to 맘)
colloquial contracted form of 마음대로 ('as one pleases')
according to one's will or purpose

마음속.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) combining 마음 ("heart, mind, spirit", from Middle Korean ᄆᆞᄉᆞᆷ mosom) + 속 ("inside, interior, depths", attested in Middle Korean as 솏 swok, "inner part, core"). Literally "the interior of the heart/mind", referring to the private, unvoiced realm of a person's emotions and thoughts. By switching the order of the two morphemes, Korean also forms 속마음 ("one's hidden/true feelings").

history.meaning: heart/mind + interior, core
the depths of one's heart, one's inner mind

마음속.notes: Compare the reversible pair 마음속 ("inside one's heart", a location noun: 마음속에 담아 두다 "to keep inside one's heart") and 속마음 ("inner/true feelings", a psychological noun: 속마음을 털어놓다 "to confess one's true feelings").

rootFamily.gloss: one's true, hidden inner feelings (reversed compound)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마음속

cognates.meaning: belonging to me (first-person singular possessive determiner)

마이.etymology: Borrowed from the English first-person singular possessive determiner my, which developed in Middle English (mi) via loss of final -n before consonants from Old English min ("my, mine"), from Proto-Germanic *minaz, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European first-person oblique stem *me-. In Korean dialogue and variety television, 마이 occurs in borrowed exclamations (such as 오 마이 갓! "oh my God!") and productive Konglish compounds like 마이웨이 ("my way", acting independently regardless of others' opinions).

history.meaning: of me, belonging to me (first-person possessive)
my (in English-derived exclamations and Konglish compounds)

마이.notes: In Korean pop culture, 마이 appears constantly in exclamations (오 마이 갓!) and slang like 마이웨이 (going "my way" unbothered by social pressure); watch out for the Gyeongsang dialect homophone 마이 (a colloquial reduction of 많이 "a lot").

rootFamily.gloss: going one's own way regardless of others (from 'my way')
oh my God! (common exclamation of shock)
one's own private automobile (from Japanese/Korean 'my car')

마이크.etymology: Clipped loanword (외래어) from English microphone (or its colloquial English clipping mike/mic, reinforced via Japanese マイク maiku). English microphone was coined in the 17th–19th centuries from Neo-Latin/Greek combining forms micro- (from Ancient Greek μικρός mikros, "small") + -phone (from Ancient Greek φωνή phone, "voice, sound"), originally denoting an instrument that amplifies faint sounds. In Korean broadcasting studios, 마이크 is the universal term for all studio, lapel, and boom microphones.

history.meaning: small + voice/sound > instrument for amplifying faint sounds or converting voice to electrical signals
microphone (handheld, boom, or lapel mic in broadcasting)

마이크.notes: On Korean TV sets like The Producers, cast and crew constantly refer to specific subtypes: 핀마이크 (clip-on lavalier mic), 붐마이크 (overhead boom mic), and 와이어리스 마이크 (wireless mic).

rootFamily.gloss: clip-on lapel/lavalier microphone worn on clothing
overhead directional boom microphone on a pole

마주.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 마조, derived from the stem 맞- of 맞다 ('to face, meet') + adverbial suffix -오/-우.

history.meaning: facing each other, opposite
face to face, opposite each other

마지막.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'the last, final moment or item', formed from the stem of 마치다/맞다 ('to finish, conclude') + nominal suffix -막.

history.meaning: final point, end
the last, final

마찬가지.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어) formed by the phonological fusion of a 15th-century Middle Korean phrase attested as 마초 한가지 (machwo hankaci), composed of 마초 (adverbial derivative of 마초다, modern 맞추다 "to match, fit together, compare", causative of 맞다 "to fit, be right") + 한가지 ("one and the same kind", from 한 "one, same" + 가지 "kind, sort, branch"). Through Early Modern Korean contraction and loss of intervocalic ㅎ (마초한가지 > 마찬가지 > 마찬가지), the phrase lexicalized into an opaque single noun meaning "the exact same thing, no different".

history.meaning: matching together as one and the same kind
the exact same thing, identical situation or case

morphemes.meaning: matched together as one (contracted from Middle Korean 마초 'matching' + 한 'one')

마찬가지.notes: Although modern speakers feel 마찬가지 is a single unanalyzable word, its second half is the familiar noun 가지 ("kind/sort"), and it literally meant "matched into one kind".

rootFamily.gloss: one and the same kind; one thing
to match, compare, fit together (source of initial 마찬-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마찬가지

마치다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 마초다 and ᄆᆞᄎᆞ다 / ᄆᆞᆺ히다 (built on the intransitive Middle Korean verb root ᄆᆞᆺ- mot-, "to end, come to a close, reach completion", related to 맏 "first/extremity" and 마지막 "last" + the causative/transitive suffix -히-/-오-). With the regular merger of Middle Korean ㆍ (arae-a) into ㅏ in initial syllables and palatalization before ㅣ, ᄆᆞᆺ히다 evolved into modern 마치다 ("to finish, complete, bring to an end").

history.meaning: to come to an end > to bring to completion, finish
to finish, complete, conclude (a task, broadcast, or ceremony)

morphemes.meaning: to finish, bring to completion (from Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆺ- + transitive suffix)

마치다.notes: Do not confuse homophones 마치다 ("to finish, conclude": 방송을 마치다) and 맞히다 (pronounced identically [마치다], "to hit a target / guess an answer correctly": 정답을 맞히다).

rootFamily.gloss: finally, at long last, in the end
full stop, period punctuation mark (literally 'finishing dot')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 마치다

마침.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 마참 / 마침, related to 맞다 ('to fit the moment, hit the mark') and 마치다 ('to finish').

history.meaning: just at the right moment
just then, opportunely, as it happened

마침내.etymology: Native Korean adverb lexicalized from 마침 ('finishing, completion', nominalization of 마치다 'to finish, complete', Middle Korean ᄆᆞᄎᆞᆷ) plus 내 ('throughout, to the end'). Attested in Middle Korean as ᄆᆞᄎᆞᆷ내 ('in the end, ultimately'), it carries a sense of culmination after a long wait or sustained effort, unlike 드디어 which can mark any awaited arrival.
마침내.notes: Common in storytelling and emotional turning points.

마트.etymology: Borrowed from English mart (popularized in South Korea via discount-store chains and clipped from supermarket).

history.meaning: retail market or grocery store
supermarket, grocery store

마포대교.etymology: Sino-Korean proper noun (한자어) written 麻浦大橋 (마포대교), naming the 1.4-kilometer bridge across the Han River in Seoul linking Mapo District (마포구, 麻浦區) on the northern bank directly to Yeouido (여의도) on the southern side. Composed of 麻 (마, "hemp") + 浦 (포, "riverbank, estuary, ferry port" — 麻浦 was a major Joseon-era river port where hemp, salt, and grain ferries docked) + 大 (대, "great, large") + 橋 (교, "bridge"). Completed in 1970 as 서울대교 ("Seoul Bridge") and officially renamed 마포대교 in 1984.

history.meaning: Hemp Ferry Port along the Han River in Joseon-era Hanyang (Seoul)
Grand Mapo Bridge connecting Mapo-gu and Yeouido across the Han River

마포대교.notes: Because KBS headquarters and major financial firms sit on Yeouido right at the southern end of 마포대교, the bridge is a constant commuter landmark in broadcasting dramas like The Producers.

rootFamily.gloss: Mapo district and historic Han River ferry port (麻浦)
grand bridge, major highway bridge (大橋)
Hangang Bridge spanning the Han River (漢江大橋)

마흔.etymology: Native Korean decadal numeral for forty, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 마ᅀᆞᆫ (mason), where the medial voiced fricative ㅿ (z) subsequently lenited to zero in the 16th century and gained an aspirate-like velar/glottal onset in Early Modern Korean 마흔 (maheun). It belongs to the native Korean decadal series (스물 20, 서른 30, 마흔 40, 쉰 50) used with native classifiers for counting tangible items, people, and human age. Unlike 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물, 마흔 does not change shape when placed directly before a counter noun.

history.meaning: forty (native numeral)
forty (after loss of ㅿ and epenthetic ㅎ)
forty (used with native counters and age)

마흔.notes: Used with native counters (마흔 개 'forty pieces', 마흔 살 'forty years old'), whereas Sino-Korean 사십 (四十) is used for minutes, prices, and room numbers.

cognates.meaning: stage curtain; act of a play; shogunate tent government (bakufu)
curtain, screen; act of a play or drama

막.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written 幕 (막, "tent, curtain, screen; theatrical act"), from Middle Chinese mak (幕), a phono-semantic compound of semantic 巾 ("cloth") and phonetic 莫 (mak). In Classical Chinese, 幕 denoted an overhead canopy or military command tent (as in 幕府 막부 "tent government"); in modern East Asian theater and broadcasting, it came to designate both the stage curtain that separates scenes and each numbered "act" of a play, opera, or unfolding public drama.

history.meaning: cloth canopy, military field tent, curtain screen
stage curtain; act or phase of a theatrical performance or event

막.notes: Used in core theatrical metaphors like 막이 오르다 ("the curtain rises / an event begins") and 막을 내리다 ("to lower the curtain / bring a show or era to a close").

rootFamily.gloss: opening of a curtain, theater season, or festival (開幕)
closing of a curtain, show, or event (閉幕)
intermission or interval between theatrical acts (幕間)

막내.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) formed from the prefix 막- ("last, final, closing", derived from the verb stem 막- "to close off, block, bring to an end") + -내, a phonological reduction of 나히 / 낳이 ("one who is born", from the native verb stem 낳- "to give birth, bear", Middle Korean 낳- nah-, + the animate/person nominalizing suffix -이). Literally "the last-born person". From its kinship sense of the youngest child in a family, it extended across Korean institutional culture to mean the youngest or most junior member of any group, idol band, or TV production crew.

history.meaning: last + to bear/give birth + person nominalizer ('the last-born one')
youngest child in a family; most junior member of a team or group

morphemes.meaning: last, final, closing (from 막- 'to close off')
one born (contracted from 낳- 'to give birth' + nominalizer -이)

막내.notes: In Korean TV production (like The Producers), the 막내 PD or 막내 작가 ("maknae PD/writer") is the newest, lowest-ranking rookie responsible for errands, slate-clapping, and cue sheets.

rootFamily.gloss: to give birth to, bear (underlying verbal root of -내)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 막내

막다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 막다 ('to block, stop up, obstruct, keep out').

history.meaning: to block, obstruct, ward off
to block, stop, prevent, shield from

막말로.etymology: Native Korean adverbial phrase (고유어) composed of the compound noun 막말 ("rough speech, blunt or unfiltered talk") + the instrumental case particle -로 ("with, by means of, in"). The noun 막말 combines the native derogatory/unrestrained prefix 막- ("roughly, carelessly, without refinement or filter", etymologically related to the adverb 마구 "recklessly, randomly") + 말 ("speech, words, language", Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ / 말 mal). Used as a discourse marker meaning "speaking bluntly" or "to put it crudely".

history.meaning: unrefined, reckless, or blunt words
frankly speaking, to put it bluntly or without filter

morphemes.meaning: roughly, carelessly, without filter or refinement
instrumental particle: by way of, speaking in terms of

막말로.notes: Notice that Korean has two homophonous prefixes 막-: one means "last/final" (as in 막내, 막차 "last train"), while the one in 막말로 means "rough/unfiltered/unrefined" (as in 막노동 "rough manual labor").

rootFamily.gloss: blunt, crude, or abusive speech; unfiltered remark
to speak bluntly, roughly, or without filter

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 막말

막방.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Korean syllabic abbreviation (혼종어 / broadcasting slang) combining the native Korean prefix 막- ("last, final", from 막- "to close off" or a clipping of 마지막 "last, final") + 방 (放, clipped from Sino-Korean 방송 放送 "broadcast", composed of 放 방 "to release, emit" + 送 송 "to send, transmit"). Coined in South Korean television and K-pop fandom jargon as a punchy counterpart to 첫방 ("first broadcast"), designating the finale episode of a show or an artist's final music-show promotional stage.

history.meaning: last, final + broadcast transmission
final broadcast episode of a series or final promotional stage

막방.notes: Part of a productive Korean TV series of -방 (放) clippings: 첫방 (premiere broadcast), 막방 (final broadcast), 본방 (live original broadcast), and 재방 (rerun broadcast).

rootFamily.gloss: first broadcast, premiere episode or stage (antonym of 막방)
original live broadcast (本放, clipped from 본방송)

막상.etymology: Widely traced by Korean lexicographers to Sino-Korean 막상 (莫上, literally 'nothing above' or 'at the very pinnacle/culmination', from 莫 막 'none, not' + 上 상 'above, top'), though treated in contemporary orthography without Hanja as a fully nativized adverb; semantically it shifted from 'at the culminating point' to 'when one actually comes face-to-face with the situation itself.'

history.meaning: at the culmination; nothing higher
in actual practice; when it actually comes to the moment

막상.notes: Often paired with a contrastive clause (e.g., 막상 해 보니 'when I actually tried doing it...') to highlight how reality differs from prior expectation or hesitation.

rootFamily.gloss: unable to tell superiority; neck and neck (莫上莫下)

막아보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (*고유어*) formed from the verb stem 막- (from 막다 'to block, obstruct, prevent', attested identically in 15th-century Middle Korean as 막다) joined via the infinitive connective suffix -아 to the auxiliary verb 보다 (Middle Korean 보다 'to see', grammaticalized after -아/-어 to mean 'to try doing, attempt').

history.meaning: to obstruct, stop + to see, test by trying
to try blocking; to attempt to prevent

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb: to try doing (lit. to see)

막아보다.notes: Combines physical or figurative obstruction (막다) with tentative effort (-아 보다), often used when trying to contain a rumor, broadcast crisis, or unwanted action.

막아서다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound (*고유어*) combining 막- (stem of 막다, Middle Korean 막다 'to block, enclose, obstruct') via the connective suffix -아 with 서- (stem of 서다, Middle Korean 셔다 'to stand'), literally meaning 'to block and stand'—hence to plant oneself in front of someone or something to bar the way.

history.meaning: to obstruct + to stand upright
to stand in the way; to confront and block

막아서다.notes: Unlike simple 막다 ('to block'), 막아서다 emphasizes bodily or active interposition—stepping right into someone's path to stop them from advancing.

막아주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb (*고유어*) composed of 막- (from 막다, Middle Korean 막다 'to block, ward off, defend against'), the infinitive connective -아, and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 'to give', grammaticalized to indicate performing an action for someone else's benefit).

history.meaning: to block, ward off + to give, grant
to block, shield, or prevent on someone's behalf

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary: to do for someone (lit. give)

막아주다.notes: In workplace and media dramas like *The Producers*, 막아주다 frequently refers to higher-ups or PR teams 'killing' a scandal or shielding a celebrity from press fallout.

막히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 막히다, formed from 막다 ('to block') + passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be blocked, obstructed
to be blocked, clogged, congested, deadlocked

만.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 만 (萬, 'ten thousand, 10,000'), from Middle Chinese *mjonH; also homophonous with the native restrictive particle/bound noun 만 ('only, just; elapsed time since').

history.meaning: ten thousand, myriad
ten thousand (10,000); only/just; after an interval of

만기.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 만기 (滿期), formed from 滿 (찰 만, 'to fill, become full, reach completion', Middle Chinese *mwanX*) and 期 (기약할 기, 'appointed time, fixed period, term', Middle Chinese *gi*); literally 'the filling up (completion) of an appointed term.'

history.meaning: completion of an appointed period or cycle
expiration of a contract, military service term, or financial maturity

만기.notes: Commonly used for financial deposits (만기일 'maturity date'), contracts, and completing mandatory South Korean military service (만기 전역 'full-term discharge').

만나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 맛나다, formed from 맞- ('to face, meet') + 나다 ('to come forth, occur'), with nasal assimilation of ㅅ + ㄴ > ㄴ + ㄴ.

history.meaning: to meet, encounter
to meet, see, come across

만남.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 만나다 ('to meet') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: meeting, encounter

만년필.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 萬年筆, uniting 萬 (일만 만, 'ten thousand'), 年 (해 년, 'year'), and 筆 (붓 필, 'writing brush, pen'). Coined in late nineteenth-century East Asia to translate reservoir fountain pens, 'ten-thousand-year brush' poetically celebrated a pen carrying its own ink supply so it could write seemingly forever without dipping into an inkstone. In Korean it still carries an air of keepsake craftsmanship and handwritten letters.
만년필.notes: Takes the instrumental particle -(으)로 when indicating the writing tool (만년필로 쓰다).

만둣국.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun (*혼종어*): Sino-Korean 만두 (饅頭, 'stuffed dumpling', borrowed from Middle Chinese *mwon-duw* by the Goryeo dynasty, attested in the 14th-century song *Ssanghwajeom*) + the native genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (*사이시옷*) + native Korean 국 (Middle Korean 국 'soup, broth').

history.meaning: stuffed wheat dumpling + broth/soup
Korean dumpling soup (standardized with saisiot -ㅅ-)

만둣국.notes: Note the spelling 만둣국 with 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-): because 만두 (Sino-Korean) combines with 국 (native Korean) and triggers tensification [만둗꾹/만둔꾹], standard orthography requires the ㅅ.

만들다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 맹글다 / 만들다 ('to make, craft, build, form').

history.meaning: to make, fashion, create
to make, create, build, prepare

만들어놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (*고유어*) combining 만들- (from 만들다 'to make, produce', evolving from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆫᄃᆞᆯ다 / 밍ᄀᆞᆯ다 'to fashion, craft, make') + connective suffix -어 + aspectual auxiliary verb 놓다 (Middle Korean 놓다 'to release, put down, set', grammaticalized to express completing an action and keeping its resulting state in place).

history.meaning: to craft, make + to put down, let go
to make beforehand and leave ready; to turn into a certain state

morphemes.meaning: resultative auxiliary: to do in advance and keep the state (lit. put)

만들어놓다.notes: Adding -어 놓다 stresses that the result of making or setting something up persists for future use—or, in complaints, that someone has 'made a mess of things and left it that way.'

rootFamily.gloss: to put, place, leave in a state

만들어주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb (*고유어*) formed from 만들- (from 만들다, Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆫᄃᆞᆯ다 'to make, build, fashion') linked by the connective suffix -어 to the benefactive auxiliary 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 'to give'), expressing the act of making, building, or creating something for another person's benefit.

history.meaning: to make, fashion + to give
to make or build for someone

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary: to do for someone (lit. give)

만들어주다.notes: When the recipient is of higher social status, 주다 is replaced by its honorific suppletive counterpart 드리다 (만들어 드리다).

rootFamily.gloss: the way something is made, build quality
to give; to do for someone

만들어지다.etymology: Native Korean syntactic passive/inchoative verb (*고유어*) formed from 만들- (from 만들다, Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆫᄃᆞᆯ다 'to make, craft') + connective suffix -어 + auxiliary verb 지다 (Middle Korean 디다 'to fall; to become'), grammaticalized to convert transitive action verbs into passives or spontaneous inchoatives ('to be made, come into being').

history.meaning: to make, fashion + to fall, become
to be made, produced, or formed

morphemes.meaning: passive/inchoative auxiliary: to become, get done

만들어지다.notes: Because 만들다 lacks a morphological passive suffix (*만들리다 is ungrammatical in standard Korean), 만들어지다 is the standard way to express 'is made' or 'gets produced.'

만만하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive adjective (*고유어*) built on the reduplicated root 만만- (originally expressing tactile softness, pliability, and lack of resistance when chewed or handled, attested in Early Modern Korean as 만만ᄒᆞ다 'soft, tender; yielding') + adjective-forming light verb -하다; semantically extended from 'physically soft and yielding' to 'easy to deal with, unintimidating, or easily pushover-like.'

history.meaning: to be soft, pliable, tender; to be yielding and manageable
to be easy to handle, unintimidating, or a pushover; to be soft/pliable

morphemes.meaning: soft, pliable, yielding, easily handled (reduplicated root)

만만하다.notes: Applied to a person (내가 만만해 보여? 'Do I look like a pushover to you?'), it carries a sharp nuance of being underestimated or treated as an easy target; in negation (만만치 않다), it means 'formidable, no easy matter.'

rootFamily.gloss: lightly, as if easy to deal with
not easy to deal with, formidable (contracted < 만만하지 않다)

만만히.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb (*고유어*) formed by attaching the deadjectival adverbial suffix -히 (standard after roots ending in a resonant or originally associated with -하다 adjectives) to the reduplicated descriptive root 만만- (from 만만하다 'to be soft, pliable; to be easy to deal with, unintimidating').

history.meaning: softly, pliably; without difficulty or intimidation
lightly, easily, as if dealing with a pushover

morphemes.meaning: soft, pliable, easy to handle, unintimidating

만만히.notes: Almost always collocated with verbs of perception or treatment like 보다 ('to look upon / regard'): 누군가를 만만히 보다 means 'to underestimate someone' or 'to take someone lightly.'

rootFamily.gloss: to be easy to deal with, unintimidating, soft
formidable, no easy matter (< 만만하지 않다)

만세.etymology: Sino-Korean exclamation 萬歲, composed of 萬 (일만 만, 'ten thousand') and 歲 (해 세, 'years of age, years'). Originally an East Asian court acclamation wishing a ruler 'ten thousand years' of life, it gained deep civic resonance in Korea during the 1919 March First Independence Movement (만세 운동). In everyday modern Korean speech, 만세 functions warmly and playfully as a spontaneous cheer of 'hooray!' or triumph when a tricky task succeeds.
만세.notes: Used both as a standalone interjection (만세!) and as a noun in 만세를 부르다 ('to shout hooray').

만실.etymology: Sino-Korean 만실 (滿室), compounding 만 (滿, 'full') and 실 (室, 'room, guestroom').

history.meaning: all rooms filled
no vacancy, all rooms booked/full

만약.etymology: Sino-Korean 만약 (萬若), compounding 만 (萬, 'ten thousand [possibilities]') and 약 (若, 'if, suppose').

history.meaning: if by one chance in ten thousand
if, in case, by any chance

만점.etymology: Sino-Korean 만점 (滿點), compounding 만 (滿, 'full, complete') and 점 (點, 'point, score, mark').

history.meaning: full score
full marks, perfect score, ten out of ten

만지다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to touch, feel, or handle with the hand', attested in Early Modern Korean as 만지다 alongside Middle Korean 만히다 ('to stroke, rub, touch').

history.meaning: to stroke, rub, touch with the hand
to touch, feel, handle

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 만지다

만큼.etymology: Native Korean bound noun and postpositional particle (*고유어*) grammaticalized from Middle Korean 만 ('extent, degree, size', related to 만ᄒᆞ다 'to be of the size/amount of') + the degree/extent suffix -큼 (attested in Early Modern Korean as 만콤 > 만큼, historically linked to the nominalized stem 크- 'to be big/great in extent' + nominalizer -ㅁ).

history.meaning: extent, degree + degree-nominalizing suffix ('to the extent of')
history.stage: Late Middle / Early Modern Korean (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: as much as, to the extent that; since/inasmuch as

만큼.notes: Spacing depends on syntax: after a noun or pronoun it attaches directly as a particle (나만큼 'as much as me'), whereas after an adnominal verb/adjective clause it is written with a space as a bound noun (노력한 만큼 'as much as one worked hard').

rootFamily.gloss: to be of the size or level of (만한 < 만하다)

만하다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary adjective ('worth doing, big enough to') formed from the bound noun 만 ('extent, degree, comparable size', Middle Korean 만) plus the adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be of such an extent or worth
to be worth doing; to be the size of

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 만하다

많다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 만ᄒᆞ다 ('to be many, abundant'), contracted by syncope of the vowel ᆞ between ㄴ and ㅎ.

history.meaning: to be many, abundant, plentiful
many, much, numerous

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 많다

많아지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative compound verb (*고유어*) formed from 많- (stem of 많다 'to be many, much, abundant', contracted from 15th-century Middle Korean 만ᄒᆞ다 'to be abundant, numerous') + connective suffix -아 + the inchoative auxiliary verb 지다 (Middle Korean 디다 'to become'), literally 'to become many/much.'

history.meaning: to be abundant/numerous + to become
to increase in number or quantity; to become abundant/excessive

morphemes.meaning: to be many, much, abundant (< Middle Korean 만ᄒᆞ-)

많아지다.notes: The silent ㅎ in 많다/많아지다 is the historical remnant of Middle Korean 만ᄒᆞ다 (where 만 'abundance' combined with ᄒᆞ다); in pronunciation, ㅎ aspirates a following plain stop (많다 [만타]) or deletes intervocalically (많아지다 [마나지다]).

rootFamily.gloss: at most, no matter how many (기껏해야 많아야)
