많이.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the adjective stem 많- ('many, much') plus the productive adverbial suffix -이 (Middle Korean 만히).

history.meaning: abundantly, in large numbers
much, a lot, plentifully

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 많이

morphemes.meaning: in such a manner or degree

말.etymology: Core native Korean noun with three major homophonous lineages: (1) 'speech, word, language' (Middle Korean 말, low-rising tone); (2) 'horse' (Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆯ); and (3) a traditional dry volume measure equal to ten 되 (~18 liters, Middle Korean 말).

history.meaning: speech, language (말); horse (ᄆᆞᆯ); dry measure (말)
word, speech, language; horse; unit of measure

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 말

말고.etymology: Grammaticalized connective form of the native Korean negative/prohibitive verb 말다 (*고유어*, Middle Korean 말다 'to desist, stop, refrain from, avoid'), consisting of the verb stem 말- plus the coordinative suffix -고 ('and'); used both after verbal -지 (-지 말고 'do not do X, and instead...') and directly after nouns (N 말고 'setting aside N; not N, but...').

history.meaning: to desist from, refrain from + and
not X (but Y); besides, other than; do not ... and instead

말고.notes: Always written with a space after the preceding noun or verb (이거 말고 저거 'not this one, that one'; 걱정하지 말고 'don't worry, and...') because it remains an inflected form of the verb 말다 rather than an attached postposition.

rootFamily.gloss: whether one does or not (-거나 말거나)

말다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb representing two distinct Middle Korean roots: (1) auxiliary and main verb 'to stop, cease, refrain from' (used in prohibitions with -지 말다, Middle Korean 말다); and (2) 'to roll up, wrap' or 'to mix rice or noodles into broth' (Middle Korean 몰다 / 말다).

history.meaning: to cease, refrain from; to roll up
to stop, refrain from (-지 말다); to roll up; to steep in broth

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 말다

말리다.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized causative verb formed from the intransitive stem 마르다 ('to dry up, become dry', Middle Korean ᄆᆞᄅᆞ다) plus the causative suffix -이-/-리-, yielding 말리다 ('to make dry'). When vowel-initial endings attach to the stem 말리-, ㅣ + 어 contracts smoothly into 말려요 and 말렸어요. Korean shares this phonological shape with two homophones—말리다 ('to stop/dissuade someone', from 말다) and 말리다 ('to be rolled up', passive of 말다)—distinguished cleanly by context.
말리다.notes: Past adnominal 말린 ('dried', as in 말린 꽃 'dried flowers', 말린 과일 'dried fruit') is extremely common.

말썽.etymology: Compound formation based on native Korean 말 (Middle Korean 말 'speech, words, talk, dispute') combined with -썽, analyzed by Korean historical linguists either as post-liquid tensification of Sino-Korean 성 (性, 성품 성 'nature, disposition, temper', i.e. 말 + 性 > 말썽 'quarrelsome disposition in speech') or an expressive native suffix; originally denoted 'noisy disputes and complaints' before broadening to 'trouble, fuss, or malfunction.'

history.meaning: argumentative talk; quarrelsome disposition in words
trouble, fuss, complication, or mechanical acting up

morphemes.meaning: nature, disposition, or trouble-making quality (< 性 성 with tensification after ㄹ)

말썽.notes: Used both for people causing scandals or headaches (말썽을 부리다/피우다 'to make trouble', 말썽꾸러기 'troublemaker') and for machines or plans acting up (컴퓨터가 또 말썽이다 'the computer is acting up again').

말씀.etymology: Native Korean noun derived from 말 ('speech, words') with the historical nominalizing suffix -ᄊᆞᆷ / -씀, attested in 15th-century Hunminjeongeum texts as 말ᄊᆞᆷ.
말씀.notes: In modern Korean, 말씀 both elevates an elder's or guest's words (선생님 말씀) and humbles one's own (제가 말씀드릴게요).

history.meaning: words, language
words (honorific or humble)

말씀드리는.etymology: Native Korean humble compound verb in its present adnominal form (*고유어*): 말씀 (Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ 'words, speech', derived from 말 'speech' + nominal suffix -ᄊᆞᆷ, which in Modern Korean bifurcated into honorific 'a superior's words' and humble 'one's own words to a superior') + 드리- (Middle Korean 드리다 'to offer/present to a superior', originally causative of 들다 'to enter') + present adnominal suffix -는.

history.meaning: words, speech (neutral/deferential) + to offer in to a superior
speaking humbly; telling or addressing (a respected listener) (adnominal)

morphemes.meaning: to offer/give humbly to a superior (드리다)

말씀드리는.notes: 말씀 has dual polarity: with 시다 (선생님께서 말씀하시다) it elevates the speaker's words, whereas with 드리다 (제가 말씀드리다) it humbles one's own speech toward a respected listener.

rootFamily.gloss: to give, offer humbly to a superior

말씀드리다.etymology: Humble compound verb meaning 'to speak or tell (to a respected person)', combining native Korean 말씀 ('words, speech', from Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ) with the humble benefactive verb 드리다 ('to give/offer to a superior').

history.meaning: speech/words + to offer humbly
to speak/tell (humble)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 말씀드리다

morphemes.meaning: to give or offer to a superior

말씀하다.etymology: Verb formed from native Korean 말씀 ('words, speech', from Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ, originally a general nominalization of 말 'speech' + -ᄊᆞᆷ that later specialized for honorific and humble registers) plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to speak, converse
to speak, say (honorific as 말씀하시다 or humble)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 말씀하다

말투.etymology: Hybrid compound noun (*혼종어*) combining native Korean 말 (Middle Korean 말 'speech, language, words') with Sino-Korean 투 (套, 틀 투 'mold, case, conventional pattern, style', Middle Chinese *thawH*); literally 'the mold or habitual style of one's speech.'

history.meaning: speech, words + set pattern, mold, style
way of speaking, tone of voice, phrasing style

말투.notes: Focuses on a person's characteristic manner of phrasing, intonation, and attitude in speech (e.g., 퉁명스러운 말투 'a curt way of speaking'), rather than regional accent alone (억양/사투리).

rootFamily.gloss: tone and manner of speaking or writing (語套)

말하다.etymology: Transparent native Korean verb combining 말 ('word, speech, language', Middle Korean 말) with the verbalizer -하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to speak, talk
to speak, say, tell

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 말하다

말해보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (*고유어*) formed from 말하다 ('to speak, say', from Middle Korean 말 'speech, words' + light verb ᄒᆞ다 'to do, say') in its infinitive form 말해 (< 말하여 < 말ᄒᆞ야) followed by the auxiliary verb 보다 (Middle Korean 보다 'to see', grammaticalized to mean 'to try doing, attempt').

history.meaning: to speak, say + to see, test by trying
to try saying; to speak up and see what happens; to tell

morphemes.meaning: infinitive form of light verb 하다 ('to do/say', < 하여)
auxiliary verb: to try doing (lit. to see)

말해보다.notes: In imperatives like 솔직히 말해 봐 ('Tell me honestly / Spit it out'), -아/어 보다 softens or prompts the listener to go ahead and speak their mind.

맑다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean ᄆᆞᇰ다 ('clear, limpid, pure, sunny'), with regular shift of ᆞ to ㅏ.

history.meaning: clear, limpid, pure
clear, clean, fresh, sunny

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맑다

맘.etymology: Syncopated monosyllabic contraction of native Korean 마음 ('heart, mind, intention'), which evolved from Early Middle Korean *ᄆᆞᄉᆞᆷ > 15th-century Middle Korean ᄆᆞᅀᆞᆷ > 16th-century ᄆᆞᄋᆞᆷ (after the loss of the voiced spirant ᅀ /z/) > Modern Korean 마음, with the resulting vowel hiatus [ma.ɯm] contracting naturally in colloquial speech to 맘 [mam].

history.meaning: heart, mind, spirit, inner disposition
heart, mind, feeling, inclination (colloquial contraction)

morphemes.meaning: heart, mind, intention (contracted from 마음 < Middle Korean ᄆᆞᅀᆞᆷ)

맘.notes: Extremely common in spoken Korean and fixed idioms like 맘에 들다 ('to like, find appealing', literally 'to enter one's heart') and 내 맘대로 ('as I please').

rootFamily.gloss: as one pleases, to one's heart's content (< 마음대로)

맙소사.etymology: Fossilized native Korean interjection (*고유어*) lexicalized from an archaic supplicative/optative inflection of 말다 (Middle Korean 말다 'to desist, refrain from, not allow'): stem 말- (with regular liquid deletion before a labial/coronal suffix -> 마-) + humble/polite prefinal suffix -옵- (< Middle Korean -ᄉᆞᆸ-/-ᅀᆞᆸ- > -압-/-옵-) + archaic deferential optative ending -소서 (altered expressively to -소사); literally 'May You [Heaven/God] forbid it!'

history.meaning: please refrain from doing so; may it not be so!
good grief! heaven forbid! oh my god! (interjection of shock or dismay)

morphemes.meaning: to refrain from, forbid, not allow (말다, with ㄹ-deletion)

맙소사.notes: Often preceded by 하늘이시여 ('O Heavens!') or 세상에 ('In the world!') in dramatic exclamations: 세상에, 맙소사! ('Good grief / Oh my gosh!').

rootFamily.gloss: not X, but Y; don't do X and...

맛.etymology: Native Korean noun descending directly from Middle Korean 맛 ('taste, flavor, relish').

history.meaning: taste, flavor
taste, flavor, savor

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맛

맛보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 맛 ('taste, flavor') and 보다 ('to see, try, experience'), attested since Middle Korean 맛보다.

history.meaning: to taste, sample food
to taste, sample; to experience

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맛보다

맛없다.etymology: Native Korean compound descriptive adjective (*고유어*) formed by univerbating 맛 (15th-century Middle Korean 맛 'taste, flavor, relish') and 없다 (Middle Korean 업다 [əp-ta], written 업스- before vowels, 'to not exist, be lacking'); literally 'to lack flavor' or 'to have no taste.'

history.meaning: taste, flavor + to be non-existent, lacking
to taste bad, be unpalatable, or be flavorless

morphemes.meaning: to not exist, lack (Middle Korean 업다)

맛없다.notes: Pronounced [마덥따] (not *[마섭따]), because 맛 is an independent noun boundary whose final ㅅ neutralizes to [ㄷ] before the vowel-initial root 없- (contrast 멋있다 [머딛따/머싣따] and 맛있다 [마딛따/마싣따], where [ㅅ] is also permitted by exception, whereas 맛없다 is strictly [마덥따] in standard orthoepy).

맛있다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective literally meaning 'taste exists' or 'having flavor', formed from 맛 ('taste, flavor') + 있다 ('to exist, have').

history.meaning: to have flavor, be tasty
delicious, tasty

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맛있다

망가뜨리다.etymology: Transitive causative verb formed on the bound stem 망가- (shared with intransitive 망가지다 'to break down, be ruined', historically reshaped from Sino-Korean 망 亡 'to perish, be ruined' + velar/connective extension) plus the native intensive transitive/causative suffix -뜨리- (alternating with -트리-), which systematically pairs with -지다 inchoatives (e.g., 깨지다 : 깨뜨리다, 넘어지다 : 넘어뜨리다).

history.meaning: stem of ruin/breakdown + intensive transitive causative suffix
to ruin, wreck, break, or destroy (transitively)

morphemes.meaning: bound root: to break down, be ruined (reshaped from 亡 망)

망가뜨리다.notes: Both 망가뜨리다 (with fortis ㄸ) and 망가트리다 (with aspirated ㅌ) are recognized as standard Korean forms with identical meaning ('to wreck, ruin').

rootFamily.gloss: to get ruined, break down (intransitive counterpart)

망가지다.etymology: Intransitive/inchoative verb built from the bound root 망가- (widely analyzed by Korean philologists as a colloquial phonological reshaping of Sino-Korean 망하- 亡하- 'to perish, be ruined, be destroyed' via velar hardening/assimilation before the auxiliary, or a dialectal extension of 亡) + the native Korean inchoative/passive auxiliary 지다 (Middle Korean 디다 'to fall, become').

history.meaning: to be ruined, destroyed + inchoative 'to become'
to break down, get ruined, fall into disrepair, or let go of one's image

morphemes.meaning: bound root: to be ruined, broken (reshaped from 亡 망)
inchoative/passive auxiliary: to become, fall into a state

망가지다.notes: In entertainment and variety-show contexts (*The Producers*), 망가지다 is famously used when a glamorous actor or idol 'lets themselves look ridiculous/slapstick' for comedic effect.

rootFamily.gloss: to fail, go bankrupt, be ruined (亡하다)

cognates.meaning: ruining oneself; losing one's life or standing

망신.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 망신 (亡身), derived from Classical Chinese 亡 (망할 망, 'to lose, ruin, perish', Middle Chinese *mjang*) + 身 (몸 신, 'body, person, social self', Middle Chinese *sjin*); in Classical Chinese 亡身 meant 'to lose one's life or ruin one's person', which in Korean specialized into 'losing face, public disgrace, or humiliation.'

history.meaning: to ruin one's person or lose one's life through recklessness
public disgrace, loss of face, humiliation, embarrassment

망신.notes: Gives rise to the vivid Korean idiom 망신살이 뻗치다 ('to be struck by a streak of public humiliation') and the phrase 국제 망신 ('international embarrassment').

rootFamily.gloss: one's own body, social status, or safety (保身)

망언.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 망언 (妄言), from 妄 (망령될 망, 'absurd, reckless, false, rash, deluded', Middle Chinese *mjangH*) and 言 (말씀 언, 'speech, word, statement', Middle Chinese *ngjon*); attested in Classical Chinese and Buddhist texts (where 妄言 is one of the precepts against false/reckless speech) before becoming standard news and everyday vocabulary for an 'outrageous or gaffe-ridden remark.'

history.meaning: false, deluded, or reckless speech (Classical Chinese & Buddhist precept)
outrageous remark, reckless public statement, offensive gaffe

망언.notes: A staple of Korean media headlines whenever a politician or celebrity makes an offensive or wildly tone-deaf public statement (망언을 쏟아내다 'to spew outrageous remarks').

망치.etymology: Native Korean tool noun 망치, developed from earlier Korean 마치 ('hammer, mallet', attested in Middle Korean as 마치) through expressive nasal insertion (-ㅇ-) in the first syllable. Korean tool vocabulary traditionally distinguishes sizes of striking tools: 마치/망치 for a standard hand hammer, 장도리 for a nail-pulling claw hammer, and 메 (or 떡메) for a heavy two-handed mallet or sledge. From 망치 comes the action noun 망치질 ('hammering').
망치.notes: Combines with suffix -질 in 망치질 ('hammering') and 망치질하다 ('to hammer').

망치질.etymology: Native Korean derived noun (*고유어*) composed of 망치 ('hammer', an expressive heavy-tool variant with nasal insertion -ㅇ- from Middle Korean 마치 'hammer, mallet', which survives in Modern Korean 마치 'small hammer') + the native Korean action suffix -질 (denoting a repetitive physical motion, tool operation, or craft).

history.meaning: mallet/hammer (with expressive velar nasal insertion) + suffix of repetitive tool action
the act of hammering; striking repeatedly with a hammer

morphemes.meaning: hammer (< Middle Korean 마치 with nasal insertion)
repetitive physical action or tool-use suffix

망치질.notes: The suffix -질 productively turns tool nouns into action nouns (가위질 'scissoring', 바늘질 > 바느질 'sewing', 빗질 'combing', 망치질 'hammering').

rootFamily.gloss: small hammer, mallet (direct reflex of Middle Korean 마치)

cognates.meaning: to perish, fall, cease to exist

망하다.etymology: Sino-Korean hybrid verb (*한자어* root + native light verb) formed from Sino-Korean 망 (亡, 망할 망 'to perish, be destroyed, flee, cease to exist', Middle Chinese *mjang*, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts as 亡ᄒᆞ다) + the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 'to do, be').

history.meaning: (of a state, house, or person) to perish, fall, be destroyed
to go bankrupt, fail, flop; (in adnominal/exclamatory use) wretched, blasted, ruined

망하다.notes: Beyond literal bankruptcy or ruin, 망하다 (and its contracted adnominal 망할 'blasted, damned!') is ubiquitous in everyday Korean for bombing an exam, a TV show flopping in ratings, or ruining a situation (나 완전 망했어 'I'm totally screwed').

rootFamily.gloss: ruin, downfall of a nation (亡國)
to fail and collapse utterly (暴亡하다, slang/colloquial)
rise and fall, prosperity and ruin (興亡)

망한.etymology: Past/perfective adnominal participle of the Sino-Korean verb 망하다 (亡하다, 'to fail, perish, go bankrupt, flop'), composed of Sino-Korean 망 (亡, 망할 망 'to perish, be destroyed') + light verb stem -하- + the past/perfective adnominal modifier suffix -ㄴ (하- + -ㄴ -> 한).

history.meaning: perished, fallen, ruined (of a state or family)
ruined, failed, bankrupt; (of a broadcast or project) flopped

망한.notes: Contrast 망한 ('which has already failed/flopped', past adnominal, e.g. 망한 프로그램 'a flopped show') with 망할 ('which will fail' -> lexicalized as a curse modifier meaning 'blasted, damned', e.g. 이 망할 놈 'this blasted guy').

rootFamily.gloss: to fail, be ruined, go bankrupt (亡하다)

망해서.etymology: Causal and sequential connective form of the Sino-Korean verb 망하다 (亡하다, 'to fail, go bankrupt, flop'), consisting of Sino-Korean 망 (亡, 망할 망 'to perish, be ruined') + -해 (contracted from 하여 < Middle Korean ᄒᆞ야, infinitive of 하다) + the causal/sequential suffix -서 (grammaticalized from Middle Korean 셔, infinitive of 셔다 'to stand/be').

history.meaning: having perished/been ruined, and so...
because it failed/flopped; having gone bankrupt and...

morphemes.meaning: infinitive of light verb 하다 (< 하여)

망해서.notes: In broadcasting industry slang (*The Producers*), 프로그램이 망해서 means 'because the show flopped (in ratings or sponsorship).'

맞다.etymology: Native Korean verb from Middle Korean 맞다 ('to meet, face; to match, be correct; to be struck by'), underlying a family of causative derivatives (맞추다, 맞히다) and compounds (맞이하다).

history.meaning: to meet, match, be right, be hit
to be correct/right; to fit; to greet; to be hit

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맞다

맞이하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from 맞이 ('act of welcoming or receiving', derived from 맞다 'to meet, greet' + nominalizing suffix -이) plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to go out to meet, welcome
to welcome, greet, usher in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맞이하다

맞추다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 맞- ('to fit, match, meet') plus the causative/transitive suffix -추- (Middle Korean 마초다), meaning 'to bring into alignment, adjust, assemble, or custom-order'.

history.meaning: to match together, compare, fit
to fit, adjust, set, assemble, order custom-made

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맞추다

맞춰달라다.etymology: Complex native Korean compound and contracted quotative verb (*고유어*): 맞추- (Middle Korean 맛초다 'to make match, fit together, adjust', morphological causative of 맞다 'to fit, be right' + causative suffix -추-) + connective -어 (contracted to 맞춰) + 달- (suppletive imperative stem of the benefactive auxiliary 주다 used when the grammatical subject and recipient of the request are coreferential) + -라다 (contracted from indirect imperative quotation -라고 하다 'to ask/tell someone to give/do for oneself').

history.meaning: to make fit, align + to ask to give/do for the speaker

history.form: 맞춰 달라다 / 맞춰달라다 (< 맞춰 달라고 하다)
history.meaning: to ask (someone) to adjust, align, or accommodate for them

morphemes.meaning: causative suffix ('to make fit, adjust, align') + connective -어 -> -춰
suppletive imperative benefactive auxiliary: give/do for the requester (달다)
contracted indirect imperative quotative ending (< -라고 하다)

맞춰달라다.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes 주다 vs. 달다 in indirect requests: 'He asked me to adjust the schedule for him' MUST use 맞춰 달라다 (< 맞춰 달라고 하다), whereas 맞춰 주라다 means 'He told me to adjust it for a third party.'

rootFamily.gloss: to adjust, align, match, accommodate (< 맛초다)

맞춰주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb formed from 맞추다 ('to fit, adjust, align', the morphological causative of 맞다 < 15th-century Middle Korean 맞다 'to meet, fit, hit the mark' with the causative suffix -추-) connected via the infinitive linker -어 (contracted from 맞추어 to 맞춰) to the auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to perform an action for someone's benefit' < Middle Korean 주다). Together it literally means 'to adjust oneself and give [accommodation] to another'.

history.meaning: to fit, meet; to make fit, align
to adjust or align something for someone's benefit
to accommodate, humor, coordinate with, or align with someone

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make fit, adjust, align
infinitive connective (contracted with ㅜ to ㅝ)
auxiliary verb: to give, do for someone's benefit

맞춰주다.notes: In workplace and broadcasting contexts, 비위를 맞춰주다 or 스케줄을 맞춰주다 means bending one's own pace or standards to accommodate a colleague, star, or client.

맞히다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 맞- ('to be correct; to be struck') plus the causative suffix -히- (Middle Korean 마키다 / 맛치다), meaning 'to hit a target, guess an answer correctly, or expose to rain/snow'.

history.meaning: to hit a mark, cause to be struck
to guess right, hit the mark

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맞히다

맡겨놓다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) aspectual compound verb formed from 맡기다 ('to entrust, leave in someone's care', the morphological causative of 맡다 < Middle Korean 맡다 'to take charge of, undertake' with the causative suffix -기-) linked by the infinitive suffix -어 (맡기어 contracted to 맡겨) to the auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put down, release; to complete an action in advance and leave the resulting state intact' < Middle Korean 놓다).

history.meaning: to take charge of; to entrust to another
to entrust something and leave it in that state
to leave someone in charge of something; to deposit in someone's care

morphemes.meaning: causative: to entrust, commit to someone's care
infinitive connective (contracted with ㅣ to ㅕ)
auxiliary verb: to put; to leave an action's result in place

맡겨놓다.notes: Adding the auxiliary -어 놓다 emphasizes that once the task or person is entrusted to someone else, the subject leaves the state as-is (often implying hands-off reliance or abandonment of responsibility).

rootFamily.gloss: to take charge of, handle, be responsible for
to entrust, leave in someone's care
to take sole responsibility for, monopolize a task

맡기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 맡- ('to take charge of, undertake') plus the causative suffix -기- (Middle Korean 맛기다), meaning 'to entrust, leave in another's care, deposit'.

history.meaning: to entrust, commit to someone's care
to entrust, leave with, check in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맡기다

맡다.etymology: Native Korean verb uniting two Middle Korean verbs that merged in Modern Korean orthography: (1) 맛다 ('to take charge of, undertake responsibility for') and (2) 맡다 ('to smell, sniff, perceive an odor').

history.meaning: to take charge of; to smell, sniff
to take charge of, handle; to smell, sniff

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맡다

매끄럽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'smooth, sleek, slippery', formed from an expressive root 매끌-/미끌- (compare 미끄럽다 'slippery' and 매끈하다 'sleek') plus the adjective-forming suffix -업다/-럽다.

history.meaning: slippery, smooth
smooth, sleek, fluent

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매끄럽다

매끈하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built on the ideophonic root 매끈- ('smooth, sleek, free of roughness') plus -하다. It belongs to a rich sound-symbolic family with 미끄럽다 ('slippery') and 매끄럽다 ('smooth, fluent'), where the bright vowel ㅐ conveys a clean, firm, pleasingly even surface such as well-kneaded bread dough or polished wood.
매끈하다.notes: Often appears in the reduplicated adverb 매끈매끈 ('smoothly').

cognates.meaning: way of doing something; (plural) polite social conduct

매너.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English manner (specifically targeting the plural sense manners 'polite social deportment and etiquette', often mediated via Japanese マナー manā). The English word entered Middle English via Anglo-Norman manere and Old French maniere from Vulgar Latin *manaria ('way of handling, method'), the substantivized feminine of Latin manuarius ('of or belonging to the hand'), ultimately from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: hand; belonging to the hand, manual
customary practice; polite social conduct and etiquette
manners, courtesy, considerate etiquette

매너.notes: Unlike English, which requires the plural 'manners' to mean etiquette, Korean uses the singular form 매너 (e.g., 매너가 좋다 'to have good manners', 매너 손 'courteous hover-hand').

rootFamily.gloss: mannerism, falling into a creative rut
silent/vibrate mode on a mobile phone (literally 'manner mode')

매년.etymology: Sino-Korean time noun and adverb 매년 (每年), meaning 'every year, annually', composed of 每 (매, 'each, every') + 年 (년, 'year').

history.meaning: each year
every year, annually

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매년

매니저.etymology: Borrowed from English manager ('person who manages a business, store, team, or performer').

history.meaning: person responsible for controlling or administering an organization
manager

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매니저

매다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ᄆᆡ다 ('to tie, bind, fasten; to weed'), with regular monophthongization of ㆎ (ᆞㅣ) to ㅐ.

history.meaning: to tie, bind, fasten
to tie, fasten, tighten (a shoelace, belt, or strap)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매다

매달다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb uniting 매다 ('to tie, bind with cord', Middle Korean ᄆᆡ다) and 달다 ('to hang, suspend, attach', Middle Korean 달다). Because its second element has a liquid ㄹ-final stem, 매달다 follows the regular Korean ㄹ-deletion rule before ㄴ, ㅂ, and ㅅ—giving 매답니다, 매단, and 매다세요 while keeping ㄹ before vowels in 매달아요 and 매달았어요. Its passive/middle counterpart 매달리다 means both 'to dangle from' and 'to devote oneself wholeheartedly to'.
매달다.notes: ㄹ-irregular stem: formal present is 매답니다 (not *매달습니다), adnominal past is 매단.

매달리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 매달다 ('to tie and hang up', a compound of 매다 'to tie' + 달다 'to suspend') plus the passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be hung up, dangle
to hang from, cling to, be absorbed in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매달리다

매듭.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Middle Korean as ᄆᆡ듭 ('knot in cord, joint of bamboo'), derived from the verb root 맺- (Middle Korean ᄆᆡᆺ-, 'to tie a knot, bear fruit, conclude') plus a nominalizing suffix -읍/-듭. In traditional Korean craft, 매듭 also names ornamental decorative knotting (전통 매듭) braided from dyed silk cords. Beyond physical ropework, phrases like 매듭을 짓다 ('to tie the knot on a matter') mean bringing an affair to a neat, settled close.
매듭.notes: Commonly pairs with 짓다 ('tie a knot / wrap up a task') and 풀다 ('untie a knot').

매력.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 魅 (매, 'bewitching spirit, mountain demon; to enchant, fascinate, captivate') + 力 (력, 'power, strength, force'). Originally referring to a supernatural spirit's power to bewitch humans, the compound was popularized in modern East Asia (via Meiji/Taisho Japanese 魅力 miryoku) in a secularized psychological sense meaning 'personal magnetism, charisma, charm, or aesthetic appeal'.

history.meaning: bewitching spirit / demon + physical or spiritual power
power to attract and fascinate; personal or artistic charm
charm, appeal, attractiveness, charisma

매력.notes: Commonly collocates with 있다/없다 (매력이 있다 'to be charming') or 터지다/넘치다 (매력이 넘치다 'to be overflowing with charm').

cognates.word: 魅力的 (みりょくてき, miryokuteki)

매력적.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) derived noun and determiner formed from 매력 (魅力, 'charm, appeal', from 魅 'to enchant, bewitch' + 力 'power, strength') + the Sino-Korean attributive/adjectival suffix -적 (的, 적, classically meaning 'white target center, bullseye, clear', grammaticalized in modern Sino-Japanese and Sino-Korean to translate Indo-European adjectival suffixes such as -tic, -ive, and -al).

history.meaning: charm/magnetism + target/attributive marker
having the quality of charm; attractive, alluring
attractive, charming, appealing

morphemes.meaning: having the quality or character of (-ive, -tic)

매력적.notes: Like other -적 (的) words in Korean, 매력적 cannot conjugate directly with -다; it takes the copula 이다 (매력적이다 'is attractive') or modifies a noun directly (매력적인 사람 'an attractive person').

매물.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 매물 (賣物), literally 'an article or property put up for sale', formed from 賣 (매, 'to sell') + 物 (물, 'thing, object, property').

history.meaning: goods or property offered for sale
item for sale, real estate listing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매물

매수자.etymology: Sino-Korean legal and commercial term 매수자 (買受者), meaning 'buyer, purchaser', formed from 매수 (買受, 'buying and taking delivery') + agent suffix -자 (者, 'person').

history.meaning: person who buys and receives property
buyer, purchaser

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매수자

매실.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 梅 (매, 'Chinese plum, Japanese apricot, Prunus mume') + 實 (실, 'fruit, seed, kernel; real substance'). Whereas 매화 (梅花) designates the tree's early-spring blossoms celebrated by classical literati as one of the Four Gentlemen (사군자), 매실 (梅實) specifically denotes the tart green stone fruit harvested in late spring and early summer for culinary and medicinal extracts.

history.meaning: fruit of the Chinese plum tree (Prunus mume)
green plum fruit used in traditional medicine and preserves
green plum, Japanese apricot

매실.notes: In Korea, 매실 is rarely eaten raw because of its intense tartness and amygdalin content in the unripe seed; instead it is steeped in sugar to make 매실청 (green plum syrup), a household remedy for indigestion.

매실차.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) trimorphemic compound noun formed from 매실 (梅實, 'green plum fruit', from 梅 'Chinese plum, Prunus mume' + 實 'fruit, seed') + 차 (茶, 차/다, 'tea, herbal infusion'). Note that the character 茶 has two Sino-Korean readings: 차 (reflecting a later northern Chinese vernacular pronunciation, used for beverages) and 다 (reflecting the older Middle Chinese layer, used in formal compounds like 다도 茶道 'tea ceremony').

history.meaning: Chinese plum fruit + tea leaf / infusion
sweet-tart beverage made by diluting fermented green plum syrup in water

매실차.notes: Served hot or iced in Korean cafes and homes, 매실차 is a go-to after-meal drink whenever someone has an upset stomach or feels bloated after overeating.

매연.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 煤 (매, 'soot, coal, cinders') + 煙 (연, 'smoke, fumes, vapor'). In pre-industrial East Asia, 煤煙 denoted black soot and smoke rising from wood or coal fires; with industrialization and motorization in the 20th century, Korean 매연 narrowed primarily to dark exhaust fumes and particulate emissions discharged by automobiles and factory smokestacks.

history.meaning: soot and dark smoke from burning fuel or coal
soot-laden smoke, industrial smoke, vehicle exhaust fumes

매연.notes: In everyday Korean, 매연 specifically evokes dirty, polluting black vehicle exhaust (자동차 매연), whereas general gaseous emissions are called 배기가스 (exhaust gas).

매일.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 매일 (每日), meaning 'every day, daily', from 每 (매, 'each, every') + 日 (일, 'day').

history.meaning: each day
every day, daily

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매일

매주.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 매주 (每週), meaning 'every week, weekly', from 每 (매, 'each, every') + 週 (주, 'week, cycle').

history.meaning: each week
every week, weekly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 매주

cognates.meaning: supernatural art; part of the trademark Magic Marker
felt-tip permanent marker (clipped from マジックインキ); magic

매직.etymology: Loanword (외래어) clipped from 매직펜 (Magic Pen) or 매직잉크 (Magic Ink), borrowed via Japanese マジックインキ (Majikku Inki, a felt-tip marker brand launched in Japan in 1953 by Uchida Yoko/Teranishi Chemical, modeled after Sidney Rosenthal's 1952 American invention Magic Marker, so named because its ink could write 'magically' on any surface). The English word magic derives via Old French magique and Latin magicus from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós, 'of the Magi'), from Old Persian maguš.

history.meaning: pertaining to the Magian priests or sorcery

history.form: Magic Marker / マジックインキ (Majikku Inki)
history.meaning: proprietary brand of felt-tip indelible ink marker (1952–1953)
felt-tip permanent marker; hair straightening perm (매직 스트레이트)

매직.notes: A classic genericized trademark in Korean: asking for a 매직 in a Korean office or TV studio means a thick felt-tip marker (used for writing on cue cards or whiteboards), never a magic trick (which is 마술).

매체.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 媒 (매, 'matchmaker, go-between, intermediary') + 體 (체, 'body, substance, form, vessel'). Coined in modern East Asian lexicon (alongside Japanese 媒体 baitai) as a semantic calque of English medium / media (from Latin medium 'middle, intermediary space'), literally denoting an 'intermediary body or vessel' that transmits information or artistic expression between sender and audience.

history.meaning: marriage go-between / intermediary + physical body / substance
intermediary substance, communication medium
media, news outlet, communication channel, medium

매체.notes: While 미디어 (loanword from English 'media') is common in casual talk, 매체 (媒體) is the standard formal term for news outlets (언론 매체), broadcasting channels (방송 매체), and mass media (대중 매체).

rootFamily.gloss: mediation, acting as an intermediary (媒介)

매칭.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English matching, the verbal noun/gerund of match ('to pair up, correspond, fit together as equals'). The English word derives from Middle English macche and Old English ġemæċċa ('mate, spouse, companion, equal'), from Proto-Germanic *gamakjô ('one who fits together'), built on the collective prefix *ga- + *makō ('fitting, suitable', cognate with English make).

history.meaning: mate, companion, one of a pair
pairing up, making two things or people correspond
matching, pairing up (of cast partners, outfits, or data)

매칭.notes: On Korean variety and dating shows (like those in 프로듀사), 매칭 refers specifically to pairing up male and female guests as couples or partners for games (커플 매칭).

매형.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) kinship compound from 妹 (매, classically 'younger sister', broadened in Sino-Korean marital compounds to mean 'sister') + 兄 (형, 'elder brother; respectful title for a male relative of one's own generation'). In Korean kinship terminology, a man or woman addresses or refers to their older sister's husband respectfully as 매형 (妹兄, literally 'sister-elder-brother'), whereas a younger sister's husband is called 매제 (妹弟, 'sister-younger-brother').

history.meaning: sister + elder brother
older sister's husband (respectful kinship term and title of address)

morphemes.meaning: elder brother; respectful title for a male peer/brother-in-law

매형.notes: While a male speaker usually calls his older sister's husband 매형 (or 자형), a female speaker more commonly calls her older sister's husband 형부 (兄夫).

rootFamily.gloss: brother and sister, male and female siblings (男妹)

cognates.meaning: beer, barley liquor (formal/written term alongside ビール)

맥주.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 麥 (맥, 'barley, wheat, grain') + 酒 (주, 'alcoholic beverage, fermented liquor, wine'), literally 'barley liquor'. Adopted in the late 19th century across East Asia (alongside Japanese 麦酒 bakushu / bīru) to designate Western-style beer brewed from malted barley (대맥 大麥), contrasting with traditional rice-based Korean alcoholic drinks like 막걸리 and 청주.

history.meaning: fermented liquor brewed from barley grain
history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese / Meiji Japanese coinage

history.meaning: beer (Western-style barley-malt beer)

맥주.notes: In Korean drinking culture, 맥주 is frequently combined into portmanteaus like 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주, fried chicken and beer) and 소맥 (소주 + 맥주, a soju-and-beer bomb cocktail).

맨.etymology: Native Korean determiner from Middle Korean ᄆᆡᆫ, used in two related senses: (1) before nouns of position or order to mean 'the very, the extreme/topmost' (e.g., 맨 위 'the very top', 맨 처음 'the very beginning'); and (2) as a prefixal determiner meaning 'bare, unmixed' (e.g., 맨손 'bare hands').

history.meaning: bare, unmixed; extreme, very
the very (first/last/top); bare

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 맨

맨날.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound adverb derived from 매날, which combines Sino-Korean 매- (每, 'each, every', as in 매일 每日 'every day') + native Korean 날 ('day' < Middle Korean 날). Through expressive nasal gemination/epenthesis (매날 > 맨날) and folk-etymological reinforcement from the native Korean prefix 맨- ('nothing but, pure, bare'), 맨날 became an emphatic colloquial adverb meaning 'every single day, all the time, invariably'. Initially treated as a non-standard variant of 만날, 맨날 was officially recognized as standard Korean (표준어) in 2011.

history.meaning: every + day (hybrid calque of 每日)
every single day, always, constantly

morphemes.meaning: every, always (< 每 매 + nasal gemination ㄴ)

맨날.notes: Often carries a slightly exasperated or hyperbolic tone in conversation ('always, every single time!'), as in 맨날 늦다 ('you're always late').

rootFamily.gloss: every day (每日, formal Sino-Korean equivalent)
every day, day by day (native Korean)
the day before yesterday, a few days ago

맨입.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun formed from the native determiner prefix 맨- ('bare, empty, unaccompanied, nothing but' < Middle Korean 맨) + the noun 입 ('mouth' < Middle Korean 입). Literally denoting 'a bare/empty mouth'—either a mouth that has eaten nothing or a mouth offering mere words without a material treat, meal, or gift—it developed the idiomatic sense of asking a favor or thanking someone 'with words alone / empty-handed'.

history.meaning: bare, unmixed + mouth
an empty mouth (without eating food); offering only words without treating someone

맨입.notes: Most commonly heard in the playful negotiation phrase 맨입으로? ('With an empty mouth? / You expect me to do this for free without buying me a meal or drink?').

rootFamily.gloss: plain steamed rice with no side dishes

맵다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) p-irregular descriptive verb (ㅂ-불규칙 형용사, stem 맵- alternating with 매운/매워 before vowels) inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 맵다 (prevocalic stem 매ㅸ- > 매오- / 매운), meaning 'pungent, acrid, sharp-tasting, biting'. Prior to the late 16th-century arrival of New World chili peppers (고추) in Korea, 맵다 described the sharp pungency of garlic, mustard, ginger, radish, and acrid smoke, as well as fierce cold or a harsh temperament.

history.meaning: pungent, acrid, biting, fierce (of taste, smoke, cold, or disposition)
spicy, hot (especially of chili peppers); biting, severe

맵다.notes: Beyond food, 맵다 retains its older sense of 'harsh/biting' in expressions like 손끝이 맵다 (a slap/hit that stings fiercely) and 매운맛을 보여주다 ('to teach someone a harsh lesson').

rootFamily.gloss: spicy taste; a harsh lesson or 'hard mode'
fierce, biting, severe (of wind, cold, or gaze)

맹수.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 猛 (맹, 'fierce, ferocious, violent, valiant') + 獸 (수, 'four-legged wild mammal, beast'). Attested in Classical Chinese historical and philosophical texts (such as Mencius, 홍수맹수 洪水猛獸 'floods and fierce beasts'), 맹수 denotes large carnivorous predators like tigers, lions, leopards, and bears.

history.meaning: fierce, predatory wild quadruped (such as a tiger or leopard)
wild beast, fierce animal, predator

맹수.notes: In Korean variety shows, aggressive or physically dominant cast members are often humorously compared to a 맹수 ('wild predator') on the prowl.

머그잔.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining English loanword 머그 (mug) with Sino-Korean 잔 (盞, 'cup, goblet') to specify a handled cylindrical mug.

history.meaning: English 'mug' + Sino-Korean 'cup'
mug, coffee mug

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 머그잔

머리.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'head; hair on the head; mind; top/beginning', descending from Middle Korean 마리 ('head') through vowel assimilation (마리 > 머리).

history.meaning: head, top
head; hair; intellect; beginning

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 머리

머리글자.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound built as a transparent formation for 'head-letter / initial': native Korean 머리 ('head, top, beginning', Middle Korean 머리) + 글자 ('letter, written character', itself combining native 글 'writing, script' with Sino-Korean 자 字 'character').

history.meaning: head + writing + character
initial letter, initials

머리글자.notes: Native-led counterpart to the English loan 이니셜 ('initials') and Sino-Korean 두문자 (頭文字); pronounced [머리글짜] with tensification of ㅈ after ㄹ.

머무르다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 머믈다 (memulta, 'to halt, tarry, stay in a place'), which developed the extended 르-irregular variant 머무르다 (meomureuda) alongside the shorter consonant-stem 머물다 (meomulda) in Modern Korean. Both stems are standard in contemporary Korean: before vowel-initial endings, 머무르다 conjugates as 머물러요/머물렀어요, sharing the exact same conjugated forms as 머물다. In hospitality contexts, it is a warm, polite verb for a guest staying at an inn or guesthouse.

history.meaning: to stop, tarry, remain in a place
to stay, lodge, linger

머무르다.notes: Both 머무르다 and 머물다 share the polite present 머물러요 and past 머물렀어요; before consonant-initial endings like -고, both 머무르고 and 머물고 are grammatical.

머물다.etymology: Native Korean verb (contracted variant of 머무르다) meaning 'to stay, remain, lodge, linger', descending from Middle Korean 머믈다 ('to halt, stay, tarry').

history.meaning: to stop, stay, remain
to stay, lodge, linger

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 머물다

머신.etymology: Direct loanword from English machine, commonly used in compounds such as 커피 머신 ('coffee/espresso machine') or 러닝머신 ('treadmill').

history.meaning: mechanical or electrical apparatus
machine, appliance

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 머신

먹다.etymology: Core native Korean verb meaning 'to eat, consume, take in', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 먹다.

history.meaning: to eat, drink, consume
to eat, have (food/drink), absorb

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 먹다

먹어보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) experiential/conative compound verb formed from 먹다 ('to eat, consume' < 15th-century Middle Korean 먹다) connected by the infinitive suffix -어 to the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see, look at; to try doing an action and observe/experience the outcome' < Middle Korean 보다). Cross-linguistically common in East and Mainland Southeast Asian languages, grammaticalization of 'see' (보다) after an action verb yields 'try V-ing / have the experience of V-ing'.

history.meaning: to eat + to see, look at, test
to try eating, taste, have the experience of eating

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb: to see; to try/experience doing

먹어보다.notes: Used both for sampling food right now (한번 먹어봐 'try a bite!') and for recounting life experience in the past tense (그거 먹어봤어요? 'Have you ever tried eating that?').

먹이다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) morphological causative verb formed from the transitive root 먹- ('to eat, drink, take in' < Middle Korean 먹다) + the native causative suffix -이- (attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 머기다 in morphophonemic spelling, later standardized to morphophonemic 먹이다). Literally meaning 'to cause to eat, to feed', it also developed rich figurative senses of bribing, scoring a point, or landing a blow.

history.meaning: to cause to eat, feed, nourish
to feed, raise livestock; (figurative) to bribe, land a blow, or trick someone

먹이다.notes: Watch out for colloquial idioms: 한 방 먹이다 means 'to land a punch / deal a heavy blow', 겁을 먹이다 means 'to intimidate', and 골탕을 먹이다 means 'to play a nasty trick on someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: animal feed, food, prey (nominalized from 먹이다)
to be eaten; to work/appeal to an audience

먹히다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) morphological passive verb formed from the transitive verb stem 먹- ('to eat, absorb, bite into' < Middle Korean 먹다) + the passive suffix -히- (attested in Middle Korean as 머키다, reflecting aspiration of ㄱ + ㅎ > ㅋ). From its concrete meaning 'to be eaten or swallowed' and mechanical sense 'for ink/dye to soak in' or 'for a gear/brake to catch and bite', 먹히다 evolved in modern colloquial Korean to mean 'to gain traction, be accepted, sell well, or work effectively on an audience'.

history.meaning: to be eaten, devoured, or swallowed
to be eaten; for dye/ink to absorb; for a tool/brake to catch or engage
to be eaten; (colloquial) to appeal to an audience, work, sell, be persuasive

morphemes.meaning: passive: to be eaten, be absorbed, take hold

먹히다.notes: In TV production and marketing (as in 프로듀사), 대중한테 먹히다 means 'to hit the mark with the public / sell well', derived from the idiom 씨알이 먹히다 ('for an argument or charm to work on someone').

rootFamily.gloss: food and drink, things to eat

먼저.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'first, ahead, beforehand', descending from Middle Korean 몬져 ('first, before others').

history.meaning: first, ahead of others
first, beforehand, earlier

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 먼저

먼지.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'dust, fine dirt particles', attested in Early Modern Korean as 먼지 (replacing earlier Middle Korean 믜리 / 드틀).

history.meaning: dust, fine particles
dust, speck of dirt

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 먼지

멀다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) l-irregular descriptive verb (ㄹ-불규칙 형용사, stem 멀- dropping ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ) with a phonemically long vowel [mɘːlda], inherited directly from 15th-century Middle Korean 멀다 (marked with two side-dots for rising tone, the historical source of Modern Korean vowel length), meaning 'far, distant in space or time, remote'. Note that its homograph 멀다 'to go blind' (눈이 멀다) had a low/short tone in Middle Korean and is prosodically distinct.

history.meaning: far, distant in space or time, remote
far off, distant, remote; a long way from completion

멀다.notes: In the past tense (아직 멀었다 'it's still far off!'), 멀다 is widely used idiomatically to mean 'you still have a long way to go' or 'it's nowhere near ready/good enough yet'.

멀리.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'far, far away, in the distance', derived from the adjective stem 멀- (멀다, 'to be far') plus the adverbial suffix -리, attested in Middle Korean as 멀리.

history.meaning: far away, distantly
far, afar, a long way off

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멀리

멀리서.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adverbial formed from 멀리 ('far away, at a distance' < 15th-century Middle Korean 멀리, derived from the adjective root 멀- 'far, distant' + the deadjectival adverbial suffix -리) + the ablative/locative postpositional particle -서 (contracted from -에서, 'from, at'). Together, 멀리서 literally means 'from a distant place' or 'from afar'.

history.meaning: far away, at a great distance
from afar, from a distance

멀리서.notes: Pairs naturally with perception verbs like 보이다/보다 (멀리서 보니까 'looking at it from afar') and 들리다 (멀리서 들리는 소리 'a sound heard from afar').

rootFamily.gloss: to keep at arm's length, shun, avoid

멀미하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb formed from the noun 멀미 ('motion sickness, vertigo, nausea') + the light verb 하다 ('to do, suffer from'). The noun 멀미 is attested in Early Modern Korean as 머리미 / 멀미, most plausibly derived from either 머리 ('head' < Middle Korean 머리) or the verb stem 멀- ('to grow dim, dizzy, or blind', as in 눈이 멀다) + nominalizing suffix -미, referring to the dizzy, spinning sensation in the head caused by the rocking motion of a boat, palanquin, or vehicle.

history.meaning: dizziness in the head, seasickness, motion sickness
to get motion sick, feel carsick or seasick

morphemes.meaning: light verb stem: to do, experience, suffer from

멀미하다.notes: Korean expresses getting motion sick with three common verbs: 멀미하다 ('to experience motion sickness'), 멀미가 나다 ('for motion sickness to arise'), and 멀미를 타다 ('to be prone to motion sickness').

멀쩡하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'completely intact, unharmed, perfectly fine, or shamelessly composed', formed from the expressive root 멀쩡- (dark-vowel counterpart of 말짱-) plus -하다.

history.meaning: unblemished, intact, sound
perfectly fine, unscathed, intact

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멀쩡하다

멈추다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to stop, halt, cease', historically derived from the intransitive root 멎- ('to cease, stop') with a causative/intensive suffix (Middle Korean 머추다, later nasalized to 멈추다).

history.meaning: to stop, halt, cause to cease
to stop, halt, pause

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멈추다

멋있다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound descriptive verb formed from the noun 멋 ('refined taste, flair, charm, style, savanna') + the existential verb 있다 ('to exist, have, possess' < Middle Korean 잇다 / 읻다). The noun 멋 emerged in Early Modern Korean via vowel ablaut (ㅏ ~ ㅓ) from 맛 ('taste, flavor' < 15th-century Middle Korean 맛), undergoing a semantic shift from physical gustatory flavor ('taste') to aesthetic sensibility, elegance, and personal panache ('good taste, style, coolness').

history.meaning: taste, flavor + to exist, have
aesthetic taste, flair, style + to have
cool, stylish, handsome, admirable, wonderful

morphemes.meaning: style, flair, charm, refined taste (< 맛 'flavor')

멋있다.notes: Both pronunciations [머딛따] (standard liaison after coda ㅅ neutralization to [t]) and [머싣따] (reanalyzed phonemic /ㅅ/) are officially accepted as standard Korean pronunciation!

멋지다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective meaning 'stylish, wonderful, splendid, cool', formed from 멋 ('style, charm, refined taste, flair') + -지다 ('to be endowed with, full of').

history.meaning: full of charm or refined taste
stylish, wonderful, cool, admirable

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멋지다

멍들다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound intransitive verb formed from the noun 멍 ('bruise, contusion, dark discoloration on skin after a blow') + the l-irregular verb 들다 ('to enter, penetrate, set in, dye/stain' < 15th-century Middle Korean 들다, used for colors, illnesses, or states permeating an object, as in 물이 들다 'to be dyed' or 병이 들다 'to fall ill'). Literally meaning 'for a bruise to enter/set into the flesh', it also extends metaphorically to emotional hurt (가슴에 멍이 들다).

history.meaning: bruise/contusion + to enter, permeate, set in
to bruise, get a bruise; (figurative) to be emotionally wounded or scarred

morphemes.meaning: bruise, contusion, dark mark on skin
to enter, set in, permeate, stain (l-irregular stem)

멍들다.notes: Can be used as a single compound verb (팔이 멍들었다 'my arm bruised') or split with the subject particle (팔에 멍이 들었다 'a bruise formed on my arm').

rootFamily.gloss: to be dyed, stained, or colored

멍청하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the ideophonic/expressive root 멍청- ('dull-witted, dazed, blank, foolish, slow on the uptake') + the adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be'). The root 멍청- expands the native mimetic root 멍- ('blank, dazed, spaced out', as in 멍하다), describing someone whose senses and wits are dulled and unresponsive, historically reinforced in folk etymology by association with Sino-Korean 맹청 (盲聽, 'blind and deaf').

history.meaning: to be blank, dazed, unresponsive, dull-witted
foolish, stupid, dim-witted, absent-mindedly blank

멍청하다.notes: Whereas 바보 ('fool') can sound affectionate or teasing, 멍청하다 / 멍청이 emphasizes acting dim-witted, clueless, or zoning out when sharpness is needed.

rootFamily.gloss: to be blank, dazed, spaced out
to zone out, stare blankly into space (slang)

멎다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to stop, cease, abate' (especially of rain, snow, wind, bleeding, or sound), descending directly from Middle Korean 멎다.

history.meaning: to stop, cease, come to a halt
to stop, let up, subside

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멎다

메뉴.etymology: Borrowed from English and French menu ('bill of fare in a restaurant; list of options'), ultimately from Latin minutus ('small, detailed list').

history.meaning: detailed list of dishes served at a meal
menu, dish on a menu

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 메뉴

메뉴판.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining the loanword 메뉴 (menu) with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 'board, plaque, sheet'), denoting a physical menu board or printed menu card.

history.meaning: menu + board/plaque
menu board, physical menu

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 메뉴판

메모.etymology: Borrowed from English memo (clipping of memorandum, 'something to be remembered; brief written note').

history.meaning: short written note or memorandum
memo, note, jotting

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 메모

cognates.meaning: method, especially method acting or programming method

메소드.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English method ( often mediated via Japanese メソッド mesoddo, which renders English /θ/ as /s/ and /ə/ by spelling pronunciation as /o/). The English word came via Middle French methode and Latin methodus from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, 'pursuit of knowledge, mode of inquiry, system'), a compound of μετά (metá, 'after, in quest of') + ὁδός (hodós, 'way, road, journey'). In Korean television and film, 메소드 most frequently refers to 'method acting' (메소드 연기).

history.meaning: pursuit of a path, systematic inquiry (meta 'after' + hodos 'road')
systematic procedure; Stanislavski/Strasberg psychological acting technique
method; especially deep psychological immersion in acting (메소드 연기)

메소드.notes: Although the National Institute of Korean Language (국립국어원) prescribes 메서드 as the standard loanword spelling, 메소드 remains overwhelmingly dominant in entertainment and acting parlance (메소드 연기 'method acting').

rootFamily.gloss: method acting (total emotional immersion in a role)

메시지.etymology: Borrowed from English message ('verbal, written, or electronic communication; underlying theme'), ultimately from Old French message.

history.meaning: communication sent to a recipient
message, text message

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 메시지

메아리.etymology: Native Korean, from Middle Korean 뫼ᅀᅡ리 (mwǒyzàlí), which Wiktionary analyses as 'one who lives in the mountains' (뫼 'mountain' + 살- 'live' + agentive -이).
메아리.notes: The echo was pictured as a voice answering from the mountains.

cognates.meaning: cosmetics applied to the face; stage styling

메이크업.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English makeup / make-up ('cosmetics applied to the face; theatrical costuming and paint'), a 19th-century nominalization of the English phrasal verb make up ('to put together, prepare, dress or paint a performer for the stage'). The verb make derives from Middle English maken and Old English macian ('to make, fashion, construct', from Proto-Germanic *makōną) + up (from Old English up 'upward, completely').

history.meaning: to construct, assemble, prepare completely
stage paint and costume; facial cosmetics (attested from 1880s)
cosmetic makeup, professional styling for broadcast or fashion

메이크업.notes: While 화장 (化粧) is the everyday Sino-Korean word for putting on makeup, 메이크업 (often shortened to 메이크 or paired in 헤어 메이크업 'hair and makeup') is preferred in broadcasting studios, salons, and beauty industry contexts.

메인.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English main ('chief, principal, primary, most important'), which evolved from Middle English main and Old English mæġen ('physical strength, power, force') reinforced by Old Norse meginn ('strong, mighty, main'), both from Proto-Germanic *maginą ('power, might'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *magʰ- ('to be able, have power'). In Korean, 메인 functions as both a prenominal modifier ('chief, lead') and an independent noun ('the lead person, headliner, or main dish').

history.meaning: physical strength, power, mighty force
chief, principal, primary in rank or importance
main, chief, lead (e.g., lead PD, head writer, main MC, or main dish)

메인.notes: In Korean television production (central to 프로듀사), staff and performers are strictly tiered into 메인 ('lead/chief', e.g., 메인 PD, 메인 작가, 메인 MC) versus 서브 ('sub/assistant', e.g., 서브 작가).

rootFamily.gloss: main vocalist of an idol group

cognates.meaning: public statement; spoken remark (source words of the clipped suffix -ment)
comment, spoken remark (source of broadcasting jargon)
cognates.word: コメント (komento) / アナウンスメント

멘트.etymology: Korean pseudo-anglicism (콩글리시) and clipped loanword (외래어) formed in Korean broadcasting jargon by apheresis (front-clipping) of English announcement (어나운스먼트) and/or comment (코멘트). In this clipping, the bound English nominalizing suffix -ment (inherited via Old French -ment from Latin -mentum, forming nouns of result or instrument from verbs) was reanalyzed in Korean as a standalone noun meaning 'a host's spoken line, scripted commentary, transition remark, or conversational pickup line'.

history.meaning: Latin/French suffix forming nouns of action or result; public statement or remark
broadcast announcer's spoken line or commentary (clipped studio jargon)
spoken commentary, MC script line, remark, or romantic pickup line

멘트.notes: A classic Korean TV/radio false friend: English speakers do not know the word 'ment' on its own! In Korean, 오프닝 멘트 means 'opening remarks', 멘트를 치다 means 'to deliver a line/quip', and 작업 멘트 means 'a cheesy pickup line'.

rootFamily.gloss: opening remarks on a broadcast or show
closing remarks on a broadcast or show

멜로디.etymology: Borrowed from English melody ('sequence of musical notes forming a tune'), ultimately from Ancient Greek μελῳδία (melōidía, 'choral song').

history.meaning: musical tune
melody, tune

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 멜로디

cognates.meaning: individual belonging to a group or organization
member of a group, cast, or team

멤버.etymology: Borrowed from English member, which derives via Anglo-Norman and Old French membre from Latin membrum ('limb, bodily organ, constituent part of a whole'). In modern Korean broadcasting and entertainment usage, it underwent semantic specialization to denote the regular cast members of a variety show or the performers in an idol group.

history.meaning: limb, bodily organ, part of a whole
individual belonging to a body, society, or cast
group member, regular variety show cast member

멤버.notes: In Korean TV production (such as 1박 2일 in The Producers), 멤버 specifically refers to the regular on-screen cast rather than behind-the-scenes crew (스태프).

cognates.meaning: member of a group or cast

멤버분.etymology: A hybrid Korean compound combining the English loanword 멤버 (member, 'cast member') with the native Korean honorific suffix/bound noun -분 ('esteemed person'). The honorific element 분 is attested in Middle Korean as 분 ('person of standing') and serves as the deferential counterpart to 사람 ('person') and 명 ('person counter').

history.meaning: esteemed person, individual of rank
respected member, honored cast member

morphemes.meaning: honorific suffix for an esteemed person

멤버분.notes: Production staff frequently attach -분 (or plural -분들) to loanwords like 멤버 or 게스트 to maintain polite workplace register toward celebrity talent.

멧돼지.etymology: Native Korean compound (*고유어 합성어*) formed from 메 ('mountain', from Middle Korean 뫼 mwoy) + the genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, historically the Middle Korean genitive particle ㅅ) + 돼지 ('pig', contracted from 도야지, from Middle Korean 도옫 twoyath 'pig' + diminutive animal suffix -아지). Literally 'mountain pig'.

history.meaning: pig of the mountain, wild swine
wild boar
wild boar (Sus scrofa)

멧돼지.notes: Preserves the archaic native Korean noun 메 ('mountain', largely replaced by Sino-Korean 산 山 in standalone use) inside natural-history compounds like 멧돼지 and 메아리 ('echo').

며느리.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun (*고유어*), directly attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447) as 며느리 (myenuli, 'son's wife, daughter-in-law'). Before vowel-initial native suffixes, its bound stem allomorph 며늘- surfaces (as in 며늘아기), pointing to an older stem *myenul plus the nominal suffix -i.

history.meaning: son's wife, daughter-in-law
daughter-in-law

며느리.notes: In traditional and colloquial speech, the shortened stem 며늘아 is used as an intimate vocative ('O daughter-in-law!') when parents-in-law address her directly.

rootFamily.gloss: new daughter-in-law, newlywed bride in the family

며칠.etymology: Native Korean noun (*고유어*), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 며츨 (myechul, 'which date, how many days'), formed from the interrogative/indefinite root 몃 (myech, Modern 몇 'how many, several') + the native day-counting suffix -을/-읠 (seen in 사흘 'three days', 나흘 'four days'). Subsequent palatalization and vowel fronting (며츨 > 며칠) caused folk association with Sino-Korean 일 (日 'day'), but South Korean orthography mandates 며칠 to reflect its unbroken native phonology [며칠] rather than *[몃일/면닐].

history.meaning: which day of the month, how many days
how many days, what date, a few days

며칠.notes: One of Korean's most famous spelling traps: *몇일 is always incorrect in standard Korean, whether asking the date ('오늘이 며칠이지?') or saying 'a few days' ('며칠 동안').

면.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun 綿 (솜 면, 'floss, raw cotton, spun cotton fiber'), written with the silk/thread radical 糸 alongside 帛 ('fine cloth'). Originally designating fine silk floss in classical Chinese before shifting to cotton fiber as cotton cultivation spread across East Asia, 면 serves in modern Korean for cotton textiles and archival rag paper (면 종이, 순면). It stands beside native Korean 솜 ('cotton batting, wadding') and shares its pronunciation with 面 ('face, surface') and 麵 ('noodles').
면.notes: Used as a modifier before fabric or paper nouns (면 종이 'cotton rag paper', 면 수건 'cotton towel'); pure cotton is 순면 (純綿).

면포.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 綿布, joining 綿 (솜 면, 'cotton floss, soft fibre') and 布 (베 포, 'woven cloth, fabric'). Historically used in Korean textiles to distinguish woven cotton cloth from hemp (마포) and silk (비단), in modern culinary Korean 면포 specifically refers to an unbleached square of breathable cotton fabric used to cover rising dough or strain clear broth.
면포.notes: Standard baking and cooking term for a dampproofing cloth or strainer cloth.

멸치김밥.etymology: Compound culinary noun formed from 멸치 ('anchovy', from early modern 멸/며래 + the native fish-naming suffix -치 seen in 갈치, 참치) + 김밥 ('seaweed rice roll', a native compound of 김 'edible laver, Porphyra' + 밥 'cooked grain/rice'). Designates gimbap filled with sweet-and-savory stir-fried dried anchovies (멸치볶음), often paired with spicy green chili peppers.

history.meaning: anchovy and seaweed-wrapped cooked rice
anchovy gimbap (seaweed rice roll filled with stir-fried anchovies)

멸치김밥.notes: Along with 참치김밥 (tuna) and 치즈김밥 (cheese), 멸치김밥 is a classic 분식 (snack shop) staple frequently ordered in bulk for late-night television editing sessions.

명.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and classifier 명 (名) used to count people ('person, people'), originally meaning 'name, roll entry'; also used as an independent Sino-Korean noun meaning 'name, renown' (名) or 'life, fate, command' (命).

history.meaning: name; person on a roster -> classifier for people
counter for people; name; life/order (命)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 명

명세서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (*한자어*) written 明細書, composed of 명세 (明細, 'clear details, itemization', from 明 명 'bright, clear, explicit' + 細 세 'fine, minute, detailed') and the documentary suffix -서 (書, 'writing, document, certificate'). Standardized in modern East Asian legal and accounting terminology to denote an itemized financial breakdown.

history.meaning: clear and minute details
itemized statement, detailed specification document

명세서.notes: Most commonly encountered in workplace contexts as 급여명세서 ('pay stub / salary statement') or 거래명세서 ('itemized transaction invoice').

rootFamily.gloss: pay stub, salary statement (給與明細書)
detailed breakdown, particulars (세부 내역, sharing 細)

cognates.meaning: engraving in one's heart, keeping in mind
engraved on the heart (as in 刻骨銘心)

명심하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from the verbal noun 명심 (銘心, literally 'to engrave upon the heart/mind', from 銘 명 'inscribe, carve into bronze or stone' + 心 심 'heart, mind') plus the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). Rooted in the Classical Chinese epigraphic metaphor of carving solemn admonitions into sacrificial bronze vessels so they are never forgotten.

history.meaning: carving an admonition upon one's heart
to bear in mind, take to heart, remember well

morphemes.meaning: engrave, inscribe on metal or stone

명심하다.notes: Note the Hanja 銘 ('engrave', as in 좌우명 座右銘 'motto'), not 明 ('bright') or 名 ('name')—so 명심하다 literally means 'carve it into your heart', carrying a weightier tone than simply 기억하다 ('remember').

rootFamily.gloss: engraving in the mind, keeping in heart (銘心)
personal motto kept by one's seat (座右銘)

명절.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 名節, joining 名 (이름 명, 'renowned, notable') and 節 (마디 절, 'bamboo joint, seasonal division, festival'). Just as bamboo nodes mark regular intervals along a stalk, 節 came to mark the turning points of the lunar-solar calendar, and 名節 singled out the most cherished annual observances. In Korea, 명절 refers above all to 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok harvest festival), when families gather to share seasonal food.
명절.notes: Refers primarily to traditional calendar holidays like 설날 and 추석 rather than ordinary weekend days off (휴일).

명쾌하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjectival verb combining 명쾌 (明快, from 明 명 'bright, clear, lucid' + 快 쾌 'brisk, refreshing, decisive, pleasing') with the native light verb -하다 ('to be'). Combines visual clarity (明) with the psychological relief of a clean, decisive cut (快) to describe logic, explanations, or answers that resolve all doubt.

history.meaning: lucid and brisk, clear and refreshing
to be crystal-clear, incisive, and decisive

명쾌하다.notes: Unlike 분명하다 or 명확하다 (which focus purely on factual clarity), 명쾌하다 adds an aesthetic nuance of refreshing, satisfying decisiveness (as in 명쾌한 해답, 'a crisp, satisfying answer').

명판.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 명판 (銘板 / 名板), meaning 'nameplate, identification plate, inscribed plaque', formed from 銘 (명, 'inscribe, engraving') or 名 (명, 'name') + 板 (판, 'plate, board').

history.meaning: inscribed plate or nameplate
nameplate, plaque

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 명판

명패.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 名牌, combining 名 (이름 명, 'name, title') with 牌 (패 패, 'wooden tablet, signboard, plaque'). In Joseon administrative practice, 牌 named carved wooden or metal tallies and identification tablets such as 호패 (號牌); paired with 名, it came to designate an engraved desk nameplate, doorplate, or dedication plaque on a bench or building. Today 명패 appears both on office desks and as small memorial brass plates on park benches.
명패.notes: Used for desk nameplates, house doorplates (문패), and engraved dedication plaques on benches or trees.

명함.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 名銜, composed of 名 (명, 'name') + 銜 (함, originally 'horse's metal bit', extended in Imperial Chinese bureaucracy to denote the 'official rank or title' held by a magistrate, as in 官銜 관함). Historically referred to the formal visiting strip bearing a scholar-official's name and court rank; in modern Korean it designates a printed business card.

history.meaning: official's name and bureaucratic title inscribed on a calling strip
business card, calling card; professional status

명함.notes: Used idiomatically in 명함도 못 내밀다 ('cannot even present one's business card'), meaning one's skill or status pales so badly next to an expert that one cannot even compete.

몇.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite determiner meaning 'how many; a few, several', descending from Middle Korean 몃.

history.meaning: how many, several
how many; a few, several

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 몇

몇십.etymology: Hybrid compound numeral combining native Korean 몇 ('how many; several') with Sino-Korean 십 (十, 'ten'), meaning 'several tens, dozens, or how many tens'.

history.meaning: several/how many + ten
dozens, several tens

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 몇십

모금.etymology: Native Korean classifier noun meaning 'a mouthful, sip (of liquid), or puff (of smoke)', derived by vowel shift from Middle Korean 머굼, the nominalized form (-움) of 머금다 ('to hold in the mouth'). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 모금 (募金, 'fundraising').

history.meaning: mouthful (from 머금다 'to hold in the mouth')
sip, mouthful, draught; fundraising (募金)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모금

cognates.meaning: neurotransmitter class containing one amino group

모노아.etymology: Colloquial truncated utterance of the biochemical loanword 모노아민 (monoamine, from English monoamine, a compound of Greek monos 'single, alone' + amine, derived from ammonia). In The Producers (프로듀사), it occurs as an echoic stumble ('모노아... 뭐?' / 'mono-a-what?') when a speaker tries and fails to recall the neurochemical term 모노아민 cited in an explanation of romantic infatuation.

history.meaning: organic compound / neurotransmitter with a single amine group
truncated conversational fragment ('mono-a-[what?]')

모노아.notes: A humorous conversational truncation in drama dialogue showing how technical loanwords (모노아민) get garbled by laypeople in everyday banter.

cognates.meaning: display screen; one who oversees or checks

모니터.etymology: Borrowed from English monitor, which comes from Classical Latin monitor ('one who reminds, warns, or oversees'), an agent noun from the verb monere ('to warn, advise, remind', from Proto-Indo-European *men- 'to think'). In Korean television production, it refers both to studio display screens and to the critical review of broadcast footage or viewer reactions.

history.meaning: adviser, overseer, one who reminds
studio check-screen; broadcast checker
display screen; broadcast review or viewer feedback panelist

morphemes.meaning: monitor screen; broadcast review (from English monitor)

모니터.notes: In Korean broadcasting jargon, 모니터하다 (or 모니터링하다) often means checking real-time viewer comments, ratings, or rough-cut edits to gauge how a show is landing.

rootFamily.gloss: monitoring, reviewing a broadcast or public reaction
to review a broadcast, to check on a monitor screen
viewer feedback panelist for a TV network

모닝빵.etymology: South Korean hybrid compound combining English loanword 모닝 (morning) with 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese パン from Portuguese pão), denoting a small, soft, slightly sweet dinner/breakfast roll.

history.meaning: morning + bread roll
soft dinner roll, breakfast roll

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모닝빵

모닝커피.etymology: Compound loanword from English morning coffee ('a cup of coffee drunk in the morning to start the day').

history.meaning: coffee drunk in the morning
morning coffee

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모닝커피

모두.etymology: Native Korean adverb and noun meaning 'all, everyone, everything', descending from Middle Korean 모도 ('all together'), an adverbial derivation from the verb root 믇- / 모도- ('to gather, assemble').

history.meaning: all together, in total
all, everyone, everything

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모두

모든.etymology: Native Korean determiner meaning 'all, every', fossilized from the adnominal form (모ᄃᆞᆫ) of the Middle Korean intransitive verb 몯다 ('to come together, gather, assemble').

history.meaning: gathered, assembled -> all, every
all, every

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모든

모래.etymology: Native Korean noun (*고유어*), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 모래 (mwolay, e.g. in Yongbieocheonga, 1447, and Hunminjeongeum Haerye, 1446). Dialectal forms such as 몰개 and 모래기 preserve an internal velar consonant, pointing to a Proto-Koreanic reconstruction *mwolkay ('sand'), from which standard Middle Korean lost intervocalic *-k- before the diphthong -ay.

history.meaning: sand, fine gravel
sand
sand

모래.notes: Do not confuse the pronunciation of 모래 ('sand', [모래]) with 모레 ('the day after tomorrow', from Middle Korean 모뢰 mwolwoy).

rootFamily.gloss: sandy beach, sandbank (with Sino-Korean 沙場)

모르고.etymology: Inflected connective form of the native Korean verb 모르다 ('not to know, to be unaware of', Middle Korean 모르다 mwolota), composed of the verb stem 모르- plus the coordinate/manner connective suffix -고 ('and; while in a state of'). Frequently functions adverbially before another verb to mean 'without knowing, unwittingly, by mistake'.

history.meaning: not knowing and; without knowing
not knowing and; unwittingly, accidentally

morphemes.meaning: not to know, be ignorant of
coordinate and manner connective suffix ('and, without')

모르고.notes: When placed directly before an action verb (e.g. 모르고 지웠다 'I deleted it by mistake'), 모르고 acts like a single adverb meaning 'inadvertently / by accident'.

rootFamily.gloss: not to know, to be unaware of

모르는.etymology: Present adnominal (noun-modifying) form of the native Korean verb 모르다 ('not to know, to be unfamiliar with', Middle Korean 모르다 mwolota), formed by attaching the dynamic adnominal suffix -는 to the stem 모르-. Modifies a following noun either actively ('[someone] who does not know') or passivized in perspective ('unknown, unfamiliar', as in 모르는 번호 'an unfamiliar number').

history.meaning: not to know, be unaware of
not knowing; unknown, unfamiliar (adnominal)

morphemes.meaning: not to know, be unaware of

모르는.notes: In Korean, 모르는 사람 can mean either 'a person who doesn't know' or 'a stranger (a person whom I don't know)', depending on context.

rootFamily.gloss: to pretend not to know, feign ignorance

모르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular verb meaning 'not to know, be unaware of, be unable to tell', descending from Middle Korean 모ᄅᆞ다.

history.meaning: not to know, be ignorant of
not to know, be unaware of

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모르다

모면.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 謀免, formed from 謀 (꾀할 모, 'to plan, contrive, seek a way') and 免 (면할 면, 'to escape, be spared, avoid'). Originally meaning 'to find a way out of danger or blame', it is overwhelmingly used in modern Korean with 위기 ('crisis') in the set phrase 위기 모면 ('crisis averted; narrow escape') or as the verb 모면하다.
모면.notes: Most commonly heard in the collocation 위기 모면 ('crisis averted').

모서리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'corner, sharp edge (of a table, box, or stone)', formed from 모 ('angle, corner', Middle Korean 모ㅎ) + 서리 ('edge, border, area around').

history.meaning: angle/corner + edge/border
corner, edge

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모서리

모서리용.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining native Korean 모서리 ('corner, edge') with the Sino-Korean suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of'), meaning 'for corners, corner-use (e.g., corner guards or corner shelves)'.

history.meaning: corner + for the use of
for corners, corner-use

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모서리용

모셔놓고.etymology: Serial verb construction combining the native Korean object-exalting verb 모시다 ('to respectfully invite, escort, or seat an honored person', from Middle Korean 뫼시다 mwoysita) + the infinitive linker -어 (fused as 모셔) + the resultative auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put, leave in a resulting state', Middle Korean 놓다 nwohta) + the connective ending -고 ('and'). Expresses having brought or seated an esteemed person and leaving them in that state prior to the next action.

history.meaning: to attend upon a superior + to place/leave
having respectfully invited/seated someone and (leaving them waiting)

morphemes.meaning: attend upon, respectfully invite or seat (humble/object-exalting)
infinitive linker (contracted with stem to 모셔)
keep or leave in a resulting state

모셔놓고.notes: Frequently used with a nuance of apology or urgency when an honored guest or senior celebrity has been invited onto set and kept waiting (어른을 모셔놓고 뭐 하는 거야?).

rootFamily.gloss: to escort, attend on, respectfully invite (humble)
to respectfully bring or invite someone here
to respectfully escort someone to a destination

모셔다드리다.etymology: Compound deferential verb formed from native Korean 모시다 ('to escort or accompany a respected person', from Middle Korean 뫼시다 mwoysita) + the transferentive connective -어다 (reduced from -어다가, indicating performing an action and moving to another location) + the humble benefactive auxiliary verb 드리다 ('to humbly give or do for a superior', Middle Korean 드리다 tulita) + citation ending -다.

history.meaning: to attend upon a superior + to offer up humbly
to humbly escort or give a ride to an honored person

morphemes.meaning: humbly do for an esteemed person

모셔다드리다.notes: The polite, object-exalting counterpart of 데려다주다 ('to take/drive someone somewhere'); essential workplace etiquette when offering a ride home to a senior colleague or VIP guest.

rootFamily.gloss: to give, offer (humble verb and auxiliary)
to take/escort a peer or junior somewhere (plain counterpart)

모습.etymology: Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 모솝 (mwosop, e.g. in Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447, and Wolin Seokbo, 1459) meaning 'bodily form, shape, countenance'. Regular unrounding of the second-syllable vowel ㆍ (o) to ㅡ (u) after a labial consonant yielded Modern Korean 모습. While classified in standard lexicons as native Korean (*고유어*), some historical linguists compare it to 몸 ('body') or an early nativized borrowing.

history.meaning: bodily figure, outward form, countenance
appearance, figure, aspect, true self

morphemes.meaning: figure, appearance, aspect of a person or thing

모습.notes: Unlike 외모 (which refers strictly to physical looks/attractiveness), 모습 encompasses a person's whole demeanor, posture, and inner character as revealed in action (e.g. 프로다운 모습 'a professional side/demeanor').

rootFamily.gloss: figure seen from behind, retreating figure
side profile, side view of a person

모시다.etymology: Native Korean object-exalting (humble) verb (*고유어*), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 뫼시다 (mwoysita, 'to attend upon, serve, accompany a superior', related to the older transitive stem 뫼호다). Following the early modern monophthongization of 뫼- to 모- after the bilabial nasal ㅁ, 뫼시다 became Modern Korean 모시다, functioning as the suppletive honorific counterpart to 데리다 ('to bring/accompany').

history.meaning: to attend upon, serve, accompany a superior
to escort, accompany, serve, or live with (an honored person)

morphemes.meaning: attend upon, escort, serve an esteemed person

모시다.notes: Covers a wide semantic range of deference: escorting a guest (손님을 모시다), working under a boss (선배님을 모시다), caring for aging parents (부모님을 모시다), and enshrining ancestors.

rootFamily.gloss: to respectfully bring or invite someone here
to humbly escort someone to a destination

모아놓으면.etymology: Conditional serial verb form built from the native Korean transitive verb 모으다 ('to gather, collect, bring together', derived from Middle Korean 모호다 mwohota, the causative counterpart of intransitive 모드다 'to assemble') + infinitive linker -아 (forming 모아) + the resultative auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put, keep in a state') + conditional suffix -으면 ('if, when'). Literally 'if one gathers and puts (them) together'.
