history.meaning: to gather together + to set/leave in place
if/when one gathers and keeps (them) together

morphemes.meaning: leave or keep in a resulting state

모아놓으면.notes: Often used when contrasting individual items or people with the collective impression they make once assembled in one room (다 모아놓으면 대단하다 'when you put them all together, it's quite something').

cognates.meaning: pattern, design; state of affairs, look of things

모양.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 模樣, compounded from 模 (모, 'model, mold, pattern, form') and 樣 (양, 'shape, manner, appearance, kind'). Beyond its concrete lexical meaning of 'outward shape or form', it grammaticalized in modern Korean predicate constructions (-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다) as an evidential marker meaning 'it appears that... / it looks like...'.

history.meaning: physical shape, pattern, outward appearance
shape, form; evidential construction ('it seems to be')

모양.notes: In -(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다 ('it seems that...'), the speaker infers a situation from external signs, so it cannot ordinarily be used to describe the speaker's own first-person feelings (*나는 바쁜 모양이다 is unnatural).

rootFamily.gloss: outward appearance, how a situation looks (+ suffix -새)

모으다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to gather, collect, save up, assemble', descending from Middle Korean 모호다 ('to bring together', causative counterpart of 믇다 'to gather').

history.meaning: to gather, collect, bring together
to gather, collect, save

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모으다

모이다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb meaning 'to gather, assemble, come together', descending from Middle Korean 모히다 (derived from 모호다 'to gather' + passive suffix -이-).

history.meaning: to be gathered, come together
to gather, assemble, congregate

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모이다

모임.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun regularly derived from the intransitive verb 모이다 ('to gather, assemble, come together', passive/intransitive of 모으다 'to collect') by adding the nominalizing suffix -ㅁ. It denotes a gathering of people for a shared purpose, ranging from casual neighborhood meetups and book clubs to formal club meetings, contrasting with the Sino-Korean 회의 (會議, 'business meeting') or 동호회 (同好會, 'hobby club').
모임.notes: Often combined with nouns like 가족 모임 ('family gathering') and 독서 모임 ('reading club').

모자.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 帽子, formed from 帽 (모, 'headgear, cap, hat', containing the cloth radical 巾) + the nominal suffix 子 (자, originally 'child', grammaticalized in Tang–Song vernacular Chinese as a general noun-forming suffix). Adopted into Korean to denote caps and hats generally, alongside specific traditional terms like 갓 and 관 (冠).

history.meaning: cloth headgear, cap
cap, hat (of any style)

모자.notes: Korean 모자 (帽子, 'hat/cap') is a complete homophone of 모자 (母子, 'mother and son/child') and 모자 (某字, 'a certain letter'), distinguished by context.

cognates.meaning: some kind of, a certain type of

모종.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 某種, compounded from the indefinite pronoun/determiner 某 (모, 'a certain, unspecified, unnamed') + 種 (종, 'kind, sort, species, type'). Literally 'a certain unspecified kind', it almost always combines with the genitive particle 의 (모종의...) to denote a covert, behind-the-scenes, or intentionally undisclosed arrangement.

history.meaning: a certain unspecified kind or category
some covert, undisclosed, or ulterior kind of

모종.notes: Almost exclusively used in the phrase 모종의 + noun (e.g. 모종의 거래 'a backroom deal', 모종의 합의 'a tacit agreement'); do not confuse with the homophonous native Korean word 모종 ('seedling for transplanting').

모텔.etymology: Borrowed from American English motel, a 1925 syllabic blend (portmanteau) coined by architect Arthur Heineman for the Milestone Mo-Tel in San Luis Obispo, California, from motor (from Latin motor 'mover') + hotel (from French hotel, from Medieval Latin hospitale 'inn, guesthouse'). Borrowed into late 20th-century Korean for budget and short-stay lodging establishments.

history.meaning: motorists' hotel along a highway
motel, short-stay urban or roadside lodging establishment

모텔.notes: In South Korea, 모텔 refers not just to highway inns for drivers but predominantly to urban multistorey short-stay or overnight lodging establishments, replacing older 여관 (旅館 'inn').

rootFamily.gloss: cluster or district of motels (+ 村)

모퉁이.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'corner, bend, turn (of a street, wall, or building)', derived from 모 ('angle, corner', Middle Korean 모ㅎ, which carries final ㅎ accounting for the aspirated ㅌ) plus the locative/expressive suffix -웅이.

history.meaning: street corner, bend, angle of a wall
corner, turn, bend

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 모퉁이

모험.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 冒險, combining 冒 (무릅쓸 모, 'to brave, risk, push forward into') and 險 (험할 험, 'steep danger, peril, difficulty'). Originally a stark literal word for 'braving physical peril', it softened over time into the modern everyday Korean word for a thrilling escapade, a leap into the unknown, or an exciting new undertaking like a treasure hunt or a novel recipe.
모험.notes: Takes the verb -하다 in 모험하다 ('to go on an adventure, take a risk').

목.etymology: Core native Korean anatomical noun (*고유어*), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 목 (mwok, e.g. in Hunminjeongeum Haerye, 1446, and Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447) denoting both the external neck and the internal throat/vocal passage. By metaphorical extension, it also denotes the narrowest part of a limb or garment (손목 'wrist', 발목 'ankle') and a strategic bottleneck in a road (길목).

history.meaning: neck, throat; narrow passage
neck, throat, voice; bottleneck, narrow joint

morphemes.meaning: neck, throat; narrow passage or joint

목.notes: Korean uses the single word 목 for both the outer 'neck' (목이 길다 'to have a long neck') and the inner 'throat/voice' (목이 아프다 'to have a sore throat', 목이 쉬다 'to lose one's voice').

목공풀.etymology: Hybrid compound of Sino-Korean 목공 (木工, 'woodworking, carpentry') and native 풀 ('glue, paste').
목공풀.notes: Pronounced [목꽁풀] with compound tensification of 목 + 공.

목록.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 목록 (目錄), meaning 'list, catalog, inventory, table of contents', from 目 (목, 'eye; item, heading') + 錄 (록, 'record, register, copy').

history.meaning: written register of items or headings
list, catalog, inventory

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 목록

목소리.etymology: Native Korean compound of 목 ('throat, neck') and 소리 ('sound').
목소리.notes: Distinguishes a human speaking or singing voice from general 소리 ('sound, noise').

목수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 목수 (木手), meaning 'carpenter, woodworker', attested since Joseon-era records, from 木 (목, 'wood, timber') + 手 (수, 'hand; skilled craftsperson').

history.meaning: wood-hand -> artisan working in timber
carpenter, joiner

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 목수

목요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 목요일 (木曜日), built from 목 (木, 'tree, wood / Jupiter'), 요 (曜, 'luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day').
목요일.notes: Pronounced [모교일] via smooth liaison of final ㄱ onto initial ㅇ.

목적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 目的, composed of 目 (목, 'eye, gaze') + 的 (적, originally 'bright white center of an archery target'). Literally 'the target bull's-eye upon which the archer's eye is fixed', it was popularized in Meiji-era Japan (mokuteki 目的) as a translation for Western philosophical and legal terms such as German Zweck and English purpose/objective, and subsequently adopted into Korean and Chinese.

history.meaning: target spot fixed upon by the eye; translations of 'purpose, objective'
history.stage: Meiji Japanese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: purpose, ultimate aim, objective

목적.notes: Compare 목적 and 목표: 목적 (目的) is the overarching abstract 'purpose' or 'why' (삶의 목적 'the purpose of life'), whereas 목표 (目標) is a concrete, measurable 'target' or milestone on the way there.

목조.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 목조 (木造), meaning 'wooden construction, built of wood', formed from 木 (목, 'wood, timber') + 造 (조, 'make, build, construct').

history.meaning: made or constructed of wood
wooden construction, timber-framed

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 목조

목탄.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 木炭, uniting 木 (나무 목, 'tree, wood') with 炭 (숯 탄, 'charcoal, carbon, coal'). While the native Korean word 숯 refers to charcoal used for grilling food or traditional heating, 목탄 specifically denotes artists' drawing charcoal (often willow or vine charcoal) or industrial wood charcoal, appearing most often in art contexts like 목탄화 ('charcoal drawing').
목탄.notes: Used primarily in art (charcoal sticks for drawing); compare native 숯 ('grilling/heating charcoal').

목표.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (*한자어*) written 目標, compounded from 目 (목, 'eye, visual attention') + 標 (표, 'treetop, signpost, beacon, visible mark'). Literally 'a visible signpost or landmark toward which one directs the eye', it came to denote a concrete target, milestone, or quantifiable goal toward which effort is directed.

history.meaning: visual landmark, signpost, target mark
goal, concrete target, objective

목표.notes: In television production, 목표 frequently pairs with quantifiable metrics such as 목표 시청률 ('target viewership rating') or 목표 달성 ('achieving a target').

rootFamily.gloss: target numerical value, goal figure (目標値)

몫.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'share, allotted portion, role, quota', descending from Middle Korean 몫 / 몯 ('share, division, lot').

history.meaning: allotted share, portion
share, portion, one's part/role

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 몫

몰라보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (*고유어 합성어*) formed from 모르다 ('not to know', whose liquid-doubling stem 모르- becomes 몰ㄹ- before the infinitive linker -아, yielding 몰라) + 보다 ('to see, look at', Middle Korean 보다 pwota). Literally 'to look at without knowing', lexicalized as 'to fail to recognize someone' (after a change in appearance) or 'to underestimate/fail to see someone's true worth'.

history.meaning: not to know + to see, look at
to fail to recognize; to misjudge or underestimate someone's worth

몰라보다.notes: The adverbial form 몰라보게 ('beyond recognition, remarkably', as in 몰라보게 예뻐졌다 'became prettier beyond recognition') is a high-frequency compliment for dramatic positive change.

rootFamily.gloss: not to know, be unaware of
to recognize someone; to investigate (exact antonym)
to fail to appreciate someone's feelings or effort

몰라서.etymology: Causal inflected form of the native Korean verb 모르다 ('not to know, to be unaware of', Middle Korean 모르다 mwolota). Before the vowel-initial causal connective suffix -아서 ('because, since', historically grammaticalized from infinitive -아 + 이셔 'existing and'), the liquid-irregular (르-불규칙) stem 모르- doubles its liquid to 몰ㄹ-, producing 몰라서 ('because one does not know').

history.meaning: not knowing and being in that state (causal)
because (one) does not know, out of ignorance

morphemes.meaning: not to know, be ignorant of (allomorph 몰ㄹ-)
causal and sequential connective suffix ('because, since')

몰라서.notes: Often used in rhetorical questions like 몰라서 물어? ('Are you asking because you genuinely don't know?'), which chides the listener for asking the obvious.

rootFamily.gloss: on one's own, knowing what to do (from 알다 + -아서)

몰라주다.etymology: Native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction combining 모르다 ('not to know, fail to recognize', liquid-irregular stem 모르- + -아 -> 몰라) + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, do for someone', Middle Korean 주다 cwuta). Constructed as the negative-polarity counterpart of 알아주다 ('to acknowledge/appreciate someone's worth'), where -주다 highlights the interpersonal emotional stake the speaker has in being understood.

history.meaning: not to know + to give/grant
to fail to appreciate, ignore someone's devotion or effort

morphemes.meaning: not to know, fail to recognize (allomorph 몰ㄹ-)

몰라주다.notes: Even though -주다 normally marks doing a favor for someone, in 몰라주다 it expresses emotional disappointment that the other person withholds empathy or recognition (내 마음을 몰라주다 'to fail to appreciate my feelings').

rootFamily.gloss: to recognize, appreciate someone's effort or value (antonym)
to fail to recognize someone's face or worth

몰래.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'secretly, stealthily, on the sly', historically fossilized from the stem 모르- (모르다, 'not to know') + adverbial suffix -애 (Middle Korean 몰래, literally 'without others knowing').

history.meaning: unknowingly, secretly (from 모ᄅᆞ다 'not to know')
secretly, stealthily, quietly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 몰래

몰래카메라.etymology: A late-20th-century hybrid compound (혼종어) combining the native Korean adverb 몰래 ("secretly, stealthily", derived from the verb stem 모르- "not to know" + adverbial suffix -애, Middle Korean 모ᄅᆞ게) and the English loanword 카메라 ("camera", from New Latin camera obscura "dark chamber"). Coined in South Korean broadcasting in the early 1990s as an adaptation of the American "Candid Camera" hidden-camera television prank format.

history.meaning: without knowing, secretly
secretly + photographic apparatus
hidden camera, candid camera television prank

몰래카메라.notes: In variety shows like The Producers, 몰래카메라 refers to a lighthearted TV prank, whereas its clipped form 몰카 now strongly connotes illegal spycam filming in everyday news.

rootFamily.gloss: to not know, to be unaware

몰려다니다.etymology: A native Korean syntactic compound verb (고유어 합성동사) formed from the passive/intransitive stem 몰리- ("to be driven together, to flock, to crowd", derived from transitive 몰- "to drive, to herd" + passive suffix -리-), the infinitive connective -어, and the ambulatory verb 다니- ("to go around, to move about repeatedly", Middle Korean ᄃᆞ니다). Literally meaning "to go about while crowded together".

history.meaning: to be driven together + to go about
to flock around together, to move about in a pack or crowd

몰려다니다.notes: Often used with a slightly critical or exasperated nuance when describing fans, reporters, or cliques moving around in a noisy pack.

rootFamily.gloss: to be crowded, to be cornered
to surge in, to crowd into a place
to drive, to herd, to steer

몰리다.etymology: A native Korean passive and intransitive verb (고유어 파생동사) derived from the transitive verb stem 몰- ("to drive, to herd, to chase", Middle Korean 몰다) plus the passive suffix -리-. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 몰리다, it developed two closely linked senses: being physically or psychologically driven into a corner, and gathering or surging together in one place.

history.meaning: to drive, to chase, to herd
to be chased, to be driven together
to flock/crowd together; to be cornered or pressed

morphemes.meaning: to drive, to herd, to chase

몰리다.notes: Watch the dual meaning in context: 사람이 몰리다 means "people crowd/flock in", whereas 궁지에 몰리다 means "to be driven into a corner".

rootFamily.gloss: to drive, to herd, to corner
to drive toward, to frame/corner someone
to surge in, to flock into

몰아가다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb (고유어 합성동사) combining the transitive verb stem 몰- ("to drive, to herd livestock, to push in a direction", Middle Korean 몰다), the гармониc connective suffix -아, and the directional auxiliary verb 가- ("to go, to continue progressively", Middle Korean 가다). From the pastoral image of driving animals toward an enclosure, it evolved metaphorically into steering a conversation or framing someone as a culprit.

history.meaning: to drive or herd (livestock/people) onward
to drive toward; to corner someone or steer a narrative

morphemes.meaning: to drive, to herd, to push

몰아가다.notes: In Korean variety shows and office banter, 분위기 몰아가다 ("steering the mood") or 범인으로 몰아가다 ("painting someone as the culprit") is a staple comedic and rhetorical trope.

rootFamily.gloss: to drive, to herd, to steer
to press hard, to corner relentlessly

몸.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'body; physical health; main part', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 몸.

history.meaning: body, person
body, physique, health

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 몸

몸무게.etymology: A transparent native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성명사) formed from 몸 ("physical body", Middle Korean 몸) and 무게 ("weight", nominalized from the descriptive verb 무겁다 "to be heavy"). It serves as the everyday, vernacular counterpart to the formal Sino-Korean term 체중 (體重, "body weight").

history.meaning: body + weight/heaviness
body weight

몸무게.notes: 몸무게 is preferred in everyday conversation ("몸무게가 늘었다" — I gained weight), while 체중 (體重) appears on medical charts and scales (체중계).

몸싸움.etymology: A native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성명사) composed of 몸 ("body", Middle Korean 몸) and 싸움 ("fight, struggle, brawl", derived from the verb stem 싸우- "to fight", Middle Korean ᄊᆞ호다, + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ, Middle Korean ᄊᆞ홈). Literally "a fight with one's body", referring to unarmed pushing, grappling, or physical scuffling.

history.meaning: body + fighting/combat
physical scuffle, jostling, unarmed tussle

몸싸움.notes: Used both for actual shoving matches (e.g. between protesters or athletes jockeying for position) and for crowded jostling in subways or press scrums.

몸통.etymology: A hybrid Korean compound noun (혼종어) combining native Korean 몸 ("body", Middle Korean 몸) with the suffixal element -통 (from Sino-Korean 桶 "barrel, cylinder, bulk" or associated with 胴 "torso, trunk"), denoting the main cylindrical trunk or torso of a body or object. In modern journalism and politics, it also developed the figurative meaning of the "mastermind" or "core organization" behind a scandal (as opposed to the "tail", 꼬리).

history.meaning: body + barrel-like trunk or bulk
torso, main body/fuselage; central mastermind of an affair

몸통.notes: In Korean news and workplace drama, 몸통 ("the main body/mastermind") is frequently contrasted with 깃털 ("a mere feather") or 꼬리 ("the tail/scapegoat").

못.etymology: Native Korean negative adverb meaning 'cannot, unable to' (descending from Middle Korean 몯). Homophonous with native Korean nouns 못 ('nail, spike, peg', Middle Korean 못) and 못 ('pond, pool', Middle Korean 못).

history.meaning: cannot, unable to (몯); nail, peg; pond (못)
cannot, unable to; nail; pond

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 못

못하다.etymology: Native Korean verb and auxiliary verb meaning 'to be unable to do; to fall short of, be inferior to; to do poorly', formed by fusing the negative adverb 못 (Middle Korean 몯, 'cannot') with 하다 ('to do, be').

history.meaning: to be unable to do; to be inferior
cannot do; to be worse at / inferior to

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 못하다

묘하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 묘 (妙, 'subtle, mysterious, exquisite, peculiar') plus the adjective-forming verb -하다.

history.meaning: subtle, wondrous, mysterious
strange, curious, subtle, exquisite

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 묘하다

무겁다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'heavy, weighty, grave', descending directly from Middle Korean 무겁다.

history.meaning: heavy, weighty
heavy, weighty, serious

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무겁다

무게.etymology: A native Korean deadjectival noun (고유어 파생명사) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 무게 ("weight"). It derives from the root of the descriptive verb 무겁다 ("to be heavy", Middle Korean 무겁다, stem 무거우-) combined with the measure-noun derivational suffix -에/-게 (parallel to 두껍다 "thick" → 두께 "thickness" and 크다 "big" → 키 "stature"). Metaphorically, it extends from physical mass to social gravitas and emotional burden.

history.meaning: physical heaviness, weight
weight; figurative burden, importance, or gravitas

무게.notes: The idiom 무게(를) 잡다 ("to put on weight/gravitas") means to act serious, dignified, or pompous to impress others.

무궁무진하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from the four-character idiom 무궁무진 (無窮無盡, "without limit and without exhaustion") plus the native adjectival suffix -하다. The Sino-Korean stem pairs 무궁 (無窮: 無 "without" + 窮 "extremity, limit, exhaustion") with 무진 (無盡: 無 "without" + 盡 "to empty out, to use up completely"), creating a reduplicative intensive meaning "boundless and inexhaustible".

history.meaning: having no limit + having no exhaustion in Literary Chinese
to be boundless, inexhaustible, endless in potential or supply

morphemes.meaning: to exhaust, to use up completely

무궁무진하다.notes: Frequently used to praise someone's boundless potential (가능성이 무궁무진하다) or an endless trove of story ideas and resources.

rootFamily.gloss: Rose of Sharon, Korea's national flower (literally endless flower, 無窮花)

무너지다.etymology: A native Korean intransitive verb (고유어) evolving from 15th-century Middle Korean 믈어디다 / 므너디다 ("to crumble down, to collapse"). It was compounded from the transitive verb stem 믈- / 므느- ("to tear down, to demolish") + connective -어 + inchoative auxiliary 디다 (> modern 지다, "to fall, to become"). Through nasal assimilation (믈어 > 므너 > 무너) and palatalization (디다 > 지다), it yielded modern 무너지다.

history.meaning: to crumble down, to collapse
to collapse, to fall into ruin
to collapse, to crumble; to break down emotionally or professionally

morphemes.meaning: to crumble, to come down (from Middle Korean 믈-/므느-)

무너지다.notes: Beyond buildings collapsing, 무너지다 vividly describes a person's composure, health, or pride breaking down (자존심이 무너지다).

rootFamily.gloss: to collapse, to crumble away (synonymous compound)

무늬.etymology: A nativized Sino-Korean word (귀화어) attested in Middle Korean as 무늬 and 문위 ("pattern, decorative figure"). It originated from Sino-Korean 문 (紋 / 文, Middle Chinese *mjun*, "streaks, lines, ornamental pattern on silk or jade") extended with a vocalic suffix -의/-위, eventually losing its perceived Sino-Korean identity and functioning as a native Korean noun.

history.meaning: streak, line, ornamental pattern
decorative pattern on fabric or objects
pattern, print, design; superficial appearance (in 무늬만)

morphemes.meaning: ornamental pattern, streak (nativized from 紋/文)

무늬.notes: The colloquial expression 무늬만 X ("X in pattern only") is a favorite idiom meaning "X in name only / a fake X" (e.g., 무늬만 휴가 — a vacation in name only).

무대.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun (한자어) written 무대 (舞臺), combining 무 (舞, "to dance, posture, theatrical performance") and 대 (臺, "elevated platform, terrace, viewing tower"). In classical East Asia it denoted an open-air raised terrace for court or ritual dances; in modern Korean it designates any theatrical, concert, or broadcast stage, as well as a figurative arena of action.

history.meaning: elevated terrace for ritual or court dance
theatrical/broadcast performance stage; figurative arena of activity

무대.notes: In K-pop and broadcasting (like Music Bank in The Producers), 무대 refers both to the physical stage and to a single song performance ("첫 무대" — debut performance).

무뚝뚝하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'blunt, brusque, curt, uncommunicative', formed from an expressive stem 무뚝뚝- (intensifying prefix 무- + reduplicated ideophone 뚝뚝 'abrupt, gruff') plus -하다.

history.meaning: blunt, gruff in manner
blunt, brusque, taciturn, gruff

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무뚝뚝하다

cognates.word: 無力化 (むりょくか, muryokuka)

무력화시키다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean causative verb formed from 무력화 (無力化, "neutralization, rendering powerless") plus the native Korean causative light verb -시키다 ("to cause to become, to make"). The Sino-Korean stem comprises 무 (無, "without, lacking"), 력 (力, "power, strength, effectiveness"), and the productive suffix -화 (化, "-ification, transformation into").

history.meaning: powerlessness + transformation (-ification)
to neutralize, to incapacitate, to render powerless or ineffective

morphemes.meaning: causative light verb: to make/cause to be

무력화시키다.notes: Used heavily in strategic, legal, and media contexts when one party disarms an opponent's argument, tactic, or authority.

rootFamily.gloss: to be neutralized, rendered powerless (無力化-)

무렵.etymology: Native Korean bound noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 무렵 (mwulyep), designating an approximate temporal boundary or the transitional period when a season or time of day sets in. Unlike exact clock counters, 무렵 portrays time as an atmospheric threshold—such as twilight (저녁 무렵), daybreak (새벽 무렵), or the turn of a season. It must always be preceded by a modifying temporal noun or a prospective adnominal verb clause ending in -(으)ㄹ.

history.meaning: approximate time, temporal juncture or threshold
around the time of, toward (bound noun)

무렵.notes: Particularly natural with times of day and transitions: 저녁 무렵 ('around dusk/evening') and 잠들 무렵 ('just as one is falling asleep').

무료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 무료 (無料), meaning 'free of charge, complimentary, no fee', composed of 無 (무, 'without, none') + 料 (료, 'fee, charge, fare').

history.meaning: without fee or charge
free of charge, complimentary

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무료

무르다.etymology: A native Korean action verb (고유어) descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 므르다 ("to step back, to retreat, to restore something to its previous state"). Through labial vowel rounding (므 > 무 after bilabial ㅁ in the Early Modern period), 므르다 became modern 무르다, meaning to undo a move in a board game, take back a promise, or return a purchase. (Distinct from its homophone 무르다 "to be soft/overripe".)

history.meaning: to step back, to retreat, to turn back
to undo a move, to back out of a deal, to take back

morphemes.meaning: to turn back, to undo, to rescind

무르다.notes: In everyday games, bets, and playful negotiations, "무르기 없기!" ("No take-backs! / No backing out!") is a set phrase every learner hears in K-dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to step back, to resign, to withdraw
to return an item, to postpone, to make someone undo

무릎.etymology: A native Korean anatomical noun (고유어) attested in the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446) and 15th-century Middle Korean texts as 무룹 ("knee"). During the Early Modern Korean transition, the second-syllable vowel unrounded from 우 to 으 and the final bilabial stop -ㅂ underwent aspiration to -ㅍ (무룹 > 무릎), reflecting coalescence with an ancient final aspirate element (-ㅎ) found in several Korean body-part nouns (compare 코 < 고ㅎ "nose", 팔 < ᄇᆞᆯㅎ "arm").

history.meaning: knee
knee
knee; lap (when sitting)

무릎.notes: The idiom 무릎(을) 꿇다 ("to kneel down") means both physically kneeling and figuratively surrendering or humbling oneself before someone.

rootFamily.gloss: to kneel, to bow in submission

무리.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written 무리 (無理), composed of the negative prefix 무 (無, "without, lacking") and 리 (理, "reason, natural principle, internal pattern of jade"). Originally denoting behavior or arguments "contrary to reason" in Classical Chinese, it expanded in Korean (and Japanese) to mean an excessive demand, an impossible task, or overexerting one's health and capacity. (Homophonous with native Korean 무리 "crowd, flock".)

history.meaning: lacking reason or principle, irrationality
unreasonableness, excessive strain, asking too much

무리.notes: Saying "그건 좀 무리예요" ("That's a bit unreasonable / asking too much") is a polite, indirect way to decline a request, while "무리하지 마세요" means "Don't overwork yourself!".

rootFamily.gloss: to overdo it, to strain oneself; to be unreasonable (無理-)
an overplay in Baduk; a reckless/unreasonable move (無理手)

무사하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 무사 (無事, literally 'without incident or trouble') plus -하다, meaning 'safe, unharmed, peaceful'.

history.meaning: without untoward incident
safe, well, without incident

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무사하다

cognates.meaning: free from trouble, safe and sound

무사히.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean adverb formed from the Sino-Korean stem 무사 (無事, "without incident, safe and sound", composed of 무 無 "without" and 사 事 "affair, trouble, incident") plus the native Korean deadjectival adverbial suffix -히 (derived from 무사하다 "to be safe"). In classical texts 無事 meant peace from war or state affairs; in everyday Korean it means arriving or finishing "safely and without mishap".

history.meaning: absence of trouble, peace from state incidents
safely, without mishap or incident

무사히.notes: Whereas 안전하게 ("safely") focuses on following safety precautions, 무사히 focuses on the relieved outcome of getting through a trip, broadcast, or ordeal without any trouble.

rootFamily.gloss: to be safe and sound, free from mishap (無事-)

무서워지는지.etymology: An inflected native Korean verb form built on the descriptive verb 무섭다 ("to be scary, frightening", Middle Korean 무셥다, derived from the older verb stem 무싀- "to fear, to dread" + adjectival suffix -업-). Here the stem 무섭- undergoes regular ㅂ-irregular lenition before the connective -어 (무서워), combines with the inchoative auxiliary 지- ("to become", from Middle Korean 디다), and takes the indirect interrogative clausal ending -는지 ("how / whether it becomes").

history.meaning: to be fearful, terrifying
whether or how frightening (something) becomes

무서워지는지.notes: Adding -어지다 turns a static quality (무섭다 "is scary") into a gradual change of state (무서워지다 "gets scary"), and -는지 embeds it as an indirect question ("...how scary a person can get").

무서워하다.etymology: A native Korean psychological transitive verb (고유어 파생동사) formed from the descriptive verb stem 무섭- ("to be scary, fearful", Middle Korean 무셥다 < 무싀- "to fear" + -업-) + infinitive connective -어 (yielding 무서워 via ㅂ-lenition) + the psychological verbalizer -하다 ("to feel or display an emotion toward an object"). It converts an internal adjective of fear into an observable transitive action ("to fear X, to be scared of X").

history.meaning: to be fearful, frightening (descriptive verb)
to be afraid of, to fear, to show fear toward

무서워하다.notes: Korean grammar rule of thumb: use 무섭다 for your own immediate feeling ("나 무서워!" — I'm scared!), but use 무서워하다 when describing a third person's fear or taking a direct object with 을/를 ("그 선배를 무서워한다").

무섭다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'scary, frightening; fearful, afraid', descending from Middle Korean 무셥다 ('fearsome, dreadful').

history.meaning: fearsome, frightening, afraid
scary, frightening, afraid

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무섭다

무쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound of 쇠 ('iron, metal', Middle Korean 쇠). The first element 무- derives historically from 물- (cognate with 물 'water' or 무르다 'to be soft, melted'), describing molten pig iron poured into a cast. Following regular Korean liquid-deletion rules, the ㄹ dropped before the coronal ㅅ of 쇠 (물쇠 > 무쇠). It names heavy, durable cast iron, famously used in traditional Korean cauldrons (가마솥) and sturdy rings or heavy pans.
무쇠.notes: Common in compounds like 무쇠솥 ('cast-iron cauldron') and 무쇠 냄비 ('cast-iron pot').

무슨.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite determiner meaning 'what, what kind of, some', descending from Middle Korean 무슨 / 므슴 (adnominal derivative of the interrogative root 므스- 'what').

history.meaning: what kind of, what
what, what kind of; some, any

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무슨

무시당하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean passive verb combining 무시 (無視, "disregard, ignoring, looking down on", from 무 無 "nothing, not" + 시 視 "to look at, to regard") with the adversative passive verbalizer -당하다 (當-, from Sino-Korean 당 當 "to face, to undergo, to suffer" + native -하다). Literally "to suffer being treated as nothing".

history.meaning: treating as nonexistent + undergoing/suffering
to be ignored, to be slighted or looked down upon

무시당하다.notes: Unlike the neutral passive 무시되다 ("to be disregarded/overlooked", used for rules or data), 무시당하다 carries strong emotional sting ("to be disrespected, slighted, or looked down on" as a person).

rootFamily.gloss: to ignore, to disregard, to look down on (無視-)
to be disregarded, overlooked (neutral passive, 無視-)

cognates.word: 無視する (むしする, mushi suru)

무시하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed from 무시 (無視, "ignoring, disregarding") and the native light verb -하다 ("to do"). The Sino-Korean noun consists of 무 (無, "not, nothing") and 시 (視, "to look at, to inspect, to regard"), literally meaning "to look upon as nothing" — hence either paying no attention to something or belittling someone's worth.

history.meaning: to regard as nothing, to disregard
to ignore, to disregard; to look down on or belittle someone

무시하다.notes: Be careful with human objects: "날 무시하는 거야?" doesn't just mean "Are you ignoring me?", it usually means "Are you looking down on me / underestimating me?".

rootFamily.gloss: to be ignored, to be looked down on (無視當-)
to slight, to make light of (輕視-)
to attach great importance to, to value highly (重視-)

무언가.etymology: A native Korean indefinite pronoun (고유어 대명사) contracted from the phrase 무엇인가 ("something, whatever it may be"). It comprises the interrogative/indefinite pronoun 무엇 ("what, thing", from Middle Korean 므슷 / 므스), the copula stem -이- ("to be"), and the dubitative/indefinite ending -ㄴ가. Intervocalic loss of the final -ㅅ of 무엇 (무엇인가 > 무어인가 > 무언가) produced the modern literary and conversational form.

history.meaning: what, which thing
what it may be, something unspecified
something (indefinite pronoun)

무언가.notes: 무언가 has a slightly more reflective, narrative, or literary feel than its everyday spoken contraction 뭔가 ("something").

무엇.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite pronoun meaning 'what, something', contracted from Middle Korean 므스것 (므스 'what' + 것 'thing' -> 므엇 -> 무엇).

history.meaning: what thing -> what
what, something

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무엇

무염.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 무염 (無鹽), meaning 'unsalted, salt-free' (frequently used of culinary ingredients such as 무염 버터 'unsalted butter'), formed from 無 (무, 'without') + 鹽 (염, 'salt').

history.meaning: without salt, unsalted
unsalted, salt-free

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 무염

cognates.word: 無条件 (むじょうけん, mujōken)

무조건.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun and adverb (한자어) written 무조건 (無條件), formed from the negative prefix 무 (無, "without, lacking") and 조건 (條件, "condition, proviso, terms", from 조 條 "article, clause, branch" + 건 件 "item, matter"). Adopted in modern legal and diplomatic prose for "unconditional" (e.g., unconditional surrender), it broadened in spoken Korean into a high-frequency emphatic adverb meaning "without fail, no matter what, automatically".

history.meaning: without + articles/conditions
unconditionally; (colloquial) no matter what, without fail, 100%

무조건.notes: In casual conversation, 무조건 is much more playful and common than English "unconditionally"—it translates naturally as "no matter what", "hands down", or "without fail".

무지.etymology: A colloquial Korean intensifier adverb derived by clipping and semantic bleaching from 무지하게 ("ignorantly; tremendously") and 무지무지 ("extremely"), rooted in Sino-Korean 무지 (無知, "ignorance, knowing no bounds", from 무 無 "without" + 지 知 "knowledge, awareness"). Just as English "awfully" or "terribly" shifted from negative evaluation to degree intensification, acting "without knowing limits" evolved into an everyday adverb meaning "awfully, super, really".

history.meaning: lack of knowledge, ignorance
recklessly, boundlessly, tremendously
awfully, extremely, really hard (colloquial intensifier)

무지.notes: As an adverb ("무지 힘들다" — It's awfully hard), 무지 is strictly informal/conversational; in formal writing, the noun 무지 (無知) still means "ignorance".

rootFamily.gloss: to be ignorant; (colloquial) to be tremendous/extreme (無知-)

묵다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 묵다 ('to stay overnight, lodge; to remain long, age, become old or fermented').

history.meaning: to stay over, remain long, age
to stay overnight, lodge; to age, ferment

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 묵다

묵사발.etymology: A hybrid Korean compound noun (혼종어) combining native Korean 묵 ("starch jelly made from acorns or buckwheat", Middle Korean 묵) and Sino-Korean 사발 (沙鉢, "large earthenware or porcelain bowl", from 사 沙 "sand, clay" + 발 鉢 "bowl", ultimately a Buddhist borrowing from Sanskrit pātra "vessel"). Literally "a bowl of mashed acorn jelly", the image of soft, fragile jelly crushed up in a soup bowl gave rise to the vivid figurative sense "pulp, mincemeat, a total wreck".

history.meaning: acorn/buckwheat starch jelly + earthenware bowl
a bowl of crushed jelly soup; (figurative) pulp, mincemeat, shattered mess

묵사발.notes: Almost always heard in the colorful idiom 묵사발(을) 만들다 or 묵사발(이) 되다 ("to beat/crush into mincemeat" or "to get pulverized/humiliated").

묵직하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built on the ideophonic root 묵직- plus the light verb suffix -하다. As the dark-vowel counterpart to the brighter 막직-, 묵직하다 goes beyond mere physical weight (무겁다) to convey a satisfying, reassuring solidity or a deep, resonant gravity, often used for heavy brass tools, thick wooden furniture, or a deep voice.
묵직하다.notes: Conveys a positive, substantial heaviness, whereas 무겁다 ('heavy') is the neutral or burdensome antonym of 가볍다 ('light').

묶다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb 묶다 ('to tie up, bind into a bundle'), attested in Middle Korean as 믜다/묶다 and related to the noun 묶음 ('bundle, bunch'). It retains the double velar stop ㄲ in its stem across all conjugations (묶어요 [무꺼요], 묶어서 [무꺼서]).
묶다.notes: Pronounced [묵따] before consonant endings and [무꺼요] before vowel endings.

묶어달라다.etymology: A native Korean contracted quotative-benefactive verb construction built on 묶- ("to tie, to bind", from Middle Korean 믓다 / 믜다 > Early Modern 묵다 > 묶다 via expressive tensification), the connective -어, the suppletive benefactive request verb 달- ("to give/do for the speaker"), and the indirect imperative quotative ending -라(고) 하- contracted to -라- + -다. It specifically reports a request in which the original speaker asked someone to tie something for them.

history.meaning: to bind/tie + to give to the requester
to ask (someone) to tie (something) for the requester

morphemes.meaning: suppletive benefactive auxiliary: to give/do for the requester

묶어달라다.notes: In indirect speech, Korean distinguishes who benefits: 묶어달라다 means "she asked you to tie it for her (the speaker)", whereas 묶어주라다 means "she asked you to tie it for someone else".

rootFamily.gloss: to tie, to bind, to bundle

묶어드리다.etymology: A native Korean humble benefactive compound verb (고유어 합성동사) combining the transitive verb stem 묶- ("to tie, to bind", from Middle Korean 믓다 > 묶다), the infinitive connective -어, and the humble benefactive auxiliary 드리- ("to give or offer to a respected person", Middle Korean 드리다, originally the causative of 들다 "to enter", i.e. "to cause to enter a superior's presence").

history.meaning: to bind + to offer/present to a superior
to tie (something) for a respected person (humble benefactive)

morphemes.meaning: humble benefactive auxiliary: to do/give for a superior

묶어드리다.notes: Replacing -어 주다 with -어 드리다 elevates the recipient of the favor (e.g., a junior PD humbly tying a senior star's hair or shoelaces).

rootFamily.gloss: to give/offer humbly to a superior

묶어주다.etymology: A native Korean benefactive compound verb (고유어 합성동사) composed of the transitive stem 묶- ("to tie, to bind, to fasten", evolving from Middle Korean 믓다 > Early Modern Korean 묵다 > modern 묶다 through glottal tensification), the infinitive connective -어, and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주- ("to give, to perform an action for someone's benefit", Middle Korean 주다).

history.meaning: to bind/fasten + to give
to tie or fasten (something) for someone

morphemes.meaning: to tie, to bind, to fasten
benefactive auxiliary: to give, to do for someone

묶어주다.notes: In Korean, favors like tying hair (머리를 묶어주다) or shoelaces almost always require the benefactive auxiliary -어 주다 rather than bare 묶다.

rootFamily.gloss: to tie, to bind, to bundle
to tie for a respected person (humble)
to be tied, to be bound (passive)

묶이다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb meaning 'to be tied, bound, bundled, or restricted', derived from 묶다 ('to tie, bind, bundle', Middle Korean 믜다 / 묶다) plus the passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be tied up, bound
to be tied, bound, bundled, held up

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 묶이다

문.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 문 (門, Middle Chinese *mwon*), meaning 'door, gate, entrance, opening', borrowed early and serving as the standard everyday Korean word for 'door'.

history.meaning: door, gate
door, gate, entrance

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 문

문가.etymology: Compound noun joining the fully naturalized Sino-Korean noun 문 (門, mun, 'door, gate') with the native Korean spatial suffixoid 가 (ga, from Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ kos, 'edge, border, vicinity'). Like 창가 ('by the window') and 길가 ('by the road'), it denotes the immediate area beside an architectural opening rather than the door leaf itself. Because of the historical genitive boundary between the two nouns, the initial velar stop of 가 tensifies in standard speech to [문까] (munkka).

history.meaning: door + edge/vicinity
by the door, doorway area

문가.notes: Standard pronunciation is [문까]; often followed by directional -로 (문가로 'over to the doorway') or locative -에 (문가에 'by the door').

문자.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written 문자 (文字), combining 문 (文, "drawn lines, pattern, writing, graph") and 자 (字, "written character, derived graph", originally depicting a child 子 nurtured under a roof 宀). For centuries it meant "written characters or script"; in the late 1990s mobile phone era, it was clipped from 문자 메시지 ("character/text message", SMS) to become the standard everyday word for a "text message".

history.meaning: written graphs and characters, script
SMS text message on a mobile phone
text message (SMS); written character/script

문자.notes: Pronunciation tip: when 문자 means "written characters/script", it is traditionally pronounced [문짜] with tensification, whereas when it means an SMS "text message", Koreans overwhelmingly pronounce it [문자] without tensification!

rootFamily.gloss: to text, to send an SMS (文字-)

문자하다.etymology: A modern hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from 문자 (文字, "text message", clipped from 문자 메시지 "SMS text message", from 문 文 "writing" + 자 字 "character") plus the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do, to send"). Coined in late-1990s and 2000s South Korean mobile culture, it parallels 전화하다 ("to phone") as the everyday verb for texting.

history.meaning: to send a text message (full phrasal expression)
to text, to send an SMS message

morphemes.meaning: light verb: to do, to send

문자하다.notes: In contemporary Korea, 문자하다 usually refers to standard SMS texting (or texting in general), while 카톡하다 specifically refers to messaging on KakaoTalk.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a phone call (電話-)

문장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 문장 (文章), meaning 'sentence (in grammar); prose composition, writing style', from 文 (문, 'writing, characters') + 章 (장, 'section, composition, emblem').

history.meaning: literary composition, prose
sentence; writing style

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 문장

문제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 문제 (問題), meaning 'question (on a test); problem, issue, matter for discussion', from 問 (문, 'to ask, inquire') + 題 (제, 'topic, subject, heading').

history.meaning: question posed for answer or debate
problem, question, issue

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 문제

문턱.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'threshold, doorsill', combining Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door, gate') with native Korean 턱 ('raised ridge, sill, chin').

history.meaning: door threshold, raised sill
threshold, doorsill; figurative barrier to entry

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 문턱

문틈.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining Sino-Korean 문 (門, "door, gate") with native Korean 틈 ("crack, gap, crevice, opening"). The second element 틈 is attested in Middle Korean as 틈 and 틉 ("crack, cleft"), derived via the nominalizing suffix -ㅁ from the native verb 트다 ("to split open, crack, chap, break through"). Together, 문틈 literally denotes the narrow chink or crevice between a door and its frame.

history.meaning: door + split, cleft, crevice
crack or chink of a door

문틈.notes: Often used in drama scenes for eavesdropping or peeking covertly (문틈으로 엿보다, "to peek through a crack in the door").

rootFamily.gloss: window crack, chink in a window

문화유산.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 文化遺産, joining 문화 (文化, 'culture, civilization') with 유산 (遺産, 'heritage, legacy left behind by predecessors', from 遺 'leave behind' + 産 'property, patrimony'). It is the official Korean legal and civic term used by national and municipal boards to designate historic buildings, courtyards, crafts, and traditions worthy of preservation.
문화유산.notes: Standard civic term for historic landmarks and protected cultural properties.

문화유산과.etymology: Sino-Korean administrative compound 문화유산과 (文化遺産課), meaning 'Cultural Heritage Division/Section', formed from 문화 (文化, 'culture') + 유산 (遺産, 'heritage, legacy') + -과 (課, 'administrative department or section').

history.meaning: cultural heritage administrative section
Cultural Heritage Division

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 문화유산과

묻다.etymology: Native Korean verb representing three Middle Korean verbs that share the modern citation spelling 묻다: (1) ㄷ-irregular 묻다 ('to ask, inquire', stem 물어- before vowels, Middle Korean 묻다); (2) regular 묻다 ('to bury in the ground, conceal', Middle Korean 묻다); and (3) regular 묻다 ('to stick to, stain, get smeared on', Middle Korean 묻다).

history.meaning: to ask (ㄷ-stem); to bury; to adhere/stain
to ask, inquire; to bury; to get on, stain

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 묻다

물.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'water, liquid, stream', descending from Middle Korean 믈 ('water') via Early Modern Korean labial rounding of ㅡ to ㅜ after the bilabial nasal ㅁ.

history.meaning: water
water, liquid, juice

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물

물갈이하다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from 물 ("water", Middle Korean 믈) + 갈이 ("changing, replacing", the deverbal noun of 갈다 "to replace, change, renew", Middle Korean 갈다, + nominalizer -이) + the verbalizer -하다 ("to do"). Originally an aquarium and agricultural term meaning "to change stale water for fresh water", it underwent metaphorical extension in modern Korean to mean completely overhauling personnel, replacing the cast of a television show, or refreshing a political lineup.

history.meaning: water + to replace, change
to change the water (in a tank or paddy)
to overhaul personnel, replace the cast or lineup

물갈이하다.notes: In broadcasting and politics, 물갈이 refers to a sweeping replacement of older cast members or incumbents with fresh faces; it can sound blunt or ruthless when applied to people.

물건.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 물건 (物件), meaning 'thing, object, item, goods', formed from 物 (물, 'thing, object, matter') + 件 (건, 'article, item').

history.meaning: tangible article or item
thing, item, object, goods

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물건

물러가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to step back, retreat, withdraw, leave a superior's presence', combining the infinitive stem 물러- of 무르다 ('to move back, yield') with 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to retreat, withdraw
to step back, fall back, retire

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물러가다

물러서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to step back, stand back, back down, resign from a post', combining 물러- (from 무르다, 'to move back') with 서다 ('to stand', Middle Korean 셔다).

history.meaning: to step back and stand
to step back, back away, step down

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물러서다

물론.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 물론 (勿論), meaning 'of course, needless to say, not to mention', literally 'do not discuss or argue', from 勿 (물, 'do not') + 論 (론, 'discuss, debate').

history.meaning: no need to debate -> without question
of course, naturally, needless to say

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물론

물리다.etymology: A native Korean passive and causative verb derived from the transitive verb stem 물- (물다, "to bite, hold in the mouth", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 물다) combined with the native voice suffix -리- (which marks passive or causative depending on valency) and the declarative ending -다. In the passive sense it means "to be bitten" (by a dog, insect, or snake), while in the causative sense it means "to make someone hold something in the mouth".

history.meaning: to bite + passive/causative suffix
to be bitten; to clamp in the mouth

morphemes.meaning: to bite, hold in the mouth

물리다.notes: Watch out for homonyms: 물리다 can mean "to get bitten" (from 물다 "bite"), "to be made to pay damages" (from 물다 "compensate"), or "to grow sick and tired of food/something" (from 무르다/물리다).

rootFamily.gloss: to bite, hold in the mouth
to clamp tightly between the teeth or lips

물리학.etymology: Sino-Korean scholarly compound 物理學, formed from 물리 (物理, 'the inherent principles of things', from 物 'thing, matter' + 理 'principle, natural law') and the suffix -학 (學, 'study, academic discipline'). Classical East Asian thinkers used 物理 for the underlying order of nature, and in the late nineteenth century it became the standard term for modern physics.
물리학.notes: Often shortened to 물리 when referring to a school subject.

물어내다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from 물다 ("to compensate, reimburse, pay damages", attested in Middle Korean as 물다 "to make restitution, pay back") + the infinitive connector -어 + the auxiliary/directional verb 내다 ("to put out, produce, pay forth", Middle Korean 내다, causative of 나다 "to come out"). The auxiliary 내다 adds the nuance of extracting resources from one's own pocket to settle a debt or damage claim.

history.meaning: to make restitution + to put forth
to reimburse, pay damages out of pocket

물어내다.notes: Compared to simple 물다 or 물어주다, 물어내다 emphasizes the reluctant or compulsory act of coughing up money to cover a loss or penalty (e.g., 위약금을 물어내다, "to pay a contract penalty").

rootFamily.gloss: to make someone pay damages; to be fined

물어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to ask, inquire', formed from the ㄷ-irregular verb 묻다 ('to ask', conjugated as 물어-) plus the exploratory auxiliary verb 보다 ('to try, see').

history.meaning: to ask and see, inquire
to ask, inquire

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물어보다

물어주다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb composed of 물다 ("to compensate, make restitution for a loss", Middle Korean 물다) + the infinitive connector -어 + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give, do for another's benefit", Middle Korean 주다). Whereas 물다 alone denotes the obligation of restitution, attaching -어 주다 frames the compensation as an action directed toward restoring the aggrieved party.

history.meaning: to compensate + to give
to reimburse or compensate someone for damages

물어주다.notes: Do not confuse 물어주다 ("to pay damages/compensate", from 물다) with 물어봐 주다 ("to ask on someone's behalf", from 묻다 "to ask", which is irregular ㄷ and also conjugates to 물어-).

rootFamily.gloss: to pay back, compensate for damages
to cough up or pay damages
to return a purchase, get a refund

물장구.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 물 ('water') and 장구 (the traditional Korean two-headed hourglass drum, lexicalized from Sino-Korean 杖鼓). The word poetically likens the rhythmic kicking of feet or flapping of wings on the water's surface to the rapid, alternating drumbeats of a janggu player. It is the standard Korean word for children paddling or birds splashing in a shallow bath.
물장구.notes: Always paired with the verb 치다 (물장구를 치다, 'to splash/paddle in water').

물정.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 물정 (物情), formed from 물 (物, "thing, matter, the outside world, the public") and 정 (情, "feelings, disposition, actual circumstances, condition"). Attested in Classical Chinese and Joseon-era administrative prose for "the sentiments of the people" or "the actual condition of things", it stabilized in modern Korean especially in phrases like 세상 물정 ("how the real world works").

history.meaning: nature of things; public sentiment
public affairs; actual state of the world
how the world works, practical realities of life

물정.notes: Almost always collocates with 모르다 or 어둡다, as in 세상 물정을 모르다 ("to be naive / ignorant of how the world works").

rootFamily.gloss: human warmth, the ways of people (人情)

물줄기.etymology: Native Korean spatial compound joining 물 ('water') and 줄기 ('stem, stalk, trunk, steady stream'). Just as a plant has a main stalk (줄기) branching outward, Korean uses 줄기 to conceptualize continuous, directed flows of natural elements, producing vivid compounds like 물줄기 ('stream, jet of water') and 빛줄기 ('ray/shaft of light').
물줄기.notes: Collocates with 뿜어지다 ('spout out'), 쏟아지다 ('pour down'), or 뻗다 ('stretch out').

물체.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 물체 (物體), meaning 'physical object, body, material form', composed of 物 (물, 'thing, matter') + 體 (체, 'body, substance, form').

history.meaning: physical body or material object
object, body, physical form

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 물체

물통.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed from the native noun 물 ('water', Middle Korean 물) and the Sino-Korean noun 통 (桶, 'tub, bucket, barrel, cylinder'). Because 통 can refer to any cylindrical or hollow container, 물통 serves as a flexible, everyday word for a painter's water basin, a hiker's water canteen, or a large water bucket, depending entirely on the context.
물통.notes: Very context-dependent: in art it means 'water basin'; outdoors it means 'water bottle/canteen'.

물티슈.etymology: A contemporary hybrid compound combining native Korean 물 ("water, wet", from Middle Korean 믈) with the English loanword 티슈 (*tissue*, "disposable paper wipe"). The English word *tissue* itself derives from Old French *tissu* ("a ribbon or fine woven fabric", the substantivized past participle of *tistre* "to weave"), ultimately from Latin *texere* ("to weave"). Coined in South Korea as a colloquial, transparent term for pre-moistened disposable wipes (*wet wipes* / *wet tissues*).

history.meaning: water (native Korean element)

history.form: tissue (< Old French tissu < Latin texere)
history.meaning: woven cloth > thin absorbent paper (English loan element)
wet wipe, moist towelette

물티슈.notes: While English speakers usually say "wet wipes" or "baby wipes", Koreans universally call them 물티슈 ("water-tissue") in restaurants, homes, and offices.

뭉개다.etymology: A native Korean transitive verb meaning "to crush, mash, flatten out of shape", and figuratively "to gloss over, sweep under the rug, or dawdle away". It belongs to a native Korean phonesthemic cluster built on the dark-vowel root 뭉그-/뭉개- ("blunt, mashed, sluggish, rubbed down", contrasting with bright-vowel 몽개다 "to crush smaller things"), structurally formed with the causative/transitive suffix -개-/-애-.

history.meaning: to mash, crush, flatten out of shape
to squash; figuratively to gloss over a duty or dawdle in one spot

뭉개다.notes: In workplace and broadcasting slang, 뭉개다 often means "to sit on an issue / ignore an order until it blows over" or "to lounge around wasting time".

rootFamily.gloss: to get squashed, be glossed over

뭉개지다.etymology: A native Korean inchoative/passive verb derived from 뭉개다 ("to crush, mash, smudge, gloss over") + the auxiliary passive/inchoative construction -어지다 (contracted to -지다 because the stem 뭉개- already ends in the vowel -애). Literally denoting a soft object losing its shape by being squashed or smudged, it also carries the figurative sense of an issue, schedule, or responsibility getting quietly buried or glossed over.

history.meaning: to crush + to become (inchoative/passive)
to get squashed, smudged, or glossed over

뭉개지다.notes: Frequently used both for physical things (like makeup smudging or a cake getting squashed) and abstract things (like pronunciation slurring or a plan getting buried).

뭉치다.etymology: A native Korean verb meaning "to lump together, pack into a ball, unite, stick together". Attested in Early Modern Korean as 뭉치다 and related to Middle Korean 무츼다 / 뭉키다 ("to gather into a mass"), it is built on the native bound root 뭉- ("compact mass, bundle, clump") + the verbalizing and intensifying suffix -치- + -다. From the physical act of packing snow or clay into a ball, it generalized to people banding together in solidarity.

history.meaning: to gather into a clump, mass together
to lump together; to unite, band together, stick together

뭉치다.notes: Famous in the Korean proverb 뭉치면 살고 흩어지면 죽는다 ("United we stand [live], divided we fall [die]"). Also used when muscles knot up (어깨가 뭉치다).

rootFamily.gloss: to form a lump, clot, or tangle
a round lump or mass (of clay, rice, etc.)

뭐.etymology: Colloquial native Korean pronoun and interjection meaning 'what; something; well', contracted from 무엇 ('what', Middle Korean 므스것 > 므엇 > 무엇 > 무어 > 뭐).

history.meaning: contracted form of 무엇 ('what')
what, something; well (discourse marker)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뭐

뭐라다.etymology: A colloquial contracted quotative verb from 무어라고 하다 ("to say what"), where 뭐 is the phonological contraction of 무어 (from 무엇 "what", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 므슷 / 므스), combined with the indirect quotative suffix -라(고) and the light verb 하다 ("to say, do"). In casual speech, the sequence 뭐라고 하- contracts by syncopating -고 하-, yielding the lexicalized stem 뭐라- ("to say what; to scold or complain").

history.meaning: what + to say/do
to say what; to criticize or talk about
to say what; to nag, scold, or babble about

뭐라다.notes: In everyday conversation, 뭐라다 means not only "What is he saying?" (뭐라는 거야?) but also "to scold / criticize someone" (엄마가 뭐라셨어?, "Did Mom tell you off?").

rootFamily.gloss: to do what; to be awkward to say

뭐래다.etymology: A colloquial contracted quotative verb derived from 무어라고 해 (the intimate/infinitive form of 무어라고 하다 "to say what"), where 뭐 (< 무어 < 무엇 "what", Middle Korean 므슷) + quotative -라(고) + 해 (< 하- + -어) coalesced into 뭐래 ("what does [he/she] say?"), which was subsequently reanalyzed by speakers as a verb stem 뭐래- taking further endings (such as 뭐래는 거야 "what is he talking about?" or citation form 뭐래다).

history.meaning: saying what / what does one say
what is (someone) saying?; to talk nonsense

뭐래다.notes: Saying 뭐래? or 쟤 뭐래니? on its own is a sharp, dismissive retort in Korean conversation equivalent to "What is he even talking about?" or "Whatever / nonsense!"

rootFamily.gloss: to say so, to do like that (< 그러하다고 해-)

뭐하다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb and adjective formed from 뭐 (the vowel-coalesced contraction of 무어 < 무엇 "what", from 15th-century Middle Korean 므슷 / 므스) + 하다 ("to do; to be", Middle Korean 흐다). As an active verb it literally means "to do what" (frequently written spaced as 뭐 하다), whereas as a lexicalized adjective it developed a euphemistic sense: "to be somewhat awkward, delicate, or hard to put into words" (because naming the quality directly feels too blunt).

history.meaning: to do what
to do what; (adj.) to be somewhat awkward or hesitant to do/say

뭐하다.notes: As an adjective, 뭐하다 is a classic Korean hedging expression: 거절하기도 좀 뭐하다 means "It feels a bit awkward/uncomfortable to refuse, too."

뭔.etymology: A colloquial native Korean interrogative and indefinite determiner meaning "what" or "what kind of", formed by contracting 무언 (itself from 무어 "what", Middle Korean 므스 / 므슷, + the copula stem 이- + the adnominal modifier suffix -ㄴ, i.e., "which is what"), while also functioning in everyday speech as a phonological reduction of 무슨 ("what kind of", Middle Korean 므슴).

history.meaning: which is what / what kind of
what, what kind of (prenominal modifier)

뭔.notes: Strictly speaking, 무슨 is standard in formal writing, while 뭔 is ubiquitous in casual speech to express surprise or disbelief (이게 뭔 일이야?, "What on earth is going on?").

뭔가.etymology: A native Korean indefinite pronoun and adverbial form contracted from 무언가 (from 무어 "what", Middle Korean 므슷, + the copula stem 이- + the adnominal ending -ㄴ + the dubitative/interrogative particle -가). By a cross-linguistically common grammaticalization pathway whereby interrogative phrases with a dubitative particle ("what is it?") shift into existential indefinites, 무언가 > 뭔가 came to mean "something" (pronoun) or "somehow, in some way" (adverb).

history.meaning: what might it be > something
something; (adv.) somehow, somewhat

뭔가.notes: In contemporary speech, 뭔가 is very frequently used as an adverbial filler meaning "somehow" or "kind of" (오늘따라 뭔가 이상하다, "Somehow things feel strange today").

뭣도.etymology: A colloquial native Korean negative-polarity pronoun phrase formed by contracting 무엇 ("what, thing", from 15th-century Middle Korean 므슷 via 므엇) into the monosyllable 뭣 (by coalescence of ㅜ + ㅓ > ㅝ) and attaching the additive/concessive particle -도 ("also, even"). Used with negative predicates (such as 아니다, 없다, or 모르다), 뭣도 means "not anything at all, nothing whatsoever".

history.meaning: even what / anything at all
anything at all (with negative: nothing at all)

뭣도.notes: Highly idiomatic in the blunt dismissal 뭣도 모르면서 ("without knowing a single thing about it!") or 뭣도 아닌 게 ("someone/something that isn't even anything special").

뮤뱅.etymology: A South Korean broadcasting syllabic abbreviation (두음절 줄임말) of 뮤직뱅크 (*Myujikbaengkeu*, KBS2's flagship weekly live music television program *Music Bank*, launched in June 1998). Formed by clipping and combining the initial syllable of each English loanword component: 뮤 (*myu*, from 뮤직 *music*) + 뱅 (*baeng*, from 뱅크 *bank*). This two-syllable clipping pattern is standard in Korean media and K-pop fandom vernacular.

history.meaning: KBS weekly music chart television show (est. 1998)
Music Bank (colloquial and industry shorthand)

뮤뱅.notes: In *The Producers* (프로듀사), characters like Tak Ye-jin (the PD of *Music Bank*) and entertainment agency staff constantly refer to the show as 뮤뱅 in everyday production talk.

cognates.meaning: art of sound; financial institution or repository

뮤직뱅크.etymology: An English loanword compound proper noun transliterating *Music Bank*, the title of the flagship weekly live K-pop television program aired by KBS (Korean Broadcasting System) since 1998. It combines 뮤직 (from English *music*, via Old French *musique* and Latin *mūsica* from Ancient Greek *mousikē (tekhnē)*, "(art) of the Muses") and 뱅크 (from English *bank* "repository, storehouse", via Italian *banca* / Old French *banque* from Germanic *bankiz* "bench, counter").

history.form: music (< Greek mousikē) + bank (< Italian banca)
history.meaning: art of music + repository/storehouse
KBS flagship weekly live music program (premiered 1998)

뮤직뱅크.notes: In *The Producers* (프로듀사), *Music Bank* (뮤직뱅크) is the central workplace of producer Tak Ye-jin (played by Gong Hyo-jin) and top idol Cindy (played by IU).

rootFamily.gloss: music video (< Eng. music video, often clipped to 뮤비)

미꾸라지.etymology: A native Korean noun denoting the mud loach (*Misgurnus mizolepis*), attested in Early Modern Korean as 밋구라지 and 미꾸라지 (alongside the shorter variant 미꾸리, Middle Korean 밋구리). Etymologically, it is derived from the native verbal/adjectival root 믯글- / 미끌- ("to slip, be slippery", seen in 미끄럽다 "to be slippery") + the diminutive animal suffix -아지 (the same suffix found in 강아지 "puppy" and 송아지 "calf"), literally meaning "the slippery little creature".

history.meaning: mud loach (slippery fish)
mud loach (with diminutive suffix -아지)

미꾸라지.notes: Used figuratively in Korean idioms: 미꾸라지 한 마리가 온 웅덩이를 흐린다 ("One loach muddies the whole pond", i.e. one troublemaker ruins the whole group) and 미꾸라지처럼 빠져나가다 ("to slip away like a loach", for someone who wriggles out of blame).

미끄러지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to slip, slide, skid', derived from the adjective 미끄럽다 ('slippery', Middle Korean 밋그럽다) plus the inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

history.meaning: to slip, slide on a smooth surface
to slip, slide, glide

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 미끄러지다

미나.etymology: Korean female given name 미나, typically written in Sino-Korean characters such as 美娜 ('beautiful and graceful') or 美奈.

history.meaning: given name

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 미나

cognates.meaning: the future, time yet to come

미래.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun 미래 (未來), compounded from 미 (未, "not yet") and 래 (來, "to come, arrive"), literally meaning "that which has not yet come". Originally coined in Chinese Buddhist translations as a calque of Sanskrit *anāgata* ("not yet come") to designate the future world/eon within the Buddhist Three Times (삼세 三世: 과거 過去 "past", 현재 現在 "present", 미래 未來 "future"), it later secularized into the general East Asian word for "the future".

history.meaning: not yet come (calque of Sanskrit anāgata, future existence)
the future world; time yet to come
the future, future prospects

미래.notes: Alongside 장래 (將來, "one's personal future/prospects") and 앞날 (native Korean "days ahead"), 미래 is the broadest term for "the future" in general, science, and grammar (미래 시제, "future tense").

미리.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'in advance, beforehand, ahead of time', attested unchanged since Middle Korean 미리.

history.meaning: beforehand, in advance
in advance, beforehand, ahead of time

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 미리

미리미리.etymology: A native Korean reduplicated adverb formed by full reduplication of 미리 ("in advance, beforehand", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 미리). In Korean morphology, total reduplication of time and manner adverbs (미리 + 미리) adds distributive and emphatic force, shifting the meaning from a single prior action ("beforehand") to habitual, thorough, or well-timed preparation across multiple occasions ("well in advance, step by step ahead of time").

history.meaning: beforehand, in advance
well in advance, steadily ahead of time

미리미리.notes: Frequently used in advice or mild nagging (미리미리 준비해라, "Prepare well in advance [instead of cramming at the last minute]!").

rootFamily.gloss: each time, at every step (reduplicated adverb)

미발표.etymology: Sino-Korean prefixal formation 未發表, prefixing 미- (未, 'not yet, un-') to 발표 (發表, 'public presentation, publication, release'). The prefix 미- specifically indicates that something has not yet been made public (compare 미공개 'unreleased' and 미완성 'unfinished'), making 미발표 the standard musical and literary term for an unpublished composition or manuscript.
미발표.notes: Used prenominally directly before nouns such as 미발표 왈츠 ('unpublished waltz') or 미발표 곡 ('unreleased song').

미사.etymology: A loanword from Ecclesiastical Latin *missa* ("the Eucharistic liturgy, Catholic Mass"), originally the late Latin verbal noun *missa* ("dismissal") from the concluding liturgical formula *Ite, missa est* ("Go, it is the dismissal"), derived from the feminine past participle *missa* of Classical Latin *mittere* ("to send, let go, dismiss"). Introduced into Korean during the late Joseon Catholic movement via Chinese-character phonetic transcriptions (彌撒 *misa*) and reinforced by French missionaries.

history.meaning: to send/dismiss > liturgical dismissal > Eucharistic Mass
Catholic Mass (phonetic transcription in early Korean Catholic texts)
Catholic Mass

미사.notes: In Korean, Catholic services are called 미사 (미사를 드리다 / 미사에 참례하다), whereas Protestant services are strictly distinguished as 예배 (禮拜, "worship service").

rootFamily.gloss: mission, task (< Eng. mission, from the same Latin root mittere)
message (< Eng. message, ultimately from Latin missus)

미션.etymology: A direct loanword from English *mission*, which derives via Middle French *mission* from Latin *missiō* (stem *missiōn-*, "an act of sending, dispatching, or releasing"), a noun of action from *mittere* (past participle *missus*, "to send, dispatch"). Beyond its diplomatic, military, and religious senses ("Christian mission"), Korean variety television (such as *1 Night 2 Days* in *The Producers*) popularized 미션 for a game challenge or quest assigned to cast members by the production crew.

history.meaning: act of sending > diplomatic/religious mission > assigned task
mission; (broadcasting) variety show challenge or game quest

미션.notes: In Korean variety shows like *1 Night 2 Days* (1박 2일) or *Running Man*, 미션 (such as 기상 미션 "wake-up mission" or 복불복 미션) is core production jargon for every game segment.

rootFamily.gloss: Catholic Mass (< Latin missa, from the same root mittere)

cognates.word: 微笑 (びしょう) + 天使 (てんし)

미소천사.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 미소천사 (微笑天使), combining 미소 (微笑, "a gentle, silent smile", from 미 微 "subtle, slight, minute" + 소 笑 "laugh, smile") and 천사 (天使, "angel", literally "messenger of heaven", from 천 天 "heaven, sky" + 사 使 "messenger, envoy", originally denoting an imperial envoy in Classical Chinese before being adopted to translate Greek *angelos* "messenger, angel"). In contemporary Korean media, it is an affectionate epithet for someone with a radiant, constant smile.

history.meaning: faint smile + imperial/heavenly envoy (later Christian angel)
smiling angel (media nickname for a celebrity or person with a warm smile)

미소천사.notes: A staple K-pop and entertainment-show nickname for idols or actors who always smile brightly for the camera even during grueling schedules.

rootFamily.gloss: roar of laughter, burst of laughter (폭소, 爆笑)

cognates.meaning: unmarried woman's title + first letter of the alphabet

미쓰에이.etymology: The Korean phonetic rendering of *Miss A* (stylized *miss A*), the four-member South Korean-Chinese girl group formed by JYP Entertainment (active 2010–2017, featuring Bae Suzy). It combines 미쓰 (a Korean transcription of English *Miss*, itself clipped from *mistress*, written with the tense sibilant 쓰 `/s͈ɯ/` to approximate the sharp English voiceless fricative `/s/`) and 에이 (English letter *A*, standing both for "A-class" talent in all areas and for "Asia").

history.meaning: English title Miss + grade/letter A (Asia / A-class)
Miss A (JYP Entertainment K-pop girl group, debuted 2010)

미쓰에이.notes: In *The Producers* (프로듀사), CEO Byun Mi-sook (who runs Cindy's agency) constantly brags about or compares her artists to JYP's Suzy of Miss A (미쓰에이 수지). Note the spelling 미쓰 with tense ㅆ rather than standard loanword orthography 미스.

rootFamily.gloss: letter A; ace grade (< Eng. A)

미안.etymology: A Sino-Korean root noun 미안 (未安), composed of 미 (未, "not yet, un-") and 안 (安, "peaceful, tranquil, comfortable, at ease"). Originally a Classical Chinese and Joseon-era epistolary expression meaning "my heart is not at ease (because I have troubled or failed you)", it grammaticalized in Modern Korean into the standard root for feeling sorry, apologetic, or indebted toward another person, and is used standalone in casual speech ("Sorry!").

history.meaning: not at ease in mind; feeling uncomfortable or ashamed
apology, feeling sorry; (interjection) sorry!

미안.notes: Saying just 미안! (without 하다 or endings) is very casual intimate speech (반말) used only among close friends, siblings, or to much younger people; to superiors or strangers, 죄송합니다 is required instead of 미안합니다.

rootFamily.gloss: to be sorry, feel apologetic (未安하다)

미안하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean adjective formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun 미안 (未安, "feeling uneasy in one's heart toward someone", from 미 未 "not yet" + 안 安 "peaceful, tranquil") with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 ("to be", Middle Korean 흐다). In Joseon-era Korean, 미안하다 meant both "to feel uncomfortable/ill at ease" and "to feel apologetic for imposing on someone", before specializing into the primary everyday Korean word for "to be sorry".

history.meaning: to be uneasy in mind, feel ashamed or indebted
to be sorry, feel apologetic

미안하다.notes: In Korean social pragmatics, 미안하다 is less deferential than 죄송하다 (罪悚하다, lit. "to tremble with guilt"): use 미안해 / 미안해요 with peers or juniors, and 죄송합니다 in formal or workplace settings.

rootFamily.gloss: to feel sorry, show remorse (active verb)
relief, peace of mind (安心, "putting the heart at ease")

미안해하다.etymology: A derived psychological transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean adjective 미안하다 (未安하다, "to be sorry", from 미 未 "not yet" + 안 安 "peaceful, at ease" + -하다) + the native auxiliary suffix -어하다 (realized as -해하다 after 하-). Because Korean subjective emotion adjectives like 미안하다 can only directly describe a first-person speaker's internal state in declarative sentences, -어하다 converts the adjective into an active, observable verb ("to feel sorry, to act apologetic") usable with third-person subjects.

history.meaning: to be sorry + to manifest or feel an emotion
to feel sorry, show remorse (especially of a third person)

morphemes.meaning: to feel or show an emotion (-어하다)

미안해하다.notes: Essential grammar distinction: say 내가 미안해 ("I am sorry", adjective), but 그 사람도 많이 미안해해 ("He feels very sorry too", verb in -해하다) or 너무 미안해하지 마 ("Don't feel too sorry!").

rootFamily.gloss: to feel anxious or uneasy (不安해하다)

미역국.etymology: A native Korean compound noun combining 미역 ("wakame, edible brown sea mustard *Undaria pinnatifida*", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 미역) and 국 ("soup, broth", attested in Middle Korean as 국). Rich in calcium and iodine, 미역국 has been traditionally eaten by Korean mothers after childbirth to aid recovery and lactation, and consequently on every birthday thereafter to honor one's mother.

history.meaning: sea mustard (Undaria pinnatifida) + soup/broth
seaweed soup (postpartum, birthday, and everyday soup)

미역국.notes: Cultural double meaning: eating 미역국 celebrates a birthday, but the idiom 미역국을 먹다 ("to eat seaweed soup") also means "to fail an exam or get rejected" because wet 미역 is slippery (미끄러지다 = "to slip / fail a test")!

rootFamily.gloss: rice cake soup (eaten on Lunar New Year to gain a year of age)

미완성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 미완성 (未完成), attaching negative prefix 미- (未, 'not yet') to 완성 (完成, 'completion').

미움받다.etymology: A native Korean compound passive-like verb formed from 미움 ("hatred, dislike, resentment", the deverbal noun derived via the nominalizing suffix -ㅁ from the irregular ㅂ-stem adjective 밉다 "to be hateful, disliked, ugly", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 밉다, stem 믜우- / 미우-) + 받다 ("to receive, suffer", Middle Korean 받다). Literally "to receive hatred", it functions as the standard lexical passive meaning "to be hated, resented, or disliked by others".

history.meaning: to be hated/disliked + to receive
to receive dislike, be hated or resented

morphemes.meaning: to be hateful, disliked (밉-, stem 미우-)

미움받다.notes: Often paired as an antonym with 사랑받다 ("to be loved"); in workplace and family contexts, 미움받다 often translates to "getting on someone's bad side" or "being the target of resentment" (미운 털이 박히다).

rootFamily.gloss: to be disliked, hateful, ugly (ㅂ-irregular adjective)
to hate, dislike, resent someone (active verb)

미적대다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) frequentative verb formed from the ideophonic root 미적- (sliding or edging along sluggishly and hesitantly, phonesthemically linked to 밀다 'to push' and 미끄러지다 'to slide') combined with the colloquial repetitive verbalizer -대다 (a variant of -거리다 'to keep doing').

history.meaning: to edge forward sluggishly or dawdle repeatedly
to drag one's feet, dawdle, or procrastinate

미적대다.notes: More colloquial and slightly more critical in tone than its standard synonym 미적거리다; often used when scolding someone for stalling on a decision or task.

미지근하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) sensory adjective built on the yin-vowel ideophonic stem 미지근- (denoting tepid temperature, attested in Early Modern Korean as 미즈근ᄒᆞ다) plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다. From physical lukewarmness of water, it extended metaphorically to half-hearted or noncommittal attitudes.

history.meaning: to be tepid or slightly warm
to be lukewarm, tepid, or half-hearted

미지근하다.notes: Frequently used figuratively in workplace and broadcasting contexts to describe a 'lukewarm' audience reaction (반응이 미지근하다) or an indecisive stance.

미처.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) fossilized adverb grammaticalized from the infinitive/converbal form of the 15th-century Middle Korean verb 및다 (modern 미치다 'to reach, extend to') plus the connective suffix -어 (미처 < 및어, literally 'reaching to that point'). It specialized into a negative polarity item meaning '(not) yet, in time, or far enough to'.

history.meaning: to reach; reaching to the point of
beforehand, in time, (not) yet (with negation)

morphemes.meaning: to reach, extend to (from MK 및-)

미처.notes: Functions almost exclusively as a negative polarity adverb paired with 못 or 안 (e.g., 미처 몰랐다 'I did not realize in time / up to that point').

rootFamily.gloss: to reach, extend to; to exert influence
as much as, to the extent of

미치다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 미치다 (stem 미치- 'to go mad, become insane'), etymologically distinct from Middle Korean 및다 ('to reach, extend to'), though both merged phonologically in Modern Korean as 미치다 after syllable-final affricates resyllabified.

history.meaning: to become mad, lose one's sanity
to go crazy, be frantic, or be obsessed with

morphemes.meaning: to go mad, lose one's mind

미치다.notes: Korean has two homophonous verbs spelled 미치다: 'to go crazy' (intransitive) and 'to reach/affect' (seen in 영향을 미치다 'to exert an influence').

미터.etymology: Borrowed from English meter / metre ('the fundamental SI unit of length'), ultimately from French mètre and Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

history.meaning: metric unit of length
meter (m)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 미터

cognates.meaning: an assembly or gathering of people

미팅.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English meeting (gerund of meet, from Old English mētan 'to encounter, come across', Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną). In South Korean usage, the word underwent semantic bifurcation into professional workplace/production meetings and university group blind dates.

history.meaning: assembly, conference, or encounter
workplace briefing/meeting; group blind date

미팅.notes: In office and TV production settings like The Producers, 미팅 means a work or企画 (planning) meeting, whereas among college students it defaults to a group blind date (contrasting with 소개팅, a 1-on-1 blind date).

rootFamily.gloss: to hold a business meeting or blind date

믹스커피.etymology: South Korean English-derived compound (외래어/콩글리시) reversing the component order of 'coffee mix', formed from English mix (from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscēre 'to blend') + coffee (via Dutch koffie and Ottoman Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa). Coined after Dongsuh Foods invented single-serve stick pouches of instant coffee, non-dairy creamer, and sugar in 1976.

history.meaning: pre-mixed instant coffee, creamer, and sugar pouch
prepared cup or packet of sweet instant coffee mix

믹스커피.notes: A quintessential staple of Korean office culture; stirring the hot water with the flattened plastic wrapper stick itself is an iconic trope in Korean workplace dramas.
