민감하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) descriptive verb formed from 민감 (敏感, 'keennes of perception, sensitivity') + native adjective-forming suffix -하다. Composed of Hanja 敏 (민, 'quick, agile, acute, clever') and 感 (감, 'to feel, perceive, respond emotionally').

history.meaning: acute perception, quickness of feeling
to be sensitive, touchy, or responsive to stimuli

민감하다.notes: Used both for physical/skin sensitivity (민감한 피부) and for touchy social, political, or ratings-related topics (민감한 문제). Its direct antonym is 둔감하다 (鈍感하다, 'insensitive/thick-skinned').

민망하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 민망 (憫惘, combining 憫 'to grieve over, pity, be troubled' + 惘 'disconcerted, bewildered, at a loss') plus native Korean adjective-forming 하다. Originally expressed sympathetic distress or frustration before specialising in modern speech to feeling sheepish, awkward, or embarrassed.

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of

history.meaning: to feel pained, sorry, or distressed over a situation
to feel embarrassed, sheepish, or socially awkward

민망하다.notes: Captures the exact sheepishness of having to ask a favour after a mistake or receiving excessive praise — lighter than moral shame (창피하다 / 부끄럽다).

민수.etymology: Common Korean given name 민수, typically written with Sino-Korean hanja combinations such as 民秀 ('outstanding among the people') or 敏秀 ('clever and outstanding').

history.meaning: given name

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 민수

민원.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 민원 (民願), literally 'the wishes or petitions of the populace', composed of Hanja 民 (민, 'people, subjects, citizens') and 願 (원, 'wish, desire, petition'). In Joseon administrative usage it denoted subjects petitioning a magistrate; in modern South Korea it denotes any official civil service application or public complaint filed with an agency.

history.meaning: petitions or desires of the common people to the state
civil petition, administrative application, or public complaint

민원.notes: In everyday Korean, 민원 넣다 ('to file a民願') often means lodging an official complaint (about noise, illegal parking, or a controversial TV broadcast) with city hall or a regulatory board.

rootFamily.gloss: civil affairs / public service office (民願室)

민트차.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'mint tea', combining the English loanword 민트 (mint) with Sino-Korean 차 (茶, 'tea').

history.meaning: mint + tea
mint tea

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 민트차

cognates.meaning: public nuisance or administrative evil affecting the people

민폐.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 민폐 (民弊), composed of Hanja 民 (민, 'the common people, public') and 弊 (폐, 'harm, abuse, evil practice, nuisance'). In the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty (조선왕조실록), it specifically referred to corrupt official practices that burdened the peasantry; in late 20th-century colloquial Korean, it semantically broadened into being a social nuisance or burden to people around one.

history.meaning: administrative abuses causing hardship to the peasantry
trouble, nuisance, or burden inflicted on others

민폐.notes: Often used as a modifier in contemporary slang, such as 민폐 하객 ('a wedding guest who dresses so flashily they upstage the bride') or 민폐 캐릭터 ('an annoying drama character whose incompetence burdens everyone').

rootFamily.gloss: public sentiment, the hearts of the people (民心)

믿다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to believe, trust, have faith in', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 믿다.

history.meaning: to believe, trust, rely upon
to believe, trust, count on

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 믿다

밀가루.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun formed from 밀 ('wheat', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 밀 < 밀ㅎ, a lenited *h*-final stem recorded in Hunminjeongeum Haerye 1446) + 가루 ('powder, flour', Middle Korean ᄀᆞᄅᆞ / ᄀᆞᆯ, exhibiting the regular vowel shift ㆍ > ㅏ and ㅡ > ㅜ). By metonymy in everyday speech, it also refers to wheat-flour foods such as noodles and bread.

history.meaning: ground wheat powder
wheat flour; wheat-based foods (noodles, pastries)

밀가루.notes: When Koreans say 밀가루를 끊다 ('to quit wheat flour'), they mean cutting out all flour-based carbs like ramyeon, jjajangmyeon, bread, and dumplings for digestion or dieting.

밀다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb meaning 'to push, shove, slide, plane/roll out', descending directly from Middle Korean 밀다.

history.meaning: to push, shove, thrust
to push, slide, roll out (dough), shave

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밀다

밀당.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) syllabic clipping coined in late 20th-century South Korean colloquial speech from the coordinate verbal noun phrase 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'). It extracts the initial root syllables 밀- (from 밀다, Middle Korean 밀다 'to push') and 당- (from 당기다, Early Modern Korean ᄃᆞᆼ기다 'to pull'), drawing on the metaphor of reeling a fish or kite line in and out to describe strategic give-and-take in romance or negotiation.

history.meaning: pushing and pulling; strategic give-and-take
playing hard to get; psychological tug-of-war in dating or business

밀당.notes: A quintessential K-drama romance keyword: good 밀당 keeps a crush intrigued by alternating warmth and distance, whereas failed 밀당 just looks like disinterest.

rootFamily.gloss: to play push-and-pull / hard to get
to pull, draw toward oneself, appeal to

밀당하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verbal derivative formed by attaching the productive light verb -하다 ('to do') to the clipped compound noun 밀당 (from 밀고 당기기 'pushing and pulling', combining 밀다 'to push' and 당기다 'to pull'). Denotes engaging in strategic emotional or negotiating tug-of-war.

history.meaning: to push and pull back and forth
to play hard to get or engage in strategic give-and-take

밀당하다.notes: Used not only between romantic prospects but also in broadcasting and corporate negotiations (e.g., casting directors and agencies playing tug-of-war over appearance fees).

rootFamily.gloss: push and pull, playing hard to get

밀랍.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 蜜蠟, uniting 蜜 (꿀 밀, 'honey, nectar, bee') and 蠟 (밀 랍, 'wax'). Long used in East Asia for sealing documents, casting metals, and waterproofing, beeswax remains the standard meaning of 밀랍 in modern Korean. It distinguishes natural beeswax and sealing wax from paraffin (파라핀) or generic synthetic wax (왁스).
밀랍.notes: Often modifies other nouns, as in 밀랍 천 ('beeswax cloth/wrap') and 밀랍 도장 ('wax seal').

밀리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) passive verb derived from the transitive verb stem 밀- (밀다, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 밀다 'to push, shove') plus the native passive derivational suffix -리-. From the literal sense 'to be pushed back or swept along', it developed the ubiquitous modern senses of traffic, work, or payments getting backed up, delayed, or falling into arrears.

history.meaning: to be pushed, shoved back, or swept by a current
to be pushed back; to get backed up, delayed, or overdue

밀리다.notes: Extremely versatile in daily life: 차가 밀리다 means traffic is backed up, 일이 밀리다 means work is piled up, and 월세가 밀리다 means rent is overdue.

밀리미터.etymology: Borrowed from English millimeter / millimetre ('one thousandth of a meter', from Latin mille 'thousand' + meter).

history.meaning: one thousandth of a meter (mm)
millimeter (mm)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밀리미터

밀어주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb composed of 밀- (밀다, Middle Korean 밀다 'to push'), the infinitive connective suffix -어, and the auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 'to give', grammaticalized as a benefactive marker 'to do for someone's benefit'). Literally 'to push from behind for someone', it metaphorically means to back, sponsor, or promote a person or project.

history.meaning: to push something for someone's benefit
to push physically; to back, sponsor, or promote someone

밀어주다.notes: In Korean entertainment and broadcasting, 밀어주다 often refers to an agency or PD actively 'pushing' a rookie celebrity by giving them prime screen time and favourable editing.

rootFamily.gloss: to push ahead forcefully with a plan
to be pushed back or backed up

밀월여행.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) four-character compound 밀월여행 (蜜月旅行), combining 밀월 (蜜月, a late 19th-century Meiji Japanese orthographic calque of English honeymoon from 蜜 밀 'honey' + 月 월 'moon, month') and 여행 (旅行, 'travel, journey', from 旅 여 'travel, troop' + 行 행 'go, journey'). Alongside literal newlywed trips, it frequently denotes a cosy 'honeymoon period' of alliance between rivals or colleagues.

history.meaning: calque of English honeymoon trip coined in Meiji Japan
honeymoon trip; cosy getaway or period of harmonious alliance

밀월여행.notes: For an actual newlywed trip, modern Koreans almost always say 신혼여행 (新婚旅行); 밀월여행 carries a more literary, journalistic, or playful nuance of a 'secretive/cosy honeymoon-style getaway'.

밉다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) p-irregular (ㅂ-불규칙) adjective derived from the 15th-century Middle Korean transitive verb 믜다 ('to hate, detest') plus the deverbal adjectival suffix -브- (forming 믜브다 > 믜우다, with lenited bilabial fricative ㅸ). Before consonant-initial endings, the labial element hardened to -ㅂ- (믜브다 > 밉다), while before vowel-initial endings it vocalized to 우 (미워, 미운). Semantically extended from 'detestable' to 'visually unflattering, ugly'.

history.meaning: to hate; to be hateful or detestable
to be hateful, detestable, or ugly/unflattering

morphemes.meaning: hateful, ugly (from MK 믜- 'hate' + -브- adjectival suffix)

밉다.notes: As an emotive and aesthetic adjective, 밉다 contrasts directly with 곱다 ('pretty, fine, kind-hearted'), as immortalized in the proverb 미운 놈 떡 하나 더 준다 ('Give an extra rice cake to the person you dislike').

rootFamily.gloss: unlikable person or unflattering feature (밉- + 상 相)

밋밋하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated sensory adjective composed of the yin-vowel ideophonic base 밋밋- (denoting a smooth, gently tapering, or featureless contour without projections; contrasting with the brighter yang-vowel 맷맷하다) and the adjective-forming suffix -하다. From physical flatness, it extended to narratives, performances, or flavors that are plain and lack dramatic punch.

history.meaning: to be smoothly tapering or flat without protuberances
to be flat, featureless, plain, or lacking excitement/flavor

밋밋하다.notes: While 밍밍하다 describes watery liquids, 밋밋하다 describes visual flatness (a plain outfit or flat facial features), a boring storyline, or food that lacks a standout kick.

rootFamily.gloss: sleek and tall without curves (slender variant)

밍밍하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated sensory adjective formed from the yin-vowel ideophonic root 밍밍- (denoting a watery, diluted, or insipid taste lacking salt, sweetness, or alcohol strength; contrasting with yang-vowel 맹맹하다) plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to be watery and weak in taste
to be watery, diluted, bland, or insipid

밍밍하다.notes: Compare Korean's three words for 'bland': 싱겁다 means under-salted (savory food), 밋밋하다 means plain/lacking spice or visual flair, and 밍밍하다 specifically means watered-down (diluted coffee, flat beer, or watery broth).

밑.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'bottom, underside, base, foot (of a mountain or object)', descending directly from Middle Korean 밑 ('base, bottom, root').

history.meaning: base, root, bottom, underside
bottom, underneath, base

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밑

밑거름.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun composed of 밑 ('bottom, base, root', Middle Korean 밑) and 거름 ('fertilizer, manure, compost', deverbal noun derived from the adjective stem 걸- of 걸다 'to be fertile, rich in soil' + nominalizing suffix -음). Originally an agricultural term for basal fertilizer mixed into soil before sowing, it figuratively denotes the groundwork or foundation for future growth.

history.meaning: basal manure applied beneath soil prior to planting crops
basal fertilizer; foundational stepping-stone for success

밑거름.notes: Very commonly used in the idiom 성공의 밑거름이 되다 ('to become the fertilizer/foundation for success'), turning past failures or hardships into a stepping-stone.

rootFamily.gloss: top-dressing fertilizer applied after sprouting (웃 + 거름)
to be rich and fertile (of soil or broth)

밑줄.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) determinative compound noun composed of 밑 ('bottom, underneath', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 밑) and 줄 ('line, cord, stripe', Middle Korean 줄). Literally 'bottom line', coined to refer to an underscore drawn beneath written text for emphasis.

history.meaning: line beneath; underscore
underline drawn under text for emphasis

밑줄.notes: Famous in Korean pop culture from instructor Seo Han-sol's catchphrase 밑줄 쫙! ('Draw a big underline right here!'), used whenever pointing out something crucial to remember.

밑칸.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining native Korean 밑 ('bottom, lower part', Middle Korean 밑) with 칸 ('compartment, shelf, architectural bay', Middle Korean 칸 / 간, an aspirated nativized borrowing from Sino-Korean 間 간 'space, interval, room between pillars'). Denotes the bottom shelf or lower compartment of a cabinet, refrigerator, or bunk.

history.meaning: lower bay or bottom compartment
bottom shelf, lower compartment, or lower berth

밑칸.notes: Because 밑 ends in an aspirated consonant ㅌ and 칸 already starts with aspirated ㅋ, no epenthetic ㅅ (사이시옷) is inserted, unlike 윗칸 ('upper shelf').

rootFamily.gloss: top shelf, upper compartment (위 + ㅅ + 칸)
blank space, empty box on a form (빈 + 칸)
next stall or adjacent compartment (옆 + 칸)

바.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) defective/bound noun (의존명사) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 바 (an *h*-final stem 바ㅎ, surfacing as 바히 in the nominative/locative). Originally denoting a concrete 'place, locus, or spot' (preserved in 바탕 'ground, foundation'), it grammaticalized through early vernacular translations (언해) of Classical Chinese nominalizer 所 (소, 'place; that which') into a formal relative-clause head noun meaning 'the fact that, that which, or a way/means'.

history.meaning: place, locus; that which, the thing or way that (translating Classical Chinese 所)
the fact that, that which, or a way/means (formal bound noun)

morphemes.meaning: fact, way, that which (bound noun, from MK 바ㅎ 'place')

바.notes: As a bound noun, 바 must always be preceded by an adnominal modifier (e.g., 앞서 말씀드린 바와 같이 'as I mentioned earlier', 어찌할 바를 모르다 'not know what to do', or blunt 알 바 아니다 'none of my business').

rootFamily.gloss: what to do, a way out (idiomatic phrase)
a matter worth knowing / one's business

바가지.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun derived from 박 ('calabash, bottle gourd', Middle Korean 박) plus the diminutive/vessel-forming suffix -아지 (박아지 > 바가지), originally denoting a hemispherical dipper made from a halved dried gourd. The modern slang sense 'rip-off, exorbitant overcharge' (바가지를 쓰다 'to get ripped off') arose from late Joseon/early 20th-century 십인땡이 (ten-person gourd gambling) or folk mask-dance troupes where the player left holding or wearing the gourd shell had to pay the entire bill.

history.meaning: halved bottle-gourd dipper or bowl
gourd dipper; exorbitant overcharge or rip-off; nagging (바가지를 긁다)

바가지.notes: Powers two of Korean's most famous idioms: 바가지를 쓰다/씌우다 ('to get ripped off / to overcharge') and 바가지를 긁다 ('to nag one's spouse', from the grating sound of scraping a dried gourd bowl to ward off ghosts).

rootFamily.gloss: rip-off price, price gouging (바가지 + 料金)

바구니.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'woven basket', descending from Middle Korean 바고니 via vowel raising (바고니 > 바구니).

history.meaning: round woven basket
basket

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바구니

바깥.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'the outside, exterior, outdoors', historically formed as a reduplicated or intensive derivative of 밖 ('outside', Middle Korean 밧ㄱ-).

history.meaning: outer side, exterior
outside, exterior, outdoors

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바깥

바깥쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'the outside, outer side, exterior direction', formed from 바깥 ('outside, exterior') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: outside + side/direction
outer side, outside

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바깥쪽

바꾸다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to change, exchange, swap, replace', descending from Middle Korean 바꾸다 / 바꼬다 ('to barter, exchange, alter').

history.meaning: to exchange, trade, replace
to change, exchange, switch

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바꾸다

바꿔주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb formed from 바꾸- (바꾸다, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 바꼬다 'to exchange, swap, alter'), the infinitive connective suffix -어 (contracting with the stem vowel 우 into 워: 바꾸어 > 바꿔), and the auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 'to give; to do for someone').

history.meaning: to exchange or swap something for someone
to change, exchange, or hand over the phone to someone for another's benefit

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective (contracted with 우 to 워)

바꿔주다.notes: Besides exchanging merchandise at a store, 바꿔주다 is the standard everyday verb for putting someone else on the phone (e.g., 엄마 좀 바꿔줘 'Put Mom on the phone for me').

바뀌다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb meaning 'to change, be changed, shift, be replaced', derived from 바꾸다 ('to change, exchange') plus the passive suffix -이-.

history.meaning: to be exchanged, change
to change, be altered, turn into

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바뀌다

바늘.etymology: Native Korean noun 바늘, descending from Middle Korean 바ᄂᆞᆯ ('needle, pin'). From its original meaning as a sewing or knitting tool, it extended metaphorically to name any sharp, slender indicator that points the way, serving as the standard Korean word for clock hands (시곗바늘) and compass needles (나침반 바늘).
바늘.notes: Frequently compounded as 시곗바늘 ('clock hand') and 나침반 바늘 ('compass needle').

바다.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'sea, ocean', descending from Middle Korean 바닿 (and archaic variant 바ᄅᆞᆯ).

history.meaning: sea, ocean
sea, ocean

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바다

바닥.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'floor, bottom surface, ground, sole (of the foot or shoe), palm (of the hand)', attested since Early Modern Korean 바닥.

history.meaning: bottom surface, floor, sole
floor, bottom, ground

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바닥

바닷물.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 바다 ('sea, ocean', Middle Korean 바닿/바다) and 물 ('water'), linked by the genitive interfix 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-). Before the nasal consonant ㅁ of 물, the linking ㅅ assimilates to [ㄴ], so 바닷물 is pronounced [바단물]. Literally 'water of the sea', it is the quintessential Korean comparison for anything intensely salty.
바닷물.notes: Pronounced [바단물] due to nasal assimilation across the 사이시옷 boundary.

바닷물고기.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) three-noun compound composed of 바다 ('sea, ocean', Middle Korean 바다ㅎ / 바ᄅᆞᆯ) + genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, continuing the Middle Korean genitive particle -ㅅ) + 물 ('water', Middle Korean 믈, with labial vowel rounding ㅡ > ㅜ after ㅁ) + 고기 ('meat, fish', Middle Korean 고기). Literally 'seawater fish'.

history.meaning: fish living in seawater
saltwater fish, marine fish

바닷물고기.notes: Note that standalone 고기 in Modern Korean defaults to 'meat' (beef/pork), whereas 물고기 ('water-meat') means a live fish, and 바닷물고기 specifically contrasts with 민물고기 ('freshwater fish').

바득바득.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated yang-vowel ideophone (의태어/의성어, contrasting with the heavier yin-vowel 버득버득). Originally mimicking the tight, dry scraping or grinding sound of hard surfaces rubbing together, it shifted metaphorically to describe someone insisting, arguing, or striving with stubborn, unyielding persistence.

history.meaning: scraping tightly; stubbornly and persistently

바득바득.notes: Most frequently collocates with 우기다 ('to insist stubbornly', 바득바득 우기다) or 대들다 ('to talk back defiantly'), painting a vivid picture of someone refusing to back down an inch.

rootFamily.gloss: to grate or insist stubbornly and repeatedly

바라다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to wish, hope for, desire; to look toward', descending from Middle Korean 바라다 ('to hope for, gaze toward').

history.meaning: to look toward, hope for, desire
to wish, hope, want

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바라다

바라다보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 바라- (Middle Korean ᄇᆞ라다 'to look toward from afar; to hope for') + the connective suffix -다- (reduced from -다가, indicating maintenance and transfer of gaze across space) + 보다 (Middle Korean 보다 'to see, look'). Serves as an emphatic, spatialized variant of 바라보다 ('to gaze at, look out over').

history.meaning: to look out toward from a distance and see
to gaze out at, look across or down from a distance

morphemes.meaning: to look toward, gaze at (from MK ᄇᆞ라-)

바라다보다.notes: Like 쳐다보다 ('look up at'), 내려다보다 ('look down at'), and 내다보다 ('look out at'), the medial -다- syllable emphasizes directing one's line of sight across a distance.

rootFamily.gloss: to gaze at, watch steadily (standard shorter form)
to look up at, stare at (치- + -어 + -다- + 보다)
to look down upon from above (내리- + -어 + -다- + 보다)

바락바락.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated yang-vowel mimetic adverb (의태어, paired with the deeper, more explosive yin-vowel counterpart 버럭버럭). Built on the ideophonic root 바락 ('a sudden, shrill burst of temper or defiant exertion'), it depicts someone shouting, talking back, or striving in repeated, fierce, high-pitched bursts.

history.meaning: in repeated, shrill, defiant bursts of shouting or effort

morphemes.meaning: bursting out shrilly or defiantly (ideophonic base)

바락바락.notes: By Korean vowel harmony, yang-vowel 바락바락 sounds sharper, shriller, and more petulant/defiant (like a subordinate or child yelling back), whereas yin-vowel 버럭버럭 sounds deeper and more booming.

rootFamily.gloss: bellowing or flaring up in heavy angry bursts (yin-vowel counterpart)
in a single sudden defiant outburst

바람.etymology: Native Korean noun with two distinct etymologies: (1) 'wind, breeze' (descending from Middle Korean 바ᄅᆞᆷ via loss of ᆞ); and (2) 'wish, hope, expectation' (substantive derivation of 바라다 'to wish, hope' + nominalizer -ㅁ).

history.meaning: wind, air current; that which is hoped for
wind, breeze; wish, hope

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바람

바래다주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb composed of 바래- (from 바래다 'to escort, see someone off safely', historically derived from Middle Korean ᄇᆞ라다 'to watch over, gaze after' + transitive/causative suffix -이- > ᄇᆞ래다 > 바래다), the transferring connective suffix -다 (from -다가), and the auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give / do for someone'). Literally 'to escort someone to a destination for their benefit'.

history.meaning: to watch over someone's departure, see off, escort
to escort or walk/drive someone safely home or to their destination

morphemes.meaning: to escort, see off (from MK ᄇᆞ라- + -이-)

바래다주다.notes: A staple romantic gesture in Korean culture (집에 바래다주다 'to walk/drive someone home'); note that the standalone verb 바래다 ('to escort' or 'to fade in color') is distinct from 바라다 ('to hope/wish').

rootFamily.gloss: to take/accompany someone to a place (데리- + -어 + -다 + 주다)
to see someone off at departure (拝迎하다 / 배웅)

바로.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'straight, directly, right away, precisely, none other than', descending from Middle Korean 바ᄅᆞ, the adverbial derivative of 바ᄅᆞ다 ('to be straight, upright, correct').

history.meaning: straight, uprightly, directly
right, immediately, directly, exactly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바로

바로바로.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated adverb formed by doubling 바로 ('straight, directly, immediately', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 바ᄅᆞ, the regular adverbial derivative of the adjective 바ᄅᆞ다 > modern 바르다 'to be straight, upright, correct'). Reduplication adds distributive aspect, shifting 'immediately' into 'promptly each and every time without letting things pile up'.

history.meaning: straight, uprightly, directly
immediately every time, promptly on each occasion

morphemes.meaning: reduplicant marking distributive 'each and every time'

바로바로.notes: While single 바로 means 'right now' (지금 바로), reduplicated 바로바로 means handling recurring items immediately as they come in (e.g., 연락 좀 바로바로 해 'Reply to messages promptly every time!').

rootFamily.gloss: to be straight, upright, correct, honest

바르네.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean (고유어) adjective 바르다 ('to be straight, upright, proper, polite'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 바ᄅᆞ다 (Yale: palota), combined with the mirative/exclamatory sentence-final suffix -네, which expresses immediate realization or mild admiration on the speaker's part.

history.meaning: to be straight, aligned, upright, or true
is indeed upright, proper, or well-mannered!

morphemes.meaning: mirative sentence-ending expressing immediate realization or mild exclamation

바르네.notes: Often heard in the collocation 예의가 바르네 ('How polite/well-mannered they are!') when a senior praises a junior's etiquette.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 바르다

바르다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adjective derived from Middle Korean 바ᄅᆞ다 (Yale: palota, 'to be straight, upright, accurate'), first attested in Yongbieocheonga (용비어천가, 1447). Through loss of the Middle Korean vowel 아래아 (ㆍ) in the second syllable, 바ᄅᆞ다 regularly developed into Modern Korean 바르다, extending from spatial straightness to moral rectitude and social propriety.

history.meaning: to be spatially straight, direct, or morally upright
to be straight, upright, proper, or polite

바르다.notes: Do not confuse the adjective 바르다 ('to be upright/polite', from Middle Korean 바ᄅᆞ다) with its modern homophone, the transitive verb 바르다 ('to apply, spread, paste', from Middle Korean ᄇᆞᄅᆞ다). Both are 르-irregular (바르다 -> 발라).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 바르다

바보.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun denoting a fool or simpleton. Most widely analyzed by Korean historical linguists as a phonological reduction of *밥보 (from 밥 'cooked rice, meal' + the pejorative/characterizing human agent suffix -보, literally 'a person who only knows how to eat rice and do nothing else'), parallel to 먹보 ('glutton'), 잠보 ('sleepyhead'), and 울보 ('crybaby').

history.meaning: simpleton who only eats; dull-witted person
fool, idiot, simpleton

morphemes.meaning: reduced stem historically linked to 밥 (cooked rice) or dullness
human agent suffix denoting a person characterized by a trait or habit

바보.notes: While literally meaning 'idiot' or 'fool', 바보 is frequently used with affectionate teasing between friends or romantic partners, much like English 'silly' or Japanese バカ.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 바보

바보짓.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun formed from 바보 ('fool, simpleton') and 짓 ('act, gesture, behavior', from Middle Korean 짒/짓). While 짓 originally denoted any physical gesture or movement (as in 손짓 'hand gesture'), as an independent or second element in compounds it developed a strong pejorative nuance of 'unwise act' or 'antic'.

history.meaning: physical gesture, movement, or deed
foolish act, idiotic move, blunder

바보짓.notes: Because 짓 carries a critical or self-deprecating tone when referring to actions (e.g., 무슨 짓이야 'What do you think you are doing?'), 바보짓 specifically highlights a regrettable blunder.

rootFamily.gloss: hand gesture, motioning with the hand

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 짓

바쁘다.etymology: Native Korean 으-irregular adjective meaning 'busy, pressed for time', descending from Middle Korean 밧브다 ('urgent, hard-pressed, busy') via glottalization (ㅅㅂ > ㅃ).

history.meaning: urgent, hard-pressed, busy
busy, occupied

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바쁘다

바삭.etymology: Native Korean mimetic (onomatopoeic) adverb 바삭, depicting a light, dry, and pleasingly brittle crunch or snap. Featuring the bright vowel ㅏ, it suggests a lighter, crispier texture (like pastry crust, thin sugar glass, or dry autumn leaves) compared to its darker-vowel counterpart 버석, which implies a heavier, drier, or sandier crumble.
바삭.notes: Combines with -거리다 or -하다 to form verbs (바삭거리다 'to crunch', 바삭하다 'to be crispy').

바삭하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective and verb meaning 'crispy, crunchy; to rustle dryly', formed from the light-vowel mimetic root 바삭 ('sound or texture of dry leaves or crisp pastry breaking') plus -하다.

history.meaning: mimetic root for crisp crunch/rustle + -하다
crispy, crunchy, flaky

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바삭하다

morphemes.meaning: to be / make the sound of

바이올린.etymology: Modern Korean loanword borrowed from English violin, which in turn derives from Italian violino (a diminutive of viola, ultimately traced to Medieval Latin vitula, 'stringed instrument'). Introduced into Korea during the late 19th and early 20th centuries alongside Western conservatory music and hymnody, it early on displaced older Sinoxenic coinages such as 제금 (提琴) in everyday speech. Under South Korea's Foreign Word Orthography, English /vaɪəˈlɪn/ is mapped to five Hangul syllables as 바이올린 (baiollin), with /v/ adapted as ㅂ and the geminate liquid represented across syllable boundaries.

history.meaning: small viola, violin
four-stringed bowed musical instrument
violin

바이올린.notes: To play the violin in Korean is 바이올린을 켜다 (literally 'to saw/draw a bow across the violin') or more generally 바이올린을 연주하다 ('to perform on the violin').

cognates.meaning: Scandinavian seafaring raider; pirate ship ride
Viking; smorgasbord buffet or pirate ship ride

바이킹.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English Viking, which itself derives from Old Norse víkingr ('seafaring raider, pirate', likely related to vík 'inlet, fjord, bay'). In South Korean popular culture and theme park usage, 바이킹 underwent metonymic narrowing to denote the swinging pendulum amusement ride shaped like a Norse dragon ship.

history.meaning: Norse seafaring raider or pirate operating from fjords
medieval Scandinavian mariner; theme-park ship ride
Viking; swinging pirate-ship amusement park ride

바이킹.notes: At Korean amusement parks like Lotte World or Everland, asking to ride the 바이킹 always refers to the giant swinging pirate ship ride rather than historical Scandinavians.

rootFamily.gloss: Norse mythology (commonly paired cultural loan context)
pirate ship (semantic equivalent of the ride)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 바이킹

바장조.etymology: Korean musical compound meaning 'F major', combining the native Korean hangul pitch letter 바 (assigned to the note F, the sixth letter in the 가-나-다-라-마-바-사 sequence corresponding to A-B-C-D-E-F-G) with Sino-Korean 장조 (長調, 'major key').

history.meaning: pitch F + major key
F major (musical key)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바장조

바짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'closely, tightly, right up to; completely (dried up); tensely', an intensified light-vowel ideophone paired with 바싹.

history.meaning: closely, tightly, completely dry
closely, tightly, tensely, parchedly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바짝

바치다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb meaning 'to offer up, dedicate, present to a superior or deity', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 바티다 (Yale: pathita, 'to offer tribute, present upward'). Palatalization of ㅌ (tʰ) before ㅣ (i) in Early Modern Korean regularly transformed 바티다 into Modern Korean 바치다.

history.meaning: to present tribute or offer up to a ruler or deity
to dedicate, devote, offer up (one's life, youth, or gift)

바치다.notes: A classic Korean spelling trap: 바치다 means 'to dedicate/devote' (e.g., 청춘을 바치다 'devote one's youth'), whereas homophonous 받치다 (with ㄷ) means 'to prop up from underneath' or 'to hold up an umbrella'.

rootFamily.gloss: to contribute, render service (from Middle Korean 이바디)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 바치다

바퀴.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'wheel; a turn or lap around a circuit', descending from Middle Korean 바회 / 바희 ('wheel') via Early Modern Korean consonantal strengthening (ㅎ + w > ㅋw).

history.meaning: wheel
wheel; counter for revolutions or laps

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 바퀴

cognates.meaning: to moor a boat; to stay for a night

박.etymology: Represents two distinct Sino-Korean (한자어) items sharing the syllable 박: (1) the bound counter noun 泊 (머무를 박, 'to anchor a boat; to lodge overnight'), used to count nights of lodging as in 1박 2일 ('one night, two days'); and (2) the major Korean surname 朴 (성씨 박, *Park*), traditionally linked by the founding myth of Park Hyeokgeose of Silla (who hatched from a giant gourd-like egg) to the native Korean word 박 ('gourd') or 밝- ('bright, radiant').

history.meaning: to moor a vessel for the night / unadorned wood; transcription of Silla royal clan name
counter for overnight stays; the Korean surname Park

morphemes.meaning: lodge overnight (泊) or surname Park (朴)

박.notes: In *The Producers*, Baek Seung-chan works on the flagship variety show *2 Days & 1 Night* (1박 2일, 일박 이일), where 박 (泊) counts nights of stay.

rootFamily.gloss: staying out overnight away from home (外泊)
one night and two days (一泊二日)

박수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 박수 (拍手), composed of 박 (拍, 'to strike, clap, beat time') and 수 (手, 'hand'). Attested in Classical Chinese and traditional Korean texts for striking the hands together in rhythm or delight, it became the standard modern noun for audience applause. Because the final coda ㄱ of 박 is an obstruent stop, the initial lax sibilant of 수 automatically tensifies in standard Korean phonology, yielding the pronunciation [박쑤] (bakssu).

history.meaning: clapping the hands together
applause, handclapping

박수.notes: The natural collocations are 박수를 치다 ('to clap one's hands') and 박수를 보내다 ('to send/give applause to a performer').

박하.etymology: Sino-Korean botanical compound 薄荷, formed from 薄 (엷을 박, 'thin, slight, dense growth') and 荷 (연꽃 하, originally 'lotus' but extended to various leafy herbs). It is the classical East Asian name for Mentha arvensis (field mint). In modern Korean, 박하 refers to sharp, cool peppermint and wild mint, distinguishing it from milder loanword herbs like 애플민트 or 스피어민트.
박하.notes: Often modifies other nouns: 박하사탕 ('peppermint candy'), 박하 향 ('mint scent').

박하차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 박하차 (薄荷茶), meaning 'peppermint tea, mint tea', composed of 박하 (薄荷, 'peppermint, mentha') + 차 (茶, 'tea').

history.meaning: infusion made from mint leaves
peppermint tea, mint tea

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 박하차

밖.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'the outside, exterior; (with negative predicates) nothing but, only', descending from Middle Korean 밧 (with underlying stem 밧ㄱ-, attested in locative 밧긔 'outside').

history.meaning: outside, exterior
outside, exterior; beyond, except

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밖

반.etymology: Sino-Korean noun representing two common homophones: (1) 반 (半, Middle Chinese *pwanH*), meaning 'half, middle, semi-'; and (2) 반 (班, Middle Chinese *pwan*), meaning 'class, group, team, shift'.

history.meaning: half; class, squad
half (半); class, group (班)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반

반갑다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'glad, delighted, welcome (upon meeting someone or hearing news)', derived from the Middle Korean verb 반기다 ('to rejoice at meeting, welcome warmly') + adjective-forming suffix -압다/-갑다.

history.meaning: to rejoice, welcome gladly -> glad, welcome
glad to see, welcome, pleasing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반갑다

반값.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'half price', combining Sino-Korean 반 (半, 'half') with native Korean 값 ('price, value', Middle Korean 값).

history.meaning: half + price
half price

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반값

cognates.meaning: return or surrender of an item, license, or property to an authority

반납.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 返納, formed from 返 (돌아올 반, 'to return, give back, send back') and 納 (들일 납, 'to deliver, pay, turn in to a repository or superior'). Adopted across modern East Asian institutional administration to denote the formal return of borrowed equipment, books, passes, or official credentials.

history.meaning: to send back + to deliver or pay in to a storehouse
formal return of borrowed items, library books, or official property

morphemes.meaning: deliver, turn in, receive into custody

반납.notes: 반납 is used when returning something borrowed or issued (like library books, broadcasting props, or ID passes), whereas 반품 (返品) is used when returning purchased merchandise for a refund.

rootFamily.gloss: to return a borrowed or issued item (返納하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반납

cognates.meaning: to return or surrender an issued item or license
cognates.word: 返納する (へんのうする, hennō suru)

반납하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verbal derivative combining the noun 반납 (返納, from 返 'return, send back' + 納 'turn in, deliver') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, perform'). Expresses the action of turning in borrowed equipment, library books, or official credentials to their rightful institution.

history.meaning: return or delivery back to an authority or lender
to return or turn in a borrowed or issued item

반납하다.notes: Often used figuratively in colloquial Korean, such as 휴일을 반납하다 ('to give up/forfeit one's holiday to work').

rootFamily.gloss: return of a borrowed item (返納)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반납하다

cognates.word: 半年 (はんとし / はんねん)

반년.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) temporal compound noun 半年, composed of 半 (반 반, 'half, divide in two', depicting an ox 牛 split in two 八) and 年 (해 년, 'year', originally depicting a person carrying harvested grain 禾, hence an agricultural year cycle).

history.meaning: half of an annual cycle, six months
half a year, six months

반년.notes: Interchangeable with 6개월 (육 개월, 'six months') in everyday speech, though 반년 treats the six-month span as a single holistic block of time.

rootFamily.gloss: first or second half of the year (上半期 / 下半期)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반년

반대.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 反對, composed of 反 (돌이킬 반 / 반대할 반, 'to turn over, reverse, go against', originally depicting a hand turning under a cliff) and 對 (대할 대, 'to face, confront, answer, pair'). Signifies standing in direct opposition or facing the reverse direction.

history.meaning: to stand in inverse relation or answer in opposition
history.stage: Classical Chinese & Meiji-era East Asian lexicon

history.meaning: opposition, objection; the exact opposite direction or side

반대.notes: Covers both English 'the opposite' (정반대 'the exact opposite', 반대로 'conversely') and 'opposition/objection' (반대하다 'to oppose', vs. 찬성 'approval').

rootFamily.gloss: the opposite side or direction (反對편)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반대

반드시.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adverb meaning 'without fail, certainly, necessarily'. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 반ᄃᆞ기 (Yale: pantoki) and 반ᄃᆞ시 (Yale: pantosi), derived from the adjectival root 반ᄃᆞᆨ- / 반ᄃᆞᆺ- ('straight, upright, square, unswerving', surviving in Modern Korean 반듯하다 'to be straight, neat') plus the adverbial suffix -이. The semantic shift progressed from 'straightly, squarely' to 'unswervingly, without fail'.

history.meaning: straightly, squarely; without fail, necessarily
without fail, certainly, at all costs

반드시.notes: Modern Korean orthography distinguishes two words from the same historical root by spelling: 반드시 means 'certainly, without fail', whereas 반듯이 means 'straightly, neatly, without tilting'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반드시

반듯하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'straight, even, neat, upright, well-proportioned', formed from the light-vowel expressive root 반듯- ('straight and level without tilting') plus -하다.

history.meaning: straight, level, neat
straight, neat, square, upright

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반듯하다

반말.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean (혼종어) compound noun combining Sino-Korean 반 (半, 'half, incomplete') with native Korean 말 ('speech, words, language', from Middle Korean 말). Originally coined to describe utterances in which full honorific sentence endings were truncated or left 'halfway' between polite and plain levels, it generalized to denote the intimate/casual non-honorific speech level (해체/해라체).

history.meaning: halfway speech with clipped honorific endings
casual, non-honorific speech used with intimates, peers, or younger people

반말.notes: In Korean workplace and broadcasting culture, switching from 존댓말 (polite/honorific speech) to 반말 (말을 놓다 'to drop one's speech level') is a major social milestone that usually requires explicit permission or close hierarchy/age alignment.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반말

반말하다.etymology: Hybrid (혼종어) verbal compound formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, speak') to 반말 (from Sino-Korean 半 'half' + native Korean 말 'speech, language'). Means to speak in the intimate or plain non-honorific register without polite sentence endings (-요 or -습니다).

history.meaning: to use half-lowered or non-honorific speech
to speak casually or without honorifics

반말하다.notes: Using 반말하다 to an older person or a stranger without agreement is considered rude, often prompting the confrontational question 왜 반말이세요? ('Why are you speaking in banmal to me?').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반말하다

cognates.meaning: the reverse side; on the other hand, whereas
reverse side of an object; negative or opposite aspect

반면.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 反面, composed of 反 (돌이킬 반, 'reverse, opposite, turn over') and 面 (낯 면, 'face, surface, side, aspect'). Literally 'the reverse face or flip side', it grammaticalized in modern prose and speech (often as 반면에 after an adnominal clause) to express contrast: 'on the other hand, whereas'.

history.meaning: the back surface or reverse side of an object or mirror
the opposite aspect; on the other hand, whereas

반면.notes: Most commonly appears following a relative clause as -(으)ㄴ/는 반면(에) ('whereas..., on the other hand...'), contrasting two facets of the same topic or two opposing situations.

rootFamily.gloss: negative example that serves as a teacher (反面敎師)
side, flank, aspect (側面, sharing 面)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반면

반무당.etymology: Compound noun formed by prefixing Sino-Korean 반- (半, 'half, quasi-, practically') to 무당 (巫堂, 'shaman, spirit medium', attested in Middle Korean as 무당 and written with the Hanja 巫 'shaman' + 堂 'shrine/hall', though widely considered by Altaicists and Korean philologists to reflect an ancient native or areal Northeast Asian word for shaman). Denotes either a novice shaman or, colloquially, an ordinary person whose intuition or superstition makes them 'practically half a psychic'.

history.meaning: shaman, traditional Korean spirit medium
novice shaman; someone who is practically half a psychic or fortune-teller

반무당.notes: Used humorously in Korean dramas when someone guesses hidden workplace gossip with eerie accuracy or relies heavily on fortune-telling and talismans.

rootFamily.gloss: clumsy, half-baked shaman; someone with dangerous little knowledge (선무당)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반무당

cognates.meaning: written statement of self-reflection or apology
cognates.word: 反省文 (はんせいぶん, hanseibun)

반성문.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) three-morpheme compound noun 反省文, consisting of 반성 (反省, from 反 'turn back' + 省 'examine, introspect oneself') and 문 (文, 글월 문, 'writing, text, document'). Literally 'a document of self-reflection', institutionalized in modern Korean schools, homes, and workplaces as a formal written apology detailing one's wrongdoing and pledge not to repeat it.

history.meaning: moral self-examination + written composition
formal written statement of remorse and self-reflection

morphemes.meaning: examine, inspect oneself (read 성 in this sense, vs. 생 'reduce')

반성문.notes: In Korean culture, having a child, student, or even an erring spouse or employee write a 반성문 (often specified by page count) is a quintessential disciplinary punishment.

rootFamily.gloss: to reflect on one's mistakes (反省하다)
letter of apology or explanation at work (始末書)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반성문

cognates.meaning: to reflect on one's conduct, examine oneself, repent
cognates.word: 反省する (はんせいする, hansei suru)

cognates.meaning: to engage in self-reflection or introspection

반성하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb formed from 반성 (反省, 'self-examination, introspection') and the native Korean verb 하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean root combines 反 (돌이킬 반, 'to turn back') and 省 (살필 성, 'to examine closely, inspect'), rooted in Confucian moral cultivation such as Zengzi's famous statement in the *Analects* (論語): 吾日三省吾身 ('Each day I examine myself on three counts').

history.meaning: to turn inward and examine one's moral conduct
to reflect critically on one's actions or mistakes; to feel remorse

반성하다.notes: Note the dual Sino-Korean reading of 省: it is read 성 when meaning 'to examine/reflect' (반성, 성찰) or 'ministry/province', but 생 when meaning 'to omit/reduce' (생략 'omission').

rootFamily.gloss: written apology / statement of reflection (反省文)
deep introspection, self-examination (省察, sharing 省)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반성하다

반응.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 反應, composed of 反 (돌이킬 반, 'to turn back, return, counter') and 應 (응할 응, 'to respond, answer, correspond', containing 心 'heart/mind' beneath 䧹). Standardized in late 19th-century East Asian scientific terminology to translate European *reaction* (in chemistry and physiology) before broadening to denote audience, public, or interpersonal responses.

history.meaning: echoing response; modern scientific calque for 'reaction'
chemical/physical reaction; emotional, viewer, or public response

반응.notes: In broadcasting (*The Producers*), 시청자 반응 ('viewer reaction') and 실시간 반응 ('real-time online reaction') are constantly monitored alongside television ratings.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반응

반죽.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'dough, batter, kneaded mixture (of flour, clay, or mortar)', attested in Early Modern Korean as 반쥭 / 반죽.

history.meaning: kneaded flour or clay
dough, batter, paste

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반죽

반지하.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) architectural compound noun 半地下, formed from 반- (半, 'half, semi-') and 지하 (地下, from 地 'earth, ground' + 下 'below, under'). Literally 'half-underground', referring to residential units whose floor level sits partially below street grade so that only high narrow windows are visible above the pavement.

history.meaning: half + below the ground surface
semi-basement apartment unit characteristic of South Korean urban housing

반지하.notes: Originally mandated in 1970 as underground civil-defense bunkers beneath residential buildings and legalized for housing during Seoul's 1980s housing shortage, 반지하 became globally famous through the film *Parasite* (기생충).

rootFamily.gloss: subway, underground railway (地下水/地下鐵)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반지하

반짝거리다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from the mimetic/ideophonic root 반짝 ('a sudden bright flash or glint') and the frequentative verb suffix -거리다 ('to do repeatedly, keep doing'). Featuring the bright vowel ㅏ and tense bilabial ㅃ/ㅉ, it vividly evokes a continuous, delicate twinkling or sparkling on wet surfaces, stars, or polished glass, contrasting with the heavier, darker flash of 번쩍거리다.
반짝거리다.notes: Synonymous with 반짝이다; both are widely used for twinkling lights, wet glints, and shiny surfaces.

반짝반짝하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated ideophonic verb and adjective meaning 'to twinkle, sparkle, glitter continuously', formed from reduplicated mimetic 반짝반짝 ('repeated bright flashes or glints') + -하다.

history.meaning: reduplicated sparkling ideophone + -하다
to twinkle, sparkle, gleam brightly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반짝반짝하다

반짝이다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to sparkle, twinkle, glitter, shine', derived from the mimetic root 반짝 ('sudden glint or flash of light') plus the verbalizing suffix -이다.

history.meaning: to glint, sparkle
to sparkle, twinkle, gleam

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반짝이다

반쪽.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean (혼종어) compound noun combining Sino-Korean 반 (半, 'half') with native Korean 쪽 ('split piece, half-section, side, direction', attested in Middle Korean as 쯀/쪽 denoting one half of a split gourd or cloven object). Literally 'a half-piece', used both for something incomplete and metaphorically for one's 'other half' (romantic partner or spouse).

history.meaning: cloven piece, split half of a gourd or object; side
one half of a whole; an incomplete thing; one's romantic 'other half'

반쪽.notes: Depending on context, 반쪽 can be critical (반쪽짜리 성공 'a half-baked/incomplete success') or deeply affectionate (나의 반쪽 'my other half / soulmate').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반쪽

반쯤.etymology: Hybrid compound meaning 'about half, halfway', formed from Sino-Korean 반 (半, 'half') plus the native Korean approximative suffix -쯤 ('about, approximately').

history.meaning: half + approximately
about half, halfway

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 반쯤

반투명.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic noun 반투명 (半透明), formed by prefixing 반- (半, 'half, semi-') to 투명 (透明, 'transparency', from 透 'penetrate, pass through' + 明 'bright, clear'). It describes materials such as frosted glass (반투명 유리), tracing paper, or thin porcelain that allow light to pass through diffusely without permitting a clear view of shapes on the other side. In Korean syntax, it frequently modifies another noun directly (반투명 유리, 'frosted/translucent glass').

history.meaning: transparent, letting light pass clearly through
semi-transparency, translucency, frosted state

반투명.notes: Often paired with 유리 (반투명 유리) to describe frosted or etched architectural glass in traditional and modern Korean interiors.

cognates.meaning: returned goods, returning merchandise to a seller

반품.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) commercial compound noun 返品, composed of 返 (돌아올 반, 'to return, send back') and 品 (물건 품, 'goods, article, commodity, item'). Standard retail and logistics term denoting the return of purchased merchandise to a vendor or manufacturer due to defects or buyer remorse.

history.meaning: to send back + goods or articles
commercial return of purchased merchandise

반품.notes: Frequently paired with 교환 ('exchange') and 환불 ('refund') in shopping contexts: 교환 및 반품 ('exchanges and returns').

rootFamily.gloss: product, manufactured goods (製品, sharing 品)
delivery of goods (納品, sharing 品)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반품

반하다.etymology: Traditionally analyzed in Korean lexicography as a Sino-Korean (한자어) verb formed from 攀 (더위잡을 반, 'to grasp, cling to, climb up, be drawn toward') or 反 (돌이킬 반, 'to turn over, invert one's heart/mind') plus the native Korean verb 하다 ('to do, become'). From the sense of one's mind clinging to or being overturned by beauty or charm, it lexicalized in Korean to mean 'to fall in love with, be infatuated or charmed by'.

history.meaning: to cling to, yearn for, or have one's heart drawn toward someone
to fall in love, be smitten, charmed, or fascinated by

morphemes.meaning: cling to, be drawn toward (攀) or turn over (反)

반하다.notes: Always takes the dative particle -에 (누구에게/무엇에 반하다 'to fall for someone/something'), especially in the set phrase 첫눈에 반하다 ('to fall in love at first sight'). Note also the homophone 반하다 (反하다, 'to violate/go against', as in 법에 반하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to climb, scale a mountain (登攀, sharing the Hanja 攀)
clinging to a connection or affinity (攀緣, sharing 攀)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반하다

cognates.word: 反抗する (はんこうする, hankō suru)

반항하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb combining 반항 (反抗, from 反 'turn against, oppose' + 抗 'resist, defy, hold off with the hand 扌') with the native Korean verb 하다 ('to do'). Signifies actively defying or rebelling against authority, elders, or oppressive circumstances.

history.meaning: to turn against + to ward off or resist with force
to rebel, defy, talk back, or resist authority

반항하다.notes: Used across registers from political resistance to everyday teenage or junior defiance (e.g., 사춘기 반항 'adolescent rebellion', 지금 반항하는 거야? 'Are you rebelling/talking back right now?').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 반항하다

받다.etymology: Core native Korean regular verb meaning 'to receive, get, accept, take; to prop/catch from underneath', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 받다.

history.meaning: to receive, accept, hold underneath
to receive, get, accept, take

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 받다

받아가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial verb compound formed from 받- ('to receive, accept, take', from Middle Korean 받다, Yale: patta), the infinitive/connective suffix -아 (selected by vowel harmony after ㅏ), and the deictic directional verb 가다 ('to go, move away from the speaker', Middle Korean 가다). Expresses receiving an item and taking it away from the current location.

history.meaning: to receive + to go away
to receive something and take it away; to pick up and go

morphemes.meaning: go, move away from speaker/reference point

받아가다.notes: Korean directional compounds strictly track speaker perspective: 받아가다 means to receive something and go away from the reference point, whereas 받아오다 means to receive something elsewhere and bring it toward the reference point.

rootFamily.gloss: to receive and bring here; to have been receiving

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 받다

받아들이다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) lexicalized compound verb composed of 받- ('to receive', Middle Korean 받다), the connective suffix -아, and 들이다 ('to let in, bring inside', the morphological causative of 들다 'to enter' formed with the causative suffix -이-). Literally 'to receive and bring inside', it evolved from physically taking in guests or goods to abstractly accepting proposals, criticism, emotions, or reality.

history.meaning: to receive and cause to enter inside
to accept, embrace, adopt (an opinion, request, person, or situation)

morphemes.meaning: causative suffix ('cause to enter -> bring in')

받아들이다.notes: While 받다 simply means 'to receive' (a gift or call), 받아들이다 means 'to accept/embrace inwardly' (현실을 받아들이다 'to accept reality', 사과를 받아들이다 'to accept an apology').

rootFamily.gloss: to bring in, let in, invest effort
to accept or humor someone's words/feelings

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 받아들이다

받아보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb-auxiliary construction combining 받- ('to receive, take', Middle Korean 받다), the connective suffix -아, and the auxiliary verb 보다 (originally 'to see, look at', Middle Korean 보다, grammaticalized after -아/-어 to express experiential aspect 'to try doing' or 'to have the experience of doing'). Means 'to experience receiving' or 'to receive and see what it is like'.

history.meaning: to receive and look at; to experience receiving
to receive (for the first time or as an experience); to subscribe to and read

morphemes.meaning: see; auxiliary denoting trial or personal experience

받아보다.notes: In Korean, attaching -아/어 보다 softens statements and highlights lived experience, as in 첫 월급을 받아보다 ('to experience getting one's very first paycheck') or 신문을 받아보다 ('to have a newspaper delivered/subscribed').

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look at; to try doing
to take an exam or get tested (시험을 받아보다/쳐보다)

받아오다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 받- ('to receive, get', Middle Korean 받다), the connective suffix -아, and 오다 ('to come toward the speaker', Middle Korean 오다). Depending on whether 오다 functions as a directional verb of motion or a temporal aspectual auxiliary, 받아오다 means either (1) 'to receive something and bring it here' or (2) 'to have been receiving continuously up to the present'.

history.meaning: to receive and come toward the speaker
to receive and bring back here; to have been receiving up to now

morphemes.meaning: come toward speaker; continue up to the present

받아오다.notes: Notice the two distinct uses of -아 오다: 사인을 받아오다 ('to go get an autograph and bring it back') is spatial motion, whereas 사랑을 받아오다 ('to have been receiving love all along') is temporal continuation up to now.

받지.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean (고유어) transitive verb 받다 ('to receive, get, accept', Middle Korean 받다, Yale: patta) combined with the suffix -지. In negative constructions (받지 않다 'not receive', 받지 못하다 'cannot receive', 받지 말다 'do not receive'), -지 derives from the Middle Korean nominalizing/suspective suffix -디 (Yale: -ti), which underwent regular palatalization (ㄷ > ㅈ before ㅣ) in Early Modern Korean.

history.meaning: receiving (complement form before negative auxiliaries 아니ᄒᆞ다/몯ᄒᆞ다)
receive / accept (complement form before negation, or committal sentence ending)

morphemes.meaning: negative complementizer (from Middle Korean -디) or committal ending

받지.notes: Pronounced [받찌] (bat-jji) because the root-final obstruent ㄷ triggers post-obstruent tensification (경음화) on the following suffix-initial ㅈ.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 받다

받치다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to prop up, support from below, place a pad/tray underneath, hold up (an umbrella)', derived from 받- ('to receive, hold underneath') plus the intensive/causative suffix -치- (Middle Korean 받티다).

history.meaning: to support from underneath, hold up
to prop up, support, place a coaster/pad under

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 받치다

morphemes.meaning: to hold or receive from below

받침.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'support, prop, coaster, saucer, pad; (in Hangul orthography) a syllable-final consonant written underneath the vowel', derived from 받치다 ('to support from underneath') + nominalizer -ㅁ.

history.meaning: underlying support, prop; final consonant
support, coaster, pad; syllable-final consonant (batchim)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 받침

morphemes.meaning: to prop up, support from below

받침대.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed from the native verb stem 받치- (from 받치다, 'to prop up, support from underneath'), the nominalizing suffix -ㅁ, and the bound noun 대 (臺, Sino-Korean 'platform, stand, pedestal', though often merged with native 대 'pole/stalk' in modern feeling). It is a highly productive everyday term for any base, saucer, tripod, or wedge used to elevate or stabilize an object.
받침대.notes: Covers everything from a teacup saucer (찻잔 받침대) and a tripod to a heavy wooden display pedestal.

발.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'foot, paw, step, leg (of furniture)', descending unchanged from Middle Korean 발. Also homophonous with native Korean 발 ('hanging blind or screen woven of bamboo splints or reeds', Middle Korean 발).

history.meaning: foot; hanging bamboo blind
foot, paw; hanging blind

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 발

발가락.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') and 가락 ('slender stick, spindle, digit').
발가락.notes: Built on the exact same pattern as 손가락 ('finger', 손 'hand' + 가락) and 젓가락 ('chopsticks').

발걸음.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') and 걸음 ('step, gait', nominalized with -음 from 걷다 'to walk').
발걸음.notes: Describes both audible footsteps and the tempo of someone's walk.

cognates.word: 発見する (はっけんする, hakken suru)

발견하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb combining 발견 (發見, from 發 'to shoot forth, open up, uncover, reveal' + 見 'to see, perceive, become visible') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to uncover and see', bringing into view something that already existed but was previously unnoticed or unknown.

history.meaning: to become manifest; to uncover and perceive what was hidden
history.stage: Classical Chinese & modern East Asian lexicon

history.meaning: to discover, find out, spot, or detect

발견하다.notes: Contrast 발견하다 (發見하다, 'to discover' something already existing, such as a talent, clue, or planet) with 발명하다 (發明하다, 'to invent' something new that did not exist before).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전) — 발견하다

발뒤꿈치.etymology: Native Korean compound of 발 ('foot') + 뒤 ('back, rear') + 꿈치 ('protruding joint bend', cf. 팔꿈치 'elbow').
발뒤꿈치.notes: Clearly distinguishes the heel of the foot from the heel of a shoe (굽).

발라지다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) passive-inchoative compound verb formed from `발라-`, the infinitive stem of the liquid-irregular verb `바르다` (Middle Korean `ᄇᆞᄅᆞ다`, "to paste, apply, smear, coat"), combined with the auxiliary verb `-지다` ("to become, come to be"). Literally meaning "to come to be pasted or applied", it describes paper, posters, or coatings becoming stuck or plastered onto a surface.

history.meaning: to apply, smear, or paste onto a surface
to become pasted up, coated, or plastered on

morphemes.meaning: to paste, apply, smear (stem of 바르다)

발라지다.notes: Often used vividly for posters, stickers, or wallpaper being plastered all over a wall, or for ointment being smoothly applied.

발리다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) morphological passive verb derived from `바르다` (Middle Korean `ᄇᆞᄅᆞ다`, "to paste, smear, coat; to peel/debone") plus the native passive suffix `-리-` (Middle Korean `ᄇᆞᆯ리다`). From its literal sense "to be coated or smeared on", the idiom `입에 발리다` ("to be smeared on the lips") yielded the meaning "sugarcoated, flattering". In contemporary slang, from the homophonous sense of `바르다` ("to strip meat from bones"), it also means "to be utterly defeated or crushed".

history.meaning: to be smeared, pasted, or applied onto a surface
to be coated; (idiomatic) sugarcoated, flattering; (slang) to get crushed

morphemes.meaning: to paste, smear, coat; to strip/peel

발리다.notes: In drama dialogue, watch for the classic collocation `입에 발린 말` ("words coated on the lips", i.e. empty flattery or lip service) versus competitive slang `발리다` ("to get owned/beaten").

rootFamily.gloss: to paste, smear, apply; to debone
to become pasted up or coated

발목.etymology: Native Korean anatomical compound of 발 ('foot') and 목 ('neck, narrow constriction').

발버둥.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun formed from `발` (Middle Korean `발`, "foot") and the mimetic/ideophonic root `버둥` (seen in `버둥거리다` and `버둥대다`, "to thrash, flail, or kick one's limbs"). Originally describing the physical act of kicking and flailing one's feet in distress or tantrum, it broadened metaphorically to denote any frantic struggle or desperate last-ditch effort.

history.meaning: physical kicking and flailing of the feet
frantic kicking; desperate struggle or writhing effort

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic root for thrashing or flailing limbs

발버둥.notes: Almost always paired with the verb `치다` as `발버둥 치다` ("to struggle frantically, make a desperate effort to survive").

rootFamily.gloss: act of kicking and thrashing about
to thrash about, flail one's limbs

cognates.meaning: to occur, break out, be generated

발생하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean (*한자어*) verb combining the Sino-Korean noun `발생` (發生, "occurrence, outbreak, generation") with the native Korean light verb `-하다` ("to do, to happen"). In `발생` (發生), `발` (發) means "to shoot forth, emit, break out" and `생` (生) means "to be born, arise, come into existence", yielding the literal sense "to spring forth into existence".

history.meaning: coming into life, sprouting forth, or arising
to occur, break out, happen, or be generated

morphemes.meaning: to be born, arise, come into being (生)

발생하다.notes: Belongs to formal and journalistic register (used for accidents, broadcasting errors, or costs); in casual speech, native `일어나다` or `생기다` is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: place of origin, source of outbreak

발설하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean (*한자어*) verb formed from `발설` (發說, "divulging, speaking out") plus the native Korean light verb `-하다` ("to do"). The Sino-Korean compound combines `발` (發, "to open up, emit, reveal") and `설` (說, "speech, talk, words"), literally "to let words out into the open", specializing in Joseon legal and modern usage to mean disclosing a secret or blabbing confidential information.

history.meaning: uttering words or setting forth an explanation
to disclose a secret, divulge, or blab

발설하다.notes: Frequently appears in negative warnings or promises of secrecy, such as `절대 발설하지 마라` ("Never breathe a word of this to anyone").

rootFamily.gloss: to leak a secret or information
rumor, gossip, talk of the town

cognates.meaning: to vocalize, produce sound, speak out

발성.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `발성` (發聲), composed of `발` (發, "to emit, send forth, project") and `성` (聲, "voice, sound, tone"). Literally meaning "sending forth the voice", it entered modern theatrical, musical, and broadcasting vocabulary (alongside Japanese 発声 *hassei*) to denote technical vocalization, breathing support, and voice projection.

history.meaning: emitting a sound or raising one's voice
vocalization, voice projection, vocal technique

발성.notes: In Korean broadcasting and acting, `발성` (voice projection from the diaphragm) and `발음` (發音, clear articulation/pronunciation) are paired as the twin fundamentals of on-camera delivery.

rootFamily.gloss: vocal technique, method of voice projection

발소리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'sound of footsteps, footfall, tread', formed from 발 ('foot') + 소리 ('sound', pronounced [발쏘리] with tensification).

history.meaning: foot + sound
sound of footsteps, footfall

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 발소리

cognates.meaning: to make a statement, speak at a meeting
to make an official statement, speak publicly

발언.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `발언` (發言), composed of `발` (發, "to issue forth, utter, put out") and `언` (言, "words, speech, statement"). Attested since the Classical Chinese *Classic of Poetry* (*Shijing*: 發言盈庭, "uttered words fill the court"), it became the standard modern legal, parliamentary, and media term for taking the floor to make a public remark or statement.

history.meaning: opening one's mouth to utter words in court or counsel
public statement, remark, or comment in a meeting or broadcast

발언.notes: In TV production and news, controversial remarks by celebrities on air are frequently called `문제적 발언` ("problematic remarks") or `폭탄 발언` ("bombshell statements").

rootFamily.gloss: the right to speak, the floor
to make a statement, speak publicly

발전하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 발전 (發展, 'development, progress, expansion', or 發電, 'electric power generation') plus -하다.

history.meaning: to unfold and advance
to develop, progress, advance, grow

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 발전하다

발짝.etymology: Native Korean bound noun and numeral classifier derived from 발 ('foot') and -짝 (a contracted form of 자국 'footprint, trace'). While 걸음 also counts steps of walking, 발짝 specifically measures short spatial distances step by step, as in a treasure hunt or a careful backward retreat. It is always preceded by a native Korean numeral (한 발짝, 두 발짝) or a demonstrative.
발짝.notes: Used with native numbers (한 발짝, 두 발짝); often interchangeable with 걸음 but emphasizes physical distance/spacing.

발코니.etymology: Borrowed from English balcony, which traces back to Italian balcone ('large window, scaffold, gallery'), augmented with the suffix -one from Lombardic/Germanic balko ('beam, rafter'). Adapted into Korean as 발코니, it refers specifically to an elevated outdoor platform projecting from a building's wall, contrasting with 베란다 (veranda, a roofed gallery) and 테라스 (terrace, an open patio on the ground).
발코니.notes: Often confused with 베란다 in Korean apartments, but technically refers to a projecting upper-floor platform.

발판.etymology: Hybrid compound combining native 발 ('foot') with Sino-Korean 판 (板, 'wooden board, plank').
발판.notes: Refers both to a low kitchen step stool and figuratively to a stepping-stone.

발표.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `발표` (發表), composed of `발` (發, "to issue forth, uncover, disclose") and `표` (表, "outer surface, manifest, display"). Literally "bringing out to the surface", it evolved from Literary Sinitic usage for manifesting inner qualities or official facts into the standard modern East Asian term (reinforced by Meiji Japanese 発表 *happyō*) for a public announcement, release, or academic/school presentation.

history.meaning: manifesting outwardly or revealing to the public
public announcement, press release, or presentation

발표.notes: Covers everything from a classroom presentation (`수업 발표`) and a new song release (`신곡 발표`) to an official press announcement (`공식 발표`).

발표하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean (*한자어*) verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb `-하다` ("to do") to the Sino-Korean noun `발표` (發表, "announcement, presentation, publication"), which combines `발` (發, "to issue forth, disclose") and `표` (表, "outer surface, manifest display"). Literally "to make manifest on the outside", hence to announce publicly or present before an audience.

history.meaning: to make manifest outwardly or proclaim publicly
to announce publicly, release, or give a presentation

발표하다.notes: Used across media and entertainment for releasing ratings, announcing cast lineups, or debuting new albums.

rootFamily.gloss: to express or declare one's stance officially

밝다.etymology: Native Korean adjective and verb descending from Middle Korean ᄇᆞᇰ다 ('bright, luminous, clear; to dawn; to be well-versed in'), with regular shift of ᆞ to ㅏ.

history.meaning: bright, light; to dawn
bright, light, cheerful, sharp/conversant

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밝다

밟다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) verb `밟다`, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as `밣다` (`palp-ta`, "to tread on, step upon"), etymologically sharing its initial root element with `발` ("foot"). From the physical action of stepping on the ground or following directly in someone's footprints (`뒤를 밟다`), it developed figurative senses including "to go through procedural steps" (`절차를 밟다`), "to press the accelerator pedal", and "to tail or shadow someone covertly".

history.meaning: to step on, tread upon with the feet
to step on; to follow a procedure; (idiomatic) to tail or shadow someone

morphemes.meaning: to step on, tread upon, follow footsteps

밟다.notes: Pronounced `[밥따]` (`[baptta]`) in Standard Korean because the consonant cluster `ㄼ` reduces to `[ㅂ]` specifically in the verb `밟다` (unlike `넓다` `[널따]`). In detective or entertainment jargon, `(뒤를) 밟다` means "to tail/shadow".

rootFamily.gloss: to be stepped on, be trampled

밤.etymology: Native Korean noun representing two ancient homographs that were distinguished by pitch accent in Middle Korean: (1) 'night, nighttime' (Middle Korean 밤, low tone); and (2) 'chestnut' (Middle Korean 밤, long/rising tone, preserved as vowel length in standard pronunciation [밤:]).

history.form: 밤 (night, low tone) / 밤 (chestnut, rising tone)
history.meaning: night; chestnut
night, evening; chestnut

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밤

밤늦다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound descriptive verb (adjective) formed by incorporating the noun `밤` (Middle Korean `밤`, "night") into the adjective `늦다` (Middle Korean `늗다`, "to be late"). Originating from the syntactic clause `밤이 늦다` ("the night is late"), the subject marker dropped to form a single lexicalized predicate meaning "to be late into the night".

history.meaning: for the night to grow late
to be late at night, late into the night

밤늦다.notes: Most commonly encountered in its adverbialized forms `밤늦게` ("late at night") or `밤늦도록` ("until late into the night").

밤새.etymology: Native Korean compound noun and adverb meaning 'all night, throughout the night, overnight', contracted from 밤사이 (밤 'night' + 사이 'interval, duration, time between').

history.meaning: duration of the night
all night long, overnight

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밤새

밤새다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound verb combining `밤` (Middle Korean `밤`, "night") and the intransitive verb `새다` (Middle Korean `새다`, "to dawn, for daybreak to grow bright"). Originally meaning "the night gives way to dawn" (`밤이 새다`), in modern colloquial Korean it is widely used with a human subject to mean "to stay up all night until daybreak" (overlapping with the causative `밤새우다`).

history.meaning: for the night to end and dawn to break
for night to pass into dawn; (colloquial) to stay up all night

밤새다.notes: Prescriptive grammar distinguishes intransitive `밤이 새다` ("dawn breaks") from transitive/causative `밤을 새우다` ("a person stays up all night"), but in everyday speech Koreans constantly say `어제 밤샜어` ("I stayed up all night yesterday").

rootFamily.gloss: to stay up all night, pull an all-nighter
for day to break; to stay up until dawn

밤새우다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound verb formed from `밤` (Middle Korean `밤`, "night") and `새우다` (Middle Korean `새오다`), which is the morphological causative (`새-` + causative suffix `-우-`) of `새다` ("to dawn, grow bright at daybreak"). Literally meaning "to make the night pass until dawn", it is the standard transitive/causative verb for intentionally staying awake all night or pulling an all-nighter.

history.meaning: to cause the night to pass into daybreak while awake
to stay up all night, pull an all-nighter

밤새우다.notes: In Korean TV production (`프로듀사`), pulling all-nighters in the editing room (`밤새워 편집하다`) is a quintessential trope of a PD's life.

rootFamily.gloss: for night to pass; (colloquial) to stay up all night
to sit up all night until dawn
to spend the entire night awake

밤중.etymology: A hybrid Korean (*혼종어*) compound noun combining the native Korean noun `밤` (Middle Korean `밤`, "night") with the Sino-Korean bound noun `중` (中, "middle, midst, center"). Attested in Early Modern Korean as `밤듕` (reflecting the pre-palatalized pronunciation of 中 `듕`), it literally means "the middle of the night".

history.meaning: the midst of the night, midnight hours
middle of the night, dead of night

밤중.notes: Often intensified with native prefixes as `한밤중` ("the dead of night") or `오밤중` ("an ungodly hour of the night", used when someone calls or makes noise late at night).

밥.etymology: A core native Korean (*고유어*) noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as `밥` (`pap`, "cooked rice; meal") and earlier in the 12th-century Song-dynasty glossary *Gyerim Yusa* (鷄林類事) transcribed in Chinese characters as `璞` (Early Middle Korean `*pak` / `*pap`). Because steamed rice has been the staple grain of the Korean diet for millennia, `밥` underwent synecdochic broadening to mean any meal, food in general, and one's basic sustenance.

history.meaning: cooked rice
history.stage: Early Middle Korean (12th c., Gyerim Yusa)

history.meaning: cooked grain/rice; a meal
cooked rice; meal, food, daily sustenance

밥.notes: So central is `밥` to Korean social life that "Have you eaten rice?" (`밥 먹었어?`) is a standard everyday greeting equivalent to "How are you?", and "Let's eat a meal sometime" (`언제 밥 한번 먹자`) is a classic polite farewell.

rootFamily.gloss: rice bowl; one's job or livelihood

밥그릇.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun combining `밥` (Middle Korean `밥`, "cooked rice, meal") and `그릇` (Middle Korean `그릏`, "vessel, bowl, container"). Literally designating the bowl used to serve steamed rice, it developed a powerful cultural metaphor in which one's rice bowl represents one's share of food, job security, livelihood, or professional turf.

history.meaning: a bowl for holding cooked rice
rice bowl; (figurative) one's livelihood, job, or turf

밥그릇.notes: In workplace and media dramas, `밥그릇 싸움` ("fighting over rice bowls") means a turf war or争夺 over jobs/budgets, and `밥그릇을 챙기다` means looking out for one's own livelihood or self-interest.

rootFamily.gloss: vessel, dish; a person's caliber or capacity

밥맛.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun composed of `밥` (Middle Korean `밥`, "cooked rice, meal") and `맛` (Middle Korean `맛`, "taste, flavor"). Literally "the flavor of rice/food", it came to denote one's appetite for food. In 20th-century colloquial slang, from expressions like `밥맛 떨어지다` ("to lose one's appetite in disgust"), calling a person or behavior `밥맛` came to mean "off-putting, obnoxious, or gross".

history.meaning: the taste of cooked rice; one's appetite for food
appetite; (slang) an obnoxious or appetite-ruining person/trait

밥맛.notes: Pronounced `[밤맏]` (`[bammat]`) due to nasal assimilation (`ㅂ` + `ㅁ` -> `ㅁㅁ`). Watch the context: `밥맛이 없다` means "I have no appetite", whereas `진짜 밥맛이야` means "He/she is totally obnoxious/gross".

밥상.etymology: A hybrid Korean (*혼종어*) compound noun combining the native Korean noun `밥` (Middle Korean `밥`, "cooked rice, meal") with the Sino-Korean noun `상` (床, "table, low portable dining tray, couch"). Historically referring to the traditional portable low wooden table (`소반`) carried from the kitchen with a full meal arranged on it, it now denotes any dinner table or set meal spread.

history.meaning: portable low wooden dining tray set with rice and side dishes
dinner table, dining table set with a meal

밥상.notes: Featured in the famous idiom `다 된 밥상에 숟가락 얹다` ("to just lay one's spoon on an already-prepared dinner table", i.e. to take credit for work others have already completed).

rootFamily.gloss: table set with alcoholic drinks and side dishes

밧줄.etymology: Native Korean compound uniting 바 (a native noun meaning 'thick rope, cable, hawser', attested in Middle Korean as 바) with the genitive linking consonant -ㅅ- (사이시옷) and 줄 ('line, cord, string'). It designates heavy-duty, thick ropes used for tying, hauling, or climbing, distinguishing itself from lighter string (실) or thin cord (끈).
밧줄.notes: Pronounced [받쭐] with tensification of ㅈ after 사이시옷.

방.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 방 (房, Middle Chinese *bjang*), meaning 'room, chamber', borrowed early and used as the standard Korean word for an indoor room.

history.meaning: room, chamber
room

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 방

방금.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 방금 (方今), meaning 'just now, a moment ago', formed from 方 (방, 'just now, at this point') + 今 (금, 'now, the present').

history.meaning: at this very moment, just now
just now, a moment ago

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 방금
