방법.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `방법` (方法), composed of `방` (方, "square, direction, prescription, technique") and `법` (法, "law, standard, model, rule"). In Classical Chinese philosophy (such as *Mozi*), `방` (方, carpenter's square) and `법` (法, standard/model) denoted objective standards of measurement; together they evolved into the general East Asian term for a method, procedure, or practical way of achieving an end.

history.meaning: standards of measurement; medical or practical technique
way, method, means, or procedure

방법.notes: Whereas `방법` (方法) focuses on a concrete "how-to" means or solution to solve a problem, `방식` (方式) refers to an established style, mode, or system of operating.

방석.etymology: Sino-Korean 방석 (方席), from 방 (方, 'square') + 석 (席, 'woven mat, seat').
방석.notes: Originally a square sedge or silk floor mat, now used for any square chair or floor cushion.

cognates.meaning: to broadcast, play over a speaker/radio

방송.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `방송` (放送), composed of `방` (放, "to release, let go, emit outward") and `송` (送, "to send, transmit, escort"). In pre-modern Literary Sinitic and Joseon legal records (`조선왕조실록`), `방송` meant "releasing an arrested prisoner". In the 1920s, Japanese repurposed 放送 (*hōsō*, literally "emitting and transmitting outward") to translate English *broadcasting*, and this modern sense entered Korean with the founding of Gyeongseong Broadcasting Station (JODK) in 1927.

history.meaning: releasing a prisoner or letting someone go free
radio, television, or internet broadcasting; a broadcast program

morphemes.meaning: to release, emit, send out widely (放)

방송.notes: Frequently shortened to the single syllable `방` in industry compounds like `본방` (original live/first airing), `재방` (rerun), `생방` (live broadcast), and `먹방` (eating broadcast).

rootFamily.gloss: to broadcast, air; to work in broadcasting

방송국.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound noun `방송국` (放送局), formed from `방송` (放送, "broadcasting", from 放 "release, emit" + 送 "send, transmit") and the institutional suffix/noun `국` (局, "bureau, office, station, department"). Coined in the early 20th-century radio era alongside Japanese 放送局 (*hōsōkyoku*), it denotes both the physical building/complex and the organization of a radio or television network (such as KBS, MBC, or SBS).

history.meaning: radio transmission station (such as JODK in 1927)
television or radio broadcasting station/network

방송국.notes: In Korean entertainment slang, insiders often playfully refer to `방송국 놈들` ("those TV station folks/PDs") when joking about how demanding or manipulative television producers can be.

방송사고.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) four-character compound noun `방송사고` (放送事故), combining `방송` (放送, "broadcast", from 放 "emit, release" + 送 "send, transmit") with `사고` (事故, "accident, mishap, unexpected incident", from 事 "matter, affair" + 故 "reason, happening, mishap"). It designates any unintended technical failure, dead air, uncensored profanity, or on-stage mishap that goes out over the airwaves.

history.meaning: transmission failure or technical incident during radio/TV airing
on-air broadcast accident, technical glitch, or live blooper

방송사고.notes: For television PDs in *The Producers*, a `방송사고` (such as failing to deliver a master tape before airtime or airing unedited footage) is the ultimate career-threatening nightmare.

cognates.word: 放送通信委員会 (Hōsō Tsūshin Iinkai)

방송통신위원회.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) institutional compound noun `방송통신위원회` (放送通信委員會), literally "Broadcasting and Communications Commission". Created in 2008 as South Korea's presidential regulatory agency overseeing television, radio, and telecommunications (modeled in part on the US FCC), it joins `방송` (放送, "broadcasting"), `통신` (通信, "telecommunications", from 通 "pass through, connect" + 信 "message, trust"), and `위원회` (委員會, "commission/committee", from 委 "entrust" + 員 "member, official" + 會 "assembly, council").

history.form: 放送委員會 (방송위원회) + 情報通信部 (정보통신부)
history.meaning: predecessor broadcasting commission and information/communications ministry
Korea Communications Commission (established February 2008)

방송통신위원회.notes: Almost universally abbreviated in news headlines and PD conversations to its three-syllable acronym `방통위` (放通委).

방송하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean (*한자어*) verb formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun `방송` (放送, "broadcasting, transmission", from 放 "emit, release" + 送 "send, transmit") with the native Korean light verb `-하다` ("to do"). Used transitively to mean "to air or transmit a program" and intransitively in entertainment industry speech to mean "to work in broadcasting or perform on air".

history.meaning: to transmit radio signals or programs to the public
to broadcast, air on TV/radio/online; to work in broadcasting

방송하다.notes: Note the passive/intransitive counterpart `방송되다` ("to be broadcast, to air"), e.g., `매주 금요일에 방송된다` ("It airs every Friday").

방식.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `방식` (方式), composed of `방` (方, "direction, square, method") and `식` (式, "form, model, rule, style, ceremony"). In Literary Sinitic it denoted an established standard or ceremonial model; in modern Korean it designates a characteristic mode, style, or established system of doing things.

history.meaning: established rule, standard model, or formula
way, mode, style, or system of operation

방식.notes: Frequently paired with possessives or modifiers to describe someone's personal style of working or living, such as `나만의 방식` ("my own way/style") or `진행 방식` ("mode of hosting/proceeding").

cognates.meaning: to set one's mind at rest, feel relieved (false friend!)

방심하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean (*한자어*) verb combining `방심` (放心, "letting one's guard down, carelessness") with the native light verb `-하다` ("to do"). Composed of `방` (放, "to release, let go") and `심` (心, "mind, heart"), the term originates in *Mencius* (孟子, *Gaozi I*: 求放心, "seeking the lost/straying heart-mind"), where `방심` meant letting one's moral mind wander unguarded. Korean preserved this negative Confucian sense ("to relax vigilance, be careless"), whereas Mandarin shifted `放心` to a positive sense ("to feel relieved").

history.meaning: letting one's moral heart-mind stray or go unguarded (Mencius)
to let one's guard down, be off guard, become careless or complacent

morphemes.meaning: to release, let go, leave unguarded (放)

방심하다.notes: A classic East Asian false friend: in Chinese, `放心` (*fàngxīn*) means "don't worry / rest assured" (Korean `안심하다` 安心), whereas Korean `방심하다` always means "to let one's guard down / become careless"!

rootFamily.gloss: inattention, letting one's guard down (`放心`)
to feel relieved, rest assured (`安心`)

방어적.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) attributive noun/determiner `방어적` (防禦的), formed from `방어` (防禦, "defense, protection") plus the Sino-Korean suffix `-적` (的, "-ive, -ic, pertaining to"). In `방어` (防禦), `방` (防, originally "levee, embankment to hold back floodwaters") means "to ward off, guard against" and `어` (禦) means "to resist, defend against", extending from military fortification to psychological or conversational defensiveness.

history.meaning: military defense and fortification against an enemy
defensive, self-protective (in military, sports, or psychology)

morphemes.meaning: embankment; to ward off, guard against (防)

방어적.notes: Grammatically functions as a determiner before a noun (`방어적 태도`, "defensive attitude") or with the copula `이다` / particle `으로` (`방어적으로 나오다`, "to act defensively").

방울.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'drop (of water, rain, or sweat); small spherical bell; small round bulb/bead', descending from Middle Korean 방올 ('small bell; round drop') via vowel raising (오 > 우).

history.meaning: small round bell; droplet, globule
drop, droplet; small bell

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 방울

cognates.meaning: attending a trial or parliament session, auditing
to audit a class, attend a session as a non-voting observer
to audit, listen in from the side

방청.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) noun `방청` (傍聽), composed of `방` (傍, "side, beside, nearby") and `청` (聽, "to listen, hear"). Literally meaning "listening from the sidelines", it was adopted in modern East Asian legal and parliamentary vocabulary (cf. Japanese 傍聴 *bōchō*) for sitting in the public gallery of a court or assembly, and in Korean broadcasting it expanded to mean attending a live radio or television studio recording as an audience member.

history.meaning: sitting in the public gallery to listen to a court trial or assembly session
attending a courtroom/assembly gallery or a TV/radio studio audience

방청.notes: In Korean variety and music shows (like *Music Bank* in *The Producers*), viewers apply online for `방청권` (studio audience tickets) to sit in the studio as `방청객` (studio audience members).

rootFamily.gloss: studio audience member, gallery observer (`傍聽客`)
studio audience ticket, gallery admission ticket (`傍聽券`)
to attend a broadcast or hearing as an audience member

방충망.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) three-morpheme compound noun `방충망` (防蟲網), transparently constructed from `방` (防, "to ward off, prevent, keep out"), `충` (蟲, "insect, bug"), and `망` (網, "net, mesh, screen"). Literally "insect-preventing net", it denotes the fine wire, aluminum, or fiberglass mesh screen fitted into window and door frames to keep mosquitoes and flies out while letting air circulate.

history.meaning: protective mesh netting against insects
window or door insect screen

morphemes.meaning: to ward off, prevent, keep out (防)

방충망.notes: The prefix `방-` (防, "preventing/proof") is highly productive in everyday Korean household terms, such as `방수` (防水, waterproof), `방음` (防音, soundproofing), and `방한` (防寒, winter/cold protection).

방통위.etymology: A Sino-Korean (*한자어*) syllabic acronym `방통위` (放通委), formed by taking the initial Sino-Korean morphemes of each constituent word in `방송통신위원회` (放送通信委員會, "Korea Communications Commission"): `방` (放) from `방송` (放送, "broadcasting"), `통` (通) from `통신` (通信, "communications"), and `위` (委) from `위원회` (委員會, "commission"). This three-syllable clipping pattern is the standard morphological template for abbreviating government agencies and committees in modern Korean.

history.meaning: full official title of the Korea Communications Commission (founded 2008)
Korea Communications Commission (standard media/everyday acronym)

방통위.notes: In Korean TV dramas and variety shows, PDs constantly worry about getting sanctioned or fined by `방통위` (or its sister content-review board `방통심의위`) for product placement (PPL) violations or inappropriate language.

방해하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 방해 (妨害, 'hindrance, obstruction, disturbance, interference') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to hinder and harm/impede
to disturb, interrupt, hinder, get in the way

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 방해하다

방향.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 방향 (方向), composed of 方 (방, 'direction, side, region, square') and 向 (향, 'to face towards, incline, direction'). Attested in Classical Chinese for both spatial orientation and figurative course of action.

history.meaning: spatial side or orientation towards which something faces
physical direction, orientation, or conceptual course of action

방향.notes: Used both for physical navigation (방향을 바꾸다, 'to change direction') and abstract creative or policy orientation (프로그램의 방향, 'the direction of a program').

배.etymology: Polysemous Korean noun uniting three native Korean words from Middle Korean ᄇᆡ—(1) 'belly, stomach, abdomen', (2) 'boat, ship, vessel', and (3) 'pear'—alongside the Sino-Korean noun/bound noun 배 (倍, 'times, -fold, double').

history.meaning: belly; boat; pear (ᄇᆡ); times, multiple (倍)
stomach, belly; boat, ship; pear; -fold, double

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배

cognates.meaning: background, scenery, context behind an event

배경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배경 (背景), formed from 背 (배, 'back, behind') and 景 (경, 'scenery, view, light'). Originally coined in Meiji-era Japanese (背景, haikei) as a calque of English 'background' in theatrical and visual arts before expanding to social and personal background across East Asia.

history.meaning: distant scenery painted at the rear of a stage or canvas
visual backdrop, historical setting, or personal and social backing

배경.notes: In Korean, 배경 can mean 'setting/context' (시대적 배경), 'background music' (배경음악, BGM), or a person's 'influential connections/family backing' (often colloquially shortened to 빽 from English 'back').

배고프다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective meaning 'hungry', formed from the subject noun 배 ('belly, stomach', Middle Korean ᄇᆡ) + adjective 고프다 ('to be hungry, famished, empty', Middle Korean 고프다).

history.meaning: the stomach is empty/hungry
hungry, famished

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배고프다

배관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배관 (配管), meaning 'plumbing, piping, pipework', formed from 配 (배, 'distribute, lay out') + 管 (관, 'pipe, tube').

history.meaning: arrangement and installation of pipes
plumbing, piping, pipes

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배관

배꼽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun deriving from Middle Korean ᄇᆡᆺ복 (poyspok), analyzed as ᄇᆡ (poy, 'belly, abdomen') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- (-s-) + 복 (pok, 'center, hub, middle', cognate with 한복판 'dead center'). Through regressive assimilation and tensification triggered by the genitive -ㅅ-, ᄇᆡᆺ복 shifted via 뱨복/배복 to modern 배꼽.

history.meaning: center of the belly; navel
navel, bellybutton; figuratively the seat of uproarious laughter

배꼽.notes: Featured in quintessential Korean idioms for laughing hysterically: 배꼽을 잡다 ('to hold one's bellybutton') and 배꼽이 빠지다 ('one's bellybutton falls out', i.e., to laugh one's head off).

배낭.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배낭 (背囊), combining 背 (배, 'back of the body') and 囊 (낭, 'bag, sack, pouch'). Used in Literary Chinese for a pouch carried on the back and standardized in modern East Asian military and hiking terminology for a rucksack or backpack.

history.meaning: sack or pouch carried on the back
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: backpack, rucksack, knapsack for hiking or travel

배낭.notes: While 가방 (from Dutch kabas via Japanese) is a general bag and 백팩 (backpack) is used for everyday fashion/school bags, 배낭 specifically evokes hiking, camping, or backpacking travel (배낭여행).

배달.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배달 (配達), meaning 'delivery, distribution (of mail, food, or goods)', composed of 配 (배, 'distribute, allocate') + 達 (달, 'reach, deliver').

history.meaning: distributing and delivering to a destination
delivery

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배달

cognates.meaning: comic performer, actor in ancient China

배우.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배우 (俳優), from 俳 (배, 'entertainer, jester, vaudevillian') and 優 (우, 'actor, performer, excellent'). Attested in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) for court jesters and theatrical performers, and revived in the late 19th century across East Asia as the standard term for dramatic and film actors.

history.meaning: court jester, comic performer, or theatrical entertainer
stage, film, or television actor/actress

배우.notes: Gender-neutral on its own; when gender specification is needed, 여배우 (女俳優, actress) and 남자 배우 (male actor) are used, though unmodified 배우 is increasingly preferred for all genders.

rootFamily.gloss: movie star, film actor (映畵俳優)

배우다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to learn, study, acquire knowledge or a skill', descending from Middle Korean ᄇᆡ호다 ('to learn').

history.meaning: to learn, study
to learn, study

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배우다

배정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배정 (配定), formed from 配 (배, 'to distribute, apportion, match') and 定 (정, 'to fix, decide, settle'). Literally 'distributing and fixing', used in administrative and institutional contexts for allocating budgets, rooms, personnel, or school placements.

history.meaning: apportioning and settling shares or duties
official assignment or allocation of resources, tasks, or personnel

배정.notes: Commonly used for institutional allocations such as 방 배정 (room assignment), 예산 배정 (budget allocation), or 신입 PD 배정 (assigning rookie PDs to variety teams).

배정하는.etymology: Adnominal present participle of the Sino-Korean verbal compound 배정하다 (配定하다, 'to assign, to allocate'), composed of the Sino-Korean noun 배정 (配定: 配 'distribute' + 定 'fix, decide'), the native Korean light verb stem 하- ('to do'), and the present adnominal modifier suffix -는.

history.meaning: to apportion and settle
assigning, allocating (modifying a following noun)

배정하는.notes: Placed directly before a noun to form a relative clause, e.g., 예산을 배정하는 부서 ('the department that allocates the budget').

배정해.etymology: Inflected form of the Sino-Korean verb 배정하다 (配定하다, 'to assign, to allocate'), consisting of 배정 (配定: 配 'distribute, apportion' + 定 'fix, settle') plus the native light verb 하- ('to do') conjugated with the infinitive/intimate suffix -어 (하- + -여 -> 해).

history.meaning: assigning, having allocated
assign!, allocate (intimate); or connecting form before auxiliary verbs like 주다

morphemes.meaning: light verb 하- + infinitive/intimate ending -어 (contracted to 해)

배정해.notes: Frequently appears before auxiliary verbs like 주다 (배정해 주다, 'to assign for someone') or as a casual imperative/declarative ending in spoken workplace dialogue.

배짱.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed from native Korean 배 ('belly, abdomen', traditionally conceived as the anatomical seat of boldness and resolve, cf. 배가 크다) + genitive interfix -ㅅ- (triggering tensification of ㅈ to ㅉ) + Sino-Korean 장 (場, 'place, field, arena', or 臟, 'viscera, internal organs'). Literally 'belly-interior' or 'guts'.

history.meaning: seat of the abdomen; inner visceral boldness
guts, nerve, audacity, unyielding boldness

배짱.notes: Common in expressions like 배짱이 두둑하다 ('to have thick/plentiful guts', i.e., to have nerves of steel) and 배짱을 부리다 ('to bluff or act brazenly').

rootFamily.gloss: false front, nerve, pretension (배 + -ㅅ- + 심 心)

배치.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배치 (配置), composed of 配 (배, 'to distribute, apportion, arrange') and 置 (치, 'to place, set up, establish'). Used across East Asia for physical layout of objects, tactical deployment of troops, or organizational posting of personnel.

history.meaning: apportioning and setting in place
spatial arrangement, layout, or personnel deployment/posting

배치.notes: Note the homonym 배치 (背馳, 'contradiction, running counter to'). In broadcasting and business, 배치 usually refers to camera/props placement or staff assignment (인력 배치).

배치도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 배치도 (配置圖), meaning 'layout plan, floor plan, arrangement diagram', formed from 배치 (配置, 'arrangement, placement') + 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, chart').

history.meaning: diagram showing spatial placement
layout diagram, floor plan

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 배치도

cognates.meaning: battery, set of percussion instruments, artillery unit

배터리.etymology: Direct loanword (외래어) from English battery. The English word derives from Middle French batterie ('action of beating, bombardment, artillery unit'), from Old French batre ('to beat'), from Latin battuere ('to beat, strike'). Benjamin Franklin extended 'battery' in 1748 to a linked array of Leyden jars ('electrical battery').

history.meaning: to beat, strike -> artillery unit that batters fortifications
linked array of electrical condensers; portable electric cell
electric battery (for cameras, phones, cars) or baseball pitcher-catcher pair

배터리.notes: In casual speech, older speakers sometimes pronounce it with tense initials as 빳데리 (influenced by Japanese batterī), though 배터리 is the sole standard form alongside Sino-Korean 건전지 (乾電池, dry cell).

백.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 백 (百, Middle Chinese *paek*), meaning 'one hundred (100)'.

history.meaning: one hundred
hundred (100)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 백

백가지.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the Sino-Korean numeral 백 (百, 'one hundred', frequently used hyperbolically to mean 'countless, all sorts of') and the native Korean bound noun/classifier 가지 ('kind, sort, variety', originally identical to Middle Korean 가지 'tree branch', via semantic extension from branching ramification to categories).

history.meaning: a hundred branches -> a hundred sorts or kinds
history.stage: Middle Korean to Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: a hundred kinds; myriad varieties; all sorts of things

백가지.notes: In Korean numbering, 백 (百) often functions figuratively for completeness or multiplicity rather than an exact count of 100 (compare 백발백중, 'a hundred shots, a hundred hits').

rootFamily.gloss: all kinds of, every sort of (萬가지)

백날.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 백 (百, 'one hundred', used figuratively for 'countless, endlessly') + native Korean 날 ('day', Middle Korean 날). Originally a noun phrase meaning 'a hundred days / countless days', it grammaticalized into an adverb meaning 'day in and day out, no matter how long one tries (in vain)'.

history.meaning: a hundred days; many days on end
every single day, day in and day out (often implying futile repetition)

백날.notes: In colloquial speech, 백날 almost always introduces a concessive or futile action: 백날 말해 봐야 소용없다 ('You can say it day in and day out, it's no use'). Compare 만날/맨날 (萬날, 'always, every day').

rootFamily.gloss: one hundredth day celebration for a baby (百日)

cognates.meaning: one hundred years, a century, a lifetime
a hundred years, a century, an entire lifetime
a hundred years, a human lifespan

백년.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 백년 (百年), composed of 百 (백, 'one hundred') and 年 (년, 'year, harvest cycle'). In both Classical Chinese and Korean, 百年 denotes either a literal century or the metaphorical span of a full human life and enduring marriage (as in 백년가약, 百年佳約).

history.meaning: one hundred years; the full span of a human lifetime
a hundred years, a century, or a lifetime/ages

백년.notes: Appears in classic cultural idioms like 백년해로 (百年偕老, 'growing old together for a hundred years in marriage') and 백년손님 ('a hundred-year guest', an affectionate traditional term for a son-in-law).

rootFamily.gloss: vow of lifelong marriage (百年佳約)
growing old together as spouses (百年偕老)

백배.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 百倍, combining 百 (일백 백, 'one hundred') with the multiplicative classifier 倍 (곱 배, 'times, -fold'). Used both literally for a hundredfold increase and hyperbolically in everyday conversation—especially after comparative -보다 ('than')—to mean 'a hundred times better!'
백배.notes: Functions both as a noun and adverbially before adjectives like 좋다 ('a hundred times better').

백설기.etymology: Sino-Korean and native hybrid culinary term 백설기 (historically rendered in Hanja as 白雪糕 or 白雪餠), composed of 백설 (白雪, 'white snow': 白 'white' + 雪 'snow') and the culinary suffix -기 (denoting steamed earthenware rice cakes, derived either from a phonetic shift of 糕/餠 or native Korean nominalizer -기). Attested in Joseon-era cookbooks for pure white steamed rice flour cake.

history.meaning: steamed rice cake as white as snow
snow-white steamed non-glutinous rice cake, served at 100th-day and first-birthday celebrations

백설기.notes: Because of its snow-white purity and the pun between 백 (白, 'white') and 백 (百, 'hundred'), 백설기 is traditionally shared with neighbors on a baby's 100th day (백일) and first birthday (돌) to wish for longevity and sacred protection.

백설탕.etymology: Sino-Korean 백설탕 (白雪糖), prefixing 백- (白, 'white') to 설탕 (雪糖, 'snow-sugar').
백설탕.notes: Contrasts with 흑설탕 ('dark brown sugar') and 황설탕 ('golden raw sugar').

cognates.meaning: empty-handed, with bare hands, from scratch

백수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 백수 (白手), formed from 白 (백, 'white, bare, empty, unadorned') and 手 (수, 'hand'). In Classical Chinese, 白手 meant 'empty-handed' or 'without capital' (as in 白手起家, building a fortune from nothing). In 20th-century Korean, clipping of 백수건달 (白手乾達, 'penniless idler') shifted 백수 to mean an unemployed person with nothing to do.

history.meaning: bare hands, empty-handed, possessing no capital or tools
penniless loafer or idler roaming about empty-handed
unemployed person (especially an educated youth seeking work)

백수.notes: Note the homonym 백수 (白壽, 99th birthday, because 百 '100' minus 一 '1' equals 白). In contemporary slang, a female unemployed person is playfully called 백조 (白鳥, literally 'swan', contrasting with 백수).

rootFamily.gloss: invalid, blank vote; empty paper (白紙)
bare hands, empty hands (맨손, native calque)

백승찬.etymology: Sino-Korean personal name 백승찬 (白承燦), borne by the rookie variety-department PD protagonist of *The Producers* (*프로듀사*, played by Kim Soo-hyun). Follows traditional Korean three-syllable anthroponymic structure: family surname 백 (白, 'white, pure') + given name 승 (承, 'to inherit, succeed, carry on') + 찬 (燦, 'bright, radiant, splendid').

history.meaning: Korean personal name combining surname 白 with given name characters 承 ('succeed/uphold') and 燦 ('radiant')

백승찬.notes: In *The Producers*, Baek Seung-chan is a Seoul National University law graduate (법대 출신) who joins KBS's entertainment division out of a crush, embodying the earnest, awkward rookie PD archetype.

rootFamily.gloss: succession to a throne or title (承繼)

백승찬이.etymology: Inflected nominal form consisting of the Sino-Korean personal name 백승찬 (白承燦, Baek Seung-chan) suffixed with the native Korean nominative (subject) case particle -이, which attaches to consonant-final stems (inherited from Middle Korean nominative marker -이).

history.meaning: Baek Seung-chan (marked as grammatical subject)

morphemes.meaning: nominative (subject) case particle after consonant-final noun

백승찬이.notes: When addressing or referring to a close peer or junior whose name ends in a consonant, Korean also uses an identical-looking vocative/hypocoristic suffix -이 before other particles (e.g., 승찬이가, 승찬이를), though 백승찬이 with the full surname is strictly the subject-marked full name.

백퍼센트.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and English compound 백퍼센트, combining the Sino-Korean numeral 백 (百, 'one hundred') with the English loanword 퍼센트 (*percent*, ultimately from New Latin *per centum*, 'by the hundred'). Used both literally for 100% and adverbially to mean 'completely, without a doubt'.

history.meaning: one hundred parts per hundred
one hundred percent; completely, absolutely, guaranteed

백퍼센트.notes: In casual spoken Korean and variety show captions, 백퍼센트 is frequently clipped to 백프로 (via Japanese *pāsento* / *puro*) or even shorter slang 백퍼 ('100%, totally, definitely').

밸브.etymology: Borrowed from English valve ('device for regulating or stopping the flow of liquid or gas through a pipe'), ultimately from Latin valva ('leaf of a folding door').

history.meaning: flow-control device in piping or machinery
valve

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 밸브

뱉다.etymology: Native Korean verb deriving from Middle Korean 왯다 (wath-ta) and 밯다 (path-ta, 'to spit out, eject from the mouth'), which underwent vowel fronting (ㅏ -> ㅐ) through umlaut/palatal assimilation in Early Modern Korean to yield modern 뱉다. Used both for physical spitting and figuratively for blurting out words.

history.meaning: to spit out saliva or food from the mouth
to spit out; figuratively to blurt out words or disgorge ill-gotten gains

뱉다.notes: Often paired with 말을 ('words') as 말을 뱉다 or 내뱉다 ('to blurt out, spit out words'); a classic proverb warns 한번 뱉은 말은 주워 담을 수 없다 ('Words once spat out cannot be scooped back up').

rootFamily.gloss: to spit out, blurt out (intensive prefix 내- + 뱉다)

버너.etymology: Borrowed from English burner ('part of a stove, lamp, or portable camp stove that produces a flame').

history.meaning: gas burner or portable stove
burner, portable gas stove

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 버너

버라이어티.etymology: Direct loanword (외래어) from English *variety* (specifically clipped from *variety show*), which came via Middle French *variété* from Latin *varietās* ('difference, diversity, changeableness'), a noun derived from *varius* ('mottled, diverse, changing'). In Korean broadcasting, it refers specifically to unscripted comedy/game entertainment television.

history.meaning: diversity, assortment -> theatrical or broadcast program featuring diverse acts
television variety show (especially Korean reality-variety formats like *2 Days & 1 Night*)

버라이어티.notes: In Korean television jargon (central to *The Producers*), 예능 (藝能) is the broad department/genre for entertainment shows, while 리얼 버라이어티 ('real variety') denotes unscripted outdoor/game shows featuring a fixed cast. Slang adjective 버라이어티하다 means 'wildly eventful or chaotic'.

버릇.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 버릇 (pelus, 'habit, custom, manner, deportment'). It has preserved its exact phonological form and meaning into Modern Korean, where it denotes either an ingrained personal habit or proper etiquette toward elders.

history.meaning: accustomed behavior, habit, or manner of conduct
habit (often mildly negative) or manners/etiquette toward elders

버릇.notes: Unlike Sino-Korean 습관 (習慣, neutral 'habit/routine'), native 버릇 often implies an unconscious quirk or bad habit (나쁜 버릇, 손버릇, 술버릇), and in 버릇없다 ('to have no manners') it specifically means 'rude, impertinent toward elders'.

rootFamily.gloss: habitual verbal tic, pet phrase (말 + 버릇)
drinking habit, behavior when drunk (술 + 버릇)

버리다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to throw away, discard, abandon' (and as the auxiliary verb -어 버리다, marking complete or regrettable aspect), descending from Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다 ('to discard, forsake').

history.meaning: to throw away, abandon, discard
to throw away, discard; (auxiliary) finish completely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 버리다

버섯.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean medical and lexical texts (such as *Hunmong Jahoe*, 1527) as 버슷 (pesus, 'mushroom, fungus'). Through vowel harmony leveling in the second syllable (ㅡ -> ㅓ), Middle Korean 버슷 evolved into Modern Korean 버섯.

history.meaning: mushroom, fleshy fungus growing on wood or soil
mushroom, fungus

버섯.notes: Korean cuisine prizes diverse mushroom varieties named by compounding with 버섯: 송이버섯 (pine mushroom), 표고버섯 (shiitake), 팽이버섯 (enoki), and 느타리버섯 (oyster mushroom).

버스.etymology: Borrowed from English bus, which itself was clipped from omnibus. The term originated in 1820s France as voiture omnibus ('carriage for all', borrowing the Latin dative plural omnibus 'for all', from omnis 'all'). Fully integrated into modern Korean, 버스 pairs with native Korean verbs like 타다 ('to ride, board') and 내리다 ('to get off').
버스.notes: Collocates with 정류장 ('bus stop') and 기사 ('bus driver'); commonly combined as 마을버스 ('village bus') or 시내버스 ('city bus').

버터.etymology: Borrowed from English butter, following standard Korean loanword orthography based on non-rhotic vowel endings (-er -> -어).
버터.notes: Combines with Sino-Korean prefixes such as 무염 버터 ('unsalted butter').

버텨내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the main verb stem 버티- ('to endure, hold out, withstand pressure', conjugated with the infinitive linker -어 into 버텨) plus the completive auxiliary verb stem 내- ('to bring forth, accomplish to the very end', originally causative of 나다 'to come out') + citation suffix -다.

history.meaning: to hold out against pressure and see it through to completion
to endure to the end, tough it out, survive an ordeal through sheer grit

morphemes.meaning: completive auxiliary ('accomplish through to the end')

버텨내다.notes: Adding -내다 to an endurance verb highlights active triumph over adversity: whereas 버티다 means 'to hold on / last', 버텨내다 emphasizes 'successfully surviving and overcoming the ordeal'.

rootFamily.gloss: to endure through, persevere to the end (참아 + 내다)

버튼.etymology: Borrowed from English button ('push-button switch on an appliance or interface; garment fastener').

history.meaning: push-button or knob
button (switch)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 버튼

버티다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in Early Modern Korean as 버틔다 ('to prop up, brace against, withstand external force'), which underwent monophthongization of post-consonantal ㅢ to ㅣ (버틔다 -> 버티다) in the 19th–20th centuries. Originally physical ('to brace or prop up'), it broadened to psychological and situational endurance.

history.meaning: to brace, prop up, stand firm against physical force
to hold out, endure hardship, last, or stubbornly refuse to yield

버티다.notes: A core survival word in Korean workplace culture (e.g., 회사에서 버티다, 'to survive/hang in there at the company'); also gave rise to the popular slang noun 존버 ('holding on stubbornly / HODLing').

rootFamily.gloss: to endure through to the end (버티- + -어 + 내다)
prop, support, pillar of strength (버팀 + 목 木)

번.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and classifier 번 (番, Middle Chinese *phjwon*), meaning 'time, occurrence, turn; number in a series'.

history.meaning: turn, time, shift, number
time(s), turn; number

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번

번개.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'lightning, flash of lightning', descending from Middle Korean 번게 ('lightning', related to the flashing ideophonic root 번- as in 번쩍).

history.meaning: lightning
lightning, flash

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번개

번거롭다.etymology: Hybrid adjective meaning 'troublesome, complicated, cumbersome, tedious', formed from Sino-Korean 번거 (煩劇 / 煩據, centered on 煩 'vexing, complicated, irksome') plus the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -롭다.

history.meaning: complicated, vexatious, troublesome
cumbersome, troublesome, inconvenient

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번거롭다

번지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 번지 (番地), meaning 'lot number, street/house number in an address system', formed from 番 (번, 'number, order') + 地 (지, 'land, plot, site').

history.meaning: numbered plot of land
street number, lot number, address

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번지

번지다.etymology: Native Korean verb 번지다, denoting the outward diffusion, spreading, or bleeding of a substance across a surface or through a medium. It physically describes ink or watercolor bleeding into paper fibers, fire spreading through a forest, or oil spreading on water. Metaphorically, it beautifully captures a smile, a blush, or news spreading rapidly through a community.
번지다.notes: Can be both literal (잉크가 번지다 'ink smudges') and figurative (웃음이 번지다 'a smile spreads', 소문이 번지다 'a rumor spreads').

번지수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 番地數, uniting 番 (차례 번, 'turn, number in a series'), 地 (땅 지, 'land, lot'), and 數 (셀 수, 'number, count'). In the traditional land-lot (jibun) address system introduced to Korea in the early twentieth century, 番地 named the specific numbered plot of land. 번지수 refers to that numerical address. It also features in the idiom 번지수를 잘못 찾다 ('to find the wrong house number', meaning 'to bark up the wrong tree').
번지수.notes: Idiom: 번지수를 잘못 찾다 means 'to misunderstand the situation' or 'bark up the wrong tree'.

번째.etymology: Hybrid bound noun forming ordinal numbers ('-th time, -th in order'), combining Sino-Korean 번 (番, 'time, turn, order') with the native Korean ordinal suffix -째.

history.meaning: turn/order + ordinal suffix
-th (in order or sequence)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번째

번쩍이다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic (mimetic) verb formed from the dark-vowel mimetic root 번쩍 ('with a large, bold flash or sudden lift') plus the verbalizing suffix -이- (which converts ideophones into verbs of repeated or continuous action) and citation ending -다. Shows classic Korean vowel symbolism against bright-vowel 반짝이다 ('to twinkle daintily').

history.meaning: to emit a large, intense flash of light or glint repeatedly

번쩍이다.notes: Korean sound symbolism in action: 반짝이다 (bright vowel ㅏ) describes small, cute, twinkling lights (like stars), whereas 번쩍이다 (dark vowel ㅓ) describes larger, more intense flashes (like camera flashes, lightning, or fierce eyes).

rootFamily.gloss: with a sudden bright flash; lifting lightly (adverb)

번호.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 번호 (番號), meaning 'number (telephone number, room number, serial number, code)', formed from 番 (번, 'turn, sequence') + 號 (호, 'number, mark, designation').

history.meaning: identifying number in a sequence
number, code, serial number

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 번호

벌써.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'already, so soon', descending from Middle Korean 벌셔 ('already').

history.meaning: already, before expected
already, so soon

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벌써

벌이다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb derived from Middle Korean 벌다 (pel-ta, 'to spread out, line up, be arranged in a row') + morphological causative/transitive suffix -이- + -다. From the concrete sense 'to spread out or set up items in an array', it evolved to mean 'to stage an event, launch a business, or start a commotion'.

history.meaning: to be lined up / spread out -> to spread out or arrange things in a display
to set up, stage (an event, campaign, or show), or start (a business or argument)

벌이다.notes: Crucial spelling distinction for learners: 벌이다 means 'to stage/launch an activity' (사업을 벌이다, 행각을 벌이다, 전쟁을 벌이다), whereas 소리-similar 벌리다 means 'to widen a physical gap' (입을 벌리다, 'to open one's mouth wide'; 팔을 벌리다, 'to spread one's arms').

rootFamily.gloss: to happen, unfold, break out (벌어 + 지다, intransitive)
to widen a physical space or open wide (distinguished doublet)
display, spread, counter of clothes (noun derivative)

법.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun 법 (法, Middle Chinese *pjap*, Old Chinese *k.pˤap*). The ancient bronze character 灋 combined 氵 ('water', symbolizing a level surface of fairness), 廌 ('xiezhi', a mythical unicorn-like beast that butts the guilty in judicial trials), and 去 ('to cast out/remove'). Used for statutory law, Buddhist Dharma, method, and grammatical bound noun ('it is natural that...').

history.meaning: model of evenness and expelling guilt; statutory law, method, or Buddhist Dharma
law, legal code; method or way of doing something; bound noun for natural expectation (-는 법이다)

법.notes: Extremely versatile: standalone noun ('law', 법을 지키다), suffix meaning 'how to / method' (사용법, 'how to use'; 대화법, 'art of conversation'), and grammatical bound noun in -(으)ㄴ/는 법이다 ('it is the way of the world that...').

법대.etymology: Sino-Korean syllabic abbreviation 법대 (法大), clipped from 법과대학 (法科大學, 'College of Law'), combining the first syllable of 법과 (法科: 法 'law' + 科 'academic department/branch') and the first syllable of 대학 (大學: 大 'great' + 學 'learning/school').

history.meaning: university faculty or college of jurisprudence
law school, undergraduate college of law

morphemes.meaning: law, short for 법과 (法科, department of law)

법대.notes: Follows the productive Korean pattern of abbreviating university faculties as [Major] + 대 (e.g., 의대 'med school', 공대 'engineering school', 음대 'music school'). After Korea introduced graduate-level law schools in 2009, graduate programs are often called 로스쿨 (law school) or 법학전문대학원, while 법대 refers to the traditional undergraduate law major (like Baek Seung-chan's background).

rootFamily.gloss: medical school (醫大, short for 醫科大學)
engineering school (工大, short for 工科大學)

법률.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 법률 (法律), meaning 'law, statute, legislation', composed of 法 (법, 'law, rule, principle') + 律 (률, 'statute, regulation, code', pronounced [범뉼] by nasalization).

history.meaning: laws and statutes
law, statute, legislation

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 법률

법무법인.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character legal compound 법무법인 (法務法人), composed of 법무 (法務, 'legal affairs, judicial administration': 法 'law' + 務 'duty, affairs') and 법인 (法人, 'juridical person, incorporated entity', a Meiji-era calque of German *juristische Person*: 法 'law' + 人 'person'). Denotes an incorporated law firm under the Korean Attorney-at-Law Act.

history.meaning: legal affairs + juridical/corporate person
incorporated law firm, legal partnership corporation

법무법인.notes: In South Korea, official law firm names always begin with 법무법인 (e.g., 법무법인 태평양), whereas in everyday speech Koreans also frequently use the English loanword 로펌 (law firm).

법이에요.etymology: A syntactic construction combining the Sino-Korean bound noun 법 (法, 'law, rule, way, natural principle', which also translated Sanskrit dharma 'cosmic order, intrinsic nature' in Buddhist texts) with the polite informal conjugated form 이에요 of the native Korean copula 이다 ('to be', from Middle Korean 이라). Preceded by an adnominal verb or adjective clause in -(으)ㄴ/는, it expresses that an outcome or state is in accordance with natural law or how things inevitably work.

history.meaning: law, regulation, model, Buddhist dharma
it is the law or principle that...
it is natural that; it is bound to be (polite informal)

법이에요.notes: Almost always used in the grammatical pattern '-(으)ㄴ/는 법이에요' to state a general truth or life lesson ('that's just how things are').

법적.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound derived from 법적 (法的), composed of 법 (法, 'law, statute, jurisprudence') and the determinative suffix -적 (的, 'relating to, having the character of'). This formation was popularized during the late 19th and early 20th centuries across the Sinosphere (alongside Meiji Japanese 法的 hōteki) as a calque for European relational adjectives like English 'legal' or German 'rechtlich'.

history.meaning: law / statute + target / bright / possessive-relational marker
legal, pertaining to the law (Meiji-era legal neologism)
legal, juridical; legally (when used adverbially with -으로)

법적.notes: In Korean syntax, 법적 functions either as a pre-noun determiner (e.g., 법적 책임 'legal responsibility') or with the instrumental particle -으로 (법적으로 'legally').

벗기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to peel, strip off, unwrap, take off (another's clothes or a cover)', derived from 벗다 ('to take off, shed') plus the causative suffix -기- (Middle Korean 벗기다).

history.meaning: to strip off, undress, peel
to peel, strip, take off, uncover

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벗기다

벗다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to take off, remove (clothing, shoes, headgear, glasses); to shed or rid oneself of', descending directly from Middle Korean 벗다.

history.meaning: to take off, undress, shed
to take off, remove, shed

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벗다

벚꽃.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun formed from 벚 ('cherry tree', related to 버찌 'cherry fruit', attested in Early Modern and Middle Korean as 벋 or 버지) and 꽃 ('flower, blossom', from Middle Korean 곶, which underwent tensification of initial ㄱ to ㄲ and palatalization/affrication of final ㅈ/ㅊ).

history.meaning: wild cherry tree + flower / blossom
cherry blossom

벚꽃.notes: Pronounced [벋꼳] due to syllable-final neutralization of ㅈ and ㅊ to [t̚] and post-obstruent tensification of 꽃.

베개.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'pillow, headrest', derived from the verb stem 베- (베다, 'to rest one's head on', Middle Korean 볘다) plus the native instrument-forming suffix -개 ('implement for doing', Middle Korean 볘개).

history.meaning: pillow, headrest (from 볘다 'to pillow on' + -개)
pillow

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 베개

베란다.etymology: A loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English veranda (often mediated via Japanese ベランダ beranda), which entered English from Hindi varaṇḍā (वरण्डा) and Bengali bārāndā, themselves closely intertwined with Portuguese and Older Spanish varanda ('railing, balustrade, balcony', of uncertain Iberian or Vulgar Latin origin). In South Korean residential architecture, the term shifted to denote the enclosed utility balcony attached to apartment units.

history.meaning: railing, long open gallery or porch in Iberian and Anglo-Indian architecture
roofed platform along the outside of a house
apartment balcony, loggia, or veranda

베란다.notes: Architectural false friend: while architectural law distinguishes aベ란다 (stepped terrace between floors of different sizes) from a 발코니 (cantilevered extension), everyday Koreans call almost any apartment balcony a 베란다.

베이스.etymology: A loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English base, which comes via Old French base and Latin basis from Ancient Greek básis (βάσις, 'a stepping, pedestal, foundation'), a verbal noun from the root of baínō (βαίνω, 'to walk, step', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- 'to step, come'). In Korean, it spans multiple domains borrowed from English: the foundation or underlying layer (e.g., makeup, cocktails, or an ideological baseline), a baseball base, or (when rendering English bass) low-frequency sound and bass instruments.

history.meaning: footstep, pedestal, architectural base
foundation, headquarters, safe station in baseball/sports
base, foundation, baseline, baseball base; bass

베이스.notes: Korean spelling 베이스 merges both English 'base' (foundation, baseball base) and 'bass' (bass guitar, low voice), so context determines which English word is intended.

cognates.meaning: main staging area for mountaineering or expeditions

베이스캠프.etymology: A loanword (*외래어*) borrowed directly from the English compound noun base camp, combining base (from Latin basis < Ancient Greek básis 'pedestal, foundation') and camp (via French camp and Italian campo from Latin campus 'open field, level ground for military drills'). Originally a mountaineering and military term for a primary staging area and supply hub, it became ubiquitous in Korean reality-variety television (such as *1 Night 2 Days* and *The Producers*) for the cast and crew's lodging headquarters on location.

history.meaning: pedestal/foundation + open field for military exercises
main staging encampment for mountaineering or military operations
expedition base camp; variety show production lodging/headquarters

베이스캠프.notes: In Korean broadcasting jargon (especially outdoor reality shows like *1박 2일*), 베이스캠프 refers to the house or hotel where cast members gather for evening games and sleeping arrangements.

베프.etymology: A modern South Korean syllabic abbreviation (*줄임말*) coined in youth and internet slang by clipping the initial syllables of the English loanword phrase 베스트 프렌드 (beseuteu peurendeu, from English best friend, where best derives from Old English betst 'most good' and friend from Old English frēond 'friend, loved one'). It follows the productive Korean pattern of condensing four- or five-syllable loanword compounds into punchy two-syllable trochees.

history.meaning: one's closest and most trusted friend
best friend (unabbreviated loanword phrase)
bestie, BFF (clipped colloquial noun)

베프.notes: Equivalent in register and warmth to English 'bestie' or 'BFF'; another common native-Sino hybrid synonym in Korean slang is 절친 (절친한 친구, 'intimate friend').

rootFamily.gloss: boyfriend (clipped from 남자 친구, parallel slang pattern)

벤치.etymology: Borrowed from English bench, tracing back to Middle English benche and Old English benc (from Proto-Germanic *bankiz, cognate with bank). In modern Korean, 벤치 refers specifically to long, often outdoor seating found in parks, plazas, and courtyards, distinguishing itself from the generic chair 의자 or the traditional Korean wooden lounging platform 평상 (平床).

벨.etymology: Borrowed from English bell ('doorbell, buzzer, electric chime, or ringtone').

history.meaning: ringing signaling device
bell, doorbell, buzzer

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벨

벨벳.etymology: Borrowed from English velvet, which entered Middle English via Anglo-Norman/Old French velvet or veluotte, stemming from Medieval Latin velluetum and ultimately from Latin villus ('shaggy hair, tuft, nap'). In Korean, 벨벳 denotes the rich, tufted woven fabric, retaining its Western associations with elegance, stage curtains, and jewelry box linings. It stands alongside the Sino-Korean equivalent 우단 (羽緞).
벨벳.notes: Often modifies other nouns, as in 벨벳 커튼 ('velvet curtain') and 벨벳 상자 ('velvet box').

벽.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 벽 (壁, Middle Chinese *pek*), meaning 'wall, partition, barrier', deeply integrated into Korean since the Middle Korean period.

history.meaning: wall, partition
wall; figurative barrier

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벽

벽돌.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'brick', combining Sino-Korean 벽 (甓, 'brick, tile') with native Korean 돌 ('stone', Middle Korean 돌ㅎ) to reinforce the sense of a stone-like building block.

history.meaning: tile/brick + stone
brick

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 벽돌

벽지.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 벽지 (壁紙), formed from 벽 (壁, 'wall, partition, cliff', Middle Chinese pek) and 지 (紙, 'paper', Middle Chinese tsyeX). While paper has been used to line interior walls and floors in traditional Korean architecture (*한옥*) for centuries (see 도배 'papering walls'), 벽지 specifically designates decorative wall-covering paper.

history.meaning: partition wall + paper made from plant fibers
wallpaper, decorative wall covering

벽지.notes: Do not confuse with the homophonous Sino-Korean word 벽지 (僻地), which uses 僻 ('remote, secluded') and 地 ('land') to mean a 'remote, out-of-the-way area'.

cognates.meaning: Chinese surname Bian (卞 or 邊)

변.etymology: A Sino-Korean family name representing two distinct Hanja lineages: 변 (卞, Middle Chinese bjenH, originally denoting 'law, hurry' and an ancient state/county in魯 Lu, modern Shandong, China; main Korean clans are 초계 Chogye and 밀양 Miryang) and 변 (邊, Middle Chinese pen, meaning 'border, edge, margin, side'; main Korean clans are 원주 Wonju, 황주 Hwangju, and 장연 Jangyeon). Both lineages trace their Korean founding ancestors to Tang, Song, or Yuan dynasty figures who settled on the Korean peninsula during the Goryeo period.

history.meaning: ancient Shandong place name and surname / border, edge, frontier surname
Korean family name Byun / Byeon (established in Goryeo-era clan registries)

변.notes: When asking which 'Byun' someone is in Korea, people distinguish them as 초계 변씨 (卞, often explained as 'cap/hat 변') versus 원주 변씨 (邊, 'border/side 변' as in 주변).

cognates.meaning: to explain, clarify, defend oneself against an accusation

변명.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 변명 (辨明 or 辯明), composed of 변 (辨 'to distinguish, discriminate, tell apart' or 辯 'to argue, dispute, articulate', two historically cognate Chinese characters that merged in many compounds) and 명 (明, 'bright, clear, to make clear'). Originally denoting the act of clearly distinguishing right from wrong to vindicate oneself, its everyday Korean sense narrowed to 'making an excuse or self-justification'.

history.meaning: to distinguish or argue a case + to make clear or bright
vindication, explanation of one's position; excuse, pretext

변명.notes: Whereas 설명 (說明) is a neutral 'explanation', 변명 (辨明) carries the defensive nuance of making excuses for a mistake or fault.

변수.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound 변수 (變數), combining 변 (變, 'to change, alter, transform') and 수 (數, 'number, quantity, fate/destiny'). In pre-modern Chinese texts, 變數 referred to changing turns of fate or exceptional contingencies; in modern East Asia (alongside Japanese 変数 hensū), it was adopted to translate the Western mathematical and scientific concept of a 'variable' and subsequently re-entered everyday speech to mean an 'unpredictable factor or wildcard'.

history.meaning: change, mutation + number, calculation, turn of fate
mathematical variable (modern scientific translation)
mathematical/programming variable; unforeseen factor or wildcard in plans

변수.notes: Very common in Korean drama and news dialogue in the phrase 변수가 생기다 ('an unexpected variable/complication crops up').

변하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, to be', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다) to the Sino-Korean root 변 (變, 'change, alter, transform', Middle Chinese pjenH). Used primarily as an intransitive processive verb meaning 'to change, to become different, or to turn into'.

history.meaning: to change, alter, transform
to change, undergo transformation
to change, alter, spoil, become different

변하다.notes: 변하다 is usually intransitive ('something changes', e.g., 마음이 변하다 'one's heart/mind changes'), whereas 바꾸다 is the native transitive verb ('to change/replace something').

변호사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 변호사 (辯護士), meaning 'lawyer, attorney-at-law', formed from 변호 (辯護, 'pleading and defending in law') + professional suffix -사 (士, 'licensed specialist, scholar').

history.meaning: legal advocate and defender
lawyer, attorney

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 변호사

변화.etymology: A classical Sino-Korean coordinate compound 변화 (變化), pairing two near-synonymous roots: 변 (變, 'to change, alter, mutate', Middle Chinese pjenH) and 화 (化, 'to transform, convert, melt into, become', Middle Chinese xwaeH). Attested in foundational Classical Chinese texts such as the *Yijing* (Book of Changes) and *Zhuangzi* to describe the ceaseless flux and metamorphosis of nature.

history.meaning: cosmic flux, mutation and transformation of things (in Classical Chinese philosophy)
change, alteration, transition, variation

변화.notes: Often collocated with 주다 (변화를 주다 'to give a change / switch things up') or 겪다 (변화를 겪다 'to undergo change').

별.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'star, heavenly body', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 별 (with long/rising pitch [별:]). Also homophonous with the Sino-Korean determiner and prefix 별 (別, 'separate, special, extraordinary').

history.meaning: star
star; special/particular (別)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 별

별거.etymology: A colloquial phonological contraction of 별것, a hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound combining the Sino-Korean determiner/prefix 별 (別, 'separate, special, extraordinary, unusual', Middle Chinese bjet) with 거, the spoken truncated form of the native Korean bound noun 것 ('thing, object, affair', Middle Korean 것). Syllabic final -ㅅ [t̚] was dropped in casual speech, just as 이것/그것/저것 contract to 이거/그거/저거.

history.meaning: separate/special (Sino-Korean) + thing/matter (Middle Korean bound noun)
something special, a big deal (colloquial drop of final -ㅅ)

별거.notes: Most frequently used with negative predicates: 별거 아니야 ('It's no big deal / It's nothing special'). Note that homophonous 별거 (別居) is a separate Sino-Korean noun meaning 'marital separation / living apart'.

rootFamily.gloss: anything special, a big deal (uncontracted form)

별것.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun formed from the Sino-Korean determiner/prefix 별- (別, 'separate, distinct, special, out of the ordinary', Middle Chinese bjet) and the native Korean bound noun 것 ('thing, object, fact', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 것). Literally 'a distinct or extraordinary thing', it grammaticalized into a polarity-sensitive expression meaning 'anything major' or 'a big deal'.

history.meaning: to divide, separate, distinguish; other, special
an unusual thing, something of note or consequence

별것.notes: In affirmative or interrogative contexts (별것 다 보겠네 'Now I've seen everything / all sorts of weird things') it means 'all kinds of bizarre things', whereas with 아니다/없다 it means 'nothing much / no big deal'.

별로.etymology: Hybrid adverb meaning '(with negative predicates) not particularly, not very much', formed from Sino-Korean 별 (別, 'special, particular, separate') plus the native Korean instrumental particle -로 ('by way of, as').

history.meaning: specially, separately -> (with negation) not particularly
(not) particularly, (not) really

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 별로

morphemes.meaning: by way of, in terms of

별말씀.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound combining the Sino-Korean prefix/determiner 별- (別, 'special, unusual, out of the ordinary', Middle Chinese bjet) with the native Korean honorific noun 말씀 ('words, speech, remark', from Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ, derived from 말 'speech, language' + nominalizing suffix -ᄊᆞᆷ). Literally 'an extraordinary or undeserved remark'.

history.meaning: words, speech (originally neutral, later specialized as honorific/humble)
an extraordinary remark; polite formula 'don't mention it'

morphemes.meaning: words, speech (honorific native noun from 말 'speech')

별말씀.notes: Almost exclusively encountered in the set polite response 별말씀을요 ('Don't mention it! / Not at all! / You're too kind!'), literally '(You are making) an undeservedly special remark'.

별명.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 별명 (別名), composed of 별 (別, 'separate, other, secondary, special', Middle Chinese bjet) and 명 (名, 'name, appellation', Middle Chinese mjieng). Originally signifying an alternative name or alias distinct from one's formal given name (본명 本名), in modern Korean it serves as the standard everyday word for a 'nickname' or 'moniker'.

history.meaning: separate / secondary + name / title
alternative name, sobriquet, nickname

별명.notes: Often paired with 붙이다 ('to attach/give a nickname', 별명을 붙이다) or 짓다 ('to coin a nickname', 별명을 짓다).

rootFamily.gloss: real name, legal given name (本名)

별소리.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining the Sino-Korean prefix/determiner 별- (別, 'unusual, strange, all sorts of', Middle Chinese bjet) with the native Korean noun 소리 ('sound, voice, talk, remark', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 소리). Literally 'strange or outlandish talk', it developed the idiomatic senses of 'absurd remarks, complaints, fuss, or overly polite/unnecessary words'.

history.meaning: sound, voice, noise
outlandish talk, nonsense, unnecessary fuss or complaints

별소리.notes: Pronounced [별쏘리] with post-liquid tensification of ㅅ to ㅆ; frequently used in expressions like 별소리를 다 듣겠네 ('I'm hearing all kinds of ridiculous things') or casual 'don't mention it' (별소리를!).

별의별.etymology: An emphatic reduplicated determiner formed by linking two instances of the Sino-Korean determiner 별 (別, 'special, unusual, different, extraordinary', Middle Chinese bjet) with the native Korean genitive particle 의 ('of', Middle Korean ㆎ/의). Literally structured as a superlative genitive ('the unusual of the unusual', parallel to 왕 중의 왕 'king of kings'), it means 'all sorts of, every imaginable kind of'.

history.meaning: the extraordinary of the extraordinary; every conceivable kind of (emphatic reduplication)

별의별.notes: Can be further contracted in colloquial speech to 별별 ('all kinds of'). In standard Korean pronunciation, the genitive 의 here can be pronounced [의] or [에] ([벼릐별] or [벼레별]).

rootFamily.gloss: all sorts of (contracted reduplication, 別別)
anything major, all kinds of things (別것)

별점.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'star rating (for a restaurant, product, or film)', combining native Korean 별 ('star') with Sino-Korean 점 (點, 'point, score, mark'). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 별점 (星占, 'astrology, star divination').

history.meaning: star + score/point
star rating

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 별점

병.etymology: Sino-Korean noun representing two everyday homophones: (1) 병 (甁, Middle Chinese *beng*), meaning 'bottle, jar, vase'; and (2) 병 (病, Middle Chinese *bjaengH*, pronounced with a long vowel [병:]), meaning 'illness, disease, sickness'.

history.meaning: bottle, jar; disease, illness
bottle (甁); illness, disease (病)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 병

병실.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 병실 (病室), composed of 병 (病, 'illness, disease, sick person/patient', Middle Chinese bjaengH) and 실 (室, 'room, chamber, interior space', Middle Chinese syit). Originally denoting a room in a home or monastery where an ill person recuperated, in modern medical usage it refers specifically to an inpatient room or ward in a hospital.

history.meaning: illness / sick person + inner chamber / room
sickroom; inpatient hospital room or ward

병실.notes: Korean hospitals categorize 병실 by occupancy, such as 1인실 ('single-patient private room') vs. 다인실 ('multi-bed ward').

rootFamily.gloss: emergency room (應急室, sharing 室)

병원.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 병원 (病院), formed from 병 (病, 'illness, disease, ailment', Middle Chinese bjaengH) and 원 (院, 'walled courtyard, public institution, hall', Middle Chinese hjwänH). First attested in Tang-dynasty Buddhist charitable infirmaries (悲田養病坊/病院) and standardized across East Asia in the 19th century (via Meiji Japanese 病院 byōin and missionary medical institutions like Korea's 1885 제중원 濟衆院) for modern medical hospitals.

history.meaning: illness / disease + courtyard building / monastic infirmary
modern Western-style hospital or medical institution
hospital, medical clinic, doctor's office

병원.notes: In everyday Korean, 병원 covers everything from a small neighborhood doctor's office (technically 의원 醫院) to a massive university medical center (대학병원); Koreans say 병원에 가다 for 'going to see the doctor'.

rootFamily.gloss: hospitalization, being admitted (入院, sharing 院)
being discharged from the hospital (退院, sharing 院)

보고하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 보고 (報告, 'report, notification') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). The Sino-Korean root compounds 보 (報, 'to requite, reply, report, inform', Middle Chinese pawH) and 고 (告, 'to tell, announce, declare respectfully', Middle Chinese kawH).

history.meaning: to reply / requite / inform + to announce / declare to a superior
to report, give an account, brief a superior

보고하다.notes: Carries a vertical, organizational nuance: one typically 'reports' (보고하다) upward to a boss, senior producer, or institution.

rootFamily.gloss: press coverage, news report (報道, sharing 報)

보관하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 보관 (保管, 'keeping, storage, safekeeping') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to protect and manage in storage
to keep, store, hold in custody

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보관하다

보글보글.etymology: Reduplicated native Korean ideophone (의성어·의태어) imitating the sight and soft popping sound of small bubbles rising in a pot of soup or stew over gentle heat. Within Korean vowel harmony, the bright vowel ㅗ in 보글보글 depicts smaller, lighter, more cheerful bubbling than its heavy-vowel counterpart 부글부글 ('boiling furiously or seething').
보글보글.notes: Almost always modifies 끓다 ('to boil/simmer') or 익다 ('to cook').

보금자리.etymology: Native Korean compound historically referring to a bird's warm nest, formed with 자리 ('place, spot').
보금자리.notes: Used figuratively in modern Korean for a cosy home or welcoming workplace where one settles in.

보기.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) deverbal noun formed from 보-, the verb stem of 보다 ('to see, look at, watch', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 보다), plus the productive native nominalizing suffix -기 (Middle Korean -기). From its literal verbal-noun meaning 'the act of seeing or looking', it lexicalized both as 'outward appearance / how something looks' (especially with the dative/locative particle -에 as 보기에) and as 'an illustrative example or sample' on a test.

history.meaning: to see, look at + nominalizing suffix ('act of seeing')
looking, outward appearance (보기에 'from appearances'); sample, example

morphemes.meaning: to see, look at (stem of 보다)
nominalizer turning a verb into a noun or gerund

보기.notes: In conversation, 보기에 (or 보기에는 / 보기로는) means 'from the looks of it / outwardly' (e.g., 보기보다 'more than it looks'). On Korean exams, <보기> is the header for the 'Example / Reference Box'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be seen, be visible; to show (passive/causative)

보내다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to send, dispatch; to spend or pass (time); to let go', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 보내다.

history.meaning: to send, dispatch, cause to go
to send; to spend (time); to see off

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보내다

보내보다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) compound verb (main verb + exploratory auxiliary verb) composed of 보내- (stem of 보내다 'to send, dispatch; to spend time', from Middle Korean 보니다, originally causative of 보다/볻- or related to 보니-) joined via the absorbed infinitive suffix -어 to the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to try doing, to do and see how it goes', grammaticalized from the lexical verb 보다 'to see').

history.meaning: to send, dispatch + to see / to test by doing
to try sending, send as a trial; to try spending (time)

morphemes.meaning: to send, dispatch; to spend time (stem of 보내다, coalesced with -어)
to try doing, experience doing (auxiliary verb from 보다 'to see')

보내보다.notes: The auxiliary verb -아/어 보다 softens suggestions and adds an exploratory nuance ('let's try sending it and see what happens').

rootFamily.gloss: to send, dispatch; to spend time
to send for someone's benefit (보내다 + 주다)

보내주다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) benefactive compound verb formed from 보내- (stem of 보내다 'to send, dispatch, let go', from Middle Korean 보니다) linked via the coalesced infinitive ending -어 to the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to do for someone's benefit', grammaticalized from the lexical verb 주다 'to give', Middle Korean 주다).

history.meaning: to send, dispatch + to give (benefactive serial verb construction)
to send for someone, kindly send or let someone go

morphemes.meaning: to send, dispatch, let go (stem of 보내다, coalesced with -어)
to do for someone's benefit (auxiliary verb from 주다 'to give')

보내주다.notes: Depending on context, 보내주다 means either 'to send (a file, gift, message) to/for someone' or 'to let someone go / release them' (e.g., 날 좀 보내줘 'Please let me go home!'). When the recipient is of higher status, 주다 is replaced by 드리다 (보내드리다).

rootFamily.gloss: to send, dispatch; to spend time

보다.etymology: Core native Korean verb meaning 'to see, look at, watch, read; (as auxiliary -어 보다) to try doing', descending directly from Middle Korean 보다. Also used as a comparative particle and adverb meaning 'than; more' (grammaticalized from the verb 'to see/compare against').

history.meaning: to see, look at, try
to see, watch, look; (auxiliary) to try; than/more

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보다

보도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 보도 (步道), meaning 'sidewalk, pedestrian walkway, pavement', from 步 (보, 'walk, step') + 道 (도, 'road, way'); and (2) 보도 (報道), meaning 'news report, press coverage', from 報 (보, 'report, inform') + 道 (도, 'state, convey').

history.meaning: footpath; news reporting
sidewalk, pavement (步道); news report (報道)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보도

보도블록.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound merging Sino-Korean 보도 (步道, 'pedestrian walkway, sidewalk', from 步 'step, walk' + 道 'road, path') with the English loanword 블록 (block). It specifically names the interlocking concrete or stone pavers used on Korean sidewalks. Because the second element begins with heavily aspirated/fortis traits, it is written as a single compound 보도블록 (rather than hyphenated).
보도블록.notes: Often written as one word; colloquially refers to sidewalk pavers.

보람.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'sense of worth, rewarding fruit of one's effort; identifying mark or tag', descending from Middle Korean 보람 ('visible mark or sign attached to an item for later recognition', derived from 보다 'to see').

history.meaning: identifying mark, sign, token
worth, rewarding feeling, fruitful result

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보람

보람되다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) derived adjective combining the noun 보람 ('worth, rewarding result, sense of fulfillment; distinguishing mark or sign', attested in Early Modern Korean as 보람, likely derived from the verb 보다 'to see' + nominal suffix -암, originally meaning a visible mark or token placed on something to remember or identify it) with the adjective-forming suffix -되다 ('to be characterized by, to have the quality of'). From 'bearing a visible mark or proof of effort', 보람 evolved to mean 'fruitful worth or fulfillment'.

history.meaning: identifying mark, visible sign or token of an action (derived from 보다 'to see')
rewarding, worthwhile, fulfilling

morphemes.meaning: characterized by, having the quality of (adjectival suffix)

보람되다.notes: Often alternates with the native adjective 보람차다 ('full of fulfillment, rewarding') and the phrase 보람을 느끼다 ('to feel a sense of fulfillment/reward').

rootFamily.gloss: bookmark (책보람, preserving the older sense 'visible marker')

보리수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 보리수 (菩提樹), meaning 'bodhi tree, linden tree', combining 보리 (菩提, the traditional Sino-Korean Buddhist transcription of Sanskrit bodhi 'awakening, enlightenment', where 提 is read 리) + 수 (樹, 'tree').

history.meaning: tree of awakening/enlightenment
bodhi tree, linden tree

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보리수

보면대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 보면대 (譜面臺), meaning 'music stand, sheet-music rack', formed from 보면 (譜面, 'surface/page of a musical score') + 대 (臺, 'stand, platform, rack').

history.meaning: stand for holding musical scores
music stand

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보면대

보면서.etymology: An inflected form of the native Korean (*고유어*) verb 보다 ('to see, watch, look at', Middle Korean 보다), conjugated with the simultaneous conjunctive ending -면서 ('while doing, at the same time as'). The ending -면서 arose in Middle Korean as -며셔, combining the coordinate conjunctive suffix -며 ('and, while') with 셔 (the infinitive 시어 of the Middle Korean verb 시다 'to be, exist, stay').

history.meaning: seeing and being (there); while looking at
while watching, while looking at, as one sees

morphemes.meaning: to see, look at, watch (verb stem)

보면서.notes: In casual speech, -면서 is frequently shortened to -며 (보며), or used in the emphatic colloquial pattern -면서까지 ('even while doing X'). Note that both clauses linked by -면서 must share the same subject.

보물.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 寶物, joining 寶 (보배 보, 'treasure, jewel, precious thing') and 物 (만물 물, 'thing, object, matter'). Rooted deeply in classical East Asian vocabulary for hoarded wealth, jewels, or state regalia, it is the universal modern Korean word for both literal hidden treasure (like pirate gold) and metaphorical treasures like cherished family keepsakes, dear friends, or irreplaceable memories.
보물.notes: Figuratively applied to cherished people, pets, or mementos.

보물찾기.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the Sino-Korean noun 보물 (寶物, 'treasure') and the native Korean verbal noun 찾기 (from 찾다 'to search, seek, find' + nominalizer -기). It is the standard term for the classic children's game of hunting for hidden slips of paper or prizes, universally beloved in Korean school picnics (소풍) and easily extended to any playful search for clues.
보물찾기.notes: Always paired with the verb 하다 (보물찾기를 하다, 'to play a treasure hunt').

cognates.meaning: enlightened being, one whose essence is awakening

보살.etymology: A Sino-Korean Buddhist loanword 보살 (菩薩), clipped from the four-syllable Chinese phonetic transcription 보리살타 (菩提薩埵, Middle Chinese bju-dej-sat-twaX), which renders Sanskrit bodhisattva (बोधिसत्त्व)—a compound of bodhi ('awakening, enlightenment', from the root budh- 'to wake, know') and sattva ('being, essence, sentient creature'). In Korean, besides denoting a Mahayana Buddhist enlightened being or an elderly female Buddhist devotee/shaman, it is used figuratively for someone of saintly patience and compassion.

history.meaning: a being bound for enlightenment who delays nirvana to save others
bodhisattva (clipped phonetic transcription in Chinese Buddhist texts)
bodhisattva; female lay Buddhist; figuratively, a saintly or endlessly patient person

morphemes.meaning: clipped from 보리 (菩提, Sanskrit bodhi 'enlightenment')
clipped from 살타 (薩埵, Sanskrit sattva 'sentient being')

보살.notes: In everyday Korean conversation and TV dramas, calling someone a 보살 (or 살아있는 보살 'a living bodhisattva') is a humorous compliment meaning they have the patience of a saint for putting up with a difficult partner or boss.

cognates.meaning: security, preservation of public peace or safety
public security, security guard, ensuring safety

보안.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 보안 (保安), composed of 보 (保, 'to protect, preserve, guard, keep safe', Middle Chinese pawX) and 안 (安, 'peace, safety, tranquility, calm', Middle Chinese 'an). Literally 'preserving peace and safety', a classical Chinese administrative phrase that in modern Korean designates institutional confidentiality, physical security, and cybersecurity.

history.meaning: to protect / safeguard + peace / safety / stability
security, confidentiality, safeguarding of information or premises

보안.notes: While 안전 (安全) means 'safety' from accidents or physical harm, 보안 (保安) specifically means 'security' against leaks, unauthorized access, or espionage (e.g., 보안 유지 'maintaining confidentiality/security').

rootFamily.gloss: safety, security from harm (安全, sharing 安)

보안경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 保眼鏡, uniting 保 (보호할 보, 'to protect, safeguard, defend'), 眼 (눈 안, 'eye'), and 鏡 (거울 경, 'lens, mirror, glasses'). Just as 안경 (眼鏡) means 'eye-lens' (spectacles), 보안경 specifies eyewear designed to protect the eyes from dust, sparks, or bright light. It belongs to a modern technical and safety lexicon alongside 보청기 (hearing aid) and 보온병 (thermos).
보안경.notes: Takes the verb 쓰다 ('to wear [glasses, hats]') or 벗다 ('to take off').

보여주다.etymology: A native Korean (*고유어*) causative-benefactive compound verb formed from 보이- ('to show, make seen', the morphological causative of 보다 'to see' + causative suffix -이-, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 보이다), conjugated with the infinitive ending -어 (contracting 보이- + -어 to 보여-) and compounded with the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, to do for someone', Middle Korean 주다). Because simple 보이다 in Modern Korean functions primarily as a passive ('to be seen, look like'), 보여주다 took over as the standard active transitive verb meaning 'to show'.

history.meaning: to cause to see (causative of 보다) + to give (benefactive auxiliary)
to show, display, demonstrate to someone

morphemes.meaning: to see, look at (root verb stem)
causative suffix ('to make seen / show', coalesced with -어 as -여-)

보여주다.notes: In modern Korean, if you want to say 'Show me!' or 'I will show you', you must use 보여주다 (or honorific 보여드리다) rather than bare 보이다, which usually means 'to be visible' or 'to seem'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be visible, seem; to show (causative/passive stem)
to send for someone (parallel -어 주다 compound)

보이다.etymology: Native Korean passive and causative verb meaning 'to be seen, be visible, look/appear; to show, display', derived from 보다 ('to see') plus the suffix -이- (Middle Korean 보이다).

history.meaning: to be seen, appear; to show
to be visible, look; to show

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보이다

morphemes.meaning: to be seen / cause to see

보일러.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English boiler (agent/appliance noun from boil + -er, ultimately from Old French boillir and Latin bullīre 'to bubble, boil'). Adopted across Korea as modern hydronic heating replaced wood-fired underfloor flues.

history.meaning: vessel or unit for heating water and steam
household hot-water and underfloor heating boiler

보일러.notes: In South Korea, 보일러를 틀다 ('turn on the boiler') means turning on the room's underfloor 온돌 radiant heat as well as hot tap water.

보일러실.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'boiler room, heating plant room', combining the English loanword 보일러 (boiler) with Sino-Korean 실 (室, 'room').

history.meaning: boiler + room
boiler room

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보일러실

보존법.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 보존법 (保存法), meaning 'preservation law/act; method of preservation', formed from 보존 (保存, 'preservation, conservation') + 법 (法, 'law, statute, method').

history.meaning: law or method governing preservation
preservation act/law; conservation method

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보존법

보통.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 보통 (普通), meaning 'usually, normally; ordinary, average', composed of 普 (보, 'universal, widespread') + 通 (통, 'common, pass through').

history.meaning: widespread and common
usually, ordinarily; normal, average

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보통

보폭.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 步幅, combining 步 (걸음 보, 'step, pace, walking') and 幅 (너비 폭, 'width, span, breadth'). It precisely denotes the physical distance covered by one step. Used in athletics, physical therapy, and navigation, it pairs with adjectives like 넓다 ('wide/long stride') or 좁다 ('short stride') and specifies exact pacing for distances.
보폭.notes: Pairs with adjectives 넓다 ('wide/long') and 좁다 ('narrow/short'); compare 걸음 ('step, walking').

보호.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinative compound 保護, formed from 保 (보, bo, "to keep, preserve, nurture") and 護 (호, ho, "to guard, shelter, defend"). Both characters appear in Classical Chinese legal and administrative texts and were borrowed into Korean alongside shared Sinosphere vocabulary to denote active safeguarding from harm.

history.meaning: to guard, preserve, and shelter from harm
protection, safeguarding, care

보호.notes: Combines with 하다 to form the transitive verb 보호하다 ("to protect") and with 되다 for the passive 보호되다 ("to be protected").

보호받다.etymology: Hybrid compound passive verb meaning 'to be protected, receive protection', formed from Sino-Korean 보호 (保護, 'protection, care') + native Korean 받다 ('to receive').

history.meaning: protection + to receive
to be protected, receive protection

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 보호받다

보호해주다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verbal construction built from the Sino-Korean noun 보호 (保護, "protection"), the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do", conjugated in its infinitive/connective form 해), and the native benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 cwuta, "to give; to perform an action for someone's benefit").

history.meaning: to perform protection on someone's behalf
to protect someone (for their benefit)

morphemes.meaning: to give; to do for another's benefit

보호해주다.notes: Adding -아/어 주다 (here 해주다) highlights that the protection is an act of care, kindness, or duty directed toward the recipient; when the recipient is an elder or superior, 주다 is replaced by 드리다 (보호해드리다).

복도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 복도 (複道), meaning 'corridor, hallway, indoor passage', from 複 (복, 'double, covered') + 道 (도, 'way, passage, path').

history.meaning: covered passageway between rooms or buildings
corridor, hallway

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 복도

복불복.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character phrase 福不福, composed of 福 (복, bok, "good fortune, blessing") + 不 (불, bul, "not") + 福 (복, bok, "good fortune, blessing"), literally "good luck or bad luck". Originally referring to the uneven and unpredictable distribution of fate, it was popularized across South Korea by the KBS variety show 2 Days & 1 Night (1박 2일) as the signature name for chance-based penalty games (such as picking between identical-looking cups of coffee and salted canary fish sauce).

history.meaning: good fortune or lack of fortune; luck of the draw
