비교하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 비교 (比較, 비 'compare side by side' + 교 'measure against') + -하다.

비굴하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 비굴 (卑屈, 'servility, obsequiousness')—consisting of 비 (卑, 'low, base, humble') and 굴 (屈, 'to bend, bow, yield, submit')—combined with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix 하다 ('to be'). Literally 'bending low in a self-abasing manner'.

history.meaning: bowing low in a base, unprincipled, or submissive manner
to be servile, obsequious, groveling, or abjectly submissive

비굴하다.notes: Often used self-deprecatingly or humorously in Korean workplace dramas when employees flatter advertisers, executives, or top stars to get a project approved.

비뇨기.etymology: Sino-Korean medical compound 비뇨기 (泌尿器, 'urinary organs'), coined in Meiji-era Japanese anatomical terminology (泌尿器, hinyōki) and borrowed into Korean, composed of 비 (泌, 'to secrete, seep, flow'), 뇨 (尿, 'urine'), and 기 (器, 'vessel, instrument, bodily organ').

history.meaning: organs that secrete and excrete urine (kidneys, bladder, urethra)
urinary organs; urological system

비뇨기.notes: Note that 비 (泌) is read 비 in secretion terms (분비 分泌, 비뇨기 泌尿器) rather than 필, preserving its medical Sino-Korean reading.

비뇨기과.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비뇨기과 (泌尿器科, 'department of urology; urology clinic'), formed by adding the medical specialty suffix -과 (科, 'academic branch, department, medical division') to 비뇨기 (泌尿器, 'urinary organs': 泌 'secrete' + 尿 'urine' + 器 'organ').

history.meaning: medical specialty dealing with the urinary tract and male reproductive system
urology department or urology clinic

비뇨기과.notes: In 2017, South Korea's medical association officially renamed the specialty 비뇨의학과 (泌尿醫學科, 'Department of Urological Medicine') to reduce social stigma for female and general patients, though 비뇨기과 remains the everyday term.

비누.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'soap', descending from Middle Korean 비누 ('washing powder made from ground soybeans and herbs, later bar soap').

history.meaning: traditional bean-based washing cleanser; soap
soap

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비누

비눗물.etymology: Korean compound of 비누 ('soap', an early loanword via Portuguese sabão) + compound linker 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + native 물 ('water').
비눗물.notes: Pronounced [비눈물] as 사이시옷 triggers nasal insertion before ㅁ.

비다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to be empty, vacant, hollow, unoccupied', descending from Middle Korean 븨다 ('to be empty, void') via monophthongization (ㅢ > ㅣ after ㅂ).

history.meaning: to be empty, vacant
to be empty, vacant, free

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비다

비로소.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from the Middle Korean verb stem 비릇- (비릇다, 'to begin, start, originate', used vertically to translate Classical Chinese 始) plus the adverbial/instrumental suffix -오/-소, yielding Middle Korean 비르소 / 비르서 ('from the beginning; for the first time; only then').

history.meaning: to begin, originate, or take its start
for the first time; only after a condition is met (translating 始)
only then, at last, for the first time

morphemes.meaning: to begin, originate (from Middle Korean 비릇-)

비로소.notes: Shares its historical root with 비롯하다 ('to originate from, begin with') and 비롯한 ('including, headed by'); typically pairs with a preceding conditional or temporal clause ('Only after X happened did Y finally...').

rootFamily.gloss: to originate from, start with (from 비릇-)

비록.etymology: Native Korean concessive adverb attested directly in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as the Seokbo Sangjeol and Hunminjeongeum Eonhae) in the identical form 비록 ('even if, although, granting that'), used to gloss Classical Chinese concessive particles such as 雖 (수) and 縱 (종).

history.meaning: even if, although, supposing that (glossing Classical Chinese 雖)
even though, although, albeit

비록.notes: Strongly collocates with concessive verb endings later in the clause, such as -지만, -더라도, or -을지라도 (e.g., 비록 작지만 'although it is small...').

rootFamily.gloss: even if, granting that (Sino-Korean 設令)

비밀.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비밀 (秘密), meaning 'secret, mystery, confidentiality', composed of 秘 (비, 'secret, hidden') + 密 (밀, 'covert, close, confidential').

history.meaning: something kept hidden and confidential
secret

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비밀

비밀번호.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 비밀번호 (秘密番號, 'secret code number, password, PIN'), combining 비밀 (秘密, 'secret, confidentiality': 秘 'secret, hidden' + 密 'dense, covert, intimate') and 번호 (番號, 'number in a sequence, code': 番 'turn, watch, number' + 號 'mark, designation, number').

history.meaning: confidential matter + sequential identification number
numeric passcode (for bank accounts, digital door locks) or alphanumeric password

비밀번호.notes: In South Korea, where keyless digital keypad locks are standard on apartment doors, 비밀번호 (often shortened colloquially to 비번) refers equally to a home's front-door keypad code and an online account password.

비빔국수.etymology: Native Korean culinary compound formed from 비빔—the verbal noun (substantive in -ㅁ) of 비비다 ('to mix, rub, toss together ingredients with sauce')—and 국수 ('noodles', attested in Middle Korean as 국슈, likely an early borrowing from Middle Chinese 麴水 or a native formation). Literally 'mixed noodles'.

history.meaning: to rub/mix together + noodles
cold wheat or buckwheat noodles tossed in a spicy-sweet gochujang dressing

morphemes.meaning: nominalizer forming a verbal noun ('mixing, mixed')

비빔국수.notes: Parallel in formation to 비빔밥 ('mixed rice'); typically served chilled with gochujang, vinegar, sesame oil, julienned cucumber, and kimchi.

rootFamily.gloss: mixed rice with vegetables and sauce (비빔 + 밥)

비상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비상 (非常), meaning 'emergency, contingency; extraordinary', literally 'not ordinary', from 非 (비, 'not') + 常 (상, 'ordinary, constant'). Also homophonous with 비상 (飛翔, 'soaring, flight').

history.meaning: unusual, extraordinary -> state of emergency
emergency; extraordinary

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비상

cognates.word: 非常事態 / 非常事态 (fēicháng shìtài)

비상사태.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비상사태 (非常事態, 'state of emergency'), composed of 비상 (非常, 'extraordinary, unusual, emergency': 非 'not' + 常 'ordinary, constant') and 사태 (事態, 'state of affairs, situation, turn of events': 事 'matter, affair' + 態 'condition, posture, state').

history.meaning: extraordinary/unusual + state of affairs
state of emergency or acute crisis requiring urgent action

비상사태.notes: Used both for official national/public emergencies (비상사태 선포 'declaration of a state of emergency') and hyperbolically in workplaces or TV production rooms when a broadcast crisis hits.

비상상황.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 비상상황 (非常狀況, 'emergency situation'), combining 비상 (非常, 'emergency, extraordinary': 非 'not' + 常 'usual, constant') with 상황 (狀況, 'situation, circumstances, state': 狀 'form, condition' + 況 'circumstance, situation').

history.meaning: unusual/extraordinary + circumstances or condition
emergency situation or unexpected contingency

비상상황.notes: Slightly more operational and concrete than 비상사태: safety manuals and broadcast control rooms refer to handling a specific on-the-ground contingency as a 비상상황.

비상약.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비상약 (非常藥, 'emergency medicine, first-aid standby medication'), formed from 비상 (非常, 'emergency, extraordinary': 非 'not' + 常 'ordinary, routine') and 약 (藥, 'medicine, drug, remedy'). Literally 'medicine kept for extraordinary/unexpected occasions'.

history.meaning: extraordinary/unforeseen occasion + medicinal herb or remedy
emergency medication or household first-aid remedies kept on hand

비상약.notes: Pronounced [비상냑] in standard Korean due to ㄴ-insertion (ㄴ 첨가) before the ㅑ of 약 in a compound word after a consonant.

rootFamily.gloss: emergency stash of cash, slush fund (非常金)

비상용.etymology: Sino-Korean 비상 (非常, literally 'not ordinary' -> 'emergency') plus suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').
비상용.notes: Productive -용 (用) suffix also forms 가정용 ('household use') and 상업용 ('commercial use').

비속어.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비속어 (卑俗語, 'vulgar language, coarse slang, profanity'), composed of 비속 (卑俗, 'vulgar, base, coarse': 卑 'low, base' + 俗 'common, worldly, vulgar') and the linguistic suffix -어 (語, 'language, word, expression').

history.meaning: low and common/vulgar + words or speech
vulgar language, coarse slang, ordemeaning expressions

비속어.notes: A central term in Korean broadcasting regulation (방송심의): TV producers must bleep or edit out 비속어 ('vulgarisms/slang') and 욕설 ('explicit profanity') to avoid sanctions from the Korea Communications Standards Commission.

비스킷.etymology: Borrowed from English biscuit ('crisp, flat baked cookie or cracker'), ultimately from Old French bescuit ('twice-cooked bread').

history.meaning: crisp baked cookie or cracker
biscuit, cookie

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비스킷

비슷하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'similar, alike, resembling, close to', attested in Early Modern Korean as 비슷ᄒᆞ다 (from the root 비슷- + -하다).

history.meaning: similar, nearly alike
similar, alike, comparable

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비슷하다

비싸다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'expensive, costly', descending from Middle Korean 값싸다 / 빗싸다, originally a compound of 빚/값 ('price, value') + 싸다 (which in Middle Korean meant 'to be worth, have a high price'; when simplex 싸다 later shifted to 'cheap', the compound 비싸다 preserved the older sense 'high-priced, expensive').

history.meaning: high-priced, costly (from 빚 'price' + 싸다 'to be worth/costly')
expensive, costly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비싸다

비용.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 비용 (費用, 'cost, expense, expenditure'), derived from Classical Chinese 費用, a coordinate compound of 비 (費, 'to spend, expend, consume; expense', containing 貝 'cowrie shell / money') and 용 (用, 'to use, employ; outlay, expenditure').

history.meaning: to expend and use resources; financial outlay or expenditure
cost, expense, or financial outlay required for an activity

비용.notes: While 비용 is the standalone noun for 'cost/expense', its first morpheme 비 (費) functions productively as a suffix on specific expense types, such as 제작비 (製作費, 'production costs') or 식비 (食費, 'food expenses').

비우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to empty, clear out, drain, vacate', derived from 비다 ('to be empty', Middle Korean 븨다) plus the causative suffix -우- (Middle Korean 븨오다).

history.meaning: to make empty, clear out
to empty, vacate, drain

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비우다

비웃다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the pejorative/oblique prefix 비- ('awry, twisted, askance', related to 비틀다 'to twist' and 빗- 'sideways', attested in Middle Korean 비웆다) and the verb 웃다 ('to laugh, smile', from Middle Korean 웃다), literally meaning 'to laugh crookedly or askance at someone'—hence 'to sneer, mock, or deride'.

history.meaning: to laugh derisively or mockingly at someone
to sneer at, smirk at, ridicule, or scorn

비웃다.notes: Its nominalized form 비웃음 ('a sneer, derisive laughter') contrasts sharply with 웃음 ('laughter, a smile') and 미소 (微笑, 'a gentle smile').

rootFamily.gloss: to twist, wrench awry (sharing prefix 비-)

비워놓다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound composed of 비우다 ('to empty, vacate', the causative of 비다 'to be empty', from Middle Korean 뷔다 -> 뷔우다), the infinitive connective -어 (contracting with 우 to 워), and the auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put, leave in a resultant state'), meaning 'to empty or vacate beforehand and leave it that way'.

history.meaning: to make empty and leave in that state
to empty out, clear, or leave a space/schedule vacant in advance

morphemes.meaning: to be empty, vacant (from Middle Korean 뷔다)
auxiliary verb of resultant state ('to leave as is')

비워놓다.notes: Frequently used for clearing one's calendar or reserving a seat/room by keeping it empty (e.g., 시간을 비워놓다 'to keep one's schedule open').

rootFamily.gloss: empty, vacant, blank (adjectival form of 비다)

비워두다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 비우다 ('to empty, vacate', causative of 비다 'to be empty', Middle Korean 뷔다), the connective suffix -어 (forming 비워), and the auxiliary verb 두다 ('to put, keep, leave for future use or preservation', Middle Korean 두다), meaning 'to leave a place, seat, or schedule vacant/unattended'.

history.meaning: to empty or vacate and keep in that state
to leave vacant, keep open, or leave a post/seat unattended

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb of sustained state ('to keep, leave')

비워두다.notes: While 비워놓다 and 비워두다 are near-synonyms, -어 두다 places slightly stronger emphasis on intentionally preserving the vacant state over a longer period (e.g., 자리를 비워두다 'to keep a seat saved/vacant' or 'to leave one's desk unattended').

rootFamily.gloss: empty space, blank margin, room (빈 + 자리)

비워주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 비우다 ('to empty, vacate, clear out', causative of 비다 'to be empty'), the infinitive connective -어, and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's benefit', from Middle Korean 주다), meaning 'to vacate a room, home, or seat for someone else'.

history.meaning: to empty or vacate for another person
to vacate (a room, apartment, or seat) or step out to give others privacy

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary verb ('to give, do for someone')

비워주다.notes: Commonly used both in real-estate/housing contexts (집을 비워주다 'to vacate an apartment for the next occupant') and socially (자리를 비워주다 'to step out of the room so two people can talk privately').

cognates.meaning: spleen and stomach; digestive system (traditional medicine)

비위.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 비위 (脾胃), originally an East Asian traditional medical compound uniting 비 (脾, 'spleen') and 위 (胃, 'stomach'), the two core visceral organs governing digestion and appetite. In Korean, the sense evolved from 'digestive capacity / strong stomach' to 'palate, inclination, humor, or mood'.

history.meaning: the spleen and the stomach as the central organs of digestion and vitality
digestive stomach; ability to stomach unpleasant sights or foods
stomach for gross things; someone's mood, humor, or capricious favor

비위.notes: Appears in two high-frequency idioms reflecting both stages of its semantic history: 비위가 좋다/약하다 ('to have a strong/weak stomach for gross things') and 비위를 맞추다 ('to humor, flatter, or cater to someone's mood').

비율.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비율 (比率), meaning 'ratio, proportion, percentage, rate', formed from 比 (비, 'compare') + 率 (율/률, 'rate, proportion', written 율 after a vowel).

history.meaning: comparative rate or proportion
ratio, proportion, rate

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비율

cognates.meaning: pathetic and heroic; tragic, grim, resolute
solemn and stirring; tragic and heroic

비장하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 비장 (悲壯, 'solemn and heroic, tragically resolute')—a Classical Chinese compound of 비 (悲, 'sorrowful, sad, tragic, poignant') and 장 (壯, 'strong, grand, heroic, spirited')—combined with the native Korean adjective-forming light verb 하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: sorrowful yet heroic and stirring in spirit (originally describing martial poetry or music)
to be grimly resolute, solemn, heroic, or dramatically determined

비장하다.notes: Often used with humorous irony in modern Korean (e.g., 비장한 표정 'a grimly solemn expression') when someone treats a mundane task—like heading into a budget meeting or ordering late-night food—as if marching into battle.

비집다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from the bound prefixal element 비- (related to 비틀다 'to twist, wrench' and 빗- 'to slant, pry obliquely') combined with 집다 (Middle Korean 집다, 'to pinch, grasp, pick up'). Literally denoting the act of pinching or prying apart a tight seam, it evolved to mean forcing or wedging oneself into a narrow gap or crowded space.

history.meaning: to pinch, grasp, pick up with the fingers or tongs
to pry apart a narrow gap, wedge into a tight space

비집다.notes: Most frequently appears in the serial construction 비집고 들어가다 ('to wedge/squeeze one's way into a crowd or tight spot') or when tears/smiles force their way out (비집고 나오다).

비추다.etymology: Native Korean transitive/causative verb meaning 'to shine (a light) upon, illuminate, reflect in a mirror', descending from Middle Korean 비취다 / 비초다 (causative derivative built on 빛 'light').

history.meaning: to illuminate, cast light upon
to shine on, illuminate, reflect

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비추다

비치다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to shine, be reflected, show through translucently', descending from Middle Korean 비취다 ('to shine, gleam, be reflected', derived from 빛 'light').

history.meaning: to shine, be reflected, show through
to shine, be reflected, be seen through

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비치다

비켜보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) auxiliary verb construction combining 비키다 ('to step aside, clear the way', from Early Modern Korean 비끼다 and Middle Korean 빗기다, a derivative of 빗- 'to slant, move obliquely') with the infinitive connective -어 and the auxiliary verb 보다 (Middle Korean 보다, 'to see', used grammatically to mean 'to try doing').

history.meaning: to move obliquely aside + to see / try
to try stepping aside, to move out of the way for a moment

비켜보다.notes: Adding -어 보다 ('try doing') softens an abrupt command like 비켜! ('Move!') into a more tentative or polite request (잠깐만 비켜봐요, 'Try stepping aside for just a second').

rootFamily.gloss: to step aside, move out of the way
to step aside and stand clear

비키다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to step aside, move out of the way, yield passage', attested in Early Modern Korean as 비키다 (derived from the root 빗- 'oblique, sideways' + causative/verbal suffix -키-).

history.meaning: to step aside, clear the way
to step aside, move out of the way

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비키다

비타민.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed via Japanese ビタミン (bitamin) from German Vitamin, preserving the Continental European monophthongal pronunciation /bi/ rather than the English diphthong /vaɪ/. The term was coined in 1912 as vitamine by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk from Latin vita ('life') + English amine ('ammonia compound'), before the final -e was dropped once scientists realized not all vitamins contain nitrogenous amine groups.

history.meaning: life-essential amine micronutrient
vitamin; figuratively an energizing person or boost

비타민.notes: Because it entered Korean via German and Japanese medical terminology, it is pronounced bi-ta-min rather than bai-ta-min, and is often used figuratively in Korean pop culture to describe a cheerful person who energizes a group ('human vitamin').

비품실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 비품실 (備品室), meaning 'supply room, equipment storage room', formed from 비품 (備品, 'furnishings, fixtures, supplies') + 실 (室, 'room').

history.meaning: room for storing fixtures and supplies
supply room, equipment room

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 비품실

비행기.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 飛行機, adopted in the early 20th century from Meiji-era Japanese 飛行機 (hikōki), which was coined to translate English 'flying machine' or 'aeroplane'. Composed of 飛 (비, 'to fly'), 行 (행, 'to go, travel, move'), and 機 (기, 'machine, mechanism', originally denoting a complex wooden loom).

history.meaning: powered flying machine, aeroplane
airplane, aircraft

비행기.notes: Appears in the popular Korean idiom 비행기를 태우다 ('to put someone on an airplane'), which means to flatter someone excessively until they feel like they are floating high in the sky.

비호감.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) derivative 非好感, formed by attaching the negative prefix 非 (비, 'non-, un-, not') to the Sino-Korean noun 好感 (호감, 'favorable impression, fondness', from 好 호 'good, fond' + 感 감 'feeling, sensation'). Popularized in 2000s South Korean variety shows and internet discourse to denote both an unpleasant impression and a person who provokes public antipathy.

history.meaning: favorable feeling, good impression
unlikability; an unlikable or off-putting person/character

비호감.notes: In Korean media and variety television, 호감 ('likable') and 비호감 ('unlikable/off-putting') function as a core binary for describing a celebrity's public image or a persona's reception by viewers.

cognates.meaning: large spectacle; ring name of wrestler Paul Wight

빅쇼.etymology: Loanword (외래어) transliterating English Big Show (from Middle English big 'large, mighty' + Old English scēawian 'to look at, display'). In Korean television and pop-culture dialogue, it refers either to a grand special broadcast or to the ring name of American professional wrestler Paul Wight ('The Big Show'), whose entrance music and giant stature became a widely recognized meme in South Korea.

history.meaning: major spectacle; ring persona of giant American wrestler Paul Wight
grand show; The Big Show (wrestler reference in Korean pop culture)

빅쇼.notes: In *The Producers* (*프로듀사*), this appears as a comedic pop-culture reference to WWE wrestler Big Show's famous entrance theme ('Weeeeell, it's the Big Show!').

빈말.etymology: Native Korean compound uniting 빈 ('empty, hollow', the adnominal form of the verb 비다) and 말 ('words, speech, language', Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ/말). It captures the social phenomenon of saying things one does not entirely mean—either polite lip service, courteous flattery, or an empty promise. It is frequently used in the defensive phrase 빈말이 아니다 ('I really mean it; it is not just lip service').
빈말.notes: Commonly used in 빈말을 하다 ('to say empty words') or 빈말이 아니다 ('to not be just flattery / to mean it sincerely').

빈속.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun formed from 빈 (the adnominal stative/past modifier of 비다, Middle Korean 비다 'to be empty, vacant, hollow') + 속 (Middle Korean 솏, 'interior, inside'). By regular anatomical metonymy in Korean, 속 ('inside') refers specifically to the stomach and digestive tract, yielding the literal sense 'an empty stomach'.

history.meaning: empty + interior / inside
an empty stomach (before eating a meal)

빈속.notes: Commonly used with the locative particle 에 as 빈속에 ('on an empty stomach'), especially when warning against drinking alcohol or taking harsh medication without food (cf. Sino-Korean 공복 空腹 in medical contexts).

rootFamily.gloss: to have heartburn / an aching stomach

빌다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem verb descending from Middle Korean 빌다 with two principal senses: (1) 'to pray, wish for, beg, apologize'; and (2) 'to borrow, rent' (the base verb from which 빌리다 is derived).

history.meaning: to pray, beg, wish; to borrow
to pray, wish, beg for forgiveness; to borrow

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빌다

빌려드리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) humble benefactive compound verb combining 빌리다 ('to lend, to borrow', derived from Middle Korean 빌다 + suffix -리-) via the infinitive connective -어 with 드리다 ('to humbly give or do for a respected person'). The auxiliary 드리다 derives from Middle Korean 드리다, the causative of 들다 ('to enter'), originally meaning 'to cause to enter into the presence of a superior, to present/offer'.

history.meaning: to lend/borrow + to cause to enter / present to a superior
to humbly lend something to a respected person or listener

morphemes.meaning: humbly give / do for a superior

빌려드리다.notes: While standalone 빌리다 usually means 'to borrow', attaching the benefactive auxiliary 주다 (빌려주다) or its humble counterpart 드리다 (빌려드리다) unambiguously shifts the direction of transfer to 'to lend'.

빌려주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to lend, loan', formed from 빌리다 ('to borrow/lend', stem 빌려-) plus the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give').

history.meaning: to lend to someone
to lend, loan

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빌려주다

빌리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb originating from Middle Korean 빌다 ('to borrow; to beg, pray') extended with the historical causative suffix -리- (빌리다). In Middle Korean, 빌다 meant 'to borrow' while the causative 빌리다 meant 'to lend' ('cause to borrow'); in Modern Korean, 빌리다 expanded to become the standard verb for 'to borrow' (and 'to lend'), leaving 빌다 specialized mostly as 'to pray, beg for forgiveness'.

history.meaning: to borrow (빌다) / to lend, cause to borrow (빌리다)
to borrow; to lend (especially in 빌려주다)

빌리다.notes: A classic case of semantic shift: because Korean speakers increasingly used 빌리다 for both sides of a loan transaction, context (such as 돈을 빌리다 'borrow money from X' vs. 돈을 빌려주다 'lend money to Y') now disambiguates the direction.

빗물.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'rainwater', formed from 비 ('rain') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 물 ('water', Middle Korean 빗믈).

history.meaning: rainwater
rainwater

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빗물

빗방울.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 비 ('rain') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 방울 ('drop, bead').
빗방울.notes: Shares 비 + 사이시옷 with 빗물 ('rainwater') and 빗소리 ('sound of rain').

빗소리.etymology: Native Korean compound from 비 ('rain') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 소리 ('sound').
빗소리.notes: The linking ㅅ tenses the following consonant in speech: [빋쏘리].

빗속.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'in the rain, the midst of falling rain', formed from 비 ('rain') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 속 ('inside, midst').

history.meaning: rain + midst/inside
in the rain, midst of the rain

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빗속

빙글.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb. Characterized by the high, closed vowel ㅣ, 빙글 depicts a small, tight, smooth single rotation or a quiet, knowing smile. It contrasts with its broader, heavier counterparts like 뱅글 (wider turn) or 빙그르르 (continuous rolling spin). When reduplicated into 빙글빙글, it means spinning continuously in circles or wearing a lingering smile.
빙글.notes: Combines with 돌다 ('to spin, turn') or 웃다 ('to smile').

빙글빙글.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb formed by doubling 빙글. While a single 빙글 represents one smooth rotation or a quick smile, the doubled 빙글빙글 signifies continuous, effortless circular motion—like a dizzying spin, a spinning top, or a lingering, sly, or cheerful smile that refuses to fade. The repetition intensifies the duration and looping nature of the action.
빙글빙글.notes: Often paired with 돌다 ('spin around') and 웃다 ('smile lingeringly').

빙빙.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated mimetic adverb (의태어) formed by doubling the sound-symbolic root 빙, which depicts smooth, continuous circular rotation or hovering around a point. Within Korean vowel-harmony sound symbolism, the high/dark vowel in 빙빙 evokes wider, heavier, or more dizzying circles than its bright-vowel counterpart 뱅뱅 (tighter, smaller, faster spinning).

history.meaning: revolving or circling smoothly and continuously

빙빙.notes: Frequently pairs with 돌다 ('to turn/spin'): 머리가 빙빙 돌다 means 'one's head is spinning (from dizziness or confusion)', while 말을 빙빙 돌리다 means 'to beat around the bush'.

rootFamily.gloss: round and round (in smaller, tighter circles)

빚.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) monosyllabic noun inherited from Middle Korean 빋 (romanized pit, where final -ㄷ in 15th-century *8-jongseong* syllable-final spelling represented an underlying affricate /t͡ɕ/ that surfaced before vowel-initial particles, as in 비즐 'debt [acc.]'). Related to the archaic root 빋 ('price, value'), it specialized from counter-value owed in exchange into monetary or moral debt.

history.meaning: price, counter-value; debt owed to another
financial debt, loan obligation, moral indebtedness

빚.notes: Be careful not to confuse the pronunciation and spelling of 빚 ('debt', final ㅈ), 빗 ('comb', final ㅅ), and 빛 ('light', final ㅊ)—all three neutralize to [빋] in isolation, making them a classic Korean phonology minimal triplet when followed by a vowel particle (-이/-을).

rootFamily.gloss: to incur a debt, owe money or a favor

빛.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'light, ray, beam; color, hue, lustre', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 빛.

history.meaning: light, radiance, color
light, gleam, hue

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빛

빛나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to shine, gleam, sparkle, be radiant', formed from 빛 ('light, lustre') + 나다 ('to come forth, arise', Middle Korean 빛나다).

history.meaning: to emit light, shine
to shine, sparkle, be brilliant

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빛나다

빛바래다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining 빛 ('light, color, hue', Middle Korean 빛) and 바래다 ('to fade, lose color, bleach from sun and air'). While 바래다 alone carries the meaning of colors washing out or textiles being sun-bleached, adding 빛 explicitly targets the loss of original vibrancy or luster. Its past adnominal form 빛바랜 ('faded, time-worn') is an evocative, nostalgic adjective for old photographs, ink, and memories.
빛바래다.notes: The past adnominal 빛바랜 ('faded, weathered') is extremely common for old documents and memories.

빠르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular adjective meaning 'fast, quick, swift, early', descending from Middle Korean ᄈᆞᄅᆞ다 ('fast, rapid').

history.meaning: fast, swift, rapid
fast, quick, early

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빠르다

빠져나가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) multi-verb compound built from 빠지다 ('to fall out, drop out, drain away', evolving from Middle Korean 바디다 via initial fortition ㅂ > ㅃ and palatalization 디 > 지) + the infinitive connective -어 + the directional compound 나가다 (나다 'to move out, exit' + 가다 'to go away'). Literally 'to drop out and go away', it describes water draining, people slipping out of a gathering, or money being automatically deducted from an account.

history.meaning: to fall/drop out + to go out and away
to slip out, escape; to drain out or be deducted (of funds)

빠져나가다.notes: In personal finance and everyday conversation, 통장에서 돈이 빠져나가다 is the natural idiomatic way to say that bills, taxes, or automatic payments 'are deducted / drained from one's bank account'.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall into; to drop out or be omitted
to escape, come out from a trap or crowd

빠져들다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 빠지다 ('to fall into, sink into', from Middle Korean 바디다 'to fall in, submerge' via initial reinforcement ㅂ > ㅃ and palatalization 디 > 지) + the infinitive connective -어 + 들다 (Middle Korean 들다, 'to enter, go inward'). Literally 'to fall in and enter deeply', it evolved from physical sinking into mud or water to psychological immersion, fascination, or infatuation.

history.meaning: to fall into / sink + to enter inward
to sink deeply into; to become absorbed, immersed, or captivated by

빠져들다.notes: Whereas 빠지다 denotes the state or moment of falling in (사랑에 빠지다 'fall in love'), adding -어 들다 (빠져들다) highlights the gradual, irresistible process of being drawn deeper and deeper into someone's charm, a story, or a habit.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall into, be absorbed in

빠지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to fall into (water, a pit, or a state); to fall out, be omitted/missing; to be absorbed in; to drain out', descending from Middle Korean ᄢᅡ디다 ('to fall into, sink, drop out').

history.meaning: to fall into, drop out
to fall into; to fall out, be left out; to be absorbed in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빠지다

빠짐없이.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb formed from 빠짐 (the substantive -ㅁ nominalization of 빠지다 'to fall out, be omitted, be left out') and 없이 ('without', adverbial form of 없다). Literally meaning 'without any omission', it often pairs with 한 글자도 ('not even one letter') or 하나도 ('not even one') to emphasize complete, attentive coverage.
빠짐없이.notes: Frequently reinforced by 하나도 or 한 글자도 (한 글자도 빠짐없이).

빡세다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) colloquial compound adjective combining the fortis intensifying root 빡- (evoking tight, packed, unyielding pressure, related to 빡빡하다 'to be tight, cramped') with the adjective 세다 (Middle Korean 세다, 'to be strong, intense, fierce'). Originating in Gyeongsang dialect (빡시다 / 빡세다) and military/student vernacular, it entered nationwide colloquial Korean to describe grueling workloads, tough schedules, or demanding bosses.

history.meaning: to be strong, forceful, intense
to be grueling, tough, intense, demanding (of work or training)

빡세다.notes: Extremely common in everyday workplace and school conversation (오늘 일정 진짜 빡세다, 'Today's schedule is really brutal/grueling'), though best avoided in formal writing where 고되다 ('arduous') or 힘들다 ('hard') is preferred.

rootFamily.gloss: to be tight, closely packed, strict (of a schedule)

빤하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the fortis sound-symbolic root 빤- (depicting bright, unobstructed visibility through a gap or across an open space, alternating in vowel harmony with dark-vowel 뻔-) + the adjective-forming suffix -하다. From its original visual sense of 'brightly lit and clearly visible from end to end', it developed the figurative meaning 'transparently obvious, completely predictable'.

history.meaning: to be brightly lit, unobstructedly clear to the eye
to be obvious, transparent, completely predictable (of an outcome or excuse)

빤하다.notes: 빤하다 (bright vowel ㅏ) and 뻔하다 (dark vowel ㅓ) are both standard words meaning 'obvious/predictable'; 빤하다 often retains a slightly sharper nuance of seeing right through a lie or watching something happen in plain sight (cf. 빤히 쳐다보다 'to stare straight at').

rootFamily.gloss: staringly, clearly, knowingly in plain sight
to be bright, well-lit, well-versed in

빤히.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'staringly, fixedly; obviously, clearly', derived from the light-vowel adjective 빤하다 ('bright, obvious, staring', glottalized counterpart of 반하다/번하다) + adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: clearly, with a fixed gaze
staringly, fixedly; obviously

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빤히

빨간색.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'red color, bright red', combining the adnominal form 빨간 of the native Korean color adjective 빨갛다 ('bright red') with Sino-Korean 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: vivid red + color
red, red color

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빨간색

빨갛다.etymology: Native Korean ㅎ-irregular color adjective meaning 'bright red, vivid crimson', formed as the light-vowel, glottalized intensive counterpart of 발갛다 and 붉다 ('red', Middle Korean 븕다).

history.meaning: red -> bright red -> vivid crimson
bright red, deep red

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빨갛다

빨래.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) deverbal noun derived from the verb stem 빨- (from 빨다 'to wash clothes by rubbing and beating', attested in Middle Korean as 발다 before undergoing initial fortition ㅂ > ㅃ) + the archaic nominalizing suffix -애/-래 (seen also in 노래 'song' from 놀다 'to play'). Attested in Early Modern Korean texts as 발래 and 빨래, denoting both the act of washing textiles and the laundry items themselves.

history.meaning: to wash clothes > washing clothes, laundry
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (15th–18th c.)

history.meaning: laundry (both the chore of washing clothes and the clothes being washed)

빨래.notes: Spellings like 빨래 ('laundry', with ㅐ) and 걸레 ('rag/mop cloth', with ㅔ) are a classic orthographic contrast in Korean; 빨래 directly reflects the bright vowel ㅏ of its source verb 빨다 ('to wash').

rootFamily.gloss: traditional communal washing spot by a stream
pile of clothes to be laundered

빨리.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'quickly, fast, Hurry, soon', derived from the adjective stem 빠르- (빠르다, 'fast', Middle Korean ᄈᆞᄅᆞ다) plus the adverbial suffix -이 (Middle Korean ᄈᆞᆯ리).

history.meaning: quickly, swiftly
quickly, fast, soon

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빨리

빨리빨리.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated adverb formed by doubling 빨리 ('quickly, fast'), which is the regular -이 adverbial derivative of the 르-irregular adjective 빠르다 ('to be fast, swift', from Middle Korean 바르다 / 빠르다: stem 바르- + adverbial -이 > Middle Korean 발리 > Modern 빨리). Full reduplication intensifies the sense of urgency ('quickly, right away!') and gave rise to the sociological expression 빨리빨리 문화 ('hurry-hurry culture').

history.meaning: swiftly, rapidly
quickly, right away, chop-chop (urgent reduplication)

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated adverbial intensifier: right away, hurry up

빨리빨리.notes: Often cited as the single most recognizable phrase to visitors in South Korea, encapsulating the high-speed efficiency and impatience of modern Korean daily life and broadcasting production.

빵.etymology: Borrowed via Japanese パン (pan) from 16th-century Portuguese pão ('bread'), ultimately from Latin pānis.
빵.notes: One of the earliest European-root loanwords in Korean, spelled with tense ㅃ to reflect the unaspirated Romance p.

빵빵.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated onomatopoeic and mimetic adverb (의성어·의태어) formed by doubling the fortis root 빵, which imitates the loud pop of a bursting balloon, gunshot, or car horn, and visually depicts something swelling tautly to the point of bursting. In Korean television and variety-show slang, 빵빵 터지다 ('to burst pop-pop') evolved to mean 'to get explosive laughs or score big hits repeatedly'.

history.meaning: with repeated popping, honking, or bursting sounds; tautly swollen
explosively, big (of laughter, jokes, or ratings blowing up)

morphemes.meaning: ideophone of a loud pop, bang, or taut swelling
reduplicated ideophone for repeated bursting or fullness

빵빵.notes: In *The Producers* and Korean variety TV, PD and writer characters constantly hope a segment will 빵빵 터지다—literally 'burst bang-bang', meaning the audience will roar with continuous laughter.

빵빵빵빵.etymology: Quadruplicated colloquial numeral compound repeating 빵 ('zero, 0') four times to read out the four-digit sequence '0000' (such as a door-lock PIN or phone code). The colloquial numeral 빵 ('zero') arose in 20th-century Korean student and military slang from the round, hollow shape of a bread roll or bun (빵 'bread', borrowed via Japanese パン pan from Portuguese pão < Latin panis), reinforced by the onomatopoeic sense of 빵 ('pop! nothing left').

history.form: 빵 (from Portuguese pão via Japanese pan)
history.meaning: bread, bun; by visual metaphor, the round digit zero (0)
four zeros (0000), especially when reading out a passcode or score

빵빵빵빵.notes: When reading phone numbers, passcodes, or scores aloud in casual Korean, speakers frequently substitute 공 (空, 'empty/zero') or 영 (零, 'zero') with 빵 for rhythmic emphasis—hence 0000 becomes 빵빵빵빵.

rootFamily.gloss: zero points on a test or game (0點)

빵빵하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adjective derived from the reduplicated mimetic root 빵빵 ('swollen tautly, filled to bursting like an inflated tire or stuffed pouch') + the adjective-deriving suffix -하다. In late 20th- and 21st-century colloquial Korean, the physical sense of being tightly packed underwent metaphorical extension to mean 'richly funded, backed by powerful connections, having a stacked cast/lineup, or boasting booming sound'.

history.meaning: to be tautly inflated, stuffed full to bursting
to be financially well-off, powerfully backed, or impressively stacked (of a lineup or specs)

빵빵하다.notes: Versatile colloquial praise: 출연진이 빵빵하다 means 'the cast/lineup is stacked with stars', 집안이 빵빵하다 means 'their family is loaded/well-connected', and 사운드가 빵빵하다 means 'the audio system is booming'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be taut, tightly stretched, neck-and-neck

빵집.etymology: Everyday Korean compound noun joining 빵 (ppang, 'bread, pastry'—borrowed at the turn of the 20th century via Japanese pan パン from 16th-century Portuguese pão) with the native Korean noun 집 (jip, Middle Korean 집 cip, 'house, home, specialty shop'). In Korean word formation, attaching -집 to a food or craft noun productively names a neighborhood shop (빵집 'bakery', 꽃집 'flower shop', 찻집 'teahouse'). Because 빵 ends in the velar nasal ㅇ across a compound boundary, 집 is pronounced with a tense affricate [빵찝] (ppangjjip).

history.meaning: bread, baked pastry
neighborhood bakery, bread shop

빵집.notes: More conversational and affectionate than the formal Sino-Korean 제과점 (製菓店, 'confectionery/bakery').

빵표.etymology: Hybrid compound noun (혼종어) combining the colloquial Korean numeral slang 빵 ('zero, naught', derived from the round shape of 빵 'bread/bun' < Japanese パン pan < Portuguese pão and mimetic 빵 'pop/blank') with the Sino-Korean counter/noun 票 (표, 'vote, ballot, ticket'). Formed by direct analogy with 빵점 (0점, 'zero points') to mean receiving zero votes in a poll or election.

history.meaning: zero votes received in a ballot
zero votes! (colloquial/emphatic hybrid compound)

빵표.notes: Saying 빵표 ('zero votes!') instead of formal 영표 (零票) or 득표수 0 ('vote count zero') adds humorous humiliation in variety-show popularity polls and team-picking games.

rootFamily.gloss: zero points, a score of zero (0點)

빼가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial verb compound formed from 빼다 ('to pull out, extract, remove', contracted from 빼이다, the causative of Middle Korean 빠다 / 빼다 'to be pulled out, come out') + the coalesced infinitive connective -어 + the directional verb 가다 (Middle Korean 가다, 'to go away'). Literally 'to extract and take away', it developed the specialized industry meaning 'to poach or lure away talent, clients, or staff from another group'.

history.meaning: to pull out / extract + to go away
to take out and carry away; to poach or lure away (talent, staff, or resources)

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective (coalesced with stem vowel 애)
go away, take away from speaker's domain

빼가다.notes: In Korean broadcasting and corporate settings, 사람을 빼가다 is the go-to expression for when a rival show, agency, or company poaches a star writer, PD, or celebrity.

rootFamily.gloss: to extract, lure out, smuggle out
to siphon off, pilfer, divert secretly

빼놓다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 빼다 ('to pull out, extract, exclude', from the causative of Middle Korean 빠다) + the coalesced connective -어 + the auxiliary verb 놓다 (Middle Korean 놓다, 'to put down, leave in a resulting state'). Literally 'to pull out and leave aside', it means either to leave something out of a group/list or, in idioms like 넋을 빼놓다 ('to pull out and leave someone's soul'), to leave someone spellbound.

history.meaning: to pull out / exclude + to set down / leave in a state
to leave out, exclude; (with 넋/혼) to mesmerize, take one's breath away

morphemes.meaning: put, leave in a resulting state (auxiliary)

빼놓다.notes: Appears in two high-frequency expressions with very different meanings: 빼놓을 수 없다 ('cannot be left out / is essential') and 넋을 빼놓다 ('to captivate completely / take someone's breath away').

rootFamily.gloss: to put down, let go, leave in a state

빼다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to pull out, extract, remove, subtract, leave out', descending from Middle Korean ᄲᅢ다 (causative counterpart of ᄢᅡ디다 > 빠지다 'to fall out').

history.meaning: to pull out, draw out, extract
to pull out, remove, subtract, exclude

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 빼다

빼돌리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 빼다 ('to pull out, extract') + 돌리다 ('to turn, divert, circulate', the historical causative of Middle Korean 돌다 'to turn, rotate'). Literally 'to pull out from its rightful place and divert elsewhere', it developed the specialized meaning of surreptitiously pilfering, embezzling, or siphoning off goods, funds, or information.

history.meaning: to extract + to turn/divert in another direction
to pilfer, siphon off, embezzle, or spirit away secretly

빼돌리다.notes: Unlike simple 훔치다 ('to steal'), 빼돌리다 specifically implies an insider quietly diverting company supplies, funds, secrets, or someone's attention to the side.

rootFamily.gloss: to extract, smuggle out, lure out

빼먹다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 빼다 ('to pull out, extract, omit') + the coalesced connective -어 + 먹다 (Middle Korean 먹다, 'to eat, consume'). Functioning both literally ('to extract and consume') and with 먹다 as a colloquial completive/pejorative auxiliary, it splits into two main senses: (1) to omit or skip a task, meal, or word, and (2) in idioms like 단물을 다 빼먹다, to squeeze someone dry of all their value or sweet juice.

history.meaning: to pull out / omit + to eat / consume completely
to skip or omit carelessly; to bleed/squeeze dry for one's own gain

morphemes.meaning: eat, consume; colloquial pejorative completive auxiliary

빼먹다.notes: Context determines which sense is active: 글자를 빼먹다 means 'to accidentally leave out a letter', whereas 단물을 빼먹다 ('to suck out all the sweet water') means 'to exploit someone until they have nothing left to give'.

rootFamily.gloss: to forget (colloquial); to peel and eat

빼어나다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adjective formed from 빼다 ('to pull out, draw forth above others', from Middle Korean 빠이-/빼-) + the infinitive connective -어 + 나다 (Middle Korean 나다, 'to emerge, come forth, be born'). Literally 'to be drawn out and stand forth above the crowd'—a semantic parallel to Latin excellere ('to rise out above') and Sino-Korean 秀/傑出—it describes striking beauty, talent, or excellence.

history.meaning: to stand out above the rest, emerge prominently
to be striking, outstanding, excelled in beauty or talent

morphemes.meaning: draw out, stand out above others
infinitive connective (preserved in full before 나-)

빼어나다.notes: Unlike 빼가다 or 빼놓다 where the connective -어 merges into 빼-, 빼어나다 retains the explicit syllable -어- in both spelling and pronunciation, giving it an elevated, literary ring often used for physical beauty (빼어난 미모) or scenery.

rootFamily.gloss: to be born with, be innately endowed with

빼주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb combining 빼다 ('to pull out, remove, subtract, excuse') + the coalesced infinitive connective -어 + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다, 'to give, do for someone's benefit'). Literally 'to pull out or subtract for someone', it covers excusing a person from a group or duty, freeing up schedule time, removing an unwanted item, or knocking down a price.

history.meaning: to pull out / subtract + to give / do for someone
to take out, excuse/exempt, free up (time), or discount for someone

morphemes.meaning: give, do as a favor for someone (benefactive auxiliary)

빼주다.notes: Highly idiomatic across everyday situations: 저 좀 빼주세요 means 'Please count me out / excuse me from this', 시간을 빼주다 means 'to clear one's schedule for someone', and 값을 빼주다 means 'to give a discount'.

rootFamily.gloss: to give; to do for someone's benefit
to overlook, cut someone some slack

뺏기다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) passive verb contracted from 빼앗기다 ('to have something snatched away, be deprived of'), which adds the passive voice suffix -기- to the compound verb 빼앗다 (빼- 'pull out, draw away' + Middle Korean 앗다 / 앋다 'to snatch, seize by force'). Both the full form 빼앗기다 and the contracted form 뺏기다 are recognized as standard Korean.

history.meaning: to snatch away > to have something snatched away (passive)
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (15th–19th c.)

history.meaning: to have something taken away or stolen; to be deprived of or captivated by

뺏기다.notes: Used not only for losing possessions or broadcast slots to rivals (자리를 뺏기다), but also in positive or neutral psychological expressions like 마음을 뺏기다 ('to have one's heart stolen') and 시선을 뺏기다 ('to have one's gaze captured').

rootFamily.gloss: to snatch away, take by force (contracted)
to be deprived of, have snatched away (full form)

뺏다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb contracted from 빼앗다 ('to snatch away, dispossess, take by force'), which is itself a historical compound of 빼- ('to pull out, extract') and Middle Korean 앗다 / 앋다 ('to seize, snatch, rob', attested in 15th-century texts such as *Yongbieocheonga*). While standalone 앗다 became restricted to elevated literary prose, 빼앗다 and its contracted spoken/written counterpart 뺏다 became the everyday verb for seizing something from another.

history.meaning: to seize, snatch away, rob by force
to pull out and snatch away; to take someone's possession, role, or right

morphemes.meaning: snatch, seize (from 앗-, contracted with 빼- into 뺏-)

뺏다.notes: Although 빼앗다 takes the bright-vowel infinitive 빼앗아 (because the second syllable has ㅏ), the contracted stem 뺏- contains the front vowel ㅐ and therefore conjugates with the dark vowel -어 as 뺏어, 뺏었다 (never *뺏아).

rootFamily.gloss: to snatch away, take by force (uncontracted form)
to have something snatched away, be deprived of
to snatch away or claim (especially a life)

뺏어가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial compound verb contracted from 빼앗아가다, composed of 뺏다 (< 빼앗다, from 빼- 'pull out' + Middle Korean 앗다 'snatch, seize') + the infinitive connective -어 + the directional verb 가다 (Middle Korean 가다, 'to go away'). Because contracting 빼앗- to 뺏- changes the stem vowel from ㅏ to ㅐ, the connective vowel shifts from -아 (빼앗아가다) to -어 (뺏어가다), denoting the act of snatching something away and carrying it off.

history.meaning: to snatch away and take off with
to snatch away, take away someone's share, item, or person

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective (selected after vowel ㅐ of 뺏-)
go away, take away from the victim/speaker

뺏어가다.notes: Adding -어 가다 to 뺏다 emphasizes the victim's sense of loss as the snatched item, opportunity, or person is carried away out of reach (cf. 뺏어오다 'to snatch and bring here').

rootFamily.gloss: to claim or snatch away (a life, literary)

뺨.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) anatomical noun, attested in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Middle Korean as 뵘 (pyam) and 뺨 (ppyam, e.g. in the 1527 Hunmong Jahoe). The modern reinforced bilabial stop ㅃ developed through fortition of the earlier initial consonant cluster ㅸ/ㅂ before the palatal glide.

history.meaning: cheek, side of the face
cheek

뺨.notes: Unlike 볼 (which refers more softly to the fleshy lower part of the cheek), 뺨 refers to the whole side of the face and is the standard noun used in expressions for slapping or kissing someone's cheek (뺨을 때리다, 뺨에 뽀뽀하다).

rootFamily.gloss: slap on the cheek, blow to the face
fleshy part of the cheek (semantic pair)

뻑뻑하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective meaning 'stiff, tight, not sliding or turning smoothly (of a drawer, door, or hinge); dry and thick; dry (of eyes)', formed from the reduplicated dark-vowel mimetic root 뻑뻑 + -하다.

history.meaning: reduplicated root for high friction/stiffness + -하다
stiff, tight, hard to move; dry and thick

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뻑뻑하다

뻑하면.etymology: Native Korean idiomatic adverbial construction lexicalized from the mimetic adverb 뻑 (ppeok, an intensive ideophone describing a sudden, forceful impact or effortless action) combined with the light verb stem 하- (ha-, 'to do') and the conditional connective ending -면 (-myeon, 'if, whenever'). Literally 'if one so much as goes ppeok', it evolved to mean 'at the slightest provocation' or 'whenever the chance arises'.

history.meaning: if struck suddenly; whenever triggered
at the drop of a hat, habitually, at every opportunity

뻑하면.notes: Almost always followed by a negative or exasperating habitual action (e.g. 뻑하면 울다 'to cry at the drop of a hat' or 뻑하면 지각하다 'to be late all the time').

rootFamily.gloss: with a sudden thud; frequently, readily
tough, stiff, or dry and hard (related intensive root)

뻔하다.etymology: Native Korean verbal/adjectival formation representing two closely linked developments: as an auxiliary adjective in the construction -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 ('nearly did, was on the verge of'), it combines the bound noun 뻔 (ppeon, 'plausible likelihood, near-occurrence') with 하다 ('to be/do'); this bound root is historically connected to the descriptive adjective 뻔하다 ('to be obvious, transparently clear'), a fortis intensive of 번하다 ('to be bright, open, manifest').

history.meaning: to be bright, manifest, plainly visible; to be nearly so
to be obvious/predictable; (after -(으)ㄹ) to almost happen

morphemes.meaning: obvious appearance; verge or likelihood of an event

뻔하다.notes: Pay close attention to syntax: as a standalone predicate (결말이 뻔하다) it means 'the ending is obvious/predictable', whereas after the prospective modifier -(으)ㄹ (넘어질 뻔했다) it means 'almost fell / nearly did'.

rootFamily.gloss: plainly, obviously, right before one's eyes

뻔히.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb formed from the fortis descriptive root 뻔- (ppeon-, 'plainly visible, obvious, crystal clear', the tense-consonant intensive counterpart of 번- 'bright, open') plus the productive deadjectival adverbial suffix -히 (-hi). It describes knowing or witnessing something unmistakably with one's own eyes.

history.meaning: brightly, clearly, manifestly
plainly, obviously, knowingly, right before one's eyes

뻔히.notes: Frequently collocates with 알다 or 보다 (e.g. 뻔히 알면서 'knowing full well', 눈을 뻔히 뜨고 'with one's eyes wide open') to criticize someone for ignoring or lying about an obvious truth.

뻗다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to stretch out, extend, reach out, spread', descending from Middle Korean 벋다 ('to stretch, extend') with initial consonant tensification (ㅂ > ㅃ).

history.meaning: to extend, stretch out
to stretch out, extend, reach

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뻗다

뻥.etymology: Native Korean mimetic noun converted from the onomatopoeic ideophone 뻥 (ppeong), which imitates a loud, hollow popping or bursting sound (as when pressure is released or grains are puffed in 뻥튀기). By metaphorical extension—likening an exaggerated boast to hot air popping loudly with nothing inside—it came to denote a bluff, tall tale, or fib in colloquial Korean.

history.meaning: sound of a hollow pop, burst, or wide opening
a pop/boom; a bluff, fib, or exaggerated lie (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: hollow popping sound; empty boast or fib

뻥.notes: Very common in everyday spoken Korean in phrases like 뻥치지 마 ('Don't lie / Quit bluffing!') and 뻥이야 ('Just kidding / It's a fib!').

rootFamily.gloss: to tell a fib, bluff, talk big
to be wide open or pierced clean through

뽀뽀.etymology: Native Korean nursery word (유아어) of reduplicated bilabial mimetic origin, formed by repeating the tense syllable 뽀 (ppo), which iconically imitates the lip-rounding posture and light smacking sound of pressing pursed lips against a cheek or mouth.

history.meaning: child-directed mimetic word for a light peck or kiss

morphemes.meaning: sound and lip-puckering motion of a light kiss or peck

뽀뽀.notes: 뽀뽀 refers specifically to a light, affectionate peck (on the cheek or lips, among family, children, or couples), whereas the English loanword 키스 (kiseu) implies a deeper, romantic kiss.

rootFamily.gloss: to give a peck, to kiss lightly

뽀뽀하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining the reduplicated bilabial mimetic noun 뽀뽀 (ppoppo, 'a light kiss, peck') with the productive native light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do, perform').

history.meaning: to give a light kiss or peck on the cheek or lips

뽀뽀하다.notes: Takes the dative particle -에게/-한테 (or locative -에 for a body part): 아이 볼에 뽀뽀하다 ('to kiss a child on the cheek').

뽀송하다.etymology: Native Korean expressive adjective meaning 'soft, dry, and fluffy (pleasantly free of dampness, as of freshly laundered towels or dry skin)', formed as the tensified light-vowel counterpart of 보송하다 + -하다.

history.meaning: dry and soft -> pleasantly dry, fluffy, and fresh
soft and dry, fluffy, moisture-free

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뽀송하다

뽑다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to pull out, extract, uproot, draw out; to select, recruit, elect', descending from Middle Korean ᄲᅩᆸ다 ('to pull out, draw forth').

history.meaning: to pull out, uproot, extract
to pull out, extract; to pick, select, print/dispense

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뽑다

뽑아내다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb composed of 뽑- (ppop-, stem of 뽑다 'to pull out, uproot, extract, select', from Middle Korean 븝다 / 뽑다), the infinitive connective suffix -아 (-a), and the transitive auxiliary/main verb 내다 (naeda, 'to put forth, bring out, produce through effort'). Together they denote forcefully extracting or drawing out something from within.

history.meaning: to pull out, uproot and bring forth
to extract, pull out, draw forth (talent, data, or physical objects)

morphemes.meaning: to bring out, produce to completion

뽑아내다.notes: In broadcasting and creative industries (like *The Producers*), 뽑아내다 is frequently used figuratively for coaxing a great performance out of a cast member or extracting high viewership ratings.

rootFamily.gloss: to pull out, extract, recruit, print out
to be pulled out, selected, elected
drawing lots, lucky dip, claw machine game

뽑아봐.etymology: Inflected colloquial imperative/hortative phrase of the native Korean compound construction 뽑아 보다 (ppoba boda): formed from 뽑- (ppop-, stem of 뽑다 'to pull out, extract; by modern extension, to print out a document, draw from a machine, or produce/render a broadcast cut'), the connective -아 (-a), the auxiliary verb 보- (bo-, from 보다 'to see; to try doing'), and the intimate-style ending -아 (-a), which coalesces with 보- into 봐 (bwa).

history.meaning: to pull out and see / try pulling out
try pulling out; print it out; turn out (a good cut/result)

morphemes.meaning: to pull out, extract, print, produce
to try doing, to see how it turns out

뽑아봐.notes: 뽑다 is a powerhouse verb in Korean office and TV production slang: 프린트 뽑아봐 means 'print out a copy', 분량 뽑아봐 means 'get enough usable footage', and 사진 잘 뽑아봐 means 'get a great shot'.

rootFamily.gloss: to pull out, select, print, extract

뾰족하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built from the sound-symbolic root 뾰족- plus the light verb suffix -하다. Featuring the tense bilabial ㅃ and the palatalized bright vowel ㅛ, 뾰족 vividly mimics a sharp, protruding, or narrowly tapering point, like a needle or sharpened pencil. Figuratively, it describes a sharp, sensitive, or easily irritated temper (뾰족한 성격) or a clever, cutting solution (뾰족한 수).
뾰족하다.notes: Used both literally ('pointed, sharp') and figuratively ('sharp-tongued, edgy', or in 뾰족한 수 'a clever solution').

뿌듯하다.etymology: Native Korean expressive adjective meaning 'proud and deeply satisfied, fulfilled, full to capacity', formed from the tensified stem 뿌듯- (intensive counterpart of 부듯- 'tightly filled') plus -하다.

history.meaning: tightly full -> swelling with pride or satisfaction
proud, fulfilled, heartwarming, full

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뿌듯하다

morphemes.meaning: full to the brim, swelling with satisfaction

뿌리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to sprinkle, scatter, strew, spray, shower', descending from Middle Korean ᄲᅳ리다 ('to sprinkle, scatter') via labial vowel rounding (ㅡ > ㅜ after ㅃ).

history.meaning: to sprinkle, scatter, strew
to sprinkle, scatter, spray, sow

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뿌리다

뿐.etymology: Native Korean bound noun and postpositional particle meaning 'only, merely, nothing but', descending directly from Middle Korean ᄲᅮᆫ.

history.meaning: only, merely, nothing more than
only, just, merely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 뿐

뿜다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb attested in Early Modern Korean as 뿜다 (ppumda) alongside earlier 뿝다 (ppupda, Middle Korean 븝다 'to spurt, spray'). The phonological shape—tense bilabial stop ㅃ, high back rounded vowel ㅜ, and bilabial nasal ㅁ—is phonaesthetically iconic of forcefully expelling air, water, fire, or smoke through pursed lips.

history.meaning: to spray, spurt out from the mouth
to spout, spew, spit out, radiate (energy or charisma)

뿜다.notes: In modern Korean media and internet slang, 뿜다 (and the reduplicated slang noun 뿜뿜) means either 'to burst out laughing (spitting out one's drink)' or 'to radiate charm/aura effortlessly' (매력을 뿜다).

rootFamily.gloss: to be spewed forth, to gush out
to spew out, gush forth forcefully
sprayer, atomizer (mixed compound with 噴霧器 influence)

뿜어지다.etymology: Native Korean passive and spontaneous-state compound verb formed from the transitive verb stem 뿜- (ppum-, 'to spout, spew, emit'), the infinitive connective suffix -어 (-eo, selected by vowel harmony after ㅜ), and the auxiliary verb -지다 (-jida, from 지다 'to fall, become', which derives passives and inchoatives). It describes liquid, smoke, laughter, or an aura gushing forth of its own accord.

history.meaning: to be spewed forth, to gush or radiate out spontaneously

뿜어지다.notes: Often paired with 나온/나오는 (뿜어져 나오다) to describe charisma, energy, or laughter involuntarily bursting out from someone.

삐걱거리다.etymology: Native Korean sound-symbolic verb formed from the onomatopoeic root 삐걱 ('the sharp creak or squeak of rubbing wood or metal') and the productive iterative verb suffix -거리다 ('to repeatedly make a sound or motion'). The tense initial ㅃ and high front vowel ㅣ imitate a higher, tighter squeak (such as a piano key pin or floorboard) than the heavier 뻐걱거리다.
삐걱거리다.notes: Often modifies 소리 ('sound') in the present adnominal form 삐걱거리는 소리 ('squeaking sound').

삐지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to sulk, pout, or get one's feelings hurt over a trifle'. Historically a palatalized/intransitivized variant of 삐치다 (ppichida, from earlier 삐티다 / 빗디다 'to slant askew, jut out diagonally, curl one's lip'), originally depicting the physical gesture of curling out one's lower lip or turning one's head askew in displeasure. Formerly proscribed as a colloquialism for 삐치다, 삐지다 was officially recognized as standard Korean by the National Institute of Korean Language in 2011.

history.meaning: to slant askew, jut out, curl one's lip in displeasure
to sulk, pout, feel slighted

morphemes.meaning: to sulk, pout, twist askew in displeasure

삐지다.notes: In everyday conversation, 삐졌어? ('Are you sulking? / Did I hurt your feelings?') is far more natural and common than its slightly stiffer standard twin 삐쳤어?.

rootFamily.gloss: to sulk, pout; to make a sweeping diagonal stroke in calligraphy
a sulky person, someone who pouts easily (colloquial)

사.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 사 (四, Middle Chinese *sijH*), meaning 'four (4)'.

history.meaning: four
four (4)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사

사가다.etymology: Native Korean serial compound verb formed from 사- (sa-, stem of 사다 'to buy, purchase', from Middle Korean 사다), the infinitive suffix -아 (-a, which coalesces with the stem vowel ㅏ), and the directional verb 가다 (gada, 'to go', from Middle Korean 가다). It denotes buying an item and taking it away with oneself toward a destination, or progressively buying up items.

history.meaning: to buy and go away with
to buy and take away; to continue buying

morphemes.meaning: to go, take away from the speaker's point of reference

사가다.notes: Contrast directional perspective: 사 가다 ('buy and take there / take home') moves away from the current location, whereas 사 오다 ('buy and bring here') moves toward the current location or home.

rootFamily.gloss: to buy in advance and keep ready

사각.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 四角, uniting 四 (넉 사, 'four') and 角 (뿔/모 각, 'horn, angle, corner'). It translates geometrically to a quadrangle or square, serving as the base for derived terms like 사각형 (四角形, 'square, rectangle') and 정사각형 ('perfect square'). Korean also possesses homophones for 사각, including 死角 ('blind spot', literally 'dead angle') and the mimetic adverb 사각사각 (the crisp sound of crunching a fresh apple or stepping on dry snow).
사각.notes: Forms compounds like 사각형 ('rectangle/square') and 사각 별 ('four-pointed star'). Distinguish from 사각지대 ('blind spot').

사건.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 事 (일 사, sa, 'matter, affair, business, event') and 件 (사건/물건 건, geon, 'item, discrete case, article', a character graphically composed of 人 'person' and 牛 'ox', originally signifying dividing up items or enumerating distinct matters). Widely established across modern East Asian legal and journalistic registers to denote a notable incident or legal case.

history.meaning: specific matter, item of business, affair
incident, criminal/legal case, notable event

사건.notes: 사건 and 사고 are often paired as 사건 사고 ('incidents and accidents' on the news): 사건 implies an event involving human agency, drama, or crime, whereas 사고 implies an unintended mishap or crash.

사고.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun from 事 (일 사, sa, 'matter, affair, occurrence') and 故 (연고 고, go, 'cause, reason, unforeseen event, mishap'). Attested in Classical Chinese texts (such as the Zhouli and Mengzi) in the broader sense of 'a reason for action' or 'an untoward occurrence', it narrowed in modern Korean to denote an unexpected accident or mishap (note its homophone 思考 사고, 'thought, reflection').

history.meaning: reason, cause; unexpected event or trouble in state/family affairs
accident, mishap, trouble

사고.notes: In broadcasting (*The Producers*), 방송 사고 (broadcasting accident—dead air, a mic failure, or an unedited blooper airing live) is a producer's worst nightmare; colloquially, 사고를 치다 means 'to cause trouble / mess up big time'.

rootFamily.gloss: traffic accident (交 + 通 + 事 + 故)

사과.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 사과 (沙果), meaning 'apple' (literally 'sandy/crisp-textured fruit', from 沙 'sand/granular' + 果 'fruit'); and (2) 사과 (謝過), meaning 'apology' (from 謝 'apologize, express regret' + 過 'fault, transgression').

history.meaning: crisp fruit; acknowledging a fault
apple (沙果); apology (謝過)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사과

사과드리다.etymology: Hybrid humble compound verb meaning 'to apologize, offer an apology (to a respected person)', combining Sino-Korean 사과 (謝過, 'apology') with the native Korean humble benefactive verb 드리다 ('to give/offer to a superior').

history.meaning: apology + to offer humbly
to apologize (humble)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사과드리다

morphemes.meaning: to offer, give to a superior

사과잼.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'apple jam', combining Sino-Korean 사과 (沙果, 'apple') with the English loanword 잼 (jam).

history.meaning: apple + jam
apple jam

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사과잼

사과하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 사과 (謝過, sagwa, 'apology') and the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do'). The Sino-Korean root combines 謝 (사례할/사죄할 사, sa, 'to apologize, express gratitude, acknowledge') and 過 (허물 과, gwa, 'fault, transgression, error, passing beyond bounds'), literally 'to acknowledge one's transgression'.

history.meaning: to acknowledge and apologize for a fault or transgression
to apologize, express regret for a mistake

사과하다.notes: Do not confuse the noun 사과 (謝過, 'apology') with its exact homophone 사과 (沙果, 'apple')—a classic source of Korean puns (such as handing someone an apple when apologizing).

rootFamily.gloss: to apologize deeply for a grave offense or sin (謝 + 罪)

사교성.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) trimorphemic noun composed of 사교 (社交, sagyo, 'socializing, social intercourse') plus the abstract quality suffix -성 (性, -seong, 'nature, disposition, propensity'). The base compound combines 社 (모일 사, sa, originally 'altar of the soil god', extended to 'community, society, association') and 交 (사귈 교, gyo, 'to cross, mingle, associate with').

history.meaning: disposition toward social intercourse in community life
sociability, outgoingness, social skills

사교성.notes: Typically used in the idiom 사교성이 좋다 ('to be sociable / a people person') or 사교성이 부족하다 ('to lack social skills').

사귀다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 사괴다 (sagoyda, e.g. in the 1447 Seokbo Sangjeol), meaning 'to associate with, become close to, or form a bond with someone'. During the transition from Early Modern to Contemporary Korean, the labialized diphthong ㅚ (oy) after the velar stop ㄱ shifted to ㅟ (wi), yielding modern 사귀다 (sagwida).

history.meaning: to associate with, befriend, mingle closely
to make friends with; to date romantically, go out with

사귀다.notes: Context and object determine whether 사귀다 is platonic or romantic: 친구를 사귀다 means 'to make friends', whereas 온전히 with a person or symmetrically (우리 사귀자 / 둘이 사귄대) means 'Let's go out / They are dating'.

rootFamily.gloss: the traditional Sino-Korean character gloss for 交 (사귈 교)

사그라들다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb formed from the bound verbal root 사그라- (sageura-, related to 삭다 'to subside, ferment, decompose, settle down' and 스러지다 'to vanish, wear away') combined with the directional auxiliary verb 들다 (deulda, 'to enter, shrink inward', from Middle Korean 들다). It vividly portrays physical or emotional intensity—such as flames, swelling, foam, or anger—subsiding and shrinking inward until nearly gone.

history.meaning: to subside and draw inward
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean roots

history.meaning: to die down, subside, dwindle away (of fire, passion, anger, or bubbles)

사그라들다.notes: Interchangeable in many contexts with 사그라지다, though 사그라들다 emphasizes the gradual inward shrinking of energy, anger (화가 사그라들다), or flames (불길이 사그라들다).

rootFamily.gloss: to die down, subside, crumble away
to subside, digest, ferment, weather away
to calm down, abate (of anger or fever)

사내.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 社內 (sanae), formed from 社 (모일/회사 사, sa, originally 'altar of the deity of the soil', extended in modern East Asia to 'company, corporation, society') and 內 (안 내, nae, 'inside, interior, within'). Literally 'inside the company', it functions as a noun and prenominal modifier meaning 'in-house' or 'intracompany'.

history.meaning: within an association or commercial company
in-house, inside the company (e.g. office romance, company cafeteria)

사내.notes: Watch out for the native Korean homophone 사내 ('man, fellow, guy', from Middle Korean 사나히)! In workplace dramas like *The Producers*, 사내 almost always means 'in-house' (e.g. 사내 연애 'office romance', 사내 식당 'company cafeteria').

rootFamily.gloss: office romance, in-house dating (社 + 內 + 戀 + 愛)
outside the company, external (社 + 外)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary (표준국어대사전): 사내 (社內)

사놓다.etymology: Native Korean aspectual compound verb formed from 사- (sa-, stem of 사다 'to buy', Middle Korean 사다), the infinitive connective suffix -아 (-a, coalesced with ㅏ), and the auxiliary verb 놓다 (nota, from Middle Korean 놓다 'to put, place, release'). Used as an auxiliary after -아/-어, 놓다 grammaticalized from 'to place down' into a resultative-preparatory marker meaning 'to do something in advance and leave it in that state for future use'.

history.meaning: to buy and set down / keep ready
to buy beforehand, stock up on in advance

morphemes.meaning: to put/keep in a completed state in advance

사놓다.notes: Nearly synonymous with 사 두다 (sa duda): both mean 'to buy in advance and keep on hand', perfect for saying you already bought snacks or supplies ahead of time.

rootFamily.gloss: to buy and keep for later use
to prepare in advance and leave ready

사다.etymology: Core native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to buy, purchase', attested unchanged in form and sense since Middle Korean 사다.

history.meaning: to buy, purchase
to buy, purchase, earn (goodwill or resentment)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사다

사다리.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'ladder', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄃᆞ리 ('wooden ladder or steps', structurally linked to 서다 'to stand/climb' + 다리 'bridge, leg').

history.meaning: ladder
ladder

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사다리

사드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble benefactive compound verb composed of 사- (sa-, stem of 사다 'to buy', Middle Korean 사다), the infinitive connective suffix -아 (-a, coalesced), and the humble benefactive auxiliary verb 드리다 (deurida, 'to give or offer respectfully to an elder or social superior', from Middle Korean 드리다, originally causative of 들다 'to enter', i.e. 'to cause to enter a superior's presence, present up').

history.meaning: to buy and respectfully present to a superior
to buy for someone (humble/respectful benefactive)

morphemes.meaning: to give/do respectfully for an elder or superior

사드리다.notes: Be careful not to confuse 사 드리다 ('to buy for an elder/superior', humble of 사 주다) with its exact homophone 사들이다 ('to buy up / purchase in bulk')!

rootFamily.gloss: to buy for someone (peer or younger)
to give/offer respectfully to a superior

사들이다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb formed from 사- (sa-, stem of 사다 'to buy', Middle Korean 사다), the infinitive connective suffix -아 (-a, coalesced), and 들이다 (deurida, the morphological causative of 들다 'to enter', formed with the causative suffix -이-, meaning 'to bring in, take inside'). Together they mean 'to buy and bring into one's possession', especially purchasing goods, land, or assets in large quantities.

history.meaning: to buy and bring inside
to buy up, purchase (in quantity or systematically)

morphemes.meaning: to cause to enter, bring in

사들이다.notes: Unlike simple 사다 ('to buy'), 사들이다 implies acquiring things into an inventory, collection, or company portfolio (e.g. 주식을 사들이다 'to buy up shares', 장비를 사들이다 'to procure equipment'). Pronounced [사드리다], identical to 사 드리다 ('buy for an elder').

rootFamily.gloss: to bring in, let in, invest effort
to bring in from outside (거두어 + 들이다)

사라지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 사라디다 (saradida), originally a compound of the verb stem 살- (sal-, 'to burn away, melt, dissolve, be consumed'—historically distinct from long-vowel 살다 'to live') + the infinitive suffix -아 (-a) + the inchoative/passive auxiliary verb 디다 (dida > Modern Korean 지다, 'to fall, become'). Through palatalization of ㄷ > ㅈ before ㅣ and semantic generalization, 사라디다 became modern 사라지다 ('to vanish, disappear without a trace').

history.meaning: to melt away, be consumed, vanish
to disappear, vanish, fade away

morphemes.meaning: to dissolve, consume, burn away (historical 살-)
to become, pass into a state (from 디다 > 지다)

사라지다.notes: Even though its spelling looks like 살아 ('living') + 지다, etymologically it comes from the homophonous Middle Korean verb 살다 ('to burn up / melt away')—which is why snow, smoke, and people 'melt/fade away' when they 사라지다!

rootFamily.gloss: to burn up, consume with fire (preserved transitive form 사르다)
to fade away, vanish, collapse (ablaut/vowel variant)

사람.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'person, human being', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄅᆞᆷ ('person, human'), historically derived from the verb stem 살- (살다, 'to live') plus the substantive nominalizing suffix -ᄋᆞᆷ.

history.meaning: living being, person, human
person, human being, people

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사람

사랑.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) abstract noun attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 사랑 (sarang, e.g. in the 1447 Yongbieocheonga and Seokbo Sangjeol), where it meant both 'deep thought, reflection, consideration' and 'affection, love, cherishing'. Most Korean historical linguists analyze it as a native nominalization in -앙 (-ang) from the verb stem 살- / 사르- ('to think, reckon, discern', also related to 살피다 'to examine closely, care for'), while an older competing hypothesis suggested early nativization from Sino-Korean 思量 (사량, saryang, 'to ponder, consider'). By the Early Modern period, the cognitive sense 'thought' was taken over by 생각, leaving 사랑 exclusively with the meaning 'love'.

history.meaning: deep thought, reflection, consideration; affection, love
love, affection, devotion

사랑.notes: In 15th-century texts, 사랑하다 meant 'to think about' as well as 'to love'—showing that in Korean linguistic history, to love someone literally grew out of holding them constantly in one's thoughts.

rootFamily.gloss: wisdom tooth (literally 'love-tooth', from the ache of first love)

사랑받다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed by combining the noun 사랑 (sarang, 'love, affection', Middle Korean 사랑) with the transitive verb 받다 (batda, 'to receive, accept', from Middle Korean 받다). In Korean grammar, compounding action or emotion nouns with 받다 serves as the primary lexical passive counterpart to 하다 compounds (hence 사랑하다 'to love' → 사랑받다 'to receive love, to be loved').

history.meaning: to receive affection or love
to be loved, to be popular and cherished

사랑받다.notes: widely used not only for personal relationships (부모님께 사랑받다 'to be loved by one's parents') but also in media and entertainment for shows or stars loved by the public (시청자들에게 사랑받는 프로그램).

사랑스러움.etymology: Native Korean derived abstract noun formed by nominalizing the descriptive adjective 사랑스럽다 (sarangseureopda, 'lovable, lovely') with the productive nominalizing suffix -(으)ㅁ (-eum). Because the suffix -스럽- (-seureop-) is a ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) stem—reflecting the historical Middle Korean voiced bilabial fricative ㅸ (-스르ㅸ-)—the stem-final ㅂ vocalizes to 우 (u) before the vowel-initial suffix -음, coalescing into 사랑스러움 (sarangseureoum).

history.meaning: state or quality of being worthy of affection
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean morphological pattern

history.meaning: loveliness, adorableness, charm

사랑스러움.notes: Illustrates the classic ㅂ-irregular noun derivation pattern in Korean: 아름답다 → 아름다움 ('beauty'), 고맙다 → 고마움 ('gratitude'), 사랑스럽다 → 사랑스러움 ('loveliness').

사랑스럽다.etymology: Native Korean derived descriptive adjective formed from the noun 사랑 (sarang, 'love, affection', Middle Korean 사랑) and the productive native deadjectival suffix -스럽다 (-seureopda, from Middle Korean -스르ㅸ다, meaning 'having the appearance or quality of, evoking, worthy of'). It describes someone or something whose demeanor naturally inspires affection.

history.meaning: evoking affection, worthy of love, lovely

morphemes.meaning: having the quality of, worthy of (-some, -able, -ly)

사랑스럽다.notes: Conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before vowel endings, ㅂ turns into 우 (사랑스러워요 'is lovely', 사랑스러운 미소 'a lovely smile').

사랑하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining the noun 사랑 (sarang, 'love, affection; in Middle Korean, also deep thought or consideration') with the native light verb 하다 (hada, from Middle Korean 흐다 'to do, make, feel'). Attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean texts (such as the 1447 Seokbo Sangjeol and 1481 Samgang Haengsildo) as 사랑흐다, where it meant both 'to ponder deeply, think upon' and 'to cherish, love dearly'.

history.meaning: to think deeply upon, ponder; to cherish, hold dear, love
to love, cherish, hold dear

사랑하다.notes: Although English speakers often treat 'to love' as a stative verb, Korean 사랑하다 is an active transitive verb taking the object particle -을/-를 (너를 사랑해) and forming present progressive or attributive forms with -는 (사랑하는 사람 'the person I love').

사무소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사무소 (事務所), meaning 'office, agency, bureau', formed from 사무 (事務, 'office work, administrative business') + 소 (所, 'place, institution').

history.meaning: establishment where business or administrative affairs are handled
office, agency, bureau

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사무소
