사무실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사무실 (事務室), meaning 'office room, workplace', formed from 사무 (事務, 'office work, administrative duties') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: room for conducting office work
office (room)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사무실

사발.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사발 (沙鉢), meaning 'large ceramic bowl (for rice, soup, or traditional drinks)', formed from 沙 (사, 'sand, porcelain/earthenware') + 鉢 (발, 'bowl', originally a Buddhist transcription of Sanskrit pātra 'alms bowl').

history.meaning: ceramic bowl
large bowl

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사발

cognates.meaning: judicial apprentice / legal trainee (at the Legal Training and Research Institute)

사법연수생.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) five-morpheme institutional compound: 사법 (司法, sabeop, 'judiciary, administration of justice', from 司 맡을 사 'to take charge of, administer' + 法 법 법 'law') + 연수 (研修, yeonsu, 'training, research and cultivation', from 硏 갈 연 'to grind, polish, study deeply' + 修 닦을 수 'to cultivate, practice, master') + 생 (生, 날/학생 생, saeng, 'student, trainee, person engaged in learning'). Specifically denotes a trainee who passed the former Korean national bar examination (사법시험) and entered the two-year program at the Judicial Research and Training Institute (사법연수원) before becoming a judge, prosecutor, or attorney.

history.form: 司法 (shihō / sabeop) + 研修 (kenshū / yeonsu) + 生 (sei / saeng)
history.meaning: institutional compound for a trainee in judicial administration and legal practice
history.stage: Modern East Asian Legal Terminology (20th c.)

history.meaning: judicial trainee at the Judicial Research and Training Institute (사법연수원)

morphemes.meaning: to administer, govern, take charge of

사법연수생.notes: Pronounced [사범년수생] due to ㄴ-insertion (연수 → 년수) and nasal assimilation of ㅂ before ㄴ (법 + 년 → 범년). Passing the grueling 사법시험 to become a 사법연수생 was traditionally considered the ultimate symbol of academic prestige in Korea (prior to the full transition to the law school system).

rootFamily.gloss: Judicial Research and Training Institute (司 + 法 + 硏 + 修 + 院)
national bar examination (司 + 法 + 試 + 驗)
trainee, participant in a training program (硏 + 修 + 生)

사생활.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 사 (私, 'private, personal') and 생활 (生活, 'living, livelihood, daily life', itself from 生 'to live, birth' + 活 'to be alive, active'). Adopted across the modern East Asian lexical sphere to distinguish an individual's personal domestic sphere from public or professional duties.

history.meaning: personal sphere combined with livelihood and daily subsistence
private life, personal affairs outside public scrutiny

사생활.notes: Frequently used in media and entertainment contexts (such as celebrity scandals) in expressions like 사생활 침해 ('invasion of privacy').

사실.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 사실 (事實), meaning 'fact, reality, truth; in fact, actually', composed of 事 (사, 'matter, affair, event') + 實 (실, 'real, true, actual').

history.meaning: actual state of affairs, truth
fact, truth; in fact, actually

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사실

사실상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound derived from 사실 (事實, 'fact, truth, reality', from 事 'matter, affair' + 實 'fruit, real, true') plus the relational suffix -상 (-上, 'on the surface of, from the standpoint of, in terms of'). It functions both as a noun and adverbially to mean 'in reality', 'practically', or 'de facto'.

history.meaning: actual reality + upon / in respect of
in fact, virtually, for all practical purposes

사실상.notes: Often functions adverbially without a particle to translate English 'virtually' or 'de facto' (e.g., 사실상 끝났다 'it is virtually over').

사심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 사 (私, 'private, personal, selfish') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind, intention'). Originally in Classical Chinese philosophical prose it contrasted personal bias or self-interest (私心) with impartial public-mindedness (公心); in modern Korean entertainment slang, it also refers to indulging personal romantic or fan interest while ostensibly working.

history.meaning: partial or selfish mind, personal bias
ulterior personal motive; personal romantic or fan interest

사심.notes: In broadcasting and K-pop variety shows, 사심을 채우다 ('to fulfill one's personal desires') is playfully used when a producer or host casts or favors a celebrity they personally admire.

사십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 사십 (四十), meaning 'forty (40)', formed from 四 (사, 'four') + 十 (십, 'ten').

history.meaning: four tens -> forty
forty (40)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사십

사십오.etymology: Sino-Korean multiplicative-additive numeral compound composed of 사 (四, 'four'), 십 (十, 'ten'), and 오 (五, 'five'), literally 'four tens and five'. Derived from Middle Chinese numerals (*sijH-dzyip-nguX) and used in Korean for dates, money, measurements, math, and sequential numbering.

history.meaning: four tens and five (forty-five)
forty-five (Sino-Korean numeral)

사십오.notes: Contrast with the native Korean numeral 마흔다섯, which is used when counting age (마흔다섯 살) or physical objects with native counters.

사안.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 사 (事, 'matter, affair, business') and 안 (案, 'wooden desk, legal case record, proposal, issue'). Originally referring to an official dossier or case laid upon a magistrate's desk (案), it evolved into an administrative and journalistic term for a specific issue or matter requiring consideration.

history.meaning: affair + official table or documented case file
matter, issue, case under discussion

사안.notes: Belongs to formal or administrative register (e.g., 중대한 사안 'a grave matter/issue'), often heard in newsrooms, corporate meetings, and legal discussions.

사업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 사업 (事業), composed of 사 (事, 'affair, matter, undertaking') and 업 (業, 'occupation, profession, enterprise'). In Classical Chinese (already in the *Book of Changes*, *Yijing*), 事業 denoted a great public undertaking or life's work. In Modern Korean, it designates both commercial business ventures (사업을 하다, 'to run a business') and organized public or institutional projects.

history.meaning: great undertaking, public work, vocation
commercial business, enterprise, or public project

사업.notes: Commonly paired with 계획 in 사업 계획 ('business plan').

사업하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the noun 사업 (事業, from 事 'affair, undertaking' + 業 'occupation, enterprise, karma/work', attested in the *Book of Changes* / *Yijing*) combined with the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ('to do'). It denotes running a commercial enterprise or engaging in business operations.

history.meaning: great undertaking, public achievement, occupation
to run a business, to engage in commercial enterprise

사업하다.notes: While 사업 in public administration can mean a 'public project' (공공사업), the verb 사업하다 almost always means running one's own commercial business.

사용료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound combining 사용 (使用, 'use, utilization', from 使 'to employ, cause' + 用 'to use') with the suffix -료 (-料, originally 'to measure grain', later 'material, fee, charge'). It designates a fee paid for the right to use property, facilities, copyrighted works, or equipment.

history.meaning: to employ and use + measured grain/payment
usage fee, rental charge, royalty

사용료.notes: The suffix -료 (料) productively forms fee words across Korean, such as 입장료 ('admission fee'), 수업료 ('tuition fee'), and 임대료 ('rent/lease fee').

사용하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from 사용 (使用, from 使 'to command, employ, make use of' + 用 'to use, employ') and the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do'). It serves as the standard, slightly formal counterpart to the native Korean verb 쓰다 ('to use').

history.meaning: to employ, to put into service
to use, to utilize, to operate

사용하다.notes: More formal and explicit than native 쓰다 (which also means 'to write', 'to wear a hat', or 'to be bitter'), making 사용하다 preferred in instructions, notices, and formal speech.

사위.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun derived from Middle Korean 사외 (saoy) or 사회 (sahoy), attested in 15th-century texts such as the *Seokbo Sangjeol* (1447) meaning 'son-in-law'. Through regular labialization and diphthong restructuring after the loss of medial /h/ or glide assimilation, Middle Korean *saoy/sahoy* evolved into Early Modern Korean 사위.

history.meaning: daughter's husband, son-in-law
son-in-law

사위.notes: In traditional Korean culture, a son-in-law is treated as an honored guest by his wife's parents, encapsulated in the proverb 사위는 백년손님 ('a son-in-law is a guest for a hundred years').

rootFamily.gloss: taking a husband / welcoming a son-in-law

사이.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'space between, interval (of space or time), gap; relationship between people', descending from Middle Korean ᄉᆞ이 ('interval, gap, space between').

history.meaning: space between, interval
space between, interval, relationship

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사이

cognates.meaning: exterior side-view mirror on a vehicle

사이드미러.etymology: Modern Korean loanword borrowed from English *side mirror* (often mediated or reinforced via Japanese automotive terminology サイドミラー *saidomirā*), combining English *side* (from Old English *side*, 'flank, edge') and *mirror* (from Old French *mireor*, from Latin *mirari*, 'to wonder at, look at'). Refers specifically to the exterior wing mirrors mounted on the sides of a motor vehicle.

history.meaning: lateral flank + reflecting glass surface
automobile exterior side-view mirror

사이드미러.notes: Compare with 백미러 ('rear-view mirror inside the cabin', from pseudo-anglicism *back mirror*), whereas 사이드미러 specifically denotes the exterior mirrors on the left and right doors.

사이즈.etymology: Borrowed from English size ('physical dimensions, magnitude, or standardized measurement of clothing/objects').

history.meaning: dimensions or standardized measurement
size

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사이즈

사이트.etymology: Unadapted loanword from English *site*, functioning primarily in modern Korean as an ellipsis of *website* (웹사이트). English *site* itself derives via Anglo-Norman from Latin *situs* ('local position, situation'), a past-participial noun from *sinere* ('to leave, let lie, place').

history.meaning: local position, placement, situation
spatial location; internet domain location on the World Wide Web
website, internet portal

사이트.notes: In everyday Korean conversation, 사이트 almost exclusively means an internet website (e.g., 포털 사이트 'portal site'), rather than a physical construction or camping site.

사자성어.etymology: Sino-Korean four-morpheme compound formed from 사 (四, 'four'), 자 (字, 'character, letter'), 성 (成, 'completed, established'), and 어 (語, 'word, expression, saying'). It refers to traditional four-character Classical Chinese idiomatic expressions (such as 일석이조 一石二鳥, 'killing two birds with one stone') deeply embedded in Korean rhetoric and education.

history.meaning: four characters + established expression/idiom
four-character Sino-Korean idiom

사자성어.notes: Often used interchangeably with 고사성어 (故事成語, 'idiom derived from a historical anecdote'), though 사자성어 emphasizes the four-syllable structural form regardless of whether a historical story lies behind it.

사장.etymology: Sino-Korean 사장 (社長), from 사 (社, 'company, enterprise') + 장 (長, 'head, chief').
사장.notes: With honorific -님 (사장님), it is the universal polite title for shop, café, and guesthouse owners.

사장님.etymology: Combines Sino-Korean 사장 (社長, 'company president, shop proprietor') with the native honorific suffix -님.
사장님.notes: In everyday Seoul life, 사장님 politely addresses both a workplace boss and any café, restaurant, or shop owner.

사장조.etymology: Korean musical key name joining pitch letter 사 ('G', 7th of 가나다라마바사 = A–G) with Sino-Korean 장조 (長調, 'major key').
사장조.notes: Contrasts with 사단조 (g minor, 短調).

사적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun formed from 사 (私, 'private, personal, individual') and the adjectival/attributive suffix -적 (-的, originally 'bright, target', popularized in modern East Asia to form relational adjectives on the model of Western *-ic* / *-al*). It contrasts directly with 공적 (公的, 'public, official').

history.meaning: private/personal + relational attribute marker
personal, private, unofficial

사적.notes: Usually appears as са적인 (modifying a noun, e.g. 사적인 감정을 넣다 'to bring personal feelings into it') or adverbially as 사적으로 ('privately, off the record'). Do not confuse with the homographs 사적 (史蹟, 'historical site') or 사적 (史籍, 'historical records').

cognates.meaning: in advance, beforehand, prior to an event

사전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound composed of 사 (事, 'matter, affair, event') and 전 (前, 'front, before, prior'). Literally meaning 'before the event takes place', it is used both as a standalone noun (especially with -에 as 사전에, 'in advance') and as a productive prefix meaning 'pre-' or 'advance' (as in 사전녹화 'pre-recording' or 사전투표 'early voting').

history.meaning: prior to the occurrence of an affair or incident
advance, beforehand, prior (antonym of 사후 事後)

사전.notes: Be careful with the very common homophone 사전 (辭典/字典, 'dictionary'); context or the following noun (e.g., 사전 예약 'advance reservation' vs. 영어 사전 'English dictionary') immediately distinguishes them.

rootFamily.gloss: after the fact, ex post facto (事後)

cognates.word: 事前収録 (jizen shūroku) / 事前録画 (jizen rokuga)

사전녹화.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound uniting 사전 (事前, 'prior to the event, in advance', from 事 'event' + 前 'before') and 녹화 (錄畫, 'video recording', from 錄 'to record, copy, inscribe' + 畫 'picture, image'). In television broadcasting, it designates taping a segment or musical performance ahead of the live broadcast.

history.meaning: prior to the event + recording images
pre-recording of a television broadcast or stage performance

사전녹화.notes: In K-pop music show and TV production culture, 사전녹화 is ubiquitious and almost universally abbreviated by fans and staff to the two-syllable acronym 사녹 (sanok).

사정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 사 (事, 'affair, matter, business') and 정 (情, 'feeling, disposition, actual condition/truth of a matter'). In Classical Chinese, 情 meant not only 'emotion' but 'the genuine reality or underlying conditions of something', yielding 事情 ('the actual state and reasons behind an affair'), which in Korean means 'circumstances, situation, or personal reasons'.

history.meaning: the actual conditions and underlying reality of an affair
circumstances, internal situation, personal reasons for acting

사정.notes: A classic false friend with Mandarin 事情 (shìqing, which simply means any 'thing, matter, or business'); in Korean, 사정 specifically implies underlying circumstances or private constraints (e.g., 개인 사정으로 'due to personal circumstances', 사정이 있다 'there is a reason/story behind it').

사주다.etymology: Native Korean serial/compound benefactive verb formed from 사다 ('to buy', Middle Korean 사다 *sada*) linked via the infinitive/connective suffix -아 (contracted after stem vowel /a/) to the auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give', Middle Korean 주다 *cwuda*). The construction V-아/어 주다 grammaticalizes 'giving' into a benefactive marker ('to do V for someone's benefit').

history.meaning: to purchase + to give to someone
to buy something for someone, to treat someone to a purchase

사주다.notes: When treating a elder or person of higher status, the auxiliary 주다 must be replaced by its honorific suppletive counterpart 드리다, yielding 사드리다 ('to buy for an esteemed person'). In social life, 밥 사주다 ('to buy someone a meal') is a foundational expression of warmth and mentorship.

사진.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사진 (寫眞), meaning 'photograph, picture', literally 'copying the true likeness', from 寫 (사, 'depict, copy') + 眞 (진, 'truth, reality'). Used in Classical Chinese and Joseon Korea for lifelike portrait paintings before being adopted in the late 19th century for camera photography.

history.meaning: lifelike portrait painting
photograph, photo

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사진

사채.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 사 (私, 'private, non-governmental') and 채 (債, 'debt, loan', composed of 人 'person' + 責 'duty, financial obligation'). While originally contrasting private or corporate debt with public government bonds (공채 公債), in everyday South Korean usage it strongly connotes high-interest private moneylending and loan sharking outside the regulated banking sector.

history.meaning: private/personal + monetary debt or obligation
private loan; high-interest unregulated moneylending (loan sharking)

사채.notes: In Korean dramas and daily speech, 사채업자 ('private moneylender') almost always refers to an aggressive loan shark, and 사채를 쓰다 ('to take out a private loan') signals severe financial desperation.

rootFamily.gloss: loan shark, private moneylender (私債業者)

사천.etymology: Sino-Korean multiplicative numeral compound formed from 사 (四, 'four', Middle Chinese *sijH) and 천 (千, 'thousand', Middle Chinese *tshen). Because native Korean numerals only run up to ninety-nine (with the archaic native word 즈믄 'thousand' having fallen out of use after Middle Korean), all numbers in the thousands use the Sino-Korean system.

history.meaning: four thousand
four thousand (Sino-Korean numeral)

사천.notes: Also a common homograph for Sichuan province in China (四川, 사천), famous in Korea for spicy Sichuan cuisine (사천요리, 사천짜장).

사촌.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship term 사촌 (四寸), literally 'four joints/degrees of kinship'.
사촌.notes: Traditional Korean kinship counts degrees (촌): parents-to-child is 1, siblings are 2, aunts/uncles are 3, and first cousins are 4 (사촌).

사촌분.etymology: Polite compound noun joining 사촌 (四寸, sachon, 'first cousin') with the native Korean honorific classifier and suffix -분 (-bun, 'esteemed person'). In traditional Korean kinship measurement (촌수, 寸數), degree of collateral consanguinity is counted in 'inches/nodes' (촌, 寸): parents and children are 1-chon, siblings are 2-chon, aunts/uncles are 3-chon, and first cousins are 4-chon (사촌, 四寸). Appending -분 elevates the reference when speaking respectfully of someone else's cousin.

history.meaning: fourth-degree collateral relative; first cousin
cousin (respectful/honorific reference)

사촌분.notes: Adding -분 to relationship or neighborhood nouns (사촌분, 이웃분, 손님분) is a hallmark of warm, courteous Korean service and neighborhood speech.

사춘기.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound borrowed from Meiji Japanese medical and psychological terminology 思春期 (*shishunki*), combining 사춘 (思春, from 思 'to think of, long for' + 春 'springtime', where 'spring' is a classical Chinese metaphor for romantic awakening and amorous desire, as in 懷春) with the suffix -기 (-期, 'period, stage, phase').

history.meaning: longing for spring (classical metaphor for awakening romantic/sexual feelings)
period of puberty and adolescence (translation of Latin *pubertas*)
puberty, adolescence; rebellious or emotionally sensitive phase

사춘기.notes: In colloquial Korean, asking someone 사춘기야? ('Are you going through puberty?') is a teasing way to call out an adult who is acting moody, prickly, melodramatic, or rebelliously stubborn; middle-aged existential angst is similarly called 오춘기 ('fifth puberty').

사탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound written 糖 or 沙糖, from 사 (砂/沙, 'sand, gravel', referring to crystalline granules) and 당/탕 (糖, 'sugar, sweet confection'). Notably, 糖 has the standard Sino-Korean reading 당 (as in 당분 'sugar content'), but in 사탕 it preserves an older vernacular Sino-Korean aspirated reading *탕* reflecting Middle Chinese palatal/dental phonology or direct Ming/Qing vernaculuar borrowing. Semantic narrowing shifted its Korean meaning from 'granulated sugar' (now 설탕 雪糖) to 'hard candy'.

history.meaning: sand-like granulated cane sugar
refined crystalline sugar, sweet confection
hard candy, boiled sweets

사탕.notes: A major false friend with Japanese 砂糖 (*satō*) and Chinese 砂糖 (*shātáng*): in Japanese and Chinese it still means 'granulated culinary sugar', whereas in Korean culinary sugar is 설탕 (雪糖, literally 'snow sugar') and 사탕 strictly means 'candy / sweets'. Also used figuratively in 사탕발림 ('sugar-coating / empty flattery').

사태.etymology: Sino-Korean compound composed of 사 (事, 'affair, event, incident') and 태 (態, 'posture, appearance, condition, state'). It denotes the unfolding condition or posture of events, typically carrying a serious or urgent nuance such as an escalating crisis or grave turn of events.

history.meaning: affair/incident + condition or posture
state of affairs, unfolding situation, emergency/crisis

사태.notes: Unlike 중립적 words for situation like 상황 (狀況), 사태 almost always implies an undesirable, alarming, or critical development (e.g., 비상사태 'state of emergency', 사태의 심각성 'the gravity of the situation'). Do not confuse with the native Korean homonym 사태 ('landslide/avalanche', as in 산사태, or 'beef shank').

사포질.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'sanding, smoothing a surface with sandpaper', combining Sino-Korean 사포 (沙布, 'sandpaper, emery cloth', from 沙 'sand' + 布 'cloth') with the native Korean action suffix -질 ('repetitive work with a tool').

history.meaning: sandpaper + tool-action suffix
sanding

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사포질

morphemes.meaning: act of working with an implement

사포질하다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb meaning 'to sand, smooth with sandpaper', formed from 사포질 ('sanding', from 사포 沙布 'sandpaper' + -질) plus the verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: sanding + to do
to sand, smooth with sandpaper

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사포질하다

사항.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 사 (事, 'matter, affair, fact') and 항 (項, 'nape of the neck; itemized entry, clause, category'). Because classical Chinese administrative documents divided subjects into numbered clauses or headings (項), 事項 came to denote individual items, particulars, or points of instruction within a document or regulation.

history.meaning: affair/matter + itemized clause or category
item, detail, matter, point of notice

사항.notes: Extremely common in compounds on forms, signs, and contracts: 주의사항 ('precautions / points to note'), 공지사항 ('announcements / notices'), 요구사항 ('requirements / demands'), and 특이사항 ('special notes / anomalies').

rootFamily.gloss: precautions, points of caution (注意事項)

사호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사호실 (四號室), meaning 'Room 4, Room No. 4', formed from 四 (사, 'four') + 號 (호, 'number, designation') + 室 (실, 'room').

history.meaning: Room Number Four
Room 4

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사호실

사회.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 사 (社, originally 'altar to the god of the soil', composed of 示 'altar/deity' + 土 'earth', hence 'local community shrine and village association') and 회 (會, 'gathering, assembly, meeting'). In Tang–Song China, 社會 meant a seasonal village festival or guild gathering around the local earth deity's shrine; in 1870s Meiji Japan (notably by Fukuzawa Yukichi), 社會 was repurposed to translate English *society*, a semantic shift soon adopted into Korean and Chinese. (Note: a distinct homograph 司會 means 'emceeing/hosting a ceremony or show').

history.meaning: communal gathering or festival around the local earth-god shrine (社)
society, civil body politic (translation of English *society*)
society, the public world outside school/home

사회.notes: In broadcasting contexts like *The Producers*, be aware of the frequent homonym 사회 (司會, from 司 'to preside over' + 會 'meeting'), meaning 'master of ceremonies / hosting an event' (e.g., 사회를 보다 'to host/emcee a show', 사회자 'host/MC').

사회생활.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound combining 사회 (社會, 'society', from 社 'community' + 會 'assembly') and 생활 (生活, 'life, living', from 生 'live' + 活 'active'). While literally 'life as a member of society', in contemporary South Korean usage it has specialized to mean navigating interpersonal hierarchy, office politics, and professional etiquette in adult working life.

history.meaning: human society + daily living and subsistence
adult working life; workplace interpersonal tact and office navigation

사회생활.notes: A classic false friend with English 'social life' (hanging out with friends or partying): in Korean, 사회생활을 잘한다 ('is good at 사회생활') means someone is tactful with bosses, polite to seniors, laughs at the director's jokes, and knows how to survive in a hierarchical workplace.

rootFamily.gloss: newcomer to the workforce (社會初年生)

사흘.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'three days (or the third day of the month)', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄒᆞᆯ ('three days'), built from the native Korean numeral root 사-/서- ('three') plus the native day-counting suffix -ᄒᆞᆯ (compare 하루, 이틀, 나흘).

history.meaning: three days
three days; third day of the month

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사흘

산.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 산 (山, Middle Chinese *srean*), meaning 'mountain, hill', which gradually replaced the native Middle Korean word 뫼 ('mountain') in everyday speech.

history.meaning: mountain, hill
mountain, hill

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 산

산길.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining Sino-Korean 산 (山, 'mountain, hill', replacing the older native Korean word 뫼 *moy* in most compounds) with native Korean 길 ('road, path, way', from Middle Korean 길ㅎ *kilh* with final *h*-consonant). Tensification (사이시옷 effect) causes 길 to be pronounced [낄] in [산낄].

history.meaning: mountain + path, road, way
mountain path, hiking trail

산길.notes: Pronounced [산낄] with tensification of /k/ to [kk] because a compound boundary links a nasal-final noun (산) and a native noun beginning with a lax obstruent (길).

rootFamily.gloss: night road / walking at night (밤 + 길)

산꿀.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 산 (山, 'mountain') with native 꿀 ('honey').
산꿀.notes: Refers to dark, aromatic wildflower and chestnut honey harvested from mountain apiaries.

산낙지.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 산, the adnominal (perfective/stative) participle of 살다 ('to live, be alive', Middle Korean 살다 *salda*, where stem-final /l/ drops before the adnominal suffix -ㄴ), modifying 낙지 ('long-armed small octopus', *Octopus minor*, attested in Joseon-era encyclopedias such as *Jibong Yuseol* and *Jasaneobo* as 낙제/낙지). In culinary usage, it denotes raw, freshly chopped or whole live small octopus eaten while still wriggling.

history.meaning: living, alive + small mudflat octopus (*Octopus minor*)
live octopus; dish of freshly chopped squirming octopus seasoned with sesame oil

산낙지.notes: Do not confuse the first syllable 산 ('live', from 살다 'to live') with 산 (山, 'mountain')! Also distinguish 낙지 (small mudflat octopus with long thin arms) from 문어 (giant octopus) and 오징어 (squid).

산들바람.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining the ideophonic root 산들- (seen in 산들산들 'blowing softly and refreshingly') with 바람 ('wind, breeze', Middle Korean ᄇᆞᄅᆞᆷ). Within Korean vowel harmony, the bright vowel ㅏ in 산들바람 evokes a light, gentle, pleasant breeze brushing past leaves on a mild afternoon.
산들바람.notes: Commonly collocates with 불다 or 불어오다 ('a gentle breeze blows in').

산딸기.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 산 (山, 뫼 산, 'mountain, uncultivated hills') with the native Korean noun 딸기 ('berry, strawberry', attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄯᆞᆯ기). Literally 'mountain berry', it serves as the general culinary and everyday Korean name for bramble fruits (Rubus species, especially Rubus crataegifolius) as well as red raspberries in baking and preserves. Because wild brambles ripen on sunny hillsides in early summer, 산딸기 strongly evokes tart-sweet summer fruit.
산딸기.notes: Pronounced [산딸기]; in baking recipes it routinely translates English 'raspberry' alongside 라즈베리.

산소.etymology: Sino-Korean scientific term borrowed from Japanese 酸素 (*sanso*), coined in the late Edo/early Meiji period (building on Udagawa Yōan's 1834 *Seimi Kaisō*) as a calque of Dutch *zuurstof* / German *Sauerstoff* (itself calquing Lavoisier's French *oxygène*, from Greek *oxys* 'sharp, acid' + *-genes* 'producer', because Lavoisier believed oxygen was the essential constituent of all acids). Composed of 산 (酸, 'sour, acid') and 소 (素, 'undyed silk; fundamental element').

history.meaning: acid-former / acid-substance (Lavoisier's chemical nomenclature)
chemical element oxygen (acid + element)
oxygen (O2)

산소.notes: Has an important everyday homophone in Korean: 산소 (山所, literally 'mountain place'), which means an ancestral grave or family tomb mound. Context (breathing vs. visiting ancestors on Chuseok) makes the meaning unmistakable. Also contrasted with Chinese, which uses 氧 / 氧氣 (*yǎngqì*) for oxygen.

산소호흡기.etymology: Sino-Korean five-morpheme compound combining 산소 (酸素, 'oxygen', from 酸 'acid' + 素 'element'), 호흡 (呼吸, 'breathing, respiration', from 呼 'to exhale, call out' + 吸 'to inhale, draw in'), and the instrument suffix -기 (-器, 'vessel, apparatus, device'). It designates a medical oxygen mask, ventilator, or breathing apparatus.

history.meaning: oxygen + exhaling and inhaling + mechanical apparatus
oxygen mask, medical respirator, life-support breathing apparatus

산소호흡기.notes: In Korean media and colloquial speech, 산소호흡기를 달다 ('to put on an oxygen respirator') or 산소호흡기를 떼다 ('to pull the plug / remove the respirator') is frequently used figuratively for keeping a failing TV program, company, or project barely alive on life support.

산수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 산 (算, 'bamboo counting rods; to calculate, reckon', composed of 竹 'bamboo' + 具 'implement') and 수 (數, 'number, calculation, count'). Attested in Classical Chinese since the Han dynasty for calculating numbers with counting rods, in modern Korean and Japanese education it refers specifically to elementary arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), as opposed to higher mathematics (수학 數學).

history.meaning: reckoning numbers with bamboo counting rods; numerical calculation
elementary arithmetic, basic number calculation

산수.notes: When someone makes a simple calculation mistake with money or numbers in daily life, Koreans tease them by saying 수학도 아니고 산수잖아! ('That's not even higher math [수학], it's basic arithmetic [산수]!'). Also note the common homonym 산수 (山水, 'mountains and water / landscape').

산악회.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 山岳 (산악, "mountains and lofty peaks", from 山 산 "mountain" + 岳 악 "high peak") and the associative suffix 會 (회, "gathering, society, club"). Coined in the modern era alongside Japanese 山岳会 (sangakukai) to denote organized mountaineering or hiking clubs.

history.meaning: mountains and towering peaks
mountaineering society, hiking club

산악회.notes: In Korean culture, neighbourhood and workplace 산악회 are ubiquitous social institutions known as much for fellowship and post-hike dining as for trekking.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 산악회

산책.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 散策, formed from 散 (흩을 산, 'to scatter, loosen, roam at leisure') and 策 (지팡이 책, 'bamboo staff, walking stick'). In classical Chinese poetic prose, 散策 meant tapping a walking stick along a quiet path without a fixed errand or hurry. Modern Korean uses 산책 for any unhurried recreational walk through a neighbourhood, park, or garden.
산책.notes: Combines with 하다 (산책하다 'to take a walk') or 나가다/가다 ('to go out for a walk').

산책하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 산책 (散策, "leisurely stroll", literally "walking with a staff at ease", from 散 산 "scatter, leisurely, unrestrained" + 策 책 "bamboo staff, walking stick") with the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do"). Literally "to tap a walking stick about at leisure", an idiom originating in Classical Chinese literati poetry.

history.meaning: to walk at leisure leaning on a bamboo staff
a stroll, promenade
to take a walk, to stroll

산책하다.notes: The second Hanja 策 (책) means "walking stick" here rather than its common modern sense "policy/plan" (as in 대책), preserving the poetic image of a scholar strolling with a staff.

산토끼.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining Sino-Korean 산 (山, "mountain, wild") with native Korean 토끼 ("rabbit, hare", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 톳기 thoski). Specifies the indigenous Korean hare (Lepus coreanus) inhabiting mountains and forests in contrast to domesticated rabbits (집토끼).

history.meaning: hare, rabbit
rabbit, hare (with reinforcement of tensified 끼)
wild mountain hare (Lepus coreanus)

산토끼.notes: Immortalized in Korean cultural memory by Lee Il-rae's 1928 children's song "산토끼 토끼야" (Mountain Hare, Little Hare), which virtually every Korean speaker knows by heart.

살.etymology: Core native Korean noun representing three Middle Korean words of the form 살: (1) 'flesh, muscle, skin, meat of fruit/fish'; (2) the native bound classifier for 'years of age' (etymologically connected to 살다 'to live'); and (3) 'arrow, spoke of a wheel, lattice bar, ray of light'.

history.meaning: flesh; year of age; arrow, spoke, lattice strip
flesh, skin; years old; spoke, lattice bar, ray

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살

살다.etymology: Core native Korean ㄹ-stem verb meaning 'to live, be alive, dwell, reside', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 살다.

history.meaning: to live, be alive, reside
to live, dwell, survive

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살다

살리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to save (a life), keep alive, revive; to make the most of, bring out (a feature or flavor)', derived from 살다 ('to live') plus the causative suffix -리- (Middle Korean 살리다).

history.meaning: to make live, save a life, revive
to save, keep alive, revive, highlight/bring out

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살리다

morphemes.meaning: to cause to live / bring to life

살림하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 살림 ("housekeeping, livelihood, household management") + 하다 ("to do"). The noun 살림 derives from the native verb 살다 ("to live") via the causative stem 살리다 ("to make live, sustain life") plus the nominalizing suffix -ㅁ (-m), originally signifying "means of sustaining life" before specializing into managing a household.

history.meaning: to live / to cause to live, sustain life
livelihood; household management, housekeeping
to keep house, manage a household

살림하다.notes: Connected to 살다 ("to live"): keeping house (살림) is literally the act of keeping a family alive and thriving. Often reduplicated or paired as 살림살이.

rootFamily.gloss: to save a life, keep alive

살벌하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb combining 살벌 (殺伐, "killing and attacking; brutal, fierce, cutthroat", from 殺 살 "kill" + 伐 벌 "strike, attack, subjugate") with the native adjective-forming verb 하다. Originally described the ruthless devastation of warfare and the bleakness of autumn/winter winds in Classical Chinese before extending to fierce workplace or social atmospheres.

history.meaning: slaughter and military campaigning; bleak, deadly severity
brutality, warlike savagery
to be brutal, fierce, cutthroat, or chillingly tense

살벌하다.notes: Frequently used hyperbolically in everyday Korean to describe a freezing-cold room, a cutthroat competition, or an intimidating boss's mood (분위기가 살벌하다).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 살벌하다

살살.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb meaning 'gently, softly, lightly, carefully, little by little', formed by reduplicating the light-vowel ideophonic root 살-.

history.meaning: gently, softly, cautiously
gently, softly, lightly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살살

살아나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 살다 (salda, Middle Korean 살다 salta, 'to live, be alive') linked via -아 (-a) to the auxiliary-like verb 나다 (nada, Middle Korean 나다 nata, 'to emerge, spring forth, come into being'). Literally 'to emerge into life', it is attested from Middle Korean onward for recovering from illness or danger and extends naturally in Modern Korean to spaces, traditions, flavors, or musical instruments coming back to life after neglect.

history.meaning: to come back to life, revive, survive
to revive, come alive again (of people, rooms, flavors, or music)

cognates.meaning: to revive, come back to life

살아나다.notes: Often paired with 다시 ('again') in 다시 살아나다 ('to come back to life, be revived').

살아보다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb construction composed of 살다 ("to live, survive", Middle Korean 살다 sal-da), the infinitive connective -아 (-a), and the auxiliary verb 보다 ("to see; to try doing"). Literally "to live and see", idiomatized as "to try living, experience life, or endeavour to survive".

history.meaning: to live + to see / try
to try living, experience life, strive to survive

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb of trial or experience (to try doing)

살아보다.notes: Whether written spaced (살아 보다, standard orthography for main verb + auxiliary) or unspaced (살아보다), the auxiliary -아/어 보다 adds the nuance of experiencing something firsthand or making a concerted effort to get by.

rootFamily.gloss: to get by, live day to day

살짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'slightly, lightly, gently, stealthily, just a bit', attested in Early Modern Korean as 살짝.

history.meaning: lightly, slightly, on the sly
slightly, gently, discreetly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살짝

살찌다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed by univerbation of the noun 살 ("flesh, bodily tissue", Middle Korean 샆 salh) and the intransitive verb 찌다 ("to grow plump, become fat or full", Middle Korean 찌다 pci-da). Originally a subject-predicate phrase meaning "one's flesh grows plump", lexicalized into a single verb meaning "to gain weight".

history.meaning: flesh + to grow plump, fatten
to put on flesh, gain weight, grow fat

살찌다.notes: Its direct antonym is 살빠지다 ("to lose weight", literally "flesh falls out"). Note that 살 ("flesh") had a final -ㅎ in Middle Korean (샆), which survives in compounds like 살코기 ("lean meat").

살펴보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to examine closely, look around carefully, check on', combining 살피다 ('to inspect, observe, look into carefully', Middle Korean ᄉᆞᆯ피다) with the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see, try').

history.meaning: to inspect and see, examine closely
to examine, look around, check carefully

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살펴보다

삶.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun derived from the verb stem 살- (from 살다, "to live, be alive") plus the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ (-m). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 삷 (salm, with rising tone), representing the regular morphological process that turns action/state verbs into abstract nouns (compare 알다 "to know" -> 앎 "knowledge", 자다 "to sleep" -> 잠 "sleep").

history.meaning: living, life, existence
human life, existence, way of living

삶.notes: Pronounced [삼] (sam) in isolation because the consonant cluster ㄻ reduces to [ㅁ] in coda position, though the ㄹ resurfaces before vowel-initial particles (삶이 [살미], 삶을 [살믈]). Contrast with Sino-Korean 생명 (生命, biological life) and 인생 (人生, course of human life).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삶

삼.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 삼 (三, Middle Chinese *sam*), meaning 'three (3)'. Also homophonous with native Korean 삼 ('hemp', Middle Korean 삼) and Sino-Korean 삼 (蔘, 'ginseng').

history.meaning: three
three (3)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼

삼가다.etymology: Native Korean verb inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 삼가다 (samka-da, "to be cautious, act prudently, refrain from"). Historically a transitive and intransitive verb denoting reverent self-restraint and circumspection in speech or conduct; often mistakenly conjugated as *삼가하다 due to confusion with Sino-Korean -하다 verbs, though 삼가다 is a pure native verb.

history.meaning: to be cautious, exercise prudence, refrain from
to refrain from, abstain from; to be discreet and reverent

morphemes.meaning: to refrain from, be prudent and cautious

삼가다.notes: A classic Korean grammar pitfall: because people mistake 삼가 for a Sino-Korean noun, they often say *삼가해 주세요, which is non-standard. The correct imperative is 삼가 주세요 (since the stem is 삼가-). The adverbial form 삼가 ("reverently, respectfully") comes from the infinitive of this verb.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삼가다

삼각.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 三角 (삼각, "three corners, triangle"), composed of 三 (삼, "three") + 角 (각, "horn, corner, angle"). Used both as an independent noun meaning "triangle" and as a productive modifier in geometric, geographic, and social compounds such as 삼각관계 ("love triangle").

history.meaning: three-cornered, three-angled
triangle; three-way, triangular

삼각.notes: In K-dramas like *The Producers*, 삼각 alone or in 삼각관계 (三角關係) almost always refers to a romantic love triangle. Also familiar from 삼각김밥 (triangular seaweed rice balls).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삼각

삼나무.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'cedar, Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica)', combining Sino-Korean 삼 (杉, 'cryptomeria, cedar') with native Korean 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모).

history.meaning: cedar + tree/wood
cedar, cryptomeria

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼나무

삼만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼만 (三萬), meaning 'thirty thousand (30,000)', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 萬 (만, 'ten thousand').

history.meaning: three ten-thousands -> thirty thousand
thirty thousand (30,000)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼만

삼베.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 삼 ("hemp, Cannabis sativa", Middle Korean 삼 sam) and 베 ("woven cloth, linen/hemp fabric", Middle Korean 뵈 poy). Denotes coarse, breathable cloth woven from hemp bast fibres, which served as the primary everyday and mourning textile of commoners in pre-modern Korea prior to the widespread cultivation of cotton.

history.meaning: hemp plant + woven bast cloth
hemp cloth, coarse hempen fabric

삼베.notes: Traditionally associated with both summer workwear (due to its stiff, airy weave) and Korean funeral mourning attire (상복, 喪服) as well as burial shrouds (수의, 壽衣).

삼사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 三社 (삼사, "three companies"), composed of the numeral 三 (삼, "three") and the counter/noun 社 (사, "company, corporation, society", originally "altar of the soil god"). In South Korean broadcasting and media parlance, shortened from 지상파 방송 삼사 (地上波放送三社) to refer specifically to the "Big Three" terrestrial networks: KBS, MBC, and SBS.

history.meaning: altar of the god of the soil; local community association
three companies or corporations
the three major terrestrial television networks (KBS, MBC, SBS) or three major telecom/card firms

삼사.notes: In the television industry setting of *The Producers*, 삼사 invariably means the three legacy terrestrial broadcasters (KBS, MBC, SBS), though in telecommunications it refers to SKT, KT, and LG U+.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삼사

삼선짜장.etymology: Sino-Korean and Mandarin-loan culinary compound combining Sino-Korean 삼선 (三鮮, "three fresh delicacies", from 三 삼 "three" + 鮮 선 "fresh, savoury ingredients") with 짜장 (from Mandarin 炸醬 zhájiàng, "fried bean sauce", formally written 자장 in Korean standards until 짜장 was recognized as standard in 2011). Originally denoted three prized ingredients from land, sea, and sky in Shandong-Korean Chinese cuisine, now meaning a premium seafood version of jajangmyeon.

history.meaning: three fresh delicacies + fried bean-sauce noodles in Shandong cuisine
deluxe jajangmyeon made with three or more premium seafood ingredients (shrimp, squid, sea cucumber)

삼선짜장.notes: For decades the National Institute of Korean Language insisted on 자장면 as the sole standard spelling, before finally accepting 짜장면 and 삼선짜장 as standard in 2011 to match universal pronunciation.

rootFamily.gloss: deluxe three-delicacy spicy seafood noodle soup

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삼선자장면

삼십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼십 (三十), meaning 'thirty (30)', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 十 (십, 'ten').

history.meaning: three tens -> thirty
thirty (30)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼십

삼십오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼십오 (三十五), meaning 'thirty-five (35)', composed of 三 (삼, 'three') + 十 (십, 'ten') + 五 (오, 'five').

history.meaning: thirty-five
thirty-five (35)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼십오

삼십육억.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral from 三十六億 (삼십육억, "thirty-six hundred million", i.e., 3.6 billion), composed of 三 (삼, "three") + 十 (십, "ten") + 六 (육, "six") + 億 (억, "one hundred million, 10^8"). Reflects the East Asian myriad-based (만/억, 10^4 / 10^8) grouping system rather than the Western thousand-based (10^3 / 10^9) system.

history.meaning: one hundred thousand (archaic) -> one hundred million (10^8)
thirty-six hundred million (3,600,000,000; 3.6 billion)

삼십육억.notes: Pronounced [삼심뉴걱] (sam-sim-nyu-geok) due to nasalization of ㅂ before nasal insertion of ㄴ in 십육 [심뉵]. When translating between Korean and English, remember that 1억 is 100 million, so 10억 is 1 billion and 36억 is 3.6 billion.

삼안.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 三案 (삼안, "third proposal, plan three, option C"), composed of 三 (삼, "three, third") and 案 (안, "proposal, draft plan, desk"). In Classical Chinese, 案 originally denoted a wooden tray or magistrate's desk, which metonymically came to mean the official documents, legal cases, or proposals laid upon the desk.

history.meaning: wooden serving tray; official's desk -> legal case or written proposal on a desk
third draft, option three, Plan C in planning meetings

삼안.notes: Standard Korean corporate and TV production jargon: when pitching ideas or budgets, teams prepare 일안 (1안, Option 1), 이안 (2안, Option 2), and 삼안 (3안, Option 3).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 안 (案)

삼인조.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 三人組 (삼인조, "three-person group, trio"), composed of 三 (삼, "three") + 人 (인, "person") + 組 (조, "braided cord; group, team, crew, squad"). Borrowed via or reinforced by Meiji-era Japanese organizational usage of 組 (kumi / -gumi) to classify small teams, musical trios, or criminal gangs by member count.

history.meaning: woven silk ribbon or cord; to weave together, organize
three-person group, trio, three-member squad or band

삼인조.notes: Commonly used in two very different contexts: pop music (e.g., 삼인조 그룹 "a three-member idol group") and crime reporting (e.g., 삼인조 강도 "a three-person robbery gang").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 조 (組)

cognates.meaning: three days; the third day of the month

삼일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun and numeral from 三日 (삼일, "three days" or "the third day of the month"), composed of 三 (삼, "three") + 日 (일, "sun, day"). Coexists alongside the native Korean word 사흘 ("three days", Middle Korean 사흘 sahul), with Sino-Korean 삼일 preferred in formal, administrative, and historical contexts (such as 삼일절, the March 1st Independence Movement Day).

history.meaning: three days; the third day
three days; the third day of the month

삼일.notes: Famous in the proverb 작심삼일 (作心三日, "a resolution lasts only three days") and the national holiday 삼일절 (三一節, March 1st Movement Day). Its native Korean synonym for a duration of three days is 사흘.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 삼일

삼촌.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship compound 삼촌 (三寸), meaning 'uncle (especially father's brother)', literally 'three degrees/joints of kinship' in the traditional Korean 촌수 (寸數) system of reckoning collateral consanguinity (where parent to child is 1촌, siblings are 2촌, and a parent's sibling is 3촌).

history.meaning: third degree of kinship -> parent's brother
uncle

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼촌

삼층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 삼층 (三層), meaning 'third floor, three stories', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 層 (층, 'story, floor, tier').

history.meaning: third level or story of a building
third floor, three stories

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼층

상.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 賞 (상, "reward, award, prize"), whose Hanja character combines the phonetic element 尚 (상, "esteem, high") with the semantic radical 貝 (패, "cowrie shell, money, valuables"). In Classical Chinese, it denoted bestowing wealth or honours upon a meritorious subject, evolving in modern Korean into "award, prize, or trophy" (as in 연예대상, the Entertainment Grand Prize).

history.meaning: to bestow valuables for merit; reward, bounty
award, prize, commendation, trophy

상.notes: Be careful with homophones: 상 can represent 賞 (award), 上 (top/above), 床 (table, as in 밥상), 像 (statue/image), or 喪 (mourning). With awards, collocations are 상을 받다/타다 ("to receive/win an award") and 상을 주다 ("to give an award").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상 (賞)

cognates.meaning: shopping street, commercial district; merchant house

상가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun representing 商街 (상가, "commercial street, shopping arcade, commercial complex", from 商 상 "commerce, merchant" + 街 가 "street, district") or 商家 (상가, "merchant shops", from 商 상 "commerce" + 家 가 "house, establishment"). In contemporary South Korean urban architecture, it specifically refers to a multi-story commercial building or the retail shopping complex attached to an apartment estate.

history.meaning: merchant house / commercial street
commercial building, shopping arcade, retail shops

상가.notes: Note the pronunciation distinction between homographs: 상가 [상가] (商街, commercial shopping complex) has a plain ㄱ, whereas 상가 [상까] (喪家, house in mourning) triggers tensification of ㄱ! Every Korean apartment complex has an 아파트 상가 housing laundries, realtors, and academies.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상가

상갓집.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining Sino-Korean 상가 (喪家, "house in mourning", from 喪 상 "mourning, bereavement, funeral" + 家 가 "house, family"), the native Korean genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷), and native Korean 집 ("house, home"). Because speakers ceased perceiving 가 (家) as transparently meaning "house", native 집 ("house") was pleonastically suffixed to reinforce the sense of a bereaved household or funeral parlor.

history.meaning: bereaved family, household in mourning
mourning house + house (pleonastic reinforcement)
house in mourning, funeral hall wake

상갓집.notes: Like 역전앞 ("in front of the station front") or 처갓집 ("wife's family's house"), 상갓집 literally contains "house" twice (家 + 집), yet 상갓집 is fully accepted as standard Korean.>? In modern Korea, most wakes take place in hospital funeral halls (장례식장), which are still called 상갓집 in speech.

rootFamily.gloss: house in mourning; chief mourner's family

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상갓집

상관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 相關 (상관, "mutual relation, relevance, involvement"), composed of 相 (상, "mutually, each other") + 關 (관, "wooden bolt of a gate; to connect, concern, involve"). Originally meant two things being interlocked like the bolt of a gate, evolving in Korean to mean both formal "correlation" (상관관계) and everyday "concern, business, or meddling" (내 알 바 아니다 / 무슨 상관이야).

history.meaning: to be mutually connected or interrelated; to concern one another
relation, relevance, concern, involvement

morphemes.meaning: gate bolt; to concern, relate, connect

상관.notes: Extremely common in spoken rhetorical questions like 무슨 상관이야? ("What does it matter? / What business is it of yours?") and 상관하지 마 ("Mind your own business / Don't interfere"). Also watch out for the homophone 상관 (上官, superior officer).

rootFamily.gloss: not to matter, to be irrelevant

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상관

상관없다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound adjective formed by univerbation of Sino-Korean 상관 (相關, "mutual relation, relevance, concern") and the native Korean existential-negative adjective 없다 ("to not exist, be lacking", Middle Korean 업다 ep-ta). Literally "there is no connection or relevance", idiomatized as "it doesn't matter, not caring, or regardless of".

history.meaning: relevance, connection + does not exist
to have nothing to do with; to not matter, be fine either way

상관없다.notes: Written as a single word (상관없다) in standard Korean when used as a fixed predicate meaning "it doesn't matter / I don't mind" (난 상관없어). Its adverbial form 상관없이 ("regardless of, irrespective of") is indispensable in both casual and formal Korean.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상관없다

상대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 相對 (상대, "facing each other; counterpart, partner, opponent"), composed of 相 (상, "mutually, each other") + 對 (대, "to face, respond, pair, oppose"). In Classical Chinese, 相對 described two people sitting or standing face-to-face; in modern Korean it denotes the person one is interacting with—whether a conversation partner (대화 상대), romantic prospect, or rival.

history.meaning: to face each other directly; mutually opposing or paired
counterpart, partner, companion, opponent; relativity

상대.notes: Depending on context, 상대 can be friendly or adversarial: 대화 상대 is "someone to talk to", 결혼 상대 is a "marriage partner", and 경쟁 상대 is a "competitor/opponent". With 하다 (상대하다), it means "to deal with, face, or take on someone".

rootFamily.gloss: the other party, the other person
co-star, acting partner in a drama or film

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상대

상대방.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 相對方 (상대방, "the other side, the other person, counterpart"), formed by adding the directional/personal suffix 方 (방, "direction, side, party") to 相對 (상대, "facing each other, counterpart", from 相 상 "mutually" + 對 대 "face, match"). Explicitly personalizes 상대 to refer to the person or party on the other side of a conversation, relationship, or negotiation.

history.meaning: facing each other + direction, side, party
the other person, counterpart, the other party in an interaction

상대방.notes: While English speakers simply say "the other person" or "them", Korean heavily relies on 상대방 whenever discussing interpersonal etiquette, dating, or negotiations (e.g., 상대방의 기분을 배려하다, "to be considerate of the other person's feelings").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상대방

cognates.meaning: first half of the year or fiscal period

상반기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 上半期 (상반기, "first half of a period/year"), composed of 上 (상, "upper, first, earlier") + 半 (반, "half") + 期 (기, "period, term, season"). Reflects the traditional vertical conceptualization of time in East Asia, where earlier periods are "upper" (上, 상) and later periods are "lower" (下, 하).

history.meaning: upper/earlier half + appointed period of time
first half of the year (January–June) or fiscal/broadcasting season

상반기.notes: Paired with its antonym 하반기 (下半期, "second half of the year", July–December). Essential vocabulary in Korean corporate hiring (상반기 공채, spring recruitment) and broadcasting schedules.

rootFamily.gloss: second half of the year (lower half period)
first ten days of a month; early part

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상반기

상봉.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상봉 (相逢), meaning 'reunion, meeting each other after separation', formed from 相 (상, 'mutually, each other') + 逢 (봉, 'meet, encounter'); also used as a place and station name in eastern Seoul (上鳳, 상봉).

history.meaning: meeting one another, reunion
reunion, meeting; Sangbong (toponym)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상봉

상사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 上司 (상사, "higher official, workplace superior, boss"), composed of 上 (상, "upper, higher, above") + 司 (사, "to administer, take charge of; official bureau, officer"). Originally designated higher-ranking government magistrates or administrative bureaus in imperial China and Joseon Korea before broadening to any workplace boss or supervisor.

history.meaning: higher-ranking government official or administrative bureau
workplace boss, supervisor, superior officer

상사.notes: Used to refer to a boss in the third person (e.g., 직장 상사 "one's boss at work"), never as a direct title of address (where 직함 like 팀장님 or 국장님 is used instead). Note homophones: 상사 (商社, trading company), 상사 (上士, master sergeant), and 상사병 (相思病, lovesickness).

rootFamily.gloss: subordinate, person working under one (lower + under)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상사 (上司)

상상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 想像 (상상, "imagination, mental visualization"), composed of 想 (상, "to think, ponder, long for", from 相 phonetic + 心 "heart/mind") and 像 (상, "likeness, image, figure", originally from 象 "elephant", as ancient Chinese scholars reconstructed the appearance of live elephants from their fossilized bones). Literally "to form a mental image in the mind".

history.meaning: to visualize an unseen figure in the mind's eye (attested in Han Fei Zi and Chu Ci)
imagination, mental conception, fancy

morphemes.meaning: to think, conceive in the mind

상상.notes: According to the classical philosopher Han Fei Zi (韓非子), 像/象 ("image/imagination") arose because people in central China rarely saw live elephants (象), so they sketched mental pictures from elephant bones—hence "imagining the unseen".

rootFamily.gloss: to imagine, picture in the mind

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상상 (想像)

상아색.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 象牙色, combining 象 (코끼리 상, 'elephant'), 牙 (어금니 아, 'tusk, fang'), and 色 (빛 색, 'colour, hue'). First lexicalized as 상아 (象牙, 'ivory') and then suffixed with -색 ('colour'), it names a warm, creamy off-white with subtle yellow undertones. In Korean design, stationery, and interior decoration, 상아색 coexists with the English loanword 아이보리.
상아색.notes: Often modifies nouns directly without a particle, as in 상아색 카드 ('ivory card') or 상아색 종이 ('ivory paper').

상업용.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상업용 (商業用), meaning 'for commercial use, commercial-grade', formed from 상업 (商業, 'commerce, business') + suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').

history.meaning: intended for commercial or business use
for commercial use, commercial

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상업용

상인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상인 (商人), meaning 'merchant, trader, shopkeeper', composed of 商 (상, 'commerce, trade') + 人 (인, 'person').

history.meaning: person engaged in trade
merchant, trader, shopkeeper

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상인

상자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상자 (箱子), meaning 'box, case, chest, carton', composed of 箱 (상, 'box, chest, trunk') + nominal suffix 子 (자).

history.meaning: woven or wooden box, chest
box, case, carton

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상자

상징.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 象徵 (상징, "symbol, emblem"), composed of 象 (상, "elephant; image, form, figure, likeness") + 徵 (징, "sign, token, evidence, manifestation"). Coined as a philosophical translation of French symbole / English symbol by Japanese aestheticians (notably Nakae Chōmin in his 1883 translation *Ishi Bigaku*) by repurposing classical roots meaning "outward form (象) and manifest sign (徵)", and subsequently adopted into Korean and Chinese.

history.meaning: visible figure/image + manifest sign or proof
symbol (Meiji philosophical coinage translating French symbole)
symbol, emblem, representation

상징.notes: Combines 象 ("visible form/image", as in 현상 "phenomenon") with 徵 ("characteristic sign", as in 특징 "feature"). Used as a verb with 하다 (상징하다, "to symbolize") and as a modifier with 적 (상징적, "symbolic").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상징

상처.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상처 (傷處), meaning 'wound, injury, scar; emotional hurt', literally 'injured place', from 傷 (상, 'wound, hurt, damage') + 處 (처, 'place, spot').

history.meaning: wounded spot on the body
wound, injury, cut, emotional hurt

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상처

상처받다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 상처 (傷處, "wound, injury, scar", from 傷 상 "wound, injure, grieve" + 處 처 "place, spot") and the native Korean transitive verb 받다 ("to receive, suffer", Middle Korean 받다 pat-ta). Literally "to receive a wounded spot", used predominantly in modern Korean for suffering emotional hurt or psychological pain.

history.meaning: wounded place on the body + to receive
to get hurt (especially emotionally), have one's feelings wounded

상처받다.notes: Korean distinguishes physical and emotional injuries via verb collocation: 상처를 입다 usually refers to sustaining a physical wound, whereas 상처(를) 받다 almost always means having one's feelings hurt. Its causative counterpart is 상처(를) 주다 ("to hurt someone's feelings").

rootFamily.gloss: to hurt someone's feelings (give a wound)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상처 (傷處)

상쾌하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean root 상쾌 (爽快), joining 爽 (시원할 상, 'clear, crisp, bracing') and 快 (쾌할 쾌, 'pleasant, brisk, gladdening'), plus the native adjective-forming verb -하다. Both Hanja evoke clearing away stuffiness or heaviness, whether in weather or mood. In everyday Korean it describes crisp morning air, a cool breeze, or the clear-headed feeling after good sleep or exercise.
상쾌하다.notes: Pairs naturally with 공기 ('air'), 아침 ('morning'), 바람 ('breeze'), and 기분 ('mood').

상큼하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built on the sound-symbolic root 상큼- ('pleasantly crisp, citrusy, invigorating') plus -하다. Featuring the bright vowel ㅏ and aspirated velar ㅋ, it is the signature Korean descriptor for the bright aroma and tang of fresh lemons, green apples, or cool morning air.
상큼하다.notes: Standard culinary word for bright citrus flavour and aroma.

상태.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 狀態 (상태, "condition, state, status"), composed of 狀 (상/장, "form, appearance, shape, condition", originally containing 犬 "dog" to denote the physical build of a hound) and 態 (태, "posture, bearing, demeanour, state", from 能 "bear/ability" + 心 "heart/mind"). Combines outward physical form (狀) with inner disposition or posture (態) to denote the overall condition of a person or thing.

history.meaning: outward appearance and demeanour; condition or form of things
state, condition, status (physical, mental, or operational)

상태.notes: Notice that the Hanja 狀 is read 상 in words meaning "condition/situation" (상태 狀態, 상황 狀況, 현상 現狀), but read 장 when it means "document/certificate" (상장 賞狀 "award certificate", 초대장 招待狀 "invitation letter"). In colloquial speech, 상태가 안 좋다 can jokingly mean someone is acting weird or hungover.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상태

상하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean root 상 (傷, 'wound, injure, damage, grieve') and the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do, to be'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 샹ᄒᆞ다 (syanghota), the verb broadened from physical injury to emotional distress (such as bruised pride) and the spoilage of food.

history.meaning: to wound, injure, harm, or grieve
to be injured, harmed, or damaged
to be hurt, damaged, emotionally bruised, or spoiled (of food)

morphemes.meaning: to do, to be in a state of

상하다.notes: Used across three key domains in everyday Korean: emotional hurt (마음이/자존심이 상하다, 'feelings/pride are hurt'), physical fatigue or weight loss (얼굴이 상하다, 'to look haggard'), and food going bad (음식이 상하다).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상하다

상황.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 상황 (狀況), composed of 상 (狀, 'form, appearance, state, condition') and 황 (況, 'circumstance, situation, state of affairs'). Both characters denote an observable state or condition in Classical Chinese, combining to express the overall circumstances or unfolding state of affairs surrounding an event.

history.meaning: appearance/form + circumstance/condition
overall state of affairs, situation, or circumstances

상황.notes: Unlike 상태 (狀態), which focuses on the internal condition of a specific person or object, 상황 (狀況) refers to the broader external circumstances or unfolding scene around someone.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 상황

상황에.etymology: Inflected adverbial phrase consisting of the Sino-Korean compound noun 상황 (狀況, from 狀 'form, state' + 況 'circumstance, situation') followed by the native Korean locative/dative postpositional particle -에 ('in, at, under'). The particle -에 derives from 15th-century Middle Korean locative -에 (-ey), situating an action within a specific set of circumstances.

history.meaning: state of affairs + locative marker 'in/at'
in a situation; under (such) circumstances

상황에.notes: Frequently paired with verbs of adaptation or judgment such as 상황에 맞다 ('to fit the situation') or 상황에 따라 ('depending on the circumstances').

rootFamily.gloss: recent situation, how one has been (近況)

상황이라면.etymology: Polymorphemic conditional construction combining the Sino-Korean noun 상황 (狀況, 狀 'state, condition' + 況 'circumstance, situation') with the native Korean copula stem -이- ('to be', realized with the retrospective/declarative stem allomorph -이라- after a consonant-final noun) and the conditional connective suffix -면 ('if, provided that'). Literally means 'if it be the situation (that)'.

history.meaning: copula stem + conditional suffix 'if it be'
if it is a situation where; in that case

morphemes.meaning: if, when, in the case that

상황이라면.notes: Adding -이라면 rather than simple -이면 adds hypothetical weight ('if it really is the case that we are in such a situation'), often preceded by a modifying clause like 이런 상황이라면 ('if it is a situation like this').

새.etymology: Core native Korean determiner meaning 'new, fresh, brand-new', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 새. Also homophonous with native Korean nouns 새 ('bird', Middle Korean 새) and 새 (contraction of 사이 'space/time between').

history.meaning: new, fresh; bird
new; bird; interval (사이)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새

새것.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'a new thing, brand-new item', formed from the native determiner 새 ('new') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

history.meaning: new + thing
new item, brand-new thing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새것

새기다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to carve, engrave, inscribe, etch (into wood, stone, metal, or one's heart)', descending from Middle Korean 사기다 ('to carve, engrave; to interpret') via regressive vowel fronting (사기다 > 새기다).

history.meaning: to carve, engrave; to gloss/translate
to carve, engrave, inscribe, bear in mind

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새기다

새다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb uniting two Middle Korean verbs: (1) 샏다 / 새다 ('to leak out, escape', of water, gas, light, or secrets); and (2) 새다 ('to dawn, grow bright as night ends', related to 새벽 'dawn').

history.meaning: to leak out; to break (of dawn)
to leak, escape; to dawn, stay up all night

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새다

새로.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adverb formed from the noun and prenominal root 새 ('newness, something new', Middle Korean 새, say) combined with the instrumental/directive particle -로 ('as, into, by way of', Middle Korean -로, -lwo). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts such as the Seokbo Sangjeol (1447) as 새로 (saylwo), fossilized into a standalone lexical adverb meaning 'anew, freshly, newly'.

history.meaning: anew, newly, for the first time
anew, freshly, newly

morphemes.meaning: in the manner of, anew, into

새로.notes: Do not confuse 새로 (adverb modifying verbs, e.g., 새로 시작하다 'to start anew') with 새 (prenominal determiner modifying nouns, e.g., 새 신발 'new shoes') or 새로이 (a more literary variant adverb).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새로

새롭다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb (adjective) derived from the root 새 ('new', Middle Korean 새, say) and the productive deadjectival suffix -롭다 (Middle Korean -롭다, -lwopta, a ㅂ-irregular suffix meaning 'characterized by, full of'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 새롭다 (saylwopta), it functions as the predicative counterpart to the prenominal determiner 새.

history.meaning: new + having the quality of
to be new, fresh, novel, or vivid anew

morphemes.meaning: characterized by, having the nature of (ㅂ-irregular)

새롭다.notes: Because 새롭다 is a ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) adjective, the final ㅂ lenites to 우/오 before vowel-initial endings: 새로운 (modifying a noun, 'new/novel') and 새로워요 (polite present). Use 새 for concrete newly acquired items (새 차 'a new car') and 새로운 for abstract novelty (새로운 생각 'a novel idea').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새롭다

새벽.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'dawn, daybreak, the small hours of the morning', descending from Middle Korean 새배 ('dawn, daybreak', formed from the root 새- 'to dawn, grow light' + 밝-/배 'bright, morning').

history.meaning: daybreak, dawn
dawn, daybreak, early morning

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새벽

새소리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'birdsong, chirping or singing of birds', formed from 새 ('bird') + 소리 ('sound, voice').

history.meaning: bird + sound
birdsong, chirping of birds

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새소리

새우다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) causative verb formed from the intransitive verb 새다 ('for the night to end, for daybreak to come', Middle Korean 새다, sayta) plus the native causative suffix -우- (-wu-) and verbal ending -다. Attested in Middle Korean as 새오다/새우다 (saywota/saywuta), it literally means 'to make the night dawn (while remaining awake)', hence 'to stay up all night'.

history.meaning: to dawn, to grow light at daybreak
to see the night through until dawn; to stay up all night
history.stage: Middle Korean to Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: to stay up all night, to sit up through the night

morphemes.meaning: to cause to, to pass through

새우다.notes: Almost always collocated with 밤 ('night') as 밤을 새우다 (or contracted in casual speech to 밤을 새다, using the intransitive base verb transitively) to describe pulling an all-nighter in editing suites or study rooms. Homophonous with the noun 새우 ('shrimp') + copula -다, which is a frequent source of Korean puns.

rootFamily.gloss: to dawn, for day to break; (colloquial) to stay up all night
staying up all night, an all-nighter (밤 + 새움)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새우다

새집.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun composed of the prenominal determiner 새 ('new', Middle Korean 새, say) and the native noun 집 ('house, home, dwelling', Middle Korean 집, cip). In Korean orthography, 새집 written without a space can represent either the lexicalized compound 'new house / new home' (contrasted with 헌집 'old house') or the homophonous compound 'birdhouse, bird's nest' (from 새 'bird' + 집 'house').

history.meaning: new + house/dwelling
a newly built or newly moved-into home (or homophonously, a birdhouse)

새집.notes: Famous in Korean culture from the children's toad song '헌집 줄게 새집 다오' ('I will give you an old house, give me a new house') and modern medical term 새집증후군 ('sick building syndrome / new house syndrome'). Note the homonym 새집 ('birdhouse / messy bedhead hair that looks like a bird's nest').

rootFamily.gloss: moving into a new house, housewarming
family members living in the same house

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새집

새콤하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built from the sound-symbolic root 새콤- plus -하다, historically linked to the basic adjective 시다 ('to be sour'). Following Korean vowel-harmony symbolism, the bright vowels ㅐ and ㅗ in 새콤하다 portray an appetizing, lively fruit tang, whereas dark-vowel 시큼하다 suggests sharper or fermented sourness. It frequently joins 달콤하다 ('sweet') in the compound 새콤달콤하다 ('sweet and tangy').
새콤하다.notes: Used exclusively as a positive culinary descriptor for berries, citrus, vinaigrettes, and fruit desserts.

새파랗다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) intensive color adjective formed by attaching the yang-vowel intensive prefix 새- (sae-, 'vividly, glaringly, deeply') to the base color adjective 파랗다 ('to be bright blue or green', Middle Korean 파랗다, phalatha). Just as English uses 'green' for an unseasoned novice, Korean extends the image of vivid, unripened green shoots to describe someone who is callow, inexperienced, or vastly younger in age or rank.

history.meaning: to be bright blue or green
vividly blue/green; ghastly pale (of face); greenhorn, callow, much younger

morphemes.meaning: to be bright blue or green (ㅎ-irregular)

새파랗다.notes: Exhibits Korean vowel-harmony sound symbolism: 새파랗다 (with bright/yang vowels ㅐ/ㅏ) feels sharp, glaring, and youthful (e.g., 새파란 신입 'a greenhorn rookie' or 새파랗게 젊다 'to be in the very prime of youth'), whereas its yin-vowel counterpart 시퍼렇다 (with dark vowels ㅣ/ㅓ) feels heavier, menacing, or bruised.

rootFamily.gloss: to be deep/dark blue or menacingly livid (yin-vowel counterpart)
to be vividly red (sharing the intensive prefix 새-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새파랗다

새하얗다.etymology: Native Korean intensifying colour prefix 새- ('vividly, dazzlingly') + 하얗다 ('white').

새하얘지다.etymology: Native Korean compound inchoative verb meaning 'to become dazzlingly/pure white, turn pale', formed from the intensified color adjective 새하얗다 (prefix 새- 'vividly, completely' + 하얗다 'white') plus the inchoative auxiliary -어지다 (새하얗- + -어지다 -> 새하얘지다).

history.meaning: vividly white + to become
to turn pure white, become snow-white

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새하얘지다

색깔.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'color, hue, tint', formed from Sino-Korean 색 (色, 'color') plus the native Korean bound element -깔 (tensified from 갈 'quality, aspect, look', seen also in 빛깔 'hue', 맛깔 'savory quality', and 성깔 'temper').

history.meaning: color + aspect/quality
color, hue, shade

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 색깔

색칠하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 색칠 (色漆), combining 色 (빛 색, 'colour, pigment') and 漆 (옻 칠, 'lacquer, coat of paint'), plus the verbalizer -하다. Because 칠하다 alone already means 'to apply a coat of paint or varnish', prefixing 색 emphasizes filling a surface or drawing with hues. Modern Korean uses 색칠하다 both for colouring illustrations with pencils or watercolours and for painting craftwork.
색칠하다.notes: Passive participle 색칠된 ('painted, coloured in') is formed with 색칠되다.

cognates.meaning: food item consisting of fillings between slices of bread

샌드위치.etymology: Modern loanword (외래어) borrowed from English sandwich. The English word is an eponym honoring John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718–1792), an English statesman and avid card player who reportedly ordered roast beef served between two slices of toasted bread so he could eat without leaving the gaming table; the Kentish place name Sandwich derives from Old English Sandwic ('sandy trading center / sandy harbor', from sand + wic).

history.meaning: sandy harbor / sandy trading settlement (toponym in Kent)
slices of bread with meat or filling between them (named after the 4th Earl of Sandwich, c. 1762)
sandwich; figuratively, being caught in the middle between two pressures

샌드위치.notes: Beyond the food itself, Korean workplace and media slang frequently uses 샌드위치 figuratively: 샌드위치 신세 ('being stuck in the middle' between senior bosses and junior staff) and 샌드위치 연휴 (a workday 'sandwiched' between a public holiday and a weekend).

rootFamily.gloss: insulated sandwich panel used in construction (샌드위치 + 패널)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 샌드위치

생각.etymology: Korean noun meaning 'thought, idea, opinion, memory, intention', attested since Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각 (traditionally traced to a nativized Sino-Korean compound 生覺, 'arising of awareness/perception', from 生 'arise' + 覺 'perceive, realize').

history.meaning: thought, reflection, recollection
thought, idea, opinion

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생각

생각나다.etymology: Compound verb formed from 생각 ('thought, idea, memory'; attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄉᆡᆼ각, soyngkak, traditionally analyzed as a Korean-coined Sino-Korean compound 生覺 'arising of awareness/perception', though treated synchronically as an unanalyzable root) and the native Korean intransitive verb 나다 ('to sprout, arise, come out, occur', Middle Korean 나다, nata). Literally means 'for a thought or memory to surface of its own accord'.

history.meaning: thought/reflection + to arise/come forth
to come to mind, to be remembered, to occur to someone

생각나다.notes: Because 나다 is an intransitive verb of spontaneous occurrence, 생각나다 takes the nominative/subject particle 이/가 on the thing remembered (그 사람이 생각나다, 'that person comes to mind / I miss that person'), unlike 생각하다 which takes the object particle 을/를. Pronounced [생강나다] due to nasal assimilation of ㄱ before ㄴ.

rootFamily.gloss: to be thought, to seem, to be deemed

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생각나다

생각되다.etymology: Compound passive/evidential verb formed from 생각 ('thought, judgment, reflection'; Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각, soyngkak, associated with Sino-Korean 生覺 'arising of awareness') and the native Korean verb 되다 ('to become, to be formed', Middle Korean 되다, toyta, functioning as the passive counterpart to -하다). It expresses that an idea or conclusion comes to be held naturally ('is thought, is deemed, would seem').

history.meaning: thought + to become / be made into
to be thought, to be considered, to seem

생각되다.notes: Frequently used with the quotative/adverbial particles -고 or -로 (e.g., ~라고 생각되다 'it would seem that / it is thought that') to soften an opinion and make it sound objective or polite in meetings and broadcasts.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생각되다

생각하다.etymology: Verb meaning 'to think, consider, ponder, remember', formed from 생각 ('thought, idea', Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각) plus the verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to think, reflect upon
to think, consider, suppose

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생각하다

생각해보다.etymology: Serial/auxiliary verb construction combining 생각하다 ('to think, ponder'; from 생각, Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각 soyngkak + verbalizer -하다, inflected with the infinitive/connective suffix -어/-여 contracted to 해) and the native Korean auxiliary verb 보다 ('to try doing, to experience doing', grammaticalized from the lexical verb 보다 'to see, look at', Middle Korean 보다, pwota). Literally 'to think and see', hence 'to think over, reflect upon, give something some thought'.

history.meaning: to think + to see / try doing
to think over, to mull over, to consider and see

morphemes.meaning: to try doing, to test and see

생각해보다.notes: In standard orthography, auxiliary 보다 is spaced as 생각해 보다 (with unspaced 생각해보다 also permitted by the optional spacing rule for -아/-어 auxiliary verbs). In conversation, '생각해 볼게요' ('I will think it over') often serves as a polite, indirect refusal or deferral.
