생기다.etymology: Intransitive verb meaning 'to come into being, form, arise, occur, be acquired; to look a certain way', attested from Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ기다 (built on Sino-Korean 生 'be born, arise' or native 살-/ᄉᆡᆼ- plus the native suffix -기다).

history.meaning: to be formed, come into existence
to arise, happen, be formed; to look (a certain way)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생기다

생나무.etymology: Hybrid compound combining Sino-Korean prefix 생- (生, 'raw, unseasoned, bare') with native 나무 ('tree, wood').
생나무.notes: Refers either to freshly cut green timber or to bare wood with no lacquer or paint.

생뚱맞다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) expressive adjective formed from the bound ideophonic/descriptive root 생뚱- (saengttung-, evoking something abruptly popping out without context or connection, related to 생뚱하다 'to be sudden and incongruous' and possibly reinforced by the prefix 생- 'raw, unprompted') plus the native adjective-deriving suffix -맞다 ('having the character of, prone to', grammaticalized from the verb 맞다 'to hit the mark, to meet'). Denotes words or actions that are random, out of the blue, and detached from the surrounding situation.

history.meaning: abrupt/unconnected root + suffix denoting a behavioral trait
to be random, out of the blue, absurdly out of context

morphemes.meaning: exhibiting the trait or manner of

생뚱맞다.notes: Often used adverbially as 생뚱맞게 ('out of the blue, randomly') when someone asks a completely unrelated question in the middle of a serious conversation. Compare 뜬금없다 ('apropos of nothing, without prior context'), which is a near-synonym.

rootFamily.gloss: to be incongruous, abrupt, unconnected to the situation
to be absurd, preposterous (sharing the suffix -맞다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생뚱맞다

생명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 생명 (生命), from 생 (生, 'birth, living, life, vitality') and 명 (命, 'life, mandate of heaven, allotted lifespan, decree'). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical texts such as the Mencius and Zhuangzi, the compound entered Korean both as the standard term for biological life and as a metaphor for the indispensable 'lifeblood' or core essence of an endeavor.

history.meaning: living/birth + allotted lifespan/decree
biological life; vital essence or lifeblood of a craft or broadcast

생명.notes: In Korean television and workplace idioms, 'X는 Y가 생명이다' ('For X, Y is its lifeblood / everything') is a staple expression—for example, 예능은 편집이 생명이다 ('Editing is the lifeblood of a variety show').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생명

생방.etymology: Sino-Korean syllabic clipping (준말) of 생방송 (生放送, 'live broadcast'), composed of 생 (生, 'raw, live, unedited') and 방 (放, 'to release, emit, broadcast'), with the final syllable 송 (送, 'to send, transmit') truncated. Formed by Korean broadcasting professionals and popularized nationwide as television and live streaming culture expanded.

history.meaning: live radio or television broadcast (from 生 'live/raw' + 放送 'broadcast')
live broadcast, live show (clipped industry and colloquial form)

morphemes.kind: root (Sino-Korean, clipped from 방송 放送)

생방.notes: Broadcast station jargon in shows like 프로듀사 (The Producers) relies heavily on two-syllable clippings ending in -방 (放): 생방 ('live broadcast', from 생방송), 본방 ('original airing', from 본방송), 재방 ('rerun', from 재방송), and 결방 ('broadcast cancellation', from 결방송).

rootFamily.gloss: original live airing of a show (本放)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 생방

생색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 생색 (生色), from 생 (生, 'to generate, produce, give rise to') and 색 (色, 'color, countenance, luster, prestige'). In Classical Chinese (attested in the Zhan Guo Ce and Gongyang Zhuan), 生色 meant 'to add luster or vitality to something' or 'to take on a proud countenance'. In Korean, this shifted semantically toward 'enhancing one's own prestige or demanding credit/gratitude in front of others after doing a favor'.

history.meaning: to bring forth color/luster; to show a proud countenance
face, prestige, or visible credit gained from a deed
ostentatious display of generosity; credit claimed for doing a favor

morphemes.meaning: to produce, generate, give rise to (生)

생색.notes: Almost always used in phrases revolving around claiming credit for favors: 생색을 내다 ('to make a show of one's generosity / lord a favor over someone') or 남의 돈으로 생색내다 ('to take credit using someone else's money/effort').

rootFamily.gloss: to take credit ostentatiously, to make a show of generosity

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생색

생색내다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 생색 (生色, from 生 'to produce' + 色 'color, countenance, prestige', meaning 'visible credit or show of generosity') with the native Korean transitive verb 내다 ('to put forth, bring out, produce', Middle Korean 내다, nayta, causative of 나다 'to come out'). Literally 'to put on a display of prestige/credit'.

history.meaning: prestige/luster + to bring forth/display
to make a show of one's generosity; to fishingly claim credit for a favor

생색내다.notes: Carries a mildly critical or teasing nuance: if someone buys coffee once and keeps reminding everyone about it, Koreans say '생색내지 마' ('Stop making such a big deal of your generosity / stop fishing for gratitude'). Pronounced [생생내다] due to nasal assimilation of ㄱ before ㄴ.

rootFamily.gloss: credit, ostentatious display of generosity (生色)
doing something merely for show or credit (생색 + 내기)
to put on airs, to show off (티 + 내다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생색내다

생음악.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 생음악 (生音樂), meaning 'live music (performed in person rather than played from a recording)', formed from the prefix 생- (生, 'live, raw, direct') + 음악 (音樂, 'music').

history.meaning: live, unrecorded musical performance
live music

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생음악

cognates.meaning: birthday (literary; 誕生日 tanjōbi is more common in speech)

생일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 생일 (生日), composed of 생 (生, 'to be born, birth, life') and 일 (日, 'day, sun'). Attested since Tang-dynasty Classical Chinese and recorded in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄉᆡᆼ일 (soyngil), it serves as the standard everyday Korean word for 'birthday'.

history.meaning: day of one's birth
birthday
birthday (standard modern term)

생일.notes: Korean has a strict three-tier honorific hierarchy for 'birthday': 생일 (生日) for peers, juniors, or oneself; 생신 (生辰, where 辰 means 'time/auspicious occasion') for respected elders such as parents or grandparents; and 탄신일 (誕辰日) for historical figures or royalty.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생일

생일날.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean pleonastic compound noun formed by attaching the native Korean noun 날 ('day', Middle Korean 날, nal) to the Sino-Korean noun 생일 (生日, from 生 'birth' + 日 'day'). Even though 일 (日) already means 'day', Korean speakers naturally append native 날 to emphasize the specific calendar day or occasion of one's birthday, triggering liquid assimilation so that 생일날 is pronounced [생일랄].

history.meaning: birthday (Sino-Korean) + day (native Korean)
on one's birthday, the day of one's birthday

생일날.notes: A classic example of Korean Sino-native semantic doubling (중복어), alongside words like 초가집 (草家집, where 가 家 and 집 both mean 'house') and 역전앞 (驛前앞, where 전 前 and 앞 both mean 'front'). Unlike 역전앞, 생일날 is fully accepted as a single standard headword in the National Institute of Korean Language dictionary.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생일날

생지.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary and craft term 생지 (生地), meaning 'unbaked pastry dough, raw dough (or unbleached cloth / unfired clay body)', adopted via the Sino-Korean reading of Japanese 生地 (kiji, 'raw material, unbaked dough'), from 生 (생, 'raw, unworked') + 地 (지, 'ground, base material').

history.meaning: raw base material, unbaked dough
raw pastry dough, unbaked dough

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생지

생활.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 생활 (生活), from 생 (生, 'life, living, birth') and 활 (活, 'to live, survive, be active'). Attested in Classical Chinese (notably in the Mencius, 民非水火不生活, 'The people cannot live without water and fire'), the compound denotes not biological existence itself (생명), but one's ongoing mode of living, daily routine, livelihood, or life within a social institution.

history.meaning: to live and survive; livelihood
livelihood, sustenance, way of living
daily life, lifestyle, institutional or professional life (career life)

생활.notes: In Korean, adding 생활 after an institution or role means 'one's life/career spent in that sphere': 직장 생활 ('office/working life, career'), 방송국 생활 ('life working at a broadcasting station'), 학교 생활 ('school life'), and 사회 생활 ('navigating adult work/social life').

rootFamily.gloss: cost of living, living expenses (生活費)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 생활

샤워.etymology: Borrowed from English shower ('bath in which water is sprayed from overhead').

history.meaning: overhead water spray for bathing
shower

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 샤워

샤워기.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'showerhead, shower fixture', combining the English loanword 샤워 (shower) with Sino-Korean 기 (器 / 機, 'apparatus, fixture, device').

history.meaning: shower + apparatus/fixture
showerhead, shower unit

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 샤워기

cognates.meaning: movable frame holding windowpanes (direct source via Japanese)
frame, window frame, chassis (source of English sash)

cognates.word: サッシ / シャッシ (sasshi / shasshi)

샷시.etymology: Loanword (외래어) referring to a metal or PVC sliding window frame, borrowed via Japanese shasshi/sasshi (シャッシ / サッシ) from English sash ('sliding frame holding glass panes'). Notably, English window sash itself arose in the late 17th century as an alteration (by folk etymology with sash 'waistband') of French châssis ('frame, framework'), which derives from Old French chas ('enclosure, frame') and ultimately Latin capsa ('box, case, holder'), making 샷시 an etymological doublet of automotive 샤시/섀시 ('chassis').

history.meaning: box/case -> wooden or metal frame
sliding window frame (borrowed into Japanese construction terminology)
aluminum or PVC sliding window frame (especially balcony enclosures)

샷시.notes: Although the National Institute of Korean Language prescribes 새시 (saesi, based on English 'sash') as the normative spelling, virtually all Korean homeowners, interior contractors, and TV dramas say and write 샷시 (syassi), especially when discussing enclosing an apartment balcony (베란다 샷시 시공).

rootFamily.gloss: normative standard spelling for window sash/frame
automotive chassis (etymological doublet from French châssis)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 새시 (normative entry for 샷시)

서너.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound numeric determiner meaning 'three or four, a few', formed by juxtaposing 서- (the prenominal combinatory stem of 셋 'three', Middle Korean 서, se) and 너- (the prenominal combinatory stem of 넷 'four', Middle Korean 너, ne). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts as 서너 (sene), it preserves the archaic vocalism (ㅓ rather than ㅔ) of the native Korean numerals three and four before classifiers.

history.meaning: three or four (approximate numeric determiner)
three or four, about three or four (used before measure words/nouns)

서너.notes: Part of a systematic series of native Korean approximate number compounds: 한두 ('one or two'), 두서너 ('two, three, or four'), 서너 ('three or four'), 너더댓 ('four or five'), and 대여섯 ('five or six'). Remember that 서너 is a prenominal determiner (서너 명 'three or four people'), whereas the standalone noun/pronoun form is 서넛 ('three or four of them').

rootFamily.gloss: three Doe (measure) or three Mal (preserving archaic 서- 'three')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 서너

서다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to stand, stand up; to stop, come to a halt; to be erected or established', descending from Middle Korean 셔다 ('to stand') via regular loss of the palatal glide after ㅅ.

history.meaning: to stand, rise, be erected
to stand; to stop/halt; to be set up

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서다

서두르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular verb meaning 'to hurry, rush, hasten, make haste', descending from Early Modern Korean 셔두르다 / 서두르다.

history.meaning: to hurry, act in haste
to hurry, rush, hasten

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서두르다

서랍.etymology: Korean noun meaning 'drawer (of a desk, table, or chest)', descending from Early Modern Korean 셜합 / 설합 (舌盒, literally 'tongue-like sliding box', from 舌 'tongue' + 盒 'covered box') through liquid-aspirate simplification (설합 > 서랍).

history.meaning: sliding drawer box
drawer

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서랍

서랍장.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun composed of 서랍 ('sliding drawer') and the Sino-Korean bound noun -장 (欌, 'cabinet, wardrobe, chest'). The first element 서랍 derives from Early Modern Korean 설합 (seolhap), historically written in Hanja as 舌盒 ('tongue box', from 舌 'tongue' + 盒 'small box/case', because a drawer slides in and out of its frame like a tongue), which underwent lenition/loss of ㅎ and resyllabification to modern 서랍.

history.meaning: sliding drawer (literally 'tongue-box' that slides in and out)
drawer + cabinet/chest
chest of drawers, dresser, bureau

서랍장.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -장 (欌) forms an entire family of Korean furniture words: 옷장 ('wardrobe/clothes closet'), 책장 ('bookshelf/bookcase'), 신발장 ('shoe cabinet'), and 찬장 ('kitchen cupboard').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 서랍장

서로.etymology: Native Korean reciprocal adverb descending from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 서르 ('mutually, each other', attested in Seokbo Sangjeol and Worin Seokbo), which shifted to 서로 in Early Modern Korean through vowel rounding of final -으 to -오.

history.meaning: mutually, one another
each other, mutually

서로.notes: Used most often right before a verb without a particle (서로 돕다, 서로 말 안 하다), though it can also take case particles as a noun (서로를 믿다).

서류.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서류 (書類), meaning 'documents, papers, official paperwork', formed from 書 (서, 'writing, document') + 類 (류, 'category, class, collection').

history.meaning: written documents and papers
document, papers, paperwork

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서류

서류철.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서류철 (書類綴), meaning 'document binder, file folder', formed from 서류 (書類, 'documents, papers') + 철 (綴, 'bind together, stitch, file').

history.meaning: bound file of documents
file folder, document binder

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서류철

서른다섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral meaning 'thirty-five (35)', combining 서른 ('thirty', Middle Korean 설흔) + 다섯 ('five', Middle Korean 다ᄉᆞᆺ).

history.meaning: thirty + five
thirty-five (35)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서른다섯

서리다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested in Early Modern Korean, etymologically linked to the root of 서리 (seori, Middle Korean 서리 seli, 'hoarfrost, condensed dew') and the verb 서리다 ('to coil, gather in a mist or haze'). Its core image is fine vapor, smoke, or frost settling in a thin, cloudy film across a cool surface such as a windowpane or eyeglasses. Metaphorically it also describes emotion or sorrow gathering in a person's eyes (눈물이 서리다).

history.meaning: hoarfrost, condensed vapor on a cold surface (nominal cognate)
to fog up, mist over, gather (of steam, moisture, or tears)

morphemes.meaning: to condense, mist over, gather in a fine layer

rootFamily.gloss: to gather faintly (of tears or light)

서리다.notes: Almost always collocated with the subject 김 ('steam, vapor'): 안경에 김이 서리다 ('one's glasses fog up with steam').

서명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서명 (署名), meaning 'signature, autograph, signing one's name', composed of 署 (서, 'write down, sign, public office') + 名 (명, 'name').

history.meaning: writing one's name on a document
signature, signing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서명

서명하다.etymology: Built from the Sino-Korean noun 서명 (署名), uniting 署 (마을 서 / 쓸 서, 'public office; to inscribe officially') and 名 (이름 명, 'personal name'), followed by -하다. In traditional East Asian chancery practice, 署名 denoted formally inscribing one's name on an official register or memorial. In contemporary Korean it is the standard polite verb for signing contracts, receipts, petitions, or book inscriptions, contrasting with casual 사인하다 for autographs or card slips.
서명하다.notes: Takes the locative particle -에 on the document or line where one signs (서류에 서명하다).

서비스.etymology: Borrowed from English service ('assistance or work provided to customers'; in South Korean restaurant and retail usage, also extended to mean 'a complimentary item or dish on the house').

history.meaning: work or assistance performed for customers
service; complimentary item ('on the house')

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서비스

cognates.meaning: to inhabit, to live in a habitat (of animals/plants)
cognates.word: 生息する / 棲息する (seisoku suru)

cognates.meaning: to dwell, to inhabit, to roost and rest

서식하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 서식 (棲息, 'inhabiting, dwelling') and the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean stem combines 서 (棲, 'to perch, roost in a tree, dwell') and 식 (息, 'to breathe, rest, live'), originally describing birds roosting and resting in their natural habitat before becoming the standard ecological verb for 'to inhabit'.

history.meaning: to perch/roost + to rest/breathe (to dwell in a habitat)
to inhabit, to live in a biological habitat; (humorous) to camp out in a place

morphemes.meaning: to do, to be in a state of

서식하다.notes: Literally a biological/ecological term for wildlife ('Tigers inhabit the forest'), 서식하다 is frequently used in Korean workplace humor (including in *The Producers*) like a nature documentary narration to describe overworked PDs or staff who practically live in the editing room or night-duty lounge (편집실에 서식하다). Note also the homophone 서식 (書式, 'document form/template').

rootFamily.gloss: inhabiting, dwelling in a habitat (棲息)
rest, repose, break (休息, sharing 식 息)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 서식하다

서울.etymology: Native Korean proper name meaning 'capital city', widely connected by historical linguists through Middle Korean 셔ᄫᅳᆯ (syeweul) to Old Korean 서라벌 (Seorabeol), the capital of Silla.
서울.notes: Uniquely among East Asian capitals, 서울 is a native vernacular word rather than a Sino-Korean character compound.

history.meaning: capital domain
capital city
Seoul

서재.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서재 (書齋), meaning 'study, private library, reading room', formed from 書 (서, 'book, writing') + 齋 (재, 'study room, quiet studio').

history.meaning: scholar's room for reading and writing
study, home library

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서재

서점.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 서점 (書店), composed of 서 (書, 'book, writing, volume') and 점 (店, 'shop, commercial storehouse'). Adopted across East Asia in the modern era as the standard designation for a retail bookstore, it pairs with the more intimate hybrid word 책방 (冊房, 'book room/shop'). In contemporary Korean, -점 (店) is a highly productive suffix for retail establishments, as seen in 서점 ('bookstore'), 제과점 ('bakery'), and 상점 ('store').

history.meaning: commercial bookshop, bookstore
bookstore, bookshop

서점.notes: Neighborhood independent bookstores in Korea are affectionately called 동네 서점 or 동네 책방.

cognates.word: thời đại đồ đá / thạch khí thời đại

석기시대.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 석기시대 (石器時代, 'Stone Age'), composed of 석기 (石器, from 石 'stone, rock' + 器 'implement, tool, vessel') and 시대 (時代, from 時 'time, season' + 代 'generation, era, epoch'). Coined in Meiji-era Japanese scholarship (sekki jidai) as a calque of English Stone Age (from Danish archaeologist Christian Jürgensen Thomsen's three-age system, Steenalderen, 1836) and borrowed into Korean academic and general usage.

history.meaning: Sino-Xenic archaeological compound calquing European 'Stone Age'
Stone Age (prehistoric period; colloquially, an ancient or outdated time)

석기시대.notes: In everyday banter, Koreans use 석기시대 hyperbolically to tease someone about outdated habits, old-fashioned mindsets, or ancient technology (e.g., '석기시대 사람도 아니고' — 'It is not like you are from the Stone Age!').

rootFamily.gloss: Paleolithic Era, Old Stone Age (舊石器時代)
Neolithic Era, New Stone Age (新石器時代)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 석기시대

섞다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb meaning 'to mix, blend, mingle, shuffle'. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 섯다 (sesta, with stem 섯- / 섟-, where a velar element followed a sibilant cluster) and 셕다 (syekta). Through Early Modern Korean, the stem-final consonant cluster underwent metathesis and tensification into the geminate velar ㄲ, yielding modern 섞다 (seokda).

history.meaning: to mix, mingle, blend together
to mix, blend, shuffle; to exchange (words or glances)

섞다.notes: Beyond mixing physical ingredients or shuffling cards (카드를 섞다), 섞다 forms the crucial interpersonal idiom 말을 섞다 ('to mix words', i.e., 'to converse or engage in talk with someone'), often used in the negative (말도 섞기 싫다, 'I do not even want to exchange a single word with them'). Pronounced [석따].

rootFamily.gloss: to be mixed, blended, mingled (passive verb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 섞다

섞어보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial/auxiliary verb construction composed of the transitive verb 섞다 ('to mix, blend, exchange', Middle Korean 섯다 sesta / 셕다 syekta) conjugated with the infinitive/connective suffix -어 (-eo, required by vowel harmony after the yin vowel ㅓ) and the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to try doing, to test by experience', from Middle Korean 보다 pwota 'to see'). Literally 'to mix and see'.

history.meaning: to mix/mingle + connective + to see/try
to try mixing together; to try exchanging (words/conversation)

morphemes.meaning: to try doing, to experience and see

섞어보다.notes: When paired with 말 ('words, speech') as 말을 섞어보다 ('to try exchanging words with someone / to try talking to someone for a bit'), it expresses testing out what someone is like by actually having a conversation with them (e.g., '몇 마디 섞어보니까 알겠더라' — 'After trying to exchange a few words with them, I could tell what they were like').

rootFamily.gloss: to be mixed or mingled together (passive)
randomly mixed or jumbled together (뒤 + 섞다)

선.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 선 (線), meaning 'line, thread, wire, route, boundary'. Derived from Middle Chinese sjenH (線, also written with its orthographic variant 綫), a phono-semantic compound combining the silk/thread radical (糸, 'fine silk thread') with the phonetic component 泉/戋. Originally denoting a spun thread or measuring cord, it extended in Classical Chinese and East Asian modernity to geometric lines, electrical cables, railway lines, and social boundaries.

history.meaning: silk thread, measuring cord, drawn line
thread, cord, line
line, wire, route, interpersonal boundary or limit

선.notes: Central to Korean expressions of social etiquette and personal boundaries: 선을 긋다 ('to draw a line / keep someone at arm's length'), 선을 넘다 ('to cross the line / go too far', whence the popular slang noun 선넘규/선넘네), and 선을 지키다 ('to respect boundaries'). Note also the common homophone 선 (先, 'first/senior' or 善, 'goodness' or arranged marriage meeting 선을 보다).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 선 (線)

cognates.meaning: selection of music or songs for a program or concert
to select music tracks; song selection

선곡.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 선곡 (選曲, 'song selection, choosing musical tracks'), composed of 선 (選, 'to choose, select, pick out') and 곡 (曲, 'melody, tune, song, musical piece'). Built on a Classical Chinese verb-object structure ('to select a tune') and lexicalized across modern Korean and Japanese broadcasting and music production as a noun for curating a playlist or program soundtrack.

history.meaning: to choose + musical piece or melody
selection of songs or background music for a broadcast, concert, or album

선곡.notes: In Korean radio and television production (such as KBS's *Music Bank* or radio booths in *The Producers*), 선곡 and 선곡표 (選曲表, 'playlist / cue sheet of selected tracks') are daily professional vocabulary, as the emotional impact of a scene or radio segment depends heavily on the PD's or DJ's 선곡 센스 ('sense for song selection').

rootFamily.gloss: song selection list, broadcast playlist (選曲表)
selection, choice (選擇, sharing 선 選)
musical composition, songwriting (作曲, sharing 곡 曲)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 선곡

선명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 선명 (鮮明, 선 'fresh, vivid' + 명 'bright, clear') + -하다.
선명하다.notes: Describes vivid paint colours, sharp photographs, or crisp lettering.

cognates.meaning: gift; side dish presented on a tray
prepared food or delicacies for presentation

선물.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 선물 (膳物), composed of 선 (膳, 'prepared food, meal, tray of delicacies presented to a superior') and 물 (物, 'thing, object, article'). Originally denoting food or delicacies offered respectfully to a guest or superior, its meaning broadened in Korean to designate any gift or present.

history.meaning: delicacies or prepared food offered on a tray
gift, present

선물.notes: Combines with 하다 to form 선물하다 ('to give as a gift'); for honorific recipients, the Sino-Korean word 선배 or elders take 드리다 rather than 주다 (선물을 드리다).

rootFamily.gloss: royal meal table in the Joseon court (from 膳)

선반.etymology: Sino-Korean-derived noun 선반 (懸板 / 宣盤), meaning 'shelf, ledge, rack mounted on a wall or inside a cabinet', attested in Early Modern Korean as 션반.

history.meaning: wall-mounted shelf or rack
shelf, ledge, rack

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 선반

선배.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 선배 (先輩), formed from 선 (先, 'first, ahead, former, prior') and 배 (輩, 'generation, peer group, cohort, rank'). Attested in Classical Chinese for those of an earlier generation or elders in scholarship, and reinforced in modern institutional usage for anyone who entered a school, university, or workplace earlier.

history.meaning: elders, scholars of an earlier generation
senior colleague, upperclassman in school or profession

선배.notes: In Korean workplaces and broadcasting stations, 선배 is based strictly on year of entry (기수/입사 연도) rather than biological age, though age hierarchy still interacts delicately with it.

rootFamily.gloss: peer of the same cohort or age group (同輩)

선배님.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean formation combining the Sino-Korean noun 선배 (先輩, 'senior colleague or upperclassman', from 先 'earlier' + 輩 'cohort') with the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (from Middle Korean 님 'lord, master, esteemed person'). Used to address or refer respectfully to a senior in school or a profession.

history.meaning: senior cohort + esteemed master/lord
respected senior colleague or upperclassman

선배님.notes: In Korean office and media culture (such as broadcasting divisions), juniors routinely address their immediate mentors and older colleagues directly as 선배님 rather than by name.

cognates.word: 先輩たち (せんぱいたち)

선배님들.etymology: Polymorphemic hybrid noun phrase consisting of Sino-Korean 선배 (先輩, 'senior, elder cohort', from 先 'first, prior' + 輩 'rank, peer group'), the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (from Middle Korean 님 'master, lord'), and the native Korean plural marker -들 (from Middle Korean 들 'two, several, group').

history.meaning: respected senior colleague
respected seniors (plural address or reference)

선배님들.notes: While Korean nouns often omit plural marking when number is clear from context, adding -들 to honorific vocatives (선배님들!) is standard when addressing a group of seniors collectively.

선생님.etymology: Hybrid respectful title combining Sino-Korean 선생 (先生, literally 'born earlier', i.e. teacher/elder) with the native Korean honorific suffix -님.
선생님.notes: Addresses teachers, doctors, and respected older guests warmly and politely.

cognates.meaning: selected athlete, team player, representative competitor

선수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 선수 (選手), from 선 (選, 'to choose, select, elect') and 수 (手, 'hand; person skilled in a craft or activity'). Originally coined in the modern East Asian lexicon to denote an athlete or representative player chosen for competition, it developed a lively colloquial Korean secondary sense of a 'seasoned pro', 'expert', or 'smooth operator' in romance or social maneuvering.

history.meaning: selected competitor or representative player in sports and games
athlete, player; (colloquial) smooth operator, seasoned pro at dating or work

선수.notes: In K-dramas and everyday speech, calling someone a 선수 ('선수끼리 왜 이래?' — 'Why act like this among pros/players?') playfully implies they are a skilled flirt or veteran schemer.

rootFamily.gloss: singer, vocalist (歌手, using agentive 手)

선을.etymology: Inflected accusative form consisting of the Sino-Korean noun 선 (線, 'thread, wire, line, boundary', composed of the silk radical 糸 and phonetic 泉) followed by the native Korean consonant-stem object particle -을. In social and interpersonal contexts, 선 denotes an unspoken boundary of propriety or personal space.

history.meaning: spun thread, cord, geometric line
line, boundary (direct object form, especially in idioms of social boundaries)

선을.notes: Frequently appears in the high-frequency social idioms 선을 넘다 ('to cross the line / overstep boundaries') and 선을 긋다 ('to draw a line / keep someone at arm's length').

선택.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 선택 (選擇), meaning 'choice, selection, option', composed of two synonymous morphemes: 選 (선, 'choose, select') + 擇 (택, 'pick out, select').

history.meaning: choosing and picking out
choice, selection, option

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 선택

cognates.word: 選択する (せんたくする)

선택하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from 선택 (選擇, 'selection, choice') and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean stem combines 선 (選, 'to choose, select, sift') and 택 (擇, 'to pick out, select, discriminate'), a classic synonym-compound (병렬 합성어) attested since Classical Chinese texts such as the *Mencius*.

history.meaning: to pick out and choose between alternatives
to choose, select, make a choice

선택하다.notes: While 고르다 is the everyday native Korean verb for picking out items (like clothes or food from a menu), 선택하다 is preferred for weightier life decisions, career paths, or formal options.

rootFamily.gloss: to select one alternative over others (擇一)

선풍기.etymology: Sino-Korean 선풍기 (扇風機), combining 선 (扇, 'fan') + 풍 (風, 'wind') + 기 (機, 'machine').
선풍기.notes: Pronounced [선풍기]; contrasts with 부채 (handheld paper/bamboo fan).

cognates.meaning: seniors and juniors (expressed as 先輩後輩)
cognates.word: 先輩後輩 (せんぱいこうはい)

선후배.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound 선후배 (先後輩), contracting 선배 (先輩, 'senior') and 후배 (後輩, 'junior') around their shared head morpheme 배 (輩, 'generation, cohort, rank'). Built from 선 (先, 'first, ahead'), 후 (後, 'after, behind'), and 배 (輩, 'peer group'), encapsulating the vertical hierarchy of Korean school and workplace cohorts.

history.meaning: earlier cohort and later cohort
seniors and juniors; vertical relationship between cohorts

선후배.notes: Often paired with 사이 ('relationship') or 관계 ('relation') in phrases like 돈독한 선후배 사이 ('a close senior-junior bond').

rootFamily.gloss: before and after; front and back; context (前後)

섣부르다.etymology: Native Korean compound adjective derived from the stem 섣- (a bound allomorph of 설다, 'to be unripe, half-cooked, unfamiliar, clumsy', with /l/ > /t/ before a labial stop) combined with 부르다 ('to be full, swollen, bulging', or an adjectival formative). Literally evoking something swollen or puffed up while still half-baked or unripe, hence 'rash, premature, half-baked, ill-considered'.

history.meaning: to be unripe/unskilled + to be full/swollen
rash, premature, clumsy, half-baked in action or judgment

섣부르다.notes: Conjugates as a 르-irregular (르 불규칙) adjective: 섣부르다 -> 섣불러서, and is most frequently seen in the adnominal form 섣부른 판단 ('a rash/premature judgment') or adverbial 섣불리 ('rashly, hastily').

rootFamily.gloss: to be clumsy, sloppy, half-baked (설- + 투르다)

설거지하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from the noun 설거지 ('dishwashing, cleaning up after a meal') plus the light verb -하다. The noun 설거지 derives from the obsolete and dialectal verb 설겆다 (attested in Early Modern Korean as 설것다, 'to put utensils and tools in order, to clear away and tidy up equipment, or to finish up farming preparations after rain') nominalized with the suffix -이. Over the 20th century, its sense narrowed specifically to washing dishes and kitchenware after a meal.

history.meaning: to put utensils and tools in order; to clear away and tidy up
putting tableware in order; washing dishes after a meal
to wash the dishes, do the dishes

morphemes.meaning: to tidy up utensils, clear away (설겆-)
deverbal noun suffix (-이, spelled phonemically as 설거지)

설거지하다.notes: Because the root verb 설겆다 is no longer actively conjugated by modern speakers, the 1988 Korean orthography reform standardized the noun spelling phonemically as 설거지 (rather than morphophonemic *설겆이).

rootFamily.gloss: water used for washing dishes; dishwater

설계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 설계 (設計), combining 설 (設, 'to set up, establish, arrange') and 계 (計, 'to calculate, measure, devise a plan'). In Classical Chinese, 設計 originally meant 'to devise a stratagem or plan', and during the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was standardized across East Asia to translate technical, architectural, and engineering 'design'. Unlike the loanword 디자인 (visual/fashion styling), 설계 specifically emphasizes structural, spatial, or acoustic planning and blueprints.

history.meaning: to lay out a plan or stratagem
architectural, structural, or acoustic design and planning

설계.notes: Combines with -하다 to form the verb 설계하다 ('to design, draw up plans for a building or system').

설계도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 설계도 (設計圖), meaning 'blueprint, architectural or engineering design plan', formed from 설계 (設計, 'design, plan') + 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, chart').

history.meaning: diagram or blueprint of a planned structure
blueprint, design drawing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설계도

설계하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 설계 (設計, 'design, planning, layout', from 設 'set up, establish' + 計 'calculate, plan') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to plan and lay out a structure or system
to design, plan, engineer

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설계하다

설득하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 설득 (說得, 'persuasion') with -하다 ('to do'). Composed of 설 (說, 'to speak, explain, expound', which also has the classical reading 세 'to canvass or persuade rulers', though read 설 in modern Korean 설득) and 득 (得, 'to obtain, succeed, get through'), literally 'to explain so as to win over or gain understanding'.

history.meaning: to explain and win over someone's mind
to persuade, convince

설득하다.notes: Note the dual Hanja readings of 說 in Korean: it is read 설 in 설명 (說明) and 설득 (說得), but 열 when meaning 'to rejoice' (悅/說) and 세 in 유세 (遊說, 'political campaigning/canvassing').

설레다.etymology: Native Korean verb 설레다 ('to flutter, throb with excitement or restlessness, wave back and forth'), attested in Early Modern Korean as 설레다 and related to the ideophonic/mimetic root 설레설레 ('shaking or waving gently from side to side'). Originally describing physical agitation such as wind stirring waves or branches, it metaphorically came to express the fluttering of the heart (마음이나 가슴이 설레다) in anticipation or romance.

history.meaning: to wave, stir, be agitated physically or emotionally
to flutter, throb with excitement, anticipation, or romance

morphemes.meaning: to stir, wave, flutter with excitement (설레-)

설레다.notes: A classic Korean spelling trap: the base verb is 설레다 (NOT *설레이다), so 'my heart flutters' is 마음이 설렌다 (past 설렜다), though the derived noun 설렘 ('fluttering excitement') is very common in K-pop and drama titles.

rootFamily.gloss: gently shaking one's head or waving from side to side (mimetic adverb)
making a fuss or bustling about restlessly

cognates.word: 設令 (せつれい / たとい)

설령.etymology: Sino-Korean concessive adverb 설령 (設令), composed of 설 (設, 'to establish, set up, suppose hypothetically') and 령 (令, 'to cause, command, let it be that'). Borrowed from Classical Chinese hypothetical constructions where 設令 literally meant 'supposing that we let [X be the case]', used to introduce an extreme or counterfactual concession.

history.meaning: supposing that one causes or allows it to be so
even if, even supposing that (paired with concessive verb endings)

설령.notes: Grammatically requires a concessive verb ending later in the clause, such as -더라도, -아도/-어도, or -ㄹ지라도 (e.g., 설령 실패하더라도 'even if we should fail'). Closely synonymous with 설사 (設使).

설마.etymology: Native Korean modal adverb expressing strong doubt or disbelief ('surely not, no way, could it possibly be that...'), descending from Middle Korean 셜마.

history.meaning: surely not, hardly
surely not, by no means, no way

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설마

설명.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 설명 (說明), composed of 설 (說, 'to speak, state, expound') and 명 (明, 'bright, clear, to make clear'). Attested in Classical Chinese commentaries with the literal resultative sense of 'speaking so as to make something clear and intelligible', hence 'explanation, elucidation'.

history.meaning: to clarify or illuminate a text or principle through speech
explanation, description, account

설명.notes: Combines productively with suffixes like -서 ('document') to form 설명서 ('instruction manual') and -회 ('meeting') to form 설명회 ('briefing session').

설명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 설명 (說明, 'explanation, elucidation', literally 'speaking to make clear') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to explain and make clear
to explain, describe, account for

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설명하다

cognates.meaning: to explain for someone (説明する + くれる/あげる)
cognates.word: 説明してくれる (せつめいしてくれる)

설명해주다.etymology: Compound benefactive verb constructed from the Sino-Korean noun 설명 (說明, 'explanation', from 說 'speak, expound' + 明 'make clear'), the light verb stem 하- conjugated with the infinitive/connective ending -여 (contracted to 해), and the native Korean auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's benefit'). Literally 'to give the act of explaining'.

history.meaning: to make clear by speaking + do and give
to explain for someone, give an explanation to someone

설명해주다.notes: Under standard Korean spacing rules, main verb + auxiliary verb can be spaced (설명해 주다) or written together as a single orthographic unit (설명해주다); when explaining to an elder or senior, 주다 shifts to 드리다 (설명해 드리다).

cognates.meaning: adding frost upon snow; making matters worse
cognates.word: 雪上加霜 (せつじょうかそう)

cognates.meaning: adding frost on top of snow; one disaster after another

설상가상.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean idiom (사자성어) 설상가상 (雪上加霜), composed of 설 (雪, 'snow'), 상 (上, 'top, upon'), 가 (加, 'to add'), and 상 (霜, 'frost'). Originating in Song-dynasty Chan (Zen) Buddhist literature such as the *Transmission of the Lamp* (*景德傳燈錄*), it literally depicts 'adding frost on top of snow', serving as a vivid metaphor for one misfortune piling directly onto another.

history.meaning: adding frost on top of snow (Chan Buddhist metaphor for redundant or compounded trouble)
to make matters worse; misfortune on top of misfortune

설상가상.notes: Frequently used with the instrumental particle -으로 as a sentence-initial adverbial: 설상가상으로 ('To make matters worse, ...'). Its native Korean proverbial equivalent is 엎친 데 덮친 격 ('like being covered/pinned down right after falling face-down').

cognates.meaning: establishment, creation, setting, fictional premise/character setup
to set up, configure; setting, premise

설정.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 설정 (設定), composed of 설 (設, 'to establish, set up, arrange') and 정 (定, 'to fix, decide, settle'). Beyond its technical sense of 'configuration' or 'system settings', in Korean broadcasting, drama writing, and pop culture it denotes a 'character premise, fictional setup, or staged persona' adopted for a show.

history.meaning: to establish and fix rules, institutions, or conditions
setting, configuration; fictional premise, staged concept or role-play in variety/drama

설정.notes: In Korean variety shows and internet slang, calling someone's behavior 설정 ('이거 설정 아니야?' — 'Isn't this staged/a bit?') or 설정샷 ('a staged photo pretending to be candid') is ubiquitous.

rootFamily.gloss: to set up, configure, establish a premise (設定하다)
staged photo pretending to be candid (設定 + shot)

설탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 설탕 (雪糖), literally 'snow sugar', from 설 (雪, 'snow') and 당/탕 (糖, 'sugar').
설탕.notes: Named for the fine white crystals of refined sugar resembling fresh snow.

섬세하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb combining 섬세 (纖細, 'delicate, fine, subtle') with the native suffix -하다. Both Hanja characters share the silk/thread radical (糸): 섬 (纖, 'fine silk thread, slender, minute') and 세 (細, 'thin, fine, detailed, minute'). Originally describing finely woven textiles or slender physical features, it extended to describe meticulous artistic craftsmanship and thoughtful, sensitive attention to emotional detail.

history.meaning: fine and thin like delicate silk threads; slender
delicate, exquisite, finely detailed; thoughtful and sensitive to subtle feelings

섬세하다.notes: Used as high praise in Korean for both artistic direction (섬세한 연출 'delicate/nuanced directing') and interpersonal warmth (배려가 섬세하다 'to be thoughtfully attentive to detail').

섭섭하다.etymology: Native Korean psychological adjective formed from the reduplicated root 섭섭- (expressing a lingering sense of emptiness, regret at parting, or mild emotional hurt when expectations of affection are unmet) and the adjectival suffix -하다. Attested in Early Modern Korean texts (such as the 17th–18th century *Yeogeo Yuhae* 譯語類解) as 섭섭흐다.

history.meaning: to feel regretful at parting or wistfully unsatisfied
to feel sad at parting; to feel hurt, let down, or mildly disappointed by someone's lack of consideration

morphemes.meaning: feeling wistful, regretful, or emotionally let down (섭섭-)

섭섭하다.notes: Encapsulates two distinct culturally rich nuances in Korean: (1) wistful sadness when saying goodbye to someone dear, and (2) feeling slightly hurt or neglected when a friend or colleague isn't as warm or considerate as expected (closely akin to 서운하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel hurt or show disappointment (externalized verb)
bittersweet; feeling both relieved and sad (시원- + 섭섭하다)

섭섭해하다.etymology: Native Korean derived psychological verb formed by attaching the psychological verbalizer construction -어하다 (here -여하다 > -해하다) to the descriptive adjective 섭섭하다 ('to be hurt, disappointed, sad at parting'). In Korean grammar, internal-state adjectives like 섭섭하다 cannot directly take third-person subjects in declarative sentences without -어하다, which externalizes the feeling into an observable emotional reaction ('to feel/act hurt').

history.meaning: to manifest regretful or hurt feelings
to feel hurt, take offense mildly, or show disappointment

섭섭해하다.notes: Use 섭섭하다 for first-person feelings ('나는 섭섭해' — 'I feel hurt') or second-person questions, and 섭섭해하다 when describing a third person's feelings ('선배가 섭섭해할 거야' — 'Senior will feel hurt').

rootFamily.gloss: to feel hurt or disappointed (near-synonym from 서운하다)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 섭섭하다 (파생어 섭섭해하다)

cognates.meaning: public relations, external liaison, client relations

섭외.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 섭외 (涉外), composed of 섭 (涉, 'to wade across water; to pass through, engage with, negotiate') and 외 (外, 'outside, external'). Coined in modern Japanese (渉外, shōgai) and adopted into Korean to mean 'external liaison, public relations, or negotiation with outside parties', it underwent a distinctive semantic specialization in the South Korean entertainment and broadcasting industry to mean 'casting, booking, or recruiting guests, actors, or filming locations'.

history.meaning: external relations, liaison with outside organizations or foreign parties
external liaison; (broadcasting/media) casting, booking guests, talent, or locations

morphemes.meaning: to wade across; to engage with, negotiate (涉)

섭외.notes: A quintessential *The Producers* (*프로듀사*) broadcasting term: whereas English uses 'casting' for actors and 'booking' for variety/talk-show guests or venues, Korean PDs and writers use 섭외 for all of them (게스트 섭외, 장소 섭외).

rootFamily.gloss: to cast, book guests or locations; to liaise externally (涉外하다)

섭외하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from 섭외 (涉外, 'external liaison; casting, booking', from 涉 'to wade across, engage with, negotiate' + 外 'outside, external') and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). In Korean media production, it specifically denotes the process of contacting, negotiating with, and securing celebrities, guests, or venues for a program.

history.meaning: to conduct external relations or negotiate with outside parties
to cast actors, book guests/celebrities, or secure filming locations for a broadcast

섭외하다.notes: In Korean TV production, PDs and writers distinguish 캐스팅하다 (often used for main drama roles) from 섭외하다 (used broadly for variety show guests, cameo appearances, interviewees, and shooting locations).

cognates.meaning: to ingest, absorb, take in (nutrients or culture)
cognates.word: 摂取する (せっしゅする)

cognates.meaning: to absorb, take in, ingest (nutrients); to photograph

섭취하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 섭취 (攝取, 'ingestion, intake, absorption') with -하다 ('to do'). Built from 섭 (攝, 'to draw in, gather, hold, assist, nourish') and 취 (取, 'to take, grasp, obtain'). Originally a Buddhist term (섭취불사 攝取不捨, a Buddha gathering in and never forsaking sentient beings), it was repurposed in modern East Asian physiology and nutrition for biological intake of food, water, and nutrients.

history.meaning: to gather in and embrace (Buddhist); to draw in and take
to ingest, consume, take in nutrients, calories, or fluids

섭취하다.notes: Because 섭취하다 sounds clinical and nutritional ('to ingest/take in nutrients'), using it in everyday conversation instead of 먹다 ('to eat') often creates a humorous, health-obsessed, or stiffly formal tone.

rootFamily.gloss: taking care of one's health, nutrition (攝生)

성격.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성격 (性格), composed of 성 (性, 'inborn nature, disposition, mind', formed from the heart radical 忄 and phonetic 生 'birth, life') and 격 (格, 'standard, pattern, frame, status, character'). Popularized in modern East Asian psychology (translating German *Charakter* / English *personality*) to denote an individual's enduring psychological traits and behavioral pattern.

history.meaning: natural disposition and standard of character; psychological personality
personality, character; nature or characteristic of an event or organization

성격.notes: Compare the three common 'character/nature' words in this set: 성격 is standard psychological 'personality', 성질 is 'inherent property' or colloquial 'bad temper', and 성품 is elevated 'moral character/temperament'.

성공.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성공 (成功), from 성 (成, 'to complete, accomplish, become') and 공 (功, 'merit, achievement, work, result'). Attested in early Classical Chinese texts (such as the *Book of Documents* 書經 and *Shiji* 史記) as a verb-object construction meaning 'to accomplish a meritorious work or bring an endeavor to completion', later nominalized as 'success'.

history.meaning: to accomplish a task or achieve meritorious results
success, achievement, prosperity

성공.notes: Its direct antonym is 실패 (失敗, 'failure'); in modern Korean slang, 성덕 (성공한 덕후) means a 'successful fan' who gets to meet or work with their idol (like Cindy's fans in *The Producers*).

성당.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성당 (聖堂), composed of 성 (聖, 'holy, sacred, sage') and 당 (堂, 'hall, large building, temple'). Historically used in Confucianism for the shrine hall honoring Confucius (문묘 성당), it became standardized in Korean Christian terminology Specifically to designate a Roman Catholic church or cathedral, contrasting with 교회 (敎會, 'house of teaching/assembly') used by Protestant denominations.

history.meaning: sacred hall; shrine hall dedicated to sages or holy figures
Catholic church or cathedral

성당.notes: A vital cultural distinction in Korea: going to 성당 (성당에 다니다) immediately identifies someone as Roman Catholic (천주교), whereas going to 교회 (교회에 다니다) identifies someone as Protestant (개신교).

rootFamily.gloss: dining hall, restaurant (食堂, sharing 堂)

성민.etymology: Common Korean given name 성민, typically written with Sino-Korean hanja combinations such as 成民 ('accomplished among the people') or 聖旼 ('wise and gentle').

history.meaning: given name

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 성민

cognates.word: 成長する (せいちょうする)

성장하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 성장 (成長, 'growth, maturation') with the native light verb -하다 ('to do'). Formed from 성 (成, 'to become, complete, form, mature') and 장 (長, 'to grow, increase, develop; long, elder'). Used for biological maturation of living organisms, personal and emotional development of characters, and macroeconomic expansion.

history.meaning: to grow to maturity, develop in stature and form
to grow, mature, develop (physically, personally, or economically)

성장하다.notes: Whereas native Korean 자라다 ('to grow') and 크다 ('to get big/grow up') are used in everyday speech for children, plants, or hair, 성장하다 carries a more reflective or formal tone for personal maturation or economic growth (경제 성장).

rootFamily.gloss: growth, development of a child or plant (發育)

cognates.word: 成績表 (せいせきひょう)

cognates.meaning: report card, transcript (commonly 成績單, also 成績表)

성적표.etymology: Three-morpheme Sino-Korean compound 성적표 (成績表), built from 성적 (成績, 'results, grades, performance record') and the suffixoid 표 (表, 'table, chart, surface, list'). In 성적, 성 (成, 'to accomplish, complete') combines with 적 (績, 'to spin hemp/silk thread; accumulated achievement or merit', sharing the thread radical 糸). Literally 'a chart of accomplished merits/results'.

history.meaning: achieved merit/results + tabular chart or document
report card, academic transcript; metaphorical scorecard of performance (such as TV ratings)

성적표.notes: In Korean broadcasting and journalism, morning viewership ratings (시청률) are routinely referred to metaphorically as a PD's or drama's 성적표 ('report card').

rootFamily.gloss: grades, academic record, performance results (成績)
timetable, schedule (時間表, sharing 表)

성질.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성질 (性質), composed of 성 (性, 'inborn nature, disposition') and 질 (質, 'substance, matter, inherent quality, constitution'). In scientific and formal contexts it denotes the 'intrinsic property or nature' of a substance or phenomenon (물리적 성질), while in colloquial Korean speech it underwent pejorative narrowing to mean 'fiery temper, irritability, or outburst of anger'.

history.meaning: inborn nature and essential substance of a person or thing
intrinsic property or quality; (colloquial) temper, irritability, outburst of anger

성질.notes: Be careful with register: saying someone has a good/bad 성격 refers neutrally to their personality, whereas idioms like 성질 내다 ('to lose one's temper'), 성질 부리다 ('to throw a fit'), or 성질이 급하다 ('to be hot-tempered/impatient') focus on volatility.

성품.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성품 (性品), formed from 성 (性, 'inborn nature, human disposition') and 품 (品, 'grade, class, moral quality, character, demeanor'). Attested in Neo-Confucian and Joseon-era prose to describe the refined moral quality and innate temperament of a person's nature, carrying a more dignified and evaluative tone than everyday 성격.

history.meaning: innate disposition and moral grade of human nature
moral character, innate temperament, personal disposition

성품.notes: Usually collocates with positive or evaluative adjectives such as 성품이 곱다 ('to have a gentle/fine character') or 성품이 인자하다 ('to have a benevolent nature'), though it can also be used ironically when someone reveals a harsh side.

성함.etymology: Sino-Korean honorific compound 성함 (姓銜), meaning 'esteemed name (polite/honorific word for another person's name)', formed from 姓 (성, 'surname, family name') + 銜 (함, 'official title, respected name').

history.meaning: surname and respected title/name
name (honorific)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 성함

성형.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 성형 (成形), composed of 성 (成, 'to accomplish, become, form') and 형 (形, 'shape, form, appearance'). In modern Korean, it functions almost exclusively as an ellipsis of 성형수술 (成形手術, 'plastic or reconstructive surgery'), especially cosmetic procedures altering facial features.

history.meaning: forming a shape; bringing into physical form
reconstructive or plastic surgery
cosmetic or plastic surgery

성형.notes: While 整形 (정형) is used for orthopedics (정형외과), Korean uses 成形 (성형) for cosmetic and plastic surgery (성형외과), unlike Japanese where 美容整形 uses 整形.

rootFamily.gloss: plastic or cosmetic surgery (成形手術)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 성형 (成形)

세.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral meaning 'three (3)' used before nouns and classifiers (e.g., 세 개, 세 번), derived by pre-consonantal final drop from 셋 ('three', Middle Korean 세ㅎ / 셋). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 세 (歲 'years of age'; 貰 'rent').

history.meaning: three (adnominal)
three (before nouns/counters)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세

세계.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 세계 (世界), combining 세 (世, 'generation, age, temporal flow') and 계 (界, 'boundary, realm, spatial extent'). Originating in Chinese Buddhist translations (such as the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) as a semantic calque of Sanskrit lokadhātu ('world-realm'), it united time (世) and space (界) to denote the entire cosmos before generalizing to the secular world or a specific sphere of activity.

history.meaning: world-realm, cosmos in Buddhist cosmology
totality of past/present/future time (世) and directional space (界); the universe
the world, global society, or a specific domain/field

세계.notes: Whereas 세상 (世上) emphasizes the human, lived social world ('in the world of people'), 세계 (世界) refers to the objective globe, international arena, or a specialized domain (e.g., 방송 세계, 'the broadcasting world').

세금.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 稅金, combining 稅 (세금 세, 'grain levy, tax', written with the grain radical 禾) and 金 (쇠 금, 'metal, money'). While classical fiscal documents used 稅 alone for agricultural tribute, modern Korean combines it with 금 to denote monetary taxes.

세다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'strong, powerful, forceful, intense', descending from Middle Korean 셰다 ('strong, fierce'). Also homophonous with native Korean verbs 세다 ('to count', from Middle Korean 헤다) and 세다 ('to turn gray/white of hair', from Middle Korean 싀다).

history.meaning: to be strong; to count; to turn white
strong, powerful, intense; to count; to turn gray

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세다

세대교체.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 세대교체 (世代交替), formed from 세대 (世代, 'generation, era', from 世 'thirty-year span, generation' + 代 'substitute, era') and 교체 (交替, 'replacement, alternation', from 交 'to exchange, intersect' + 替 'to replace, substitute'). It denotes the transition of leadership, talent, or cultural dominance from an older cohort to a younger one.

history.meaning: succession of eras + mutual replacement
generational turnover in politics, sports, or entertainment

세대교체.notes: Frequently used in Korean broadcasting, sports, and politics when veteran cast members or players are replaced by younger newcomers to refresh ratings or performance.

세리머니.etymology: Borrowed from English ceremony (ultimately from Latin caerimōnia, 'sacredness, ritual awe'). In contemporary South Korean usage, alongside its general sense of a formal ritual (such as an opening or awards ceremony), it underwent semantic specialization in sports and entertainment media to denote an expressive celebratory gesture or victory routine—most famously a soccer player's goal celebration (골 세리머니) or a celebrity's pledge performance.

history.meaning: religious worship, sacred ritual
formal ritual or public observance
formal ceremony; expressive victory or goal celebration in sports and media

morphemes.meaning: ceremony; celebratory gesture or routine (from English ceremony)

세리머니.notes: A classic false friend for English speakers: in Korean sports and variety shows, 골 세리머니 means 'goal celebration' (the dance or gesture after scoring), not a formal award ceremony.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 세리머니

세상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 세상 (世上), meaning 'the world, society, life among people', composed of 世 (세, 'world, age, generation') + 上 (상, 'upon, realm').

history.meaning: the world of living people
the world, society, life

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세상

세상에.etymology: Lexicalized interjection formed from the Sino-Korean noun 세상 (世上, literally 'upon the world', from 世 'world, generation' + 上 'above, upon') combined with the native Korean locative particle -에 ('in, at, on'). Literally meaning 'in the world!', it grammaticalized as an exclamation of astonishment, disbelief, or sympathy ('Goodness!', 'Oh my!', 'What in the world!').

history.meaning: in the world, among living people
in the world (locative phrase) > exclamation of surprise or shock ('goodness!', 'oh my!')

세상에.notes: Intonation determines the emotion: a rising-falling contour expresses sympathetic shock ('Oh dear, how awful!'), while a sharp drop expresses incredulity ('No way!'). Often expanded to 어머 세상에 ('Oh my goodness!').

rootFamily.gloss: world affairs, ways of the world (世上事)

세상에나.etymology: Lexicalized Korean exclamation formed from 세상 (世上, 'the world', from 世 'generation, age' and 上 'upon, realm'), the locative particle -에 ('in'), and the emotive particle -나 expressing surprise at something beyond expectation. Literally 'in this world even!', it intensifies the already common interjection 세상에 ('oh my word!'). Speakers use it warmly when delighted, astonished, or struck by an uncanny coincidence.
세상에나.notes: Stands at the start of a clause followed by a comma; warmer and slightly more expressive than plain 세상에.

cognates.meaning: to wash one's hands; (euphemistic) to use the toilet
washing hands; restroom (as お手洗い)

세수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 세수 (洗手), composed of 세 (洗, 'to wash, rinse') and 수 (手, 'hand'). Although the Hanja literally denote 'washing one's hands' (a sense preserved in Chinese 洗手), in Korean the compound underwent semantic widening and shift to mean 'washing one's face (and hands)', replacing or competing with the more formal 세면 (洗面, 'washing the face').

history.meaning: washing the hands (often before rituals or meals)
washing the hands and face
washing one's face in daily hygiene

세수.notes: Despite containing 수 (手, 'hand'), 세수하다 in everyday Korean specifically means 'to wash one's face' (washing hands alone is 손 씻다). Compare Chinese 洗手間 (xǐshǒujiān, 'washroom/toilet').

rootFamily.gloss: washbasin, sink for washing the face (洗手臺)
washing the face, formal register (洗面)

세우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to make stand, erect, build, set up; to stop or park (a vehicle); to establish (a plan or rule)', descending from Middle Korean 셰우다 / 세오다 (causative of 셔다 > 서다 'to stand').

history.meaning: to make stand, erect, establish
to stand up, erect, build, stop (a car), form (a plan)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세우다

세워주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 세우다 ('to make stand, erect, stop a vehicle', the morphological causative of 서다 'to stand', from Middle Korean 셔다 'to stand' + causative suffix -이-/-우- yielding 셰다 > 세우다), linked by the infinitive/connective suffix -어 to the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone', Middle Korean 주다). In transit contexts, it means 'to pull over or stop a vehicle for someone'.

history.meaning: to cause to stand / erect + to give
to erect, establish, or bring a moving vehicle to a halt for someone's benefit

morphemes.meaning: to make stand, bring to a halt, establish

세워주다.notes: Essential phrase for Korean taxis and buses: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요 ('Driver, please let me off / stop the car here'). Polite honorific requests replace 주다 with 드리다 or 주세요.

rootFamily.gloss: to stand, to come to a stop
to make stand, to park/stop a car, to establish a plan
to stand up straight, to erect

세워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb meaning 'to be erected, be built, be established, be set up', formed from the causative verb 세우다 ('to erect, set up') plus the passive/inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

history.meaning: to erect + passive auxiliary
to be erected, built, established

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세워지다

세월.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 세월 (歲月), meaning 'time, years and months, the flow of time', composed of 歲 (세, 'year') + 月 (월, 'month').

history.meaning: years and months -> the passage of time
time, years, passing time

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세월

cognates.meaning: group of matching items; theatrical or film stage scenery

세트.etymology: Borrowed from English set (in its nominal senses derived from the Old English verb settan 'to cause to sit or place' and partially merged with Old French sette 'sequence, group'). In Korean broadcasting and film production (such as *The Producers*), it refers specifically to a constructed studio stage set (세트장), while in commerce and dining it denotes a bundled combo meal or matched assortment.

history.meaning: collection of things belonging together; theatrical scenery constructed for a production
broadcast/film studio set; combo meal or matched product package; tennis/volleyball set

morphemes.meaning: stage set, matched group, combo (from English set)

세트.notes: In Korean TV production, an indoor constructed filming stage is called a 세트 or 세트장 (set + 場 'place'), contrasted with 야외 촬영 ('outdoor location shooting'). Often pronounced with tense [쎄트] in colloquial speech.

rootFamily.gloss: combo meal at a restaurant (set + menu)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 세트

cognates.meaning: act of placing, arranging, or configuring

세팅.etymology: Borrowed from the English verbal noun setting (from set + -ing). In Korean, rather than meaning 'narrative backdrop or environment' (which is usually 배경, 背景), 세팅 denotes the active preparation, arrangement, or configuration of equipment, stage props, dining tables, computer systems, or hair and makeup styling before an event or broadcast.

history.meaning: action of putting in place, mounting, or adjusting equipment and hair
setup of broadcast gear/cameras, table arrangement, or hair/makeup styling

morphemes.meaning: to place, arrange, configure (from English set)
action or result of arranging (from English -ing)

세팅.notes: In Korean TV stations and salons, 세팅 always implies active preparation ('getting things set up' or 'having one's hair styled/permed'), never the literary setting of a story. Colloquially pronounced [쎄팅].

rootFamily.gloss: to set up, arrange, style (setting + 하다)
stage set, matched group (from English set)
hair perm using heated rollers (setting + perm)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 세팅

세팅하다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb combining the English loanword 세팅 (setting, 'setup, arrangement, configuration, styling') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, make', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). It functions as the standard transitive and intransitive verb for setting up broadcast equipment, laying out a table, configuring software, or styling hair and wardrobe for filming.

history.meaning: English verbal noun setting + native Korean light verb 'to do'
to set up equipment, arrange a venue/table, or finish hair and makeup styling

세팅하다.notes: Used heavily on film sets (e.g., 카메라 세팅하다 'to set up the cameras', 조명 세팅하다 'to rig the lighting') as well as in restaurants (테이블 세팅하다 'to set the table').

rootFamily.gloss: to be set up or prepared (setting + 되다)
stage set, matched group (from English set)

cognates.meaning: faculty of perception, intuitive knack or judgment
good taste, flair, knack, stylistic sensibility

센스.etymology: Borrowed from English sense (from Middle French sens, from Latin sēnsus 'perception, feeling, meaning', from sentīre 'to feel, perceive'), heavily influenced by Japanese センス (sensu). In Korean, 센스 specifically denotes social perceptiveness, quick wit, aesthetic flair, or tactful situational awareness rather than the five physical senses (which are 감각, 感覺) or semantic meaning (의미, 意味).

history.meaning: faculty of perceiving, feeling, thought, or meaning
intuitive knack, aesthetic judgment, or flair (narrowed in Japanese and Korean)
wit, tact, aesthetic flair, or quick situational intuition

morphemes.meaning: wit, flair, tact, sensibility (from English sense)

센스.notes: The idiomatic expression 센스 있다 ('to have sense') is high praise in Korean workplace and social life, meaning someone is perceptive, considerate, witty, or anticipates what is needed without being told.

rootFamily.gloss: to be witty, perceptive, stylish, or tactful (sense + 있다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 센스

센터.etymology: Borrowed from English center / centre ('central point; facility or organization dedicated to a particular activity or service').

history.meaning: central facility or hub
center (community center, service center)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 센터

센티.etymology: Clipped loanword from 센티미터 (from English centimeter / French centimètre, coined from Latin centum 'hundred' + French mètre, from Greek métron 'measure'). Following the East Asian pattern of truncating long metric compounds to their prefix (compare Japanese センチ senchi and キロ kiro), Korean routinely uses 센티 in spoken language as a standalone unit noun for 'centimeter'. (In a separate homophonous clipping, 센티하다 derives from English sentimental.)

history.meaning: metric unit equal to one hundredth of a meter
centimeter (colloquial truncation of the metric unit)

morphemes.meaning: centimeter (truncated from 센티미터, from Latin centi- 'hundredth')

센티.notes: In everyday Korean speech, people say 몇 센티예요? ('How many centimeters is it?') rather than the full 몇 센티미터예요?, frequently pronouncing it [쎈티] or colloquially [쎈치] (under older Japanese influence).

rootFamily.gloss: centimeter, full standard form (from English centimeter)
to feel sentimental or melancholic (from English sentimental + 하다)
millimeter, often clipped to 밀리 (from English millimeter)

센티미터.etymology: Borrowed from English centimeter / centimetre ('one hundredth of a meter, cm', from French centimètre).

history.meaning: one hundredth of a meter (cm)
centimeter (cm)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 센티미터

셈.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun derived from the verb stem 세- (세다, 'to count, reckon, calculate', evolving from 15th-century Middle Korean 헤다 'to count, ponder' via palatalized 셰다 > 세다) plus the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ. From its concrete sense of 'counting, calculation, arithmetic', 셈 grammaticalized into a bound (dependent) noun in the construction -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다, meaning 'it amounts to, it counts as, or in effect it is'.

history.meaning: to count, reckon, think > act of counting or reckoning
calculation, reckoning, account; conjecture or supposition
calculation; dependent noun meaning 'amounts to, practically counts as' (in -ㄴ/는 셈이다)

morphemes.meaning: substantive nominalizer forming nouns from verb stems

셈.notes: In drama dialogue, -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 ('it amounts to X / it's practically X') and -(으)ㄹ 셈이다 ('to intend/plan to do X') are high-frequency grammatical patterns built on the metaphor of mental calculation.

rootFamily.gloss: to calculate, settle accounts, consider (from Middle Korean 헤아리다)

셋.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'three (3)', descending from Middle Korean 셋 / 세ㅎ ('three').

history.meaning: three
three (3)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셋

셋째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral and noun meaning 'third (3rd); the third child', formed from 셋 ('three', Middle Korean 셋) plus the native ordinal suffix -째.

history.meaning: three + ordinal suffix
third (3rd); third child

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셋째

셔츠.etymology: Borrowed from English shirt / shirts ('collared upper-body garment with sleeves', entered via the plural form shirts).

history.meaning: buttoned or collared upper garment
shirt, dress shirt

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셔츠

셔터.etymology: Borrowed from English shutter ('rolling metal security door over a shopfront or window; mechanical or electronic camera shutter').

history.meaning: hinged or rolling cover for an opening; camera shutter
rolling storefront shutter; camera shutter

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셔터

셰프님.etymology: Hybrid honorific noun meaning 'Chef (respectful title of address or reference)', combining the French/English loanword 셰프 (chef, 'head cook') with the native Korean honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: professional chef + honorific suffix
Chef (polite/respectful address)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셰프님

소감.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 소감 (所感), composed of theClassical Chinese pronominal relativizer 소 (所, 'that which, place') and 감 (感, 'to feel, be moved, emotion'). Literally meaning 'that which is felt' or 'what one has experienced emotionally', it denotes one's personal impressions, reflections, or acceptance remarks upon winning an award or completing a project.

history.meaning: that which moves the heart; what one feels or perceives
personal impressions, thoughts, or acceptance speech remarks

morphemes.meaning: that which, place, object of action (所)

소감.notes: A staple word in Korean broadcasting and award shows: 수상 소감 (受賞所感) means 'award acceptance speech/remarks', and interviewers routinely ask 소감이 어떠세요? ('How do you feel about it? / What are your thoughts?').

rootFamily.gloss: emotion, deep impression, being moved (感動)
impression, review after reading or watching (感想)

소개팅.etymology: South Korean neologism and morphological blend (portmanteau) coined in the late 20th century from Sino-Korean 소개 (紹介, 'introduction', from 紹 'to connect, continue' + 介 'to mediate, lie between') and the clipped English suffixoid -팅 (extracted from 미팅 meeting, which in Korean university slang meant a group blind date). Thus 소개팅 specifically denotes a one-on-one blind date arranged through a mutual acquaintance's introduction.

history.meaning: personal introduction + group social gathering/blind date
one-on-one blind date set up by a mutual friend or matchmaker

morphemes.meaning: social gathering or date (clipped from English meeting 미팅)

소개팅.notes: Korean distinguishes three types of arranged dates: 소개팅 (casual one-on-one blind date introduced by a friend), 미팅 (group blind date, often among college students), and 맞선 or 선 (formal matchmaking meeting aimed directly at marriage).

rootFamily.gloss: to go on a one-on-one blind date (紹介ting + 하다)
meeting; group blind date (from English meeting)

소개팅하다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, perform', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다) to the South Korean blend noun 소개팅 (소개 紹介 'introduction' + -팅 from English meeting). It means to go on or participate in a one-on-one blind date arranged by a third party.

history.meaning: one-on-one blind date + native light verb 'to do'
to go on a blind date arranged through a mutual acquaintance

소개팅하다.notes: In colloquial Korean, alongside 소개팅하다, speakers frequently say 소개팅에 나가다 ('to go out to a blind date') or 소개팅을 주선하다 ('to set up/arrange a blind date for someone').

소개하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb combining 소개 (紹介, 'introduction, mediation', from 紹 'to continue, connect' + 介 'to lie between, act as intermediary') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). In Classical Chinese (such as the *Records of the Grand Historian*), 紹介 referred to intermediary attendants who relayed messages between host and guest during formal rituals, before generalizing to introducing people, ideas, or romantic partners.

history.meaning: ritual intermediary who relays messages between host and guest; to mediate
to introduce people to one another or present a topic
to introduce, present, or set someone up with a romantic partner or job

소개하다.notes: Note that Mandarin Chinese reverses the two characters as 介紹 (jièshào) and Vietnamese uses giới thiệu (介紹介), whereas Korean and Japanese preserve the Classical Chinese order 紹介 (소개 / shōkai). When followed by 주다 (소개해 주다), it often means 'to set someone up on a date'.

rootFamily.gloss: letter of introduction or cover letter (紹介書)

소고기김밥.etymology: Native Korean four-part compound noun: 소고기 ('beef', composed of 소 'cow, ox, cattle' [from Middle Korean 쇼] + 고기 'meat, flesh' [from Middle Korean 고기]) + 김밥 ('seaweed rice roll', composed of 김 'edible laver/seaweed, Porphyra' + 밥 'cooked grain/rice' [from Middle Korean 밥]). Both 소고기 and 쇠고기 (where 쇠- reflects 소 + genitive particle -ㅅ/-의) are recognized as standard Korean forms for 'beef'.

history.meaning: ox/cattle + flesh/meat; laver seaweed + cooked rice
cooked rice and seasoned beef rolled in dried laver seaweed

morphemes.meaning: cow, ox, cattle (from Middle Korean 쇼)

소고기김밥.notes: A ubiquitous, quick meal on busy Korean television production sets (*프로듀사*) when staff have no time for a sit-down meal. Both 소고기 and 쇠고기 are official standard Korean spellings for beef.

cognates.meaning: under the jurisdiction or administration of

소관.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 소관 (所管), formed from the Classical Chinese object-relativizing particle 소 (所, 'that which') and 관 (管, 'bamboo pipe, key, to govern, administer, take charge of'). Literally meaning 'that which one governs or manages', it denotes official jurisdiction, administrative purview, or sphere of responsibility within a bureaucracy or organization.

history.meaning: that which is under one's administrative control or custody
official jurisdiction, administrative responsibility, or departmental purview

morphemes.meaning: that which, place, object of action (所)
to govern, manage, control; bamboo tube (管)

소관.notes: Frequently heard in bureaucratic or office dialogue to deflect or claim responsibility: 그건 내 소관이 아니야 ('That's not in my jurisdiction / That's not my department').

rootFamily.gloss: jurisdiction, control over a territory or sphere (管轄)
taking charge of, hosting, or subjectivity (主管)

소금.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'salt', descending from Middle Korean 소곰 ('salt') through unrounding/delabialization of the second-syllable vowel (소곰 > 소금).

history.meaning: salt
salt

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소금

소독.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소독 (消毒), composed of 소 (消, 'to melt away, extinguish, eliminate') and 독 (毒, 'poison, toxin, harmful agent'). Originally used in traditional Chinese medicine for neutralizing toxins or pathogenic heat in the body, it was adopted in modern East Asian medicine (via Meiji-era Japanese 消毒 *shōdoku*) to translate Western concepts of medical disinfection, sterilization, and sanitization.

history.meaning: dispelling or neutralizing bodily toxins and venom in traditional medicine
destruction of pathogenic microorganisms; medical disinfection and sterilization
history.stage: Modern East Asian medical terminology (19th–20th c.)

소독.notes: Used both literally for medical/hygienic sanitization (손 소독제 'hand sanitizer', 상처 소독 'disinfecting a wound') and jokingly in colloquial speech (알코올 소독 'alcohol disinfection', i.e., going out for drinks).

rootFamily.gloss: disinfectant, antiseptic, hand sanitizer (消毒藥 / 消毒劑)

소독하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 소독 (消毒, 'disinfection, sanitization', from 消 'to eliminate, extinguish' + 毒 'poison, pathogen') combined with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, perform', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). It means to disinfect a wound, sterilize medical instruments, or sanitize surfaces and hands against germs.

history.meaning: to neutralize poison/pathogens + native light verb 'to do'
to disinfect a wound, sanitize hands/surfaces, or fumigate against pests

소독하다.notes: Covers everything from dabbing antiseptic on a scrape (상처를 소독하다) to boiling baby bottles (열탕 소독하다) and municipal pest fumigation (방역 소독하다).

소라.etymology: Korean female given name 소라, homonymous with the native Korean noun 소라 ('horned turban shell, conch', attested since Middle Korean 소라).

history.meaning: turban shell; female given name

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소라

소리.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'sound, voice, noise, song, remark', descending from Middle Korean 소리 ('sound, voice').

history.meaning: sound, voice, cry
sound, voice, noise

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소리

소리치다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to shout, yell, cry out loudly', formed from 소리 ('loud voice, cry') + 치다 ('to strike, utter or emit forcefully').

history.meaning: voice/cry + to emit forcefully
to shout, yell, exclaim

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소리치다

cognates.meaning: that which one hopes for or looks toward

소망하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 소망 (所望, 'that which is hoped for; earnest wish or aspiration', composed of the Classical Chinese object-relativizer 所 'that which' + 望 'to gaze from afar, hope, expect') plus the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). It expresses a deep, earnest longing or heartfelt aspiration.

history.meaning: that toward which one gazes or places one's hopes; expectation or desire
to earnestly wish for, long for, or aspire to

morphemes.meaning: to gaze into the distance, hope, expect (望)

소망하다.notes: Carries an elevated, literary, or spiritual tone compared to everyday 바라다 ('to hope/want') or 원하다 ('to want'); in Korean Protestant tradition, 믿음, 소망, 사랑 translates 'faith, hope, and love' (1 Corinthians 13:13).

소매.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'sleeve (of a garment)', descending from Middle Korean 소매 ('sleeve', historically linked to 손 'hand, arm' + -매). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 소매 (小賣, 'retail sale').

history.meaning: sleeve of a garment
sleeve; retail (小賣)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소매

cognates.meaning: what one has heard, hearsay, information
what one hears, firsthand/secondhand report (often in 所見所聞)
