소문.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 소문 (所聞), composed of the Classical Chinese object-relativizing particle 소 (所, 'that which') and 문 (聞, 'to hear, news, reputation'). Literally meaning 'that which is heard', it evolved in Korean from neutral 'hearsay or tidings' into the standard everyday word for 'rumor, gossip, or word-of-mouth reputation'.

history.meaning: that which has been heard; reports or tidings reaching the ear
rumor, gossip, word of mouth circulating among the public

소문.notes: While 소문 often translates to 'rumor' or 'gossip' (헛소문 'false rumor'), it can also mean positive word-of-mouth fame, as in 소문난 맛집 ('a restaurant famous by word of mouth').

rootFamily.gloss: for a rumor or reputation to spread (所聞나다)
to spread a rumor or word of mouth (所聞내다)

소문나다.etymology: Hybrid compound intransitive verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 소문 (所聞, 'rumor, word of mouth', from 所 'that which' + 聞 'to hear') with the native Korean verb 나다 ('to come out, arise, sprout, break out', Middle Korean 나다). Literally meaning 'for a rumor to come out/emerge', it means for word to get out, for gossip to circulate, or to become widely known.

history.meaning: that which is heard (rumor) + native verb 'to come out, arise'
for a rumor to spread; to become famous or notorious by word of mouth

morphemes.meaning: to come out, arise, occur (from 나다)

소문나다.notes: Forms an intransitive/transitive pair with 소문내다: 소문나다 is intransitive ('word gets out / rumor spreads'), while 소문내다 is transitive ('someone spreads a rumor'). The adnominal form 소문난 ('renowned, famous') is extremely common.

rootFamily.gloss: rumor, gossip, word of mouth (所聞)
to spread a rumor, tell everyone (所聞내다)
for a rumor to circulate widely (所聞이 돌다)

소문내다.etymology: Hybrid compound transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 소문 (所聞, 'rumor, hearsay', from 所 'that which' + 聞 'to hear') and the native Korean causative/transitive verb 내다 ('to put forth, make come out, produce', derived in Middle Korean from 나다 'to come out' + causative suffix -이- yielding 내다). It means to actively spread a rumor, broadcast a secret, or publicize news by word of mouth.

history.meaning: rumor/hearsay + native causative verb 'to make come out, put forth'
to spread rumors, blab a secret, or publicize by word of mouth

morphemes.meaning: to put out, cause to emerge, spread (causative of 나다)

소문내다.notes: In workplace and drama dialogue, 동네방네 소문내다 ('to spread the rumor to every neighborhood') is a vivid idiom used when scolding someone for blabbing a secret to everyone.

rootFamily.gloss: rumor, hearsay, word of mouth (所聞)
for a rumor to spread, to become well-known (所聞나다)
word of mouth, literally 'mouth rumor' (입所聞)

소박하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 소박 (素朴, 'simple, plain, unadorned, artless', from 素 'uncolored silk, plain' + 朴 'unworked wood, honest') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: plain and unpretentious like unworked wood
simple, modest, unadorned, homely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소박하다

소설.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소설 (小說), composed of 소 (小, 'small, minor, trivial') and 설 (說, 'speech, discourse, narrative, persuasion'). First attested in the *Zhuangzi* (莊子) for petty or inconsequential talk contrasted with grand philosophical truth, and used by Ban Gu in the *Book of Han* (漢書) for street-corner anecdotes collected by minor officials (패관, 稗官), it developed through Tang–Ming vernacular tales and was repurposed in late 19th-century Japan (by Tsubouchi Shōyō in *Shōsetsu Shinzui*, 1885) as the standard East Asian translation for the Western literary 'novel'.

history.meaning: petty talk, minor persuasions, or street-corner folklore/anecdotes (Zhuangzi, Hanshu)
classical and vernacular narrative tales (such as Kim Si-seup's Geumo Sinhwa)
modern literary novel or prose fiction; (colloquial) an invented story or fabrication

소설.notes: In colloquial Korean conversation, 소설 쓰다 (literally 'to write a novel', e.g., 또 소설 쓰네!) is a witty idiom meaning 'to make things up, spin wild conspiracy theories, or exaggerate'.

cognates.meaning: affiliation, belonging to (used in 所属事務所 for talent agency)
that to which one belongs or is affiliated

소속사.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 소속사 (所屬社), formed from 소속 (所屬, 'affiliation, belonging to', from 所 'that which, place' + 屬 'to belong to, be attached to') and the nominal suffix 사 (社, 'company, firm, society', clipped from 회사 會社). In contemporary South Korea, it is the standard term for an entertainment management agency representing actors, singers, or K-pop idols.

history.meaning: place/group to which one belongs + commercial company/firm
affiliated company; specifically a talent or entertainment management agency

morphemes.meaning: to belong to, be affiliated with (屬)

소속사.notes: Central vocabulary in K-pop and Korean drama culture (*The Producers*): when referring to an idol's or actor's management company, Koreans almost always say 소속사 rather than 기획사 (企劃社, 'planning/production agency') when emphasizing who the artist is signed under.

rootFamily.gloss: affiliation, belonging to an organization (所屬)

소송.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소송 (訴訟), composed of two near-synonymous legal characters: 소 (訴, 'to accuse, complain, appeal, inform') and 송 (訟, 'to dispute in court, litigate, demand justice'). Attested in Classical Chinese legal and historical texts (such as the *Book of Later Han*), it denotes formal litigation or a lawsuit brought before a court of law to resolve civil, administrative, or criminal disputes.

history.meaning: presenting a grievance and arguing a dispute before a magistrate or official court
formal judicial lawsuit or litigation (civil, criminal, or administrative)
history.stage: Joseon Legal Korean to Modern Korean

morphemes.meaning: to litigate, dispute before a court (訟)

소송.notes: Distinguish 소송 (訴訟, generally a civil or administrative 'lawsuit', as in 민사소송 'civil suit' or 손해배상 소송 'damages lawsuit') from 고소 (告訴, filing a 'criminal complaint' with police or prosecutors). Common collocation: 소송을 걸다 ('to file a lawsuit against someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to sue, file a lawsuit, litigate (訴訟하다)
criminal complaint or accusation to authorities (告訴)
indictment, prosecution by a public prosecutor (起訴)

소송하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb combining 소송 (訴訟, 'lawsuit, litigation', from 訴 'to accuse, appeal' + 訟 'to litigate, argue in court') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, perform', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). It means to bring legal action, file a lawsuit, or engage in court litigation against another party.

history.meaning: to litigate a legal dispute + native light verb 'to do'
to sue, file a lawsuit, or conduct litigation in court

소송하다.notes: In entertainment industry disputes (such as contract termination battles with a 소속사 or defamation claims), speakers use both 소송하다 ('to sue') and 소송을 제기하다 / 소송을 걸다 ('to file/initiate a lawsuit').

rootFamily.gloss: to file a criminal complaint (告訴하다)

cognates.meaning: cylindrical minced meat food in a casing

소시지.etymology: Borrowed from English sausage, which entered Middle English (sausige) from Old North French saussiche (modern French saucisse), from Vulgar Latin salsīcia ('seasoned with salt'), a substantivized feminine plural of Late Latin salsīcius, from Latin salsus ('salted', past participle of sallere 'to salt', from sāl 'salt'). Standardized in South Korean orthography as 소시지 (replacing older colloquial spellings like 소세지 influenced by Japanese ソーセージ sōsēji).

history.meaning: salted > salted and seasoned meat preparation
minced and seasoned meat stuffed into a cylindrical casing
history.stage: Old North French to Modern English

history.meaning: Western-style pork/meat sausage or processed fish-paste snack sausage in Korea

morphemes.meaning: sausage (from English sausage, ultimately from Latin salsus 'salted')

소시지.notes: While the official National Institute of Korean Language (NIKL) spelling is 소시지, many Koreans colloquially pronounce and write it as 소세지 ([쏘세지]), especially when referring to retro pink lunchbox sausages (분홍 소시지). Native Korean blood sausage is called 순대.

rootFamily.gloss: hot dog, corn dog (from English hot dog)
stir-fried sausage and vegetables, a classic Korean side dish (소시지 + 야채볶음)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 소시지

소식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소식 (消息), meaning 'news, word, tidings, update', from 消 (소, 'wane, disappear') + 息 (식, 'wax, grow, breathe'), which in Classical Chinese meant 'waxing and waning of things, how matters stand' and hence 'news of someone's condition'.

history.meaning: changes in circumstance -> tidings, news
news, word, tidings

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소식

소용돌이.etymology: A native Korean compound whose second element derives from the verb stem 돌- (Middle Korean 돌다, 'to turn, spin, revolve') plus the deverbal nominalizing suffix -이. The initial element 소용- (attested in Early Modern Korean as 소옴- in 소옴돌이 and dialectally as 소용/소옴) is likely related to the verbal root 솟- ('to surge, gush up') or a noun meaning 'deep pool, surging water', literally describing water that wells up and spins in a vortex.

history.meaning: to turn, revolve, spin
whirling water, eddy, whirlpool
whirlpool, vortex; figuratively a maelstrom of events

소용돌이.notes: Frequently used figuratively in drama and journalism (e.g., 감정의 소용돌이, 'a whirlwind/maelstrom of emotions') as well as in the verbal derivative 소용돌이치다 ('to swirl, eddy').

rootFamily.gloss: to swirl, rage like a whirlpool

소유권.etymology: Sino-Korean legal compound 소유권 (所有權), meaning 'ownership, property right, legal title', formed from 소유 (所有, 'possession, ownership') + 권 (權, 'right, authority').

history.meaning: legal right to possess and dispose of property
ownership, property right, title

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소유권

소음.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소음 (騷音), meaning 'noise, din, unwanted or disruptive sound', formed from 騷 (소, 'disturb, commotion, uproar') + 音 (음, 'sound').

history.meaning: disturbing or clamorous sound
noise, unwanted sound

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소음

소재.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 所在 (소재, 'locus, whereabouts, place where something resides'), composed of 所 (소, 'place, that which', functioning as a locative/relative nominalizer in Classical Chinese) and 在 (재, 'to exist, reside, be located at'). Note the common homograph 素材 (소재, 'raw material, subject matter'), which is equally frequent in television and literary contexts.

history.meaning: place where someone or something is located
locus, whereabouts, location; (as 素材) subject matter, material

소재.notes: Distinguish between the two major homographs: 所在 ('location, whereabouts', as in 소재 파악 'identifying someone's whereabouts') and 素材 ('material, story subject/topic', as in 드라마 소재 'drama subject matter').

cognates.word: 焼酎 (しょうちゅう, shōchū)

소주.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 燒酒 (소주), literally 'burned (i.e., distilled) liquor', from 燒 (소, 'to burn, heat, roast') + 酒 (주, 'alcoholic beverage, wine'). Distillation technology was introduced to the Korean peninsula during the late Goryeo dynasty (13th–14th centuries) via Mongol (Yuan dynasty) military encampments, where it was also known as 아락주 (阿剌吉酒, from Arabic ʿaraq 'perspiration; distilled spirit').

history.meaning: distilled spirit heated over fire
distilled grain liquor
soju, clear Korean distilled spirit

소주.notes: Central to Korean socializing and workplace culture (회식); traditionally distilled from rice (증류식 소주), though modern green-bottle commercial soju is mostly diluted ethanol flavored with sweeteners (희석식 소주).

소중하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 소중 (所重, literally 'that which is held weighty or dear') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: held in high regard or importance
precious, valuable, cherished, dear

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소중하다

소중함.etymology: Derived noun formed from the Sino-Korean root 소중 (所重, 'that which is weighty, cherished, of great importance', from 所 소 'that which' + 重 중 'heavy, weighty, important'), combined with the native Korean adjective-deriving suffix -하- and the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: that which is held as weighty or important
to be precious, valuable, cherished
preciousness, the state of being cherished

소중함.notes: Adding -ㅁ to descriptive verb stems (소중하- → 소중함) turns a quality into an abstract noun, often used with 깨닫다 ('to realize the preciousness of...').

cognates.meaning: upholstered couch with back and arms
raised platform, long bench of stone or wood covered with cushions

소파.etymology: Loanword borrowed in the 20th century from English sofa, which entered European languages via French and Italian from Ottoman Turkish sofa ('raised sitting area covered with carpets and cushions'), ultimately from Arabic ṣuffa (صُفَّة, 'raised platform, bench').

history.meaning: raised platform or cushioned bench
upholstered couch for multiple people
sofa, couch

소파.notes: Since Korean lacks the labiodental fricative /f/, English 'f' is systematically adapted using the aspirated bilabial stop ㅍ (/pʰ/), yielding 소파 rather than *소화.

cognates.meaning: small article; short literary sketch; stage prop (小品)

소품.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 小品 (소품), from 小 (소, 'small, minor') + 品 (품, 'article, item, goods, work'). Originally a Buddhist and literary term in China for abridged sutras or short, informal essays and paintings, it expanded in modern East Asian theater, film, and television to denote stage props and small personal accessories.

history.meaning: abridged text; short literary composition or small painting
stage prop; small decorative item or accessory; short artistic piece

소품.notes: In broadcasting and filmmaking (*프로듀사* context), 소품 specifically means 'stage/set props' (managed by the 소품팀, 'prop department'), whereas in everyday shopping it refers to small interior decor items or fashion accessories.

rootFamily.gloss: prop room in a studio or theater (小品室)

소화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 消化 (소화), formed from 消 (소, 'to melt, dissolve, cause to disappear') + 化 (화, 'to transform, change, convert'). Originally a traditional Chinese medical and alchemical term describing the dissolving and transformation of food in the stomach, later adopted as the standard translation for physiological digestion and figurative assimilation.

history.meaning: dissolving and transforming food or matter
physiological digestion; figurative mastery or execution of a task/role

소화.notes: Notice the common homograph 消火 (소화, 'extinguishing fire', from 火 'fire'), seen on every 소화기 ('fire extinguisher')—whereas 消化기 (소화기, 消化器) means 'digestive organs'!

rootFamily.gloss: to digest; to pull off a role or schedule (消化하다)

cognates.meaning: to digest; to work through a schedule or master a skill (消化する)
cognates.word: 消化する (しょうかする, shōka suru)

소화하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 소화 (消化, from 消 소 'to dissolve, melt away' + 化 화 'to transform') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Beyond literal biological digestion of food, it underwent a vivid semantic extension in modern Korean to mean 'to absorb knowledge, carry out a demanding schedule, or pull off a costume/character role'.

history.meaning: to dissolve and digest food in the stomach
to digest food; to master, fulfill, or pull off (a role, outfit, or schedule)

소화하다.notes: In entertainment and media Korean, 소화하다 is constantly used for 'pulling off' a concept, outfit, or role (배역을 완벽하게 소화하다, 'to pull off the role perfectly') or 'getting through' a grueling schedule (스케줄을 소화하다).

속.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'inside, interior, core; stomach; inner mind or feelings', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 속.

history.meaning: inside, interior, heart/mind
inside, interior; stomach; inner thoughts

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 속

속도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 速度 (속도), composed of 速 (속, 'fast, rapid, quick') + 度 (도, 'degree, measure, standard'). Popularized across East Asia during the Meiji-era standardization of scientific and physical terminology to translate English 'speed' and 'velocity'.

history.meaning: degree of rapidity; rate of motion
speed, velocity, pace

속도.notes: Pairs naturally with verbs like 내다 ('to pick up speed', 속도를 내다) and 줄이다 ('to slow down', 속도를 줄이다), as well as the colloquial expression 속도위반 ('speeding; premarital pregnancy').

속뜻.etymology: Native Korean determinative compound formed from 속 (Middle Korean 속, 'inside, interior, inner mind') and 뜻 (Middle Korean  [ptɨt], 'meaning, intention, will'). Literally 'inner meaning', referring to the unstated intention or hidden significance beneath surface words or actions.

history.meaning: interior/inside + mind/meaning/intention
inner meaning, hidden intention, underlying significance

속뜻.notes: Pronounced [속똧] with tensification of ㄷ after the unreleased velar stop ㄱ; belongs to a productive series of 속- ('inner') compounds describing concealed thoughts, such as 속마음 ('true inner feelings') and 속내 ('inner thoughts').

속삭이다.etymology: Native Korean verb derived from the mimetic root 속삭- (seen in the reduplicated adverb 속삭속삭, imitating hushed sibilant speech) plus the verbalizing suffix -이다, which regularly turns sound-symbolic roots into action verbs (compare 반짝이다, 중얼거리다). The repeated initial ㅅ mirrors the breathy friction of speaking under one's breath. Beyond human speech, poetic Korean also applies 속삭이다 to rustling leaves or a gentle stream.
속삭이다.notes: Forms the derived noun 속삭임 ('a whisper, murmuring').

속살.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 속 ('interior, inside', Middle Korean 속) and 살 ('flesh, skin, soft tissue', Middle Korean ᄉᆞᆯ). Originally referring to skin normally covered by clothing, 속살 broadened naturally to the soft, pale interior beneath a peel, shell, bark, or baked crust. In Korean food writing it vividly describes the tender inner crumb of cakes and bread, roasted chestnuts, fruit pulp, or crabmeat.
속살.notes: Pronounced [속쌀] with tensification of ㅅ after final ㄱ; contrasts with 겉면 or 껍질 ('outer surface, crust, peel').

속상하다.etymology: Lexicalized hybrid compound adjective originally arising from the subject-predicate clause 속(이) 상하다, combining native Korean 속 (Middle Korean 속, 'inside, stomach, inner heart/mind') with the Sino-Korean verb 상하다 (傷하다, from 傷 상 'to wound, injure, damage' + native light verb 하다). Literally 'one's insides/heart are wounded or bruised'.

history.meaning: for one's insides or inner mind to be damaged/hurt
to be upset, distressed, vexed, heart-sore

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of, do

속상하다.notes: Korean uses 속 ('inside/stomach/heart') as the seat of emotional distress: compare 속이 타다 ('one's insides burn' = to be worried sick) and 속이 시원하다 ('one's insides feel cool/refreshed' = to feel relieved).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel upset, show distress (verb form)

속상해하다.etymology: Psychological process verb derived from the hybrid adjective 속상하다 ('to be upset, distressed', from native 속 'inner heart' + Sino-Korean 傷 상 'wound, hurt' + -하-) by attaching the auxiliary verbal construction -어하다 (-아하다/-여하다), which converts internal subjective adjectives into observable behavioral verbs.

history.meaning: to be upset, distressed (subjective state)
to feel upset, manifest distress, grieve over something

속상해하다.notes: Crucial Korean grammar point: subjective emotion adjectives like 속상하다 cannot take a third-person subject in declarative present-tense statements (*그녀는 속상하다 is unnatural in conversation); speakers must use the -어하다 verb form (그녀는 속상해한다, 'she feels/is acting upset') or take a direct object with 을/를.

속성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 屬性 (속성), composed of 屬 (속, 'to belong to, be attached to, category') + 性 (성, 'nature, quality, innate character'). Literally 'a quality that belongs to a thing', adopted in modern East Asian philosophy, logic, and computing as the standard equivalent of Latin attributum ('attribute, inherent property').

history.meaning: characteristic quality belonging to an entity; philosophical attribute
history.stage: Literary Chinese / Modern East Asian Philosophy

history.meaning: inherent nature, attribute, property (of a person, genre, or data object)

morphemes.meaning: to belong to, be affiliated with

속성.notes: Beware the common homograph 速成 (속성, 'rapid completion, crash course', from 速 'fast' + 成 'accomplish'), as in 속성 과외 ('crash tutoring'). Context distinguishes 'inherent attribute' (屬性) from 'fast-track' (速成).

rootFamily.gloss: to belong to, be affiliated with (屬하다)

속앓이.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 속 (Middle Korean 속, 'inside, interior, heart/mind'), the verb stem 앓- (Middle Korean 앏다 [alp-ta], 'to ache, suffer from illness, be in pain'), and the deverbal nominalizing suffix -이. Literally 'an aching of the insides', denoting either an internal ailment or silent emotional anguish and pining.

history.meaning: interior/heart + to ache/be ill + nominalizer
internal illness; silent heartache, worrying or pining away inside

속앓이.notes: Pronounced [소갈이] → [소가리] because the ㅎ of the cluster ㅀ is silent before a vowel-initial suffix while ㄹ resyllabifies; commonly paired with 하다 (속앓이를 하다, 'to suffer in silence, pine away inwardly').

rootFamily.gloss: to suffer from an illness, ache, agonize over
lovesickness, pining for someone (相思병 / 가슴앓이)

cognates.meaning: to belong to, be affiliated with (属する)

속하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the single Hanja morpheme 屬 (속, 'to belong to, be attached to, be subordinate to, fall under a category') plus the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, be'). In Classical Chinese, 屬 originally depicted a tail attached to a body, whence 'to be joined, attached, or subordinate to'.

history.meaning: to be joined, attached; to belong to a category or jurisdiction
to belong to, be subordinate to
to belong to, be affiliated with, fall under

morphemes.meaning: to belong to, be attached to, category
to do, be in the state of

속하다.notes: Pronounced [소카다] because the final ㄱ of 속 merges with the initial ㅎ of 하다 to produce aspirated ㅋ (/kʰ/); always takes the dative/locative particle -에 (예능국에 속하다, 'to belong to the variety department').

손.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'hand; manual effort, labor, help', descending unchanged from Middle Korean 손. Also homophonous with native Korean 손 ('guest, visitor; wandering spirit', Middle Korean 손, the root of 손님).

history.meaning: hand; guest, visitor
hand, labor/help; guest

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손

손가락.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 손 ('hand') and 가락 ('slender stick, spindle, or digit').
손가락.notes: The same native element 가락 appears in 발가락 ('toe'), 젓가락 ('chopsticks'), and 숟가락 ('spoon').

손글씨.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 손 ('hand') and 글씨 ('written letters, handwriting', derived from 글 'writing').
손글씨.notes: Contrasts personal pen-and-pencil script with printed type.

손길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'touch or movement of a hand; helping hand, care', formed from 손 ('hand') + 길 ('way, path, course of movement').

history.meaning: hand + path/movement
touch of a hand, helping hand

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손길

손님.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'guest, visitor, customer, passenger', formed from native Korean 손 ('guest, visitor', Middle Korean 손) plus the honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: honored guest or visitor
guest, visitor, customer

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손님

손대다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to touch, lay a hand on, start working on, meddle with', formed from 손 ('hand') + 대다 ('to bring into contact, touch').

history.meaning: hand + to put in contact
to touch, lay hands on, begin or dabble in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손대다

손목.etymology: Native Korean anatomical compound of 손 (Middle Korean 손, 'hand') + 목 (Middle Korean 목, 'neck; narrow constricted part connecting two structures'). Korean anatomically metaphors the narrow joint connecting an extremity to the limb as a 'neck' (목): thus 손목 ('hand-neck' = wrist) and 발목 ('foot-neck' = ankle).

history.meaning: hand + neck; wrist
wrist

손목.notes: Compare the parallel anatomical compound 발목 ('foot-neck' = ankle); in Korean dramas, 손목을 잡다 ('to grab someone by the wrist') is a famously recurring dramatic trope.

손목시계.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the native Korean body-part compound 손목 ('wrist', literally 'hand-neck') with the Sino-Korean noun 시계 (時計, 'timepiece, clock'). Korean distinguishes timepieces by where they sit: 손목시계 ('wristwatch'), 벽시계 ('wall clock'), and 회중시계 ('pocket watch').
손목시계.notes: Takes the verb 차다 ('to wear/fasten on the wrist').

손바닥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 손 (Middle Korean 손, 'hand') and 바닥 (Middle Korean 바닥, 'bottom, floor, flat underside or surface'). Literally 'the flat bottom surface of the hand', parallel to 발바닥 ('sole of the foot').

history.meaning: palm of the hand (hand + flat bottom surface)
palm of the hand

손바닥.notes: Pronounced [손빠닥] with saisiot (genitive compound) tensification of ㅂ to ㅃ; appears in vivid proverbs like 손바닥으로 하늘을 가리다 ('to cover the sky with one's palm' = to try in vain to hide an obvious truth) and 손바닥 뒤집듯 ('like flipping one's palm' = changing one's mind/attitude effortlessly).

손뼉.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'palm of the hand, flat of the hand (especially when clapping, as in 손뼉을 치다)', descending from Middle Korean 손벽 (from 손 'hand' + 벽 'flat surface', with tensification [손뼉] reflected in modern spelling).

history.meaning: palm, flat of the hand
palm of the hand (in clapping)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손뼉

손수.etymology: Native Korean adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 손조 (and later Early Modern Korean 손소), formed from 손 ('hand') plus an archaic emphatic/instrumental adverbial suffix -조 / -소 ('by oneself, with one's own'). In Modern Korean, vowel rounding shifted 손소 to 손수, which was subsequently folk-etymologized as a tautological hybrid of native 손 ('hand') + Sino-Korean 手 (수, 'hand').

history.meaning: with one's own hands, personally
history.stage: Middle Korean (15th c., e.g. Seokbo Sangjeol)

history.meaning: with one's own hands, in person
with one's own hands, personally, by oneself

morphemes.meaning: archaic instrumental/emphatic suffix (< MK -조 > -소 > -수, often folk-associated with 手)

손수.notes: Used exclusively as an adverb modifying action verbs to emphasize personal effort and care (e.g., 어머니가 손수 만드신 도시락, 'a lunchbox Mom made with her own hands').

rootFamily.gloss: one's own handwriting, autograph (親筆 / 손글씨)

손자.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship compound 손자 (孫子), meaning 'grandson', composed of 孫 (손, 'grandchild, descendant') + 子 (자, 'son, child').

history.meaning: grandson
grandson

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손자

손잡이.etymology: Native Korean synthetic compound from 손 ('hand') + 잡- ('grip, hold') + nominalizing suffix -이: literally 'hand-holder'.
손잡이.notes: Covers door handles, suitcase handles, and teacup handles alike.

손전등.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'flashlight, hand-held electric torch', combining native Korean 손 ('hand') with Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈, 'electric light/lamp', from 電 'electricity' + 燈 'lamp').

history.meaning: hand + electric lamp
flashlight, torch

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손전등

손질.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 손 ('hand') and the action-noun suffix -질 ('skilled activity or repeated motion with an instrument or body part'). Literally 'hand-work', 손질 denotes cleaning, trimming, and prepping raw ingredients in the kitchen, as well as grooming plants or maintaining tools.
손질.notes: Combines with -하다 to form 손질하다 ('to prep ingredients, trim, maintain').

cognates.meaning: to damage, injure; harm, loss (損害)

손해.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 損害 (손해), composed of 損 (손, 'to diminish, decrease, lose, damage') + 害 (해, 'harm, injury, detriment'). Attested in Classical Chinese legal and philosophical texts, it denotes both material/financial loss and general harm or disadvantage.

history.meaning: to diminish and injure; harm, detriment
financial loss, damage, disadvantage

손해.notes: In idiomatic Korean, one 'sees' a loss: 손해를 보다 ('to suffer a loss / get the short end of the stick'), contrasting directly with 이익을 보다 or 이득을 보다 ('to make a profit / gain an advantage').

솔솔.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb meaning 'gently, softly, smoothly (of a cool breeze blowing, a pleasant scent wafting, powder sprinkling, or water trickling)', formed by reduplicating the light-vowel ideophone 솔-.

history.meaning: gently blowing, wafting, or trickling
gently, softly, smoothly (wafting or sprinkling)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔솔

솔직하게.etymology: Derived adverb from the Sino-Korean adjective 솔직하다 (率直하다, 'to be honest, frank, candid'), formed from 率 (솔, 'to lead; unreserved, straightforward, natural') + 直 (직, 'straight, upright, direct') + adjective-forming light verb -하- + productive adverbial suffix -게 ('in a ... manner').

history.meaning: unreserved and upright; frank, candid in character
history.stage: Classical Chinese (e.g., Records of the Grand Historian)

history.meaning: to be honest, frank, straightforward
honestly, frankly, candidly

솔직하게.notes: Interchangeable in many contexts with the lexicalized adverb 솔직히 ('frankly speaking'), though 솔직하게 emphasizes the manner of an action (솔직하게 말하다, 'to speak candidly'), whereas 솔직히 often functions as a sentence-initial discourse marker ('To be honest, ...').

솔직하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 솔직 (率直, 'frank, candid, honest, straightforward', from 率 'unreserved, direct' + 直 'straight, upright') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: unreserved and straightforward
honest, frank, candid

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직하다

솔직해지다.etymology: Hybrid compound inchoative verb meaning 'to become honest/frank, open up candidly', formed from the Sino-Korean adjective 솔직하다 ('frank, honest', stem 솔직해-) plus the native Korean inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

history.meaning: to be frank + to become
to become frank/honest, open up

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직해지다

솔직히.etymology: Hybrid adverb meaning 'frankly, honestly, candidly', formed from Sino-Korean 솔직 (率直, 'frank, straightforward') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: frank/honest + adverbial suffix
frankly, honestly, to be honest

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직히

솜씨.etymology: Native Korean noun tracing back to fifteenth-century Middle Korean 손ㅿㅣ, a compound of 손 ('hand') and -ㅿㅣ/-씨 ('manner, style, cultivated knack', compare 말씨 'way of speaking' and 글씨 'handwriting'). Over Early Modern Korean, alveolar 손 assimilated in place to labial 솜 before the tense sibilant 씨, yielding modern 솜씨. Because of its literal origin in 'the way of one's hands', 솜씨 specifically praises practical artistry in cooking, sewing, drawing, or carpentry.
솜씨.notes: Commonly evaluated with 좋다 ('skilled, deft') or 뛰어나다 ('outstanding craftsmanship').

쇠.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'iron, metal', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 쇠 ('iron, metal, ore').

history.meaning: iron, metal
iron, metal

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠

쇠걸쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'iron latch, metal hook or catch (on a door, window, or box)', formed from 쇠 ('iron, metal') + 걸쇠 ('latch, hook', itself a compound of 걸다 'to hang/hook' + 쇠 'metal fixture').

history.meaning: iron + metal hook/latch
iron latch, metal hasp/hook

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠걸쇠

쇠고리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'iron ring, metal loop or eye', formed from 쇠 ('iron, metal') + 고리 ('ring, loop', Middle Korean 고리).

history.meaning: iron + ring/loop
iron ring, metal loop

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠고리

쇠지렛대.etymology: Native Korean three-part compound formed from 쇠 ('iron, metal', Middle Korean 쇠) plus 지렛대 ('lever, pry bar'), itself composed of 지레 ('lever', related to 지르다 'to brace, thrust under'), the compound marker -ㅅ- (사이시옷), and 대 ('rod, pole, bar'). While wooden levers were traditionally used to shift garden stones or timber, prefixing 쇠 specifies a forged steel pry bar or crowbar used in carpentry and masonry.
쇠지렛대.notes: Pronounced [쇠지렏때] or [쉐지렏때] due to the saisiot -ㅅ- before 대.

쇼.etymology: 20th-century loanword from English show (from Middle English shewen, Old English scēawian, 'to look at, inspect, display', from Proto-Germanic *skauwōną). Adopted into Korean for both television/stage variety programs and colloquial expressions meaning 'a staged pretense or dramatic scene'.

history.meaning: to look at > to display > public spectacle or broadcast program
television/stage show; ostentatious display or pretense

쇼.notes: Used both literally in broadcasting compounds (토크쇼 'talk show', 라디오 쇼 'radio show') and idiomatically in 쇼하다 ('to put on an act, make a scene, fake it').

rootFamily.gloss: to put on an act, make a dramatic scene

cognates.meaning: causing sudden surprise, dismay, or outrage

쇼킹하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword adjective combining English shocking (participial adjective of shock, borrowed via French choquer 'to strike against, jolt') with the native Korean adjectival light verb 하다 ('to be in the state of').

history.meaning: striking with sudden surprise or scandal
to be shocking, sensational, startling (colloquial/media register)

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of

쇼킹하다.notes: Favored in entertainment television, gossip journalism, and casual speech for dramatic flair; in formal writing or news broadcasts, the Sino-Korean equivalent 충격적이다 (衝擊的이다) is preferred.

수.etymology: Polysemous Korean noun: (1) native Korean bound noun 수 ('way, method, possibility, ability', used in -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 'can / cannot', descending from Middle Korean 수 'means, way'); (2) Sino-Korean 수 (數, 'number, count, quantity; fate, luck'); and (3) Sino-Korean 수 (手, 'move in a game, skill, means').

history.meaning: means, ability; number, count
way, possibility (-ㄹ 수 있다); number (數); move/skill (手)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수

수건.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수건 (手巾), meaning 'towel, hand towel, cloth', composed of 手 (수, 'hand') + 巾 (건, 'cloth, kerchief, towel').

history.meaning: cloth for wiping the hands or face
towel

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수건

수고.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 受苦 (수고), composed of 受 (수, 'to receive, undergo, suffer') + 苦 (고, 'bitterness, hardship, pain, toil'). Originating in Chinese Buddhist terminology for undergoing worldly suffering (dukkha), it was secularized in Korean into an everyday noun denoting the trouble, effort, and hard work expended on a task.

history.meaning: to undergo suffering or hardship (Buddhist/Vernacular Chinese)
pains, trouble, hard work, effort

수고.notes: Forms the backbone of Korean workplace greetings: 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work' / 'thank you for your effort') and 수고하셨습니다 ('thank you for your hard work'). Note that saying 수고하세요 to a social superior is considered impolite—use 고생하셨습니다 or 감사드립니다 instead.

rootFamily.gloss: to work hard, take pains (受苦하다)

수고하다.etymology: Verb meaning 'to work hard, take pains, go to trouble', formed from 수고 ('hard work, trouble, effort', attested in Middle Korean as 수고 and traditionally linked to Sino-Korean 受苦, 'undergoing toil/hardship') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to undergo hardship, take pains
to work hard, take trouble (used in thanks/greetings)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수고하다

수군거림.etymology: Native Korean mimetic (ideophonic) verbal noun derived from the onomatopoeic/mimetic root 수군 (as in 수군수군, depicting the low, secretive murmur of people whispering to one another), followed by the frequentative verbal suffix -거리- ('to repeatedly make the sound/motion of') and the substantive nominalizer -ㅁ.

history.meaning: to whisper covertly, murmur in low voices
whispering, covert murmuring, gossiping behind someone's back

수군거림.notes: Korean sound symbolism features vowel harmony: the dark-vowel form 수군거리다 (with ㅜ) evokes conspiratorial, hushed whispering among adults, whereas the bright-vowel counterpart 소곤거리다 (with ㅗ) feels lighter, gentler, and more intimate.

rootFamily.gloss: in a low, secretive whisper (mimetic adverb)

수도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 수도 (水道), meaning 'waterworks, running water system, water conduit' (from 水 'water' + 道 'channel, way'); and (2) 수도 (首都), meaning 'capital city' (from 首 'head, chief' + 都 'metropolis').

history.form: 水道 (water supply) / 首都 (capital city)
history.meaning: water conduit; chief metropolis
running water, waterworks (水道); capital city (首都)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도

수도관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수도관 (水道管), meaning 'water pipe, water main, plumbing pipe', formed from 수도 (水道, 'water supply, water conduit') + 관 (管, 'pipe, tube').

history.meaning: pipe carrying running water
water pipe

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도관

수도꼭지.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'faucet, water tap, spigot', combining Sino-Korean 수도 (水道, 'running water system') with native Korean 꼭지 ('knob, spout, stem, tip', Middle Korean 곡지).

history.meaning: water supply + knob/spout
faucet, water tap

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도꼭지

수레.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 술위 and 수레 ('wheeled cart, carriage'). Historically, 수레 served as the native gloss (훈) for the Hanja 車 ('수레 거/차') and referred to everything from wooden ox-carts to royal palanquins on wheels. In modern urban Korean it typically denotes a two- or four-wheeled wooden display cart, garden barrow, or delivery handcart (손수레).
수레.notes: Takes 끌다 ('to pull a cart') or 밀다 ('to push a cart').

cognates.word: 修理費 (しゅうりひ, shūrihi)

수리비.etymology: Three-morpheme Sino-Korean compound 修理費 (수리비), consisting of 수리 (修理, 'repair, mending', from 修 수 'to mend, cultivate, put in order' + 理 리 'to put in order, manage, polish jade') plus the productive suffixoid 비 (費, 'expense, cost, fee').

history.meaning: putting in order/repairing + expense/fee
repair cost, maintenance charges

morphemes.meaning: to put in order, manage, regulate

수리비.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -비 (費) productively forms cost compounds across Korean: 교통비 ('transportation cost'), 식비 ('food expenses'), 치료비 ('medical treatment cost'), and 제작비 ('production budget').

cognates.word: 修理する (しゅうりする, shūri suru)

수리하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 수리 (修理, from 修 수 'to mend, restore, cultivate' + 理 리 'to put in order, dress jade, regulate') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Attested in Classical Chinese for putting state affairs or buildings in order, and used in modern Korean for repairing machinery, vehicles, or facilities.

history.meaning: to put in order, restore, mend (buildings, governance, or utensils)
to repair, mend, fix (machines, cars, appliances, buildings)

morphemes.meaning: to put in order, manage, regulate

수리하다.notes: Compare with native Korean 고치다 ('to fix, mend, cure, correct'): 수리하다 is somewhat more formal and used specifically for physical objects, vehicles, and facilities, whereas 고치다 can also apply to habits (버릇을 고치다) or illnesses (병을 고치다).

rootFamily.gloss: renovation, remodeling, repair of clothing/houses (修繕)

수많다.etymology: Lexicalized hybrid compound adjective formed from the Sino-Korean noun 수 (數, 'number, count') and the native Korean adjective 많다 (Middle Korean 만ᄒᆞ다 [man-hʌ-ta], 'to be many, abundant'), originating from the subject-predicate phrase 수가 많다 ('the number is large').

history.meaning: number/count + to be many/abundant
to be countless, numerous, multitudinous

수많다.notes: Almost overwhelmingly encountered in its adnominal modifier form 수많은 ('countless, numerous', e.g., 수많은 사람들 'countless people', 수많은 시행착오 'countless trials and errors').

수명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 壽命 (수명), composed of 壽 (수, 'longevity, long life, age') + 命 (명, 'life, fate, Heaven's decree'). Attested in Classical Chinese since the Warring States period, referring both to the allotted span of a living being's life and figuratively to the useful service life of an object or program.

history.meaning: allotted span of life, longevity decreed by Heaven
lifespan, life expectancy; service life of a product or show

수명.notes: Used both biologically (수명이 길다/짧다, 'to have a long/short lifespan'; 수명이 단축되다, 'for one's lifespan to be shortened [by stress]') and for batteries, appliances, or television programs.

cognates.meaning: technique, style; trick, modus operandi (手法)

수법.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 手法 (수법), formed from 手 (수, 'hand, manual skill') + 法 (법, 'method, way, law, technique'). Originally an artistic and literary term for brushwork or compositional technique ('hand-method'), in modern Korean it frequently carries a pejorative nuance of 'trick, scheme, or criminal modus operandi'.

history.meaning: manual skill, artistic brushwork or literary technique
artistic technique; (more commonly) scheme, trick, modus operandi

morphemes.meaning: hand, manual skill, person skilled in an art

수법.notes: While 수법 can still mean 'artistic/literary technique' (표현 수법), in everyday speech and crime reporting it strongly implies a deceptive scheme or modus operandi (사기 수법 'scam technique', 뻔한 수법 'an obvious trick'). For neutral 'method', use 방법 (方法) or 기법 (技法).

cognates.meaning: defense, garrison, fielding in baseball (守備)

수비.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 守備 (수비), composed of 守 (수, 'to guard, defend, protect, keep') + 備 (비, 'to prepare, provide against, equip'). Originally a Classical Chinese military term for garrisoning and defending a stronghold, it was extended in modern Korean to sports (especially baseball and soccer defense/fielding).

history.meaning: to guard and prepare defenses; military garrison
military defense; defensive play or fielding in sports; figurative self-defense in conversation

수비.notes: Forms an antonymic pair with 공격 (攻擊, 'attack, offense'); in sports and everyday banter, 수비수 (守備手) means 'defender/fielder', while 방어 (防禦) is preferred for abstract psychological defense or biological immunity.

수상하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 수상 (殊常, literally 'different from the ordinary, unusual') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다, meaning 'suspicious, fishy, questionable, strange'.

history.meaning: out of the ordinary, suspicious
suspicious, shady, strange

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수상하다

수석.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 首席, uniting 首 (머리 수, 'head, leader, first') and 席 (자리 석, 'woven mat, seat, official post'). Literally 'the head seat' at an assembly or banquet, it came to designate either the person holding the highest rank among peers—such as chief judge (수석 심사위원) or principal musician—or graduating at the very top of an examination list (수석 졸업). Notice the unrelated homograph 수석 (壽石/水石, 'viewing stone').
수석.notes: Placed directly before a role title as a prenominal modifier, e.g. 수석 심사위원 ('chief judge') or 수석 연구원 ('senior/chief researcher').

수성.etymology: Sino-Korean 수성 (水性), compounding 수 (水, 'water') + 성 (性, 'nature, property').
수성.notes: Used before 페인트 ('water-based paint') and 펜 ('water-based ink pen').

수수께끼.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Early Modern Korean texts in forms such as 수수격기 and 수수겻기 ('verbal guessing game, riddle'), built with expressive reduplicated 수수- and a nominalised verbal element with tensification of ㄱ to ㄲ.

history.meaning: verbal riddle, guessing puzzle
riddle; puzzling mystery

수수께끼.notes: Used both for children's word riddles (수수께끼를 내다, 'to pose a riddle') and figuratively for an intriguing mystery or cryptic note.

cognates.meaning: order of moves in Go; procedure, sequence of steps
order of moves in board games; sequence of steps

수순.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 수순 (手順), borrowed via Japanese 手順 (tejun) during the modern era and read with Sino-Korean pronunciations: 手 (수, 'hand; move in a board game') + 順 (순, 'order, sequence, follow'). Originally a technical term in Go (바둑) denoting the exact sequence in which stones are played, it broadened in general Korean prose and broadcasting/political registers to mean a 'standard procedure' or 'expected sequence of steps'.

history.meaning: sequence of hand movements; order of plays in Go (baduk)
order of moves in Go; prescribed procedure or expected sequence of steps

수순.notes: Often used with the verb 밟다 (수순을 밟다, 'to go through the standard steps/follow a predictable course'), especially in news and workplace contexts.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (수순)

수습.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 수습 (收拾), meaning 'bringing a situation under control, settling, sorting out, clearing up' (from 收 'gather' + 拾 'pick up, put in order'); and (2) 수습 (修習), meaning 'probation, apprenticeship, practical training' (from 修 'cultivate' + 習 'practice').

history.form: 收拾 (settling/sorting out) / 修習 (probationary training)
history.meaning: putting in order; practical training
remedying/controlling a situation (收拾); probation/training (修習)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수습

수습생.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic noun 수습생 (修習生), formed from 수습 (修習, 'cultivating and practicing a craft on the job', from 修 'cultivate, train' + 習 'practice, learn by doing') plus the personal suffix -생 (生, 'student, trainee, person in training'). Historically used in guilds, workshops, legal professions, and kitchens, it designates a novice who learns practical skills under a master's supervision. In Sora's kitchen, calling Mina and Minsu her 주방 수습생 ('kitchen apprentices') is an affectionate nod to their baking help.

history.meaning: practical training and cultivation of a craft
apprentice, trainee learning on the job

수습생.notes: Pronounced [수습쌩] with automatic tensification of ㅅ after the bilabial stop coda ㅂ.

cognates.meaning: hand signal, flag or manual signaling

수신호.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 수신호 (手信號), formed by prefixing 手 (수, 'hand') to the disyllabic Sino-Korean noun 신호 (信號, 'signal, sign'), itself composed of 信 (신, 'trust, message, sign') and 號 (호, 'mark, call, designation'). In television production and traffic control, it denotes non-verbal manual cues used when live microphones prohibit spoken directions.

history.meaning: established sign, beacon, or communicative signal
manual cue or hand signal used in traffic, military, or studio directing

수신호.notes: Essential television studio jargon: floor directors (FD) rely on 수신호 to cue cast members without being picked up by live audio mics.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (수신호)

수업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수업 (授業), meaning 'class, lesson, academic instruction', composed of 授 (수, 'confer, impart, teach') + 業 (업, 'study, coursework').

history.meaning: imparting instruction in a course of study
class, lesson

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수업

수영장.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 수영장 (水泳場), combining 수영 (水泳, 'swimming', from 水 수 'water' + 泳 영 'swim, move through water') with the locative suffix 장 (場, 'place, ground, venue, arena'). Modeled on Meiji-era Japanese compound formations for modern athletic facilities, it designates an artificial pool or designated venue for swimming.

history.meaning: moving or floating through water; swimming
designated facility or pool for swimming

수영장.notes: While 수영장 is the standard term for a public or athletic swimming pool, hotel or resort pools are also casually called 풀장 (pool + 場).

수요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수요일 (水曜日), meaning 'Wednesday', formed from 수요 (水曜, 'the planet Mercury, the Water Star' in traditional East Asian seven-luminary astronomy) + 일 (日, 'day').

history.meaning: day of the Water Star (Mercury)
Wednesday

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수요일

수정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound 수정하다 (修正하다), formed from the Sino-Korean noun 수정 (修正, 'revision, amendment') plus the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ('to do, make'). The Hanja root 修正 combines 修 (수, 'cultivate, repair, embellish') and 正 (정, 'straight, upright, correct'), attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., *Liji*) for rectifying one's conduct before shifting in modern usage to editing texts, scripts, or video cuts.

history.meaning: to rectify conduct; to set right what is flawed
to revise, edit, amend, or touch up a text, plan, or broadcast cut

수정하다.notes: In broadcasting and makeup alike, 수정하다 covers both revising a script/edit (대본을 수정하다) and touching up makeup on set (화장을 수정하다).

cognates.meaning: patty of ground beef served in a bun (short for hamburger)

수제버거.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and English compound 수제버거 (手製 + burger). The first element is Sino-Korean 수제 (手製, 'handmade, crafted by hand', from 手 수 'hand' + 製 제 'make, manufacture, fashion'); the second element is the English loanword 버거 (*burger*, clipped by reanalysis from *hamburger*, originally 'from Hamburg, Germany'). In contemporary Korean dining, it denotes an artisanal gourmet burger as opposed to mass-produced fast food.

history.meaning: hand-crafted manufacture + Hamburg-style beef steak sandwich
artisanal or gourmet handmade hamburger

수제버거.notes: In South Korea, 수제버거 implies a sit-down gourmet burger made with fresh, non-frozen patties, contrasting sharply with franchise 햄버거.

수제버거집.etymology: Three-part hybrid compound 수제버거집 (手製 + burger + 집), combining Sino-Korean 수제 (手製, 手 'hand' + 製 'manufacture'), the English loanword 버거 (*burger*), and the native Korean noun 집 ('house; shop, restaurant', from Middle Korean 집 *cip*). In Korean morphology, native 집 productively attaches to food nouns to denote a specialized eatery or restaurant serving that dish.

history.meaning: dwelling, house, building
specialty restaurant or joint serving gourmet handmade burgers

morphemes.meaning: house; specialty shop or restaurant (native Korean)

수제버거집.notes: The suffix -집 ('house') is the everyday conversational way to name restaurants by their signature dish (e.g., 고깃집 'BBQ restaurant', 술집 'bar').

수채화.etymology: Sino-Korean three-morpheme art term 水彩畵, composed of 水 (물 수, 'water'), 彩 (채색 채, 'pigment, colour'), and 畵 (그림 화, 'picture, painting'). Coined in modern East Asian fine-arts terminology to translate Western 'watercolour painting', it contrasts structurally with 유화 (油畵, 'oil painting') and 목탄화 (木炭畵, 'charcoal drawing'). In Korean it refers both to the medium itself and to an individual finished watercolour work.
수채화.notes: Combines with 물감 in 수채화 물감 ('watercolour paints') and 종이 in 수채화 종이 ('watercolour paper').

수첩.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수첩 (手帖), combining 수 (手, 'hand') and 첩 (帖, 'folded booklet, register').
수첩.notes: Literally a 'hand-booklet' small enough to slip into a coat or apron pocket.

수평.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 수평 (水平), composed of 수 (水, 'water') and 평 (平, 'flat, even, level'). Already in Classical Chinese (*radically 'level as still water'*), builders and carpenters used troughs of still water to establish a true horizontal plane before spirit levels existed. In Modern Korean carpentry and everyday life, 수평을 맞추다 ('to align the water-level') is the idiomatic expression for leveling a wobbly table or shelf.

history.meaning: as level as still water; water-level gauge used in construction
horizontal level, even balance

수평.notes: Key carpentry collocations: 수평을 맞추다 ('to level something') and 수평이 맞다 ('to be level/even').

수프.etymology: Borrowed from English soup ('savory liquid dish made by simmering ingredients in stock or water').

history.meaning: liquid dish, broth
soup (especially Western-style soup)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수프

수프용.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'for soup, soup-use (e.g., a soup bowl or soup spoon)', combining the English loanword 수프 (soup) with the Sino-Korean suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').

history.meaning: soup + for the use of
for soup, soup-use

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수프용

cognates.meaning: predestined fate; previous life in Buddhist usage
predestined fate, karma from a past life

숙명.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 숙명 (宿命), composed of 宿 (숙, 'lodge overnight; old, long-standing, from a previous existence') and 命 (명, 'life, decree, fate'). Originally a Chinese Buddhist translation of Sanskrit *pūrva-janman* or *pūrva-nivāsa* ('previous life, karmic condition from a former existence'), it secularized across East Asia to mean an inescapable, predetermined destiny.

history.meaning: former lives and karmic conditions carried over from past existences
inescapable destiny or predetermined fate from birth

morphemes.meaning: lodge; former, from a previous life (宿)

숙명.notes: Carries a heavier, more dramatic tone of inescapable karmic fate than 운명 (運命), which can include shifting luck or fortune.

숙박.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박 (宿泊), meaning 'lodging, staying overnight, accommodation', composed of 宿 (숙, 'stay overnight, lodge') + 泊 (박, 'moor, stay for the night').

history.meaning: staying overnight at an inn or lodging
lodging, overnight stay, accommodation

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙박

숙박부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박부 (宿泊簿), from 숙박 (宿泊, 'lodging overnight') and 부 (簿, 'ledger, register book').
숙박부.notes: Shares 부 (簿, 'record book') with 장부 (帳簿, 'account ledger').

숙박비.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박비 (宿泊費), meaning 'lodging expenses, cost of accommodation', formed from 숙박 (宿泊, 'overnight lodging') + 비 (費, 'cost, expense, fee').

history.meaning: fee or expense for overnight lodging
lodging fee, accommodation cost

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙박비

숙소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙소 (宿所), meaning 'lodging, quarters, accommodation, place to stay', formed from 宿 (숙, 'lodge, stay overnight') + 所 (소, 'place').

history.meaning: place where one lodges overnight
lodging, quarters, accommodation

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙소

숙직실.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 숙직실 (宿直室), formed from 숙직 (宿直, 'staying overnight on duty', from 宿 숙 'lodge overnight' + 直 직 'be on duty, keep watch, direct') and the locative suffix 실 (室, 'room, chamber'). Attested in traditional East Asian bureaucratic usage for palace guards and officials keeping night watch, it now refers to the on-call sleeping room in broadcasting stations, hospitals, and offices.

history.meaning: spending the night on guard or official duty at a court office
night-duty room or on-call sleeping quarters in a workplace

숙직실.notes: In Korean broadcasting stations, PDs and editors pulling all-nighters in the editing bay frequently crash in the station's 숙직실.

순간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 순간 (瞬間), from 순 (瞬, 'blink of an eye') and 간 (間, 'interval of time').
순간.notes: Literally 'the space of a single blink'.

cognates.meaning: blood sausage; intestine stuffed with blood (senggi 'blood' + duha 'intestine')

순대.etymology: Korean culinary noun 순대, attested in Late Joseon cookbooks such as the 19th-century *Siuijeonseo* (시의전서) as 슌대 (*syuntay*). Philologists widely derive it as a Jurchen-Manchu loanword connected to Manchu *senggi duha* ('stuffed blood intestine', from *senggi* 'blood' + *duha* 'intestine, casings'), reflecting northern pastoral sausage-making traditions adopted into Korean cuisine and adapted with glass noodles (당면) in the 20th century.

history.meaning: animal intestine stuffed with blood and roasted or boiled
pig or cow intestine stuffed with seasoned blood, bean sprouts, and grains
Korean blood sausage stuffed with coagulated pig blood, glass noodles, and vegetables

순대.notes: A beloved Korean street food and late-night comfort dish; in Seoul it is dipped in salt with chili powder, while in southern provinces it is dipped in fermented bean paste (막장) or vinegar-chili paste (초장).

rootFamily.gloss: stir-fried blood sausage and vegetables (순대 + 볶음)

순댓국.etymology: Compound culinary noun 순댓국, formed from 순대 ('Korean blood sausage'), the genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, marking compounds where a vowel-final noun precedes a lax consonant and triggers tensification to [순댇꾹]), and the native Korean noun 국 ('soup, broth', attested in Middle Korean as 국 *kwuk*). It designates a hearty pork-bone broth simmered with sliced blood sausage and offal.

history.meaning: boiled soup or broth served alongside rice
rich pork-bone soup boiled with slices of blood sausage and offal

순댓국.notes: Under South Korean Hangul orthography rules, the 사이시옷 (ㅅ) is mandatory between 순대 and 국 because the initial ㄱ of 국 tensifies in pronunciation ([순댇꾹]).

rootFamily.gloss: soup with rice mixed in (국 + 밥)

순서.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound 순서 (順序), composed of 順 (순, 'follow along, obey, in proper alignment') and 序 (서, 'sequence, arrangement, east-west wing wall of a school, preface'). Both characters denote orderly progression; together they signify a sequential arrangement, turn, or in broadcasting and performance contexts, a program lineup or billing order.

history.meaning: harmonious progression or sequential arrangement
order, sequence, turn, or program lineup/billing sequence

순서.notes: In television and stage production, 순서 often refers specifically to a segment's slot in the cue sheet or an actor's billing order in credits.

순수하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) 순수하다 (純粹하다), combining the Sino-Korean noun 순수 (純粹, 'purity, unmixedness') with the native adjective-forming suffix -하다. In Classical Chinese, 純 (순) originally denoted 'unmixed raw silk' (from 糸 'silk' + 屯 phonetic) and 粹 (수) denoted 'unadulterated, hulled grain' (from 米 'rice' + 卒 phonetic). From literal material purity, it extended to moral innocence and non-calculating, platonic affection.

history.meaning: unmixed silk and unadulterated grain; complete material or philosophical purity
to be pure, unmixed, genuine, or free of ulterior motives (platonic/innocent)

순수하다.notes: Unlike 순진하다 (which can imply gullible naivety), 순수하다 is consistently positive, praising someone's uncorrupted heart or genuine motives.

순전히.etymology: Hybrid adverb meaning 'purely, entirely, wholly, solely', formed from Sino-Korean 순전 (純全, 'pure and complete', from 純 'pure, unmixed' + 全 'whole, entire') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: pure and whole + adverbial suffix
purely, entirely, solely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 순전히

순진하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb 순진하다 (純眞하다), derived from the Sino-Korean noun 순진 (純眞) + native suffix -하다 ('to be'). Composed of 純 (순, 'pure silk, unmixed, simple') and 眞 (진, 'true, genuine, unadorned, natural'), the compound originally praised Taoist and literary ideals of unspoiled naturalness before acquiring the modern conversational nuance of being worldly-inexperienced or gullibly naive.

history.meaning: unadorned natural truth and unspoiled simplicity of character
to be innocent, simple-hearted, or naive about worldly schemes

순진하다.notes: Watch the nuance: calling an adult 순진하다 often implies they are gullible or clueless about how the world works, whereas 순수하다 means pure-hearted.

rootFamily.gloss: utterly naive and innocent (純眞無垢하다)

숟가락.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'spoon', descending from Middle Korean 술가락, formed from 술 ('spoon; spoonful', Middle Korean 술) + 가락 ('slender stick, rod, or utensil', Middle Korean 가락), with pre-consonantal coronal neutralization spelled ㄷ in Modern Korean orthography.

history.meaning: spoon (from 술 'spoon' + 가락 'slender stick')
spoon

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숟가락

술.etymology: Native Korean noun 술 ('alcoholic beverage, liquor, wine'), contracted from Middle Korean 수울 (*swuwul*, attested in the 1446 *Hunminjeongeum Haerye* and 1447 *Yongbieocheonga*) via the intermediate 16th-century form 수을 (*swuul*). The loss of intervocalic *-w-* and vowel contraction (*swuwul* > *swuul* > *swul*) is a regular phonological development in the transition from Middle to Modern Korean. Internal reconstruction links Old Korean *suwul* to the process of fermenting grain mash.

history.meaning: fermented grain liquor; alcoholic drink
alcoholic beverage, rice wine or distilled spirits
alcoholic drink of any kind (beer, soju, wine, rice wine)

술.notes: 술 is the umbrella word for all alcohol in Korean; asking '술 마실래?' ('Want to get a drink?') covers everything from soju and beer to wine.

rootFamily.gloss: spoon (historically related tool for liquid/food) or 술잔 'drinking glass' (술 + 잔)

술버릇.etymology: Native Korean determinative compound 술버릇, combining 술 ('alcoholic beverage', from Middle Korean 수울 *swuwul*) and 버릇 ('habit, custom, mannerism', from Middle Korean 버릇 *pelus*, attested in the 15th-century *Seokbo Sangjeol*). Literally 'liquor-habit', it denotes the recurring behavioral quirks or antics a person exhibits specifically when intoxicated.

history.meaning: fermented liquor + accustomed habit or manner
characteristic habit or behavior displayed when drunk

술버릇.notes: A staple topic in Korean drinking culture (회식); its Sino-Korean synonym 주사 (酒邪, literally 'alcohol wickedness') specifically implies bad or unruly drunken behavior, whereas 술버릇 can be harmless (like falling asleep or paying the bill).

rootFamily.gloss: habit of talking, verbal tic (말 + 버릇)

술친구.etymology: Hybrid Korean-Sino-Korean compound noun 술친구 (술親舊), joining the native Korean noun 술 ('alcoholic drink', from Middle Korean 수울 *swuwul*) with the Sino-Korean noun 친구 (親舊, 'friend', from 親 친 'intimate, close, relatives' + 舊 구 'old, long-standing acquaintance'). Originally 親舊 in Classical Chinese meant 'relatives and old acquaintances', narrowing in Korean to 'friend' and here specifying a companion with whom one shares drinks and candid conversation.

history.meaning: liquor + relatives and old acquaintances
drinking buddy; friend one meets over drinks

술친구.notes: In Korean social life, asking someone to be a 술친구 is a warm, low-pressure way to seek companionship or comfort after a rough day at work.

숨.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'breath, respiration', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 숨.

history.meaning: breath, respiration
breath

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨

숨겨오다.etymology: Native Korean serial/auxiliary verb construction 숨겨오다, formed from 숨기- (the causative stem of 숨다 'to hide oneself', from Middle Korean 숨다 *swumta* + causative suffix -기- *-ki-*), the infinitive/connective ending -어 (*-e*), and the deictic motion verb 오다 ('to come', Middle Korean 오다 *wota*) functioning as an aspectual auxiliary denoting an action continued from the past up to the present ('to have kept hiding until now').

history.meaning: to cause to be hidden + to come toward the speaker
to have kept something concealed continuously up to the present moment

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective ending (fused with -기- as 겨)
auxiliary verb of continuous action up to the present ('come')

숨겨오다.notes: The auxiliary -어 오다 expresses a state or action sustained from the past up to right now, contrasting with -어 가다 (continuing from now into the future).

숨겨지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb meaning 'to be hidden, be concealed', formed from the causative/transitive verb 숨기다 ('to hide, conceal', stem 숨겨-) plus the passive/inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

history.meaning: to conceal + passive auxiliary
to be hidden, be concealed

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨겨지다

숨기다.etymology: Native Korean causative/transitive verb meaning 'to hide, conceal, keep secret', derived from the intransitive verb 숨다 ('to hide oneself') plus the causative suffix -기- (Middle Korean 숨기다).

history.meaning: to hide, conceal something
to hide, conceal

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨기다

숨다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to hide oneself, go into hiding, lurk out of sight', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 숨다.

history.meaning: to hide oneself, conceal oneself
to hide, lurk

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨다

숫기.etymology: Hybrid native and Sino-Korean noun 숫기 (숫氣). Standard philological analysis derives it from the native Korean prefixal element 숫- (historically related to 수 'male, vigorous, forward' + compound marker -ㅅ-, or 숫- 'unspoiled, pure, lively') combined with Sino-Korean 기 (氣, 'breath, vital energy, spirit, disposition'). From 'forward/virile spirit', it came to denote social boldness, outgoing confidence, and lack of shyness around strangers.

history.meaning: vigorous, forward, or unabashed temperament
social confidence, outgoingness, or lack of shyness around others

morphemes.meaning: forward, vigorous, pure (native Korean prefixal stem with ㅅ)

숫기.notes: Almost always used in negative or comparative expressions like 숫기가 없다 ('to be shy/lack social confidence') or 숫기가 좋다 ('to be outgoing/bold').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (숫기)

숫자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숫자 (數字), meaning 'number, numeral, figure, digit', formed from 數 (수, 'number, count') + 字 (자, 'character, symbol'), written in South Korean orthography with the genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) as one of the six exceptional two-hanja words that take 사이시옷 (곳간, 셋방, 숫자, 찻간, 툇간, 횟수).

history.meaning: written numeral or figure
number, numeral, digit, figure

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숫자

숲.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'forest, woods, grove', descending from Middle Korean 수플 ('woods, thicket', historically related to 숳 'thicket' + 풀 'vegetation') via syncope/apocope of the final syllable into an aspirated labial stop (수플 > 숖 > 숲).

history.meaning: forest, woods, thicket
forest, woods

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숲

숲길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun 숲길, formed from 숲 ('forest, woods, grove', contracted from Middle Korean 수플 *swuphul*, 15th c.) and 길 ('road, path, way', from Middle Korean 길 *kil*, with stem-final aspirate *길ㅎ* *kilh* in oblique cases). The loss of the second-syllable vowel and apocope of *-l* in *swuphul* > *swuph* (숲) is a well-documented sound change in Early Modern Korean.

history.meaning: thicket or forest + path or road
forest path, woodland trail, or tree-lined walkway

숲길.notes: Pronounced [숩낄] with automatic tensification of ㄱ to [ㄲ] after the obstruent coda of 숲. Often evokes a peaceful, healing walk away from city stress.

숲속.etymology: Native Korean compound noun 숲속, combining 숲 ('forest, woods', from Middle Korean 수플 *swuphul*, attested in the 1445 *Yongbieocheonga*) and 속 ('interior, inside, heart', from Middle Korean 속 *swok*). Written without a space as a lexicalized compound in Standard Korean, it designates the deep interior of a forest or woodland.

history.meaning: dense thicket or woods + interior space
the interior of a forest; deep in the woods

숲속.notes: Registered as a single compound word in the Standard Korean Dictionary (so written 숲속 without a space, unlike many other noun + 속 phrases).

쉬다.etymology: Native Korean verb uniting two Middle Korean verbs: (1) 쉬다 ('to rest, take a break, relax; to breathe', as in 숨을 쉬다 'to draw breath'); and (2) 싀다 > 쉬다 ('to go sour or spoil of food; to become hoarse of the voice').

history.meaning: to rest, breathe; to turn sour or hoarse
to rest, take time off; to breathe; to spoil/go sour; to get hoarse

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쉬다

쉬어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction 쉬어보다, composed of the verb stem 쉬- (from 쉬다 'to rest, take a breather', Middle Korean 쉬다 *swuyta*, originally connected to drawing breath, cf. 숨을 쉬다), the infinitive connective ending -어 (*-e*), and the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to try doing, experience doing', grammaticalized from the lexical verb 보다 *pwota* 'to see, look at'). Literally 'to rest and see how it is'.

history.meaning: to breathe/cease labor + to look at or observe
to try resting; to take some time off and see how it feels

morphemes.meaning: auxiliary verb of attempt or experience ('try doing', lit. 'see')

쉬어보다.notes: The -어 보다 construction softens suggestions or describes past experiences ('tried resting'), very common in overworked Korean workplace dialogue.

rootFamily.gloss: to rest, take a break; to breathe

쉽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'easy, simple, effortless; likely/apt to', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 쉽다.

history.meaning: easy, not difficult
easy, simple

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쉽다

슈거파우더.etymology: Compound loanword from English sugar and powder ('finely ground confectioners' sugar or icing sugar dusted over pastries and desserts').

history.meaning: finely powdered sugar
powdered sugar, icing sugar

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슈거파우더

슈퍼.etymology: Loanword 슈퍼, clipped from 슈퍼마켓 (from English *supermarket*, itself a 20th-century American English compound of Latin *super-* 'above, beyond' + *market*, from Latin *mercātus* 'trade, marketplace'). This clipping parallels Japanese スーパー (*sūpā* < *sūpāmāketto*) and in South Korean usage specifically came to denote a neighborhood grocery or corner market (동네 슈퍼) rather than a massive hypermarket.

history.meaning: large self-service retail grocery store
neighborhood grocery store or corner market

morphemes.meaning: supermarket, neighborhood grocery store (clipped from English 'supermarket')

슈퍼.notes: In Korea, a 슈퍼 usually means a small neighborhood mom-and-pop grocery store (슈퍼마켓), whereas huge big-box supermarkets are called 마트 (mart) and 24-hour chains are 편의점 (convenience stores).

cognates.meaning: clever, quick-witted, neat and stylish in appearance

스마트하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword descriptive verb 스마트하다, combining the English loanword 스마트 (*smart*, ultimately from Old English *smeart* 'sharp, stinging, brisk, quick', Proto-Germanic **smartaz*) with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be'). In Korean, it retains both the American English sense of 'clever, intelligent, tech-savvy' and the British/Commonwealth sense of 'sharp, neat, and polished in manner or dress'.

history.meaning: causing sharp pain > brisk, quick-witted, neat and trim in attire
to be clever, sharp-witted, sleek, or polished in style and work

스마트하다.notes: Describing a coworker or PD as 스마트하다 compliments not just their IQ, but their crisp, efficient, and well-groomed professional demeanor.

스며들다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining the infinitive stem 스며- of 스미다 ('to soak, ooze, permeate', Middle Korean 스믜다) with the directional verb 들다 ('to enter, go inward'). Adding 들다 highlights inward penetration into a porous material or space—syrup soaking into sponge cake, rain seeping into stone, or evening light and aroma filling a room. Because the second stem is 들-, it follows Korean ㄹ-deletion before ㄴ, ㅂ, and ㅅ (스며듭니다, 스며드는).
스며들다.notes: Takes -에 or -으로/-로 to mark the medium or space penetrated (종이에 스며들다).

스무.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral meaning 'twenty (20)' used before nouns and classifiers (e.g., 스무 살 'twenty years old', 스무 개 'twenty items'), derived by regular pre-consonantal final ㄹ loss from 스물 ('twenty', Middle Korean 스믈).

history.meaning: twenty (adnominal form before nouns)
twenty (adnominal)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스무

스물.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'twenty (20)', descending from Middle Korean 스믈 ('twenty') via Early Modern Korean labial vowel rounding of ㅡ to ㅜ after ㅁ.

history.meaning: twenty
twenty (20)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물

스물네.etymology: Native Korean compound adnominal numeral meaning 'twenty-four (24)' used before nouns and classifiers, combining 스물 ('twenty') + 네 (adnominal form of 넷 'four').

history.meaning: twenty + four (adnominal)
twenty-four (before a counter)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물네

스물다섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral meaning 'twenty-five (25)', combining 스물 ('twenty', Middle Korean 스믈) + 다섯 ('five', Middle Korean 다ᄉᆞᆺ).

history.meaning: twenty + five
twenty-five (25)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물다섯

스물두개.etymology: Compound numeral-classifier expression 스물두개, composed of the native Korean decimal numeral 스물 ('twenty', from Middle Korean 스믈 *sumul*, 15th c., prior to labial vowel rounding *u* > *wu* after bilabial *m*), the prenominal determiner form 두 ('two', reduced from native Korean 둘 *twul* before classifiers), and the Sino-Korean general classifier 개 (個, 'individual item, piece', originally 'bamboo stalk').

history.meaning: twenty + two + individual bamboo tally or item counter
twenty-two items or pieces

morphemes.meaning: two (prenominal form of 둘 before a counter)

스물두개.notes: Notice how 스물 ('20') keeps its final ㄹ before 두 ('2') in 스물두 개, whereas 스물 drops its ㄹ directly before counters or certain words (e.g., 스무 살 '20 years old', 스무 개 '20 items').

스물셋.etymology: Native Korean additive compound numeral 스물셋 ('twenty-three'), formed by juxtaposing 스물 ('twenty', from Middle Korean 스믈 *sumul*, which underwent labial vowel rounding of the second syllable *으* > *우* after *ㅁ* in Early Modern Korean) and 셋 ('three', substantive numeral form from Middle Korean 세 *sey* / 셋 *seys*, attested in the 15th-century *Hunminjeongeum* and *Seokbo Sangjeol*). Used as a standalone noun or age expression without a classifier.

history.meaning: two tens (twenty) + three
the number twenty-three; twenty-three years of age (in colloquial speech)

스물셋.notes: When used directly before a counter like 살 ('years of age') or 개 ('items'), 셋 shortens to its determiner form 세: 스물세 살 ('23 years old'). Without the counter, Koreans simply say 스물셋 ('I'm 23').

스물여덟.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral 스물여덟 ('twenty-eight'), combining 스물 ('twenty', Middle Korean 스믈 *sumul*) and 여덟 ('eight', Middle Korean 여듧 *yetulp*, attested in 15th-century texts with a complex *-lp* coda cluster). Etymologists have long analyzed Old/Middle Korean *yetulp* ('eight') as a subtractive formation related to 열 (*yel*, 'ten') minus 둘 (*twul*, 'two'), i.e., 'two from ten'.

history.meaning: twenty + eight (two short of ten)
twenty-eight; twenty-eight years old in conversational Korean

스물여덟.notes: Pronounced [스물려덜] in standard speech (with liquidization/n-insertion and reduction of the ㄼ cluster to [ㄹ] before a pause or consonant). Unlike 둘/셋/넷, 여덟 does not change shape before counters (스물여덟 살).

rootFamily.gloss: eighty (native Korean numeral, related to 여덟)

스물여덟째.etymology: Native Korean compound ordinal numeral meaning 'twenty-eighth (28th)', formed from 스물 ('twenty') + 여덟 ('eight', Middle Korean 여듧) + ordinal suffix -째.

history.meaning: twenty + eight + ordinal suffix
twenty-eighth (28th)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물여덟째

스스로.etymology: Native Korean reflexive noun and adverb 스스로 ('by oneself, on one's own accord, spontaneously'), inherited from Middle Korean 스스로 (*susu-lwo*, attested in the 1447 *Seokbo Sangjeol* and 1459 *Worin Seokbo*, alongside dialectal/earlier 시스로 *sisulwo*). Morphologically formed from a reduplicated reflexive/spontaneous base 스스- (*susu-*) plus the native instrumental suffix -로 (*-lwo*, 'by means of, as').

history.meaning: of one's own accord, spontaneously, by oneself
by oneself, on one's own, voluntarily; oneself (as a reflexive noun)

스스로.notes: Functions both as an adverb ('스스로 해결하다', to solve by oneself) and as a noun that can take case particles ('스스로를 믿다', to believe in oneself).

rootFamily.gloss: for oneself, by itself (저절로, parallel -로 adverbial formation)
each by oneself, separately (따로, native -로 adverb)

스웨터.etymology: Borrowed from English sweater ('knitted garment worn on the upper body').

history.meaning: knitted pullover or cardigan
sweater

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스웨터

스위치.etymology: Borrowed from English switch ('device for making and breaking an electrical connection').

history.meaning: electrical control switch
switch

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스위치

cognates.meaning: publicly disgraceful event or rumor; moral outrage

스캔들.etymology: Loanword 스캔들, borrowed from English *scandal*, which entered Middle English via Old French *escandle* from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin *scandalum* ('cause of offense, stumbling block'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek *skándalon* (σκάνδαλον, 'trap, snare, trigger stick of a trap, stumbling block'). In contemporary South Korean entertainment and media discourse, it frequently narrows to mean a celebrity dating rumor or romantic exposé.

history.meaning: spring-stick of a trap; stumbling block or moral temptation
disgraceful publicized misconduct or defamatory rumor
public scandal, or specifically a celebrity romantic rumor/dating news story

스캔들.notes: False friend alert: in K-pop and K-drama entertainment news (연예계), 스캔들 very often just means 'dating rumor' (열애설) between two celebrities, even when nothing illegal or unethical happened!

rootFamily.gloss: dating rumor, romantic news report (熱愛說, native Sino-Korean equivalent)
scandal, disgraceful affair (醜聞, Sino-Korean equivalent)

스케줄.etymology: Loanword 스케줄, borrowed from American English *schedule* ([ˈskɛdʒuːl]), which came via Middle English *sedule* and Old French *cedule* from Late Latin *schedula* ('small slip of paper, note'), the diminutive of Latin *scheda* from Ancient Greek *skhédē* (σχέδη, 'strip of papyrus leaf', related to *skhízō* 'to split, cleave'). In Korean broadcasting and entertainment, it refers both to an overall timetable and to an individual work booking or shoot.

history.meaning: strip of papyrus > small slip of paper or appended scroll note
tabulated timetable or planned sequence of appointments
timetable, itinerary, or a celebrity's individual filming/appearance booking

스케줄.notes: Orthography & usage tip: Korean spells it 스케줄 (with 줄, NEVER *스케쥴), and in entertainment jargon it is countable for individual gigs ('오늘 스케줄 세 개 뛰었다' = 'I ran three work bookings today').

스케줄표부터.etymology: Polymorphemic hybrid form 스케줄표부터, combining the English loanword 스케줄 (*schedule*, from Late Latin *schedula* 'small slip of paper'), the Sino-Korean bound suffix 표 (表, 'surface, chart, table, list'), and the native Korean delimiter particle 부터 ('from, starting with'). The particle 부터 grammaticalized from Middle Korean 브터 (*puthe*, 15th c.), originally the infinitive form (*붙- + -어*) of the verb 붙다 ('to adhere, stick to, originate at').

history.meaning: adhering to / starting from + written table or memorial list
starting with the schedule sheet; the schedule chart first

morphemes.meaning: starting from, first (native Korean delimiter particle)

스케줄표부터.notes: When attached to an object rather than a time/place, -부터 means 'starting with X first (before doing anything else)', e.g., '스케줄표부터 확인하자' ('Let's check the schedule sheet first').

rootFamily.gloss: timetable, class or train schedule (時間表)
