스케치.etymology: Borrowed from English sketch, which entered English via Dutch schets from Italian schizzo ('a quick splash, rough preliminary drawing'), ultimately tracing back through Latin schedius to Ancient Greek skhedios ('done on the spur of the moment, improvised'). Korean adapts the consonant cluster sk- with epenthetic 으 as 스- and final -ch as -치, yielding three open syllables (스케치). It is standard in Korean art, architecture, and everyday speech alongside the native compound 밑그림 ('under-drawing').
스케치.notes: Forms the verb 스케치하다 ('to sketch') and compound 스케치북 ('sketchbook').

스케치북.etymology: Borrowed from English 'sketchbook', a compound of 'sketch' (via Dutch 'schets' and Italian 'schizzo' from Latin 'schedius', 'made suddenly or offhand', from Ancient Greek 'σχέδιος') and 'book' (from Old English 'bōc'). In Korean broadcasting, beyond a drawing pad, it denotes large flip-pad cue books and the title of KBS's flagship live music talk show '유희열의 스케치북' (You Hee-yeol's Sketchbook).

history.meaning: rough impromptu drawing; written tablet or tome (Italian / Old English)
pad or book of blank paper for sketching
sketchbook; studio cue-book or music program title

스케치북.notes: In Korean TV production, PDs and writers often use a large physical 스케치북 instead of printed cue cards to write big, spontaneous prompts for cast members during filming.

rootFamily.gloss: sketch; rough draft or short comedy scene

스크램블드에그.etymology: Compound loanword from English scrambled eggs ('dish of beaten eggs gently stirred while cooking in a pan').

history.meaning: pan-cooked stirred beaten eggs
scrambled eggs

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스크램블드에그

스크롤.etymology: Borrowed from English 'scroll', from Middle English 'scrolle' (altered from 'scrowe' under the influence of 'rolle'), from Anglo-Norman 'escrowe' ('strip of parchment'), ultimately from Frankish '*skrōda' ('shred, strip'). Adopted into Korean broadcasting and computing terminology for text moving vertically or horizontally across a screen, especially the end-credit roll ('엔딩 스크롤') of a television program or film.

history.meaning: roll of parchment or paper containing writing
parchment roll; continuous movement of text across a display screen
screen scrolling; broadcast end-credit roll

스크롤.notes: In Korean TV variety and drama production, '스크롤 올라간다' ('the scroll is going up') is standard jargon for the final moments of a broadcast when the end credits roll.

스타.etymology: Borrowed from English 'star', from Middle English 'sterre', from Old English 'steorra', from Proto-Germanic '*sterrō', ultimately from Proto-Indo-European '*h₂stḗr' ('star'). Korean borrowed the word primarily in its 19th- and 20th-century theatrical and cinematic metaphorical sense of a celebrated performer, top entertainer, or public luminary, whereas the astronomical body is usually called native Korean '별' (byeol).

history.meaning: celestial body visible in the night sky
celestial body; leading actor or famous celebrity (since ~1820s)
celebrity, top entertainer, famous sports or media figure

스타.notes: For literal stars in the sky, Korean uses native '별' (byeol) or Sino-Korean '항성' (恒星); '스타' is reserved almost exclusively for celebrities, top athletes, or iconic figures.

스타일리시.etymology: Borrowed from English 'stylish', derived from 'style' (via Old French 'stile' from Latin 'stilus', originally a pointed stake or Roman writing implement for wax tablets, extended to manner of writing and mode of expression) plus the adjectival suffix '-ish'. In Korean, English adjectives are borrowed as bound or autonomous nominal stems that can be used directly in titles/modifiers or combined with '-하다'.

history.meaning: pointed writing instrument; manner of composition
fashionably elegant, conforming to current style
stylishness; stylish (used as a nominal modifier or root)

스타일리시.notes: Under South Korean loanword orthography, English word-final '-sh' after a vowel is transcribed as '시' (not '쉬'), yielding '스타일리시' rather than the colloquial spelling '스타일리쉬'.

스타일리시하다.etymology: A hybrid descriptive verb (adjective) formed in Modern Korean by combining the English loanword stem '스타일리시' (from English 'stylish', ultimately from Latin 'stilus' 'writing tool, manner of expression' + English '-ish') with the native Korean light verb/adjective-forming suffix '-하다' (from Middle Korean 'ᄒᆞ다' 'to do, to be'). This morphological pattern integrates foreign adjectives into Korean predicate syntax.

history.meaning: having elegance or fashionable flair
loanword stem joined with native Korean deadjectival/deverbal predicator
to be stylish, chic, and fashionably sophisticated

morphemes.meaning: to be / to do (native Korean adjective-deriving suffix)

스타일리시하다.notes: When modifying a noun directly in a sentence, conjugate it with the adjectival determiner ending '-한' ('스타일리시한 옷', 'stylish clothes') rather than using bare '스타일리시'.

스탠드.etymology: Borrowed from English stand ('upright support or holder; desk lamp or floor lamp; spectator stands').

history.meaning: upright support, lamp stand, stadium seating
desk/floor lamp; stand, holder

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스탠드

스탠바이.etymology: Borrowed from English 'standby', nominalized from the phrasal verb 'stand by' (from Old English 'standan' 'to stand' + 'bī' 'near, by'), originally a nautical command meaning to remain near at hand and ready to assist another vessel or man a station. In Korean broadcasting and film sets, it is the universal floor director's cue ordering cast and crew into final readiness right before cameras roll.

history.meaning: to remain present and ready to act (originally nautical)
state of readiness or alert before action or transmission
on-set readiness cue before filming; waiting state

스탠바이.notes: On Korean drama and variety sets, the floor director shouts '스탠바이!' followed by '큐!' (Cue!) or '액션!' (Action!); '스탠바이하다' means to wait on set in full costume and makeup.

rootFamily.gloss: to stand by, wait in readiness to film

스트레스받다.etymology: A hybrid compound verb combining the English loanword '스트레스' ('stress', from Middle English 'stresse', partly shortened from 'distresse' and partly from Old French 'estrece' 'narrowness, oppression', from Vulgar Latin '*strictia', from Latin 'strictus', past participle of 'stringere' 'to draw tight') with the native Korean verb '받다' (Middle Korean '받다' 'pat-ta', 'to receive, take, suffer'). Literally 'to receive stress'.

history.meaning: to draw tight; tightness, hardship, psychological or physical strain
to receive, accept, undergo (attested in 15th-century Hangul texts)
to get stressed, experience mental or emotional strain

morphemes.meaning: stress, mental or physical pressure (from English)

스트레스받다.notes: In Korean, stress is idiomatically 'received' ('스트레스(를) 받다'), relieved by 'untying/releasing' ('스트레스를 풀다'), and inflicted by 'giving' ('스트레스를 주다').

스펀지.etymology: Borrowed from English sponge ('soft, porous, water-absorbent pad used for cleaning, baking, or cushioning'), ultimately from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).

history.meaning: absorbent porous material or pad
sponge

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스펀지

스페셜.etymology: Borrowed from English 'special', via Middle English and Old French 'especial' from Latin 'speciālis' ('individual, particular, belonging to a specific kind'), derived from 'speciēs' ('appearance, form, sort, kind'), itself from 'specere' ('to look at, behold'). In Korean television jargon, '스페셜' functions as a noun meaning a special broadcast, holiday edition, or highlight compilation episode.

history.meaning: particular, belonging to a specific sort or species
distinguished from what is ordinary; a special television program
special edition, television special, or highlight episode

스페셜.notes: While Sino-Korean '특별' (特別) is used in formal compounds ('특별 기획'), '스페셜' is preferred in TV scheduling for highlight episodes aired when regular filming is preempted.

스푼.etymology: Borrowed from English spoon ('utensil with a small shallow bowl on a handle, used for eating, stirring, or measuring').

history.meaning: eating or measuring spoon
spoon, teaspoon/tablespoon

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스푼

스프레이.etymology: Borrowed from English 'spray' ('liquid dispersed in fine droplets, or an atomizer device'), borrowed in Early Modern English from Middle Dutch 'sprāien' ('to sprinkle, scatter'), from Proto-West Germanic '*spraijan' ('to scatter, strew, dash in drops'). In Korean, it refers both to pressurized aerosol cans (such as hairspray or insect spray) and manual misting bottles.

history.meaning: to sprinkle, scatter liquid droplets
fine mist of liquid; pressurized aerosol dispenser or mist bottle
spray bottle, aerosol spray (especially hairspray or mist)

스프레이.notes: Korean pairs '스프레이' with the native verb '뿌리다' ('to sprinkle/scatter'): '스프레이를 뿌리다' ('to spray with a spray bottle or aerosol can').

rootFamily.gloss: spring (coil/season, sharing English initial spr- loan adaptation)

스피커.etymology: Borrowed from English 'speaker' (specifically the clipped form of 'loudspeaker', coined in the late 19th and early 20th centuries for an electroacoustic transducer), derived from the verb 'speak' (from Old English 'specan', variant of 'sprecan', from Proto-West Germanic '*sprekan') plus the agentive suffix '-er'. In Korean, it almost always means an audio loudspeaker rather than an orator.

history.meaning: to utter words, converse, make a speech
orator; electroacoustic device that converts electrical audio signals into sound
audio speaker, loudspeaker, public address horn

스피커.notes: A human speaker at a lecture or parliament is called '연사' (演士), '발표자' (發表者), or '의장' (議長); '스피커' in everyday Korean refers to audio hardware (or figuratively a 'mouthpiece').

rootFamily.gloss: speech, public address or promo talk

슬쩍.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'stealthily, discreetly, lightly, casually in passing', an intensified counterpart of 슬적.

history.meaning: quietly, discreetly, with a light motion
stealthily, discreetly, lightly

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슬쩍

슬쩍슬쩍.etymology: A native Korean reduplicated mimetic/ideophonic adverb (의태어) formed by doubling '슬쩍' (seuljjeok, 'stealthily, surreptitiously, with a quick effortless motion'). Within Korean sound symbolism, the dark/yin vowel 'ㅡ/ㅓ' in '슬쩍슬쩍' conveys a Slightly larger, heavier, or more covert and sly action than its bright/yang vowel counterpart '살짝살짝' (saljjak-saljjak, 'lightly, tiptoeing, barely touching'). Reduplication indicates repeated or intermittent stealthy actions.

history.meaning: with a single quick, unobtrusive, or sly motion
history.stage: Early Modern & Modern Korean base ideophone

history.meaning: repeatedly and surreptitiously; glancing or acting on the sly again and again

morphemes.meaning: stealthily, with a quick sly motion
reduplicated stem expressing repeated or ongoing sly action

슬쩍슬쩍.notes: Compare vowel harmony: '살짝살짝' feels cute, delicate, or light, whereas '슬쩍슬쩍' feels sneakier, more nonchalant, or sly (e.g., peeking at someone's answers or slipping out of work).

rootFamily.gloss: stealthily, on the sly, with a quick light brush (single action)
to slip away or pass over something on the sly

슬프다.etymology: Native Korean 으-irregular adjective meaning 'sad, sorrowful, mournful', descending from Middle Korean 슬프다, derived from the verb stem 슳- (슳다, 'to grieve, feel sorrow') plus the adjective-forming suffix -브다 (> -프다 after final ㅎ).

history.meaning: to grieve -> sad, sorrowful
sad, sorrowful

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슬프다

슬픔.etymology: A native Korean deverbal noun derived from the adjective stem '슬프-' (from '슬프다', 'to be sad, sorrowful') plus the substantive nominalizing suffix '-ㅁ' (-m). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean (such as the 'Seokbo Sangjeol', 1447, and 'Worin Seokbo', 1459) as '슬프다' (seul-pheu-da) and the related verb '슳다' (seulh-ta, 'to grieve, feel sorrow or physical/emotional ache'), nominalized via '-움/-음' as '슬픔'.

history.meaning: to grieve, lament, feel bitter pain or sorrow in the heart
sorrow, grief, sadness (nominalized with -ㅁ)

morphemes.meaning: to be sad, sorrowful (stem of 슬프다)

슬픔.notes: Formed by the productive native nominalizer '-ㅁ/-음', just like '기쁨' ('joy' < '기쁘다' 'to be joyful') and '아픔' ('pain' < '아프다' 'to hurt').

rootFamily.gloss: to grieve, mourn, feel sad (psychological action verb)
mournfully, pitifully, sorrowfully (derived from archaic root 슳-)

습기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 습기 (濕氣), meaning 'moisture, dampness, humidity', composed of 濕 (습, 'wet, damp, moist') + 氣 (기, 'air, vapor').

history.meaning: moist vapor or dampness in the air
moisture, dampness, humidity

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 습기

승강장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 승강장 (乘降場), meaning 'platform, boarding and alighting area (at a train, subway, or bus station)', formed from 승강 (乘降, 'boarding and alighting') + 장 (場, 'place, area').

history.meaning: place for getting on and off vehicles
platform, boarding area

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 승강장

cognates.meaning: victory or defeat; match, bout, contest
victory and defeat, outcome of a contest

승부.etymology: A Sino-Korean dvandva (coordinate) compound from Hanja '勝負' (승부), combining '勝' (이길 승, 'to win, triumph, surpass') and '負' (질 부, 'to lose, suffer defeat; originally to carry a burden on the back'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., 'Sunzi's Art of War'), '勝負' meant the two possible outcomes of battle—'victory or defeat'—which subsequently shifted by metonymy in Korean and Japanese to mean a decisive match, contest, or gamble itself.

history.meaning: victory and defeat; who wins and who loses in war or competition
outcome of a contest; a match, bout, showdown, or decisive bet/gamble

morphemes.meaning: 勝 (이길 승): victory, to win, prevail
負 (질 부): defeat, to lose, bear on the back

승부.notes: Key collocations include '승부를 가리다' ('to decide the winner'), '승부를 걸다' ('to stake everything / make a bold bet'), and '승부수' (勝負手, 'a decisive, game-changing move').

rootFamily.gloss: competitive spirit, desire to win (勝負 + 欲)
decisive move in a game or negotiation (勝負 + 手)

승부차기.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun coined in modern Korean sports terminology: Sino-Korean '勝負' (승부, 'victory or defeat; deciding the winner', from '勝' 'win' + '負' 'lose') combined with native Korean '차기' (chagi, 'kicking', nominalized from the verb stem '차-' of '차다' 'to kick' + nominalizer '-기'). Literally 'a kick to decide victory or defeat', created to distinguish a tie-breaking penalty shootout from an in-game penalty kick ('페널티킥').

history.meaning: deciding victory/defeat + native Korean verb 'to kick' (Middle Korean '차다')
tie-breaking penalty shootout in football (soccer)

morphemes.meaning: to kick (stem of native Korean verb 차다)

승부차기.notes: Do not confuse '승부차기' (the tie-breaking penalty shootout after extra time) with '페널티킥' (a single penalty kick awarded for a foul inside the penalty box during regular play).

rootFamily.gloss: victory or defeat; match, showdown (勝負)
to kick, strike with the foot
free kick in football (自由 + 차기, North Korean/puristic equivalent) or 제기차기 (shuttlecock kicking)

승용차.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '乘用車' (승용차), composed of '乘' (탈 승, 'to ride, mount, board a vehicle'), '用' (쓸 용, 'to use, for the purpose of'), and '車' (수레 차, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, automobile'). Coined in modern East Asian transport terminology (alongside Japanese '乗用車' jōyōsha) to designate a private vehicle built for riding passengers (typically a sedan or coupe seating six or fewer people), in contrast to commercial trucks or buses.

history.meaning: for riding use + wheeled carriage or vehicle
passenger car, private automobile, sedan

morphemes.meaning: 乘 (탈 승): to ride, mount, board
用 (쓸 용): to use, for the use of

승용차.notes: In Korean traffic and vehicle law, '승용차' specifically means a standard passenger car/sedan, contrasting with '승합차' (乘合車, 'van/minibus') and '화물차' (貨物車, 'cargo truck').

rootFamily.gloss: boarding, getting into a vehicle (乘車)

승인되다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 승인 (承認, combining 承 'receive, accede to' and 認 'recognize, authorize') plus the passive inchoative verb -되다 ('to become, be done'). It is the standard official and administrative verb for a permit, review, or proposal being formally approved.
승인되다.notes: Contracted in polite past speech as 승인됐어요.

승진시키다.etymology: Hybrid causative verb meaning 'to promote (someone to a higher rank or office)', combining Sino-Korean 승진 (昇進, 'promotion, advancement in rank', from 昇 'rise' + 進 'advance') with the native Korean causative verb -시키다.

history.meaning: promotion + causative verb
to promote (an employee or officer)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 승진시키다

승진하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound joining 승진 (昇進, from 昇 'ascend, rise' + 進 'advance') with native light verb -하다.
승진하다.notes: Used seriously for workplace promotions and playfully for 'getting promoted' to taste tester.

승질.etymology: A colloquial and dialectal phonological variant of the Sino-Korean noun '성질' (性質, seongjil, 'nature, disposition, temper'), composed of Hanja '性' (성품 성, 'inborn nature, character') and '質' (바탕 질, 'substance, essence, disposition'). Through vowel raising of '/ㅓ/' (eo) to '/ㅡ/' (eu) before the velar nasal '/ㅇ/'—a frequent sound change in colloquial Korean—'성질' became '승질', narrowing semantically to mean a fiery temper, irritability, or outburst of anger.

history.meaning: inherent nature, quality, or personal temperament
bad temper, flare of anger, irritable disposition (via vowel raising ㅓ > ㅡ)

morphemes.meaning: 性 (성품 성, colloquial 승): inborn nature, temperament, temper
質 (바탕 질): fundamental substance, disposition, quality

승질.notes: While '성질' can neutrally mean the 'chemical/physical property' of an object or a person's 'nature', the colloquial pronunciation '승질' almost always means a hot temper ('승질 내다', 'to lose one's temper').

rootFamily.gloss: nature, property, temperament, temper (standard form 性質)
hot-tempered person, someone with a nasty temper (colloquial)

시.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and bound classifier representing three everyday homophones: (1) 시 (時, Middle Chinese *dzyi*), bound counter for 'hour, o'clock' and noun 'time'; (2) 시 (市, Middle Chinese *dzyijX*), 'city, municipality'; and (3) 시 (詩, Middle Chinese *syi*), 'poem, poetry'.

history.meaning: o'clock, time; city; poem
o'clock, hour (時); city (市); poem, poetry (詩)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시

시간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시간 (時間), from 시 (時, 'time, hour') and 간 (間, 'interval, space between').
시간.notes: Means both 'time' in general and a duration of hours when preceded by a native Korean number (두 시간, 'two hours').

cognates.meaning: time zone; broadcasting timeslot or time period of day

시간대.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '時間帶' (시간대), formed from '時間' (시간, 'time, hour, interval of time', from '時' 'time, season' + '間' 'space, interval') plus the suffixoid '帶' (띠 대, originally 'girdle, sash, belt', extended in modern geography and scheduling to mean 'zone, band, or bracket'). It denotes either a geographical time zone (more often '표준시') or a specific block/timeslot of the day in broadcasting and traffic analysis.

history.meaning: interval of time + belt, band, or zone
time band, broadcasting timeslot, or geographical time zone

morphemes.meaning: 帶 (띠 대): belt, zone, band, range

시간대.notes: Essential TV industry vocabulary: '황금 시간대' ('golden timeband' = prime time), '심야 시간대' ('late-night timeslot'), and '동시간대 1위' ('No. 1 in the same timeslot').

시간표.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 시간표 (時間表): 시간 ('time') + 표 (表, 'chart, table').
시간표.notes: Used for train timetables, bus schedules, and school class schedules.

시계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시계 (時計), literally 'time-measurer', from 시 (時, 'time') + 계 (計, 'measure, gauge').
시계.notes: Covers both wall clocks and wristwatches.

시계바늘.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 시계 (時計, 'timepiece, clock', from 時 'time, hour' and 計 'measure, gauge') with the native Korean noun 바늘 ('needle', Middle Korean 바ᄂᆞᆯ). Just as European languages metaphorically call timepiece pointers 'hands' or 'needles' (compare French aiguille), Korean likens the slender metal pointers sweeping round a dial to sewing needles. Specific hands are distinguished by Sino-Korean compounds such as 시침 ('hour hand') and 분침 ('minute hand').
시계바늘.notes: Often pronounced [시계빠늘] or [시게빠늘] with compound tensification of ㅂ.

시계탑.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시계탑 (時計塔), meaning 'clock tower', formed from 시계 (時計, 'clock, timepiece', from 時 'time' + 計 'measure') + 탑 (塔, 'tower, pagoda').

history.meaning: tower fitted with a large clock
clock tower

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시계탑

시기.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '時期' (시기), combining '時' (때 시, 'time, season, oportunidad') and '期' (기약할 기, 'appointed time, fixed period, cycle, to await'). Used across East Asian literary and modern registers to denote a specific phase, historical period, seasonal juncture, or opportune moment in time.

history.meaning: appointed season or fixed period of time
time, period, phase, critical juncture, or season for doing something

morphemes.meaning: 期 (기약할 기): appointed time, period, phase, cycle

시기.notes: Watch out for two major homophones: '時期' (시기, 'time, period, juncture'), '時機' (시기, 'opportune moment, timing'), and '猜忌' (시기, 'jealousy, envy').

시끄럽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'noisy, loud, clamorous, boisterous', attested in Early Modern Korean as 식그럽다 / 시끄럽다 (built on an ideophonic/expressive stem 시끌- + adjective suffix -업다/-럽다).

history.meaning: noisy, tumultuous, loud
noisy, loud, rowdy

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시끄럽다

시나몬.etymology: Borrowed from English cinnamon ('aromatic inner bark of Cinnamomum trees used as a culinary spice', alongside Sino-Korean 계피 桂皮).

history.meaning: sweet aromatic bark spice
cinnamon

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시나몬

시내.etymology: Korean noun representing two distinct etymologies: (1) Sino-Korean 시내 (市內, pronounced with a long initial vowel [시:내]), meaning 'downtown, city center, within the city' (from 市 'city' + 內 'inside'); and (2) native Korean 시내, meaning 'stream, brook, creek' (descending unchanged from Middle Korean 시내).

history.form: 市內 (within the city) / 시내 (brook, stream)
history.meaning: downtown, city interior; stream, creek
downtown, city center (市內); stream, brook

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시내

시다.etymology: Core native Korean taste adjective attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 싀다 ('to be sour, acid'), belonging to the primary five-taste set alongside 달다 ('sweet'), 짜다 ('salty'), 쓰다 ('bitter'), and 맵다 ('spicy'). Its adnominal form 신 appears in lexicalized compounds such as 신맛 ('sour taste') and 신김치 ('well-fermented sour kimchi'), and its root spun off the sensory derivatives 시큼하다 and 새콤하다. A secondary somatic sense describes eyes smarting from bright glare or cold wind (눈이 시다).
시다.notes: Conjugates 시 + 어요 -> 셔요 (or uncontracted 시어요) and adnominal 신 (신 과일 'sour fruit').

시대.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '時代' (시대), formed from '時' (때 시, 'time, season, epoch') and '代' (대신할 대 / 대 대, 'to replace, succeed; generation, dynasty, historical period'). Originally referring to the succession of times and dynasties, it became the standard East Asian term for a historical era, epoch, or the prevailing zeitgeist of an age.

history.meaning: successive generations or dynastic periods of time
historical era, age, epoch, or contemporary times

morphemes.meaning: 代 (대 대): generation, dynasty, era, succession

시대.notes: While '시기' (時期) is a shorter phase or juncture (e.g., adolescence or a fiscal quarter), '시대' (時代) refers to a grand historical era or cultural age ('조선 시대' 'Joseon Dynasty era', '디지털 시대' 'digital age').

rootFamily.gloss: spirit of the times, zeitgeist (時代精神)

cognates.meaning: starting an engine or machine, activation

시동.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '始動' (시동), combining '始' (비로소 시, 'beginning, to start, initiate') and '動' (움직일 동, 'to move, set in motion, operate'). Coined in modern Sino-Japanese and Sino-Korean engineering terminology ('始動', shidō / sidong) for putting a mechanical engine or motor into initial motion, and universally used in everyday Korean for a vehicle's ignition.

history.meaning: to begin + to move or act
starting a machine or motor; vehicle engine ignition and warm-up

morphemes.meaning: 始 (비로소 시): beginning, to start, initiate
動 (움직일 동): to move, operate, set in motion

시동.notes: Learn the core automotive idioms: '시동을 걸다' ('to start the engine / turn the ignition on'), '시동을 끄다' ('to turn off the engine'), and '시동이 꺼지다' ('for the engine to stall/die'). Also used figuratively for warming up to a task!

rootFamily.gloss: operation, running of a machine or system (稼動)

시럽.etymology: Borrowed from English syrup ('thick sweet liquid made by dissolving sugar in water or fruit juice'), ultimately from Medieval Latin sirupus and Arabic شراب (sharāb, 'beverage, sweet drink').

history.meaning: viscous sweetened liquid
syrup

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시럽

시련.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '試鍊' (also written '試練', 시련), composed of '試' (시험 시, 'to test, try, examine') and '鍊' (불릴 련, 'to smelt, refine metal in fire, temper steel'; or '練' 익힐 련, 'to boil and bleach raw silk, to drill, train'). Originally a metallurgical and ascetic metaphor—testing and tempering metal through intense fire—it came to denote a severe life ordeal, tribulation, or hardship that tests one's fortitude.

history.meaning: testing and refining metal by fire (or softening silk by boiling)
hardship, severe trial, tribulation, or ordeal that tests a person

morphemes.meaning: 試 (시험 시): to test, try, examine
鍊 (불릴 련): to smelt, temper metal in fire, refine through hardship

시련.notes: Do not confuse '시련' (試鍊, 'trials, hardship, ordeal') with the near-homophone '실연' (失戀, [시련], 'heartbreak, unrequited or lost love')—though in Korean dramas characters often suffer both at once!

시뮬레이션.etymology: Borrowed from English 'simulation', from Middle French 'simulation', from Latin 'simulātiō' ('an imitating, feigning, copying'), noun of action from the past participial stem of 'simulāre' ('to make like, imitate, copy, represent'), itself derived from the Latin adjective 'similis' ('like, resembling, of the same kind'). In Korean, it refers to computer modeling, rehearsal run-throughs in broadcasting, or mentally playing out scenarios in advance.

history.meaning: like, similar > to copy or feign > act of imitating or modeling
imitation of the operation of a real-world process or system over time
computer simulation; pre-broadcast rehearsal or mental scenario run-through

morphemes.meaning: simulate (to model, imitate, or rehearse a process)

시뮬레이션.notes: In Korean variety shows and everyday speech, '시뮬레이션을 돌리다' ('to run a simulation') often means mentally rehearsing a conversation, confession, or game strategy in one's head before doing it for real.

rootFamily.gloss: similar, simulation-like (related English loan family in gaming: 시뮬, abbreviation of 시뮬레이션)

시민.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 市民, formed from 市 (저자 시, 'market, municipality, city') and 民 (백성 민, 'people, citizenry'). Whereas classical East Asian texts used 市人 for urban market-dwellers, 市民 gained modern civic currency in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries to denote both the residents of a municipality (such as 서울 시민, 'residents of Seoul') and rights-bearing members of civil society.
시민.notes: Pairs with city names (서울 시민, 부산 시민) and civic compounds like 시민 공원 ('citizens' park').

cognates.meaning: right and wrong; pros and cons; by all means
right and wrong; quarrel, dispute, gossip

시비.etymology: A Sino-Korean dvandva compound from Hanja '是非' (시비), combining '是' (옳을 시, 'this, right, correct') and '非' (아닐 비, 'not, wrong, fault'). In Classical Chinese philosophy (such as 'Zhuangzi' and 'Mencius'), '是非' meant distinguishing moral right from wrong. From 'arguing over who is right and who is wrong', its meaning evolved in Korean and Chinese into 'verbal dispute, wrangling, quarrel, or picking a fight'.

history.meaning: right and wrong; moral judgment between truth and error
judging right and wrong; a quarrel, dispute, or picking a fight

morphemes.meaning: 非 (아닐 비): wrong, not, fault, error

시비.notes: The classic idiom is '시비를 걸다' ('to pick a fight / start a quarrel with someone') and '시비가 붙다' ('for a quarrel/brawl to break out'). Compare the four-character idiom '시시비비' (是是非非, 'sorting out every right and wrong').

rootFamily.gloss: judging what is right and what is wrong (是是非非)
to argue, nitpick, or dispute right and wrong (是非하다)

cognates.meaning: preview screening of a film or television program

시사하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed from '試寫' (시사, 'preview screening') plus the native Korean verb-deriving suffix '-하다' ('to do'). '試寫' combines Hanja '試' (시험 시, 'to test, try out') and '寫' (베낄 사, originally 'to sketch, copy, transcribe', extended in modern media to 'photograph, project on a screen', as in '寫眞' 'photograph' and '映寫' 'film projection'). In Korean broadcasting and cinema, '시사하다' means to preview or test-screen edited footage before public release.

history.meaning: to test or try + to copy, depict, or project images
history.stage: Sino-Korean / Modern East Asian media roots

history.meaning: to preview or test-screen a film or broadcast episode before airing

morphemes.meaning: 寫 (베낄 사): to copy, project, screen images

시사하다.notes: In 'The Producers' (프로듀사), PDs constantly '시사하다' (試寫하다, 'preview/screen the edited episode in the editing room before broadcast'). Do not confuse with its common homophone '시사하다' (示唆하다, 'to imply, suggest, hint at')!

rootFamily.gloss: preview room, screening room at a TV station (試寫室)

시선.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '視線' (시선), composed of '視' (볼 시, 'to look at, inspect, regard, vision') and '線' (줄 선, 'thread, wire, line'). Originally coined in modern East Asian optical and anatomical vocabulary to translate European 'line of sight' or 'visual axis', it rapidly expanded in everyday Korean to mean a person's gaze, eye contact, or figurative societal perspective and scrutiny.

history.meaning: to look at, vision + thread or geometrical line
optical line of sight; one's gaze, eyes, or public perspective/viewpoint

morphemes.meaning: 視 (볼 시): to look at, see, vision, gaze

시선.notes: Used both for literal eye direction ('시선을 마주치다' 'to lock eyes', '시선을 피하다' 'to avert one's gaze') and for how others view someone ('따가운 시선' 'stinging/critical eyes', '사회의 시선' 'society's perspective').

rootFamily.gloss: eye contact, gaze, attention (注目 / 눈길, or 視線 처리 'handling where one looks on camera')

시설.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시설 (施設), meaning 'facility, installation, equipment, institution', composed of 施 (시, 'carry out, put in place') + 設 (설, 'establish, set up').

history.meaning: setting up and equipping an installation
facility, installation, amenities

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시설

시스템.etymology: Borrowed from English 'system', from Early Modern French 'système' or Late Latin 'systēma' ('an arrangement, musical interval, or organized whole'), borrowed from Ancient Greek 'σύστημα' (sústēma, 'an organized whole compounded of several parts'), from 'σύν' (sún, 'together, with') + the root of 'ἵστημι' (hístēmi, 'to cause to stand, set up', from PIE '*steh₂-'). Used in Korean for both technical/computer architectures and organizational workflows.

history.meaning: whole compounded of several parts standing together
organized set of interacting components, rules, or computing equipment
computer/technical system; institutional workflow or organizational structure

morphemes.meaning: system, organized structure or technical setup

시스템.notes: While Sino-Korean '체계' (體系) is used for theoretical or academic frameworks and '제도' (制度) for laws/policies, '시스템' is the everyday word for both IT hardware/software and how a workplace or TV station operates.

rootFamily.gloss: to systematize, turn into a routine system (시스템 + 化)

시식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시식 (試食), from 시 (試, 'test, try') and 식 (食, 'eat, food').
시식.notes: Parallel to 시음 (試飮, 'drink tasting') and 시연 (試演, 'trial performance').

시원섭섭하다.etymology: A native Korean oxymoronic coordinate compound adjective formed by joining the stem '시원-' (from '시원하다', 'to be cool, refreshing, relieved, unburdened') and the ideophonic/emotive stem '섭섭-' (from '섭섭하다', 'to feel sad at parting, regretful, wistful, disappointed') with the adjective-forming suffix '-하다'. It lexicalizes a quintessential Korean emotional blend: feeling relieved that a long, arduous task is over, yet simultaneously wistful and sad to part ways.

history.meaning: to feel cool/relieved + to feel wistful/regretful at parting
to feel bittersweet (simultaneously relieved and sad/nostalgic at an ending)

morphemes.meaning: wistful, sorry to part, regretful (stem of 섭섭하다)

시원섭섭하다.notes: A classic culturally resonant Korean expression used at graduations, retirements, or a drama/variety show's final wrap party ('종방연'), capturing the mix of 'glad the hard work is done' ('시원') and 'sad to say goodbye' ('섭섭').

rootFamily.gloss: to feel sad at parting, wistful, disappointed

시원하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'cool, refreshing (of air, wind, or a hot broth that brings relief); relieving, satisfying, unhindered', attested in Early Modern Korean as 시원ᄒᆞ다.

history.meaning: refreshing, cool, relieving
cool, refreshing, relieving, forthright

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시원하다

cognates.meaning: demonstration, show of force, protest march
to demonstrate, hold a protest march, show force
to demonstrate, make a show of force

시위.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from Hanja '示威' (시위), composed of '示' (보일 시, 'to show, display, manifest') and '威' (위엄 위, 'might, power, authority, awe-inspiring dignity'). Originally a Classical Chinese military expression ('示威', verb-object: 'to display military might to awe an adversary'), it was adapted in modern East Asian political vocabulary to translate Western 'demonstration'—a public rally, march, or picket showing collective resolve.

history.meaning: to display military power or authority to intimidate an opponent
public protest, political demonstration, or picket rally

morphemes.meaning: 示 (보일 시): to show, display, manifest
威 (위엄 위): power, might, authority, collective force

시위.notes: Often used in '1인 시위' ('one-person protest with a placard', seen in 'The Producers' in front of the broadcasting station). Note also the native Korean homophone '시위' ('bowstring', as in '시위를 당기다').

rootFamily.gloss: to protest, stage a demonstration (示威하다)

시작.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시작 (始作), meaning 'beginning, start, commencement', formed from 始 (시, 'begin, initial') + 作 (작, 'make, do, undertake').

history.meaning: beginning an action or work
start, beginning

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작

시작되다.etymology: Hybrid passive/intransitive verb meaning 'to begin, be started, commence', formed from Sino-Korean 시작 (始作, 'beginning, start') plus the native Korean passive/inchoative verb -되다 ('to become, be done').

history.meaning: beginning + to become/be done
to begin, start (intransitive/passive)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작되다

시작하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb meaning 'to begin, start, commence', formed from 시작 (始作, 'beginning, start') plus the verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to begin, initiate
to start, begin

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작하다

시장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시장 (市場), meaning 'market, marketplace, bazaar', formed from 市 (시, 'market, city') + 場 (장, 'place, ground'). Also homophonous with 시장 (市長, 'mayor of a city') and 시장 (腸, 'feeling of hunger').

history.meaning: place where goods are traded
market, marketplace (市場); mayor (市長)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시장

시장통.etymology: A compound noun formed from Sino-Korean '市場' (시장, 'market, marketplace', from '市' 저자 시 'market, trade, city' + '場' 마당 장 'open ground, site, arena') and the Korean bound noun/suffix '-통' (-tong, 'amidst a crowded, noisy place or chaotic commotion', historically linked to Sino-Korean '通' 'thoroughfare, street' and the native/colloquial spatial noun '통' denoting a bustling environment or turmoil). It vividly evokes the noisy, crowded heart of a traditional street market.

history.meaning: marketplace, open ground where goods are traded
the bustling, noisy middle of a marketplace; a chaotic market-like scene

morphemes.meaning: 場 (마당 장): open ground, place, arena
bustling street, crowded midst, or noisy commotion (통)

시장통.notes: Adding '-통' to '시장' shifts the nuance from a neutral economic/geographic 'market' ('시장') to a sensory scene of crowds, shouting vendors, and lively chaos ('교실이 완전 시장통이다' = 'the classroom is like a noisy marketplace').

rootFamily.gloss: amidst the chaos of war, war-torn turmoil (亂離 + 통)
bustling narrow alley or backstreet (골목 + 통)

시절.etymology: Sino-Korean 시절 (時節), combining 시 (時, 'time, era') + 절 (節, 'bamboo joint, seasonal node, division of time'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese where 時節 denoted a season of the year, and extended in Korean to a fondly remembered period of one's life.

history.meaning: season of the year, juncture of time
season, era; days of one's life (어린 시절 'childhood')

시절.notes: In Korean, 어린 시절 ('young days') is the warmest everyday way to say 'childhood', alongside Sino-Korean 유년기.

시즌.etymology: Borrowed from English 'season', from Middle English 'sesoun', from Old French 'seson' ('proper time, season of planting'), from Latin 'satiōnem' (accusative of 'satiō', 'a sowing, planting'), derived from the past participial stem of 'serere' ('to sow, plant seeds', from PIE '*seh₁-'). While the four natural seasons are called Sino-Korean '계절' (季節), '시즌' is used in Korean for sports leagues, holiday peak periods, and television show broadcast runs ('시즌 1, 시즌 2').

history.meaning: act of sowing seeds > time of year for planting crops (Latin to Old French)
division of the year; recurrent period for sports, theater, or television series
broadcast season of a TV show; sports season or peak commercial period

morphemes.meaning: season (broadcast run, sports league period, or peak time of year)

시즌.notes: Use '계절' (季節) or '철' for spring/summer/autumn/winter weather, and '시즌' for TV series ('시즌제 드라마' 'seasonal drama'), sports ('야구 시즌'), or peak travel times ('휴가 시즌').

rootFamily.gloss: seasonal system in TV broadcasting (시즌 + 制)
season ticket or ski season pass (시즌 + 券)

시청.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시청 (市廳), from 시 (市, 'city, municipality') and 청 (廳, 'government hall, administrative office').
시청.notes: In Seoul, 시청 refers both to City Hall itself and the major subway junction beside Seoul Plaza.

시청률.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 시청 (視聽, 'watching and listening; audiovisual viewing', from 視 'look at, inspect' + 聽 'listen, hear') and the suffix -률 (率, 'rate, ratio, proportion'), which is spelled and pronounced -률 rather than -율 after a syllable ending in ㅇ (ng) per Korean orthographic rules. Coined in the twentieth-century broadcasting era (paralleling Japanese 視聴率 shichōritsu) to quantify the percentage of television households or individuals tuned in to a given program.

history.meaning: to look at + to listen to + rate or ratio
broadcasting audience measurement ratio
viewer ratings, television viewership percentage

시청률.notes: Under the South Korean Du-eum Beopchik (initial sound rule), 率 is written 열/율 after vowels or ㄴ, but retains its liquid initial 률 after all other consonants (including ㅇ in 시청률). In K-drama production rooms like in The Producers, minute-by-minute real-time ratings (분당 시청률) dictate a show's survival.

rootFamily.gloss: to watch TV, view a broadcast (視聽)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 시청률

시청률표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed by suffixing 표 (表, 'surface, chart, table, schedule') to 시청률 (視聽率, 'viewer ratings', from 視 'look at' + 聽 'listen' + 率 'rate, ratio'). Literally 'audiovisual viewing-rate table', referring to the daily or minute-by-minute statistical report sheets distributed by rating agencies (such as Nielsen Korea or TNMS) to television producers.

history.meaning: viewing-and-listening rate + tabular chart or list
ratings chart, television viewership table

시청률표.notes: In Korean television broadcasting, producers arrive at the station early in the morning specifically to check the overnight 시청률표 broken down by metropolitan area, age demographic, and commercial target.

시청자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound derived from 시청 (視聽, 'watching and listening; viewing a broadcast', from 視 'look at, see' + 聽 'listen, hear') plus the agentive suffix -자 (者, 'person who does, one who'). Adopted in modern broadcasting terminology (alongside Japanese 視聴者 shichōsha) to designate television and multimedia audiences who both watch and hear a program, in contrast to radio 청취자 (聽取者, 'listeners') or theater 관객 (觀客, 'spectators').

history.meaning: looking and listening + person/agent
broadcast viewer, television audience member
viewer, television audience

시청자.notes: Korean media distinguishes audience types strictly by sensory medium: 시청자 (視聽者) for TV/video, 청취자 (聽取者) for radio, 독자 (讀者) for print, and 관객 (觀客) for cinema or live stage.

cognates.meaning: circumstance, state of affairs, dramatic scenario

시추에이션.etymology: Direct modern loanword (외래어) from English situation, itself borrowed from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio ('position, site, arrangement'), a noun of action from Latin situare ('to place, locate'), from situs ('a place, position, site'), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *tḱey- ('to settle, dwell'). In Korean television and variety production jargon, 시추에이션 is frequently used for a scripted or semi-improvised dramatic setup (as in 시추에이션 코미디 'sitcom' or 시추에이션 드라마).

history.meaning: spatial placement, site, location
set of circumstances, dramatic setup in theater/TV
situation, staged scenario or dramatic premise in broadcasting

시추에이션.notes: While everyday 'situation' is normally expressed by the Sino-Korean 상황 (狀況), entertainment industry insiders use the English loanword 시추에이션 when referring to a contrived scenario, role-play setup, or sitcom premise.

rootFamily.gloss: sitcom, situation comedy (shortened from 시추에이션 코미디)

시켜달라다.etymology: Polymorphemic native Korean verbal construction composed of 시키다 ('to make someone do, order, assign, allow to participate', historically a causative derivative of Middle Korean 시다 'to exist/do' or related to 치다/시키다), the infinitive/connective suffix -어 (yielding 시켜), the suppletive benefactive/request auxiliary verb 달다 ('to give to the speaker', used in imperatives and indirect quotations in place of 주다), and the contracted indirect imperative quotative ending -라다 (contracted from -라고 하다, 'to say/ask someone to do'). Literally 'to say/ask [someone] to make/let [one] do it'.

history.meaning: to cause to do + connective + give to me + quote imperative + declarative
to ask/demand to be made/allowed to do something or have something ordered/assigned

morphemes.meaning: infinitive linker (-어 fused with ㅣ to -여)
give to the speaker, do for the speaker (suppletive to 주다)

시켜달라다.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes benefactive requests by recipient: in indirect speech ('she asked them to let her do it / cast her'), when the beneficiary is the subject of the quoting verb, 달다 (-달라고 하다 / -달라다) must be used instead of 주다 (-주라고 하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to make do, order, assign, commission
to assign for someone, let someone do, order for someone
to ask someone to give (contracted from 달라고 하다)

시켜주다.etymology: Compound native Korean verb formed from the causative/factitive verb stem 시키- (from 시키다, 'to make someone do, assign a role, order food/work'), the infinitive connective suffix -어 (contracting with 시키- to 시켜), and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, to do as a favor for someone', from Middle Korean 주다 'to give'). Together, 시켜주다 means 'to assign a task/role for someone's benefit', 'to let/allow someone do something', or 'to order (food/service) for someone'.

history.meaning: to give, bestow
to cause to do / order + for the benefit of another
to assign to someone, let someone do, or order for someone

시켜주다.notes: Depending on context, 시켜주다 can mean granting someone a coveted opportunity or role ('cast me in the show / let me do the job'), or simply ordering a meal/drink on someone's behalf ('buy/order for you').

시키다.etymology: Native Korean transitive and causative verb meaning 'to make or have someone do something; to order (food, drinks, or goods)', descending from Middle Korean 시키다 / 시기다 ('to cause to do, command').

history.meaning: to cause someone to do, instruct
to make/let do, order (a meal or delivery)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시키다

시트.etymology: Borrowed from English sheet ('bedsheet, baking/parchment sheet, flat layer of material') and English seat ('chair or vehicle seat').

history.meaning: flat sheet of cloth/paper; seat
sheet (bedsheet, baking sheet); seat

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시트

시합하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 시합 (試合, 'match, bout, game, contest', from 試 'test, try' + 合 'come together, bout') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to meet and test skill in a match
to compete in a match, have a game/bout

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시합하다

시험.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 시험 (試驗), a classical compound of 시 (試, 'to try, test, examine, put to use') and 험 (驗, 'to verify, inspect, prove, effect'). Already attested in Classical Chinese texts (such as the Qianfu Lun and historical annals) in the sense of 'trying out and verifying efficacy', it later became the standard East Asian term for academic examinations, civil service tests, and personal trials.

history.meaning: to try out and verify; practical verification of ability or efficacy
trial, verification, state examination
exam, test, trial, ordeal

시험.notes: In Korean, you do not 'take' (받다) an exam passively; the idiomatic collocations are 시험을 보다 ('to see/sit an exam') or 시험을 치르다 ('to undergo/pay off an exam'). In Christian and metaphorical contexts, 시험 also means 'temptation' or 'tribulation'.

cognates.meaning: test stand, testing bench, proving ground

시험대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 시험 (試驗, 'test, trial, examination', from 試 'try, test' + 驗 'verify, inspect') and the suffix/noun 대 (臺, 'platform, stand, stage, pedestal, workbench'). Originally denoting a physical laboratory bench or mechanical test stand on which apparatus is mounted for testing, it underwent metaphorical extension to mean a 'proving ground' or public scrutiny where a person's competence or a project's viability is put to the test.

history.meaning: testing/verification + raised platform or workbench
laboratory test bench; figuratively, a proving ground or public test of capability

시험대.notes: Almost always used figuratively in journalism and workplace speech in the phrase 시험대에 오르다 ('to ascend onto the testing bench', i.e., 'to be put to the test' or 'come under scrutiny').

rootFamily.gloss: chopping board, surface of public criticism (도마 / 俎臺)

시험하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 시험 (試驗, 'test, examination, trial, experiment', from 試 'try, test' + 驗 'verify, examine') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to try out and verify
to test, examine, try out

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시험하다

식.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun and suffix from Hanja 식 (式, 'model, pattern, rule, method, style, ceremony'), derived from Old Chinese *hljɯk, originally denoting a carpenter's rule, standard pattern, or the crossbar of a carriage used in ritual salutation. In Korean, 식 functions both as a suffix/bound noun meaning 'style, manner, way, type of' (as in 한국식 'Korean style' or 이런 식 'this kind of way') and 'ceremony, ritual' (as in 결혼식 'wedding ceremony').

history.meaning: standard model, rule, ritual pattern, carriage crossbar
established rule, ceremony, style or manner of doing
kind of, style of, manner, way; ceremony, mathematical formula

식.notes: In conversational Korean, 이런 식으로 ('in this manner / like this') and 그런 식 ('that kind of way') are ubiquitous for characterizing someone's behavior or attitude, often with a critical edge ('if you keep acting like that...').

식구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식구 (食口), meaning 'family member, household member, fellow member of a close group', literally 'mouths that eat together under one roof', from 食 (식, 'eat, meals') + 口 (구, 'mouth, person').

history.meaning: mouths sharing meals in a household
family member, household member

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식구

식다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to cool down, grow cold (of hot food, liquid, or enthusiasm)', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 식다.

history.meaning: to cool down, become cold
to cool, get cold, subside (of passion)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식다

식당.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식당 (食堂), meaning 'restaurant, dining hall, cafeteria, dining room', composed of 食 (식, 'eat, meal, food') + 堂 (당, 'hall, building, room').

history.meaning: hall or room for taking meals
restaurant, cafeteria, dining room

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식당

식물.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 植物, combining 植 (심을 식, 'to plant, set upright in soil', written with the tree radical 木) and 物 (만물 물, 'thing, living creature'). While classical Chinese writings already paired 動物 ('moving creatures, animals') and 植物 ('rooted things, plants'), the compound was standardized across modern East Asia as the scientific and everyday word for botanical life.
식물.notes: Pronounced [싱물] via nasal assimilation of ㄱ before ㅁ; pairs with 키우다 or 기르다 ('to grow plants').

식빵.etymology: Hybrid compound prefixing Sino-Korean 식- (食, 'meal, staple food') to 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese pan from Portuguese pão).
식빵.notes: Refers specifically to an unsweetened rectangular loaf sliced for toast or sandwiches.

식사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식사 (食事), meaning 'meal, dining', composed of 食 (식, 'eat, food') + 事 (사, 'matter, act, business').

history.meaning: act or affair of taking a meal
meal, dining

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식사

식사하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 식사 (食事, 'meal, dining', composed of 食 'to eat, food, meal' + 事 'affair, matter, business, act') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to do the business/act of eating', 식사 (食事) provides a polite, formal register alternative to the native Korean 밥 먹다 ('to eat cooked rice/a meal').

history.meaning: matters concerning food and agricultural sustenance; act of taking a meal
to partake of a meal, dine formally
to have a meal, dine

식사하다.notes: 식사하셨어요? ('Have you had a meal?') is a classic Korean workplace and polite social greeting. For higher honorifics toward elders or superiors, 식사하다 is elevated to 진지 드시다, whereas among close friends 밥 먹다 is used.

cognates.meaning: indigestion, Dyspepsia, getting tired of food

식상하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) combining the Sino-Korean noun 식상 (食傷, literally 'injury/harm from food', from 食 'eat, food' + 傷 'wound, injure, harm, sicken') with the native suffix 하다 ('to be in the state of'). Originating in traditional East Asian medicine (such as Heo Jun's Dongui Bogam) for dyspepsia or revulsion toward food caused by overeating the same dish, it shifted metaphorically to mean feeling fed up with something trite, stale, cliché, or overdone.

history.meaning: internal injury or indigestion from overeating (traditional Chinese/Korean medicine)
to suffer indigestion; to feel sick of eating the same food
to be stale, trite, hackneyed, overdone; to be fed up with

식상하다.notes: Just as English 'fed up' and French 'dégoûté' derive from overeating and distaste for food, 식상하다 (食傷하다) literally means 'food-injured'. In K-drama and variety production, a plot twist or gag that audiences have seen too many times is criticized as 식상한 설정 ('a stale/cliché setup').

식초.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식초 (食醋), from 식 (食, 'edible, food') and 초 (醋, 'vinegar, sour liquor').
식초.notes: Adding 식 (食) clarifies culinary vinegar in spoken Korean.

식탁.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식탁 (食卓), meaning 'dining table, kitchen table', composed of 食 (식, 'meal, food') + 卓 (탁, 'table, desk').

history.meaning: table for eating meals
dining table

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식탁

식탁보.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식탁보 (食卓褓), meaning 'tablecloth', formed from 식탁 (食卓, 'dining table') + 보 (褓, 'cloth cover, wrapping cloth', also the base of 보자기).

history.meaning: cloth covering for a dining table
tablecloth

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식탁보

식히다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to cool (something) down, let cool', derived from the intransitive verb 식다 ('to cool down') plus the causative suffix -히- (Middle Korean 식히다 / 시기다).

history.meaning: to make cool, cool down
to cool, let cool down

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식히다

식힘망.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'cooling rack (wire mesh rack used to cool freshly baked bread or pastries)', combining the native Korean verbal noun 식힘 ('cooling', from 식히다 'to cool' + nominalizer -ㅁ) with Sino-Korean 망 (網, 'net, wire mesh').

history.meaning: cooling + wire mesh/rack
wire cooling rack

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식힘망

신경.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 신경 (神經), composed of 신 (神, 'spirit, mind, vital psychic energy') and 경 (經, 'warp threads, meridian channel, pathway'). Famous as an 18th-century Sino-Japanese anatomical neologism coined by Sugita Genpaku and his colleagues in Kaitai Shinsho (解體新書, 1774) to translate Dutch zenuw ('nerve'), synthesizing the Sino-medical concept of 신기 (神氣, 'vital spirit') with 경맥 (經脈, 'meridian vessels'). Borrowed into Korean and Chinese, it expanded from anatomical 'nerve' to everyday psychological 'attention, care, concern, sensitivity'.

history.form: 神氣 + 經脈 > 神經 (shinkei)
history.meaning: anatomical nerve (translation of Dutch zenuw in 1774 Kaitai Shinsho)
anatomical nerve; psychological sensitivity, mind, concern

신경.notes: One of the most productive idiomatic nouns in Korean: 신경 쓰다 ('to use one's nerves' = to pay attention, care about, or bother with), 신경이 쓰이다 ('to have something weigh on one's mind'), and 신경전 (神經戰, 'war of nerves').

rootFamily.gloss: war of nerves, psychological battle (神經戰)

신고.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신고 (申告), meaning 'report, declaration, formal notification (to police, government, or authorities)', composed of 申 (신, 'state, report to a superior') + 告 (고, 'inform, declare').

history.meaning: stating and reporting formally
report, declaration, filing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신고

cognates.meaning: official report, declaration, tax return, filing
to report officially to a higher authority, declare

신고하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining 신고 (申告, 'official report, statement, or notification to authorities', from 申 'to state, explain, report to a superior, stretch out' + 告 'to tell, announce, inform, accuse') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Already attested in Classical Chinese administrative prose for reporting upward to a magistrate or sovereign, in modern Korean it specifically denotes filing an official report with the police, customs, tax office, or civil registry.

history.meaning: to state and announce formally to a higher authority
to report to the police or authorities, declare officially (taxes, birth, marriage)

morphemes.meaning: state, report to a superior, extend (申)

신고하다.notes: Do not confuse 신고하다 (申告하다, 'to file an official report with authorities/police, or register a marriage/birth') with 보고하다 (報告하다, 'to report work progress to a boss'). Also note the colloquial idiom 신고식을 치르다 ('to undergo a hazing/initiation ceremony as a newcomer').

cognates.meaning: new building, new wing of a library/museum/complex

신관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 신관 (新館), composed of 신 (新, 'new, recent, fresh') and 관 (館, 'public building, hall, lodge, pavilion, institutional edifice'). Literally 'new hall/building', it designates a newly constructed wing or annex added to an existing institutional complex—such as a broadcasting headquarters (like the KBS 신관 in Yeouido featured in The Producers), university, hospital, or department store—in contrast to the 본관 (本館, 'main/original building') or 구관 (舊館, 'old wing').

history.meaning: new + large public hall or lodging house
new wing, annex, newly constructed institutional building

신관.notes: At the KBS headquarters in Yeouido (the real-life setting of The Producers), television variety and drama departments operate out of the KBS 신관 (New Wing), making it a daily landmark in Korean broadcasting life. Note the homonym 신관 (神官, 'priest') and 구관이 명관이다 ('the old official [舊官] is the wise official [明官]').

신기하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 신기 (神奇, 'marvellous, wondrous, strange and fascinating', from 神 'miraculous, divine' + 奇 'unusual, curious') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: wondrous and extraordinary
marvellous, amazing, fascinating, curious

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신기하다

신나다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb lexicalized from the noun phrase 신(이) 나다, combining 신 (derived from Sino-Korean 神, 'spirit, divine energy, shamanic possession/enthusiasm', specialized in Korean folk culture to mean 'high spirits, exhilarating gusto, rhythmic excitement', akin to 신명 神明) and the native Korean intransitive verb 나다 ('to sprout, arise, break out, come forth', Middle Korean 나다). Literally 'for one's spirit/enthusiasm to well up', hence 'to become excited, thrilled, elated, or merry'.

history.meaning: vital/shamanic spirit + to come forth, arise
history.stage: Middle and Early Modern Korean constituents

history.meaning: for high spirits/enthusiasm to arise; to get excited, feel thrilled and merry

신나다.notes: Because 신나다 is grammatically an action/process verb (동사) rather than an adjective (형용사), its adnominal modifier meaning 'exciting/fun' uses the present-tense active participle 신나는 (e.g., 신나는 노래 'an exciting song'), never *신난 노래 for general characterization.

rootFamily.gloss: anger arises, to get angry (火 + 나다)

신다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to put on, wear (shoes, boots, slippers, or socks on the feet)', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 신다 (verbal counterpart of the noun 신 'footwear').

history.meaning: to wear on the feet
to put on / wear (shoes or socks)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신다

cognates.meaning: female given name (diminutive of Cynthia or Lucinda)
woman of Mount Cynthus (epithet of Artemis)

신디.etymology: Korean transliteration (신디) of the English female given name Cindy, which arose as a hypocoristic (pet form) of Cynthia (from Latin Cynthia, from Ancient Greek Κυνθία Kynthía, 'woman from Mount Cynthus on Delos', classical epithet of the moon goddess Artemis) and secondarily of Lucinda (an elaboration of Lucia, from Latin lux 'light') or Cinderella. In the 2015 K-drama The Producers (프로듀사), 신디 (Cindy) is the stage name of the aloof top K-pop idol played by IU.

history.meaning: of Mount Cynthus; epithet of the Greek goddess Artemis
English diminutive female given name
Cindy (transliterated given name / stage name of K-pop star in The Producers)

신디.notes: In South Korean pop culture, English hypocoristic names like 신디 (Cindy), 제니 (Jennie), and 웬디 (Wendy) are widely adopted as two-syllable idol stage names because they fit naturally into Korean prosody and international marketing.

rootFamily.gloss: Cinderella (often shortened to 신디 in pop culture references)

신문사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 신문사 (新聞社), formed from 신문 (新聞, 'newspaper', literally 'newly heard things / news', from 新 'new' + 聞 'to hear, news') and the institutional suffix -사 (社, 'company, society, association', originally 'altar of the soil god' and the village community gathered around it in Old Chinese). Modeled in the late nineteenth century alongside Meiji Japanese 新聞社 (shinbunsha) to denote a modern newspaper publishing corporation.

history.meaning: newly heard tidings + community association or commercial firm
history.stage: Classical Chinese constituents / Meiji Sino-Japanese coinage

history.meaning: newspaper company, press publisher (such as Hansung Sunbo or Dongnipsinmun offices)
history.stage: Late Joseon / Enlightenment Period Korean (late 19th century)

history.meaning: newspaper company, press corporation

신문사.notes: Whereas 신문 (新聞) means 'news' in Mandarin and Japanese (in compounds like 新聞局), in Korean 신문 alone strictly means 'newspaper' (print publication), while 'news' is expressed by the English loanword 뉴스 or 소식 (消息). A broadcasting network is a 방송사 (放送社), while a newspaper is a 신문사 (新聞社).

신문지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신문지 (新聞紙), adding 지 (紙, 'paper') to 신문 (新聞, literally 'newly heard things' -> 'newspaper').
신문지.notes: Distinguishes physical sheets of newsprint (used for wrapping pottery or vegetables) from 신문 as a publication.

신발.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'shoes, footwear', formed from 신 ('shoe, footwear', Middle Korean 신) + 발 ('foot', or collective suffix -발).

history.meaning: shoe + foot
shoes, footwear

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신발

신발끈.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of 신발 ('footwear, shoes', itself a compound of Middle Korean 신 'shoe, footwear' + 발 'foot') and 끈 ('string, cord, lace, strap', attested in Middle Korean as 끈 / 근 'string, tether'). Note that Middle Korean 신 ('shoe') + 발 ('foot') originally formed a coordinate or especificar compound designating footwear covering the foot, to which 끈 ('string/lace') was added to denote 'shoelace'.

history.meaning: footwear + foot + binding cord or string
shoelace, shoe string

신발끈.notes: In Korean cultural superstition and romantic tropes (frequently seen in K-dramas like The Producers), an untied 신발끈 means someone is thinking of you, and kneeling to tie another person's shoelace is a classic gesture of affection. Also used in the idiom 신발끈을 조여 매다 ('to tighten one's shoelaces' = to brace oneself for a challenge).

rootFamily.gloss: to wear on the feet (shoes, socks)

cognates.meaning: one's person, personal affairs, personal safety/circumstances
at one's side, with oneself, personal proximity

신변.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 신변 (身邊), formed from 신 (身, 'body, person, self') and 변 (邊, 'side, edge, margin, immediate surroundings'). Literally 'the area beside one's body', it evolved from physical proximity to denote a person's immediate life circumstances, personal affairs, or physical security and safety (as in 신변 보호 'personal protection').

history.meaning: beside one's body; immediate personal surroundings or possessions on one's person
one's personal safety, personal affairs, or immediate life circumstances

신변.notes: Most frequently encountered in two high-frequency collocations: 신변 보호 (身邊保護, 'personal safety/police protection') and 신변 정리 (身邊整理, 'putting one's personal affairs in order', used both for clearing out relationships/belongings before a major move and darkly in crime dramas).

rootFamily.gloss: personal life, one's lot in life (身世)

신비로움.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean derived abstract noun built on the Sino-Korean root 신비 (神秘, 'divine mystery', from 神 'god, spirit, miraculous, unfathomable' + 秘 'secret, hidden, esoteric'), extended with the native Korean adjectival derivational suffix -롭- (Middle Korean -롭-, forming descriptive verbs meaning 'characterized by, full of', whose ㅂ vocalizes to ㅜ before a vowel) and nominalized by the native substantivizing suffix -ㅁ/-음. Thus 신비 + -롭- + -음 yields 신비로움 ('the quality of being mysterious; mystique, aura of mystery').

history.meaning: divinely hidden, abstruse, miraculous and secret
to be mysterious, mystical, enigmatic
history.stage: Early Modern and Modern Korean adjective derivation

history.meaning: mystique, mysteriousness, enigmatic quality

morphemes.meaning: characterized by, full of (-롭- > -로우- before vowel)

신비로움.notes: While 신비 (神秘) is the bare noun 'mystery', Korean speakers prefer the derived nominalization 신비로움 when describing the subjective 'mystique' or 'aura' of an artist or phenomenon. In K-pop and entertainment management, maintaining an idol's aloofness by limiting variety appearances is called 신비주의 (神秘主義, 'mysticism / mystique marketing strategy').

rootFamily.gloss: mysticism; celebrity mystique strategy (神秘主義)

신선하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 신선 (新鮮, 'fresh, crisp, new', from 新 'new' + 鮮 'fresh, bright') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: new and fresh
fresh (of ingredients, air, or ideas)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신선하다

cognates.meaning: one's lot in life, personal circumstances (archaic/literary)
one's life experience, family background, lot in life
one's life story and social lot

신세.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 신세 (身世), composed of 신 (身, 'one's body, person, self') and 세 (世, 'world, generation, lifetime, human society'). In Classical Chinese poetry and prose, 身世 denoted 'one's personal life and encounters in the world' or 'one's lot in life, often marked by hardship'. In Korean, this branched into two distinct everyday senses: (1) one's (often pitiful) personal circumstances or plight (as in 내 신세야 'oh, my wretched plight!'), and (2) being indebted to someone's care, hospitality, or favor in navigating life (as in 신세를 지다 'to incur a debt of gratitude / impose on someone's hospitality').

history.meaning: one's self and the world; the vicissitudes of one's personal lifetime
one's personal lot or plight in life; social indebtedness or reliance on another's favor

신세.notes: One of Korean's most culturally loaded words, bridging two seemingly opposite contexts: 신세 한탄 (身世恨歎, 'lamenting one's miserable lot in life') and 신세를 지다 ('to owe someone a favor / stay as a guest imposing on someone's hospitality', functionally equivalent to Japanese 世話になる sewa ni naru).

rootFamily.gloss: to owe a favor, impose on someone's hospitality (身世를 지다)
lamenting one's lot in life (身世恨歎)

신세계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 신세계 (新世界), formed by prefixing 신 (新, 'new, fresh') to 세계 (世界, 'the world, universe, realm', originally a Buddhist Sanskrit calque of lokadhātu where 世 'time, generations' translates loka and 界 'spatial boundary, realm' translates dhātu). Initially coined in modern East Asia to translate European geographical 'New World' (Novus Mundus, the Americas), in colloquial Korean it also means a 'whole new world'—a revelatory, eye-opening experience or domain one had never encountered before.

history.meaning: the temporal and spatial cosmos; the world
the geographical New World (the Americas); a newly opened realm
New World; a whole new world, eye-opening experience or domain

신세계.notes: In everyday slang, Koreans exclaim 신세계다! or 신세계를 맛보다 ('to taste a whole new world') when trying a life-changing convenience, gadget, or food for the first time. It is also the name of South Korea's iconic department store chain, Shinsegae (新世界).

신인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 신인 (新人), composed of 신 (新, 'new, recent, fresh') and 인 (人, 'person, human being'). In Classical Chinese (such as the Book of Documents and Tang poetry), 新人 could mean 'a person renewed in virtue', 'a new acquaintance', or 'a new bride'. In modern Korean, it specialized to designate a professional 'newcomer, debutant, or rookie' in arts, literature, entertainment, or sports (such as a 신인 배우 'rookie actor' or 신인 가수 'debuting singer').

history.meaning: new person, newly wedded bride, or morally renewed person
newcomer, debutant artist, rookie athlete or entertainer

신인.notes: Korean distinguishes between 신인 (新人) and 신입 (新入): 신인 is used for public-facing creative, entertainment, or athletic professions (actors, singers, writers, baseball players, e.g., 신인상 'Rookie of the Year Award'), whereas 신입 is used for someone newly entering an organization, school, or company (like a TV station PD).

rootFamily.gloss: Rookie of the Year Award, Best New Artist Award (新人賞)
veteran, established figure, old hand (元老 / 舊人)

신입.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신입 (新入), meaning 'newcomer, new entrant, new employee or student', composed of 新 (신, 'new') + 入 (입, 'enter').

history.meaning: newly entering an organization or school
newcomer, new member/employee

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신입

신입도.etymology: Inflected/particle-attached form consisting of the Sino-Korean noun 신입 (新入, 'new entrant, rookie, new recruit', literally 'newly entering', from 新 'new' + 入 'to enter, join', frequently clipped from 신입사원 新入社員 'new company employee' or 신입생 新入生 'new student') plus the native Korean inclusive auxiliary particle -도 ('also, too, even', Middle Korean -도). Literally 'even the rookie' or 'the new recruit too'.

history.meaning: new entry/entrant + inclusive particle 'also, even'
even the rookie, the new recruit too

신입도.notes: In Korean corporate and broadcasting culture, 신입 (新入) is routinely used as a standalone noun (short for 신입사원 or 신입 PD) to refer to the newest cohort of recruits, and attaching -도 ('even a rookie...') often highlights either surprising competence or universal workplace obligations.

rootFamily.gloss: new entrant, rookie, new recruit (新入)

신입사원.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound noun from 신입사원 (新入社員), combining 신입 (新入, 'newly entering, new entry', from 新 'new' + 入 'to enter') and 사원 (社員, 'company employee, staff member', from 社 'company, corporation, society' + 員 'member, personnel'). Modeled parallel to modern Japanese 新入社員 (shinnyū shain), it denotes an entry-level employee newly hired into a corporation or broadcasting network, typically via open recruitment (공채, 公採).

history.meaning: newly entering + member of a company/society
new company employee, entry-level corporate recruit

신입사원.notes: In The Producers, Baek Seung-chan (played by Kim Soo-hyun) is a quintessential KBS 예능국 신입사원 (or 신입 PD), navigating Korea's rigid seniority hierarchy where rookies handle everything from coffee runs to editing room all-nighters. Often contrasted with 경력사원 (經歷社員, 'experienced hire').

신입이.etymology: Composed of the Sino-Korean noun 신입 (新入, 'new entrant, new recruit, rookie', from 新 'new' + 入 'to enter', clipped from 신입사원 新入社員) followed by -이, which functions either as the native Korean nominative case particle -이 ('[the rookie] as subject', Middle Korean -이) after a consonant-final noun, or as the native colloquial person-identifying suffix -이 attached to titles/nicknames before another particle. Literally 'the rookie (subject)'.

history.meaning: new entrant/recruit + subject marker (or person suffix)
the rookie (as grammatical subject), the new recruit

morphemes.meaning: nominative subject marker (after consonant) or colloquial person suffix

신입이.notes: Because 신입 ends in the consonant ㅂ (p), it takes the consonant-after allomorph -이 of the subject particle (-이/-가), producing 신입이 [시니비] via liaison (연음). Senior producers frequently refer to the youngest team member simply as 우리 신입이 ('our rookie').

cognates.meaning: to apply for, file an application, petition

신청.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 신청 (申請), composed of 신 (申, 'to state, explain, report upward to an authority') and 청 (請, 'to request, ask for, petition, invite'). Attested in Classical Chinese official administrative documents (such as Song and Ming dynasty memorials) for 'stating a matter and requesting permission from a higher office', it became the standard modern East Asian word for formal applications, subscriptions, course enrollments, and viewer song/ticket requests.

history.meaning: to state a case upward to a superior authority and request approval
history.stage: Classical and Imperial Chinese administrative usage

history.meaning: formal application, enrollment, subscription, or viewer/listener request

신청.notes: Used across both formal bureaucracy (비자 신청 'visa application', 수강 신청 'course enrollment') and broadcasting (방청 신청 'applying for studio audience tickets', 신청곡 'a listener-requested song'). Note that the 신 here is 申 ('to state/report'), not 新 ('new').

rootFamily.gloss: to apply for, request, enroll in (申請하다)

신호.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 신호 (信號), composed of 신 (信, 'trustworthy message, token, sign, dispatch') and 호 (號, 'mark, symbol, call, designation, command signal'). Originally used in pre-modern Chinese military contexts for agreed-upon visual or acoustic battle signals (flags, beacons, gongs, passwords), it was adapted in the modern industrial era to translate English signal—covering traffic lights, telecommunication waves, broadcasting cues, and figurative interpersonal hints.

history.meaning: agreed military token, beacon, or password sign
railway/traffic signal, telegraph/broadcast signal, cue
signal, traffic light, cue, sign

신호.notes: Covers everything from traffic lights (신호등 信號燈, 신호를 건너다 'to cross at the light'), broadcast transmission (방송 신호), and a director's cue on set, to romantic hints (호감의 신호 'a signal of affection') and bodily urgency ('nature's call': 배에서 신호가 오다).

rootFamily.gloss: starting pistol / first signal of a trend (信號彈)

cognates.word: 新婚夫婦 / 新婚夫妇 (xīnhūn fūfù)

신혼부부.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound noun from 신혼부부 (新婚夫婦), combining 신혼 (新魂/新婚: 新 'new, recent' + 婚 'marriage, wedlock') and 부부 (夫婦: 夫 'husband, married man' + 婦 'wife, married woman'). Both 新婚 ('newly wedded') and 夫婦 ('husband and wife') are ancient Classical Chinese compounds attested since the Six Dynasties and Tang poetry (e.g., Du Fu's 新婚別 'Parting of the Newlyweds'); their four-character combination designates a newlywed married couple.

history.meaning: newly married + husband and wife
newlywed couple, newlyweds

신혼부부.notes: In Korean teasing and variety television, any two people (even coworkers or roommates like in The Producers) who bicker affectionately or act overly domestic together are jokingly compared to a 신혼부부 ('newlyweds'). Note that the two 부 syllables represent different Hanja: 夫 ('husband') and 婦 ('wife').

rootFamily.gloss: husband and wife, married couple (夫婦)

싣다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (ㄷ-irregular conjugation: 싣다, 실어, 실으니) directly inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 싣다 (stem 실- / 싣-, 'to load onto a vehicle, boat, or pack animal; to carry on board'), attested in early Hangul texts such as Yongbieocheonga (1447) and Worin Seokbo (1459). In the modern era, its core sense of 'loading cargo onto a vehicle or vessel' expanded metaphorically to 'publishing/printing an article or photo in a newspaper or broadcast' and 'putting emotion or weight into one's voice or gesture'.

history.meaning: to load cargo or passengers onto a cart, horse, or boat
to load onto a vehicle/vessel; to publish/carry an article in print; to imbue with emotion or force

morphemes.meaning: load onto a vehicle, carry, publish in print (alternates with 실- before vowels)

싣다.notes: A classic ㄷ-irregular (ㄷ 불규칙) verb: the stem-final ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowel-initial endings (싣다 -> 짐을 실어 'load the luggage', 실으니), which preserves its historical Middle Korean liquid stem consonant. Its passive counterpart is 실리다 ('to be loaded' or 'to be published in a newspaper/magazine').

rootFamily.gloss: to be loaded onto a vehicle; to be published/printed in media (passive of 싣다)
freight, cargo, load (싣- + -음 nominalization in compounds / 짐)

실.etymology: Native Korean monosyllabic noun 실 ('thread, yarn, string'), attested in Middle Korean as 실 (sìl) with a rising tone. Used since antiquity for spun cotton, hemp, or silk thread as well as kitchen twine used to bundle herbs.
실.notes: With instrumental particle -로, the liquid geminates to 실로 ('with thread/string').

실감.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 實感, composed of 實 (실, "fruit, substance, reality, truth") and 感 (감, "to feel, emotion, sensation"). Popularized in modern East Asian lexicon via Japanese 実感 (jikkan) to denote an acute, tangible sense of reality experienced firsthand rather than merely understood in the abstract.

history.meaning: solid substance/truth + emotional stirring or perception
tangible sense of reality, acute realization

실감.notes: Most commonly paired with the verb 나다 in the expression 실감이 나다 ("to feel real / to truly sink in") or negated as 실감이 안 나다 ("it still doesn't feel real").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실내.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실내 (室內), meaning 'indoors, inside a room, interior', composed of 室 (실, 'room, chamber') + 內 (내, 'inside, interior', pronounced [실래] by liquidization).

history.meaning: inside a room or building
indoors, interior

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실내

실뜨기하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the noun 실 ("thread, string", from Middle Korean 실) + 뜨- (stem of 뜨다, "to scoop up, knit, weave, or take up loops of thread") + nominalizing suffix -기 + light verb 하다 ("to do"). Literally "to do string-looping," referring to the traditional two-player game of cat's cradle where players take turns lifting and transferring woven patterns of string between their fingers.

history.meaning: thread/string + to scoop up or weave loops
to play cat's cradle by transferring string figures between hands

morphemes.meaning: to knit, loop, or scoop up

실뜨기하다.notes: In Korean culture and drama dialogue, 실뜨기 often serves as a metaphor for back-and-forth reciprocity, teamwork, or passing a delicate situation back and forth between two people.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실려가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 실리- (passive stem of 싣다, "to load onto a vehicle or vessel," from Middle Korean 싣다 sitta, with passive derivational suffix -리-) + connective ending -어 + directional auxiliary verb 가다 ("to go away from the speaker"). Literally "to be loaded onto a conveyance and taken away," used both for cargo and for a person being rushed off in an ambulance or stretcher.

history.meaning: to load onto a cart or boat + to go
to be loaded/placed onto a vehicle and carried away

실려가다.notes: When referring to people (e.g., 병원에 실려가다), it vividly implies the person collapsed, was injured, or was incapacitated and had to be carried away to the hospital by ambulance.

rootFamily.gloss: to load, to carry on a vehicle
to be loaded, to be carried or published
to load/carry for someone, to lend weight to

실력.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 實力, formed from 實 (실, "fruit, substance, reality, genuine") and 力 (력, "physical strength, power, capability").
