Originally denoting actual military or political power in Classical Chinese texts, it came to signify a person's genuine competence or tested skill in contrast to mere credentials, seniority, or luck.

history.meaning: actual strength or substantial power
genuine skill, proficiency, or proven ability

실력.notes: Add the Sino-Korean agent suffix -파 (派, "faction/type") to form 실력파 ("a person of true talent," often used for singers or actors whose success rests on skill rather than looks).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실례.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실례 (失禮), literally 'losing courtesy' or 'a breach of etiquette'.
실례.notes: Pronounced [실례] by liquidization of ㄴ+ㄹ -> ㄹ+ㄹ; used in 실례합니다 and 실례지만 ('excuse me').

실례하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 실례 (失禮, 'breach of etiquette, rudeness, excusing oneself', literally 'losing courtesy', from 失 'lose' + 禮 'courtesy') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to commit a breach of courtesy -> to excuse oneself
to excuse oneself, intrude politely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실례하다

cognates.meaning: real thing, original object, in the flesh

실물.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 實物, uniting 實 (실, "real, actual, genuine") and 物 (물, "thing, physical object, creature"). Originally used in economics and administration for physical goods in kind (as opposed to money or paper records), in modern colloquial Korean and entertainment culture it broadened to mean a person's actual appearance in the flesh as opposed to on camera or in photographs.

history.meaning: actual physical object or goods in kind
the real article; a person's real-life appearance in person

실물.notes: A staple compliment in Korean celebrity culture is 실물이 훨씬 낫다 ("You look much better in person/real life than on screen").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실밥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 실 ("thread," from Middle Korean 실) and 밥 (originally "cooked grain/rice," from Middle Korean 밥, which developed a secondary morphological sense in Korean compounds such as 톱밥 "sawdust" or 빗밥 "hair clippings in a comb" denoting small bits, flecks, or visible remnants left by working a material). Thus 실밥 literally means "bits/traces of thread," referring to visible seam stitches or medical sutures.

history.meaning: thread + cooked grain / small remnants or particles
visible stitches in cloth; surgical sutures

morphemes.meaning: cooked rice; flecks, bits, or visible remnants

실밥.notes: Used both for clothing (실밥이 터지다, "the seam stitches burst open") and in medicine (실밥을 풀다/뽑다, "to have one's surgical stitches removed").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실수 (失手), meaning 'mistake, blunder, slip, oversight', literally 'a slip of the hand (originally in baduk/chess or manual craft)', from 失 (실, 'miss, err, lose') + 手 (수, 'hand, move').

history.meaning: slip of the hand or faulty move
mistake, blunder, error

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실수

실수하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb meaning 'to make a mistake, blunder, slip up', formed from 실수 (失手, 'mistake, slip') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to make a slip or error
to make a mistake

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실수하다

실시간.etymology: Modern Sino-Korean compound noun 實時間, formed as a semantic calque of English "real-time" by combining 實 (실, "real, actual") with 時間 (시간, "time," itself from 時 시, "time, hour" + 間 간, "interval, space"). Adopted in late twentieth-century computing and television broadcasting, it became ubiquitous in Korean internet culture through live search rankings and streaming broadcasts.

history.meaning: processing or transmitting data instantaneously as events occur
real-time, live and simultaneous transmission or updates

실시간.notes: Often abbreviated in internet slang and TV variety show captions as 실검 (from 실시간 검색어, "real-time trending search terms").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실어주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 싣- (stem of the ㄷ-irregular verb 싣다, "to load onto a vehicle, to place weight/content into," from Middle Korean 싣다 sitta, whose final -ㄷ mutates to -ㄹ before vowel-initial endings) + infinitive connective -어 + benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give, to do on someone's behalf"). Literally "to load or carry for someone," and figuratively (as in 힘을 실어주다) "to lend weight, authority, or support to someone."

history.meaning: to load onto a conveyance + to give
to give someone a lift; to lend support or backing to someone

morphemes.meaning: to load, carry, or invest weight in (ㄷ-irregular stem)
to give, to do for someone's benefit

실어주다.notes: In workplace and political dramas like *The Producers*, 힘을 실어주다 ("to lend strength/backing to someone") is a key idiom for empowering a colleague or project.

rootFamily.gloss: to load, to publish, to put weight into
to be loaded, to be carried or published
to be carried off (in a vehicle/ambulance)

cognates.meaning: slip of the tongue, verbal gaffe
to make a slip of the tongue, speak indiscreetly

실언하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 失言 (실언) with the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ("to do"). 失言 consists of 失 (실, "to lose, miss, err, let slip") and 言 (언, "words, speech, saying"), a classical compound attested in the *Analects* of Confucius (論語, *Weilinggong*: "Not to speak to a man who is capable of being spoken to is to lose the man; to speak to a man who is not capable of being spoken to is to lose/waste one's words [失言]"), which evolved to mean making an indiscreet remark or verbal blunder.

history.meaning: to waste words or err in speech
to make a slip of the tongue, speak out of turn, or commit a verbal gaffe

실언하다.notes: More formal than 말실수하다 ("to make a speaking mistake"); 실언하다 is frequently used in apologies by public figures, broadcasters, or subordinates who spoke out of turn.

실외기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 室外機, composed of 室 (실, "room, chamber, interior space"), 外 (외, "outside, exterior"), and 機 (기, "machine, apparatus, mechanism"). Coined in modern East Asian industrial terminology to designate the exterior compressor-condenser unit of a split-system air conditioner or heat pump, contrasting with 실내기 (室內機, "indoor unit").

history.meaning: outside a room/building + mechanical apparatus
the outdoor condenser/compressor unit of an air conditioner

실외기.notes: In densely packed Korean apartment complexes and urban buildings, 실외기 units mounted on exterior walls or balconies are a familiar architectural feature and occasional source of neighborhood heat/noise complaints.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: head of an office, room, or division

실장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 室長, formed from 室 (실, "room, chamber, office, specialized division") and 長 (장, "elder, chief, head, leader"). In modern Korean organizational hierarchies, a 실 (室) is typically a specialized office or division (such as 기획실 "planning office" or 비서실 "secretariat"), making the 실장 its presiding director or manager.

history.meaning: chamber/household room + elder or chief
head of an office, studio, or corporate division; senior manager in salons or agencies

실장.notes: Beyond corporate offices (like 비서실장 "chief of staff"), 실장 is widely used in entertainment agencies, hair/makeup salons, and clinics for senior managers overseeing client operations.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

실장님.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean title combining 실장 (室長, from 室 실, "office, division, room" + 長 장, "head, chief") with the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (from Middle Korean 님 nim, "lord, master, esteemed person"). In Korean workplace etiquette, professional titles are almost never used bare when addressing a superior; attaching -님 converts the bare rank into a respectful form of address or reference.

history.meaning: division/office head + master/esteemed lord
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean components

history.meaning: Director, Manager, Head of Office (polite title of address)

실장님.notes: In Korean dramas, "실장님" became a classic trope for the suave, capable corporate director or entertainment agency manager who supports the lead character.

실제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 實際, composed of 實 (실, "truth, reality, substance") and 際 (제, "border, limit, juncture, occasion"). Originally coined in Chinese Buddhist translations (such as Kumārajīva's works) to render Sanskrit bhūta-koṭi ("the utmost limit of reality" or "ultimate truth"), it was later secularized across East Asia to mean the concrete, actual state of affairs in contrast to theory, fiction, or supposition.

history.meaning: the ultimate boundary or apex of true reality
actuality, real life, the true state of facts

실제.notes: Can stand directly before another noun without a particle as an adnominal modifier (e.g., 실제 상황 "an actual situation / not a drill", 실제 이야기 "a true story").

실제로.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 실제 (實際, "actuality, reality," from 實 실, "real, true" + 際 제, "boundary, state, juncture") followed by the native Korean instrumental/adverbial postposition -로 (from Middle Korean 로, marking manner, means, or role). Together they mean "in reality, in actual fact, or in practice."

history.meaning: actuality + by means of / in the manner of
in fact, actually, in real life

실제로.notes: Whereas 사실 (事實) often introduces a speaker's confession ("To tell the truth..."), 실제로 emphasizes empirical verification ("In actual practice / When tested in real life...").

cognates.meaning: practice, to put into practice, fulfill

실천.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 實踐, uniting 實 (실, "real, true, substantive") and 踐 (천, "to tread upon, walk, step on, carry out, fulfill"). Rooted in Neo-Confucian moral philosophy (where "treading the path in reality" meant embodying ethical principles through concrete conduct rather than mere book learning), it also came in modern usage to translate Western philosophical "praxis" and everyday "putting plans into action."

history.meaning: treading upon and fulfilling moral duties in actual conduct
practice, execution, putting theory or resolutions into action

morphemes.meaning: to tread upon, step, carry out, fulfill

실천.notes: Frequently paired with 옮기다 ("to move/transfer") in the idiom 실천에 옮기다 ("to put into practice / translate into action").

rootFamily.gloss: to put into practice, carry out

실패.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound noun 失敗, composed of 失 (실, "to lose, miss, let slip, err") and 敗 (패, "to be defeated, ruined, spoiled, smashed"—originally depicting a cowrie shell 貝 struck by a hand/weapon 攵). Attested in Classical Chinese historical texts (such as the *Records of the Grand Historian* 史記) for military or strategic defeat and ruin, it now serves as the standard general word for failure in any endeavor.

history.meaning: loss and defeat in battle or statecraft
failure, falling short of an intended goal or plan

실패.notes: Note the homophone 실패 ("spool, bobbin for thread," from 실 "thread" + 패). In the sense of "failure," its antonym is 성공 (成功, "success"), as in the proverb 실패는 성공의 어머니 ("Failure is the mother of success").

싫다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) descending from Middle Korean 슳다 (sulhta), which originally meant both "to be sad, sorrowful, or pained in heart" (sharing its root with 슬프다 "to be sad," from Middle Korean 슬프다 sulhphuda) and "to feel reluctant, weary, or averse." Over the transition to Modern Korean, the vowel ㅡ (u) fronted to ㅣ (i) after the sibilant ㅅ (슳다 > 싫다), and the meaning specialized to "to be disliked, unpleasant, or unwilling."

history.meaning: to be grieved, sorrowful, or reluctant/averse
history.stage: Middle Korean (15th c., Yongbieocheonga & Seokbo Sangjeol)

history.meaning: to be disliked, unpleasant, hateful, or unwilling

싫다.notes: Grammatically, 싫다 is a descriptive verb (adjective), so in the 1st person takes the subject particle 이/가 on the disliked object (나는 그것이 싫다 "To me, that is unpleasant"). To use it transitively with object marker 을/를, add -어하다 to form the action verb 싫어하다 ("to dislike").

rootFamily.gloss: because one dislikes, not wanting to
disliking, weariness, boredom (as in 싫증이 나다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

싫어서.etymology: Inflected causal/connective form of the native Korean descriptive verb 싫다 ("to be disliked, unpleasant, reluctant," from Middle Korean 슳다 sulhta, "to grieve, feel averse"), combining the stem 싫- with the causal/sequential connective suffix -어서 (which follows non-ㅏ/ㅗ stems and derives from the Middle Korean infinitive -어 plus 셔, reduced from 이셔 "existing/being"). Literally "being unpleasant/reluctant, and so..." or "because one dislikes it."

history.meaning: grieving or feeling averse, and therefore...
because one dislikes it; out of reluctance or aversion

싫어서.notes: Notice the pronunciation [시러서]: the ㅎ of 싫- is silent before a vowel-initial suffix, and the ㄹ resyllabifies into the following syllable. Also frequently follows the -기 nominalizer in하기 싫어서 ("because I don't want to do it").

싫어하다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to dislike, hate, be averse to', derived from the subjective adjective 싫다 ('to be displeasing, disliked', Middle Korean 슬다 / 싫다) plus the psychological verb-forming auxiliary -어하다.

history.meaning: displeasing + to feel/show
to dislike, hate

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싫어하다

싫은.etymology: Inflected adnominal (relative) form of the native Korean descriptive verb 싫다 ("to be disliked, unpleasant," from Middle Korean 슳다 sulhta, "to be sorrowful, feel averse"), consisting of the stem 싫- and the consonant-after adnominal suffix -은 (from Middle Korean -은). Used before nouns to modify them ("unpleasant, disliked, reluctant") or before bound nouns such as 것 ("thing") and 기색 ("sign/expression").

history.meaning: sorrowful, painful, or averse (modifying a noun)
disliked, unpleasant, unwelcome, reluctant (modifying a noun)

싫은.notes: Appears in the common idiom 싫은 소리 ("unpleasant/critical words," e.g., 싫은 소리를 하다 "to say something harsh/unwelcome that needs to be said"). Pronounced [시른] due to ㅎ-deletion before a vowel.

심각하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 심각 (深刻, 'serious, grave, acute, severe', literally 'deeply carved/incisive', from 深 'deep' + 刻 'carve, engrave') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: deeply engraved -> acute, grave
serious, grave, severe

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심각하다

심다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to plant (a tree, flower, or seed); to instill (an idea or hope)', descending from Middle Korean 심다 / 심그다 ('to plant').

history.meaning: to plant in the ground
to plant; to instill

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심다

cognates.meaning: perturbed in mind, anxious and confused

심란하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb combining 心亂 (심란) with the native Korean adjective-forming auxiliary 하다. 心亂 consists of 心 (심, "heart, mind, spirit") and 亂 (란, "disorder, chaos, rebellion, tangling"—originally depicting two hands untangling silk threads on a spool). Literally "one's heart/mind is in disorder," describing a state of emotional agitation, distraction, and unsettled anxiety.

history.meaning: the mind or heart thrown into confusion and disorder
history.stage: Classical Chinese (attested in Tang poetry & Buddhist texts)

history.meaning: to be mentally agitated, disturbed, troubled, or in emotional turmoil

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of (descriptive verbalizer)

심란하다.notes: Whereas 불안하다 (不安하다) focuses on nervous fear about what might happen, 심란하다 emphasizes a cluttered, unsettled, or chaotic state of mind when too many worries or complicated emotions pile up.

rootFamily.gloss: one's inner feelings, state of mind

심리적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner 心理的, formed from 心理 (심리, "psychology, mentality," composed of 心 심, "heart, mind" + 理 리, "inner pattern, principle, reason") and the determiner/adjectival suffix -적 (的, "relating to, having the character of, -ic/-ical"). While 心理 existed in Neo-Confucian philosophy for "the moral principles of the mind," Meiji-era Japanese scholars (notably Nishi Amane) repurposed 心理学 (shinrigaku) to translate Western "psychology," and 心理的 entered Korean to render "psychological."

history.meaning: the inherent moral principles and workings of the heart-mind
psychological, mental (translating English psychological)

심리적.notes: As a -적 (的) word, it modifies nouns either directly (심리적 부담 "psychological burden") or with the copula particle 인 (심리적인 압박 "psychological pressure"), and becomes an adverb with -으로 (심리적으로 "psychologically").

심부름.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 심브름 and 힘부름. Korean historical linguists derive it from a compound of 힘 ("strength, labor, physical effort," from Middle Korean 힘, which underwent palatalization/spirantization 힘 > 심 in many dialects and compounds) + 부름 (the verbal noun in -음 of 부리다, "to employ, command, wield, or make someone work," from Middle Korean 브리다). Literally "the commanding or exercising of someone's labor," hence an errand or chore performed at another's bidding.

history.meaning: exercising or commanding physical labor/service
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Korean (17th–18th c.)

history.meaning: an errand, message delivery, or chore done for someone else

morphemes.meaning: to employ, command, make someone work

심부름.notes: Despite beginning with 심-, this is a pure native Korean word (고유어), not a Sino-Korean word with 心 ("heart"). Add the native suffix -꾼 ("person who does") to get 심부름꾼 ("errand boy, gofer").

rootFamily.gloss: to employ, command, wield, or work someone

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

심사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 審査, combining 審 (살필 심, 'examine in detail, judge') and 査 (조사할 사, 'inspect, verify'). Used across civic administration, cultural heritage boards, and competitions for an official evaluation against set criteria.
심사.notes: Pairs with 통과하다 ('pass a review') and 심사하다 ('to review, judge').

심사위원.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean title 審査委員, formed from 심사 (審査, 'close examination and judging', from 審 'inspect thoroughly' and 査 'investigate') plus 위원 (委員, 'committee member', from 委 'entrust' and 員 'member, official'). Unlike 재판관 or 판사 for a courtroom judge, 심사위원 specifically designates an appointed evaluator on a competition jury, audition panel, or municipal review board.
심사위원.notes: Often addressed politely in speech with the honorific suffix -님 as 심사위원님.

cognates.meaning: ordinary, commonplace (as in 尋常ではない "extraordinary")

심상치.etymology: Contracted adverbial stem from 심상하지 (尋常하지), almost exclusively used in the negative idiom 심상치 않다 ("to be unusual, extraordinary, or ominous"). The Sino-Korean root 尋常 (심상) combines two ancient Chinese linear measurements: 尋 (심, a span of eight 尺 cheok, roughly the distance of two outstretched arms) and 常 (상, double a 尋, or sixteen 尺). Because a 尋 and a 常 were modest, everyday lengths in Classical Chinese, 尋常 came metaphorically to mean "ordinary, commonplace, nothing out of the ordinary." With -하지 contracted to -치 before 않다, 심상치 않다 means "not ordinary; portending something serious."

history.meaning: eight-foot span + sixteen-foot span -> a modest, everyday measurement; ordinary, usual
(with 않다) not ordinary, unusual, ominous, foreboding

morphemes.meaning: contracted form of -하지 (descriptive verbalizer 하- + negative connective -지)

심상치.notes: In modern Korean, 심상하다 is rarely used in the affirmative; it survives almost entirely in the negative construction 심상치 않다 (e.g., 분위기가 심상치 않다 "The atmosphere looks ominous / Something unusual is brewing").

cognates.meaning: body and mind (also reversed as 身心 shēnxīn)

심신.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound noun 心身, juxtaposing 心 (심, "heart, mind, spirit") and 身 (신, "body, physical self, person"). Rooted in Classical Chinese and Buddhist philosophical discourse on the interdependence of mental consciousness and the physical form, it serves in modern Korean as a formal, legal, and medical term for a person's holistic mental and physical condition.

history.meaning: heart-mind and physical body
mind and body as an integrated whole

심신.notes: Frequently encountered in expressions like 심신이 지치다 ("to be exhausted in mind and body") and in Korean legal terminology such as 심신미약 (心身微弱, "diminished mental and physical capacity").

rootFamily.gloss: one's inner feelings, state of mind
devotion of body and mind, dedication

심심하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'bored, having nothing to do; slightly bland or undersalted in flavor', formed from the reduplicated root 심심- + -하다. Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 심심하다 (甚深-, 'profound, deep', used in formal expressions of gratitude or sympathy).

history.meaning: bored, listless; bland in taste
bored; bland/lightly seasoned; profound (甚深-)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심심하다

심의.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 審議, composed of 審 (심, "to examine closely, investigate, scrutinize, judge"—depicting a roof 宀 over 番, sorting footprints/grains carefully) and 議 (의, "to discuss, deliberate, consult, evaluate"). Used in East Asian governance and administration for formal committee deliberation, in the Korean broadcasting and entertainment industry (such as KBS in *The Producers*) it specifically denotes regulatory content screening and broadcast standards review.

history.meaning: careful investigation and official deliberation
formal legislative deliberation; regulatory screening and censorship review in broadcasting

심의.notes: In Korean TV and music production, passing 심의 (broadcast standards review—checking for profanity, brand names, or inappropriate content) is a constant hurdle for producers, often referred to as 방송 심의 ("broadcast review") or 심의에 걸리다 ("to get flagged by the review board").

심장.etymology: Sino-Korean anatomical compound 심장 (心臟), meaning 'the heart (organ)', composed of 心 (심, 'heart, mind') + 臟 (장, 'internal organ, viscera').

history.meaning: visceral organ of the heart
heart

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심장

cognates.meaning: sentiment, feelings, psychology, frame of mind
mood, frame of mind, emotional state

심정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 心情, formed from 心 (심, "heart, mind") and 情 (정, "feeling, emotion, affection, inner disposition"). Attested in Classical Chinese poetry and prose for the genuine emotional state residing within the heart, it denotes in modern Korean one's personal, empathetic inner feelings or emotional plight in a specific situation.

history.meaning: inner disposition and emotional stirrings of the heart
one's personal feelings, emotional state, or heartfelt frame of mind

심정.notes: Unlike 감정 (感情, general or objective "emotions"), 심정 highlights the subjective, relatable inner plight of a person in a particular predicament (e.g., 지푸라기라도 잡는 심정으로 "with the desperate feeling of clutching at straws").

심지어.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb 심지어 (甚至於), meaning 'even, going so far as to, to the extreme that', borrowed from the Classical Chinese connective phrase 甚至於 (甚 'extremely, even' + 至 'reach' + 於 'to, at').

history.meaning: reaching even to the point of
even, what is more, so much so that

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심지어

심하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 심 (甚, 'extreme, excessive, severe, intense') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다 (Middle Korean 심ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: extreme, severe, excessive
severe, harsh, excessive, intense

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심하다

심호흡.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 深呼吸, prefixing 深 (깊을 심, 'deep') to 호흡 (呼吸, 'breathing, respiration', literally 呼 'exhale' + 吸 'inhale'). In everyday Korean, 심호흡을 하다 or 심호흡을 크게 하다 is the standard phrase for taking a calming deep breath before a big moment.
심호흡.notes: Collocates with 크게 하다 ('take a big deep breath').

십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 십 (十, Middle Chinese *dzyip*), meaning 'ten (10)'.

history.meaning: ten
ten (10)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십

cognates.meaning: ten tenths, fully, very (with 鐘: ten minutes)

십분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 十分, composed of 十 (십, "ten") and 分 (분, "to divide; a tenth part, fraction; a minute of time or arc"). In modern timekeeping, 分 renders the sixty-part division of an hour ("minute"), making 십분 "ten minutes." Historically in Classical Sinitic measurement, where a whole was divided into ten 分 (tenths), 十分 meant "ten parts out of ten" (100%), giving rise to the homographic Korean adverb 십분 meaning "to the fullest, thoroughly."

history.meaning: ten tenths (one hundred percent, completely)
(1) ten minutes of time; (2) adverbially: fully, one hundred percent (as in 십분 이해하다)

십분.notes: Pronounced [십뿐] with tense [ㅃ] due to post-obstruent tensification. While everyday 십분 means "ten minutes," you will also hear the formal adverbial sense in phrases like 십분 활용하다 ("to utilize to the fullest") or 그 심정을 십분 이해한다 ("I understand that feeling 100%").

십사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십사 (十四), meaning 'fourteen (14)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 四 (사, 'four').

history.meaning: ten and four -> fourteen
fourteen (14)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십사

십오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십오 (十五), meaning 'fifteen (15)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 五 (오, 'five').

history.meaning: ten and five -> fifteen
fifteen (15)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십오

십이.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십이 (十二), meaning 'twelve (12)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 二 (이, 'two').

history.meaning: ten and two -> twelve
twelve (12)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십이

cognates.word: 十全大補湯 / 十全大补汤 (shíquán dàbǔ tāng)

십전대보탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 十全大補湯, composed of 十 (십, "ten"), 全 (전, "complete, whole, perfect"), 大 (대, "great"), 補 (보, "to supplement, nourish, tonify, restore"), and 湯 (탕, "hot water, decoction, medicinal soup/tea"). First recorded in the Song dynasty imperial medical formulary *Taiping Huimin Heji Jufang* (太平惠民和劑局方) and canonicalized in Joseon Korea's *Dongui Bogam* (東醫寶鑑, 1613), the formula combines the four qi-tonifying herbs of 사군자탕 (四君子湯) and the four blood-tonifying herbs of 사물탕 (四物湯) with astragalus root (황기) and cinnamon bark (육계) to make ten herbs that comprehensively replenish both vital energy (氣) and blood (血).

history.form: 十全大補湯 (in Taiping Huimin Heji Jufang)
history.meaning: ten-herb complete great tonifying medicinal decoction
history.stage: Song Dynasty Chinese (12th c.) & Joseon Korean (Dongui Bogam, 1613)

history.meaning: traditional ten-herb restorative tonic tea/decoction, also sold in Korean cafes and herbal shops

십전대보탕.notes: In Korean everyday life and dramas, ordering or gifting 십전대보탕 instead of coffee is a humorous sign of either middle-aged health consciousness or extreme physical exhaustion from overwork.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

cognates.meaning: single person; single record; single room

싱글.etymology: Modern loanword (외래어) borrowed from English "single," which derives via Old French sengle from Latin singulus ("one each, individual, separate, alone"), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *sem- ("one, together"). In contemporary Korean, 싱글 is widely used to denote an unmarried or romantically unattached person, a single-track music release, a single room or bed, or a single-digit handicap in golf.

history.meaning: one at a time, separate, individual, unmarried
an unmarried/unattached person; a single album release; a single bed/room

싱글.notes: While traditional Sino-Korean 독신 (獨身) or 미혼 (未婚, "unmarried") sounds formal or demographic, 싱글 (and compounds like 싱글족 "the single-lifestyle demographic" or 돌싱, short for 돌아온 싱글 "returned single / divorcee") carries a modern, lifestyle-oriented nuance.

rootFamily.gloss: single people as a lifestyle demographic (single + clan/group 族)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

싱싱하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'fresh, crisp, lively, full of vitality (of vegetables, fruit, fish, trees, or youth)', formed from the reduplicated expressive root 싱싱- plus -하다.

history.meaning: fresh, unwithering, lively
fresh, crisp, vibrant

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싱싱하다

싱크대.etymology: Hybrid English and Sino-Korean compound noun formed in Korean by combining the English loanword 싱크 ("sink," from Old English sincan, "to become submerged, subside," from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną) with the Sino-Korean noun and suffix -대 (臺, "platform, stand, counter, table,台"). Rather than referring solely to the metal basin itself (which is called 개수대,  개수臺), 싱크대 refers to the entire built-in kitchen counter, cabinetry, and sink unit as a single fixture.

history.meaning: plumbed basin + raised stand or counter unit
kitchen sink and its integrated countertop/cabinet unit

싱크대.notes: Notice how productive the Sino-Korean suffix -대 (臺, "stand/platform/table") is across Korean household furniture: 침대 (寢臺, "bed"), 화장대 (化粧臺, "dressing table / vanity"), and 식탁/조리대 (調理臺, "kitchen prep counter"). Bathroom sinks are NOT called 싱크대; a bathroom washbasin is called 세면대 (洗面臺).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

싶다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary adjective meaning 'to want to, wish to (after -고)' or 'to seem, feel like, wonder if (after clause endings)', descending from Middle Korean 식브다 / 십다 ('to feel inclined, seem').

history.meaning: to wish, feel inclined, seem
to want to (-고 싶다); to think/seem that

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싶다

싶으면.etymology: Conditional inflected form of the native Korean (*고유어*) auxiliary adjective 싶다 (to want to, to feel like, to seem), combining the stem 싶- with the conditional connective ending -으면 (if, when). Attested in 15th- and 16th-century Middle Korean as 싀브다 and 싚다 (conditional 싀브면), the stem underwent vowel monophthongization (ㅢ > ㅣ) and aspiration of the labial-velar/lenis cluster to yield modern 싶다. Following declarative or quotative clauses (-는가 싶으면, -다 싶으면), it shifts from volition ('if one wants') to epistemic conjecture ('if one thinks/senses that').

history.meaning: if one feels inclined; if it seems that
if one thinks that; if one wants to

싶으면.notes: After a verb in -고 (-고 싶으면), it means 'if you want to do X'; after a clause in -다/-는가 (-다 싶으면), it means 'if you think/sense that X is the case'.

rootFamily.gloss: to want to; to seem or feel like

싸가지.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) colloquial and originally southwestern/central dialectal noun derived from 싹 (sprout, bud, shoot; Middle Korean 싻) plus the diminutive suffix -아지 (found in young-animal and diminutive nouns such as 강아지, 송아지, 망아지). Resyllabification of 싹 + -아지 produced the phonetic spelling 싸가지. Originally denoting a promising young shoot showing potential for healthy growth (parallel to 싹수), it metaphorically came to mean basic manners, consideration, or promising character, and by ellipsis of 싸가지 없는 놈 ('one lacking manners/promise'), a rude brat.

history.meaning: sprout, bud, new shoot of a plant
young shoot; promising potential or basic manners
basic manners, courtesy; (by ellipsis) an ill-mannered brat

morphemes.meaning: diminutive suffix forming nouns of young or small things

싸가지.notes: Almost always paired with 없다 ('싸가지 없다', rude/bratty); using 싸가지 alone as a noun for a person is rough slang for an insolent brat.

rootFamily.gloss: promise or potential of a sprout; manners

싸다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adjective uniting three Middle Korean words spelled ᄡᅡ다: (1) transitive verb 'to wrap, pack, bundle'; (2) adjective 'cheap, inexpensive' (which in Middle Korean meant 'to be worth its price' before shifting to 'low-priced, cheap'); and (3) verb 'to excrete, discharge'.

history.meaning: to wrap up; to be worth/cheap; to excrete
to wrap, pack; cheap, inexpensive

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싸다

싸안다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound verb formed from 싸다 (to wrap, envelop, bundle up; Middle Korean 싸다, stem 싸-) connected via -아 (collapsed by identical vowel deletion) to 안다 (to hug, embrace, hold in one's arms; Middle Korean 안다, stem 안-). From the literal physical action of wrapping something up and clasping it against one's chest, the compound developed the protective figurative sense of sheltering someone in one's embrace or taking full responsibility for a burden.

history.meaning: to wrap up and to hold in the arms
to wrap in one's arms; to embrace protectively or shoulder a burden

morphemes.meaning: to hug, hold in one's arms

싸안다.notes: Used both physically ('wrapping a child in one's arms') and figuratively ('embracing a flawed colleague or taking on all the risk oneself').

rootFamily.gloss: to hug, embrace, hold in the arms
to pull close into one's embrace

싸우다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) verb meaning to fight, quarrel, or contend. Well attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as *Yongbieocheonga* and *Seokbo Sangjeol*) as 싸호다 (stem 싸호-, nominalized as 싸홈). During the transition to Early Modern Korean, intervocalic ㅎ was lenited and lost between vowels (싸호다 > 싸오다), followed by vowel raising (ㅗ > ㅜ) in non-initial syllables to yield modern 싸우다.

history.meaning: to wage war, fight in battle, contend
to fight, quarrel, struggle
to fight, brawl, argue, compete

싸우다.notes: Covers the entire spectrum from verbal bickering between friends or coworkers to physical brawls and military combat.

싸인.etymology: Colloquial orthographic variant (reflecting the widespread tensified pronunciation [싸인]) of 사인, borrowed from English sign ('signature, autograph; signal or gesture').

history.meaning: signature, autograph, signal
signature, autograph; signal

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싸인

싹.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) mimetic and ideophonic adverb (*의태어* / *의성어*). Built on Korean sound symbolism with initial fortis sibilant ㅆ (conveying swift, sharp, decisive intensity), bright vowel ㅏ (conveying a clean, crisp, outward or complete sweep, contrasted with dark-vowel 쓱), and final velar stop ㄱ (abrupt completion). Originally imitating the crisp sound and motion of wiping, cutting, or sweeping a surface in a single stroke, it grammaticalized into an emphatic degree adverb meaning 'completely, clean away, in a flash'.

history.meaning: with a single swift sweep or stroke
completely, cleanly, in a flash, without leaving a trace

싹.notes: Frequently reinforced with 다 ('싹 다', every last bit) or used before verbs of disappearing, wiping, or changing mood instantly.

rootFamily.gloss: rubbing or sweeping back and forth briskly
sweeping everything away; a clean sweep

cognates.meaning: third plaque; comic relief actor in kabuki; buffoon role
cognates.word: 三枚目 (さんまいめ, sanmaime)

쌈마이.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from Japanese theatrical jargon 三枚目 (*sanmaime*, さんまいめ, literally 'the third wooden plaque/billboard'). In Edo- and Meiji-period kabuki theater, actors' names were posted on wooden boards outside the venue: the first board (*ichimaime*) featured the lead star, the second (*nimaime*) the handsome romantic actor, and the third (*sanmaime*) the comic relief or clown. Borrowed into Korean film, stage, and broadcasting slang with initial fortition (s- > ㅆ) and apocope of the final syllable (-me), 쌈마이 came to designate campy, B-grade, low-budget, or delightfully unpretentious slapstick entertainment.

history.meaning: third name-plaque in kabuki theater; comic relief actor
third-rate, B-grade, lowbrow, or campy comic style in film/TV jargon

morphemes.meaning: flat counter / plaque (Japanese mai, 枚) + ordinal (-me, 目)

쌈마이.notes: In broadcasting and variety-show slang, 쌈마이 isn't always an insult—it often affectionately describes scrappy, B-grade, unpretentious comic charm.

rootFamily.gloss: stage/set props and production slang from Japanese jargon

쌈박하다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) expressive adjective formed from the ideophonic root 쌈박 (a fortis, colloquial variant of 삼박, depicting something cutting cleanly, crisply, or fitting together with a sharp click) plus the adjective-deriving suffix -하다. Originally dialectal and colloquial (standard dictionary base 삼박하다 / 산뜻하다), the tensified initial ㅆ intensifies the sense of freshness, sharpness, and punchy appeal, making 쌈박하다 a favorite media and advertising word for ideas or designs that feel refreshingly clever and striking.

history.meaning: clean-cut, crisp, unhesitating, neat
fresh and punchy, strikingly clever, crisp and neat

morphemes.meaning: cleanly, crisply, with a sharp punchy feel

쌈박하다.notes: Producers and writers love using 쌈박하다 when pitching: '쌈박한 아이템' means a fresh, punchy, clever concept that grabs attention immediately.

쌍둥이.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'twins', combining Sino-Korean 쌍 (雙, 'pair, couple, twin', Middle Korean 솽) with the native Korean person-forming suffix -둥이 ('child or person born with a given trait', Middle Korean 솽동이).

history.meaning: twin child
twins

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌍둥이

쌍소리.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound (*혼종어*) combining the tensified prefix 쌍- (from Sino-Korean 상 常, meaning 'common, ordinary, vulgar, base-born', as in 상놈 'commoner/lowborn fellow' and 상스럽다 'vulgar', which underwent expressive initial tensification 상 > 쌍 to convey crudeness) with the native Korean noun 소리 (sound, voice, speech, words; Middle Korean 소리). Literally 'vulgar/lowborn speech', it denotes coarse profanity, swearing, and abusive language.

history.meaning: common/vulgar speech or words
vulgar language, crude curses, profanity

morphemes.meaning: vulgar, coarse, lowborn (expressive tensification of 常 상)

쌍소리.notes: Do not confuse this prefix 쌍- (from 常 'vulgar') with homophonous 쌍- (雙 'pair/twin'); 상소리 and 쌍소리 are both standard, with 쌍소리 sounding much harsher.

쌓다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to pile up, stack, build up, accumulate (stones, snow, wealth, or experience)', descending from Middle Korean 샇다 ('to pile up, build') with initial glottalization (ㅅ > ㅆ).

history.meaning: to pile up, heap, build
to stack, pile up, accumulate

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌓다

쌓이다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb meaning 'to be piled up, accumulate, build up', descending from Middle Korean 사히다 (derived from 샇다 > 쌓다 'to pile up' + passive suffix -이-).

history.meaning: to be piled up, accumulate
to pile up, accumulate, be stacked

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌓이다

써드리다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) humble benefactive compound verb composed of 써 (infinitive of 쓰다 'to write' or 'to use', from Middle Korean 쓰다 + connective -어) plus the humble auxiliary verb 드리다 ('to give/offer to a respected person', grammaticalized from the causative of 들다 'to enter', i.e. 들- + causative -이- > 드리다 'to cause to enter / present upward to a superior'). Together, 써드리다 expresses humbly writing (a script, letter, signature) or using something for the benefit of an addressee of higher status.

history.meaning: to write/use + to present or offer inward to a superior
to humbly write or use something for a respected person

morphemes.meaning: to humbly do for a superior (benefactive auxiliary)

써드리다.notes: The humble counterpart of 써주다; use 써드리다 when offering to write a recommendation, autograph, or document for a senior or client.

rootFamily.gloss: to humbly give or offer; benefactive auxiliary
to write/use for someone (equal or lower status)

써오다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound/serial verb combining 써 (infinitive of 쓰다 'to write, compose'; Middle Korean 쓰다, stem 쓰- + connective -어) and 오다 ('to come'; Middle Korean 오다). As a directional serial verb, it means 'to write something up and bring it along (to the speaker's location)'; as an aspectual auxiliary construction, it also expresses having continuously written up to the present moment.

history.meaning: to write + to come
to write up and bring in; to have been writing up to now

morphemes.meaning: to come; aspectual continuation toward the present

써오다.notes: In TV production rooms, '대본 써오다' means drafting the script beforehand and bringing the finished draft in to the meeting.

rootFamily.gloss: to come; to continue doing up to the present
to write down and take away; to continue writing forward

써주다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) benefactive compound verb formed from 써 (infinitive of 쓰다 'to use, employ; to write, compose'; Middle Korean 쓰다 + connective -어) and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, to do for someone's benefit'; Middle Korean 주다). Depending on which homophonous stem 쓰다 is active in context, 써주다 means either 'to use/employ (a person, item, or song) as a favor' or 'to write something for someone'.

history.meaning: to use or write + to give
to use/employ or write for someone's benefit

morphemes.meaning: to give; to do for someone's benefit (benefactive)

써주다.notes: Because 쓰다 means both 'to use/hire' and 'to write', 써주다 can mean either 'use this product/cast this person for me' or 'write this for me'.

rootFamily.gloss: to use, spend, employ; to write
to humbly write/use for a respected person

썩이다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) morphological causative verb derived from the intransitive stem 썩- (썩다 'to rot, decay, spoil, fester'; attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 셕다) plus the productive causative suffix -이- (Middle Korean 셕이다 > 썩이다). While literally meaning 'to cause organic matter to rot or decompose', in modern Korean it is overwhelmingly used metaphorically in psychological expressions such as 속을 썩이다 or 골치를 썩이다 ('to make someone's insides or brains fester with worry; to torment or distress deeply').

history.meaning: to rot, decay / to cause to rot or spoil
to cause to rot; (figuratively) to worry, distress, or torment someone's heart/mind

썩이다.notes: Rarely used for literal food spoilage in everyday speech; almost always heard in '속(을) 썩이다' (to drive parents, bosses, or partners crazy with worry).

rootFamily.gloss: to rot, decay; (of one's insides) to be deeply troubled
to worry someone sick, cause heartache

썰다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem transitive verb meaning 'to slice, chop, dice, cut into pieces', descending from Middle Korean 섨다 / 썰다 ('to slice, chop').

history.meaning: to cut into slices or pieces
to slice, chop, cut

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 썰다

cognates.meaning: an unspecified or unstated thing; a special spark between people

썸.etymology: Contemporary South Korean neologism and clipped pseudo-anglicism (*외래어* / *신조어*) derived from English *something* (borrowed earlier as 썸씽 in the phrase '우리 사이에 썸씽이 있다', 'there is something going on between us'). Clipped to its first syllable with expressive fortition of initial /s/ to ㅆ (썸) and popularized nationwide by the 2014 duet *Some* (썸) by Soyou and Junggigo, it denotes mutual romantic tension, flirting, or a situationship prior to official dating.

history.meaning: an unspoken romantic spark or affair between two people
mutual flirting stage before officially dating; a romantic fling or situationship

썸.notes: Used in the collocation '썸(을) 타다' (to be in a mutual talking/flirting stage), and creates compounds like 썸남 (guy one is flirting with) and 썸녀 (girl one is flirting with).

rootFamily.gloss: a guy with whom one has a mutual romantic spark (썸 + 男)
a woman with whom one has a mutual romantic spark (썸 + 女)
a special romantic spark or untold event (from English something)

쏘다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 쏘다 (stem 쏘-), originally meaning 'to shoot (an arrow or projectile)' or 'to sting/bite (of insects)'. In late 20th-century colloquial South Korean usage, 쏘다 developed the lively figurative sense 'to treat others generously to a meal or drinks; to pick up the whole tab' (as in '오늘 내가 쏜다!'), extending the image of firing a decisive, big-spending shot for the group.

history.meaning: to shoot an arrow; to sting or pierce
to shoot a weapon; (colloquial) to treat someone generously to food or drinks

morphemes.meaning: shoot, fire; treat generously to a meal

쏘다.notes: Saying '내가 쏠게!' ('I'm shooting!' = 'It's on me!') is the most natural casual way to announce you are paying for everyone's meal or coffee.

rootFamily.gloss: to be struck by / exposed to wind or light (from 쏘이다)
shooting, gunfire; a sharp sting or burst
to snap at someone sharply with words

쏙.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) mimetic adverb (*의태어*). Formed with initial fortis ㅆ (denoting compact, focused precision), bright rounded vowel ㅗ (denoting a small, neat, snug fit, in vowel-harmonic contrast with the larger, heavier movement of dark-vowel 쑥), and final stop ㄱ (clean completion). It depicts something sliding, sinking, or fitting neatly and deeply all the way into (or out of) an opening, and figuratively entering one's heart or mind effortlessly ('마음에 쏙 들다').

history.meaning: snugly and cleanly slipping in or popping out
cleanly right in/out; snugly; completely to one's liking

쏙.notes: Essential in the idiom '마음에 쏙 들다' (to fit right into one's heart = to be 100% to one's liking) and '쏙 빼닮다' (to be the spitting image of).

rootFamily.gloss: deeply or abruptly thrusting in/out (dark-vowel counterpart)
slipping in and out repeatedly or neatly

쏟다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to pour out, spill, empty out; to pour (one's heart, effort, or attention) into', descending from Middle Korean 쏫다 ('to pour out, spill').

history.meaning: to pour out, spill
to pour out, spill, devote (effort/affection)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쏟다

쏟아붓다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound verb uniting 쏟아 (infinitive of 쏟다 'to pour out, spill, empty out'; Middle Korean 쏫다, stem 쏫- + connective -아) with 붓다 ('to pour liquid into a container'; Middle Korean 븟다, s-irregular stem 붓-/부-). By combining 'emptying out from the source' (쏟다) and 'pouring into the target' (붓다), the compound intensifies into 'to pour down in torrents' or figuratively 'to pour all of one's passion, money, or effort into something'.

history.meaning: to spill/empty out + to pour liquid into a vessel
to pour down torrentially; to pour all one's energy, funds, or emotion into

쏟아붓다.notes: Note that 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular (ㅅ 불규칙) verb, so 쏟아붓다 conjugates as 쏟아부어, 쏟아부으니, 쏟아부었다 (dropping the ㅅ before vowels).

rootFamily.gloss: to pour out, spill, devote (열정을 쏟다)
to pour liquid into; to pay installments
to pour down, cascade out in torrents

쏟아지다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb meaning 'to pour down (of heavy rain or sunlight), gush out, spill over, flood in (of questions or sleepiness)', formed from 쏟다 ('to pour out') plus the inchoative/passive auxiliary -아지다.

history.meaning: to be poured out, gush forth
to pour down, spill out, cascade

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쏟아지다

쐬다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) verb, contracted from 쏘이다 (passive/causative of 쏘다 'to shoot, strike, shine upon'; Middle Korean 쏘이다, from stem 쏘- + passive/causative suffix -이-). Through regular diphthong contraction (ㅗ + ㅣ > ㅚ), 쏘이다 became 쐬다. From the original sense of 'being struck or touched by rays of light, smoke, or currents of air', it specialized into the everyday experiential verb meaning to expose oneself to fresh air or catch a breeze ('바람을 쐬다').

history.meaning: to be struck or shot by (arrows, rays, wind, smoke)
to expose oneself to or catch (a breeze, sunlight, fresh air)

morphemes.meaning: to be exposed to air/light (contracted from 쏘- + -이-)

쐬다.notes: Almost always heard in the collocation '바람(을) 쐬다'—which means not just feeling wind, but going outside for a breather or a short getaway trip to clear one's head.

rootFamily.gloss: to shoot, strike, sting; uncontracted base of 쐬다
going out for fresh air or a change of scenery

쑥.etymology: Native Korean sound-symbolic (ideophonic) adverb 쑥 portraying smooth, unobstructed motion plunging inward, pulling outward, or shooting upward in one clean stroke. Within Korean vowel harmony, dark-vowel 쑥 conveys a broader, deeper, or heavier movement than its bright-vowel twin 쏙 ('snugly, neatly right in'). Do not confuse this adverb with the unrelated homophonous native noun 쑥 ('mugwort').
쑥.notes: Commonly modifies 들어가다 ('go right in'), 빠지다 ('come right out'), 내밀다 ('stick out'), and 자라다/크다 ('grow noticeably').

쓰다.etymology: Core native Korean 으-irregular verb and adjective uniting four Middle Korean words: (1) 쓰다 ('to write, compose'); (2) ᄡᅳ다 ('to use, employ, spend money'); (3) 쓰다 ('to wear on the head—a hat, glasses, mask—or hold overhead like an umbrella'); and (4) adjective ᄡᅳ다 ('bitter in taste').

history.form: 쓰다 (write; wear on head) / ᄡᅳ다 (use, spend; bitter)
history.meaning: to write; to wear on the head; to use; to be bitter
to write; to use/spend; to wear (hat/glasses); bitter

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쓰다

쓰레기.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) noun derived from the verb stem 쓸- (쓸다 'to sweep with a broom'; attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 쓸다) plus the nominalizing suffix -에기 (a front-vowel variant of -아기/-어기, which forms nouns denoting fragments, scraps, or residue resulting from an action, cf. 부스러기 'crumbs'). Recorded in Early Modern Korean as 쓸에기 and resyllabified as 쓰레기, it literally means 'sweepings—the dust and refuse gathered up by sweeping'.

history.meaning: to sweep with a broom, brush away
sweepings, floor dust and refuse swept together
garbage, trash, waste; (figuratively) a trashy person or worthless thing

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix denoting scraps, remnants, or sweepings

쓰레기.notes: Knowing that 쓰레기 comes from 쓸다 ('to sweep') + -에기 ('remnants') makes it easy to connect with 빗자루로 쓸다 ('to sweep with a broom') and 쓰레받기 ('dustpan').

쓰레기통.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'trash can, wastebasket, garbage bin', combining native Korean 쓰레기 ('rubbish, trash, sweepings', derived from 쓸다 'to sweep' + nominal suffix -에기) with Sino-Korean 통 (桶, 'tub, bin, container').

history.meaning: sweepings/trash + bin/tub
trash can, wastebasket, dustbin

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쓰레기통

쓸데없다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) lexicalized compound adjective composed of 쓸 (prospective adnominal modifier of 쓰다 'to use': stem 쓰- + adnominal ending -ㄹ; Middle Korean 쓸), the bound noun 데 ('place, occasion, circumstance, purpose'; from Middle Korean ᄃᆡ 'place'), and 없다 ('to not exist, to lack'; Middle Korean 업다). Literally meaning 'there is no place or occasion where it can be used', it fused into a single adjective meaning 'useless, unnecessary, pointless, or uncalled-for'.

history.meaning: there is no place or occasion to use it
useless, unnecessary, pointless, uncalled-for

쓸데없다.notes: Often modifies nouns as 쓸데없는 ('쓸데없는 소리 하지 마' = 'Stop talking nonsense/unnecessary chatter', '쓸데없는 걱정' = 'pointless worry').

쓸데없이.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) derived adverb formed by attaching the productive adverb-deriving suffix -이 (Middle Korean -이) to the compound adjective stem 쓸데없- (from 쓸 'to be used', prospective modifier of 쓰다 'to use', + bound noun 데 'place, occasion, purpose', Middle Korean ᄃᆡ, + 없- 'to lack', Middle Korean 업다). Literally 'without any place or purpose to be used', it functions as a sentence or manner adverb meaning 'needlessly, pointlessly, in vain, or for no good reason'.

history.meaning: without any place or occasion for use; in vain
needlessly, pointlessly, unnecessarily, for no reason

쓸데없이.notes: In workplace comedy, '쓸데없이 고퀄리티' ('needlessly high-quality') is a famous meme for pouring immense talent into something completely trivial.

쓸모없어지다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound inchoative verb built from 쓸모 ('usefulness, utility, worth', a compound of 쓸, prospective adnominal form of 쓰다 'to use', + 모 'corner, angle, aspect, capacity', Middle Korean 모ㅎ), combined with 없- ('to lack, not exist'; Middle Korean 업다) and the inchoative auxiliary construction -어지다 (-어 + 지다 'to become'). Literally 'to become lacking in usable aspect', it expresses the transition of a person or thing into obsolescence or uselessness.

history.meaning: use + angle/aspect + to lack + to become
to become useless, obsolete, or no longer needed

쓸모없어지다.notes: Whereas 쓸데없다 focuses on an action or remark being 'unnecessary/uncalled-for', 쓸모없어지다 focuses on a tool or person losing practical value and becoming obsolete.

rootFamily.gloss: useless, worthless, of no practical use
useful, handy, of good practical value

씌우다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) causative verb formed from the transitive verb 쓰다 ('to wear on the head, to hold an umbrella over oneself, to be covered with'; Middle Korean 쓰다, distinct in sense from homophonous 쓰다 'to write' and 'to be bitter') plus the double causative suffix sequence -이- + -우- (쓰- + -이- + -우- + -다 > 씌우다; Middle Korean 씌오다). It means 'to cause someone else to wear or be covered by (a hat, glasses, mask, or umbrella)', and figuratively 'to pin blame or a false charge on someone' (누명을 씌우다).

history.meaning: to put a head-covering on another; to cover over
to put (a hat/glasses) on someone; to hold (an umbrella) over someone; to frame or cover

morphemes.meaning: to wear on the head, cover with an umbrella/hat

씌우다.notes: In Korean romance tropes, '우산을 씌워 주다' (holding an umbrella over someone else so they don't get wet) is the quintessential gesture of quiet affection.

rootFamily.gloss: to wear on the head (hat, glasses); to use an umbrella; to take blame
to be covered or possessed by (passive/intransitive)

씨.etymology: Polysemous Korean word representing two common lineages: (1) Sino-Korean bound honorific noun 씨 (氏, Middle Chinese *dzyeX*), used after a full or given name to mean 'Mr., Ms., -san' (or after a surname for 'clan, family'); and (2) native Korean noun 씨 ('seed, kernel, pit, stock/lineage'), descending from Middle Korean ᄡᅵ.

history.meaning: polite title, clan name (氏); seed, kernel (ᄡᅵ)
Mr./Ms. (polite address, 氏); seed, pit

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 씨

씨씨티비.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) consisting of the Hangul letter-by-letter phonetic transcription of the English initialism *CCTV* (*Closed-Circuit Television*: *closed*, from Old French *clos* / Latin *clausus*, + *circuit*, from Latin *circuitus* 'a going around', + *television*, from Greek *tēle-* 'far' + Latin *vīsiō* 'sight'). Unlike American English (which commonly says 'security camera'), South Korean usage universally employs 씨씨티비 (CCTV) in everyday speech, news reports, and police investigations for any surveillance or security camera.

history.meaning: non-broadcast television transmitted to a limited set of monitors
security camera, surveillance camera system

씨씨티비.notes: In Korea, nobody says '보안 카메라' in casual conversation—everyone says 씨씨티비 (or '씨씨티비 돌려보다', to check the security camera footage).

cognates.meaning: chief producer; executive head overseeing television producers

씨피.etymology: South Korean broadcasting initialism (*외래어* / *방송 용어*) transcribing the English acronym *CP* (*Chief Producer*: *chief*, from Old French *chief* < Latin *caput* 'head', + *producer*, from Latin *prōdūcere* 'to lead or bring forth'). In the hierarchy of Korean television networks such as KBS (the setting of *The Producers*), a 씨피 (CP) sits above individual program directors (피디, PDs) and below the department head (국장), overseeing multiple shows, budgets, casting approvals, and network-level crises.

history.meaning: supervising or executive producer in broadcasting
chief producer overseeing multiple television programs and PDs in a Korean network

씨피.notes: In Korean TV station hierarchy: 막내 피디 (junior PD) -> 메인 피디 (main PD directing one show) -> 씨피 (CP overseeing several shows) -> 국장 (division director).

rootFamily.gloss: floor director on a studio set (FD)

씩씩하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'energetic, brave, spirited, vigorous, plucky', descending from Middle Korean 식식ᄒᆞ다 ('imposing, spirited, vigorous') via expressive initial tensification (ㅅ > ㅆ).

history.meaning: imposing, vigorous, spirited
energetic, brave, spirited, lively

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 씩씩하다

씹다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 씹다 (stem 씹-, 'to chew, masticate with the teeth'). From the physical act of grinding something between one's teeth, colloquial Korean developed two vivid metaphorical extensions: first, 'to badmouth, trash-talk, or tear someone apart verbally behind their back' (남을 씹다); and second, 'to chew up and swallow someone's words or text messages without replying—i.e., to blatantly ignore' (말을/문자를 씹다).

history.meaning: to chew, masticate food with the teeth
to chew; (slang) to badmouth someone or blatantly ignore a message/remark

씹다.notes: Gave rise to the ubiquitous texting slang 읽씹 (읽고 씹다, 'leaving someone on read') and 안읽씹 (안 읽고 씹다, 'ignoring without even opening the message').

rootFamily.gloss: to be chewed; (slang) to be ignored or trashed
to ruminate, chew over repeatedly (memories or words)
reading a message and ignoring it (읽고 씹다)

씻다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 씻다, where the stem alternated lenitingly before vowels (시서 'washing'). By Early Modern Korean, paradigm leveling restored stem-final ㅅ throughout all inflected forms, making modern 씻다 a completely regular ㅅ-final verb (씻어, 씻으니) unlike irregular 짓다 ('to build, make' -> 지어). It is the everyday verb for washing hands, face, dishes, or fresh produce, whereas laundry takes 빨다 or 세탁하다.
씻다.notes: Pronounced [씯따] in citation form; keeps ㅅ before vowel endings (씻어요 [씨서요]).

rootFamily.gloss: to wash one's face and hands

아.etymology: Primary native Korean vocalic interjection expressing sudden realization, recollection, surprise, or mild dismay ('ah!, oh!'), attested from Middle Korean texts onward.

history.meaning: exclamation of emotion, realization, or surprise
ah!, oh! (interjection)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아

아가씨.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'young lady, unmarried woman, miss', descending from Early Modern Korean 아기씨 / 아가씨, originally a respectful compound of 아기/아가 ('young daughter of a household') plus the honorific suffix -씨 (氏).

history.meaning: respected young unmarried daughter; young lady
young lady, miss; husband's younger sister

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아가씨

아까.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb meaning 'a little while ago, earlier (today), just now', descending from Middle Korean 아까 / 악가.

history.meaning: a short while ago
a little while ago, earlier

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아까

아깝다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) p-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) adjective attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 앗갑다 (stem 앗갑-, inflecting as 앗가온 / 앗가와). It shares the root 앗- / 앚- with the transitive verb 앗기다 (modern 아끼다 'to cherish, value, spare, begrudge') plus the adjective-forming suffix -갑-/-압- (seen in 차갑다, 따갑다). Regular post-lenis tensification of the cluster ㅅㄱ > ㄲ yielded modern 아깝다, expressing regret that something valuable is wasted, lost, or too good for its recipient.

history.meaning: to be precious, regrettable to lose or waste
regrettable, a waste, too good to lose, narrowly missed

morphemes.meaning: cherish, begrudge losing (from Middle Korean 앗-)

아깝다.notes: Used in three key situations: wasted resources ('시간/돈이 아깝다', what a waste of time/money), narrow misses ('아깝게 지다', to lose by a hair), and mismatches ('그 사람이 아깝다', they're way too good for their partner).

rootFamily.gloss: to cherish, treasure, save, begrudge spending (from 앗기다)
regrettably, narrowly, by a hair's breadth
without sparing or holding back (앗김업시 > 아낌없이)

아끼다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to cherish, treasure, value dearly; to save, use sparingly, begrudge spending', descending from Middle Korean 앗기다 ('to spare, begrudge, hold dear') via assimilation/glottalization (ㅅㄱ > ㄲ).

history.meaning: to spare, begrudge, hold dear
to cherish, treasure; to save, economize on

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아끼다

아나운서.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English *announcer* (from *announce* + agent suffix *-er*; *announce* derives via Old French *anoncier* from Latin *annūntiāre* 'to bring news, proclaim', composed of *ad-* 'to' + *nūntiāre* 'to report', from *nūntius* 'messenger'). Introduced into Korean with the birth of radio broadcasting in the late 1920s, in South Korea 아나운서 specifically denotes a full-time staff newsreader, host, or presenter recruited and employed by a broadcasting network.

history.meaning: one who proclaims news; radio/television presenter
staff broadcast newsreader, anchor, or television/radio host in Korea

아나운서.notes: In Korean TV culture, an 아나운서 is an elite salaried network employee (who hosts news, culture, and variety shows); if they quit the network to go freelance, they are called a 프리랜서 방송인.

rootFamily.gloss: announcing, vocal articulation and delivery in broadcasting
main news desk anchor (from English anchor)
master of ceremonies, show host (from English MC)

아뇨.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) polite negative interjection, formed as the contracted colloquial pronunciation and spelling of 아니요, which combines the negative noun/adverb stem 아니 ('not, no'; attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 아니) with the informal-polite (*해요체*) sentence-final particle -요 (Middle Korean -이요). Diphthongization and coalescence of 아니 + -요 (ni + yo > nyo) produced 아뇨, recognized alongside 아니요 as standard Korean.

history.meaning: not, no (negative stem)
no (informal polite response or modest denial)

morphemes.meaning: informal polite addressee-honorific particle (-요 coalesced as -뇨)

아뇨.notes: Do not confuse 아뇨 (contracted from 아니요, polite 'No!') with 아니오 (the old-fashioned blunt/authoritative 하오체 predicate ending meaning 'It is not').

아늑하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'cozy, snug, sheltered, quietly warm and comfortable', formed from the light-vowel expressive root 아늑- (counterpart of 어늑-) plus -하다.

history.meaning: sheltered, snug, cozy
cozy, snug, peaceful

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아늑하다

아니.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) negative particle, adverb, and discourse interjection. Attested throughout 15th-century Middle Korean as 아니 ('not, no', also contracting with 하다 to form 안다/않다 and with 이다 to form 아니다), and cognate with the negative prefix 안- (from 아니). In spoken Korean, beyond answering 'no' in intimate speech (*반말*), 아니 grammaticalized into a ubiquitous discourse marker expressing sudden surprise, bafflement, protest, or a conversational pivot ('Wait a minute!', 'Hold on, why—?').

history.meaning: not (pre-verbal negative adverb and negative noun)
no (intimate); wait, well, hold on (discourse interjection of surprise or protest)

아니.notes: When a Korean speaker starts a sentence with an emphatic '아니, ...', they aren't answering a yes/no question—they are expressing disbelief, mild exasperation, or 'Wait, seriously, listen to this!'.

rootFamily.gloss: not (shortened pre-verbal negative adverb from 아니)

아니다.etymology: Core native Korean negative copula (classified in Korean grammar as an adjective) meaning 'not to be, be not', descending from Middle Korean 아니다, formed by fusing the negative noun/adverb 아니 ('not') with the copula -이다 ('to be').

history.meaning: not to be
to not be, be not

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니다

아니라고.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) inflected quotative form of the negative copula 아니다 ('to not be', grammaticalized from the Middle Korean negative noun 아니 'not' + copula -이다) combined with the indirect declarative quotative ending -라고 (from copular declarative -이라 + quotative particle -고). Used mid-sentence, it reports a negative statement ('saying that it is not'); used sentence-finally (often with -요), it serves as an emphatic, exasperated reassertion ('I already told you it's not!').

history.meaning: saying that it is not (negative noun + copula + quotative)
that it is not; I'm telling you it's not!

morphemes.meaning: copular declarative quotative ending (that it is / I tell you it is)

아니라고.notes: Ending a sentence with '아니라고(요)!' ('I said NO / It's NOT like that!') is a classic flustered denial when someone teases you about having a crush or a secret.

rootFamily.gloss: saying that it is not (contracted colloquial quotative 아니라고 해 > 아니래)

아니면.etymology: Native Korean conjunction and adverb meaning 'or, otherwise, if not', grammaticalized from the conditional form of the negative copula 아니다 (stem 아니- + conditional connective ending -면, literally 'if it is not').

history.meaning: if it is not -> otherwise, or
or, otherwise, if not

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니면

아니요.etymology: Polite native Korean negative response interjection meaning 'no', formed from the negative root 아니 ('no, not') plus the polite addressee particle -요.

history.meaning: no + polite particle
no (polite)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니요

아들.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun derived from Middle Korean 아ᄃᆞᆯ (atòl), amply attested in 15th-century Hangul monuments including Yongbi Eocheonga (1445) and Seokbo Sangjeol (1447). Earlier transcribed in the Song-dynasty glossary Jilin leishi (1103) as 阿得, reflecting an Early Middle Korean form *atər, before the loss of the vowel ㆍ (araea) merged the second syllable into 들.

history.meaning: male offspring, son
son
son

아들.notes: Unlike Sino-Korean 자 (子) or 아자 (兒子), 아들 is the everyday native term; for polite reference to someone else's son, 아드님 is used instead.

아들이.etymology: Inflected nominative form of the native Korean noun 아들 ('son', from Middle Korean 아ᄃᆞᆯ) combined with the post-consonantal subject case marker -이. In 15th-century Middle Korean orthography, which followed phonemic liaison spelling (이어쓰기), this sequence was written directly as 아ᄃᆞ리.

history.meaning: the son (nominative case)
son (as grammatical subject)

morphemes.meaning: nominative case marker after consonant-final stems

아들이.notes: Because 아들 ends in the liquid consonant ㄹ, it always takes the full vowel subject marker -이 (아들이) rather than -가.

아래.etymology: Core native Korean locative noun meaning 'bottom, lower part, underneath, below', descending from Middle Korean 아래, originally a fossilized locative form combining the archaic noun 알 ('bottom, underside') with the locative particle -애 ('at, in').

history.meaning: at the bottom -> below, underneath
bottom, below, underneath, downstairs

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래

아래쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'lower side, bottom part, downward direction', formed from 아래 ('bottom, below') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: below/bottom + side/direction
lower side, bottom part

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래쪽

아래층.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'lower floor, downstairs', combining native Korean 아래 ('below, lower part') with Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'floor, story, level').

history.meaning: lower part + floor/story
downstairs, floor below

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래층

아랫길.etymology: Native Korean spatial compound joining 아래 ('lower part, down-slope', Middle Korean 아래) and 길 ('road, lane, street') with the genitive interfix 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-). In hilly Korean neighbourhoods, streets are naturally distinguished as 윗길 ('upper lane') and 아랫길 ('lower lane, further down the street').
아랫길.notes: Pronounced [아랟낄] / [아랠길] with tensification of ㄱ to [ㄲ].

아랫사람.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (합성어) formed from 아래 ('bottom, lower part, subordinate position', from Middle Korean 아래), the genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, continuing the Middle Korean genitive particle ㅅ), and 사람 ('person', from Middle Korean 사ᄅᆞᆷ). Literally 'a person positioned below', shifting from spatial lowness to social or organizational rank.

history.meaning: person below in position or status
subordinate, junior in age or workplace rank

아랫사람.notes: Pronounced [아랟싸람] with tensification of ㅅ caused by the saisiot; its direct hierarchical antonym in Korean workplace culture is 윗사람 ('senior, superior').

아랫줄.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 아래 ('lower part, bottom', Middle Korean 아래), the genitive compound marker -ㅅ- (사이시옷), and 줄 ('line, row, cord', Middle Korean 줄). Orthographically, Korean inserts 사이시옷 between a vowel-final native noun and 줄, producing 아랫줄 alongside 윗줄 ('top line') and 가운뎃줄 ('middle row'). It refers equally to a line of written text on a page, a shelf row, or a seated row.
아랫줄.notes: Pronounced [아랟쭐] with tensification of ㅈ; frequently preceded by 맨 ('the very bottom line', 맨 아랫줄).

아름답다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'beautiful, lovely, admirable', descending from Middle Korean 아ᄅᆞᆷ답다, formed from the Middle Korean noun 아ᄅᆞᆷ ('one's own self/character, worth, beauty', related to 알다 'to know/understand') plus the adjective-forming suffix -답다 ('having the true quality of').

history.meaning: worthy, admirable, beautiful
beautiful, lovely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아름답다

아마.etymology: Native Korean epistemic modal adverb meaning 'probably, perhaps, maybe, likely', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 아마.

history.meaning: perhaps, probably
probably, maybe, perhaps

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아마

아마추어.etymology: Modern loanword (외래어) borrowed from English amateur, which entered English via French amateur ('lover of arts, devotee') from Latin amātor ('lover, admirer'), an agent noun derived from the verb amāre ('to love'). In Korean workplace and broadcasting contexts, it often carries a critical nuance of lacking professional polish.

history.meaning: lover, devoted admirer
one who cultivates an art for love rather than money; non-professional
amateur, non-professional; someone acting unprofessionally

아마추어.notes: Often contrasted with 프로 ('pro/professional'); saying 아마추어같이 왜 이래? ('Why are you acting like an amateur?') is a classic Korean workplace rebuke.

아몬드.etymology: Borrowed from English almond ('edible oval nut/seed of the almond tree, Prunus amygdalus').

history.meaning: edible kernel of Prunus amygdalus
almond

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아몬드

아무.etymology: Native Korean indefinite pronoun and determiner meaning 'any, anyone, anybody (typically used with negative or concessive predicates)', descending from Middle Korean 아모 ('anyone, any').

history.meaning: anyone, any
any, anyone, anybody

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아무

아무거.etymology: Colloquial spoken contraction of the native Korean indefinite pronoun 아무것 ('anything at all'), composed of the indefinite determiner 아무 ('any, unspecified', from Middle Korean 아모) and 거, the weakened colloquial form of the bound noun 것 ('thing, object', from Middle Korean 것). Drop of final ㅅ before vowels or in casual speech yielded 아무거.

history.meaning: any thing whatsoever
anything (standard written form)
anything at all (colloquial spoken form)

아무거.notes: Rarely stands bare without a particle in natural speech; it almost always combines with particles like -나 (아무거나) or -도 (아무것도).

아무거나.etymology: Colloquial native Korean indefinite pronoun contracted from 아무것이나 ('anything whatsoever'), combining the indefinite determiner 아무 ('any', Middle Korean 아모), the colloquial bound noun 거 ('thing', from 것), and the post-vocalic allomorph of the concessive/free-choice particle -(이)나 ('or whatever, regardless of choice').

history.meaning: whatever thing it may be
anything at all (uncontracted form)
anything; whatever (colloquial standard)

아무거나.notes: The classic indecisive answer to 'What do you want to eat?' (뭐 먹을래? — 아무거나!); applies only to inanimate things, whereas 'anyone' is 아무나.

아무것.etymology: Native Korean compound indefinite pronoun meaning 'anything (or, with negative predicates, nothing at all)', formed from the determiner 아무 ('any', Middle Korean 아모) + bound noun 것 ('thing').

history.meaning: anything
anything; (with 도 + negation) nothing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아무것

아무도.etymology: Lexicalized negative-polarity pronoun combining the native Korean indefinite root 아무 (amu, Middle Korean 아모 amo, 'any person, whoever') with the concessive/inclusive particle -도 (-do, 'even, also'). Literally meaning 'even anyone', it obligatorily pairs with a negative predicate (such as 없다, 안 가다, 싫어하다, or 모르다) to express universal negation ('not a single person, nobody'). This construction exemplifies Korean's regular formation of negative pronouns via interrogative/indefinite stem + -도.

history.meaning: not even anyone, nobody (with negative predicate)
nobody, no one

아무도.notes: Always paired with a negative verb or negative psychological verb (e.g., 아무도 안 왔어요 'nobody came', 아무도 모른다 'nobody knows').

아무래도.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean sentential adverb contracted from 아무러하여도 ('no matter how one does or views it'), derived from the Middle Korean indefinite adjective 아모라ᄒᆞ다 ('to be in any way or state') inflected with the infinitive -아/-어 and the concessive particle -도 ('even if'). Over time, 아무러해도 underwent regular ㅎ-deletion and vowel coalescence into 아무래도.

history.meaning: however it may be done or considered
no matter how one looks at it
after all, by all appearances, no matter what

morphemes.meaning: to be in any way (contracted stem)
infinitive connective ending (triggers ㅎ-drop and vowel fusion to 애)

아무래도.notes: Used when the speaker reaches an unavoidable conclusion after weighing the situation ('Come to think of it / All things considered, I think...').

rootFamily.gloss: to be in any way; to feel bothered

아무렇다.etymology: Native Korean indefinite demonstrative adjective (지시 형용사) continuing Middle Korean 아모라ᄒᆞ다 ('to be of any sort or state'), formed from the indefinite root 아모 ('any') + -라- + light adjective ᄒᆞ다 ('to be/do'). Phonological reduction of -라ᄒᆞ- yielded the modern ㅎ-irregular stem 아무렇-, paralleling 이렇다 ('to be like this') and 그렇다 ('to be like that').

history.meaning: to be in any state or manner whatsoever
to be of any kind; to feel affected
to be in any way; to feel bothered or affected

morphemes.meaning: adjectival formative (from -라 하다, 'to be in such a state')

아무렇다.notes: Almost always occurs as a negative polarity item in phrases like 아무렇지도 않다 ('to feel completely fine / not bothered at all').

아무리.etymology: Native Korean concessive adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as Seokbo Sangjeol and Wolin Seokbo) as 아모리 ('in whatever way, no matter how'). Derived from the indefinite root 아모 (modern 아무, 'any, whatever') and the adverbial derivational suffix -리 (compare 이리 'this way', 그리 'that way', 저리 'that way over there').

history.meaning: in whatever manner, however much
no matter how much, regardless of degree

아무리.notes: Virtually always pairs with a concessive clause ending in -아도/-어도 or -(으)나마나 (e.g., 아무리 바빠도 'no matter how busy one is').

아무튼.etymology: Native Korean discourse adverb contracted from 아무렇든지 or 아무려튼지 ('however it may be'), formed from the indefinite adjectival stem 아무렇- ('to be in any state', from Middle Korean 아모라ᄒᆞ-) and the concessive ending -든지 ('whether or not, regardless of'). Syncope of the medial syllable and aspiration from stem-final ㅎ produced 아무튼.

history.meaning: however it may turn out
regardless of how it is; in any case
anyway, in any case, at any rate

morphemes.meaning: to be in any way (reduced stem of 아무렇-)

아무튼.notes: Functions in conversation as a topic-closer or pivot ('Anyway...') alongside its close synonyms 어쨌든 and 하여튼.

rootFamily.gloss: to be in any way; bothered

아버님.etymology: Native Korean honorific kinship term continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 아바님 (àpàním), attested in Yongbi Eocheonga (1445) and Seokbo Sangjeol (1447). Composed of the kinship root 아바/아버- ('father', related to 아비) and the honorific personal suffix -님 (from Middle Korean 님, 'lord, esteemed person'). Vowel raising in the second syllable shifted 아바님 to 아버님.

history.meaning: esteemed father (honorific)
honored father; father-in-law; respectful address for an older man

morphemes.meaning: father (bound stem from Middle Korean 아바)

아버님.notes: Used to address or refer to one's father-in-law, someone else's father, or one's own father in formal/filial contexts; service staff also use it for male customers with children.

아버지.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun derived from the Middle Korean paternal root 아바 / 아비 ('father', recorded in Hunminjeongeum Haerye 1446) combined with the kinship formative suffix -지 (which originally carried respectful or diminutive-endearing force, also preserved in 할아버지 'grandfather' and 아저씨 from 아자비). Early Modern Korean 아바지 underwent vowel centralization of the second syllable to 아버지.

history.meaning: father
father (polite familial form)
father

아버지.notes: The standard polite word for 'father' used by adults; the older bare root 아비 survives today only as a lowering or literary word.

아빠.etymology: Native Korean nursery and intimate kinship term (유아어) derived from the Middle Korean vocative/familial stem 아바 ('papa, father') via expressive consonant reinforcement (tensification of lenient ㅂ to tense bilabial ㅃ). This cross-linguistically widespread bilabial Lallwort pattern parallels 엄마 ('mom', from 어미/어마).

history.meaning: papa, father (vocative and intimate stem)
dad, daddy

아빠.notes: Originally children's speech, 아빠 is now commonly used by grown sons and daughters in warm, close families, as well as by wives referring to their husbands via their children (e.g., 애 아빠).

아쉽게도.etymology: Native Korean sentence adverb meaning 'unfortunately, regrettably, to one's regret', derived from the adjective 아쉽다 ('regrettable, leaving something to be desired, sorry to part', Middle Korean 아싀엽다) + adverbial ending -게 + particle -도 ('even/indeed').

history.meaning: regrettably + particle
unfortunately, regrettably

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아쉽게도

아쉽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 아싀엽다 and its contracted variant 아싚다 ('to feel lacking, to feel inconvenienced or regretful over an absence'), attested in Seokbo Sangjeol (1447) and Wolin Seokbo (1459). Built on an obsolete verb/noun base 아싀- ('lack, yearning') plus the deadjectival suffix -업다/-브다, which regularly yields modern -ㅂ다 adjectives.

history.meaning: to feel a lack; to find regrettable or unsatisfied
regrettable, leaving one wanting more, sad to part with

morphemes.meaning: lacking, regrettable, leaving one wanting more
