아쉽다.notes: Covers a uniquely Korean emotional range from mild disappointment ('It's a shame we lost') to fond reluctance ('It's sad to say goodbye so soon') and feeling the pinch of something missing (돈이 아쉽다).

rootFamily.gloss: sense of regret, lingering fondness, or lack
to feel regretful or miss sorely

아야.etymology: Native Korean interjection expressing sudden sharp physical pain ('ouch!, ow!'), attested since Early Modern Korean.

history.meaning: exclamation of sudden pain
ouch!, ow!

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아야

아예.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'from the very beginning, altogether, completely, at all (especially with negative or resolute statements)', descending from Early Modern Korean 아예 / 아이에.

history.meaning: from the outset, altogether
from the start, altogether, at all

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아예

아우.etymology: Native Korean primary interjection (감탄사) of spontaneous vocalic-phonesthemic origin, imitating a groaned breath or sigh to express sudden annoyance, frustration, physical discomfort, or cringing embarrassment. Completely distinct in etymology from its homograph 아우 ('younger sibling', which derives from Middle Korean 아ᄋᆞ).

history.meaning: exclamation of frustration, groaning, or embarrassment ('ugh, aw')

아우.notes: Follows Korean vowel-harmony sound symbolism: bright-vowel 아우 feels sharper or more petulant ('Ugh, seriously!'), while dark-vowel 어우 sounds heavier or more visceral ('Ugh / Whew').

아유.etymology: Native Korean colloquial interjection (감탄사) arising as a palatalized, phonetically softened variant of 아이고 / 아이구 and 아우. By leniting the velar stop ㄱ of 아이구 into a glide (아이구 > 아유), speakers convey milder exasperation, bashful modesty when praised, or warm sympathy.

history.meaning: exclamation of startlement, pain, or lament
softened exclamation of mild frustration, modesty, or sympathy ('oh goodness')

아유.notes: Extremely common at the start of a turn to deflect compliments politely (아유, 별말씀을요 'Oh goodness, don't mention it') or express gentle exasperation (아유, 진짜 'Oh, honestly!').

아이.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'child, kid, youngster', descending from Middle Korean 아히 ('child') via loss of intervocalic ㅎ (아히 > 아이). Also used as an exclamation of mild dismay or surprise.

history.meaning: child
child, kid

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이

아이고.etymology: Classic native Korean interjection expressing pain, grief, exhaustion, surprise, or relief ('oh my!, alas!, dear me!, whew!'), attested from Middle Korean 아이고 onward.

history.meaning: exclamation of grief, pain, or surprise
oh my!, dear me!, goodness!

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이고

아이고야.etymology: Native Korean compound interjection formed from the traditional exclamation 아이고 ('alas, oh my', recorded since the Joseon period as an outcry of pain, grief, exhaustion, or startlement) extended with the vocative/exclamatory particle -야. The final -야 heightens the dramatic or regional flavor of the lament.

history.meaning: outcry of grief, pain, or startlement
emphatic exclamation of dismay, fatigue, or surprise ('oh dear!, oh boy!')

morphemes.meaning: alas, oh my (exclamation of pain or surprise)

아이고야.notes: Especially vibrant in Gyeongsang and Jeolla conversational styles and among older speakers when sitting down with aching bones or reacting to a sudden mess.

아이구.etymology: Expressive variant of the native Korean interjection 아이고 ('oh my!, goodness!, whew!'), formed by raising the final vowel (오 > 우) for a softer or more colloquial nuance.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, relief, or ache
oh my!, goodness!, whew!

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이구

아이돌.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English idol, which came via Old French idole and Late Latin īdōlum from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, 'image, phantom, figure, idol'), a derivative of εἶδος (eîdos, 'form, visible shape'). Its modern Korean entertainment sense ('agency-trained K-pop group star') developed alongside Japanese アイドル (aidoru) before becoming a global K-pop term in its own right.

history.meaning: image, likeness, cult statue
venerated image; adored celebrity or matinee star
K-pop idol performer or group member

아이돌.notes: In Korean entertainment, 아이돌 specifically denotes agency-trained pop performers (as opposed to ballad singers or indie musicians), and its second syllable -돌 acts as a productive slang suffix (e.g., 연기돌 'acting idol').

아이디어.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English idea, from Late Latin idea ('Platonic archetype or form'), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, 'form, look, pattern, nature'), derived from the verb ἰδεῖν (ideîn, 'to see', from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- 'to see, know'). In Korean TV production (프로듀사), it refers concrete-pragmatically to show concepts, segment pitches, and comedic gags.

history.meaning: visual form, appearance, ideal archetype
mental conception, plan, or creative thought
idea, creative concept, show pitch

아이디어.notes: While Sino-Korean 생각 or 구상 (構想) cover general thoughts, 아이디어 specifically implies a clever, actionable, or creative pitch in meetings.

아이스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) from English ice (and phonetically reducediced), ultimately from Old English īs and Proto-Germanic *īsą ('ice'). In contemporary Korean café culture, 아이스 underwent semantic ellipsis from phrases like 아이스 커피 ('iced coffee') and 아이스 아메리카노 to function as an independent noun meaning 'an iced beverage' (contrasted with 핫 'hot drink').

history.meaning: frozen water, ice
iced drink (elliptical noun); ice cream popsicle; iced (modifier)

아이스.notes: When ordering at Korean cafés, staff routinely ask 핫으로 드릴까요, 아이스로 드릴까요? ('Would you like that hot or iced?'), and 'Iced Americano' is famously abbreviated to 아아.

아이쿠.etymology: Native Korean interjection uttered when suddenly startled, stumbling, dropping something, or realizing a mistake ('whoops!, oops!, oh dear!'), formed as an aspirated expressive variant of 아이구/아이고.

history.meaning: aspirated exclamation of sudden startle or slip
whoops!, oops!, oh my!

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이쿠

cognates.meaning: distinct article or unit in a list

아이템.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English item, which originated as the Latin adverb item ('likewise, also, in the same manner', from id 'it' + adverbial suffix -tem) used to introduce successive entries in an inventory. In Korean broadcasting and journalism jargon (방송·언론 용어), 아이템 underwent specialized semantic shift to mean a 'program topic, episode concept, or news story angle'.

history.meaning: likewise, moreover (introducing inventory entries)
individual entry, article, or object in a collection
item, product; video-game equipment; TV episode topic or segment pitch

아이템.notes: In Korean variety and newsrooms, 아이템을 발제하다 means 'to pitch a story/segment topic'; in everyday youth slang, its final syllable -템 is a ubiquitous suffix (e.g., 인생템 'holy-grail item', 꿀템 'awesome item').

아저씨.etymology: Native Korean kinship and social noun meaning 'uncle (parent's brother or aunt's husband); middle-aged man, mister', descending from Middle Korean 아자비 ('uncle') reshaped in Early Modern Korean with the honorific suffix -씨 (아자비 + -씨 > 아저씨).

history.meaning: uncle
uncle; middle-aged man, mister

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아저씨

아주.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb meaning 'very, extremely; completely, for good', descending from Middle Korean 아조 ('completely, altogether, very') via vowel raising (오 > 우).

history.meaning: completely, altogether, very
very, quite; completely

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아주

아주머니.etymology: Native Korean kinship and social noun continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 아자미 ('aunt; female relative of one's parents' generation', attested in Seokbo Sangjeol 1447 and Beonyeok Sohak 1518). Formed from the collateral kinship root 아잠- (also seen in 아자비 > 아저씨 'uncle') plus the female kinship suffix -어미/-어니 (remodeled in Early Modern Korean to 아즈머니 > 아주머니 by analogy with 어머니 'mother' and 할머니 'grandmother').

history.meaning: maternal or paternal aunt; female collateral relative
aunt; married woman of one's parents' generation
aunt (by marriage); polite term for a middle-aged woman

morphemes.meaning: collateral relative of parents' generation (from Middle Korean 아잠-)
female kinship formative suffix (patterned on 어머니)

아주머니.notes: More polite and respectful than its contraction 아줌마, though many middle-aged Korean women today still prefer titles like 이모님 ('auntie') or 사장님 ('boss') in restaurants and shops.

아줌마.etymology: Colloquial native Korean noun contracted from 아주머니 ('aunt; middle-aged woman', from Middle Korean 아자미). Through syncope of the medial vowel and regressive labial assimilation (아주머니 > 아즈마니 > 아줌마), reinforced by the phonological template of 엄마 ('mom'), it became the everyday vernacular word for a married or middle-aged woman.

history.meaning: aunt, female collateral relative
aunt; married woman of one's parents' generation
auntie, ma'am, middle-aged woman (colloquial)

아줌마.notes: Calling an unfamiliar woman 아줌마 can sound blunt or age-insensitive in modern Korea; speakers often substitute 이모님 ('auntie') or 선생님 ('ma'am/teacher') to avoid offense.

아줌마들.etymology: Pluralized native Korean noun combining 아줌마 ('auntie, middle-aged woman', colloquial contraction of 아주머니 from Middle Korean 아자미) with the native plural suffix -들 (from Middle Korean -ᄃᆞᆯ, attested in 15th-century texts as the general animate/inanimate pluralizer).

history.meaning: aunts, female relatives of the parents' generation
middle-aged women, aunties

아줌마들.notes: In Korean television ratings and pop-culture commentary, 아줌마들 often refers to the influential demographic of married female viewers who drive drama viewership.

아직.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb meaning 'still, yet', descending from Middle Korean 아짇 / 아직 ('still, while yet').

history.meaning: still, yet
still, (not) yet

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아직

아치.etymology: Borrowed from English arch ('curved masonry or structural opening spanning a doorway, bridge, or passage'), ultimately from Latin arcus ('bow, arch').

history.meaning: curved structural span
arch

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아치

아치문.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'arched doorway, archway, arch gate', combining the English loanword 아치 (arch) with Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door, gate').

history.meaning: arch + door/gate
arched door, archway

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아치문

아치형.etymology: Hybrid architectural term combining the English loanword 아치 ('arch') with the productive Sino-Korean shape suffix -형 (型, 모형 형, 'mould, form, style'). Placed directly before nouns like 창문 ('window') or 출입구 ('entrance'), it describes curved masonry or woodwork.
아치형.notes: Used prenominally without a particle before architectural nouns (아치형 창문).

아침.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'morning; breakfast (morning meal)', descending from Middle Korean 아ᄎᆞᆷ ('morning; breakfast') via vowel fronting/raising (ᆞ > ㅣ after ㅊ).

history.meaning: morning; morning meal
morning; breakfast

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아침

아침밥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어 합성어) composed of 아침 ('morning', from 15th-century Middle Korean 아ᄎᆞᆷ, recorded in Hunminjeongeum Haerye 1446) and 밥 ('cooked grain, meal', from Middle Korean 밥). Literally 'morning cooked-rice meal', attested in Middle Korean as 아ᄎᆞᆷ밥 and contrasting with the Sino-Korean formal equivalent 조식 (朝食).

history.meaning: morning meal of cooked rice
breakfast

아침밥.notes: In casual speech, 아침 alone often means 'breakfast' (아침 먹었어?), while 아침밥 emphasizes a proper, hearty morning meal (especially one with rice).

cognates.meaning: creator of fine art; performing musician

아티스트.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English artist, which came via French artiste and Italian artista from Medieval Latin artista ('master of the liberal arts, craftsman'), derived from Classical Latin ars, artis ('art, skill, craft', from PIE *h₂r-ti- 'fitting together'). In Korean entertainment agencies and broadcasting, 아티스트 is the preferred prestige term for recording musicians and idols.

history.meaning: skill, craft / practitioner of a craft or liberal art
practitioner of fine arts; musical or stage performer
fine artist; recording artist, singer-songwriter, or K-pop performer

아티스트.notes: Whereas Sino-Korean 예술가 (藝術家) suggests a classical painter, sculptor, or high-art creator, 아티스트 in Korean media usually refers to pop musicians, agency performers, or makeup/tattoo specialists.

cognates.meaning: residential flat or suite of rooms

아파트.etymology: Loanword (외래어) clipped from English apartment (initially mediated through Japanese アパート apāto during the early 20th century), ultimately from French appartement and Italian appartamento ('private suite of rooms'), from appartare ('to separate, set apart', from Latin ad partem). In postwar South Korea, 아파트 underwent semantic elevation to denote large, high-rise reinforced-concrete residential complexes.

history.meaning: separated suite of rooms within a palace or house
self-contained residential flat / multi-unit dwelling
high-rise apartment unit or multi-tower residential complex

아파트.notes: Watch out for the false friend with Japanese and English: in Korea, an 아파트 is almost always a prestigious high-rise complex (5+ stories), whereas a smaller low-rise walk-up building is called a 빌라 ('villa').

아프다.etymology: Native Korean 으-irregular adjective meaning 'painful, sore, aching, sick, hurt', descending from Middle Korean 알프다 ('painful, aching'), derived from the verb stem 앓- (앓다, 'to suffer from illness or pain') plus the adjective-forming suffix -브다 (> -프다).

history.meaning: to ache/suffer -> painful, sick
painful, sore, sick, hurt

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아프다

아픔.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun (파생명사) derived from the adjective stem 아프- ('to hurt, to be painful or sick', from 15th-century Middle Korean 앐다 / 아프다, attested in Seokbo Sangjeol 1447 and Worincheongangjigok 1447) combined with the productive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ (from Middle Korean -옴/-움). Encompasses both physical pain and emotional suffering.

history.meaning: to ache, be painful / physical pain or illness
pain, ache; emotional sorrow or trauma

morphemes.meaning: to hurt, be painful, be sick

아픔.notes: While Sino-Korean 통증 (痛症) is clinical ('medical pain/ache'), native 아픔 carries deep emotional resonance and is often used for heartbreak or personal scars (이별의 아픔 'the pain of parting').

rootFamily.gloss: to hurt, be painful, be sick
to feel or show pain, grieve over

아하.etymology: Native Korean interjection expressing sudden comprehension, discovery, or realization ('aha!, I see!'), formed from 아 ('ah') + 하 ('ha').

history.meaning: exclamation of sudden realization or understanding

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아하

아홉.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'nine (9)', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 아홉.

history.meaning: nine
nine (9)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아홉

악보.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 악보 (樂譜), meaning 'sheet music, musical score', composed of 樂 (악, 'music') + 譜 (보, 'score, chart, register').

history.meaning: written notation or score of music
sheet music, musical score

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 악보

악수.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written as 握手, composed of 握 (잡을 악, 'to grasp, clench, hold firmly') and 手 (손 수, 'hand'). Already attested in Classical Chinese histories (such as the Shiji and Book of Han) for clasping hands in friendship or parting, it was standardized across modern East Asia to denote the Western social gesture of shaking hands.

history.meaning: clasping another's hand in comradeship or emotional parting
handshake; gesture of greeting or reconciliation

morphemes.meaning: to grasp, grip, hold in the hand

악수.notes: In traditional Korean etiquette, a junior shaking hands with a senior uses both hands (or supports the right forearm with the left hand); do not confuse with its homograph 악수 (惡手, 'a disastrous move in Go/baduk or negotiations').

cognates.word: 悪循環 (あくじゅんかん, akujunkan)

악순환.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (한자어) written as 惡循環, formed from prefixal modifier 惡 (악할 악, 'bad, evil, harmful, vicious') and 循環 (순환, 'circulation, cycle'), which joins 循 (돌 순, 'to follow in order, revolve') and 環 (고리 환, 'jade ring, loop, cycle'). Coined in modern East Asian Sino-Xenic vocabulary as a calque of European 'vicious circle / vicious cycle'.

history.meaning: moving continuously in a ring; natural or cosmic cycle
vicious circle (modern Sino-Xenic calque)
vicious cycle, self-reinforcing downward spiral

악순환.notes: Its direct positive antonym—frequently paired with it in Korean news and workplace discussions—is 선순환 (善循環, 'virtuous cycle').

악절.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 악절 (樂節), meaning 'musical phrase, period, or passage in a composition', composed of 樂 (악, 'music') + 節 (절, 'section, joint, phrase, measure').

history.meaning: structural section or phrase of a musical piece
musical phrase, passage, period

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 악절

cognates.meaning: malicious comment (sharing the Sinitic initial 惡/悪)
response, answer (source of the clipped element -플)

악플.etymology: Coined in early-2000s South Korean internet culture as a hybrid syllabic blend (portmanteau) of Sino-Korean 악성 (惡性, "maliciousness, malignancy", specifically its initial Hanja 악 惡 "evil, bad, malicious") and 리플 ("online comment, reply", a loanword clipped from English reply).

history.meaning: Sino-Korean root for 'evil, bad' + English noun 'response'
malicious online reply or comment
malicious online comment, hate comment

morphemes.meaning: bad, evil, malicious (from 악성 惡性)
online comment, reply (clipped from 리플 < English reply)

악플.notes: In Korean broadcasting and entertainment (like 프로듀사), 악플 contrasts with 선플 (善플, 'kind/positive comment'), and a person who habitually leaves hate comments is called an 악플러 (악플 + English agentive -er).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 악플

안.etymology: Core native Korean word representing two everyday lineages: (1) noun 안 ('inside, interior, within'), descending from Middle Korean 안ㅎ (an ㅎ-final noun, which is why 안 + 밖 'outside' yields 안팎 'inside and outside'); and (2) negative adverb 안 ('not'), contracted from 아니 (Middle Korean 아니). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 안 (案, 'plan, proposal, draft').

history.meaning: interior, inside; not
inside, interior; not (negative adverb); proposal/draft (案)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안

안경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안경 (眼鏡), literally 'eye-mirror/lens', from 안 (眼, 'eye') + 경 (鏡, 'mirror, lens').
안경.notes: Takes the verb 쓰다 ('안경을 쓰다') when putting glasses on.

안내.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 案內, composed of 案 (책상 안 / 안건 안, 'document, plan, matter at hand') and 內 (안 내, 'interior, inside details'). Originally signifying familiarity with the inner particulars of a matter or locality in East Asian epistolary prose, it became the standard modern Korean word both for escorting guests to their seats and for written visitor notices or instructions.
안내.notes: Productively forms 안내하다 ('to guide, announce'), 안내문 ('written notice/instructions'), and 안내소 ('information desk').

안내문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안내문 (案內文), meaning 'information notice, guide text, written announcement', formed from 안내 (案內, 'guidance, showing the way, information') + 문 (文, 'writing, text, notice').

history.meaning: written text providing guidance or information
information notice, guide text, announcement

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안내문

안내판.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안내판 (案內板), meaning 'information board, signboard, directory sign', formed from 안내 (案內, 'guidance, information') + 판 (板, 'board, plaque, sign').

history.meaning: signboard displaying directions or information
information board, signboard, notice board

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안내판

안녕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being'), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, safe') and 녕 (寧, 'tranquil, at ease'); used in Modern Korean as an informal greeting ('hello; goodbye').

history.meaning: peace, safety, and well-being
well-being; informal greeting ('hi; bye')

안녕하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adjective formed from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, "peace, tranquility, well-being", composed of 안 安 "peaceful, safe, calm" and 녕 寧 "tranquil, serene, at peace") combined with the native Korean adjective-deriving light verb 하다 ("to be, to do").

history.meaning: peace, stability, and freedom from turmoil
to be in peace and good health (used when inquiring after someone's well-being)
to be well, peaceful; basis of standard Korean greetings ('hello')

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving descriptive verbs: to be

안녕하다.notes: The everyday greeting 안녕하세요? is literally an interrogative asking 'Are you at peace / Are you well?', reflecting a history of hardship where inquiring after someone's safety was the primary salutation.

안녕하세요.etymology: Built from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being'), the adjective-forming verb 하다, and the polite honorific ending -세요 (contracted from -시어요). Literally asks or wishes 'Are you at peace?'.
안녕하세요.notes: Used across South Korea at any hour of the day as the standard polite greeting.

안녕히.etymology: Hybrid Korean adverb formed from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being') + native Korean adverbial suffix -히 ('in a ... manner'), used in polite greetings and farewells such as 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

history.meaning: peacefully, in good health, safely

안되다.etymology: Lexicalized univerbation of the native Korean negative adverb 안 (contracted from 아니, Middle Korean 아니 "not") and the native verb 되다 (Middle Korean 되다 "to become, to turn out, to be formed"). Written as one word without a space, it shifted from literal negation ("does not become") to an evaluative adjective/verb meaning "to turn out poorly, to be pitiful or sorry to see".

history.meaning: to not become, to not be accomplished
to fail to work out, to not be permitted
to be pitiful, sorry, unfortunate; to go poorly

안되다.notes: Korean orthography strictly distinguishes spaced 안 되다 ('is not allowed / does not work') from unspaced 안되다 ('feels pitiful / sorry for someone', as in 마음이 안되다 or 참 안됐다).

rootFamily.gloss: that is too bad, how pitiful!
to become, to work out well
to be wicked, mean-spirited, or turn out badly

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 안되다

안마당.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 안 ('inside, inner') with 마당 ('courtyard, yard').
안마당.notes: Traditional Korean courtyard houses arrange rooms around a sheltered 안마당 open to the sky.

cognates.meaning: chamber, room, monk's quarters (sharing Sinitic 房)

안방.etymology: Hybrid compound of native Korean 안 ("inside, interior", from Middle Korean ㅎ-final noun 안ㅎ "interior, inner quarters") and Sino-Korean 방 (房, "room, chamber"). The tensified pronunciation [안빵] preserves the phonological trace of the Middle Korean final -ㅎ (or genitive साई시옷) before ㅂ. Historically the inner room of a traditional 한옥 reserved for the female head of the household.

history.meaning: inner chamber of a house
women's inner quarters in a traditional Korean house; main family room
master bedroom; metaphorically the home TV viewing space

안방.notes: In Korean broadcasting jargon (frequently heard in 프로듀사), 안방 or 안방극장 ('master-bedroom theater') refers to home television viewers and the small screen, because families traditionally gathered around the TV set in the warmest main room (안방).

rootFamily.gloss: the small screen, home TV drama viewing ('living-room theater')
outer reception study for the male head of a traditional house

안색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안색 (顔色), borrowed from Classical Chinese 顔色, composed of 안 (顔, "face, forehead, countenance") and 색 (色, "color, look, expression"). While Modern Mandarin 颜色 generalized to mean "color" of any object, Korean 안색 faithfully retains the classical sense of "facial complexion or countenance".

history.meaning: color and expression of the face, countenance
facial look reflecting one's health or inner emotion
complexion, countenance, facial color

안색.notes: Commonly used in expressions like 안색이 안 좋다 ('your complexion looks pale/unwell') or 안색이 변하다 ('one's face changes color from shock or anger'); never used for the color of objects (making it a classic false friend with Mandarin 颜色).

안심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안심 (安心), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, calm') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind') — literally 'setting one's mind at rest'; also has a homonymous native culinary sense ('tenderloin, inner fillet of meat', from 안 'inside' + 힘/심 'sinew, muscle').

history.meaning: putting the mind at ease, relief
peace of mind, relief; inner tenderloin cut

안심하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean compound 안심 (安心, literally 安 'peaceful, settled' + 心 'heart, mind'—'setting one's heart at ease') and the verb suffix -하다. In the connective form 안심하고 ('with a peaceful heart, without worry'), it regularly modifies verbs like 맡기다 ('entrust') or 자다 ('sleep').
안심하다.notes: Very frequent in the adverbial connective 안심하고 ('reassuredly, without worry').

안전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안전 (安全), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, secure') and 전 (全, 'whole, intact, complete') — literally 'safe and intact'.

history.meaning: free from danger, intact and secure
safety, security

안전모.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 安全帽, built from 안전 (安全, 'safety, security', joining 安 'peaceful, secure' and 全 'intact, whole') plus the bound head-noun suffix -모 (帽, 모자 모, 'hat, cap, headgear'). Following the productive Sino-Korean pattern seen in 등산모 ('hiking hat') and 수영모 ('swim cap'), 안전모 denotes protective headgear worn on construction sites, workshops, or bicycles.
안전모.notes: Takes the headwear verb 쓰다 ('to put on/wear a helmet') and 벗다 ('to take off').

안전하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 안전 (安全, 'safety, security') + native light verb/adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: to be safe, free from danger

안정되다.etymology: Sino-Korean hybrid verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 안정 (安定, "stability, steadiness, calm", from 안 安 "peaceful, safe, settled" + 정 定 "fixed, established, settled") combined with the native Korean passive/inchoative verbalizing suffix -되다 ("to become, to be made").

history.meaning: settled and peaceful; free from disturbance
stability, composure, steadiness
to become stable, to be stabilized or settled

안정되다.notes: Often used in the adnominal past form 안정된 (e.g., 안정된 직장 'a stable job', 안정된 연기 'steady acting') because 되다 is an inchoative verb where the past modifier -된 describes an achieved resulting state ('stabilized -> stable').

안쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 안 ('inside, interior', Middle Korean 안ㅎ) + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the inside, inner side, interior

안타깝다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular descriptive verb (adjective). Korean historical linguists analyze it as a compound of 안 (Middle Korean 안ㅎ, "inside, breast, heart") + 타- ("to burn, scorch") + the adjective-forming suffix -깝다 (intensive variant of -갑다, "evoking the feeling of"), literally "making one's insides burn with frustration and pity".

history.meaning: to feel burning anxiety, pity, or frustration in one's chest
to be regrettable, frustratingly sad, or pitiable (with tensified -깝다)

morphemes.meaning: inside, chest, heart (from Middle Korean 안ㅎ)

안타깝다.notes: Unlike 슬프다 (pure sadness), 안타깝다 specifically captures the helpless, frustrating ache of watching someone struggle, miss an opportunity, or suffer undeservedly.

rootFamily.gloss: to feel sorry, frustrated, or pained for someone (transitive verb)
to be anxious, worried sick ('one's heart/bowels burn')
to be a waste, regrettable, too good to lose

안티.etymology: Borrowed from the English prefix anti- (ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀντί / antí, "against, opposite, in opposition to"). In late-1990s South Korean media and entertainment slang, 안티 was clipped from 안티팬 (anti-fan) to function as an independent noun meaning an "anti-fan, hater, or organized detractor".

history.meaning: against, opposite to (prefix)
detractor opposed to a specific celebrity or public figure
anti-fan, hater; public hostility toward a celebrity

안티.notes: In Korean entertainment shows, celebrities often joke about an action or broadcast edit 'producing more anti-fans' (안티를 부르다 / 안티가 늘다), using 안티 as a countable/measurable noun.

안티카페.etymology: South Korean internet compound combining 안티 (from English anti-, "anti-fan, detractor") and 카페 (from French café, "coffeehouse"). Following the launch of Daum Café (1999) and Naver Café (2003), 카페 acquired the Korean-specific sense of an "online web forum/community", making 안티카페 an online forum organized by detractors of a celebrity.

history.meaning: English prefix 'against' + French noun 'coffeehouse'
membership-based online community forum on Korean web portals
online anti-fan forum dedicated to criticizing a celebrity

안티카페.notes: In *The Producers* (*프로듀사*), Cindy (IU)'s storyline directly revolves around the president of her 안티카페—highlighting how Korean portal 'cafés' function like Reddit communities or fan/anti-fan clubs rather than physical coffee shops.

rootFamily.gloss: official or fan-run online fan community forum

cognates.meaning: detractor of a celebrity (re-borrowed into global English via K-pop)

안티팬.etymology: Korean loanword compound combining English anti- ("against, opposed to", from Ancient Greek ἀντί) and fan ("devotee, enthusiast", clipped from English fanatic, from Latin fānāticus "inspired by a god, frenzied", from fānum "temple"). Popularized in late-1990s South Korean K-pop fandom culture and subsequently exported into global English fandom vocabulary.

history.meaning: Greek 'against' + Latin 'temple devotee' -> English 'enthusiast'
person who actively opposes, boycotts, or criticizes a celebrity

안티팬.notes: While formed from English roots, 안티팬 was popularized in South Korea during the late 1990s first-generation idol era and was later borrowed into English K-pop journalism as 'anti-fan'.

앉다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 앉다 ('to sit, take a seat').

history.meaning: to sit down
to sit, perch, settle

않다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary negation verb/adjective, contracted from 아니하다 ('not to do, not to be'), itself from negative adverb 아니 ('not') + 하다 ('to do, be').

history.meaning: not to do or be
auxiliary verb/adjective of negation

않을.etymology: Inflected prospective/irrealis adnominal form of the native Korean negative auxiliary verb 않다 ("to not do, to not be"), which is a phonological contraction of 아니하다 (from Middle Korean negative adverb 아니 "not" + light verb ᄒᆞ다 "to do"). The contracted stem 않- (where ㄴ + ㅎ forms the aspirated cluster ㄶ) takes the epenthetic vowel -으- and prospective adnominal suffix -ㄹ.

history.meaning: that will not do / not being (adnominal modifier)
syncope of medial vowels producing the contracted stem 않- + -을
will not; not (prospective adnominal modifier form of 않다)

morphemes.meaning: negative auxiliary stem: to not do/be (contracted from 아니하-)

않을.notes: Frequently appears in core grammatical patterns like -지 않을 수 없다 ('cannot help but do', double negative) and -지 않을까 싶다 ('I wonder if it might not be...'). Always spelled with ㄶ (않을), never 안을 (which is from 안다 'to hug').

rootFamily.gloss: to not do, to not be (negative auxiliary)
to not do, to not be (uncontracted formal form)

알.etymology: Native Korean core noun 알 ("egg, spawn, roe; grain, small spherical object"), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as Worin Seokbo, 1459) as 알 with a rising tone (상성), which in Korean historical phonology points to an earlier disyllabic or complex proto-form. By metaphor, it extended to any small, round, kernel-like unit (pills, berries, eyeglass lenses).

history.meaning: egg, bird's egg, fish roe, small round grain or berry
egg, roe; small spherical unit (pill, grape, eyeglass lens)

morphemes.meaning: egg, roe, small round unit or kernel

알.notes: While 알 is the general word for any egg (bird, reptile, fish, insect), a chicken egg in everyday cooking is specifically called 달걀 (historically contracted from 닭의 알 'hen's egg') or Sino-Korean 계란 (鷄卵).

알다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 알다 ('to know, understand, recognize').

history.meaning: to know, perceive
to know, understand, be aware of

알람.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed in the 20th century from English alarm (ultimately from Italian all'arme! 'to arms!').

history.meaning: wake-up alarm clock or warning signal

알려드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble benefactive compound verb formed from 알리다 ("to inform, make known", the morphological causative of 알다 "to know", Middle Korean 알다 + causative suffix -리-) linked via the infinitive -어 (알리- + -어 -> 알려) to the humble benefactive auxiliary verb 드리다 (Middle Korean 드리다 "to offer up to a superior").

history.form: 알리다 (to make known) + 드리다 (to offer up)
history.meaning: causative verb of knowing + verb of offering to a respected person
to inform, notify, or let (a respected person/listener) know

morphemes.meaning: humble benefactive auxiliary: to give/offer to a superior

알려드리다.notes: Essential in Korean broadcasting, customer service, and workplace speech (e.g., 안내 말씀 알려드립니다 'We would like to inform you...'): use 알려드리다 when informing a senior, viewer, or stranger, and 알려주다 with equals or juniors.

rootFamily.gloss: to let someone know, tell, teach (plain benefactive)

알려주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb combining 알리다 ("to inform, make known", causative of 알다 "to know", from Middle Korean 알다 + causative suffix -리-) via the infinitive linker -어 (알려) with the native benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다 "to give"). Literally "to give the making-known of something to someone".

history.meaning: to cause to know + to give as a benefit
to let someone know, inform, tell, or teach

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary: to give, do for someone

알려주다.notes: Do not confuse 알려주다 ('to let someone know / inform', built on causative 알리다) with 알아주다 ('to recognize / appreciate someone's worth', built directly on 알다). In casual speech, 알려주다 often translates English 'teach me' or 'tell me' (예: 번호 좀 알려줘).

rootFamily.gloss: to acknowledge, appreciate someone's effort or value

알려지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed by adding the inchoative/passive auxiliary -어지다 (from infinitive -어 + Middle Korean 디다 > 지다 "to fall, to become") to the stem 알리- ("to make known / be known", from 알다 "to know" + suffix -리-). Morphologically a double-marked passive/inchoative (알-리-어-지-다) that grammaticalized as the standard modern passive "to become known".

history.form: 알다 (to know) -> 알리다 (to make known / be known)
history.meaning: synthetic causative/passive derivation in Middle Korean
to come to be known, to become widely known or publicized

알려지다.notes: Although Korean grammar prescriptivists historically debated whether 알려지다 is a 'double passive' (이중 피동), it is completely standard and indispensable in Modern Korean for 'to become known to the public' (예: 세상에 널리 알려지다).

알리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 알외다 / 알리다, formed from 알다 ('to know') + causative suffix -리- ('to cause to know').

history.meaning: to make known, inform, notify, announce

cognates.meaning: part-time job (clipped in Japanese from アルバイト arubaito)

알바.etymology: Two-syllable Korean contraction of 아르바이트 ("part-time job, side gig"), which was borrowed via 20th-century Japanese student slang アルバイト (arubaito, "student side job") from German Arbeit ("work, labor", from Middle High German arbeit, Old High German arabeit "toil, hardship, labor"). While Japanese clipped it to the final syllables バイト (baito), Korean contracted the initial and medial syllables into 알바.

history.meaning: work, labor, employment
student part-time job or side work
part-time job, side gig; part-time worker

morphemes.meaning: contracted first element of 아르바이트 (< German Ar-)
clipped second element of 아르바이트 (< German -beit)

알바.notes: Notice the divergent clipping patterns between Korean and Japanese: from 아르바이트 / アルバイト (Arbeit), Korean kept the front syllables to coin 알바, whereas Japanese kept the back syllables to coin バイト (baito). In Korean, 알바 can refer both to the gig itself and to the worker (or 알바생).

rootFamily.gloss: part-time job, side work (full loanword form)
short-term lucrative or desirable part-time gig ('honey gig')

알아내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, learn") linked by the harmonizing infinitive suffix -아 to the completive auxiliary verb 내다 (Middle Korean 내다 "to bring forth, put out, produce", originally the causative of 나다 "to come out"). As an auxiliary, -아/어 내다 expresses extracting or achieving a result through active effort.

history.meaning: to know + to bring forth / extract
to find out, discover, uncover through effort or investigation

morphemes.meaning: completive auxiliary: to bring out, achieve through effort

알아내다.notes: The auxiliary -아/어 내다 adds a nuance of overcoming secrecy or difficulty: whereas 알다 is simply knowing and 알게 되다 is coming to know naturally, 알아내다 implies actively digging up or ferreting out information (e.g., 비밀을 알아내다).

rootFamily.gloss: to track down, find out through searching
to dig up, pry out (a secret or truth)

알아놓다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, find out") + infinitive linker -아 + the preparatory/resultative auxiliary verb 놓다 (Middle Korean 놓다, "to put down, set in place, leave as is"). Grammaticalized from "to put down and leave in place", the auxiliary -아/어 놓다 indicates performing an action beforehand and maintaining its result for future readiness.

history.form: 알다 (to know) + 놓다 (to set down, leave)
history.meaning: to know + to place and leave in state
to find out in advance, make sure to know beforehand for future use

morphemes.meaning: preparatory/resultative auxiliary: to set in place beforehand

알아놓다.notes: Closely synonymous with 알아두다 ('to keep in mind / learn for future reference'): both -아 놓다 and -아 두다 express doing something in advance so the knowledge or preparation remains ready when needed.

rootFamily.gloss: to learn/find out and keep in mind for later
to do in advance and leave ready
to write down and keep for reference

알아듣다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, comprehend") + infinitive linker -아 + 듣다 (Middle Korean 듣다, ㄷ-irregular verb "to hear, listen", conjugating as 들어, 들으니). Literally "to hear comprehendingly", it lexicalized as a single transitive verb meaning "to understand spoken words, catch someone's meaning, or follow what is said".

history.meaning: to comprehend + to hear/listen
to understand what is said, catch someone's meaning

알아듣다.notes: Notice the sensory pairing in Korean compound verbs with 알다: 알아듣다 means 'to understand by hearing' (spoken words, a hint, a foreign language), whereas 알아보다 means 'to recognize by seeing' (a person's face, written text) or 'to look into'.

rootFamily.gloss: to recognize by sight; to look into, inquire
to listen attentively ('listen putting it in one's ear')

알아보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 알다 ('to know, recognize', conjunctive form 알아) + auxiliary/exploratory verb 보다 ('to see, try').

history.meaning: to recognize; to inquire into, check out, investigate

알아주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, recognize") + infinitive linker -아 + the benefactive verb 주다 (Middle Korean 주다, "to give"). Built directly on transitive 알다 (rather than causative 알리다), it literally means "to give recognition or understanding to someone", hence "to acknowledge someone's worth/hardships, appreciate, or give credit to".

history.meaning: to know + to give/grant
to recognize someone's value or effort, appreciate; to be widely renowned for something

알아주다.notes: A classic learner pitfall is confusing 알아주다 ('to appreciate/acknowledge someone's effort', e.g., 누가 내 마음을 알아주나 'Who would understand/appreciate my feelings?') with 알려주다 ('to inform/tell someone'). Colloquially, 알아주다 also means 'to be famous/unrivaled for' (예: 고집 하나는 알아줘야 해).

rootFamily.gloss: to let know, inform, tell (built on causative 알리다)
to overlook a fault, cut someone some slack ('give a pass by looking')

알았다고.etymology: Inflected quotative/emphatic form of native Korean 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, understand"), consisting of the root 알- + past/perfective marker -았- (grammaticalized from Middle Korean periphrastic resultative -아 잇다 "to be in the state of having done") + plain declarative ending -다 + indirect quotative suffix -고 ("saying that"). Used either to report that someone understood or, at the end of a sentence, to emphatically repeat "I said I got it!".

history.meaning: to be in a state of having come to know (resultative)
came to know; understood, got it
that one understood; 'I told you I got it!' (quotative/emphatic)

morphemes.meaning: quotative/emphatic particle ('saying that / I told you')

알았다고.notes: When used as a standalone utterance (예: 아, 알았다고! 'Ugh, I said I got it!'), the quotative suffix -고(요) signals mild exasperation because the speaker feels they are repeating an acknowledgment they already gave.

알았어.etymology: Informal intimate (반말 / 해체) past-tense form of native Korean 알다 (Middle Korean 알다, "to know, understand"), composed of the verb stem 알- + the past/perfective marker -았- (historically contracted from Middle Korean -아 잇다 "to be in the state of having come to know") + the informal sentence-final suffix -어 (grammaticalized from the infinitive converb -어).

history.meaning: to be in the state of having come to know
got it; okay, I understand (informal)

알았어.notes: In Korean, saying present-tense 알아 ('I know') to an instruction or request sounds dismissive ('Yeah, I already know that'), whereas past-tense 알았어 ('I have now understood what you said') or conjectural 알겠어 ('I get it / will do') is the natural way to say 'Got it / Okay'.

rootFamily.gloss: got it; okay, I understand (polite 해요체)
I said I got it! (emphatic quotative)
I get it, I understand (more accommodating/deferential)

앓다.etymology: Native Korean verb 앓다 ("to suffer from an illness, ache, ail, agonize over"), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 앏다 / 앓다 (e.g., in Seokbo Sangjeol and Hunminjeongeum Eonhae). It shares a deep internal Korean root with the Middle Korean adjective 앏다 (> Modern Korean 아프다 "to hurt, be painful"), reflecting an old voice/transitivity differentiation between the state of pain (앏다 > 아프다) and the process of enduring/suffering an illness (앓다).

history.meaning: to be sick, suffer pain, endure an illness
to suffer from (a disease), ache, agonize over

morphemes.meaning: to ail, suffer from illness, ache

앓다.notes: While 아프다 is an adjective ('to be painful/sick'), 앓다 is an active verb that can take a direct object naming the illness or emotional torment (예: 독감을 앓다 'to suffer from the flu', 속앓이를 하다 'to suffer inwardly'). Its nominalized form -앓이 is also popular in drama fandoms (예: 백승찬 앓이 'being lovesick/obsessed over Baek Seung-chan').

rootFamily.gloss: suffering, aching; obsessive infatuation over a character/person (-앓이)
to hurt, be painful, be sick (etymological doublet)

암.etymology: Sino-Korean medical noun 암 (癌, "cancer, malignant tumor"). The character 癌 combines the illness radical 疒 ("sickness, disease") with the phonetic/semantic component 嵒 (a variant of 巖 암, "craggy rock, cliff, precipice"). First recorded in Song-dynasty Chinese medical treatises to describe hard, uneven breast tumors that felt like craggy rock to the touch, and standardized in modern East Asian medicine to translate "cancer / carcinoma".

history.form: 癌 (from 疒 'illness' + 嵒/巖 'craggy rock')
history.meaning: rock-hard ulcerous tumor or abscess (especially of the breast)
malignant neoplasm, carcinoma, cancer
cancer; metaphorically a person or situation causing extreme frustration

암.notes: In colloquial Korean internet and TV slang, expressions like 암 걸리겠다 ('it's going to give me cancer') or 발암 캐릭터 ('carcinogenic character') are hyperbolically used for frustrating plotlines or maddeningly clueless characters. Note also the native Korean homonym 암 ('female of an animal').

암튼.etymology: Colloquial and digital syncope (contraction) of the standard native Korean discourse adverb 아무튼 ("anyway, in any case, at any rate"). 아무튼 itself grammaticalized from the Middle Korean indefinite pronoun/determiner 아모 (> Modern 아무, "any, whatever") + the concessive verb form ᄒᆞ든 (> 하든(지), "however one does / whatever it may be"). Dropping the unstressed medial vowel ㅜ reduces three-syllable 아무튼 to brisk two-syllable 암튼.

history.meaning: whatever one does, however it may be
anyway, in any case, at any rate (standard adverb)
anyway, anyhow (casual spoken and texting contraction)

morphemes.meaning: concessive ending: however it be (from 하든)

암튼.notes: Very common in casual conversation, variety shows, and KakaoTalk messages to pivot topics or wrap up a tangent ('Anyway...'); in formal writing or news broadcasts, always use the uncontracted standard form 아무튼 or 어쨌든.

rootFamily.gloss: anyway, in any case, at any rate (standard form)
in any case, anyhow (Sino-Korean hybrid synonym)
no matter how one looks at it, probably

압도적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun 압도적 (壓倒的, "overwhelming"), formed from 압도 (壓倒, "overwhelming, crushing, outshining", composed of 압 壓 "to press down, crush" + 도 倒 "to topple, knock over, fall") plus the adnominal/adjectival suffix -적 (的, "having the quality of, -ic/-ive", popularized in modern Sino-Japanese and Sino-Korean). Literally "of a pressing-down-and-toppling nature".

history.meaning: to press down and topple; (in Tang literary criticism) to outshine all other poets
overwhelming, crushing (with adjectival suffix -的)
overwhelming, by a landslide

압도적.notes: Syntactically, words ending in -적 (的) take -으로 to function as adverbs (압도적으로 'overwhelmingly'), or -이다/-인 to modify nouns (압도적인 시청률 'overwhelming viewership ratings').

압력.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 압력 (壓力), joining 압 (壓, 'to press down, crush') and 력 (力, 'force, power, strength').

history.meaning: pressing force, physical or social pressure

앞.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 앞 ('front, forepart; presence').

history.meaning: front, space in front
front, ahead; the future

앞길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 앞 (Middle Korean 앒, "front, ahead, future") and 길 (Middle Korean 길ㅎ, "road, way, path"). Literally "the road in front", it denotes both the physical path ahead of someone walking and, metaphorically, a person's future life, career prospects, or trajectory.

history.meaning: the road or path ahead
the way ahead; one's future path, career prospects, or life ahead

앞길.notes: Frequently used in idioms about someone's career or future prospects, such as 앞길이 창창하다 ('to have a bright, wide-open future ahead') or 남의 앞길을 막다 ('to block someone's future/career path').

rootFamily.gloss: the path ahead to go (갈 길)

앞당겨지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 앞당기다 ('to pull forward, move a date/time earlier', from 앞 'front' + 당기다 'to pull') + passive auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to be moved forward or brought earlier in schedule

cognates.meaning: ridgepole; counter for large buildings or apartment blocks

앞동.etymology: Hybrid compound of native Korean 앞 (Middle Korean 앒, "front") and Sino-Korean 동 (棟, originally "main roof beam, ridgepole" in Classical Chinese, which evolved in Korean and Japanese architecture into a noun and classifier for an individual "building block" within an apartment complex, campus, or hospital). Thus 앞동 means "the apartment building block right in front".

history.meaning: native noun 'front' + Sino-Korean architectural term 'ridgepole / building'
the apartment building block situated directly in front of one's own building

앞동.notes: Note the crucial homonym distinction in Korean residential addresses: 동 (洞) is a neighborhood/ward (e.g., 신사동), whereas 동 (棟) is a specific apartment building number within a complex (e.g., 101동, 앞동 'the building in front', 옆동 'the building next door').

rootFamily.gloss: the adjacent apartment building block next door

앞두다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb formed by incorporating the spatial/temporal noun 앞 (Middle Korean 앒, "front, ahead") into the verb 두다 (Middle Korean 두다, "to put, place, keep, leave"). Derived from the phrase 앞에 두다 ("to place/have in front of oneself"), it lexicalized to mean "to have an upcoming event, broadcast, or deadline right ahead".

history.meaning: to place or have in front
to have (an event, milestone, or deadline) ahead of one; to be on the verge of

앞두다.notes: Almost always used either in the converb form -을/-를 앞두고 ('ahead of / just before [an event]', e.g., 첫 방송을 앞두고 'ahead of the premiere broadcast') or the adnominal modifier form 앞둔 ('facing/approaching').

rootFamily.gloss: to take the lead, stand at the forefront
to put forward, push to the front

앞면.etymology: Hybrid Korean spatial compound combining the native Korean noun 앞 ('front, forepart', Middle Korean 앞) with Sino-Korean 면 (面, 낯 면, 'face, surface, side'). Korean systematically pairs native positional nouns with 면 to name the faces of flat or three-dimensional objects: 앞면 ('front side'), 뒷면 ('back side'), 윗면 ('top surface'), and 옆면 ('side surface').
앞면.notes: Standard pronunciation is [암면], because final ㅍ neutralizes to [ㅂ] and assimilates nasally before ㅁ.

앞부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound pairing the native Korean noun 앞 ('front, forepart, earlier section', Middle Korean 앞) with the Sino-Korean noun 부분 (部分, 'part, section'). Together with its antonym 뒷부분 ('back part, second half'), it is the standard everyday way to refer to the opening half of a piece of music, book, or film.
앞부분.notes: Pronounced [압뿌분] with neutralization of ㅍ to [ㅂ] and tensification of ㅂ to [ㅃ].

앞세우다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb combining 앞 (Middle Korean 앒, "front, forefront") and 세우다 ("to make stand, set up, position", which is the historical causative of 서다 "to stand", from Middle Korean 셔다 "to stand" -> causative 셰우다 / 셰다). Literally "to make someone or something stand in front", hence "to push to the front, use as a front/pretext, or put first".

history.meaning: to make stand in front or go ahead
to push to the front, put at the forefront (a person, excuse, or emotion); to outlive a child/younger person

morphemes.meaning: causative suffix fusing with 서- to form 세우- ('to make stand')

앞세우다.notes: Used both literally/rhetorically for pushing someone or an emotion to the front (예: 감정을 앞세우다 'to let one's emotions get ahead of reason', 남을 방패막이로 앞세우다 'to use someone as a human shield') and as a poignant Korean euphemism for a parent losing a child before their own death (자식을 먼저 앞세우다 'to send one's child ahead first').

rootFamily.gloss: to put forward, tout, assert prominently
to take the lead, stand at the head of a group
to stand up, erect, establish, formulate

앞으로.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) lexicalized adverbial form composed of the noun 앞 ("front, forepart, future"; from Middle Korean 앒, *alph*) and the directional/instrumental case particle -으로 ("toward, in the direction of"; Middle Korean -으로, *-uro*). Literally meaning "toward the front", it underwent the cross-linguistically regular spatio-temporal shift from spatial forward motion ("ahead, forward") to future temporal reference ("from now on, hereafter, in the future").

history.meaning: toward the front, ahead
forward; from now on, in the future

앞으로.notes: Used both spatially ("step forward", 앞으로 나오세요) and temporally ("from now on", 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다, "please take care of me from now on").

앞자리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 앞 ('front') + 자리 ('seat, place, position, digit place').

history.meaning: front seat; leading digit of a number

앞장서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 앞장 ('the very head or vanguard of a group', from 앞 'front' + 장) + 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand at the head, take the lead, walk in front

앞쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 앞 ('front') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the front side, forward direction

앞치마.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound noun joining 앞 (ap, Middle Korean 앞 aph, 'front, forepart') and 치마 (chima, Middle Korean 치마 chima, 'skirt, wraparound lower garment'). Literally meaning a 'front-skirt', the term originated in traditional Korean dress for a protective cloth tied over the front of a hanbok chima while cooking or washing, and now designates any kitchen, café, or workshop apron. Because 앞 ends in an unreleased bilabial stop [ㅂ] in coda position, the compound is pronounced [압치마] (apchima).

history.meaning: front protective overskirt worn for kitchen work
apron (for cooking, baking, or craft work)

앞치마.notes: To put on or tie an apron is 앞치마를 매다 or 앞치마를 두르다; to take it off is 앞치마를 벗다.

앞표지.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound prefixing native 앞 ('front') to Sino-Korean 표지 (表紙, 'book cover', from 表 'outer surface, exterior' and 紙 'paper'). While 표지 alone often refers to a magazine or book cover in general, 앞표지 explicitly singles out the front cover in contrast to 뒤표지 ('back cover') and 책등 ('book spine'). Note that unlike 뒷면/윗면, 뒤표지 is written without 사이시옷 because 표 begins with an aspirated consonant.
앞표지.notes: Pronounced [압표지] as coda ㅍ neutralizes to [ㅂ] before aspirated ㅍ.

애.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) colloquial noun formed by vowel monophthongization (/ai/ > /ɛ/) of 아이 ("child"), which descends from Middle Korean 아ᄒᆡ (*ahoy*, "child"). While a homophonous native noun 애 ("anxious mind, effort", originally "intestines" in Middle Korean, as in 애쓰다) exists, in the sense of "kid, young person, guy/girl" it is strictly the contracted form of 아이.

history.meaning: child, youth
child
kid, young person, peer (colloquial)

애.notes: In everyday conversation among adults, 애 (especially in 착한 애, "a good person/kid", or 그 애 / 걔, "that guy/girl") refers casually to peers, friends, or junior colleagues, not just literal children.

애교.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 愛嬌, composed of 愛 (애, "love, affection, fondness") and 嬌 (교, "charming, winsome, graceful, coquettish"). Originally a Classical Chinese poetic expression describing natural winsome grace in a woman or child, in modern Korean it specializes to denote performative cuteness, baby-talk, or endearing gestures used to win affection or soften a request.

history.meaning: lovable and graceful charm, winsomeness
cutesy charm, winsome behavior, affectionate playfulness

애교.notes: Commonly paired with the verb 부리다 or 떨다 (애교를 부리다/떨다, "to act cute / turn on the charm"); figuratively used as 애교로 봐주다 ("to overlook a minor flaw as something cute/harmless").

애기.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) colloquial and dialectal variant of 아기 ("baby, infant"), produced by regressive i-umlaut (fronting of the back vowel /a/ to /ɛ/ before the high front vowel /i/ in the following syllable). The standard form 아기 is attested directly in Middle Korean as 아기 (*aki*, "baby, child"). In affectionate colloquial speech, 애기 extends to romantic partners, youngest team members, or even prized possessions (such as a cherished designer bag).

history.meaning: baby, young child
baby, infant (standard)
baby, darling, precious one (colloquial umlauted form)

애기.notes: While 아기 is the prescriptive standard spelling for "infant", 애기 is ubiquitous in spoken Korean as a term of endearment for a baby, a younger partner, or a treasured object ("my baby").

애들.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) plural noun composed of 애 ("kid, young person", contracted from 아이 < Middle Korean 아ᄒᆡ *ahoy*, "child") and the plural suffix -들 (from Middle Korean -ᄃᆞᆯ *-tol*). In casual spoken Korean, its semantic range broadens from literal "children" to "the guys/girls", "our friends/peers", or "the junior staff/team members".

history.meaning: children
children
kids, guys, friends, peers (colloquial)

애들.notes: When a senior producer or manager says 애들 ("the kids"), it affectionately or casually refers to the junior writers, assistant directors, or cast members on their team.

애로사항.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) four-character compound 隘路事項, formed from 애로 (隘路, "narrow defile, mountain pass, bottleneck, obstacle", from 隘 애 "narrow, confined, pass" + 路 로 "road, path") and 사항 (事項, "matter, item, point", from 事 사 "matter, affair" + 項 항 "item, clause, nape"). Literally "bottleneck items", it became entrenched in Korean institutional, military, and corporate usage to denote practical difficulties, grievances, or pain points on the job.

history.meaning: narrow defile, obstructed mountain path
matters of difficulty, practical obstacles, workplace grievances

애로사항.notes: A classic piece of Korean office and military vocabulary: superiors routinely ask subordinates, 애로사항 있으면 말해 ("If you have any difficulties/grievances, let me know").

애매하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) root 애매 (曖昧, "dim, obscure, vague, ambiguous") combined with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 ("to be"). Both 曖 (애, "dim sunlight, obscured by clouds") and 昧 (매, "pre-dawn darkness, dim, indistinct") denote lack of light and clarity in Classical Chinese, compounding into 曖昧 ("shadowy, indistinct, equivocal"). In contemporary Korean, it describes anything borderline, hard to classify, or awkwardly non-committal.

history.meaning: dim, shadowy, obscure, indistinct
to be vague, ambiguous, borderline, awkward to decide

애매하다.notes: In everyday Korean, 애매하다 often means "in an awkward middle ground" or "borderline" (e.g., 시간이 애매하다, "the timing is awkward—neither enough time to go home nor short enough to just wait").

애쓰다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) idiomatic compound verb formed from the noun 애 ("anxious mind, painstaking effort", originally meaning "intestines, bowels, viscera" in Middle Korean 애, viewed traditionally as the bodily seat of deep emotion and worry) and the verb 쓰다 ("to use, expend"; Middle Korean ᄡᅳ다 *psuta*). Literally "to expend one's guts/viscera", it lexicalized into "to exert oneself, take great pains, struggle hard".

history.meaning: to expend one's bowels / inner vitality
to agonize, exert oneself, take pains
to try hard, make a strenuous effort, struggle

애쓰다.notes: Can express genuine appreciation (애쓰셨습니다, "thank you for your hard work/trouble") or ironic teasing when someone tries too hard (참 애쓴다, "look how hard you're trying").

rootFamily.gloss: to be worried sick, anxious (literally one's bowels burn)
to have a hard time, suffer trouble

애정.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 愛情, composed of 愛 (애, "love, cherish, fondness") and 情 (정, "feeling, emotion, sentiment, warmth"). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and literary texts as the synthesis of tender fondness (愛) and deep emotional bond (情), it denotes warm affection, attachment, or devotion toward a person, work, or object.

history.meaning: feelings of love and fondness, emotional attachment
affection, love, tender attachment

애정.notes: Unlike Mandarin 愛情 (which usually means romantic love between partners), Korean 애정 covers broad fondness—for a junior colleague, a TV program, a pet, or a romantic partner (e.g., 애정이 있다, "to have affection/care for").

애프터.etymology: Loanword (외래어) and Korean-coined English expression (콩글리시) clipped from English *after* (ultimate origin Old English *æfter*, "behind, later in time"). In South Korean blind-date (소개팅 / 미팅) culture, 애프터 (clipped from phrases like *after-meeting* or *after-service*) underwent semantic specialization to mean a "follow-up second date" requested after a first blind date, or an informal "after-party" following an official event.

history.meaning: behind, later in time, following
subsequent to, following in time
follow-up date after a blind date; after-party; after-sales service

morphemes.meaning: after; follow-up date or after-party (from English after)

애프터.notes: In Korean dating slang, 애프터 신청 ("applying for an after") means asking someone out for a second date after a blind date (소개팅), which is the decisive signal that the first meeting went well.

rootFamily.gloss: asking for a follow-up date after a blind date

액기스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed via Japanese エキス (*ekisu*, "extract, essence, concentrate"), which was borrowed during the Edo-period Rangaku (Dutch studies) era as an abbreviation of Dutch *extract*, ultimately from Medieval Latin *extractum* ("that which is drawn out", from Latin *ex-* "out" + *trahere* "to draw, pull"). In Korean, the velar stop was tensified (/ekisu/ > /ɛk'isɯ/, spelled 액기스 or 엑기스), possibly reinforced by folk-etymological association with Sino-Korean 액 (液, "liquid").

history.meaning: that which is drawn out, extracted substance
concentrated medical or culinary extract
extract, essence, concentrate
concentrated fruit/herbal syrup or extract; core essence

morphemes.meaning: extract, concentrate, essence (via Japanese エキス from Dutch extract)

액기스.notes: Used both in kitchens for fermented fruit syrups/concentrates (like 매실 액기스, "plum extract syrup") and figuratively in study or work for "the distilled core/highlights" (액기스만 뽑다, "to extract only the essentials").

액자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 額子, joining 額 (이마 액 / 현판 액, 'forehead; horizontal inscribed wooden plaque hung under eaves') with the nominalizing diminutive suffix 子 (아들 자, seen in household nouns like 의자 'chair' and 상자 'box'). From traditional framed calligraphy tablets hung high on lintels, 액자 generalized in modern Korean to any wooden, metal, or glass frame holding a painting, photograph, or certificate—as well as the framed piece as a whole.
액자.notes: Pronounced [액짜] with automatic tensification of ㅈ after coda ㄱ; takes 걸다 ('to hang a frame').

액젓.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean (혼종어) compound combining Sino-Korean 액 (液, "liquid, fluid, juice") and native Korean 젓 ("salted and fermented seafood", attested in Middle Korean as 졷 *cyos*). Literally "liquid salted-seafood ferment", it designates the clear, umami-rich amber liquid strained from salted, fermented fish (such as anchovies or sand lance), indispensable for seasoning kimchi and Korean soups.

history.meaning: salted fermented fish or shellfish
liquid fermented fish sauce

액젓.notes: Unlike solid 젓갈 (whole fermented shrimp or squid eaten as a side dish), 액젓 is a strained liquid fish sauce—most famously 멸치액젓 (anchovy sauce) and 까나리액젓 (sand lance sauce).

rootFamily.gloss: salted and fermented seafood side dish

cognates.meaning: book for photographs or collection of musical recordings

앨범.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English *album* ("book for photographs or autographs; collection of musical recordings"), which derives from Classical Latin *album* ("white tablet on which public notices or lists were inscribed; blank tablet"), the neuter substantive of *albus* ("white", from Proto-Indo-European *\*h₂elbʰós*, "white"). In 17th-century Europe, scholars kept *alba amicorum* ("blank books of friends") for autographs, which evolved into photo albums and later phonograph record sleeves.

history.meaning: white tablet for public notices, blank register
blank book for keepsakes/photos; multi-track music release
photo album; recorded music album

morphemes.meaning: photo album; musical album (from English album)

앨범.notes: In Korean music and broadcasting (like *The Producers*), 앨범를 내다 ("to release an album") is the standard phrase for a singer's comeback or debut record, alongside 음반 (音盤).

야.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) informal vocative interjection ("Hey!", "Look here!") and post-vocalic vocative case particle, originating as a primary acoustic attention-calling exclamation. In Middle Korean, -야 / -아 functioned as the intimate vocative particle attached to names and nouns, and standalone 야 grammaticalized as a direct, uninhibited call used toward friends, children, or social inferiors.

history.meaning: vocative particle and exclamation calling attention
hey! (informal vocative interjection and particle)

야.notes: Strictly 반말 (informal/intimate speech): calling 야! to someone older or of higher status is considered rude and confrontational, whereas among close friends of the same age it is the most natural way to say "Hey!".

rootFamily.gloss: hey kid!, hey you! (contracted from 이 아이야)

야간.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 夜間, composed of 夜 (야, "night, darkness") and 間 (간, "interval, space between, time period"). Literally "the interval of night", it serves as the formal Sino-Korean noun and modifier for "nighttime" in institutional, scheduling, and broadcasting contexts (such as 야간 촬영, "night filming", in contrast to 주간, 晝間, "daytime").

history.meaning: during the night, interval of night
nighttime, at night (formal/institutional modifier)

야간.notes: While 밤 is the everyday native word for "night", 야간 is used for official schedules and services: 야간 근무 ("night shift"), 야간 촬영 ("night shoot"), and 야간 진료 ("nighttime medical clinic").

rootFamily.gloss: late at night, dead of night (深夜)

야단.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun traditionally traced to the Buddhist four-character expression 야단법석 (野壇法席, from 野 야 "open field, outdoors" + 壇 단 "altar platform" + 法 법 "Buddhist dharma" + 席 석 "seat, assembly"), which denoted a massive, noisy outdoor preaching assembly when a temple courtyard could not hold the crowd. By clipping to 야단 (野壇), the meaning shifted from "crowded outdoor altar" to "noisy commotion, uproar, fuss" and subsequently to "loudly scolding or reprimanding someone" (also recorded in some late Joseon sources with the characters 惹端, "stirring up trouble").

history.meaning: open-air dharma assembly platform gathered by large crowds
noisy commotion, big fuss, uproar
uproar, trouble; sharp scolding or reprimand

야단.notes: Pairs symmetrically with voice-distinguishing verbs: 야단치다 means "to scold / tell off", while 야단맞다 means "to get scolded"; meanwhile 야단났다 means "all hell broke loose / we're in big trouble!".

rootFamily.gloss: to be scolded, get told off

야생.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 野生, composed of 野 (야, "open field, wilderness, uncultivated, untamed") and 生 (생, "living, growing, birth, life"). Literally "growing or living in the wild fields", contrasting with domesticated (가축, 家畜) or cultivated (재배, 栽培) organisms. In South Korean broadcasting, it gained iconic pop-culture currency through *2 Days & 1 Night* (1박 2일, featured in *The Producers*) and its tagline 리얼 야생 로드 버라이어티 ("real wild road variety").

history.meaning: growing or living uncultivated in the open wild
the wild; wild, untamed, undomesticated

야생.notes: Don't confuse 야생 (野生, "living in the wild", e.g., 야생동물 "wild animals") with its homophone 야성 (野性, "wild nature / untamed instinct", e.g., 야성미 "rugged, untamed charm").

야생화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 野生花, formed from 야생 (野生, 'living or growing in the wild', combining 野 'open field, uncultivated countryside' and 生 'to grow, be born') plus -화 (花, 꽃 화, 'flower, blossom'). It contrasts cultivated greenhouse or garden blooms (원예화) with uncultivated native flora, and also appears frequently in culinary names such as 야생화 꿀 ('wildflower honey') and 야생화 차 ('wildflower tea').
야생화.notes: Pairs with native Korean 들꽃 ('field flower, wildflower'), which carries a slightly more lyrical everyday tone.

cognates.meaning: late-night meal, supper eaten at night

야식.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 夜食, composed of 夜 (야, "night, nighttime") and 食 (식, "food, meal, eating"). Literally "night meal", attested in Classical Chinese and East Asian monastic/court records for food taken during night watches or study sessions, and central to modern South Korean delivery culture for late-night comfort foods (such as fried chicken, jokbal, or ramyeon).

history.meaning: food or meal eaten during the night
late-night meal, midnight snack

야식.notes: Part of the productive -식 (食, "meal") series: 조식 (breakfast, formal), 중식 (lunch), 석식 (dinner), 간식 (between-meal snack), and 야식 (late-night meal, especially popular among TV crews editing overnight).

cognates.meaning: open country, out in the field

야외.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 野外, composed of 野 (야, "open field, plain, countryside") and 外 (외, "outside, exterior, beyond"). In Classical Chinese, it denoted the open countryside beyond city outskirts; in modern Korean, it functions as the standard noun and modifier for "outdoors, in the open air" (as opposed to 실내, 室內, "indoors").

history.meaning: open plains and fields outside a town
outdoors, open air

야외.notes: In Korean variety shows like *2 Days & 1 Night*, 야외 취침 ("sleeping outdoors in a tent") vs. 실내 취침 ("sleeping indoors") is the classic game penalty distinction, alongside 야외 촬영 ("outdoor location shoot").

rootFamily.gloss: the wild, living in the wild (野生)

야하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) root 야 (冶, "to smelt metal; to deck out, adorn seductively, alluring") combined with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 ("to be"). In Classical Chinese—most famously in the *I Ching* (易經) maxim 冶容誨淫 ("seductive adornment invites licentiousness") and the compound 妖冶 (요야, "bewitchingly alluring")—the character 冶 evolved metaphorically from "melting/fusing metal" to "meltingly charming, heavily made-up, voluptuous". In modern Korean, 야하다 means "risqué, racy, revealing, sexually suggestive", or (of colors/clothes) "loud and flashy".

history.meaning: to smelt metal; seductively adorned, alluring (as in 冶容, 妖冶)
to be bewitchingly dressed, gaudy, loud
to be racy, risqué, revealing, sexually suggestive

야하다.notes: Covers everything from mildly revealing outfits (옷이 좀 야하다, "the outfit is a bit revealing") and racy jokes (야한 농담, "dirty joke") to loud, neon colors; in broadcasting, overly 야한 scenes risk censorship by standards boards.

rootFamily.gloss: meltingly or subtly suggestive, peculiar, odd
metallurgy, smelting (冶金, retaining the literal sense of 冶)

cognates.meaning: some, a few, a little, slightly
a certain number or amount, several

약간.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 若干, composed of 若 (약, "like, such, as if, or") and 干 (간, "stem, shield; a certain number, how many"). Attested in Classical Chinese (including the *Book of Rites* and *Records of the Grand Historian*) as an indefinite numeral quantifier meaning "such-and-such a count, a certain amount, several". In modern Korean, it functions primarily as a degree adverb meaning "a little, slightly, somewhat" and as a noun/modifier (약간의, "a small amount of").

history.meaning: how many; a certain unspecified number or amount
a little, slightly, somewhat; a small amount

약간.notes: In casual spoken Korean, 약간 is also widely used as a conversational hedge—much like English "kind of" or "sort of" (e.g., 약간 어색해, "it's kind of awkward").

rootFamily.gloss: a few people, a small number of people (若干名)

약국.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 약국 (藥局), joining 약 (藥, 'medicine, medicinal herb, drug') and 국 (局, 'office, bureau, shop, dispensary').

history.meaning: dispensary, pharmacy, drugstore

약사님.etymology: Polite occupational title combining the Sino-Korean noun 약사 (藥師, yaksa, 'pharmacist', from 藥 'medicine, healing herb' + 師 'master, licensed specialist') with the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (-nim). In Korean social address, professional titles are rarely used bare when speaking to or respectfully about a community professional; attaching -님 creates the courteous everyday form of address 약사님. Pronounced [약싸님] (yakssanim) due to post-obstruent tensification of ㅅ after ㄱ.

history.meaning: master of medicine; licensed pharmacist
pharmacist (respectful title and address)

약사님.notes: In Korean neighborhoods, local shopkeepers and specialists are warmly referred to by their role + -님 (약사님, 사장님, 셰프님).

약속.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 약속 (約束), combining 약 (約, 'bind, agree') and 속 (束, 'tie, bundle').
약속.notes: Covers both a personal promise ('약속해요!') and a scheduled appointment or plan with someone.

약속하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 약속 (約束, 'promise, appointment, pact', from 約 'to bind, make a covenant' + 束 'to tie in a bundle, restrain') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to make a promise or appointment

약점.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 弱點, composed of 弱 (약, "weak, fragile, deficient") and 點 (점, "point, spot, dot, aspect"). Literally "weak point", used across East Asian languages to translate both a personal flaw or strategic vulnerability and, in Korean idiomatic usage (약점을 잡다, "to seize someone's weak point"), compromising secrets or "dirt" that gives someone leverage over another.

history.meaning: point of weakness or deficiency
weakness, flaw, vulnerability; compromising dirt/leverage

약점.notes: Learn the high-frequency idiom 약점을 잡다 ("to have dirt on someone / hold someone's weakness as leverage") and its passive counterpart 약점을 잡히다 ("to have someone hold dirt over you").

약하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 약 (弱, 'weak, fragile, slender') + native adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to be weak, frail, mild

얇다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 얣겁다 / 엷다 (bright-vowel variant 얇다, 'to be thin, not thick, of flat objects').

history.meaning: to be thin, slender in thickness
to be thin (of paper, cloth, ice, slices)

얌전히.etymology: Derived Korean adverb combining the descriptive root 얌전- (attested in Early Modern Korean as 얌젼ᄒᆞ다, 'modest, composed, gentle in manner') with the productive adverbial suffix -히. Under Standard Korean orthography, -하다 adjectives whose stems end in ㄴ vary between -히 and -하게, and 얌전히 is lexicalized with -히 alongside 여전히 and 부지런히. Applied to people or pets it means 'politely, without fuss', and applied figuratively to objects it evokes sitting undisturbed and neatly in place.
얌전히.notes: Modifies verbs of posture, waiting, or placing such as 앉다, 기다리다, 놓이다, and 접다.

양.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) single-character noun 量 (량 / 양, "quantity, amount, volume, measure, portion"). Under South Korea's Initial Sound Rule (두음법칙), the historical Sino-Korean reading 량 (*ryang*) drops its initial liquid-glide sequence in word-initial position to become 양 (*yang*), while preserving 량 when appearing as a non-initial element inside compounds (such as 분량 "portion/screen time" or 용량 "capacity").

history.meaning: measure, capacity, quantity, amount
amount, quantity, portion size (word-initial form under 두음법칙)

양.notes: When talking about food, 양이 많다 / 적다 means "the portion size is big / small"; when talking about a person, 양이 적다 means "they have a small appetite / eat little".

rootFamily.gloss: amount, portion; broadcast screen time (分量)

양갱.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) culinary term 羊羹, composed of 羊 (양, "sheep, mutton") and 羹 (갱, "thick soup, broth, stew"). In medieval China, 羊羹 was literally a savory mutton broth that congealed into a jelly when cooled due to animal gelatin. Zen Buddhist monks, bound by vegetarian precepts, introduced the dish to Japan during the Kamakura and Muromachi periods and substituted azuki red beans, wheat flour, sugar, and later agar (*kanten*) for the mutton, creating the sweet confection *yōkan* (羊羹), which entered modern Korean in its Sino-Korean reading 양갱.

history.meaning: savory gelled soup made from mutton broth
sweet vegetarian confection of red-bean paste set with agar
sweet red-bean jelly bar

양갱.notes: Despite its literal Hanja meaning "sheep soup" (羊羹), modern 양갱 contains zero meat—it is a sweet vegan-friendly jelly made of red bean paste and agar (most famously sold in Korea as 연양갱 or 밤양갱, "chestnut red-bean jelly").

양다리.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean (혼종어) compound combining Sino-Korean 양 (兩, "both, two, a pair"; historically 량 before the Initial Sound Rule) and native Korean 다리 ("leg; bridge", attested in Middle Korean as 다리 *tari*). Literally "both legs", it derives its figurative sense from the idiom 양다리를 걸치다 ("to straddle one leg onto each of two sides"), which shifted from opportunistically hedging one's bets between two rival camps to romantic "two-timing" (secretly dating two people at once).

history.meaning: both legs
both legs; straddling two factions; romantic two-timing

양다리.notes: Almost always used with the verb 걸치다 ("to drape/straddle across"): 양다리를 걸치다 means "to two-time (romantically)" or "to have a foot in both camps".

양동이.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed in the late 19th–early 20th century from Sino-Korean prefix 양- (洋-, 'Western, foreign, across the ocean') + native Korean 동이 ('large round earthenware water jar') — literally 'Western-style metal bucket'.

history.meaning: metal or plastic bucket, pail

양모.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 양모 (羊毛), from 양 (羊, 'sheep') and 모 (毛, 'hair, wool, fur').
양모.notes: Dense compressed 양모 forms the felt hammers inside acoustic pianos.

양복.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 洋服, composed of 洋 (양, "ocean; Western, Occidental", elliptic for 西洋 서양 "the Western world") and 服 (복, "clothing, garment, dress"). Coined in late 19th-century East Asia to distinguish imported Western attire (洋服) from traditional national dress (such as Korean 한복 韓服 or Japanese 화복 和服). While Japanese *yōfuku* still means any Western clothing, in contemporary Korean 양복 narrowed specifically to a tailored Western business suit (especially a men's suit).

history.meaning: Western-style garments (as opposed to traditional East Asian dress)
Western-style clothes; tailored business suit

양복.notes: False friend alert with Japanese: Japanese 洋服 (*yōfuku*) means any everyday Western clothes (jeans, T-shirts, dresses), whereas Korean 양복 specifically means a formal tailored suit (synonymous with 정장, 正裝).

양심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 良心, uniting 良 (어질 량, 'innately good, upright, virtuous') and 心 (마음 심, 'heart, mind'). The term originates in classical Confucian philosophy—specifically Mencius (孟子, Gaozi I), who used 良心 for the innate moral heart that naturally recognizes right and wrong—and later became the standard East Asian translation for Western ethical 'conscience'. Word-initial 량 regularly loses its liquid before ㅣ/ㅑ in South Korean orthography (두음법칙), yielding 양심.
양심.notes: Appears in everyday idioms like 양심에 찔리다 ('to feel a prick of conscience') and 양심 규칙 ('honour rule').

양쪽.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 양 (兩, 'both, pair, two') + native Korean 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: both sides, both parties

양철.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 양철 (洋鐵), formed from 양 (洋, 'ocean, Western, foreign') and 철 (鐵, 'iron'). Coined in the late 19th century when tin-plated sheet iron was imported into East Asia from Europe and North America, the term literally means 'Western iron'. In Korean material culture, 양철 evokes nostalgic biscuit tins, tea canisters, pencil cases, and painted tin roofs.

history.meaning: imported Western tin-plated iron sheet
tinplate, tin (used for canisters, boxes, and roofs)

양철.notes: Because tinplate resists rust when sealed, a small 양철 통 ('tin canister') was a classic household vessel for homemade time capsules.
