양파.etymology: Hybrid botanical and culinary compound prefixing Sino-Korean 양- (洋, 큰바다 양, 'ocean, Western') to the native Korean noun 파 ('scallion, welsh onion', Middle Korean 파). When round bulb onions were introduced to Korea in the late nineteenth century, speakers named them 'Western scallions' (양파) in contrast to native green onions (대파, 쪽파).
양파.notes: Standard word for round cooking onions; green onions/scallions are 파 or 대파.

얘.etymology: Contracted colloquial Korean noun and interjection from 이 아이 ('this child, this kid'), used to call a child or close younger friend ('hey, listen') or refer to 'this person/kid'.

history.meaning: this child, this friend; 'hey!'

얘기.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) contracted noun derived from 이야기 ("story, talk, conversation") via syncope and glide coalescence (/ijagi/ > /jɛgi/). The uncontracted form 이야기 is attested in Early Modern Korean as 니야기 (*niyaki*) and 이야기, which historical linguists generally analyze as a nominalization derived from the Middle Korean verb stem 니르- / 닐- ("to say, tell, recount"). In modern Korean, 얘기 is the default spoken form for "talk, chat, story, or point under discussion".

history.meaning: story, narrative, account, talk
story, tale, conversation (uncontracted standard form)
talk, chat, conversation, story (contracted form)

얘기.notes: Both 이야기 and 얘기 are accepted in standard Korean, but 이야기 feels slightly more literary or narrative ("a fairy tale / story"), whereas 얘기 is far more natural in everyday conversation ("having a chat / what someone said").

얘기를.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) inflected noun form consisting of 얘기 ("talk, story, conversation", contracted from 이야기 < Early Modern Korean 니야기 *niyaki*) and the post-vocalic accusative (direct object) case particle -를 (from Middle Korean -를 / -ᄅᆞᆯ). It serves as the direct object in ubiquitous conversational collocations such as 얘기를 하다 ("to talk / tell a story"), 얘기를 나누다 ("to share a conversation"), and 얘기를 듣다 ("to hear a story / listen to what someone says").

history.meaning: story, talk (accusative)
story, conversation (uncontracted accusative)
talk, story (contracted accusative)

morphemes.meaning: accusative (direct object) marker after a vowel

얘기를.notes: In fast spoken Korean, 얘기를 often contracts even further to 얘길 (e.g., 무슨 얘길 그렇게 해?, "What are you talking about like that?").

rootFamily.gloss: talk, story (further contracted spoken object form)

얘기입니까.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) inflected predicate phrase composed of the noun 얘기 ("talk, story, point, matter", contracted from 이야기 < Early Modern Korean 니야기), the copula stem -이- ("to be", Middle Korean -이-), and the deferential/formal polite (하십시오체) interrogative ending -ㅂ니까 (evolved from the Middle Korean object-humble suffix -ᄉᆞᆸ- + indicative -니- + interrogative -까/-가). Literally "Is it the talk/statement that...?", used in formal workplace or broadcast settings to ask pointedly what someone means ("Are you saying that...?" / "Is it a matter of...?").

history.meaning: is it a story/statement? (deferential question)
is it a story / matter of...? (uncontracted formal polite question)
is it talk / a matter of...? (contracted formal polite question)

얘기입니까.notes: Combine the colloquial stem 얘기 with the formal polite ending -입니까 to create a crisp, natural spoken workplace question, such as 그게 무슨 얘기입니까? ("What do you mean by that?" / "What kind of talk is that?").

rootFamily.gloss: is it a story/matter? (uncontracted formal question)
it is a story/matter (formal polite declarative)

얘기하고.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) conjugated verb form composed of the noun 얘기 ("talk, conversation", contracted from 이야기 < Early Modern Korean 니야기), the verbalizing light verb stem -하- ("to do", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ- *ho-*), and the conjunctive suffix -고 ("and; -ing", Middle Korean -고). It functions both as a coordinate clause linker ("talk and...") and as the progressive participle before 있다 (얘기하고 있다, "to be talking").

history.meaning: talking and; telling a story and
talking and (uncontracted form)
talking and; talking (contracted form)

얘기하고.notes: Be careful to distinguish the verb form 얘기하고 ("talk and...", from 얘기하다) from the noun + comitative particle homograph 얘기하고 ("with the story/talk", where -하고 means "with/and").

얘기하니.etymology: Inflected form of colloquial native Korean verb 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, tell'), contracted from 이야기하다 (iyagihada). Formed by attaching the suffix -니 (-ni), which marks either a causal/sequential connective ('since one talks, upon talking') or an intimate/plain interrogative ending ('do you talk?'). 이야기 (iyagi) derives from Early Modern Korean 니야기 (niyagi), nominalized from middle Korean 니르다 (nireuda, 'to say, tell').

history.meaning: to say, tell; story, tale
to converse, tell a story
since one talks; do you talk?

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving verbs from nouns ('to do')
causal/discovery connective or intimate question ending

얘기하니.notes: Depending on intonation and clause position, -니 can connect a reason/discovery ('when I talked to them...') or ask a friendly question to a younger/equal interlocutor ('are you talking about...?').

얘기하다.etymology: Contracted colloquial verb from native Korean 이야기하다 (iyagihada, 'to talk, converse, tell a story'), composed of 얘기 (yaegi, syncopated from 이야기 iyagi via vowel coalescence of -iya- > -yae-) plus the productive light verb suffix -하다 (-hada, 'to do'). The noun 이야기 is attested in Early Modern Korean as 니야기 (niyagi), before initial n-deletion before /i/ or /j/ (두음법칙), likely derived from Middle Korean verb 니르다 (nireuda, 'to say, speak').

history.meaning: to recount a tale, speak
to tell a story, converse
to talk, chat, tell (colloquial standard)

얘기하다.notes: While 이야기하다 is preferred in formal prose, 얘기하다 is overwhelmingly dominant in everyday conversation and broadcast dialogue.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (얘기하다)

얘기하란다고.etymology: Complex quotative-rhetorical inflection of native Korean 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, tell', from 이야기하다). Built from stem 얘기하- plus -란다 (-randa, contracted indirect imperative quotative from -(으)라고 한다, 'someone tells one to do') and connective -고 (-go), forming the idiomatic construction -란다고 ('just because someone tells you to [speak]...'). Used to chide someone for taking an instruction too literally.

history.meaning: to tell a story, speak
saying that someone tells one to speak (uncontracted)
just because someone tells you to talk/say it

얘기하란다고.notes: Often echoed with the same verb in the main clause (e.g., 얘기하란다고 진짜 다 얘기하냐? 'Just because they told you to talk, do you really tell them everything?').

얘기하자.etymology: Hortative form of native Korean 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, converse'), contracted from 이야기하다 (iyagihada). Composed of the noun 얘기 (yaegi < 이야기 iyagi < Early Modern Korean 니야기 niyagi, 'story, talk'), the verbalizing suffix -하- (-ha-), and the plain-style cohortative sentence-final suffix -자 (-ja, 'let us'). Also serves as the stem for the connective 얘기하자면 ('if we are to speak of...').

history.meaning: let us speak / recount
let us converse / talk together
let's talk (colloquial hortative)

얘기하자.notes: In workplace or drama dialogues like *The Producers*, 잠깐 얘기하자 ('let's talk for a second') signals a private one-on-one conversation from a senior or peer in banmal (반말).

얘기할.etymology: Prospective adnominal (participle) form of native Korean 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, tell', contracted from 이야기하다 iyagihada). Formed from 얘기하- plus the prospective/irrealis determiner suffix -ㄹ (-l, after vowel stems), which derives from Middle Korean future/prospective adnominal marker -ㄹ (-l). Modifies a following noun or bound noun to express 'to talk about, that will speak, or time/person to talk'.

history.meaning: to speak, that will recount
to converse, prospective modifier
to talk (modifying noun); when talking

얘기할.notes: Frequently combines with grammatical bound nouns such as 때 (얘기할 때 'when talking'), 것 (얘기할 거 'something to talk about'), or 시간 (얘기할 시간 'time to talk').

얘기할게.etymology: Promissory first-person future form of native Korean 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, tell' < 이야기하다 iyagihada). Constructed from the stem 얘기하- plus the intimate/informal volitional-promissory ending -ㄹ게 (-lge), historically grammaticalized from the prospective adnominal suffix -ㄹ (-l) + bound noun 것 (geot, 'thing, fact') + copula/predicative particle, expressing the speaker's cooperative commitment to the listener ('I will talk [for you / as promised]').

history.meaning: it is something I shall speak of (analytic periphrasis)
I will tell/talk (uncontracted promissory)
I'll talk to them; I'll tell you (colloquial)

얘기할게.notes: Unlike -(으)ㄹ 거야 (which states a simple plan regardless of the listener), -ㄹ게 specifically reassures or involves the listener ('I'll talk to them for you' or 'I'll tell you later'). Adding -요 (얘기할게요) makes it polite.

얘기해서.etymology: Causal and sequential connective form of native Korean 얘기하다 (yaegihada, 'to talk, tell' < 이야기하다 iyagihada). Formed from 얘기하- plus the infinitive/connective suffix -아서/-어서 (-aseo/-eoseo, which coalesces with 하- ha- into 해- hae- via historic 하여서 hayeoseo > 해서 haeseo). Indicates either means/cause ('by talking, because one talked') or sequential action ('talk and then').

history.meaning: having spoken, by speaking (from 흐야 + 셔)
by conversing, because one told
by talking; because one talked (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: causal/sequential connective (coalesced with 하- as 해서)

얘기해서.notes: In Korean phonology, 하 + -아서 becomes 하여서 in literary prose and contracts to 해서 in everyday speech and writing.

어.etymology: Natural native Korean exclamation uttered when suddenly noticing something, hesitating, or expressing mild surprise ('oh, uh, hey').

history.meaning: interjection of sudden realization, surprise, or informal affirmation

어깨.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 어께 ('shoulder').

history.meaning: shoulder
shoulder

어느.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite determiner descending from Middle Korean 어느 ('which, what, some').

history.meaning: which, what, any
which, some, a certain

어느새.etymology: Univerbated native Korean compound adverb formed from the interrogative/indefinite determiner 어느 (eoneu, 'which, some', from Middle Korean 어느 eoneu) and 새 (sae, contracted from 사이 sai, 'interval, space, time between', from Middle Korean 스이 seui). Literally 'in which interval of time', shifting semantically to 'in no time at all, before one knew it, already'.

history.meaning: in which interval / space of time
at some point in between, before one noticed (uncontracted phrase)
before one knew it, already, in the blink of an eye

morphemes.meaning: interval, gap in time (contracted from 사이)

어느새.notes: Spelled as a single word (어느새) because it has lexicalized into an adverb meaning 'before one realized', whereas the literal phrase 어느 사이 ('which gap') is spaced. Closely synonymous with 어느덧.

rootFamily.gloss: before one knows it, unawares (synonymous compound)
in the meantime, during that brief interval

어두워지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative compound verb formed from the p-irregular descriptive verb 어둡다 (eodupda, 'to be dark, dim', Middle Korean 어듭다 eodeupda / 어둡다 eodupda) in its infinitive stem 어두워- (eoduwo-, where stem-final -ㅂ vocalizes to -우- before a vowel) plus the auxiliary inchoative verb -지다 (-jida, 'to become, come to be', originally from 지다 jida 'to fall, set'). Literally 'to become dark'.

history.meaning: to be dark; to grow dark
to become dark, grow dim or gloomy

morphemes.meaning: to be dark (p-irregular stem 어둡- > 어두우-)

어두워지다.notes: Demonstrates two core Korean morphophonological rules at once: ㅂ-irregular lenition (어둡- + -어 -> 어두워) and vowel harmony infringement where polysyllabic ㅂ-stems take -워 rather than -와 in modern standard Korean. Used both for nightfall and for someone's facial expression darkening (표정이 어두워지다).

rootFamily.gloss: to be dark, dim, ignorant of

어둡다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어듭다 ('to be dark, dim, gloomy').

history.meaning: to be dark, unlit
to be dark, dim, poorly informed about

어디.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 어드메 / 어디 ('where, what place, somewhere').

history.meaning: what place, where
where; somewhere, anywhere

어디선가.etymology: Native Korean compound indefinite adverb formed by contracting 어디에서인가 (eodieseoinga, 'from somewhere or other'). Consists of 어디 (eodi, 'where, somewhere', from Middle Korean 어듸 eodeui), the ablative/dynamic locative case marker -서 (-seo, shortened from -에서 -eseo, 'from, at'), and the indefinite/dubitative copular suffix -ㄴ가 (-n'ga, contracted from -인가 -in'ga, 'is it?, some...').

history.meaning: from where, at what place
at or from somewhere (uncontracted analytic form)
from somewhere, somewhere or other

어디선가.notes: Adding -ㄴ가 turns a question word + particle into an existential indefinite ('from somewhere' rather than 'from where?'), parallel to 누군가 ('someone'), 언젠가 ('someday'), and 뭔가를 ('something').

어디에나.etymology: Native Korean adverbial phrase formed from 어디 ('where, any place') + locative particle -에 ('at, in') + inclusive particle -나 ('or, regardless of, every').

history.meaning: everywhere, in any place whatever

어딨다.etymology: Colloquial phonological contraction of the native Korean phrase 어디에 있다 (eodie itda) or 어디 있다 (eodi itda, 'where is [it]?, to be somewhere'). Formed through vowel coalescence of the final /i/ of 어디 (eodi, 'where', Middle Korean 어듸 eodeui) and the initial /i/ of 있다 (itda, 'to exist, be located', Middle Korean 잇다 isda).

history.meaning: to be located where / somewhere
where is it?; to be somewhere (uncontracted phrase)
where is it? (colloquial contracted predicate)

morphemes.meaning: to exist, be at a location (있다)

어딨다.notes: Almost always encountered in conjugated spoken forms like 어딨어? ('Where are you? / Where is it?'), 어딨니?, or 어딨지?; in formal writing, it should be written spaced as 어디 있어 or 어디에 있어.

어떡하다.etymology: Phonological contraction in spoken and standard Korean of 어떠하게 하다 / 어떻게 하다 ('to do how, what to do about something').

history.meaning: to do what, how to handle a situation

어떤.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner contracted from 어떠하- (어떻다, 'to be of what kind') + adnominal suffix -ㄴ.

history.meaning: what kind of, which; some, a certain

어떻게.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 어떠하게, adverbial form (-게) of 어떠하다 / 어떻다 ('to be how, be in what state').

history.meaning: in what way, how

어떻게든.etymology: Native Korean compound adverb formed from 어떻게 (eotteoke, 'how, in what way', adverbial derivation in -게 from 어떻다 eotteota, contracted from 어떠하다 eotteohada, Middle Korean 어뗘흐다 eottyeoheuda) plus the concessive/indefinite suffix -든 (-deun, shortened from -든지 -deunji, 'no matter what, whether or not'). Literally 'no matter how', hence 'somehow or other, by hook or by crook, at any cost'.

history.meaning: in what manner, how
in whatever way, by any means (full form)
somehow or other, no matter what

morphemes.meaning: to be how, in what state (from 어떠하-)

어떻게든.notes: Frequently paired with resilient future expressions in K-dramas, such as 어떻게든 되겠지 ('Things will work out somehow or other') or 어떻게든 해 볼게요 ('I'll pull it off somehow').

rootFamily.gloss: to be how, what kind of state

어떻다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb contracted from 어떠하다 (Middle Korean 어떠하다, 'to be how, be of what sort or state').

history.meaning: to be in what state or manner
to be how, be like what

cognates.meaning: to put in order, adapt musically, or organize behind the scenes
musical arrangement, styling adaptation, or coordination (borrowed in parallel)

어레인지.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English *arrange* (or reinforced via Japanese broadcast/music jargon アレンジ *arenji*), which ultimately derives from Old French *arengier* ('to put in a row, line up in battle order'), from *a-* (Latin *ad-*) + *reng* ('rank, row', of Frankish origin *hring* 'ring, circle'). In Korean television and music industry jargon, the English verb *arrange* was nominalized to mean either 'musical arrangement' or behind-the-scenes 'scheduling, coordination, and fixing of appearances/deals'.

history.meaning: to set in a row, draw up battle lines
to put in order, plan, adapt a musical composition
coordination/fixing of schedules or deals; musical arrangement

어레인지.notes: In *The Producers* (*프로듀사*) and entertainment industry parlance, 어레인지하다 often means 'to set up a meeting, broker a casting deal, or smooth things over behind the scenes' (corresponding to Sino-Korean 조율하다 or 주선하다), whereas in music it corresponds to 편곡 (編曲).

rootFamily.gloss: to arrange, coordinate, broker, or adapt musically

어렵다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective (descriptive verb), inherited from Middle Korean 어렵다 (eoryeopda). In 15th-century Middle Korean, 어렵다 primarily meant 'to be cautious, hesitant, deferential, or fearful of imposing' (the sense of modern 조심스럽다 or 꺼리다), while 'difficult, hard' was expressed by 버겁다 or 힘듦; over the Early Modern period, the psychological sense 'daunting, intimidating to approach' broadened into the general modern meaning 'difficult, hard, arduous', while also retaining the deferential sense ('feeling awkward/deferential around a superior').

history.meaning: to feel hesitant, deferential, or intimidated; to be difficult
to be difficult, hard; to be deferential/uncomfortable around someone; to be impoverished

어렵다.notes: Besides 'difficult' (반대말: 쉽다 'easy'), 어렵다 is still used in social contexts (그 선배는 좀 어려워 'I feel a bit intimidated/formal around that senior') and economic contexts (집안 형편이 어렵다 'the family's finances are tight'). Its ㅂ-irregular stem becomes 어려워 (eoryeowo) before -어.

rootFamily.gloss: with difficulty, barely, after much trouble (adverb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어렵다)

어르신.etymology: Native Korean honorific noun derived from 어른 ('adult, elder', Middle Korean 얼운, originally the past adnominal of 얼우다/얼다) blended with the honorific stem formative -으시-. It is the most gracious, respectful everyday word in modern Korean for addressing or referring to an older person whom one does not know by family title.
어르신.notes: Takes honorific counter 분 (어르신 한 분) and honorific verbs (계시다, 하시다).

어른.etymology: Native Korean noun inherited from Middle Korean 어른 (eoreun, also attested as 얼운 eorun in 15th-century texts). Etymologically derived as the past/perfective adnominal participle (얼운 eorun) of the Middle Korean verb 얼다 (eolda, 'to marry, consummate marriage, pair up'), because in traditional Korean society an individual was recognized as a full adult only upon marriage and the capping ceremony (관례). Semantic bleaching of the verb 얼다 ('to marry') left 어른 as the standard noun for 'adult, grown-up, elder'.

history.meaning: one who has married -> married person, full-fledged adult
adult, grown-up; respected elder of a household or community

morphemes.meaning: adult, elder (historically from Middle Korean 얼- 'to marry' + participle -운)

어른.notes: In Korean culture, 어른 means both 'chronological adult' (opposite of 아이/어린이) and 'senior/elder worthy of deference' (웃어른, 집안 어른). Its honorific counterpart is 어르신 (eoreusin).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어른)

어리다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어리다; famously meant 'to be foolish, naive, simple-minded' in 15th-century Middle Korean (as in the opening preface of the Hunminjeongeum, 어린 백성 'unlettered/simple common folk') before shifting to 'to be young in age, tender'.

history.meaning: to be naive, foolish, unlearned
to be young in years, juvenile

어리바리하다.etymology: Colloquial native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the mimetic root 어리바리 (eoribari, an ablaut/rhyming sound-symbolic formation built on the root 어리- eori-, 'dazed, muddled, foolish, naive', seen in 어리석다 and 어리둥절하다) plus the descriptive verbalizer -하다 (-hada). Standard Korean dictionaries prescribe 어리버리하다 (eoribeorihada) as the normative form, with 어리바리하다 being a widespread vowel-alternant colloquialism expressing a slightly lighter, more bumbling or clueless nuance.

history.meaning: to be foolish, naive, dim-witted
to look muddled, slow-witted, or unsure of oneself (standard form)
to be bumbling, clueless, scatterbrained, or rookie-like (colloquial variant)

morphemes.meaning: bumbling, muddled, clueless (ideophonic reduplication on 어리-)

어리바리하다.notes: In *The Producers*, rookie PD Baek Seung-chan is frequently teased as 어리바리하다 ('bumbling, wide-eyed, cluelessly clumsy'). In formal writing, use the standard spelling 어리버리하다.

rootFamily.gloss: to be muddled, bumbling, slow on the uptake (standard spelling)
to be bewildered, dazed and confused

어리석다.etymology: Native Korean compound descriptive verb derived from Middle Korean 어리다 (eorida, which in 15th-century Korean meant 'to be foolish, stupid, ignorant', as preserved in King Sejong's *Hunminjeongeum* preface 어린 백성 eorin baekseong, 'foolish/unlettered commoners') combined with the suffix or root -석다 (-seokda, likely related to 석다/설다 'unripe, lax, lacking'). As simple 어리다 shifted semantically in Early Modern Korean from 'foolish' to 'young in age', the suffixed form 어리석다 took over the original sense 'foolish, unwise, silly'.

history.meaning: to be foolish, ignorant, simple-minded
to be foolish, unwise, lacking discernment (disambiguated from 어리다 'young')

morphemes.meaning: adjective-forming element indicating deficiency or state

어리석다.notes: A classic example of Korean semantic shift: in 1446, King Sejong's famous phrase 어엿비 너겨 ('taking pity on') 어린 백성 ('foolish/uneducated people') used 어리다 in the sense now carried by 어리석다! Today 어리다 means only 'young', while 어리석다 means 'foolish'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be young, immature (historic semantic split)

어린이.etymology: Native Korean compound noun coined and popularized in 1920 by Korean children's rights pioneer and author Bang Jeong-hwan (방정환, 1899–1931, pen name 소파 小波) to accord children dignity as autonomous persons. Formed from 어린 (eorin, adnominal participle of 어리다 eorida, 'to be young') + bound noun 이 (i, 'person', historically used with respect, on par with 늙은이 'elder' and 젊은이 'youth'), replacing the older, somewhat dismissive terms 아이/애 or 어린애. (Note that in 16th-century Korean, 어린 이 had meant 'foolish person' before 어리다 shifted to 'young'.)

history.meaning: foolish person (when 어리다 meant 'foolish') / young person
child, young person (dignified neologism popularized by Bang Jeong-hwan in 1920)

morphemes.meaning: to be young, tender in age

어린이.notes: More respectful and public/official in register than 아이 or 애 ('kid'). Used in official designations like 어린이날 (Children's Day, May 5, also founded by Bang Jeong-hwan) and 어린이집 (daycare center).

rootFamily.gloss: youth, young adult (parallel formation with 이 'person')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어린이)

어마어마하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated emphatic adjective formed from the ideophonic/exclamatory root 어마어마 (eoma-eoma) + -하다 (-hada). The base 어마 is widely analyzed by Korean philologists as originating from the startled exclamation 어마! (eoma!, originally invoking 'Mother!' < 어마/어머니 when shocked or awestruck by something overwhelming), reduplicated to express awe-inspiring scale ('staggering, colossal, tremendous, unimaginable').

history.meaning: exclamation of shock or awe (from 'mother!')
to be enormous, tremendous, staggering in scale or degree

어마어마하다.notes: Can describe either physical immensity (어마어마한 건물 'a colossal building'), huge quantities/costs, or high social clout/stardom (어마어마한 인기 'tremendous popularity'). In youth slang, it is playfully blended with 무시무시하다 ('formidable') into 어마무시하다.

rootFamily.gloss: colossal and formidable (colloquial blend of 어마어마하다 + 무시무시하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어마어마하다)

어머.etymology: Native Korean exclamation of surprise or mild dismay, originating as a shortened vocative of 어머니 / 엄마 ('mother!, oh my!').

history.meaning: oh my!, goodness!

어머나.etymology: Native Korean interjection of surprise formed from 어머 ('oh my!') + expressive exclamatory particle -나.

history.meaning: oh my goodness!, dear me!

어머니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun descending from Middle Korean 어마님 / 어미 ('mother', built on the ancient maternal root 엄-/어마 plus honorific suffix -니).

history.meaning: mother (respectful standard form)

어머님.etymology: Native Korean honorific kinship noun formed from 어머니 (eomeoni, 'mother', from Middle Korean 어미 eomi 'mother' + honorific/affectionate kinship suffix -니 -ni, attested as 어마님 eomanim in 15th-century texts) plus the honorific suffix -님 (-nim, from Middle Korean 님 nim, 'lord, master, respected person'). The vowel sequence underwent assimilation or syncope (어마님 > 어머님, or 어머니 + -님 > 어머님).

history.meaning: mother; respected mother (honorific)
honored mother; mother-in-law; polite address for someone else's mother or an older woman

어머님.notes: Used in four distinct ways: (1) addressing or referring to one's mother-in-law (시어머니 or 장모님), (2) referring politely to someone else's mother, (3) addressing one's own mother with high formality (e.g. in letters), or (4) in service/school settings to address a child's mother or an older female customer.

cognates.meaning: fish cake stew (whose borrowing 오뎅 prompted the Korean purification coinage 어묵)

어묵탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (魚묵湯 / 어묵탕) combining the Korean language-purification neologism 어묵 (eomuk, coined in the mid-20th century to replace the Japanese loanword 오뎅 *oden*, from Sino-Korean 어 魚 'fish' + native Korean 묵 muk 'jelly/cake made from starch') with Sino-Korean 탕 (湯 tang, 'hot water, broth, soup'). Literally 'fish-cake soup'.

history.meaning: hot water, decoction, broth, soup
processed fish cake (coined from 魚 'fish' + 묵 'jellied cake' to replace Japanese 오뎅)
fish-cake soup (simmered in radish, kelp, and anchovy broth)

morphemes.meaning: jellied cake/paste (native Korean noun, as in 도토리묵)

어묵탕.notes: 어묵탕 is the standard broadcast-approved term (since Korean TV networks like KBS discourage Japanese loanwords on air), though in casual street-food stalls and pojangmacha bars many speakers still call it 오뎅탕 (odeng-tang).

rootFamily.gloss: ginseng chicken soup (蔘雞湯, sharing 湯 'soup')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어묵탕)

cognates.meaning: linguistic difficulty; awkwardness in phrasing (Sino-Japanese cognate)

어색하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from 어색 (語塞, eosaek) + -하다 (-hada, 'to be'). The Sino-Korean root 語塞 is composed of 어 (語, 'words, speech, language') and 색 (塞, 'to block, stopper, obstruct; blocked', read 색 saek in the sense 'blocked/stifled' and 변방 새 sae in the sense 'frontier fortress'). Originally a literary Chinese compound meaning 'speech is blocked; to be at a loss for words' or 'phrasing is stilted and unnatural', it generalized in Korean to describe any awkward, stilted, or unnatural social atmosphere, relationship, or appearance.

history.meaning: speech-blocked; tongue-tied, unable to find words; stilted phrasing
to be tongue-tied; to be unnatural in speech or manner
to be awkward, uncomfortable, unnatural, or stilted

morphemes.meaning: to block, obstruct, be stifled (Hanja: 塞)

어색하다.notes: Because speakers rarely realize 어색하다 is Sino-Korean (語塞, literally 'speech-blocked'), it is a surprising etymology for learners! Notice how 塞 is read 색 (saek) when meaning 'blocked' (색전증 'embolism', 어색 'awkward') and 새 (sae) when meaning 'border fortress' (요새 要塞 'fortress'). In youth slang, 어색한 사이 ('awkward relationship') is shortened to 어사.

rootFamily.gloss: blockade, sealing off (封鎖/閉塞, cf. 폐색 閉塞 sharing 塞 'block')

어색해지다.etymology: Inchoative compound verb formed from Sino-Korean descriptive verb 어색하다 (語塞하다, eosaekhada, 'to be awkward, stilted, uncomfortable', from 語 'speech' + 塞 'blocked, obstructed') in its infinitive stem 어색해- (eosaekhae-, contracted from 어색하여) plus the native Korean auxiliary verb -지다 (-jida, 'to become, come to be'). Literally 'to become tongue-tied/blocked in speech', hence 'to grow awkward or strained'.

history.meaning: speech is blocked; tongue-tied or stilted in expression
to be awkward, unnatural, uncomfortable
to grow awkward, become strained (of a mood or relationship)

어색해지다.notes: A quintessential K-drama relationship verb:气氛/분위기가 어색해지다 ('the atmosphere grows awkward') or 우리 사이가 어색해졌다 ('things became awkward between us', e.g., after an unrequited confession).

어서.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 어서 ('quickly, promptly, without delay; welcomingly').

history.meaning: quickly, right away
quickly, promptly; gladly/welcomingly (어서 오세요)

어설프다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb. Attested in Early Modern Korean as 어설프다 (eoseolpeuda) and analyzed as containing the prefixal or root element 어- (eo-, seen in words denoting imperfection or misalignment like 어긋나다, 어중간하다) + 설- (seol-, stem of 설다 seolda, 'to be unripe, half-cooked, unfamiliar, lacking mastery', from Middle Korean 설다 seolda) + the adjectival suffix -프다 (-peuda, seen in 고프다, 가엾다/가엾브다). Originally 'unripe, poorly finished, sloppy', evolving to 'clumsy, half-baked, shoddy, amateurish'.

history.meaning: to be unripe, undercooked, unfamiliar, unskillful
to be sloppy, crudely made, lacking thoroughness
to be clumsy, half-baked, amateurish, poorly executed

어설프다.notes: Conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular adjective: 어설프- + -어 drops ㅡ and takes -어 to become 어설퍼 (eoseolpeo). Often used as an adverbial modifier 어설프게 ('half-bakedly, clumsily'), as in 어설프게 거짓말하다 ('to tell a clumsy, unconvincing lie').

rootFamily.gloss: to be half-cooked, unripe, or imprecise (설- + 익다 'ripen')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어설프다)

어우.etymology: Native Korean primary vocalic interjection (감탄사) of spontaneous emotion, formed from the open-mid back/central vowel 어 (eo) lengthened and rounded into 우 (u). Part of a rich sound-symbolic paradigm of Korean exclamations built on vowel gradation (어이, 어유, 어우, 아우, 아이구) that express visceral physical or emotional reactions ranging from frustration, disgust, or cringe to relief, sympathy, or sensation of heat/cold.

history.meaning: spontaneous vocalic exclamation of exasperation, relief, disgust, or physical sensation

morphemes.meaning: expressive vocalic interjection of visceral reaction or exasperation

어우.notes: Highly intonation-dependent in spoken Korean: said with a sigh (어우, 진짜! 'Ugh, seriously!'), it expresses annoyance or embarrassment; said when eating hot broth or stepping into cold air (어우, 추워! 'Brr, it's cold!' / 어우, 시원하다! 'Ah, how refreshing!'), it conveys immediate physical sensation.

rootFamily.gloss: oh my goodness, alas (traditional exclamation of叹/effort)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어우)

어울리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 어울다 / 어우르다 ('to join together, mingle, match harmoniously'), derived from the passive/causative stem 어울리-.

history.meaning: to mingle, harmonize
to suit, match well, look good on; to socialize with

어이.etymology: Native Korean primary interjection (감탄사) inherited from Middle Korean 어이 (eoi). Formed as a natural vocalic call combining the open vowel 어 (eo) with a high front off-glide 이 (i) to project the voice across a distance or express a sharp sigh. Historically used both as an exclamation of lament/astonishment and as a direct vocative call ('Hey!, Oy!') to get the attention of an equal or social junior. (Homophonous with the archaic noun 어이 meaning 'handle' or 'spirit/wits' in 어이없다 'dumbfounded'.)

history.meaning: alas!, oh! (exclamation of sorrow or surprise); hey!
hey!, yo! (familiar attention-getting call to a peer or subordinate)

어이.notes: As a call ('Hey!'), 어이 is strictly informal (반말 register) and used by seniors calling juniors (e.g., 어이, 신입! 'Hey, rookie!') or between close friends; using it toward a stranger or superior sounds rude or confrontational. Do not confuse with the noun 어이 in 어이없다 ('to be dumbfounded/absurd').

rootFamily.gloss: hey there, excuse me (slightly more polite attention-getter)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어이)

어제.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 어제 ('yesterday').

history.meaning: yesterday
yesterday

어젯밤.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 어제 ('yesterday') + genitive/compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 밤 ('night').

history.meaning: last night, yesterday evening

어쨌든.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized discourse adverb contracted from 어찌하였든 (eojjihayeotdeun, 'however one acted, no matter how it happened') via 어찌했든 (eojjihaetdeun) > 어쨌든 (eojjaetdeun). Built from the Middle Korean interrogative adverb 어찌 (eojji < 어찌/어듸, 'how, why') + light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do/be') + past/perfective marker -었- (-eot-) + concessive suffix -든 (-deun, shortened from -든지 -deunji, 'regardless of'). Literally 'regardless of how it was done', hence 'anyway, in any case, at any rate'.

history.meaning: regardless of how one did it / how it turned out
no matter how it was done (uncontracted literary form)
anyway, in any case, regardless (contracted standard adverb)

morphemes.meaning: to do how / be how (contracted from 어찌하-)

어쨌든.notes: A staple Korean conversation pivot used to wrap up a tangent or move to the bottom line ('Anyway...'). Avoid the common spelling error *어쨋든 (with ㅅ instead of ㅆ): because it contains the past-tense morpheme -었-, it must be written with double ㅆ (어쨌든), just like 아무튼/어쩌면.

rootFamily.gloss: to do what, do how (base verb contracted from 어찌하다)
anyway, whether this way or that (synonymous phrase)
in any case, one way or another (expanded variant)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어쨌든)

어쩌고.etymology: Inflected connective/quotative form of the native Korean pro-verb 어쩌다 (eojjeoda, 'to do how, do what', contracted from 어찌하다 eojjihada, from adverb 어찌 'how, why' + 하다 'to do/say'). Formed from stem 어쩌- + connective/quotative suffix -고 (-go). When reduplicated or paired with its distal demonstrative counterpart 저쩌고 (jeojjeogo < 저찌하고, 'doing/saying that way'), it functions as an idiomatic pro-clause meaning 'saying this and that; blah blah blah; and so forth'.

history.meaning: doing how and; saying what (uncontracted)
what to do; saying this and that, blah blah (especially in 어쩌고저쩌고)

morphemes.meaning: to do/say how or what (contracted from 어찌하-)
coordinate or quotative connective suffix ('and; saying that')

어쩌고.notes: Used in two main ways in dialogue: (1) dismissively summarizing someone's long-winded excuse or chatter as 어쩌고저쩌고 ('blah blah, yadda yadda'), or (2) echoing a remark incredulously: 뭐가 어쩌고 어째? ('What did you just say?!').

rootFamily.gloss: blah blah, saying this and that (compound with 저쩌고)
to do what, how to act; by chance (base verb/adverb)

어쩌다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adverb contracted from 어찌하다 ('to do how, do what'); as an adverb (short for 어쩌다가), means 'by chance, accidentally, once in a while'.

history.meaning: to do what; by chance, unintentionally, occasionally

어쩌면.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean modal adverb derived as the conditional form of the pro-verb 어쩌다 (eojjeoda, 'to do or turn out in some way', contracted from 어찌하다 eojjihada, from Middle Korean 어찌 'how' + 흐다 'to do/be') plus the conditional connective suffix -면 (-myeon, 'if'). Literally 'if it turns out in some way', which grammaticalized into two distinct modal senses: epistemic possibility ('perhaps, maybe, possibly') and exclamatory wonder ('how on earth, how can it be that...').

history.meaning: if one does how; if it turns out somehow
perhaps, maybe (epistemic); how in the world (exclamatory)

morphemes.meaning: to do/be how or in some way (contracted from 어찌하-)

어쩌면.notes: Watch the two meanings: paired with a conjectural ending like -ㄹ지도 모르다 or -겠다 (어쩌면 비가 올지도 몰라 'Perhaps it might rain'), it means 'maybe/perhaps'; paired with 그렇게/이리 ('so, like this'), it means 'how on earth' (and often contracts further to 어쩜!).

rootFamily.gloss: how on earth!, my goodness! (contracted exclamatory adverb)
by chance, accidentally; to do what (base verb/adverb)
anyway, in any case (past concessive form)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어쩌면)

어쩐지.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 어찌한지 ('for what reason it may be, somehow'), from 어찌하다 + indirect question ending -ㄴ지.

history.meaning: somehow, for some reason; no wonder!

어쩜.etymology: Colloquial syncopated contraction of the native Korean adverb 어쩌면 (eojjeomyeon, 'how on earth, perhaps', itself contracted from 어찌하면 eojjihamyeon, 'if one does how', from 어찌 'how' + 하다 'to do/be' + conditional -면). Through syncope of the glide-vowel sequence -yeo- in rapid expressive speech (어쩌면 > 어쩜), the contracted form 어쩜 specialized predominantly in the exclamatory sense 'how on earth!, how can it be so...!' or as a standalone interjection of amazement ('Oh my!, No way!').

history.meaning: if one does how / in what way
perhaps; how on earth (uncontracted adverb)
how on earth!, my goodness! (syncopated exclamatory adverb/interjection)

어쩜.notes: While full 어쩌면 usually means 'perhaps/maybe', contracted 어쩜 almost always expresses emotional amazement or disbelief—either positive (어쩜 이렇게 예뻐! 'How on earth is it this pretty!') or negative (어쩜 사람이 그래? 'How on earth can a person act like that?').

rootFamily.gloss: perhaps; how in the world (uncontracted form)
to do how; by chance (base pro-verb/adverb)
why, for what reason (contracted from 어찌하여서)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 표준국어대사전 (어쩜)

cognates.meaning: at this and that (Classical Chinese elements)
here and there (sharing 此彼 characters)

어차피.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb constructed from the Classical Chinese characters 於 (어, preposition meaning 'at, in, by'), 此 (차, demonstrative pronoun 'this'), and 彼 (피, demonstrative pronoun 'that'). Literally meaning 'whether in this way or in that way', it lexicalized in Korean as an adverb expressing inevitability regardless of which alternative is chosen ('anyway, in any case').

history.meaning: in this or that case; either way
either way, in any case, anyway

어차피.notes: Frequently paired with statements of resignation or pragmatic acceptance (e.g., 'Since it will happen anyway...').

rootFamily.gloss: this time, the present occasion (此番)
that side and this side; both parties (彼此)

어처구니.etymology: Native Korean noun whose exact origin is debated among philologists. Traditionally explained via folk and material-culture etymology as denoting the wooden handle of a stone hand-mill (맷돌 손잡이) or the clay figurines placed on palace roof ridges (잡상); if a miller picks up a heavy millstone only to find the handle missing, they are left dumbfounded. An alternative philological hypothesis links it to Early Modern Korean 어척 ('measure, yardstick', from Sino-Korean 於尺) plus a diminutive or nominal suffix, originally meaning 'something beyond all measure or bounds'.

history.meaning: to be beyond measure; to be utterly absurd or dumbfounding
an imaginably huge thing; absurdity (in negative idioms)

morphemes.meaning: boundless thing; millstone handle; sense of proportion

어처구니.notes: Almost never used in the affirmative in everyday speech; it appears overwhelmingly in 어처구니없다 or 어처구니가 없다 ('to be dumbfounded, absurd, preposterous').

rootFamily.gloss: to be dumbfounded (synonymous idiom from 'blocked speech')

어플.etymology: Late-2000s South Korean clipped loanword (외래어) shortened from the first two syllables of 어플리케이션, a colloquial transcription of English 'application' (ultimately from Latin applicātiō, from applicāre 'to attach to, apply'). Coined during the early smartphone boom to denote a mobile software application.

history.meaning: computer software program designed for end users
software application program
smartphone app

어플.notes: While the National Institute of Korean Language prescribes 앱 (app) or 애플리케이션, 어플 remains pervasive in casual South Korean conversation.

cognates.meaning: to make an earnest request or attract interest
to showcase one's charm or make an appeal

어필해보다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb (혼종어) combining the English loanword 어필 (from English 'appeal', via Anglo-Norman apeler and Latin appellāre 'to accost, address, call upon'), the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', conjugated in its infinitive/connective form 해), and the native auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing'). In Korean broadcasting and everyday usage, 어필하다 shifted from legal/formal pleading to actively showcasing one's charm, talent, or selling points to win someone over.

history.meaning: to call upon; to be attractive or interesting
to showcase one's appeal; to pitch or highlight strengths
to try making an appeal; to try pitching oneself

morphemes.meaning: to do (infinitive form of light verb 하다)

어필해보다.notes: Unlike English 'appeal to someone' (which often takes the viewer as subject: 'It appeals to me'), Korean 어필하다 is used transitively/actively by the person pitching their own charm ('I will try appealing to them').

rootFamily.gloss: to appeal, to showcase one's strengths

어휴.etymology: Native Korean expressive interjection (감탄사) of vocal-mimetic origin, directly imitating the audible exhalation of a heavy sigh when relieved, exhausted, exasperated, or overwhelmed. It participates in Korean vowel-harmony ablaut alongside the brighter-vowel variant 아휴 and the unaspirated variant 어유.

history.meaning: expressive vocalization of sighing in relief or frustration

morphemes.meaning: mimetic sigh of relief, exhaustion, or exasperation

어휴.notes: Depending on intonation, 어휴 can express either 'Phew, what a relief!' (falling, relaxed) or 'Ugh, good grief!' at someone's antics (sharp, drawn-out).

rootFamily.gloss: alas, oh dear (classic exclamation of fatigue or dismay)

억울하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from the Sino-Korean bound root 억울 (抑鬱, combining 抑 억 'to press down, restrain, suppress' and 鬱 울 'luxuriant, dense, blocked up, gloomy, melancholic') plus the native Korean adjectival suffix -하다. While the Chinese and Japanese cognates (抑鬱) denote clinical or emotional depression, Korean underwent a distinctive semantic specialization from 'pent-up and stifled' to 'feeling deeply wronged, falsely accused, or treated unfairly'.

history.meaning: suppressed and stifled in spirit; pent-up frustration
to feel stifled with resentment over an injustice
to feel wronged, treated unfairly, or falsely accused

억울하다.notes: Watch out for a classic East Asian false friend: Japanese 抑鬱 (yokuutsu) and Chinese 抑鬱 (yìyù) mean 'clinical depression', whereas Korean 억울하다 specifically describes the burning indignation of being unfairly blamed or wronged.

억지로.etymology: Lexicalized Korean adverb built from the noun 억지 ('stubborn insistence, forcing what is unnatural', traditionally associated with Sino-Korean 臆志, from 臆 'subjective will, chest' and 志 'intent') plus the directional-instrumental particle -로 ('by means of'). It covers two closely linked nuances: applying physical force to a stuck mechanism or lid (억지로 열다), and compelling oneself or someone else emotionally against natural inclination (억지로 웃다 'force a smile').
억지로.notes: Pronounced [억찌로] with automatic tensification of ㅈ after ㄱ; contrasts with 저절로 or 자연스럽게.

언니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun (attested from Early Modern Korean 언니) used by a female speaker to address or refer to an older sister (and formerly also used between males for an elder brother in Seoul speech), extended to friendly older female acquaintances.

history.meaning: older sister (of a female); friendly address to an older woman

언덕.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 언덕 ('hill, bank, slope, rising ground').

history.meaning: embankment, hill, slope
hill, gentle slope

언뜻.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic/mimetic adverb describing an image, thought, or figure flashing momentarily across one's vision or mind ('in a flash, fleetingly, at first glance'). It belongs to a native Korean sound-symbolic series with 언뜩 (tense-stop intensive variant) and 안뜩 (bright-vowel variant).

history.meaning: in a fleeting flash; momentarily passing before the eyes or mind

morphemes.meaning: fleetingly, in a flash, at first glance

언뜻.notes: Very commonly collocates with 보기에는 (언뜻 보기에는, 'at first glance') or 생각나다 (언뜻 생각나다, 'to suddenly cross one's mind').

rootFamily.gloss: suddenly, in a sharp flash (intensive variant)

cognates.meaning: the press, speech and discussion; arbitration; committee (cognate Sino-Japanese components)
cognates.word: 言論 (genron) / 仲裁 (chūsai) / 委員会 (iinkai)

언론중재위원회.etymology: Sino-Korean institutional compound noun (言論仲裁委員會) designating South Korea's statutory Press Arbitration Commission, established in 1981 to mediate disputes over defamation and factual inaccuracies in news reporting. Composed of 언론 (言論, 'speech and discussion; the press/media'), 중재 (仲裁, 'arbitration, mediation between parties'), and 위원회 (委員會, 'committee, commission').

history.form: 言論 + 仲裁 + 委員會
history.meaning: Sino-Korean legal and administrative nouns for press, arbitration, and commission
Press Arbitration Commission of South Korea (established 1981)

morphemes.meaning: words, speech (言) + discussion, discourse (論) -> the press, media
middle, intermediary (仲) + judge, regulate (裁) -> arbitration, mediation
entrust (委) + member, official (員) + assembly, council (會) -> commission, committee

언론중재위원회.notes: Often abbreviated in Korean newsrooms and legal contexts as 언중위 (言仲委); in K-dramas about broadcasting, characters threaten to file complaints here over unfair media coverage.

rootFamily.gloss: the press, media, public speech (言論)

cognates.meaning: the press, speech (shared Sino-Japanese first component)
strategic action or maneuver (source of second component)

언론플레이.etymology: South Korean hybrid compound noun (혼종어) coined in late-20th-century political and entertainment journalism by combining Sino-Korean 언론 (言論, from 言 언 'speech, word' + 論 론 'discuss, argue', meaning 'the press, mass media') with the English loanword 플레이 ('play', in the sense of a calculated tactical move or maneuver). It denotes the strategic leaking or staging of stories to manipulate public opinion ('media spin').

history.meaning: the press/media + tactical maneuver or game play
strategic manipulation of news coverage; media spin

morphemes.meaning: the press, mass media (言論: speech + discussion)

언론플레이.notes: Frequently clipped to 언플 in entertainment news and netizen slang when accusing celebrity agencies or politicians of planting stories to sway public sympathy.

rootFamily.gloss: teamwork, cooperative play (hybrid compound with 플레이)

언제.etymology: Native Korean interrogative noun and adverb meaning 'when, at what time'. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 어느제, a transparent compound of the interrogative determiner 어느 ('which, what') and the bound temporal noun 제 ('time, occasion', related to 젹 'time'). Syncope of the medial vowel ㅡ in 어느제 regularly produced the contracted form 언제.

history.meaning: which time, at what time
when, what time (contracted via medial vowel syncope)

언제.notes: Depending on sentence intonation and context, 언제 can function either as a direct question ('When?') or as an indefinite temporal pronoun ('sometime, at some point').

rootFamily.gloss: which, what (interrogative determiner preserving the full stem)
someday, at some point (언제 + indefinite interrogative -ㄴ가)

언제나.etymology: Native Korean adverb lexicalized from the interrogative temporal noun 언제 ('when', from Middle Korean 어느제 'which time') combined with the postpositional particle -나 (allomorph of -이나 after a vowel), which converts interrogative pronouns into universal quantifiers ('whatever time, at all times, always').

history.meaning: at whichever time, whenever
always, at all times, whenever

morphemes.meaning: when, what time (from Middle Korean 어느제)

언제나.notes: This productive pattern of [interrogative pronoun + -(이)나] yields universal ('every/any') meanings across Korean: 누구 ('who') -> 누구나 ('everyone'), 어디 ('where') -> 어디나 ('everywhere'), 언제 ('when') -> 언제나 ('always').

언제든.etymology: Formed from the native Korean temporal interrogative 언제 ('when') and the free-choice particle -든 (shortened from -든지, 'regardless of which/when'). Adding -든 converts an interrogative word into a welcoming universal expression: 언제든 ('at any time, whenever'), 어디든 ('anywhere'), and 누구든 ('anyone').
언제든.notes: Interchangeable with the slightly fuller form 언제든지.

언젠가.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 언제 ('when', from Middle Korean 어느제 'which time') plus the indefinite interrogative copula ending -인가 (copula stem -이- + interrogative suffix -ㄴ가). Adding -인가 to an interrogative pronoun turns it into an existential indefinite ('at some unknown time -> someday, once').

history.meaning: at some unspecified time (analytic form)
someday, one day; at some point in the past

morphemes.meaning: indefinite interrogative copula ending (-인가 contracted to -ㄴ가)

언젠가.notes: Unlike English 'someday' (which only looks to the future), Korean 언젠가 can refer either to an unspecified future time ('someday') or an unspecified past occasion ('some time ago, once before') depending on the verb tense.

얹혀살다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 얹혀 (the infinitive/connective form of 얹히다, passive of 얹다 'to place on top, lay upon') and 살다 ('to live, dwell', Middle Korean 살다). Literally meaning 'to live placed atop someone else', the metaphor depicts a dependent or freeloader as extra weight resting on another person's household or livelihood.

history.meaning: to be placed upon + to live/reside
to live as a dependent in another's home; to freeload or crash

morphemes.meaning: passive suffix -히- + infinitive connective -어 -> 얹혀 ('being placed upon')

얹혀살다.notes: Carries a self-deprecating or critical nuance of being a burden or sponge in someone else's home, stronger than simply 'staying as a guest'.

rootFamily.gloss: to place on top, put upon
to be placed on top; to freeload; to have indigestion
to live off someone, sponge off (synonymous compound with 붙다 'stick to')

얹히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from the transitive verb stem 얹- (얹다, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 엏다 and 얹다 'to place on top, lay upon') plus the native passive derivational suffix -히-. From the literal physical sense 'to be laid on top of something', it developed two major figurative extensions: (1) food sitting unmoving on top of the stomach ('to suffer acute indigestion'), and (2) a person resting their livelihood on another's household ('to stay as a freeloader or dependent').

history.meaning: to place on top, set upon (transitive root)
to be placed upon; to suffer indigestion; to live off another

morphemes.meaning: to place on top, lay upon (stem of 얹다)

얹히다.notes: Notice the dual everyday idioms: 속이 얹히다 means 'to have food sit heavy on one's stomach (indigestion)', while 남의 집에 얹히다 means 'to crash/freeload at someone else's house'.

rootFamily.gloss: to place on top, put upon (base transitive verb)
to live as a freeloader/dependent (얹혀 + 살다)
to put on top of, lay over (얹어 + 놓다)

얻다.etymology: Core native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to get, obtain, acquire, gain'. Directly inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 얻다 (stem 얻-), which already carried the full range of senses from acquiring material objects to winning people, brides, or abstract prestige. In compound verbs, its infinitive 얻어- productively grammaticalized into a prefixoid meaning 'by receiving from outside' (often unwelcome or free).

history.meaning: to obtain, acquire, get, take in marriage
to get, gain, obtain, win

morphemes.meaning: to get, obtain, gain (native verb stem)

얻다.notes: Beyond simple acquisition ('get a room' 방을 얻다, 'gain popularity' 인기를 얻다), 얻어- serves as the first element of many vivid compound verbs denoting things received passively from others (얻어맞다 'get hit', 얻어먹다 'get fed for free / get cursed at').

rootFamily.gloss: to manage to get, extract through effort (얻어 + 내다)
to get hit, take a beating (얻어 + 맞다)
to hear by chance or overhear (얻어 + 듣다)

얻어내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 얻다 ('to get, obtain', Middle Korean 얻다) linked via the infinitive connective -어 to the auxiliary/transitive verb 내다 ('to put forth, bring out, accomplish through effort', Middle Korean 내다). The auxiliary -어 내다 adds a completive, extractive nuance: securing a desired result or concession through persistence despite resistance.

history.meaning: to obtain + to bring out / accomplish
to extract, wring out, or manage to obtain through effort

morphemes.meaning: to bring out, achieve through effort (내다)

얻어내다.notes: Whereas 얻다 simply means 'to get', 얻어내다 implies active persuasion, negotiation, or persistence—such as a TV producer finally getting a reluctant celebrity's approval or securing a budget.

rootFamily.gloss: to pull out, extract, accomplish (auxiliary/main verb)
to win, clinch, secure a prize or contract (따 + 내다)

얻어맞다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 얻어- (the infinitive form of 얻다 'to get, acquire, receive', used here as an adversative-receptive prefixoid) with 맞다 ('to be struck, hit, beaten', Middle Korean 맞다 'to meet, be hit by a projectile'). Literally meaning 'to acquire a hitting', it emphasizes being on the receiving end of blows.

history.meaning: to receive/get + to be struck by a blow
to get hit, take a beating, be battered

얻어맞다.notes: Often used figuratively in workplace and media contexts for taking a battering from critics, ratings, or superiors (e.g., 'getting clobbered by rival shows').

rootFamily.gloss: to be hit, struck; to face/meet
to get beaten harshly (synonymous intensive compound with 두들기다)

얻어먹고.etymology: Conjunctive form (-고 'and') of the native Korean compound verb 얻어먹다, composed of 얻어- (infinitive of 얻다 'to get, obtain from others') and 먹다 ('to eat, consume', Middle Korean 먹다). Literally 'to get food from others and eat it (for free)', it also participates in the ubiquitous Korean metaphor of 'eating' verbal abuse (욕을 얻어먹다 'to swallow insults, catch flak, get chewed out').

history.meaning: to obtain + to eat
to eat at another's expense; (with 욕) to be scolded or catch flak, and...

morphemes.meaning: to get, receive from others (infinitive of 얻다)
to eat, consume, take in (stem of 먹다)

얻어먹고.notes: Pay close attention to the direct object: 밥을 얻어먹다 means 'to get treated to a free meal (or sponge off someone)', whereas 욕을 얻어먹다 means 'to catch flak / get cursed out'.

rootFamily.gloss: to get fed for free; to catch flak (dictionary form)

얼굴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 얼굴; originally meant 'overall bodily shape, figure, form, appearance' in 15th-century Middle Korean (while 낯 meant 'face'), before narrowing in Early Modern Korean to 'human face, countenance'.

history.meaning: bodily shape, overall figure or form
face, countenance

얼룩.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 어루기 / 얼룩 ('mottled pattern, spot, dapple, stain').

history.meaning: mottled spot, blotch, stain

얼른.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/expressive adverb meaning 'in a flash, quickly, right away, without hesitation'.

history.meaning: quickly, promptly, in a flash

얼마.etymology: Native Korean noun and pronoun of quantity, price, or duration ('how much; an indefinite or short amount of time/quantity'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 어느마, a compound of the interrogative determiner 어느 ('which, what') and the bound noun 마 ('measure, degree, extent'). Syncope of the medial vowel ㅡ produced Early Modern Korean 언마, which then underwent regressive liquid assimilation (ㄴ + ㅁ -> ㄹ + ㅁ) to yield Modern Korean 얼마.

history.meaning: what measure, what extent, how much
how much, what amount (via medial vowel syncope)
how much; a short while or small amount (in negative/indefinite contexts)

morphemes.meaning: which, what (from Middle Korean 어느, assimilated to 얼-)

얼마.notes: Before a negative predicate (e.g., 얼마 안 되다, 얼마 전에), 얼마 shifts from a question ('how much?') to a minimize-quantity sense ('not much; only a short while ago').

rootFamily.gloss: as much as one wants, anytime (얼마 + -든지)
how much, to what extent (얼마 + adverbial -나)
only that much, to that extent (그 'that' + 마 'measure' + -만큼)

얼마나.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from 얼마 ('how much, how many, what quantity', from Middle Korean 언마) + emphatic particle -나.

history.meaning: how much, to what degree, how very!

얼마든지.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed by combining the quantity/degree noun 얼마 ('how much, whatever amount', from Middle Korean 어느마 'what measure') with the concessive auxiliary particle -든지 ('whether, regardless of, no matter which'). Together they lexicalized to mean 'no matter how much -> as much as you want, anytime, without restriction'.

history.meaning: whatever amount + regardless of choice
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean construction

history.meaning: as much as one likes, anytime, readily

morphemes.meaning: how much, whatever amount (from Middle Korean 어느마)

얼마든지.notes: Frequently used as an enthusiastic, hospitable reply ('Of course! Anytime! As much as you like!') when someone asks for a favor or permission.

얼음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 얼다 ('to freeze') + nominalizing suffix -음.
얼음.notes: Retains morphophonemic spelling 얼음 (pronounced [어름]) showing its derivation from 얼-.

얼음물.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 얼음 ('ice', nominalization in -음 of 얼다 'to freeze') + 물 ('water').

history.meaning: ice water, iced water

얼음장.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 얼음 ('ice') + Sino-Korean/classifier 장 (張/場, 'flat sheet or slab') — literally 'a thick sheet or slab of ice'.

history.meaning: sheet or cake of ice; something icy cold

cognates.meaning: chief, head, leader (source of 짱 via 長)

얼짱.etymology: Late-1990s South Korean internet slang blend combining 얼-, clipped from the native Korean noun 얼굴 ('face', Middle Korean 얼굴 'shape, body, form'), with the youth slang noun/suffix 짱 ('the best, top, boss', derived via expressive consonant tensification from Sino-Korean 장 長 'head, chief, leader'). Literally 'face-best', referring to someone famous online or in school for extraordinary facial attractiveness.

history.meaning: face + the best / chief
person with the best-looking face; internet visual celebrity

morphemes.meaning: the best, top, champion (slang tensification of 長 장 'chief')

얼짱.notes: 얼짱 spawned an entire 2000s South Korean pop-culture paradigm of X-짱 compounds, such as 몸짱 ('best body / fitness icon') and 얼짱 각도 ('the flattering 45-degree selfie angle').

rootFamily.gloss: person with a great physique (몸 'body' + 짱 'best')
the best, awesome; boss (slang noun from 長)

얼추.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'roughly, approximately, nearly all'. It shares the native initial element 얼- ('approximate outline, rough frame, partial degree', seen in 얼핏 'fleetingly', 얼추잡다 'to estimate roughly', and 어림 'rough estimate') combined with an adverbial formative -추. It denotes reaching a close approximation of a whole without exact calculation.

history.meaning: in rough outline; approximately, nearly

얼추.notes: Often paired with 다 ('all') or 끝나다 ('to finish')—e.g., 얼추 다 끝났다 ('It is roughly all finished / almost done')—when a task is 80–90% complete.

rootFamily.gloss: to estimate roughly, make a ballpark guess
at a fleeting glance, dimly (sharing the native 얼- initial)

엄격하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 엄격 (嚴格), combining 嚴 (엄할 엄, 'stern, solemn, unyielding') and 格 (격식 격, 'standard, measure, proper form'), plus the native adjective suffix -하다. Rather than mere harshness, 엄격하다 emphasizes holding unwaveringly to clear rules, standards, or proportions. Phonologically, stem-final ㄱ merges with the ㅎ of -하다 to aspirate as [엄겨카다 / 엄겨캐요].
엄격하다.notes: Adverbial forms are 엄격히 and 엄격하게 ('strictly, rigorously').

엄마.etymology: Native Korean affectionate/informal kinship noun ('mom, mommy'), descending from the nursery and vocative root 어마 (cf. Middle Korean 어미 / 어마님).

history.meaning: mom, mommy

엄지손가락.etymology: Native Korean three-morpheme compound joining 엄지 ('thumb, big toe, foremost digit', built on the ancient native root 엄-/어미 'mother, main, largest', compare 어금니 'molar' and 엄나무) with 손가락 ('finger', from 손 'hand' plus 가락 'slender stick, spindle, digit'). Korean names all five fingers symmetrically by prefixing role descriptors to 손가락, pairing 엄지손가락 ('thumb') with 집게손가락 ('index finger') and 새끼손가락 ('little finger', literally 'baby finger').
엄지손가락.notes: Often shortened in casual speech to 엄지 ('thumb'); 엄지손가락을 치켜세우다 means 'to give a thumbs-up'.

엄청.etymology: Adverb derived by clipping and back-formation from the adjective stem of 엄청나다 ('to be absurdly beyond measure; enormous, massive'). Originally associated with 어림청 ('rough estimate or measure', so that exceeding it was 'preposterous, unthinkable'), 엄청 grammaticalized in late-20th-century colloquial Korean into a general high-frequency degree intensifier ('hugely, super, really, very').

history.meaning: to exceed all reasonable estimate; preposterous, prodigious
hugely, enormously, super, very (degree adverb)

morphemes.meaning: to an enormous or absurd degree (clipped from 엄청나다)

엄청.notes: In contemporary spoken Korean, 엄청 has lost any negative nuance of 'absurdity' and functions just like English 'super' or 'really' (e.g., 엄청 맛있다 'super delicious').

엄청나다.etymology: Korean adjective formed from the bound stem 엄청- plus the native verb/adjective formative 나다 ('to come out, arise, exceed bounds'). Philologists connect 엄청- to a contraction of 어림청 ('ballpark measure, rough calculation'), originally describing something that 'goes clean outside any conceivable estimate' ('preposterous, absurdly out of proportion'), which then broadened into general magnitude ('enormous, massive, tremendous').

history.meaning: to be absurdly beyond all measure or expectation
enormous, massive, tremendous, prodigious

엄청나다.notes: Always conjugates with verb-like present attributive -는 (엄청난 사건 'a massive incident' in past/completed state, or 엄청나게 'enormously') because its second element is historically the verb 나다.

rootFamily.gloss: to be out of the question, absurdly far off (어림 'estimate' + 없다)
to be extraordinary, stand out (별 'special' + 나다)

업무.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (業務) composed of Hanja 業 (업, 'occupation, profession, enterprise, business; originally the wooden crossboard of a bell stand') and 務 (무, 'task, affair, duty; to devote oneself to'). Shared across the East Asian Sinosphere to denote continuous duties and operations carried out within an organization or profession.

history.meaning: tasks and duties pertaining to one's occupation or enterprise
official work, business duties, operations

업무.notes: While 일 is any general 'work or matter', 업무 specifically refers to formal workplace tasks, institutional duties, or office operations.

rootFamily.gloss: for official business, in the course of duty (業務上)

cognates.meaning: in the course of business, for official duty (e.g., gyōmujō kashitsu)
cognates.word: 業務上 (ぎょうむじょう, gyōmujō)
業務上 / 业务上 (yèwù shàng)

업무상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (業務上) formed from 업무 (業務, from 業 업 'business, occupation' + 務 무 'duty, task') and the productive Sino-Korean relational suffix -상 (上, literally 'above, upon', used abstractly to mean 'from the standpoint of, in the course of, with respect to'). Literally 'upon business duties', i.e., 'in the course of official work'.

history.meaning: business duties + in the domain/course of
for official work, in the line of duty, professionally

morphemes.meaning: business, profession (業) + duty, task (務) -> official work
in terms of, in the course of, from the standpoint of (上)

업무상.notes: Used both in everyday office excuses ('I met them strictly for work' 업무상 만났다) and in formal Korean law (업무상 과실 'professional negligence', 업무상 횡령 'occupational embezzlement').

rootFamily.gloss: for convenience, as a matter of convenience (便宜上)

cognates.meaning: in a higher position or elevated mood/level
to raise, boost, or upgrade (parallel loanword construction)

업시켜.etymology: Inflected infinitive/connective form (업시켜) of the South Korean hybrid verb 업시키다, formed by combining the English loanword 업 ('up', used in Korean to mean an elevated mood, energy level, or glamorous styling) with the Korean causative light verb -시키다 ('to cause to do, make happen', historically derived from Middle Korean 시키다). Literally 'to cause to go up', hence 'to hype up, cheer up, boost (the mood)'.

history.meaning: elevated state/mood + to cause to become
history.stage: Component loanword and Korean causative verb

history.meaning: to boost, hype up, elevate mood or styling
history.stage: Modern South Korean colloquial hybrid verb

morphemes.meaning: elevated mood, energy, or level (from English 'up')
causative light verb -시키다 conjugated in infinitive form (-시켜)

업시켜.notes: Extremely common in broadcasting and variety-show jargon in the phrase 분위기를 업시키다 ('to hype up the atmosphere / lift the mood on set') and 기분을 업시키다 ('to cheer someone up').

rootFamily.gloss: to become hyped up, get in high spirits (업 + 되다)
to make someone move or get excited (causative construction)

업체.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun (業體) formed from Hanja 業 (업, 'business, trade, industry, enterprise') and 體 (체, 'body, substance, organizational entity'). Distinctively lexicalized in Korean commercial and administrative usage to denote an individual business establishment, vendor, contractor, or service company.

history.meaning: business/industry + organizational body/entity
business enterprise, commercial firm, vendor, service company

업체.notes: In Korean workplaces (including TV production), 업체 usually refers to an external vendor, subcontractor, or specialized service firm (e.g., 협력 업체 'partner vendor', 청소 업체 'cleaning company', 외주 업체 'outsourcing production company').

없다.etymology: Native Korean existential negation adjective descending from Middle Korean 없다 ('not to exist, be lacking, not to have').

history.meaning: not to exist, be absent
to not be, not exist, not have

없애다.etymology: Native Korean transitive/causative verb derived from the negative existential adjective/verb stem 없- (없다, attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 업다 / 없다 'to not exist, be lacking') plus the native causative derivational suffix -애- (historically from -오/우- + -이-). Literally meaning 'to cause not to exist', it evolved to mean 'to eliminate, get rid of, abolish, scrap, or cancel'.

history.meaning: to not exist, be absent or lacking
to make non-existent; to do away with, eliminate, scrap

morphemes.meaning: to not exist, be lacking (stem of 없다)

없애다.notes: In Korean broadcasting and corporate settings, 프로그램을 없애다 is the blunt, colloquial way of saying 'to axe / scrap / cancel a TV show' (as opposed to the formal Sino-Korean 폐지하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to not exist, be lacking, not have (base stem)
to disappear, vanish, be cancelled (inchoative passive counterpart)

없어지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative intransitive verb formed from 없어 (the infinitive/connective form of 없다, Middle Korean 업다 / 없다 'to not exist') combined with the grammaticalized auxiliary verb -지다 (from 지다 'to fall; to become, come to be in a state'). Literally 'to become non-existent', hence 'to disappear, vanish, run out, or be abolished/cancelled'.

history.meaning: to not exist + to become (change-of-state auxiliary)
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean components

history.meaning: to cease to exist, disappear, vanish, be scrapped/cancelled

morphemes.meaning: to not exist, be lacking (stem of 없다)

없어지다.notes: Forms a neat causative/inchoative pair with 없애다: 없애다 is transitive ('someone scraps/eliminates X'), while 없어지다 is intransitive ('X disappears / gets cancelled').

rootFamily.gloss: to not exist, be lacking (base stem)
to eliminate, get rid of, scrap (transitive counterpart)
to vanish, fade away (synonymous verb with 스러지다/사라지다)

없이.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 업시, formed from the stem 없- (없다, 'not to exist, lack') + adverbial suffix -이.

history.meaning: without
without, lacking

에.etymology: Native Korean locative/dative/allative case particle descending from Middle Korean 애 / 에 / 예 (which harmonized with the preceding vowel), marking static location ('in, at, on'), time ('at'), or destination ('to').

history.meaning: locative and directional postposition
in, at, on, to (locative/temporal/goal particle)

에서.etymology: Native Korean ablative and dynamic-locative case particle descending from Middle Korean 애셔 / 에셔, grammaticalized from locative particle 에 + 서 (converbal form 시어 of 이시다 / 있다 'to be, exist' — literally 'being at [a place], from').

history.meaning: being at -> at (place of action); from (point of departure)
at, in (where an action happens); from

cognates.meaning: online platform for building social networks

에스엔에스.etymology: Korean Hangul phonetic spelling of the English initialism SNS, abbreviated from social networking service (from English social < Latin sociālis 'allied, companionable', network, and service < Old French servise < Latin servitium). Popularized in South Korea and Japan since the mid-2000s (initially with Cyworld and later applied to Twitter, Instagram, and Facebook) as the standard everyday term for social media platforms.

history.meaning: online platform for building social relations among users
initialism for social networking service
social media, social networking service

에스엔에스.notes: Whereas English speakers normally say 'social media', Koreans almost universally use 에스엔에스 (SNS) in both news broadcasts and casual speech.

에이.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) expressive interjection (감탄사) of playful dismissal, mild irritation, disappointment, or disbelief ('come on', 'no way', 'oh please'). Formed by diphthongal lengthening of the primary exclamation 에 (e) with the high front glide -이 (-i), creating a drawn-out vocal gesture used in colloquial conversation to wave off an exaggeration, tease, or implausible claim.

history.meaning: short exclamation of surprise, regret, or dismissal
come on, no way, oh please (dismissive or chiding interjection)

morphemes.meaning: dismissive or chiding exclamation ('come on, no way')

에이.notes: Often accompanied by a wave of the hand when brushing off flattery or a ridiculous excuse ('에이, 설마!' — 'Come on, no way!').

rootFamily.gloss: eh, hey (short interjection of dismissal or surprise)
oh my, dear me (exclamation of fatigue or dismay)
ah well, what the heck (resigned exclamation)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 에이

cognates.meaning: closing sequence or theme of a broadcast

엔딩.etymology: Borrowed from English ending, the verbal noun of end (from Old English endian 'to bring to an end, finish', from Proto-Germanic *andijōną, derived from *andijaz 'end, boundary') + gerund suffix -ing. In South Korean television drama and variety production (프로듀사), it refers specifically to the closing scene, final cliffhanger freeze-frame, or closing credits of an episode.

history.meaning: to bring to a conclusion; finishing, termination
final part or conclusion of a story, play, or broadcast
ending scene, finale, or closing sequence of a broadcast/drama

엔딩.notes: In K-drama and K-pop broadcasting jargon, 엔딩 is central to phrases like 엔딩 맛집 ('a show famous for great cliffhanger endings') and 엔딩 요정 ('ending fairy', the idol caught in the final close-up shot).

엔진.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed in the 20th century from English engine (ultimately from Latin ingenium 'innate talent, clever contrivance').

history.meaning: mechanical engine, motor

cognates.meaning: mechanical lift for passengers or freight

엘리베이터.etymology: Borrowed from American English elevator ('mechanical passenger lift'), coined in the mid-19th century as an instrument noun from English elevate, from Latin ēlevātus, past participle of ēlevāre ('to lift up, raise, lighten', formed from ex- 'out, up' + levāre 'to lighten, raise', from levis 'light in weight').

history.meaning: to lift up, raise, alleviate
thing that raises; mechanical hoist or lift for buildings
elevator, passenger lift

morphemes.meaning: to lift up, raise (from English elevate < Latin ēlevāre)

엘리베이터.notes: In casual spoken Korean, 엘리베이터 is very frequently clipped to the two-syllable slang abbreviation 엘베 (elbe).

엠비에이.etymology: Korean Hangul phonetic transcription of the American English academic initialism MBA, standing for Master of Business Administration (first established as a graduate degree at Harvard University in 1908; from English master < Latin magister 'chief, teacher', business < Old English bisignis 'care, occupation', and administration < Latin administrātiō 'management, direction').

history.meaning: postgraduate degree in business management
initialism for Master of Business Administration
an MBA degree or MBA program

엠비에이.notes: Often written in Latin letters as MBA in Korean text, with the Sino-Korean equivalent 경영학 석사 (經營學碩士) used in formal academic diplomas.

cognates.meaning: master of ceremonies, host of a show or event

엠씨.etymology: Korean Hangul phonetic transcription of the English initialism MC (emcee), abbreviated from Master of Ceremonies (from Latin magister 'master, director' and caerimōnia 'sacred rite, ceremony'). The second syllable is spelled and pronounced with tense ㅆ (씨) to reflect the sharp English voiceless sibilant onset of the letter name C (/siː/). In Korean broadcasting, it denotes the host or presenter of a variety or talk show.

history.meaning: official host presiding over a formal event or entertainment
stage, radio, or television host; hip-hop vocalist
television variety show host, event presenter, or emcee

엠씨.notes: In Korean television (such as in *The Producers*), 엠씨 specifically means a variety/talk show host (e.g., 유재석 as 국민 엠씨 'Nation's MC'), alongside the native/Sino-Korean term 진행자 (進行者).

cognates.meaning: state of belonging to a group or organization

엠티.etymology: South Korean pseudo-anglicism (Konglish initialism) MT, abbreviated from English membership training (from member < Old French membre < Latin membrum 'limb, part' + -ship, and train < Old French trainer 'to draw, drag, instruct' + -ing). Coined in Korean university and corporate culture to denote an overnight group retreat or bonding trip where students, club members, or colleagues travel together to build camaraderie.

history.meaning: group membership and instructional training
overnight university or company bonding retreat

엠티.notes: A classic Konglish cultural term: an English speaker will not recognize 'MT' or 'membership training', which in natural English corresponds to a 'college retreat', 'team-building trip', or 'offsite'.

rootFamily.gloss: orientation (OT) for new students or employees

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 엠티

여기.etymology: Native Korean proximal place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 예 / 여기 ('this place, here', built on proximal demonstrative root 이-/여- + place suffix -기).

history.meaning: this place, here

여기서.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) contracted locative adverb formed from the proximal spatial pronoun 여기 (yeogi, 'this place, here', descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 이ᅌᅥ긔 iNgekuy, built on the proximal demonstrative root 이 i 'this' + locative noun element 어긔 ekuy) combined with the locative/ablative case particle 에서 (-eseo, 'at, in, from', shortened to -서 -seo after the high front vowel -이).

history.meaning: at this place, from here
here, from this place
here, right here, from here

morphemes.meaning: at, in, from (contracted form of 에서)

여기서.notes: Contracted from 여기에서; in spoken Korean 여기서 is far more natural and frequent than the uncontracted four-syllable form.

rootFamily.gloss: over there, at/from that place yonder

여기저기.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) coordinate compound adverb pairing the proximal locative pronoun 여기 (yeogi, 'here, this place', from Middle Korean 이ᅌᅥ긔 iNgekuy, based on 이 'this') with the distal locative pronoun 저기 (jeogi, 'over there, that place yonder', from Middle Korean 뎌ᅌᅥ긔 tyeNgekuy, based on 뎌 'that over there'). By juxtaposing near and far spatial deictics, the compound expresses 'here and there, in various places, everywhere'.

history.meaning: this place and that place yonder
here and there, all over the place, everywhere

여기저기.notes: Korean omits the conjunction 'and' in spatial pairs, placing near before far (여기저기 'here and there', 이곳저곳 'this place and that place').

rootFamily.gloss: this place and that place, everywhere

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여기저기

여덟.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 여듧 ('eight').

history.meaning: eight
eight (native Korean number)

cognates.meaning: born together, born at the same time

여동생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (女同生), formed by prefixing 여- (女, Middle Korean 녀 nye, 'woman, female', with initial n- deleted in South Korean standard orthography via the initial sound rule 두음법칙) to 동생 (同生, literally 'born together [of the same parents]', from 同 동 'same, together' + 生 생 'birth, born'). In Korean, 同生 (동생) underwent semantic narrowing from 'sibling born of the same parents' to specifically mean 'younger sibling'.

history.meaning: sibling born of the same parents; younger sibling
female younger sibling, younger sister
younger sister (whether of a male or female speaker)

여동생.notes: Unlike older sibling terms (언니/누나/오빠/형), which depend on the speaker's gender, 여동생 ('younger sister') and 남동생 ('younger brother') are used identically by both men and women.

여러.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) pre-noun / determiner (관형사) meaning 'several, many, various', directly continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 여러 (yele, 'many, several'). Internally related to the bound numeral/plural root 엳- / 열- (yelh-, seen in the substantive noun 여럿 'several' and etymologically connected to the native numeral 열 yelh 'ten, a full count or multitude').

history.meaning: many, several, various (pre-nominal modifier)
several, various, a number of

여러.notes: Because 여러 is a pure determiner (관형사), it can never stand alone as a subject or object and must always precede a noun or counter (e.g., 여러 사람 'several people', 여러 번 'several times'); use 여럿 when a standalone noun is needed.

rootFamily.gloss: several (people or things, as a noun)
in many ways, from various angles

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여러

여러모로.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adverb formed from the determiner 여러 (yeoreo, Middle Korean 여러 yele, 'several, many, various') + the native noun 모 (mo, Middle Korean 모 mwo < *mwoh, originally meaning 'corner, angle, facet', and by extension 'aspect, side, respect') + the instrumental/directional case particle -로 (-ro, 'by, in, through'). Literally 'by many angles' or 'from various facets', hence 'in many ways, in various respects'.

history.meaning: by several angles or facets
in many ways, in various respects, from many angles

여러모로.notes: Frequently used in expressions of gratitude or polite assessment, such as '여러모로 도와주셔서 감사합니다' ('Thank you for helping me in so many ways').

rootFamily.gloss: in this way and that, in various ways

여러분.etymology: Native Korean honorific second-person plural pronoun formed from 여러 ('many, several, various', Middle Korean 여러) + honorific person classifier 분 ('esteemed person').

history.meaning: everyone, ladies and gentlemen, all of you
