여럿.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) substantive noun meaning 'a number of people or things, several together', derived from the Middle Korean plural/multitude stem 여러 / 엳- (yele / yelh-, 'several, many') + the native nominalizing suffix -ㅅ (-s), which converts determiner or numeral stems into independent count nouns. Attested in Middle Korean with the stem 엳- before case markers (e.g., 엳시 yelh-i 'several [as subject]').

history.meaning: a multitude, several people or things together
several (people or things) as a group

morphemes.meaning: substantive nominalizer forming an independent noun

여럿.notes: While 여러 must modify a following noun (여러 명 'several people'), 여럿 functions as a noun itself and takes particles directly (여럿이 모이다 'several gather together').

rootFamily.gloss: in many ways, from many angles
together in a group of several (adverb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여럿

여름.etymology: Native Korean seasonal noun descending from Middle Korean 녀름 ('summer'); in 15th-century Middle Korean, 녀름 also meant 'fruits of the earth, harvest, farming' (derived from 녈- / 열다 'to bear fruit'), because summer is the growing season.

history.meaning: summer; farming, harvest
summer

여리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb (형용사) meaning 'soft, tender, delicate, fragile, frail', directly continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 여리다 (yelita, 'to be soft, weak, lacking stiffness or harshness'). Etymologically connected via Korean vowel harmony / ablaut sets to 어리다 (eorida, Middle Korean 어리다 elita, originally 'foolish, naive, tender/young') and 여위다 (yeowida, 'to grow thin, frail').

history.meaning: to be soft, weak, tender, or fragile
to be tender, delicate, soft, or emotionally gentle/frail

여리다.notes: Used both physically (피부가 여리다 'to have delicate/sensitive skin') and emotionally (마음이 여리다 'to be tender-hearted / easily moved to tears').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여리다

여리여리하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated descriptive verb (형용사) formed by full ideophonic/stem reduplication (첩어) of 여리- (from 여리다 yeorida, Middle Korean 여리다 yelita, 'to be soft, tender, delicate') combined with the adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). The reduplication vividly evokes a slender, dainty, and fragile physique or appearance.

history.meaning: to be soft, weak, or tender
to be delicately slender, dainty, and fragile in build or appearance

여리여리하다.notes: A favorite compliment in modern Korean fashion and beauty contexts to describe a graceful, petite, or willow-slender silhouette (여리여리한 핏 'a dainty, slender fit').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여리여리하다

여백.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 餘白, uniting 餘 (남을 여, 'remaining, left over, spare') and 白 (흰 백, 'white, uninked, blank'). In printing and bookmaking it designates the unprinted border around text or illustrations, while in traditional Korean and East Asian ink painting and ceramics it names intentional negative space—celebrated aesthetically in the phrase 여백의 미 ('the beauty of empty space').
여백.notes: Used both literally for page margins and figuratively for breathing room in design or conversation.

여보.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) vocative pronoun and term of endearment between married spouses ('honey, dear, darling'), arising in Early Modern Korean as a rapid-speech phonological contraction of 여기 보오 (yeogi boo, literally 'look here!'), composed of the proximal locative pronoun 여기 (yeogi, 'here') + the verb stem 보- (bo-, from 보다 boda, Middle Korean 보다 pwota, 'to look, see') + the blunt/intimate semiformal imperative ending -오 (-o).

history.meaning: look here! (attention-calling phrase)
hey there, look here (vocative call to an equal or spouse)
honey, dear, darling (mutual address between husband and wife)

morphemes.meaning: to look, see (from 보다, fused with imperative -오)

여보.notes: In modern Korea, 여보 is used almost exclusively between married couples (whereas unmarried couples use 자기야 or 오빠); it shares its exact origin ('look here!') with the telephone greeting 여보세요.

rootFamily.gloss: hello (when answering the phone; literally 'please look here')
hey there, my friend (familiar address to an equal or younger adult)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여보

여보세요.etymology: Native Korean attention-getting interjection and standard telephone greeting, contracted from 여기 보셔요 / 여기 보세요 ('look here, excuse me', from 여기 'here' + 보시다 'to look [honorific]').

history.meaning: look here!, excuse me!; hello? (on the telephone)

여분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 여분 (餘分), joining 여 (餘, 'surplus, remainder, left over') and 분 (分, 'share, portion, part').

history.meaning: extra portion, surplus, spare

여섯.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 여슷 ('six').

history.meaning: six
six (native Korean number)

여성분.etymology: Polite compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 여성 (女性, 'woman, female gender', from 女 'woman' + 性 'sex, nature') + native Korean honorific person classifier 분 ('esteemed person').

history.meaning: lady, woman (polite/respectful reference)

여우짓.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun combining 여우 (yeou, 'fox', evolving from 15th-century Middle Korean 여ᅀᆞ yezo via loss of the voiced fricative ㅿ /z/ > 여오 > 여우) and 짓 (jit, Middle Korean 짛 cilh, 'act, gesture, behavior, antic', often carrying a disparaging nuance). Because the fox (specifically the mythical nine-tailed fox 구미호) symbolizes seductive cunning and bewitchment in Korean folklore, 여우짓 literally means 'fox antics' — sly, coy, or calculating flirting.

history.meaning: fox + act/behavior
fox-like behavior; sly, coy flirting or manipulative charm

morphemes.meaning: fox (metaphorically a sly or coy person)

여우짓.notes: In Korean slang and dramas, calling someone a 여우 ('fox') vs. 곰 ('bear') contrasts a socially shrewd, coyly charming person with a blunt, guileless one; 여우짓 refers specifically to calculated flirting to win someone's attention.

여유롭다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 여유 (餘裕, 'surplus, room to spare, composure', from 餘 'surplus' + 裕 'abundant, unhurried') + native adjectival suffix -롭다 ('characterized by').

history.meaning: to be unhurried, relaxed, composed, having plenty to spare

여의도.etymology: Sino-Korean toponym (汝矣島) denoting the large island in the Han River in Seoul, composed of 汝 (여, 'you'), 矣 (의, classical Chinese final emphatic particle), and 島 (도, 'island'). Historically recorded in the Joseon dynasty as 汝矣島 (여의도) or 仍火島 (잉화도), where 汝矣 served both as an Idu phonetic transcription of an older native Korean name (나의섬 / 너의섬) and as a witty folk-etymological pun meaning 'You may have it!' ('너나 가져라'), because the low-lying sandy island flooded every summer before its 1968 embankment reclamation. Today it is South Korea's financial, political, and broadcasting center, housing the National Assembly and KBS headquarters (the setting of *The Producers*).

history.meaning: sandy river island in the Han River southwest of Hanyang
Yeouido Island ('You-may-have-it Island', used for royal livestock pasture and later Seoul's first airstrip)
Yeouido (Seoul's Manhattan: hub of finance, politics, and major television networks like KBS)

여의도.notes: In Korean media and news, '여의도' is used as a metonym for both national politics (the National Assembly) and the television broadcasting industry (centered around KBS).

여자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (女子), continuing Middle Korean 녀자 (nyeca), borrowed from Classical Chinese 女子 (nǚzǐ, 'woman, female, daughter'), composed of 女 (여 / 녀, 'woman, female', originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a kneeling figure with crossed hands) + 子 (자, originally 'child, offspring', functioning here as a general nominal suffix for persons). In South Korean standard orthography, word-initial 녀 (nyeo) lost its nasal onset via the initial sound rule (두음법칙) to become 여 (yeo), while North Korean Cultural Language retains 녀자.

history.meaning: daughter, young woman, female person
woman, female person
woman, female, girl, girlfriend/wife (in possessive contexts)

여자.notes: 여자 is the standard everyday word for 'woman', whereas 여성 (女性) is more formal/institutional ('female, women') and 여인 (女人) is literary/poetic.

여자가.etymology: Inflected nominative noun phrase composed of the Sino-Korean noun 여자 (女子, yeoja, Middle Korean 녀자 nyeca, 'woman, female', from 女 'woman' + 子 'person') + the native Korean post-vocalic nominative/subject case particle -가 (-ga). Historically, 15th-century Middle Korean used only -이 (-i) as the subject marker (hence 녀재 nyeca-y), and the particle -가 (-ga) emerged in the late 16th to 17th centuries after vowel-final nouns to preserve stem clarity and prevent hiatus.

history.meaning: woman (as grammatical subject)
woman (as grammatical subject with post-vocalic marker -가)
a woman / the woman (subject form)

morphemes.meaning: nominative/subject case marker after vowel-final stems

여자가.notes: Contrasts with 여자는 (topic marker -는, 'as for a woman / women in general'); 여자가 singles out a specific woman as the subject or introduces new focus ('it is a woman who...').

여자라니까.etymology: Inflected predicate phrase combining the Sino-Korean noun 여자 (女子, yeoja, 'woman', from 女 'woman' + 子 'person') + the post-vocalic copula stem -(이)라- (-(i)ra-, from the native copula 이다 ida, Middle Korean 이다 ita, 'to be', which drops 이- after a vowel) + the emphatic causal and assertive connective ending -니까 (-nikka, 'because, since, I'm telling you that...'). Iconic in South Korean pop culture as the title hook of Lee Seung-gi's 2004 debut ballad '내 여자라니까' ('Because You're My Woman'), a recurring older-woman/younger-man (누나) anthem referenced in *The Producers*.

history.meaning: because (she) is a woman / I tell you (she) is a woman
because she is (my) woman! / I'm telling you, she's a woman!

morphemes.meaning: post-vocalic copula stem ('to be', from 이다)
emphatic causal/reassuring connective ending ('because, I tell you')

여자라니까.notes: In Korean grammar, -라니까 works both as an emphatic 'because' ('내 여자라니까' — 'Because you're my woman') and as an insistent reminder when repeating oneself ('여자라니까!' — 'I told you, it's a woman!').

rootFamily.gloss: because (he) is a man / I tell you he's a man

여자애.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 여자 (女子, yeoja, 'woman, female', from 女 'woman' + 子 'person') and the native Korean colloquial noun 애 (ae, 'child, kid, young person, friend'). The element 애 is a vowel-fronted monophthongization of 아이 (ai, 'child'), which descends from 15th-century Middle Korean 아히 (ahi) / 아ᄒᆡ (ahoy, 'child'). Literally 'female child', used colloquially for 'girl' or 'young woman'.

history.meaning: female + child
female child, girl
girl, young woman (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: child, kid, young person (contracted from 아이 < Middle Korean 아ᄒᆡ)

여자애.notes: Among young speakers and in casual dialogue, 여자애 (and its male counterpart 남자애) doesn't just mean a small child — peers regularly use it to mean 'a girl / young woman (around our age or younger)'.

여전히.etymology: Derived from the Sino-Korean descriptive stem 여전- (如前, composed of 如 'like, resembling' and 前 'before, former times', literally 'just like before') plus the native adverbial suffix -히. Unlike 아직 ('still, yet'), which often implies an expected change has not yet happened, 여전히 emphasizes continuity across time—that a quality, habit, or warmth remains unchanged despite years or shifting circumstances.
여전히.notes: Pairs naturally with concessive clauses ending in -는데도 or -지만 ('even though ..., still as ever').

여쭤보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) deferential/humble compound verb (겸양어) meaning 'to politely ask or inquire of a superior', contracted from 여쭈어 보다 (yeojjueo boda). The main verb 여쭙다 / 여쭈다 (yeojjuda, 'to humbly tell or ask a senior') descends from 15th-century Middle Korean 엳줍다 (yetcwupta), originally formed from the verb stem 엳- + the object-exalting humble suffix -줍- (-cwup-, a post-coronal allomorph of -ᅀᆞᆸ- -zop-) + -다; the second element is the native auxiliary verb 보다 (boda, Middle Korean 보다 pwota, 'to see; to try doing'), which softens the inquiry into a polite attempt ('may I venture to ask').

history.meaning: to humbly report, tell, or ask a social superior (object-exalting verb)
to humbly venture to ask a superior
to ask, inquire (humble/deferential form toward elders or superiors)

morphemes.meaning: to humbly ask or inform a superior (contracted infinitive 여쭈어 from 여쭙다/여쭈다)
to try doing, to see (auxiliary verb stem from 보다)

여쭤보다.notes: The essential humble counterpart to 물어보다 ('to ask'): when speaking to a boss, senior producer, professor, or elder, Korean workplace etiquette requires 여쭤보다 ('제가 선배님께 여쭤볼 게 있는데요').

rootFamily.gloss: to humbly ask or inform a superior
to humbly give or offer (드려- + 보다)

여태.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) temporal adverb meaning 'up until now, still, to this very moment', originating as a phonological alteration of 이때 (ittae, 'this time', composed of the proximal demonstrative 이 i 'this' + the noun 때 ttae 'time', from Middle Korean ㅿ대 pstai / ᄠᅢ ptay 'time, season') via palatalization/diphthongization of the first syllable (이때 > 여때) and aspiration of the medial fortis stop (여때 > 여태).

history.meaning: this time, this moment
up to this time, until now
still, up until now, all this time

morphemes.meaning: this (phonologically altered from proximal demonstrative 이-)

여태.notes: Almost always used when mildly chiding or expressing surprise that something still hasn't happened ('여태 안 자고 뭐 해?' — 'What are you doing still awake until now?').

rootFamily.gloss: all the way up until now (emphatic with -껏)
up until this time, until now

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 여태

여행.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 여행 (旅行), joining 여 (旅, 'travel, journey, troop') and 행 (行, 'to go, walk, travel').

history.meaning: going on a journey, travel, trip

여행책.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 여행 (旅行, 'travel, trip') + 책 (冊, 'book, volume').

history.meaning: travel book, guidebook

여행하다.etymology: Built from Sino-Korean 여행 (旅行), joining 旅 (나그네 려, 'wayfarer, sojourn away from home') and 行 (다닐 행, 'to walk, go, journey'), plus the native verb -하다. Word-initial 려 regularly drops its initial liquid before ㅕ under South Korean 두음법칙 to become 여 (contrast compound-internal 신혼여행 'honeymoon trip' or 여객 'passenger'). In modern Korean it covers everything from a weekend countryside trip to extended international travel.
여행하다.notes: Can take an accusative place object (해안 마을을 여행하다 'travel through coastal towns') or -로 여행을 가다.

역.etymology: Sino-Korean morpheme 역 (驛, originally 'mounted post-horse relay station' in premodern East Asia, adapted in the late 19th century for a railway or subway 'station'; also 役 'role, part, service' or 域 'area, zone').

history.meaning: post-horse relay station
train or subway station; role/part (役)

역사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (歷史), attested in Classical Chinese 歷史 (lìshǐ, 'chronicle of past ages, annals', e.g., in the *Sanguozhi* commentary) and repurposed in Meiji-era Japan as 歴史 (rekishi) to translate the Western concept of 'history' (from Greek historia), then re-adopted into Late Joseon / Modern Korean. Composed of 歷 (역 / 력, 'to pass through, undergo, successive', with initial r/l dropped in South Korea by 두음법칙) + 史 (사, 'chronicle, annals, court historian', originally a pictograph of a hand holding a tally or record).

history.meaning: chronicles of successive dynasties, historical annals
history (as both past human events and the academic discipline)
history.stage: Late 19th-century East Asian / Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: history, historical record or tradition

역사.notes: Note the South Korean initial sound law (두음법칙): 歷 is pronounced 력 (ryeok) inside compounds like 이력서 (履歷書 'resume/CV'), but becomes 역 (yeok) at the start of a word in 역사 (歷史). North Korea spells and pronounces it 력사.

cognates.meaning: also, likewise, as expected (semantic parallel written with 矢張/亦)

역시.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (亦是), borrowed from Classical and Literary Chinese 亦是 (yìshì, literally 'also is [so], is indeed right'), composed of 亦 (역, 'also, too, likewise') + 是 (시, 'this; to be right, indeed, truly', functioning as an emphatic copula in post-Classical Chinese). In Korean, 亦是 (역시) retained both its literal additive sense ('also, too') and evolved into a high-frequency modal adverb meaning 'indeed, just as expected, sure enough'.

history.meaning: is also so, is indeed thus
likewise, also; indeed, as expected
as expected, sure enough; also, too

역시.notes: 역시 has two distinct everyday uses depending on context: placed after a noun ('나 역시 그렇게 생각해' — 'I also think so') vs. used as an exclamation of admiration or confirmation ('역시 백승찬!' — 'Just as expected of Baek Seung-chan!').

역효과.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (逆效果), formed by prefixing 역- (逆, yeok, 'reverse, opposite, contrary, to go against the grain') to the noun 효과 (效果, hyogwa, 'effect, efficacy, result', composed of 效 효 'to prove effective, imitate, exert' + 果 과 'fruit, outcome, result'). Literally 'contrary outcome', denoting an action that backfires and produces the exact opposite of the intended effect.

history.meaning: efficacious result, effect, outcome
reverse effect, counterproductive outcome, backfire

역효과.notes: Pronounced [여쿅꽈] (yeokyokkwa), because the final ㄱ of 역 (逆) merges with the initial ㅎ of 효과 (效果) into aspirated ㅋ, and 과 undergoes tensification to 꽈. Commonly used with 내다 or 나다 ('역효과가 나다' — 'to backfire').

엮다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb meaning originally 'to weave, plait, braid, or string together (straw, reeds, bamboo strips, or threads)', directly continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 엯다 (yekta, 'to weave, plait, bind in a row', already attested with the complex velar cluster ㄲ /sk/ or /kk/). From the concrete sense of weaving separate strands into a single mat or garland, it developed figurative meanings: 'to compile (a book or anthology)', 'to frame or implicate someone in a plot', and in modern television/fandom slang, 'to pair up or ship two people romantically'.

history.meaning: to weave, plait, or string together (straw, reeds, or cords)
to weave together; to compile (writings); to entangle or pair people up

morphemes.meaning: to weave, plait, bind, or link together

엮다.notes: In Korean variety shows (*The Producers*) and everyday gossip, '둘이 엮다' means to tease or set up two cast members into a romantic 'loveline' (러브라인), while the passive '엮이다' means 'to get entangled/mixed up with someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to be woven; to get entangled or paired up with someone (passive)
to weave together, to compile or produce a story

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 엮다

연결되다.etymology: Hybrid passive verb formed from Sino-Korean 연결 (連結, 'connection, linking', from 連 'to link, join continuously' + 結 'to tie, bind') + native passive/inchoative verb 되다 ('to become, be made').

history.meaning: to be connected, linked, joined together

연구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 硏究, combining 硏 (갈 연, 'to grind, rub fine on an inkstone, polish', written with the stone radical 石) and 究 (궁구할 구, 'to examine to the very end, probe a cavern'). Together the two metaphors—grinding fine and probing to the bottom—yield the classical and modern East Asian noun for thorough scholarly, scientific, or culinary investigation.
연구.notes: Forms 연구하다 ('to research, study'), 연구원 ('researcher'), and 연구소 ('research institute, lab').

연구소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 硏究所, formed by attaching the noun-suffix 所 (바 소, 'place, office, institution') to 연구 (硏究, 'research'). It is the standard official designation for both vast national laboratories and small specialized research bodies, but in everyday speech it is playfully applied to a kitchen or workshop where someone is obsessively experimenting with a recipe or craft.
연구소.notes: Often attaches directly to a field of study, as in 과학 연구소 ('science laboratory').

연구하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 연구 (硏究, 'research, deep study', from 硏 'to grind, polish, rub fine' + 究 'to examine thoroughly, probe to the bottom') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to research, study in depth, investigate

연기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (演技), popularized in modern East Asian theatrical and cinematic vocabulary via Meiji Japanese 演技 (engi, 'acting, performance'), composed of 演 (연, 'to perform, practice, flow out, expound', built with the water radical 氵 signifying an expansive flow) + 技 (기, 'skill, art, craft, technique', built with the hand radical 扌). Literally 'the art/skill of performing', referring to dramatic acting on stage or screen as well as feigned behavior in real life.

history.meaning: to practice/perform + skill/craft
theatrical or cinematic acting, dramatic performance
acting, performance; pretending or putting on an act

연기.notes: Beware of Korean homophones: 연기 can mean 'acting' (演技, with a short vowel), 'postponement/delay' (延期, with a long vowel: 방송 연기 'broadcast postponement'), or 'smoke' (煙氣, with a long vowel).

rootFamily.gloss: directing, production of a show/play (演出)

cognates.meaning: to act, to perform a role

연기하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verb formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun 연기 (演技, yeongi, 'acting, performance', from 演 연 'to perform, enact' + 技 기 'skill, craft, art') with the native Korean light verb -하다 (-hada, from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, 'to do, make, perform'). Used both for an actor portraying a character in a drama or film and figuratively for someone pretending or putting on an act in everyday social situations.

history.meaning: to perform dramatic acting (Sino-Korean noun + native light verb)
to act, play a role; to pretend, put on an act

연기하다.notes: Just like the noun 연기, the verb 연기하다 can mean either 'to act / put on an act' (演技하다) or 'to postpone / delay' (延期하다) — context and object ('배역을 연기하다' 'act a role' vs. '일정을 연기하다' 'postpone a schedule') make the meaning clear.

rootFamily.gloss: to direct or stage a production (演出하다)
to perform publicly in a show or concert (公演하다)

연락.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연락 (連絡 / 聯絡), joining 연 (連/聯, 'to link, join in a row') and 락 (絡, 'thread, network, connect').

history.meaning: connection, keeping in touch, communication, contact

cognates.meaning: to contact, get in touch (聯絡)

연락드리다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean humble compound verb formed from 연락 (連絡, 'connection, contact', from 連 연 'to connect, join in a row' + 絡 락 'to entwine, bind, network') combined with the native Korean humble light verb -드리다 ('to offer, present to a superior', from Middle Korean 드리다).

history.meaning: to link together, connect in a continuous network
to offer or present humbly to an honored person
to contact or get in touch with (humble/deferential)

morphemes.meaning: humbly give or do for a superior

연락드리다.notes: Replacing -하다 with -드리다 elevates the verb into a deferential promise ('I will contact you') used constantly in Korean workplace and broadcasting settings.

rootFamily.gloss: contact details, address or phone number
to offer, tell humbly to a superior

연락처.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 연락처 (連絡處), formed from 연락 (連絡, 'connection, communication', from 連 연 'to join, link' + 絡 락 'silk thread, network') suffixed with 처 (處, 'place, location, point, department'). Literally 'place of contact', it shifted from a physical liaison office to a person's phone number or email.

history.meaning: liaison point; place where connections meet
contact address, phone number, or contact details

연락처.notes: In modern Korean social and dating contexts, asking for someone's 연락처 specifically means asking for their mobile number or KakaoTalk ID.

rootFamily.gloss: reception desk, point of application (接受處)

연락하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb composed of the Sino-Korean noun 연락 (連絡, 'connection, liaison, communication', from 連 연 'to link, join continuously' + 絡 락 'to wind silk, entwine, network') and the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do, make'). Note the liquid assimilation /n/ + /l/ -> [ll] yielding [열라카다].

history.meaning: to join together in a continuous thread or network
to link up, maintain communication
to contact, get in touch with

연락하다.notes: Pronounced [열라카다] due to liquid assimilation of ㄴ+ㄹ to [ll] and aspiration of ㄱ+ㅎ to [kʰ].

연령층.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 연령층 (年齡層), built from 연령 (年齡, 'age, years of life', from 年 연 'year, harvest cycle' + 齡 령 'years of age', originally containing the tooth radical 齒 because age was judged by teeth) and the sociological suffixoid 층 (層, 'story, layer, stratum, demographic bracket').

history.meaning: the count of a person's years of life
demographic layer or stratum defined by age
age group, age bracket (especially in TV ratings and marketing)

연령층.notes: Heavily used in broadcasting and media analytics (such as TV ratings in *The Producers*) alongside 시청자층 ('viewer demographic').

cognates.meaning: older in years, senior in age (年上)

연상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연상 (年上), composed of 연 (年, 'year, age', originally a pictograph of a person carrying a ripe grain harvest) and 상 (上, 'above, upper, superior, older'). In contemporary Korean relationship terminology, it specializes to denote an older romantic partner (especially an older woman dating a younger man, or vice versa).

history.meaning: above in years; older in age
person who is older than oneself; an older romantic partner

연상.notes: Contrasts directly with 연하 (年下, 'younger partner') and 동갑 (同甲, 'same-age peer'); do not confuse with the homophone 연상 (聯想, 'mental association').

rootFamily.gloss: younger person, younger romantic partner (年下)
older woman in a relationship (年上女)

연설문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연설문 (演說文), joining 연설 (演說, 'public speech, address', from 演 'to expound, perform' + 說 'to speak, explain') and 문 (文, 'writing, text').

history.meaning: written text or script of a public speech

cognates.meaning: entertainment trainee (練習生, borrowed from Korean/Japanese)

연습생.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 연습생 (練習生), from 연습 (練習, 'practice, drill', composed of 練 연 'to boil and soften raw silk, refine by training' + 習 습 'young bird flapping wings repeatedly to learn to fly') + the agentive/status suffix 생 (生, 'student, trainee, person in training').

history.meaning: to train repeatedly and master a skill
apprentice or student undergoing practical training
trainee (especially an idol or entertainment agency trainee before debut)

연습생.notes: Central to the K-pop industry ecosystem, where aspiring idols spend years as 연습생 at entertainment agencies before officially debuting.

연습실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연습실 (練習室), formed from 연습 (練習, 'practice, rehearsal', from 練 연 'to refine silk, drill' + 習 습 'to practice repeatedly') and the locative suffixoid 실 (室, 'room, chamber, studio'). Literally 'room for repeated training and rehearsal'.

history.meaning: chamber or room dedicated to skill practice
practice room, rehearsal studio (for music, dance, or script reading)

연습실.notes: The suffix -실 (室) productively forms names of specialized rooms across broadcasting stations, such as 편집실 ('editing room') and 대기실 ('waiting/green room').

연습하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 연습 (練習, 'practice, drill, rehearsal', from 練 'to boil and bleach raw silk, train, drill' + 習 'to flap wings repeatedly, practice') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to practice, rehearse, drill

cognates.meaning: coastal area, along the shore (沿岸)

연안.etymology: Sino-Korean geographical compound 연안 (沿岸), composed of 연 (沿, 'to follow along a watercourse or shoreline, border upon') and 안 (岸, 'steep bank, cliff, shore, coast'). Literally 'following along the shore', denoting littoral waters or coastal regions (and also the place name Yeonan).

history.meaning: stretching along the bank of a river or sea
coast, littoral zone, coastal waters

morphemes.meaning: follow along a course or shore (沿)

연안.notes: Often paired with 해안 (海岸, 'seashore/coastline') and 연근해 (沿近海, 'coastal and adjacent seas') in news broadcasts and maritime reports.

rootFamily.gloss: along a railway or road (沿線)

연애.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 연애 (戀愛), composed of 연 (戀, 'to yearn for, pine after, feel romantic attachment') and 애 (愛, 'love, affection, cherish'). While both characters are ancient Chinese, the compound 戀愛 was popularized in Meiji-era Japan (ren'ai) to translate Western notions of free romantic love and courtship, then borrowed into Early Modern Korean.

history.meaning: deep affectionate attachment or longing
romantic love between two individuals (calquing English 'love/romance')
romantic love, courtship, dating

연애.notes: Unlike 사랑 ('love' in general, native Korean), 연애 specifically refers to the active practice of romantic dating and courtship.

rootFamily.gloss: to date, be in a romantic relationship

cognates.meaning: to be in love, date romantically (恋愛する)
to date, be in a romantic relationship (談戀愛)

연애하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do') to the Sino-Korean noun 연애 (戀愛, 'romantic love, courtship', from 戀 연 'to yearn for, dote on' + 愛 애 'to love, cherish'). It denotes engaging in romantic courtship or being in a dating relationship.

history.meaning: modern romantic courtship and love
to date, carry on a romance, be in a relationship

연애하다.notes: Can be used intransitively ('to be dating someone in general', 요즘 연애해?) or with the comitative particle -와/과 ('to date [someone]').

rootFamily.gloss: to cling to, dwell on (戀戀하다)

cognates.meaning: fondly attached, unable to let go (恋々)
reluctant to part, deeply attached (戀戀)

연연하다.etymology: Sino-Korean reduplicated descriptive/stative verb 연연하다 (戀戀하다), formed from the Literary Chinese reduplication 연연 (戀戀, from 戀 연 'to yearn for, feel lingering attachment, be tangled in emotion') plus the native Korean verbalizer -하다. The initial ल/r-sound (련련) undergoes standard South Korean initial law (두음법칙) to become 연연.

history.meaning: feeling deep, lingering attachment; reluctant to part with someone
to cling to, dwell on, be overly attached to or obsessed with (fame, past, results)

morphemes.meaning: to be, act in such a state

연연하다.notes: Almost always takes the dative/locative particle -에 (e.g., 시청률에 연연하다 'to obsess/dwell over viewer ratings') and frequently appears in negative constructions (-에 연연하지 않다).

cognates.meaning: entertainment district/world (芸能界) + relay broadcast (中継)
cognates.word: げいのう (geinō) / ちゅうけい (chūkei)

연예가중계.etymology: Sino-Korean broadcast program title 연예가중계 (演藝街中繼, KBS's iconic *Entertainment Weekly*, 1984–2019), compounded from 연예 (演藝, 'performing arts, show business', from 演 연 'perform' + 藝 예 'art') + 가 (街, 'street, quarter, world/scene', as in 대학가 or 월가) + 중계 (中繼, 'relay broadcast, live transmission', from 中 중 'intermediary' + 繼 계 'connect, succeed'). Literally 'Live Relay from the Street of Show Business'.

history.meaning: performing arts district + intermediary relay transmission
Entertainment Weekly (flagship KBS entertainment news program featured in *The Producers*)

연예가중계.notes: In *The Producers* (*프로듀사*), Tak Ye-jin and Baek Seung-chan work with KBS variety and entertainment news teams where *연예가중계* represents the quintessential celebrity coverage show.

연예가중계야.etymology: Inflected casual predicate phrase formed from the Sino-Korean television program title 연예가중계 (演藝街中繼, 'Entertainment Weekly', composed of 演藝 연예 'entertainment' + 街 가 'street, scene' + 中繼 중계 'relay broadcast') plus -야, the post-vocalic casual (반말) declarative/interrogative realization of the native Korean copula 이다 ('to be').

history.meaning: copula 'to be' reducing to -ya after vowel-final stems in intimate speech
it is Entertainment Weekly! / are you Entertainment Weekly? (casual)

연예가중계야.notes: In Korean drama dialogue, saying '너 연예가중계야?' ('What are you, *Entertainment Weekly*?') is a witty idiom for teasing someone who gossips or pries into others' private lives like a celebrity reporter.

연예인.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 연예인 (演藝人), formed from 연예 (演藝, 'performing arts, entertainment', from 演 연 'to perform, practice, flow out' + 藝 예 'skill, art, talent, originally planting') and the agentive suffix 인 (人, 'person'). Literally 'a person of the performing arts'.

history.meaning: stage performer or practitioner of theatrical and musical arts
celebrity, TV personality, singer, or actor in the entertainment industry

연예인.notes: Covers singers, actors, comedians, and variety personalities alike, whereas 방송인 (放送人) emphasizes television broadcasters and hosts.

연장.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 연장 (延長), composed of 연 (延, 'to stretch out, prolong, lengthen, postpone') and 장 (長, 'long, extended in space or time'). Originally referring to physical lengthening in Literary Chinese, it applies equally to extending time limits, contracts, broadcasts, or visa renewals.

history.meaning: to stretch out in length or duration
extension of time, contract renewal, or prolongation

연장.notes: Watch out for the native/older homophone 연장 ('hand tool, implement, weapon'): 연장 (延長, 'extension') has a long initial vowel in conservative speech and takes -하다 to mean 'to extend'.

cognates.meaning: overtime match, extra time (延長賽 / 延長戰)

연장전.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 연장전 (延長戰), built from 연장 (延長, 'extension, prolongation', from 延 연 'stretch out, prolong' + 長 장 'long') and the suffixoid 전 (戰, 'battle, combat, match, game'). Coined for modern sports to denote a match extended beyond regulation time to break a tie, and used figuratively in daily life.

history.meaning: extended contest or extra-innings match in athletics
overtime, extra time (in sports or figuratively in prolonged work/drinking)

연장전.notes: Frequently used metaphorically in Korean workplace and social banter when a meeting, filming shoot, or company dinner (회식) continues past its scheduled end into a 'second round'.

rootFamily.gloss: first half of a game (前半戰)
second half of a game (後半戰)

연장하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 연장 (延長, 'extension, prolongation', from 延 연 'to stretch out, lengthen' + 長 장 'long') combined with the native Korean transitive/intransitive verbalizer -하다 ('to do, make'). It denotes lengthening a deadline, renewing a contract, or adding episodes to a television drama run.

history.meaning: to stretch out or lengthen
to extend (time, hours, episodes) or renew (a contract or visa)

연장하다.notes: In Korean television production, popular dramas often '연장하다' (extend their broadcast run by 2–4 extra episodes), whereas struggling shows face 조기종영 ('early cancellation').

rootFamily.gloss: eldest person, senior by age (年長者)

연주.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연주 (演奏), joining 연 (演, 'to perform, unfold, practice') and 주 (奏, 'to play music, present to a ruler').

history.meaning: musical performance, playing an instrument

연주하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 연주 (演奏, 'musical performance') and the native verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean stem combines 연 (演, 'to practice, perform, unfold') and 주 (奏, 'to play music, present to a sovereign'). While Korean uses instrument-specific verbs in casual speech—such as 피아노를 치다 ('to strike the piano') or 바이올린을 켜다 ('to bow the violin')—연주하다 is the universal verb for performing a piece of music on any instrument.

history.meaning: performing music on instruments
to play or perform music

cognates.meaning: to perform on a musical instrument

연주하다.notes: Can take either a musical instrument (피아노를 연주하다) or a musical piece (왈츠를 연주하다) as its direct object.

연체료.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 연체료 (延滯料), derived from 연체 (延滯, 'arrears, delay in payment or return', from 延 연 'to delay, postpone, stretch' + 滯 체 'to stagnate, be blocked, fall behind') and the financial suffixoid 료 (料, 'fee, charge, toll, material'). Literally 'fee for delayed stagnation of payment'.

history.meaning: to be delayed and held up; to fall into arrears
monetary surcharge imposed for overdue bills or late returns

연체료.notes: Applies to everything from overdue library books and DVD rentals to late utility bills and credit card payments.

rootFamily.gloss: delinquent payer, person in arrears (延滯者)

연출.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 연출 (演出), composed of 연 (演, 'to develop, expand, practice, perform') and 출 (出, 'to come out, bring forth, produce'). While in Chinese 演出 means 'to perform on stage', in Japanese (enshutsu) and Korean (연출) it specialized in theatrical and broadcasting terminology to mean 'artistic direction, staging, or the director (PD) of a show'.

history.meaning: to draw out, deduce, or bring forth a performance
theatrical staging and artistic direction of a play, film, or broadcast
direction, staging, production; director (on TV credits)

연출.notes: At the end of Korean TV episodes (including *The Producers*), the main director's credit appears on screen simply as '연출: [Name]'.

cognates.meaning: to direct, stage, produce (演出する)

연출하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from 연출 (演出, 'direction, staging, production', from 演 연 'to perform, unfold' + 出 출 'to bring forth, put out') and the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). It means both to direct a broadcast, film, or play, and more broadly to orchestrate a particular atmosphere or scene.

history.meaning: to direct and stage a dramatic or broadcast production
to direct (a show/film); to create or stage (a mood, look, or situation)

연출하다.notes: Beyond TV and film directing, Korean fashion and lifestyle writing uses 연출하다 for 'styling/creating a look or vibe' (e.g., 자연스러운 분위기를 연출하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to make an appearance on a show (出演하다)

연필.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연필 (鉛筆), joining 연 (鉛, 'lead metal') and 필 (筆, 'writing brush, pen') — literally 'lead brush' (historically used in China for lead styluses, and adapted in the late 19th century as a calque of European 'lead pencil').

history.meaning: lead brush -> graphite pencil

열.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 열 ('ten', pre-noun form 열); also homonymous with Sino-Korean 열 (熱, 'heat, fever, enthusiasm') and 열 (列, 'row, line').

history.meaning: ten (native numeral); also 熱 ('heat, fever')

열기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 열기 (熱氣), joining 열 (熱, 'heat, hot') and 기 (氣, 'air, vapor, energy, atmosphere').

history.meaning: hot air, heat; heated enthusiasm or excitement

열다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 열다 ('to open a door, lid, or passage; to unlock, begin').

history.meaning: to open
to open, unlock, hold (an event)

열다섯.etymology: Native Korean numeral formed by transparently compounding 열 ('ten', Middle Korean 열) and 다섯 ('five', Middle Korean 다ᄉᆞᆺ). Used for counting discrete objects with native counters (개, 권, 장) or for telling one's age (열다섯 살, 'fifteen years old'). Unlike 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 which drop their final consonant before a counter, the -섯 in 열다섯 does not change form (열다섯 개).

열두.etymology: Native Korean pre-nominal compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 두 (adnominal form of 둘 'two', Middle Korean 열둘).

history.meaning: twelve (before a counter or noun)

열리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 열이다, formed from 열다 ('to open') + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be opened, open by itself, be held (of a meeting or market)

열받다.etymology: Colloquial hybrid compound verb 열받다, combining the Sino-Korean noun 열 (熱, 'heat, fever, bodily warmth') with the native Korean verb 받다 ('to receive, take, be subjected to', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 받다). Literally 'to receive heat' or 'to get heated up in the head', metaphorically lexicalized as losing one's temper or getting furious.

history.meaning: to absorb physical heat or suffer a feverish rise in temperature
to get worked up, lose one's temper, become furious or aggravated

열받다.notes: A vivid colloquial physiological metaphor for anger; its causative counterpart 열받게 하다 means 'to piss someone off / make someone's blood boil'.

rootFamily.gloss: to receive stress, be stressed out

열세살.etymology: Native Korean numeral-counter phrase 열세살 ('thirteen years old'), composed of the native Korean numeral 열 ('ten', Middle Korean 엻), the prenominal modifier form 세 ('three', from 셋, Middle Korean 셓, dropping its final consonant before a noun/counter), and the native Korean age counter 살 ('year of age', Middle Korean 삸).

history.meaning: ten + three + years of age (thirteen years old)
thirteen years old

열세살.notes: Native Korean numerals drop their final consonants before counters for 1 (한), 2 (두), 3 (세), 4 (네), and 20 (스무), so '13 years old' is 열세 살, never *열셋 살.

열쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound built from the prospective stem 열- of 열다 ('to open') and 쇠 ('iron, metal'): literally 'opening-metal'.
열쇠.notes: Pairs naturally with 잠그다 ('to lock') and 열다 ('to open').

열심히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adverb 열심히, derived from the Sino-Korean noun 열심 (熱心, 'ardor, zeal, enthusiasm, fervent heart', from 熱 열 'hot, fervent' + 心 심 'heart, mind') suffixed with the native Korean deadjectival/denominal adverb-forming suffix -히 (from Middle Korean -히, related to ᄒᆞ다 'to do/be'). Literally 'with a hot, fervent heart'.

history.meaning: a fervent, ardent, or eager heart and mind
zealously, earnestly, with wholehearted devotion
diligently, hard, earnestly, enthusiastically

열심히.notes: One of the most culturally salient adverbs in Korean daily life; '열심히 하겠습니다!' ('I will work hard / give it my all!') is the universal pledge of every rookie PD and idol trainee.

열아홉.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 아홉 ('nine', Middle Korean 아홉).

history.meaning: nineteen (native Korean number)

열어주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb 열어주다, formed from the verb stem 열- (열다, 'to open, unlock, inaugurate, pave the way', Middle Korean 열다 / 엶다) linked via the infinitive/connective suffix -어 to the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, do for someone's benefit', Middle Korean 주다). Literally 'to open [a door, path, or opportunity] for someone'.

history.meaning: to open + to give
to open (something) for someone; figuratively, to pave the way or open doors for someone

morphemes.meaning: to give, do for the benefit of

열어주다.notes: Used both literally (문을 열어주다 'to open the door for someone') and idiomatically (길을 열어주다 'to pave the way / open up a path for someone').

열여덟.etymology: Native Korean numeral joining 열 ('ten') and 여덟 ('eight', Middle Korean 여듧). Its pronunciation involves fascinating phonological rules: the final ㄹㅂ cluster of 여덟 loses its ㅂ before silence or a consonant (여덟 개 [여덜 깨]), and when 열 and 여덟 combine, a ㄴ is inserted and immediately assimilates to the preceding liquid, yielding the standard pronunciation [열려덜]. Used for counting age and native counters (걸음, 명, 개).
열여덟.notes: Crucially pronounced [열려덜] in isolation or before a counter.

열여섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 여섯 ('six', Middle Korean 여슷), pronounced [열려섣] with [n]-insertion and liquidization.

history.meaning: sixteen (native Korean number)

열한.etymology: Native Korean pre-nominal compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 한 (adnominal form of 하나 'one', Middle Korean 열하나).

history.meaning: eleven (before a counter or noun)

엽서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 엽서 (葉書), joining 엽 (葉, 'leaf, thin flat sheet') and 서 (書, 'letter, writing') — literally 'leaf-letter', coined in Meiji Japan (hagaki) and adopted into Korean for a postal card.

history.meaning: single-sheet postal card, postcard

엿보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 엿보다 ('to peep, spy on, watch for an opportunity'), from verb stem 엿- ('to lurk, watch stealthily') + 보다 ('to look, see').

history.meaning: to peep through a crack, spy on, watch for a chance

영.etymology: Emphatic Korean adverb 영 ('really, altogether, quite, [not] at all'), traditionally traced to the Sino-Korean reading of 永 (영, 'perpetually, forever, completely') or influenced in negative contexts by 零 (영, 'zero, nought'). From an original sense of 'permanently, all the way through', it bleached into a colloquial intensifier with negative or dissatisfied predicates ('totally off, not at all good').

history.meaning: perpetually, for good, all the way through
altogether, quite, really, (not) at all (colloquial emphatic adverb)

영.notes: Almost always precedes a negative verb or an unfavourable evaluation (e.g., 기분이 영 별로다 'my mood is really not great at all', 영 마음에 안 들다 'I don't like it at all').

영광.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 영광 (榮光), composed of 영 (榮, 'flourishing, blooming, honor, glory', originally depicting torchlight or flowering trees) and 광 (光, 'light, radiance, brilliance, honor'). Literally 'flourishing radiance', used in Classical Chinese for auspicious splendor and in modern Korean for high honor or glory.

history.meaning: radiant splendor, auspicious light, high honor
glory, honor, privilege

영광.notes: The set phrase '영광입니다' ('It is an honor!') is the standard polite expression when meeting an admired celebrity, senior director, or receiving an award.

영리하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 영리 (伶俐), combining 伶 (영리할/악공 령, 'nimble, clever, performing artist') and 俐 (영리할 리, 'bright, quick-witted, smooth'), plus the native -하다. Originally describing actors or servants who were quick on their feet and observant, it came to describe bright, astute cleverness in problem-solving. In modern Korean it is generously applied to sharp-witted children, intelligent pets, and resourceful ideas.
영리하다.notes: Word-initial 령 becomes 영 under South Korean pronunciation rules (두음법칙).

영미.etymology: Korean female given name 영미 (commonly written in Hanja as 英美, combining 英 'flower petal, outstanding, brilliant' and 美 'beautiful', or 永美 'eternal beauty').

history.meaning: Korean female personal name (Yeong-mi)

cognates.meaning: image, reflection, video footage (映像 / 影像)

영상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 영상 (映像), composed of 영 (映, 'to shine upon, reflect light, project an image') and 상 (像, 'likeness, figure, image, portrait'). Originally denoting an optical reflection in water or a mirror, in 20th-century film and broadcasting it came to denote projected visual media, video footage, and clips.

history.meaning: reflected image or optical figure cast by light
cinematic or television visual image, video footage, clip

영상.notes: In modern Korean, 영상 is the default everyday word for any 'video clip' or 'footage' (e.g., 유튜브 영상, 예고 영상), replacing older terms like 비디오.

영수증.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 영수증 (領受證), joining 영수 (領受, 'receiving and taking into possession', from 領 'to lead, receive' + 受 'to receive') and 증 (證, 'certificate, proof, voucher').

history.meaning: written proof of payment received, receipt

영어.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 영어 (英語, 'English language'), formed from 영 (英, the first character of the phonetic transliteration 英吉利 Yeonggilli / Yīngjílì for 'England', itself meaning 'flower petal, outstanding, brave') and 어 (語, 'language, speech, words').Literally 'the language of England (영국, 英國)'.

history.meaning: phonetic transcription of 'English/England' abbreviated + 'language'
history.stage: Qing Dynasty Chinese / Meiji Japanese (19th c.)

history.meaning: the English language

morphemes.meaning: England, British (abbreviation of 英吉利) (英)

영어.notes: The same country-prefix 영 (英) appears in 영국 (英國, 'United Kingdom / England') and 영문 (英文, 'English writing/text').

영업하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 영업 (營業, 영 'manage, run' + 업 'business, trade') + -하다.
영업하다.notes: Standard term on Korean shopfront signs (영업중 'Open', 매일 영업합니다 'Open Daily').

영영.etymology: Sino-Korean reduplicated adverb 영영 (永永), formed by doubling the character 영 (永, 'long, perpetual, eternal', originally an ancient pictograph of a long, continuously flowing river current). Reduplication intensifies the sense of permanence into 'forever, for good, once and for all, never to return'.

history.meaning: endlessly, perpetually through the ages
forever, for good, permanently (especially of parting, vanishing, or irreversible change)

영영.notes: Unlike 영원히 ('eternally, forever' in idealistic or romantic vows), 영영 typically carries a sense of finality or irreversible loss (e.g., 영영 떠나다 'to leave for good', 영영 못 보다 'to never see again').

영웅.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 영웅 (英雄), joining 영 (英, 'outstanding blossom, person of exceptional talent') and 웅 (雄, 'male bird, vigorous leader, champion').

history.meaning: person of extraordinary valor and ability, hero

영원하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) 영원하다 (永遠하다), composed of the Sino-Korean noun 영원 (永遠, 'eternity, perpetuity', from 永 영 'long-flowing, perpetual, eternal' + 遠 원 'far, distant in space or time') and the native Korean adjectival verbalizer -하다 ('to be'). Literally 'to be unendingly long and distant in time'.

history.meaning: stretching far and long in time; perpetual and unending
to be eternal, everlasting, timeless, forever

영원하다.notes: Functions as a descriptive verb (adjective) in Korean, taking the modifier form 영원한 ('eternal', as in 영원한 사랑 'eternal love') and adverbial form 영원히 ('forever').

영입하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from 영입 (迎入, "welcoming and bringing in"), combining 迎 (맞이할 영, "to welcome, meet, receive") and 入 (들 입, "to enter, bring in"), suffixed with the native light verb 하다 ("to do"). Originally used for welcoming guests or inducting scholars, in modern Korean it specifically denotes recruiting talent, executives, or star cast members into an organization.

history.meaning: welcoming and receiving inside
to recruit, scout, or induct talent into an organization or team

영입하다.notes: Unlike 일반 채용 (general hiring via open applications), 영입하다 implies actively scouting and courting an established talent or star to join a team or show.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 영입하다

cognates.word: 零點二 / 零点二 (líng diǎn èr)

영점이.etymology: A Sino-Korean decimal numeral expression composed of 영 (零, "zero, fractional remainder, raindrops"), 점 (點, "dot, decimal point"), and 이 (二, "two"). In Korean broadcasting and statistics, decimal expressions use Sino-Korean numerals exclusively on both sides of 점 (點).

history.meaning: raindrop or remainder / black dot / two
zero point two (0.2)

영점이.notes: In Korean TV production, small decimal numbers like 영점이 (0.2%) frequently appear in tense discussions of viewer ratings (시청률) differentials.

cognates.word: 零點七 / 零点七 (líng diǎn qī)

영점칠.etymology: A Sino-Korean decimal numeral compound built from 영 (零, "zero, naught"), 점 (點, "dot, decimal point"), and 칠 (七, "seven"). The use of 點 to mark the radix point entered East Asian mathematical terminology during the late nineteenth-century adoption of Western decimal notation.

history.meaning: remainder / dot or mark / seven
zero point seven (0.7)

영점칠.notes: While zero in phone numbers is usually read 공 (空), in decimal numbers and temperatures before 점 (點) it is almost always read 영 (零).

영화.etymology: A Sino-Korean loan from Meiji-era Japanese 映画 (eiga, literally "projected picture"), compounded from 映 (비칠 영, "to reflect, shine, project light") and 畫 (그림 화, "picture, drawing, image"). In early twentieth-century Korea, it displaced the earlier term 활동사진 (活動寫眞, "moving photograph") as the standard word for motion pictures.

history.meaning: projected lantern slide or motion picture
movie, motion picture, cinema

영화.notes: Do not confuse 영화 (映畫, "movie") with its homophone 영화 (榮華, "glory and splendor"), which differs in both Hanja and historical vowel length.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 영화

영화관.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound combining 영화 (映畫, "movie, motion picture", from 映 "project light" + 畫 "picture") with the architectural suffix 관 (館, 집 관, "public building, hall, lodge"). It literally denotes a dedicated hall for screening projected motion pictures.

history.meaning: guest lodge, public hall, official building
movie theater, cinema hall

영화관.notes: In everyday speech, 영화관 is interchangeable with 극장 (劇場, "theater"), though 극장 can also refer to a live stage playhouse.

영화배우.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound joining 영화 (映畫, "motion picture") and 배우 (俳優, "actor, performer"). The noun 배우 (俳優) derives from Classical Chinese 俳 (광대 배, "jester, comic performer") and 優 (광대 우, "actor, theatrical entertainer"), originally referring to court entertainers and stage players before broadening in modern East Asia to dramatic and screen actors.

history.meaning: court jester, theatrical player, comic entertainer
motion picture actor or actress

영화배우.notes: Korean industry culture sometimes distinguishes 영화배우 (film actors, traditionally seen as having high prestige) from 탤런트 (TV drama actors).

옅다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Middle Korean as 엳다 or 옅다. Its core spatial meaning 'to be shallow' (옅은 물 'shallow water', contrasting with 깊다 'deep') naturally extended to sensory gradients, denoting pale or light colours (옅은 색), faint scents, or thin fog, contrasting with 짙다 ('deep, thick, rich'). As a regular ㅌ-stem, it conjugates seamlessly before vowels (옅어, 옅으니).
옅다.notes: Commonly modifies 색 ('colour') or 향기 ('scent') in its adnominal form 옅은.

옆.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 옆 ('side, flank of the body, space beside').

history.meaning: flank, side, space beside
side, next to, beside

옆구리.etymology: Native Korean anatomical compound descending from Middle Korean 옆구리, formed from 옆 ('side') + 구리 (bound root denoting a curved flank or hollow of the torso).

history.meaning: side of the torso between ribs and hip, flank

옆면.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 옆 ('side') + Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface, side').

history.meaning: side surface, lateral face, profile

옆집.etymology: A native Korean (고유어) determinative compound of 옆 ("side, flank", attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 엳 / 옆, originally an anatomic noun meaning "rib, flank") and 집 ("house, home, shop", Middle Korean 집). By metonymy, it signifies the house, apartment, or shop immediately adjacent to one's own, as well as the neighbors living there.

history.meaning: flank or side + house
next-door house, adjacent shop, or next-door neighbor

옆집.notes: Because of tensification (경음화) after the obstruent coda ㅍ [p̚], 옆집 is always pronounced [엽찝]. It refers equally to a residential neighbor's home or the business next door.

예.etymology: A polite native Korean interjection of affirmation and attentiveness ("yes, I hear you"), attested in Early Modern Korean alongside 네. It developed from a deferential response particle acknowledging a superior's call, distinct from the Sino-Korean noun 예 (禮, "courtesy") or 예 (例, "example"), though reinforced in formal register by associations with respectful deportment.

history.meaning: polite affirmative response to a elder or superior
yes (polite/formal); pardon? (when spoken with rising intonation)

예.notes: In workplace settings like a broadcasting station, 예 often sounds slightly more formal, crisp, and deferential than 네, though both are standard polite "yes".

예고.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from 예고 (豫告), consisting of 豫 (미리 예, "beforehand, in advance, prepare") and 告 (고할 고, "to announce, inform, tell"). Originally an administrative and legal term for prior notification, in modern media it also denotes a broadcast preview or teaser announcement for an upcoming episode.

history.meaning: to notify or announce beforehand
advance notice; broadcast preview or teaser

예고.notes: In TV production jargon, cutting the 예고 (next-episode preview) at the end of a broadcast is critical for retaining next week's ratings.

예고편.etymology: A Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound formed from 예고 (豫告, "advance notice, preview", from 豫 "beforehand" + 告 "announce") and the classifier/suffix 편 (篇, 책 편, "chapter, bound bamboo slips, literary piece, film reel/episode"). It literally means "advance-announcement segment" or "preview reel".

history.meaning: bundle of bamboo slips, book section, literary composition
trailer or preview clip for an upcoming film or television episode

예고편.notes: While 예고 can refer to the act of announcing or a short TV spot, 예고편 specifically refers to the edited video clip or theatrical trailer itself.

예능.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from 예능 (藝能), combining 藝 (재주 예, "art, craft, skill", originally a pictograph of a person planting a seedling, signifying cultivated skill) and 能 (능할 능, "ability, talent, competence"). Historically meaning artistic and martial accomplishments, in contemporary South Korean broadcasting it functions as shorthand for 예능 프로그램 ("variety entertainment programs").

history.meaning: cultivated artistic skills and practical talents
performing arts; television variety entertainment shows

예능.notes: In Korean TV culture, 예능 specifically contrasts with 드라마 (scripted drama) and 교양/시사 (educational/current-affairs programming); saying someone has 예능감 means they have a knack for being funny on variety shows.

예능국.etymology: A Sino-Korean institutional compound combining 예능 (藝能, "variety entertainment", from 藝 "art, skill" + 能 "talent") and 국 (局, 판 국 / 부서 국, "bureau, department, office, board"). At Korean television networks such as KBS, the 예능국 is the administrative division responsible for producing comedy, talk, reality, and variety shows.

history.meaning: chessboard square; government bureau or division office
variety entertainment department at a broadcasting network

예능국.notes: In *The Producers* (프로듀사), the KBS 예능국 (Variety Department) is the central workplace setting where the main PDs plan and edit their shows.

예능국인데요.etymology: An inflected conversational phrase built on the Sino-Korean noun 예능국 (藝能局, "variety entertainment department", from 藝 "art" + 能 "talent" + 局 "bureau/department"), followed by the native Korean copula stem -이- ("to be") and the polite background-explanatory sentence-final ending -ㄴ데요 (from adnominal -ㄴ + bound noun 데 "place/circumstance" + polite particle 요). It is the standard Korean telephone or doorway self-identification formula ("This is the Variety Department speaking...").

history.meaning: noun + copula + circumstantial clause ending + polite particle
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean grammar

history.meaning: This is the Variety Department (speaking / calling), and...

morphemes.meaning: polite circumstantial/explanatory ending (sets up context or invites response)

예능국인데요.notes: Ending a self-introduction on the phone with -인데요 rather than -입니다 softens the statement and signals that you are about to state your business or waiting for the listener's acknowledgment.

cognates.word: 前売り (maeuri, semantic parallel) / 予売

예매.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from 예매 (豫賣), uniting 豫 (미리 예, "beforehand, in advance") and 賣 (팔 매, "to sell", which in commercial ticket compounds functions reciprocally from the consumer's perspective as "advance ticket purchase/booking"). Originally referring to the vendor's advance sale of tickets, in everyday Korean usage it denotes buying or booking tickets in advance for movies, concerts, or trains.

history.meaning: selling goods or tickets beforehand
advance ticket booking or purchase (for films, concerts, trains)

예매.notes: Use 예매 specifically for buying tickets in advance (movies, concerts, KTX trains), whereas 예약 (豫約) is used for general reservations (restaurants, hotels, hospitals).

예민하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from 예민 (銳敏, "sharp and quick, acute") plus the native adjective-forming suffix 하다. The Sino-Korean stem combines 銳 (날카로울 예, "sharp-edged, pointed, keen", containing the metal radical 金) and 敏 (민첩할 민, "quick, agile, perceptive"). Metaphorically extended from a sharp blade and quick reflexes, it describes heightened sensory acuity or a touchy, high-strung temperament.

history.meaning: sharp-edged and quick-witted, keen, acute
to be sensitive, acute, touchy, or high-strung

예민하다.notes: When describing a person's mood or personality, 예민하다 usually carries the nuance of being "touchy, edgy, or easily irritated" (e.g., before a broadcast deadline) rather than empathetically "sensitive".

예방.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun from 예방 (豫防), compounded from 豫 (미리 예, "beforehand, in advance") and 防 (막을 방, "to dike, embankment, defend against, ward off", containing the mound radical 阜). Literally meaning "building a barrier beforehand", it denotes warding off illness, accidents, or crises before they occur.

history.meaning: guarding against or warding off danger beforehand
prevention, precaution, prophylaxis

예방.notes: Commonly paired with 접종 in 예방 접종 (vaccination) or used in the proverb 사후약방문보다 예방이 낫다 ("prevention is better than a prescription after death").

예배.etymology: A Sino-Korean religious term from 예배 (禮拜, originally 례배 prior to the South Korean Initial Sound Rule 두음법칙), composed of 禮 (예도 례, "ritual, propriety, reverence") and 拜 (절 배, "to bow with clasped hands, do obeisance"). Originally a Buddhist and Confucian term for ritual bowing before sacred images or elders, it was adopted by Korean Protestantism as the standard term for a Christian worship service.

history.meaning: reverent bowing before a deity, Buddha, or revered figure
Christian worship service, divine service

예배.notes: In South Korea, attending a Protestant service is called 예배를 드리다 (or 예배를 보다), whereas a Catholic Mass is called 미사 (Missa) and a Buddhist service is 법회 (法會).

예쁘다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어엿브다; in 15th-century Middle Korean (famously in the Hunminjeongeum preface, 내 이를 위하야 어엿비 너겨 'I, feeling pity for them on this account'), 어엿브다 meant 'pitiful, touching, arousing tender compassion', which shifted in Early Modern Korean to 'endearing, lovely, pretty'.

history.meaning: pitiful, arousing tender sympathy
lovely, pretty, sweet

예산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예산 (豫算), combining 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 산 (算, 'count, calculate').
예산.notes: Shares the calculation root 산 (算) with 계산 ('payment / calculation').

예상.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from 예상 (豫想), combining 豫 (미리 예, "beforehand, in advance") and 想 (생각 상, "to think, conceive, imagine", formed from 相 "mutual/observe" over 心 "heart-mind"). It literally signifies "picturing in the mind beforehand", hence an expectation, estimate, or forecast of how events will unfold.

history.meaning: to conceive or conjecture in advance
expectation, anticipation, forecast, estimate

예상.notes: Frequently used in phrases like 예상외로 ("contrary to expectations / unexpectedly") and 예상 시청률 ("projected viewer ratings").

예술.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound from 예술 (藝術), uniting 藝 (재주 예, "art, cultivated skill, accomplishment") and 術 (재주 술, "method, technique, art, discipline"). In premodern East Asia, 藝術 referred broadly to scholarly, technical, and divinatory crafts (such as the Six Arts 六藝); in the late nineteenth century, it was repurposed to translate the Western aesthetic concept of "fine arts". In colloquial Korean, it is also used predicatively ("예술이다!") to mean "It's a masterpiece! / It's amazing!".

history.meaning: cultivated skills, classical arts, and technical disciplines
fine arts, artistic creation; (colloquial) a work of art, perfection

예술.notes: In casual conversation, exclaiming "와, 예술이다!" (or "예술이네!") is a vibrant idiom praising anything—from a scenic view to a delicious dish or a great camera shot—as "an absolute work of art!".

예약.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예약 (豫約), from 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 약 (約, 'agreement, booking').
예약.notes: Standard noun for hotel, restaurant, and train reservations; pairs with 하다 ('예약하다').

예약하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 예약 (豫約, 'advance booking or pledge', from 豫 'beforehand, in advance' + 約 'agreement, promise') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to book in advance, make a reservation

예언.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 豫言, composed of 豫 (미리 예, 'beforehand, in advance, prepare') and 言 (말씀 언, 'word, speech, statement'). Although traditionally associated with grand religious or mythological prophecies, modern everyday Korean playfully uses 예언 for any accurate foresight, hunch, or weather prediction made by a perceptive friend or neighbour.
예언.notes: Forms 예언하다 ('to prophesy, predict') and 예언자 ('prophet, seer').

예의.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun from 예의 (禮儀, historically 례의 before initial ㄹ loss), combining 禮 (예도 례, "ritual propriety, ethical courtesy") and 儀 (거동 의, "demeanor, ceremony, model conduct"). Rooted in core Confucian social philosophy (such as the *Book of Rites* 禮記), where inner reverence (禮) is expressed through proper outward bearing (儀), in modern Korean it denotes everyday manners, politeness, and social courtesy.

history.meaning: Confucian ritual propriety and ceremonial demeanor
manners, courtesy, politeness, etiquette

예의.notes: The diphthong 의 in 예의 (When non-initial) is canonically pronounced [예이] in natural standard speech. It pairs constantly with 바르다 ("예의가 바르다", to be well-mannered) or 없다 ("예의가 없다", to be rude).

예의가.etymology: An inflected nominative form consisting of the Sino-Korean noun 예의 (禮儀, "manners, courtesy, etiquette", from 禮 "ritual propriety" + 儀 "demeanor") and the native Korean subject particle -가 (which emerged in Early Modern Korean around the sixteenth–seventeenth centuries after vowel-final stems, complementing Middle Korean -이). It routinely serves as the grammatical subject of predicates like 바르다 ("to be well-mannered"), 있다 ("to have manners"), or 없다 ("to lack manners").

history.meaning: ritual propriety + nominative case marker
manners, courtesy (as grammatical subject)

예의가.notes: In Korean, "He is polite" or "He is rude" is structured as a double-subject construction using 예의가: "그 사람은 예의가 바르다 / 예의가 없다."

예의라는.etymology: An adnominal quotative construction built on the Sino-Korean noun 예의 (禮儀, "manners, courtesy", from 禮 "propriety" + 儀 "demeanor") suffixed with the contracted quotative modifier -라는 (from copula -(이)라 + quotative -고 하- + adnominal modifier -는, literally "that is called"). Followed by a bound noun like 것 ("thing"), 예의라는 것 expresses rhetorical emphasis: "a thing called courtesy" or "such a thing as manners".

history.meaning: that which is called propriety or courtesy
called courtesy; such a thing as manners (adnominal modifier)

예의라는.notes: Attaching -라는 것 ("a thing called X") to an abstract noun like 예의 is a classic rhetorical device in Korean scolding: "너는 예의라는 것도 모르니?" ("Do you not even know a thing called manners?").

예전.etymology: Hybrid temporal noun formed from native Korean 예 ('olden times, the past', Middle Korean 녜) + Sino-Korean 전 (前, 'before, former times').

history.meaning: former times, the old days, before

옛.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner descending from Middle Korean 녯, formed from 녜 ('olden times, antiquity') + genitive particle -ㅅ.

history.meaning: of olden times, old, former
old, ancient, former, bygone

옛날.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 녯날, formed from 녯 / 옛 ('of old') + 날 ('day, time').

history.meaning: olden days, long ago, once upon a time

옜다.etymology: A native Korean exclamation formed by the phonological contraction of the deictic phrase 여기 있다 ("Here it is!"), via the intermediate colloquial contraction 여깄다 -> 옜다. Over time it grammaticalized into a standalone interjection used when tossing, handing over, or begrudgingly granting an item or favor to someone ("Here, take this!").

history.meaning: it is right here
Here, take this! / Here you go! (interjection when handing something over)

morphemes.meaning: to exist, be here (contraction of 있-)

옜다.notes: 옜다 is strictly informal (반말) and often carries a playful, gruff, or magnanimous nuance—like a senior colleague tossing a treat or a favor to a junior while pretending not to care.

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to be, to have

오.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 오 (五, 'five'), from Middle Chinese *nguX; also used as a natural Korean exclamation 오 ('oh!, ah!').

history.meaning: five (Sino-Korean number)

오가다.etymology: A native Korean coordinate (dvandva) compound verb formed by directly serializing the verb stem 오- (from 오다, Middle Korean 오다, "to come") and 가- (from 가다, Middle Korean 가다, "to go") without an intervening conjunctive suffix. It denotes reciprocal movement back and forth between places, or the mutual exchange of words, glances, or feelings between people.

history.meaning: to come and to go
to come and go, go back and forth, be exchanged between people

오가다.notes: Beyond physical commuting ("집과 방송국을 오가다"), 오가다 frequently describes abstract exchanges such as conversation ("대화가 오가다") or affection ("정이 오가다").

rootFamily.gloss: in passing, while coming and going

오그라들다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb joining the sound-symbolic/descriptive stem 오그라- (seen in 오그라지다 'to curl up, shrivel, contract', with dark-vowel twin 우그러지다) and the directional auxiliary 들다 ('to go inward'). It physically describes paper curling in a fire, leaves shriveling in autumn, or hands puckering in water. In modern slang, 손발이 오그라들다 ('one's hands and feet curl inward') vividly translates the bodily sensation of secondhand embarrassment or cringing at cheesy dialogue.
오그라들다.notes: As an ㄹ-stem, 들다 drops ㄹ before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ: 오그라듭니다, 오그라드는.

오냐오냐.etymology: A native Korean reduplicated ideophonic adverb derived from the interjection 오냐 ("Yes, alright, there-there!"), an affectionate and indulgent affirmative used by elders or parents when granting a child's or junior's wish. By repeating 오냐 twice (오냐오냐), the form lexicalized into an adverb meaning "indulging every whim, pamperingly, spoilingly".

history.meaning: affirmative interjection used by an elder to a younger person ("yes, alright")
pamperingly, indulgently, yielding to every whim

오냐오냐.notes: Almost always combined with 해 주다 or 받아 주다 (e.g., "오냐오냐해 주다") to warn that spoiling someone or humoring their every demand will make them arrogant.

오년.etymology: A Sino-Korean numeral-classifier compound from 오년 (五年), combining 오 (五, 다섯 오, "five") and 년 (年, 해 년, "year, harvest cycle", originally an ideograph of a person carrying a ripe grain sheaf). In Korean, the Sino-Korean counter 년 (年) exclusively selects Sino-Korean numerals (일, 이, 삼, 사, 오...), whereas the native counter 해 ("year") selects native numerals (한 해, 두 해, 다섯 해).

history.meaning: five years or five harvest cycles
five years

오년.notes: Remember the numeral-counter matching rule: say 오 년 (Sino-Korean 五 + 年), never 다섯 년; with the native noun 해, say 다섯 해.

오늘.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 오늘 ('today', analyzed historically as proximal deictic root 오- 'this' + 날/늘 'day').

history.meaning: this day, today
today, the present day

오늘치.etymology: A native Korean derivative noun formed from 오늘 ("today", attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 오늘) and the native Korean bound suffix -치 ("allotted share, portion, quota, worth"). It denotes the specific portion of work, food, filming, or wages allocated for today.

history.meaning: this day, today
today's share, today's quota or portion of work

오늘치.notes: The suffix -치 attaches productively to time words and quantities to mean "worth/quota of": 오늘치 ("today's quota of work/footage"), 한 달치 ("a month's worth"), 이틀치 ("two days' worth").

오다.etymology: Native Korean basic motion verb descending from Middle Korean 오다 ('to come, move toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come
to come, arrive; (of rain or snow) to fall

오다가다.etymology: A native Korean compound adverb lexicalized from the parallel transferentive verb phrase 오다가 가다가 ("while coming and while going"), where 오- ("to come") and 가- ("to go") each take the interrupted/simultaneous action suffix -다가, with the first -가 elided by haplology (오다가 + 가다가 > 오다가다). It means "in passing, casually along the way, or by chance while coming and going".

history.meaning: while in the middle of coming and while in the middle of going
in passing, casually along the way, occasionally by chance

오다가다.notes: Often shortened even further in rapid speech to 오가다 or paired with 마주치다 ("오다가다 마주치다", to bump into someone in passing in the hallway or neighborhood).

rootFamily.gloss: to come and go, go back and forth

오돌뼈.etymology: A native Korean compound noun combining the mimetic/ideophonic root 오돌- (from 오돌오돌 / 오도독, mimicking a firm, crunchy, bumpy, or gristly texture when chewed) and the native noun 뼈 ("bone, cartilage", attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as ㅿ벼 / 뼈). In Korean cuisine and pojangmacha (street-stall) culture, it refers both to crunchy pork cartilage and to the popular spicy stir-fried dish made with finely chopped pork cartilage.

history.meaning: bone, skeletal frame
crunchy cartilage (especially pork cartilage) or spicy stir-fried pork cartilage dish

오돌뼈.notes: In Korean drinking culture (포장마차 / 실내포차), 오돌뼈 is a classic fiery late-night 안주 (drinking snack), typically served with rice balls (주먹밥) to temper the heat.

rootFamily.gloss: crunchily, with a firm chewing sound (ideophone)

오래.etymology: A native Korean temporal adverb meaning "for a long time", derived from the Middle Korean adjective stem 오라- (dictionary form 오라다, "to be long in time, to take a long while") plus the productive adverb-deriving suffix -이 (오라- + -이 > 오래). Although the base adjective 오라다 became obsolete in Modern Korean, its stem survives in the adverb 오래, the adnominal modifier 오랜 ("long-standing", from 오란), and compounds like 오래간만 ("after a long time").

history.meaning: for a long duration of time (adverbial of 오라다 "to be long in time")
for a long time, at length

morphemes.meaning: long in time (bound stem from Middle Korean 오라다)

오래.notes: Because the original adjective 오라다 died out, modern Korean uses the verb 오래되다 ("to become old/long-standing") for predicates, while keeping 오래 as an adverb ("오래 기다리다") and 오랜 as a noun modifier ("오랜 친구").

rootFamily.gloss: after a long time, long time no see

오래다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb formed from the adverb/noun root 오래 ('a long time', Middle Korean 오라다 'to be long in time').

history.meaning: to be of long standing, take a long time

오래되다.etymology: Native Korean compound descriptive/intransitive verb formed from 오래 ('for a long time') + 되다 ('to become, pass, elapse').

history.meaning: to be old, date back a long time

오래오래.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic and emphatic full reduplication of the adverb 오래 (orae, 'for a long time'), which is attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 오래 (woray) and derives from the native qualitative verb 오라다 (worata, 'to be long in duration, to take a long time') plus the adverbial derivational suffix -이 (-i). Full reduplication intensifies the temporal duration to express enduring longevity or heartfelt wishes.

history.meaning: to be long in time or duration
for a long time, at length
for a very long time, everlastingly

오래오래.notes: Frequently used in warm blessings and farewells—such as 오래오래 행복하세요 ('be happy for a long, long time')—giving a softer, more affectionate tone than simple 오래.

rootFamily.gloss: after a long time; long time no see

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오래오래

오랜만.etymology: Native Korean compound noun contracted from 오래간만 (oraeganman, 'an interval after a long time'), itself formed from the adnominal form 오랜 (oraen, from 오래다 'to be long in time' + adnominal suffix -ㄴ) modifying the bound noun 만 (man, 'elapsed time, interval since an event', from Middle Korean 만 indicating extent or duration). Historically used with the copula (오랜만이다) or locative particle (오랜만에) to greet someone after a long separation.

history.meaning: to be long in time + bound noun of temporal extent
an interval of a long time
after a long time; long time no see

morphemes.meaning: interval of time elapsed since an event

오랜만.notes: Watch the spelling distinction: 오랜만에 ('after a long time', noun 오랜만 + particle 에) vs. 오랫동안 ('for a long duration', adverbial compound with saisiot ㅅ); *오랜동안 is a common native-speaker misspelling.

rootFamily.gloss: for a long period of time

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오랜만

오렌지.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English orange (ultimately via Old French, Italian, Arabic, and Persian from Sanskrit naranga).

history.meaning: sweet orange fruit; orange color

오로지.etymology: Native Korean adverb derived from Middle Korean 오로 (wolo, 'wholly, intactly, solely'), which is formed from the native root *올- / 오올- (wol- / wowol-, 'whole, complete, sound, undivided', also seen in 온 'all, whole') followed by the instrumental/adverbial suffix -로 and later reinforced with the adverbial suffix -지. The semantic shift progressed from 'in an undivided, intact state' to 'exclusively, solely, with single-minded focus'.

history.meaning: to be whole, complete, intact
wholly, entirely, exclusively
history.stage: Middle Korean to Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: solely, exclusively, only

오로지.notes: Compared to 오직 ('only, merely'), 오로지 emphasizes single-minded devotion or undivided exclusivity (e.g., 오로지 너만 생각했어, 'I thought solely of you without distraction').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오로지

오르다.etymology: Native Korean verb inherited from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 오르다 (woluta, 'to ascend, climb, mount, rise'). It belongs to the 르-irregular (르 불규칙) verb class, alternating its stem between 오르- before consonants and 올라- (Middle Korean 올아-) before vowel-initial endings. Semantically it covers physical ascent, mounting a vehicle or stage, and quantitative increases such as prices or TV ratings.

history.meaning: to ascend, climb, rise up
to go up, rise, climb, advance (in rank, price, or ratings)

오르다.notes: In broadcasting dramas like The Producers, 오르다 is constantly paired with 시청률 ('viewer ratings')—시청률이 오르다 means 'the ratings go up', whereas transitive 올리다 means 'to raise/boost'.

rootFamily.gloss: to go up, ascend (compound with 가다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오르다

오른쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 오른 (adnominal form of 옳다 'to be right, proper, straight', Middle Korean 옳-) + 쪽 ('side, direction') — just like English 'right' and French 'droit', linking moral/practical 'rightness' with the right-hand side.

history.meaning: the right-hand side

오만.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 오만 (五萬, 'fifty thousand', joining 五 'five' + 萬 'ten thousand'); homonymous with Sino-Korean 오만 (傲慢, 'arrogance, haughtiness').

history.meaning: five ten-thousands, fifty thousand

오버.etymology: Loanword borrowed from English over (via or reinforced by Japanese Wasei-eigo オーバー ōbā), specifically clipped from theatrical and broadcasting compound expressions such as overaction (오버액션, 'exaggerated acting') and overdo. In contemporary Korean it functions as an independent noun (and verbal noun with 하다) meaning 'exaggeration, overreaction, or going too far beyond social norms'.

history.meaning: beyond a limit; exaggerated theatrical acting
exaggerated gesture or dramatic overacting
overreaction, exaggeration, going overboard

오버.notes: Colloquially used both as a noun (오버 좀 하지 마, 'stop overreacting') and as a verb (오버하다, 'to go overboard / make a fuss'); in baseball or golf it also retains the literal sense of 'over par / over the fence'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오버

오븐.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English oven (from Old English ofen 'furnace, baking chamber').
