history.meaning: baking oven

오빠.etymology: Native Korean kinship term meaning 'older brother of a female speaker', resulting from nursery or hypocoristic contraction and labial assimilation of Early Modern Korean 오라바님 (orabanim) / 오라비 (orabi), attested in Middle Korean as 올아비 (wol.api). The Middle Korean compound combines *올- (wol-, a kinship prefix marking family/collateral relation, cf. 올케) and 아비 (api, 'father, adult male'). In modern society, it extended from blood kinship to an affectionate address term for older male friends, seniors, and romantic partners.

history.meaning: older brother of a woman
esteemed older brother (of a female)
older brother of a female; older male friend, colleague, or boyfriend

morphemes.meaning: male/brother stem (assimilated with tense labial from 아비/바)

오빠.notes: Strictly a female-speaker perspective kinship term (men call an older brother 형); in Korean workplace and campus culture, women often use 오빠 for close older male seniors or boyfriends, while 오라버니 survives as a formal or playfully archaic variant.

rootFamily.gloss: older brother of a female (slightly formal/traditional)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오빠

오성급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 오성급 (五星級), joining 오 (五, 'five'), 성 (星, 'star'), and 급 (級, 'grade, class, rank') — a calque of international 'five-star rating'.

history.meaning: five-star class or rating (especially of a hotel)

오십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 오십 (五十), joining 오 (五, 'five') and 십 (十, 'ten').

history.meaning: five tens, fifty

오월.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 오월 (五月), joining 오 (五, 'five') and 월 (月, 'month, moon') — literally 'fifth month'.

history.meaning: the month of May

오전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 午前, composed of 午 (오, o, 'noon, midday; seventh of the Twelve Earthly Branches corresponding to the Horse, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.') and 前 (전, jeon, 'before, front, prior'). In traditional East Asian timekeeping, 午 marked the solar zenith at midday, so 午前 literally denotes the period from midnight to noon (ante meridiem, a.m.).

history.meaning: before the hour of the Horse (midday)
forenoon, morning, a.m. (00:00 to 12:00)

오전.notes: Contrast 오전 (午前, 'before noon / a.m.') with 오후 (午後, 'after noon / p.m.') and 정오 (正午, 'exact noon / 12:00 p.m.'); unlike native 아침 ('morning after waking'), 오전 is an exact clock-time division.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오전

오죽하면.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized conditional adverbial phrase formed from the rhetorical degree adverb 오죽 ('how much, to what an extreme extent', attested in Early Modern Korean as 오쥭 / 오죽) plus the light verb stem 하- ('to be/do so') and the conditional connective ending -면 ('if'). Literally meaning 'if the situation is so extreme that...', it introduces a clause explaining that an extreme action or state happened for a very understandable, compelling reason ('no wonder, small wonder').

history.meaning: to what degree, how very much (in rhetorical or negative contexts)
if things are so extreme; no wonder, for good reason

morphemes.meaning: how much, to such an extreme degree

오죽하면.notes: Almost always pairs with a rhetorical past-future or conjectural ending (-았/었겠어?, -았/었을까?) at the end of the sentence: 오죽하면 그랬겠어? ('Just think how desperate they must have been to do that! / No wonder they did that!').

rootFamily.gloss: to be extreme enough to warrant sympathy

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오죽하다

오지라퍼.etymology: Twenty-first-century South Korean colloquial hybrid neologism formed by attaching the English agentive suffix -er (adapted as -어, triggering resyllabification of the final ㅍ [p] of 오지랖 to aspirated [pʰ] in 라퍼) to the native Korean noun 오지랖 (ojirap, 'front outer flap of a garment', figuratively 'meddling in others' affairs' from the idiom 오지랖이 넓다). Coined in variety television and internet culture to playfully label a chronic busybody.

history.meaning: to have a wide garment flap; to meddle in everything
a busybody, nosy meddler (hybrid slang with English -er)

morphemes.meaning: front flap of a garment; meddling streak

오지라퍼.notes: Notice how the underlying ㅍ of 오지랖 surfaces phonetically as [퍼] before the vowel-initial suffix -어, yielding the spelling 오지라퍼; a classic example of productive Korean-English hybrid word formation in TV variety banter.

rootFamily.gloss: front lapel/flap of a coat; meddling tendency
to be nosy, to meddle in everyone's affairs (idiom)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 오지라퍼

오지랖.etymology: Native Korean tailoring term originally denoting the wide front outer flap or lapel (겉자락) of an upper garment such as a hanbok jeogori or overcoat that wraps across the chest. Attested in Early Modern Korean lexicography in forms such as 오쟛 and 오지랖. Through the metaphor of an overly wide coat flap wrapping around things it need not cover, the idiom 오지랖이 넓다 ('one's front flap is wide') became lexicalized to mean 'unsolicited meddling or nosiness'.

history.meaning: front outer flap of a traditional upper garment
garment front flap; (figuratively) meddling streak, nosiness into others' business

오지랖.notes: In modern speech, few speakers use 오지랖 for literal clothing; it appears almost exclusively in the figurative sense of nosy interference (sometimes well-intentioned but unwelcome), especially in 오지랖이 넓다 or 오지랖 부리다.

rootFamily.gloss: hem or flap of a garment

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오지랖

오직.etymology: Native Korean restrictive adverb inherited directly from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 오직 (wocik, 'only, solely, merely'). Internally related to the native Korean root *오- / *올- ('single, whole, undivided', also seen in 오로지 'solely' and 외- 'single/alone') plus an archaic adverbial formative *-직. Used in translation of Classical Chinese particles such as 唯 and 惟 ('only') since the earliest Hangul texts of the 1440s.

history.meaning: only, solely, merely (glossing Classical Chinese 唯/惟)
only, solely, exclusively

오직.notes: Often co-occurs with the restrictive particle 만 ('only') in the same clause for strong emphasis (e.g., 오직 당신만, 'only and exclusively you'), and sounds slightly more literary or elevated than simple 단지 or 그냥.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오직

오케이.etymology: Loanword borrowed from American English okay / OK, which originated in 1839 in Boston newspaper journalism as a humorous initialism for oll korrect (a facetious spelling of all correct) and was popularized during Martin Van Buren's 1840 presidential campaign (Old Kinderhook). Borrowed into Korean in the mid-twentieth century as both an everyday interjection of agreement and a broadcasting/filming noun meaning 'a director's approval of a take'.

history.meaning: all correct, approved
okay, all right; approval of a broadcast/film take

오케이.notes: In Korean TV and film production (central to The Producers), 오케이 (or 오케이 컷) is technical studio jargon for a director's approved take, and 오케이하다 means 'to give the green light / approve'.

rootFamily.gloss: to approve, give the green light, agree

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오케이

cognates.meaning: early 20th-century term for a motorized bicycle or motorcycle

오토바이.etymology: Loanword borrowed via Japanese オートバイ (ōtobai), a Meiji/Taishō-era Wasei-eigo (Japanese-coined English) clipping of the early twentieth-century English compound auto-bicycle ('motorized bicycle', combining auto- 'self-propelled' and bicycle). Entering Korean during the twentieth century, 오토바이 became the standard everyday word for any motorcycle or motor scooter, though official legal terminology prefers 이륜자동차 (二輪自動車, 'two-wheeled motor vehicle').

history.meaning: motorized two-wheeled cycle
motorcycle (clipped Wasei-eigo compound)
motorcycle, motorbike, scooter

오토바이.notes: A classic false friend for English speakers: 'autobike' or 'autobi' is not standard English, whereas 바이크 (baikeu, from bike) is increasingly used in Korea by hobbyists for high-displacement motorcycles.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오토바이

오해.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 誤解, formed from 誤 (그르칠 오, o, 'to err, mistake, be mistaken') and 解 (풀 해, hae, 'to untie, loosen, analyze, understand'). Literally 'mistaken untangling/interpretation', it denotes construing someone's words, intentions, or actions in an incorrect way. Shared across the East Asian Sinosphere (Chinese wùjiě, Japanese gokai).

history.meaning: erroneous interpretation or explanation
misunderstanding, misapprehension

오해.notes: Because 解 literally means 'to untie a knot', Korean idioms say 오해를 풀다 ('to untie/clear up a misunderstanding') and 오해가 쌓이다 ('misunderstandings pile up').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오해

오해하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by combining the Sino-Korean verbal noun 오해 (誤解, 'misunderstanding', from 誤 'err, mistake' + 解 'untie, understand') with the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do, perform, think'). It functions both transitively (taking an object with 을/를 or a source with 에 대해) and intransitively in conversational disclaimers such as 오해하지 마세요 ('please do not get the wrong idea').

history.meaning: to interpret erroneously, to misunderstand
to misunderstand, misjudge, get the wrong idea

morphemes.meaning: to do, make, think (native light verb)

오해하다.notes: To say 'be misunderstood', replace active 하다 with passive 받다 or 사다: 오해를 받다 ('to be misunderstood') or 오해를 사다 ('to invite/provoke misunderstanding').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오해하다

오후.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 오후 (午後), joining 오 (午, 'noon, seventh Earthly Branch 11 a.m.–1 p.m.') and 후 (後, 'after, behind') — literally 'after noon'.

history.meaning: afternoon, p.m.

오히려.etymology: Native Korean counter-expectational adverb inherited directly from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 오히려 (wohilye). In Middle Korean texts (such as Yongbieocheonga and Seokbo Sangjeol), 오히려 carried both the continuative temporal sense 'still, yet' (glossing Classical Chinese 猶 and 尚) and the adversative sense 'rather, on the contrary, instead' (glossing 反). By Modern Korean, the adversative meaning became primary, while the 'still' sense was taken over by 아직.

history.meaning: still, yet; rather, on the contrary (glossing 猶, 尚, 反)
on the contrary, rather, instead of what was expected

오히려.notes: Used when an outcome is the exact opposite of expectation—often in a surprisingly positive way, as in contemporary slang 오히려 좋아 ('Actually, that's even better / on the contrary, it works out in my favor!').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 오히려

옥타브.etymology: Modern musical loanword borrowed from English octave or French octave (ultimately from Latin octava 'eighth').

history.meaning: musical octave (interval of eight diatonic degrees)

온갖.etymology: Native Korean prenominal determiner evolved by vowel apocope and palatal-to-alveolar coda neutralization from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 온가지 (wonkaci, 'all kinds, a hundred varieties'). This compound joins the native numeral/determiner 온 (won, originally meaning 'one hundred' and by extension 'all, whole, complete') with the noun 가지 (kaci, 'branch; kind, sort, variety'). Dropping the final vowel -이 turned the noun phrase 온가지 into the invariable determiner 온갖.

history.meaning: one hundred kinds; all sorts and varieties
all manner of, every kind of (with apocope of final vowel)
all manner of, all sorts of, every conceivable

morphemes.meaning: all, whole, one hundred (native determiner 온)

온갖.notes: Phonologically pronounced [온갇] because final ㅈ neutralizes to [t] in coda position; historically 온 meant '100' (cf. 즈믄 for '1,000'), explaining why 온갖 evokes 'a hundred different kinds'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 온갖

온기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 온기 (溫氣), joining 온 (溫, 'warm, gentle') and 기 (氣, 'air, breath, energy').
온기.notes: Shares 온 (溫) with 온실 ('conservatory / greenhouse', 溫室).

온몸.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from the native prenominal determiner 온 (on, from Middle Korean 온 won, 'whole, entire, all; originally one hundred') and the native noun 몸 (mom, from Middle Korean 몸 mwom, 'body'). Written as a single fused compound word without a space because 온 + 몸 has lexicalized as a standard anatomical totality term ('the entire body from head to toe').

history.meaning: the whole body, entire physical frame
one's whole body, from head to toe

온몸.notes: Pairs naturally with physical sensation or total effort—e.g., 온몸이 쑤시다 ('my whole body aches') or 온몸을 던지다 ('to throw one's whole body/self into something'); its Sino-Korean counterpart is 전신 (全身).

rootFamily.gloss: all manner of, every kind of

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 온몸

온수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 온수 (溫水), joining 온 (溫, 'warm, lukewarm') and 수 (水, 'water').

history.meaning: warm or hot water (for bathing or washing)

온실.etymology: Sino-Korean 온실 (溫室), combining 온 (溫, 'warm, gentle heat') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber'). Originally named a heated palace chamber in Han-dynasty China and was adopted across modern East Asia to render Western glass greenhouses and conservatories.

history.meaning: warmed indoor chamber
glass greenhouse, conservatory, sunroom

온실.notes: Names both botanical glasshouses and sunny glass-enclosed courtyard rooms; the bound morpheme 실 (室, 'room') recurs in 객실 ('guest room'), 욕실 ('bathroom'), and 사무실 ('office').

올드하다.etymology: Hybrid loanword adjective combining the English adjective old (borrowed into Korean as 올드, oldeu) with the native Korean adjectival formative light verb 하다 (hada, 'to be in the state of'). Rather than referring to chronological age of people or objects (for which native 늙다 or 오래되다 are used), 올드하다 underwent semantic specialization in Korean media, fashion, and broadcasting to mean 'old-fashioned, dated, cheesy, or out of touch with current trends'.

history.meaning: having lived or existed for a long time; old-fashioned
to be old-fashioned, dated, retro, or behind the times in style/sensibility

올드하다.notes: Never use 올드하다 to state someone's literal age (*그 할아버지는 올드하다 is unnatural); it specifically critiques sensibilities, jokes, fashion, or directing styles as 'dated/old-school' (e.g., 연출이 좀 올드하다, 'the directing style feels a bit dated').

rootFamily.gloss: an veteran/senior member or old-timer (from old boy)
classic pop music from earlier decades (from old pop)
a veteran fan from the early days (from old fan)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 올드하다

올라가다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb descending from Middle Korean 올아가다, formed from 오르다 ('to rise, climb, ascend', conjunctive 올라) + deictic motion verb 가다 ('to go away from the speaker').

history.meaning: to go up, climb, ascend, rise (in price or temperature)

올라오다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb descending from Middle Korean 올아오다, formed from 오르다 ('to rise, ascend', conjunctive 올라) + deictic motion verb 오다 ('to come toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come up, climb up toward here

올려다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 올리다 ('to raise, lift up', conjunctive 올려) + directive particle -다 + 보다 ('to look at').

history.meaning: to look up at, gaze upward

올리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 올이다, formed from 오르다 ('to go up, rise') + causative suffix -리- ('to cause to rise, raise').

history.meaning: to raise, lift up, place on top, offer respectfully, post online

올리브유.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining the English loanword 올리브 (olive) + Sino-Korean 유 (油, 'oil').

history.meaning: olive oil

올해.etymology: Native Korean compound noun attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 올해 (wolhay, 'this year'). Morphologically composed of 올- (wol-, originally the prospective adnominal form 올 of 오다 'to come', designating the currently arriving/present cycle, also seen in 올가을 'this autumn' and 올봄 'this spring') and 해 (hay, 'year; sun'). It serves as the native Korean equivalent of Sino-Korean 금년 (今年) and 본년 (本年).

history.meaning: this year, the current year
this year

morphemes.meaning: this/current cycle (from prospective adnominal of 오다 'to come')

올해.notes: Observe the native Korean temporal series for years: 지난해 ('last year'), 올해 ('this year'), 다음 해 / 이듬해 ('next year'), alongside Sino-Korean 작년 (昨年), 금년 (今年), 내년 (來年).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 올해

옮겨드리다.etymology: Native Korean humble-benefactive compound verb formed from 옮기- (omgi-, 'to move, shift, transfer', the morphological causative of Middle Korean 옮다 womta 'to move/shift location' + causative suffix -기-), linked via the infinitive connector -어 (-eo, coalescing with 옮기- as 옮겨-) to the humble benefactive auxiliary verb 드리다 (deurida, 'to give/do for an esteemed person', from Middle Korean 드리다 'to offer up'). Literally 'to move/transfer [something] as a humble service for you'.

history.meaning: to move (intransitive) → to move, transfer (transitive/causative)
to move, relocate, or transfer (something/someone) humbly for a respected person

morphemes.meaning: humble benefactive auxiliary ('do for an honored person')

옮겨드리다.notes: In polite workplace or service Korean (such as a PD or assistant speaking to a senior guest or cast member), 자리 옮겨드릴까요? means 'Shall I move your seat / escort you to another spot?'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 옮기다

옮기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 옮기다, formed from 옮다 ('to move from one place to another, shift, spread') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to move something to another place, transfer, translate

cognates.meaning: choice, optional feature or contractual clause

옵션.etymology: Loanword borrowed from English option (ultimately from Latin optiō, 'free choice, preference', from optāre 'to choose, wish for'). While retaining the general sense of 'a choice or alternative', 옵션 underwent marked semantic narrowing in South Korean commercial, real-estate, automotive, and entertainment-contract usage to mean 'an included appliance/feature, extra add-on perk, or supplementary condition attached to a main deal'.

history.meaning: act of choosing; optional feature or contractual right
choice; extra feature, included studio appliance (풀옵션), or add-on bonus condition

옵션.notes: In Korean apartment hunting, 풀옵션 (full option) means a studio comes fully equipped with a washer, fridge, and A/C; in colloquial banter, 옵션이 붙다 means 'an extra condition or add-on perk is attached'.

rootFamily.gloss: fully equipped with appliances/extras (Konglish full option)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 옵션

옷.etymology: Core native Korean monosyllabic noun inherited directly from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 옷 (wos, 'clothes, garment, attire') and attested earlier in twelfth-century Early Middle Korean (Jilin leishi / 계림유사) with a final sibilant coda. Historically its stem final -ㅅ was pronounced as a true sibilant [s] before vowel-initial case markers (e.g., Middle Korean 오시 [wosi] for modern 옷이 [osi]).

history.meaning: clothes, garment, outer attire
clothes, outfit, garment

옷.notes: In Korean phonology, 옷 illustrates coda neutralization: in isolation or before a consonant it is pronounced [옫] ([ot]), before a vowel-initial grammatical particle (옷이, 옷을) the ㅅ resyllabifies as [오시, 오슬], and before a vowel-initial lexical compound (옷안) it reduces to [오단].

rootFamily.gloss: clothing, attire, style of dress (옷 + 차림)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 옷

와.etymology: Native Korean primary expressive interjection (감탄사) formed with an open-mouth labial-velar glide [wa], iconically vocalizing a sudden intake or release of breath upon experiencing awe, surprise, delight, or crowd excitement. In contemporary speech, its exclamatory use is phonetically and pragmatically reinforced by English wow (와우) and pan-East Asian exclamations such as Chinese 哇 (wā) and Japanese わあ (wā).

history.meaning: expressive cry of a crowd or exclamation of astonishment/delight

와.notes: Intonation determines the nuance: a high, rising-falling 와! expresses genuine amazement or joy ('Wow!'), whereas a flat, drawn-out 와... with a sigh expresses disbelief or exasperation ('Whoa, seriously...').

rootFamily.gloss: in a sudden rushing crowd or collapse (ideophone)
uproariously, with a loud collective roar (와글와글)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 와

와닿다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed by fusing 와 (wa, the infinitive/connective form of 오다 oda, 'to come', from Middle Korean 오다 wota) with 닿다 (data, 'to touch, reach, make contact', from Middle Korean 다히다 / 닿다). While the literal physical sense 'to come and touch' exists, the fused verb 와닿다 has undergone metaphorical internalization to mean that words, emotions, or artistic works 'reach and touch one's heart—i.e., resonate deeply, hit home, or feel tangibly real'.

history.meaning: to come + to reach or make physical contact
to come into contact; (figuratively) to hit home, resonate, feel real to the heart

와닿다.notes: Frequently modified by 마음에 ('to the heart') or 피부로 ('through the skin / viscerally'), as in 그 대사가 마음에 확 와닿았어 ('That line of dialogue really hit home for me').

rootFamily.gloss: to touch, reach, arrive at contact
to make contact, reach out (맞 + 닿다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 와닿다

와보다.etymology: Native Korean serial and auxiliary verb construction combining 와 (wa, the infinitive form of 오다 oda, 'to come', from Middle Korean 오다 wota) with 보다 (boda, 'to see, look at', or as an auxiliary verb 'to try doing, experience', from Middle Korean 보다 pwota). Depending on context and prosody, it either means literally 'to come and look' (serial verbs: 와서 보다) or experientially 'to try coming / have the experience of coming here' (main verb + auxiliary 보다).

history.meaning: to come + to see / to try doing (auxiliary)
to come and see; to try coming or have visited before

morphemes.meaning: to see, look; to try or experience doing

와보다.notes: In imperatives like 이리 와 봐! ('Come here and look!' or 'Come over here for a second!'), 보다 softens the command or invites inspection; in past tense 여기 와 봤어? ('Have you been here before?'), it marks past experience.

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look; to try doing
to go and see; to have been somewhere (가 + 보다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 보다

cognates.meaning: exclamation of astonishment, admiration, or excitement

와우.etymology: Loanword interjection borrowed directly from English wow (originally attested in sixteenth-century Scots and popularized worldwide in twentieth-century American English as an expressive exclamation of astonishment, admiration, or pleasure). Adopted into modern colloquial Korean and television entertainment banter as a breezy, playful, or slightly theatrical alternative to native 와 (wa) or 우와 (uwa).

history.meaning: natural exclamation of wonder, surprise, or admiration
wow! (colloquial and playful exclamation of admiration or surprise)

와우.notes: Compared to native 와! or 우와!, saying 와우 (wau) in Korean sounds intentionally hip, playful, or slightly ironic/theatrical, often accompanied by a thumbs-up or English-style reaction in variety shows.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 와우

와이프.etymology: Loanword borrowed from English wife (which evolved from Middle English wif and Old English wīf, 'woman, female, wife', from Proto-Germanic *wībą). Borrowed into late twentieth-century South Korean conversational speech, 와이프 became widely used by husbands in casual and workplace settings to refer to their own wife (or a colleague's wife), chosen by many speakers as a modern, neutral middle ground between formal 아내/부인 and slightly blunt/old-fashioned 마누라 or 집사람.

history.meaning: woman → female spouse, married woman
one's wife (casual modern conversational term)

와이프.notes: In Korean workplace conversation, men frequently say 우리 와이프 ('my wife') to peers; for formal occasions, use 아내 (for one's own wife) or 부인 / 사모님 (respectfully for someone else's wife).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 와이프

와주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb formed by linking 와 (wa, the infinitive/connective form of 오다 oda, 'to come', from Middle Korean 오다 wota) with the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, literally 'to give', from Middle Korean 주다 cwuta). In Korean grammar, attaching -아/어 주다 frames the action of coming not merely as physical motion, but as a welcome favor, kindness, or emotional support directed toward the speaker or beneficiary.

history.meaning: to come + to give / do for someone's benefit
to come for someone's sake, to grace someone with one's presence

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary ('give / do as a favor for someone')

와주다.notes: In Korean etiquette, thanking someone for attending an event or visiting requires the benefactive 와 주셔서 감사합니다 ('Thank you for coming [for my sake]')—saying bare *와서 감사합니다 sounds unnatural and ungrateful.

rootFamily.gloss: to give; to do as a favor for someone
to come for an honored person (polite/humble counterpart)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 주다

cognates.meaning: in the vortex of, in the midst of turmoil or controversy

와중.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 渦中, composed of 渦 (소용돌이 와, wa, 'whirlpool, eddy, vortex, swirling water') and 中 (가운데 중, jung, 'middle, center, inside'). Literally meaning 'inside a swirling whirlpool', it evolved metaphorically into a high-frequency noun (almost always followed by the locative particle 에 or 에도) denoting 'in the midst of a chaotic, hectic, or turbulent situation'.

history.meaning: the center of a whirlpool or swirling eddy
the thick of turmoil; in the middle of a busy or chaotic situation

와중.notes: Used almost exclusively with an adnominal clause and locative particle—e.g., 바쁜 와중에도 ('even in the midst of being hectic') or 그 와중에 ('even in the middle of all that chaos').

rootFamily.gloss: in the middle of, during (Sino-Korean 途中)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 와중

완료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 完了, pairing 完 (완전할 완, 'whole, complete, intact') with 了 (마칠 료, 'finish, conclude'). Frequently used as a concise status marker at the end of checklist items ('done, completed') as well as with -하다/-되다 in formal announcements.
완료.notes: Commonly called out after a task noun on a checklist (준비 완료 'prep complete').

완만하다.etymology: Built from Sino-Korean 완만 (緩慢), uniting 緩 (느슨할 완, 'gentle, loose, slack, unhurried') and 慢 (더딜 만, 'slow, sluggish'), plus the native adjective suffix -하다. While it can describe a sluggish pace in economics (완만한 회복 'gradual recovery'), its most common physical use in Korean is topographical: describing a gentle, easy incline or curve (완만한 경사, 완만한 언덕) in contrast to a steep precipice (가파르다).
완만하다.notes: Takes the adnominal form 완만한 before nouns like 언덕 ('hill') or 경사 ('slope').

완벽하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 완벽 (完璧, 'flawlessness, perfection', from a classical Chinese historical idiom 完璧歸趙 meaning 'to return the priceless Heshibi jade disc whole and unscathed [完] to the State of Zhao') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.form: 完璧 ('unscathed jade disc') -> 완벽 + -하다 -> 완벽하다
history.meaning: to be flawless, complete, perfect

완성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 完成, composed of 完 (완, 'whole, complete, intact') and 成 (성, 'to accomplish, to become, to achieve'). Borrowed from Literary Chinese 完成 ('to bring to completion'), where two near-synonymous telic verbs reinforce the sense of bringing a work or project to its final, intact state.

history.meaning: to bring to completion, to make whole and accomplished
completion, finishing, perfection of a work

완성.notes: Frequently combines with 하다 (완성하다, transitive 'to complete') and 되다 (완성되다, intransitive/passive 'to be completed'), and appears in media production as 완성도 (degree of perfection/polish).

완성되다.etymology: Hybrid passive/inchoative verb formed from Sino-Korean 완성 (完成, 'completion, perfection', from 完 'whole, complete' + 成 'to accomplish, achieve') + native 되다 ('to become, be made').

history.meaning: to be completed, finished, brought to perfection

완성하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb formed from Sino-Korean 완성 (完成, 'completion', from 完 'complete' + 成 'accomplish') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to complete, finish, accomplish fully

완전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 完全, uniting 完 (완, 'whole, intact, undamaged') and 全 (전, 'all, entire, complete'). Originally a stative noun in Literary Chinese meaning 'intactness without defect', it came to be used adverbially in colloquial Modern Korean (alongside 완전히) as an emphatic intensifier meaning 'totally' or 'completely'.

history.meaning: intact, whole, preserved without flaw or damage
completeness, perfection (noun)
completely, totally, utterly (colloquial adverb)

완전.notes: In formal writing, the derived adverb 완전히 ('completely') or descriptive verb 완전하다 ('to be complete') is preferred; bare 완전 as an adverb ('totally!') is a hallmark of lively spoken Korean.

완전히.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 완전 (完全, 'completeness, wholeness', from 完 'whole' + 全 'intact, entire') + native adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: completely, wholly, entirely

완충재.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 완충재 (緩衝材), joining 완충 (緩衝, 'buffering, softening a shock', from 緩 'slack, gentle, slow' + 衝 'collision, impact') and 재 (材, 'material, timber').

history.meaning: shock-absorbing packing material, cushioning (such as bubble wrap or styrofoam)

왈츠.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed via English waltz from German Walzer ('triple-time ballroom dance', derived from walzen 'to revolve, roll, glide').

history.meaning: waltz dance or music in 3/4 time

왕따.etymology: Late-1990s South Korean student slang blend combining the Sino-Korean augmentative prefix 왕- (王, literally 'king', used productively to mean 'supreme, extreme, mega-') with 따, the clipped initial syllable of the native Korean noun 따돌림 ('ostracism, bullying, shunning', nominalized from 따돌리다 'to isolate, to leave out in the cold').

history.meaning: to alienate, to ostracize / group ostracism
severe group ostracism, or the outcast/loner targeted by it

왕따.notes: Denotes both the act of collective ostracism (왕따를 시키다 'to ostracize someone') and the person subjected to it (왕따가 되다 'to become an outcast'). Related slang includes 은따 (subtle ostracism) and 전따 (school-wide outcast).

rootFamily.gloss: to ostracize, to leave out, to alienate

왕싸가지.etymology: Hybrid colloquial compound formed from the Sino-Korean intensifying prefix 왕- (王, 'king, supreme, utter') attached to native Korean 싸가지 ('manners, courtesy, promising character'). 싸가지 itself derives via tensification and palatalization from 싹아지, a diminutive of 싹 ('sprout, shoot, bud' < Middle Korean 싀악/싹) + diminutive suffix -아지, via the agrarian metaphor of judging a plant's future yield from its young sprout (싹수).

history.meaning: young sprout, shoot; nascent promise or character in a youth
basic manners, consideración for others (chiefly in negative expressions)
utterly ill-mannered person, total brat

morphemes.meaning: sprout, bud; figuratively manners or promise (< 싹)

왕싸가지.notes: While 싸가지가 없다 means 'to have no manners / to be rude', prefixing 왕- turns the noun itself into a character label for someone who is notoriously arrogant or bratty.

rootFamily.gloss: promise, sign of future success; basic manners

왜.etymology: Native Korean interrogative adverb ('why, for what reason'), contracted in Early Modern Korean from Middle Korean 오🆈 / 어이 ('how, why').

history.meaning: why, for what reason

왜냐면.etymology: Colloquial contracted conjunction from 왜냐하면 ('if one asks why it is so; because'), grammaticalized from the interrogative adverb 왜 ('why' < Middle Korean 오ㆎ, a contraction of 어이 'how/why'), the copula stem -이-, the interrogative quotative ending -냐, the pro-verb 하- ('to say/do'), and the conditional connective ending -면 ('if'). Dropping the medial syllable -하- yields the conversational form 왜냐면.

history.meaning: why, for what reason
if you ask why; because, for the reason that
because (conversational contraction)

왜냐면.notes: Prescriptively paired with a clause ending in -기 때문이다 ('Because... it is due to...'), though in casual speech speakers simply end the sentence with -거든(요) or a regular polite ending.

왠지.etymology: Standard contracted adverb from 왜인지 ('whether/what the reason is; for some unknown reason'), composed of the interrogative 왜 ('why' < Middle Korean 오ㆎ), the copula stem -이- ('to be'), and the indirect question / uncertainty suffix -ㄴ지. The sequence 왜 + 이- coalesces into the single syllable 왠-, expressing vague intuition or inexplicable feeling ('somehow').

history.meaning: what the reason might be, for whatever reason
somehow, for some reason, inexplicably

왠지.notes: A classic Korean spelling trap: 왠지 ('somehow' = 왜인지) is the ONLY word spelled with 왠; every other occurrence is spelled 웬 (from 어찌 된, e.g., 웬일 'what matter', 웬만하면 'if possible').

rootFamily.gloss: what sort of, for what reason (distinct root < 어찌 된)

외곽.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 外郭, consisting of 外 (외, 'outside, outer, external') and 郭 (곽, 'outer city wall, rampart, rim'). In traditional East Asian urban architecture, 城 (성) denoted the inner citadel wall while 郭 (곽) denoted the outer defensive ring wall; from 'outer fortification ring' the meaning generalized to the 'outskirts, periphery, or outer suburbs' of a city.

history.meaning: outer defensive wall encircling an inner walled city (城)
outer rampart; outskirts, periphery, outer suburbs of a metropolis

외곽.notes: Commonly heard in urban geography and traffic reports, such as 서울 외곽 ('the outskirts of Seoul') or 외곽 순환 도로 ('outer ring road / beltway').

외국.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 外國, formed from 外 (외, 'outside, external, beyond') and 國 (국, 'country, state, realm'). Attested in Classical Chinese for states lying outside one's own polity or dynasty, and adopted into Korean to denote any foreign nation or 'abroad' in contrast to 국내 (國內, 'domestic') or 한국 (韓國, 'Korea').

history.meaning: states or realms outside the central domain
foreign country, overseas, abroad

외국.notes: Whereas 해외 (海外, 'overseas') emphasizes crossing the sea or international reach, 외국 (外國) focuses on the cultural and political status of being another nation (hence 외국인 'foreigner' and 외국어 'foreign language').

외국계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 外國系, combining 외국 (外國, 'foreign country', from 外 'outside' + 國 'country') with the Sino-Korean bound suffix -계 (系, 'system, lineage, affiliation, thread'). Modeled on modern East Asian corporate and sociological terminology to classify businesses, capital, or individuals by their institutional or ancestral lineage.

history.meaning: foreign country + lineage/affiliation
foreign-affiliated, foreign-invested (especially of corporations)

외국계.notes: Most frequently modifies 기업 or 회사 in expressions like 외국계 기업 ('foreign-affiliated company' or multinational subsidiary operating in Korea).

외로워지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative verb formed from the descriptive verb stem 외롭- ('to be lonely, solitary', irregular ㅂ-stem) + infinitive linker -어 + inchoative auxiliary verb 지다 ('to become') + declarative suffix -다. The adjective 외롭다 is attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 외롭다 (woylwopta), derived from the native noun/prefix 외- (woy, 'single, solitary, one-sided, isolated') plus the deadjectival suffix -롭- ('characterized by').

history.meaning: to be solitary, isolated, or lonely
to become lonely, to grow lonesome

외로워지다.notes: Note that the initial 외- in 외롭다 is a pure native Korean root meaning 'single/alone' (as in 외아들 'only son' or 외길 'single path'), not the Sino-Korean Hanja 外 ('outside').

외모.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 外貌, composed of 外 (외, 'outside, external, outward') and 貌 (모, 'countenance, facial features, appearance, demeanor'). In Literary Chinese, 外貌 contrasted a person's visible physical bearing and facial features with their inner disposition (內心, 내심).

history.meaning: outward countenance, physical bearing and facial appearance
outward looks, physical attractiveness or appearance

외모.notes: Central to cultural discussions in Korea such as 외모 지상주의 (外貌至上主義, 'lookism' or the belief that physical appearance is supreme).

rootFamily.gloss: appearance, aspect, figure (Sino-Korean + native blend origin)

cognates.meaning: staying out overnight away from home or barracks

외박.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 外泊, formed from 外 (외, 'outside, away from home') and 泊 (박, 'to anchor a boat for the night, to lodge, to stay overnight'). Originally a maritime verb in Classical Chinese meaning 'to moor a vessel in shallow water', 泊 generalized to lodging overnight, and 外泊 came to mean spending the night away from one's household, dormitory, or military base.

history.meaning: to moor a boat; to lodge for the night
staying out overnight away from home, dorm, or barracks

외박.notes: Carries two distinct everyday nuances in Korea: an authorized overnight leave pass for military conscripts or dorm students, and in family/relationship contexts, staying out all night without coming home.

rootFamily.gloss: lodging, staying overnight at an inn or hotel
two days and one night (1 night, 2 days)

외박하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining the Sino-Korean action noun 외박 (外泊, from 外 'outside, away from home' + 泊 'to lodge overnight, to moor') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, to perform'). Literally 'to do an outside-lodging', i.e., to sleep away from one's own home or quarters overnight.

history.meaning: overnight stay outside + light verb 'to do'
to stay out overnight, to sleep away from home

외박하다.notes: In Korean family dramas and variety shows like *The Producers*, adults living with their parents are still playfully scolded for 외박하다 ('staying out all night').

rootFamily.gloss: going out, leaving the house temporarily

외우다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 외오다 ('to recite from memory, learn by heart').

history.meaning: to recite aloud from memory
to memorize, learn by heart, recite

외제차.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound from 外製車, composed of 외제 (外製, 'foreign-made', from 外 'outside, foreign' + 製 'to manufacture, to make, to tailor') and 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, automobile'). Contrasts directly with 국산차 (國産車, 'domestically produced car').

history.meaning: foreign-manufactured + vehicle
imported car, foreign-made automobile

외제차.notes: In older South Korean usage, 외제 ('foreign-made goods') and 외제차 carried strong prestige and luxury connotations due to strict import tariffs; today 수입차 (輸入車, 'imported car') is equally common in formal media.

왼손.etymology: Native Korean compound of adnominal prefix 왼- ('left') and 손 ('hand').
왼손.notes: Pairs with 오른손 ('right hand') and 왼쪽 ('left side').

왼쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 왼 ('left-hand; originally twisted, reversed, wrong way', adnominal of Middle Korean 외다 'to be wrong, reversed') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the left-hand side

요.etymology: Native Korean proximal demonstrative determiner formed by Korean sound symbolism (음상징) from the neutral proximal determiner 이 ('this, near the speaker'). By shifting the neutral high vowel ㅣ (i) to the bright/yang rounded vowel ㅛ (yo), Korean creates a diminutive, affective, or immediacy-highlighting variant meaning 'this little, this very, these immediate (past few days/things)'. Also fossilized in temporal compounds like 요새 and 요즘.

history.meaning: this (right here, immediate, diminutive, or pejorative/endearing)

morphemes.meaning: proximal demonstrative determiner ('this very / these immediate')

요.notes: The entire Korean demonstrative system has bright-vowel diminutive/affective counterparts: 이 → 요 ('this right here'), 그 → 고 ('that little'), 저 → 조 ('that little over there'). Used before time words (요 며칠 'these past few days'), it stresses immediacy.

요거.etymology: Colloquial native Korean pronoun contracted from 요것 ('this little/cute thing right here'), which combines the sound-symbolic proximal determiner 요 ('this little, this immediate', bright-vowel shift from 이 'this') with the bound noun 것 ('thing, object'). In spoken Korean, final -ㅅ before a pause or non-subject particle regularly drops in casual pronouns (이것 > 이거, 그것 > 그거, 요것 > 요거).

history.meaning: this little thing, this immediate object
this little one, this cute/handy thing right here (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: bound noun ('thing, object', contracted from 것)

요거.notes: Adds a nuance of endearment, playfulness, or cheeky familiarity compared to neutral 이거 ('this thing')—ideal when pointing at a cute snack, a cherished item ('this little egg of mine'), or a clever trick.

cognates.meaning: to demand, to request, to require

요구하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound from 要求 (요구, 'demand, claim, request') + native light verb 하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean stem combines 要 (요, 'to seek, to demand, to need; essential') and 求 (구, 'to seek, to ask for, to request'), an established Classical Chinese coordinate compound meaning 'to seek and claim as necessary'.

history.meaning: to seek, to ask for, to claim as necessary
to demand, to require, to call for

morphemes.meaning: to seek, to request, to ask for

요구하다.notes: Stronger and more assertive than 부탁하다 ('to ask a favor') or 요청하다 (要請하다, 'to formally request'); 요구하다 implies demanding something one considers a right, condition, or necessity.

요금.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 料金, formed from 料 (료 > 요 via the Korean initial law 두음법칙, 'to measure grain, to calculate, material, allowance') and 金 (금, 'metal, gold, money'). Coined in Meiji-era Japan as 料金 (ryōkin) to denote a measured monetary fee or tariff for a service (such as transit, utilities, or telecommunications) and borrowed into Korean via Sino-Korean reading.

history.meaning: calculated monetary fee or rate for a service
fee, fare, charge, utility/service rate
history.stage: Modern Korean (South Korean standard with initial law)

morphemes.meaning: to measure, calculate, material, fee (from 료 via initial law)

요금.notes: Used specifically for metered utilities, fares, and public/commercial service rates (버스 요금 'bus fare', 전기 요금 'electricity bill', 통신 요금 'phone charges'), whereas school tuition is 등록금 and admission tickets are 입장료.

cognates.meaning: gist, essentials; knack, trick of the trade

요령.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 要領, joining 要 (요, 'waistband of a garment; pivotal point, essential', original graph for 腰 'waist') and 領 (령, 'neckband or collar of a robe; to lead'). Derived from a Classical Chinese metaphor in the *Book of Rites* (禮記): when lifting or folding heavy robes, one grasps the waistband (要) and collar (領) to control the whole garment effortlessly—hence 'the essential point' and by extension 'practical knack, savvy, or street smarts'.

history.meaning: waistband and collar of a garment; the pivotal essentials of a matter
essential gist; practical knack, know-how, or clever shortcut

요령.notes: Can be positive (요령이 있다 'to have the knack / work smartly') or slightly negative (요령을 피우다 'to cut corners / shirk hard work using clever tricks').

요리.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 요리 (料理), joining 료/요 (料, 'to measure grain, calculate, ingredients, material') and 리 (理, 'to dress jade, put in order, manage'); originally meant 'arranging and managing affairs', then specialized in East Asian usage to 'preparing food, cooking, dish'.

history.meaning: measuring and managing -> culinary preparation, cooking, dish

요새.etymology: Native Korean compound contraction from 요사이 ('these days, recently'), composed of the proximal determiner 요 ('this immediate', sound-symbolic variant of 이 'this') and the native noun 사이 ('interval, space, time between' < Middle Korean 사ㅿㅣ, where medial ㅿ z was lost). The two syllables of 사이 contracted into the single front-vowel syllable 새 (as also seen in 밤새 < 밤사이 'overnight').

history.meaning: this immediate interval of time; recently
history.stage: Late Middle to Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: these days, lately, nowadays (noun and adverb)

morphemes.meaning: this immediate, recent (from proximal determiner 이)
interval, span of time (contracted from 사이)

요새.notes: Be careful not to confuse native Korean 요새 ('these days, lately') with its Sino-Korean homograph 요새 (要塞, 'fortress, stronghold'). In conversation, 요새 and 요즘 are virtually interchangeable.

요정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 妖精, combining 妖 (요, 'bewitching, supernatural, enchanting, eerie') and 精 (정, 'essence, spirit, vital energy, sprite'). In traditional Chinese folklore (such as *Journey to the West*), 妖精 denoted a shape-shifting nature spirit or seductive demon; in the modern era, via Japanese translation of European folklore (妖精, yōsei), it was repurposed in Korean and Japanese to translate Western 'fairy, pixie, or elf'.

history.meaning: bewitching nature spirit, shape-shifting sprite or goblin
fairy, sprite, pixie; figuratively a charming K-pop idol or star

요정.notes: In Korean pop culture and variety broadcasting, 요정 ('fairy') is affectionately used as a title for first-generation girl groups (like S.E.S. and Fin.K.L.) or for cast members who bring ratings luck (시청률 요정 'ratings fairy').

요즘.etymology: Native Korean temporal compound contracted from 요즈음 ('these days, nowadays'), formed from the proximal determiner 요 ('this immediate', sound-symbolic variant of 이 'this') and the native noun 즈음 ('approximate time, occasion, juncture'). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 요ㅿㅡᆷ (yozum, from 이/요 + ㅿㅡᆷ 'time/interval'), where the lenited sibilant ㅿ (z) later shifted to ㅈ (j) in Early Modern Korean, yielding 요즈음 and its contracted standard form 요즘.

history.meaning: around this time, recently, these days
this approximate period of time, lately
nowadays, these days, recently

morphemes.meaning: this immediate, near (from proximal determiner 이)

요즘.notes: Both 요즘 and uncontracted 요즈음 are standard Korean, though 요즘 is overwhelmingly preferred in everyday speech and writing. Often used directly before nouns (요즘 사람들 'people these days') or as a sentence-initial adverb.

rootFamily.gloss: around the time of, approximate juncture

욕.etymology: Sino-Korean single-character noun from 辱 (욕, 'disgrace, humiliation, insult, verbal abuse'). The character 辱 combines 辰 (a shell sickle used in weeding) and 寸 (hand), originally depicting agricultural labor or punishment under threat of disgrace. In Korean, 욕 underwent semantic specialization from 'humiliation/dishonor' to 'profanity, curse words, swearing, and harsh criticism'.

history.meaning: disgrace, humiliation, dishonor, to insult
humiliation; verbal abuse, profanity, swearing, harsh criticism

욕.notes: Do not confuse 욕 (辱, 'insult, swearing') with its Sino-Korean homophones 욕 (慾, 'desire, greed', as in 욕심) and 욕 (浴, 'bathing', as in 목욕 and 욕실). In Korean, 욕 covers everything from mild scolding/criticism to actual profanity (욕설).

욕먹다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean idiomatic compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 욕 (辱, 'insult, verbal abuse, criticism') and the native Korean verb 먹다 ('to eat, to consume, to take in' < Middle Korean 먹다 mekta). Korean productively uses 먹다 as a patient-receiving light verb for unpleasant or experiential things one 'absorbs' (e.g., 나이를 먹다 'to grow a year older', 겁을 먹다 'to get scared', 욕을 먹다 'to be cursed at / criticized').

history.meaning: insult/abuse + to eat/absorb > to be on the receiving end of abuse
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean idiom

history.meaning: to be criticized, to get cursed out, to take flak

morphemes.meaning: to eat, to absorb, to suffer/receive (verb stem)

욕먹다.notes: In Korea, there is a famous humorous folk belief that 욕을 많이 먹으면 오래 산다 ('If you get criticized/cursed at a lot, you will live a long life'), often used to comfort someone who is taking public flak.

rootFamily.gloss: to swear, to badmouth, to insult
to eat; to absorb or take in (age, fear, criticism)

욕실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 욕실 (浴室), joining 욕 (浴, 'to bathe, wash the body') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: bathing room, bathroom

욕실용.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 浴室用, consisting of 욕실 (浴室, 'bathroom', from 浴 'to bathe, wash' + 室 'room, chamber') and the Sino-Korean bound suffix -용 (用, 'use, purpose, intended for'). The suffix -용 (用) attaches productively to nouns to indicate functional designation ('for use in/by X').

history.meaning: bathing room + for the use of
for bathroom use, bathroom-grade (slippers, mats, organizers)

욕실용.notes: Note that 욕 here is 浴 ('bathing'), not 辱 ('insult'). In Korean households, 욕실용 슬리퍼 ('bathroom slippers') are a quintessential daily item kept at the bathroom threshold.

욕심내다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 욕심 (慾心, 'greed, covetousness, strong desire', from 慾 'desire, appetite' + 心 'heart, mind') + native Korean 내다 ('to put forth, produce, show').

history.meaning: to show greed, covet, be ambitious for more

욕을.etymology: Inflected accusative phrase consisting of the Sino-Korean noun 욕 (辱, 'insult, profanity, criticism') followed by the native Korean postpositional object marker -을 (used after consonant-final nouns; < Middle Korean -을/-으란). Appears as the direct object of verbs of speaking or receiving, such as 욕을 하다 ('to hurl insults / badmouth') and 욕을 먹다 ('to receive criticism / take flak').

history.meaning: disgrace/insult + accusative case marker
insults, profanity, criticism (as grammatical direct object)

morphemes.meaning: accusative (direct object) case marker after a consonant

욕을.notes: Pronounced [요글] via regular Korean liaison (연음), where the final velar stop ㄱ of 욕 moves into the onset of the vowel-initial particle -을.

rootFamily.gloss: to swear, to badmouth, to criticize
to get criticized, to be cursed at

욕하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 욕 (辱, 'insult, disgrace, profanity, verbal abuse') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, to say'). While Classical Chinese used 辱 transitively to mean 'to disgrace or humiliate', Korean 욕하다 specifically denotes uttering profanity, cursing, or badmouthing someone behind their back or to their face.

history.meaning: insult/profanity + light verb 'to do/say'
to swear, to curse, to badmouth, to revile

욕하다.notes: Pronounced [요카다] because the final ㄱ of 욕 and the initial ㅎ of 하다 coalesce into aspirated ㅋ [kʰ] by regular Korean consonant aspiration (거센소리되기).

rootFamily.gloss: to get criticized, to take flak

용감하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 용감 (勇敢), combining 勇 (날랠 용, 'brave, valiant, courageous') and 敢 (감히 감, 'daring, bold, venturing'), plus the native adjective suffix -하다. It translates universally as 'brave' or 'courageous', encompassing both heroic physical courage and the cheerful, everyday boldness required to step forward, volunteer, or try an intimidating new recipe.

cognates.meaning: business, matter to attend to, errand

용건.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 用件, combining 用 (용, 'use, function, business, task to perform') and 件 (건, 'item, matter, affair, document'). Originally coalesced in modern Japanese-influenced Sino-administrative usage (用件, yōken) to mean 'a specific matter of business or errand that requires attention or communication'.

history.meaning: item of business, matter to be attended to
history.stage: Early Modern East Asian administrative term

history.meaning: business at hand, specific reason for calling, visiting, or texting

용건.notes: Often used when cutting to the chase in phone calls, messages, or meetings: 용건만 간단히 말하다 ('to state only one's business briefly / get straight to the point').

용기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 勇氣, formed from 勇 (용, 'brave, valiant, bold, forceful') and 氣 (기, 'breath, vital energy, spirit, morale'). Attested in Classical Chinese military and philosophical texts, where 勇氣 denoted the inner vital spirit (氣) that empowers a person to act bravely without fear.

history.meaning: valiant vital energy, martial spirit, boldness
courage, bravery, nerve (both moral and physical)

용기.notes: Collocates natively with 내다 ('to put forth, muster'): 용기를 내다 ('to muster up courage'). Also has a common Sino-Korean homophone 용기 (容器, 'container, vessel, Tupperware').

cognates.meaning: to tolerate, to accept, to sanction
to hold, to contain, to tolerate, to accommodate

용납하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound from 容納 (용납, 'acceptance, tolerance, accommodation') + native light verb 하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean stem combines 容 (용, 'to contain, to hold, to allow, to forgive') and 納 (납, 'to receive, to admit, to take in'). In Literary Chinese, 容納 meant both physically holding/containing a volume and figuratively receiving someone's words or faults with broad-minded forbearance.

history.meaning: to contain, to take in; to receive with forbearance and tolerance
to tolerate, to pardon, to accept or brook (transgressions or behavior)

morphemes.meaning: to receive, admit, accept, take in

용납하다.notes: Used predominantly in negative or rhetorical constructions (용납할 수 없다 'cannot tolerate / will not stand for it', 용납이 안 되다 'to be unacceptable/unforgivable').

용달.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 용달 (用達), from Hanja 用 (용, 'to use, employ, function') and 達 (달, 'to reach, deliver, accomplish'). Borrowed and specialized via Meiji/Shōwa Japanese 用達 (yōtatsu, 'transacting business, supplying goods, delivery errand'), in modern South Korean usage it functions primarily as an ellipsis of 용달차 (用達車), denoting a small commercial pickup truck or light moving van hired for short-haul freight and studio prop transport.

history.meaning: fulfilling orders, purveying supplies, commercial delivery service
small moving van or light commercial freight service on call

용달.notes: For a studio apartment or dorm move with minimal furniture, Koreans hire a 용달 (typically a 1-ton Porter or Bongo truck) rather than a full-service 이삿짐센터 (moving company).

rootFamily.gloss: light commercial delivery truck, moving van

우기다.etymology: Native Korean verb 우기다 ('to insist stubbornly, press one's point'), morphologically analyzed as a fossilized causative derivation from the native verb stem 욱- (욱다, 'to bend inward, be dented, yield under pressure') plus the causative suffix -이- and infinitive ending -다. The original physical sense 'to force inward, overpower, press down' underwent semantic shift in Early Modern Korean toward 'to force one's claim through against reason or opposition'.

history.meaning: to press inward, overpower, force down
to insist stubbornly, assert unreasonably

morphemes.meaning: make, cause to be forced through

우기다.notes: Carries a distinctly negative or playful nuance of stubbornly pushing an unreasonable claim (생떼를 쓰며 우기다), unlike 주장하다 ('to argue/assert' neutrally).

rootFamily.gloss: to be dented, curved inward, overpowered

우렁차다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb formed from the mimetic root 우렁- (evoking a deep, booming, resonant sound, as in 우렁우렁) + adjective-forming root 차다 ('to be full of').

history.meaning: to be booming, sonorous, loud and resonant

우르르.etymology: Native Korean ideophone and mimetic adverb (의성어·의태어) 우르르, formed by an expressive dark-vowel initial syllable 우- followed by reduplicated liquid syllables -르르 depicting continuous rolling, rumbling, or swarming motion. In Korean sound symbolism, it contrasts with its bright-vowel counterpart 와르르 (which suggests a sharper, louder, or more sudden crash or collapse), whereas 우르르 evokes a heavy crowd rushing together, thunder rolling, or water coming to a sudden boil.

history.meaning: rumblingly, rushing or swarming all at once
in a big pack, swarming all together, with a rumble

morphemes.meaning: heavy rushing, rumbling, or swarming motion

우르르.notes: Pairs with vowel-harmonic 와르르 ('crashing down loudly'); in workplace and TV production slang, 우르르 몰려다니다 describes an entourage or crew moving around in a big pack.

rootFamily.gloss: crashing down all at once (bright-vowelablaut counterpart)
with a sudden rumble or shiver (intensive variant)

우리.etymology: Native Korean first-person plural pronoun descending from Middle Korean 우리 ('we, us, our', related to 울 / 우리 'enclosure, fence, fold, group sharing one enclosure').

history.meaning: we, our group
we, us, our (often used for shared family, home, or country)

우리나라.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized compound noun 우리나라 ('our country, Korea'), composed of the first-person plural pronoun 우리 (Middle Korean 우리, 'we, our') and 나라 (Middle Korean 나라해 / 나랗, with final -ㅎ stem, 'country, state, kingdom'). Because Korean cultural and linguistic norms favor collective first-person plural possession (우리) over singular 내 ('my') for shared in-group institutions, 우리나라 became the standard idiomatic self-designation for Korea by native speakers.

history.meaning: our country, our kingdom (Joseon)
our country, Korea (lexicalized single-word noun)

우리나라.notes: Written as a single solid word without a space in standard Korean orthography, and used exclusively by Koreans to refer to Korea itself (alongside 한국).

우산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우산 (雨傘), joining 우 (雨, 'rain') and 산 (傘, 'umbrella, parasol').

history.meaning: rain umbrella

우산값.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun 우산값 ('the price of an umbrella'), formed from Sino-Korean 우산 (雨傘, from 雨 우 'rain' + 傘 산 'umbrella, parasol') and native Korean 값 (Middle Korean 값, 'price, value, cost'). Morphophonemically, an unwritten genitive interfix (-ㅅ-, 사이시옷) triggers post-nasal tensification of the following velar obstruent, yielding the pronunciation [우산깝].

history.meaning: rain parasol + price, worth
price or cost of an umbrella

우산값.notes: Pronounced [우산깝] with automatic tensification of 값 ([깝]) when attached as the head of a compound noun (compare 찻값, 집값, 밥값).

rootFamily.gloss: cost of a meal, earning one's keep

우상.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 우상 (偶像), from Hanja 偶 (우, 'carved wooden or clay human figure, puppet, mate') and 像 (상, 'likeness, image, statue'). Attested in Classical Chinese (such as the Shiji 史記) for wooden or earthen effigies, it was adopted in modern East Asian Christian and philosophical translations to render Greek eidōlon ('idol, false image') before broadening to mean any revered role model or pop-culture idol.

history.meaning: carved wooden or clay human figure, statuette
religious idol, venerated icon, idealized figure

우상.notes: While English loanword 아이돌 refers specifically to K-pop idol singers, 우상 refers either to a deeply admired personal hero ('나의 우상') or a religious/ideological idol.

rootFamily.gloss: to idolize, deify, put on a pedestal

우선.etymology: Sino-Korean compound adverb 우선 (于先 / 優先), joining 우 (于 'at, in' or 優 'surpassing, priority') and 선 (先, 'first, before, ahead').

history.meaning: first of all, before anything else, for now

우세하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjectival verb 우세하다 (優勢하다), formed from the Sino-Korean noun 우세 (優勢, from 優 우 'abundant, superior, excellent' + 勢 세 'power, force, momentum, position') combined with the native adjective-forming light verb -하다 ('to be'). Literally 'to possess superior momentum or force', it describes holding the upper hand in a contest, ratings battle, or election.

history.meaning: superior force or strategic advantage
to be dominant, hold the lead, predominate

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of

우세하다.notes: Frequently used in news broadcasts, sports, and TV ratings analysis (예: 동시간대 시청률에서 우세하다, 'to dominate in same-time-slot viewership ratings'); its direct antonym is 열세하다 (劣勢하다).

우습다.etymology: Native Korean irregular ㅂ-stem adjective 우습다 ('to be funny, laughable, ridiculous'), descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 우〯습다〯 (also attested as 웃브다). It is transparently derived from the native verb stem 웃- ('to laugh') plus the deverbal adjectival suffix -브-/-습- ('worthy of, prone to'), literally meaning 'laugh-worthy'. In modern Korean it means both 'amusing' and 'contemptibly ridiculous or easy to underestimate'.

history.meaning: laugh-worthy, amusing, laughable
funny, comical; ridiculous, trifling, easily looked down on

우습다.notes: In idiomatic expressions like 우습게 보다 ('to look down on, take lightly') or 내가 우스워 보여? ('Do I look like a joke to you?'), it means 'trifling/contemptible' rather than 'humorous'.

우승자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 優勝者, composed of 우승 (優勝, 'overall victory or championship', from 優 'superior, excelling' and 勝 'win, triumph') and the agent suffix -자 (者, 사람 자, 'person'). Unlike 승리자 ('victor' in a battle or single match), 우승자 specifically denotes the champion who takes first place at the end of a tournament, contest (대회), or judged competition.
우승자.notes: Collocates with 뽑다 ('to pick/choose a winner') or 발표하다 ('to announce the winner').

우아하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective 우아하다 (優雅하다), formed from Sino-Korean 우아 (優雅, from Hanja 優 우 'gentle, leisurely, refined, superior' + 雅 아 'courtly, graceful, refined, classical') and the native adjectival suffix -하다. In Classical Chinese poetics, 雅 denoted courtly elegance (as in the Daya 大雅 and Xiaoya 小雅 odes of the Shijing 詩經), and the compound 優雅 came to describe poised, dignified aesthetic grace.

history.meaning: courtly refinement, leisurely grace and elegance
to be elegant, graceful, poised and refined

morphemes.meaning: to be in the state of

우아하다.notes: Often used both sincerely for high-class poise and ironically in variety shows (like the famous metaphor of a swan looking 우아하다 above water while paddling furiously underneath).

우연히.etymology: Sino-Korean derived adverb 우연히 (偶然히), formed from the Sino-Korean root 우연 (偶然, from Hanja 偶 우 'to meet unexpectedly, pair up by chance' + 然 연 'thus, so, state/adverbial suffix') and the native Korean adverb-deriving suffix -히. In Classical Chinese, 偶 moved from 'two figurines facing each other' to 'an unplanned encounter', making 偶然 the standard term for fortuitous coincidence.

history.meaning: happening unexpectedly, by coincidence, fortuitously
by chance, accidentally, coincidentally

morphemes.meaning: so, thus, in such a state

우연히.notes: Contrast 우연히 ('by coincidence/chance', neutral or pleasant, e.g., 우연히 마주치다 'to bump into someone by chance') with 실수로 ('by mistake/error').

우와.etymology: Natural Korean expressive interjection (variant of 와) voicing sudden amazement, admiration, or awe ('wow!, whoa!').

history.meaning: exclamation of wonder or excitement ('wow!')

우유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우유 (牛乳), joining 우 (牛, 'cow, cattle') and 유 (乳, 'breast, milk').

history.meaning: cow's milk

우정.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 우정 (友情), from Hanja 友 (우, 'friend, companion', originally an ideogram of two hands 又 working together in harmony) and 情 (정, 'feeling, affection, inner sentiment'). Literally 'the affection between friends', it designates bond and loyalty between peers as distinct from familial affection (가족애) or romantic love (애정).

history.meaning: sentiment or bond between friends
friendship, camaraderie, fraternal loyalty

우정.notes: In Korean broadcasting and film, a cameo appearance done out of personal loyalty to the director or lead actor is called 우정 출연 (友情出演, 'friendship appearance').

우체부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우체부 (郵遞夫), joining 우 (郵, 'post station, mail'), 체 (遞, 'to hand over in relay, deliver'), and 부 (夫, 'working man, carrier').

history.meaning: mail carrier, postman

우편.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우편 (郵便), joining 우 (郵, 'posthouse, mail relay') and 편 (便, 'convenience, dispatch, message, opportunity') — adopted in late 19th-century East Asian postal reforms for the modern postal service.

history.meaning: postal service, mail

우편물.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 郵便物, formed from 우편 (郵便, 'postal service', from 郵 'post-stage relay' + 便 'convenience, dispatch') and the collective suffix -물 (物, 만물 물, 'things, physical items'). Whereas 편지 refers specifically to a personal letter, 우편물 encompasses all delivered mail including official envelopes, postcards, and parcels.
우편물.notes: Standard collective noun for letters, notices, and packages delivered by post.

우편함.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 우편함 (郵便函), combining 우편 (郵便, 'postal service, mail', from 郵 'post-station, mail relay' + 便 'convenience, dispatch') with the suffixoid 함 (函, 'wooden or metal box, case'). While 우체통 (郵遞筒) usually refers to the red public pillar box on the street where outgoing letters are dropped, 우편함 specifically designates a home's or building's receiving letterbox mounted by the gate or front door.

history.meaning: postal mail + receiving box
household mailbox, letterbox at a gate or entrance

우편함.notes: Distinguish 우편함 (the household letterbox where incoming mail arrives) from 우체통 (the street postbox for mailing letters).

욱하다.etymology: Native Korean verb 욱하다 ('to flare up in sudden anger, lose one's temper impulsively'), formed from the monosyllabic mimetic root 욱 (depicting a sudden upward surge of fiery temper, blood rushing to the head, or a wave of nausea rising in the throat) and the native light verb -하다 ('to do, act'). Its short, clipped closed syllable (-ㄱ coda) iconically mirrors a sharp, explosive burst of emotion.

history.meaning: to surge up suddenly (of anger or nausea)

morphemes.meaning: sudden upward surge of temper or heat

욱하다.notes: The adnominal phrase 욱하는 성질 ('a quick, hot-headed temper that flares up on impulse') is a staple character trait in Korean dramas and variety shows.

rootFamily.gloss: with a sudden surge of heat, anger, or emotion (intensive variant)
flaring up or surging repeatedly (bright-vowel variant)
a sudden burst of temper (adverbial usage)

운.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 운 (運, 'revolving movement of heaven and earth, fate, fortune, luck'; also 韻 'rhyme, resonance').

history.meaning: revolving destiny, fortune, luck

운동.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 운동 (運動), from Hanja 運 (운, 'to revolve, transport, circulate') and 動 (동, 'to move, stir, act'). While attested in Classical Chinese for the revolution of heavenly bodies, it was repurposed in Meiji Japan (運動 undō) to translate Western scientific 'motion' (in physics), 'bodily exercise/athletics', and 'political/social movement', entering modern Korean with all three senses intact.

history.meaning: revolving motion, circulation of celestial bodies or qi
physical motion; athletic exercise; organized social or political campaign
physical exercise, workout, sports; social/political movement; physical motion

운동.notes: Covers everything from working out at the gym (운동하다) to historical campaigns like the March First Independence Movement (삼일운동 三一運動).

운수.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 운수 (運數), from Hanja 運 (운, 'revolving cycle of fate, fortune, luck') and 數 (수, 'number, calculation, Heaven-allotted destiny'). Rooted in traditional East Asian cosmology where human fortune unfolds according to cyclical numerical proportions (기수 氣數 and 역수 曆數), it came to mean everyday luck or one's lot in life.

history.meaning: cosmological cycle and numerical allotment of fate
luck, fortune, destiny, turn of luck in daily life

운수.notes: Immortalized in Korean literature by Hyun Jin-geon's ironic 1924 realist short story 운수 좋은 날 ('A Lucky Day'), and heard in the everyday exclamation 운수 대통 (運數大通, 'hitting the jackpot of good luck').

운영진.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound noun 운영진 (運營陣), formed from 운영 (運營, 'management, operation, administration', from 運 운 'to move, wield, circulate' + 營 영 'to lay out a camp, plan, manage') plus the collective suffixoid -진 (陣, originally 'military battle formation or ranks', extended in modern Korean and Japanese to mean 'lineup, team, staff, corps'). In internet and fan-cafe culture, it specifically denotes the administrators and moderators running an online community.

history.meaning: operating management + lineup/corps of personnel
management team, organizing committee, online forum administrators/moderators

운영진.notes: In Korean fan cafes (팬카페) and online communities, 운영진 (often abbreviated 운진 or paired with singular 운영자 'admin/mod') holds the power to approve membership levels (등업) and police posts.

cognates.meaning: to revolve, orbit, operate (of machinery or systems)

운전하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb 운전하다 (運轉하다), composed of 운전 (運轉, from Hanja 運 운 'to move, convey, revolve' + 轉 전 'to turn, roll, rotate, wheel') and the native verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). In Classical Chinese and traditional Korean texts, 運轉 referred to the rotation of heavenly bodies, wheels, or capital; in modern Meiji-influenced usage, it narrowed to operating powered machinery and specifically driving an automobile or train.

history.meaning: to revolve, rotate, circulate continuously
to drive a motor vehicle, steer, or operate heavy machinery

morphemes.meaning: turn, roll, revolve (with wheel radical 車)

운전하다.notes: Notice the character 轉 (전) contains the chariot/wheel radical (車), making 운전하다 literally 'to move and turn the wheels'.

울고불고.etymology: Native Korean rhyming coordinate adverbial phrase 울고불고 ('weeping and wailing, crying one's eyes out'), formed by pairing 울고 (from the verb stem 울- 'to cry, weep' + conjunctive suffix -고 'and') with the echoic/rhyming element 불고 (historically associated with 부르짖다/불- 'to cry out, bellow, blow' + -고, reinforced by Korean labial-initial rhyming reduplication like 갈팡질팡 or 오순도순). Together they express loud, unrestrained sobbing and commotion.

history.meaning: crying and wailing loudly in tandem

울고불고.notes: Almost always followed by verbs of commotion such as 난리를 치다 ('to make a huge scene weeping and wailing') or 매달리다 ('to cling while bawling').

rootFamily.gloss: a crybaby, person who cries easily

울다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 울다 ('to cry, weep; of birds, beasts, wind, or bells, to call out, sing, ring').

history.meaning: to weep, cry; (of animals or bells) to sound
to cry, weep, chime, ring

울리다.etymology: Native Korean causative/intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 울이다, formed from 울다 ('to cry, sound, ring') + suffix -리- ('to make cry; to cause to ring, resound, echo').

history.meaning: to make someone cry; to ring, echo, reverberate

울림.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun formed from 울리다 ('to ring, resound, reverberate') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: resonance, reverberation, echo, emotional resonance

울타리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun 울타리 ('fence, hedge, protective enclosure'), analyzed historically as Middle Korean 울 ('fence, palisade, woven enclosure, cage') compounded with the bound noun element 타리 (attested in Early Modern Korean 울타리, likely related to 틀 'frame' or 다래/타래 'woven bundle, coil, wickerwork'). Metaphorically, it extends from a woven twig or wooden barrier around a homestead to a protective social or familial circle.

history.meaning: fence, enclosure, palisade
woven fence or hedge enclosing a yard; protective boundary or shelter

울타리.notes: Frequently used figuratively for a protective institution or family circle, as in 가족이라는 든든한 울타리 ('the sturdy protective shelter called family').

움직이다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 움즈기다 ('to move, stir, shift'), formed on the mimetic root 움즉- ('stirring, budging slightly') + verbalizer -이다.

history.meaning: to stir, move
to move, stir, operate

웃기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb 웃기다 ('to make someone laugh; to be funny, hilarious, or absurd'), derived transparently from the native verb stem 웃- (Middle Korean 웃-, 'to laugh, smile') plus the productive native causative suffix -기- and citation ending -다. In contemporary colloquial Korean, the active/participial forms 웃긴다 and 웃기는 function practically as adjectives meaning 'hilarious' or sarcastically 'ridiculous, preposterous'.

history.meaning: to cause to laugh, amuse
to make someone laugh; (colloquially) to be funny, hilarious, or preposterous

웃기다.notes: Depending on tone of voice, 진짜 웃긴다! can mean 'That's genuinely hilarious!' or 'How ridiculous / You've got to be kidding me!' (similar to 웃기지 마 'Don't make me laugh / Stop talking nonsense').

웃다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 웃다 (stem 웃-, 'to laugh, smile').

history.meaning: to laugh, smile
to laugh, smile

웃음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun 웃음 ('laughter, a laugh, a smile'), descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 우〯숨 (wuswum), formed from the native verb stem 웃- ('to laugh, smile') and the substantive nominalizing suffix -움/-음. Earlier phonemic spelling 우숨 reflected the surface resyllabification of stem-final -ㅅ before the vowel-initial suffix before 20th-century morphophonemic orthography restored the underlying stem spelling 웃음.

history.meaning: laughter, smiling
laugh, laughter, smile

웃음.notes: Korean 웃음 covers both audible 'laughter' and silent 'smiling' (though 미소 微笑 specifically singles out a quiet smile); thus 눈웃음 means 'smiling with one's eyes'.

웃음꽃.etymology: Native Korean metaphorical compound noun 웃음꽃 ('blossoms of laughter, radiant shared joy'), composed of 웃음 ('laughter, smiling', from verb stem 웃- + nominalizer -음) and 꽃 ('flower, blossom', from Middle Korean 곶 koc). Built on the poetic conceit that bright faces breaking into laughter around a room resemble flowers bursting into bloom, it is prototypically used with the verb 피다 ('to bloom').

history.meaning: laughter + blossom (historical constituent roots)
blossoms of laughter, lively atmosphere of shared merriment

웃음꽃.notes: Almost exclusively appears in the collocation 웃음꽃이 피다 ('blossoms of laughter bloom') or 웃음꽃을 피우다 ('to make laughter bloom' during a warm conversation).

rootFamily.gloss: blossoms of lively conversation (parallel idiom: 이야기꽃을 피우다)

웃음소리.etymology: Native Korean determinative compound noun 웃음소리 ('the sound of laughter'), formed from 웃음 ('laughter', from Middle Korean 우〯숨 < 웃- 'to laugh' + nominalizer -음) and 소리 ('sound, voice', from Middle Korean 소리〯). Morphophonemically, an underlying genitive interfix causes post-nasal fortition of the initial fricative of 소리, resulting in the standard pronunciation [우슴쏘리].

history.meaning: laughter + sound/voice
sound of laughter, peal of laughter

웃음소리.notes: Pronounced [우슴쏘리] with tensification of ㅅ to ㅆ because of the compound-internal genitive boundary (사이시옷 phenomenon), just like 울음소리 [우름쏘리] ('sound of crying') and 발걸음소리 [발꺼름쏘리] ('sound of footsteps').

워낙.etymology: Korean degree and modal adverb 워낙 ('by nature, from the start, so very, all too'), phonologically reshaped via resyllabification and vowel assimilation from the earlier attested form 원악 ('originally, extraordinarily, to an extreme degree'). Philologists trace 원악 either to a Sino-Korean compound such as 元惡/遠惡 whose literal sense bleached into an intensive adverb, or to a blend with 원체 (元體, 'originally, fundamentally, by nature'), with [wʌ.nak] spelled phonemically as 워낙 in modern standard Korean.

history.meaning: originally, from the outset; to an extraordinary or extreme degree
by nature, fundamentally; so very, to such a high degree that

morphemes.meaning: by nature, originally, to an extraordinary degree (from earlier 원악)

워낙.notes: Typically sets up a causal explanation for why something is inevitable (예: 워낙 바빠서 얼굴 보기도 힘들다, 'Because they are so very busy to begin with, it's hard even to see their face').

rootFamily.gloss: so very, originally, by nature (emphatic variant with -에)
originally, fundamentally, by very nature (functional synonym)

워낙에.etymology: Korean emphatic adverb 워낙에 ('so remarkably, by its very nature, all too'), formed by attaching the native locative/emphatic adverbial particle -에 to the degree adverb 워낙 (itself from Early Modern Korean 원악, 'from the outset, extraordinarily'). Just as 일찍 ('early') forms emphatic 일찍이/일찍에 and 원체 ('originally') forms 원체에 in colloquial speech, -에 reinforces the speaker's assessment that a quality holds true from the very start.

history.meaning: originally, by its very nature; to such a remarkable degree

워낙에.notes: Slightly more colloquial and conversational than bare 워낙, often used when giving background praise or excuses (예: 워낙에 성격이 좋아서, 'since they have such a remarkably good personality to begin with').

원.etymology: Sino-Korean morpheme 원: as the Korean currency unit ('won'), derived from 圓 ('round, round silver coin', cognate with Chinese yuan and Japanese yen); also represents 願 ('wish, desire') or 院 ('courtyard building, institute').

history.meaning: round coin -> base unit of Korean currency (KRW)

cognates.meaning: manuscript fee, payment for writing, royalties per page

원고료.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound noun 원고료 (原稿料, 'manuscript fee, scriptwriter's payment'), composed of 원고 (原稿, 'manuscript, draft, script', from 原 원 'original, source' + 稿 고 'grain stalk, rough straw draft, manuscript') plus the suffixoid -료 (料, 'fee, charge, compensation, material'). Historically calculated per 200-character squared manuscript sheet (원고지 原稿紙), in television and radio it denotes a writer's per-episode script fee.

history.meaning: original manuscript/draft + monetary fee
author's manuscript fee, broadcast scriptwriting payment per episode or article

원고료.notes: In Korean broadcasting, drama and variety writers (작가) are typically paid 원고료 per aired episode rather than a standard monthly salary, whilst performers receive 출연료 (出演料, 'appearance fee').

rootFamily.gloss: squared manuscript paper (traditionally 200 characters per sheet)

cognates.meaning: principal sum, capital (as opposed to interest)

원금.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 원금 (元金, 'principal sum of money'), from Hanja 元 (원, 'head, origin, primary, fundamental') and 金 (금, 'metal, gold, money'). Literally 'the original/primary money', it designates the initial capital lent, borrowed, or invested before the accrual of interest (이자 利子) or profit, a distinction central to traditional East Asian and modern banking law.

history.meaning: initial capital or principal sum of a loan or investment
principal (of a loan, deposit, or investment, contrasted with interest)

원금.notes: Often paired with 이자 (利子, 'interest') in the compound 원리금 (元利金, 'principal and interest combined'), or in warnings about investment risk: 원금 손실 ('loss of principal').

rootFamily.gloss: principal and interest combined (blend of 원금 + 이자)

원래.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 원래 (原來), joining 원 (原, 'source, origin, high plain') and 래 (來, 'coming from, since') — literally 'coming from the origin'.

history.meaning: from the very beginning, originally, by nature

cognates.meaning: to harbor resentment, nurse a grievance, reproach

원망.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 원망 (怨望, 'resentment, reproach, blame'), from Hanja 怨 (원, 'hatred, grievance, resentment', showing a person turning in bed 夗 over a heart 心) and 望 (망, 'to gaze from afar, expect, reproach or blame when paired with 怨'). Already lexicalized in Classical Chinese histories such as Sima Qian's Shiji (史記) to mean 'nursing a grievance and blaming someone for failing one's expectations', it entered Middle Korean as 원〯망.

history.meaning: to harbor a grievance and reproach a superior or peer
resentment, bitter reproach, grievance
resentment, blame, holding a grudge against someone

원망.notes: Unlike 복수 (復讐, active 'revenge'), 원망 focuses on the emotional bitterness of blaming someone who let you down or wronged you (예: 남을 원망하기 전에, 'before blaming/resenting others').

rootFamily.gloss: resentful, worthy of blame or grievance

cognates.meaning: unmilled log, raw timber, natural solid wood
