raw log, undressed timber, solid natural wood

원목.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 원목 (原木, 'raw timber, unmilled log, solid hardwood'), from Hanja 原 (원, 'source, origin, raw, unprocessed') and 木 (목, 'tree, wood, lumber'). Originally a forestry and lumber-trade term denoting felled logs before sawmilling, in modern interior design and furniture vocabulary it designates solid natural wood (원목 가구) in contrast to composite boards such as plywood (합판) or MDF.

history.meaning: unmilled felled logs, raw timber from the forest
raw log; solid natural wood (in furniture and interior construction)

원목.notes: In Korean home shopping and real-estate/interior contexts, 원목 is prized as a marker of quality and eco-friendliness ('solid wood' vs. 시트지/합판 veneer or particle board).

cognates.meaning: original text, master copy, script original
original manuscript, master edition, source text

원본.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 원본 (原本, 'original text, master copy, raw unedited footage/file'), from Hanja 原 (원, 'source, origin, original') and 本 (본, 'tree root, foundation, codex/book, version'). In traditional East Asian textual scholarship and woodblock printing, 原本 denoted the exemplar manuscript or first edition from which copies (사본 寫本) or translations (역본 譯本) were made; in modern broadcasting and digital media, it denotes unedited raw camera footage or an unretouched master file.

history.meaning: root foundation; original master manuscript or exemplar text in bibliography
original document; master recording, unedited raw footage or unretouched digital file

원본.notes: In TV production (like *The Producers*), 원본 (or 원본 테이프/원본 파일) refers to the raw unedited camera footage before cuts, captions (자막), or mosaic blurring are applied—contrasted with 편집본 (編輯本, 'edited version').

rootFamily.gloss: edited version, final cut (in broadcasting and publishing)

원수.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 원수 (怨讎, 'mortal enemy, sworn foe, nemesis'), from Hanja 怨 (원, 'hatred, resentment, grievance') and 讎 (수, historically read 구, 'to answer back, rival, enemy, avenge', depicting two birds 隹 facing off around speech 言). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 원〯슈〯, the second character underwent a lexicalized reading shift in Korean from expected *구 to 슈 > 수 exclusively in this word and 복수 (復讎/復讐, 'revenge'). In colloquial speech, it often appears in the umlauted form 웬수.

history.meaning: bitter enmity, blood feud, sworn adversary
mortal enemy, object of vengeance
mortal enemy, nemesis; (affectionately/exasperatedly) troublesome spouse or child in one's life

원수.notes: Do not confuse with its exact homographs 원수 (元首, 'head of state') and 원수 (元帥, 'five-star general/field marshal'). In everyday banter, Koreans often use the fronted colloquial pronunciation 웬수 ('유머러스한 애증의 대상', e.g., 전생의 웬수 'my nemesis from a past life').

rootFamily.gloss: revenge, vengeance (shares the irregular reading 수 for 讎/讐)
deep grudge, bitter resentment and hatred

원조.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 元祖 (원조), composed of 元 (으뜸 원, "first, primary, origin, head") and 祖 (조상 조, "ancestor, forebear, founder"). Originally denoting the founding ancestor of a lineage or religious sect in Classical Chinese, it underwent semantic broadening in modern Korean to designate the original creator of a genre, trend, or dish—especially ubiquitous on restaurant signage claiming to be the authentic originator.

history.meaning: primogenitor, founding ancestor of a clan or school
founder, pioneer, original creator
the original, pioneer, authentic founder (of a dish or trend)

원조.notes: Do not confuse with the homophonous Sino-Korean word 원조 (援助, "aid, financial assistance"); on Korean street signs and in pop culture, 원조 (元祖) means "the OG / the original."

rootFamily.gloss: head of state, supreme leader (元首)
founder of a sect or dynasty (시조, 始祖)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (원조)

원피스.etymology: 20th-century loanword from English one-piece (short for one-piece dress), designating a woman's dress in which bodice and skirt form a single garment.

history.meaning: one-piece dress

원하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb formed from Sino-Korean 원 (願, 'wish, desire, vow') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to wish for, want, desire

원형.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 圓形, joining 圓 (둥글 원, 'circle, round') and 形 (모양 형, 'shape, form'). It describes mathematically circular geometry, rounded architectural features, or baking tins (원형 틀, 'round cake tin'). The term is a true homograph with 원형 (原型, 'prototype, original form', from 原 'origin'), so context easily distinguishes the 'round' baking pan from the 'original' recipe.
원형.notes: Frequently acts as a prenominal modifier, as in 원형 탁자 ('round table') or 원형 틀 ('round tin').

원흉.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 元兇 or 元凶 (원흉), formed from 元 (으뜸 원, "chief, head, principal") and 兇/凶 (흉할 흉, "fierce, evil, baleful, villain"). Attested in the Classical Chinese Book of Documents (書經, Shujing) to denote the arch-criminal or ringleader of a rebellion, the term entered Korean bureaucratic and literary prose and now refers both to a chief perpetrator and figuratively to the root cause of a disaster.

history.meaning: arch-villain, chief rebel leader
ringleader of a crime or treasonous plot
prime culprit, main instigator, root cause of a problem

원흉.notes: Often used with dramatic flair in news broadcasts and workplace banter alike (e.g., 패배의 원흉, "the prime culprit behind the defeat").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (원흉)

월급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 月給 (월급), combining 月 (달 월, "moon, month") and 給 (줄 급, "supply, provide, grant, pay"). Standardized across East Asia during late 19th-century administrative and industrial modernization (parallel to Meiji Japanese 月給 gekkyū), it replaced traditional Joseon-era stipend terms such as 녹봉 (祿俸) as salaried monthly employment became the norm.

history.meaning: monthly provision or allowance issued by an office
monthly wage paid to modern civil servants and company workers
monthly salary, regular paycheck

월급.notes: Forms the basis of popular Korean office slang such as 월급루팡 ("salary Lupin," a worker who collects a paycheck while doing nothing) and 월급날 ("payday").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (월급)

월등히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adverb formed from the Sino-Korean root 越等 (월등, "surpassing a rank or grade"), composed of 越 (넘을 월, "cross over, exceed, transcend") and 等 (등급 등, "rank, class, grade, tier"), plus the productive native Korean adverb-deriving suffix -히 (-hi). Originally referring in Joseon civil service administration to promoting an official across multiple ranks at once, it generalized to mean "incomparably, by far, far and away."

history.meaning: skipping over grades or ranks in official promotion
to be far superior, to stand head and shoulders above
far more, by far, overwhelmingly

월등히.notes: Pairs naturally with comparative adjectives and verbs of superiority, such as 월등히 높다 ("to be far higher") or 월등히 앞서다 ("to be way ahead").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (월등히)

cognates.meaning: to rent, lease, borrow on credit (classical)

월세.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 月貰 (월세), uniting 月 (달 월, "month") and 貰 (세낼 세, "to rent, lease, hire on credit"). While 貰 is an ancient Classical Chinese character for leasing or buying on credit (attested in the Han-era Shuowen Jiezi), the compound 月貰 was coined within Korean legal and real-estate practice to distinguish monthly rental payments from 전세 (傳貰), Korea's lump-sum deposit lease system.

history.meaning: to lease, hire, or buy on credit
monthly property rent paid in cash
monthly rent (as opposed to lump-sum deposit 전세)

월세.notes: In Korean housing culture, 월세 (monthly rent with a smaller deposit) is constantly contrasted with 전세 (傳貰, a massive refundable key-money deposit with zero monthly rent).

rootFamily.gloss: room for rent, rental housing (셋방, 貰房)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (월세)

월요일.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 월요일 (月曜日), joining 월 (月, 'Moon'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day') — literally 'Day of the Moon' (matching Latin dies Lunae).

history.meaning: Monday

cognates.word: 月次 (げつじ, getsuji / つきなみ, tsukinami)

월차.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 月次 (월차), clipped from the labor-law compound 월차유급휴가 (月次有給休暇, "monthly paid leave"). Composed of 月 (달 월, "month") and 次 (차례 차, "order, sequence, recurring interval"), it was borrowed via modern Japanese administrative vocabulary (月次 getsuji, "monthly installment/occurrence") and specialized in Korean workplace usage to mean a monthly accrued day off.

history.meaning: monthly sequence, occurring each month

history.form: 월차 유급 휴가 (月次有給休暇)
history.meaning: statutory monthly paid day off work
monthly paid leave, personal day off

월차.notes: Although South Korean labor law officially merged statutory 월차 (monthly leave) into 연차 (年次, annual leave) in 2004, office workers still colloquially say 월차 내다 for taking a single monthly personal day off.

rootFamily.gloss: annual paid leave, year of seniority (연차, 年次)
next time, second in rank (차기, 次期)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (월차)

웬.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and exclamatory determiner (관형사) 웬 (wen, "what sort of, why on earth"). Historically contracted from the Early Modern Korean adnominal form 어짼 (eojjaen, from 어찌 "how/why" + adnominal suffix -ㄴ) via labialized variants 왱이 / 왼 (oen), before unrounding and lowering to 웬 in central Seoul speech by the late 19th century.

history.meaning: how is it that, what kind of
what sort of, what unexpected
what sort of, why on earth (expressing surprise)

웬.notes: One of the most frequent Korean spelling traps: always spell 웬 with ㅜ+ㅔ (웬), except in 왠지 ("for some reason," which contracts 왜인지 "why is it that").

rootFamily.gloss: what brings you here?, what on earth?
fairly passable, in most ordinary cases
somehow, for some unknown reason (from 왜인지)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (웬)

웬만하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective 웬만하다 (wenmanhada), attested in Early Modern Korean as 우연만하다 (uyeonmanhada, from 우연 偶然 "chance, ordinary occurrence" + delimiter -만 "to the degree of" + -하다) which contracted phonologically through 왼만하다 (oenmanhada) to modern 웬만하다. It denotes reaching a passable, tolerable standard or applying to almost all ordinary cases short of extremes.

history.meaning: to be of an ordinary or tolerable degree
to be fairly good, passable; to be within normal bounds (in most cases)

웬만하다.notes: In conditional forms like 웬만하면 ("if at all possible / in most cases"), it signals pragmatic moderation—doing something unless extraordinary circumstances prevent it.

rootFamily.gloss: unless something extraordinary happens, in most cases
to a passable degree, fairly well

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (웬만하다)

웬수.etymology: Colloquial and dialectal vowel-fronted form of Sino-Korean 원수 (怨讐, wonsu, "mortal enemy, object of resentment"), from 怨 (원망할 원, "resentment, grievance, blame") and 讐 (원수 수, "enemy, vengeance, reprisal"). Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 원수 (wonsu), the spoken variant 웬수 (wensu) arose via expressive fronting of /wʌ/ to /we/ and underwent semantic amelioration in everyday speech to mean "troublesome pest, bane of my existence, the one to blame."

history.meaning: bitter enmity, mortal foe deserving vengeance
sworn enemy, avenger, object of a blood feud
troublesome person, bane of one's life, culprit to blame (colloquial)

morphemes.meaning: resentment, grievance, blame (怨, fronted from 원)

웬수.notes: While standard 원수 (怨讐) refers to a serious enemy, spelling and pronouncing it 웬수 softens it into affectionate exasperation—commonly used by parents or spouses (e.g., 이 웬수야!, "You little troublemaker!").

rootFamily.gloss: mortal enemy, foe (standard form, 怨讐)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (웬수)

웬일.etymology: Native Korean compound noun 웬일 (pronounced [웬닐] via ㄴ-insertion), lexicalized from the interrogative prenoun 웬 (wen, "what sort of, for what unexpected reason," < Early Modern Korean 왼 < 어짼) and the native noun 일 (il, < Middle Korean 일, "work, matter, affair, event"). Literally meaning "what sort of affair," it expresses surprise at an unexpected visit or turn of events.

history.meaning: what manner of affair or occurrence
what unexpected matter, what brings you here?

웬일.notes: Written as a single word without a space (웬일) and pronounced [웬닐] with mandatory nasal insertion; frequently used as a warm greeting when someone drops by unexpectedly (이게 웬일이야?, "What a surprise! What brings you here?").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (웬일)

위.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 우ㅎ ('top, upper part, above', which acquired the vowel -ㅣ from locative 우희 > 위에).

history.meaning: top, above, upper part
top, above, on, superior rank

위기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 危機 (위기), composed of 危 (위태할 위, "high and precarious, perilous, dangerous") and 機 (틀 기, "crossbow trigger, pivot, crucial mechanism, critical moment"). Attested in Tang-dynasty literary Chinese (such as the Wenxuan anthology) for a hidden trap or perilous turning point, it became the standard modern East Asian equivalent of English "crisis."

history.meaning: perilous trigger-point, hidden danger, critical juncture
decisive and dangerous turning point, emergency, crisis

위기.notes: Popular folk etymology claims 危機 combines "danger" (危) + "opportunity" (機 as in 機會 기회), though philologically 機 here originally meant a "critical pivot or trigger point" rather than a lucky opportunity.

rootFamily.gloss: sense of crisis, feeling of urgency (위기감, 危機感)
critical moment, decisive turning point (고비 / 계기, 契機)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위기)

cognates.meaning: sense of crisis, feeling of impending danger
sense of crisis, feeling of urgency

위기감.etymology: Trimorphemic Sino-Korean noun from 危機感 (위기감), built by suffixing 感 (느낄 감, "feeling, sense, perception, awareness") to the compound 危機 (위기, "crisis, critical juncture," from 危 "precarious, perilous" + 機 "pivot, critical moment"). It denotes the psychological awareness of impending danger or professional urgency.

history.meaning: perilous turning point, crisis
sense of crisis, psychological feeling of urgency or threat

위기감.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -감 (感, "sense of") is highly productive for psychological states, forming parallels like 책임감 (責任感, "sense of responsibility") and 해방감 (解放感, "sense of liberation").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위기감)

cognates.meaning: consolation, recognition of someone's hard work or services
to console, express sympathy and appreciation for hard work
to comfort, console and reward troops

위로.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 慰勞 (위로), combining 慰 (위로할 위, "soothe, pacify, calm, comfort") and 勞 (일할 로 / 위로할 로, "toil, labor; to acknowledge and soothe someone's toil"). In Classical Chinese histories such as the Zuo Zhuan and Shiji, 慰勞 described a ruler or general visiting troops to commend their hardships; in Korean it broadened into general emotional solace and consolation.

history.meaning: to soothe and reward soldiers or envoys for their arduous toil
acknowledging someone's hardship with warm words or gifts
comfort, consolation, emotional solace

위로.notes: Notice that the homograph 위로 can also be the native Korean noun 위 ("top, above") + directional particle -로 ("upward"); context and pitch/phrasing immediately distinguish "consolation" (慰勞) from "upward."

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위로)

cognates.word: 違約金 (いやくきん, iyakukin)

cognates.meaning: penalty for breach of contract, liquidated damages

위약금.etymology: Trimorphemic Sino-Korean legal and commercial compound from 違約金 (위약금), consisting of 違 (어길 위, "go against, violate, disobey"), 約 (맺을 약, "bind, covenant, promise, contract"), and 金 (쇠 금 / 돈 금, "metal, gold, money"). Built on the classical verb-object compound 違約 ("to break a covenant"), it denotes monetary damages stipulated for breaking an agreement.

history.meaning: to violate a treaty or break a sworn promise
stipulated monetary penalty for breach of contract

위약금.notes: A staple plot device in Korean entertainment and K-dramas (including *The Producers*), where celebrity talent agencies and advertisers constantly invoke massive 위약금 clauses over scandals or broken endorsement deals.

rootFamily.gloss: violation of law or rules (위반, 違反)
contract deposit, down payment (계약금, 契約金)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위약금)

cognates.meaning: to give priority to, take as the main thing

위주.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 爲主 (위주), originating as a Classical Chinese verb-object predicate composed of 爲 (삼을 위 / 할 위, "to make, take as, serve as") and 主 (주인 주 / 주장할 주, "master, host, principal element"). Literally meaning "making [something] the primary focus," it functions in Korean after a noun (often followed by -로) to mean "centered on, mainly around, prioritizing."

history.meaning: to act as host/master; to treat as the principal element
putting first, centering mainly around a given element

위주.notes: Almost always used postpositionally after another noun in the pattern [Noun] + 위주로 ("mainly around [Noun]," e.g., 예능 위주로 "mainly around variety shows").

rootFamily.gloss: leading role, taking the initiative (주도, 主導)
focusing mainly on, centering on (중심, 中心)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위주)

위쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 위 ('top, above') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the upper side, upward direction, top part

위층.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 위 ('top, upper') + Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'story, floor, layer').

history.meaning: upper floor, upstairs

위치.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 位置 (위치), combining 位 (자리 위, "seat of honor, court rank, standing, place") and 置 (둘 치, "to set up, place, arrange, establish"). In Classical Chinese it referred to the ritual arrangement of seats or official ranks at court; in modern Korean it encompasses both physical geographic location and abstract social or professional standing.

history.meaning: court seating arrangement, official rank and placement
spatial position, geographical location, social standing

위치.notes: Covers both physical coordinates (위치 추적, "location tracking") and workplace hierarchy (내 위치가 애매하다, "My position/standing in the office is awkward").

rootFamily.gloss: status, social standing, position (지위, 地位)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위치)

위하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 위 (爲, 'to act for the sake of, serve, benefit') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to do for the sake of, care for, honor

위험하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from the compound root 危險 (위험, "danger, peril") plus the native adjective-forming suffix -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean stem joins 危 (위태할 위, "high and tottering, precarious, perilous") and 險 (험할 험, "precipitous mountain defile, rugged, hazardous"), literally evoking a steep, treacherous cliff before generalizing to all physical and abstract risks.

history.meaning: precipitous and treacherous terrain; perilous state
danger, hazard, risk of harm or loss
to be dangerous, perilous, risky, unsafe

위험하다.notes: While 험하다 (險-) alone still describes rugged terrain or rough weather/language (험한 길, "a rugged road"), 위험하다 (危險-) is the general word for "dangerous."

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (위험하다)

윗면.etymology: Hybrid Korean spatial compound linking the native noun 위 ('top, upper part', Middle Korean 우ㅎ) with the Sino-Korean noun 면 (面, 낯 면, 'face, surface, side') via the genitive/compound marker 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-). It designates the exposed top face of any object, from a cake to a box or desk. Phonologically, the 사이시옷 neutralizes to [ㄷ] and then assimilates to the nasal ㅁ, making the standard pronunciation [윈면].
윗면.notes: Contrasts systematically with 밑면/아랫면 ('bottom surface') and 옆면 ('side surface').

윗부분.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining the native prefix 윗- (formed from 위 'top' + -ㅅ-) and the Sino-Korean noun 부분 (部分, 'part, portion, section', from 部 'division, section' and 分 'share, divide'). While 윗면 specifies a two-dimensional flat top surface, 윗부분 refers volumetrically to the upper half or top section of an object, document, or building.
윗부분.notes: Pronounced [윋뿌분] due to tensification of ㅂ after the neutralized 사이시옷 [ㄷ].

윗줄.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 위 ('top, upper') + compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 줄 ('line, row, string').

history.meaning: top line, upper row

유난.etymology: Korean noun 유난 (yunan, "unusual fuss, eccentricity, pickiness"), traditionally recorded in Korean lexicons with the Hanja 有難, from 有 (있을 유, "to have, possess") and 難 (어려울 난, "difficulty, trouble, fastidiousness"). Originally signifying behavior that "has difficulty/pickiness" beyond ordinary norms, it developed inside Korean into an expressive noun for making an exaggerated fuss or acting exceptionally finicky.

history.meaning: having difficulty or unusual fastidiousness in conduct
fuss, eccentricity, overdramatic or finicky behavior

유난.notes: Commonly paired with the verb 떨다 ("to shake/display") in the idiom 유난을 떨다 ("to make a huge fuss / be overly dramatic about nothing").

rootFamily.gloss: picky, fastidious, hard to please (까다롭다 / 난감하다, 難堪-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유난)

유난스럽다.etymology: Hybrid Korean adjective derived from the noun root 유난 (有難, yunan, "fussiness, unusual particularity," from 有 "have" + 難 "difficulty, fastidiousness") combined with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -스럽다 (-seureopda, "giving the impression of, characterized by," which conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular stem). It describes speech, taste, or conduct that is overly dramatic, finicky, or ostentatiously different.

history.meaning: unusual pickiness, fussiness
to be fussy, overdramatic, eccentric, making a big deal

morphemes.meaning: native adjective suffix meaning characterized by (-스럽다)

유난스럽다.notes: Carries a mildly critical or teasing nuance toward someone who overreacts to ordinary situations, whereas the related adverb 유난히 ("unusually, especially") is often completely neutral.

rootFamily.gloss: boisterous, making a noisy fuss (요란스럽다, 擾亂-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유난스럽다)

유난히.etymology: Hybrid Korean adverb formed by attaching the native Korean adverbial suffix -히 (-hi) to the stem 유난 (有難, yunan, "unusual particularity, standing out from the norm," from 有 "have" + 難 "difficulty/fastidiousness"). While the base noun 유난 implies fussiness, the derived adverb 유난히 bleached semantically into a general intensifier meaning "unusually, remarkably, especially, more than usual."

history.meaning: in a noticeably finicky or unusual manner
unusually, particularly, especially, remarkably

유난히.notes: Unlike 유난 ("fuss") and 유난스럽다 ("overdramatic"), 유난히 is frequently used in warm, poetic, or neutral descriptions (e.g., 오늘따라 별이 유난히 밝다, "The stars are unusually bright tonight").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유난히)

cognates.meaning: influential, powerful, leading, strong (candidate or clue)

유력하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 有力 (유력, yuryeok) + native adjective verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean root combines 有 (있을 유, "to have, possess") and 力 (힘 력, "physical strength, power, influence, efficacy"). Attested in Classical Chinese for possessing political clout or physical might, it extended in modern journalistic Korean to mean "most likely, leading, strong" (as of a contender, hypothesis, or piece of evidence).

history.meaning: possessing strength, wealth, or political influence
to be influential and powerful; to be a leading or highly probable contender/theory

유력하다.notes: A favorite word in Korean news and entertainment reporting for front-runners and prime suspects: 유력한 후보 ("the leading candidate") or 유력한 용의자 ("the prime suspect").

rootFamily.gloss: influential person, person of clout (유력자, 有力者)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유력하다)

유리.etymology: Sino-Korean 琉璃, borrowed from Chinese 琉璃 'glass, glaze'.
유리.notes: Found in 유리창 'glass window' and 유리컵 'drinking glass'.

유리방.etymology: Sino-Korean/hybrid compound noun formed from 유리 (琉璃, 'glass') + 방 (房, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: glass-enclosed room or booth

유리병.etymology: Compound of 유리 (琉璃, an ancient Buddhist Sanskrit loanword via Classical Chinese meaning 'lapis / glass') and 병 (瓶, 'bottle, jar').
유리병.notes: Used in everyday Korean for both narrow-necked glass bottles and wide-mouthed honey or jam jars.

유리창.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 유리창 (琉璃窓), joining 유리 (琉璃, 'lapis lazuli, colored glaze, glass', itself an ancient Chinese transcription via Prakrit veluriya of Sanskrit vaidurya 'beryl, cat's-eye gem') and 창 (窓, 'window').

history.meaning: glass window, windowpane

cognates.meaning: lapis lazuli, colored glass (historic Buddhist loan)
beryl, cat's-eye gem, lapis lazuli (source of 琉璃)

유리창용.etymology: Polymorphemic Sino-Korean compound noun 琉璃窓用 (유리창용), built from 유리 (琉璃, "glass") + 창 (窓, 창문 창, "window") + suffixoid 용 (用, 쓸 용, "for the use of"). Remarkably, 유리 (琉璃 < Middle Korean 류리 ryuri < Middle Chinese *ljuw-lje) is an ancient Silk Road loanword ultimately borrowed via Prakrit (*veḷuriya) from Sanskrit vaiḍūrya ("beryl, cat's-eye quartz"), which shifted from precious colored glaze to clear window glass in modern Korean.

history.meaning: beryl, lapis lazuli, translucent colored glass glaze
glass windowpane (replacing traditional paper-covered lattice windows)
intended or designated for windowpanes

morphemes.meaning: for the use or purpose of (用)

유리창용.notes: The suffix -용 (用, "for use in/by") attaches to almost any noun to specify intended purpose, such as 가정용 ("for household use"), 방송용 ("suitable for broadcast"), or 유리창용 ("for windowpanes").

유리컵.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining Sino-Korean 유리 (琉璃, 'glass') + English loanword 컵 (cup).

history.meaning: drinking glass, glass tumbler

유명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean compound adjective formed from 유명 (有名), uniting 有 (있을 유, 'to exist, to have') and 名 (이름 명, 'name, reputation, renown'), plus the native suffix -하다. Literally 'having a name' or 'possessing renown', it is the ubiquitous everyday Korean word for being famous. It corresponds to classical equivalents but has broadened to cover anything from a globally renowned scientist to a locally popular bakery.
유명하다.notes: Takes the particle -로 to mark the reason for fame (산딸기 케이크로 유명하다 'famous for raspberry cake').

유서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 由緖, joining 由 (말미암을 유, 'origin, cause, provenance') and 緖 (실마리 서, 'end of a silk thread, lineage, continuing tradition'). Literally 'the thread of origin running down through time', it appears almost exclusively before 깊다 ('deep') in the set phrase 유서 깊은 ('steeped in history, time-honoured').
유서.notes: Nearly always followed by 깊은 ('deep') -> 유서 깊은 ('historic, steeped in tradition').

cognates.meaning: influence, power; (as 遊説) political canvassing, stumping
cognates.word: 有勢 / 遊説 (ゆうぜい, yūzei)

cognates.meaning: to go around campaigning or lobbying rulers (Classical 遊說)

유세하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 유세 + -하다 (-hada), reflecting a convergence of two Classical Sino-Korean roots: 有勢 (유세, from 有 있을 유 "have" + 勢 권세 세 "power, authority, clout," meaning "possessing influence") and 遊說 (유세, from 遊 놀 유 "travel about" + 說 달랠 세 "persuade," referring to Warring States strategists canvassing rulers). In colloquial Korean, 유세하다 (and 유세 부리다/떨다) means to flaunt one's clout, favors, or status and throw one's weight around.

history.meaning: possessing authority and clout (有勢); traveling to persuade rulers (遊說)
to campaign politically; (colloquially) to boast of one's influence and throw one's weight around

유세하다.notes: Notice the reading of 說: when meaning "explain/theory" it is read 설 (설명 說明), when meaning "rejoice" it is 열 (기뻐할 열), and when meaning "persuade/lobby" it is read 세 (유세 遊說), which blended in everyday speech with 유세 (有勢, "wielding clout").

rootFamily.gloss: bragging, bluffing, putting on airs (허세, 虛勢)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유세하다)

유월.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar noun from 六月 (유월), composed of 六 (여섯 륙/육, "six") and 月 (달 월, "moon, month"). Originally pronounced 륙월 (ryugwol) in Middle Korean, it underwent two regular phonological changes: initial liquid drop (두음법칙, 륙 > 육) and deletion of the syllable-final velar stop ㄱ (/k/) before the labiovelar glide /w/ of 월 (육월 > 유월) to ease articulation.

history.meaning: the sixth month of the lunar calendar
the sixth month of the year
June (the sixth month of the Gregorian calendar)

유월.notes: In Korean calendar months, exactly two months lose their final consonant in both pronunciation and spelling: 유월 (六月, June—not *육월) and 시월 (十月, October—not *십월).

rootFamily.gloss: October (十月, showing parallel consonant drop from 십월)
January, the first month (일월, 一月)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유월)

유일하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 唯一 (유일, yuil) + native adjective verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean root unites 唯 (오직 유, "only, solely, exclusively") and 一 (한 일, "one, single, unified"). Prominent in Chinese Buddhist translations (such as the Lotus Sutra's 唯一佛乘, "the one and only Buddha-vehicle") and expressions like 唯一無二 ("one and only, without a second"), it became the standard Korean word for "sole, unique."

history.meaning: solely one, exclusive and without a second (especially in Buddhist scripture)
to be the only one, sole, unique

유일하다.notes: Often reinforced in the four-character idiom 유일무이하다 (唯一無二-, "to be one of a kind, literally solely one and without a second").

rootFamily.gloss: one and only, unique (유일무이, 唯一無二)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유일하다)

유지하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb from 維持 (유지, yuji) + native verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean root combines 維 (바 유 / 맬 유, "heavy cord, guy-rope, to tie fast, hold together") and 持 (가질 지, "to grasp, hold up, sustain, support"). Originally evoking securing a tent or carriage with sturdy ropes and holding it steady, it generalized in Classical Chinese and Korean to maintaining order, status, or physical condition.

history.meaning: to tie fast with cords and hold steady; to uphold and support
to maintain, preserve, keep a state or condition unchanged

유지하다.notes: The noun 유지 (維持) also appears in maintenance costs (유지비 維持費) and the status quo (현상 유지 現狀維持). Do not confuse with the homonym 유지 (有志, "a local notable or community leader").

rootFamily.gloss: maintenance cost, upkeep fee (유지비, 維持費)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유지하다)

cognates.meaning: outflow, leakage (of data, talent, or capital)
cognates.word: 流出 (りゅうしゅつ, ryūshutsu)

cognates.meaning: to flow out, drain away, leak out

유출되다.etymology: Sino-Korean passive verb formed from 流出 (유출, yuchul) + native Korean passive verbalizer -되다 (-doeda, "to become, be done"). The Sino-Korean stem combines 流 (흐를 류/유, "to flow, stream, drift, circulate," showing initial liquid drop from 류 to 유) and 出 (날 출, "to go out, emerge, issue"). Literally "to be caused to flow out," it extended metaphorically from liquids to confidential information, broadcast scripts, or personal data leaking to the public.

history.meaning: water or liquid flowing out from a source
outflow of water, capital, cultural artifacts, or secrets
to be leaked out, disclosed unauthorizedly, or drained away

morphemes.meaning: native passive verb-deriving suffix (to become / be done)

유출되다.notes: In Korean media and IT contexts, 유출되다 is the standard term for unauthorized leaks of confidential data, exam questions, or spoilers (개인정보 유출, 대본 유출), whereas 누출되다 (漏出-) is preferred for physical gas or radiation leaks.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유출되다)

유치하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective from 幼稚 (유치, yuchi) + native adjective verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean stem pairs 幼 (어릴 유, "young, tender, minor") and 稚 (어릴 치, "young grain, late-planted crop, fledgling, infantile"). In Classical Chinese (such as the Guanzi and Han histories), 幼稚 neutrally described young children; as an adjective in modern Korean, 유치하다 acquired a pejorative nuance of "childish, juvenile, corny, tacky."

history.meaning: young and tender in years, young children collectively
to be immature in thought; childish, juvenile, tacky, corny

유치하다.notes: Although 유치원 (幼稚園, "kindergarten," literally "garden for young children") uses the exact same Hanja 幼稚 neutrally, calling someone's behavior or a TV gag 유치하다 is always disparaging ("childish, cheesy, juvenile").

rootFamily.gloss: baby tooth, milk tooth (유치, 乳齒 — homophone!)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유치하다)

유혹하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb from 誘惑 (유혹, yuhok) + native verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean root unites 誘 (꾈 유, "to beckon, coax, entice, lure") and 惑 (미혹할 혹, "to confuse, delude, beguile, lead astray"). Originally describing leading someone into moral or intellectual delusion through sweet words, it now spans romantic seduction, commercial enticement, and winning someone over with an irresistible offer.

history.meaning: to coax and delude, to lead someone astray with enticements
to tempt, seduce, allure, entice or win over

유혹하다.notes: Used both for romantic/moral temptation and in workplace or broadcasting contexts for "courting/winning over" a star writer, producer, or cast member with lucrative terms.

rootFamily.gloss: inducement, guidance; judo (유도, 誘導 / 柔道)
bewitchment, fascination, infatuation (미혹, 迷惑 / 매혹, 魅惑)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — 표준국어대사전 (유혹하다)

육.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 육 (六, 'six', initial form of 륙 before pause or vowel), from Middle Chinese *ljuwk.

history.meaning: six (Sino-Korean number)

cognates.word: 六ヶ月 / 六箇月 (ろっかげつ, rokkagetsu)
六個月 / 六个月 (liù gè yuè)

육개월.etymology: Trimorphemic Sino-Korean numeral-classifier compound from 六個月 (육개월, yukgaewol), composed of 六 (여섯 륙/육, "six," with regular word-initial loss of r-), 個 (낱 개, "bamboo tally, individual unit, general counter"), and 月 (달 월, "month"). Unlike 유월 (六月, "June"), the intervening classifier 개 (個) blocks consonant deletion of 육 and marks a measured duration ("six months") rather than a calendar name.

history.meaning: a span of six individual months
duration of six months (or the sixth month of a multi-month period)

육개월.notes: Crucial learner distinction: 유월 (六月) means "June" (the 6th month of the year), whereas 육개월 (六個月, or native 여섯 달) means a duration of "six months" and retains the final ㄱ of 육.

rootFamily.gloss: June, the sixth calendar month (유월, 六月)

육수.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary compound 肉水, combining 肉 (고기 육, 'meat') and 水 (물 수, 'water, liquid'). Although originally denoting simmered meat broth in royal and traditional Korean cuisine, in modern cooking 육수 has broadened to mean any flavourful culinary stock or broth—including vegetable, mushroom, or kelp stock (채소 육수, 다시마 육수).
육수.notes: Pronounced [육쑤] with conventional tensification in culinary usage.

육십분.etymology: Sino-Korean numerical measure compound formed from 육십 (六十, 'sixty', composed of 六 'six' + 十 'ten') and the bound counter 분 (分, originally 'to divide, a tenth/fraction', adopted in East Asian modernity for 'minute' as a sixtieth division of an hour). In Korean broadcasting culture, it famously evokes KBS's flagship investigative journalism program 추적 60분 ('In Depth 60 Minutes').

history.meaning: six tens; a fractional division or share
sixty parts; sixty minutes (equivalent to one hour)
sixty minutes; shorthand allusion to investigative documentary television

육십분.notes: While एक한 시간 (han sigan) is the everyday way to say 'one hour', 육십분 (60 minutes) stresses exact duration and in Korean media banter often alludes to KBS's investigative program 추적 60분.

rootFamily.gloss: minute hand; minutes and seconds (分秒)

육점팔.etymology: Sino-Korean decimal number expression composed of 육 (六, 'six'), 점 (點, literally 'black dot, speck, point', used mathematically as the decimal point separator), and 팔 (八, 'eight'). In Korean television production, decimal figures read with Sino-Korean numerals are standardly used to report viewer rating percentages (시청률), such as 6.8%.

history.meaning: six; black dot or mark; eight
the decimal figure 6.8; 6.8 percent ratings in broadcasting jargon

육점팔.notes: Korean always reads decimal numbers using Sino-Korean numerals with 점 (點) for 'point'; in broadcasting drama contexts, a bare decimal like 육점팔 (6.8) immediately refers to episode viewership ratings (시청률 6.8%).

육포.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary compound from 육포 (肉脯), combining 육 (肉, 'flesh, meat') and 포 (脯, 'dried and seasoned slices of meat'). Recorded in classical Chinese ritual canons such as the Zhouli and Liji as preserved strips of spiced meat offered at ancestral rites, the dish became a staple of Joseon royal court cuisine, wedding 폐백 (pyebaek) trays, and modern drinking snacks (안주).

history.meaning: sliced meat cured and dried with spices for preservation and ritual offerings
thinly sliced beef marinated in soy sauce and dried, used for ancestral rites and banquets
beef jerky, eaten both as a traditional ceremonial delicacy and a casual snack with alcohol

육포.notes: In Korea, 육포 ranges from high-end ceremonial gifts presented at weddings (폐백) to convenience-store snacks paired with beer (맥주 안주).

육호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 육호실 (六號室), joining 육 (六, 'six'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room').

history.meaning: Room No. 6

윤기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 潤氣, combining 潤 (윤택할 윤, 'moist, sleek, glossy') with 氣 (기운 기, 'aura, quality, appearance'). It describes a warm, moist, healthy sheen—whether on glazed pastry, silky lemon curd, polished wood, or glossy hair—and regularly pairs with 나다 ('shine forth') or 흐르다 ('flow').
윤기.notes: Collocates with 나다: 윤기가 나다 / 윤기 나게 ('to be glossy / glossily').

윤여정.etymology: Korean personal name of the acclaimed South Korean film and television actress Youn Yuh-jung (윤여정, 尹汝貞, born 1947). Composed of the Korean clan surname 윤 (尹, historically meaning 'governor, magistrate', specifically the Papyeong Yun clan) and the Sino-Korean given name 여정 (汝 'you, graceful' + 貞 'virtuous, steadfast, chaste'). She famously appeared as herself in episodes 1 and 2 of The Producers.

history.meaning: magistrate/governor (surname); thou/graceful; upright/chaste
Youn Yuh-jung, veteran South Korean screen actress and later Academy Award winner

윤여정.notes: Youn Yuh-jung (윤여정) is a towering figure in Korean cinema and television (and the first Korean actor to win an Academy Award, for Minari); in The Producers, her cameo highlights Korean broadcasting's reverence for veteran 'senior teachers' (선생님).

윤전기.etymology: Sino-Korean technical noun 윤전기 (輪轉機), borrowed during the late enlightenment/colonial era via Meiji Japanese 輪転機 (rintenki), which coined the term to translate English 'rotary printing press'. Built from 輪 (윤, 'wheel, cylinder'), 轉 (전, 'to revolve, rotate'), and 機 (기, 'machine, mechanism'), referring to high-speed newspaper presses that print on continuous paper rolls between rotating cylinders.

history.meaning: rotary printing press using cylindrical rollers for mass newspaper printing
rotary printing press; metonym for newspaper press deadlines in journalism

윤전기.notes: In Korean entertainment and media dramas, 'stopping the 윤전기' (윤전기를 세우다) is a classic journalistic trope for killing a scandal story right before the morning newspapers go to print.

으으.etymology: Natural Korean vocalic interjection expressing a shiver from cold, a groan of pain or effort, or revulsion ('brrr!, ugh!').

history.meaning: groan or shiver of cold, pain, or disgust

은.etymology: Native Korean topic/contrastive marker attached to consonant-final nouns (allomorph of 는 after vowels), descending from Middle Korean 은 / 으란; also homonymous with Sino-Korean noun 은 (銀, 'silver').

history.meaning: topic and contrast particle after consonants; also 銀 ('silver')

은색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 은색 (銀色), joining 은 (銀, 'silver metal') and 색 (色, 'color, hue').

history.meaning: silver color

은신처.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 은신처 (隱身處), formed from the verbal noun 은신 (隱身, 'hiding one's body/person', from 隱 'to hide, conceal' + 身 'body, self') plus the locative suffix 처 (處, 'place, site, location'). Literally 'a place to conceal one's body', it denotes a secret refuge, safe house, or hideout from pursuers or the public eye.

history.meaning: to conceal oneself; to withdraw from public office into seclusion
secret hiding place, refuge, or safe house away from pursuers or reporters

은신처.notes: In celebrity and tabloid contexts, 은신처 often refers slightly melodramatically to the secret apartment or retreat where a scandal-ridden star hides from paparazzi.

은어.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 은어 (隱語), combining 은 (隱, 'hidden, secret, veiled') and 어 (語, 'language, speech, word'). In Classical Chinese (such as Liu Xie's Wenxin Diaolong), 隱語 meant 'riddle, enigmatic expression, veiled allegory'; in modern East Asian linguistics and everyday usage, it shifted to mean 'argot, cant, or secret insider jargon' used within a closed group or profession (such as TV producers) so outsiders cannot easily understand.

history.meaning: riddle, veiled speech, or enigmatic allusion in classical rhetoric
insider jargon, occupational cant, or subcultural slang opaque to outsiders

은어.notes: Unlike 속어 (俗語, general colloquial slang) or 비어 (卑語, vulgar slang), 은어 (隱語) specifically refers to insider jargon or coded vocabulary used by a specific group—like broadcasting PDs, teenagers, or gamers. (Note: a homonym 은어 銀魚 means 'sweetfish'.)

은은하다.etymology: Formed from the reduplicated Sino-Korean root 은은 (隱隱, combining 隱 '숨을 은, hidden, veiled, subtle' twice for emphasis) plus the native adjective suffix -하다. Rather than meaning completely invisible, 은은 describes a sensory stimulus that is subdued, softly lingering, and pleasantly unobtrusive. It perfectly captures warm, dim lighting, a delicate floral tea aroma, or a faint bell tolling in the distance.
은은하다.notes: Highly poetic yet common in everyday aesthetics; pairs with 빛 ('light'), 향기/냄새 ('scent'), and 소리 ('sound').

은퇴.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 隱退, uniting 隱 (숨을 은, 'to hide, conceal, withdraw from public') and 退 (물러날 퇴, 'to step back, retreat, retire'). Rooted in the classical East Asian ideal of the scholar-official withdrawing from courtly affairs to live quietly in the countryside, 은퇴 is now the standard modern term for ending one's career or stepping down from a professional role due to age.
은퇴.notes: Often combines with -하다 (은퇴하다 'to retire') or forms nouns like 은퇴식 ('retirement ceremony').

은퇴하다.etymology: Formed by attaching the native verbalizer -하다 to the Sino-Korean noun 은퇴 (隱退, from 隱 'withdraw, hide' and 退 'step back'). While classical usages leaned toward reclusion, modern 은퇴하다 strictly denotes concluding one's lifelong career or professional sports life. It contrasts with 사직하다 ('to resign prematurely') and 퇴직하다 ('to leave a company/post', often for another job).
은퇴하다.notes: Takes the honorific -시- when referring to elders (은퇴하셨어요). Takes -에서 ('from') for the field left behind.

은행.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 은행 (銀行), composed of 은 (銀, 'silver, money') and 행 (行, 'merchant guild, commercial establishment, row'). Historically attested in Tang/Song Chinese for a 'silver-smiths' guild' and adopted in 1872 Meiji Japan (銀行, ginkō) to translate English 'bank' under the National Bank Act, before spreading into Korean during the late Joseon Enlightenment reforms. (Note that 行 is read 행 here in the commercial sense, distinct from its homograph 은행 銀杏 'ginkgo'.)

history.meaning: guild or commercial house dealing in silver bullion and exchange
modern financial institution for deposits, credit, and currency issuance (translating English 'bank')
bank; modern financial institution

morphemes.meaning: commercial firm, guild, line of business (行)

은행.notes: Beware of the exact homonym 은행 (銀杏, 'silver apricot'), which means 'ginkgo tree / ginkgo nut'—a classic source of Korean puns because ginkgo trees line many city streets right in front of banks.

은행길.etymology: Compound street name formed from Sino-Korean 은행 (either 銀杏 'ginkgo tree' or 銀行 'bank') + native Korean 길 ('road, street, way') — 'Ginkgo Street' or 'Bank Street'.

history.meaning: Ginkgo-tree Street / Bank Street

은혜.etymology: Sino-Korean synonym-compound 은혜 (恩惠), uniting 은 (恩, 'kindness, grace, affection', graphically 因 'cause/rely' over 心 'heart') and 혜 (惠, 'favor, benevolence, charity'). Deeply rooted in Confucian and Buddhist ethics of reciprocal moral obligation (보은, 報恩), it denotes benevolent favor bestowed by parents, teachers, mentors, or heaven, and the resulting debt of gratitude felt by the recipient.

history.meaning: imperial or parental benevolence, grace, and charitable favor
benevolent grace or favor received from superiors/parents, and the moral debt of gratitude it creates

은혜.notes: In Korean culture, 은혜 is not merely the feeling of 'gratitude' (감사), but the weighty 'favor or grace received' that one is morally bound to repay—as in 은혜를 갚다 ('to repay a kindness') or 은혜를 입다 ('to be indebted to someone's kindness').

을.etymology: Native Korean accusative (direct object) case particle attached to consonant-final nouns (allomorph of 를 after vowels), descending from Middle Korean 을 / 알.

history.meaning: direct object marker after consonants
accusative particle (post-consonantal)

음.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 음 (音, 'sound, tone, musical note, pronunciation') and the natural Korean nasal vocalization 음 ('hmm, well', uttered while pondering or agreeing).

history.meaning: sound, musical pitch, speech sound; also contemplative interjection ('hmm')

음계.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 음계 (音階), joining 음 (音, 'sound, musical note') and 계 (階, 'steps, stairs, gradations') — literally 'staircase of notes'.

history.meaning: musical scale

음성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음성 (音聲), uniting 음 (音, 'sound') and 성 (聲, 'voice').
음성.notes: Used in technical or formal contexts like 음성 메시지 ('voice message'), whereas native 목소리 is everyday spoken 'voice'.

cognates.meaning: eating and drinking; food and beverage

음식.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinative compound 음식 (飮食), pairing 음 (飮, 'to drink; beverage') and 식 (食, 'to eat; food, cooked grain'). Attested since the Classic of Changes (Yijing) and Mencius for 'drinking and eating', the compound underwent semantic narrowing in everyday Korean to serve as the standard general noun for prepared 'food, cuisine, or dishes'.

history.meaning: drinking and eating; beverages and victuals collectively
food and drink; prepared dishes and culinary fare

음식.notes: Although literally 'drink and food' (飮 + 食), modern Korean 음식 refers primarily to prepared food or cuisine (whereas native Korean 밥 means cooked rice or a meal, and 식품 食品 refers to commercial food products/groceries).

음식물.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 음식물 (飮食物), derived by suffixing 물 (物, 'thing, physical substance, matter') to 음식 (飮食, 'food and drink'). While literally denoting 'edible substances or foodstuffs', in contemporary South Korean civic and household usage it overwhelmingly appears in the collocation 음식물 쓰레기 ('food waste'), referring to organic kitchen scraps regulated under mandatory municipal recycling laws.

history.meaning: drinking and eating + physical matter/things
foodstuffs, physical food matter (especially in administrative and sanitation contexts like food waste)

음식물.notes: You rarely order 음식물 at a table; adding -물 (物, 'physical matter') makes it sound clinical or administrative, so Koreans use it mainly for 음식물 쓰레기 ('food waste') or medical/legal contexts.

음식점.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음식점 (飮食店), formed from 음식 (飮食, 'food and drink') and the commercial suffix 점 (店, 'shop, store, inn'). Borrowed and popularized in modern administrative and commercial Korean alongside Japanese 飲食店 (inshokuten), it serves as the formal and regulatory term for any restaurant or dining establishment.

history.meaning: food and drink + inn or shopfront
restaurant, commercial dining establishment

음식점.notes: In casual conversation Koreans often say 식당 (食堂) or 맛집 ('tasty place'), whereas 음식점 (飮食店) is slightly more formal or official (e.g., on business licenses as 일반음식점 'general restaurant').

음악.etymology: Sino-Korean 음악 (音樂), combining 음 (音, 'voice, pitched tone, sound') + 악 (樂, 'instrumental music, harmony'). Rooted in Classical Chinese musical philosophy (such as the Yueji / Record of Music) and established across East Asia as the general word for music.

history.meaning: tones and instrumental music
music

음악.notes: Notice how the character 樂 has three readings in Sino-Korean depending on sense: 악 ('music', 음악), 락/낙 ('pleasure', 오락), and 요 ('to delight in').

음악가.etymology: Sino-Korean occupational noun 음악가 (音樂家), formed from 음악 (音樂, 'music', combining 音 'sound, tone' and 樂 'music, harmony') plus the agentive suffix -가 (家, originally 'house, family', extended since Classical Chinese 諸子百家 to denote a 'master, school, or professional specialist in an art or scholarly field').

history.meaning: musical tones and harmony + household or master of a school/art
professional musician, composer, or musical artist

음악가.notes: The suffix -가 (家) carries prestige and artistry (음악가 'musician', 예술가 'artist', 소설가 'novelist'), whereas popular singers or band members are more commonly called 가수 (歌手) or 뮤지션 ('musician').

음악회.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음악회 (音樂會), joining 음악 (音樂, 'music', from 音 'sound' + 樂 'music') and 회 (會, 'gathering, assembly, recital').

history.meaning: musical concert, recital

음주단속.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 음주단속 (飮酒團束), joining 음주 (飮酒, 'drinking alcohol', from 飮 'drink' + 酒 'liquor, wine') and 단속 (團束, 'binding together, regulation, policing, crackdown', from 團 'gather, round group' + 束 'bind, tie in a bundle, restrain'). In modern South Korea, it specifically denotes police roadside sobriety checkpoints and breathalyzer enforcement against drunk driving (음주운전 단속).

history.form: 飮酒 (ʔjimH tsyuwX) + 團束 (dwan syowk)
history.meaning: drinking wine/liquor + binding together or maintaining discipline
police sobriety checkpoint; crackdown on drunk driving

음주단속.notes: In Korean media, getting caught at an 음주단속 (sobriety checkpoint) is an instant career-ending scandal for celebrities and a recurring headache for TV producers whose cast members get pulled over.

음표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음표 (音標), combining 음 (音, 'sound, musical tone') and 표 (標, 'mark, symbol').
음표.notes: Shares 음 (音) with 음악 ('music') and 표 (標) with 화살표 ('arrow mark').

음향.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음향 (音響), joining 음 (音, 'sound, tone') and 향 (響, 'echo, resonance, reverberation').

history.meaning: sound, acoustics, sound effects

응.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) vocalic-nasal interjection 응, originating as a natural closed-mouth velar nasal murmur (/ɯŋ/) signaling attentive backchanneling, recognition, or casual affirmation ('yeah, uh-huh, mm-hmm'). Paralleled typologically across languages (compare Japanese うん un, Mandarin 嗯 ng, English uh-huh), it has a reduplicated variant 으응 and contrasts in register with polite 네 / 예.

history.meaning: natural nasal exclamation of acknowledgment, response, or realization
yeah, uh-huh (intimate/informal affirmative response or backchannel)

응.notes: Strictly 반말 (intimate/casual speech): use 응 only with close friends, younger people, or family; saying 응 to a boss or senior in a Korean workplace instead of 네 is a major breach of etiquette.

cognates.meaning: to support, back up; fan support (應援)

응원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 응원 (應援), composed of 응 (應, 'to respond, answer, correspond') and 원 (援, 'to pull by the hand, rescue, aid, reinforce'). In Classical Chinese military historiography, 應援 meant 'sending relief troops in response to an ally's call for help'; in modern Japanese (応援, ōen) and Korean, it broadened to athletic cheering, rooting for a team, and moral or fan support for a person's endeavors.

history.meaning: to respond to a call for military aid and dispatch reinforcement troops
military reinforcement; cheering at sports events; rooting for or supporting someone's success

응원.notes: Originally a military term for 'reinforcements', 응원 now spans everything from stadium cheerleaders (응원단) and K-pop lightsticks (응원봉) to everyday encouragement like 응원할게요! ('I'll be rooting for you!').

의.etymology: Sino-Korean root noun 의 (衣, 'clothing, upper garment, apparel'), derived from the Old Chinese pictograph depicting the overlapping lapels and sleeves of a traditional upper robe. In Korean, while native 옷 is the everyday standalone word for clothes, Sino-Korean 의 (衣) appears independently when enumerating the foundational spheres of human life—most notably 의, 식, 주 (衣·食·住, 'clothing, food, and shelter').

history.meaning: upper garment, robe; clothing in general
clothing, attire (used in formal enumerations like 의·식·주 and Sino-Korean compounds)

의.notes: In everyday speech Koreans say 옷 for 'clothes', using single-syllable 의 (衣) only in formal categorizations like 의·식·주 ('clothing, food, and shelter') or compounds like 의류 (衣類, 'apparel') and 의복 (衣服, 'garments').

의견.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의견 (意見), formed from 의 (意, 'thought, mind, intention', graphically 音 'sound' over 心 'heart') and 견 (見, 'to see, perceive; view, judgment'). Attested in medieval Chinese historical memorials and Buddhist texts for 'what is perceived in the mind; personal view or proposal', it is the standard Korean noun for an 'opinion, viewpoint, or suggestion'.

history.meaning: thoughts and views held in the mind; a formal proposal or judgment
personal or collective opinion, viewpoint, or suggestion

의견.notes: Unlike Mandarin 意見 (yìjiàn), which often implies 'complaint or objection' (as in 有意見), Korean 의견 (意見) is completely neutral and positive, meaning 'opinion, idea, or feedback' in meetings.

의도하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb 의도하다, combining the Sino-Korean noun 의도 (意圖, 'intention, design, aim', from 意 'mind, thought, will' + 圖 'map, diagram, plan, scheme') with the productive native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do, make'). Literally 'to map out in the mind', it means 'to intend, plan deliberately, or aim at a specific effect'.

history.meaning: mental plan, scheme, or deliberate intention
to intend, purpose, or deliberately design an action or message

의도하다.notes: In TV and film production, 기획 의도 ('planning intention') and 의도하다 ('to intend [an edit or scene]') are constant buzzwords when PDs explain why they shot or edited a scene a certain way.

의미.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의미 (意味), formed from 의 (意, 'thought, mind, purport') and 미 (味, 'taste, flavor, savor'). In Classical Chinese literary and Buddhist aesthetics, 意味 originally referred to the 'lingering flavor, aesthetic overtone, or subtle purport' of a poem or teaching; in modern Japanese (意味, imi) and Korean, it grammaticalized into the core noun for 'meaning, significance, or semantic sense'.

history.meaning: subtle flavor, aesthetic mood, or inner purport of words and thoughts
meaning, linguistic sense, significance, or symbolic value

의미.notes: Compare Sino-Korean 의미 (意味) with native Korean 뜻: both mean 'meaning', but 뜻 also covers 'will/intention' (뜻이 있다), while 의미 focuses on 'significance, symbolic value, or definition' (의미가 깊다 'deeply meaningful').

의미하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean transitive verb 의미하다, derived by attaching the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do, make') to the Sino-Korean noun 의미 (意味, 'meaning, significance', from 意 'thought, intent' + 味 'flavor, sense'). It functions in formal, journalistic, and analytical Korean prose as the direct equivalent of English 'to mean, signify, or imply'.

history.meaning: inner purport or lingering flavor of an expression
to mean, signify, denote, or imply

의미하다.notes: 의미하다 is a transitive verb taking the object marker -을/를 (예: 이것은 성공을 의미한다 'This signifies success'); in casual conversation, speakers more often say ~라는 뜻이다 ('it means that...').

의사.etymology: Sino-Korean occupational title 의사 (醫師), combining 의 (醫, 'medicine, healing, physician', whose traditional character contains 酉 'fermented elixir/medicinal alcohol' at the bottom alongside arrows and ritual healing implements) and 사 (師, 'master, teacher, specialist'). Recorded as early as the Zhouli (Rites of Zhou) for the chief court physician overseeing medical officers, it is the standard modern Korean word for a licensed medical doctor.

history.meaning: master physician overseeing medical administration at the royal court (Zhouli)
licensed medical doctor, physician

의사.notes: 의사 has several major Sino-Korean homographs: 의사 (醫師 'medical doctor'), 의사 (意思 'intention/willingness'), and 의사 (義士 'righteous patriot/martyr', such as Ahn Jung-geun). When addressing a doctor directly, Koreans say 의사 선생님 ('Doctor-teacher').

의상.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinative compound 의상 (衣裳), pairing 의 (衣, 'upper garment, jacket, robe') and 상 (裳, 'lower garment, skirt, pleated apron'). Famous from the Book of Changes (Yijing) and Classic of Poetry (Shijing) formula 黃帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治 ('The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let hang their upper robes and lower skirts, and the world was governed'), in modern Korean it specializes to mean 'stage costume, broadcast wardrobe, or formal fashion attire'.

history.meaning: upper robe and lower skirt; ceremonial attire as a symbol of civilized order
formal garments; stage costume, broadcast outfit, or fashion wardrobe

의상.notes: While 옷 is everyday clothing, 의상 (衣裳) refers to curated outfits, designer dresses, or stage/broadcast wardrobe—for instance, K-pop stage outfits are called 무대 의상, and wardrobe sponsors are 의상 협찬.

cognates.meaning: food, clothing, and shelter; the necessities of life
clothing, food, shelter, and transport (basic necessities)

의식주.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character coordinative compound 의식주 (衣食住), concatenating 의 (衣, 'clothing, apparel'), 식 (食, 'food, nourishment'), and 주 (住, 'dwelling, housing, shelter'). Together they encapsulate the three fundamental material necessities required for human survival and livelihood.

history.meaning: garments; food/eating; dwelling/residing
clothing, food, and shelter; the three basic necessities of human life

의식주.notes: Notice the fixed East Asian order: Korean and Japanese say 의식주 (衣食住, 'clothing, food, shelter'), whereas English typically puts food first ('food, clothing, and shelter') and Chinese adds transport as 衣食住行.

의심스럽다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) 의심스럽다, formed by attaching the native Korean adjectival suffix -스럽다 ('eliciting the feeling or impression of, -some, -ish', attested in Middle Korean as -스ㅿ럽다 / -스럽다) to the Sino-Korean noun 의심 (疑心, 'doubt, suspicion', literally 疑 'doubt, hesitate' + 心 'heart, mind'). It describes someone or something that arouses doubt or looks suspicious.

history.meaning: doubting mind + native suffix denoting 'having the quality or appearance of'
history.stage: Middle Chinese root + Middle Korean suffix

history.meaning: suspicious, doubtful, dubious, arousing mistrust

morphemes.meaning: giving the impression of, worthy of (-스럽다)

의심스럽다.notes: Like all ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) adjectives ending in -스럽다, the final ㅂ turns into 우 before a vowel: 의심스럽다 -> 의심스러워요 ('it looks suspicious'), 의심스러운 ('suspicious [modifier]').

의외.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의외 (意外), combining 의 (意, 'thought, expectation, anticipation') and 외 (外, 'outside, beyond'). Literally 'outside of one's thoughts or expectations', it is attested since the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi) and Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) for events that fall beyond what was anticipated, and is used in Korean as a noun or adnominal modifier (의외의) meaning 'unexpectedness, a surprise turn'.

history.meaning: beyond what was thought or anticipated; an unforeseen contingency
something unexpected or surprising (often in 의외이다 'to be unexpected' or 의외의 'unexpected')

의외.notes: Be careful of a partial false friend with Mandarin: in Chinese, 意外 (yìwài) as a noun often means 'an accident or mishap', whereas Korean 의외 (意外) simply means 'something unexpected or surprising' (frequently pleasant!).

cognates.word: 意外と / 意外に (igai to / igai ni)

의외로.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean adverb 의외로, formed from the Sino-Korean noun 의외 (意外, 'outside of expectation', from 意 'thought, expectation' + 外 'outside, beyond') followed by the native Korean directional/instrumental particle -로 ('by way of, as, into', Middle Korean -으로/-로). Literally 'by way of unexpectedness', it lexicalized into a high-frequency sentence adverb meaning 'unexpectedly, surprisingly, contrary to what one might think'.

history.meaning: beyond expectation + native Korean adverbial/instrumental case marker
unexpectedly, surprisingly, more than expected

morphemes.meaning: by way of, in the manner of (-로)

의외로.notes: 의외로 is a favorite conversational adverb when someone defies a stereotype or expectation (예: 의외로 요리 잘하네! 'You're surprisingly good at cooking!').

의자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의자 (椅子), joining 의 (椅, 'catalpa tree; wooden chair with a backrest') and diminutive/nominal suffix 자 (子).

history.meaning: chair, seat

의전하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb 의전하다, combining the Sino-Korean noun 의전 (儀典, 'ceremonial protocol, state etiquette', from 儀 'ceremony, deportment, model' + 典 'canon, standard statute, solemn rite') with the native light verb -하다 ('to do, perform'). Historically denoting state diplomatic or courtly ceremonial rules, in modern Korean corporate and broadcasting culture 의전하다 also means 'to provide VIP protocol, escort, and hospitality for high-ranking guests or top-tier celebrities'.

history.meaning: canonical rules and statutes governing court ceremonies and state rites
to conduct diplomatic/official protocol; to escort and attend to VIPs with formal courtesy

의전하다.notes: In Korean broadcasting and politics, 의전 (protocol/VIP handling) is a high-stakes art: junior PDs are often tasked with 의전하다—waiting at the parking lot to escort veteran stars or executives and ensuring seating and waiting-room hierarchy are flawless.

의지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의지 (意志), composed of 의 (意, 'mind, thought, intent') and 지 (志, 'ambition, resolve, direction of the heart', graphically 士/之 'go forward' over 心 'heart'). Already paired in Classical Chinese texts for 'purpose and aspiration', the compound was reinforced in late 19th-century Meiji Japanese philosophy (意志, ishi) to translate German Wille / English 'will, volition' (as in Schopenhauer's Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung), denoting firm mental resolve and willpower.

history.meaning: purpose, inclination of the mind, and moral aspiration
philosophical and psychological 'will' or 'volition' (translating German Wille / English will)
willpower, resolve, determination to carry out a goal

morphemes.meaning: resolve, ambition, direction of the heart (志)

의지.notes: Do not confuse the two common homonyms spelled 의지: 의지 (意志) means 'willpower, resolve' (의지가 강하다 'strong-willed'), whereas 의지 (依支) means 'reliance, leaning on someone' (의지하다 'to rely on').

rootFamily.gloss: comrade sharing the same resolve (同志)向/同志

이.etymology: Native Korean proximal demonstrative determiner ('this', Middle Korean 이), post-consonantal nominative case particle (-이), and native noun 이 ('tooth', Middle Korean 니); also Sino-Korean numeral 이 (二, 'two').

history.meaning: this; subject marker; tooth; two

이거.etymology: Colloquial spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing, this one'), formed from proximal demonstrative 이 ('this') + bound noun 거 (< 것 'thing').

history.meaning: this thing, this one (informal/spoken)

이거예요.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) colloquial copular phrase 이거예요, contracted from 이것이에요 ('it is this thing'). Built from the proximal demonstrative determiner 이 ('this', Middle Korean 이), the bound noun 거 (< 것, 'thing, fact, point', Middle Korean 것), and the polite informal (해요체) copula ending -예요 (the post-vocalic contraction of -이에요, from copula stem 이- + polite suffix -어요). In emphatic discourse, it means 'this is it!' or 'this is the exact point!'.

history.meaning: it is this thing (proximal demonstrative 이 + bound noun 것 + copula 이-)
it is this; this is the point (with colloquial final -ㅅ deletion in 것 > 거 and vowel-after copula contraction -이에요 > -예요)

morphemes.meaning: is, equals (contracted from -이에요 after a vowel)

이거예요.notes: Orthography trap: because 이거 ends in a vowel, the polite copula must be spelled -예요 (이거예요, contracted from 이거 + 이에요), never *이거에요! In pitches and meetings, 바로 이거예요! means 'That's it! / Bingo!'.

이거저거.etymology: Colloquial native Korean (*고유어*) coordinate pronoun contracted from 이것저것 ("this thing and that thing") through the regular casual deletion of the final coda -ㅅ in the bound noun 것 ("thing"), combining the proximal demonstrative 이 ("this") and the distal demonstrative 저 ("that over there").

history.meaning: this thing and that thing
this and that, various things
this and that indiscriminately (colloquial)

이거저거.notes: Used primarily in casual spoken Korean; in formal writing or broadcasts, the uncontracted form 이것저것 is preferred.

이것.etymology: Native Korean compound demonstrative pronoun descending from Middle Korean 이것, formed from proximal determiner 이 ('this') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

history.meaning: this thing, this

이것저것.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) coordinate compound pairing 이것 ("this thing", from proximal determiner 이 + bound noun 것) with 저것 ("that thing", from distal determiner 저, Middle Korean 뎌 + bound noun 것). The symmetric reduplication of 것 expresses an open-ended assortment of items or topics.

history.meaning: this thing / that thing over there
this and that, an assortment of things

이것저것.notes: Korean demonstrative compounds pair proximal 이- ("near speaker") with distal 저- ("far from both") rather than medial 그- when expressing "this and that" (e.g., 이것저것, 이리저리, 이곳저곳).

이겨내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 이기다 ('to win, overcome', conjunctive 이겨) + completive auxiliary verb 내다 ('to carry through to the end, manage to').

history.meaning: to overcome, endure and triumph over a hardship

이곳.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound formed from the proximal demonstrative determiner 이 ("this", Middle Korean 이) and the noun 곳 ("place, locality", Middle Korean 곧), which lexicalized into a single spatial pronoun referring to the speaker's immediate location.

history.meaning: this place, this spot
this place, here

이곳.notes: More formal and descriptive than 여기 ("here"); often used in broadcast narration, writing, and introductions (e.g., 이곳은 KBS입니다 "This place is KBS").

이기다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 이기다 ('to win, defeat an opponent, master, knead dough thoroughly').

history.meaning: to prevail over, defeat, win
to win, beat, overcome

이날따라.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) adverbial formation combining 이날 ("this day, that very day", from proximal 이 + 날 "day", Middle Korean 날) with the postpositional particle -따라 ("of all times/people, unusually on"), which grammaticalized from the infinitive form 따라 of the verb 따르다 ("to follow, accord with").

history.meaning: following this day
on this day of all days, unusually on this day

이날따라.notes: The particle -따라 attaches to time or person nouns (오늘따라 "today of all days", 그날따라 "that day of all days") to highlight an unexpected coincidence or uncharacteristic event.

이다.etymology: Native Korean predicative copula ('to be [something]') descending from Middle Korean 이라 / 이다, attaching directly to nouns; also a homonymous native verb 이다 ('to carry on the head; to roof a house').

history.meaning: predicative copula ('to be'); also 'to carry on the head'

이대로.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) adverb lexicalized from the proximal determiner 이 ("this") plus the bound noun 대로 ("in accordance with, in the same state as", derived from 대 "stalk, frame, standard" + instrumental particle -로), meaning "in this exact state without change".

history.meaning: according to this, in this manner
just as it is, just like this

morphemes.meaning: in the state of, in accordance with

이대로.notes: Written as one word when meaning "as things stand now" (이대로 가다 "to go on like this"), parallel to 그대로 ("as it is") and 저대로 ("like that").

rootFamily.gloss: at one's own will, as one pleases

이동.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 移動, formed from 移 (옮길 이, "to shift, transplant, change place", originally depicting grain 禾 swaying or being transplanted) and 動 (움직일 동, "to move, stir, act", from 重 "heavy" + 力 "strength"). Widely used for physical transit, data transfer, and crew repositioning on broadcast sets.

history.meaning: shifting position, moving from one place to another
movement, transfer, transit, migration

이동.notes: In TV production and everyday life, 이동하다 is the standard term for changing locations between shoots or commuting between venues.

이따가.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) temporal adverb derived through fortition and phonological reduction from Early Modern Korean 잇다가, the stem of 있다 (Middle Korean 잇다, "to stay, remain, exist") inflected with the transferentive connective suffix -다가 ("after remaining for a short while, and then").

history.meaning: after staying/remaining for a while
in a little while, a bit later today

이따가.notes: Refers only to a short time later on the same day (often shortened to 이따 in speech); do not confuse with 나중에 ("later on, at some future time").

rootFamily.gloss: to be, to stay, to exist

이딴.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) derogatory adnominal determiner contracted from 이따위인 or formed directly from the proximal determiner 이 ("this") + derogatory bound noun 따위 ("ilk, sort, paltry kind", related to 따 "earth, ground, separate") + adnominal suffix -ㄴ.

history.meaning: this sort, this ilk
this trashy kind of, this pathetic sort of

이딴.notes: Carries strong contempt or self-deprecation (e.g., 이딴 거 "this piece of junk"); avoid in polite conversation unless deliberately expressing anger or frustration.

이때.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) compound noun formed from the proximal determiner 이 ("this", Middle Korean 이) and the noun 때 ("time, moment, juncture", Middle Korean ㅿㅐ / ᄠᅢ), lexicalized to denote "this exact moment" or "this time of day".

history.meaning: this time, this season
this moment, this hour, at this juncture

이때.notes: Frequently combines with emphasis particles such as 이때다 ("now is the moment!") or 이때쯤 ("around this time").

rootFamily.gloss: until now, up to this time

이래서.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) conjunctive adverb contracted from 이러하여서, the stem of 이러하다 ("to be like this, to act this way", from proximal manner root 이러 + light verb 하-) combined with the causal connective ending -여서 ("because it is like this").

history.meaning: because it is like this, by doing thus
this is why, for this reason, so

이래서.notes: Often used in spoken Korean to point to an immediate situation as proof of a general complaint ("See, this is why...").

rootFamily.gloss: to do this, to be like this

이러다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) demonstrative verb contracted from 이러하다 ("to do thus, to act like this"), composed of the proximal manner stem 이러- (from proximal 이 "this") and the productive verb-forming suffix -하다 ("to do, to be"). When used as an action verb, it takes processive inflections (이러니, 이러면, 이러다가).

history.meaning: to be like this, to act thus
to do this, to act like this, to end up doing

이러다.notes: In conditional or transferentive forms like 이러다(가) ("if we keep doing this..."), it warns of an impending unintended consequence.

rootFamily.gloss: to do that, to be like that

이런.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner contracted from 이러하- (이렇다, 'to be like this, be such') + adnominal suffix -ㄴ; also used as a mild exclamation of surprise or regret ('oh dear, my goodness').

history.meaning: such, like this; 'oh dear!'

이렇게.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 이러하게, adverbial form (-게) of 이러하다 / 이렇다 ('to be like this').

history.meaning: like this, in this way, so

이렇다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb contracted from 이러하다 (Middle Korean 이러하다, 'to be like this, be so', built on proximal deictic root 이-).

history.meaning: to be like this, be so

이루다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (Middle Korean 이루다), originally a causative derivative of the Middle Korean intransitive 일다 ('to arise, come into being', root of 일어나다 'to stand up') plus the causative suffix -우-. Thus 이루다 literally means 'to bring into being' or 'to cause to rise'. Today it serves as a highly poetic and standard verb for fulfilling a dream (꿈을 이루다), accomplishing a goal, or forming a harmonious whole.
이루다.notes: Conjugates 이루 + 어요 -> 이뤄요 (or uncontracted 이루어요). The passive/inchoative is 이루어지다 ('to be accomplished, come true').

이루어지다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) passive and inchoative compound verb built from 이루다 ("to accomplish, achieve, form", Middle Korean 일우다, the causative derivation of 일다 "to rise, come into being, happen") plus the infinitive linker -어 and the auxiliary passive/inchoative verb 지다 ("to become, come to be").

history.meaning: to come into being > to cause to come into being, accomplish
to be accomplished, to be fulfilled, to come true, to consist of

이루어지다.notes: Frequently contracted to 이뤄지다 in both speech and writing; means both "to come true" (꿈이 이루어지다) and "to be composed of" (~로 이루어지다).

rootFamily.gloss: to rise, happen, come into being

이르다.etymology: Convergence of three native Korean verbs from distinct Middle Korean stems: (1) adjective 이르다 ('to be early', Middle Korean 이르다); (2) verb 이르다 ('to reach, arrive at', Middle Korean 니르다, ל-irregular); and (3) verb 이르다 ('to say, tell, inform on', Middle Korean 니르다).

history.meaning: to be early; to reach a place; to tell or report

이름.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 일홈 ('name, appellation'), nominalization in -옴/-움 of 니르다 / 일컫다 ('to call, name, say').

history.meaning: that by which something is called, name
name, given name, renown

이름표.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 이름 ('name') + Sino-Korean 표 (票/標, 'tag, label, ticket').

history.meaning: name tag, name badge, label

이리.etymology: Native Korean directional/manner adverb descending from Middle Korean 이리 ('this way, toward here; in this manner'), formed from proximal demonstrative root 이- + directional suffix -리.

history.meaning: this way, over here; thus, so

이마.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 니마ㅎ ('forehead, brow').

history.meaning: forehead, brow
forehead, brow

이만.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) numeral compound 二萬, formed from 二 (두 이, "two") and 萬 (일만 만, "ten thousand, myriad", originally a pictograph of a scorpion borrowed phonetically in Old Chinese for "ten thousand"). Literally "two myriads", i.e., twenty thousand.

history.meaning: two myriads, twenty thousand
twenty thousand

이만.notes: Whereas 일만 (10,000) usually drops 일 to become simply 만, multiples from 20,000 upward require the leading multiplier (이만, 삼만). Also a homograph of the native Korean adverb 이만 ("this much, stopping here", as in 오늘은 이만 "that's all for today").

이만큼.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) degree adverb and pronoun formed from the proximal determiner 이 ("this", Middle Korean 이) and 만큼 ("extent, degree, as much as"), which itself arose in Early Modern Korean from the bound noun 만 ("extent, size") plus 큼 (the substantive nominalization of 크다 "to be big, great").

history.meaning: to this size, to this extent
this much, to this extent

이만큼.notes: Often accompanied by a hand gesture showing size or quantity, or used emotionally to emphasize how much effort or affection one has invested.

이면지.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 裏面紙, composed of 裏 (속 리/이, "inside, lining, reverse side", with initial ㄹ lost in South Korean word-initial position by the *두음법칙* initial-sound law), 面 (낯 면, "face, surface, side"), and 紙 (종이 지, "paper"). Literally "reverse-side paper", referring to single-sided printouts reused on the blank back for drafts or notes.

history.meaning: reverse surface + paper
scrap paper, reused one-sided printout

이면지.notes: A quintessential Korean office and broadcasting-station word: television writers and PDs go through stacks of script drafts and reuse the blank backs as 이면지.

rootFamily.gloss: reverse side, hidden side, underside (裏面)
manuscript paper, squared writing paper (原稿紙)

이모.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) kinship term 姨母, compounded from 姨 (이모 이, "mother's sister, wife's sister") and 母 (어미 모, "mother"). From its literal sense of "mother's sister", Korean kinship-based social deixis extended the word into an affectionate, respectful vocative for middle-aged female restaurant workers or family friends.

history.meaning: mother's sister, maternal aunt
maternal aunt; friendly address for a female server or middle-aged woman

이모.notes: Calling a woman at a casual Korean restaurant or *pojangmacha* 이모 ("Auntie!") feels warmer and more familial than 아주머니, because in Korean culture a maternal aunt is traditionally perceived as the closest, kindest relative after one's mother.

이미.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb inherited from fifteenth-century Middle Korean 이미 / 이믜 ('already, beforehand'), regularly used in Joseon-dynasty vernacular glosses (언해) to translate Classical Chinese 已 and 旣 ('already').

history.meaning: already, previously
already

이미.notes: Compare 이미 and 벌써: 이미 calmly reports a completed fact ('the bread is already in the oven'), whereas 벌써 expresses surprise ('finished already?!').

이미지.etymology: Modern loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English image, which entered Middle English via Old French image from Latin imago (stem imagin-, "likeness, statue, representation, mental picture"), related to imitari ("to copy, imitate"). In Korean media and entertainment discourse, it specifically denotes a celebrity's or public figure's perceived persona.

history.meaning: statue, likeness, representation
mental representation, visual likeness, public reputation
public image, persona, mental impression

이미지.notes: In Korean entertainment and workplace culture, 이미지 관리 ("image management" — curating one's public reputation) is a ubiquitous phrase.

이백.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 二百, joining 二 (두 이, 'two') and 百 (일백 백, 'hundred'). Sino-Korean numerals are used universally in modern Korean for reading mathematical figures, dates, money (이백 원), and metric measurements (이백 그램, 이백 미터), as well as time units like seconds and minutes, whereas native Korean numerals (스물, 두) are typically reserved for counting discrete objects (두 개) and hours (두 시).
이백.notes: Pronounced [이백]. When counting native objects, 이백 개 ('two hundred items') uses Sino-Korean, as native numerals over 100 are obsolete.

이백팔십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이백팔십 (二百八十), joining 이백 (二百, 'two hundred') and 팔십 (八十, 'eighty').

history.meaning: two hundred eighty (280)

이번.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean proximal determiner 이 ('this') + Sino-Korean counter 번 (番, 'turn, time, occasion').
