history.meaning: this time, this occasion, the current...

cognates.meaning: to part, leave each other, separation

이별.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 離別, formed from 離 (떠날 리/이, "to leave, depart from, be separated", with word-initial ㄹ becoming ㅇ in South Korean standard orthography) and 別 (나눌 별, "to divide, separate, part ways"). Denotes both a solemn parting of ways and a romantic breakup.

history.meaning: parting from loved ones, separation
parting, farewell, romantic breakup

이별.notes: More poetic and emotionally weighty than the native Korean verb 헤어지다 ("to break up, part ways"); pervasive in K-pop ballad titles and K-drama dialogue.

이별에도.etymology: Agglutinative inflected form built on the Sino-Korean noun 이별 (離別, "parting, separation, romantic breakup", from 離 "to leave, separate" + 別 "to divide, part") followed by the native Korean locative/dative postposition -에 ("in, at, upon") and the inclusive auxiliary particle -도 ("even, also, too").

history.meaning: even in parting, in separation as well
even in a breakup, even in parting

이별에도.notes: Korean stacks postpositional particles directly onto nouns: -에 marks the situation or domain ("in a breakup") while -도 adds concession or inclusion ("even in a breakup, [courtesy/etiquette is needed]").

rootFamily.gloss: to break up, to part ways (離別-)

이분.etymology: Compound pronoun combining the native Korean proximal determiner 이 ("this", Middle Korean 이) with the honorific bound noun 분 ("esteemed person", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 분, traditionally linked to Sino-Korean 分 "lot, status, personage" or native honorific grammaticalization). Serves as the polite/honorific counterpart of 이 사람 ("this person").

history.meaning: this esteemed personage
this person (honorific), this gentleman/lady

이분.notes: Written as one word when used as a pronoun meaning "this esteemed person" (이분은 피디님입니다), but with a space when 분 counters a numeral (이 두 분 "these two people").

이불장.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 이불 ('bedding quilt, comforter', Middle Korean 니블, from 닙다/입다 'to cover, wear') + Sino-Korean 장 (欌, 'wardrobe, cabinet, chest').

history.meaning: bedding closet or wardrobe for storing quilts and blankets

이뻐지다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) inchoative verb formed from 이쁘- (the vowel-raised colloquial and expressive variant of standard 예쁘다 "to be pretty", ultimately from Middle Korean 어엿브다 "to be pitiable, tender") plus the infinitive suffix -어 and the auxiliary inchoative verb 지다 ("to become").

history.meaning: to be pitiable > to be lovable, pretty
history.stage: Middle Korean to Early Modern Korean

history.meaning: to become prettier, to grow pretty (colloquial/affectionate)

이뻐지다.notes: Although 예뻐지다 was long the sole prescriptive standard, the National Institute of Korean Language officially recognized 이쁘다/이뻐지다 as a standard form in 2015 due to its universal usage in everyday conversation.

이쁘다.etymology: Native Korean (*고유어*) adjective raised from 예쁘다 via initial vowel raising (예 > 이). Both trace back to 15th-century Middle Korean 어엿브다 ("to be pitiable, pathetic, moving one to compassion", from 어엿- + adjective suffix -브-). Over the Early Modern period, "eliciting tender pity" underwent semantic amelioration to "endearing, lovely, pretty", while the older sense "pitiable" split off into 가엾다 / 어엾다.

history.meaning: to be pitiable, pathetic, worthy of compassion
to be endearing, lovely, pretty
to be pretty, cute, adorable

이쁘다.notes: A classic example of semantic amelioration in Korean: in King Sejong's 1446 *Hunminjeongeum* preface, 어엿비 너겨 meant "feeling pity/compassion for [the people]", not "thinking them pretty"! Also used beyond visual beauty to praise a child's or junior's admirable behavior (말도 이쁘게 한다).

rootFamily.gloss: to dote on, to adore, to treat affectionately

이사.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 移徙, formed from 移 (옮길 이, "to move, shift, transfer") and 徙 (옮길 사, "to move one's residence, relocate on foot", containing the crossroads/foot radical 彳 and 止). In Korean, 移徙 became the everyday word for moving house.

history.meaning: changing one's dwelling place, migrating
moving house, household relocation

이사.notes: Can be used either as a verbal noun with 하다 (이사하다) or as an object with 가다/오다 (이사 가다 "to move away", 이사 오다 "to move in"). Note the homophone 이사 (理事, "board director").

rootFamily.gloss: moving luggage, household goods packed for moving

이사하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 이사 (移徙, "moving house, changing residence", from 移 "to shift" + 徙 "to relocate") with the native Korean light verb 하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: to relocate one's dwelling
to move house, to relocate

이사하다.notes: In Korean drama plots and everyday life, moving day (이사하는 날) is traditionally celebrated by ordering *jjajangmyeon* (black-bean noodles) amid unpacked boxes.

이삼.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) approximative numeral compound 二三, juxtaposing adjacent numerals 二 (두 이, "two") and 三 (석 삼, "three") without a conjunction to express an approximate count of "two or three".

history.meaning: two or three, a couple of
two or three (used before Sino-Korean counters)

이삼.notes: Used before Sino-Korean counters like 일 ("days", 이삼 일 "two or three days"), 주 ("weeks"), or 년 ("years"), whereas native Korean 두세 ("two or three") precedes native counters like 번 ("times") or 개 ("items").

이삿짐.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native compound combining Sino-Korean 이사 (移徙, "moving house, relocation", from 移 "to shift" + 徙 "to move residence") + the genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (*사이시옷*, marking tense pronunciation [이샄찜/이사찜]) + native Korean 짐 ("load, pack, luggage", Middle Korean 짐, derived from 지다 "to carry on the back").

history.meaning: relocation + genitive marker + load/luggage
household goods packed for moving house

이삿짐.notes: Korean orthography inserts *사이시옷* (-ㅅ-) in hybrid Sino-Korean + native Korean compounds when the first element ends in a vowel and triggers tensification of the following consonant (이사 + 짐 -> 이삿짐 [이사찜]).

이삿짐센터.etymology: Three-part hybrid compound combining Sino-Korean 이사 (移徙, 'moving house, relocation', from 移 'to move' + 徙 'to shift residence') + compound interfix -ㅅ- + native Korean 짐 ('luggage, household load') + English loanword 센터 (center).

history.meaning: moving company, household movers

cognates.meaning: more than, above (以上) / abnormal, unusual (異常)
more than, above (以上) / abnormal (異常)

이상.etymology: Convergent Sino-Korean (*한자어*) homophone pair: (1) 以上 ("more than, beyond, the above"), from 以 (써 이, "by means of, starting from") + 上 (윗 상, "above, upper, beyond"); and (2) 異常 ("abnormal, strange, something wrong"), from 異 (다를 이, "different, unusual") + 常 (항상 상, "constant, normal, ordinary"). Both are pronounced 이상 in Korean.

history.meaning: from this upward / departing from the norm
more than, beyond, that is all (以上); abnormality, strangeness (異常)

morphemes.meaning: from, by means of (以) / different, unusual (異)

이상.notes: A high-frequency Sino-Korean homophone: 이상 (以上) means "more than / since / over and out", 이상 (異常) means "abnormality / strange" (as in 이상하다 "to be strange" or 이상 무 "nothing abnormal / all clear"), and 이상 (理想) means "an ideal".

이상하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 이상 (異常, 'unusualness, abnormality', from 異 'different, strange' + 常 'ordinary, constant') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.form: 異常 (이상, 'different from the norm') + -하다 -> 이상하다
history.meaning: to be strange, odd, unusual, weird

이상형.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 理想型, formed from 理想 (다스릴 리/이 理 "principle, reason" + 생각 상 想 "thought, conception", coined in Meiji Japan by Nishi Amane to translate Western philosophical *ideal*) plus 型 (모형 형, "mold, model, type", originally a clay casting mold). Originally a sociological term (translating Max Weber's *Idealtypus*), it became everyday Korean for one's romantic "ideal partner type".

history.meaning: philosophical or sociological ideal type (Idealtypus)
one's ideal romantic partner type

이상형.notes: A staple question on Korean variety shows and blind dates (*sogaeting*): "이상형이 어떻게 되세요?" ("What is your ideal type?").

rootFamily.gloss: blood type (血液型) / model type (-型)

이성.etymology: Sino-Korean (*한자어*) compound 異性, formed from 異 (다를 이, "different, other") and 性 (성품 성, "inborn nature, character, sex, gender", from 心 "heart/mind" + 生 "birth/life"). Originally meaning "different nature" in Classical Chinese, it was specialized in modern East Asian lexicon to mean "the opposite sex".

history.meaning: different nature or disposition
the opposite sex, a person of the opposite gender

이성.notes: Watch out for the exact homophone 이성 (理性, "reason, rationality", as in 이성적이다 "to be rational"): context determines whether someone is talking about romance with the opposite sex (異性) or keeping a cool head (理性).

rootFamily.gloss: friend of the opposite sex (異性親舊)

이슈.etymology: Modern loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English issue ("a matter of public debate or concern"), which came via Middle English and Old French issue ("way out, outcome, final result") from Vulgar Latin *exuta and Classical Latin exitus ("departure, outlet, result", from exire "to go out"). In Korean journalism and broadcasting, it narrowed specifically to mean a "hot topic, media buzz, or viral controversy".

history.meaning: going out, outlet, outcome
point in question, matter of public debate, publication
hot topic, media buzz, trending controversy or news item

morphemes.meaning: hot topic, public issue (from English issue)

이슈.notes: In Korean entertainment and newsrooms, 이슈가 되다 ("to become an issue") does not necessarily mean a problem—it often means "to go viral, attract media attention, or become a hot topic".

rootFamily.gloss: to turn into a hot topic / media issue (issue + 化)
newsmaker, someone who generates buzz (issue maker)

이슬비.etymology: Native Korean compound of 이슬 ('morning dew') and 비 ('rain').
이슬비.notes: Evokes a mist-like drizzle gentler than 소나기 ('passing shower') or 폭우 ('downpour').

이십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이십 (二十), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 십 (十, 'ten').

history.meaning: twenty

이십구.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이십구 (二十九), joining 이십 (二十, 'twenty') and 구 (九, 'nine').

history.meaning: twenty-nine (29)

이십분.etymology: Sino-Korean numerical time compound 二十分, formed from the numeral 이십 (二十, 'twenty' — composed of 이 二 'two' and 십 十 'ten') and the bound counter 분 (分, 'minute; fraction, one-sixtieth of an hour', from Middle Chinese *pjun, originally meaning 'to divide'). In the modern Korean dual numeral system, Sino-Korean numerals are strictly required before the Sino-Korean minute counter 분 (分), contrasting with native Korean numerals used before 시 (時, 'o'clock').

history.meaning: twenty parts; twenty divisions
twenty minutes

이십분.notes: When telling time in Korean, hours use native numerals (예: 두 시 '2 o'clock') while minutes always use Sino-Korean numerals like 이십분 ('20 minutes').

이십사시간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 二十四時間, combining the numeral 이십사 (二十四, 'twenty-four': 이 二 'two' + 십 十 'ten' + 사 四 'four') with 시간 (時間, 'hour(s), duration of time', from 시 時 'time, hour' + 간 間 'interval, space'). While native Korean 스물네 시간 is standard in everyday speech for counting duration, the fully Sino-Korean form 이십사시간 is common in rapid broadcast speech, written schedules, and idiomatic expressions meaning 'around the clock, 24/7'.

history.meaning: twenty-four + interval of time
twenty-four hours; around the clock

이십사시간.notes: Although 시간 ('hour duration') normally takes native Korean numbers (스물네 시간), the all-Sino-Korean 이십사시간 is widely used when emphasizing 'nonstop / 24 hours a day'.

이십오.etymology: Sino-Korean additive-multiplicative compound numeral 二十五 ('twenty-five'), transparently constructed from 이 (二, 'two', Middle Chinese *nyijH), 십 (十, 'ten', Middle Chinese *dzyip), and 오 (五, 'five', Middle Chinese *nguX). It belongs to the Sino-Korean numeral stratum borrowed during the Three Kingdoms and Unified Silla periods and exists alongside the native Korean equivalent 스물다섯.

history.meaning: twenty-five (two tens and five)
twenty-five

이십오.notes: Used for dates, money, phone numbers, minutes, and percentages, whereas native Korean 스물다섯 (스물다섯 살) is used when counting age in years or physical objects.

이안.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 二案 ('second proposal, option two, Plan B'), formed from 이 (二, 'two, second') and 안 (案, 'plan, proposal, draft, desk', from Middle Chinese *'anH, originally denoting a small wooden table or magistrate's desk, whence the documents placed upon it and by extension a formal proposal or bill). Widely used in corporate, bureaucratic, and television production planning meetings to contrast with 일안 (一案, 'option one').

history.meaning: wooden table; official document on a magistrate's desk
second draft or proposal
option two; second plan

이안.notes: In Korean office and broadcasting meetings, proposals are routinely labeled 일안 (一案, Plan A), 이안 (二案, Plan B), and 삼안 (三案, Plan C).

이야.etymology: Native Korean expressive interjection 이야, formed as a vocalic lengthening and intensification of the exclamation 야 ('hey!, wow!'). Across Korean varieties, open-vowel exclamations beginning with 이- or 으- followed by -야 express sudden admiration, surprise, or mock awe when witnessing something impressive or unexpected.

history.meaning: expressive exclamation of surprise or admiration

이야.notes: Pronounced with a long rising-falling intonation (이~야!), it conveys genuine admiration ('Wow, impressive!') or teasing surprise depending on context.

이야기.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Early Modern Korean 니야기 / 이야기 ('story, tale, conversation', likely derived from 니르다 'to tell, speak').

history.meaning: spoken account, tale, talk
story, tale, conversation, chat

이야기하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from 이야기 ('story, talk, conversation') + light verb -하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to talk, converse, tell a story

이어지다.etymology: Formed from the native Korean ㅅ-irregular verb 잇다 ('to join, link, continue', Middle Korean 닛다, whose stem-final ㅅ drops before vowels to yield 이어-) combined with the auxiliary suffix -어지다. It expresses how two musical phrases, roads, or generations link seamlessly into a continuous whole.
이어지다.notes: Past adnominal 이어진 means 'connected, continuous across time or space'.

이어폰.etymology: Twentieth-century loanword borrowed from English earphone (a compound of ear, from Old English eare, and -phone, from Ancient Greek phone 'voice, sound'). Adapted into Korean phonology as 이어폰 (i-eo-pon), with English non-rhotic /ɪə(r)/ rendered as disyllabic 이어 and /f/ mapped to aspirated bilabial /pʰ/ (ㅍ) since Korean lacks a labiodental fricative.

history.meaning: ear + voice/sound (audio receiver worn at the ear)
earphones, earbuds

이어폰.notes: In Korean, 이어폰 refers specifically to in-ear wired or wireless earbuds, whereas over-ear models are called 헤드폰 ('headphones').

이억.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 二億 ('two hundred million'), composed of 이 (二, 'two') and 억 (億, 'one hundred million, 10^8', from Middle Chinese *'ik). In Archaic Chinese, 億 originally meant 'one hundred thousand' (10^5) or simply 'a vast, incalculable number; peace of mind', before stabilizing in the East Asian myriad-based (만 萬 = 10^4) place-value system as 10^4 × 10^4 = 10^8.

history.meaning: a hundred thousand; myriad myriads (10^8)
two hundred million (200,000,000)

이억.notes: East Asian large numbers group by fours (만 = 10,000; 억 = 100,000,000) rather than threes, so learners must mentally translate 이억 directly as '200 million' rather than '2 billion'.

rootFamily.gloss: hundreds of millions of won (億臺)

이왕.etymology: Sino-Korean word 已往, composed of 이 (已, 'already, finished', Middle Chinese *yiX) and 왕 (往, 'to go, past, bygone', Middle Chinese *hjwangX). Originally a noun meaning 'things that have already passed; the past', in Korean it grammaticalized into a discourse adverb meaning 'since things have already gone this far; since one is doing it anyway; might as well'.

history.meaning: what has already gone by; the past
the past; already
since already; while one is at it

이왕.notes: Frequently paired with 조건 expressions like 이왕 이렇게 된 거 ('Since it has already turned out this way...') or 이왕이면 ('If we're doing it anyway, preferably...').

rootFamily.gloss: if one is doing it anyway (已往-)
round trip, going and coming (往復)

이웃.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 이우즛 / 이웃 ('neighbor, neighboring house', related to 잇다 'to join, connect consecutively').

history.meaning: adjoining house, neighbor
neighbor, neighborhood

이웃분.etymology: Respectful native Korean compound formed by attaching the honorific person suffix -분 (-bun, 'esteemed person') to 이웃 (iut, Middle Korean 이윳 iyus, 'neighbor, adjoining household'). In Middle Korean, 이윳 was related to the verb 잇- (is-, 'to join, connect, adjoin'), denoting those whose eaves and walls stood next to one's own. Adding -분 allows speakers to refer warmly and courteously to an individual neighbor in polite conversation.

history.meaning: adjoining house, neighbor
neighbor (respectful singular/plural reference)

이웃분.notes: Because ㅅ in coda position neutralizes to [ㄷ], the initial consonant of -분 tensifies in pronunciation to [이욷뿐].

이월.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 二月 ('February'), formed from 이 (二, 'two, second') and 월 (月, 'moon, month', from Middle Chinese *ngjwot). Historically in Joseon Korea, 二月 denoted the second month of the traditional lunisolar calendar; following the solar calendar reform (건양 Geonyang era, 1896), it came to designate February in the Gregorian calendar.

history.meaning: second month of the lunar year
February (second month of the Gregorian year)

이월.notes: Unlike 유월 (June, from 육월) and 시월 (October, from 십월) which drop their final consonants for ease of pronunciation, 이월 is completely regular.

이유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이유 (理由), joining 리/이 (理, 'principle, reason, logic') and 유 (由, 'cause, origin, from').

history.meaning: reason, ground, motive, excuse

이음새.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 이음 ('joining, connection', verbal noun in -음 of 잇다 'to join, link together') + suffix -새 ('manner, appearance, seam').

history.meaning: joint, seam, point where two pieces are joined

cognates.meaning: two days; the second day of the month
second day of the month; two days

이일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 二日 ('two days; the second day of the month'), formed from 이 (二, 'two, second') and 일 (日, 'sun, day', from Middle Chinese *nyit). It coexists with the native Korean word 이틀 ('two days; the second day'), with Sino-Korean 이일 preferred in formal announcements, written schedules, and calendar dates (예: 오월 이일 'May 2nd').

history.meaning: two days; the second day
two days; the 2nd of the month

이일.notes: In everyday conversation, Koreans often prefer native Korean 이틀 for 'a two-day duration' (이틀 동안), reserving 이일 primarily for calendar dates ('the 2nd') or formal schedules (일박 이일 '1 night, 2 days').

rootFamily.gloss: one night and two days (一泊二日)

이자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 利子 ('financial interest'), composed of 이 (利, historic/underlying 리, 'profit, benefit, sharpness', from Middle Chinese *lijH, originally depicting grain 禾 cut with a knife 刀) and 자 (子, 'child, offspring, small thing, seed', Middle Chinese *tsiX). By classical Chinese economic metaphor, the principal sum is the 'mother' (모금 母金) and the interest generated from it is the 'offspring of profit' (利子). Word-initial /l/ (ㄹ) regularly becomes ø (ㅇ) before /i/ in standard South Korean (두음법칙).

history.meaning: profit-offspring; financial yield on principal
interest on a loan
interest (on a debt or deposit)

이자.notes: Notice the word-initial sound law (두음법칙): 利 is pronounced 이 at the start of a word (이자 'interest', 이익 'profit') but 리 inside a word (금리 'interest rate', 복리 'compound interest').

이전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이전 (以前, 'before this, previous times', from 以 'by, from' + 前 'before, prior'; also 移轉 'moving to a new location, transfer of rights').

history.meaning: prior time, before; relocation or transfer

이제.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 이제 ('now, this moment', formed from proximal demonstrative 이 'this' + 적/제 'time, occasion').

history.meaning: this time, now
now, from now on

이제야.etymology: Native Korean emphatic temporal adverb formed from 이제 ('now') + emphatic particle -야 ('only when, at last').

history.meaning: only now, at long last

이중적.etymology: Sino-Korean derived noun/adnominal 二重的 ('dual, double, two-faced'), formed from 이중 (二重, 'double, two layers': 이 二 'two' + 중 重 'layer, fold, repeat', Middle Chinese *drjung) plus the Sino-Korean adjectival-nominal suffix -적 (的, 'having the quality of, -ic'). From the literal sense of 'two-layered', it developed the psychological and moral sense of 'duplicitous, hypocritical, two-faced'.

history.meaning: two layers, double fold
dual, two-fold; two-faced, duplicitous

이중적.notes: Can be used neutrally for 'dual nature' (이중적 구조 'dual structure') or critically for a person's behavior meaning 'two-faced, hypocritical' (이중적인 태도).

이중주.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 이중주 (二重奏), joining 이 (二, 'two'), 중 (重, 'fold, layer'), and 주 (奏, 'musical performance') — literally 'two-part instrumental performance'.

history.meaning: instrumental duet

이쪽.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative compound 이쪽 ('this side, this direction; our side / your side'), formed from the proximal demonstrative determiner 이 ('this', Middle Korean 이) and the bound noun 쪽 ('side, direction, piece', from Middle Korean 쟉 'piece, half of a split whole', which underwent palatalization and tensification to 쪽). In conversational Korean, 이쪽 also functions as a polite or indirect personal pronoun meaning 'this person, I/we' or 'your side'.

history.meaning: this + piece/side
this side, this way; this party/person

이쪽.notes: Part of the classic Korean three-way deictic system: 이쪽 ('this side / near me'), 그쪽 ('that side / near you; you'), and 저쪽 ('that side over there').

이쯤.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative-approximative compound 이쯤 ('around here, about this much, at this point'), combining the proximal demonstrative pronoun 이 ('this', Middle Korean 이) with the approximative suffix -쯤 ('around, approximately, to the degree of', derived from the native noun 즈음, Middle Korean 즈음 'interval of time or space, juncture'). Phonological contraction and tensification turned 즈음 into the productive bound suffix -쯤.

history.meaning: interval, juncture of time or space
around this point, to this extent

morphemes.meaning: approximately, around the point of (from 즈음)

이쯤.notes: Frequently used to wrap up a meeting, broadcast segment, or argument: 이쯤에서 마무리합시다 ('Let's wrap things up right about here').

cognates.meaning: second time, secondary; after-party (二次会 nijikai)

이차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 二次 ('second time, secondary stage; round two'), composed of 이 (二, 'two, second') and 차 (次, 'order, sequence, time, next', from Middle Chinese *tshijH). In South Korean workplace and dining culture (회식), 이차 specifically designates the 'second round' of an evening outing—moving from the first restaurant (일차) to a bar, pub, or karaoke room (노래방).

history.meaning: second in sequence; second time
secondary stage; round two of a social gathering

이차.notes: In Korean social life and K-dramas, "이차 가자!" ('Let's go to round two!') is the classic phrase for relocating to a bar or noraebang after dinner.

rootFamily.gloss: next time, next in order (次例)

이천.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이천 (二千), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 천 (千, 'thousand').

history.meaning: two thousand (2,000)

이층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이층 (二層), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 층 (層, 'story, level, floor').

history.meaning: second floor, two stories

이틀.etymology: Native Korean day-count noun descending from Middle Korean 이틀 ('two days; the second day of the month', built on an archaic native root 이트- 'two' + 날 'day').

history.meaning: two days; second day of a month

이해.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 理解 ('understanding, comprehension'), formed from 이 (理, historic/underlying 리, 'principle, reason, pattern in jade', from Middle Chinese *liX) and 해 (解, 'to untie, loosen, dissect, explain', from Middle Chinese *kaeX, graphically depicting a knife 刀 separating a cow's 牛 horn 角). Originally meaning 'to analyze according to principle', it was popularized in Meiji-era Japan and late 19th-century Korea as the standard philosophical and everyday term for intellectual and empathetic 'understanding'. Word-initial /l/ drops before /i/ in South Korean.

history.meaning: to untie/analyze according to natural principle
comprehension, understanding
understanding, sympathy, comprehension

이해.notes: Don't confuse 이해 (理解, 'understanding', pronounced with a short vowel) with its homograph 이해 (利害, 'gains and losses, interests', as in 이해관계 'conflict of interest').

이해하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 이해 (理解, 'understanding, comprehension', from 理 'principle, reason' + 解 'to untie, loosen, solve') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to understand, comprehend, figure out

이후.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이후 (以後), joining 이 (以, 'from, by') and 후 (後, 'after, behind, later').

history.meaning: after this, from then on, afterward, since

익다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 익다 ('to ripen, become thoroughly cooked, ferment, become familiar or skilled through practice').

history.meaning: to ripen, cook through, become practiced
to ripen, be cooked, grow familiar

익숙하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb combining the native Korean verb stem 익- (익다, 'to grow familiar or practiced') + Sino-Korean 숙 (熟, 'ripe, cooked, skilled, familiar') + native adjective suffix -하다 — a tautological native + Sino-Korean synonym compound.

history.meaning: to be accustomed to, familiar with, skilled at

익숙해지다.etymology: Hybrid Korean inchoative verb 익숙해지다 ('to become accustomed to, to grow used to'), derived from the descriptive verb 익숙하다 ('to be familiar, skilled, accustomed') plus the auxiliary inchoative construction -어지다 ('to become'). The stem 익숙 comes from Middle Korean 닉숙ᄒᆞ다, itself a blend of the native Korean verb root 닉- (modern 익다 'to ripen, be cooked, become familiar through practice') and the Sino-Korean morpheme 숙 (熟, 'ripe, cooked, thoroughly familiar', Middle Chinese *dzyuwk)—a striking tautological native+Sino-Korean compound where both halves mean 'ripe/familiar'.

history.meaning: to be ripe/well-practiced + Sino-Korean 'ripe/familiar' → to be skilled, accustomed
to grow accustomed to, to get used to

morphemes.meaning: to ripen, become familiar (native root 익-, Middle Korean 닉-)

익숙해지다.notes: Always takes the dative/locative particle -에 for the thing one gets used to: 새 환경에 익숙해지다 ('to get used to a new environment').

인간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 人間 ('human being; the human realm'), formed from 인 (人, 'person, human', Middle Chinese *nyin) and 간 (間, 'interval, space, among', Middle Chinese *kean). In Classical Chinese and early Buddhist texts (translating Sanskrit manuṣyaloka), 人間 meant 'among people; the mortal world' (as opposed to heaven or the underworld). In both Korean and Japanese, the meaning shifted metonymically from 'the realm among humans' to 'an individual human being' and 'humanity as a species'.

history.meaning: among people; the secular/mortal world (Sanskrit manuṣyaloka)
the mortal world; human relationships; a human being
human being, mortal; (colloquially) 'that guy/person'

인간.notes: In high register, 인간 means 'human being, mankind', but in casual frustration ("저 인간이 정말!" — 'That guy, seriously!'), calling someone 저 인간 or 이 인간 is a exasperated, slightly derogatory way to say 'this/that person'.

인간적.etymology: Sino-Korean derived noun/adnominal 人間的 ('human, humane, relatable, down-to-earth'), composed of 인간 (人間, 'human being', from 인 人 'person' + 간 間 'realm, among') and the Sino-Korean adjectival suffix -적 (的, 'having the quality of, -ic'). It denotes both the objective property of pertaining to humans and the warm, empathetic quality of showing genuine human flaws, warmth, and compassion.

history.meaning: human being + -ic (characteristic of a human)
human, humane, warm, relatable

인간적.notes: Used very frequently as a sentence adverb 인간적으로 ('Speaking as a decent human being / Honestly, between us humans...').

인구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 人口 ('population'), formed from 인 (人, 'person, human', Middle Chinese *nyin) and 구 (口, 'mouth, opening', Middle Chinese *khuwX). In Imperial Chinese and Joseon administrative censuses, subjects were enumerated by 'mouths to feed' (구 口, synecdochically representing an individual person), making 人口 literally 'the number of human mouths' in a territory.

history.meaning: human mouths (individuals counted in a household or state tax census)
population; number of inhabitants

morphemes.meaning: mouth; individual counted in a census (口)

인구.notes: The same 'mouths to feed' metaphor appears in 식구 (食口, literally 'eating mouths'), the warm everyday Korean word for 'family members / household members'.

인기도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 人氣度 ('popularity rating, degree of popularity'), formed from 인기 (人氣, 'popularity, public favor': 인 人 'person, people' + 기 氣 'breath, spirit, energy, aura', Middle Chinese *khj+jH) and the Sino-Korean suffix -도 (度, 'degree, measure, extent', Middle Chinese *duH). In television broadcasting and entertainment, 인기도 specifically measures a celebrity's or program's public appeal and recognition index.

history.meaning: human aura/vitality; public sentiment and favor
history.stage: Classical to Early Modern East Asian coined usage

history.meaning: degree of popularity; popularity rating

인기도.notes: In broadcasting (like in *The Producers*), 인기도 ('popularity rating') is often paired with 인지도 (認知度, 'public awareness/recognition rating').

인류.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 人類 ('humankind, the human race'), composed of 인 (人, 'person, human', Middle Chinese *nyin) and 류 (類, 'kind, category, species, class', Middle Chinese *ljwijH). Attested in Classical Chinese for 'the category of human beings' as distinct from birds and beasts, it was reinforced in the late 19th century as the scientific and anthropological term for Homo sapiens / humankind.

history.meaning: the class/category of human beings
humankind, humanity, the human species

인류.notes: Because of liquid assimilation in Korean phonology, /n/ + /r/ (인 + 류) is pronounced [일류] (illyu), making it a homophone of 일류 (一流, 'first-class, top-tier').

인마.etymology: Native Korean colloquial vocative interjection 인마 ('hey you!, brat!, punk!'), formed by rapid allegro contraction and nasal assimilation of the phrase 이놈아: proximal demonstrative 이 ('this') + pejorative bound noun 놈 ('fellow, guy, bastard', from Middle Korean 놈 'ordinary person, commoner, man') + intimate/blunt vocative particle -아. Specifically, 이놈아 [inoma] dropped the medial vowel /o/ to yield *인마 [inma] (alongside variant 임마 [imma] via labial assimilation).

history.meaning: hey, this fellow/commoner!
hey brat!, you punk!, man! (blunt/affectionate vocative)

인마.notes: Strictly informal (반말): used either when scolding a younger subordinate or affectionately/playfully banter-teasing a close friend ("야 인마!" — 'Hey, man! / You brat!'). Often pronounced and spelled 임마 as well.

인맥.etymology: Sino-Korean metaphorical compound 人脈 ('personal connections, network of contacts'), formed from 인 (人, 'person, human', Middle Chinese *nyin) and 맥 (脈, 'blood vessel, pulse, mountain range, mineral vein', Middle Chinese *mreak). Just as blood vessels (혈맥 血脈) circulate vitality through a body or mineral veins (광맥 鑛脈) run through rock, 人脈 conceptualizes interpersonal relationships and patronage networks as invisible 'human veins' running through society.

history.meaning: blood vessel, pulse; branching vein
network of personal connections and professional contacts

인맥.notes: In Korean corporate and entertainment life, having wide connections is expressed as 인맥이 넓다 ('one's network is wide') or colloquially 발이 넓다 ('one's feet are wide').

cognates.meaning: human affairs; personnel; ways of the world

인사.etymology: Sino-Korean polysemous compound 人事 (plus homophonous 人士 'prominent figure'), composed of 인 (人, 'person, human') and 사 (事, 'affair, matter, duty', Middle Chinese *dzriH). From the broad Classical Chinese sense of 'human affairs and social obligations', Korean developed the specific everyday sense of 'social courtesy, greeting, bowing' (인사하다 'to greet'), alongside the institutional sense of 'personnel administration, HR' (인사과 'HR department'). Homophonous 인사 (人士, with 사 士 'scholar, notable person') means 'prominent public figure, VIP'.

history.meaning: human affairs, duties, and social etiquette; (also 人士 'scholar-gentleman')
social etiquette, manners; greeting, salutation; personnel management

morphemes.meaning: affair, duty, etiquette (事); or scholar/figure (士)

인사.notes: One spelling covers three vital meanings in drama workplace settings: 1) greeting/bowing (인사하다), 2) HR/personnel appointments (인사 이동), and 3) VIP/notable figure (유명 인사, written 人士).

rootFamily.gloss: to greet, bow, say hello (人事-)

인사말.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 인사 (人事, 'courtesy greeting, salutation') with the native Korean noun 말 ('spoken words, speech'). According to standard Korean orthography, no 사이시옷 is written in 인사말 (even though some speakers insert a nasal in pronunciation), parallel to 머리말 ('foreword').
인사말.notes: Often paired with 환영 ('welcome') as 환영 인사말 ('welcome speech/remarks').

인사불성.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character idiom (사자성어) 人事不省 ('unconsciousness; dead drunk, out cold'), composed of 인사 (人事, 'human affairs, awareness of one's surroundings': 인 人 'person' + 사 事 'affair'), 불 (不, 'not', Middle Chinese *pjuw), and 성 (省, 'to examine, be aware of, reflect upon', Middle Chinese *sengX). Reordering the Classical Chinese verb-object phrase 不省人事 ('not aware of human affairs'), it literally means 'unable to recognize human affairs'—originally describing a coma or faint, and colloquially used for drinking oneself into total stupor.

history.form: 不省人事 / 人事不省
history.meaning: unable to perceive human affairs; in a coma or faint
unconscious; dead drunk, blacked out from alcohol

morphemes.meaning: to perceive, reflect, be conscious of (省)

인사불성.notes: Note that 省 is read 성 (seong) when it means 'to reflect/be conscious of' (반성, 성찰, 인사불성), but 생 (saeng) when it means 'to omit/save' (생략 'omission').

인사하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 인사 (人事, originally 'human affairs, social courtesy and etiquette', from 人 'person' + 事 'affair, service') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to greet, bow in greeting, say hello or goodbye

인생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 인생 (人生), joining 인 (人, 'human being, person') and 생 (生, 'life, birth, living').

history.meaning: human life, one's lifetime

인생에.etymology: Inflected noun phrase 인생에 ('in [one's] life'), consisting of the Sino-Korean compound noun 인생 (人生, 'human life, one's lifetime': 인 人 'person, human', Middle Chinese *nyin + 생 生 'birth, life, living', Middle Chinese *sraeng) followed by the native Korean locative/dative postpositional particle -에 ('in, at, to', Middle Korean -에). Unlike 생명 (生命, biological life force) or 생활 (生活, daily living/livelihood), 인생 specifically denotes the narrative arc and existential journey of a person's lifetime.

history.meaning: human life, a mortal's lifetime
in (one's) human life / lifetime

인생에.notes: Korean distinguishes three words for 'life': 인생 (人生, the philosophical journey of one's lifetime), 생명 (生命, biological life vs. death), and 생활 (生活, daily routine/living).

rootFamily.gloss: view of life, philosophy of life (人生觀)

인쇄되다.etymology: Formed by attaching the native passive/inchoative verb 되다 (doeda, 'to become, be done') to the Sino-Korean noun 인쇄 (印刷, 'printing', from 印 'stamp, seal, imprint' + 刷 'brush, ink-rub, print'). In Korean morphology, Sino-Korean action nouns regularly form active transitive verbs with -하다 (인쇄하다, 'to print') and passive verbs with -되다 (인쇄되다, 'to be printed'). Its past adnominal form 인쇄된 ('printed') frequently modifies nouns such as 종이 ('printed page') or 책 ('printed book').

history.meaning: imprinting with seals and brushing ink onto paper
to be printed

인쇄되다.notes: Commonly encountered in the adnominal modifier form 인쇄된 ('printed', e.g., 인쇄된 종이 'a printed sheet of paper').

인쇄하다.etymology: Active transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 인쇄 (印刷, 'printing') and the light verb -하다 (-hada, 'to do'). The two hanja characters 印 ('to press a seal or block') and 刷 ('to brush ink across woodblocks or movable type') directly reflect traditional East Asian woodblock and movable metal-type printing, in which Korea was a world pioneer during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties. Today 인쇄하다 covers everything from desktop laser printing to commercial book publishing.

history.meaning: pressing type/blocks and brushing ink to print
to print (documents, menus, or books)

인쇄하다.notes: In everyday office and home use, 인쇄하다 and 프린트하다 ('to print out') are interchangeable.

cognates.meaning: karmic cause and condition; predestined relationship

인연.etymology: Sino-Korean Buddhist compound 因緣 ('fate, destiny, karmic bond, interpersonal connection'), composed of 인 (因, 'direct cause, primary seed', Middle Chinese *'jin, translating Sanskrit hetu) and 연 (緣, 'indirect condition, hem of a garment, affinity', Middle Chinese *ywen, translating Sanskrit pratyaya). In Buddhist philosophy, hetu-pratyaya (因緣) explains how all phenomena arise from the convergence of inner causes (因) and external conditions (緣); in everyday Korean, it came to mean a 'meant-to-be bond' or fateful connection between people.

history.meaning: direct cause (hetu) and auxiliary condition (pratyaya) in Buddhist causality
karmic destiny; fateful bond or relationship between people

인연.notes: Central to Korean cultural views of relationships: meeting someone special is 인연이 닿다 ('for a fateful bond to reach/connect'), while parting ways is 인연이 아니다 ('it wasn't meant to be').

인정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound 認定하다 ('to acknowledge, admit, recognize, give credit'), formed from the Sino-Korean noun 인정 (認定: 인 認 'to recognize, know, admit', Middle Chinese *nyinH + 정 定 'to fix, settle, determine', Middle Chinese *dengH) and the native light verb -하다 ('to do'). Literally meaning 'to recognize and establish as settled fact', it spans legal/official certification as well as conversational admission of a truth or another's skill.

history.meaning: to recognize and establish definitely
to admit, acknowledge, recognize, give credit to

인정하다.notes: In modern Korean slang, the noun alone—"인정!" ('Admitted! / Fair enough! / I agree!') or "ㅇㅈ"—is constantly used as a standalone exclamation meaning 'Facts! / Can't argue with that!'. Also note homophone 인정 (人情, 'human warmth, compassion').

인터넷.etymology: Late 20th-century loanword borrowed from English Internet, itself a shortening of internetwork ( coined in the 1970s ARPANET/TCP-IP era from Latin prefix inter- 'between, among' + English network, from net + work). Adapted into Korean orthography as 인터넷 (in-teo-net), with non-rhotic English /ˈɪntə(r)nɛt/ rendered with final coda -ㅅ (realized as unreleased alveolar stop [t̚] at the end of a word or [s] before vowel-initial case particles like 인터넷에 [in.tʰʌ.ne.se]).

history.meaning: interconnected computer network
the internet

인터넷.notes: In casual Korean and online slang, 인터넷 is very frequently clipped to 인넷 or simply 넷 (as in 네티즌 'netizen', a portmanteau of net + citizen that remains mainstream in Korean).

인테리어.etymology: Borrowed from English interior (ultimately from Latin interior, comparative of inter 'within, between'), elliptically clipped in Korean (parallel to Japanese インテリア) from phrases like interior design or interior decoration to mean indoor decor or remodeling.

history.meaning: inner, situated within
inside of a building; indoor decoration
interior design, indoor remodeling or decor

인테리어.notes: In Korean usage, 인테리어 rarely means simply 'the inside' in abstract contexts; it specifically refers to interior design, home decor, or renovation work.

rootFamily.gloss: to remodel or decorate an interior

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 인테리어

인테리어하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed by combining the English loanword 인테리어 (from English interior, used for 'interior design or renovation') with the productive native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ('to do, to make').

history.meaning: inner part of a building; indoor design
to decorate or remodel the interior of a space

인테리어하다.notes: In everyday Korean speech, both 인테리어하다 and 인테리어를 하다 ('to do interior remodeling') are used interchangeably when talking about renovating an apartment or office.

인형.etymology: Sino-Korean word from 人形 (인형), composed of 人 (인, 'person, human') and 形 (형, 'form, shape, figure'). While the compound existed in Classical Chinese meaning 'human shape or effigy', its modern sense of 'doll, puppet, or plush toy' was reinforced by orthographic borrowing from Japanese 人形 (ningyō).

history.meaning: human form, human-shaped effigy or statue
doll, puppet, figurine
doll, puppet, stuffed animal or plush toy

인형.notes: Although literally 'human shape' (人形), 인형 in Korean covers not only human dolls but also animal plush toys (봉제 인형, 곰 인형 'teddy bear') and claw-machine prizes (인형 뽑기).

일.etymology: Convergence of two high-frequency words: (1) native Korean noun 일 ('work, task, matter, event', descending from Middle Korean 일); and (2) Sino-Korean numeral 일 (一, 'one') or calendar counter 일 (日, 'day').

history.meaning: work, job, affair; one; day

일곱.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 닐굽 ('seven').

history.meaning: seven
seven (native Korean number)

일관성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一貫性 (일관성), formed from 一貫 (일관, 'threading through with one strand, running consistently from start to finish', ultimately alluding to Confucius's Analects 4.15: 吾道一以貫之 'My way is threaded together by one single principle') plus the abstract noun suffix -性 (성, 'nature, quality').

history.meaning: to pierce or thread through with one single cord; unifying principle
consistency, coherence from beginning to end

morphemes.meaning: to pierce through, to string together

일관성.notes: Commonly collocated with 있다/없다 as 일관성이 있다 ('to be consistent') or 일관성이 없다 ('to be inconsistent, erratic').

rootFamily.gloss: to be consistent from start to finish

일광욕실.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean architectural compound 日光浴室, formed from 일광욕 (日光浴, 'sunbathing', from 日光 'sunlight' + 浴 'bathe, bask') and the room suffix -실 (室, 집 실, 'room, chamber'). Literally a 'sunlight-basking room', it designates a glass-enclosed sunroom or conservatory designed to catch afternoon light.

일기예보.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 일기예보 (日氣豫報), joining 일기 (日氣, 'daily weather') with 예보 (豫報, 'advance report, forecast').
일기예보.notes: Standard broadcast and everyday term for a weather forecast.

cognates.meaning: once; for the time being, first of all
in a single day; once (something happens)

일단.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb and noun from 一旦 (일단), literally 'one morning' or 'a single daybreak', composed of 一 (일, 'one, single') and 旦 (단, 'morning, dawn', pictographically the sun 日 rising above the horizon 一). From 'in a single morning', the meaning developed into 'once (an action occurs)' and, in Korean and Japanese, 'first of all, for now, setting other things aside'.

history.meaning: one morning; in a single day; once, if ever
first of all, for the time being; once (an action is taken)

일단.notes: In spoken Korean, 일단 is a ubiquitous discourse marker meaning 'first of all / for now, let's...', used to prioritize an immediate step before worrying about later details.

rootFamily.gloss: New Year's Day, the first morning of the year

cognates.meaning: first class, first rank, first place

일등.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一等 (일등), combining 一 (일, 'one, first') and 等 (등, 'grade, rank, class', originally bamboo slips 竹 aligned in order at a government office 寺). It denotes the highest rank, grade, or first place in a competition.

history.meaning: first grade, top tier in official rank or classification
first place, top rank, first class

일등.notes: While 일등 (一等) and 일위 (一位) both mean 'first place', 일등 feels more colloquial and competitive (e.g., school exams, lottery prizes), whereas 일위 is preferred in formal charts, ratings, and broadcast rankings.

rootFamily.gloss: ranking, order of grades or places

일러주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the 르-irregular verb 이르다 ('to tell, inform, teach, explain', from Middle Korean 니르다 niruda 'to say, speak, tell'), combined via its infinitive stem 일러- with the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, to do for someone').

history.meaning: to say, speak, tell, proclaim
to tell or explain for someone's benefit

morphemes.meaning: to tell, inform, instruct (stem of 이르다)
to give; to do for someone

일러주다.notes: Do not confuse the three homophonous Korean verbs spelled 이르다: (1) 'to tell/inform' (르-irregular: 일러, as in 일러주다), (2) 'to be early' (르-irregular: 일러), and (3) 'to reach/arrive at' (러-irregular: 이르러).

rootFamily.gloss: to tell, inform, instruct; or to tattle
to admonish, advise, or explain gently in detail
to tip off or tell someone what to do beforehand

cognates.meaning: one side, one aspect; front page of a newspaper

일면.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一面 (일면), composed of 一 (일, 'one, first') and 面 (면, 'face, surface, side, page'). In modern journalism and media, it specializes to mean 'page one, the front page of a newspaper', alongside its older senses of 'one side/aspect of a matter' and 'the whole surface'.

history.meaning: one face, one side or aspect; a single meeting
front page (page 1) of a newspaper; one side or aspect

일면.notes: In media and entertainment contexts (such as *The Producers*), 일면 almost always refers to the front page of a newspaper (1면 기사 'front-page article'), whereas in essayistic prose it means 'one aspect/on the one hand'.

rootFamily.gloss: acquaintance, having met at least once

cognates.meaning: to moor or stay for a night

일박.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一泊 (일박), combining 一 (일, 'one') and 泊 (박, 'to moor a boat for the night; to lodge or stay overnight', composed of the water radical 氵 and 白 phonetic). Originally referring to anchoring a vessel overnight, 泊 broadened to mean any overnight lodging on a trip.

history.meaning: to anchor a boat overnight; to stop and lodge for one night
a one-night stay (at a hotel, inn, or campsite)

일박.notes: Famous in Korean pop culture through the flagship KBS variety show *1박 2일* (일박 이일, '1 Night 2 Days'), the standard Korean phrasing for a weekend overnight trip.

rootFamily.gloss: lodging, staying overnight at an inn or hotel
staying out overnight away from home
two days and one night (1 night, 2 days)

일반.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一般 (일반), composed of 一 (일, 'one, same') and 般 (반, 'sort, kind, class, way', originally 'to turn or transport by boat'). In Middle Chinese and Tang–Song vernacular (often popularized in Buddhist texts), 一般 meant 'of the same kind, alike', which later evolved in East Asian usage to mean 'in general, universal, ordinary, standard'.

history.meaning: of one and the same kind; alike, identical
general, universal, ordinary (as opposed to special)
general, ordinary, standard, common

일반.notes: Used constantly as an attributive modifier before nouns (e.g., 일반 승객 'regular passenger', 일반 우편 'standard mail', 일반 상식 'common sense') to contrast with special, VIP, or professional categories.

cognates.meaning: ordinary person, member of the general public, non-celebrity

일반인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一般人 (일반인), formed by adding the person suffix -人 (인, 'person') to 一般 (일반, 'general, ordinary, common', from 一 'one, same' + 般 'kind, class'). It denotes a member of the general public or a layperson outside a specialized group.

history.meaning: member of the general public, ordinary citizen or layperson
ordinary person; layperson; non-celebrity civilian (in broadcasting)

일반인.notes: In Korean TV broadcasting and entertainment (like *The Producers*), 일반인 specifically means a 'non-celebrity / civilian' (as opposed to 연예인 'celebrity/entertainer'), such as when a celebrity dates a non-celebrity or a variety show features ordinary viewers.

일반적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun from 一般的 (일반적), derived from 一般 (일반, 'general, ordinary, common', from 一 'one, same' + 般 'kind, sort') plus the adnominal/attributive suffix -的 (적, 'of the nature of, -ic, -al').

history.meaning: general, universal, conventional (coined in Meiji-era translation of European 'general')
general, common, typical, ordinary

morphemes.meaning: attributive suffix (-ic, -al, having the quality of)

일반적.notes: Like other -적 (的) words in Korean, 일반적 cannot directly modify a noun on its own without -인 (일반적인 생각 'a common thought') and takes -으로 to form the adverb 일반적으로 ('generally, commonly').

일방적.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一方的 (일방적), formed from 一方 (일방, 'one side, one direction, one party', from 一 'one' + 方 'direction, side, party') and the attributive suffix -的 (적, '-al, -ic, characterized by'). It describes actions or feelings directed from only one side without mutual consent or reciprocity.

history.meaning: one direction, one region, one side or party
unilateral, one-sided
one-sided, unilateral, unreciprocated

일방적.notes: Used both in formal/legal contexts (일방적인 계약 파기 'unilateral breach of contract') and interpersonal contexts (일방적인 통보 'one-sided notification', 일방적인 사랑 'unrequited/one-sided love').

rootFamily.gloss: one-way traffic, one-way street or communication

일본식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 日本式 (일본식), combining 日本 (일본, 'Japan', literally 'origin of the sun', from 日 'sun' + 本 'root, origin') and the suffix -式 (식, 'style, mode, ceremony, system').

history.meaning: Land of the Rising Sun, Japan (adopted as official state name in the 7th century)
Japanese style, Japanese manner or culinary/architectural mode

일본식.notes: Whereas 일식 (日式) is the clipped culinary noun specifically meaning 'Japanese cuisine/food' (alongside 한식, 중식, 양식), 일본식 (日本式) means 'Japanese-style' more broadly (e.g., 일본식 카레 'Japanese-style curry', 일본식 정원 'Japanese-style garden').

일부러.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Early Modern Korean 일부러 ('on purpose, intentionally, going out of one's way').

history.meaning: deliberately, on purpose, специально

cognates.meaning: one minute; one point; one tenth

일분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一分 (일분), combining the Sino-Korean numeral 一 (일, 'one') with the counter 分 (분, 'minute; part, fraction, division', originally depicting a knife 刀 dividing something 八 into pieces). In modern timekeeping, 分 translates the Western 'minute' (a sixtieth part of an hour).

history.meaning: one part, one tenth, a tiny fraction
one minute (60 seconds); one part or fraction

일분.notes: Remember that Korean uses native Korean numerals for hours (한 시 '1 o'clock') but Sino-Korean numerals for minutes and seconds (일 분 '1 minute', 일 초 '1 second'). In TV production, 분당 (分當, 'per minute') ratings are tracked down to every 일분 (1분 단위로 'by the minute').

rootFamily.gloss: every single minute and second (idiom for urgency)

일시불.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一時拂 (일시불), composed of 一時 (일시, 'one time, all at once', from 一 'one' + 時 'time') and 拂 (불, 'to pay, clear, disburse', originally 'to brush away or shake off' with the hand radical 扌, extended in East Asian commercial usage via Japanese 払う harau to mean 'to pay off money').

history.form: 一時 + 拂 (一時払い ichijibarai)
history.meaning: paying the entire sum at one time
lump-sum payment, paying in full at once (as opposed to installments)

일시불.notes: At any shop or restaurant in Korea when paying by credit card, cashiers routinely ask "일시불로 해 드릴까요, 할부로 해 드릴까요?" ('Shall I put it on a single lump-sum payment, or in monthly installments [할부]?').

일시적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun from 一時的 (일시적), formed from 一時 (일시, 'one time, a brief moment, temporary', from 一 'one' + 時 'time, period') and the attributive suffix -的 (적, '-al, -ic, having the nature of').

history.meaning: one time, a single moment or brief period; simultaneously
temporary, transient, momentary, short-lived

일시적.notes: Contrast 일시적 (一時的, 'temporary, transient', e.g., 일시적인 현상 'a temporary phenomenon') with 지속적 (持續的, 'continuous, sustained') or 영구적 (永久的, 'permanent').

rootFamily.gloss: a moment, temporary; or date and time (日時)
temporary pause, pause button on media players

cognates.meaning: first proposal, plan A, one idea
one case; first proposal or draft

일안.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一案 (일안, often written 1안), composed of 一 (일, 'one, first') and 案 (안, 'proposal, plan, draft, case', originally 'a wooden writing desk or table' from 木 'wood' + 安 'peace/rest', which metonymically came to mean the official documents, drafts, and plans laid upon a desk).

history.meaning: writing table; official dossier, proposal, or plan number one
Option 1, Plan A, the first proposal or draft

일안.notes: In Korean corporate and TV production meetings (frequently written 1안, 2안, 3안), staff present multiple proposals where 일안 (1안) is 'Option 1 / Plan A' and 이안 (2안) is 'Option 2 / Plan B'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language Standard Korean Dictionary: 안 (案)

일어나다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 니러나다, formed from 일다 ('to rise, spring up', Middle Korean 닐다) + 나다 ('to come out, occur, happen').

history.meaning: to rise up, wake up, occur
to get up (from sleep or sitting), stand up, happen/break out

일어서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 니러서다, formed from 일다 ('to rise', Middle Korean 닐다) + 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand up, rise to one's feet

일요일.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 일요일 (日曜日), joining 일 (日, 'Sun'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day') — literally 'Day of the Sun' (Sunday).

history.meaning: Sunday

일위.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一位 (일위, often written 1위), combining 一 (일, 'one, first') and 位 (위, 'rank, position, seat, place', pictographically a person 亻 standing 立 at their assigned court station). It denotes the number-one position in rankings, charts, or ratings.

history.meaning: the first rank at court; one honorable person or seat
first place, #1 rank (in charts, viewership ratings, or standings)

일위.notes: In Korean broadcasting (*Music Bank* charts or TV viewership ratings 시청률), 일위 (1위) is the standard term for '#1 / first place' (e.g., 동시간대 시청률 1위 '#1 in viewership ratings in its time slot').

일인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一人 (일인, often written 1인), composed of 一 (일, 'one, single') and 人 (인, 'person, human'). While everyday counting of people uses native Korean 한 사람 or 한 명, Sino-Korean 일인 is used in formal compounds, per-capita statistics, and modifiers meaning 'one-person, solo, single-user'.

history.meaning: one person, a single individual; the sovereign alone
one person, solo, single-occupancy or per-capita modifier

일인.notes: Productively forms modern social and media terms such as 1인 가구 (일인 가구, 'single-person household'), 1인 미디어 (일인 미디어, 'solo creator/streamer media'), 1인분 (일인분, 'one-person serving'), and 1인 2역 (일인 이역, 'playing two roles by one actor').

rootFamily.gloss: one serving, portion for one person
number of one's own kind; top person in a field

cognates.meaning: one by one, in every single detail, without omission
one by one, each and every one

일일이.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb formed by reduplicating the Sino-Korean numeral 一 (일, 'one') as 一一 (일일, 'one by one, each and every one') and attaching the native Korean adverbial suffix -이 (historically from -히/-이, which derives adverbs from reduplicated or stative roots). Attested in Early Modern Korean as 일일히 before standardizing to 일일이.

history.meaning: one by one, each and every single one
one by one, in every single detail
one by one, individually, every single detail without exception

일일이.notes: A classic Korean spelling trap: because of the pronunciation of words like 꼼꼼히 or 천천히, many speakers mistakenly write *일일히, but under Hangul Orthography Rule 51 (after a syllable ending in ㄹ), only 일일이 is correct.

rootFamily.gloss: one by one, step by step (native Korean equivalent)
day by day, every day (homophonous 日日이)

일정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 日程 (일정), composed of 日 (일, 'day, daily') and 程 (정, 'journey, stage of travel, measure, schedule, order', originally a measure of grain 禾 presented to the king 呈). Originally denoting the distance traveled in a single day's journey, it evolved to mean a planned itinerary or schedule of work across days.

history.meaning: distance covered in a day's travel; daily quota of work
schedule, itinerary, agenda of events

일정.notes: In Korean entertainment and broadcasting, 일정 (日程) is the formal Korean equivalent of the loanword 스케줄 ('schedule'), used for shooting schedules (촬영 일정) and broadcast schedules (방송 일정). Note its homophone 일정 (一定, 'fixed, certain'), which forms 일정하다.

일정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjectival verb formed from 一定 (일정, 'fixed as one, settled, uniform, regular', from 一 'one, unified' + 定 'to fix, settle, determine') combined with the native Korean light verb/adjective suffix -하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: settled as one, firmly fixed, determined without variation
to be regular, fixed, constant, uniform

일정하다.notes: Do not confuse 일정하다 (一定하다, 'to be fixed, regular, constant', e.g., 일정한 간격 'regular intervals') with its homophone 일정 (日程, 'schedule, itinerary'). Also beware the Mandarin false friend 一定 (yīdìng), which usually means 'definitely, must', whereas Korean 일정하다 means 'constant/uniform' or 'a certain fixed amount'.

rootFamily.gloss: fixedness, regularity; a certain fixed amount (一定)

cognates.meaning: one kind, a sort of, a species of

일종.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一種 (일종), combining 一 (일, 'one, a') and 種 (종, 'seed, species, kind, category, sort', from 禾 'grain' + 重 'heavy'). Literally meaning 'one kind' or 'one species', it is almost always followed by the genitive particle 의 as 일종의 ('a kind of, a sort of').

history.meaning: one species of grain or plant; one kind or sort
a kind, a sort, a type (chiefly in 일종의 'a kind of')

일종.notes: In natural Korean, 일종 virtually never stands alone; it functions idiomatically in the frame 일종의 + Noun ('a kind of [Noun], a sort of [Noun]'), hedging or categorizing a concept (e.g., 일종의 직업병 'a kind of occupational hazard').

rootFamily.gloss: event, item, category (in sports or business)

일주일.etymology: Sino-Korean temporal compound 일주일 (一週日), joining 일 (一, 'one'), 주 (週, 'cycle, week'), and 일 (日, 'day').

history.meaning: one full week (seven days)

일찍.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 일즉 ('early, betimes; formerly', derived from the stem of 이르다 'to be early').

history.meaning: early, ahead of time
early

일차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 一次 (일차, often written 1차), composed of 一 (일, 'one, first') and 次 (차, 'order, sequence, stage, round, time', originally depicting a person pausing or lining up in sequence). It denotes the first stage, phase, or round in a sequence of events.

history.meaning: one time, first in sequence or order of stations
first round, phase one, primary stage; first stop in a night out

일차.notes: Beyond formal uses like 1차 면접 ('first-round interview') or 1차 산업 ('primary industry'), in Korean social and company dinner (회식) culture, 일차 (1차) specifically means 'Round 1' (usually dinner and drinks), followed by 이차 (2차, 'Round 2' at a bar or karaoke) and 삼차 (3차).

rootFamily.gloss: order, turn, sequence (derived from 次第)

일층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 일층 (一層), joining 일 (一, 'one, first') and 층 (層, 'story, floor, layer').

history.meaning: first floor (ground floor)

일하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 일하다, formed from 일 ('work, labor') + 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to work, labor

일호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 일호실 (一號室), joining 일 (一, 'one, No. 1'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room').

history.meaning: Room No. 1

읽다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닑다 ('to read aloud, recite, peruse written characters').

history.meaning: to read, recite
to read

읽어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 읽다 ('to read', Middle Korean 닑다 nilkda 'to read aloud, recite') connected via the infinitive suffix -어 to the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see', which as an auxiliary means 'to try doing, to experience doing').

history.meaning: to read + to see/try
to try reading, to read through and see; to have read before

morphemes.meaning: to try doing; to have the experience of doing (literally 'to see')

읽어보다.notes: Depending on tense, 읽어보다 means either 'to try reading / take a look at (a script, book, or message)' in imperatives and futures (한번 읽어보세요 'Please give it a read') or 'to have the experience of reading' in the past tense (읽어봤어요 'I've read it before').

rootFamily.gloss: to be read; or causative to make someone read

읽음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from the verb stem 읽- ('to read', from Middle Korean 닑다 nilkda) plus the productive nominalizing suffix -음, which turns verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns or completed-state labels.

history.meaning: the act or fact of reading
the act of reading; 'read' status indicator on digital messages and emails

읽음.notes: In modern digital communication (KakaoTalk, email, text messaging), 읽음 is the standard UI label for 'Read' (as opposed to 안 읽음 'Unread'), and gave rise to the ubiquitous Korean slang 읽씹 (읽고 씹다, 'leaving someone on read / reading a message and ignoring it').

rootFamily.gloss: to try reading, to give a read
reading a message and ignoring it ('leaving on read')

읽히다.etymology: Native Korean passive and causative verb descending from Middle Korean 닑히다, formed from 읽다 ('to read') + suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be read (easily or widely); to have someone read

잃다.etymology: Native Korean verb directly inherited from Middle Korean 잃다 (ilhda, 'to lose, to be deprived of, to forfeit'), attested since the 15th-century *Yongbieocheonga* (1447) and *Seokbo Sangjeol* (1449) with the consonant cluster stem 잃-.

history.meaning: to lose, be deprived of, miss (one's way or possession)
to lose (an object, person, direction, or attribute)

잃다.notes: Because the stem ends in the cluster ㅀ (lh), the ㅎ causes aspiration when followed by ㄱ, ㄷ, or ㅈ (so 잃고 is pronounced [일코], 잃지 is [일치]), while disappearing before a vowel (잃어 is pronounced [이러]). Learners often confuse 잃다 ('to lose an object/way', 잃어버리다) with 잊다 ('to forget a memory', 잊어버리다).

rootFamily.gloss: to lose completely, to misplace (with completive auxiliary 버리다)
to have the experience of losing something
loss, damage (native noun derived from 잃- + 손실)

잃어버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 잃다 ('to lose', Middle Korean 잃다) + completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to end up doing completely, regrettably').

history.meaning: to lose completely, misplace for good

잃어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 잃다 ('to lose, be deprived of', from Middle Korean 잃다 ilhda) linked via the infinitive suffix -어 to the experiential auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing or to have the experience of doing').

history.meaning: to lose + to see/experience
to have the experience of losing (something or someone)

morphemes.meaning: to experience, to have done before (literally 'to see')

잃어보다.notes: Because nobody intentionally 'tries' to lose something, -어 보다 attached to an involuntary verb like 잃다 almost exclusively carries the experiential meaning ('to have experienced losing something before', e.g., 잃어본 사람만 안다 'Only someone who has lost it knows').

rootFamily.gloss: to try reading / to have read before (parallel -어 보다 formation)

임대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 임대 (賃貸), joining 임 (賃, 'to hire, rent for payment') and 대 (貸, 'to lend, lease out').

history.meaning: leasing out, rental (of real estate or equipment)

임대료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 賃貸料 (임대료), composed of 賃 (임, 'to rent, hire, lease; wages', combining 任 phonetic with 貝 'cowrie shell/money'), 貸 (대, 'to lend, loan, lease out', combining 代 phonetic with 貝 'money'), and the suffix -料 (료, 'fee, charge, material', originally 'to measure grain' from 米 'rice' + 斗 'dipper').

history.meaning: fee paid for leasing or renting property or equipment
rent, lease payment, rental fee (especially for commercial or residential real estate)

임대료.notes: In Korea's real estate system, 임대료 is the formal legal and economic term for 'rent/lease fee' (especially for commercial properties, offices, and formal contracts), whereas in everyday residential conversation Koreans more often say 월세 (月貰, 'monthly rent') or 집세 ('house rent').

rootFamily.gloss: lessor, landlord, property owner who leases out

임무.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 임무 (任務), composed of 임 (任, 'entrust, appoint, bear responsibility') and 무 (務, 'affairs, duty, strive'). Adopted into modern Korean administrative and military usage during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries alongside cognate Japanese 任務 (ninmu).

history.meaning: entrusted official charge and administrative affairs
assigned duty, official mission, or task

임무.notes: Used both for serious military or official assignments and playfully in Korean variety shows like 1박 2일 for game challenges ('missions').

입.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 입 ('mouth, lips, opening').

history.meaning: mouth
mouth, lips, spoken words, eater

입구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 입구 (入口), joining 입 (入, 'to enter, go in') and 구 (口, 'mouth, opening, gate') — literally 'entering mouth/opening'.

history.meaning: entrance, way in

입다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닙다 ('to put on or wear clothing on the body; to receive a favor or suffer damage').

history.meaning: to wear clothing; to receive or suffer
to wear, put on (clothes); to suffer (harm) or receive (grace)

입맛.etymology: Native Korean Determinative compound noun 입맛, formed from 입 ('mouth', Middle Korean 입) and 맛 ('taste, flavor', Middle Korean 맛). Originally denoting the physical sensation of flavor in the mouth, it broadened semantically to mean one's appetite for food as well as personal aesthetic or culinary preference ('palate').

history.meaning: mouth and flavor/taste
appetite; culinary palate; personal taste or preference

입맛.notes: Commonly appears in idioms such as 입맛이 없다 ('to have no appetite') and 입맛에 맞다 ('to suit one's taste or preference').

입사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 입사 (入社), formed from 입 (入, 'enter') and 사 (社, 'company, society, tutelary shrine'). Coined in modern East Asian corporate vocabulary (paralleling Japanese 入社 nyūsha) as 社 shifted from traditional village altar or association to a commercial corporation (會社, 회사).

history.meaning: entering a local association or society
joining a business corporation or broadcasting company as an employee

입사.notes: In South Korean workplace culture, one's year or cohort of 입사 (입사 동기) defines seniority across broadcasting networks and conglomerates.

rootFamily.gloss: leaving or resigning from a company (退社)

cognates.word: 入社式 (にゅうしゃしき, nyūshashiki)

입사식.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 입사식 (入社式), combining 입사 (入社, 'entering a company', from 入 'enter' + 社 'company') with the suffixal noun 식 (式, 'ceremony, ritual, form'). It designates the formal corporate induction ceremony welcoming a cohort of new recruits.

history.meaning: entering a company + formal ceremony
corporate induction or onboarding ceremony for new hires

입사식.notes: The suffix -식 (式) productively forms ceremony nouns in Korean, such as 입학식 (school entrance ceremony), 졸업식 (graduation), and 결혼식 (wedding).

cognates.word: 入社する (にゅうしゃする, nyūsha suru)

입사하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative 입사하다 (入社하다), formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다) to the Sino-Korean action noun 입사 (入社, 'entering a company', from 入 'enter' + 社 'company, society').

history.meaning: to enter an association or company
to join a company; to enter corporate employment

입사하다.notes: Takes the dative/locative particle -에 to mark the employer (예: KBS에 입사하다, 'to join KBS'). Its antonym is 퇴사하다 ('to resign from a company').

rootFamily.gloss: to leave a company, resign (退社하다)
to enter a school, matriculate (入學하다)

cognates.word: 入水 (じゅすい / にゅうすい, jusui / nyūsui)

입수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 입수 (入水), composed of 입 (入, 'enter') and 수 (水, 'water'). Historically used in Literary Sinitic and Korean chronicles for entering water or drowning oneself, it was popularized in contemporary South Korean television by outdoor variety shows like 1박 2일 (2 Days & 1 Night) to mean plunging into cold water as a game penalty. Note a homophonous 입수 (入手, 'acquiring, obtaining').

history.meaning: entering water; submerging oneself in a river or sea
entering the water; plunging into cold water as a variety-show penalty

입수.notes: Do not confuse with the homophone 입수 (入手, 'obtaining information or an item', literally 'entering the hand'), which is common in news reporting.

입어주다.etymology: Native Korean compound benefactive verb 입어주다, formed from the main verb stem 입- ('to wear, put on clothing', Middle Korean 입다), the infinitive/connective suffix -어, and the auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give', Middle Korean 주다), grammaticalized here as a benefactive marker indicating that the action is performed as a favor for someone else.

history.meaning: to wear clothing + to give
to wear or put on (an outfit) for someone else's sake or benefit

morphemes.meaning: benefactive auxiliary ('to do for someone', lit. 'give')

입어주다.notes: In Korean celebrity and broadcasting culture, sponsors often ask stars or staff to '입어주다' (wear a garment as a favor) for product placement (PPL) exposure.

rootFamily.gloss: to try on clothes (lit. 'wear and see')

입원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 입원 (入院), composed of 입 (入, 'enter') and 원 (院, 'walled courtyard, public institution, hospital', here abbreviating 병원 病院 'hospital'). Adopted across modern East Asian medical terminology to denote being admitted to a hospital as an inpatient.

history.meaning: entering a monastic cloister or official courtyard institution
hospitalization; admission to a hospital as an inpatient

morphemes.meaning: institution, hospital (院, short for 病院)

입원.notes: Its direct antonym is 퇴원 (退院, 'being discharged from the hospital'), and a hospital room is called an 입원실 (入院室).

입원시키다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean causative verb 입원시키다 (入院시키다), formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun 입원 (入院, 'hospitalization', from 入 'enter' + 院 'hospital') with the native causative light verb 시키다 ('to make/cause someone to do', historically derived from Middle Korean 시기다).

history.meaning: hospitalization + to cause or order someone to do
to hospitalize someone; to have a patient admitted to a hospital

입원시키다.notes: While 입원하다 is intransitive ('to be hospitalized / check oneself in'), 입원시키다 is transitive ('to admit/hospitalize someone else').

rootFamily.gloss: to discharge a patient from the hospital (退院시키다)

cognates.word: 入院する (にゅういんする, nyūin suru)

입원하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative 입원하다 (入院하다), formed from the Sino-Korean noun 입원 (入院, 'hospitalization', composed of 入 'enter' + 院 'hospital, institution') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: to enter an institution or hospital
to be hospitalized; to check into a hospital as an inpatient

입원하다.notes: Although English uses a passive construction ('be hospitalized'), Korean uses the active intransitive verb 입원하다 ('enter the hospital').

rootFamily.gloss: to be discharged from the hospital (退院하다)

입으로는.etymology: Native Korean inflected noun phrase 입으로는, consisting of the noun 입 ('mouth', Middle Korean 입), the instrumental postpositional particle -으로 ('by means of, with', Middle Korean -으로), and the contrastive topic particle -는 ('as for, at least'). In discourse, it contrasts what someone says verbally ('with their mouth') against their true feelings or actions.

history.meaning: with the mouth (contrastive topic)
in words; verbally (often implying a gap between words and actions/feelings)

morphemes.meaning: contrastive topic marker ('as for, on the surface')

입으로는.notes: The contrastive particle -는 strongly implies an unspoken 'but': 입으로는 싫다고 하면서 ('saying they dislike it with their mouth, [while actually liking it]').

입장.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 입장 (立場), written with the Hanja 입 (立, 'stand') and 장 (場, 'place, ground, arena'). It originated as an orthographic borrowing of the Japanese native compound 立場 (tachiba, 'standing place; standpoint, position, situation'), read on the Sino-Korean pronunciations of its characters. (Note also the homophonous 입장 入場 'entering a venue').

history.meaning: place where one stands; footing; social position or standpoint
one's standpoint, position, perspective, or predicament

입장.notes: Initial الل (l/r) in 立 (립) becomes ㅇ (입) word-initially under the South Korean Initial Sound Rule (두음법칙). Commonly used in 입장 바꿔 생각하다 ('to put oneself in someone else's shoes').

cognates.meaning: moving into a residence or building

입주.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 입주 (入居), composed of 입 (入, 'enter') and 주 (居, 'reside, dwell, occupy', which has the secondary Sino-Korean reading 거 as in 거주 居住, or alternatively written 入住 with 住 'dwell'). In modern Korean real estate and office terminology, it denotes moving into a new home, apartment complex, or commercial building.

history.meaning: entering a dwelling to take up residence
moving into an apartment, house, or office building

입주.notes: Frequently paired with words like 입주자 ('resident/tenant') and 입주 청소 ('move-in deep cleaning' before occupying an apartment).

cognates.meaning: to move into a building or apartment
cognates.word: 入居する (にゅうきょする, nyūkyo suru)

입주하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative 입주하다 (入居하다 / 入住하다), formed from the Sino-Korean noun 입주 ('moving into a dwelling', from 入 'enter' + 住/居 'reside, dwell') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: to enter and dwell in a residence
to move into a house, apartment, or office building

입주하다.notes: Whereas 이사하다 ('to move house') emphasizes the relocation process itself, 입주하다 emphasizes taking occupancy of a newly built or newly leased property.

있겠냐.etymology: Inflected rhetorical question form of the native Korean existential verb 있다 ('to exist, to have', from Middle Korean 이시다 via assimilated 잇다), combining the stem 있- with the presumptive/conjectural pre-final suffix -겠- and the intimate/plain interrogative ending -냐 (variant of -느냐). Literally 'would there be?', it functions idiomatically as an emphatic rhetorical denial ('how could there possibly be?').

history.meaning: to exist, to be located, to stay
would there be?; how could there possibly be? (rhetorical question)

morphemes.meaning: to exist, to have, to be at

있겠냐.notes: In casual speech (반말), -겠냐 almost always expresses sarcastic or emphatic disbelief rather than a genuine question (예: 말이 되겠냐? 'How could that make sense?').

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to have, to stay
to not exist, to lack (originally 없- + -다)

있는.etymology: Adnominal (participial) present-tense form 있는, derived from the native Korean existential and possessive verb stem 있- ('to exist, to have, to stay', Middle Korean 이시다 / 잇다) plus the dynamic present adnominal suffix -는 (historically from Middle Korean processive -ᄂᆞ- + adnominal -ㄴ). Although 있다 behaves partly like a descriptive adjective in some paradigms, it takes the active adnominal ending -는 rather than adjectival -은.

history.meaning: which is existing; who stays at
existing; that has; who is located at (modifying a following noun)

morphemes.meaning: to exist, to have, to be at

있는.notes: Because 있다 straddles the boundary between verbs and adjectives in Korean, learners should note that its noun-modifying form is always 있는 (like action verbs), never *있은.

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to have, to be at

있다.etymology: Native Korean existential and possessive verb/adjective descending from Middle Korean 이시다 ('to exist, be in a place, have, stay').

history.meaning: to exist, be present, stay
to be (in a place), exist, have

있다더니.etymology: Inflected quotative-retrospective connective form 있다더니, built on the existential verb stem 있- ('to exist, to have', Middle Korean 이시다 / 잇다) and the contracted indirect-quotative retrospective ending -다더니 (shortened from -다고 하더니, combining declarative -다, quotative complementizer -고, verb 하- 'say', retrospective -더-, and sequential/contrastive connective -니).

history.meaning: said that there was/existed, and then (as observed)...
heard/said that there was, and (sure enough / contrary to expectation)...

morphemes.meaning: to exist, to have, to be at
retrospective connective ('as I observed, and so / yet')

있다더니.notes: Used either to confirm hearsay with firsthand observation ('I heard she had one, and sure enough she does!') or to point out an ironic contrast with what was claimed.

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to have, to stay

있어보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb 있어보다, formed from the existential/stative verb stem 있- ('to stay, remain, be in a state', Middle Korean 이시다 / 잇다), the infinitive connective -어, and the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see', Middle Korean 보다), which grammaticalized into an experiential or tentative auxiliary meaning 'to try doing' or 'to experience being'.

history.meaning: to stay/exist + to see
to try staying; to wait and see; to experience being in a place or state

morphemes.meaning: tentative/experiential auxiliary ('to try doing, wait and see')

있어보다.notes: In the imperative (가만히 좀 있어 봐! 'Hold still / stay put for a second!'), it is one of the most frequent conversational expressions in Korean dramas.

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to stay, to have

있어주다.etymology: Native Korean compound benefactive verb 있어주다, composed of the verb stem 있- ('to stay, remain, be present', Middle Korean 이시다 / 잇다), the infinitive connective -어, and the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's sake', Middle Korean 주다). It expresses remaining at someone's side or staying in a place as a supportive favor.

history.meaning: to stay/be present + to give
to stay with or remain present for someone's benefit

있어주다.notes: Often appears in emotional expressions of gratitude or comfort, such as 옆에 있어 줘서 고마워 ('Thank you for staying by my side').

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to stay, to have
to try staying, stay put and see
to do something for someone's sake

있잖아.etymology: Conversational Korean discourse marker and interjection 있잖아, grammaticalized from the intimate sentence-ending form of 있잖다, itself a phonological contraction of 있지 않다 (있- 'to exist' + -지 'negative nominalizer' + 않- 'not to be' + -아 'intimate ending'). Literally asking 'Isn't there...?' or 'You know there is...', it evolved into an attention-getting opener ('Hey, listen', 'You know what?').

history.meaning: does it not exist?; is there not? (rhetorical negative question)
you know; hey, listen; the thing is (discourse marker introducing a topic)
