morphemes.meaning: contracted negative presuppositional marker (-지 않-, 'you know that...')

있잖아.notes: Adding the polite particle -요 yields 있잖아요, a quintessential conversational opener when hesitantly bringing up a request or secret.

rootFamily.gloss: to exist, to have, to be at
isn't it so?; you know, right? (< 그렇지 않아)
didn't you say...?; as I told you (< 그렇지 않았느냐)

잉크.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English ink (ultimately via Old French enque from Late Latin encaustum < Ancient Greek enkauston 'purple ink burned in').

history.meaning: writing or printing ink

잊다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 잊다 ('to forget, let slip from memory').

history.meaning: to forget
to forget

잊어버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 잊다 ('to forget') + completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to end up doing completely').

history.meaning: to forget completely, clean forget

잎.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean as 닙 or 닢 ('leaf, petal'). Under modern South Korean orthographic rules (두음법칙), the initial ㄴ drops before ㅣ or ㅑ/ㅕ/ㅛ/ㅠ at the start of a word, yielding 잎. However, the ancient ㄴ re-emerges when combined in compounds with a preceding vowel, written via 사이시옷: 나뭇잎 (나무+ㅅ+잎, pronounced [나문닙]), 꽃잎 ([꼰닙]), 깻잎 ([깬닙]).
잎.notes: Takes counters like 장 (잎 한 장 'one leaf').

잎사귀.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Early Modern Korean 닙사귀 / 입사귀, derived from 잎 ('leaf', Middle Korean 닢) + suffix -사귀 ('foliage, individual leaf blade', cf. 귀 'ear, corner').

history.meaning: individual tree or plant leaf

자.etymology: Native Koreanhortative/prompting interjection 자 ('come on!, well now!, here we go!'); also a native Korean noun 자 ('measuring ruler, Korean foot measure', Middle Korean 자ㅎ).

history.meaning: well!, come now!, here! (interj.); ruler, foot measure (noun)

자가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 자가 (自家), formed from 자 (自, 'self, one's own') and 가 (家, 'house, home, family'). In Classical Chinese and earlier Korean, it meant 'one's own household or clan'; in modern South Korean housing and real-estate terminology, it specifically designates an owner-occupied home (as opposed to 전세 key-money lease or 월세 monthly rent).

history.meaning: one's own household, family, or school of thought
one's own house; owner-occupied property (also prefix 'self-/private', as in 자가용)

자가.notes: In Korean real estate surveys and dating banter (as seen in 프로듀사), housing status is categorized into 자가 (owner-occupied), 전세 (lump-sum deposit lease), and 월세 (monthly rent).

rootFamily.gloss: private car, for personal use (自家用)

자격.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 자격 (資格), composed of 자 (資, 'resources, endowment, innate quality, capital') and 격 (格, 'standard, status, rank, pattern'). Originally referring to a person's natural endowments and official rank in Literary Sinitic, it became the standard modern legal and social term for formal qualification, eligibility, or right to do something.

history.meaning: personal endowment and official status or rank
qualification, eligibility, credential, or right

자격.notes: Frequently used both for official credentials (자격증, 'license/certificate') and interpersonal standing (예: 네가 그럴 자격이 있어? 'Do you have the right to act like that?').

자괴감.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 자괴감 (自愧感), formed from 자괴 (自愧, 'being ashamed of oneself', composed of 自 'self' + 愧 'shame, remorse, mortification') and the suffixal noun 감 (感, 'feeling, sense, emotion'). In Literary Sinitic, 自愧 functioned as a reflexive verb phrase ('to feel shame within oneself'), which was nominalized with -감 in modern Korean psychological vocabulary.

history.meaning: to feel ashamed of oneself; inward mortification
sense of self-reproach, self-disgust, humiliation, or shame at oneself

자괴감.notes: Commonly collocated with 들다: 자괴감이 들다 ('to be overcome with a sense of self-reproach or humiliation').

자국.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 자국 / 자최 ('footprint, track, mark or stain left behind where something has pressed or passed').

history.meaning: footprint, track, trace, mark, scar, stain

자기.etymology: Sino-Korean reflexive pronoun 자기 (自己), joining 자 (自, 'self, oneself') and 기 (己, 'self, one's own person'); also used in modern colloquial Korean as an affectionate second-person pronoun between romantic partners ('honey, darling').

history.meaning: oneself (reflexive pronoun); darling/honey

자기네.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean collective pronoun 자기네 (自己네), formed by attaching the native Korean collective/group suffix -네 ('household, group, folks associated with') to the Sino-Korean reflexive pronoun 자기 (自己, 'oneself', from 自 'self' + 己 'self'). It refers to a third-person group ('they, their side, their family/company') already established in discourse.

history.meaning: oneself + collective/plural group marker
they, their group, their family/company; (Directly pre-nominal) their

morphemes.meaning: collective group / household suffix ('folks, side, group')

자기네.notes: Directly before a noun, 자기네 often functions possessively without 의 (예: 자기네 회사, 'their own company'; 자기네끼리, 'among themselves').

자기는.etymology: Topic-marked Sino-Korean pronoun 자기는 (自己는), consisting of the reflexive pronoun 자기 (自己, combining the synonymous Classical Chinese characters 自 'self' and 己 'self') and the native Korean topic/contrastive particle -는 ('as for'). In modern Korean, 자기 functions both as a third-person reflexive ('as for him/her/oneself') and, in intimate speech between couples or close friends, as a second-person pronoun ('as for you, honey').

history.meaning: one's own self (emphatic disyllabic reflexive)
as for oneself; as for him/her (reported speech); as for you/darling (intimate)

자기는.notes: Beware the dual usage of 자기: in formal or narrative contexts it means 'oneself / he / she', whereas between romantic partners (자기는 뭐 먹을래?) it means 'honey / you'.

cognates.word: 自己主張 (じこしゅちょう, jiko shuchō)
自己主張 / 自己主张 (zìjǐ zhǔzhāng)

자기주장.etymology: Sino-Korean quadrisyllabic compound 자기주장 (自己主張), combining 자기 (自己, 'oneself', from 自 'self' + 己 'self') with 주장 (主張, 'assertion, advocacy, claim', from 主 'main, host, lead' + 張 'stretch, spread, advocate'). It denotes asserting one's own opinions, convictions, or needs rather than yielding passively to others.

history.meaning: oneself + holding forth or advocating a position
self-assertion; expressing one's own convictions or opinions firmly

자기주장.notes: Commonly used in the expression 자기주장이 강하다 ('to be strongly opinionated / assertive'), which is also a humorous Korean slang phrase for having very prominent facial features (예: 이목구비가 자기주장이 강하다).

자꾸.etymology: Native Korean adverb (attested in Early Modern Korean 자고 / 자꾸) meaning 'repeatedly, over and over, persistently'.

history.meaning: repeatedly, again and again, continually

자꾸만.etymology: Native Korean emphatic adverb 자꾸만, formed by adding the delimiter particle -만 ('only, just, exclusively, emphatically') to the adverb 자꾸 ('repeatedly, incessantly, over and over', attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄌᆞᆰ고 / 자꼬, linked to the root 잦- 'to be frequent', Middle Korean 잗다). The suffix -만 intensifies the sense of unstoppable or involuntary repetition.

history.meaning: to be frequent > frequently, repeatedly
over and over again; persistently; despite oneself

자꾸만.notes: Compared to plain 자꾸, 자꾸만 carries a softer, more lyrical or emotional nuance—often used when thoughts, smiles, or feelings keep arising involuntarily (예: 자꾸만 생각이 나요, 'I just keep thinking of it').

자다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 자다 ('to sleep, go to bed').

history.meaning: to sleep
to sleep, lodge for the night; (of a clock) to stop

cognates.word: 自動振替 (じどうふりかえ, jidō furikae)

자동이체.etymology: Sino-Korean quadrisyllabic compound 자동이체 (自動移替), composed of 자동 (自動, 'automatic', from 自 'self' + 動 'move') and 이체 (移替, 'transferring funds between accounts', from 移 'move, shift' + 替 'replace, substitute, exchange'). It is the standard South Korean banking term for an automatic recurring fund transfer or direct debit.

history.meaning: self-moving (automatic) + shifting and substituting accounts
automatic bank transfer; direct debit; standing order

자동이체.notes: Whereas 계좌이체 (口座移替) is a one-time bank transfer between accounts, 자동이체 is a scheduled recurring payment for bills, rent, or subscriptions.

자라나다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb formed from 자라다 ('to grow, mature', Middle Korean 자라다) + 나다 ('to come forth, sprout, develop').

history.meaning: to grow up, spring up and mature

자라다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 자라다 ('to grow in size or age, mature; to be sufficient').

history.meaning: to grow, reach fullness
to grow up, grow (of plants, animals, children)

자락.etymology: Native Korean noun 자락 denoting the hanging flap, skirt, or lower border of a garment or cloth, extended metaphorically to the sloping foot of a mountain (산자락) and the fading tail end of a song or season. Attested in Early Modern Korean texts describing robe hems, it retains a tactile sense of flexible fabric that can be folded back or lifted.
자락.notes: Common in compounds like 옷자락 ('hem of clothes') and 산자락 ('foothill').

자랑.etymology: Native Korean noun 자랑 ('boasting, bragging, source of pride'), attested in fifteenth-century Middle Korean texts (such as the Seokbo Sangjeol, 1447) in the exact form 자랑 alongside the verb 자랑ᄒᆞ다 ('to boast, praise oneself'). It is a pure native Korean root (고유어) with no Hanja derivation.

history.meaning: boasting, praising oneself, showing off
boasting, bragging; something or someone to be proud of

자랑.notes: Unlike English 'bragging' (which is mostly negative), 자랑 can also be positive: 자랑스럽다 means 'to be proud of / worthy of pride' (예: 자랑스러운 한국인).

rootFamily.gloss: to be proud, worthy of pride
something to boast about, pride and joy (자랑 + 거리)

자료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 자료 (資料), formed from 자 (資, 'resources, capital, aid, basis') and 료 (料, 'measure, grain, material, ingredients'). Historically denoting material provisions or supplies, it became the standard modern East Asian term for reference materials, research data, documentation, or television archive footage (자료 화면).

history.meaning: material provisions, supplies, or resources for use
data, reference materials, documents, or archive footage

자료.notes: In television production (like 프로듀사), 자료 화면 ('reference/archive footage') and 자료 조사 ('background research') are everyday production terms. Word-internally, 料 retains its original r/l reading 료, whereas word-initially it becomes 요 (as in 요리 料理 'cooking').

rootFamily.gloss: resources, natural or human capital (資源)

자르다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 짤아다 / 자르다 ('to cut off, sever, chop into pieces').

history.meaning: to cut, sever
to cut, slice, chop, trim

자리.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 자리 ('woven mat for sitting or sleeping; seat, place, spot, position, trace').

history.meaning: sitting/sleeping mat; spot, seat, position
seat, place, spot, job opening, occasion

자막.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 字幕 (자막), borrowed via modern Japanese 字幕 (jimaku), which was coined during the silent film era from 字 (자, "written character, letter") + 幕 (막, "curtain, screen"). Originally referring to intertitle cards projected onto a cloth screen between scenes, it expanded to denote superimposed film subtitles and, in Korean television, expressive on-screen caption graphics.

history.meaning: written character + tent or stage curtain
silent-film intertitle screen or superimposed dialogue captions
subtitles, closed captions, or variety-show on-screen text graphics

자막.notes: In Korean variety shows like those featured in The Producers, 자막 refers not just to translation subtitles but to the colorful, witty editorial pop-up captions added by PDs and writers to punch up comedic moments.

rootFamily.gloss: opening of a play or event (開幕)
behind the scenes, inside story (內幕)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자막 (字幕)

자물쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 자믈쇠, formed from the verb stem 잠그- / 자믈- ('to lock, fasten shut', Middle Korean 자믈다) + 쇠 ('iron, metal device').

history.meaning: metal locking mechanism, padlock
lock, padlock

자빠지다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb attested in Early Modern Korean as 쟙바지다 and 자바지다. Formed from the bound root 자빠- ("to tilt or lean backward", preserved in the causative counterpart 자빠뜨리다) combined with the inchoative auxiliary verb -아/어지다 ("to become, to fall into a state"). It specifically denotes losing one's balance and falling backward onto one's back.

history.meaning: to tilt backward and fall over onto one's back
to topple backward; (vulgar/slang) to sprawl out or flop down

자빠지다.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes direction of falling: 자빠지다 means falling backward (onto one's back), whereas 엎어지다 means falling forward (onto one's face or stomach). In rough speech, 자빠지다 (e.g., 자빠져 자다) is a vulgar intensifier for sprawling out lazily.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall forward on one's face

자세히.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 자세 (仔細 / 詳細, 'minute, detailed, attentive', from 仔 'careful, minute' + 細 'fine, small, detailed') + native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: in detail, closely, minutely, carefully

자숙하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal noun 자숙 (自肅, "self-discipline, solemn self-restraint") combined with the native light verb 하다 ("to do"). Composed of 自 (자, "self, oneself") + 肅 (숙, "solemn, reverent, strict, purge"). Originally denoting quiet moral self-cultivation and austerity, in modern South Korean media it acquired the specialized institutional meaning of stepping away from broadcasting in contrite reflection after a public controversy.

history.meaning: to compose oneself with solemn reverence and strict self-discipline
to exercise self-restraint; to go on public hiatus in contrite reflection

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving active verbs (to do)

자숙하다.notes: In Korean entertainment journalism, 자숙하다 is the standard term for when a celebrity withdraws from all TV appearances following a scandal (such as a DUI or controversy) to demonstrate remorse to the public.

rootFamily.gloss: period of contrite hiatus (自肅期間)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자숙하다 (自肅하다)

자식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자식 (子息), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄌᆞ식 (子息). Composed of 子 (자, "child, son, seed") + 息 (식, originally "breath, respiration", extended in Classical Chinese to "that which grows and multiplies, offspring"). While retaining its literal meaning of "one's own children", in colloquial Korean it underwent pejoration when paired with demonstratives (이 자식, 그 자식) to mean "brat, punk, jerk, guy".

history.meaning: sons and daughters; offspring born of one's bloodline
one's children, progeny
one's children; (colloquial/derogatory) brat, jerk, fellow

자식.notes: Context determines whether 자식 is tender or vulgar: 부모와 자식 means "parents and children", whereas 이 자식아! or 그 자식들은 ranges from affectionate rough camaraderie among close friends to a sharp insult ("you punk / those jerks").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자식 (子息)

cognates.meaning: oneself, one's own body or person

자신.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자신 (自身), from Classical Chinese 自身, composed of 自 (자, originally a pictograph of a nose, hence "self, oneself") + 身 (신, originally a pictograph of a torso/pregnant body, hence "body, person, self"). Literally "one's own body or person", it functions in Korean as a reflexive pronoun ("oneself") and pre-nominal modifier ("one's own"). Distinct from the homophonous Sino-Korean noun 자신 (自信, "self-confidence").

history.meaning: one's own physical body or moral person
oneself; one's own (reflexive pronoun)

자신.notes: Watch out for the exact homophone: 자신 (自身) means "oneself / one's own" (자기 자신, "one's own self"), whereas 자신 (自信) means "self-confidence" (자신이 있다, "to be confident").

rootFamily.gloss: myself, oneself (자기 자신, 自己自身)
the person directly concerned (當事者 / 本人) or physical status (身分)
whole body, heart and soul (全身)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자신 (自身)

자신감.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 자신감 (自信感), formed from the Sino-Korean stem 자신 (自信, "believing in oneself, self-confidence", from 自 자 "self" + 信 신 "trust, believe") + the productive Sino-Korean noun suffix -감 (感, "feeling, sense, perception"). Adding -감 disambiguates the psychological feeling of confidence from the homophonous reflexive pronoun 자신 (自身, "oneself").

history.meaning: to trust or believe in one's own capability or integrity
feeling of self-confidence, self-assurance

자신감.notes: Commonly collocates with 넘치다 ("to overflow with confidence", 자신감이 넘치다), 있다/없다 ("to have/lack confidence"), and 떨어지다 ("for confidence to drop").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자신감 (自信感)

자연스럽다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adjective formed from Sino-Korean 자연 (自然, "nature, spontaneity") + the native Korean adjectival suffix -스럽다 ("having the quality of, seeming like"). In Classical Daoist philosophy (such as the Laozi), 自然 (from 自 자 "self" + 然 연 "to be so, thus") meant "self-so, occurring spontaneously without artificial coercion"; combined with -스럽다, it describes behavior, speech, or acting that feels unforced and organic.

history.meaning: self-so, spontaneously existing as it is without artifice
natural, unaffected, smooth and unforced

자연스럽다.notes: As a ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ 불규칙) adjective, the ㅂ drops and becomes 우/워 before vowel endings: 자연스럽다 -> 자연스러운 (adnominal "natural"), 자연스럽게 (adverbial "naturally"), 자연스러워요 (polite).

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자연스럽다 (自然스럽다)

자유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자유 (自由), from Classical Chinese 自由, composed of 自 (자, "self, from") + 由 (유, "cause, origin, follow, act according to"). In Han-dynasty poetry and Tang Chan (Zen) Buddhist texts, 自由 meant "acting according to one's own inclination, unrestrained". During the Meiji Enlightenment in Japan, scholars such as Fukuzawa Yukichi and Nakamura Masanao repurposed 自由 as a calque for English "freedom" and "liberty", from which the modern political and philosophical sense entered Korean.

history.meaning: acting at one's own discretion; unrestrained by external hindrance
political and philosophical liberty or freedom (translating English liberty)
freedom, liberty; free (as a pre-noun)

자유.notes: Although formally a noun, 자유 frequently acts directly as a pre-nominal modifier (e.g., 자유 시간 "free time", 자유 무역 "free trade") or adverbially with a particle (자유로이 "freely").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자유 (自由)

자유롭다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adjective derived from the Sino-Korean noun 자유 (自由, "freedom, liberty", from 自 자 "self" + 由 유 "follow, act from") + the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -롭다 (from Middle Korean -ᄅᆞ외- / -롭-, used to derive descriptive adjectives from vowel-final nouns). It converts the abstract noun "freedom" into a predicate meaning "to be free, unrestrained, or at ease".

history.meaning: characterized by being unrestrained or free
history.stage: Middle / Early Modern Korean derivational pattern

history.meaning: to be free, uninhibited, unrestricted

자유롭다.notes: The suffix -롭다 attaches after nouns ending in a vowel (자유롭다, 평화롭다, 지혜롭다), whereas -스럽다 attaches more broadly (often after consonant-final nouns like 자연스럽다, 사랑스럽다). Like -스럽다, -롭다 is ㅂ-irregular (자유로운, 자유롭게).

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자유롭다 (自由롭다)

자유분방하다.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 자유분방 (自由奔放) combined with the native light verb 하다 ("to do, to be"). Formed from 자유 (自由, "freedom, following one's own will", 自 자 "self" + 由 유 "follow") + 분방 (奔放, "galloping wildly, unbridled", from 奔 분 "run fast, rush like a steed" + 放 방 "release, let go, unrestrained"). Originally used in classical literary and calligraphy criticism for vigorous, untamed artistic style, it now characterizes a bohemian or freewheeling personality.

history.meaning: galloping unbridled like a steed; vigorous and untamed in literary style
freewheeling, bohemian, unconstrained by social convention

morphemes.meaning: light verb forming descriptive adjectives (to be)

자유분방하다.notes: Often used to describe artists, producers, or eccentric characters who ignore rigid hierarchy or dress codes; it carries a livelier, more indulgent nuance than simple 자유롭다 ("free").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자유분방하다 (自由奔放하다)

자의.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자의 (自意), composed of 自 (자, "self, oneself") + 意 (의, "mind, thought, intention, meaning", a compound ideograph of 音 "sound/voice" over 心 "heart"). Literally "one's own intention or will", it denotes acting out of personal volition rather than external compulsion.

history.meaning: one's own personal thought or intention
one's own free will, volition

자의.notes: Most famously encountered in the four-word expression 자의 반 타의 반 (自意半他意半, "half of one's own will, half by others' pressure"), used when someone is "voluntarily" nudged into a decision. Do not confuse with homophonous 자의 (字義, "literal meaning of a character").

rootFamily.gloss: another person's will or ulterior motive (他意)
arbitrary, self-serving interpretation (恣意的 — different Hanja 恣, but same 意) / intention (意圖)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자의 (自意)

자전거.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 自転車, combining 自 (스스로 자, 'self'), 轉 (구를 전, 'to revolve, roll'), and 車 (수레 거/차, 'wheeled vehicle'). Coined in Meiji-era East Asia for the pedal-driven 'self-rolling vehicle' and adopted into Korean in the late nineteenth century, it remains the universal everyday Korean word for a bicycle.
자전거.notes: Takes the verb 타다 ('to ride a bicycle').

자제하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal noun 자제 (自制, "self-control, self-restraint") combined with the native light verb 하다 ("to do"). Composed of 自 (자, "self, oneself") + 制 (제, originally "to cut or trim branches with a knife 刂", hence "to regulate, curb, govern, control"). Already attested in Classical Chinese texts such as the Xunzi (荀子), it means governing or curbing one's own desires, emotions, or actions.

history.meaning: to master or curb one's own impulses and desires
to refrain from, hold back, exercise self-restraint

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving active verbs (to do)

자제하다.notes: Used both for curbing one's own emotions (감정을 자제하다) and in polite public notices asking people to refrain from an activity (흡연을 자제해 주십시오, "please refrain from smoking").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자제하다 (自制하다)

자존감.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자존감 (自尊感), formed in modern Korean psychological discourse as a clipped blend of 자아존중감 (自我尊重感, a calque of English "self-esteem"). Composed of 自 (자, "self") + 尊 (존, originally a vessel 酋 offered with two hands 廾/寸, hence "to honor, respect, revere") + -감 (感, "feeling, sense"). It denotes an intrinsic, unconditional sense of one's own worth.

history.meaning: to honor or hold oneself in high regard

history.form: 자아존중감 (自我尊重感) -> 자존감 (自尊感)
history.meaning: psychological self-esteem, internal sense of self-worth

자존감.notes: Contemporary Korean sharply contrasts 자존감 (自尊感, healthy internal self-esteem that accepts oneself flaws and all) with 자존심 (自尊心, competitive pride or ego based on how one compares to others).

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자존감 (自尊感)

자존심.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 자존심 (自尊心), composed of 自 (자, "self, oneself") + 尊 (존, "honor, revere, noble") + 心 (심, "heart, mind"). Built on Classical Chinese 自尊 ("to hold oneself in high regard") with the psychological suffix -심 (心, "mind/disposition"), it denotes outward-facing personal pride, dignity, or ego that resists humiliation before others.

history.meaning: holding oneself in high esteem; dignified self-regard
personal pride, self-respect, competitive ego

자존심.notes: Key idioms include 자존심이 상하다 ("to have one's pride hurt"), 자존심을 세우다 ("to stand on one's pride / be stubborn"), and 자존심을 굽히다 ("to swallow one's pride").

rootFamily.gloss: competitiveness, desire to win (勝負欲 / 競爭心)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자존심 (自尊心)

자주.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adverb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as ᄌᆞ조 ("frequently, repeatedly"). Derived from the native adjective/verb stem 잗- / ᄌᆞᄌᆞ- ("to be frequent, closely spaced", modern Korean 잦다) + the deadjectival adverb-forming suffix -오. Through the regular loss of the vowel ㆍ (arae-a, merging into ㅏ in the first syllable) and vowel raising of final ㅗ to ㅜ in Early Modern Korean, ᄌᆞ조 evolved into modern 자주.

history.meaning: at short intervals, repeatedly, frequently
often, frequently

morphemes.meaning: be frequent, closely spaced (cf. modern 잦다)

자주.notes: The underlying adjectival root survives in modern Korean 잦다 ("to be frequent", e.g., 잦은 실수 "frequent mistakes", 비가 잦다 "rain is frequent"), making 자주 and 잦다 an essential native vocabulary pair.

cognates.meaning: stepping forward voluntarily, of one's own accord

자진.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자진 (自進), composed of 自 (자, "self, personally, of one's own accord") + 進 (진, "advance, step forward, present", depicting a bird 隹 moving forward on a path 辶). Literally "stepping forward by oneself", it denotes taking initiative or volunteering for an action (such as resigning, surrendering, or leaving a program) without waiting to be compelled.

history.meaning: to step forward or present oneself of one's own accord
voluntary action, stepping forward on one's own initiative

자진.notes: Frequently used right before another Sino-Korean verbal noun (or as 자진해서) to mean "voluntarily": 자진 사퇴 ("voluntary resignation"), 자진 하차 ("voluntarily stepping down from a TV show"), 자진 신고 ("voluntary reporting to authorities").

rootFamily.gloss: to volunteer, step forward willingly (自進하다)
entry, advancement into a market or round (進出)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자진 (自進)

자책감.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound 자책감 (自責感), formed from 자책 (自責, "self-reproach, blaming oneself", attested in Classical Chinese histories such as the Hanshu, from 自 자 "self" + 責 책 "blame, reprove, demand responsibility") + the suffix -감 (感, "feeling, sense"). Literally "the feeling of reproaching oneself", it denotes pangs of conscience and remorse over one's own perceived fault.

history.meaning: to reprove or hold oneself accountable for a failure or fault
sense of self-blame, remorse, or personal guilt

자책감.notes: Whereas 죄책감 (罪責感) emphasizes moral or legal guilt over a wrongdoing ("sin/crime guilt"), 자책감 (自責感) focuses on beating oneself up for a mistake or failure ("self-blame"). In soccer/sports, 자책골 (自責골) is an "own goal".

rootFamily.gloss: to blame oneself, reproach oneself (自責하다)
sense of guilt over a wrongdoing (罪責感)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자책감 (自責感)

cognates.meaning: itself, one's own body or substance

자체.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 자체 (自體), composed of 自 (자, "self, own") + 體 (체, "body, substance, form, structure"). In medieval Chinese Buddhist metaphysics, 自體 denoted the "intrinsic substance or self-nature (svabhāva)" of a phenomenon as opposed to external attributes. In modern Korean, it functions both as an emphatic post-nominal noun ("in itself, the very thing itself") and a pre-nominal modifier ("in-house, internal, one's own").

history.meaning: one's own physical body; the intrinsic substance or essence of a thing
itself, in itself; internal, in-house, self-contained

자체.notes: Placed after a noun, 자체 means "X itself" (존재 자체 "existence itself", 문제 자체 "the problem itself"). Placed before a noun in broadcasting or business, it means "in-house / internal / own" (자체 제작 "in-house production", 자체 최고 시청률 "a show's own highest viewership rating").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 자체 (自體)

자취.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as the Yongbieocheonga and Seokbo sangjeol) as 자최 ("footprint, track, vestige"). Through phonological rounding and raising of the second-syllable diphthong (ㅚ > ㅟ) during Early Modern Korean, 자최 became modern 자취. It denotes physical footprints left behind as well as figurative traces or whereabouts.

history.meaning: footprint, wheel track, physical trace left behind
footprints, traces, vestiges, whereabouts

morphemes.meaning: footprint, track, trace (from Middle Korean 자최)

자취.notes: Commonly used in expressions like 자취를 감추다 ("to hide one's tracks / vanish without a trace") and 발자취 ("footsteps, life trajectory"). Do not confuse with the homophonous Sino-Korean noun 자취 (自炊, "cooking for oneself / living alone as a student or single person").

rootFamily.gloss: trace, vestige, mark (痕跡, Sino-Korean synonym)

cognates.meaning: short coat or outer garment; record sleeve

자켓.etymology: Loanword (외래어) from English jacket, with the colloquial Korean vowel realization 자켓 (rather than the prescribed National Institute of Korean Language standard 재킷) reinforced by orthographic spelling pronunciation and Japanese ジャケット (jaketto). English jacket was borrowed from Middle French jaquet ("short tunic or coat"), diminutive of jaque ("peasant's short tunic"), traditionally linked to the personal name Jacques (used generically for a French peasant, as in the Jacquerie revolt).

history.meaning: short padded tunic worn by peasants or foot soldiers
short outer garment for the upper body; protective sleeve or cover
jacket (clothing); album cover or promotional photoshoot sleeve

morphemes.meaning: jacket (outer garment or album cover sleeve)

자켓.notes: While the official South Korean loanword orthography is 재킷, everyday speakers and K-pop/broadcasting staff overwhelmingly say and write 자켓—including in 자켓 촬영 ("album cover photoshoot", borrowed via Japanese record-industry usage of ジャケット for an LP/CD sleeve).

작가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작가 (作家), joining 작 (作, 'to make, compose, write, create') and specialist suffix 가 (家, 'master, specialist, school').

history.meaning: author, writer, artist

작가님.etymology: Polite title formed from Sino-Korean 작가 (作家, 'writer, author, artist') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: esteemed writer/author/artist (polite address or reference)

작곡가.etymology: Three-part Sino-Korean compound 작곡가 (作曲家): 작 (作, 'make, create') + 곡 (曲, 'tune, piece of music') + specialist suffix -가 (家).
작곡가.notes: Parallels 건축가 (建築家, 'architect') in using -가 (家) for an accomplished practitioner.

작곡가님.etymology: Polite title formed from Sino-Korean 작곡가 (作曲家, 'musical composer', from 作 'make, compose' + 曲 'melody, tune' + 家 'specialist') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: esteemed musical composer (polite address or reference)

작년.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작년 (昨年), composed of 昨 (작, "yesterday, past, previous", formed from 日 "sun/day" + phonetic 乍 "suddenly/just now") + 年 (년, "year", originally depicting a person carrying harvested grain 禾). In Classical Chinese, 昨 meant "yesterday" (작일 昨日) and by temporal extension "the immediately preceding year" (昨年).

history.meaning: the year that has just passed, last year
last year, the previous year

작년.notes: Due to Korean nasalization rules, 작년 [장년] is pronounced with [ㅇ] in the first syllable coda because ㄱ before ㄴ nasalizes to ㅇ (작년 -> [장년]). Its native Korean synonym is 지난해 ("the year that passed").

rootFamily.gloss: this year, the current year (今年)
next year, the coming year (來年)
the year before last (재작년, 再昨年)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 작년 (昨年)

작다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 쟉다 ('to be small in size, short in height, minor', bright-vowel counterpart of 적다 'to be few in number/quantity').

history.meaning: to be small in size
to be small, little, low in volume

작업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작업 (作業), joining 작 (作, 'to make, work, operate') and 업 (業, 'work, occupation, task').

history.meaning: work, operation, hands-on job or task

작업실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작업실 (作業室), joining 작업 (作業, 'work, artistic or manual craft') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: workshop, studio, workroom

작은방.etymology: Hybrid compound noun lexicalized from the native Korean adnominal form 작은 ("small", from the adjective stem 작- "to be small in size", Middle Korean 쟉다, + adnominal modifier suffix -은) and the Sino-Korean noun 방 (房, "room, chamber"). In traditional and contemporary Korean residential layout, it designates the smaller secondary bedroom(s) in contrast to the master bedroom (안방 or 큰방).

history.meaning: to be small + room or chamber
secondary bedroom, spare room, smaller room of a house

morphemes.meaning: be small in size or scale

작은방.notes: Written without a space (작은방) when referring to the specific architectural room category ("the secondary/spare bedroom" vs. 안방 "master bedroom"), whereas 작은 방 with a space simply means "a room that is small". Similarly, 작은아버지 ("father's younger brother") is a lexicalized compound.

rootFamily.gloss: father's married younger brother, uncle (작은 + 아버지)

작전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작전 (作戰), composed of 作 (작, "make, initiate, arise, conduct") + 戰 (전, "war, battle, fight"). Famous as the title of the second chapter of Sun Tzu's Art of War (孫子兵法 〈作戰〉, "Waging War"), where it meant mobilizing forces and conducting a military campaign. In modern Korean, it denotes both formal military operations and everyday tactical schemes, game plans, or dating/broadcasting strategies.

history.meaning: to initiate and conduct warfare; military campaigning (Sun Tzu, Art of War)
military operation; tactical plan, scheme, or game strategy

작전.notes: Used constantly in everyday Korean for playful or serious scheming: 작전을 짜다 ("to hatch a plan/strategy"), 작전 타임 ("time-out in sports to discuss tactics"), and 미인계 작전 ("honey-trap operation").

rootFamily.gloss: collaborative operation or joint scheme (합동 작전, 合同作戰)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 작전 (作戰)

cognates.meaning: work of art, opus, production, piece
work of art or literature, opus

작품.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작품 (作品), borrowed via modern Japanese 作品 (sakuhin) and shared across East Asia, composed of 作 (작, "make, create, compose, author") + 品 (품, "article, object, class, quality", originally three mouths/objects 品 representing multiple items or grades). It designates any created piece of art, literature, music, cinema, or television drama.

history.meaning: to create or compose + graded article or object
work of art, literary composition, creative piece
artistic work, opus; a film or TV drama series (in entertainment industry usage)

작품.notes: In the Korean entertainment world, actors and directors refer to the dramas or movies they work on as 작품 (e.g., 차기 작품 "next project/drama", 데뷔 작품 "debut piece", 작품을 고르다 "to choose a script/project"). Colloquially, 걸작 ("masterpiece") or "What a piece of work!" can also be expressed IRONICALLY as 작품이네!

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 작품 (作品)

잔.etymology: Sino-Korean 잔 (盞, 'small cup, winecup, glass'), borrowed from Middle Chinese 盞 ('shallow cup, goblet') and used both as an independent noun ('cup, glass') and as a counter for drinks.

history.meaning: small cup, winecup
cup, glass; counter for cupfuls

잔소리는.etymology: Topic-marked form of the native Korean (고유어) compound noun 잔소리 ("nagging, scolding, needless nitpicking") + the postpositional topic/contrastive particle -는 ("as for"). 잔소리 is compounded from 잔 (adnominal form of the native adjective 잘다 "to be fine, small, petty, trivial", Middle Korean 잗다 / 잘다) + 소리 ("sound, voice, speech, words", Middle Korean 소래). Literally "petty/small talk or nitpicking words", it lexicalized into "nagging".

history.meaning: to be fine/small + sound or voice
petty nitpicking remarks, nagging, scolding
as for nagging (topic-marked noun form)

morphemes.meaning: be fine, small, petty, trivial (stem of 잘다)
topic and contrastive postpositional particle (after vowel)

잔소리는.notes: To say "to nag" in Korean, pair 잔소리 with 하다 (잔소리를 하다) or, from the receiver's perspective, "to get nagged / hear nagging" is 잔소리를 듣다. Adding -는 (잔소리는 그만해!) sets up a contrast or exasperated dismissal ("Enough with the nagging!").

잔인하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive noun 잔인 (殘忍, "cruelty, ruthlessness") combined with the native light verb 하다 ("to be"). Composed of 殘 (잔, "injure, destroy, mutilate, ruthless", containing 歹 "bare bones/death" + 戔 "halberds/slash") + 忍 (인, "endure, harden one's heart, bear to inflict pain", depicting a blade 刃 over the heart 心). In Classical Chinese (attested in the Shiji), 殘忍 describes a person whose heart is hard enough to inflict harm without compassion.

history.meaning: ruthlessly injuring others with an unfeeling, hardened heart (Shiji)
to be cruel, brutal, merciless, heartless

morphemes.meaning: endure, harden the heart, blade over heart (忍)
light verb forming descriptive adjectives (to be)

잔인하다.notes: Notice how the character 忍 (인, "blade 刃 over heart 心") has two sides: enduring pain oneself yields 인내 (忍耐, "patience, endurance"), whereas hardening one's heart to others' pain yields 잔인하다 (殘忍하다, "to be cruel").

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 잔인하다 (殘忍하다)

잔재.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 잔재 (殘滓), composed of 殘 (잔, "remain, leftover, incomplete, remnant") + 滓 (재, "dregs, sediment, lees, sludge", containing 氵 "water/liquid" + 宰). Originally referring literally to the physical sediment or dregs left at the bottom of a liquid, it underwent metaphorical extension to denote undesirable vestiges or holdovers from a past era or regime.

history.meaning: leftover dregs, sediment, or lees of liquid or food
vestiges, remnants, undesirable holdovers of the past

잔재.notes: Almost always carries a negative or critical connotation of outdated things that ought to be cleared away, as in 일제 잔재 ("vestiges of Japanese colonial rule") or 권위주의의 잔재 ("remnants of authoritarianism"). For neutral or positive historical traces, use 유산 (遺産, "heritage") or 흔적 (痕跡, "traces").

rootFamily.gloss: remaining balance in an account (殘額)
surviving remnants or defeated troops (殘黨)

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 잔재 (殘滓)

잘.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 잘 ('well, skillfully, properly, often').

history.meaning: well, skillfully, thoroughly
well, properly, frequently

잘나가다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed by univerbation of the adverb 잘 ("well, successfully, smoothly", Middle Korean 잘) + the compound verb 나가다 ("to go out, move forward, advance, sell", itself from 나- "emerge" + 가다 "go"). Literally "to go forward well" or "to sell briskly", it lexicalized as a single headword meaning to prosper, thrive, or enjoy peak popularity and career momentum.

history.meaning: to go out or advance well; for goods to sell briskly
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean phrase

history.meaning: to be successful, thriving, popular, on a roll

잘나가다.notes: Written without a space (잘나가다) when meaning "to be successful / popular / thriving" (e.g., 요즘 제일 잘나가는 프로듀서 "the hottest/most successful producer these days"), whereas 잘 나가다 with a space literally means "to go outside well". Even though it means "to be popular/successful", it conjugates as an action verb (잘나가는, NOT *잘나간 for present state).

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, advance, progress (나- + 가다)
to turn out well, prosper, succeed (잘 + 되다)
to live well, be affluent (잘 + 살다)

잘나다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound adjective formed from the adverb 잘 ("well, finely", Middle Korean 잘) + the verb 나다 ("to be born, come into being, emerge", Middle Korean 나다). Literally "to be born well" or "to turn out finely", it originally praised someone of distinguished looks, talent, or status (as opposed to 못나다, "to be homely, foolish, or inferior"). In modern colloquial speech, however, it underwent strong pragmatic irony and is used primarily to mock pretension or self-importance.

history.meaning: to be born well; to emerge as distinguished or handsome
to be distinguished or accomplished; (ironic) to think one is special, be full of oneself

morphemes.meaning: be born, come into being, turn out

잘나다.notes: In everyday conversation, exclaiming 잘났다! or 정말 잘났어! is almost 100% sarcastic ("Oh, aren't you special!" / "Big deal!"), and 잘난 척하다 means "to act snobby / show off / act like hot stuff". Its antonym 못나다 ("to be foolish, ugly, or lacking") remains sincere.

rootFamily.gloss: to be foolish, homely, or lacking (못 + 나다)
to be born, come into the world (태어 + 나다)

잘되다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the adverb 잘 ('well, successfully') and the verb 되다 ('to become, turn out, go').

history.meaning: to go well, turn out successfully, prosper

잘라버리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining the infinitive stem 잘라- of 자르다 ("to cut, sever, chop off; (colloquial) to fire or dismiss", Middle Korean ᄌᆞᄅᆞ다, a 르-irregular verb) + the completive auxiliary verb 버리다 (originally "to throw away, discard", Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다). Grammatically, -아/어버리다 marks the complete, irreversible termination of an action, often expressing the speaker's relief, decisiveness, or frustration ("cut right off once and for all").

history.meaning: to cut or sever + to throw away or discard completely
to cut right off, sever completely, or fire/edit out decisively

morphemes.meaning: cut, sever, chop; edit out or fire (르-irregular stem of 자르다)
completive auxiliary verb (do completely, once and for all; literally throw away)

잘라버리다.notes: In TV production and workplace contexts, 자르다 / 잘라버리다 has two very common extended meanings beyond physical cutting: (1) editing/cutting a scene or cast member's footage out of a broadcast (통편집으로 잘라버리다), and (2) firing someone from a job.

rootFamily.gloss: to cut, sever; to fire/dismiss (base verb)
to be cut off; to get fired or edited out (passive)
to throw away; completive auxiliary verb

잘라주다.etymology: A native Korean benefactive serial verb compound formed from 잘라, the infinitive (아서/어서) stem of 자르다 (jareuda, "to cut, sever, chop off", from Middle Korean 쟈ᄅᆞ다, cyalota), combined with the auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, "to give, to do as a favor for someone", from Middle Korean 주다, cwuta). In broadcasting and editing contexts, it specifically refers to cutting or trimming unwanted footage on someone's behalf.

history.meaning: to sever or cut off and give
to cut or edit out for someone's benefit

morphemes.meaning: to give, to do for someone's benefit

잘라주다.notes: In television production (편집), PD and editors frequently use 잘라주다 when asking a colleague to edit out an awkward take or controversial remark in the editing room.

rootFamily.gloss: to be cut off, to get fired

잘리다.etymology: A native Korean passive verb derived from the transitive verb stem 자르- (jareu-, "to cut, sever, chop off", from Middle Korean 쟈ᄅᆞ다, cyalota) plus the native passive derivational suffix -리- (-ri-, allomorph used after 르-irregular stems) and the citation ending -다 (-da). From the literal meaning of being severed or lopped off from a whole, it developed the ubiquitous colloquial metaphor "to be axed, dismissed, or fired from a job" as well as having one's scenes cut in film editing.

history.meaning: to cut, sever, chop off
to be cut off, severed; (colloquial) to be fired or edited out

잘리다.notes: Often pronounced [짤리다] with tense reinforcement in casual speech for emotional emphasis when talking about getting fired from a company or having one's screen time cut (통편집으로 잘리다).

잘못.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the adverbs 잘 ('well, properly') and 못 ('cannot, poorly, amiss'), lexicalized both as a noun ('mistake, fault, error') and as an adverb ('wrongly, mistakenly').

history.meaning: improperly; fault, error
mistake, fault; wrongly

잘못되다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the noun/adverb 잘못 (jalmot, "mistake, fault, error; wrongly", itself a fusion of the adverb 잘 "well" and the negative adverb 못 "cannot, poorly", attested in Middle Korean as 쟐못, cyal.mwos) combined with the inchoative verb 되다 (doeda, "to become, to turn out", from Middle Korean 도외다, twoyoyta). Literally "to become not-well", hence for a plan, situation, or broadcast to go awry or turn out badly.

history.meaning: to not go well, to become amiss
to go wrong, to turn out badly, to be faulty

잘못되다.notes: Spelled as a single word when meaning "to go awry / turn out badly" (일이 잘못되다), whereas 잘못 되다 with a space is much rarer; compare 잘못하다 which focuses on an agent making a mistake.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a mistake, to blunder

잘못하다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb composed of 잘못 (jalmot, "mistake, blunder; wrongly", a lexicalized compound of 잘 "well" + 못 "cannot, unable", Middle Korean 쟐못, cyal.mwos) and the light verb 하다 (hada, "to do", Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다, hota). Originally transparent ("to not do well"), it lexicalized both as "to commit a fault or blunder" and, in conditional clauses (잘못하면 / 잘못하다가는), "if one makes a false step / if things go wrong".

history.meaning: to fail to do well, to err
to make a mistake, to do wrong; (conditional) if things go wrong

잘못하다.notes: In conditional forms like 잘못하면 or 잘못하다가는, it acts almost like an adverbial warning ("if you're not careful / at the slightest misstep, something bad will happen").

rootFamily.gloss: to go wrong, to turn out badly
to be unable to do, to do poorly

잘하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the adverb 잘 ('well, skillfully') and the verb 하다 ('to do, perform').

history.meaning: to do well, be good at, treat well

잠.etymology: A native Korean deverbal noun derived from the verb stem 자- (ja-, "to sleep", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 자다, cata) plus the substantive nominalizing suffix -ㅁ (-m, Middle Korean -옴/-움, -wom/-wum, yielding 잠, cam). It represents one of the oldest preserved lexicalized -ㅁ action nouns in Korean alongside 꿈 (dream, from 꾸다) and 춤 (dance, from 추다).

history.meaning: act of sleeping, sleep, slumber
sleep, slumber

잠.notes: Because 잠 is already a noun derived from 자다, Korean forms the cognate-object phrase 잠을 자다 ("to sleep a sleep"), alongside idioms like 잠이 오다 ("sleep comes" = to feel sleepy) and 잠을 설치다 ("to toss and turn").

잠그다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ㅭᆞᆷ그다 / 잠그다 ('to immerse in liquid, steep; to shut and lock').

history.meaning: to immerse; to lock, fasten
to lock, fasten, turn off (a valve); to soak

잠기다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 잠그다 ('to lock; to immerse') + the passive suffix -이-, attested in Middle Korean as ㅭᆞᆷ기다 / 잠기다.

history.meaning: to be submerged; to be locked
to be locked, fastened; to sink, be immersed

잠깐.etymology: Phonologically tensified form of Sino-Korean 잠간 (暫間), compounding 잠 (暫, 'briefly, temporarily') and 간 (間, 'interval, space of time').

history.meaning: brief interval, a short while
for a moment, briefly; just a second

잠들다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the noun 잠 (jam, "sleep", nominalization of 자다 "to sleep") and the verb 들다 (deulda, "to enter, to go in, to take hold", from Middle Korean 들다, tulta). Literally "for sleep to enter (one)" or "to enter into sleep", paralleling other sensory/state inchoative compounds with 들다 such as 정들다 ("to grow fond") and 병들다 ("to fall ill").

history.meaning: to enter into sleep, for sleep to set in
to fall asleep, to go to sleep

잠들다.notes: Unlike 자다 ("to sleep" as an intentional action or ongoing state), 잠들다 pinpoints the involuntary transition into sleep ("to fall asleep / drift off").

잠수.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 潛水 (잠수), composed of 潛 (잠, jam, "to submerge, dive, hide beneath water") and 水 (수, su, "water"). While its primary sense is underwater diving, late-20th and 21st-century Korean slang (especially in broadcasting, entertainment, and dating) extended "submerging underwater" to mean "going radio silent, going AWOL, cutting off all contact and disappearing from work or social circles" (잠수를 타다).

history.meaning: submerging or diving under water
underwater diving; (slang) going AWOL, ghosting, becoming unreachable

잠수.notes: In workplace and K-drama parlance, 잠수를 타다 ("to ride a dive") means to suddenly stop answering calls or showing up to the studio, while 잠수 이별 means breaking up by ghosting one's partner.

잠시.etymology: Sino-Korean 잠시 (暫時), compounding 잠 (暫, 'briefly, for a short time') and 시 (時, 'time, period').

history.meaning: short time, brief moment
a short while, a moment; briefly

cognates.meaning: disappearing without a trace, going into hiding

잠적하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verbal compound formed from 潛跡 (잠적, jamjeok, "hiding one's tracks, disappearing without a trace") and the native light verb 하다 (hada, "to do"). The Sino-Korean noun combines 潛 (잠, jam, "to hide, submerge, conceal") and 跡 (적, jeok, "footprints, traces, tracks"), literally meaning "to submerge one's footprints" so that pursuers or the public cannot locate one's whereabouts.

history.meaning: concealing one's footprints, going into hiding
to vanish without a trace, to go into hiding, to abscond

잠적하다.notes: More formal and journalistic than the slangy 잠수 타다; entertainment news reporters frequently use 잠적하다 when a celebrity or PD abruptly disappears amid a scandal or contract dispute.

잡다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 잡다 ('to grasp, hold, catch, seize').

history.meaning: to hold, grasp, catch
to catch, hold, grip, set (a date or plan)

잡무.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 雜務 (잡무), pronounced [잠무] (jammu) via regressive nasal assimilation of ㅂ before ㅁ. It is composed of 雜 (잡, jap, "mixed, sundry, miscellaneous, minor") and 務 (무, mu, "official business, duty, task, affair"). In Korean organizational culture, it denotes all the unglamorous administrative errands and sundry paperwork that fall outside one's core creative or professional role.

history.meaning: sundry administrative affairs, miscellaneous duties
odd jobs, routine office chores, miscellaneous tasks

잡무.notes: Note the mandatory nasal assimilation in pronunciation: 잡무 is always pronounced [잠무]. Compare 잡일 (a hybrid Sino-native word for manual/household odd chores), whereas 잡무 sounds more like office or administrative busywork.

잡아먹다.etymology: A native Korean serial verb compound built from 잡아, the infinitive (아서/어서) form of 잡다 (japda, "to seize, catch, butcher", Middle Korean 잡다, capta), and 먹다 (meokda, "to eat, consume", Middle Korean 먹다, mekta). Literally "to catch and eat (prey)" or "to slaughter and eat (livestock)", it evolved a vivid figurative sense in everyday speech: to chew someone out mercilessly, devour a subordinate through harsh scolding, or harbor predatory hostility toward someone.

history.meaning: to catch and devour prey; to butcher livestock for food
to catch and eat; (figurative) to eat someone alive, bully, or ruin someone

잡아먹다.notes: Frequently used hyperbolically by senior staff or parents ("내가 너를 잡아먹기라도 하니?" — "Am I going to eat you alive or something?") or to describe a fierce boss who terrorizes newcomers.

잡아주다.etymology: A native Korean benefactive compound verb combining 잡아, the infinitive stem of 잡다 (japda, "to seize, hold, secure, set, book", from Middle Korean 잡다, capta), with the auxiliary verb 주다 (juda, "to give, to do for someone's benefit", Middle Korean 주다, cwuta). Because 잡다 broadened semantically from physically grasping an object to "securing" an abstract slot (a date, hotel room, casting appearance, or concept), 잡아주다 came to mean booking a venue, locking in a schedule, or steadying someone's posture/direction for them.

history.meaning: to grasp or secure something for someone
to hold, secure, book (a room/schedule), or set up for someone

morphemes.meaning: to give, to do as a favor for someone

잡아주다.notes: Extremely versatile in production and daily life: 숙소를 잡아주다 ("to book accommodations for someone"), 스케줄을 잡아주다 ("to lock in a schedule for someone"), or 중심을 잡아주다 ("to keep things anchored/grounded for the team").

rootFamily.gloss: to be caught, to be scheduled/booked

잡일.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun formed from the Sino-Korean prefixoid root 雜 (잡, jap, "mixed, sundry, miscellaneous, trivial") and the native Korean noun 일 (il, "work, task, labor", from Middle Korean 일, il). In standard pronunciation, a consonantal ㄴ-insertion (니은 첨가) occurs at the morpheme boundary before [i], followed by nasal assimilation of ㅂ to ㅁ, yielding [잠닐] (jamnil).

history.meaning: sundry tasks, miscellaneous manual work
odd jobs, menial chores, drudgery around the house or workplace

잡일.notes: Watch the pronunciation: because 일 begins with a high front vowel across a compound boundary, ㄴ is inserted (잡 + ㄴ + 일 -> [잠닐], never *[자빌]). Youngest writers and rookie PDs (막내) are notorious for being burdened with 잡일.

잡히다.etymology: A native Korean passive and causative verb derived from the transitive root 잡- (jap-, "to seize, catch, hold, schedule", from Middle Korean 잡다, capta) plus the passive/causative derivational suffix -히- (-hi-, Middle Korean -히-, -hi-) and citation ending -다 (-da). Phonetically realized as [자피다] (japida) due to coalescence of ㅂ + ㅎ into aspirated ㅍ. It covers both physical capture ("to get caught") and abstract scheduling ("for a date/plan to be set").

history.meaning: to be seized, captured, or held; to give as collateral
to get caught, be captured; to be scheduled or grasped

잡히다.notes: Beyond "getting caught red-handed" (꼬리가 잡히다 / 현장에서 잡히다), in broadcasting it often means "a schedule/shooting date has been finalized" (일정이 잡히다) or "entering the camera frame" (카메라에 잡히다).

rootFamily.gloss: to book or secure for someone
to catch and eat; to eat alive

장.etymology: Sino-Korean monosyllable representing several common homographs: 장 (場, 'place, ground, market'), 장 (欌, 'cabinet, wardrobe'), 장 (張, classifier for flat sheets such as paper or leaves), and 장 (章, 'chapter, section').

history.form: 場 / 欌 / 張 / 章 (장)
history.meaning: market, place / cabinet / sheet counter / chapter
market; cabinet; sheet (counter); chapter

장갑.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 掌甲, combining 掌 (손바닥 장, 'palm of the hand') and 甲 (갑옷 갑, 'protective shell, casing, armour'). Originally a military or work covering for the hands, 장갑 became the universal Korean word for gloves and kitchen oven mitts (오븐 장갑). In Korean, gloves take the verb 끼다 ('to fit/slip on').
장갑.notes: Takes the verb 끼다 ('put on/wear gloves') and 벗다 ('take off gloves').

cognates.meaning: shogi, Japanese chess (cognate first character 將)

장기.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 將棋 (장기, janggi, also historically written 將棊), composed of 將 (장, jang, "general, commander, king piece") and 棋/棊 (기, gi, "board game, chess piece"). The game evolved on the Korean Peninsula from early Chinese xiangqi (象棋) during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, acquiring its name from the central role of the general (將) piece (or 宮/漢/楚) on the board. Note that Korean also has homophonous Sino-Korean words 장기: 長期 ("long term") and 長技 ("one's forte/special skill").

history.meaning: traditional Korean strategy board game ("general's chess")
janggi (Korean chess)

장기.notes: Do not confuse three common Sino-Korean homophones spelled 장기: 將棋 ("Korean chess"), 長期 ("long period of time"), and 長技 ("special talent / personal talent show, 장기자랑").

rootFamily.gloss: paduk, Go board game (棋院 = Go salon)
general, commander (將軍; also "check!" in janggi)

cognates.meaning: long period of time, long term
cognates.word: 長期間 (ちょうきかん, chōkikan)

cognates.meaning: over a long period of time

장기간.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound noun from 長期間 (장기간, janggigan), structured as 長期 (장기, "long period, long term", from 長 "long" + 期 "period, appointed time") plus 間 (간, "interval, space, duration"). It denotes an extended span of time and is frequently used adverbially without a particle to mean "for a prolonged period".

history.meaning: an extended interval or long span of time
a long period of time; for a long period

장기간.notes: Antonym is 단기간 (短期間, "a short period of time"). In Korean syntax, 장기간 often functions directly as a temporal adverb before a verb (e.g., 장기간 방영되다, "to be broadcast over a long period").

rootFamily.gloss: long-term stay at an inn/hotel (長期投宿)

장기투숙.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound noun from 長期投宿 (장기투숙, janggitusuk), combining 長期 (장기, "long term, extended period", from 長 "long" + 期 "period") with 投宿 (투숙, "checking into and lodging at an inn or hotel", from 投 "to cast oneself into, stop at" + 宿 "lodge, stay overnight"). In Classical Chinese, 投宿 originally described a traveler casting themselves into a roadside inn at nightfall.

history.meaning: to stop at an inn for the night, to take lodging
long-term stay or extended lodging at a hotel or guesthouse

morphemes.meaning: to throw in, check into, stop at (投)

장기투숙.notes: 투숙 (投宿) is the formal hotel-industry term for staying as a registered guest (hence 투숙객 "hotel guest"), while 장기투숙 refers to living out of a hotel, motel, or gosiwon for weeks or months at a discounted rate.

장난.etymology: Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 쟉난 (cyak.nan) and 쟝난 (cyang.nan, "mischievous play, prank, caper"). Most Korean historical linguists analyze it as a lexicalized Sino-Korean compound from 作亂 (작란, literally "making disorder / stirring up a ruckus", from 作 "to make, do" + 亂 "chaos, rebellion, mischief"), which underwent nasalization [장난] -> 쟝난 and semantic softening from "causing a disturbance" to "playful mischief, prank, joke, or toying around".

history.meaning: stirring up disorder; unruly play or mischievous caper
prank, joke, mischief, playful fooling around

morphemes.meaning: to make, stir up (phonologically assimilated to 장-)

장난.notes: Extremely productive in colloquial slang: besides "prank/joke", 장난 아니다 ("it's no joke") is the go-to idiom for "insanely intense, awesome, or serious".

rootFamily.gloss: to joke, kid, pull a prank

장난감.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 장난 ('play, pastime, prank', attested in early Modern Korean as 작난) + the suffixoid/noun 감 ('material, item suitable for a purpose').

history.meaning: play, amusement, prank
plaything, toy

장난치다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 장난 ('play, prank, mischief') + 치다 ('to strike, make, engage in').

history.meaning: to play a prank, fool around, joke

장난하다.etymology: A verbal compound formed from the noun 장난 (jangnan, "mischief, prank, joke", Middle Korean 쟉난/쟝난, historically from 作亂 "creating commotion") and the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, "to do", Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다, hota). In conversational Korean, it ranges from "to play around / pull a prank" to the rhetorical disbelief phrase "장난해?" ("Are you kidding me? / Are you messing with me?").

history.meaning: to engage in unruly play or mischief
to joke, kid around, pull a prank, mess with someone

장난하다.notes: In K-dramas and variety shows, "너 지금 나랑 장난하냐?" ("Are you messing with me right now?") is a classic confrontational line when someone feels disrespected or given an absurd excuse.

rootFamily.gloss: to play a prank on, to toy with (장난을 치다)

장담.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 壯談 (장담, jangdam), composed of 壯 (장, jang, "vigorous, grand, bold, stout") and 談 (담, dam, "talk, speech, statement"). Originally meaning "bold or grandiose talk / big boasting" in Classical Chinese, in Korean it shifted toward "a confident assertion, emphatic assurance, or personal guarantee" that something will or will not happen (often in negative constructions like 장담할 수 없다, "cannot guarantee").

history.meaning: bold speech, grandiloquent or confident talk
confident assurance, personal guarantee, bold assertion

장담.notes: Frequently paired with the emphatic adverb 호언 (豪言) in 호언장담하다 ("to boast confidently / swear up and down"), or used in the fixed pattern 내가 장담하는데 ("I guarantee you / mark my words...").

rootFamily.gloss: to guarantee confidently, to assure (壯談하다)
big talk and bold assurance (豪言壯談)

장담하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 장담 (壯談, 'bold talk, confident assurance', compounding 壯 'vigorous, bold' and 談 'talk, speech') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: bold assertion, confident guarantee
to assure confidently, guarantee, vouch for

장땡.etymology: A colloquial Korean term originating from traditional Korean card games (섯다, Seotda, played with 화투, Hwatu flower cards). It combines 장 (jang, designating the Month 10 maple card, 풍/단풍, which is the 10th and highest regular month in Seotda, likely from 長 "chief/ten-rank") and 땡 (ttaeng, a mimetic/slang gaming term for a matching pair of the same month, possibly from the ringing sound of a bell signaling a winning hand). Because a pair of 10s (장땡) beats all regular pairs (1땡 through 9땡), "장땡이다" became popular slang for "that's the ultimate trump card / that beats everything / nothing else matters if you have that".

history.meaning: a pair of Month 10 cards, the highest regular pair in Seotda card games
the unbeatable hand; (slang) king, the ultimate winner, all that matters

morphemes.meaning: Month 10 card in Hwatu/Seotda (highest regular rank)
a matching pair of the same month in Seotda card games

장땡.notes: Used in everyday speech in the pattern "X이면 장땡이야?" ("Do you think as long as X happens, everything is fine / it wins it all?"), e.g., 시청률만 잘 나오면 장땡이야? ("Is getting high ratings all that matters?").

rootFamily.gloss: catching a lucky break by sheer chance (땡잡다)
pair of Month 1 (pine) cards in Seotda
pair of Month 9 (chrysanthemum) cards in Seotda

cognates.meaning: scene, setting, shot (source of the modern theatrical sense)

장면.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 場面 (장면, jangmyeon), composed of 場 (장, jang, "place, ground, stage, arena") and 面 (면, myeon, "face, surface, aspect, side"). Reinforced during the modern era alongside Japanese 場面 (bamen) to translate English "scene" in theater, cinema, and television broadcasting, it refers both to a dramatic scene or shot of footage and to a memorable moment witnessed in real life.

history.meaning: the face or aspect of a stage or gathering place
history.stage: Sino-Korean / East Asian modern lexical borrowing

history.meaning: scene, shot, footage (in film/TV); a sight or moment in real life

장면.notes: Essential broadcasting vocabulary: 명장면 (名場面) means an iconic/legendary scene in a drama or variety show, and 방영 장면 refers to aired footage.

장바구니.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 장 (場, 'market, marketplace, grocery shopping') + native Korean 바구니 ('woven basket').

history.meaning: market basket, shopping bag or cart

장부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 장부 (帳簿), combining 장 (帳, 'account register') and 부 (簿, 'record book, ledger').
장부.notes: Used for traditional paper account books and guesthouse check-in ledgers.

장사.etymology: Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 댱ᄉᆞ (tyangso, "merchant, trade, commerce"), derived from the Sino-Korean compound 商賈 (상고/장사, "merchant, trade", where 商 refers to a traveling merchant and 賈 refers to a stationary shopkeeper) or 場市 ("market"). Over the Joseon period, the palatalized form 장사 (jangsa) became completely nativized, shifting primarily to mean "commercial trade, running a shop, selling goods" (and by metaphor in broadcasting, "attracting an audience / doing business with ratings").

history.meaning: merchant, peddler; commercial trade
trade, commerce, running a shop or small business

morphemes.meaning: trade, commerce, selling goods (from Middle Korean 댱ᄉᆞ)

장사.notes: Do not confuse with the Sino-Korean homophone 장사 (壯士, "person of immense physical strength", as in 천하장사). In entertainment slang, 시청률 장사 means "peddling for viewer ratings".

rootFamily.gloss: to do business, to run a shop, to trade
peddler, vendor (native suffix variant, e.g. 격장수/과일장수)

장사꾼.etymology: A native Korean derivative noun formed from 장사 (jangsa, "trade, commerce, selling", from Middle Korean 댱ᄉᆞ, tyangso) and the productive agentive suffix -꾼 (-kkun, from Middle Korean -군, denoting a person habitually or professionally engaged in an activity, compare 일꾼 "worker", 사기꾼 "con artist"). Earlier 장사 alone could mean both "trade" and "merchant", so -꾼 was added to unambiguously mark the person who trades—often with a colloquial nuance of someone calculating and profit-driven.

history.meaning: one who engages in trade, merchant, peddler
merchant, shopkeeper, peddler; (figurative) profit-minded wheeler-dealer

morphemes.meaning: agentive suffix for a specialist, habitual doer, or dealer

장사꾼.notes: While 상인 (商人) is the neutral, respectful term for a merchant or businessperson, 장사꾼 sounds earthy and colloquial, and when applied figuratively to a PD or executive ("완전 장사꾼이네"), implies they care only about profit or ratings.

rootFamily.gloss: to run a business, to trade

장사하다.etymology: A compound verb formed from 장사 (jangsa, "trade, commerce, running a shop", from Middle Korean 댱ᄉᆞ, tyangso) and the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, "to do", Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다, hota). It originally referred to buying and selling goods in a market or shop, and in modern colloquial Korean extends to operating any commercial establishment (such as a restaurant or stall) or figuratively "selling" a concept, image, or emotion to the public.

history.meaning: to engage in trade, to buy and sell goods
to run a shop/business, to engage in commerce, to peddle

장사하다.notes: Compare 사업을 하다 ("to run a corporate/entrepreneurial business") with 장사하다 ("to run a shop, restaurant, or retail trade", or colloquially "to be open for business today").

rootFamily.gloss: to be open for business (營業하다)

장소.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 場所 (장소, jangso), composed of 場 (장, jang, "open ground, arena, stage, gathering site") and 所 (소, so, "place, location, spot"). Both characters denote spatial locations, forming a synonymous coordinate compound that designates a specific physical venue, meeting spot, or filming location.

history.meaning: a specific site, ground, or location
place, location, venue, spot (for an event or shoot)

장소.notes: Whereas 곳 is the native Korean word for any general "place", 장소 refers to a designated venue or spot for an activity (e.g., 촬영 장소 "filming location", 약속 장소 "meeting spot").

cognates.meaning: longevity, living a long life; long-running (program)

장수.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 長壽 (장수, jangsu), composed of 長 (장, jang, "long, enduring") and 壽 (수, su, "lifespan, old age, longevity"). Originally referring to human biological longevity (living to a ripe old age), in modern Korean media and broadcasting it is widely used attributively before nouns like 프로그램 ("program") or 프로 ("show") to mean "long-running" (e.g., 장수 프로그램, a television show that stays on the air for many years).

history.meaning: long lifespan, living to an advanced age
longevity; (broadcasting) long-running status of a show or brand

장수.notes: Korean has several common homophones for 장수: 長壽 ("longevity / long-running"), 將帥 ("military general/commander"), and native Korean 장수 ("peddler/seller", as in 채소 장수). In *The Producers*, 장수 프로그램 refers to a flagship long-running show like *1박 2일* or *전국노래자랑*.

rootFamily.gloss: to live a long life, to be long-running (長壽하다)
short life; cancellation after a short run (短命)

장식.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 裝飾 (장식, jangsik), composed of 裝 (장, jang, "attire, dress, adorn, outfit") and 飾 (식, sik, "ornament, embellish, decorate"). Originally denoting physical adornment of clothing, architecture, or vessels, it is also used sarcastically in colloquial Korean idioms ("눈이나 귀는 장식이냐?" — "Are your eyes/ears just for decoration?") to scold someone who isn't paying attention, and in broadcasting (대미를 장식하다) for "gracing the grand finale".

history.meaning: adornment, embellishment of dress or objects
ornament, decoration; (colloquial) something merely ornamental and useless

장식.notes: In colloquial dialogue, asking "머리는 장식이야?" ("Is your head just an ornament?") or "폼으로 달고 다니는 장식" is a classic sarcastic jab meaning someone isn't using their brain, eyes, or title.

rootFamily.gloss: to decorate, adorn, grace a finale (裝飾하다)

장인.etymology: Sino-Korean 장인 (匠人), from 장 (匠, 'artisan, master woodworker') + 인 (人, 'person').
장인.notes: Honors a craftsperson who has dedicated decades to perfecting a manual craft.

cognates.word: 長所 (ちょうしょ, chōsho - parallel formation) / 長点
長處 / 长处 (chángchù - parallel) / 長點

장점.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 長點 (장점, jangjeom), composed of 長 (장, jang, "long, superior, excelling in") and 點 (점, jeom, "point, dot, aspect, feature"). In Classical Chinese, 長 already carried the extended sense of "what one excels at / a strong suit" (as in 일장일단, 一長一短, "one merit and one demerit"), and combining it with 點 ("point/aspect") yielded the standard modern term for a person's or product's strength, merit, or advantage.

history.meaning: a point of excellence, superior feature
strength, merit, advantage, strong point

장점.notes: Its direct antonym is 단점 (短點, "weakness, flaw, demerit"), and the two are compressed into the compound 장단점 (長短點, "pros and cons / strengths and weaknesses"). Pronounced [장쩜] with tensification of ㅈ in standard speech.

rootFamily.gloss: pros and cons, strengths and weaknesses (長短點)
strong point, forte ( 강점, 強點)

장하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the Sino-Korean root 壯 (장, jang, "grand, vigorous, admirable, magnificent, stout") and the native Korean adjective-forming light verb 하다 (hada, "to be", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다, hota). Attested in Middle Korean as 댱ᄒᆞ다 / 쟝ᄒᆞ다, it originally described imposing physical grandeur or heroic vigor, and in modern Korean is used both sincerely ("admirable, praiseworthy, proud of you!") and sarcastically ("참 장하다!" — "Oh, bravo, what a grand achievement!").

history.meaning: to be grand, vigorous, imposing, or heroic
to be admirable, praiseworthy, splendid; (ironic) "well done indeed!"

장하다.notes: Pay close attention to intonation: elders say "아이고, 우리 아들 장하다!" with genuine pride, whereas a peer or boss saying "참 장~하다, 장해!" after you mess up or brag about something trivial is 100% biting sarcasm.

잦다.etymology: A native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) meaning "to be frequent, repeated at short intervals", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 쟛다 (cyasta) alongside its derived adverb 자조 (caco, Modern Korean 자주, jaju, "often, frequently"). The root 잦- (jat-) originally expressed closely spaced recurrence in time, and while the adverb 자주 became the everyday word for "often", the base adjective 잦다 remains standard for modifying nouns (잦은 실수, "frequent mistakes"; 잦은 야근, "frequent late-night overtime").

history.meaning: to occur closely together in time, to be frequent
to be frequent, to happen repeatedly at short intervals

잦다.notes: Remember the pair: 잦다 is the adjective (most commonly seen in its prenominal form 잦은 + Noun, e.g., 잦은 결방 "frequent broadcast cancellations"), while 자주 is the cognate adverb ("often"). Do not confuse with 젖다 ("to get wet") or 찾다 ("to find").

재.etymology: Native Korean (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts such as the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446) as ᄌᆡ (coy, "ash, cinders"). From the literal sense of powdery residue left after fire, it developed vivid figurative idioms such as 재(를) 뿌리다 ("to scatter ashes", meaning to ruin the mood or spoil a celebration, rooted in the traditional folk taboo against scattering dirty ashes over a clean ritual or festive courtyard).

history.meaning: ash, cinders remaining after combustion
ashes; (in idioms) ruin or spoiling of a festive mood

재.notes: In drama dialogue, 찬물에 재 뿌리다 ("scattering ashes on cold water") or 잔치에 재 뿌리다 ("scattering ashes on a feast") is a quintessential idiom for being a wet blanket or ruining someone's big moment.

재개장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재개장 (再開場), joining prefix 재- (再, 'again, re-') with 개장 (開場, 'opening a venue').
재개장.notes: Used for guesthouses, theatres, markets, and halls opening their doors anew.

재계약.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 再契約, formed by attaching the Sino-Korean iterative prefix 再 (재, jae, "again, a second time, re-") to the noun 契約 (계약, gyeyak, "contract, covenant", from 契 "notched tally, deed, covenant" + 約 "bind, promise, treaty"). In ancient China, 契 referred to notched bamboo or wooden tallies split between parties as proof of a binding obligation.

history.meaning: binding covenant, formal deed or agreement
contract renewal, re-signing of an agreement

재계약.notes: In the Korean entertainment and broadcasting industry, 재계약 시즌 ("contract renewal season") is a high-stakes period when talent agencies and stars renegotiate exclusive management deals (전속 계약).

재구성하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 再構成 (재구성, jaeguseong, "reconstruction, reorganization") with the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, "to do, make"). The Sino-Korean stem consists of 再 (재, "again, re-") + 構 (구, "fit timber together, frame, construct") + 成 (성, "complete, accomplish, form"). In television production, it specifically denotes dramatizing or reconstructing real events for broadcast.

history.meaning: structural framing, composition of parts into a whole
to reconstruct, reorganize, or dramatize anew

재구성하다.notes: TV programs frequently display the disclaimer 이 프로그램은 실화를 바탕으로 재구성한 것입니다 ("This program has been reconstructed/dramatized based on a true story").

rootFamily.gloss: to compose, constitute, make up (構成-)
broadcast scriptwriter /構成 writer (構成作家)

재능.etymology: Sino-Korean 재능 (才能), compounding 재 (才, 'natural gift, talent') and 능 (能, 'ability, capability, skill').

history.meaning: natural talent and ability
talent, gift, aptitude

재다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 재다 ('to measure length, size, or quantity; to gauge').

history.meaning: to measure, gauge
to measure, weigh, size up

cognates.meaning: display of playful skill or literary sport

재롱.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound derived from 才弄 (재롱, jaerong), combining 才 (재, jae, "talent, knack, natural ability") and 弄 (롱/농, rong/nong, "play with, sport, frolic, jest"). While the Hanja literally mean "sporting with one's cleverness or skill", the word became thoroughly nativized in Korean to denote the adorable, playful movements and cute tricks performed by a toddler or pet to delight adults.

history.meaning: playful display of cleverness or tricks
cute, endearing antics or tricks of a young child or pet

재롱.notes: Usually paired with the verbs 부리다 or 떨다 (재롱을 부리다 / 재롱을 떨다, "to put on cute antics"); used ironically when an adult acts overly cute or tries too hard to please a boss.

rootFamily.gloss: endearing child who charms adults with cute tricks

재료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 材料, combining 材 (재목 재, 'timber, raw material, talent') and 料 (헤아릴 료, 'measured grain, provisions, ingredients'). In Korean, 재료 covers both culinary ingredients for cooking and baking (요리 재료, 수프 재료) and physical materials for carpentry or art.
재료.notes: The go-to kitchen word for recipe ingredients.

재미.etymology: Widely traced by Korean historical linguists to the Sino-Korean compound 滋味 (자미, jami, "rich flavor, savor, relish", from 滋 "nourishing, juicy, sapid" + 味 "taste, flavor") via regressive vowel fronting (자미 > 재미, triggered by the high front vowel /i/ of the second syllable; compare North Korean standard 자미). An alternative folk-etymological writing in late Joseon texts is 在味 ("where the flavor/interest lies"). Semantically, it shifted from palatable "savory taste" to mental "amusement, fun, and interest".

history.meaning: rich, nourishing taste; savory flavor and relish
amusement, fun, interest, enjoyment; profit or good results

morphemes.meaning: savory, nourishing, rich (fronted from 자 滋)

재미.notes: Beyond "fun", 재미 retains a commercial/idiomatic sense of "reward or good results", as in 요즘 장사 재미가 어때요? ("How is business going / are you seeing good returns lately?").

재미없다.etymology: Compound descriptive verb (adjective) univerbated from the noun 재미 (jaemi, "fun, interest, savor", from Sino-Korean 滋味 jami) and the native Korean negative existential predicate 없다 (eopda, Middle Korean 업다 epta, "to not exist, to be lacking"). Literally meaning "fun does not exist" or "lacking savor", it fused into a single lexicalized adjective meaning "boring, dull, unfunny, uninteresting".

history.meaning: to not exist, to be absent or lacking (base predicate)
to lack interest or amusement; to be boring, dull, or unfunny

재미없다.notes: Pronounced [재미업따] with tensification after the labial stop; in variety-show production (*프로듀사*), calling a segment 재미없다 ("unfunny/boring") is the ultimate verdict of failure.

재미있다.etymology: Compound descriptive verb (adjective) formed by univerbating the noun 재미 (jaemi, "fun, interest, savor", from Sino-Korean 滋味 jami) with the native Korean existential predicate 있다 (itda, Middle Korean 이시다 isita / 잇다 ista, "to exist, be present, have"). Literally "to possess fun/interest", it grammaticalized as a single adjective meaning "to be amusing, entertaining, interesting, or funny".

history.meaning: to exist, to be present (existential verb)
to be fun, interesting, amusing, or entertaining

재미있다.notes: Covers both English "interesting" (intellectually engaging) and "fun/funny" (amusing); Korean learners often overtranslate it as "funny" when "interesting" or "fun" is intended.

재밌다.etymology: Standard phonological contraction (준말) of 재미있다 (jaemiitda, "to be fun, interesting"). Because the second syllable of 재미 (mi) ends in the high front vowel /i/ and the existential stem 있- (it-) begins with the identical vowel /i/, the two adjacent /i/ vowels coalesce in rapid speech into a single syllable (미 + 있 -> 밌, pronounced [재믿따]), which is recognized as a standard lexical entry in South Korean orthography.

history.meaning: to be fun, interesting, amusing (uncontracted compound)
to be fun, interesting, amusing (coalesced standard contraction)

morphemes.meaning: fun, interest (vowel coalesced with following stem)

재밌다.notes: While 재미있다 contracts naturally to 재밌다 because both syllables share the vowel ㅣ (/i/), its antonym 재미없다 (/i/ + /ʌ/) cannot contract in standard orthography (*재몲다 is non-standard).

cognates.meaning: large family-controlled South Korean business conglomerate

재벌.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 財閥, composed of 財 (재, jae, "wealth, finance, property") and 閥 (벌, beol, "powerful clan, merit-pillar of an aristocratic house, clique, faction"). In Han-dynasty China, 閥閱 (벌열) denoted the left and right pillars outside a noble clan's gate inscribed with its merits. Adopted in modern East Asia alongside Japanese 財閥 (zaibatsu), 재벌 came to denote South Korea's family-controlled mega-conglomerates and the tycoon dynasties who run them.

history.meaning: wealthy and influential family faction
financial clique, industrial monopoly conglomerate
family-controlled business conglomerate; billionaire tycoon or plutocrat

재벌.notes: Borrowed directly into English economics and K-drama fandom as "chaebol"; in Korean popular culture, 재벌 2세 / 3세 ("second- or third-generation conglomerate heir") is a staple K-drama archetype.

rootFamily.gloss: academic clique or elite university pedigree (學閥)

재벌칠.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 재- (再, 'second time, again') + native Korean 벌 ('round, layer, set') + Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, paint, coating'), denoting a second coat of paint or plaster.

history.meaning: second coat of paint, varnish, or plaster
