재빠르다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound/prefixed adjective formed from 재- (jae-, stem of the adjective 재다 jaeda, Middle Korean 잗다 / 쟛다, meaning "nimble, agile, quick and unhesitating in movement") combined with 빠르다 (ppareuda, Middle Korean ᄲᆞᄅᆞ다 spolota, "fast, rapid, swift"). While 빠르다 measures raw speed or velocity, prefixing 재- adds the nuance of nimble, alert, and dexterous quickness in physical action or wit.

history.meaning: nimble in motion + rapid in speed
to be nimble, agile, quick-witted, and swift in movement or reaction

재빠르다.notes: Unlike 빠르다 (which can describe a fast train or internet connection), 재빠르다 describes animate agility—a cat dodging, a person reacting swiftly (재빠르게 대처하다), or nimble hands.

rootFamily.gloss: to be nimble, quick in movement or speech
to be quick-footed, prompt to act on news or opportunity

재산목록.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) four-character compound written 財産目錄, combining 財産 (재산, jaesan, "property, estate, assets", from 財 "wealth, valuables" + 産 "give birth, produce, livelihood, estate") and 目錄 (목록, mongnok, "catalog, inventory, list", from 目 "eye, heading, item" + 錄 "inscribe, register, record", with assimilation ㄱ+ㄹ -> ㅇ+ㄴ [몽녹]). Originally a formal legal and accounting term for an estate inventory, it is widely used humorously in everyday speech for one's most prized possessions.

history.meaning: formal written inventory of an estate's assets and liabilities
asset list, inventory of property; (figuratively) one's most treasured possessions

재산목록.notes: The phrase 보물 제1호 or 재산목록 1호 ("Item #1 on my asset inventory") is a beloved Korean idiom for one's single most prized possession—whether a vintage camera, a signed album, or a child.

재생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재생 (再生), combining 재 (再, 'again, a second time') and 생 (生, 'come alive, produce').
재생.notes: Means both ecological/material regeneration ('recycling, renewal') and audio/video playback ('bringing recorded sound back to life').

재수.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 財數, composed of 財 (재, jae, "wealth, money, material valuables") and 數 (수, su, "number, calculation, fate, heavenly allotment", as in 운수 運數 "luck, fortune"). Originally denoting one's fated allotment for acquiring wealth, the term broadened in colloquial Korean to mean everyday good luck (`재수가 좋다`, "to have good luck") and, in negative expressions (`재수 없다`), an unpleasant jinx or an obnoxious, repulsive person.

history.meaning: predestined fortune or luck in acquiring material wealth
daily luck or fortune; (in negative idioms) obnoxious vibe or bad omen

재수.notes: Do not confuse with the homograph 재수 (再修, "retaking the university entrance exam after a gap year"); also note that 재수 없다! in drama dialogue usually means "What a jerk! / How obnoxious!" rather than just "I'm unlucky."

rootFamily.gloss: to be unlucky; (colloquially) to be obnoxious, off-putting

재우다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) morphological causative verb derived from the intransitive verb 자다 (jada, Middle Korean 자다 cata, "to sleep") by attaching the historical stacked causative suffix sequence -이- + -우- (-i-u-, Middle Korean 자이오다 / 재오다, where 자- + -이- coalesced into 재- and -오-/-우- reinforced the causative valence). By metaphorical extension from "putting a child to sleep/rest", it also means "to let meat or cabbage rest in marinade or salt so the seasoning sinks in".

history.meaning: to sleep, to lie down to rest (base intransitive verb)
to cause to sleep, to put to bed
to put to sleep; to let someone stay overnight; to marinate food by resting it

morphemes.meaning: causative suffix sequence (causing someone to sleep)

재우다.notes: Has three everyday uses: putting a baby/drunk friend to bed (아기를 재우다), letting a guest sleep over (하룻밤 재워 주다), and marinating Korean BBQ ribs (갈비를 양념에 재우다).

재작년.etymology: Sino-Korean 재작년 (再昨年), formed from prefix 재- (再, 'again, one step further back') + 작년 (昨年, 'last year', from 昨 'yesterday, past' + 年 'year').

history.meaning: the year before last
the year before last

재정비하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 再整備 (재정비, jaejeongbi, "reorganization, overhaul, refitting") and the native verbalizer 하다 (hada, "to do"). The Sino-Korean stem comprises 再 (재, "again, re-") + 整 (정, "put in order, arrange neatly, repair") + 備 (비, "prepare, equip, make ready"). It denotes taking a system, team, or broadcast program that has fallen into disorder and overhauling it back into fighting readiness.

history.meaning: putting equipment or organization into proper order and readiness
to overhaul, reorganize, revamp, or refit anew

재정비하다.notes: In broadcasting and sports, تیم을 재정비하다 ("to overhaul/reorganize the team") or 프로그램을 재정비하다 ("to revamp the show") is used when replacing cast members or changing formats to boost ratings.

rootFamily.gloss: to service, maintain, put in order (整備-)

재치.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 才致, joining 才 (재주 재, 'natural talent, knack') with 致 (이룰 치 / 운치 치, 'delicate flair, tasteful effect'). Rather than heavy book learning, 재치 highlights nimble, charming resourcefulness—saying or designing just the right clever thing in the moment.
재치.notes: Frequently used in the adjectival phrase 재치 있다 ('to be witty, clever').

재킷.etymology: Modern Korean loanword borrowed from English 'jacket' (ultimately from Old French jaquet). Standardized by the National Institute of Korean Language as 재킷 rather than the older colloquial spelling 자켓, it denotes a tailored suit jacket, blazer, or light outer coat.
재킷.notes: Takes the verb 입다 ('to wear/put on clothing').

재활용.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 再活用, formed by prefixing 再 (재, jae, "again, a second time, re-") to 活用 (활용, hwaryong, "practical application, active utilization", from 活 "live, active, vital" + 用 "use, employ"). Literally meaning "putting back into living/practical use", it became the standard South Korean term for material recycling as nationwide municipal waste-sorting policies were instituted in the late 20th century.

history.meaning: putting to active, practical use; grammatical conjugation
recycling, reprocessing or repurposing waste materials for new use

재활용.notes: Often paired in everyday apartment life with 분리수거 (分離收去, "separated waste collection"); humorously applied to people or ideas (인간 재활용이 안 된다, "that person is beyond salvaging/recycling").

재활용일.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun written 再活用日, formed by suffixing 日 (일, il, "sun, day, designated date") to 再活用 (재활용, jaehwaryong, "recycling", from 再 "again" + 活 "active, living" + 用 "use, employ"). In South Korean urban residential culture, apartment complexes designate a specific weekly day (재활용일 or 분리수거일) when residents bring sorted plastics, glass, paper, and cans down to the courtyard collection bins.

history.meaning: recycling + appointed day
designated weekly recycling collection day

재활용일.notes: In K-dramas (including *The Producers*), taking out sorted recyclables on 재활용일 is a classic slice-of-life domestic scene where neighbors unexpectedly bump into each other in casual clothes.

재활용하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native verb formed by combining the Sino-Korean noun 再活用 (재활용, jaehwaryong, "recycling, re-utilization", from 再 "again, re-" + 活 "live, active" + 用 "use, employ") with the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, "to do, make"). Beyond sorting household recyclables, it is also used in media production for repurposing old footage, props, or storylines in a new broadcast.

history.meaning: putting discarded or used items back into practical use
to recycle waste materials; to reuse or repurpose existing resources

재활용하다.notes: Distinguish 재활용하다 ("to recycle", processing or repurposing materials for new use) from 재사용하다 (再使用하다, "to reuse" an item as-is without reprocessing).

rootFamily.gloss: to utilize, put to practical use (活用-)

잼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English jam ('sweet fruit preserve boiled with sugar').

history.meaning: fruit preserve
jam, fruit spread

쟁반.etymology: Sino-Korean 쟁반 (錚盤), compounding 쟁 (錚, 'clang of metal, flat metal gong or plate') and 반 (盤, 'tray, platter, shallow basin').

history.meaning: flat metal platter, serving tray
tray, platter, salver

쟤.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) contracted third-person demonstrative pronoun derived from the phrase 저 아이 (jeo ai, Middle Korean 뎌 아ᄒᆡ tye ahoy, "that child over there"). First, 아이 ("child, kid, young person") contracted to 애 (ae), yielding 저애 (jeo-ae, "that kid/person over there"); then the vowel sequence /ʌ/ + /ɛ/ coalesced into the single palatalized syllable 쟤 (jyae). It forms a three-way deictic set with 얘 (이 아이, "this kid/person here") and 걔 (그 아이, "that kid/person near you or just mentioned").

history.meaning: that child over there
that child, that young person over there
that kid, that guy/girl over there, he/she (casual colloquial pronoun)

쟤.notes: Strictly informal/colloquial: appropriate when referring to friends, peers, or younger people in casual speech, but rude if used to refer to a senior or elder (where 저분 is required).

rootFamily.gloss: this kid/guy/girl here (contraction of 이 아이)
that kid/guy/girl near you or mentioned (contraction of 그 아이)

저.etymology: In humble first-person usage ('I, me'), native Korean pronoun descending from Middle Korean 뎌 / 저 ('oneself; humble I'); as a distal demonstrative ('that over there'), from Middle Korean 뎌 ('that').

history.meaning: oneself, humble I / that over there
I (humble); that (distal determiner); um/well

저거.etymology: Colloquial contracted form of 저것 ('that thing over there'), composed of distal demonstrative 저 ('that') + 거 (reduced form of dependent noun 것 'thing').

history.meaning: that thing over there (spoken/informal)

저것.etymology: Native Korean compound pronoun formed from distal demonstrative 저 ('that over there', Middle Korean 뎌) + the bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

history.meaning: that thing over there
that thing, that one (away from both speaker and listener)

저기.etymology: Native Korean distal locative pronoun descending from Middle Korean 뎌긔 ('that place over there', from distal 뎌 + locative nominal element -긔).

history.meaning: that place over there
over there, that place; excuse me (attention-getter)

저녁.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 져녁 ('evening, dusk; evening meal').

history.meaning: evening, dusk
evening; dinner, supper

저녁밥.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound noun composed of 저녁 (jeonyeok, Middle Korean 져녁 cyenyek, "evening, dusk") and 밥 (bap, Middle Korean 밥 pap, "cooked grain/rice; meal"). Because cooked rice (밥) has been the foundational staple of Korean cuisine for millennia, compounding a time-of-day noun with 밥 (아침밥, 점심밥, 저녁밥) is the standard native way to name the corresponding meal of the day.

history.meaning: evening + cooked rice or meal
evening meal, dinner, supper

저녁밥.notes: In everyday speech, 저녁 alone frequently stands for 저녁밥 (e.g., 저녁 먹었어? "Did you eat dinner?"), while 저녁밥 emphasizes the actual meal or home-cooked food on the table.

저는.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) inflected pronoun phrase consisting of the humble first-person singular pronoun 저 (jeo, Middle Korean 뎌 tye, originally a distal/self-effacing reflexive pronoun meaning "that one / oneself", which grammaticalized as the humble counterpart to plain 나 na "I") followed by the post-vocalic topic/contrastive particle -는 (-neun, Middle Korean -ᄂᆞᆫ -non). In polite speech, speakers lower themselves via 저 when addressing superiors or unfamiliar listeners.

history.meaning: as for that one / as for oneself (self-effacing reference)
as for me, I (humble/polite first-person topic form)

저는.notes: Frequently contracts to 전 (jeon) in spoken Korean; remember that while 저 + 는 stays 저는, combining 저 with the subject particle 가 triggers stem suppletion to 제가 (never *저가 in standard polite Korean).

저러다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) demonstrative verb contracted from 저리하다 (jeorihada, "to act in that way over there"), which is built on the distal demonstrative root 저 (jeo, Middle Korean 뎌 tye, "that over there, visible to both speaker and listener, or emotionally distanced") + adverbial suffix -리 (-ri) + light verb 하다 (hada, "to do"). It belongs to Korean's symmetrical three-way deictic verb paradigm: 이러다 (proximal, "do like this"), 그러다 (medial/anaphoric, "do like that"), and 저러다 (distal, "do like that over there").

history.meaning: to act or do in that manner over there
to act like that (over there), to keep doing that

저러다.notes: Often used when watching someone behave bizarrely or recklessly from a distance (저러다 큰일 나지, "If they keep acting like that, they'll get into big trouble!").

rootFamily.gloss: to be like that over there (adjective counterpart)

저런.etymology: Native Korean determiner contracted from 저러한 ('such as that over there', from distal demonstrative stem 저러- + -하- + adnominal -ㄴ); also used as an exclamation of surprise or sympathy ('oh dear, my goodness').

history.meaning: such as that, like that
that kind of, such; oh my!

저렇게.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) demonstrative adverb formed by attaching the productive adverbializer -게 (-ge, "in such a manner, so as to be") to the distal demonstrative adjective stem 저렇- (jeoreot-, citation form 저렇다 jeoreota, Middle Korean 뎌러ᄒᆞ다 tyerehota, "to be like that over there"). Because the stem 저렇- ends in ㅎ (/h/), combining it with -게 triggers aspiration of the following velar stop (ㅎ + ㄱ -> ㅋ), yielding the pronunciation [저러케].

history.meaning: in that manner over there, to that extent
like that (over there), in that way, so much

morphemes.meaning: to be in such a state or manner (contracted from -러하-)

저렇게.notes: Besides pointing to a visible action ("in that way over there"), 저렇게 is used as an emotional intensifier before adjectives: 저렇게 좋을까? ("Could someone really be that happy?").

rootFamily.gloss: to be like that over there (base adjective)

저렇다.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative adjective contracted from 저러하다 ('to be like that over there'), descending from Middle Korean 뎌러하다 (built on distal root 뎌- 'that').

history.meaning: to be like that
to be like that (over there), be that way

저렴하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adjective combining the Sino-Korean root 低廉 (저렴, jeoryeom, "low-priced, inexpensive") with the native adjectivalizer 하다 (hada, "to be"). In Classical Chinese, 低 (저, jeo) means "low, bowed down" and 廉 (렴/염, ryeom/yeom) originally meant "sharp corner of a hall; morally upright, uncorrupted, not greedy". Because an uncorrupted merchant does not price-gouge, 廉 acquired the economic sense of "modest or fair in price", and 低廉 came to mean "affordably low in price".

history.meaning: low and modest in price, uninflated cost
to be inexpensive, affordable, reasonably priced

저렴하다.notes: Whereas native 싸다 ("cheap") can sometimes sound blunt or imply low quality, 저렴하다 is a polite, positive word meaning "affordable, budget-friendly, reasonably priced" (though slang uses 입이 저렴하다 humorously for "having a foul/vulgar mouth").

rootFamily.gloss: to be upright, honest, incorruptible (淸廉-)

저명하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adjective formed from the Sino-Korean compound 著名 (저명, jeomyeong, "prominent, celebrated, eminent") and the native adjectivalizer 하다 (hada, "to be"). The Hanja 著 (저, jeo) means "manifest, clearly visible, prominent; to author/publish" and 名 (명, myeong) means "name, reputation, fame". Literally meaning "possessing a clearly manifest name", it describes scholars, authors, or public figures of distinguished reputation.

history.meaning: manifest name, prominent and widely recognized reputation
to be renowned, eminent, distinguished, celebrated

저명하다.notes: Higher in register than 유명하다 ("famous"): while a pop idol or viral restaurant is 유명하다, a respected professor, critic, or statesperson is described as 저명하다 (especially in the attributive form 저명한 학자, "an eminent scholar").

rootFamily.gloss: eminent figure, notable dignitary (著名人士)
to be conspicuous, striking, marked (顯著-)

저번.etymology: Hybrid native Korean and Sino-Korean compound noun formed by combining the native Korean distal demonstrative determiner 저 (jeo, Middle Korean 뎌 tye, "that over there, that distant/past one") with the Sino-Korean bound noun and classifier 番 (번, beon, "turn, time, occasion, order in a sequence"). Literally "that (previous) turn", it lexicalized as a temporal noun meaning "last time, the previous occasion, the other day".

history.meaning: that turn or occasion
last time, the previous occasion, the other day

저번.notes: Forms a natural temporal set with 이번 ("this time") and 다음번 ("next time"), and is interchangeable in everyday speech with 지난번 ("last time, the past occasion").

rootFamily.gloss: which number/turn; once (어느 번 / 한 번)

저분.etymology: Native Korean honorific pronoun formed from distal demonstrative 저 ('that over there') + the honorific bound noun 분 ('esteemed person').

history.meaning: that person over there (honorific)

저절로.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean adverb formed from the reflexive pronoun 저 ('oneself, itself') plus 절로 ('naturally, by itself', from Middle Korean 절로, itself built with the instrumental particle -로). Together 저절로 emphasizes that an action unfolds spontaneously without anyone pushing or forcing it.
저절로.notes: Directly precedes intransitive or passive verbs such as 열리다, 펼쳐지다, or 낫다.

저한테.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) inflected pronoun phrase combining the humble first-person singular pronoun 저 (jeo, Middle Korean 뎌 tye, "I, me (humble)") with the colloquial animate dative/ablative postposition 한테 (hante, "to, at, from a person or animal"). Historical linguists trace 한테 to the contraction of 한 터에 (han teo-e, from 한 "one, same" + 터 "ground, site, place" + locative -에, literally "in the same place/presence with"), which grammaticalized into a dative marker for animate nouns.

history.meaning: in the same place or presence with (origin of postposition 한테)
to me, from me, at me (humble first-person pronoun + colloquial animate dative)

저한테.notes: Depending on the verb, 저한테 can mean either "to me" (저한테 주세요, "Please give it to me") or "from me" (저한테 들었어요, "They heard it from me"); in formal writing or speeches, use 저에게 instead.

rootFamily.gloss: to me, from me (humble, more formal/written particle)
to me, from me (plain/intimate pronoun + 한테)

저희.etymology: Native Korean humble first-person plural pronoun ('we, us, our') descending from Middle Korean 저희, formed from 저 ('oneself; humble I') + the animate plural suffix -희.

history.meaning: themselves; we (humble)
we, us, our (humble)

적.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('the time when, occasion, past experience'), descending from Middle Korean 젹 ('time, occasion'); as an independent Sino-Korean noun ('enemy, foe, rival'), borrowed from 적 (敵).

history.meaning: time, occasion / enemy, opponent
occasion, experience (bound noun); enemy, rival

적극.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 積極, combining 積 (쌓을 적, 'to pile up, build') and 極 (다할 극, 'utmost limit, pole'). Adopted in modern East Asian prose as the positive counterpart to 소극 (消極, 'passive, hesitant'), 적극 functions both as a noun in 적극적 ('proactive') and directly as an adverb before verbs of support and participation.
적극.notes: Often modifies 찬성하다, 추천하다, or 돕다.

적다.etymology: As a verb ('to write down, note, record'), native Korean descending from Middle Korean 젹다 ('to write down'); homophonous with the native Korean adjective 적다 ('to be few, small in quantity', Middle Korean 쟉다 / 젹다).

history.meaning: to write down, record; to be few, little
to write down, jot down; to be few, little

적당하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adjective formed from the Sino-Korean compound 適當 (적당, jeokdang, "suitable, fitting, proportionate") and the native adjectivalizer 하다 (hada, "to be"). Composed of 適 (적, jeok, "go toward, fit, suit, conform") and 當 (당, dang, "match, correspond, ought, bear"). In Classical Chinese, 適當 meant "matching the exact measure required", which in modern Korean covers both positive suitability ("appropriate, fitting") and measured restraint ("moderate, reasonable").

history.meaning: fitting the mark, matching what is proper and proportionate
to be suitable, appropriate, moderate, or reasonable in degree

적당하다.notes: While 적당하다 as an adjective is usually positive ("suitable, right amount", e.g., 가격이 적당하다 "the price is reasonable"), its adverbial cousin 적당히 often carries a cautionary or critical edge ("just enough / half-heartedly").

rootFamily.gloss: to be apt, appropriate, timely (適切-)
to be right, proper, natural (etymologically related via 當)

적당히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adverb formed by suffixing the native Korean adverbializer -히 (-hi, "in a ... manner, -ly", historically reduced from the stem of 하다 + adverbial -이) to the Sino-Korean root 適當 (적당, jeokdang, "fitting, proportionate, moderate", from 適 "fit, suit" + 當 "match, appropriate"). From the core sense of "proportionately, in due measure", it developed two divergent pragmatic uses in spoken Korean: positive moderation ("in moderation") and cutting corners ("just enough to get by, half-heartedly").

history.meaning: in a fitting or proportionate manner
moderately, reasonably; (colloquially) without going overboard, or perfunctorily

적당히.notes: Context is everything: 적당히 드세요 means "Enjoy in moderation", 적당히 넘어가자 means "Let's just let it slide / not make a fuss", and the sharp imperative 적당히 해! means "Know when to stop! / Don't push your luck!".

rootFamily.gloss: to be suitable, moderate, reasonable (適當-)

적시다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 젹시다 ('to make wet, moisten, soak'), historically related to 젖다 ('to get wet').

history.meaning: to wet, moisten, drench
to wet, soak, dampen

적어도.etymology: Lexicalised native Korean adverb formed from the stem 적- of 적다 ('to be few, small in quantity', from Middle Korean 젹다) plus the concessive connective ending -어도 ('even though, even if'), literally 'even if it be little / few' -> 'at least'.

history.meaning: to be few, scanty
at least, at a minimum

rootFamily.gloss: to be few, little in quantity

적어도.notes: Parallel in structure to English 'at least' or Japanese 少なくとも ('even if few'): sets either a numerical floor or a silver lining.

cognates.meaning: to adapt, to suit, to fit in

적응.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound written 適應, composed of 適 (적, jeok, "go toward, fit, suit, conform") and 應 (응, eung, "respond, answer, correspond, adapt"). Combining "conforming to conditions" (適) with "responding to stimuli" (應), the compound was standardized in modern East Asian scientific and sociological vocabulary to translate biological "adaptation" and psychological/workplace "adjustment" to a new environment.

history.meaning: conforming and responding harmoniously to external conditions
adaptation, adjustment, acclimatization to a new environment or role

적응.notes: Takes the particle 에 for the environment being adjusted to (새로운 환경에 적응을 잘하다, "to adjust well to a new environment"); a rookie employee's workplace adjustment is a central theme of *The Producers*.

rootFamily.gloss: to adapt, adjust, get used to (適應-)

적적하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native adjective formed from the reduplicated Sino-Korean root 寂寂 (적적, jeokjeok, "hushed, solitary, desolate") and the native adjectivalizer 하다 (hada, "to be"). The character 寂 (적, jeok) combines 宀 ("roof, house") and 叔 ("gather, quiet"), depicting a house with no voices heard inside. In Classical Chinese poetry, reduplicated 寂寂 evoked deep, tranquil stillness; in modern Korean, 적적하다 specifically expresses a quiet, empty, lonesome feeling when a house or room is too still.

history.meaning: deeply hushed, still, and solitary without human sound
to feel lonely, lonesome, and quietly empty in a still setting

morphemes.meaning: silent, still, solitary (reduplicated for affective intensity)

적적하다.notes: Unlike 외롭다 (which describes emotional loneliness or longing for love/company anywhere), 적적하다 describes the quiet, empty lonesomeness of an unoccupied house or solitary evening (아이들이 떠나서 집이 적적하다, "The house feels empty and lonely now that the kids have left").

rootFamily.gloss: to be desolate, dreary, and silent (寂寞-)
to be solitary and tranquil (孤寂-)

적히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 적다 ('to write down, record') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be written down, be recorded, be listed

전.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 전 (前, 'front, before, former, ago'); also represents Sino-Korean 전 (全, 'whole, complete') and 전 (煎, 'pan-fried battered food, savoury pancake').

history.meaning: before, former / whole / pan-fried dish
before, ago, former; whole; Korean savoury pancake

전골.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary term traditionally written 전골 (煎骨), combining 전 (煎, "to pan-fry, simmer in shallow liquid, decoct") and 골 (骨, "bone, meat on the bone"). Joseon-era encyclopedic records such as *Siuijeonseo* also connect the dish to 전철 (氈鐵, a wide, shallow iron pan shaped like a soldier's felt hat, 전립 氈笠), in which thinly sliced beef, offal, and vegetables were cooked tableside in rich broth.

history.meaning: shallow iron pan or meat-and-bone dish simmered at the table
elaborate Korean hotpot of meat, seafood, mushrooms, and vegetables simmered tableside

morphemes.meaning: to pan-fry, simmer in shallow liquid

전골.notes: Unlike 찌개 (a thicker everyday stew served already boiled), 전골 is a communal celebratory hotpot cooked raw at the center of the table.

rootFamily.gloss: pan-fried battered fish or vegetable fritter

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 전골

전구.etymology: Sino-Korean 전구 (電球), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity, lightning') and 구 (球, 'ball, sphere, globe').

history.meaning: electric globe, light bulb
light bulb

전날.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound (혼종어), combining the Sino-Korean root 전 (前, "before, prior, previous") with the native Korean noun 날 ("day", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 날). Literally "the day before" or "the previous day/night", contrasting with the more formal pure Sino-Korean synonym 전일 (前日).

history.meaning: prior + day (constituent elements in Middle Korean)
the day before, the previous day or eve of an event

전날.notes: Pronounced [전날] without tensification; often used before big events (e.g., 시험 전날 "the day/night before an exam").

rootFamily.gloss: the next day, the following day

전달.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 전 (傳, "to transmit, pass on, hand down, relay") and 달 (達, "to reach, arrive at, attain"). Originally denoting the relaying of an official decree or message through intermediaries until it reaches its intended recipient, it now covers both physical delivery of items and the effective communication of meaning or emotion.

history.meaning: to pass a command or message onward until it arrives
delivery, transmission, getting a message across

전달.notes: While 배달 (配達) refers to commercial courier/food delivery, 전달 (傳達) focuses on passing a message, document, or parcel from one person to another—or getting one's meaning across (의사 전달).

전달하다.etymology: Hybrid verb combining the Sino-Korean action noun 전달 (傳達, from 전 傳 "to transmit, relay" + 달 達 "to reach, arrive") with the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ("to do, make", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). Literally "to cause a transmission to reach its target", used for relaying messages, directives, feelings, or physical packages.

history.meaning: to relay an order or message to its destination
to deliver, relay, convey information or goods

전달하다.notes: In workplace and broadcasting contexts, 전달하다 is the standard polite-formal verb for "relaying" a memo, script change, or gift to a colleague.

rootFamily.gloss: to be delivered, to be conveyed (passive)
ability to get one's message across (e.g. a news anchor's diction)

전등.etymology: Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity') and 등 (燈, 'lamp, lantern, light').

history.meaning: electric lamp
electric light, lamp

전등갓.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈, 'electric lamp') + native Korean 갓 ('conical hat, canopy, shade', Middle Korean 갈 / 갓).

history.meaning: lampshade

전망.etymology: Sino-Korean 전망 (展望), compounding 전 (展, 'unfold, open up, spread out') and 망 (望, 'look into the distance, view, hope').

history.meaning: distant view, prospect, outlook
view, observation, future outlook

전면.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 전 (前, "front, fore, before") and 면 (面, "face, surface, side, aspect"), literally "the front surface" or "the forefront". Used spatially and figuratively in phrases like 전면에 나서다 ("to step to the forefront"). It is homophonous with 전면 (全面, from 全 "whole, entire" + 面 "surface"), which means "full-scale, across the board".

history.meaning: front face, forward-facing side
the front side, facade, forefront of public attention or action

전면.notes: Watch the two Hanja homophones: 전면에 나서다 uses 前面 ("step to the forefront"), whereas 전면 개편 ("full-scale overhaul") and 전면전 ("all-out war") use 全面 ("entire surface").

전문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 전 (專, "exclusive, single-minded, concentrated, originally a spindle turned by hand") and 문 (門, "gate, school of thought, lineage, branch of learning"). In Han-dynasty scholarship, 專門 described a scholar who devoted himself exclusively to one master's "gate" or school of textual exegesis, later broadening to mean any specialized field or professional domain.

history.meaning: devoting oneself exclusively to a single scholarly lineage or school
specialty, specialized field, professional domain

전문.notes: Used both as a noun ("specialty", e.g. 내 전문이다 "It's my specialty") and pre-nominally before nouns ("specialized/professional", e.g. 전문 지식 "specialized knowledge").

전문가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 전문 (專門, "specialty, specialized discipline", from 전 專 "exclusive, single-minded" + 문 門 "gate, field of study") and the agentive suffix -가 (家, originally "house, household", extended in Classical Chinese to denote an authoritative master or practitioner of a school of thought, as in 유가 儒家).

history.meaning: exclusive school of study + master/practitioner suffix
expert, specialist, authority in a field

전문가.notes: The suffix -가 (家) designates high-level creative or intellectual specialists (전문가 "expert", 예술가 "artist", 정치가 "politician"), contrasting with -사 (士/師) for licensed professionals.

전문점.etymology: Sino-Korean compound combining 전문 (專門, "specialty", from 전 專 "exclusive, dedicated" + 문 門 "gate, category, field") with the noun suffix -점 (店, "shop, store, commercial establishment"). Literally "an establishment dedicated exclusively to a single category of merchandise or cuisine".

history.meaning: exclusive category + shop/inn
specialty store, restaurant specializing in a specific dish

전문점.notes: In Korea, 전문점 is heavily used for restaurants focusing on a single signature dish (e.g., 삼겹살 전문점 "pork-belly specialty restaurant", 커피 전문점 "specialty coffee shop").

전문직.etymology: Sino-Korean compound combining 전문 (專門, "specialty, specialized field", from 전 專 "exclusive, focused" + 문 門 "gate, discipline") with the suffix -직 (職, "office, duty, occupation, employment"). Coined in modern East Asian administrative and labor terminology to classify occupations requiring advanced academic training or state licensure.

history.meaning: specialized discipline + official post or duty
specialized profession, white-collar professional occupation (e.g. doctor, lawyer, PD)

전문직.notes: In Korean social conversation (especially matchmaking and workplace talk), 전문직 specifically evokes high-status licensed or specialized careers (lawyers, doctors, CPAs, broadcasting producers) rather than general office work (사무직).

cognates.meaning: previous shift, former turn on watch

전번.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 전 (前, "before, prior, previous") and 번 (番, "turn, shift, time, occasion", originally depicting animal tracks or taking turns on guard duty). Originally denoting the preceding shift on duty, it generalized in everyday Korean to mean "the last time, the previous occasion".

history.meaning: the previous watch or prior turn on duty
the last time, the previous occasion (also used colloquially as an abbreviation of 전화번호 "phone number")

전번.notes: Context distinguishes two uses of 전번: in temporal phrases (전번에 말했듯이 "as I said last time") it is 前番 ("previous occasion"), whereas in casual texting ("전번 뭐야?") it is a clipped slang form of 전화번호 (電話番號, "phone number").

rootFamily.gloss: last time, the previous occasion (native + Sino synonym)

전부.etymology: Sino-Korean 전부 (全部), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, entire, complete') and 부 (部, 'part, section, division').

history.meaning: all parts, the whole
all, the whole, everything

전선.etymology: Sino-Korean 전선 (電線), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity') and 선 (線, 'line, thread, wire'); also homophonous with 전선 (戰線, 'battlefront, front line').

history.meaning: electric wire, power cable / battlefront
electric wire, cable; front line

전세.etymology: Uniquely Korean Sino-Korean legal-economic compound written 전세 (傳貰), from 전 (傳, "to hand over, entrust, pass on") and 세 (貰, "to lease, rent, lend on credit"). Attested from the late Goryeo and Joseon periods (when land or houses were leased against a redeemable pledge of grain or coin) and institutionalized during late 19th- and 20th-century urbanization as Korea's signature lump-sum key-money deposit lease.

history.meaning: pledging money or property in exchange for the right to use land or a dwelling
lump-sum deposit housing lease with no monthly rent, refunded at contract end

morphemes.meaning: to rent, lease, hire on credit

전세.notes: Pronounced [전쎄] with tensification; also watch its common homophone 전세 (形勢/戰勢, "the tide of battle/situation", as in 전세가 역전되다 "the tables are turned").

rootFamily.gloss: chartered or exclusively rented vehicle/plane (uses 專貰)
deposit money returned at the end of a jeonse lease

전역.etymology: Sino-Korean 전역 (全域, 'the entire area, whole region'), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, entire') and 역 (域, 'region, territory, boundary'); also homophonous with 전역 (轉役, 'transfer to the reserves, discharge from military service').

history.meaning: entire region / military discharge
the whole area, throughout; completion of military service

cognates.meaning: all members, the entire staff, everyone

전원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 전 (全, "whole, entire, complete, all") and 원 (員, "member, personnel, official", originally a round ding cauldron used as a classifier for officials). Literally "the complete roster of members", used to mean "all members of a group or cast" or "everyone".

history.meaning: the complete complement of officials or personnel
all members, the entire group or crew, everyone

morphemes.meaning: member, personnel, person in a group

전원.notes: Korean has three common homophones spelled 전원: 全員 ("all members", e.g. 전원 참석 "everyone attending"), 電源 ("electric power supply", e.g. 전원을 켜다 "turn on the power"), and 田園 ("countryside, pastoral fields", e.g. 전원주택 "country house").

rootFamily.gloss: member of a club or organization

전쟁.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound from 전 (戰, "battle, armed combat, to fight with weapons", containing the halberd radical 戈) and 쟁 (爭, "to contend, struggle, dispute, vie", originally depicting two hands pulling at an object). Together they form an intensive noun meaning "armed struggle between states or factions; war".

history.meaning: armed combat and contention between armies
war, warfare (and figuratively any fierce competition)

morphemes.meaning: battle, warfare, to fight with weapons

전쟁.notes: Frequently used figuratively in Korean broadcasting and workplace drama for cutthroat competition, such as 시청률 전쟁 ("ratings war") or 출근 전쟁 ("the morning commute battle").

전쟁터.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound (혼종어), combining Sino-Korean 전쟁 (戰爭, "war", from 전 戰 "armed battle" + 쟁 爭 "contention, struggle") with the native Korean noun 터 ("site, ground, lot, foundation", attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 터). Literally "a war ground" or "battlefield", contrasting with its pure Sino-Korean synonym 전장 (戰場).

history.meaning: warfare + ground/site
battlefield, war zone (often used metaphorically for chaotic workplaces)

전쟁터.notes: The native Korean suffix-like noun 터 ("site/ground") productively forms vivid everyday compounds like 일터 ("workplace"), 삶터 ("living space"), and 장터 ("marketplace"), making 전쟁터 feel more visceral than Sino-Korean 전장 (戰場).

전체.etymology: Sino-Korean 전체 (全體), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, complete, entire') and 체 (體, 'body, substance, system').

history.meaning: the whole body, entirety
the whole, entirety, all

전체적.etymology: Sino-Korean compound derived from 전체 (全體, "the whole body, entirety", from 전 全 "complete, whole, all" + 체 體 "body, substance, structure") and the attributive suffix -적 (的, originally "target, bright mark" in Classical Chinese, adopted across modern East Asian languages to form "-ic / -al" relational modifiers).

history.meaning: the whole body/entirety + relational modifier suffix (-ic/-al)
overall, general, comprehensive, taken as a whole

전체적.notes: In Korean grammar, -적 (的) words cannot stand directly before a noun without 이다 (전체적인 분위기 "the overall atmosphere") or before a verb without 으로 (전체적으로 좋다 "it is good overall").

전하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전 (傳, 'to transmit, hand down, pass on, deliver') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to transmit, convey, hand down
to convey, deliver, tell, pass on

전해드리다.etymology: Hybrid humble compound verb combining the Sino-Korean root 전- (傳, "to transmit, convey, pass on"), the native Korean light-verb connective -해- (contracted from -하- "to do" + infinitive -여), and the native Korean humble benefactive auxiliary 드리다 ("to offer/give to a superior", from 15th-century Middle Korean 드리다, originally the causative of 들다 "to enter", i.e. "to cause to enter a respected person's presence").

history.meaning: to transmit + doing + to humbly present into a superior's presence
to humbly pass along or convey (a message, gift, or news) to a respected recipient

morphemes.meaning: to humbly give or do for a superior

전해드리다.notes: Elevates the recipient of the message or item (not the speaker): use 전해드리다 when passing news or a gift to a senior, client, or television audience, and 전해주다 when passing it to a peer or junior.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass along (to an equal or junior)
to speak or tell humbly to a superior

전해주다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb combining the Sino-Korean root 전- (傳, "to transmit, pass on, hand down"), the native Korean verbalizer and infinitive connective -해- (contraction of -하여, from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 "to do"), and the native Korean benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give, to do for someone's benefit", from Middle Korean 주다). Literally "to do the favor of conveying (words or an object) to someone".

history.meaning: to transmit + doing + to give/perform for someone
to pass along a message, tell someone on another's behalf, hand over

morphemes.meaning: to give, do for someone's benefit

전해주다.notes: In everyday speech, "안부 전해줘" ("Pass along my regards / Say hi to them for me") is one of the most common parting phrases in Korean.

rootFamily.gloss: to pass along humbly to a superior

전혀.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 전 (全, 'wholly, completely') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -혀, attested in Middle Korean as 젼혀 ('entirely, completely', now used predominantly with negative predicates to mean 'not at all').

history.meaning: wholly, entirely, completely
(not) at all, altogether

전형적.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 전형 (典型, "archetype, model, standard pattern", from 전 典 "canon, statute, authoritative standard" + 형 型 "earthen mold for casting metal, pattern, type") and the attributive suffix -적 (的, "pertaining to, -ic, -al"). Originally referring in Classical Chinese to venerable statutes and casting molds that set the pattern for posterity, it now means "typical, textbook, quintessential".

history.meaning: authoritative statute, canonical mold or exemplar
typical, textbook, archetypal, quintessential

전형적.notes: While 전형적 (典型的) means "typical/textbook", the bare noun 전형 (典型) is also widely used in Korea for university admissions screening tracks (e.g., 수시 전형 "rolling admissions track").

전화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 전화 (電話), literally 'electric speech', coined in East Asia for the telephone.
전화.notes: Combines into 전화기 ('telephone set') and 전화번호 ('phone number').

전화기.etymology: Sino-Korean 전화기 (電話機), formed from 전화 (電話, 'telephone', from 電 'electricity' + 話 'speech, conversation') + 기 (機, 'machine, device, apparatus').

history.meaning: telephone apparatus
telephone set, phone receiver

전화번호.etymology: Sino-Korean 전화번호 (電話番號), compounding 전화 (電話, 'telephone') and 번호 (番號, 'number, numerical code', from 番 'turn, order' + 號 'mark, number').

history.meaning: telephone number
phone number

전화하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전화 (電話, 'telephone, phone call') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to make a phone call, telephone

전환.etymology: Sino-Korean 전환 (轉換), compounding 전 (轉, 'turn, revolve, shift') and 환 (換, 'exchange, replace, switch').

history.meaning: turning around, conversion, switch
conversion, transition, switch, changeover

전환하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전환 (轉換, 'conversion, switch, shift') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to convert, switch over, shift

절대.etymology: Sino-Korean 절대 (絕對), compounding 절 (絕, 'cut off, sever, surpass') and 대 (對, 'oppose, pair, compare'), originally a Buddhist philosophical term meaning 'beyond all comparison or relative opposition, absolute'.

history.meaning: severed from comparison, unconditional, absolute
absoluteness; absolutely, by no means (with negation)

절대로.etymology: Hybrid adverb combining the Sino-Korean noun 절대 (絶對, from 절 絶 "to sever, cut off, transcend" + 대 對 "opposition, pair, comparison") with the native Korean directive/instrumental particle -로 ("in the manner of, by", from Middle Korean -로). Coined in Chinese Buddhist philosophy (절대 絶對, contrasted with 상대 相對 "mutual opposition/relativity") to describe ultimate reality transcending all dualistic comparison, it developed into a strong emphatic adverb meaning "absolutely, under any circumstances".

history.meaning: severed from all relative opposition; unconditional ultimate reality (Buddhist philosophical term)
absolutely, unconditionally; never, under no circumstances (with negative predicates)

morphemes.meaning: in the manner of, by means of (adverbializer)

절대로.notes: Although 절대로 literally means "absolutely", in natural Korean it overwhelmingly functions as a negative polarity item paired with negative verbs ("never, under any circumstances", e.g. 절대로 안 돼 "No way / Never"),though emphatic affirmative uses also occur in modern speech.

절반.etymology: Sino-Korean 절반 (折半), compounding 절 (折, 'break, fold, divide') and 반 (半, 'half').

history.meaning: dividing in two, half
half

절연.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 절연 (絶緣), from 절 (絶, 'sever, cut off') and 연 (緣, 'tie, connection, edge').
절연.notes: Means severing personal ties in literary prose, and blocking electrical current ('insulation') in engineering.

절친.etymology: Modern Korean clipped noun (준말) extracted from the traditional Sino-Korean descriptive verb 절친하다 (切親하다, "to be earnestly and intimately close"), composed of 절 (切, "earnest, keen, close, urgent", originally "to cut closely to the bone") and 친 (親, "intimate, close, kin, parents"). While 절친하다 appears in Joseon-era prose for close kinship or friendship, using the bare root 절친 as a count noun ("best friend, bestie") popularized through 2000s Korean variety television and youth slang.

history.meaning: to be deeply intimate or closely related
best friend, closest buddy ("bestie")

절친.notes: Notice how the same two Hanja reversed form 친절 (親切, "kindness, friendliness toward anyone"), whereas 절친 (切親) means "deeply intimate best friend".

rootFamily.gloss: to be deeply intimate, very close

cognates.meaning: best, ideal, golden (especially in 絶好の機会 "golden opportunity")

절호.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 절 (絶, "to cut off, surpass all others, peerless, supreme") and 호 (好, "good, fine, favorable"). Here 절 (絶) operates as a superlative intensive prefix meaning "beyond comparison, matchlessly" (compare 절세 絶世 "peerless in the world" and 절경 絶景 "breathtaking scenery"), yielding the sense "supremely favorable, golden".

history.meaning: incomparably good, surpassingly fine
golden, supremely favorable (almost always in 절호의 기회/찬스)

절호.notes: Almost exclusively encountered as a fossilized genitive collocation: 절호의 기회 or 절호의 찬스 ("a golden opportunity / the chance of a lifetime").

rootFamily.gloss: peerless in the world (e.g. 절세미인 "peerless beauty")

젊다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 졈다 ('to be young, youthful').

history.meaning: to be young
to be young, youthful

점.etymology: Sino-Korean 점 (點, 'dot, spot, point, mark, aspect, score; counter for artworks or items'); also represents 점 (店, 'shop, store') and 점 (占, 'divination, fortune-telling').

history.meaning: dot, point, mark / shop / divination
point, dot, mole, score, aspect; store; fortune-telling

점검.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 점검 (點檢), from 점 (點, 'dot, itemize, check off') and 검 (檢, 'inspect, verify').
점검.notes: Originally meant checking off items one dot at a time on an inventory roll.

점검표.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 點檢表, combining 점검 (點檢, 'checking item by item', from 點 'dot, check mark' + 檢 'examine, inspect') with the suffix -표 (表, 겉 표, 'chart, table, written form'). Literally a 'dot-by-dot inspection chart', it is the exact Korean equivalent of an official checklist.
점검표.notes: Pairs with 항목 ('item on a checklist') and 확인하다 ('check/verify').

점검하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 점검 (點檢, 'checking item by item, inspection', compounding 點 'dot, check off' and 檢 'examine, inspect') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: checking off and examining, inspection
to inspect, check, examine

점수.etymology: Sino-Korean 점수 (點數), compounding 점 (點, 'point, mark') and 수 (數, 'number, count').

history.meaning: number of points, score
score, grade, points, marks

점심.etymology: Sino-Korean 점심 (點心), compounding 점 (點, 'dot, touch lightly') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind'), originally a Chinese and Zen monastic term meaning 'to stay the stomach with a light midday refreshment' (cognate with Cantonese dim sum).

history.meaning: light refreshment to touch the heart/stomach
lunch, midday meal

cognates.meaning: dim sum, light snack (cognate of the 點心 element)
light refreshment between meals, dim sum (cognate of 點心)

점심때.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound (혼종어), joining Sino-Korean 점심 (點心, "lunch", literally "dotting the heart/stomach", from 점 點 "dot, speck, to touch lightly" + 심 心 "heart, stomach") with native Korean 때 ("time, season, mealtime", from 15th-century Middle Korean ㅿ대). In Tang–Song China and Seon (Zen) Buddhist monasteries, 點心 denoted a small pastry snack taken to "dot the empty stomach" between morning and evening meals; in Korea it shifted to mean the main midday meal itself.

history.meaning: light midday snack ("dotting the stomach") + time/mealtime
lunchtime, the midday meal hour

점심때.notes: Korean 점심 (點心, "lunch") is an exact etymological cognate of English "dim sum" (borrowed from Cantonese 點心): both trace back to "putting a little dot on the heart/stomach" with a midday refreshment!

rootFamily.gloss: right on time, the proper time (especially for meals)

점심시간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound joining 점심 (點心, literally 'dotting the heart'—originally a light midday refreshment in Tang/Song China before becoming the standard Korean word for midday lunch) and 시간 (時間, 'time, period'). Together 점심시간 designates the midday meal break at workplaces, schools, and shops.
점심시간.notes: Pronounced [점심씨간] in everyday speech with compound tensification.

cognates.meaning: gradually, little by little, by degrees

점점.etymology: Sino-Korean reduplicated adverb from 점 (漸, "gradually, by degrees, originally water seeping in or advancing slowly", containing the water radical 氵). The full reduplication 점점 (漸漸) iconically mirrors steady, step-by-step accumulation over time ("little by little, gradually, more and more").

history.meaning: water seeping or advancing little by little; gradually
gradually, more and more, increasingly over time

morphemes.meaning: gradually, by degrees, to seep in slowly

점점.notes: Frequently paired with 더 ("more") as 점점 더 ("more and more") to describe ongoing change in weather, emotion, or plot tension.

rootFamily.gloss: gradually, step by step, in stages

접다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 졉다 ('to fold, double over').

history.meaning: to fold, bend over
to fold, collapse; to set aside or give up

접시.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 뎌프시 / 졉시 ('shallow plate, saucer, dish').

history.meaning: plate, dish
plate, dish, saucer

접이식.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 접이 ('folding', derived from 접다 'to fold' + nominalizer -이) + Sino-Korean 식 (式, 'style, type, system').

history.meaning: folding type, collapsible style

접질리다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to sprain, twist (a joint under pressure)', derived from the root of 접다 ('to fold, bend back') with intensive and passive suffixation.

history.meaning: to sprain, wrench, twist (an ankle, wrist, etc.)

cognates.meaning: to touch, come into contact with, receive (news)
to receive, connect, come into contact with

접하다.etymology: Hybrid verb combining the single-character Sino-Korean root 접 (接, "to touch, join, come into contact with, receive, welcome", with the hand radical 扌) and the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ("to do", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). From its primary physical meaning "to border on or touch", it developed the perceptual sense "to encounter, experience first-hand, or receive news/information".

history.meaning: to adjoin, touch, or receive a guest or message
to hear or receive (news), encounter or gain exposure to (culture/ideas), border on

접하다.notes: Pronounced [저파다] because ㅂ merges with ㅎ into aspirated ㅍ; commonly used with 소식 ("news", 소식을 접하다 "to hear the news") or 새로운 문화 ("new culture", 문화를 접하다 "to be exposed to a culture").

접히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 접다 ('to fold') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be folded, fold up, crease

젓다.etymology: Native Korean s-irregular verb (젓-, 저어) descending from Middle Korean 졋다 ('to stir, churn; to row with an oar; to wave or shake').

history.meaning: to stir; to row; to wave
to stir; to row a boat; to shake one's head or wave one's hand

정.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 정 (情, 'warmth, affection, emotional bond, attachment, sympathy'); also represents native/Sino-Korean 정 (錠, 'chisel, burin; tablet').

history.meaning: feeling, emotion, affection, human warmth
affection, emotional attachment, fondness; chisel

정각.etymology: Sino-Korean 정각 (正刻), compounding 정 (正, 'exact, right, straight') and 각 (刻, 'carved notch on a clepsydra, time mark, moment').

history.meaning: exact appointed time mark
the exact hour, o'clock sharp, on the dot

정겹다.etymology: Hybrid Korean adjective combining Sino-Korean 정 (情, 'deep human warmth, fondness, attachment') with the native Korean adjectival suffix -겹다 ('overflowing with a feeling', also seen in 흥겹다 'merry' and 눈물겹다 'moving to tears'). As a ㅂ-irregular stem, 정겹다 evokes an intimate, nostalgic warmth that fills the heart.

정공법으로.etymology: Hybrid adverbial form combining the Sino-Korean compound noun 정공법 (正攻法, from 정 正 "upright, orthodox, direct" + 공 攻 "to attack, assault, tackle" + 법 法 "method, tactic, law") with the native Korean instrumental particle -으로 ("by means of", from Middle Korean -으로). Rooted in classical East Asian military strategy (where 正 "orthodox frontal engagement" contrasts with 奇 "unorthodox surprise maneuvers"), it means tackling a challenge head-on and above board without gimmicks or evasion.

history.meaning: orthodox frontal assault tactic in military strategy and Go (baduk)
history.stage: Modern Sino-Japanese / Sino-Korean military & baduk term

history.meaning: head-on, by the direct and orthodox approach without tricks or shortcuts

정공법으로.notes: Often paired with 승부하다 or 돌파하다 (정공법으로 승부하다 / 돌파하다 "to compete or break through head-on") when a celebrity, politician, or producer addresses a crisis directly rather than dodging it with tricks (꼼수).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 정공법

정권.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 정 (政, "governance, state administration, political affairs") and 권 (權, "power, authority, right", originally "sliding weight on a steelyard balance", hence "leverage, weighing of authority"). Denotes sovereign political authority or the specific administration/regime holding state power during a given period.

history.meaning: the authority to govern the state; political leverage
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Early Modern East Asian political lexicon

history.meaning: political power, administration, ruling regime

정권.notes: Unlike English "regime" (which often carries a negative authoritarian connotation), Korean 정권 (政權) is used neutrally for any elected presidential administration (e.g. 정권 교체 "change of governing party/administration") as well as figuratively for "who holds the power" in an office or household.

정규.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 정 (正, "proper, standard, orthodox, official") and 규 (規, "compasses for drawing circles, rule, regulation, standard norm"). Literally "conforming to the official standard rule", used pre-nominally in modern Korean to mean "regular, formal, permanent, full-time".

history.meaning: proper standard, orthodox rule or regulation
regular, formal, permanent (programming, curriculum, employment, or studio album)

정규.notes: In Korean broadcasting (*The Producers*) and music, 정규 is crucial jargon: 정규 편성 means a pilot show being picked up for "regular weekly programming", 정규 앨범 means a "full-length studio album" (vs. a mini-album), and 정규직 means a "permanent full-time position" (vs. 계약직/비정규직).

정답.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 정 (正, "correct, right, true, proper") and 답 (答, "answer, reply, response"). Literally "the right answer", originating in examination and pedagogical usage before expanding into a lively conversational exclamation meaning "Bingo! Spot on! That's the right move!".

history.meaning: correct/right + answer/reply
correct answer (in tests/quizzes); the ideal choice or spot-on remark in daily life

정답.notes: On Korean variety shows, shouting "정답!" ("Answer!") is the signature way contestants buzz in on quiz segments; in life advice, "결혼에는 정답이 없다" means "There is no single right answer in marriage."

rootFamily.gloss: wrong answer, incorrect response (e.g. 오답 노트 "error review notebook")

정답다.etymology: Hybrid Korean adjective formed from Sino-Korean 정 (情, 'warmth, closeness, bond') and the productive native Korean suffix -답다 ('true to the nature of, full of'). Following the ㅂ-irregular pattern (정다워요, 정다운), it describes voices, conversations, or familiar objects that radiate gentle, companionable warmth.
정답다.notes: Prenominal form 정다운 frequently modifies 말투 ('tone of voice') or 친구 ('close friend').

정도.etymology: Sino-Korean 정도 (程度), compounding 정 (程, 'measure, standard, stage, journey') and 도 (度, 'degree, measure, limit').

history.meaning: standard measure, grade, degree
degree, extent, level; approximately, about

cognates.meaning: to arrange, tidy up, sort out, compile

정리.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate compound from 정 (整, "to arrange, put in neat order, tidy up", composed of 束 "bundle", 攵 "strike/tap", and 正 "straight") and 리 (理, "to carve jade along its natural veins, to regulate, put in rational order, manage"). Together they denote bringing systematic order to physical clutter, complex information, financial accounts, or tangled human relationships.

history.meaning: to put tangled state affairs or texts into proper order
tidying up, organization, summary; settling or ending a relationship or job

morphemes.meaning: to arrange, put in neat order, tidy
vein of jade, principle, to regulate, put in order

정리.notes: Beyond physical tidying (방 정리 "cleaning one's room") and summarizing (요점 정리 "key-point summary"), 정리 is the standard Korean euphemism for cleanly ending a romance (마음 정리 "getting over feelings") or downsizing staff (정리 해고 "layoffs").

rootFamily.gloss: neat arrangement, tidying up (often paired as 정리 정돈)

cognates.meaning: to sort out, organize, tidy up, liquidate/settle

정리하다.etymology: Hybrid verb combining the Sino-Korean verbal noun 정리 (整理, "putting in order, sorting out", from 정 整 "to arrange neatly, tidy" + 리 理 "to dress jade along its veins, regulate, manage") with the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ("to do, make", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). Spans physical tidying, conceptual summarizing, and interpersonal closure.

history.meaning: to arrange and put affairs in order
to tidy up, organize, summarize; to settle accounts or end a relationship

morphemes.meaning: to arrange, put in neat order, tidy
to regulate, manage, put in rational order

정리하다.notes: In K-dramas, when someone says "그 사람이랑 다 정리했어" ("I sorted everything out with that person") or "마음을 정리하다" ("to organize one's heart"), it means they have broken up or moved on emotionally.

rootFamily.gloss: to be sorted out, organized, settled (passive)
to put in neat order, tidy up

cognates.meaning: to arrange, to tidy up, to sort out

정리해놓다.etymology: A Sino-Korean and native Korean serial verb construction combining 정리 (整理, 'arrangement, sorting', from 整 'to put in order' + 理 'to manage, pattern'), the native light verb 하다 ('to do', conjugated as 해), and the auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put, to leave in a state', from Middle Korean 놓다). It expresses sorting or organizing something in advance and leaving it ready.

history.meaning: putting in order, regulating patterns
to put down, to release, to set in place
to sort out and leave ready in advance

morphemes.meaning: to arrange, to put in order
to put down, to keep a resulting state for later

정리해놓다.notes: The auxiliary -아/어 놓다 emphasizes that the action of tidying or organizing is completed beforehand so the resulting neat state remains available for future use.

rootFamily.gloss: to organize, to tidy up, to summarize

cognates.meaning: to put in order, to arrange

정리해주다.etymology: A benefactive compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 정리 (整理, 'putting in order, sorting', from 整 'to arrange neatly' + 理 'to regulate, order'), the light verb stem 해- (infinitive of 하다, 'to do'), and the native auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give', Middle Korean 주다), indicating that the act of organizing or summarizing is performed for someone else's benefit.

history.meaning: putting in order, regulating
to give, to grant
to tidy up or summarize for someone

morphemes.meaning: to arrange, to put in order

정리해주다.notes: Used both for physically tidying a space for someone and for mentally summarizing complex information or ending an awkward relationship on someone's behalf.

rootFamily.gloss: to be organized, to be sorted out

정말.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 정 (正, 'right, true, genuine') + native Korean 말 ('word, speech, talk'), literally 'true words, truth', used both as a noun and as an adverb ('really, truly').

history.meaning: true statement, truth
truth; really, truly, indeed

정말로.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb formed from the noun 정말 ('truth, fact, reality'), itself a compound of Sino-Korean 정 (正, 'right, true, genuine, straight') and native Korean 말 ('speech, word', Middle Korean 말ᄊᆞᆷ/말), suffixed with the native instrumental-adverbial particle -로 ('by means of, in the manner of, truly').

history.meaning: word, speech, language
true words, genuine fact, truth
truly, really, in truth

정말로.notes: Adding -로 to 정말 makes the adverb more emphatic than bare 정말, similar to English 'truly' or 'for real' versus 'really'.

정모.etymology: A late-20th-century South Korean internet slang syllabic abbreviation (두음절 줄임말) clipped from 정기 모임 (定期모임, 'regular gathering/meetup'), which combines Sino-Korean 정기 (定期, from 定 'to fix, determine' + 期 'period, appointed time') and the native Korean deverbal noun 모임 ('gathering, meeting', from 모이다 'to gather' + nominalizer -ㅁ). Coined in early PC communication (PC통신) and Daum/Naver fan cafes.

history.meaning: to come together > gathering, assembly
regularly scheduled meeting
scheduled offline meetup of an online community or fan club

morphemes.kind: clipped Sino-Korean syllable (定 from 定期)
clipped native noun syllable (모 from 모임)

정모.notes: Contrasts in Korean fan-club and online cafe culture with 번개 or 번모 ('lightning meetup', an impromptu unscheduled gathering).

정문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 正門, joining 正 (바를 정, 'principal, front-facing, proper') with 門 (문 문, 'gate, doorway'). Used across Korean architecture from palaces and universities to courtyard houses, 정문 designates the primary street-facing entrance as opposed to 후문 (後門, 'back gate').
정문.notes: Contrasts with 후문 ('rear gate') and 쪽문 ('small side door').

정사각형.etymology: Sino-Korean geometric compound 正四角形, composed of 正 (바를 정, 'regular, equal'), 四 (넉 사, 'four'), 角 (뿔 각, 'angle, corner'), and 形 (모양 형, 'shape, figure'). It specifically denotes an equilateral four-cornered square, contrasting with 직사각형 (直四角形, 'oblong rectangle').
정사각형.notes: Pairs in everyday speech with native 네모나다 ('to be square/box-shaped').

cognates.meaning: exact calculation, adjustment of fare or accounts

정산하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb composed of 정산 (精算, 'exact calculation, settlement of accounts', from 精 'fine, precise, refined, thorough' + 算 'to calculate, reckon, count with bamboo tallies') plus the native light verb 하다 ('to do'). In modern Korean business and entertainment industry usage, it specifically denotes balancing expenses and distributing revenue shares.

history.meaning: meticulous reckoning of numbers or accounts
to calculate precisely, to settle accounts or split payments/royalties

정산하다.notes: In Korean pop culture and everyday life, 정산하다 is used both for splitting bills after a group trip and for K-pop idols or TV staff receiving their settled payout from an agency.

cognates.meaning: to put on a stern or solemn countenance

정색하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb derived from 정색 (正色, 'a solemn,Composed, or stern facial expression', literally 'straightening one's countenance/color', from 正 'straight, proper, upright' + 色 'color, facial expression, look'), attested in Classical Chinese texts such as the Mencius and Analects, combined with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: pure primary color; composing one's face into a solemn, stern expression
a grave, unsmiling countenance
to drop one's smile and put on a dead-serious or stern face

정색하다.notes: Often used in conversation when someone suddenly stops laughing at a joke and gets dead-serious or visibly offended (e.g., 왜 그렇게 정색해? 'Why are you getting so serious all of a sudden?').

rootFamily.gloss: change of complexion or attitude (變色)

정성.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 정성 (精誠, 'utmost sincerity, wholehearted devotion'), combining 정 (精, 'refined essence, pure, meticulous', originally 'hulled/polished grain') and 성 (誠, 'sincerity, truthfulness, devotion', from 言 'word' + 成 'complete'). Classical Chinese locus classicus includes Zhuangzi (精誠之至 'the utmost of pure sincerity').

history.meaning: pure, unalloyed sincerity that moves heaven and earth
wholehearted devotion, earnest care put into an action or gift

정성.notes: Frequently paired with 들이다 (정성을 들이다, 'to put one's heart and care into something') or the adverb 정성껏 ('with all one's heart').

정성껏.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 정성 (精誠, 'true heart, utmost sincerity and devotion', from 精 'pure, refined' + 誠 'sincerity') + the native Korean suffix -껏 ('to the utmost of').

history.meaning: with all one's heart, wholeheartedly, with utmost care

정숙도.etymology: Sino-Korean 정숙도 (靜肅度), formed from 정숙 (靜肅, 'quietness, silence, stillness', from 靜 'quiet, still' + 肅 'solemn, hushed') + the suffix 도 (度, 'degree, level').

history.meaning: degree of quietness, noise-insulation or hush level

정식.etymology: Represents two common Sino-Korean compounds: 정식 (正式, 'formal, official, proper form', from 正 'right, proper' + 式 'form, style, ceremony') and 정식 (定食, 'fixed set meal, table d'hôte', from 定 'fixed, settled' + 食 'meal, food').

history.meaning: proper official form / fixed set meal
formality, official way; set meal, full-course meal

cognates.word: 精神力 (せいしんりょく, seishinryoku)

정신력.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound noun 정신력 (精神力, 'mental strength, willpower, fortitude'), formed from 정신 (精神, 'mind, spirit, consciousness', from 精 'vital essence' + 神 'spirit, numinous mind') and the suffixoid noun 력 (力, 'power, strength, force'). In Classical Taoist and medical texts, 精神 denoted vital essence and spirit; in Meiji/modern East Asian usage, it shifted to psychological mind and willpower.

history.meaning: vital essence and numinous spirit
mind, consciousness, soul
mental fortitude, willpower, grit

정신력.notes: Notice the phonological assimilation in standard pronunciation: 정신력 is pronounced [정신녁] because /ㄹ/ nasalizes to [ㄴ] after /ㄴ/.

정신없다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) compounded from Sino-Korean 정신 (精神, 'mind, wits, attention', from 精 'vital essence' + 神 'spirit, mind') and the native Korean existential-negative adjective 없다 ('to not exist, to lack', Middle Korean 없다). Literally 'to lack one's wits/mind', idiomatized to describe either a person who is scatterbrained/frantic or an environment that is chaotic and hectic.

history.meaning: to have no presence of mind, to lose one's wits
hectic, chaotic, frantic, scatterbrained

정신없다.notes: Can describe both a person ('I'm so swamped I can't think straight') and a situation/place ('The studio is so hectic and noisy').

rootFamily.gloss: to pull oneself together, to come to one's senses

정오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 정오 (正午), from 정 (正, 'exact, upright') and 오 (午, 'the Horse hour', 11 a.m.–1 p.m., whose midpoint is twelve noon).
정오.notes: Explains 오전 (午前, 'before noon / a.m.') and 오후 (午後, 'after noon / p.m.') as well.

정원.etymology: Sino-Korean 정원 (庭園, 'garden, landscaped yard'), compounding 정 (庭, 'courtyard, yard') and 원 (園, 'garden, orchard, park'); also homophonous with 정원 (定員, 'fixed capacity or quota of people').

history.meaning: courtyard and garden / fixed number of personnel
garden; fixed capacity

정원용.etymology: Sino-Korean 정원용 (庭園用), formed from 정원 (庭園, 'garden') + the suffix 용 (用, 'use, intended for').

history.meaning: for garden use, garden-grade

cognates.word: 正義感 (せいぎかん, seigikan)

정의감.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound noun 정의감 (正義感, 'sense of justice'), built from 정의 (正義, 'justice, righteousness', from 正 'right, straight, correct' + 義 'moral duty, righteousness, justice') and the suffixoid 감 (感, 'feeling, sense, perception'). While 正義 meant 'correct interpretation' or 'moral rectitude' in Classical Chinese, it became the standard East Asian translation for Western 'justice' in the late 19th century.

history.meaning: moral rectitude; orthodox exposition of a classic text
justice, righteousness
personal sense of justice or moral indignation at unfairness

정의감.notes: Often collocated with 불타다 (정의감에 불타다, 'to burn with a sense of justice') or 투철하다 ('to have a strong sense of justice').

정의롭다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed by attaching the native Korean adjectival suffix -롭다 ('characterized by, full of, worthy of', from Middle Korean -롭다) to the Sino-Korean noun 정의 (正義, 'justice, righteousness', from 正 'right, upright, straight' + 義 'moral duty, justice').

history.meaning: righteousness, moral rectitude, justice
having the quality or nature of (adjectival derivational suffix)
righteous, just, fair-minded

정의롭다.notes: As a ㅂ-irregular (ㅂ불규칙) adjective, the stem 정의롭- changes to 정의로워 before vowel-initial endings and 정의로운 in the adnominal modifier form.

정장.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 정장 (正裝, 'formal attire, business suit'), composed of 정 (正, 'proper, standard, formal, orthodox') and 장 (裝, 'attire, dress, outfit, adornment'). Historically denoting official court or ceremonial dress in contrast to casual attire (便服), in modern Korean it specifically refers to a Western-style tailored business suit or formal outfit.

history.meaning: official or ceremonial full dress
formal wear, business suit (jacket and trousers/skirt)

정장.notes: Whereas 양복 (洋服) usually refers specifically to a man's Western suit, 정장 (正裝) is gender-neutral and applies equally to men's and women's formal business suits.

정전.etymology: Sino-Korean 정전 (停電), combining 정 (停, 'to stop, halt, suspend') + 전 (電, 'lightning; electricity'). Coined in modern Sinospheric technical vocabulary in the late nineteenth / early twentieth century for an interruption of electrical power.

history.meaning: suspension of electric current, blackout
power outage, blackout

정전.notes: In speech, Koreans say 정전이 되다 or 정전이 나다 ('a blackout happens') alongside native 불이 나가다 ('the lights go out').

cognates.word: 訂正報道 (ていせいほうどう, teisei hōdō)

정정보도.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound noun 정정보도 (訂正報道, 'press correction, corrective broadcast/report'), combining 정정 (訂正, 'revision, correction', from 訂 'to examine, revise, edit' + 正 'to make right, correct') and 보도 (報道, 'news report, media coverage', from 報 'to report, announce' + 道 'to tell, state, way'). It is a core legal and journalistic term in Korean broadcasting law.

history.meaning: revising errors + reporting news to the public
official press correction or retraction broadcast by a media outlet

정정보도.notes: Under South Korea's Act on Press Arbitration (언론중재법), someone harmed by false factual reporting has the statutory right to demand a 정정보도 ('correction report') or 반론보도 ('rebuttal report').

정직원.etymology: Sino-Korean 정직원 (正職員), formed from prefix 정- (正, 'regular, official, full-time') + 직원 (職員, 'staff member, employee', from 職 'post, duty' + 員 'member, personnel').

history.meaning: regular full-time employee, permanent staff member

정직하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정직 (正直, 'honesty, uprightness, candor', compounding 正 'right, straight' and 直 'straight, direct, honest') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: uprightness, honesty
to be honest, upright, truthful

정체.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 正體, pairing 正 (바를 정, 'true, authentic, proper') and 體 (몸 체, 'body, form, substance'). Originally meaning the authentic form or true nature of a person or thing, it appears humorously in everyday Korean in the set phrase 정체 모를 ('of unknown identity; mystery —').
정체.notes: Very common in the idiom 정체 모를 + Noun ('mystery —, unidentified —').

cognates.meaning: to stagnate, to be bogged down

정체되다.etymology: A Sino-Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 정체 (停滯, 'stagnation, congestion, standstill', from 停 'to stop, halt, pause' + 滯 'to block, congeal, stagnate, fail to flow') and the native Korean passive/inchoative verb suffix 되다 ('to become, to get'). Originally used in Classical Chinese for blocked water or indigestion, it now describes traffic congestion, economic stagnation, or a stalled career/ratings.

history.meaning: obstruction of water flow or qi/digestion; halting in one place
stagnation, deadlock, traffic congestion
to become stagnant, stalled, or congested

정체되다.notes: Used across three common domains in Korean: highway traffic (정체 구간 'congested section'), economic growth (경기 정체 'economic stagnation'), and personal/creative progress.

rootFamily.gloss: period of stagnation or slump (停滯期)

정하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정 (定, 'to fix, settle, decide, establish') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to fix, settle, decide
to decide, set, fix, determine

정해지다.etymology: Passive/inchoative verb formed from 정하다 ('to decide, set', from Sino-Korean 定 + 하다) + the auxiliary passive construction -아/어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to be decided, be set, be determined

정확하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정확 (正確, 'accuracy, precision, exactness', compounding 正 'right, correct' and 確 'firm, certain, accurate') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: correctness and certainty, accuracy
to be accurate, exact, precise

정확히.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정확 (正確, 'accurate, exact') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: accurately, exactly, precisely

젖다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 젗다 ('to get wet, become soaked or damp').

history.meaning: to get wet, be moistened
to get wet, be soaked; to be steeped in (an emotion)

젖히다.etymology: Native Korean causative-transitive verb historically derived from 젖다 ('to lean or tilt backward', Middle Korean 졎다) plus the transitivizing suffix -히-. Because coda ㅈ meets ㅎ, standard Korean pronounces 젖히다 as [저치다], denoting the crisp motion of flipping back a cloth flap, lid, collar, or curtain.
젖히다.notes: Do not confuse spelling with 젖다 ('to get wet').

제.etymology: Primarily the contracted possessive and pre-가 nominative form of humble first-person 저 ('I, my') or reflexive 저 ('one's own', Middle Korean 졔 < 저 + 의/이); also represents Sino-Korean ordinal prefix 제- (第-, 'number, -th').

history.meaning: my (humble) / one's own; I (before subject marker)
my (humble), one's own; I (before 가); ordinal prefix (第)

cognates.meaning: offer, provision, sponsorship (of a TV program)
to provide, to supply, to offer

제공되다.etymology: A Sino-Korean passive verb combining 제공 (提供, 'provision, supplying, offering', from 提 'to carry in the hand, raise, put forward, bring up' + 供 'to supply, offer, present, furnish') with the native Korean passive suffix 되다 ('to become, to be done'). In broadcasting, 제공 also specifically denotes commercial sponsorship or provision of production support.

history.meaning: putting forward and supplying goods, information, or sponsorship
to be provided, supplied, or offered

제공되다.notes: Frequently seen in formal notices, service terms, and TV credits (e.g., 숙식이 제공되다 'room and board are provided').

rootFamily.gloss: to provide, to supply, to offer

cognates.meaning: to offer, to provide, to sponsor
cognates.word: 提供する (ていきょうする, teikyō suru)

cognates.meaning: to provide, to supply, to furnish

제공하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean active transitive verb formed from 제공 (提供, 'provision, supply, offering', from 提 'to lift, carry, put forward' + 供 'to supply, present, offer') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Adopted across modern East Asian languages to denote supplying resources, services, information, or media sponsorship.

history.meaning: putting forward and supplying resources or information
to provide, to supply, to offer

제공하다.notes: In Korean broadcasting, 제공 is the standard word heard in sponsor announcements before and after a show ('이 프로그램은 ... 제공으로 보내드립니다').

rootFamily.gloss: to be provided, to be supplied

제공해주다.etymology: A benefactive compound verb combining Sino-Korean 제공 (提供, 'provision, supply', from 提 'to put forward, bring' + 供 'to supply, offer'), the light verb stem 해- (infinitive of 하다, 'to do'), and the native Korean auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give', Middle Korean 주다), expressing the act of providing or supplying something for another person's benefit.

history.meaning: to provide, to supply
to provide or furnish something for someone

제공해주다.notes: Adding -아/어 주다 softens the formal bureaucratic tone of 제공하다 by highlighting helpfulness toward the recipient.

rootFamily.gloss: to be provided, to be offered

제대로.etymology: Native Korean adverb lexicalized from reflexive 제 ('its own proper [state or form]') + the particle/bound noun 대로 ('in accordance with, just as').

history.meaning: as it should be, properly,in good order

제목.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 제목 (題目), combining 제 (題, 'forehead, heading, inscription') and 목 (目, 'eye, item, heading').
제목.notes: Standard word for the title of a piece of sheet music, book, or article.

제발.etymology: Attested since early Modern Korean as 데발 / 제발 ('please, I beg of you'); generally traced to Sino-Korean 제발 (濟拔, a Buddhist term meaning 'to save and pull out from suffering', from 濟 'save, ferry across' + 拔 'pull out, rescue').

history.meaning: salvation from distress -> earnest plea ('please!')
please, for heaven's sake

제법.etymology: Originally a Sino-Korean noun 제법 (諸法, 'various laws, rules, or methods; all dharmas in Buddhism', from 諸 'all, various' + 法 'law, method, way, dharma'), attested in Middle Korean texts as 졔법. In Early Modern Korean, phrases meaning 'acting according to all the proper rules/methods' underwent semantic shift into an adverb and predicative noun meaning 'quite, fairly well, impressively, up to standard'.

history.meaning: all laws/methods; all dharmas (phenomena) in Buddhist philosophy
in accordance with proper form; quite well, fairly impressively

제법.notes: Used both as an adverb (제법 잘한다 'does quite well') and with the copula (제법이다 'is quite impressive / not bad at all!'), often with a nuance of pleasant surprise that someone exceeded expectations.

cognates.meaning: information tip-off, reporting news to media or authorities
cognates.word: 情報提供 (じょうほうていきょう) / 提報 (ていほう, teihō)

제보할.etymology: The prospective adnominal form (-ㄹ) of the Sino-Korean verb 제보하다 (提報하다, 'to tip off, to report news or information to the media or authorities'), compounded from 제보 (提報, from 提 'to bring forward, present, submit' + 報 'to report, inform, announce') and the native light verb 하다 ('to do') inflected with the prospective modifier suffix -ㄹ ('to..., that will...').

history.meaning: submitting a report or tip of information
to tip off, to report > (something) to report / (someone) who will tip off

morphemes.meaning: to put forward, submit, bring up

제보할.notes: In Korean journalism and TV shows, 제보 refers specifically to an informant or viewer tipping off a newsroom or investigative program (as opposed to 신고, which is reporting a crime to the police).

제빵.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 제- (製, 'making, manufacturing') + 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese pan from Portuguese pão < Latin pānis).

history.meaning: bread
bread-making, baking

제빵사.etymology: A compound of Sino-Korean 제 (製) 'make', 빵 'bread' and Sino-Korean 사 (師) 'master, specialist'.

제삼.etymology: A Sino-Korean ordinal numeral noun 제삼 (第三, 'the third'), formed from the ordinal prefix 제 (第, 'order, sequence, rank, grade', originally written with the bamboo radical 竹 representingnumbered bamboo slips) and the Sino-Korean cardinal numeral 삼 (三, 'three').

history.meaning: third in sequence or rank
the third; a third party or alternative beyond two sides

제삼.notes: Frequently appears in compounds indicating neutrality or an outside alternative, such as 제삼자 (第三者, 'a third party / outsider') and 제삼세계 (第三世界, 'the Third World').

제삼금융권.etymology: A five-character Sino-Korean economic compound 제삼금융권 (第三金融圈, 'tertiary financial sector; private moneylenders/loan sharks'), combining 제삼 (第三, 'the third', from 第 'ordinal prefix' + 三 'three'), 금융 (金融, 'finance, money circulation', from 金 'gold, money' + 融 'to melt, circulate, blend'), and 권 (圈, 'sphere, sector, circle, domain').
