Coined in South Korea to classify unlicensed or non-institutional private lending outside commercial banks (제1금융권) and non-bank financial institutions like savings banks and credit unions (제2금융권).

history.meaning: sphere of monetary circulation / financial sector
the third-tier financial sector: consumer loan companies and private moneylenders (대부업체/사채)

제삼금융권.notes: In everyday Korean conversation and K-dramas, mentioning 제삼금융권 is a euphemistic or dryly humorous way of talking about high-interest consumer loan companies (대부업) or loan sharks (사채).

제안.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 제안 (提案, 'proposal, suggestion, motion'), composed of 제 (提, 'to lift, carry in the hand, bring forward, raise a topic') and 안 (案, 'table/desk > official document, draft plan, bill, matter for consideration'). Literally 'bringing a draft plan forward onto the table for deliberation'.

history.meaning: wooden tray or desk; legal case file or official draft plan laid on a magistrate's desk
putting forward a formal motion, bill, or proposal

제안.notes: Slightly more concrete or action-oriented than 제의 (提議, 'suggestion for discussion'), 제안 covers both formal business proposals (제안서) and personal offers.

rootFamily.gloss: agenda item, bill, draft plan (案件)

cognates.word: 提案する (ていあんする, teian suru)

cognates.meaning: to put forward a motion or proposal

제안하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean transitive verb formed from 제안 (提案, 'proposal, offer, suggestion', from 提 'to bring forward, raise' + 案 'draft plan, matter on the table') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). It denotes putting forward a plan, idea, or offer for someone else to consider.

history.meaning: putting forward a draft plan or motion
to propose, to suggest, to make an offer

제안하다.notes: Commonly used in workplace and media contexts for pitching a show concept, offering a casting role, or proposing a business deal.

rootFamily.gloss: to suggest, to make an overture (提議하다)

cognates.meaning: to exclude, to leave out, apart from

제외.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun 제외 (除外, 'exclusion, exception, leaving out'), composed of 제 (除, 'to remove, eliminate, clear away, deduct', originally 'steps to a palace hall') and 외 (外, 'outside, external, beyond'). Literally 'removing something and placing it outside the count or group'.

history.meaning: to deduct and leave outside a reckoning or rule
exclusion, exception, omission from a group

제외.notes: Very frequently used in the clause connector pattern ~을/를 제외하고(는) ('except for ~ / excluding ~').

rootFamily.gloss: to be excluded, to be left out

제이.etymology: A Sino-Korean ordinal numeral noun 제이 (第二, 'the second'), formed from the ordinal prefix 제 (第, 'order, rank, sequence', written with the bamboo radical 竹 for sequenced bamboo tallies) and the Sino-Korean cardinal numeral 이 (二, 'two').

history.meaning: second in sequence or rank
the second; a successor or next iteration

제이.notes: Used with the genitive particle 의 (제이의..., written 제2의...) to mean 'the next / a second...' (e.g., 제2의 전성기 'a second heyday', 제2의 인생 'a second chapter in life').

rootFamily.gloss: the first, number one; most (第一)

제일.etymology: Sino-Korean 제일 (第一), compounding the ordinal prefix 제- (第, 'rank, order') and 일 (一, 'one, first'), used both as a noun ('number one, the first') and as a superlative adverb ('most, best').

history.meaning: the first, number one
the first, foremost; most, best

제자리.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the reflexive determiner 제 ('its own, one's own') + 자리 ('place, spot, seat, position').

history.meaning: its own place, original position, right spot

제작자.etymology: Sino-Korean agent noun 제작자 (製作者), formed from 제작 (製作, 'making, crafting, manufacturing', from 製 'cut out, fashion, manufacture' + 作 'make, create') plus the personal agentive suffix -자 (者, 'person who does'). Depending on the preceding noun, it denotes either a traditional artisan or specialist—such as 지도 제작자 ('mapmaker, cartographer') or 악기 제작자 ('instrument maker, luthier')—or a modern film/broadcast producer.

history.meaning: crafting/making + agent suffix
maker, craftsman, creator, or producer

제작자.notes: Paired with 지도 ('map'), 지도 제작자 is the natural Korean expression for a mapmaker or cartographer.

cognates.word: 制作陣 (せいさくじん, seisakujin)

제작진.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound noun 제작진 (製作陣, 'production crew, production staff'), formed from 제작 (製作, 'production, manufacture, creation', from 製 'to cut out garments, fashion, make' + 作 'to make, create, compose') and the collective suffix 진 (陣, 'battle formation, camp, lineup, team of personnel'). Literally 'the battle formation/lineup of creators'.

history.meaning: making/crafting + military battle array or camp
the production crew or staff of a film, broadcast program, or stage work

제작진.notes: The suffix -진 (陣, originally 'military formation') is productive in Korean media and sports for a whole team of specialists: 제작진 ('production crew'), 출연진 ('cast'), 보도진 ('press corps'), 의료진 ('medical team').

제정신.etymology: A hybrid native Korean and Sino-Korean compound noun 제정신 ('one's right mind, sanity, normal consciousness'), formed from the native Korean reflexive/possessive determiner 제 ('one's own, its proper', from Middle Korean 졔, reflexive pronoun 져 'oneself' + genitive -의) and Sino-Korean 정신 (精神, 'mind, spirit, consciousness', from 精 'vital essence' + 神 'spirit, mind'). Literally 'one's own proper mind'.

history.meaning: one's own mind or consciousness
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean components

history.meaning: one's right mind, sanity, sober senses

제정신.notes: Almost always used with the copula in questions or negations: 제정신이야? ('Are you in your right mind?') or 제정신이 아니다 ('to be out of one's mind').

rootFamily.gloss: at the right time, on time (제 + 때)
one's proper role or share (제 + 몫)

cognates.word: 済州島 (さいしゅうとう, Saishūtō)

제주도.etymology: A Sino-Korean proper noun 제주도 (濟州島, 'Jeju Island', or 濟州道 'Jeju Province'), combining 제주 (濟州, 'Province across the water', from 濟 'to cross a river/sea, aid' + 州 'prefecture, province') and 도 (島, 'island', or 道, 'province'). Formerly the maritime kingdom of Tamna (耽羅), it was renamed Jeju (濟州, referring to a prefecture reached by crossing the sea) during the Goryeo dynasty under King Gojong (1214–1259).

history.meaning: ancient and medieval island kingdom on Jeju
prefecture across the sea (renamed in 13th-century Goryeo)

history.form: 제주도 (濟州島 / 濟州特別自治道)
history.meaning: Jeju Island / Jeju Special Self-Governing Province

morphemes.meaning: to cross water/sea, to ferry across

제주도.notes: In Korean, 제주도 can represent two homophonous Hanja spellings: 濟州島 (the physical island, Jeju Island) and 濟州道 (the administrative province, Jeju Province, which also includes smaller surrounding islands like Udo and Marado).

져드리다.etymology: A native Korean humble benefactive compound verb formed from 지다 ('to lose, be defeated, yield', Middle Korean 지다, conjugated into its infinitive stem 져-) and the humble benefactive auxiliary verb 드리다 ('to give/do for a respected person', derived from Middle Korean 드리다 'to offer up, cause to enter'). Literally 'to lose or yield to a superior on purpose as a courtesy'.

history.meaning: to be defeated + to offer up to a superior
to intentionally lose or yield to someone of higher status

morphemes.meaning: to humbly give or do for an honored person

져드리다.notes: While 지다 ('to lose') is normally involuntary, adding -어 주다 (져주다) or its humble counterpart -어 드리다 (져드리다) means 'to let someone win on purpose / to give in graciously'.

rootFamily.gloss: to lose, to be defeated, to yield
to let someone win, to yield to someone

조.etymology: Sino-Korean monosyllable representing several common homographs: 조 (組, 'group, team, squad, set'), 조 (條, 'article, clause, item'), and 조 (兆, 'one trillion; omen'); also native Korean 조 ('foxtail millet', Middle Korean 조).

history.meaning: group, team / article, clause / trillion, omen
group, team; legal article; trillion; millet

조각.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 조각 ('broken piece, fragment, slice, shard'); homophonous with Sino-Korean 조각 (彫刻, 'carving, sculpture').

history.meaning: piece, fragment, slice
piece, slice, fragment; sculpture (彫刻)

조각하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 조각 (彫刻, joining 彫 'to carve, chisel ornamentally' and 刻 'to incise, engrave into stone or wood') plus the native light verb 하다. Note that Korean has two homophonous nouns spelled 조각: native Korean 조각 ('piece, slice') and Sino-Korean 彫刻 ('sculpture, carving'), with only the latter forming 조각하다.
조각하다.notes: Passive state is expressed with 조각되다 or 조각되어 있다 ('to be carved').

cognates.word: 朝刊新聞 (ちょうかんしんぶん, chōkan shinbun)

조간신문.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound noun 조간신문 (朝刊新聞, 'morning newspaper'), combining 조간 (朝刊, 'morning publication/edition', from 朝 'morning, dawn' + 刊 'to carve woodblocks, print, publish') and 신문 (新聞, 'newspaper', literally 'new things heard', from 新 'new' + 聞 'to hear, news'). Contrasts with 석간신문 (夕刊新聞, 'evening newspaper').

history.meaning: newly heard tidings or reports; later coined in 19th-c. East Asia for 'newspaper'
history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese / Early Modern East Asian coinage

history.meaning: morning-printed edition + newspaper

조간신문.notes: Often shortened simply to 조간 (朝刊, 'the morning paper/edition'), in contrast to 석간 (夕刊, 'the evening paper/edition').

조건.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 條件, composed of 條 (조, 'branch, clause, article, item') and 件 (건, 'matter, item, document'). In pre-modern Chinese administrative prose, 條件 denoted individual articles or stipulations itemized in a document; during the Meiji period in Japan (条件 jōken), it was repurposed to translate European legal and philosophical terms for 'condition' or 'prerequisite' (German Bedingung, English condition) and subsequently entered modern Korean.

history.meaning: itemized clauses or articles in an official document
condition, stipulation, prerequisite, terms

조건.notes: Frequently paired with 걸다 ('to attach/set conditions', 조건을 걸다) or prefixed with 무- (무조건, 'unconditionally / no matter what').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조건

조그맣다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb (ㅎ-irregular adjective), contracted from 조그마하다 ('to be rather small or tiny'). It derives from the diminutive root seen in 조금 ('a little, a small amount', 15th-century Middle Korean 죠고마 / 죠곰) combined with the adjectival formative -맣다. Its bright vowels (ㅗ and ㅏ) employ Korean sound symbolism to evoke something cute, petite, or trifling in scale, contrasting with the heavier dark-vowel counterpart 지그맣다/즈그맣다.

history.meaning: to be small, trifling, slight in size
to be tiny, small, little

조그맣다.notes: As a ㅎ-irregular adjective, the final ㅎ drops before vowel-initial endings and alters the vowel: 조그맣다 -> 조그만 ('tiny [attributive]') and 조그매서 ('because it is tiny').

rootFamily.gloss: to be rather small, tiny (uncontracted form)
to be petite, neat and small (vowel-harmonic variant)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조그맣다

조금.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 조ᄀᆞᆷ ('a little, a small amount, slightly').

history.meaning: a small amount, a little
a little, a bit, slightly

조금씩.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) polymorphemic adverb formed by attaching the distributive suffix -씩 ('each, apiece, at a time', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as -식) to the noun/adverb 조금 ('a little, a small amount', Middle Korean 죠곰, from the diminutive base 죡- + nominalizer -옴). Literally meaning 'in small portions at a time', it expresses gradual, incremental progression ('little by little, bit by bit').

history.meaning: a little bit each, in small amounts at a time
little by little, gradually, bit by bit

morphemes.meaning: distributive marker: each, at a time, in increments of

조금씩.notes: Unlike 단지 조금 ('just a little'), adding -씩 emphasizes steady, repeated increments over time or distribution across multiple recipients.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조금씩

조례.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean compounds: 조례 (條例, 'municipal ordinance, bylaw, regulation', from 條 'article, clause' + 例 'rule, regulation') and 조례 (朝禮, 'morning assembly or briefing', from 朝 'morning' + 禮 'ceremony, greeting').

history.meaning: itemized regulations, bylaw / morning ceremony
local ordinance, bylaw; morning assembly

조르다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) 르-irregular transitive verb, attested in Early Modern Korean as 조르다 / 졸으다. Its primary physical sense is 'to tighten, constrict, or bind tightly around the neck or waist' (related to 졸라매다 'to tie tightly'). Through metaphorical extension—squeezing or pressing someone until they yield—it developed the common interpersonal sense 'to pester, nag, or importune someone persistently for a favor or gift'.

history.meaning: to constrict, tighten around the throat or waist
to tighten; to pester, nag, beg persistently

morphemes.meaning: to tighten, constrict; to press or pester

조르다.notes: Conjugates as a 르-irregular verb (조르다 -> 졸라, 졸라서); in colloquial speech, the conjugated form 졸라 also spawned a coarse slang intensifier meaning 'extremely'.

rootFamily.gloss: to tie tightly, tighten one's belt
to be tightened, strangled, or pressured

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조르다

조리대.etymology: Sino-Korean 조리대 (調理臺), formed from 조리 (調理, 'cooking, culinary preparation', from 調 'season, harmonize' + 理 'arrange, prepare') + 대 (臺, 'platform, stand, counter').

history.meaning: kitchen countertop, food-preparation table

조림.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) culinary noun derived via the deverbal nominalizer -ㅁ from the transitive verb 조리다 / 졸이다 ('to simmer down, braise in a seasoned broth until the liquid reduces and glazes the ingredients'), itself the morphological causative (-이-) of the intransitive verb 졸다 ('to boil down, evaporate, shrink in volume', Middle Korean 졸다). Denotes a major category of Korean side dishes (반찬) where fish, meat, tofu, or vegetables are braised in soy sauce or spicy seasoning.

history.meaning: to boil down (intransitive) > to simmer and reduce liquid (transitive)
braised dish simmered down in seasoned sauce

morphemes.meaning: to simmer down, braise in seasoned liquid (조리다/졸이다)

조림.notes: Usually attached directly after the main ingredient to name a dish, such as 장조림 (soy-braised beef), 고등어조림 (braised mackerel), or 두부조림 (braised tofu).

rootFamily.gloss: to boil down, simmer; to fret anxiously
to boil down, diminish in volume through simmering

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조림

cognates.meaning: morning and evening; sooner or later

조만간.etymology: Sino-Korean temporal adverb from 早晩間, composed of 早 (조, 'early, morning'), 晩 (만, 'late, evening'), and 間 (간, 'interval, space between'). Literally meaning 'within the interval between early and late' (i.e., 'sooner or later, whether early or late'), in contemporary Korean usage its meaning has narrowed and shifted toward the 'early' pole to mean 'before long, shortly, in the very near future'.

history.meaning: between morning and evening; sooner or later
before long, soon, in the near future

조만간.notes: A classic semantic shift: although the Hanja literally mean 'sooner or later' (早晩), speakers today almost always use 조만간 to mean 'pretty soon / in the next few days or weeks' (머지않아).

rootFamily.gloss: late years, twilight of life (晩年)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조만간

조명.etymology: Sino-Korean 조명 (照明), compounding 조 (照, 'shine, illuminate') and 명 (明, 'bright, light').

history.meaning: shining brightly, illumination
lighting, illumination

조사.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 調査, composed of 調 (조, 'harmonize, regulate, calculate, examine') and 査 (사, 'inspect, examine, look into'). Popularized across East Asia in the late 19th century (via Meiji Japanese 調査 chōsa) as the standard administrative, legal, and scientific term for a systematic inquiry, fact-finding examination, or statistical survey.

history.meaning: official inspection, fact-finding inquiry, survey
history.stage: Meiji Japanese & Early Modern East Asian Prose

history.meaning: investigation, survey, inquiry, examination

조사.notes: Distinguish from 수사 (搜査), which specifically means a criminal investigation by police or prosecutors; 조사 (調査) covers both general surveys/research and formal questioning (조사를 받다, 'to be questioned/investigated'). Also homophonous with 조사 (助詞, grammatical particle).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조사

조성.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 조성 (調性), from 조 (調, 'melody, tune, key') and 성 (性, 'nature, quality').
조성.notes: Distinguishes musical tonality/key from unrelated homographs of 조.

조심스럽다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean descriptive verb (ㅂ-irregular adjective) formed by attaching the native Korean adjectival derivational suffix -스럽다 ('having the quality of, evoking the impression of') to the Sino-Korean noun 조심 (操心, 'caution, prudence', literally 'holding and governing one's heart/mind', from 操 조 'grasp, manage' + 心 심 'heart, mind', attested in Mencius). Describes behavior or an attitude that is cautious, circumspect, or hesitant out of care.

history.meaning: to hold fast to one's mind/principles; to take pains
to be cautious, careful, circumspect, hesitant

morphemes.meaning: native adjective-forming suffix: characterized by, seeming

조심스럽다.notes: While 조심하다 is an action verb ('to be careful / watch out'), 조심스럽다 is a descriptive adjective describing a delicate, tentative, or hesitant demeanor or situation ('to feel cautious about broaching a topic').

rootFamily.gloss: to be careful, watch out (操心하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조심스럽다

조심조심.etymology: Reduplicated Korean adverb doubling Sino-Korean 조심 (操心, from 操 'to hold, manage' and 心 'heart, mind'—literally 'holding one's mind steady'). Repeating the two-syllable noun in full turns careful attention into a step-by-step rhythm, portraying delicate hands unfolding brittle paper or carrying hot tea.
조심조심.notes: More vivid and gentle in spoken storytelling than plain 조심히.

조심하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 조심 (操心, 'caution, heedfulness', literally 'holding and governing one's mind', from 操 'hold, control' + 心 'mind, heart') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to govern one's mind, exercise caution
to be careful, watch out, take care

조심히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean adverb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 조심 (操心, 'care, caution, mindfulness', composed of 操 조 'grasp, control, manage' + 心 심 'heart, mind') and the productive native Korean adverb-forming suffix -히 ('in the manner of'). Literally meaning 'with a guarded/attentive mind', it functions as the standard adverb for 'carefully' or 'safely'.

history.meaning: holding and guarding one's mind; exercising prudence
carefully, cautiously, safely

morphemes.meaning: native adverbializing suffix: in a manner of

조심히.notes: Ubiquitous in everyday Korean farewells such as 조심히 들어가세요 ('get home safely') or 조심히 다녀오세요 ('have a safe trip and come back').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조심히

cognates.meaning: assistant directing, assistant director in theatre/broadcasting

조연출.etymology: Sino-Korean broadcasting and theatrical compound noun from 助演出, formed by prefixing 助 (조, 'assist, aid, assistant') to 연출 (演出, 'stage or broadcast directing, production', from 演 연 'perform, unfold, practice' + 出 출 'bring out, present'). Denotes either the role of assisting the main producer-director (PD) or the assistant director (AD) in television, radio, and stage productions.

history.meaning: staging and directing a performance or broadcast
assistant directing; assistant director (AD) in television or theater

조연출.notes: In Korean television (such as KBS in *The Producers*), junior PDs work as 조연출 (often colloquially called FD or 막내 PD/AD) under a main 연출 (chief/main PD) before debuting with their own program. Compare 조감독 (助監督), which is used in the film industry.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조연출

조용하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 종용 (從容, 'calm, unhurried, quiet, composed'), attested in Middle Korean as 죵용ᄒᆞ다 and evolving by dissimilation of the first nasal coda to 조용하다.

history.meaning: to be calm, composed, quiet
to be quiet, silent, peaceful

조용해지다.etymology: Inchoative verb built from the Sino-Korean descriptive adjective 조용하다 (從容하다, joyonghada, 'to be quiet, calm, unhurried') by attaching the native Korean change-of-state auxiliary suffix -아/어지다 (-eojida, 'to become, grow'). In Korean grammar, descriptive adjectives describe states rather than transitions; adding -어지다 converts 'is quiet' (조용하다) into the dynamic event 'becomes quiet / falls silent' (조용해지다).

history.meaning: to be calm, composed, quiet
to become quiet, fall silent, hush

cognates.meaning: calm, composed (same historical hanja 從容)

조용해지다.notes: Very common in past tense (조용해졌어요, 'it went quiet / hushed') to describe a room falling silent before a performance or speech.

조용히.etymology: Formed from the root of 조용하다 ('to be quiet, calm' < Sino-Korean 從容) + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: quietly, silently, calmly

조율.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조율 (調律), combining 조 (調, 'adjust, harmonize') and 율 (律, 'musical pitch, standard').
조율.notes: Used both literally for tuning stringed instruments and figuratively for coordinating plans.

조율하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 조율 (調律, 'tuning musical pitches; coordinating differing views', compounding 調 'harmonize, adjust' and 律 'musical pitch, standard') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: adjusting musical pitch, tuning
to tune (an instrument); to coordinate, mediate, fine-tune

조이다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 조이다 / 조히다 ('to tighten, bind fast, make taut; to feel anxious').

history.meaning: to tighten, press hard
to tighten, fasten firmly, screw down

조절.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 調節, composed of 調 (조, 'harmonize, blend, tune, adjust') and 節 (절, 'bamboo node, joint, moderate, restrain'). Attested in classical Chinese texts (such as the *Guanzi* and *Book of Han*) for moderating and balancing excesses or seasonal flows, it is used in modern Korean for physical, mechanical, physiological, or emotional calibration and adjustment.

history.meaning: to balance, moderate, and harmonize proportions or flows
adjustment, regulation, calibration, control

조절.notes: Used when calibrating a continuous scale or intensity—such as temperature (온도 조절), volume, weight (체중 조절), or emotional self-control (감정 조절)—whereas 조정 (調整) often implies resolving disputes or fine-tuning schedules.

rootFamily.gloss: to adjust, regulate, pace oneself (調節하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조절

조절하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean verb formed by combining the Sino-Korean verbal noun 조절 (調節, 'adjustment, regulation, moderation', from 調 조 'harmonize, tune' + 節 절 'bamboo node, moderate, restrain') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, make'). Means to regulate, calibrate, or moderate intensity, quantity, or one's own pace and stamina.

history.meaning: to harmonize and moderate proportions or extremes
to adjust, regulate, calibrate, pace oneself

morphemes.meaning: native light verb: to do, perform

조절하다.notes: In broadcasting and everyday life, 수위를 조절하다 ('to adjust the water level') is a very common idiom meaning 'to tone down or calibrate the intensity/provocativeness of remarks or content'.

rootFamily.gloss: calibrating intensity or broadcast appropriateness (水位調節)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조절하다

조합.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조합 (組合), from 조 (組, 'braid, group, pair') and 합 (合, 'join, unite').
조합.notes: Common in food talk for a winning flavour pairing (꿀조합, 좋은 조합).

조화.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 調和, composed of 調 (조, 'tune, blend, harmonize') and 和 (화, 'harmony, peace, gentle blending'). In classical Chinese texts (*Xunzi*, *Lüshi Chunqiu*), 調和 originally described the skillful blending of the five culinary flavors or the tuning of musical instruments; in modern Korean it denotes visual, aesthetic, ecological, or interpersonal harmony and balance.

history.meaning: blending of flavors or musical tones; harmonizing yin and yang
harmony, balance, accord, aesthetic coordination

조화.notes: Commonly used in the collocation 조화를 이루다 ('to achieve/form harmony'). Note the homophones 조화 (造花, 'artificial flower') and 조화 (造化, 'creation, nature, wondrous feat').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 조화

존경하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 존경 (尊敬, 'respect, reverence, esteem', compounding 尊 'honor, revere' and 敬 'respect, venerate') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: reverence and respect
to respect, look up to, esteem

존댓말.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 존대 (尊待, 'respectful treatment or address', from 尊 'honor' + 待 'treat') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + native Korean 말 ('speech, words, language').

history.meaning: honorific speech, polite language

존재.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 存在, composed of 存 (존, 'exist, survive, remain, preserve') and 在 (재, 'be located at, reside, be present'). Already used as a coordinate compound verb in Literary Chinese meaning 'to remain present or alive', it was lexicalized as an abstract noun in Meiji Japan (存在 sonzai) to translate Western philosophical terms for 'existence' or 'being' (German Sein / Existenz), and in Korean also refers metonymically to an individual being or valued person ('someone of importance, a presence').

history.meaning: to remain alive, continue to be present
existence, being; a significant person or presence

존재.notes: Beyond abstract philosophy, Korean frequently uses 존재 to describe what a person means to someone (예: 나에게 소중한 존재, 'someone precious to me') or in 존재감 (存在感, 'stage/screen presence, charisma').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of presence, charisma, impact (存在感)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 존재

cognates.meaning: to graduate from school; to outgrow

졸업하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 졸업 (卒業, 'graduation, completion of a course of study', from 卒 졸 'finish, complete, conclude' + 業 업 'study, enterprise, coursework') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). In Han-dynasty Chinese texts, 卒業 meant 'to complete one's scholarly studies'; it was institutionalized in modern East Asian school systems for formal academic graduation.

history.meaning: to finish one's scholarly curriculum or work
to graduate from an educational institution; to move past a stage

졸업하다.notes: Takes the object particle -을/를 with the school name (대학교를 졸업하다, 'to graduate from university'), unlike English which uses 'from'. Also used figuratively for 'outgrowing' or 'moving on from' a habit or phase.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 졸업하다

졸음.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) deverbal noun formed by attaching the productive nominalizing suffix -음 to the verb stem 졸- of 졸다 ('to doze, nod off, slumber lightly', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 졸다 / 조오다, and Early Modern Korean 자올다). Denotes the physical state of drowsiness or an urge to nod off.

history.meaning: to doze, nod off > drowsiness, slumber
drowsiness, sleepiness, nodding off

morphemes.meaning: to doze, nod off, feel sleepy (졸다)

졸음.notes: Frequently appears in the idiom 졸음이 쏟아지다 ('drowsiness pours down' = to be overcome with sudden sleepiness) and in road-safety warnings against 졸음운전 ('drowsy driving').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 졸음

졸이다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb formed as the morphological causative (-이-) of the intransitive verb 졸다 ('to boil down, evaporate, diminish in volume through simmering', attested in Middle Korean as 졸다, distinct from homophonous 졸다 'to doze'). Literally meaning 'to reduce a liquid by boiling or simmering', it also developed the vivid psychological idiom 마음을 졸이다 ('to shrink/boil down one's heart', i.e., to fret, be on tenterhooks, or feel anxious suspense).

history.meaning: to diminish by boiling > to boil down, simmer until reduced
to boil down, reduce by simmering; to fret or be anxious (with 마음)

morphemes.meaning: to boil down, evaporate, shrink in volume (졸다)

졸이다.notes: Standard Korean orthography distinguishes 조리다 (braising solid ingredients like fish or meat so flavor soaks in) from 졸이다 (boiling down liquid/broth to concentrate it, or fretting in 마음을 졸이다), though both share the same historical root.

rootFamily.gloss: to boil down, reduce in volume (intransitive)
braised dish simmered in seasoned sauce
to braise ingredients in seasoned sauce

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 졸이다

졸졸.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated ideophone—functioning as both an onomatopoeic adverb (의성어) and a mimetic adverb (의태어). Built on the bright vowel ㅗ for light, small-scale continuity, it depicts either the gentle, steady babbling of a narrow stream of water or the visual image of someone (such as a child, puppy, or rookie assistant) following closely and persistently right at another person's heels.

history.meaning: trickling gently in a thin stream; following closely behind

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic base for steady trickling or trailing closely
reduplicated ideophonic base indicating continuous action

졸졸.notes: Illustrates Korean vowel-and-consonant sound symbolism: bright-vowel 졸졸 is light and cute (trickling brook or tagging along behind someone), dark-vowel 줄줄 is heavier and larger in volume (pouring sweat/rain or reciting fluently), and tensed 쫄쫄 is cramped or tiny (starving, 쫄쫄 굶다).

rootFamily.gloss: flowing in a heavier stream; trailing in a line (dark-vowel counterpart)
trickling in a very thin, tight stream; going hungry (tensed counterpart)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 졸졸

좀.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 조금 ('a little, a bit'), attested since early Modern Korean and frequently used as a politeness softener ('please, just a bit').

history.meaning: a little, slightly
a little, somewhat; please (politeness mitigator)

좁다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 좁다 ('to be narrow, cramped, small in width or area').

history.meaning: to be narrow, confined
to be narrow, cramped, small

종.etymology: Sino-Korean 종 (鐘, 'bell, chime'); also represents Sino-Korean 종 (種, 'kind, species, type') and native Korean 종 ('servant, slave', Middle Korean 죵).

history.meaning: bell, gong / seed, kind, species
bell; kind, type, species; servant

종소리.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 종 (鐘, 'bell') + native Korean 소리 ('sound, voice, ringing').

history.meaning: sound of a bell, bell tolling or chiming

종이.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 죠ᄒᆡ ('paper'), evolving through 죠희 > 조히 > 종이.

history.meaning: paper
paper

종이봉투.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound pairing native Korean 종이 ('paper', from Middle Korean 죠ᄒᆡ) with Sino-Korean 봉투 (封套, from 封 'to seal' and 套 'outer sleeve, wrapper'). While 봉투 alone usually means a letter envelope, 종이봉투 is the everyday bakery and market word for a brown paper bag.
종이봉투.notes: Contrasts with 비닐봉투 ('plastic bag') and 편지 봉투 ('letter envelope').

종이책.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun combining native Korean 종이 (jong-i, from Middle Korean 조ᄒᆡ cwohoy, 'paper') with the long-naturalized Sino-Korean noun 책 (冊, chaek, 'book, bound volume'). While books were historically made of paper by definition, 종이책 became a distinct everyday compound in late 20th- and 21st-century Korean as a retronym contrasting physical printed books with digital电子 books (전자책) and screens.

history.meaning: paper + bound book
physical paper book (contrasted with digital screens or e-books)

종이책.notes: Echoes Junho's fond philosophy from Season 1 Episode 1 that paper books and paper ledgers never fail during a rainstorm or power outage.

cognates.meaning: all day long, the whole day
all day long, from morning till night

종일.etymology: Sino-Korean temporal noun and adverbial from 終日, composed of 終 (종, 'end, finish, complete, throughout') and 日 (일, 'sun, day'). Attested in Old Chinese classics including the *Analects* and *Book of Odes* with the literal verb-object structure 'to finish/exhaust the day', it entered Korean to mean 'all day long, from morning to night'.

history.meaning: to the end of the day; throughout the entire day
all day long, the whole day

종일.notes: Most frequently reinforced by the native Korean word 하루 ('one day') in the pleonastic collocation 하루 종일 ('all day long'), or extended with the suffix -토록 as 종일토록 ('throughout the entire day').

rootFamily.gloss: terminus, last stop on a line (終點)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 종일

종잡다.etymology: Korean compound transitive verb formed from 종 (traditionally traced either to Sino-Korean 宗 종 'main point, principal thread, lineage' or a bound native root denoting 'direction, clue, or outline') and the native Korean verb 잡다 ('to grasp, catch, take hold of', 15th-century Middle Korean 잡다). Literally meaning 'to grasp the main thread or outline', it means 'to pin down, fathom, or figure out the gist or direction of something'.

history.meaning: to grasp, seize > to grasp the main thread or gist of a situation

종잡다.notes: A classic negative-polarity verb in Korean: it is almost exclusively used in negative or interrogative expressions such as 종잡을 수 없다 ('impossible to pin down / unpredictable') or 도무지 종잡지 못하다 ('cannot figure out at all').

rootFamily.gloss: to pull oneself together, brace one's mind
to get hold of, keep under control (usually negative: 걷잡을 수 없다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 종잡다

cognates.meaning: various, a variety of, all sorts of
all kinds of, various sorts of

종종.etymology: Sino-Korean reduplicated adverb from 種種, doubling 種 (종, 'seed, kind, sort, species'). In Literary Chinese and Buddhist scriptures, 種種 meant 'of many different kinds, manifold, various'. While Korean dictionaries still record the literary sense 'various', in everyday spoken and written Korean it underwent a semantic shift from multiplicity of kinds to recurrence of occasions, meaning 'from time to time, occasionally, or fairly often'.

history.meaning: of various kinds, manifold, sundry
history.stage: Literary Chinese & Middle Korean Buddhist Texts

history.meaning: from time to time, occasionally, fairly often

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated root expressing plurality or recurrence (種)

종종.notes: A notable false friend with Japanese 種々 (shuju) and Chinese 種種 (zhǒngzhǒng), which still mean 'various kinds'; in Korean, 종종 is a frequency adverb intermediate between 가끔 ('sometimes') and 자주 ('often').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 종종

종편실.etymology: Sino-Korean television broadcasting compound noun, syllabically contracted from 종합편집실 (綜合編輯室, 'comprehensive editing room'). It combines 綜 (종, 'gather threads of a loom, synthesize', representing 종합 綜合 'comprehensive, composite'), 編 (편, 'weave, compile, edit', representing 편집 編輯 'editing'), and 室 (실, 'room, chamber, suite'). Denotes the final post-production edit suite where rough-cut video is combined with color grading, visual effects, subtitles (자막), and audio mixing.

history.meaning: comprehensive post-production editing room in broadcasting
final edit suite, online post-production room

morphemes.meaning: synthesize, comprehensive (綜, clipped from 綜合 종합)
weave, compile, edit (編, clipped from 編輯 편집)

종편실.notes: In Korean variety-show production (*프로듀사*), the 종편실 is the sleepless nerve center where PDs spend the final hours before broadcast adding Korean variety-style on-screen captions (자막) and sound effects after offline rough editing (가편집).

rootFamily.gloss: final post-production editing; comprehensive TV channel (綜編)
to do final post-production editing (綜編하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 종합편집실 / 종편

종편하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean broadcasting verb formed by attaching the native light verb 하다 ('to do') to 종편 (綜編), a two-syllable acronymic contraction of 종합편집 (綜合編輯, 'comprehensive editing', from 綜 종 'gather threads, synthesize' + 合 합 'join' + 編 편 'weave, edit' + 輯 집 'compile'). In television production jargon, it denotes performing the final online post-production assembly—integrating video, audio, captions, and graphics—prior to airing.

history.meaning: to perform comprehensive post-production editing
to do final post-production editing and mastering for broadcast

morphemes.meaning: synthesize, comprehensive (綜, clipped from 綜合 종합)
weave, compile, edit (編, clipped from 編輯 편집)
native light verb: to do, perform

종편하다.notes: Contrasts with 가편집하다 (假編輯하다, shortened to 가편하다), which is the preliminary 'rough cut' done by the PD before entering the final edit suite to 종편하다. Note that the noun 종편 can also abbreviate 종합편성채널 ('general programming cable TV channel').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 편집하다

좋다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 둗다 ('to be good, fine, desirable'), which underwent palatalization of initial ㄷ before ㅛ in early Modern Korean (둗다 > 죻다 > 좋다).

history.meaning: to be good, fine
to be good, nice, pleasant

좋아요.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) inflected adjective form—and in the digital era a lexicalized noun—derived from the adjective 좋다 ('to be good, pleasing, fine') conjugated with the informal polite ending -아요. In 15th-century Middle Korean, 'to be good' was 둗다 (stem 둏-), contrasting with 죻다 ('to be clean, pure'); through 17th–18th century palatalization (ㄷ > ㅈ before ㅛ) and vowel delabialization/merger (ㅛ > ㅗ), 둗다 evolved into modern 좋다. In the late 2000s, 좋아요 was adopted as the Korean translation of the social-media 'Like' button.

history.meaning: to be good, fine, pleasing
to be good, likable; 'it is good / I like it'
'Like' (social media reaction button or count of likes)

좋아요.notes: Functions both as the everyday polite predicate 'It's good / Sounds good!' and as a countable noun in online media (예: 좋아요를 누르다, 'to hit the Like button'; 좋아요 수, 'number of likes').

rootFamily.gloss: to like, be fond of (transitive verb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 좋다

좋아하다.etymology: Native Korean psychological verb formed from the adjective 좋다 ('to be good, pleasing') + the auxiliary verb construction -아 하다 ('to feel or consider [something] good, to like').

history.meaning: to like, rejoice in, be fond of
to like, be fond of, enjoy

좋진.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) contracted adjectival form of 좋지는, built from the adjective stem 좋- ('to be good, fine', from 15th-century Middle Korean 둗다 / 둏- via Early Modern palatalization 죻다), the negative complementizer suffix -지 (used before negative auxiliaries like 않다 or 못하다), and the contrastive topic marker -는 contracted to the final consonant -ㄴ. Used with a following negative auxiliary (좋진 않다) to express nuanced, hedged negation ('not particularly good, not all that great').

history.meaning: to not be good
(as for being good) not particularly good, not that great

좋진.notes: Adding the contrastive topic marker -는/-ㄴ to -지 (좋진 않다 vs. 좋지 않다) softens the negation and implies nuance: 'It's not *good*, per se (though maybe not terrible either)'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 좋다

좌르르르.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) expressive ideophone (의태어/의성어), formed by extending the standard mimetic adverb 좌르르 ('pouring, trickling, or cascading smoothly and briskly') with an additional reduplicated syllable -르 to iconically lengthen the duration and drama of the flow. Its bright diphthong ㅘ and liquid ㄹ consonants evoke a vivid, brisk cascade of liquid, sweat, grains, or even figurative charisma/magnificence pouring off someone all at once.

history.meaning: cascading, pouring, or streaming down smoothly and continuously

morphemes.meaning: mimetic base for brisk, smooth cascading or pouring
expressive reduplicative extension prolonging the motion

좌르르르.notes: In Korean ideophones, adding extra -르 syllables (좌르르 -> 좌르르르) directly stretches the perceived visual or auditory duration; in comedy and drama, it can describe either sweat/water pouring down or an aura/glossiness 'cascading' off a person.

rootFamily.gloss: pouring, cascading smoothly and briskly (standard base form)
trickling or sliding down in a heavier stream (dark-vowel counterpart)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 좌르르

좌석.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 座席, combining 座 (자리 좌, 'seat, throne, place to sit') and 席 (자리 석, 'woven mat, seat at a gathering'). Whereas 의자 refers to the physical piece of furniture ('chair') and 자리 is the everyday native word for a spot or seat, 좌석 is the formal and public-venue word for guest seating capacity and arrangements.
좌석.notes: Used in official notices, cafés, theatres, and public transport.

죄.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 罪 (죄, 'crime, sin, offense, fault, blame'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 죄 (Zwoy). In ancient Chinese paleography, the word was originally written 辠 (combining 自 'nose' and 辛 'criminal punishment', referring to the ancient penalty of nose-slitting), which Qin Shi Huang replaced by decree with 罪 (combining 网 'net' + 非 'wrong', i.e., 'caught in the net of wrongdoing') because 辠 resembled 皇 ('emperor'). In Korean, it spans legal crime, religious sin, and everyday interpersonal fault.

history.meaning: transgression, legal offense, guilt, blame
crime, sin, fault, blame
history.stage: Middle Korean (15th c.) to Modern Korean

죄.notes: While 범죄 (犯罪) means a formal legal crime, standalone 죄 is frequently used in everyday speech for personal fault or blame, as in 무슨 죄야? ('What fault is it of mine/theirs? / What did I do to deserve this?') or 죄를 짓다 ('to commit a sin/wrong').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 죄

죄송.etymology: Sino-Korean bound/root noun from 罪悚, composed of 罪 (죄, 'fault, offense, blame, transgression') and 悚 (송, 'fearful, terrified, trembling with awe or remorse', containing the heart radical 忄). Originally a formal epistolary and courtly humble compound in Choson-era Korean meaning 'trembling in fear of having committed an offense against a superior', it evolved into the standard polite root for apologizing in modern Korean.

history.meaning: trembling with fear and remorse over a transgression
feeling deeply apologetic; 'sorry' (used alone in casual ellipsis or with 하다)

죄송.notes: More deferential and formal than 미안 (未安, 'feeling uneasy/sorry'); in playful or colloquial workplace speech, speakers sometimes drop 하다 and utter the bare Sino-Korean root 죄송! as a quick, slightly sheepish 'my bad / sorry!'.

rootFamily.gloss: overwhelmed with awe or gratitude (惶悚하다, sharing 悚)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 죄송

죄송하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 죄송 (罪悚, literally 'guilty and fearful') combined with 하다.
죄송하다.notes: Standard polite expression for 'I am sorry' toward guests, strangers, and elders; casual speech prefers native 미안하다.

cognates.meaning: sense of guilt, feeling of culpability

죄책감.etymology: Sino-Korean three-morpheme compound noun from 罪責感, formed by suffixing 感 (감, 'feeling, sense, emotion') to 죄책 (罪責, 'blame and responsibility for an offense', composed of 罪 죄 'sin, crime, fault' + 責 책 'duty, responsibility, reprove'). Denotes the internal psychological feeling of guilt, self-reproach, or remorse over a real or perceived wrongdoing.

history.meaning: culpability and reproof for an offense
sense of guilt, feeling of remorse or self-reproach

죄책감.notes: Typically collocates with 느끼다 (죄책감을 느끼다, 'to feel guilt') or 시달리다 (죄책감에 시달리다, 'to be tormented by guilt'); it refers strictly to emotional remorse, whereas 유죄 (有罪) means legal 'guilt' in court.

rootFamily.gloss: guilt consciousness, sense of sin (罪意識)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 죄책감

주.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 주 (週, 'week, seven-day cycle'); also represents Sino-Korean 주 (州, 'state, province'), 주 (株, 'share of stock'), and 주 (主, 'master, main').

history.form: 週 / 州 / 株 / 主 (주)
history.meaning: week / province, state / stock share / master, main
week; state/province; stock share; main

cognates.meaning: during the week, span of a week

주간.etymology: Sino-Korean temporal noun from 週間, composed of 週 (주, 'week, cycle, revolve, return in a circle') and 間 (간, 'interval, span, period'). When the Western seven-day week was introduced to East Asia in the late 19th century, 週 ('cycle of seven days') was combined with 間 ('duration/interval', compare Japanese 週間 shūkan) to express a span of weeks (e.g., 2주간 'for a two-week span') or a weekly observance period.

history.meaning: duration of a week or number of weeks; weekly period
span of weeks, weekly period, weeklong duration

주간.notes: Watch out for two common Sino-Korean homophones: 주간 (晝間, 'daytime, day shift', contrasting with 야간 'nighttime') and 주간 (週刊, 'weekly publication', as in 주간지 'weekly magazine'). When counting a span of weeks (예: 3주간), the Hanja are 週間.

rootFamily.gloss: weekly magazine (週刊誌, sharing 週)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 주간

주거.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주거 (住居), formed from Hanja 住 (머무를 주, 'to halt, stay, reside') and 居 (살 거, 'to dwell, sit, occupy a place'). Both characters originally depicted physical posture and stationary presence in Classical Chinese before coalescing into a formal legal and administrative term for human habitation and housing.

history.meaning: to dwell and reside in a fixed place
dwelling, residence, housing

주거.notes: Used primarily in formal, legal, and real-estate contexts (such as 주거 환경 'living environment' or 주거 침입 'trespassing/breaking and entering'), whereas 집 is used in everyday speech for 'home'.

주기.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 주기 (週期), composed of Hanja 週 (돌 주, 'to revolve, cycle, week') and 期 (기약할 기, 'appointed time, period, phase'). Adopted into modern Korean scientific and general vocabulary alongside Meiji-era Japanese 週期 (shūki) to denote a regularly recurring interval of time or broadcast schedule.

history.meaning: recurring revolution or appointed time interval
cycle, period, regular interval

주기.notes: Frequently expanded with -적 (的) to form 주기적 ('periodic, cyclical') or 주기적으로 ('periodically, at regular intervals'). Do not confuse with homophones like 수기 (handwriting) or 주의 (caution).

주나.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean verb 주다 ('to give', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 주다) combined with the verbal suffix -나, which functions either as an intimate/monologic interrogative ending ('does one give?') or as an auxiliary/concessive connective expressing doubt or rhetorical skepticism ('as if they would give').

history.meaning: to give, bestow, hand over
does one give?; whether one gives; seems to give/do for

morphemes.meaning: to give, bestow (Also auxiliary: to do as a favor)

주나.notes: When attached after another verb in -아/어 주다 (e.g., 알아주나 'do they even appreciate it?'), 주- acts as a benefactive auxiliary meaning 'to do something for someone'.

주년.etymology: Sino-Korean bound counter noun 周年, combining 周 (두루 주, 'a complete circuit or cycle') with 年 (해 년, 'year'). Placed directly after Sino-Korean numerals (일 주년, 십 주년, 삼십 주년), it marks how many full annual cycles have elapsed since a founding, wedding, or historic event.
주년.notes: Always preceded by Sino-Korean numbers (십 주년, 삼십 주년), never native numbers.

주다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 주다 ('to give, hand over, bestow'), also widely used as a benefactive auxiliary verb (-아/어 주다).

history.meaning: to give, grant
to give; to do something for someone (auxiliary)

주로.etymology: Hybrid adverb lexicalized from Sino-Korean 주 (主, 'main, chief, principal part') + the native Korean instrumental particle -로 ('by way of, as').

history.meaning: mainly, mostly, chiefly, for the most part

주말.etymology: Sino-Korean 주말 (週末), compounding 주 (週, 'week') and 말 (末, 'end, close').

history.meaning: end of the week
weekend

주머니.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 주머귀 ('small drawstring pouch, bag, purse'), evolving to modern 주머니.

history.meaning: pouch, drawstring bag
pocket, pouch, small bag

주먹.etymology: Native Korean noun 주먹 ('fist'), directly attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 주먹 (e.g., in the *Hunminjeongeum Haerye* and *Seokbo Sangjeol*). Etymologically analyzed as an ancient nominalization from the native verbal root 쥐- / 줌- ('to clench, grasp in the hand', cf. 쥐다 'to grasp' and 줌 'handful') plus the archaic Korean nominalizing suffix -억.

history.meaning: clenched hand, fist
fist; metaphorically brute force or a tough guy nickname

주먹.notes: In Korean dramas and variety shows, 주먹 means both a literal 'fist' (and 'rock' in rock-paper-scissors, 주먹 가위 보) and figuratively 'brute force' or a gangster/brawler nickname.

rootFamily.gloss: to clench, grasp in the hand

주무세요.etymology: Polite honorific imperative/declarative form of the native Korean suppletive honorific verb 주무시다 ('to sleep', used of elders or respected persons). Attested in Early Modern Korean as 줌시다, which evolved through lexicalized honorification from the native root 자- ('to sleep', Middle Korean 자다) via nominal/causative-honorific stem enlargement before taking the polite sentence ending -세요 (-시- + -어요).

history.meaning: to sleep (plain / honorific)
to sleep (honorific); please sleep well / good night

주무세요.notes: Korean requires suppletive honorific verbs for elders: instead of adding -시- to 자다 (*자시다 is archaic/dialectal for eating), speakers must use 주무시다, making 안녕히 주무세요 the standard polite 'Good night'.

주무시다.etymology: Native Korean honorific verb ('to sleep') descending from Middle Korean 주무시다, historically formed with the honorific suffix -시-.

history.meaning: to sleep (honorific)
to sleep, go to bed (honorific of 자다)

주문하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 주문 (注文, 'placing an order for goods or food, request', from 注 'fix upon, note down' + 文 'writing, text') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: order for goods, custom request
to order (food, goods), place an order

주민.etymology: Sino-Korean 주민 (住民), compounding 주 (住, 'dwell, reside, live') and 민 (民, 'people, inhabitants').

history.meaning: dwelling people, inhabitants
resident, local inhabitant

주방.etymology: Sino-Korean 주방 (廚房), compounding 주 (廚, 'kitchen, cookhouse') and 방 (房, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: cooking room, kitchen
kitchen

주범.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주범 (主犯), formed from Hanja 主 (으뜸 주 / 주인 주, 'chief, principal, master') and 犯 (범할 범, 'to violate, offend, criminal'). Originally a legal term in East Asian penal codes distinguishing the principal perpetrator of a crime from an accomplice (공범 共犯), it is widely used figuratively in everyday Korean for the 'main culprit' behind any mishap.

history.meaning: principal perpetrator in a criminal offense
main culprit, primary cause, ringleader

주범.notes: Often used humorously or hyperbolically in conversation and TV variety shows (e.g., 시청률 하락의 주범 'the main culprit behind falling ratings') as well as in serious crime reporting.

주변.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주변 (周邊), composed of Hanja 周 (두루 주, 'circumference, all around, circuit') and 邊 (가 변, 'edge, margin, border, side'). From its literal geometric sense of the perimeter or outer edge of an area, it broadened in Korean to denote both physical surroundings ('the neighborhood around a place') and social circles ('the people around oneself').

history.meaning: outer perimeter, border circumference
surroundings, vicinity; people in one's immediate circle

주변.notes: In Korean, 주변 commonly modifies human relationships (주변 사람들 'people around me; friends and acquaintances') just as naturally as physical locations (역 주변 'around the station').

주사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주사 (酒邪), formed from Hanja 酒 (술 주, 'alcohol, liquor') and 邪 (간사할 사, 'perverse, awry, demonic, erratic'). Literally meaning 'alcohol-induced perversity or erratic spirit', it was coined in traditional Korean Sinographic usage to describe a person's habitual misbehavior, antics, or personality changes when intoxicated.

history.meaning: erratic or perverse behavior caused by liquor
bad drinking habit, drunken antics

주사.notes: A classic Korean homophone trap: 주사 (酒邪) means 'drunken habit/antics' (used in 주사를 부리다 'to act out when drunk'), whereas 주사 (注射) means a medical 'injection/shot'. Native Korean 술버릇 is a pure synonym for drinking habit.

sources.title: Standard Korean Language Dictionary: 주사 (酒邪)

주소.etymology: Sino-Korean 주소 (住所), compounding 주 (住, 'dwell, reside') and 소 (所, 'place, location').

history.meaning: place of residence
address, residence

주소지.etymology: Sino-Korean tri-morphemic compound 주소지 (住所地), combining 주소 (住所, 'address, domicile', from 住 머무를 주 'reside' + 所 바 소 'place') with the locative suffix Hanja 地 (땅 지, 'land, spot, location'). Used in administrative, postal, and legal registers to specify the physical location corresponding to a person's registered residential address.

history.meaning: place where one resides, dwelling place
registered home address location, domicile

주소지.notes: While 주소 (住所) can mean an email or web address as well as a street address, adding -지 (地) restricts 주소지 strictly to a physical geographic domicile or mailing location.

주스.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English juice ('liquid pressed from fruit or vegetables').

history.meaning: fruit or vegetable juice
juice

주식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주식 (株式), borrowed via Meiji-era Japanese 株式 (kabushiki, 'stock, company shares'), composed of Hanja 株 (그루 주, 'tree stump, counter for shares/guild franchises') and 式 (법 식, 'system, form, style'). In Edo-period Japan, guild licenses were called 株 (kabu, literally a 'stump/root' that stays in place and yields offshoots), which Meiji economists adapted with 式 to translate Western joint-stock equity.

history.meaning: merchant guild share -> modern corporate stock system
corporate stock, shares, equity

morphemes.meaning: tree stump, share of stock (그루 주)

주식.notes: Distinguish between the two common Sino-Korean homophones written 주식: 株式 ('financial stock/shares', as in 주식 시장 'stock market') and 主食 ('staple food', such as rice).

주어지다.etymology: Native Korean syntactic passive verb 주어지다 ('to be given, to be granted, to be assigned'), formed from the transitive verb stem 주- ('to give', Middle Korean 주다) linked by the infinitive/connective suffix -어 to the inchoative/passive auxiliary verb 지다 ('to become, come to be', from Middle Korean 지다 'to fall/become'). It grammaticalized in modern Korean to express roles, conditions, or opportunities bestowed upon someone.

history.meaning: to give + to fall/become (independent verbs)
to be given, granted, endowed, or assigned

주어지다.notes: Very common in adnominal modifier form 주어진 (e.g., 주어진 시간 'the allotted/given time', 주어진 역할 'the assigned role'). In fast speech it often contracts to 줘지다, though 주어지다 is preferred in writing.

주인.etymology: Sino-Korean 주인 (主人), compounding 주 (主, 'master, owner, host') and 인 (人, 'person').

history.meaning: master of the house, host, owner
owner, proprietor, landlord, host

주인공.etymology: Sino-Korean 주인공 (主人公), formed from 주인 (主人, 'master, host') + 공 (公, honorific title 'lord, respected figure'), originally a Zen Buddhist term for one's true inner master and in modern Korean 'main character, protagonist'.

history.meaning: true inner master; central figure
protagonist, hero/heroine, main character

주인이.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 주인 (主人, 'owner, master, proprietor, landlord, host') inflected with the native Korean nominative (subject) case particle -이. The noun 主人 is an ancient Classical Chinese compound of 主 (주인 주, 'master, host, originally a lamp flame') and 人 (사람 인, 'person'), attested in Korean since the Three Kingdoms and Middle Korean periods.

history.meaning: host of a house, master, ruler
the owner / landlord / proprietor (as grammatical subject)

morphemes.meaning: nominative (subject) case marker after a consonant

주인이.notes: In Korean housing and commerce, 주인 often means 'landlord' (집주인) or 'shop owner' (가게 주인). Adding -님 creates the polite title 주인님 or 주인장.

주전자.etymology: Sino-Korean 주전자 (酒煎子), compounding 주 (酒, 'wine, liquor'), 전 (煎, 'boil, heat, decoct'), and 자 (子, utensil suffix), originally naming a spouted metal pot for warming wine and later generalized to any kettle or teapot.

history.meaning: spouted vessel for heating wine
kettle, teapot

주제.etymology: In the colloquial sense 'one's humble station, lot, or pathetic appearance' (used with -에 as 주제에 'for someone in your position!'), 주제 derives from Early Modern Korean 조제/주제 ('personal bearing, circumstance, lot'), of native or obscured Sino-Korean origin. It is homophonous with Sino-Korean 주제 (主題: 主 으뜸 주 'main' + 題 제목 제 'topic, heading', meaning 'theme/subject'), and speakers frequently play on both words.

history.meaning: one's personal bearing, outward appearance, or social lot
one's station/position (pejorative, as in 주제에); also homophone 主題 (theme)

morphemes.meaning: one's lot, humble position, or outward bearing (pejorative)

주제.notes: When followed by -에 (e.g., 내 주제에 무슨... 'how could someone in my position...' or 네 주제에 'who do you think you are'), 주제 is strongly self-deprecating or disparaging; the phrase 주제를 알다 means 'to know one's place'.

rootFamily.gloss: main theme, subject, motif (homophone 主題)

주지.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean verb 주다 ('to give, bestow', Middle Korean 주다) combined with the suffix -지. Depending on syntactic position, -지 functions either as the long-form negation complementizer before 않다/못하다/말다 (derived from Middle Korean nominalizer -디, e.g., 주지 않다 'does not give') or as an intimate sentence-final ending expressing supposition, reassurance, or retrospective confirmation ('could have given / of course one gives').

history.meaning: giving (nominalized complement before negation)
doesn't give (with negation) / could give, of course gives (sentence-final)

morphemes.meaning: negative complementizer or committal/suppositional ending (from MK -디)

주지.notes: Do not confuse the verb form 주지 (from 주다 'to give') with the Sino-Korean noun 주지 (住持, 'chief abbot of a Buddhist temple') or 주지 (周知, 'common knowledge').

cognates.meaning: to park a vehicle, stop a car

주차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주차 (駐車), composed of Hanja 駐 (머무를 주, 'to halt a horse or carriage, station, stay temporarily', with the horse radical 馬) and 車 (수레 차, 'wheeled vehicle, carriage, car'). Originally referring in Classical Chinese to halting an imperial or military carriage, it was repurposed in modern East Asian vocabulary to denote parking an automobile.

history.meaning: to halt a horse-drawn carriage or military chariot
parking a motor vehicle

morphemes.meaning: to halt a horse/carriage, station, park (머무를 주)

주차.notes: Notice how Korean distinguishes stopping a car briefly (정차 停車, 'stopping/standing') from parking and leaving it (주차 駐車, 'parking'), often combined on street signs as 주정차 금지 ('No Parking or Stopping').

주차료.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 주차료 (駐車料), formed by suffixing Hanja 料 (헤아릴 료, 'to measure grain, material, fee, charge') to 주차 (駐車, 'parking': 駐 머무를 주 'halt/station' + 車 수레 차 'vehicle'). The suffix -료 (料) productively forms nouns denoting service fees or admission charges across modern Korean and Japanese administrative vocabulary.

history.meaning: vehicle parking + measured fee/charge
parking fee, car-park charge

morphemes.meaning: to halt a carriage, station, park (머무를 주)

주차료.notes: Because 料 (료) follows a vowel (차), the initial liquid is pronounced as 'r' (주차료 [jucharyo]) rather than shifting to 'n' as it does after consonants (e.g., 관람료 [gwallamnyo] 'admission fee'). Often interchangeable with 주차비 (駐車費).

주차장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 주차장 (駐車場), combining 주차 (駐車, 'parking': 駐 머무를 주 'to halt/station a carriage' + 車 수레 차 'vehicle') with the locative noun suffix 場 (마당 장, 'open ground, courtyard, site, arena'). Literally 'a ground for stationing vehicles', it is the universal Korean term for an outdoor parking lot or indoor parking garage.

history.meaning: designated ground for stationing vehicles
parking lot, parking garage, car park

morphemes.meaning: open ground, lot, site, venue (마당 장)

주차장.notes: Korean television stations and apartment complexes rely heavily on underground parking garages, known as 지하 주차장 (地下駐車場), a staple setting for dramatic conversations in K-dramas like *The Producers*.

주차하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verbal compound 주차하다 (駐車하다), formed from the Sino-Korean action noun 주차 (駐車, 'parking': 駐 머무를 주 'to halt/station' + 車 수레 차 'vehicle, car') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do, make', Middle Korean 하야/하다).lobbing action nouns into predicates via -하다 is the primary mechanism for verbalizing Sino-Korean nouns.

history.meaning: to perform the action of stationing/parking a vehicle

morphemes.meaning: to halt a carriage, station, park (머무를 주)

주차하다.notes: In everyday speech, speakers frequently separate the noun and verb with the object particle (주차를 하다) or use the native phrase 차를 대다 ('to pull a car up / park a car') in casual conversation.

주책.etymology: Derived via umbilical vowel fronting (umlaut: a -> ae) from Sino-Korean 주착 (主着), composed of Hanja 主 (주인 주, 'master, main principle') and 着 (붙을 착, 'to adhere, settle, fix'). Originally, 주착 meant 'a firm, settled mind or consistent principle'. Because it was overwhelmingly used in negative expressions like 주책없다 ('lacking a settled mind -> scatterbrained, tactless, meddlesome'), the noun 주책 itself underwent semantic contagion (enantiosemy) to mean 'meddlesome, silly, or inappropriate behavior'.

history.meaning: a firm, settled principle or composure of mind
fixed sense (in 주책없다) -> tactless, meddlesome, or silly behavior (in 주책이다 / 주책을 떨다)

morphemes.meaning: to adhere, settle, fix (붙을 착 -> fronted to 책)

주책.notes: A fascinating case of Korean auto-antonymy: because 주책 ursprünglich meant 'good sense', both 주책없다 ('lacking sense') and 주책이다 ('being silly/meddlesome') mean almost the same negative thing in modern Korean!

죽다.etymology: Core native Korean verb 죽다 ('to die, pass away, perish, stop functioning'), directly inherited from 15th-century Middle Korean 죽다 (attested in *Worin Seokbo*, *Seokbo Sangjeol*, etc.) and Old Korean. In addition to biological death, it developed rich metaphorical extensions in Korean for extinguished fire/spirit, flat batteries or clocks, and extreme hyperbolic intensity ('to die of exhaustion/cuteness/laughter').

history.meaning: to die, perish, lose life
to die; to stop working; (hyperbolic) to be extremely tired/hungry/etc.

죽다.notes: Extremely frequent in colloquial hyperbole: 배고파 죽겠다 ('I'm starving to death'), 좋아 죽다 ('to be head over heels / dying of happiness'). For respected elders, the honorific 돌아가시다 ('to pass away') replaces 죽다.

rootFamily.gloss: to kill, murder; (slang) to be awesome
to kill off completely, finish off

죽여버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound transitive verb 죽여버리다 ('to kill off completely, to finish someone off'), formed from 죽여 (the infinitive/connective form of 죽이다 'to kill', itself the morphological causative of 죽다 'to die' + -어) and the telic/completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to throw away, discard, finish completely', Middle Korean 버리다). Combining a transitive verb with -어 버리다 adds strong emotional finality, relief, or ruthless completion.

history.meaning: to cause to die + to throw away/discard
to kill off completely, finish off, wipe out

morphemes.meaning: causative marker ('to cause to die -> kill') + infinitive -어 -> -여
completive auxiliary ('completely, once and for all', literally 'throw away')

죽여버리다.notes: In Korean TV dramas and everyday banter, 죽여버린다 ('I'll finish you off!') is frequently used as an exaggerated threat among close friends or frustrated coworkers rather than literal violence.

rootFamily.gloss: to kill, put to death; to axe a program
to throw away, discard; to do completely

죽이다.etymology: Native Korean morphological causative verb 죽이다 ('to kill, to put to death, to murder; to suppress or axe'), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 죽이다 (and phonetically spelled 주기다). Derived directly from the intransitive verb stem 죽- ('to die') plus the productive Korean causative suffix -이- ('to cause to') and the citation ending -다. In broadcasting and colloquial slang, it extended to mean 'to axe/cancel a program', 'to mute/dim', or 'to be killer/awesome'.

history.meaning: to cause to die, to kill, to slay
to kill; to hold one's breath (숨을 죽이다); to axe/scrap a show; (slang) to be fantastic

죽이다.notes: Beyond 'to kill', 죽이다 has two vital idiomatic uses: in broadcasting/office jargon, 프로그램을 죽이다 means 'to axe/cancel a show' (opposite of 살리다 'to save/bring alive'); in slang, 죽인다! means 'That's killer / awesome!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to kill off completely, finish off

준모.etymology: Sino-Korean masculine given name 준모 (Joon-mo), notably borne by Ra Joon-mo (라준모, played by Cha Tae-hyun), the veteran variety-show PD in *The Producers* (*프로듀사*). Follows the classic two-syllable Korean anthroponymic pattern combining Sino-Korean generational and virtue characters, typically 俊 (준걸 준, 'talented, outstanding person') or 準 (법도 준, 'standard, criterion') with 模 (법 모, 'model, exemplar') or 謨 (꾀 모, 'plan, wise counsel').

history.form: 俊模 / 準模 (Sino-Korean Personal Name)
history.meaning: outstanding model / exemplar of talent (traditional two-Hanja naming structure)
male given name (Ra Joon-mo in KBS drama The Producers)

morphemes.meaning: talented, eminent (俊 준걸 준) or standard (準 법도 준)
model, exemplar (模 법 모) or counsel (謨 꾀 모)

준모.notes: When addressing or referring to a peer or junior by given name in Korean, a consonant-final name like 준모 takes the vocative particle -야 (준모야!) or the polite suffix -씨 (준모 씨), and in workplace settings a title like 준모 피디 (PD Joon-mo).

준비.etymology: Sino-Korean 준비 (準備), compounding 준 (準, 'level, standard, prepare') and 비 (備, 'prepare, provide, equip').

history.meaning: preparation, readiness
preparation, arrangements

준비되다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 준비 (準備, 'preparation') + the native passive/inchoative verb 되다 ('to become, be made').

history.meaning: to be prepared, get ready

준비하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 준비 (準備, 'preparation') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to prepare, get ready

준호.etymology: Korean masculine given name of Sino-Korean origin, typically written with hanja combinations such as 俊浩 or 準鎬 (compounding 준 俊 'talented, outstanding' or 準 'standard, level' with 호 浩 'vast, grand' or 鎬 'bright, shining').

history.meaning: Korean masculine given name (Jun-ho)

줄.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 줄 ('cord, rope, string, line, row').

history.meaning: cord, rope, line
rope, string, cord, line, queue; bound noun for ability/fact ('how to, that')

줄기.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 줄기 ('plant stem, stalk, trunk; mountain ridge or stream'), derived from 줄 ('line, cord').

history.meaning: stem, stalk, continuous line or stream
stem, stalk, trunk; stream, ray, main thread

줄이다.etymology: Native Korean morphological causative verb 줄이다 ('to reduce, decrease, shorten, shrink, turn down volume'), formed from the intransitive verb stem 줄- ('to decrease, shrink, diminish', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 줄다) plus the productive transitive/causative suffix -이- and ending -다. Attested in Middle and Early Modern Korean as 주리다 / 줄이다.

history.meaning: to shrink/diminish (intransitive) -> to cause to shrink or decrease (transitive)
to reduce, cut down, abbreviate, turn down (volume/speed)

줄이다.notes: Carefully distinguish transitive 줄이다 ('to reduce something / turn down the volume', e.g., 소리를 줄이다) from intransitive 줄다 or 줄어들다 ('to shrink or decrease on its own'), and from homophonous 굶주리다/주리다 ('to starve').

줄자.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 줄 ('string, cord, flexible strip') + 자 ('ruler, measuring rod', Middle Korean 자).

history.meaning: tape measure

줄줄이.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb 줄줄이 ('in a continuous row, one after another, in strings'), formed by reduplicating the native noun 줄 ('rope, cord, line, row', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 줄) into 줄줄 and adding the productive adverb-forming suffix -이. The reduplication iconically mirrors a series of items linked or emerging in an unbroken sequence.

history.meaning: cord, rope, line, row
in a continuous line, one after another, in succession

morphemes.meaning: plural/continuous sequence of lines or rows
in the manner of, one by one

줄줄이.notes: Used both for physical items strung together (like 줄줄이 소시지 'Vienna sausages linked in a chain') and for events happening in rapid succession (예능 프로그램이 줄줄이 결방되다 'variety shows are canceled one after another').

rootFamily.gloss: flowing or reciting smoothly and continuously (adverb)

줍다.etymology: Native Korean verb 줍다 ('to pick up from the ground, glean, gather, find a lost item'), descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 쥽다 (with a voiced bilabial fricative ㅸ before vowel-initial endings, e.g., 주워 < 쥬워). This historical intervocalic lenition of *p > *β > w explains why 줍다 is a classic ㅂ-irregular verb (ㅂ 불규칙 동사) in modern Korean, conjugating as 주워, 주우니, 주워서 rather than *줍어.

history.meaning: to pick up, gather from the ground, glean
to pick up, gather, find (something dropped or lost)

morphemes.meaning: to pick up, glean, gather (ㅂ-irregular stem: 줍- ~ 주우-)

줍다.notes: Watch out for the ㅂ-irregular conjugation and false friends: 줍다 ('to pick up') conjugates as 주워 / 주워서, whereas the adjective 춥다 ('to be cold') conjugates as 추워, and 좁다 ('to be narrow') is regular (좁아).

rootFamily.gloss: to pick up and eat (slang 줄임말: 줍줍)
gathering, gleaning (e.g., 이삭줍기 'gleaning ears of grain')
to take care of, gather together, pack

중.etymology: Sino-Korean bound/dependent noun 중 (中, 가운데 중), derived from the ancient Chinese pictograph 中 depicting a flagpole or target drum pierced right through the center. Borrowed into Korean with two primary grammaticalized functions: a partitive sense ('among, out of a group') and a progressive/temporal sense ('in the middle of, during, currently under way').

history.meaning: center, middle, inside; midway through
middle; among (out of); during / in the middle of doing something

morphemes.meaning: middle, center; among; in the process of (가운데 중)

중.notes: After an action noun or a verb in -는, 중 expresses an ongoing action (회의 중 'in a meeting', 촬영 중 'filming in progress', 생각하는 중 'in the middle of thinking'). Also has a native Korean homophone 중 meaning 'Buddhist monk'.

rootFamily.gloss: on the way, in the middle of an action

중간.etymology: Sino-Korean 중간 (中間), compounding 중 (中, 'middle, center') and 간 (間, 'space, interval, between').

history.meaning: space in between, middle
middle, center, midway

중국어.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 중국어 (中國語), composed of 중국 (中國, 'China', literally 'Central State/Middle Kingdom': 中 가운데 중 'center' + 國 나라 국 'country, state') and the bound Hanja suffix -어 (語, 말씀 어, 'language, speech, tongue'). Literally 'the language of the Central State', it is the standard modern Korean designation for the Chinese language.

history.meaning: Central State (China) + language/speech
the Chinese language (especially Standard Mandarin)

중국어.notes: In Korean, adding -어 (語) to a country name regularly forms the language name: 한국어 (Korean), 일본어 (Japanese), 중국어 (Chinese). Classical/literary Chinese written in Hanja is called 한문 (漢文) rather than 중국어.

중국집.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun 중국집 (中國집), combining Sino-Korean 중국 (中國, 'China': 中 가운데 중 'center' + 國 나라 국 'country') with the native Korean noun 집 ('house, home, shop, restaurant', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 집). In Korean word formation, attaching 집 to a food or cuisine type productively denotes a restaurant specializing in that fare.

history.meaning: China + house/establishment
Chinese restaurant (specifically Korean-Chinese cuisine restaurant)

중국집.notes: In Korea, a 중국집 serves distinctive Korean-Chinese cuisine (중화요리)—famous for 짜장면 (black-bean noodles), 짬뽕 (spicy seafood noodle soup), and 탕수육 (sweet-and-sour pork)—and is iconic in K-dramas for fast delivery straight to TV editing rooms and offices.

중독.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 중독 (中毒), formed from Hanja 中 (맞을 중, here in its classical verbal reading 'to be hit by, struck by, afflicted with'—corresponding to Mandarin falling-tone zhòng—rather than 'center') and 毒 (독 독, 'poison, toxin, venom'). Originally a Classical Chinese medical term meaning 'to be struck by poison / food or chemical poisoning', it expanded in modern Korean and Japanese to encompass psychological or physiological 'addiction'.

history.meaning: to be struck or afflicted by poison/toxin
medical poisoning (food/gas); psychological or substance addiction

morphemes.meaning: to be hit by, struck by, afflicted with (맞을 중)

중독.notes: Covers both medical 'poisoning' (식중독 'food poisoning', 일산화탄소 중독 'carbon monoxide poisoning') and behavioral/substance 'addiction' (알코올 중독 'alcoholism', 일 중독 'workaholism', 스마트폰 중독 'smartphone addiction').

중딩.etymology: Late 20th-century South Korean youth and internet slang clipping of the Sino-Korean compound 중학생 (中學生, 'middle-school student'), formed by combining the initial syllable 중 (中, 'middle') with the playful slang suffix -딩 (derived by phonological alteration of -생 [生, 'student'] in 1990s PC communication networks alongside 초딩 and 고딩).

history.meaning: middle school student
middle-schooler (colloquial/slang)

morphemes.meaning: colloquial slang suffix denoting a student or member of a group

중딩.notes: Belongs to the productive '-딩' age-group slang series: 초딩 (elementary schooler), 중딩 (middle schooler), 고딩 (high schooler), 대딩 (college student), and 직딩 (office worker). Can sound slightly dismissive or immature when applied to adults ('acting like a middle-schooler').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary) – 중딩

중심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 중심 (中心), composed of 중 (中, 'middle, interior, center') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind, core'). Literally 'the heart at the center,' attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and literary texts and used across East Asia for both spatial centers and the focal pivot of an organization or narrative.

history.meaning: the inner heart or mind; central core
physical center; focal point, core, or balance

중심.notes: Used both concretely in 중심을 잡다 ('to keep one's physical balance') and abstractly as a suffix-like modifier in 자기중심적 ('self-centered') or 인물 중심 ('character-driven').

중요하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 중요 (重要, 'importance, weightiness', compounding 重 'heavy, weighty' and 要 'essential, vital') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: weighty and essential, important
to be important, significant, essential

cognates.meaning: middle school student, junior high school student
cognates.word: 中学生 (ちゅうがくせい, chūgakusei)

중학생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 중학생 (中學生), combining 중학 (中學, 'middle school,' from 中 'middle' + 學 'learning, school') and the agentive noun suffix 생 (生, 'student, scholar, person born'). Adopted during late 19th- and early 20th-century educational modernization alongside Japanese chūgakusei (中学生) to denote a student in lower secondary education.

history.meaning: student of a modern secondary/middle school
middle-schooler, junior high school student (grades 7–9)

중학생.notes: In South Korea's 6-3-3-4 school system, a 중학생 attends three years of middle school (중학교, roughly ages 13–15). In casual speech, it is frequently shortened to the slang form 중딩.

줘버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction contracted from 주어 버리다, combining the transitive verb 주다 ('to give,' Middle Korean 주다) + infinitive connective -어 + the completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to throw away, discard; to do completely,' Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다). The auxiliary 버리다 grammaticalized from physical disposal into an aspectual marker indicating an irreversible, complete, and often rash or regrettable action.

history.meaning: to give away and cast off completely
to give away completely (often rashly or for good)

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective ending (contracted with 주- to 줘)
completive auxiliary verb ('completely, away, for good')

줘버리다.notes: Adding -어 버리다 to 주다 emphasizes finality and emotional attitude—either relief at getting rid of something ('just hand it over and be done with it') or frustration that someone gave something away rashly.

줘보다.etymology: Native Korean serial/auxiliary verb construction contracted from 주어 보다, combining 주다 ('to give,' Middle Korean 주다) + infinitive connective -어 + the auxiliary/main verb 보다 ('to see, look; to try doing,' Middle Korean 보다). Literally 'try giving [it to me]' or 'give [it] so I can see,' used constantly in spoken Korean to ask someone to hand an object over for inspection.

history.meaning: to try giving; to give and see
to try giving; (imperative 줘 봐) hand it over and let me see

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective ending (contracted with 주- to 줘)
experiential/tentative auxiliary verb ('to try doing; to see')

줘보다.notes: In imperative forms like 줘 봐 ('let me have a look / hand it here'), the auxiliary 보다 softens a blunt command (줘! 'Give it!') into a tentative request ('try giving it to me for a moment').

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look; to try doing

쥐.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어), attested in the very first Hangul promulgation text, the 15th-century Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446), as 쥐 (jwi, 'mouse, rat'). A core monosyllabic native Korean zoological term that encompasses both mice and rats without lexical distinction unless specified by a modifier (such as 생쥐 'mouse' or 시궁쥐 'sewer rat').

history.meaning: mouse, rat (translating Chinese 鼠)
mouse, rat; muscle cramp (by metaphor of a mouse crawling under the skin)

쥐.notes: Besides the rodent, 쥐가 나다 ('a mouse comes out') is the standard Korean idiom for getting a muscle cramp or pins and needles (compare Latin musculus 'little mouse' -> 'muscle'). Also appears in numerous proverbs like 쥐구멍에도 볕 들 날 있다 ('even a mouse hole gets sunshine someday').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 쥐

쥐다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 쥐다 (jwida, 'to grasp in the hand, clench the fist'). From the concrete physical action of closing one's fingers tightly around an object, the verb extended metaphorically to holding authority (권력을 쥐다), secrets, or a person's weakness in one's grasp.

history.meaning: to grasp in the hand, clench
to grip, hold tightly; to hold power or control over

morphemes.meaning: to grip, grasp, clench in the hand

쥐다.notes: Contrast 쥐다 ('to grip/clench inside the palm or fist,' e.g., 손을 쥐다 'clench one's fist') with 잡다 ('to catch, grab, or hold' more generally) and 들다 ('to lift/carry in the hand').

rootFamily.gloss: to place into someone's hand (causative compound)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 쥐다

즉.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb Derived from Classical Chinese 즉 (卽 / 即, 'to approach; thereupon; namely, that is to say'). In oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, 卽 depicted a kneeling person (卩) approaching a food vessel (皀) to eat; from 'to come right up to,' it grammaticalized in Classical Chinese into an immediacy marker ('at once') and a logical equative connective ('namely, in other words').
