history.meaning: to approach food; thereupon; namely, that is to say
namely, in other words, that is to say

즉.notes: Functions as a crisp, slightly formal discourse marker equivalent to English 'i.e.', 'namely', or 'in other words'—its native Korean conversational counterpart is 곧.

즐겁다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 즐겁다 ('to be joyful, happy, pleasant'), derived from the verb stem 즐기- ('to enjoy, take pleasure in') + the adjectival suffix -업-.

history.meaning: to be joyful, delightful
to be pleasant, joyful, enjoyable, happy

즐기다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 즐기다 (jeulgida, 'to rejoice in, take pleasure in, enjoy'). Derived from the same native Korean root *즐- ('joy, pleasure') that produced the descriptive verb 즐겁다 (Middle Korean 즐겁다, 'to be joyful, pleasant').

history.meaning: to rejoice, delight in, enjoy
to enjoy, take pleasure in, savor

morphemes.meaning: to enjoy, take pleasure in (from root *즐- 'joy')

즐기다.notes: Keep the transitivity pair straight: 즐겁다 is an intransitive adjective ('to be enjoyable/pleasant,' e.g., 시간이 즐겁다), whereas 즐기다 is an active transitive verb taking -을/를 ('to enjoy something,' e.g., 시간을 즐기다). The participle 즐겨 ('enjoyingly -> frequently/fondly') forms 즐겨찾기 ('browser bookmarks/favorites').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 즐기다

증명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 증명 (證明), combining 증 (證, 'to testify, verify, evidence') and 명 (明, 'bright, clear; to clarify'). Literally 'making clear through testimony or evidence,' attested in Classical Chinese legal and Buddhist logical treatises before becoming the standard modern East Asian term for logical, scientific, and administrative proof.

history.meaning: to clarify or substantiate through testimony; Buddhist logical verification
proof, verification, official certification

증명.notes: Used both for abstract logical/scientific proof (수학적 증명, 'mathematical proof') and concrete administrative documents or notices (재직 증명, 'proof of employment'; 내용 증명, 'certified-contents legal notice').

cognates.word: 証明する (しょうめいする, shōmei suru)

증명하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 증명 (證明, 'proof, verification,' from 證 'testify, evidence' + 明 'make clear') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to perform verification' or 'to make clear by evidence.'

history.meaning: to verify, substantiate, or certify
to prove, demonstrate, certify

증명하다.notes: Can take either a proposition/fact (결백을 증명하다, 'prove one's innocence') or reflexive/personal worth (스스로를 증명하다, 'prove oneself') as its direct object.

증인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 증인 (證人), composed of 증 (證, 'to testify, bear witness, evidence') and 인 (人, 'person'). Literally 'a person who bears witness,' attested in Classical Chinese legal codes and used in Korean law and everyday speech for someone who testifies to the truth of an event.

history.meaning: person who testifies to a transaction or legal dispute
witness (in court, contracts, or everyday situations)

증인.notes: Distinguish 증인 (證人, a 'witness' who vouches for a fact or testifies in court/conversation) from 목격자 (目擊者, an 'eyewitness' who physically saw an accident or crime happen with their own eyes).

지.etymology: Native Korean dependent/bound noun (의존 명사) used after the past/completive adnominal suffix -(으)ㄴ to denote the time elapsed since an action took place ('since doing X'). Historically derived from 15th-century Middle Korean 디 (di, a bound noun meaning 'fact, state, or elapsed interval'), which underwent regular Early Modern Korean palatalization of ㄷ > ㅈ before the high front vowel ㅣ (디 > 지).

history.meaning: bound noun indicating an abstract fact, state, or time interval
bound noun indicating time elapsed since an event ('since')

morphemes.meaning: bound noun indicating elapsed time since an action occurred

지.notes: Orthography trap: when 지 means 'since' (elapsed time, e.g., 만난 지 3년 'three years since we met'), it is a bound noun and MUST be written with a space after -(으)ㄴ. When -는지/-은지 expresses an indirect question ('whether/what,' e.g., 얼마인지 모르겠다), it is part of the verbal ending and is written WITHOUT a space.

rootFamily.gloss: indirect question ending ('whether/what,' from the same historical 디)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지 (bound noun)

지각하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'being late for an appointed time, tardiness', compounding 遲 'slow, late' and 刻 'appointed time, moment') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: arriving past the appointed time, tardiness
to be late (for school, work, or an appointment)

지갑.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 紙匣, formed from 紙 (종이 지, 'paper, banknotes') and 匣 (갑 갑, 'small hinged box or folding case'). Originally referring to a folded case made of oiled paper or leather for carrying paper notes and calling cards, 지갑 became the standard modern Korean word for any pocket wallet or billfold.
지갑.notes: Commonly collocates with 열다 ('open one's wallet') and 잃어버리다 ('lose one's wallet').

지겹다.etymology: Native Korean irregular ㅂ-stem descriptive verb (형용사), attested in Early Modern Korean as 디겹다 / 지겹다, built on a native root expressing weariness and mental saturation from prolonged repetition. Phonaesthetically and etymologically connected to the native root cluster 지긋- ('wearisomely persistent') and 지치다 ('to grow exhausted').

history.meaning: to be tedious, wearisome, tiresome
to be sick and tired of, fed up with, intolerably tedious

morphemes.meaning: to be tedious, wearisome, sick and tired of (ㅂ-irregular stem)

지겹다.notes: Stronger and more emotionally exasperated than 지루하다 ('boring/dull'): 지루하다 describes a slow movie or lecture, whereas 지겹다 means you have experienced something so many times that you are 'sick and tired of it.' Conjugates as a ㅂ-irregular adjective (지겹다 -> 지겨워, 지겨운).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel sick and tired of (transitive psych-verb)
to be utterly sick to death of (reduplicated emphatic)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지겹다

지금.etymology: Sino-Korean 지금 (只今), compounding 지 (只, 'only, just') and 금 (今, 'now, the present'), attested since Middle Korean for 'right now, the present time'.

history.meaning: just now, the present moment
now, at present

지긋지긋하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated descriptive verb formed by doubling the ideophonic/expressive root 지긋- (denoting heavy, lingering, oppressive persistence) and attaching the native adjective-forming light verb 하다. The full reduplication (첩어, 지긋지긋) dramatically intensifies the feeling of inescapable, drawn-out tedium and revulsion ('sick to death of').

history.meaning: to be oppressively persistent and tiresome
to be utterly sick and tired of, fed up to the teeth with

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic root of heavy, lingering persistence or weariness
reduplicated root intensifying the sense of oppressive repetition

지긋지긋하다.notes: Expresses visceral exhaustion with a recurring nuisance—such as nagging, debt, or an inescapable workplace routine ('I am sick to death of this'). Curiously, the unreduplicated adverb 지긋이 has a calm, positive nuance ('gently and patiently pressing/closing,' as in 눈을 지긋이 감다 'close one's eyes gently').

rootFamily.gloss: to be tired of, fed up with
gently, quietly and patiently (adverb from the same root of steady pressure)
to be disgusted and sick to death of

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지긋지긋하다

지나가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지나다 ('to pass by, cross, elapse') + the directional verb 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to pass by, go past
to pass by, go past, blow over

지나다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 디나다 ('to pass through, cross over, elapse'), with regular early Modern Korean palatalization of initial 디- to 지-.

history.meaning: to pass by, elapse, exceed
to pass, go by, elapse

지나다니다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지나다 ('to pass by') + 다니다 ('to go back and forth, walk around, commute').

history.meaning: to pass by regularly, walk or travel back and forth past a place

지난겨울.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 지난 ('past, last', past adnominal participle of 지나다 'to pass') + 겨울 ('winter', Middle Korean 겨슬 / 겨을).

history.meaning: last winter

지난번.etymology: Hybrid native-Sino Korean compound noun formed from 지난 (the past adnominal modifier form of the native Korean verb 지나다, 'to pass by,' Middle Korean 디나다) + the Sino-Korean bound noun/counter 번 (番, 'turn, time, occasion'). Literally 'the occasion that has passed,' lexicalized as a single compound word for 'last time.'

history.meaning: to pass by + turn/occasion
last time, the previous occasion

지난번.notes: Forms a symmetrical three-way temporal series with 이번 ('this time') and 다음번 ('next time'). Similarly, the prefix-like modifier 지난- combines with time units to form 지난달 ('last month'), 지난주 ('last week'), and 지난밤 ('last night').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지난번

지난봄.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean temporal noun fusing 지난 (past adnominal form of 지나다 'to pass by') with 봄 ('spring', Middle Korean 봄, historically linked to 보다 'to see' as the season of fresh budding). Written without a space in standard Korean orthography alongside 지난여름, 지난가을, and 지난겨울.
지난봄.notes: Written as one solid word (지난봄), unlike 다음 봄 ('next spring').

지난주.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 지난 ('past, last', past adnominal participle of 지나다 'to pass') + Sino-Korean 주 (週, 'week').

history.meaning: last week

지내다.etymology: Native Korean verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 디내다 (dinaeda). Morphologically derived from 디나다 (modern 지나다, 'to pass, cross over') + the causative/transitive suffix -이- (디나- + -이- > 디내다 > 지내다 via regular Early Modern palatalization 디 > 지). From 'to cause time to pass' or 'spend time,' it evolved to mean 'to live, get along, or associate with someone.'

history.meaning: to cause to pass; to spend time, pass one's days, perform a rite
to spend time, live, get along (with someone), fare

morphemes.meaning: to spend time, live, get along (historically 지나- 'pass' + causative -이-)

지내다.notes: A cornerstone of Korean greetings and social life: 잘 지냈어? ('Have you been doing well?') asks how someone has been spending their days, while 친하게 지내다 ('to get along closely') describes maintaining a friendly relationship. Also used for holding ancestral rites (제사를 지내다).

rootFamily.gloss: to pass by, elapse (intransitive base verb)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지내다

지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 디다 (dida, 'to fall down, drop, sink, set; to be defeated'), which became 지다 via regular 17th–18th century palatalization (디 > 지). The competitive sense 'to lose (a game, battle, or argument)' developed metaphorically from physical falling or sinking (as when the sun sets or leaves fall)—the vanquished falls while the victor rises.

history.meaning: to fall down, drop, set (of the sun); to be defeated in battle or contest
to lose, be defeated; to set (of the sun/moon); to wither/fall (of blossoms)

morphemes.meaning: to fall, sink; to be defeated, lose

지다.notes: Korean has three major homophonous verbs 지다: (1) 'to fall / set / lose a contest' (Middle Korean 디다, opposite of 이기다 'to win'); (2) 'to carry on one's back / bear a burden' (Middle Korean 지다, as in 책임을 지다 'take responsibility'); and (3) the passive/inchoative auxiliary -어지다 ('to become').

rootFamily.gloss: to fall, drop down (compound preserving physical 'fall' sense)
to erase (historically the causative 디우다 'cause to fall off')

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지다

지도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 지도 (地圖), composed of 지 (地, 'earth, land, territory') and 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, chart'). Attested across Classical Chinese and Joseon-era Korean cartography—most famously in Kim Jeong-ho's monumental 1861 woodblock map Daedongyeojido (大東輿地圖)—it has been the standard Korean word for a geographical map for centuries. Note that it is homophonous with 지도 (指導, 'guidance, instruction'), distinguished in context by meaning and collocations such as 지도를 그리다 ('to draw a map') or 지도를 보다 ('to read a map').

history.meaning: geographical chart or map of the land
map, geographical chart

지도.notes: Commonly paired with 그리다 ('to draw a map'), 펼치다 ('to unfold a map'), or 보다 ('to look at a map').

지도학.etymology: Sino-Korean scholarly compound 地圖學, adding the disciplinary suffix -학 (學, 배울 학, 'science, field of study') onto 지도 (地圖, 'earth-chart, map'). Following the productive pattern of 건축학 ('architecture') and 식물학 ('botany'), 지도학 denotes the art and science of surveying and drawing maps.
지도학.notes: Pairs with 교수 ('cartography professor') or 연구 ('cartographic study').

지령.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지령 (指令), composed of 지 (指, 'finger; to point, indicate, direct') and 령 (令, 'command, order, decree'). Originally a formal military and administrative term for an authoritative directive issued by a headquarters, in modern South Korean pop culture and variety shows (like 1 Night 2 Days in The Producers) it often evokes a covert 'secret mission order.'

history.meaning: official administrative or military directive
directive, operational order; secret mission order (in espionage or variety shows)

지령.notes: While 지시 (指示) is everyday workplace 'instructions' and 명령 (命令) is a general 'command,' 지령 (指令) carries a dramatic, covert, or high-command ring—used for labor-union strike directives, espionage missions, or secret PD orders to cast members on Korean variety shows.

지루하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 지리ᄒᆞ다 ('to be long and drawn-out, tedious, wearisome'), evolving through 지류하다 to modern 지루하다.

history.meaning: to be drawn-out, tedious, tiresome
to be boring, tedious, dull

지름길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 지름 (nominalization of 지르다, 'to cut directly across, take the shortest line', also seen in 가로지르다 'to cut across' and 지름 'diameter of a circle') with 길 ('road, path'). Just as a circle's diameter cuts straight from rim to rim, a 지름길 cuts straight across winding streets.
지름길.notes: Pronounced [지름낄] with compound tensification of ㄱ.

지리.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지리 (地理), composed of 지 (地, 'earth, land, ground') and 리 (理, 'pattern, principle, vein in jade'). First attested in the commentary to the Classical Chinese Book of Changes (Yijing: 'looking up to contemplate the patterns of heaven [天文], looking down to examine the patterns of earth [地理]'), it denoted topography and geomancy before being adopted in modern East Asia to translate Western 'geography.'

history.meaning: natural patterns and configuration of the earth; geomancy (풍수지리)
geography; local layout and streets of an area

지리.notes: Beyond the school subject ('geography'), 지리 is constantly used in everyday Korean to mean 'the lay of the land / local streets' of a neighborhood, as in 여기는 내가 지리를 잘 안다 ('I know my way around this area well').

rootFamily.gloss: traditional geomancy / feng shui (lit. 'wind, water, and earth-patterns')

cognates.meaning: aspiration, desired choice of school or career

지망이.etymology: Inflected nominative form consisting of the Sino-Korean noun 지망 (志望, 'aspiration, desired option,' from 志 'will, ambition, intent' + 望 'to hope, look toward from afar') followed by the native Korean nominative/subject case particle -이. Adopted in modern Korean academic and organizational usage (alongside Japanese shibō 志望) to denote a candidate's ranked preference of school, major, or department.

history.meaning: fixing one's ambition and hope upon a goal; desired choice
desired choice, preference (as grammatical subject)

지망이.notes: In Korean college admissions and company recruitments (like new KBS producers choosing which program team to join), applicants rank their choices as 1지망 ('first choice'), 2지망 ('second choice'), and 3지망 ('third choice').

rootFamily.gloss: aspirant, hopeful, wannabe (e.g., 가수 지망생 'aspiring singer')

cognates.meaning: to aspire to, apply for as one's desired choice
cognates.word: 志望する (しぼうする, shibō suru)

지망하고.etymology: Conjugated coordinate form of the hybrid Sino-Korean verb 지망하다 (志望하다), combining the Sino-Korean noun 지망 (志望, from 志 'will, intent, ambition' + 望 'to hope, look toward'), the native verbalizing suffix 하- ('to do'), and the conjunctive ending -고 ('and, and then'). Literally 'setting one's sights on / applying for as one's desired choice and...'

history.meaning: to aspire to or select as one's preferred school/department
applying for / choosing as one's desired option and...

지망하고.notes: While 지원하다 (志願하다) means formally submitting an application, 지망하다 (志望하다) emphasizes the applicant's personal preference or aspiration toward a specific field, school, or division (e.g., 예능국을 지망하다 'to aspire to/choose the Variety Department').

rootFamily.gloss: to aspire to, apply for as one's choice (citation form)

지명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지명 (地名), composed of 지 (地, 'earth, land, place') and 명 (名, 'name'). Literally 'the name of a place' (toponym), attested across Classical Chinese geographical treatises and Korean gazetteers (such as the geographic treatises in the Samguk Sagi and Goryeosa).

history.meaning: geographical place name, toponym
place name, toponym

지명.notes: Watch out for three common Sino-Korean homographs spelled 지명: (1) 地名 ('place name, toponym'), (2) 指名 ('nominating/calling on a specific person by name,' e.g., 지명타자 'designated hitter'), and (3) 知名 ('being well-known,' as in 지명도 'name recognition/fame').

cognates.meaning: proprietary modular lightweight camera crane system

지미집.etymology: Direct English loanword (외래어) from the American proprietary brand name Jimmy Jib (invented by Jimmy Stanton of Stanton Video Services in the 1980s, combining the personal name Jimmy + English jib, 'the projecting counterweighted arm of a crane'). In South Korean television production jargon, the trademark underwent genericization to refer to any large counterweighted camera crane with a remote-controlled pan-tilt head.

history.meaning: modular tubular camera crane trademarked by Stanton Video Services
crane camera / jib arm used for sweeping high-angle broadcast shots

morphemes.meaning: proper name element from the Stanton 'Jimmy Jib' camera crane trademark
projecting arm of a crane (from English 'jib')

지미집.notes: A classic example of Korean broadcasting Konglish/jargon via trademark genericization (like 포크레인 'Poclain -> excavator' or 스카치테이프 'Scotch tape'). Because 집 sounds identical to native Korean 집 ('house'), laypeople hearing 지미집 for the first time often humorously mistake it for 'Jimmy's house.'

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Urimalsaem) – 지미집

cognates.meaning: place, local region, province (vs. central government)

지방.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지방 (地方), composed of 지 (地, 'earth, land') and 방 (方, 'square, direction, quarter, region'). Originating in the ancient Chinese cosmological phrase 천원지방 (天圓地方, 'Heaven is round, Earth is square'), it came to denote the four quarters of the realm and, in centralized East Asian states, local regions outside the capital city.

history.meaning: the squareness of the earth; quarters/regions of a territory
the provinces, local regions outside the Seoul Capital Area (수도권)

지방.notes: In Seoul-centric South Korean usage, 지방 ('the provinces') refers to anywhere outside the Seoul Metropolitan Area (서울·경기·인천)—even major metropolises like Busan or Daegu! Also note the common homograph 지방 (脂肪, 'fat, lipids'). In slang, '꺼라, 지방방송!' ('Turn off the regional broadcast!') means 'Stop the side chatter while someone is speaking!'

rootFamily.gloss: region, area (more neutral term than 지방)
regional broadcast; slang for noisy side chatter

지불하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive verb formed from 지불 (支拂, 'payment, disbursement') + native light verb 하다 ('to do'). The Sino-Korean compound 지불 (支拂, from 支 'to support, branch out, disburse' + 拂 'to brush away, clear off, pay out') entered modern Korean commercial and legal usage as an orthographic borrowing of Meiji Japanese shiharai (支払い / 支拂い, from the native Japanese compound verb shiharau).

history.form: 支拂ひ / 支拂う (shiharai / shiharau)
history.meaning: to disburse, pay out money, settle an account
to pay (money, a bill, or a price)

morphemes.meaning: to clear off, brush away, pay out

지불하다.notes: Although Korean language purists and statutory editors often recommend 지급하다 (支給하다) or 치르다 because 지불 (支拂) originated as a Japanese reading, 지불하다 remains completely natural and standard in everyday Korean for paying a bill, fee, or price (비용을 지불하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to pay, provide, issue (official/statutory preferred term)

지붕.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 집우희 / 지븡 ('roof'), historically a compound of 집 ('house') and 우희 / 우 ('top, upper part', modern 위), literally 'the top of the house'.

history.meaning: top of a house, roof
roof

지수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지수 (指數), composed of 지 (指, 'finger; to point, indicate') and 수 (數, 'number, figure, count'). Literally 'an indicating number,' coined in modern East Asian scientific and statistical vocabulary (via Japanese shisū 指数) to translate both mathematical 'exponent' and statistical 'index' (such as a price index, UV index, or humorous 'affection/stress meter' in variety TV).

history.meaning: pointing number; mathematical exponent or statistical index
index, meter, quotient; mathematical exponent

지수.notes: Beyond economics (물가지수 'price index') and weather (불쾌지수 'discomfort/humidity index'), Korean TV captions playfully attach 지수 to emotions or traits (e.g., 호감 지수 'affection meter', 허당 지수 'clumsiness index') to quantify a character's mood on screen.

지시하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 지시 (指示, 'pointing out, instruction, direction', compounding 指 'finger, point' and 示 'show, indicate') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: pointing out, directing, instruction
to instruct, direct, order, indicate

지우다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어), attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 디우다 (diuda, 'to cause to fall or drop off; to wipe away'), formed as the morphological causative of 디다 (modern 지다, 'to fall, drop, fade, disappear') with the causative suffix -우-. Via regular Early Modern palatalization (디 > 지), 디우다 became 지우다, meaning 'to cause [marks, writing, or memories] to disappear,' hence 'to erase, wipe off, or delete.'

history.meaning: to cause to fall or drop; to miscarry; to wipe away, blot out
to erase, wipe off (makeup/writing), delete (files/texts), blot out (memories)

morphemes.meaning: to erase, wipe out, delete (historically 지- 'fall/fade' + causative -우-)

지우다.notes: Covers a wide range of English verbs depending on the object: 글씨를 지우다 ('erase pencil writing'), 화장을 지우다 ('remove/wipe off makeup'), 번호를 지우다 ('delete a phone number'), and 기억을 지우다 ('blot out a memory'). Note the homonym 지우다 meaning 'to put a burden on someone' (causative of 지다 'to carry on the back').

rootFamily.gloss: to be erased, wiped away, fade out (passive)
to fall, fade, come out (of stains: 얼룩이 지다/빠지다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language – 지우다

지워버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound/auxiliary verb construction contracted from 지우어 버리다, combining the transitive verb 지우다 ('to erase, delete,' from Middle Korean 디우다) + infinitive connective -어 + the completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to throw away; to do completely and irrevocably,' Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다). Expresses wiping out, deleting, or erasing something thoroughly and for good.

history.meaning: to wipe away or cast off completely
to erase completely, wipe right out, delete once and for all

morphemes.meaning: infinitive connective ending (contracted with 지우- to 지워)
completive auxiliary verb ('completely, once and for all')

지워버리다.notes: While 지우다 simply states the action of erasing or deleting, 지워버리다 adds strong emotional finality—whether decisively deleting an embarrassing video/message so no one can ever see it, or accidentally wiping out important footage.

rootFamily.gloss: to throw away, discard; completive auxiliary

지워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 지우다 ('to erase, wipe away, blot out') + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to be erased, rub off, fade away

지장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 지장 (支障), composed of 지 (支, 'branch; to diverge, prop up, obstruct') and 장 (障, 'barrier, screen; to block, hinder'). Originally a Chinese Buddhist term for karmic or mental impediments (alongside 장애 障礙) and later reinforced by modern Japanese administrative usage (shishō 支障), it denotes a practical hindrance, disruption, or adverse effect on normal operations.

history.meaning: obstruction, impediment, barrier
hindrance, interference, problem affecting work or daily life

지장.notes: Almost exclusively used in fixed collocations with the dative particle -에 and verbs like 있다/없다 or 주다/초래하다: 방송에 지장이 없다 ('there is no hindrance/problem for the broadcast') or 업무에 지장을 주다 ('to interfere with/hamper work').

지적사항.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound (指摘事項) combining 지적 (指摘, 'pointing out faults or key points', from 指 'finger, point' + 摘 'pick, expose, point out') and 사항 (事項, 'item, matter, article', from 事 'affair, matter' + 項 'nape, item, clause'). In bureaucratic and broadcasting contexts, it denotes specific flaws, revisions, or compliance notes flagged during review.

history.meaning: to point out errors + itemized affairs or clauses
pointed-out item; review note or issue flagged for correction

지적사항.notes: Frequently used in workplace, administrative, and broadcasting review meetings (such as script or broadcast deliberations) to refer to specific points requiring correction.

지정석.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (指定席) formed from 지정 (指定, 'designation, appointment', from 指 'point, indicate' + 定 'fix, settle, decide') and the bound noun/suffix -석 (席, 'woven mat, seat, place'). Originally adopted across East Asian rail and theater systems in the modern era to distinguish reserved seating from unreserved seating (자유석, 自由席).

history.meaning: to point out and fix + sitting mat or seat
assigned or reserved seat in transit, theaters, or offices

지정석.notes: Contrasts directly with 자유석 (自由席, 'unassigned/open seating'); also used humorously in daily life for someone's habitual spot at a table or café.

지켜내다.etymology: Native Korean verb-verb compound combining 지키다 ('to guard, protect, keep', from Middle Korean 디키다 via palatalization of *di- > ji-) via the infinitive linker -어 with the auxiliary/main verb 내다 ('to put forth, bring out, accomplish through effort', Middle Korean 내다). The auxiliary -어 내다 adds an aspectual nuance of persevering through hardship to successfully defend or preserve something to the very end.

history.meaning: to guard or watch over + to bring forth or extract
to guard and carry through to completion after palatalization (디 > 지)
to successfully protect or defend to the end despite adversity

morphemes.meaning: accomplish, see through to the end

지켜내다.notes: Unlike simple 지키다 ('to protect'), the compound 지켜내다 emphasizes overcoming obstacles, pressure, or threats to successfully safeguard someone or something.

지켜보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지키다 ('to guard, watch over') + 보다 ('to look at, see, watch').

history.meaning: to watch closely, keep an eye on, observe

지켜주다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지키다 ('to guard, protect, keep', descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 디키다) joined by the connective suffix -어 to the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do for someone's benefit', Middle Korean 주다). The construction expresses protective action performed out of care or devotion toward another person.

history.meaning: to watch over, guard + to give or bestow
to protect, stand by, and safeguard someone

morphemes.meaning: connective suffix linking main and auxiliary verbs
give; perform an action for another's benefit

지켜주다.notes: A staple expression in Korean dramas and ballads (e.g., 내가 널 지켜줄게, 'I will protect you'), carrying warm interpersonal devotion rather than institutional security.

rootFamily.gloss: to successfully defend to the end

지켜지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 지키다 ('to guard, defend, keep a promise or contract') plus the passive auxiliary -어지다 (contracted from 지키어지다 to 지켜지다). It highlights that a cherished place, lease, or promise has been successfully safeguarded.
지켜지다.notes: Active counterpart is 지키다 ('to protect, keep').

지키다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 디키다 ('to guard, protect, watch over, keep'), with regular palatalization of initial 디- to 지-.

history.meaning: to guard, keep watch, protect
to protect, guard, keep (a promise or rule)

지퍼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from American English zipper ('interlocking slide fastener').

history.meaning: slide fastener
zipper

지하실.etymology: Sino-Korean 지하실 (地下室), formed from 지하 (地下, 'underground, below the ground', from 地 'earth, ground' + 下 'below, under') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: underground room
basement, cellar

지훈.etymology: Korean masculine given name of Sino-Korean origin, commonly written with hanja such as 智勳 or 志勳 (compounding 지 智 'wisdom' or 志 'noble will, ambition' with 훈 勳 'meritorious achievement').

history.meaning: Korean masculine given name (Ji-hoon)

지휘권.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 指揮權, joining 지휘 (指揮, from 指 'to point a finger' and 揮 'to wave a banner or baton'—conducting an orchestra or directing an expedition) with the suffix -권 (權, 권세 권, 'authority, right'). Used seriously in leadership and playfully among friends for whoever holds the map!
지휘권.notes: Pronounced [지휘꿘]; collocates with 넘기다 ('hand over command') and 잡다 ('take command').

지휘하다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 지휘 (指揮, combining 指 'point with a finger' and 揮 'wave a signal flag or baton, direct troops') plus -하다. Originally denoting a general directing troops with hand and banner signals, it became the standard modern Korean word for conducting a symphony orchestra—and by affectionate extension, directing a busy kitchen.

직속.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (直屬) composed of 직 (直, 'straight, direct, unmediated') and 속 (屬, 'belong to, be subordinate to, category'). It denotes an organizational relationship in which a person or unit reports directly to a superior or headquarters without intermediate hierarchy.

history.meaning: being directly attached or subordinate to a higher office
direct affiliation; directly under someone's supervision (e.g., 직속 선배/상사)

직속.notes: Commonly modifies organizational nouns such as 직속 상사 ('immediate boss') or 직속 선배 ('direct senior in one's exact department or team line').

직업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (職業) combining 직 (職, 'official duty, post, responsibility') and 업 (業, 'work, enterprise, livelihood, karma'). While both characters appeared in Classical Chinese to denote one's allotted station and work, the compound was popularized across modern East Asia to translate Western concepts of 'profession', 'vocation', and 'occupation'.

history.meaning: official post or duty + livelihood or enterprise
profession, occupation, regular paid livelihood

직업.notes: Refers to one's societal calling or line of work ('profession'), whereas 직장 (職場) refers to the specific workplace or company where one is employed.

직원.etymology: Sino-Korean 직원 (職員), compounding 직 (職, 'office, post, duty, occupation') and 원 (員, 'member, personnel').

history.meaning: office personnel, staff member
employee, staff member, clerk

직접.etymology: Sino-Korean 직접 (直接), compounding 직 (直, 'straight, direct, immediate') and 접 (接, 'touch, contact, meet').

history.meaning: direct contact, immediacy
directly, in person, firsthand

직조.etymology: Sino-Korean 직조 (織造), compounding 직 (織, 'weave, knit') and 조 (造, 'make, manufacture').

history.meaning: weaving cloth, textile manufacture
weaving, fabric weave

진국.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean compound formed from Sino-Korean 진- (眞, 'true, genuine, undiluted'; cf. 진하다 'to be thick, rich, concentrated') and native Korean 국 ('soup, broth', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 국). Literally denoting a rich, deeply simmered broth boiled down without artificial dilution, it underwent metaphorical extension to describe a person of genuine, unpretentious integrity or the 'real deal'.

history.meaning: soup, boiled broth
thick, undiluted, richly boiled broth or stock
rich broth; metaphorically a genuine gem of a person or authentic article

진국.notes: Calling someone 진국이다 ('they are rich broth') is high praise in Korean, meaning they are loyal, authentic, and admirable once you truly get to know them.

rootFamily.gloss: to be thick, rich, deep in flavor or color (眞-)
soup, broth, liquid part of soup

진단.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (診斷) consisting of 진 (診, 'examine a patient, observe symptoms, feel the pulse', with the speech/inquiry radical 言) and 단 (斷, 'cut, sever, decide, judge'). Originally a medical term for examining symptoms and determining the nature of an illness, it also extends to analytical assessments of social, economic, or organizational problems.

history.meaning: to examine pulse/symptoms + to judge or decide
clinical medical diagnosis; critical evaluation of a situation or system

진단.notes: Paired with 처방 (處方, 'prescription/remedy') in both literal medicine and figurative commentary (e.g., diagnosing why a TV show's ratings fell).

진돗개.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Korean toponym 진도 (珍島, 'Precious Island', an island county off the southwestern coast of South Jeolla Province, from 珍 'precious, treasure' + 島 'island'), the native genitive/compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, marking a locative-attributive relationship), and native Korean 개 ('dog', evolving from Middle Korean 가히 via loss of intervocalic -h- and monophthongization a+i > ae). Refers to the indigenous Korean hunting breed renowned for fierce loyalty and homing instinct.

history.meaning: dog (undergoing lenition of intervocalic ㅎ and vowel contraction)
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean (15th–18th c.)

history.meaning: the native dog breed originating from Jindo Island, designated Natural Monument No. 53

morphemes.meaning: dog (native Korean, from Middle Korean 가히)

진돗개.notes: Because of theJindo dog's legendary tenacity and single-owner loyalty, Koreans often compare someone who bites down on a task and never lets go to a 진돗개.

rootFamily.gloss: Sapsali, shaggy native Korean dog breed

진동.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (振動) formed from 진 (振, 'shake, wave, rouse, oscillate', with the hand radical 扌) and 동 (動, 'move, stir, set in motion'). Used in classical prose for shaking or stirring movement, it was standardized in modern physics for mechanical oscillation and later adopted in telecommunications as the standard term for a mobile phone's 'vibrate mode'.

history.meaning: shaking, stirring, or trembling motion
mechanical vibration; smartphone vibrate mode (진동 모드)

진동.notes: In everyday conversation, 진동 most frequently refers to setting one's phone to vibrate (진동으로 해 놓다) or to a strong smell 'shaking' the room (냄새가 진동하다, though historically influenced by 震動).

rootFamily.gloss: to shake, swing, oscillate (振子, pendulum)

진실.etymology: Sino-Korean 진실 (眞實), compounding 진 (眞, 'true, genuine, real') and 실 (實, 'fruit, substance, reality, fact').

history.meaning: truth, genuineness, reality
truth, fact, sincerity

진실하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjectival derivative combining the noun 진실 (眞實, 'truth, genuineness', from 眞 'true, real, authentic' + 實 'fruit, seed, substance, fact') with the native Korean light verb/adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be, to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다). The compound unites the Daoist/Buddhist concept of 'unfeigned reality' (眞) with concrete 'fullness of substance' (實).

history.meaning: to be true, substantive, and without falsehood
to be truthful, sincere, honest, and genuine

진실하다.notes: Describes a person's sincere character or heartfelt expression (진실한 사랑, 'true/sincere love'), whereas the related form 진실되다 emphasizes being factual and untainted by lies.

진심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (眞心) formed from 진 (眞, 'true, genuine, unfeigned') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind, intention'). Originally a Buddhist and Classical Chinese noun denoting an untainted, authentic mind free of delusion or deceit, in contemporary colloquial Korean it frequently functions adverbially (as a shortened form of 진심으로) meaning 'genuinely, seriously, for real'.

history.meaning: the true, unfeigned mind or original nature in Buddhist and classical thought
sincerity, true feelings (noun); genuinely, seriously, no joke (colloquial adverb)

진심.notes: In standard grammar 진심 is a noun ('sincerity') that takes -으로 ('sincerely'), but in casual speech and variety shows people drop the particle and use 진심 directly before adjectives or verbs (e.g., 진심 대박이다, 'it is seriously awesome').

cognates.meaning: entry, approach, pulling into a station or lane

진입하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative combining 진입 (進入, 'advancing and entering', from 進 'advance, move forward' + 入 'enter, go in') with the native verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Unlike simple 들어가다 ('to go in'), 진입하다 conveys a formal, directional progression into a bounded zone, such as a highway lane, a new market, a broadcast rankings chart, or a restricted stage.

history.meaning: to advance forward + to enter within
to enter, penetrate, or advance into a road, market, phase, or top tier

진입하다.notes: Used for vehicles merging onto a road (진입로, 'access ramp'), companies entering a market (시장 진입), or songs/shows breaking into top rankings (차트 진입).

진정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (鎭靜) composed of 진 (鎭, 'weigh down with metal, press down, pacify, quell') and 정 (靜, 'quiet, still, tranquil, serene'). Originally referring to quelling unrest or weighing down turbulent forces so that stillness returns, it now denotes emotional composure ('calming down') as well as medical sedation or soothing irritated skin.

history.meaning: pressing down commotion and restoring stillness or peace
calming down, composure, soothing, or medical sedation

진정.notes: Watch out for homophones: 진정 (鎭靜) means 'calming down' (진정해!, 'Calm down!'), whereas 진정 (眞正) means 'truly/genuinely' and 진정 (陳情) means 'filing a petition'.

rootFamily.gloss: to calm down, soothe, quell (鎭靜하다)
suppression of a riot or fire (鎭壓)

진정하다.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean formations: as a verb ('to calm down, settle, subside'), from 진정 (鎭靜, 'quelling and quieting', from 鎭 'press down, pacify' + 靜 'quiet, still') + 하다; as an adjective ('to be genuine, true'), from 진정 (眞正, 'true and right') + 하다.

history.meaning: calming down / genuineness
to calm down, compose oneself; to be genuine, true

진지하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjectival derivative formed from 진지 (眞摯, 'earnestness, seriousness', from 眞 'true, genuine' + 摯 'grasp firmly, hold fast, sincere, earnest', containing the hand radical 手) plus the native adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be'). It characterizes an attitude that takes a matter to heart with gravity and sincerity rather than joking around.

history.meaning: genuine and earnestly grasping or holding fast to sincerity
to be serious, earnest, and grave in attitude or tone

진지하다.notes: Describes a person's demeanor or tone ('earnest, serious, not joking'), unlike 심각하다 (深刻하다), which describes a situation or problem being 'severe, critical, or dire'. (Also popularized in slang: 진지충, 'someone who takes every joke way too seriously'.)

진짜.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 진 (眞, 'true, real, genuine') + the native/bound suffixoid -짜 ('article, item, person of a given quality'; compare 가짜 'fake').

history.meaning: genuine article, real thing; really, truly

진하다.etymology: Attested in Middle Korean as 진ᄒᆞ다 ('to be thick, viscous, deep in color or flavor'), formed from Sino-Korean 진 (津, 'sap, rich fluid', or 眞 'pure, concentrated') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be thick, concentrated, dark
to be dark (in color), strong/rich (in flavor or scent), thick, deep

cognates.meaning: progress, advance, emceeing/directing a program or meeting
to advance, to carry out, to be in progress

진행.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (進行) combining 진 (進, 'advance, move forward') and 행 (行, 'go, walk, carry out, conduct'). From the literal spatial sense of 'marching or moving forward', it broadened to mean the ongoing execution of a process or event, and in Korean broadcasting and events it specifically denotes 'hosting, emceeing, or running a program'.

history.meaning: moving or marching forward; advancing along a path
progression of work or events; hosting and steering a broadcast or meeting

진행.notes: In Korean television and radio (*The Producers* context), 진행 refers specifically to the MC's skill at keeping a show flowing smoothly (진행을 잘 보다 / 진행 솜씨).

rootFamily.gloss: to be carried out, to take place (進行되다)

cognates.meaning: to be underway, to be carried out

진행되다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean passive/intransitive verb formed by attaching the native Korean passive/inchoative formative -되다 ('to become, to be done', from Middle Korean 되다) to the Sino-Korean verbal noun 진행 (進行, 'progress, execution', from 進 'advance' + 行 'go, conduct'). It expresses that an event, broadcast shoot, or project is underway or taking place.

history.meaning: advance/conduct + to become or come into being
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern Korean formation

history.meaning: to be carried out, to proceed, to take place, to be underway

morphemes.meaning: passive/inchoative verb-deriving suffix ('to be done, become')

진행되다.notes: While 진행하다 is transitive ('someone conducts/hosts X'), 진행되다 is intransitive/passive ('X takes place / is currently underway', e.g., 녹화가 진행되다, 'the recording takes place').

rootFamily.gloss: to conduct, carry out, host (進行하다)

진회색.etymology: Compound formed from 진- ('dark, deep', root of 진하다) + Sino-Korean 회색 (灰色, 'gray color', from 灰 'ash' + 色 'color').

history.meaning: dark gray, charcoal gray

질리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb morphologically derived from the stem 지르- ('to thrust, pierce, choke, or strike forcefully', Middle Korean 지르다) plus the passive suffix -리-. Originally denoting physical choking, suffocation, or being stunned/overwhelmed by a sudden shock, it developed the psychological sense of being completely surfeited, fed up, or sick and tired of something through overexposure.

history.meaning: to be pierced, choked, or struck; to becomebluish/pale from shock or cold
to be intimidated or stunned; to be thoroughly sick and tired of something from excess

질리다.notes: Can describe both being intimidated/scared pale (겁에 질리다, 'paralyzed with fear') and being utterly fed up with repetitive food, work, or behavior (완전 질렸어, 'I am totally sick of it').

rootFamily.gloss: to pierce, thrust, shout, or bet
to be daunting, intimidating, or overwhelming (진절머리/질리다)
tedium, being sick and tired of something (싫증)

질문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (質問) composed of 질 (質, 'substance, pledge, verify, confront and inquire') and 문 (問, 'ask, inquire'). In Classical Chinese (attested in the *Book of Rites* and *Hanshu*), 質問 meant to present a doubt before an authority to verify the truth; in modern Korean and Japanese it serves as the neutral everyday word for 'question'.

history.meaning: to bring a matter before someone and ask in order to verify its truth
question, inquiry (in classrooms, interviews, and daily life)

질문.notes: False friend alert with Mandarin: in Korean (and Japanese), 질문 (質問) is a polite, neutral 'question', whereas in Mandarin 質问 (zhìwèn) means an aggressive 'interrogation or calling someone to account'. For a hostile grilling in Korean, use 추궁 (追窮) or 힐문 (詰問).

질색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (窒塞) formed from 질 (窒, 'stop up, obstruct, suffocate') and 색 (塞, 'block, plug up, border'). In traditional Korean medicine and older literary usage, 질색 denoted a sudden blockage of breath and blood flow causing a person to turn pale or faint in shock; in modern Korean it shifted to express extreme revulsion, disgust, or abhorrence toward something.

history.meaning: obstruction or choking of breath/qi; turning pale from sudden shock
history.stage: Traditional Sino-Korean medical and literary usage

history.meaning: extreme aversion, loathing, or detesting something (질색이다 / 질색하다)

질색.notes: Note the sino-reading: 塞 is read 색 when meaning 'to block/plug' (as in 질색 窒塞, 색전증 塞栓症) and 요새 (要塞) when meaning 'fortress'. Often intensified as 질색팔색하다 in colloquial speech.

rootFamily.gloss: to detest, loathe, be utterly averse to (窒塞하다)
turning pale with shock or horror (失色)

질서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (秩序) combining 질 (秩, 'orderly rank, regular arrangement, official stipend', originally from the grain radical 禾 suggesting neat rows of sheaves) and 서 (序, 'sequence, precedence, east-west school walls, preface'). Attested in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*), it denotes harmonious hierarchy, sequential regularity, and public or social order.

history.meaning: regularity of rank, rite, and sequence in governance and nature
public order, social discipline, or systematic arrangement

질서.notes: Frequently paired with the verb 지키다 in public campaigns (질서를 지키다, 'to keep/observe public order') or negated with 무- (無秩序, 무질서, 'disorder, chaos').

짊어지다.etymology: Native Korean pleonastic compound verb built from 짊어- (the infinitive of 짊다, 'to tie up and carry a load on the back', itself derived from the noun 짐 'load, burden', Middle Korean 딤, which came from the verb 디다/지다) and 지다 ('to carry on the back', Middle Korean 디다). By stacking the denominal verb 짊다 onto its own root verb 지다, the compound vividly emphasizes hoisting and bearing a heavy load or responsibility on one's shoulders.

history.meaning: to carry on the back > a load carried on the back > to bundle and load onto the back
to shoulder a physical pack; metaphorically to bear a heavy duty, debt, or responsibility

짊어지다.notes: Used both literally for strapping on a heavy backpack and figuratively for shouldering burdens such as family livelihood, guilt, or team responsibility (책임을 짊어지다).

rootFamily.gloss: load, luggage, burden (from Middle Korean 딤)
to carry on the back, bear, or owe

짐.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 짐 ('load carried on the back or head, pack, burden'), related to the verb 지다 ('to carry on the back').

history.meaning: that which is carried on the back, load, pack
luggage, baggage, load, burden

짐승.etymology: Nativized Korean word that originated as the Sino-Korean Buddhist compound 중생 (衆生, 'all sentient beings, the multitude of living creatures', translating Sanskrit *sattva* or *jana*, from 衆 'multitude, crowd' + 生 'living being, birth'). In 15th-century Middle Korean, the vernacular phonetic form 즘숌 / 즘생 diverged from the scholarly reading 중생, later undergoing vowel raising (즈 > 지) and unrounding to become 짐승 while narrowing semantically from 'all sentient beings' to 'non-human beast or animal'.

history.meaning: all living/sentient beings in Buddhist cosmology > non-human living creatures or beasts
beast, animal, brute (fully nativized and dissociated from Hanja 衆生)

morphemes.meaning: nativized reflex of Buddhist Sino-Korean 衆生 ('living creature, beast')

짐승.notes: A classic example of a lexical doublet in Korean: the exact same Hanja compound 衆生 survives both as the learned Buddhist term 중생 ('sentient beings/mortals') and the fully nativized everyday word 짐승 ('beast, animal').

rootFamily.gloss: sentient beings, mortals (learned Sino-Korean doublet 衆生)

cognates.meaning: taking into consideration, making allowances for
to consider, deliberate, pour wine carefully
to consider carefully, weigh pros and cons

짐작하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative combining 짐작 (斟酌, 'estimating, guessing', from 斟 'ladle out, pour liquid' + 酌 'pour wine, deliberate, consult', both sharing the wine-vessel/ladle radical 斗/酉) with the native light verb -하다 ('to do'). Literally meaning to gauge how much wine or broth to ladle into a cup, it metaphorically evolved in Classical Chinese and Korean into 'measuring circumstances in one's mind to estimate or guess'.

history.meaning: to ladle out and pour wine according to appropriate measure; to deliberate carefully
to gauge, estimate, conjecture, or figure out from context

짐작하다.notes: Because its phonetic shape feels native and colloquial, many Koreans are surprised to learn that 짐작 (斟酌) is a poetic Sino-Korean metaphor from pouring wine! (Compare Japanese *shinshaku* 斟酌, which kept the sense of 'making allowances/consideration'.)

rootFamily.gloss: to consider, take into account circumstances (參酌하다)

집.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 집 ('house, home, dwelling, family; protective case or sheath').

history.meaning: house, home, household
house, home, dwelling

집다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 집다 ('to pick up with the fingers, chopsticks, or tongs; to pinch').

history.meaning: to pick up, pinch
to pick up, pluck, point out

집들이하다.etymology: Native Korean verbal compound formed from the noun 집들이 ('moving into a new house; housewarming party') plus the light verb -하다 ('to do'). The noun 집들이 itself comprises 집 ('house, home', Middle Korean 집), the verb stem 들- ('to enter, go inside', Middle Korean 들다), and the action-nominalizing suffix -이 ('the act of entering a house'). Traditionally referring to the ritual of moving into a new residence, it now primarily denotes hosting friends and colleagues for a housewarming meal.

history.meaning: the act of moving one's household into a newly built or acquired home
to hold a housewarming party after moving into a new home

집들이하다.notes: At traditional Korean housewarmings (집들이), guests famously bring laundry detergent or rolls of toilet paper as gifts, symbolizing wishes that the host's good fortune will 'bubble up' and 'unroll smoothly' (술술 풀리다).

rootFamily.gloss: housewarming party, moving into a house
entering the bride's/in-laws' house after a wedding (新行 / 신행)
autumn harvesting and bringing crops into the house (가을걷이)

집밥.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining 집 ('house, home', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 집) and 밥 ('cooked grain/rice, meal', attested in Middle Korean as 밥). Transparency of its two core native roots gives it strong emotional resonance in contemporary Korean culture, contrasting wholesome, comforting meals prepared at home with commercial restaurant or delivery food (외식/배달음식).

history.meaning: house/home + cooked rice or meal
home-cooked meal (associated with family warmth and everyday comfort food)

집밥.notes: For single-person households and busy broadcasting staff eating takeout on set, 집밥 carries deep nostalgia for a mother's cooking and unpretentious nourishment.

집세.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 집 ('house, home') + Sino-Korean 세 (貰, 'rent, lease payment, hire').

history.meaning: house rent

집안.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 집 ('house, dwelling', Middle Korean 집) and 안 ('inside, interior', Middle Korean 안ㅎ, an h-final noun). From its literal spatial sense of 'the interior of a house', it underwent metonymic extension to denote the domestic household, a family's lineage, clan standing, and internal family affairs.

history.meaning: the inside of a house; the household and family members within it
inside the house; household, family lineage, or clan background

집안.notes: Depending on context, 집안 can mean the physical interior of a home (집안이 깨끗하다, 'the house is clean inside'), housework (집안일, 'chores'), or family pedigree/background (집안이 좋다, 'comes from a prestigious family').

rootFamily.gloss: family member, household (食口, literally 'mouths to feed')
inside and outside, domestic and external; husband and wife (안 + 밖)

집주인.etymology: Hybrid native–Sino-Korean compound combining native Korean 집 ('house, home', Middle Korean 집) with Sino-Korean 주인 (主人, 'master, owner, host', from 主 'lord, master, owner, host' + 人 'person'). It designates either the legal owner of a residential property or the landlord who leases a home to tenants (세입자).

history.meaning: house (native) + master or host of a household (Sino-Korean)
homeowner; landlord or landlady in a jeonse or monthly rental contract

집주인.notes: In modern Korean housing contexts (especially 전세 *jeonse* lump-sum deposit leases and 월세 monthly rent), 집주인 almost always refers to the 'landlord/lessor', paired opposite 세입자 (貰入者, 'tenant'). Also commonly inverted as 주인집 when referring to the landlord's household.

cognates.meaning: to cling to, be obsessed with, persistent

집착.etymology: Sino-Korean compound (執着 / 執著) formed from 집 (執, 'grasp in the hand, hold fast, maintain stubbornly') and 착 (着/著, 'attach, adhere, stick to, reach'). Coined in Chinese Buddhist translations of Sanskrit *abhinivesa* and *upadana* to denote the deluded mental clinging to worldly phenomena or ego that causes suffering, it broadened into everyday psychological vocabulary for 'obsession, fixation, or possessive attachment'.

history.meaning: mental clinging or grasping onto phenomena as permanent (translating Sanskrit Buddhist terms)
psychological obsession, fixation, or possessive attachment to a person, goal, or object

집착.notes: Notice the dual Hanja readings of 着: it is read 착 when meaning 'attach/arrive' (집착 執着, 도착 到着, 정착 定着) and 자 in a few older compounds, while 執 is always 집 ('grasp', as in 고집 固執, 'stubbornness').

rootFamily.gloss: to obsess over, cling to (執着하다)

cognates.meaning: to cling to, be obsessed with
to be persistent or obsessed with

집착하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal derivative combining the Buddhist-origin Sino-Korean noun 집착 (執着, 'clinging, obsession', from 執 'grasp firmly' + 着 'adhere, stick to') with the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). It takes the dative/locative particle -에 (X-에 집착하다) to express fixating on or clinging excessively to a person, outcome, or idea.

history.meaning: to cling to worldly attachments or fixed notions in Buddhist discourse
to obsess over, fixate on, or be overly possessive of someone or something

집착하다.notes: Always takes the particle -에 on the target of obsession (e.g., 시청률에 집착하다, 'to obsess over viewer ratings'; 과거에 집착하다, 'to dwell/fixate on the past').

rootFamily.gloss: single-minded devotion or concentration on one thing (執念)

집토끼.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) formed from 집 (Middle Korean 집, "house, home") and 토끼 (Middle Korean 톳기, "rabbit, hare"). Literally denoting a domesticated rabbit raised at home in contrast to 산토끼 ("wild mountain hare"), the compound underwent metaphorical extension in modern Korean political, business, and television broadcasting discourse to refer to an already-secured core audience, loyal regular viewers, or reliable supporter base.

history.meaning: house / home + rabbit / hare
domesticated rabbit; (figurative) loyal regular audience or core fanbase

집토끼.notes: Often paired with 산토끼 ("wild rabbit", i.e., floating voters or uncaptured viewers): broadcasting PDs talk about holding onto 집토끼 (loyal regulars) while hunting 산토끼 (new viewers).

rootFamily.gloss: wild mountain rabbit; uncaptured audience or swing voters
pet dog, family dog kept at home

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 집토끼

짓.etymology: Native Korean noun (고유어) descending from Middle Korean 짒 (ciz, "act, gesture, bodily movement"), deverbal nominalization of the verb stem 짓- (Middle Korean 짛다, ciz-ta, "to make, construct, perform"). While neutral in Middle Korean for any physical gesture or action, in Modern Korean 짓 underwent strong pejoration to denote a foolish, mischievous, awkward, or reprehensible act or stunt.

history.meaning: bodily gesture, movement, or deed (neutral)
foolish act, stunt, antics, or questionable behavior

짓.notes: Carries a strongly disparaging nuance in standalone use (e.g., 무슨 짓이야? "What kind of stunt are you pulling?"), though neutral in fossilized compounds like 몸짓 ("body gesture") and 손짓 ("hand signal").

rootFamily.gloss: hand gesture, motioning with the hand

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짓

짓다.etymology: Native Korean ㅅ-irregular verb (고유어) from Middle Korean 짛다 (ciz-ta, "to make, build, compose, prepare"), whose stem-final voiced fricative ㅿ (z) lenited to zero before vowels (지어) and merged with -ㅅ (-t) before consonants (짓고). Originally denoting skilled creation—building a house (집을 짓다), cooking rice (밥을 짓다), or composing poetry (시를 짓다)—it broadened to forming facial expressions (표정을 짓다, 미소를 짓다) and concluding matters (결론을 짓다).

history.meaning: to build, construct, prepare, or compose
to build, make, compose, or form (an expression or smile)

짓다.notes: As a ㅅ-irregular (ㅅ 불규칙) verb, the stem-final ㅅ drops before vowel-initial endings: 짓 + -어 -> 지어 (not *짓어), 짓 + -으니 -> 지으니.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짓다

cognates.meaning: spell, curse, bringer of bad luck

징크스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed in the 20th century (partly mediated via Japanese ジンクス, jinkusu) from English jinx ("a person or thing that brings bad luck"), which derives via 17th-century English jyng and Latin iynx from Ancient Greek ἴυγξ (íunx, the Eurasian wryneck bird, bound to a revolving wheel in ancient Greek witchcraft and divination). In Korean, it refers not only to a bad-luck curse but also to any recurring superstition or pre-broadcast omen.

history.meaning: wryneck bird used in magical charms and divination
bringer of bad luck, hoodoo, curse
jinx, ominous pattern, or personal superstition

징크스.notes: Unlike English "jinx" (which is strictly negative), Korean 징크스 is often used neutrally for any superstitious correlation (even a positive one, e.g., "Whenever it rains on premiere day, our ratings skyrocket").

rootFamily.gloss: to break a jinx or curse

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 징크스

짚다.etymology: Native Korean verb (고유어) continuing Middle Korean 짒다 (cip-ta, "to lean on a staff, prop oneself up with a hand, press one's fingers onto a surface"). From the tactile physical gesture of placing one's fingers on a wrist to feel a pulse (맥을 짚다) or touching a spot on a map, the verb developed the cognitive sense of pinpointing, guessing, or clarifying an issue before moving on (짚고 넘어가다).

history.meaning: to lean on a cane or place one's hand on a surface for support
to touch, lean on; to pinpoint, guess, or point out a fact

짚다.notes: Extremely common in workplace and drama dialogue in the phrase 짚고 넘어가다 ("to point something out / clarify a point before moving on") and 헛다리 짚다 ("to bark up the wrong tree", lit. "to grab the wrong leg").

rootFamily.gloss: to guess, reckon, put one's finger on
to retrace one's steps or memories

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짚다

짜다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어) from Middle Korean ㅭ다 (pza-ta, "to weave cloth on a loom, interlace threads"), whose initial consonant cluster ㅭ- (pz-) regularly simplified to the tense affricate ㅉ- (cc-) in Early Modern Korean. From weaving warp and weft threads into fabric (베를 짜다) and joining wooden pieces into a frame (틀을 짜다), it evolved metaphorically to mean structuring a plan, schedule, team, or broadcast lineup (계획을 짜다, 판을 짜다).

history.meaning: to weave cloth, interlace threads on a loom
to weave, assemble a frame; to organize, devise, or put together a plan

짜다.notes: Korean has three homophonous verbs spelled 짜다 from different Middle Korean consonant clusters: 1) "to weave / plan" (< ㅭ다 pza-ta), 2) "to squeeze / wring out" (< ㅿ다 > 짜다), and 3) the adjective "to be salty" (< ㅭ다 pca-ta).

rootFamily.gloss: pre-arranged script or rigged setup (짜고 치는 고스톱)
to be woven or organized together (passive)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짜다

짜장면.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary loanword adapted from Shandong Mandarin 炸醬麵 (zhájiàngmiàn, "fried-sauce noodles": 炸 zhá "deep-fry in oil", 醬 jiàng "fermented soybean paste", 麵 miàn "wheat noodles"), introduced by Shandong Chinese immigrants in Incheon's Chinatown during the late 19th century and localized with sweet caramel-roasted chunjang (춘장). Because Mandarin retroflex voiced/unaspirated zh- [ʈʂ] was perceived by Korean speakers as fortis ㅉ [tɕ͈], it was universally pronounced 짜장면 alongside the traditional Sino-Korean reading 자장면 (炸醬麵).

history.meaning: wheat noodles topped with stir-fried fermented soybean paste and pork
Korean-Chinese black-bean-sauce noodles

짜장면.notes: For decades, prescriptive orthography recognized only 자장면, turning 짜장면 vs. 자장면 into a famous national debate until the National Institute of Korean Language officially accepted 짜장면 as a standard form in August 2011.

rootFamily.gloss: rice topped with black-bean sauce and stir-fried vegetables (炸醬飯)
spicy seafood noodle soup (another Incheon Korean-Chinese classic)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짜장면

짜증.etymology: Attested in Early Modern Korean (19th century) as 짜정 and 짜증 ("fretfulness, peevishness, temper"), widely analyzed by Korean philologists as a phonologically altered Sino-Korean medical compound ending in -증 (症, "symptom, ailment"), most likely from 燀症 (단증 > 짠증 > 짜증, "feverish/burning irritation") or 積症 (적증, "pent-up indigestion/blockage symptom"), which underwent palatalization and initial fortition and shifted from physical fretfulness in children to general psychological annoyance.

history.meaning: feverish fretfulness, peevishness, or physical crankiness
irritation, annoyance, crankiness, frustration

짜증.notes: Distinguish 짜증이 나다 ("to feel annoyed / irritated", involuntary state) from 짜증을 내다 ("to vent one's irritation / snap at someone", deliberate action).

rootFamily.gloss: to get irritated, for annoyance to arise

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짜증

짝.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 짝 / 쨕 ('one of a pair, partner, mate, matching half').

history.meaning: mate, partner, one of a pair
pair, partner, mate, match

짝사랑.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) composed of the prefixal noun 짝- (from Middle Korean 짝, "one of a pair, a single unmatched member without its counterpart") and 사랑 (Middle Korean 사랑, "thought, longing, affection, love"). Just as 짝- in compounds like 짝눈 ("uneven eyes") or 짝귀 ("unmatched ears") denotes asymmetry or incompleteness of a pair, 짝사랑 literally signifies "one-half love"—affection felt by only one side without reciprocation.

history.meaning: single member of a pair + longing / affection
unrequited love, one-sided crush

morphemes.meaning: unpaired, one-sided, single member of a pair

짝사랑.notes: While standalone 짝 means a "partner" or "matched pair" (환상의 짝꿍), as a prefix 짝- paradoxically means "unpaired / lopsided" because a single half of a pair lacks its match!

rootFamily.gloss: to love unrequitedly, to pine for someone one-sidedly

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짝사랑

짝짓기.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (고유어) formed from 짝 (Middle Korean 짝, "pair, mate, partner"), the verb stem 짓- (Middle Korean 짛다, "to make, form"), and the deverbal nominalizer -기. Originally a literal expression for forming pairs and standard biological terminology for animal mating, it is widely used in Korean variety shows (예능 프로그램) with tongue-in-cheek humor to describe romantic coupling games or matchmaking segments among cast members.

history.meaning: forming a pair or mate
animal mating; (humorous/broadcasting) romantic pairing or matchmaking

짝짓기.notes: Because 짝짓기 is the standard biological term for animal mating on nature documentaries (동물의 왕국), calling a human dating or variety-show segment 짝짓기 adds a dry, documentary-style comedic tone.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짝짓기

짠하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic verb (고유어) representing the convergence of two distinct formations: (1) as an action verb meaning "to clink glasses in a toast", it combines the onomatopoeic interjection 짠 (mimicking the ringing clink of glass cups striking together, or a "ta-da!" reveal) with the light verb -하다 ("to do/make"); (2) as a homophonous descriptive verb (adjective) meaning "to be poignant, heart-wrenching, or sympathetically stung", it entered standard Korean from Jeolla/Chungcheong dialect 짠하다, historically related to 짜다 ("salty, stinging to the nose/eyes").

history.meaning: to make a ringing clink or sudden reveal; (dialectal) to feel a stinging ache of pity
(verb) to clink glasses in a toast; (adjective) to feel poignant or heart-wrenched

morphemes.meaning: clinking sound of glasses ("cheers!") / stinging poignancy
to do, to make, to be

짠하다.notes: In Korean drinking culture (회식), saying "짠!" or "우리 짠하자!" means "Let's clink glasses / Cheers!", whereas saying "마음이 짠하다" uses the homophonous adjective meaning "My heart aches with sympathy."

rootFamily.gloss: ta-da! / cheers! (interjection when revealing something or clinking glasses)
salty, stinging (etymological root of the poignant sense)
miser, stingy person (related colloquial root 짠-)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 짠하다

짤.etymology: Early-2000s Korean internet neologism clipped from 짤방, itself an acronym of 짤림 방지 ("deletion prevention"), combining 짤림—the colloquial tensed (fortis) nominalization of 잘리다 ("to be cut off, deleted", passive of native Korean 자르다, Middle Korean 쟛다)—and Sino-Korean 방지 (防止, "prevention": 防 방 "defend/ward off" + 止 지 "stop"). Originating on DC Inside forums for an unrelated photo attached so moderators would not delete a text-only post, 짤 evolved to denote any reaction meme, funny screenshot, or animated GIF clip.

history.meaning: mandatory image attached to a forum post to prevent moderator deletion
reaction meme, humorous screenshot, animated GIF, or short video clip

morphemes.meaning: clipped from 짤림 (< 잘리다, to be cut/deleted) + 방지 (防止, prevention)

짤.notes: An essential broadcasting and social-media buzzword: 움직이는 짤 is shortened to 움짤 ("animated GIF"), and generating viral reaction memes from a show is called 짤을 생성하다.

rootFamily.gloss: original acronym ("deletion-prevention image") from which 짤 was clipped
animated GIF or short looping video clip (< 움직이는 짤방)
to be cut, fired, or deleted (colloquial tensed form: 짤리다)

짧다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 뎌르다 / 쟑다 ('to be short in length or duration').

history.meaning: to be short
to be short, brief

짧아지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative compound verb (고유어) formed from 짧- (stem of 짧다, from Middle Korean 쟛다 / 쟗다, cyalp-ta, "to be short, brief"), the infinitive connective -아, and the auxiliary verb -지다 ("to become", grammaticalized from 지다 "to fall/be formed"). Literally meaning "to grow shorter", in the idiomatic expression 말이 짧아지다 ("one's speech gets shorter") it refers to dropping polite sentence endings (-요, -습니다) and slipping into informal 반말.

history.meaning: to be short in length or duration
to become shorter; (of speech, 말이 짧아지다) to become casual or drop honorifics

짧아지다.notes: Because Korean polite speech (존댓말) adds final syllables like -요 or -습니다 at the end of verbs, dropping them literally makes sentences physically shorter—hence "어, 말이 짧아진다?" ("Huh, your speech is getting casual/short with me?").

rootFamily.gloss: short track speed skating / short-form content (contrasted loanword usage) or 단말 (short word)

짭짤하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated taste adjective formed from the root of 짜다 ('to be salty', Middle Korean ㅭᆞ다 / 짜다) + the adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be pleasantly salty, savory; to be tidy/lucrative (of income)

쨍.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic adverb featuring the tense palatal affricate ㅉ and bright vowel ㅐ closed by velar nasal ㅇ, iconically capturing a high, resonant impact on glass, porcelain, ice, or caramelized sugar. In Korean sound symbolism, tense initials like ㅉ convey crisp, unyielding sharpness compared with plain 쟁.
쨍.notes: Also appears in 쨍하다 ('to glare brightly, ring sharply') and 쨍그랑 ('shattering crash').

쩔다.etymology: Modern Korean slang verb and adjective formed by expressive initial fortition (tensification ㅈ > ㅉ) from standard native Korean 절다 (Middle Korean 절다, cel-ta, "to be salted, pickled, soaked, or saturated in brine or sweat"). From the literal sense of being thoroughly steeped or drenched in something (e.g., 땀에 절다 "drenched in sweat", 오글거림에 쩔다 "dripping with cringe"), youth slang extended 쩔다 in the 2000s to mean "to be overwhelmingly intense, awesome, or next-level".

history.meaning: to become salted, pickled, or thoroughly soaked in liquid
(slang) to be steeped/dripping with; to be insanely good, intense, or overwhelming

morphemes.meaning: be steeped, soaked, saturated; (slang) be extreme/awesome (< 절-)

쩔다.notes: Conjugates like a ㄹ-irregular verb: before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ, the stem-final ㄹ drops, giving 쩐다! ("That's sick! / It's dripping with...") in the present indicative.

rootFamily.gloss: to be salted, pickled, or soaked in sweat/grease (standard source verb)
to pickle or salt vegetables (causative, e.g., 배추를 절이다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 절다

쪼이다.etymology: Colloquial tensed (fortis) variant of native Korean 조이다 (Middle Korean 조이다, "to tighten, constrict, squeeze", passive/causative related to 죄다). By shifting the initial lax affricate ㅈ [tɕ] to fortis ㅉ [tɕ͈] (쪼이다), speakers iconically intensify the physical sensation of tight squeezing or constriction; in contemporary slang (especially 심장이 쪼이다, "one's heart is squeezed tight"), it means to be nerve-wracking, suspenseful, or nail-biting.

history.meaning: to tighten, bind, or constrict physically
to be tightly squeezed; (slang) to be nerve-wracking, tense, or nail-biting

morphemes.meaning: tighten, squeeze, constrict (tensed form of 조이-)

쪼이다.notes: Frequently used in variety/drama production rooms when waiting for live ratings or a cliffhanger: "아, 진짜 쪼인다!" ("Ah, this is seriously nerve-wracking!"). Not to be confused with homophonous 쪼이다 (< 쪼다, "to be pecked by a bird") or 쬐다 ("to bask in sunlight").

rootFamily.gloss: to tighten, fasten, or feel anxious (standard lax form)
to tighten, constrict, or press someone hard (contracted form)
to pressure or nag someone relentlessly (colloquial transitive variant)

쪽.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 쯼 / 쪽 ('split half, piece, slice; side, direction').

history.meaning: split piece, half, side
direction, side, way; page; piece, clove

쪽지.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 쪽 ('small piece, slip, fragment') + Sino-Korean 지 (紙, 'paper').

history.meaning: small slip of paper, short note, memo

쪽팔리다.etymology: Colloquial Korean slang compound combining 쪽—an argot noun meaning "face, countenance, dignity" (traced by Korean lexicographers either to a specialization of native 쪽 "side, direction, piece/profile" or early-20th-century underworld slang for the face)—with 팔리다 ("to be sold", passive of native Korean 팔다, Middle Korean 팔다). Literally meaning "to have one's face sold off in public" (structurally parallel to standard 얼굴이 팔리다 and 체면이 깎이다), it denotes losing face or feeling acute humiliation.

history.meaning: to be sold or put on display
(slang) to lose face, feel humiliated, or be embarrassed in front of others

쪽팔리다.notes: Very common in casual spoken Korean ("아, 쪽팔려!" = "Ugh, how embarrassing!"), but considered slang/vulgar in formal settings—use 창피하다 or 부끄럽다 in polite or official contexts.

rootFamily.gloss: to be sold; (of one's face/name) to become widely known or exposed
unable to lift one's face out of shame (slang sharing 쪽 "face")
rootFamily.word: 쪽도 못 쓰다 (to be utterly outmatched/humiliated)

쫄다.etymology: Colloquial Korean verb formed via expressive initial fortition (ㅈ > ㅉ) from native Korean 졸다 (Middle Korean 졸다, col-ta, "to boil down, evaporate, shrink in volume"). Just as soup or sauce boils down and shrinks in a pot (국물이 졸다), the tensed slang derivative 쫄다 vividly portrays a person's spirit, courage, or posture shrinking back in fear, meaning to cower, chicken out, or feel intimidated.

history.meaning: to boil down, diminish in volume, or shrink
(colloquial/slang) to cower, shrink back in fear, or be intimidated

morphemes.meaning: shrink back, cower, be intimidated (< 졸- "boil down/shrink")

쫄다.notes: Often heard in teasing challenges like "쫄았냐?" ("Did you chicken out? / Are you scared?") or "쫄지 마!" ("Don't be intimidated!"). Not to be confused with the homophonous standard verb 졸다 ("to doze off").

rootFamily.gloss: to boil down, shrink in volume (standard lax verb)
to simmer or boil down in sauce (causative)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 졸다

쫄쫄.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic/ideophonic adverb (의태어/의성어), serving as the fortis (tensed ㅉ), bright-vowel (ㅗ) counterpart in the Korean sound-symbolic series 졸졸 / 줄줄 / 쫄쫄 / 쭐쭐. In the collocation 쫄쫄 굶다 ("to starve on a completely empty stomach"), it iconically evokes the shrunken, pinched, and rumbling state of an empty belly (connected to the root of 쫄다, "to shrink/boil down"), whereas with verbs of flowing it depicts water trickling in a thin, tight stream.

history.meaning: trickling in a narrow stream; shrunken and pinched from hunger

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic root evoking a thin trickle or shrunken/pinched emptiness (reduplicated)

쫄쫄.notes: Almost always paired with 굶다 ("to go hungry/skip meals") as the idiomatic intensifier 쫄쫄 굶다 ("to starve completely / go without a single bite all day").

rootFamily.gloss: gently trickling (of a brook); tagging along closely (lax counterpart)
pouring or flowing continuously in streams (dark-vowel lax counterpart)
chewy, elastic, tightly contracted texture (related ideophonic root)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 쫄쫄

쫓겨나다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (고유어) formed from 쫓기- (the passive stem of 쫓다, Middle Korean 쯫다, "to drive away, pursue, expel", derived with the passive suffix -기-), the infinitive connective -어, and the directional movement verb 나다 (Middle Korean 나다, "to go out, exit, emerge"). Literally meaning "to be chased and go out", it denotes being involuntarily driven out, evicted, or kicked out of a place or position.

history.meaning: to pursue/drive away + to go out/exit
to be driven out, expelled, evicted, or kicked out

쫓겨나다.notes: The passive counterpart of 쫓아내다 ("to kick someone out"): 집에서 쫓겨나다 means "to get kicked out of the house". Do not confuse 쫓다 ("to chase/expel", with ㅊ) with 좇다 ("to follow a goal/ideal", with ㅈ).

rootFamily.gloss: to be chased, to be pressed (for time: 시간에 쫓기다)
to chase out, expel, kick out (active transitive counterpart)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 쫓겨나다

쫓아가다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound joining 쫓다 ('to chase, pursue rapidly', Middle Korean 좇다/쫓다, distinct in modern spelling from 좇다 'to follow an ideal or principle') via infinitive -아 with directional 가다 ('to go away from the speaker'). Together 쫓아가다 depicts hurrying forward in pursuit of someone or something moving ahead.
쫓아가다.notes: Contrasts with 쫓아오다 ('to chase toward the speaker').

쫓아내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb (고유어) combining the transitive verb stem 쫓- (Middle Korean 쯫다, pcwoch-ta, "to pursue, drive away, expel"), the infinitive connective -아, and the transitive directional verb 내다 (Middle Korean 내다, causative of 나다, "to put out, make exit, drive forth"). Literally "to chase and put outside", it means to expel, banish, or kick someone out.

history.meaning: to drive away/pursue + to put forth/make exit
to chase out, drive away, evict, or expel

morphemes.meaning: put out, make exit (causative of 나다)

쫓아내다.notes: Forms a clean active/passive pair with 쫓겨나다: the landlord or boss 쫓아내다 (kicks someone out), while the tenant or employee 쫓겨나다 (gets kicked out).

rootFamily.gloss: to get kicked out, be expelled (passive counterpart)
to chase after, catch up with (쫓- + -아 + 가다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 쫓아내다

쫓아다니다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb combining 쫓아 (infinitive stem of 쫓다, 'to pursue') with 다니다 ('to go about from place to place'). Whereas 쫓아가다 describes a single straight pursuit, adding 다니다 adds multi-directional, ongoing motion—following clues, shadows, or someone's footsteps all around town.
쫓아다니다.notes: Takes object particle -을/-를 on the thing being pursued.

쫙.etymology: Native Korean single-syllable ideophonic adverb (의태어/의성어), contracted from 쭈악 with expressive initial fortition (ㅉ) and the bright (양성) diphthong ㅘ (wa). In Korean sound symbolism, bright-vowel 쫙 contrasts with dark-vowel 쭉: whereas 쭉 depicts steady linear extension in one direction, 쫙 vividly depicts something unfolding, spreading out wide, tearing open, or sweeping across a surface all at once.

history.meaning: ideophone of tearing, spreading wide, or sweeping out all at once

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic root depicting rapid, wide spreading or sweeping action

쫙.notes: Compare the vowel-harmony pair: 쫙 펴다 means "to spread out wide/flat all at once" (like a fan, map, or shoulders), whereas 쭉 뻗다 means "to stretch out straight and long" (like a road or legs).

rootFamily.gloss: straight, continuously in a line (dark-vowel counterpart)
spreading or tearing in wide strokes (reduplicated form)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 쫙

쭉.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/ideophonic adverb expressing straight, uninterrupted extension in space or time ('straight through, all the way, in a row, in one draught').

history.meaning: straight, continuously, all the way, in one gulp

찌르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular transitive verb (고유어) descending from Middle Korean 지르다 (cilu-ta, "to pierce, stab, thrust, prod"), which underwent expressive initial fortition (ㅈ > ㅉ) in Early Modern Korean to become 찌르다 for the sharp, puncturing sense ("to stab, prick, poke, prod"), while the original lax initial survives in 지르다 for broader thrusting actions ("to kick/thrust, set fire, yell out").

history.meaning: to pierce, stab, thrust, or prod
to stab, prick, poke, prod, or pierce sharply

찌르다.notes: Conjugates as a 르-irregular (르 불규칙) verb: before -어/-아, the vowel ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles, yielding 찔러 (찔러보다 "to probe / test the waters") and passive 찔리다 ("to be stabbed; to have a guilty conscience").

rootFamily.gloss: to be stabbed; to feel a twinge of guilt (도둑이 제 발 저리듯 양심이 찔리다)
to thrust, kick, set fire, or shout out (lax etymological doublet)
to probe, poke around to test someone's reaction (찌르- + -어 + 보다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찌르다

찌르릉.etymology: Native Korean mimetic-onomatopoeic word built with tense initial ㅉ for a sharp metallic start, liquid ㄹ across the middle syllable for rapid mechanical vibration, and final velar nasal ㅇ for lingering resonance. It is the classic Korean sound word for old-fashioned desk buzzers, doorbells, and bicycle bells.
찌르릉.notes: Often repeated (찌르릉 찌르릉) for a double ring.

찌푸리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from early Modern Korean 쯰푸리다 / 찌푸리다 ('to knit one's brows, frown; for the weather to become overcast').

history.meaning: to frown, scowl, cloud over
to frown, grimace, scowl; to become overcast
