찍다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어) from Middle Korean 찍다 / 찦다 ("to stamp, imprint, peck, chop, mark with a dot"). Originally denoting a sharp downward impact that leaves a mark—such as stamping a seal in red ink (도장을 찍다), printing movable type onto paper (글자를 찍다), or dotting a point (점을 찍다)—it was semantically extended with the arrival of photography and cinema in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to "imprinting" an image onto film (사진을 찍다, 영화를 찍다).

history.meaning: to stamp, chop, peck, or imprint a mark upon a surface
to stamp, print, dot, dip in sauce; to take a photograph or shoot film/video

찍다.notes: One of the most versatile verbs in Korean: besides filming a show (방송을 찍다) or taking a photo (사진을 찍다), it also means to stamp a seal (도장을 찍다), dip food in sauce (소스에 찍어 먹다), and guess an answer on a multiple-choice test (답을 찍다)!

rootFamily.gloss: to be stamped, imprinted, or photographed; to be on a boss's bad side (눈도장/미운털이 찍히다)
to try filming or taking a photo (찍- + -어 + 보다)
to film on location and bring the footage back (찍- + -어 + 오다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찍다

찍어보다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb construction (고유어) combining 찍- (from Middle Korean 찍다, "to stamp, imprint"; modern "to photograph, film, shoot video"), the infinitive connective -어, and the experiential/conative auxiliary verb 보다 (from Middle Korean 보다, "to see, look at", which grammaticalized after -어/-아 into an auxiliary meaning "to try doing" or "to have the experience of doing").

history.meaning: to try stamping/imprinting or test by marking
to try taking a photo/video, or to have experience shooting footage

찍어보다.notes: In past or interrogative frames like "예능 찍어봤어요?" ("Have you ever shot a variety show before?"), -어 보다 expresses life experience ("have you ever...") rather than a mere attempt.

rootFamily.gloss: to stamp, print; to take a photo or shoot video
to film on location and bring the footage back
to eat by dipping into sauce (찍- + -어 + 먹다, "dip-eating")

찍어오다.etymology: Native Korean directional serial verb compound (고유어) formed from 찍- (Middle Korean 찍다, "to stamp, imprint"; modern "to photograph, shoot video"), the infinitive connective -어, and the deictic motion verb 오다 (Middle Korean 오다, o-ta, "to come, move toward the speaker"). In television production, it denotes going out into the field to shoot footage and bringing the recorded material back to the editing room.

history.meaning: to imprint/mark and come back
to shoot photos or video footage on location and bring it back

morphemes.meaning: come, bring toward the speaker's location

찍어오다.notes: In broadcasting jargon, senior PDs frequently tell junior PDs (막내 PD) or VJs "이거 찍어와" ("Go shoot this footage and bring it back to the editing bay").

rootFamily.gloss: to stamp; to photograph or film
to try filming or have experience shooting footage
to buy and bring back (parallel -어/아 오다 compound)

찍히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 찍다 ('to stamp, imprint, dot, take a picture, chop') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be stamped, be imprinted, be photographed, be singled out

찡그리다.etymology: Native Korean verb ('to wince, grimace, screw up one's face or eyes') attested since early Modern Korean, expressively related to 찌푸리다 ('to frown').

history.meaning: to screw up one's face, wince
to frown, grimace, wince

찢다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb 찢다 ('to rend, rip apart paper or cloth'), descended from Middle Korean 찟다/찢다 with initial tense affricate ㅉ iconically evoking the sharp parting of fibres. Its intransitive counterpart 찢어지다 ('to get torn') is formed productively with the auxiliary -어지다.
찢다.notes: Commonly collocates with 반으로 ('tear in half') or 갈기갈기 ('tear to shreds').

찢어지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 찢다 ('to tear, rip, rend', Middle Korean 찟다) + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다.

history.meaning: to tear, rip
to be torn, get ripped, split apart

차.etymology: Represents two core Sino-Korean nouns borrowed from Middle Chinese: 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, car, train') and 차 (茶, 'tea'); also represents 차 (差, 'difference, gap') and 차 (次, 'order, next, for the purpose of').

history.form: 車 / 茶 / 差 / 次 (차)
history.meaning: vehicle, carriage / tea / difference / order, occasion
car, vehicle; tea; difference; bound noun for purpose/occasion

차갑다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective derived from the stem of 차다 ('to be cold, icy', Middle Korean ᄎᆞ다) + the adjectival suffix -갑-.

history.meaning: to be cold
to be cold to the touch, chilly, cold-hearted

차다.etymology: Convergence of several native Korean verbs and adjectives from Middle Korean: (1) 츠다 > 차다 ('to kick'), (2) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to become full, be filled'), (3) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to be cold, icy'), and (4) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to wear or fasten at the waist or wrist').

history.meaning: to kick / to be full; to be cold; to wear at the waist
to kick; to be full; to be cold; to wear (a watch or belt)

차라리.etymology: Native Korean modal adverb (고유어) descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 챀히 (chalh-i) and 차라리 (chalali, "rather, preferably, instead"), derived from the obsolete verbal root 챀- (chalh-, "to choose, prefer, select as better") suffixed with the adverbializer -이 / -리. Through liquid assimilation and vowel reanalysis (챀히 > 차라히 > 차라리), it grammaticalized into a standalone adverb introducing a preferable second-best choice or lesser evil.

history.meaning: by choosing as better; rather, preferably
rather, preferably, instead (choosing a lesser evil)

morphemes.meaning: historical root *챀- (to choose, prefer) + adverbial suffix -리 (fused in Modern Korean)

차라리.notes: Unlike English "preferably" (which can sound optimistic), 차라리 almost always implies that the current situation is so bad that you would rather endure a different (often dramatic) alternative: "차라리 날 죽여라!" ("Just kill me instead!").

rootFamily.gloss: rather than that, if that's the case (frequent collocation)
at least, if nothing else (semantic companion in concession clauses)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차라리

차례.etymology: Sino-Korean 차례 (次例), compounding 차 (次, 'order, sequence, next') and 례 (例, 'rule, custom, precedent'); homophonous with 차례 (茶禮, 'traditional holiday ancestral memorial rite').

history.meaning: sequential order / ancestral tea rite
order, turn, table of contents; ancestral rite

차리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb (고유어) continuing 15th-century Middle Korean 차리다 (chali-ta, "to prepare, equip, arrange, put in order, gather one's wits"). Spanning both material arrangement—setting a meal table (밥상을 차리다), opening a shop (가게를 차리다), or dressing up (차려입다)—and psychological or social composure, it forms core idioms for regaining mental focus (정신을 차리다) and observing proper etiquette (예의를 차리다, 격식을 차리다).

history.meaning: to prepare, equip, arrange in order, or collect one's mind
to set (a table), open (a business), dress up, or pull together (one's wits/manners)

차리다.notes: The military and school command "차렷!" ("Attention!") is the direct imperative/abrupt root form of 차리다 (short for 정신/자세를 차려, "pull your posture/wits together!").

rootFamily.gloss: table setting, menu spread, outfit/attire (deverbal noun)
to dress up, deck oneself out (차리- + -어 + 입다)
table setting, full meal spread (상 + 차림)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차리다

차림.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun formed from 차리다 ('to prepare, set out, dress up, equip') + the substantive suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: dress, attire, outfit; table setting or preparation

차분하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from the root 차분- ('calm, settled, composed') + the adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be calm, composed, quiet and steady

차원.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written as 次元, composed of 차 (次, "order, sequence, degree, tier") and 원 (元, "origin, fundamental element, basis"). Originally coined in Meiji-era Japanese (次元, jigen) to translate English/Latin mathematical and physical dimension (as in 3차원, "three dimensions", corresponding to algebraic degree/order 次 of a fundamental variable 元) and borrowed into Korean, where it expanded into everyday administrative and conversational usage to mean "level, tier, scope, or perspective" (e.g., 팀 차원에서, "at the team level").

history.meaning: mathematical and spatial dimension (coined translation of Latin dimensio)
spatial/mathematical dimension; institutional level, scope, or plane of comparison

차원.notes: Very frequent in workplace Korean in the pattern [Noun] 차원에서 ("at the [team/company/preventive] level" or "as a matter of...") and in the idiom 차원이 다르다 ("to be on a whole different level").

rootFamily.gloss: four-dimensional; (slang) quirky, eccentric person living in their own world

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차원

차이.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) from Literary Sinitic 差異, a coordinate compound of 차 (差, "to diverge, fall short, differ; discrepancy") and 이 (異, "different, distinct, other"). Attested in Classical Chinese philosophical and historical treatises (such as the Xunzi and Book of Han) and borrowed into Korean, where it serves as the primary everyday noun for any quantitative gap, margin, or qualitative difference between things.

history.meaning: divergence, discrepancy, or distinction between things
difference, gap, disparity, or margin

차이.notes: Often shortened to just 차 (差) when attached directly after another noun: 나이 차이 -> 나이 차 ("age gap"), 시간 차이 -> 시차 ("time difference / jet lag"), 점수 차 ("score margin").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차이

차주.etymology: Sino-Korean noun (한자어) written as 車主, compounded from 차 (車, "wheeled vehicle, cart, carriage; automobile") and 주 (主, "master, owner, host, principal"). While 車 originally denoted horse-drawn carts or chariots in Classical Chinese, in Modern Korean 차주 specifically refers to the registered owner or driver of an automobile.

history.meaning: owner of a cart, wagon, or carriage
registered owner or driver of a motor vehicle

차주.notes: Watch out for a common workplace homophone: 차주 (車主, "car owner") vs. 차주 (次週, "next week", used in formal schedules and broadcasting meetings alongside 금주 "this week" and 전주 "last week").

rootFamily.gloss: landlord, building owner (家主 / 建物主, sharing -주 主 "owner")
advertiser, sponsor (廣告主, sharing -주 主)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차주

차지하다.etymology: Formed from 차지 ('taking possession, share, charge', attested in Joseon administrative usage as 차디 次知 'person in charge, custody') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: custody, charge, taking possession
to occupy, take possession of, win, account for

cognates.meaning: selecting and dispatching personnel for a special task

차출되다.etymology: Sino-Korean passive verb formed from 차출 (差出, "selecting and dispatching personnel for a special duty"), composed of Hanja 差 (차, "to dispatch, send on an errand, select") and 出 (출, "to go out, send out"), combined with the native Korean passive-inchoative suffix -되다 ("to become, to be done"). In institutional and broadcasting contexts, it denotes being drafted or pulled from one's regular team to staff an urgent project or new program.

history.meaning: selecting and sending out officials or soldiers for a specific duty
to be drafted, seconded, or reassigned to a special task

차출되다.notes: Often used in workplace and TV production settings when staff or assistant directors (FDs/PDs) are involuntarily pulled onto a struggling show or special broadcast.

rootFamily.gloss: selection and dispatch for special duty

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 차출되다

착각하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 착각 (錯覺, "illusion, misapprehension, mistaken belief"), composed of Hanja 錯 (착, "intertwined, disorderly, mistaken, wrong") and 覺 (각, "to perceive, awaken, sense"), plus the native light verb suffix -하다 ("to do"). Originally coined in East Asian psychology to translate perceptual illusion (German Sinnestäuschung), it broadened in everyday speech to mean laboring under a mistaken impression.

history.meaning: perceptual illusion or confused awareness
to misperceive, be mistaken, or harbor a delusion

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving active verbs (to do)

착각하다.notes: In K-dramas and everyday banter, 착각하지 마 ("Don't flatter yourself / Don't get the wrong idea") is a classic retort when someone misreads politeness as romantic interest.

착석.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 착석 (着席, "taking one's seat"), composed of Hanja 着 (착, "to attach, reach, arrive at, put on", a variant of 著) and 席 (석, "woven mat, seat, place"). Because traditional East Asian seating used floor mats (席), "arriving at one's mat" naturally lexicalized into taking one's assigned seat at a ceremony, banquet, or broadcast hall.

history.meaning: reaching and sitting upon one's mat at an assembly
taking one's seat (in formal venues, auditoriums, or transit)

morphemes.meaning: to arrive at, attach, come into contact with
mat, seat, place at a gathering

착석.notes: Belongs to formal and institutional register—commonly heard in award-show cues, auditorium announcements ("착석해 주시기 바랍니다"), and aviation prompts.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 착석

착오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 착오 (錯誤, "mistake, error, mix-up"), formed from two near-synonymous Hanja roots: 錯 (착, "to cross, mix up, go awry, err") and 誤 (오, "to err, mistake, miss, deceive"). Already attested in Classical Chinese histories (such as the Book of Han) for administrative orcalculative blunders, it entered Korean as an analytical term for procedural errors or plans going awry.

history.meaning: intertwined error; administrative or factual blunder
mistake, mix-up, or miscalculation in planning or execution

착오.notes: Frequently paired with 시행 (試行) in the four-character expression 시행착오 (試行錯誤, "trial and error"), or used with 생기다/빚어지다 when a scheduling or administrative mix-up occurs.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 착오

착하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb (adjective) evolving from Early Modern and Late Middle Korean 챡ᄒᆞ다 (chyakhoda) / 댝ᄒᆞ다 (tyakhoda), originally meaning "to be upright, proper, and closely adhering to what is right." Some Korean historical linguists connect the root 댝-/챡- to Sino-Korean 着 (착/댝, "to adhere, be settled"), though in Modern Korean it functions purely as a native stem meaning "good-natured, kind-hearted, gentle, well-behaved."

history.meaning: to be upright, proper, and honest in conduct
history.stage: Late Middle / Early Modern Korean (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: to be kind-hearted, gentle, mild, and well-behaved

착하다.notes: Beyond praising children or kind people, 착하다 is used in contemporary slang for consumer-friendly prices ("착한 가격", an affordable/fair price).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 착하다

찬물.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 찬 ('cold', adnominal participle of 차다 'to be cold', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆫ) + 물 ('water', Middle Korean 믈).

history.meaning: cold water
cold water

찬바람.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 찬 (adnominal form of 차다, "to be cold, chilly", from Middle Korean ᄎᆞ다) + 바람 ("wind, breeze", from Middle Korean ᄇᆞᄅᆞᆷ). Literally "cold wind," it denotes both an autumn/winter chill and, figuratively, a frosty atmosphere, harsh reception, or sudden downturn in interpersonal or professional warmth.

history.meaning: cold wind blowing in autumn or winter
cold breeze; figuratively, an icy atmosphere or cold shoulder

morphemes.meaning: adnominal modifier suffix for descriptive verbs

찬바람.notes: The idiom 찬바람이 불다 ("a cold wind blows") vividly describes a tense office mood, a struggling economy, or someone giving the cold shoulder ("찬바람이 쌩쌩 불다").

rootFamily.gloss: to be cold to the touch or in temperature

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찬바람

찬성하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 찬성 (贊成, joining 贊 'to assist, praise, endorse' and 成 'to accomplish, bring to completion'—helping a proposal succeed) plus native 하다. In both formal votes and everyday conversation, 찬성하다 is the direct antonym of 반대하다 (反對하다, 'to oppose').
찬성하다.notes: Takes dative particle -에 on the proposal or plan supported (계획에 찬성하다).

찬스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed in the 20th century from English chance (frequently reinforced via Japanese チャンス, chansu), which itself derives from Old French cheance ("fall of the dice, fortune, befalling") and ultimately from Late Latin cadentia ("a falling", from Classical Latin cadere, "to fall"). In Korean, its semantic range narrowed from neutral "probability" to a specifically positive "golden opportunity" or a special lifeline/perk in games and variety shows.

history.meaning: falling of dice; random fortune or probability
favorable opportunity, scoring break, or special lifeline/perk

찬스.notes: Unlike English "chance" (which can mean neutral probability or risk), Korean 찬스 almost always means a favorable opportunity, a sports scoring break, or a variety-show lifeline (e.g., 지인 찬스, "calling-a-friend perk", or 엄카 찬스, "using Mom's credit card").

rootFamily.gloss: using a friend or connection as a lifeline/favor

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찬스

찰떡.etymology: Native Korean compound noun composed of the determiner prefix 찰- ("glutinous, sticky, cohesive", derived from the root of 차지다/찰지다, Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆯ-) + 떡 ("steamed or pounded rice cake", Middle Korean ᄯᅥᆨ). Because pounded glutinous rice (찹쌀) binds together with extraordinary elasticity and adhesion, 찰떡 became the archetypal Korean metaphor for inseparable closeness, Chemistry, and spot-on fit.

history.meaning: pounded rice cake made from glutinous grain
glutinous rice cake; metaphor for perfect harmony or fit

찰떡.notes: In contemporary Korean pop culture, 찰떡 is used predicatively ("완전 찰떡이다!") to mean a role, outfit, or hairstyle suits someone to perfection, and in 찰떡궁합 ("sticky-rice-cake marital harmony") for an unbeatable duo.

rootFamily.gloss: to be sticky, glutinous, or delightfully punchy in texture/speech

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찰떡

찰떡같이.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb formed from the compound noun 찰떡 ("glutinous rice cake", from 찰- "sticky" + 떡 "rice cake") + the comparative adjective stem 같- (from 같다, "to be like, identical to", Middle Korean ᄀᆞᇀ다) + the adverbializer suffix -이. Literally "like sticky rice cake," it evokes the way glutinous rice dough adheres firmly and seamlessly, evolving into an idiomatic adverb meaning "with spot-on accuracy, seamlessly, or with instant comprehension."

history.meaning: sticking fast like glutinous rice cake; firmly and seamlessly

찰떡같이.notes: Famous in the proverb 개떡같이 말해도 찰떡같이 알아듣다 ("Even if someone speaks like a coarse bran cake [badly/vaguely], you understand it like a fine sticky rice cake [spot-on]")—essential praise for a sharp junior PD or assistant!

rootFamily.gloss: like a coarse/messy rice cake (sloppily, vaguely)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찰떡같이

참.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ ('truth, reality; truly, really, very'); also used as an interjection upon sudden recollection ('oh, by the way!').

history.meaning: truth, genuineness; truly
really, truly, very; truth; oh! (interjection)

참나.etymology: Colloquial native Korean compound interjection coalescing from the discourse interjection 참 ("truly, really, honestly!", from Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ, "truth, reality") and the first-person singular pronoun 나 ("I, me", Middle Korean 나), elliptically truncating a bewildered self-directed clause such as "참, 나(는 기가 막혀서)..." ("Truly, I [am left speechless]..."). It expresses exasperation, disbelief, or scoffing amusement at someone's audacity or absurdity.

history.meaning: truth/truly + I (literal lexical components)
Unbelievable! Well, I never! (elliptical exclamation of dumbfoundedness)

morphemes.meaning: truly, really, for crying out loud

참나.notes: Often preceded by 아 or 어이없어서 ("아, 참나, 어이가 없어서!") accompanied by a short, dry scoff when someone says something brazen or nonsensical.

참나무.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 참 ('true, genuine, fine', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ) + 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모), literally 'true tree', designating oak trees (genus Quercus).

history.meaning: oak tree
oak, oakwood

참다.etymology: Native Korean transitive and intransitive verb directly inherited from Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ다 (chomda, "to endure, bear, hold back, restrain oneself"), attested in 15th-century texts such as the Seokbo Sangjeol (1447) and Worin Seokbo (1459). With the loss of the vowel ㆍ (arae-a) in Early Modern Korean, ᄎᆞᆷ다 regularly shifted to 참다, maintaining its core meaning of suppressing an impulse (laughter, anger, tears, bodily urges) or enduring hardship.

history.meaning: to bear, endure, restrain an impulse or suffering
to endure, put up with, hold back, suppress

참다.notes: Used both for enduring external mistreatment (고통을 참다) and physically holding back internal reactions (웃음을 참다 "hold back laughter", 눈물을 참다 "hold back tears", 화를 참다 "keep one's temper").

rootFamily.gloss: while holding back reluctantly; unable to bear it any longer

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 참다

참새.etymology: Native Korean compound noun combining the prefix 참- ('true, genuine, quintessential', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ-, also seen in 참나무 'oak' and 참기름 'sesame oil') with 새 ('bird'). Because tree sparrows nested under every Korean eave and courtyard roof, they were named the quintessential everyday 'true bird'.
참새.notes: Featured in the famous proverb 참새가 방앗간을 그냥 지나치랴 ('Can a sparrow pass a mill without stopping?').

cognates.meaning: attendance at a meeting or ceremony

참석하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 참석 (參席, "attendance at a meeting or seat"), composed of Hanja 參 (참, "to participate, join, attend, consult") and 席 (석, "woven mat, seat, assembly place"), followed by the native verbalizer -하다 ("to do"). It literally signifies joining the mats/seats of an assembly and is the standard formal verb for attending conferences, ceremonies, press briefings, or weddings.

history.meaning: joining the seats of a formal gathering or council
to attend, be present at a meeting or official event

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving active verbs (to do)

참석하다.notes: Takes the locative particle -에 (회의에 참석하다, "attend a meeting"). Contrast with 참여하다 (參與하다, "to participate/take active part in an activity") and 참가하다 (參加하다, "to enter a contest or event").

rootFamily.gloss: absence from a meeting or seat

찻숟가락.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 차 (茶, 'tea') via the native genitive linking consonant ㅅ (사이시옷, as in 찻잔 'teacup' and 찻주전자 'teapot') with native Korean 숟가락 ('spoon', from Middle Korean 술 'spoon' + 가락 'slender stick'). Together 찻숟가락 names both a small spoon for stirring tea and the baking measure.
찻숟가락.notes: Also called 티스푼 in modern café menus and recipes.

찻잔.etymology: Compound of Sino-Korean 차 (茶, 'tea') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 잔 (盞, 'cup').
찻잔.notes: Written with linking ㅅ because both nouns are established monosyllabic Sino-Korean roots acting like native compounds.

찻주전자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 차 (茶, 'tea') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 주전자 (酒煎子, 'spouted kettle or pot').

history.meaning: teapot

찻집.etymology: A compound of 차 'tea' and native 집 'house', joined by the linking ㅅ (사이시옷) written under 차.
찻집.notes: The same linking ㅅ appears in 찻잔 'teacup'.

창가.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window') + native Korean 가 ('edge, border, side', Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ).

history.meaning: by the window, windowside

창고.etymology: Sino-Korean 창고 (倉庫), compounding 창 (倉, 'granary, storehouse') and 고 (庫, 'storehouse, depot, treasury').

history.meaning: granary and storehouse
warehouse, storeroom, shed

창문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 창문 (窓門), joining 창 (窓, 'window') and 문 (門, 'door, opening').
창문.notes: Traditional Korean architecture built lattice windows that swing or slide like small doors, making 창문 completely natural.

창밖.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window') + native Korean 밖 ('outside, exterior').

history.meaning: outside the window

창피하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb derived from 창피 (猖披, originally written 猖披 or 昌披 in Classical Chinese, notably in Qu Yuan's Chuci / Li Sao), composed of Hanja 猖 (창, "mad, wild, unrestrained") and 披 (피, "to spread open, dishevel, wear loosely unfastened"), plus -하다. In Classical Chinese, 猖披 described walking about with one's robes unfastened and hair disheveled in frantic disorder; in Korean, the image of public dishabille shifted semantically to the social mortification and embarrassment of being seen in an unseemly state.

history.meaning: with garments unfastened and hair disheveled; wild and disorderly in appearance
to be shameful, unsightly, or socially embarrassing

창피하다.notes: Although speakers today feel 창피하다 as an everyday native-like word for "embarrassing/humiliating," its origin in Classical Chinese 猖披 ("garments flying open") explains why expressions like 창피를 당하다 ("suffer public embarrassment") carry such strong visual stigma of "losing face."

rootFamily.gloss: to feel ashamed or embarrassed (psychological verb)

창피해하다.etymology: Derived psychological action verb constructed from the Sino-Korean adjective 창피하다 (猖披하다, "to be embarrassing, shameful") + the psychological verbalizer construction -어하다 (realized as -여하다 > -해하다 after 하다), which converts subjective internal-state adjectives into observable transitive/action verbs usable with third-person subjects. Thus, while 창피하다 describes a state ("I am embarrassed / It is embarrassing"), 창피해하다 describes someone actively feeling or showing embarrassment ("He feels ashamed of...").

history.meaning: to feel or manifest embarrassment/shame toward something

창피해하다.notes: Korean grammar restricts bare subjective adjectives (창피하다, 슬프다, 기쁘다) to 1st-person statements or 2nd-person questions; to say a 3rd person "feels embarrassed by X" (or to use the object marker -을/를), you must use 창피해하다.

rootFamily.gloss: to be embarrassed or bashful (native synonym)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 창피하다

찾다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 찿다 ('to seek, look for, find, visit').

history.meaning: to look for, seek, visit
to look for, find, retrieve, visit

찾아가다.etymology: Native Korean serial-verb compound formed from 찾다 ("to seek, look for, visit", from Middle Korean 챳다, chatda) + the infinitive/connective suffix -아 + the directional verb 가다 ("to go", Middle Korean 가다). Literally "to seek and go," it lexicalized into a single verb meaning "to go visit someone/somewhere with a purpose" or "to go claim/retrieve something."

history.meaning: to seek out and go toward a person or place
to go visit, call on someone, or go retrieve

morphemes.meaning: to go (away from speaker's deictic center)

찾아가다.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes deictic direction in visiting verbs: 찾아가다 means going away from the current location to visit someone, whereas 찾아오다 means someone coming to visit the speaker's location.

rootFamily.gloss: to look for, seek, visit, withdraw (money)
to come visit, come looking for
to try looking for, search for, visit and see

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찾아가다

찾아보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 찾다 ("to look for, search, seek", Middle Korean 챳다) + connective suffix -아 + the auxiliary/experiential verb 보다 ("to see, to try doing", Middle Korean 보다). Combining the action of searching with the tentative aspect of -아/어 보다 ("try doing and see"), it means "to look up (information), search around for, or pay a visit to see someone."

history.meaning: to try searching for; to seek out and see

찾아보다.notes: Has two high-frequency senses: (1) searching for information/items ("인터넷에서 찾아보다", look it up online) and (2) paying a polite visit to an elder or superior ("선생님을 찾아뵙다/찾아보다").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찾아보다

찾아오다.etymology: Native Korean serial-verb compound formed from 찾다 ("to seek, look for, visit", from Middle Korean 챳다) + connective suffix -아 + the deictic motion verb 오다 ("to come", Middle Korean 오다). Literally "to seek and come," it denotes someone coming toward the speaker's location to visit, seek help, or reclaim an object, or figuratively a season or state (like peace or crisis) arriving.

history.meaning: to come seeking a person or object
to come visit, come looking for, or arrive (of a season/moment)

찾아오다.notes: Frequently used metaphorically for abstract arrivals: 봄이 찾아오다 ("spring comes calling"), 위기가 찾아오다 ("a crisis arrives"). In workplace dramas, 누군가 찾아왔는데요 means "Someone has come here looking for you."

rootFamily.gloss: to search for; to pay a visit

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 찾아오다

채.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('while still in the state of, just as it is'), descending from Middle Korean 채; also a native Korean counter for buildings or houses, blankets, and hand-pulled vehicles.

history.meaning: intact state, just as it is; counter for houses or curtains
while/with (state intact); counter for buildings; whip/rod

채널.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English channel, which came via Old French chanel ("bed of a waterway, pipe, groove") from Latin canalis ("water pipe, groove, canal", a derivative of canna, "reed, hollow tube"). Adopted into Korean alongside radio and television broadcasting in the mid-20th century to denote a broadcast frequency band or station, and later extended to communication pathways and online streaming accounts.

history.meaning: reed pipe, water conduit, navigable strait, communication band
television/radio broadcast channel, communication avenue, or media stream

morphemes.meaning: broadcast or communication channel (from English channel)

채널.notes: In Korean TV industry jargon (as in *The Producers*), 채널을 돌리다 means "to change/flip the channel" (originally from turning a rotary dial on older TV sets), and 채널 고정 ("Keep it locked on this channel!") is the classic host catchphrase before a commercial break.

rootFamily.gloss: locking onto a channel ("Don't touch that dial!")
channel surfing / flipping rights (slang: remote-control power)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 채널

채소.etymology: Sino-Korean 채소 (菜蔬), compounding 채 (菜, 'edible greens, vegetables') and 소 (蔬, 'edible herbs, greens').

history.meaning: edible greens and herbs, vegetables
vegetables, greens

채우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 채오다 / 채우다, derived from 차다 ('to become full' and 'to wear/fasten').

history.meaning: to make full, fill; to fasten
to fill up, satisfy; to lock, button, or buckle

채워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb built by layering the auxiliary passive construction -어지다 onto the transitive causative verb 채우다 ("to fill, make full"), which itself derives from the intransitive verb 차다 ("to become full, be filled", Middle Korean ᄎᆞ다) + the causative suffix -이우- (Middle Korean ᄎᆡ오다 / ᄎᆡ우다). Literally "to become filled," it highlights either a resulting state of fullness or an external filling process (such as a broadcast runtime, quota, or emotional void being filled).

history.meaning: to be full > to cause to be full, to fill up
to be filled up, become fulfilled or replenished

채워지다.notes: Although 차다 is already intransitive ("to get full"), speakers prefer 채워지다 when emphasizing that an intentional slot, quota, air-time, or emotional emptiness has been filled by something or someone.

rootFamily.gloss: full, 가득 차다 (to be brimming full)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 채우다

책.etymology: Sino-Korean 책 (冊, 'book, volume, register'), originally depicting bound bamboo or wooden writing slips in Old Chinese.

history.meaning: bound writing tablets, book, volume
book

책갈피.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound pairing Sino-Korean 책 (冊, 'book') with native Korean 갈피 ('the narrow gap, fold, or boundary between overlapping layers', also preserved in 갈피를 못 잡다 'unable to get one's bearings'). Originally denoting the space between two leaves of a book where pressed flowers or notes rest, 책갈피 also came to mean a physical bookmark.

책꽂이.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining Sino-Korean 책 (冊, 'book') with native Korean 꽂이 (formed from the verb root 꽂- 'to insert upright, stick in' plus instrument/place suffix -이, as in 연필꽂이 'pencil holder' and 옷걸이 'coat hanger'). Unlike a floor-to-ceiling 책장, 책꽂이 highlights a compact shelf or rack where books slot neatly side by side.

책등.etymology: Hybrid anatomical metaphor combining Sino-Korean 책 (冊, 'book') with native Korean 등 ('human or animal back, ridge'). Just as English speaks of a book's 'spine' and French of its 'dos', Korean names the bound outer ridge where pages hinge together 책등 ('book-back').
책등.notes: Pronounced [책뜽] with regular tensification after coda ㄱ.

책상.etymology: Sino-Korean 책상 (冊床), compounding 책 (冊, 'book') and 상 (床, 'table, low platform, stand').

history.meaning: reading and writing table
desk

책임.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 책임 (責任, "responsibility, duty, accountability"), composed of Hanja 責 (책, "to demand, exact, reprove, duty, charge") and 任 (임, "to entrust, bear a load, office, duty"). While both characters carried senses of official duty in Classical Chinese, the compound 責任 was popularized across East Asia during the late 19th century (via Meiji Japanese legal and philosophical translations of English responsibility and German Verantwortung) to denote moral, legal, and institutional accountability.

history.meaning: demanding fulfillment of an entrusted official charge; legal and moral responsibility
responsibility, duty, accountability, or person in charge (in compounds)

morphemes.meaning: duty, charge, to hold accountable, reprove
to entrust, bear a burden, official post

책임.notes: In Korean broadcasting, 책임 프로듀서 (CP, Chief Producer) translates "Executive/Chief Producer"—literally the producer who bears ultimate institutional responsibility (책임) for a group of programs.

rootFamily.gloss: to take responsibility, bear the blame/duty
person in charge, chief responsible officer

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 책임

책임감.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic noun 책임감 (責任感, "sense of responsibility"), formed by suffixing the productive Sino-Korean noun 감 (感, "feeling, sense, perception") to 책임 (責任, "responsibility, duty", from 責 "duty, demand" + 任 "entrusted burden, office"). It denotes the subjective moral conscientiousness that compels a person to see an entrusted task through to completion.

history.meaning: subjective feeling or awareness of one's duty and accountability
sense of responsibility, conscientiousness

책임감.notes: Idiomatically paired with 강하다 or 투철하다 ("책임감이 강하다/투철하다", to have a strong/thoroughgoing sense of responsibility) or 무겁다 ("책임감이 무겁다", to feel the heavy weight of responsibility).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 책임감

책임지다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 책임 (責任, "responsibility, accountability", from 責 "duty, reproof" + 任 "entrusted load") + the native Korean transitive verb 지다 ("to carry on one's back, bear a load, owe", from Middle Korean 지다). Because 任 originally meant carrying a burden on a shoulder pole, combining 책임 with native 지다 ("to shoulder on the back") preserves the concrete metaphor of carrying a weight on one's own shoulders.

history.meaning: to shoulder a duty on one's back; to take full accountability for outcomes

morphemes.meaning: to carry on the back, bear a burden, shoulder

책임지다.notes: A staple of K-drama dialogue: "내가 책임질게" ("I'll take responsibility / I'll see it through") can range from a boss covering for a team's broadcast mistake to an old-fashioned romantic pledge to take care of someone.

rootFamily.gloss: to carry luggage/burden on one's back; to bear a load

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 책임지다

책장.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean compounds: 책장 (冊欌, 'bookcase, bookshelf', from 冊 'book' + 欌 'cabinet, cupboard') and 책장 (冊張, 'page or leaf of a book', from 冊 'book' + 張 'sheet').

history.meaning: book cabinet / sheet of a book
bookcase, bookshelf; page of a book

챙겨주다.etymology: Native Korean benefactive compound verb composed of 챙기다 ("to gather up, pack in order, look after, take care of", derived from Early Modern Korean 챵기다, related to keeping things neat and complete without omission) + connective suffix -어 (contracted with -기- to -겨) + the benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give, to do for someone's benefit", Middle Korean 주다). Together it expresses thoughtfully looking out for someone, making sure they eat or have what they need.

history.meaning: to gather and put in order > to thoughtfully look after or pack things for someone

morphemes.meaning: to pack, gather without omission, look after
benefactive auxiliary (to give, do for someone)

챙겨주다.notes: A culturally central warmth word in Korean workplaces and families: "잘 챙겨주다" describes a senior (선배) or colleague who remembers your meals, covers your blind spots, and looks out for your well-being.

rootFamily.gloss: to pack, keep track of, look after, take for oneself
to make sure to eat (a meal) properly

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 챙기다

챙기다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested since early Modern Korean as 챵기다 / 챙기다 ('to gather and pack tightly, make sure to take along; to look after').

history.meaning: to put in order, gather up, pack
to pack, remember to bring; to take care of, look after

처리.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 처리 (處理, "handling, processing, settlement, disposal"), composed of Hanja 處 (처, "to dwell, situate, manage, decide, deal with") and 理 (리/이, "veins in jade, pattern, principle, to put in order, regulate"). Attested in Tang-era Classical Chinese for managing official affairs according to proper order, it now covers everything from administrative paperwork and waste disposal to computer data processing and audio/video post-production (e.g., mosaic or bleeping edits).

history.meaning: managing and putting affairs in proper order; adjudicating matters
handling, processing (tasks, data, edits, or waste), settlement

morphemes.meaning: to manage, deal with, situate, decide
to put in order, regulate, principle

처리.notes: In TV editing (*The Producers*), 처리 appears constantly in technical compounds like 모자이크 처리 ("blurring/pixelating a face on screen"), 삐 처리 ("bleeping out profanity"), and 편집 처리 ("handling an issue via editing").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 처리

처음.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 처섬 ('beginning, start, first time'), evolving through 처엄 to modern 처음 via loss of intervocalic ㅿ.

history.meaning: beginning, start, first time
beginning, first time; for the first time

처음이야.etymology: Native Korean inflected predicative phrase consisting of the noun 처음 ("the beginning, the first time") + the informal (반말) copula -이야 (composed of the copula stem 이- after a consonant + the intimate/informal indicative ending -야, reduced from -아). The noun 처음 itself evolved regularly from 15th-century Middle Korean 처섬 (cheseom, "beginning, start") via the loss of intervocalic ㅅ (ㅿ) in the 16th century (처섬 > 처엄 > 처음).

history.meaning: the beginning, outset, first time (via loss of medial ㅅ/ㅿ)
history.stage: Middle Korean (15th c.) to Modern Korean

history.meaning: it is the first time; you are the first (informal copular predicate)

morphemes.meaning: beginning, first time (from Middle Korean 처섬)

처음이야.notes: A quintessential K-drama trope line: "이런 기분 처음이야" ("This is the first time I've ever felt this way") or "너 같은 사람은 처음이야" ("You're the first person like this I've ever met"). Politer equivalents are 처음이에요 and 처음입니다.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 처음

처지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 처지 (處地, "situation, circumstances, plight, standing"), formed from Hanja 處 (처, "to dwell, be situated in, place") and 地 (지, "earth, ground, place, position"). Literally "the ground/place where one is situated," it developed primarily in Korean usage to denote a person's social footing, predicament, or the awkward position one finds oneself in relative to others.

history.meaning: the place or ground in which one resides or stands
one's personal situation, social standing, or plight

처지.notes: Often carries a nuance of humble or constrained circumstances, as in "내 처지에 무슨..." ("In my position/plight, how could I possibly afford/do...") or the idiom 동병상련의 처지 ("being in the same boat / sharing the same plight").

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 처지

척.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('pretense, feigned air', used in -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다), attested since early Modern Korean (쳑 / 척); also Sino-Korean 척 (隻, counter for ships) and 척 (尺, traditional foot unit).

history.meaning: feigned appearance, pretense
act of pretending (bound noun); counter for boats (隻)

척척.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic/ideophonic adverb describing actions carried out smoothly, briskly, and without a hitch ('smoothly, right away, one after another').

history.meaning: smoothly and promptly, without hesitation; sticking closely

척하다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary verb formed from the bound noun 척 ('pretense, outward show') + the verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to pretend, feign, act as though

천.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 천 (千, 'one thousand'); homophonous with native Korean noun 천 ('woven cloth, fabric') and Sino-Korean 천 (天, 'sky, heaven').

history.meaning: one thousand
thousand; cloth, fabric

천년보살.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound noun 천년보살 (千年菩薩, literally "thousand-year Bodhisattva"), combining 천년 (千年, from 千 천 "thousand" + 年 년 "year") with 보살 (菩薩, abbreviation of 보리살타 菩提薩埵, the Middle Chinese phonetic transcription of Sanskrit bodhisattva, "a being bound for enlightenment who acts with infinite compassion and forbearance"). In colloquial Korean, calling someone a 보살 (or intensified as 천년보살) humorously praises—or marvels at—someone who endures outrageous provocation with saintly, millennia-deep patience.

history.form: bodhisattva > 菩提薩埵 > 菩薩 (보살)
history.meaning: enlightened compassionate being in Mahayana Buddhism
thousand-year Bodhisattva; figuratively, a person of saintly, superhuman patience

morphemes.meaning: Bodhisattva (from 菩提薩埵 < Sanskrit bodhisattva); saintly person or female Buddhist layperson/shaman

천년보살.notes: In Korean variety shows and everyday slang, 보살 ("Bodhisattva/saint") is used whenever someone puts up with an impossible boss, partner, or teammate without losing their temper; adding 천년 ("a thousand years") exaggerates their ancient, unshakable serenity. Also used by fortune-tellers as a title.

rootFamily.gloss: Bodhisattva; figuratively, a saintly, infinitely patient person

천만다행.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character expression 천만다행 (千萬多幸), compounding 천만 (千萬, 'ten million, myriad, exceedingly') and 다행 (多幸, 'great good fortune, lucky', from 多 'much' + 幸 'fortune').

history.meaning: a stroke of immense good fortune
great relief, stroke of huge luck ('thank goodness')

천박하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from 천박 (淺薄, "shallow and thin; superficial, vulgar, base"), composed of Hanja 淺 (천, "shallow, not deep, superficial") and 薄 (박, "thin, meager, frivolous, ungenerous"), plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다. In Classical Chinese, 淺薄 primarily described shallow scholarship or meager virtue; in Modern Korean, it additionally took on a strong social-register judgment meaning "vulgar, tacky, crass, or lacking refinement" (often mentally associated by speakers with 賤 천, "lowly/cheap", though etymologically spelled 淺薄).

history.meaning: shallow in water or depth; superficial in learning or thin in virtue
to be shallow, superficial, vulgar, crass, or lowbrow

천박하다.notes: A sharp, cutting word used to criticize speech, humor, or taste as "crass, lowbrow, or shallow" (e.g., 천박한 농담 "a vulgar joke", 자본주의의 천박함 "the crassness of commercialism").

천이백육호.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral-classifier compound 천이백육호 (千二百六號, "Room/Unit 1206"), constructed regularly from Sino-Korean cardinal numerals 千 (천, "1,000") + 二 (이, "2") + 百 (백, "100") + 六 (육/륙, "6") + the bound noun classifier 號 (호, "number, mark, designation, room/unit/issue"). Note the phonological rule whereby 백 (baek) + 육 (yuk) undergoes ㄴ-insertion and nasalization in standard pronunciation as [처니뱅뉵호 / cheonibaengnyukho] when read as a full thousand-hundred number, though apartment units are also frequently read digit-by-digit in casual speech (일동 이백육호 or 천이백육호).

history.meaning: designated number 1,206 (used for rooms, apartment units, or serials)

morphemes.meaning: number, room/apartment unit, issue, train car

천이백육호.notes: In Korean apartment complexes, unit numbers (호, 號) combine the floor number and the unit number: 천이백육호 (1206호) means the 12th floor (12층), unit 06 (6호). Watch the pronunciation: 백 + 육 triggers ㄴ-insertion and velar nasalization → [뱅뉵호].

rootFamily.gloss: room number, unit number, issue number

천장.etymology: Sino-Korean 天障, literally the 'sky screen' above a room.

천재적.etymology: Sino-Korean derivative 天才的, formed by adding the determiner-noun suffix -적 (的, 'having the quality of') to 천재 (天才, 'heaven-bestowed talent, genius', from 天 'heaven, innate' + 才 'talent, ability'). In Korean syntax, 천재적 combines with the copula 이다 (천재적이다, 천재적이라고) or the adnominal 의 (천재적인) to mean 'brilliant, a stroke of genius'.

천천히.etymology: Attested in Middle and early Modern Korean as 쳔쳔히 ('slowly, unhurriedly'), formed from reduplicated 천천 (originally linked to Sino-Korean 儃儃 'leisurely, unhurried') + the native adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: leisurely, unhurriedly, slowly
slowly, unhurriedly, take one's time

철대문.etymology: Sino-Korean 철대문 (鐵大門), formed from 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') + 대문 (大門, 'main gate of a house', from 大 'large, main' + 門 'gate, door').

history.meaning: iron main gate

철문.etymology: Sino-Korean 철문 (鐵門), compounding 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') and 문 (門, 'door, gate').

history.meaning: iron gate, steel door
iron door, heavy metal gate

철물점.etymology: Sino-Korean 철물점 (鐵物店), formed from 철물 (鐵物, 'ironware, hardware, metal tools', from 鐵 'iron' + 物 'articles, goods') + 점 (店, 'shop, store').

history.meaning: hardware store

철사.etymology: Sino-Korean 철사 (鐵絲), compounding 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') and 사 (絲, 'thread, filament, wire').

history.meaning: iron thread, metal wire
wire, metal wire

cognates.meaning: thoroughness, completeness, going all the way to the bottom
thorough, complete, to the very bottom (chèdǐ)

철저하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from 철저 (徹底, "penetrating all the way to the bottom; thoroughness"), composed of Hanja 徹 (철, "to penetrate, pierce through, pervade, clear") and 底 (저, "bottom, base, foundation, underneath"), plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다. Originally a vivid Classical Chinese visual image of clear water seen all the way to the riverbed (徹見底), it metaphorically evolved across East Asia to mean "exhaustive, rigorous, leaving nothing overlooked."

history.meaning: piercing or seeing clear through to the very bottom of water or a vessel
to be thorough, exhaustive, scrupulous, and uncompromising

철저하다.notes: Both adverbial idioms 철저히 and 철저하게 ("thoroughly, strictly") are high-frequency in professional contexts—such as 보안이 철저하다 ("security is airtight") or 자기관리가 철저하다 ("to be rigorously disciplined in self-management", a key compliment for celebrities).

rootFamily.gloss: staying up all night (piercing through the night)

철저히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean adverb formed from the Sino-Korean root 철저 (徹底, 'penetrating all the way to the bottom'), composed of 철 (徹, 'to pierce, penetrate, go through') and 저 (底, 'bottom, base, foundation'), combined with the productive native Korean adverbial suffix -히 (derived from the light verb stem 하- plus adverbial -이). Literally 'so as to reach the very bottom', hence 'thoroughly, strictly, exhaustively'.

history.meaning: reaching to the very bottom of water or a vessel (Classical Chinese metaphor for exhaustiveness)
thoroughly, strictly, completely

철저히.notes: Pairs naturally with verbs of preparation, investigation, or secrecy (e.g., 철저히 준비하다 'prepare thoroughly', 철저히 숨기다 'hide strictly'); its adjectival counterpart is 철저하다.

rootFamily.gloss: staying up all night (piercing the night, 徹夜)

cognates.meaning: hatred that pierces the heavens; mortal enmity
cognates.word: 徹天之怨 / 彻天之冤

철천지원수.etymology: Sino-Korean four-plus-two-character idiomatic compound 철천지원수 (徹天之怨讐), composed of 철 (徹, 'pierce, penetrate'), 천 (天, 'heaven, sky'), the Classical Chinese associative particle 지 (之, 'of, that which'), 원 (怨, 'resentment, grievance'), and 수 (讐, 'enemy, foe', historically read 수 from Middle Korean 원싀 < 怨讎). Literally 'an enemy whose caused resentment pierces all the way to heaven', denoting a mortal or sworn enemy.

history.meaning: bitter enemy, object of resentment
an enemy toward whom one's grievance pierces heaven; mortal enemy

철천지원수.notes: Although gravely dramatic in origin, in modern K-dramas and everyday speech it is frequently used hyperbolically for bickering rivals, ex-partners, or siblings.

rootFamily.gloss: grievance that pierces heaven (徹天之恨)

철칙.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 철칙 (鐵則), formed from 철 (鐵, 'iron', used metaphorically for unyielding hardness and permanence) and 칙 (則, 'rule, law, principle'; read 칙 rather than 즉 when meaning 'rule'). Borrowed into modern Korean alongside Meiji/Taisho Japanese 鉄則 (tessoku) as a calque of European expressions like German 'ehernes Gesetz' ('iron law'), denoting an inviolable rule.

history.meaning: unbreakable law or principle, hard as iron
ironclad rule, absolute principle

철칙.notes: Notice the dual Sino-Korean reading of 則: it is read 칙 (chik) in nouns meaning 'rule' (규칙, 원칙, 철칙) but 즉 (jeuk) as a formal conjunction meaning 'namely, immediately'.

첫.etymology: Native Korean determiner descending from Middle Korean 첫 ('first, initial'), sharing a historical root with 처음 ('beginning, first time').

history.meaning: first, initial
first, maiden, initial

첫날.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 첫 ('first') + 날 ('day', Middle Korean 날).

history.meaning: the first day
the first day, opening day

첫방.etymology: Hybrid broadcasting abbreviation combining the native Korean determiner 첫 ('first', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 첫, derived from the root 첮- 'beginning') with 방 (放), the clipped initial syllable of the Sino-Korean noun 방송 (放送, 'broadcast, transmission', literally 'releasing and sending out'). Coined in television and radio industry jargon for a program's premiere episode.

history.meaning: first broadcast of a program
premiere broadcast, debut airing

morphemes.kind: clipped root (Hanja 放 from 放送)

첫방.notes: Part of a productive television/idol-industry clipping series in -방 (-放): 첫방 ('premiere broadcast'), 막방 ('final broadcast', from 마지막 방송), 본방 ('live/original broadcast', 本放), and 재방 ('rerun', 再放).

첫사랑.etymology: Native Korean compound noun (*고유어*) composed of the pre-noun determiner 첫 ('first', Middle Korean 첫) and the noun 사랑 ('love, affection', from Middle Korean ᄉᆞ랑 'thought, reflection, affection', nominalized from the verb stem ᄉᆞ랑ᄒᆞ- 'to think of fondly, to love'). Literally 'first love', referring to one's earliest romantic attachment.

history.meaning: first + thought, longing, affection
first romantic love

첫사랑.notes: Pronounced [첟싸랑] with automatic post-obstruent tensification of ㅅ to ㅆ after the final stop [ㄷ] of 첫; a quintessential trope across Korean cinema and television dramas.

첫째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral formed from 첫 ('first') + the ordinal suffix -째 ('-th in order').

history.meaning: first, firstly; eldest child

청구하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 청구 (請求, 'request, claim, demand for payment'), formed from 청 (請, 'to ask, request, invite') and 구 (求, 'to seek, demand, strive for'), with the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). In modern legal and commercial usage, it specialized from 'politely asking and seeking' into 'filing a formal claim' or 'billing an expense'.

history.meaning: to request earnestly, seek something from another
to bill, charge, claim formally (damages, expenses, rights)

청구하다.notes: Used in everyday life for billing receipts and expense reimbursements (비용을 청구하다) as well as legal/insurance claims (손해배상을 청구하다).

청동.etymology: Sino-Korean metallurgy compound 靑銅, joining 靑 (푸를 청, 'blue-green, patina-coloured') and 銅 (구리 동, 'copper'). Named in classical East Asian antiquity after the distinctive bluish-green patina that tin-copper alloy develops over centuries, 청동 contrasts with 황동 (黃銅, 'yellow copper = brass') and 적동 ('red copper').
청동.notes: Compare 황동 ('brass') used for the guesthouse keys and pocket compass.

cognates.meaning: liquidation, settlement of accounts or past affairs
to clear accounts, liquidate, settle scores

청산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 청산 (清算), composed of 청 (清, 'clear, pure, clean') and 산 (算, 'to calculate, reckon, count with counting rods'). Originally a bookkeeping term meaning 'to tally and clear all outstanding accounts cleanly', it broadened metaphorically to mean liquidating a business, paying off debts, or making a clean break with a troubled past or relationship.

history.meaning: calculating and settling financial accounts completely
settling debts, liquidation; wiping the slate clean of past ties or history

청산.notes: Don't confuse with homophones 청산 (青山, 'green mountains') or 청산 (青酸, 'prussic acid/cyanide'); in drama dialogue, 과거를 청산하다 means 'to make a clean break with one's past'.

rootFamily.gloss: to liquidate, settle accounts or the past
calculation, reckoning, paying the bill (計算)

청소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 청소 (清掃), formed from 청 (清, 'clear, clean, pure') and 소 (掃, 'to sweep with a broom, brush away', written with the hand radical 扌 and broom 帚). Literally 'making clean by sweeping', serving as the standard everyday Korean noun for housecleaning or tidying a space.

history.meaning: sweeping away dirt to make a place pure and clean
cleaning, sweeping, tidying up a room or area

청소.notes: While 세탁 (洗濯) or 빨래 refers to washing laundry and 설거지 refers to washing dishes, 청소 specifically covers sweeping, vacuuming, wiping, and tidying rooms or buildings.

cognates.word: 青少年期 (せいしょうねんき, seishōnenki)

청소년기.etymology: Sino-Korean four-morpheme compound 청소년기 (青少年期), built from 청소년 (青少年, 'youth and adolescents' — itself condensing 청년 青年 'green/young years, young adult' and 소년 少年 'few years, boy/juvenile') plus the temporal bound morpheme -기 (期, 'period, phase, stage'). Literally 'the life stage of green and few years', i.e., adolescence.

history.meaning: young people, juveniles and young adults
the period of adolescence, teenage developmental stage

청소년기.notes: Unlike 사춘기 (思春期, 'puberty / rebellious teen phase'), 청소년기 is a neutral developmental, sociological, and legal term for the entire adolescent period (roughly ages 9–24 under Korean youth law, or teenage years generally).

cognates.word: 清掃する (せいそうする, seisō suru)

청소하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do') to the Sino-Korean noun 청소 (清掃, from 清 'clean, clear' + 掃 'to sweep with a broom'). Literally 'to do cleaning and sweeping', serving as the standard transitive and intransitive verb for cleaning a room, house, or workplace.

history.meaning: to sweep and make clean
to clean, tidy up, vacuum or sweep a space

청소하다.notes: Can be used either as a single compound verb taking a location as direct object (방을 청소하다 'to clean the room') or separated with an object particle (청소를 하다 'to do the cleaning').

청춘.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 청춘 (青春), composed of 청 (青, 'blue-green, verdant') and 춘 (春, 'spring'). Derived from traditional Chinese Five Phases (五行) cosmology, in which the season of spring corresponds to the eastern direction, the wood element, and the color blue-green (青) of sprouting vegetation; 'verdant spring' came to signify the prime springtime of human life, i.e., youth.

history.meaning: verdant springtime (in Five Elements cosmology and Classical Chinese poetry)
youth, the springtime or prime of one's life

청춘.notes: Evokes a poetic, nostalgic, or passionate nuance ('the springtime of life') compared to the matter-of-fact 청년 ('young adult') or native 젊음 ('youthfulness').

cognates.word: 体育大会 (たいいくたいかい, taiiku taikai)

체육대회.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 체육대회 (體育大會), joining 체육 (體育, 'physical education, athletics', from 體 'body' + 育 'nurture, cultivate, educate') with 대회 (大會, 'grand assembly, tournament, meet', from 大 'great, large' + 會 'gathering, meeting'). Refers to a school, company, or community sports day or athletic festival.

history.meaning: physical cultivation + grand gathering/tournament
sports day, intramural or company athletic meet

체육대회.notes: In Korean workplace culture (featured prominently in *The Producers*), a 사내 체육대회 ('company sports day') is a major team-building event where departments compete fiercely in tug-of-war, foot volleyball (족구), and relay races.

rootFamily.gloss: school sports day, field day (運動會)

체인지.etymology: Direct loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English *change* (which entered Middle English from Old French *changier*, ultimately from Late Latin *cambiāre* 'to barter, exchange', of Gaulish/Celtic origin). Adapted to Korean phonology as 체인지 by breaking the consonant clusters and diphthong /eɪ/ into disyllabic 체인- and inserting epenthetic -지 for final /-dʒ/.

history.meaning: to barter, exchange, alter
swap, substitution, switch (of roles, players, partners, or image)

체인지.notes: While general 'change' is expressed by native 바꾸다 or Sino-Korean 변화 (變化)/교체 (交替), 체인지 is used in entertainment, sports, and variety shows for swapping partners, roles, or style makeovers.

체크.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English *check* (ultimately from Old French *eschec*, Persian *šāh* 'king' in chess, where calling 'check' meant arresting or verifying the king's position, later broadening to 'control, verify, mark off'). Adapted into Korean with aspirated ㄱ (ㅋ) and an epenthetic vowel ㅡ to resolve the final voiceless velar stop /k/.

history.meaning: chess check -> restraint -> verification, tick mark, checkered pattern
verification, checking, tick mark; plaid/checkered pattern; hotel check-in/out

체크.notes: Covers both 'verification/inspection' (스케줄 체크 'schedule check', 마이크 체크 'mic check') and 'plaid/checkered fabric' (체크무늬 'checkered pattern'), though 'bank check' is Sino-Korean 수표 (手票).

체크인.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English check-in ('registration upon arrival at a hotel, airport, or venue').

history.meaning: arrival registration at a hotel or airport
check-in

체크인하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from the English loanword 체크인 (check-in) + the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to check in (at a hotel or airport)

체크하다.etymology: Hybrid verbal construction combining the English loanword 체크 (*check*, from Old French *eschec* < Persian *šāh*) with the productive native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). Used across workplace, media production, and everyday registers to mean 'to check, verify, monitor, or tick off'.

history.meaning: to do a check, verify, mark off

체크하다.notes: In office and broadcasting settings, 체크하다 is slightly brisker and more casual than Sino-Korean 확인하다 (確認하다, 'to confirm/verify') or 점검하다 (點檢하다, 'to inspect').

체하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the single-character Sino-Korean root 체 (滯, 'to stagnate, block up, obstruct, fail to circulate') and the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do/be'). Originating in traditional East Asian medicine where 식체 (食滯, 'food stagnation') describes undigested food blocking the stomach's qi flow, 체하다 means 'to suffer acute indigestion or feel food stuck in one's chest/stomach'.

history.meaning: to become blocked or stagnant in digestion
to have an upset stomach or acute indigestion (feeling food sitting heavy in the stomach)

morphemes.meaning: to be in a state of, do

체하다.notes: Do not confuse with the homonym 체하다 ('to pretend, feign', as in 아는 체하다 'pretend to know', derived from 體 'form/manner'); culturally, Koreans often prick the thumb when someone 체하다 ('gets acute indigestion from eating too fast or under stress').

쳐놓다.etymology: Native Korean serial verb compound (*고유어*) combining 쳐 — the contracted infinitive form (치- + -어) of the polysemous native verb 치다 (Middle Korean 치다, 'to strike, pitch a tent/net, draw a line, or cause/commit an incident', as in 사고를 치다 'cause an accident/mess') — with the auxiliary verb 놓다 (Middle Korean 놓다, 'to put down, leave in a resulting state'). Literally 'to strike/cause/set up and leave it in that state'.

history.meaning: to pitch/strike/make and leave in place
to have set up beforehand (a net, curtain, barrier) or to have caused/perpetrated (trouble) with lasting consequences

morphemes.meaning: connective (-어 contracted with 치- to 쳐)
put, leave a resulting state in place

쳐놓다.notes: With 사고 (事故, 'accident/trouble'), 사고를 쳐놓다 means 'to have gone and caused a big mess (that now has to be cleaned up)'; with physical objects like 커튼 or 그물, it means 'to keep curtains drawn / a net pitched'.

rootFamily.gloss: to put, release; auxiliary of resultant state
to put aside, leave done (치- + -어 + 두다)

쳐다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 치어다보다, formed from 치- ('upward') + connective -어다 + 보다 ('to look, see').

history.meaning: to look upward at, gaze at
to look up at, look squarely at, stare at

쳐들어가다.etymology: Native Korean trimorphemic compound verb (*고유어*) formed from 쳐 (치- 'to strike, attack, storm' + infinitive -어), 들- (from 들다, Middle Korean 들다 'to enter, go inside', connected via -어), and 가다 (Middle Korean 가다 'to go'). Originally a military expression meaning 'to attack and advance into enemy territory', it broadened in everyday speech to mean 'to barge in, storm into someone's room, house, or office unannounced'.

history.meaning: to attack and advance into (a fortress or territory)
to invade, raid; (colloquial) to barge in, storm into a place

쳐들어가다.notes: Contrast directional pair 쳐들어가다 ('barge in [going there]') with 쳐들어오다 ('barge in [coming here toward the speaker]').

rootFamily.gloss: to invade, barge in toward the speaker (치- + 들어오다)

쳐지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb construction combining 쳐 — the contracted infinitive (치- + -어) of the transitive verb 치다 ('to draw a line/mark, pitch a tent/curtain, or strike') — with the inchoative/passive auxiliary verb -지다 (Middle Korean 지다, 'to fall, become'). Literally 'to come to be drawn, marked, or pitched' (e.g., 밑줄이 쳐지다 'an underline gets drawn', 커튼이 쳐지다 'a curtain is drawn').

history.meaning: to become struck, pitched, or drawn
to be drawn/marked (of lines), to be pitched/put up (of curtains/nets); also a frequent non-standard spelling of 처지다 ('to sag, lag behind')

쳐지다.notes: Important orthography trap: when passive of 치다 ('a line is drawn' 줄이 쳐지다 / 'a curtain is drawn' 커튼이 쳐지다), it is spelled 쳐지다; when meaning 'to droop, sag, feel down, or lag behind', standard Korean orthography requires 처지다 (without ㅕ).

rootFamily.gloss: to draw a line, pitch a tent, strike
to droop, sag, lag behind (standard spelling)

초.etymology: Represents several common words: (1) native/nativized 초 ('candle', Middle Korean 초, early borrowing from Chinese 燭 'torch, candle'), (2) Sino-Korean 초 (秒, 'second of time'), (3) Sino-Korean 초 (初, 'beginning, early part'), and (4) Sino-Korean 초 (醋, 'vinegar').

history.form: 초 (< 燭) / 秒 / 初 / 醋 (초)
history.meaning: candle / second / beginning / vinegar
candle; second (unit of time); beginning of a period; vinegar

cognates.word: 招待する (しょうたいする, shōtai suru)

초대하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound combining 초대 (招待, 'invitation'), formed from 초 (招, 'to beckon with the hand, summon, invite') and 대 (待, 'to wait for, treat, entertain hospitably'), with the native Korean light verb -하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to beckon a guest and treat them hospitably', hence 'to invite'.

history.meaning: beckoning a guest and entertaining them hospitably
to invite (someone to a home, event, broadcast, or gathering)

초대하다.notes: Whereas 초대하다 is used for social, personal, or festive invitations (parties, homes, weddings, talk-show guests), 초청하다 (招請하다) is more formal and institutional (official speakers, state guests).

cognates.meaning: elementary school (historical/formal term for primary level)
cognates.word: 初等学校 (しょとうがっこう, shotō gakkō)

초등학교.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 초등학교 (初等學校), composed of 초등 (初等, 'primary grade, elementary level', from 初 'beginning, first' + 等 'rank, grade, level') and 학교 (學校, 'school', from 學 'study, learn' + 校 'school, enclosure'). Adopted officially in South Korea in 1996 to replace 국민학교 (國民學校, a colonial-era calque of German *Volksschule* via Japanese).

history.form: 國民學校 (국민학교) -> 初等學校 (초등학교)
history.meaning: replaced colonial-era 'national school' with 'elementary-grade school' in 1996
elementary school, primary school (grades 1–6 in South Korea)

초등학교.notes: Because South Korea changed 국민학교 to 초등학교 on March 1, 1996, Koreans often joke about generational divides based on whether someone graduated from a 국민학교 or a 초등학교.

초딩.etymology: Colloquial South Korean slang abbreviation coined in early 1990s PC telecom chatrooms (originally modeled on 고딩 from 고등학교/고등학생, where 등 等 'grade' was playfully altered by vowel fronting to -딩). Formed from 초 (初, 'elementary', clipped from 초등학교 初等學校 or 초등학생 初等學生) plus the slang suffix -딩 ('schooler, student'). Literally 'grade-schooler', often used figuratively for someone acting childishly.

history.meaning: elementary school student (clipped and suffixed with slang -딩)
grade-schooler, elementary kid; (figurative/teasing) childish or immature person/taste

morphemes.kind: clipped root (Hanja 初 from 初等學生)

초딩.notes: Frequently used as a teasing modifier for childish behavior or sweet/simple food preferences (e.g., 초딩 입맛 'having a grade-schooler's palate' — loving sweet sauces, sausages, and hating bitter vegetables).

초라하다.etymology: Descriptive adjective built from the bound root 초라- ('shabby, worn-out, meager, pitiful in appearance') and the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (Early Modern Korean 초라ᄒᆞ다). While treated synchronically as a native word (*고유어*), philologists note a likely phonological reduction from Sino-Korean 초췌하다 (憔悴하다, 'haggard, gaunt, withered') or 소략하다 (疎略하다, 'rough, meager'), reshaped into native root structure.

history.meaning: to be shabby, worn-out, or scant in appearance
shabby, dingy, pitiful, humble or lonely in appearance

morphemes.meaning: to be in a state of

초라하다.notes: Describes both physical shabbiness (초라한 행색 'shabby attire') and emotional vulnerability when one's situation looks small or pathetic next to splendid surroundings (초라해 보이다 'to look pitiful/small').

rootFamily.gloss: to become shabby or feel small/pitiful (초라해 + -지다)

초록.etymology: Sino-Korean 초록 (草綠), compounding 초 (草, 'grass, plants') and 록 (綠, 'green'), literally 'grass green'.

history.meaning: grass green
green, grass green

초록색.etymology: Sino-Korean 초록색 (草綠色), formed from 초록 (草綠, 'grass green') + 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: green color

초벌칠.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 초- (初, 'first, initial') + native Korean 벌 ('round, layer, set') + Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, paint, coating').

history.meaning: first coat of paint or plaster, primer coat, undercoat

초인종.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 초인종 (招人鐘): 초 (招, 'summon, invite') + 인 (人, 'person') + 종 (鐘, 'bell').
초인종.notes: Literally 'a bell for calling someone'—the everyday Korean word for a doorbell or room buzzer.

초조.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 초조 (焦燥), formed from 초 (焦, 'to scorch, char, burn over fire', written with 隹 'bird' over 灬 'fire') and 조 (燥, 'dry, parched, arid', written with 火 'fire'). Literally 'scorched and parched', a vivid physiological metaphor for the burning, dry-mouthed restlessness and fretful anxiety one feels while waiting nervously for an outcome.

history.meaning: scorched and parched by heat; burning with impatience or worry
nervousness, fretfulness, anxious impatience

초조.notes: Unlike 불안 (不安, general 'unease/insecurity') or 긴장 (緊張, 'tension/stage fright'), 초조 specifically captures the restless, clock-watching fretfulness of waiting for results (e.g., TV viewership ratings or exam scores).

초조해하다.etymology: Derived psychological verb formed from the Sino-Korean descriptive adjective 초조하다 (焦燥하다, 'to be anxious, fretful', from 焦 'scorch/fret' + 燥 'parched/restless') by attaching the auxiliary verbalizer -어하다 (-하- + -어 + -하다 -> -해하다). In Korean grammar, adding -어하다 converts an internal subjective emotion adjective into an active, observable behavioral verb meaning 'to feel and show anxiety'.

history.meaning: to be fretful, anxious (subjective state adjective)
to feel anxious, act fretfully, show nervousness (observable third-person or active process verb)

초조해하다.notes: Korean emotion adjectives like 초조하다 cannot directly describe a third person's inner state in declarative sentences (*그가 초조하다 sounds like narration); speakers use the -해하다 verb form (그가 초조해한다 'he is feeling/acting anxious') instead.

초짜리.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Korean bound counter noun 초 (秒, 'second of time or arc', originally denoting the fine beard/awn at the tip of a grain of rice 禾, hence a minute fraction) with the native Korean suffix -짜리 ('something worth, lasting, or measuring [X]', historically derived from Middle Korean 쟉 'measure/pair' + nominal suffix). Used after a number (e.g., 5초짜리 'a 5-second-long [clip]') to denote something lasting only a given number of seconds.

history.meaning: a unit measuring N seconds in duration or value

morphemes.meaning: having the duration, value, or age of

초짜리.notes: In television editing and advertising, N초짜리 (e.g., 15초짜리 예고편 'a 15-second teaser', 3초짜리 카메오 'a 3-second cameo') emphasizes how brief a segment or cut is.

rootFamily.gloss: second hand of a watch (秒針)

초콜릿.etymology: Loanword (*외래어*) borrowed from English *chocolate*, which came via Spanish *chocolate* from Classical Nahuatl *xocolātl* (traditionally analyzed from *xococ* 'bitter' + *ātl* 'water', referring to the spiced Mesoamerican cacao drink). Standardized in South Korean orthography as 초콜릿 (representing English /-lɪt/), replacing older Japanese-influenced variants like 초코렛.

history.meaning: bitter cacao drink -> solid or liquid cacao confection
chocolate (standardized spelling in 1986 loanword orthography)

초콜릿.notes: While the full word is spelled 초콜릿, in compounds and casual speech it is regularly clipped to 초코 (e.g., 초코우유 'chocolate milk', 초코파이 'Choco Pie', 민트초코 'mint chocolate').

cognates.meaning: tactile sense; feelers/antennae (used in 'stretching one's feelers')
cognates.word: 触覚 / 触 (しょっかく / しょく)

촉.etymology: Colloquial single-syllable noun clipped from Sino-Korean 촉감 (觸感, 'sense of touch, tactile impression') or 촉각 (觸覺, 'sense of touch; insect antenna/feeler'), written with the Hanja 촉 (觸, originally 'to butt with horns' 角 + 蜀, extended to 'to touch, contact, feel'). Metaphorically likens human intuition or a gut hunch to sensitive antennae detecting subtle signals.

history.meaning: tactile sense, feelers/antennae of an organism
hunch, gut instinct, intuitive sixth sense (as in 촉이 좋다 / 촉이 오다)

촉.notes: Extremely common in Korean variety shows, detective dramas, and daily conversation in the idioms 촉이 오다 ('to get a hunch/vibe') and 촉이 좋다 ('to have sharp intuition/sixth sense'); homophonous with native 촉 ('nib, tip, arrowhead').

rootFamily.gloss: sense of touch, tactile feeling (觸感)

촉촉하다.etymology: Native Korean sensory adjective built on the reduplicated mimetic root 촉촉- ('pleasantly damp, dewy, tender without wetness') plus -하다. Unlike 젖다 ('soaked, wet') or 습하다 ('uncomfortably humid'), 촉촉하다 carries warm positive connotations—celebrating tender baked crumb, morning dew on leaves, or eyes misting with emotion.
촉촉하다.notes: Adverbial form 촉촉이 or 촉촉하게 is ubiquitous in Korean baking.

촛불.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from 초 ('candle', nativized in Early Modern Korean from Middle Korean 쵹, the Sino-Korean reading of 燭 'torch, candle'), the native Korean genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (*사이시옷*, from Middle Korean genitive particle ㅅ), and native Korean 불 ('fire, light', Middle Korean 블). Literally 'candle's fire', hence 'candlelight' or a lit candle flame.

history.meaning: flame of a wax or tallow candle
candlelight, candle flame (also symbolic of peaceful vigils)

촛불.notes: Because 초 ('candle', historically from 燭) was fully nativized after losing its final ㄱ, Korean spelling rules treat 초 + 불 as a native-type compound and insert the *sai-siot* (ㅅ), yielding 촛불 [촏뿔 / 초뿔]; culturally iconic in 촛불집회 ('candlelight vigils').

촬영.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 촬영 (撮影), composed of 촬 (撮, 'to pinch with fingers, gather, take/capture an image', written with the hand radical 扌 and 最) and 영 (影, 'shadow, reflection, image, figure'). Coined in 19th-century East Asia as photography entered the region, literally meaning 'to capture a shadow/reflection', now the universal Korean noun for filming television/movies or taking professional photographs.

history.meaning: capturing a shadow/image on a photographic plate (19th-century photographic neologism)
filming, video shooting, cinema/TV production shoot, or professional photography

촬영.notes: Core vocabulary in *The Producers* (*프로듀사*): while casual phone snapshots are usually called 사진을 찍다, any television, film, YouTube, or studio shoot is referred to as 촬영 (e.g., 야외 촬영 'outdoor shoot', 촬영장 'filming set').

cognates.word: 撮影場 (さつえいじょう)

촬영장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 촬영 (撮影, "photographing, filming") and the locative suffix 장 (場, "place, ground, arena"). Coined in the modern era via Meiji Japanese 撮影 (satsuei, literally "capturing shadows/reflections") combined with 場 to designate a dedicated studio lot or active film set.

history.meaning: to pinch/gather + shadow/reflection + open ground/site

history.form: 撮影場 (さつえいじょう)
history.meaning: photographic studio or motion-picture shooting ground
filming set, studio lot, shooting site

촬영장.notes: Refers specifically to the active working production site or studio set where cameras and crew are operating, unlike 촬영지 which emphasizes the geographic destination.

rootFamily.gloss: filming location, tourist spot where a show was shot

촬영지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound combining 촬영 (撮影, "filming, photography", from 撮 "capture" + 影 "shadow/image") with the geographic suffix 지 (地, "earth, land, locality"). While 촬영 (撮影) entered Korean through modern Japanese photographic terminology, attaching 지 (地) specifies a geographical locale where a movie or drama was shot on location.

history.meaning: to gather/capture + shadow/image + land/locality
geographical site of photography or filming
filming location, on-location shooting site

촬영지.notes: Often used in Korean tourism and media (e.g., 드라마 촬영지, "drama filming location") when fans visit real-world neighborhoods or landmarks featured on screen.

cognates.word: 撮影する (さつえいする)

촬영하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ("to do") to the Sino-Korean verbal noun 촬영 (撮影, "photography, filming"). 撮影 was coined in 19th-century Japan from Classical Chinese 撮 ("to pinch together, gather, capture") and 影 ("shadow, optical image") to translate Western photography and later cinematography.

history.meaning: capturing an optical image; photography
photography, motion picture filming
to film, shoot, or photograph

촬영하다.notes: More formal and technical than native 찍다 ("to snap/shoot"); broadcast crews say 촬영하다 for scheduled production shoots, whereas casual speakers use 사진을 찍다 for everyday snapshots.

최고.etymology: Sino-Korean 최고 (最高), compounding the superlative prefix 최- (最, 'most, supreme') and 고 (高, 'high, tall, lofty').

history.meaning: highest, supreme
the highest, the best, top-notch

최근.etymology: Sino-Korean word from 최근 (最近), composed of the superlative prefix 최 (最, "most, extreme, utmost") and 근 (近, "near, close"). Originally denoting spatial or temporal proximity ("nearest, closest") in Classical and Middle Chinese, it became specialized in modern East Asian usage to mean "recent times" or "recently".

history.meaning: closest in distance or time; most proximate
the most recent period, lately, nowadays

최근.notes: Functions both as a noun ("recent times", often with 에 as 최근에 "recently") and adnominally before nouns; slightly more formal than native Korean 요즘 ("these days").

최소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 최소 (最小), formed from the superlative prefix 최 (最, "most, utmost") and 소 (小, "small, little, minor"). Attested in Classical Chinese for "the smallest in size or scale", it also acquired the quantitative and adverbial sense "minimum" or "at least" in modern Korean usage.

history.meaning: smallest in size, youngest in age, least in scale
minimum quantity/degree; adverbially "at least"

최소.notes: Distinguish 최소 (最小, smallest in size/scale or minimum threshold) from its homophone 최소 (最少, smallest in countable number, "fewest"), though 최소한 (最小限) covers "at least" generally.

rootFamily.gloss: at the very least, minimum limit (最小限)

최소한.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 最小限, formed from superlative prefix 最 (가장 최, 'most'), 小 (작을 소, 'small'), and 限 (한계 한, 'boundary, limit'). Literally 'the smallest possible limit', it functions adverbially in spoken Korean right before numbers or quantities to set a floor ('at the very least').
최소한.notes: Antonym is 최대한 (最大限, 'at most, to the fullest extent').

최악.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 최악 (最惡), combining the superlative prefix 최 (最, "most, extreme") and 악 (惡, "bad, evil, foul, unfavorable"). From meaning "the most wicked or dire" in literary Sinitic, it broadened in everyday Korean and Japanese to express any worst-case scenario or colloquially "the absolute worst!".

history.meaning: most wicked, foulest, worst in moral or material quality
worst-case scenario; colloquially "the worst!"

최악.notes: Used both in formal expressions like 최악의 상황 ("the worst-case situation") and as a standalone colloquial exclamation (최악이다! "It's the worst!") parallels to its antonym 최고 ("the best!").

추가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 추가 (追加), composed of 추 (追, "to pursue, follow after, retroactively supplement") and 가 (加, "to add, increase, attach"). Here 추 (追) carries the sense of "following up subsequently" (as in 추후 追後), so 추가 literally denotes "adding on afterward" to an existing amount, order, or document.

history.meaning: to confer or append subsequently after an initial act
addition, supplement, extra order or item

morphemes.meaning: to follow after, pursue, supplement subsequently (追)

추가.notes: Extremely common on Korean restaurant menus (e.g., 사리 추가 "add extra noodles") as well as in office and software contexts ("add file/item").

cognates.meaning: to add, to append, to supplement
