추가하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 추가 (追加, "addition, supplement", from 追 "follow after, subsequently" + 加 "add, increase") and the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do"). Signifies adding something afterward onto an already existing baseline, list, or order.

history.meaning: subsequent addition or supplementation
to add, append, or order extra

추가하다.notes: Unlike 더하다 ("to add together in arithmetic or general degree"), 추가하다 specifically implies appending an extra item, clause, or order onto what is already there.

cognates.meaning: to pursue, to seek after (a goal or ideal)
cognates.word: 追求する (ついきゅうする)

cognates.meaning: to pursue, to seek, to woo

추구하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining 추구 (追求, "pursuit, quest") with the native Korean verb-forming suffix -하다 ("to do"). The Sino-Korean root pairs 추 (追, "to chase, follow after") with 구 (求, "to seek, request, strive for"), originally describing physical or earnest seeking in Classical Chinese and now used primarily for abstract goals, ideals, or values.

history.meaning: to chase after and seek to obtain
earnest pursuit of an aim, value, or happiness
to pursue, seek after (an ideal, profit, or artistic style)

추구하다.notes: Used for abstract objects like happiness (행복을 추구하다), profit (이익을 추구하다), or artistic vision; for physically chasing a suspect or target, Korean uses 추적하다 instead.

추레하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb built from an expressive root 추레- ("shabby, bedraggled, worn-out and untidy") and the adjectival suffix -하다. Related by vowel-harmony and sound-symbolic alternation to 초라하다 ("shabby, poor-looking, pitiful") and dialectal/older forms like 추리하다, evoking a limp, damp, or unkempt physical appearance.

history.meaning: worn-out, shabby, wretched in appearance
shabby, scruffy, haggard, bedraggled

추레하다.notes: Describes clothes or a person's physical state looking rumpled, grimy, or haggard (e.g., after pulling an all-nighter in an editing room), whereas 초라하다 emphasizes looking pitifully poor or unimpressive in scale.

cognates.meaning: to deduce, to infer, to reason

추리하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining 추리 (推理, "inference, deduction, reasoning") with the native verb-forming suffix -하다 ("to do"). The Sino-Korean compound pairs 추 (推, originally "to push forward", extended in philosophical Chinese to "to extrapolate, extend a principle") with 리 (理, "pattern, principle, logic, reason"), meaning to push known facts forward to uncover hidden logic.

history.meaning: to extend a principle in order to judge or fathom a matter
logical inference, deductive reasoning, detective deduction
to deduce, infer logically, or sleuth out clues

추리하다.notes: Used both in formal logic and very frequently in pop culture for detective sleuthing (e.g., 추리 소설 "detective/mystery novel", 추리 예능 "mystery variety show").

추스르다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb 추스르다, historically attested in Early Modern Korean as 추슬우다 and 추스리다, formed from the upward/gathering verbal prefix 추- (seen in 추켜세우다 "to hoist/praise up" and 추어올리다 "to lift up") combined with a root related to 스르다/슬다 ("to gather, sort out, soothe"). Literally "to hitch up and put in order", it evolved to mean tending to one's body, clothes, or composure.

history.meaning: to hitch up, gather together, and set in order
to pull together (one's body, emotions, or affairs); to recover composure

morphemes.meaning: to gather, tend to, put in order (르-irregular stem)

추스르다.notes: A 르-irregular verb (conjugates as 추슬러, 추슬렀다); frequently collocates with 몸 ("body/health", 몸을 추스르다) or 마음/감정 ("emotions", 마음을 추스르다 "to pull oneself together emotionally").

rootFamily.gloss: to hoist up, to flatter/praise highly
to govern, manage, control (one's mind or realm)

추신.etymology: Sino-Korean epistolary term 追伸, combining 追 (쫓을 추, 'to follow after, append subsequently') and 伸 (펼 신, 'to unfold, set forth one's words'). Historically used at the close of traditional East Asian letters for an afterthought added once the main body and signature were finished, 추신 corresponds directly to Latin-derived English 'postscript (P.S.)'.
추신.notes: Written 추신: at the bottom of Korean letters and postcards.

추억.etymology: Sino-Korean 추억 (追憶), compounding 추 (追, 'follow back, retrace') and 억 (憶, 'remember, call to mind').

history.meaning: looking back and remembering, recollection
fond memory, reminiscence

cognates.word: 追越 (おいこし / ついえつ)

추월하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from 추월 (追越, "overtaking, passing") and the native verb suffix -하다 ("to do"). The Sino-Korean compound combines 추 (追, "to chase, pursue from behind") and 월 (越, "to cross over, pass beyond, exceed"), literally depicting chasing after a vehicle or competitor ahead and passing beyond them.

history.meaning: to chase after + to cross over/surpass
overtaking a vehicle or surpassing a rival from behind
to overtake, pass (in traffic or competition)

morphemes.meaning: to cross over, pass beyond, exceed (越)

추월하다.notes: Standard traffic term for passing another car in a lane (추월 차선 "passing lane"), and also used figuratively when a TV show's ratings or a company's sales overtake a rival's.

cognates.meaning: to track, to trace, to pursue
cognates.word: 追蹤 / 追踪 (zhuīzōng) / 追跡 (zhuījì)

추적.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 추적 (追跡), formed from 추 (追, "to chase, pursue") and 적 (跡, "footprint, track, trace"). Literally meaning "to follow footprints", it evolved from tracking game or fugitives on foot to investigative reporting, police pursuit, and data tracking.

history.meaning: to follow someone's footprints or trail; to pursue closely
tracking, hot pursuit, investigative tracing

추적.notes: A staple word in Korean investigative journalism and current-affairs TV titles (e.g., 추적 60분 "Tracking 60 Minutes"), emphasizing doggedly following a trail of evidence.

cognates.meaning: to speculate, to conjecture, to surmise

추측.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 추측 (推測), combining 추 (推, "to push forward, extrapolate, infer") and 측 (測, "to fathom, measure depth, gauge"). Originally drawing on the metaphor of sounding water depth (測) by extending from what is known (推), it denotes mental conjecture, speculation, or an educated guess.

history.meaning: to extrapolate from known signs and fathom what is unknown
conjecture, speculation, supposition, guess

추측.notes: Unlike 추리 (推理, rigorous logical deduction), 추측 (推測) implies an unverified guess or speculation (e.g., 추측성 기사 "speculative news article").

추후.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 추후 (追後), composed of 추 (追, "to follow after, subsequently") and 후 (後, "behind, later, after"). Used extensively in Joseon-era administrative documents and modern official notices to mean "at a later date" or "subsequently following the current action".

history.meaning: following afterward; at a subsequent time
later, at a future date, subsequently (often in official notices)

추후.notes: Belongs to formal and administrative register—very common in phrases like 추후 공지 ("to be announced at a later date") or 추후 일정 ("subsequent schedule").

축.etymology: Borrowed from Sino-Korean 축 (軸, "wheel axle, pivot, roller for a scroll"). From the concrete sense of a central axle or spindle around which things revolve or are grouped (and a counter for bundled scrolls), Korean grammaticalized 축 as a bound noun meaning "a group, party, or category of people/things sharing a trait" (e.g., 빠른 축에 속하다, "to belong to the fast category/group").

history.meaning: wheel axle; central pivot; roller for a mounted scroll
axis, pivot; bundle of scrolls or dried fish (counter)
group, cohort, or category on a spectrum (bound noun, especially with -에 속하다/끼다)

morphemes.meaning: axle, axis, pivot; extended to group/category (軸)

축.notes: In everyday speech, -(으)ㄴ/는 축에 속하다 (or 들다/끼다) is an idiomatic way to say someone "falls on the [adjective] side" or "counts among the [adjective] group" (e.g., 젊은 축에 속한다 "counts among the younger ones").

cognates.word: 祝歌 (しゅくか / しゅっか)

축가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 축가 (祝歌), formed from 축 (祝, "to pray for blessings, congratulate, celebrate") and 가 (歌, "song, singing"). While literally denoting any song of celebration or blessing, in contemporary South Korean culture it has become strongly specialized to mean a celebratory song performed live for the bride and groom at a wedding ceremony.

history.meaning: to invoke blessings/congratulate + song
celebratory or congratulatory song; specifically a wedding song

축가.notes: When Koreans say 축가를 부르다 ("to sing a 축가") without further context, it almost always refers to singing a special congratulatory ballad for friends or colleagues at their wedding.

cognates.word: 蹴球大会 (しゅうきゅうたいかい)
蹴球大會 / 蹴球大会 (cùqiú dàhuì)

축구대회.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 축구대회 (蹴球大會), combining 축구 (蹴球, "soccer/football", from 蹴 "to kick, tread" + 球 "ball, sphere") with 대회 (大會, "grand assembly, tournament, competition", from 大 "great, large" + 會 "gathering, meeting"). 蹴球 was coined in Meiji Japan to translate English association football and became the standard everyday word for soccer in Korean.

history.meaning: kicking a ball + great gathering/assembly

history.form: 蹴球大会 (しゅうきゅうたいかい)
history.meaning: football/soccer tournament or meet
soccer tournament, championship, or organized match event

축구대회.notes: While Japanese largely replaced 蹴球 (shūkyū) with the English loanword サッカー (sakkā) and Chinese uses 足球 (zúqiú), Korean retains 축구 (蹴球) as the universal everyday word for soccer.

rootFamily.gloss: athletic meet, sports day (體育大會)

cognates.word: 蹴球する (しゅうきゅうする)

축구하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from 축구 (蹴球, "soccer, football", composed of 蹴 "to kick" + 球 "ball") and the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do, play"). 蹴球 draws on the Classical Chinese term 蹴鞠 (cùjū, an ancient Chinese ball-kicking game), adapted in modern East Asia with 球 ("sphere/ball") to designate modern association football.

history.meaning: ancient Chinese and Korean game of kicking a stuffed leather ball
modern association football (soccer)
to play soccer

축구하다.notes: In Korean, ball sports ending in -구 (球) like 축구 (soccer), 야구 (baseball), 농구 (basketball), and 배구 (volleyball) all form verbs simply by adding -하다 (or using 치다/하다 depending on the sport).

축배.etymology: Sino-Korean 축배 (祝杯), from 축 (祝, 'celebrate, felicitate') + 배 (杯, 'cup, goblet').
축배.notes: Idiomatic in 축배를 들다 ('raise a celebratory glass / celebrate victory').

축제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 축제 (祝祭), composed of 축 (祝, "to invoke blessings, celebrate") and 제 (祭, "ritual sacrifice, solemn ceremony, festival"). Originally referring to religious or state rituals combining celebratory prayers (祝) and ceremonial offerings (祭), it broadened in modern Korean to denote any festive celebration, campus festival, or cultural carnival.

history.meaning: invocation of blessings + sacrificial rite/ceremony
national celebration and ceremonial feast day
festival, carnival, public or university celebration

축제.notes: Covers everything from university festivals (대학 축제) and film festivals (영화제) to lively neighborhood street festivals; carries a joyful, communal nuance despite 제 (祭) also appearing in 제사 ("ancestral memorial rite").

축축해지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative verb formed from the ideophonic adjective 축축하다 ('to be damp, moist, clammy') + the auxiliary construction -어지다 ('to become, grow').

history.meaning: to become damp, get moist or soggy

축하.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 축하 (祝賀), combining 축 (祝, "to pray for good fortune, invoke blessings, celebrate") and 하 (賀, "to congratulate, offer gifts in celebration"). Attested in Classical Chinese for offering formal felicitations on auspicious occasions, it is now the universal everyday Korean word for "congratulations" and "celebration".

history.meaning: to offer prayers of blessing and formal felicitations
congratulations, celebration of a happy occasion

축하.notes: Forms the ubiquitous greeting 축하합니다 / 축하해요 ("Congratulations!"), often paired with 생일 ("birthday"), 결혼 ("wedding"), or 승진 ("promotion").

축하드리다.etymology: Polite hybrid compound verb combining Sino-Korean 축하 (祝賀, 'celebration and felicitation', from 祝 'pray for blessing' + 賀 'congratulate with gifts') with the native Korean humble benefactive verb 드리다 ('to humbly offer or give to a respected person'). Replacing plain -하다 with -드리다 creates the warmest respectful way to congratulate an elder, colleague, or host.
축하드리다.notes: 축하드려요 and 축하드립니다 are the standard polite formulas for 'Congratulations!'

축하하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 축하 (祝賀, 'congratulation, celebration', compounding 祝 'pray for blessing, felicitate' and 賀 'congratulate, celebrate') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: felicitation and congratulation
to congratulate, celebrate

cognates.meaning: going to work, reporting to the office
to turn out for work, attendance rate

출근.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출근 (出勤), composed of 출 (出, "to go out, come forth, appear") and 근 (勤, "to toil, work diligently, perform official duty"). Literally "going out to perform one's duty", it pairs directly with its antonym 퇴근 (退勤, "withdrawing from duty / leaving work") to frame the daily workday commute.

history.meaning: to go forth + diligent labor/official service
reporting for duty at a government bureau or company office
going to work, clocking in at the workplace, morning commute

morphemes.meaning: to go out, appear, come forth (出)

출근.notes: Frequently combined with its opposite 퇴근 in the compound 출퇴근 ("commuting to and from work", e.g., 출퇴근 시간 "rush hour").

rootFamily.gloss: to go to work, report for duty

cognates.meaning: to go to work, to report to the office
cognates.word: 出勤する (しゅっきんする)

출근하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean verb-forming suffix -하다 ("to do") to 출근 (出勤, "going to work, reporting for duty", from 出 "go out, appear" + 勤 "work, official service"). Expresses both the act of commuting to the workplace and arriving on site to begin one's shift.

history.meaning: going forth to perform official duty or workplace labor
to go to work, commute to the office, report for duty

출근하다.notes: In Korean broadcasting and entertainment (like in *The Producers*), celebrity guests or idols arriving at a studio in the morning are playfully described as doing 출근길 ("the walk to work").

rootFamily.gloss: going to work, attendance at work (出勤)
to leave work for the day (退勤-)

cognates.meaning: presence, appearance in person (at a court or police station)
to show one's face, to rise above others, to appear publicly

출두.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출두 (出頭), literally "putting forth one's head", from 출 (出, "to put out, come forth") and 두 (頭, "head"). In Vernacular Chinese and traditional Korean/Japanese legal administration, "showing one's head" specialized to mean presenting oneself in person before a magistrate, investigative board, or government office, and in Joseon history also denoted the dramatic surprise appearance of a royal secret inspector (암행어사 출두).

history.meaning: to show one's face; to appear in person before a public authority
history.stage: Tang–Song Vernacular Chinese / Joseon administrative Korean

history.meaning: appearing in person before a court, prosecutor, or disciplinary board

morphemes.meaning: to come out, put forth, appear (出)

출두.notes: Carries a weighty, authoritative, or disciplinary ring (e.g., 검찰 출두 "appearing before prosecutors" or being summoned before a broadcasting ethics committee); also famous from the historical cry "암행어사 출두요!" ("The Royal Secret Inspector appears!").

rootFamily.gloss: to appear in person before an authority
advent, appearance of a prominent figure or thing (出現)
vanguard, the head/front of a line (先頭)

출력.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출력 (出力), composed of 출 (出, "to put out, emit, send forth") and 력 (力, "power, force, energy"). In Classical Chinese 出力 meant "to exert one's physical strength", whereas in modern East Asian engineering and computing it was adapted to translate English "output" (engine power output, audio/video signal output, and printing out documents on a printer).

history.meaning: to put forth physical strength or effort
mechanical or electrical power output; data output
power/signal output; printing out a document from a computer

morphemes.meaning: to put out, emit, send forth (出)

출력.notes: In Korean office life (such as TV station writers preparing scripts), 출력하다 / 출력물 almost always means "to print out on paper" / "a printout", alongside 프린트하다.

cognates.meaning: to set out, to depart, to start off

출발.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출발 (出發), formed from two synonymous directional verbs: 출 (出, "to go out, exit, emerge") and 발 (發, "to shoot forth, set out, dispatch, start"). Attested in Classical Chinese for troops or travelers setting forth on a journey, it serves in modern Korean as the standard noun for both physical departure and the beginning of an enterprise or broadcast.

history.meaning: to go forth and set out on a march or journey
departure of a person or vehicle; start of an event or venture

출발.notes: Used both literally for travel/vehicles (pairs with 도착 到著 "arrival") and figuratively for fresh starts (새 출발 "a new start") or energetic show titles (e.g., 출발! 드림팀 "Let's Go! Dream Team").

cognates.meaning: to depart, to set out, to start
cognates.word: 出発する (しゅっぱつする)

출발하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining 출발 (出發, "departure, setting out", from 出 "go out" + 發 "launch, set forth") with the native Korean light verb suffix -하다 ("to do"). Expresses leaving a starting point for a destination or beginning a race, journey, or new project.

history.meaning: setting forth on a journey; departure
to depart, head out, start off

출발하다.notes: In everyday conversation, 출발하다 is used not only for trains and planes ("to depart") but also casually among friends or production crews for "heading out now" (지금 출발해요 "I'm heading out now").

rootFamily.gloss: departure of a flight or ship (出航)
to depart, leave for a post or trip (出程-)

cognates.meaning: attendance, presence (at a meeting or class)
to attend, to be present at a meeting or banquet

출석.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출석 (出席), composed of 출 (出, "to come out, appear") and 석 (席, "woven mat, seat, place at a gathering"). Since people in traditional East Asia sat on woven mats (席) during assemblies and lectures, "coming out to one's mat/seat" came to mean formal attendance at school, a parliament session, or an official hearing.

history.meaning: to come forth + woven sitting mat / assigned seat
taking one's seat at an assembly, classroom, or tribunal; attendance
attendance at school or a meeting; appearing in response to an official summons

morphemes.meaning: woven mat, seat, place at a meeting (席)

출석.notes: Used both for classroom roll call (출석을 부르다 "to call roll", colloquially shortened by students to 출첵 from 출석 체크) and for legal/parliamentary summons (출석 요구서 "written summons to appear").

cognates.meaning: to appear in a performance or film, to act in a role

출연.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 출연 (出演), formed from 출 (出, "to come out, step forth, appear") and 연 (演, "to flow out, practice, perform, act"). Coined in modern theatrical and broadcasting vocabulary (via Meiji Japanese 出演 shutsuen) to denote stepping out onto a stage or in front of cameras to perform in a play, film, or television program.

history.meaning: to come forth + to expound, practice, or perform an art
stepping onto a stage to perform before an audience
appearing or performing in a play, film, or broadcast program

출연.notes: Core broadcasting vocabulary in *The Producers*: yields key industry compounds like 출연자 ("cast member / guest on a show"), 출연료 ("appearance fee"), and 특별 출연 ("cameo / special appearance").

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on a show, perform in a film/play

출연료.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 출연 (出演, "stage or broadcast appearance", from 出 "to come out, step forth" + 演 "to perform, practice, act") and the Sino-Korean suffix -료 (料, "fee, charge, material"). Coined in the modern era alongside Japanese 出演料 (shutsuenryō) to denote contractual compensation paid to actors, guests, and talents in theater and broadcasting.

history.meaning: to go out; to perform/practice; measured grain or fee
appearance fee or performance remuneration in theater and broadcasting

출연료.notes: The suffix -료 (料) productively forms fee nouns across Korean (e.g., 수업료 "tuition fee", 입장료 "admission fee"); in Korean TV production, 출연료 is typically negotiated per episode (회당 출연료).

rootFamily.gloss: to appear in a show or performance

출연시키다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean causative verb combining 출연 (出演, "stage or broadcast appearance", composed of 出 "to exit, step out" and 演 "to perform, act") with the native Korean causative verbalizer -시키다 ("to make or cause someone to do", derived from Middle Korean 시키다 "to cause to do, order").

history.meaning: to cause to do, to order or commission
to cast someone or have someone appear on a program or stage

출연시키다.notes: Replacing -하다 with -시키다 turns intransitive or active Sino-Korean action nouns into causatives: 출연하다 ("to appear on a show") becomes 출연시키다 ("to put/cast someone on a show").

rootFamily.gloss: to appear in a broadcast or play

cognates.meaning: performer, cast member, guest on a show

출연자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 출연 (出演, "performing before the public", from 出 "to come out" + 演 "to act, perform") and the bound agentive suffix -자 (者, "person who does"). Parallel to modern Japanese 出演者 (shutsuensha), referring to anyone appearing on screen or stage.

history.meaning: to step forth; to perform; agentive nominalizer (one who)
performer, cast member, or guest appearing on a program

출연자.notes: Covers scripted actors, variety show regulars, and talk-show guests alike; contrast with 제작진 (production crew), who work behind the camera.

rootFamily.gloss: to appear on a show or stage

출연진을.etymology: Accusative-marked noun phrase consisting of Sino-Korean 출연진 (出演陣, "the cast, lineup of performers", from 出 "to step forth", 演 "to perform", and 陣 "military battle formation, array, roster") followed by the native Korean postpositional object marker -을 (Middle Korean -을). The military character 陣 ("battle array") metaphorically denotes an organized team or roster.

history.meaning: military rank, battle formation, camp
the cast/lineup of performers (direct object)

출연진을.notes: The suffix -진 (陣, originally "battle formation") is widely used in media Korean to refer to a collective group or roster: 출연진 ("the cast"), 제작진 ("production crew"), 보도진 ("press corps").

cognates.meaning: to appear on stage or in a broadcast
to appear in a play or film, to perform

출연하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 출연 (出演, "appearing before the public to perform", composed of 出 "to go out, emerge" and 演 "to flow out, practice, perform") and the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do", from Middle Korean 호다 / 하다).

history.meaning: to emerge; to expound, practice, or perform
to make an appearance in a play, film, or broadcast program

출연하다.notes: Takes the locative particle -에 for the program, film, or stage appeared in (e.g., 드라마에 출연하다 "to appear in a drama"). To speaks of a cameo or special guest turn, Korean uses 특별 출연하다.

출입구.etymology: Three-character Sino-Korean compound 出入口, formed from 출입 (出入, 'going out and coming in', from 出 'exit' + 入 'enter') and the aperture suffix -구 (口, 입 구, 'mouth, opening, doorway'). Whereas 입구 means 'entrance' and 출구 means 'exit', 출입구 designates a main doorway or gate used for both entering and leaving.
출입구.notes: Standard architectural and safety-inspection term for an access doorway or gate.

출입문.etymology: Sino-Korean 출입문 (出入門), formed from 출입 (出入, 'going out and coming in, entry and exit', from 出 'go out' + 入 'enter') + 문 (門, 'door, gate').

history.meaning: entrance and exit door, doorway

cognates.meaning: business trip, official out-of-office duty, on-site service

출장.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 출장 (出張), composed of 出 ("to go out, depart") and 張 ("to stretch a bowstring, spread a tent or canopy, set up"). Originally denoted pitching a military or official tent outside headquarters; in modern usage (reinforced by Japanese 出張 shutchō) it denotes both an employee's business trip and an on-site service such as catering (출장 뷔페).

history.meaning: going out to pitch a camp or temporary administrative post
business trip; on-site service or catering dispatched to a client's location

morphemes.meaning: to spread, pitch a tent, extend

출장.notes: While 출장 alone usually means a "business trip" (출장을 가다), before another noun it means "mobile/on-site service" — e.g., 출장 뷔페 (on-site buffet catering, often shortened simply to 출장 in colloquial speech) or 출장 요리 (on-site cooking).

rootFamily.gloss: going to work, commuting to the office
departure (of a train, plane, or team)

출출하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the reduplicated ideophonic root 출출 (evoking a slightly hollow, slack, or gently rumbling sensation in an empty stomach) and the adjective-forming suffix -하다. Part of Korean's extensive sound-symbolic (의태어) system where vowel harmony distinguishes nuances of bodily sensations.

history.meaning: having a slightly empty or hollow bodily sensation
to feel peckish, mildly hungry between meals

morphemes.meaning: ideophone for mild emptiness in the stomach

출출하다.notes: Describes mild, pleasant or manageable hunger ("feeling peckish", wanting a late-night snack or 야식), whereas 배고프다 is general hunger and 굶주리다 means to starve.

rootFamily.gloss: in a slightly hungry, peckish manner (adverb)
liquid sloshing or overflowing abundantly (related ideophone)

춤추다.etymology: Native Korean cognate-object compound verb descending from Middle Korean 춤츠다, formed from the verbal noun 춤 ('dance', from 추- + -ㅁ) and the verb 추다 ('to dance').

history.meaning: to dance a dance
to dance

춥다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 춥다 ('to be cold [of weather, air, or one's body feeling the cold]').

history.meaning: to be cold (weather/feeling)
to be cold, chilly

충격.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 충격 (衝擊), a compound of 衝 ("to rush against, collide, thrust forward") and 擊 ("to strike, hit, beat"). In Classical Chinese military texts, 衝擊 described cavalry or infantry charging and striking enemy formations; in modern East Asian usage, it broadened to physical impact in physics and emotional or psychological shock.

history.meaning: to charge and strike an enemy line in battle
physical impact; severe emotional or psychological shock

충격.notes: In Korean collocations, one "receives" a shock: 충격을 받다 ("to be shocked", literally "to receive shock") and 충격을 주다 ("to shock someone", literally "to give shock").

충분하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 충분 (充分, 'fullness, sufficiency', compounding 充 'fill, full' and 分 'measure, share, portion') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: full measure, sufficiency
to be enough, sufficient, ample

충분히.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 충분 (充分, 'sufficient, ample') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: sufficiently, enough, fully, amply

충성.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Classical Chinese 충성 (忠誠), a coordinative compound of 忠 ("loyalty, unswerving devotion", composed of 中 "centered, unbending" over 心 "heart") and 誠 ("sincerity, truthfulness", composed of 言 "speech" and 成 "to fulfill, complete"). Literally "an unswerving heart and true words".

history.meaning: wholehearted devotion and sincerity toward one's sovereign or principle
loyalty, allegiance; standard military salute motto; (humorous) sycophantic devotion to a boss

충성.notes: Because "충성!" is the official salute cry of the Republic of Korea Army, Korean office workers and variety-show cast members often snap a mock salute and say "충성!" (or use 충성하다) to joke about sucking up or showing total obedience to a senior or boss.

취소되다.etymology: Passive compound verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 취소 (取消, 'cancellation, revocation', from 取 'take back' + 消 'extinguish, erase, annul') with the native passive/inchoative verbalizer -되다 (-doeda, 'to become, be done'). While 취소하다 is used when an agent actively cancels a reservation or order, 취소되다 is used when a train, flight, concert, or appointment is called off.

history.meaning: revocation, cancellation, annulment
to be cancelled, called off

cognates.word: 取り消す / 取消 (torikesu / torikeshi)

취소되다.notes: In travel and hospitality contexts, 기차가 취소되다 ('the train is cancelled') and 예약이 취소되다 ('the booking is cancelled') are essential expressions.

취소하다.etymology: Hybrid verb from Sino-Korean 취소 (取消, "cancellation, revocation", composed of 取 "to take back" and 消 "to erase, extinguish, make disappear") plus native Korean -하다 ("to do"). The compound 取消 originated as an orthographic rendering of the native Japanese compound verb 取り消す (torikesu, nominalized as 取消 torikeshi, "to take back and erase") and entered Korean and Chinese via modern administrative terminology.

history.meaning: taking back and erasing a statement or official decision
to cancel, revoke, or call off a reservation, broadcast, or legal act

취소하다.notes: The passive counterpart is 취소되다 ("to be canceled", e.g., 방송이 취소되다 "the broadcast is canceled"). Don't confuse 취소 (取消, cancellation) with 축소 (縮小, reduction/scaling down).

cognates.meaning: news gathering, press coverage, interviewing for a story
to draw materials or inspiration for an artistic work

취재하다.etymology: Hybrid verb combining Sino-Korean 취재 (取材, from 取 "to take, select" + 材 "timber, raw material, subject matter") and the native verbalizer -하다 ("to do"). In Classical Chinese, 取材 meant selecting timber or choosing themes for literature; in modern Japanese (取材 shuzai) and Korean journalism, it specialized to collecting facts, interviewing sources, and covering a story on site.

history.meaning: to select timber, raw materials, or talented personnel; to choose literary themes
to gather news material, investigate a story, or cover an event as a journalist or producer

취재하다.notes: Essential media vocabulary: journalists and TV producers go out to 취재하다 ("gather material / cover a story"), and the resulting press pack is called 취재진 ("press corps / reporting team").

취조.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 취조 (取調), composed of 取 ("to take, obtain") and 調 ("to examine, investigate, harmonize"). Borrowed into Korean via modern Japanese legal and police terminology 取調 / 取り調べ (torishirabe, nominalization of 取り調べる "to investigate thoroughly, interrogate a suspect"), pronounced with Sino-Korean readings.

history.meaning: official investigation or questioning of a suspect by authorities
police interrogation or intensive questioning

취조.notes: In contemporary South Korean legal usage, official police questioning is more formally called 조사 (調査) or 신문 (訊問), while 취조 (and 취조실 "interrogation room") carries a dramatic, coercive nuance often used figuratively when a partner or boss grills someone with rapid-fire questions.

취중구라.etymology: Humorous hybrid compound blending Sino-Korean 취중 (醉中, "in the midst of drunkenness, while intoxicated", from 醉 "drunk" + 中 "middle, inside") with the colloquial slang noun 구라 ("lie, bluff, tall tale", widely derived in Korean lexicography from early 20th-century underworld slang or Japanese くらま kurama "trick, deception"). Coined as a comic parody of the four-character idiom 취중진담 (醉中眞談, "truth spoken while drunk / in vino veritas").

history.meaning: sincere truth spoken while under the influence of alcohol (model idiom)
blatant lies or wild bluffs told while drunk (humorous nickname/blend)

취중구라.notes: A witty play on the beloved Korean phrase 취중진담 (醉中眞談, "truth spoken while drunk"): replacing 진담 ("true talk") with the slang word 구라 ("fib/lie") creates a mock four-syllable title for someone who makes up outrageous stories or false promises when tipsy.

rootFamily.gloss: truth spoken while drunk (in vino veritas)

cognates.meaning: going to bed, retiring for the night, lights-out
to retire for the night, go to bed (formal)

취침.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Classical Chinese 취침 (就寢), composed of the verb 就 ("to approach, proceed toward, enter upon") and the noun/verb 寢 ("inner sleeping quarters, bedchamber; to lie down to sleep"). Literally "retiring to the bedchamber", attested in classical ritual and historical texts.

history.meaning: to proceed to the inner bedchamber to sleep
going to sleep, bedtime, lights-out in institutional or variety-show contexts

morphemes.meaning: to approach, go toward, enter upon
bedchamber, to lie down to sleep

취침.notes: A formal institutional word paired with 기상 (起床, "waking up / reveille") in military barracks, dormitories, and Korean variety shows like *2 Days & 1 Night* (where losing a game leads to 야외취침 "sleeping outdoors" vs. 실내취침 "sleeping indoors").

rootFamily.gloss: to go to sleep, retire for the night

cognates.meaning: to go to bed, retire for the night

취침하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 취침 (就寢, "retiring to bed", from 就 "to approach, enter upon" + 寢 "sleeping quarters, to sleep") and the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ("to do").

history.meaning: to retire to the sleeping quarters
to go to bed, retire for the night, be asleep (formal or humorous register)

취침하다.notes: In everyday conversation, Koreans say 자다 (plain) or 주무시다 (honorific) for sleeping; using 취침하다 in casual speech sounds deliberately stiff, military-like, or playful (like a variety-show caption reporting on a cast member's status).

cognates.meaning: to get drunk; to feel motion sickness; to be elated
cognates.word: 酔う (you, written with 醉/酔)

취하다.etymology: Hybrid verb combining the single-character Sino-Korean root 취 (醉, "to become intoxicated", composed of the semantic radical 酉 "fermented millet wine jar" and the phonetic/semantic component 卒 "soldier; to finish, reach one's limit") with the native Korean verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to drink wine to one's limit, to become intoxicated
to get drunk on alcohol; to be overcome by motion sickness or enchanted by an atmosphere

취하다.notes: Like Japanese 酔う, 취하다 (醉하다) covers three related senses with the particle -에: getting drunk on alcohol (술에 취하다), getting motion sickness (배/차에 취하다), and being intoxicated by a mood, music, or one's own narcissism (분위기에/자아에 취하다). Note also the homonym 취하다 (取하다, "to take, adopt").

rootFamily.gloss: sobriety test, breathalyzer check; state of drunkenness

cognates.meaning: side, party, faction (e.g., 会社側 kaishagawa "the company's side")

측.etymology: Sino-Korean bound noun from 측 (側, "side, flank, margin"), a compound ideograph/phono-semantic character of 人 ("person") and 則 ("rule, standard; phonetic element"). Originally denoted leaning to one side or standing beside someone; in modern journalistic and legal Korean, it functions as a postnominal marker meaning "party, camp, or representatives of".

history.meaning: oblique, leaning to the side, flank
side, party, faction, or official representatives in a dispute or statement

측.notes: Ubiquitous in entertainment news and broadcasting when reporting official statements via a representative rather than quoting a celebrity directly: 소속사 측 ("the agency's side/reps"), 제작진 측 ("the production team's side").

rootFamily.gloss: close aide, confidant (literally "one at one's side")

층.etymology: Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'story of a building, floor, tier, layer, stratum').

history.meaning: story, tier, layer
floor, story (of a building), layer, level

층계참.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 층계 (層階, 'stairs, flight of steps', from 層 'tier, story' + 階 'steps, stairs') + 참 ('resting stage, post station', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ / 站), literally 'resting stage on a staircase'.

history.meaning: staircase landing

치다.etymology: Native Korean polysemous verb descending from Middle Korean 치다 ('to strike, hit, beat, play [an instrument], pitch [a tent or screen]') and 츠다 ('to raise animals; to prune branches').

history.meaning: to strike, beat, put up a screen / to rear, prune
to hit, strike, play, take (a test), draw (a curtain), raise (livestock)

치대다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the prefix/verb stem 치- ('upward, hard, repeatedly') + 대다 ('to touch, press against, apply').

history.meaning: to knead vigorously, work dough; to rub or lean against

치명적.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and determiner formed from 치명 (致命, composed of 致 "to deliver, surrender, cause to reach" and 命 "life, fate") plus the adjectival suffix -적 (的). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Analects* 19:1 見危致命), 致命 meant "to lay down one's life in the face of danger"; it later shifted to "costing one's life, fatal, mortal".

history.meaning: to devote or surrender one's life to duty or a sovereign
causing loss of life, mortal, lethal (as in 치명상 "mortal wound")
fatal, devastating, critical; (colloquial) dangerously alluring, femme-fatale-like

morphemes.meaning: to deliver, cause to reach, surrender

치명적.notes: Besides its serious meaning of "fatal" or "devastating" (치명적인 실수 "a fatal mistake"), in Korean pop culture and variety shows 치명적 (often pronounced playfully as 치명치명) describes someone posing in a sultry, dangerously seductive "femme/homme fatale" way (치명적인 매력 "fatal charm").

치사하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb traditionally traced to Sino-Korean 치사 (恥事, literally "shameful matter or affair", from 恥 "shame, disgrace" + 事 "matter, deed, behavior") combined with the native adjective suffix -하다. Over time, the sense narrowed from "disgraceful or beneath one's dignity" to "petty, stingy, mean-spirited, or playing dirty".

history.meaning: to be a shameful or disgraceful affair beneath a person of honor
to be petty, stingy, underhanded, or ungenerous in one's dealings

치사하다.notes: Often paired with 더럽다 ("dirty") in the classic Korean workplace rant "치사하고 더러워서 못 해먹겠다!" ("It's so petty and demeaning I can't stand doing this job!"). Beware of the homonym 치사하다 (致謝하다, "to express gratitude/praise", formal).

rootFamily.gloss: sense of shame, conscience (as in 파렴치 "shameless")

치수.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 치 ('Korean inch, tenth of a 자', Middle Korean 치) + interfix -ㅅ- + Sino-Korean 수 (數, 'number, figure'), literally 'number of inches'.

history.meaning: measurement, dimensions, size

치아시드.etymology: Contemporary Korean loanword (외래어) borrowed from English *chia seed*. English *chia* comes via Mexican Spanish *chía* from Classical Nahuatl *chian* (or *chīan*), denoting the oily seed of *Salvia hispanica*, while *seed* derives from Old English *sǣd* (Proto-Germanic *sēdiz*, "that which is sown").

history.meaning: oily sage seed (Salvia hispanica) cultivated in Mesoamerica
edible superfood seed of Salvia hispanica
chia seeds (imported health and diet food)

치아시드.notes: Entered Korean popular vocabulary in the mid-2010s during the health-food and celebrity diet boom (since chia seeds swell in water to give a feeling of fullness), as well as through Korean skincare products marketing moisture retention. Do not confuse the loanword 치아 in 치아시드 with Sino-Korean 치아 (齒牙, "teeth").

rootFamily.gloss: flaxseed, linseed (often paired with chia seeds)

치약.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 치 (齒, "tooth, molar", an ancient pictograph depicting front teeth inside an open mouth) and 약 (藥, "medicinal herb, drug, chemical preparation", composed of 艸 "grass/plant" over 樂 "music/pleasure, phonetic"). Originally denoted medicinal tooth powder or dental analgesic before shifting to modern toothpaste.

history.meaning: tooth; medicinal preparation or herbal remedy
tooth powder or dental medicine; modern commercial toothpaste

치약.notes: Notice the Hanja root 치 (齒, "tooth") in medical/hygiene words like 치약 ("toothpaste"), 치과 (齒科, "dentistry"), and 치아 (齒牙, "teeth"), whereas everyday native Korean uses 이 or 이빨 for "tooth" and 칫솔 ("toothbrush", from native 솔 "brush").

치욕.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Classical Chinese 치욕 (恥辱), a coordinative compound pairing two near-synonyms: 恥 ("inward shame, blushing of the heart", composed of 耳 "ear turning red" and 心 "heart") and 辱 ("public humiliation, insult, disgrace", originally depicting a farming tool 辰 held in the hand 寸, extended to servitude and disgrace).

history.meaning: moral shame and public humiliation or dishonor
disgrace, mortifying humiliation, indignity

치욕.notes: A strong, dramatic word for humiliation (치욕을 당하다 "to suffer humiliation", 치욕스럽다 "to be mortifying/humiliating"), frequently used Either seriously in historical contexts or hyperbolically in Korean dramas and variety shows over minor embarrassments.

치우다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb derived from Middle Korean 치우다 / 치오다 ("to remove, put aside, clear away"), morphologically formed as a causative/intensive derivative of the native root 치- (related to 치다 "to clear out, scoop away, push aside") with the causative suffix -우-.

history.meaning: to move out of the way, clear aside
to tidy up, clean up a mess, clear the table, or get rid of something

치우다.notes: Whereas 청소하다 (淸掃하다) means cleaning a room (sweeping, vacuuming, scrubbing), 치우다 specifically means "clearing away clutter or putting things away" (방 좀 치워라 "tidy up your room", 상을 치우다 "clear the dining table"). Also used as an auxiliary verb -어 치우다 meaning "to get something done and over with".

rootFamily.gloss: to push or lean to one side, be biased (related root)
to clear out, scoop out (mud, snow, clutter)

치즈.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cheese ('food made from pressed curds of milk').

history.meaning: cheese
cheese

친구.etymology: Sino-Korean 친구 (親舊), compounding 친 (親, 'intimate, close, relative') and 구 (舊, 'old, long-standing acquaintance').

history.meaning: relatives and old friends; close companion
friend, peer

cognates.word: 親近 (shinkin, as in 親近感 shinkinkan)

cognates.meaning: to be close to, intimate, approachable

친근하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 친근 (親近, "intimate and close", a Classical Chinese coordinative compound of 親 "intimate, familial, close" and 近 "near in distance or relationship") plus the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to draw near to and be on intimate terms with someone
to feel familiar, warm, approachable, and friendly

친근하다.notes: Whereas 친하다 describes an existing close interpersonal relationship between two people ("we are close friends"), 친근하다 describes a person's warm, approachable demeanor or a feeling of familiarity toward someone (e.g., 친근한 이미지 "an approachable, neighborly image", 친근감 "a sense of familiarity").

rootFamily.gloss: sense of familiarity, feeling of closeness
to be close friends, on intimate terms
close aide, inner circle; nearby area

친절.etymology: Sino-Korean 친절 (親切), compounding 친 (親, 'intimate, close, warm') and 절 (切, 'earnest, keen, thorough').

history.meaning: warm closeness and earnestness, kindness
kindness, friendliness, courtesy

cognates.meaning: intimate, close, friendly (built on the same Hanja 親)

친하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb combining the single-character Sino-Korean root 친 (親, "intimate, close, parents, in person", composed of 亲 "close/hazel tree" and 見 "to see regularly face-to-face") with the native Korean adjective-forming suffix -하다 (Middle Korean 친호다).

history.meaning: parents, blood kin; to be intimately close to
to be on close, friendly, or intimate terms with someone

친하다.notes: One of the most common relationship words in Korean: "Are you two close?" is simply "둘이 친해요?", and a "close friend / bestie" is often abbreviated in slang as 절친 (short for 절친한 친구). Takes the comitative particle -와/-과 or -하고 (누구와 친하다).

친해지다.etymology: Inchoative verb formed from 친하다 ('to be close, intimate', from Sino-Korean 親 'close, intimate' + 하다) + the auxiliary construction -어지다 ('to become, grow').

history.meaning: to become close friends, grow familiar with one another

칠.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 칠 (七, 'seven'); homophonous with Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, varnish, coat of paint').

history.meaning: seven / lacquer, paint
seven; lacquer, paint coating

칠만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 칠만 (七萬, "70,000"), composed of 칠 (七, "seven") and 만 (萬, "ten thousand, myriad", originally a pictograph of a scorpion borrowed phonetically in Old Chinese for the number 10,000). Follows the East Asian myriad-based ($10^4$) place-value system.

history.meaning: seven + myriad (ten thousand) = seventy thousand
seventy thousand (70,000)

칠만.notes: Because Korean groups large numbers by units of 만 (萬, 10,000) rather than thousands (1,000), 70,000 is conceptualized as "7 myriads" (칠만 = 7 × 10,000). 칠만 원 (70,000 KRW) is roughly $50–$65 USD depending on exchange rates.

rootFamily.gloss: ten thousand; one hundred million (만 and 억)

칠십만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 칠십만 (七十萬, "700,000"), composed of 칠 (七, "seven"), 십 (十, "ten"), and 만 (萬, "ten thousand, myriad"). Literally structured as "seventy myriads" (70 × 10,000) under the traditional East Asian myriad ($10^4$) grouping system.

history.meaning: seventy myriads (seven hundred thousand)
seven hundred thousand (700,000)

칠십만.notes: Notice the nasal assimilation in pronunciation: 칠십만 is pronounced [칠심만] because the final bilabial stop ㅂ of 십 assimilates to [ㅁ] before the nasal ㅁ of 만. To convert X십만 into English quickly, multiply X by 100,000 (칠십만 = 700,000).

cognates.word: 七十五萬 / 七十五万 (qīshíwǔwàn)

칠십오만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 칠십오만 (七十五萬, "750,000"), composed of 칠 (七, "seven"), 십 (十, "ten"), 오 (五, "five"), and 만 (萬, "ten thousand, myriad"). Literally "seventy-five ten-thousands" (75 × 10,000).

history.meaning: seventy-five myriads (seven hundred fifty thousand)
seven hundred fifty thousand (750,000)

칠십오만.notes: When mental-translating Korean money or numbers into English, mentally move the comma one digit to the left: 75,0000 (칠십오만 = 75 만) becomes 750,000 ("seven hundred fifty thousand").

칠칠맞다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the root 칠칠- (from 칠칠하다, "neat, well-grown, capable") and the derivational suffix -맞다 ("having the look or quality of"). Although originally synonymous with 칠칠하다 ("neat and capable"), because it was overwhelmingly used in the negative phrase 칠칠맞지 못하다 ("not neat, sloppy") and because the suffix -맞다 frequently attaches to negative traits (like 궁상맞다, 방정맞다), in everyday modern Korean 칠칠맞다 underwent semantic inversion (Jespersen-like negative contamination) to mean "clumsy, sloppy, careless".

history.meaning: displaying a neat, brisk, and capable manner (original prescriptive sense)
clumsy, sloppy, careless, scatterbrained (via contamination from the negative construction and pejorative -맞다)

morphemes.meaning: originally neat/capable; reanalyzed in speech as sloppy/careless
adjective suffix indicating a characteristic trait or demeanor

칠칠맞다.notes: A famous Korean "contranym" (auto-antonym): prescriptive dictionaries long defined 칠칠맞다 as "neat and capable" (same as 칠칠하다), yet in actual spoken Korean and TV dramas, "칠칠맞게 왜 이래?" ("Why are you being so clumsy/sloppy?") is universally used as a shortening of 칠칠맞지 못하게 ("sloppily, carelessly").

칠칠하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the reduplicated sound-symbolic root 칠칠 (originally describing plants, hair, or children growing lush, tall, and sleek without blemish) plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다. Extended metaphorically from healthy, unobstructed physical growth to a person whose work and demeanor are neat, thorough, and capable.

history.meaning: growing lush, long, and vigorous without defect (of plants or hair)
neat, capable, thorough, and well-put-together in one's work and appearance

morphemes.meaning: sleek, lushly grown, neat and capable

칠칠하다.notes: Most frequently heard in the negative form 칠칠하지 못하다 (contracted to 칠칠치 못하다), meaning "sloppy, careless, or scatterbrained". Unlike 칠칠맞다, positive 칠칠하다 still retains its positive sense ("neat, capable"), though it sounds somewhat traditional.

rootFamily.gloss: clumsy, sloppy (in colloquial usage; originally neat)
in a neat, sleek, or capable manner (adverb)

칠하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, varnish, paint') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, apply').

history.meaning: to apply lacquer or paint
to paint, coat, varnish, color in

칠호실.etymology: Sino-Korean 칠호실 (七號室), compounding 칠 (七, 'seven'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: Room 7, Room No. 7

침대.etymology: Sino-Korean 침대 (寢臺), compounding 침 (寢, 'sleep, lie down') and 대 (臺, 'raised platform, stand, frame').

history.meaning: sleeping platform, bedstead
bed

침착하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 침착 (沈着, 'composure, self-possession, steadiness', compounding 沈 'sink deep, settle' and 着 'attach, settle firmly') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: settled and unflustered, composed
to be calm, composed, level-headed

침체기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 침체 (沈滯, 'stagnation, slump, depression') and the suffix -기 (期, 'period, phase, season'). 침체 combines 沈 (잠길 침, 'to sink, submerge') and 滯 (막힐 체, 'to stagnate, be obstructed, accumulate without flowing'), literally describing a period when activity or momentum sinks and fails to move forward.

history.meaning: period of sinking and non-circulation; prolonged slump or downturn

침체기.notes: Commonly used for economic downturns (경기 침체기) as well as a creative, career, or ratings slump in entertainment.

rootFamily.gloss: to stagnate, be in a slump (沈滯하다)

칫솔.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound with the genitive interfix -ㅅ- (saisiot): formed from Sino-Korean 치 (齒, 'tooth, teeth') + -ㅅ- + native Korean 솔 ('brush', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 솔, originally identical with 솔 'pine needles', which were bound together to make traditional brushes).

history.meaning: pine; brush made of bundled fibres or needles
brush for cleaning the teeth; toothbrush

칫솔.notes: Because of the saisiot (ㅅ), the pronunciation tenses the following consonant to [칟쏠 / 칫쏠]; compare 치약 (齒藥, 'toothpaste'), which shares the Sino-Korean root 치 (齒).

칭찬하다.etymology: Active transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 칭찬 (稱讚, 'praise, commendation') and the verbalizer -하다 (-hada). The Sino-Korean stem pairs two synonymous Classical Chinese roots: 칭 (稱, 'to acclaim, speak well of, extol') and 찬 (讚, 'to praise, eulogize, admire'). Attested in Korean literary and vernacular texts since the Joseon period, 칭찬하다 is the standard everyday verb for complimenting someone's work, cooking, or kindness.

history.meaning: acclaiming and praising someone's virtue or skill
to praise, compliment, commend

rootFamily.gloss: words of high praise, tribute (讚辭)

칭찬하다.notes: Can be used either as 칭찬하다 ('to praise') or as the noun-verb phrase 칭찬을 하다 / 칭찬을 받다 ('to give / receive praise').

카더라.etymology: Colloquial nominalized form derived from the Gyeongsang dialectal retrospective quotative verb ending ~카더라 ('someone said that ~ / I heard tell that ~'), a phonological contraction of standard Korean ~(이)라고 하더라 ('they say that ~'). Used as a noun or modifier to denote unverified grapevine rumors.

history.meaning: (I recall that) someone said ~
unverified hearsay, 'someone-said-so' rumor mill

카더라.notes: Most famously paired with 통신 ('news agency/communications') in the satirical phrase 카더라 통신 ('the Radio Free Hearsay / rumor mill').

rootFamily.gloss: the rumor mill, grapevine news (lit. 'they-said-so news agency')
they say that ~ / I heard that ~ (standard form)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 카더라 통신

카드.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English card ('playing card, greeting card, identification or payment card').

history.meaning: stiff paper card, playing card, credit/debit card
card (greeting card, credit card, playing card)

cognates.meaning: optical device for recording images or video

카메라.etymology: Borrowed from English camera, itself an ellipsis of New Latin camera obscura ('dark chamber'), from Latin camera ('vaulted room, arched chamber'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kamara ('anything with an arched cover, vaulted chamber').

history.meaning: darkened optical chamber; photographic apparatus
photographic or television camera

카메라.notes: In Korean broadcasting, 카메라 is used for television/film cameras, while a still photographer's camera is also colloquially called 사진기 (寫眞機).

카모마일.etymology: Borrowed from English chamomile ('aromatic daisy-like herb used in infusions', from Old French camomille < Late Latin chamomilla < Ancient Greek χαμαίμηλον 'earth-apple').

history.meaning: aromatic herb used for tea
chamomile, chamomile tea

카운터.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English counter ('long service table or checkout desk in a shop, hotel, or restaurant; counting device').

history.meaning: service desk, checkout counter; counting device
counter, reception or checkout desk

카운트다운.etymology: Borrowed from English countdown ('backward counting of time to zero preceding a launch or event').

history.meaning: counting backward to zero
countdown

카페.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from French café ('coffee; coffeehouse', also reinforced via English café and Japanese カフェ), tracing back through Italian caffè and Ottoman Turkish kahve to Arabic qahwa (قَهْوَة, 'dark brew, coffee').

history.meaning: coffee
coffee; coffeehouse
café, coffeehouse

rootFamily.gloss: coffee (drink, borrowed separately via English coffee)

카페.notes: Korean neatly splits the European word family into 카페 (from French café) for the neighbourhood coffee shop and 커피 (from English coffee) for the drink itself.

카펫.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English carpet ('thick woven floor covering').

history.meaning: woven floor covering, rug
carpet, rug

칸.etymology: Nativized aspirated form of Sino-Korean 간 (間, 'space between two pillars, architectural bay, compartment, room'), attested since Middle Korean as 칸 / 간.

history.meaning: space between pillars, bay, room
compartment, booth, section, blank space or square

칸막이.etymology: Compound formed from 칸 ('compartment, room section' < 間) + 막이 ('partition, screen, blocker', derived from 막다 'to block, divide' + nominalizer -이).

history.meaning: partition, room divider, cubicle wall

칼.etymology: Native Korean word meaning 'knife, blade, sword'. Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 갈 (kal, with a final implosive/aspirated stem alternating as 갈ㅎ kalh before vowels), which underwent expressive word-initial aspiration (ㄱ > ㅋ) in Early Modern Korean to yield modern 칼.

history.meaning: knife, sword, cutting blade
knife, blade; figuratively sharpness or strictness

칼.notes: Used as a prefix or modifier to mean 'razor-sharp' or 'strictly on time', as in 칼퇴근 ('clocking out on the dot') or 칼군무 ('razor-sharp synchronized group dance').

rootFamily.gloss: blade edge of a knife or sword
leaving work right on the dot (칼 + 退勤)

칼자루.etymology: Native Korean compound of 칼 ('knife, sword', Middle Korean 갈 kalh) and 자루 ('handle, grip, haft of a tool', Middle Korean 자로 caro). Literally 'the handle of a knife', it developed the figurative meaning 'decisive authority or leverage' by contrast with 칼날 ('the bare blade').

history.meaning: hilt or wooden handle of a blade
knife handle; figuratively, the seat of control or authority

칼자루.notes: Almost always encountered in the idiom 칼자루를 쥐다 ('to hold the hilt of the knife' = to have the upper hand or final say in negotiations).

cognates.meaning: distinctive nature; fictional role or persona

캐릭터.etymology: Borrowed from English character, which derives via Old French caractere and Latin character from Ancient Greek kharakter ('engraved mark, stamp, distinctive nature'), an agent/instrument noun from kharassein ('to sharpen, cut into furrows, engrave').

history.meaning: stamped mark, defining trait, dramatic role
fictional character; a performer's signature variety-show persona; mascot design

캐릭터.notes: In Korean variety shows (예능), 캐릭터 specifically refers to a cast member's recurring comedic persona or archetype (e.g., the 'betrayer' or 'clumsy' character).

rootFamily.gloss: licensed mascot or character merchandise (캐릭터 + 商品)
overlapping personas among cast members (캐릭터 + 겹치다)

cognates.meaning: selection of actors for roles; street scouting

캐스팅.etymology: Borrowed from English casting, the verbal noun of cast ('to assign parts in a play or film', originally 'to throw' or 'to pour molten metal into a mold'), itself borrowed into Middle English from Old Norse kasta ('to throw, hurl').

history.meaning: to throw; to mold; to assign theatrical roles to actors
selecting and signing actors or guests for a broadcast, film, or agency

morphemes.meaning: to throw, mold, assign a role (English cast)

캐스팅.notes: In Korea, 길거리 캐스팅 ('street casting') is a well-known entertainment term for talent scouts recruiting idol trainees or actors directly on the street.

rootFamily.gloss: to cast an actor or recruit talent

캐스팅하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed by attaching the native Korean verbalizing suffix -하다 ('to do, make') to the English loanword 캐스팅 (casting, 'the selection and assignment of performers to roles in a drama, film, or show', ultimately from Old Norse kasta 'to throw').

history.meaning: to cast an actor in a role; to scout or recruit talent

morphemes.meaning: native Korean verbalizing light verb ('to do')

캐스팅하다.notes: Korean routinely borrows English verbal nouns in -ing (캐스팅, 편집/커팅, 코칭) rather than bare verb stems when forming -하다 verbs in media jargon.

rootFamily.gloss: to be cast in a role (passive with 되다)

커드.etymology: Borrowed from English curd ('coagulated milk solids or thickened fruit spread such as lemon curd').

history.meaning: coagulated milk curd; creamy fruit spread
curd (cheese curd or fruit curd)

커버.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cover ('protective casing, slipcover, lid, or musical cover version').

history.meaning: protective cover, jacket, lid
cover, slipcover, casing

cognates.meaning: an act of cutting; film shot or edit transition

커트.etymology: Borrowed from English cut (Middle English cutten, 'to sever or incise with a sharp instrument', of North Germanic origin) with epenthetic final vowel -ㅡ (-eu) following the word-final stop. Coexists as a doublet with the newer single-syllable spelling 컷.

history.meaning: to slice, sever; an edited film strip or haircut style
film/broadcasting shot or edit cut; haircut; table-tennis chop stroke

커트.notes: While 커트 is the traditional prescriptive spelling used for haircuts (커트 머리) and editing, the monosyllabic doublet 컷 is more common on film sets and in casual speech.

rootFamily.gloss: cut, shot, comic panel, cutoff threshold (monosyllabic doublet)
to cut out, edit out, or reject
minimum passing score or cutoff line (cutline)

커튼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English curtain ('hanging cloth screen for a window or stage').

history.meaning: window or stage drapery
curtain, drapes

cognates.meaning: pair; two people in a romantic relationship

커플.etymology: Borrowed from English couple, which entered Middle English via Old French cople from Latin copula ('a tie, bond, link, connection', formed from co- 'together' + apere 'to fasten, join'). In Korean, its meaning narrowed specifically to a romantic or paired duo.

history.meaning: fastening bond; pair of linked things or partners
romantic couple; paired duo on a television program

커플.notes: Unlike English 'a couple of' (meaning 'two or a few'), Korean 커플 is never used as a quantifier—it strictly means a romantic pair or matched duo (e.g., 커플티, matching couple T-shirts).

rootFamily.gloss: matching outfits worn by a romantic couple (couple look)
matching rings worn by a couple (couple ring)
matchmaker or dating agency consultant (couple manager)

커피.etymology: Borrowed from English coffee, adapted to Korean phonology with ㅋ (k) for initial c and ㅍ (p) for English f (since Korean lacks a labiodental fricative).
커피.notes: Replaced the older late-19th-century phonetic transcription 가배 (珈琲) in modern Korean.

커피잔.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from the English loanword 커피 (coffee) + Sino-Korean 잔 (盞, 'cup').

history.meaning: coffee cup

cognates.meaning: abstract idea; overarching theme or design plan

컨셉.etymology: Borrowed from English concept, from Medieval Latin conceptum ('something conceived in the mind'), neuter past participle of Latin concipere ('to take in, conceive', from com- 'together' + capere 'to take'). Borrowed into colloquial Korean with reduction of the final consonant cluster -pt to -p (ㅂ).

history.meaning: mental conception, general notion, thematic design
overarching theme, styling direction, or adopted persona angle

컨셉.notes: Although the National Institute of Korean Language prescribes 콘셉트, everyday speakers and K-pop/broadcasting professionals overwhelmingly say and write 컨셉 (e.g., 컨셉을 잡다, 'to settle on a theme/persona').

rootFamily.gloss: acting in character or putting on a contrived persona (컨셉 + -질)

컨테이너.etymology: Borrowed from English container (from contain + agent/instrument suffix -er; contain derives via Old French contenir from Latin continere 'to hold together, enclose', from com- 'together' + tenere 'to hold'). In Korean, the loanword underwent semantic narrowing to denote large freight containers or modular box structures.

history.meaning: any receptacle; standardized intermodal freight container (20th c.)
large steel shipping container, moving storage box, or makeshift modular office/shelter

컨테이너.notes: False friend alert: small kitchen food containers are called 용기 (容器) or 반찬통 in Korean; 컨테이너 refers specifically to huge steel shipping/moving boxes or temporary prefab structures.

rootFamily.gloss: steel shipping container or prefab modular unit (container box)

cognates.meaning: full of color; vivid and varied

컬러풀하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb (adjective) combining the English loanword 컬러풀 (colorful, from color [Latin color] + adjectival suffix -ful) with the native Korean adjectival suffix -하다 ('to be characterized by').

history.meaning: to be brightly colored, visually vivid, or richly varied

컬러풀하다.notes: Used both literally for bright, multi-colored outfits or set designs and figuratively for a lively, varied array of personalities or styles.

rootFamily.gloss: color; distinctive character or style (English color)

컴퓨터.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English computer ('programmable electronic computing machine').

history.meaning: electronic computer
computer

컵.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cup ('drinking vessel, glass, mug').

history.meaning: drinking vessel
cup, glass, mug, tumbler

컵라면.etymology: Hybrid compound of the English loanword 컵 (cup, from Old English cuppe and Late Latin cuppa 'drinking vessel') and 라면 (拉麵, 'instant noodles', borrowed via Japanese ラーメン ramen from Mandarin lamian 'hand-pulled wheat noodles', from 拉 la 'to pull, stretch' + 麵 mian 'wheat flour, noodles'). Modeled after Japanese カップラーメン (1971).

history.form: 拉麵 (Mandarin lamian) > ラーメン (Japanese) > 라면 (Korean)
history.meaning: hand-pulled noodles > instant fried noodle soup
instant noodles packaged in a disposable heat-resistant cup

컵라면.notes: Due to Korean nasal assimilation (비음화), ㅂ before ㄹ assimilates so that 컵라면 is pronounced [컴나면] (keomnamyeon), never *[컵라면].

rootFamily.gloss: instant noodles sold in a wide bowl container (사발 + 라면)

cognates.meaning: director's command to stop filming; single camera shot; edit

컷.etymology: Single-syllable loanword from English cut (Middle English cutten), adapting the English short vowel and final alveolar stop into a closed Korean syllable (컷) without vowel epenthesis. Serves as a sleeker, modern doublet of two-syllable 커트 in film, webtoons, and colloquial slang.

history.meaning: director's cue to stop rolling; individual shot or comic frame; elimination threshold
director's 'Cut!'; individual camera shot or photo frame; summary rejection or cutoff

컷.notes: Beyond the film-set command '컷!', it acts as a classifier for photos/webtoon panels (사진 한 컷, 'one snapshot') and in slang for swiftly eliminating or rejecting something (일차 컷, 'eliminated in round one').

rootFamily.gloss: an A-cut or best selected photo/take (A + cut)
rough edited assembly of footage (가편집 + 컷)

cognates.meaning: interpersonal rapport, mutual attraction or spark (chemistry)

케미.etymology: Clipped neologism formed in South Korean entertainment media by truncating the first two syllables of the English loanword 케미스트리 (chemistry, in its figurative sense of 'natural interpersonal rapport or spark between two people', ultimately from chemist + -ry, via New Latin alchimia and Arabic al-kimiya).

history.meaning: interpersonal attraction, rapport, or dynamic synergy between people
on-screen chemistry or banter between co-stars, hosts, or characters

케미.notes: Almost always collocated with 맞다 ('to match well', 케미가 잘 맞다), 좋다 ('to be good'), or 터지다 ('to burst/explode with chemistry', 케미가 터지다).

rootFamily.gloss: playful bickering chemistry between two characters (티격태격 + 케미)

케어.etymology: Borrowed from English care ('serious attention, protection, supervision, looking after someone'), which descends from Old English caru / cearu ('sorrow, anxiety, grief; perhatian, charge, oversight'), from Proto-Germanic *karo ('cry, lament, care').

history.meaning: grief, concern > attentive looking after, maintenance, or supervision
looking after a person (client, artist, junior, or patient), skin/health maintenance, or crisis management

케어.notes: In Korean entertainment and office culture, 멘탈 케어 ('mental care', looking after someone's emotional state) and 신인 케어 ('looking after a rookie') are ubiquitous expressions.

rootFamily.gloss: to look after, tend to, or manage someone attentively
looking after someone's emotional resilience (mental + care)

케이크.etymology: Borrowed from English cake, adding epenthetic 으 (-크) because Korean syllables do not end in an aspirated ㅋ release.
케이크.notes: Often shortened in casual speech to 케익, though 케이크 is the standard spelling.

켜다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 혀다 ('to light a lamp or fire; to pull, saw wood, play a bowed instrument'), which underwent palatalization and aspiration (혀다 > 켜다).

history.meaning: to light (a fire/lamp); to pull, saw
to turn on, switch on, light (a lamp or appliance); to saw or play strings

켜지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 켜다 ('to light, turn on, switch on') + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다.

history.meaning: to be turned on, come on, light up

켤레.etymology: Native Korean classifier/counter for pairs of footwear, socks, or gloves, attested since early Modern Korean as 켤네 / 켤레.

history.meaning: counter for a pair of shoes or socks
pair (counter for shoes, socks, gloves)

코.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 고 (고ㅎ, an h-final noun meaning 'nose, snout, spout, tip'), which acquired initial aspiration from the internal *h* (고ㅎ > 코).

history.meaning: nose, snout, projecting tip
nose; spout; stitch loop in knitting

코끝.etymology: Native Korean body-part compound joining 코 ('nose', Middle Korean 고ㅎ) directly with 끝 ('tip, extremity', Middle Korean 귿). Beyond literal anatomy—such as reading glasses sliding down one's nose—Korean uses 코끝 figuratively for catching delicate aromas and for feeling a sudden prickle of emotion (코끝이 찡하다).

코끼리.etymology: Native Korean descriptive compound attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 고키리 (kokhiri) and 코키리 (khokhiri). Formed from 코 ('nose, trunk', Middle Korean 고 ko) + 기리 (kiri, modern 길이 'length; that which is long', derived from 길- 'to be long' + nominalizer -이), literally designating the animal as 'the long-nosed one'.

history.meaning: elephant (literally 'long-nose')
elephant (with fortition of medial ㄱ > ㄲ)

morphemes.meaning: to be long (길다, with compound tensification ㄲ)

코끼리.notes: A classic example of transparent native Korean word-formation replacing an older Sino-Korean term (상 象, 'elephant'); also famous on Korean variety shows for the 'elephant spin' game (코끼리 코, holding one's nose and spinning around).

rootFamily.gloss: variety-show game posture of holding one's nose to form an elephant trunk

cognates.meaning: insulated electrical cable; string or rope
cipher, system of rules or shared sensibility; musical chord

코드.etymology: Homophonous Korean loanword merging three English words due to non-rhotic vowel lengthening and syllable adaptation: (1) English cord ('flexible insulated electrical cable with a plug', via Old French corde and Latin chorda from Greek khorde 'gut, string'); (2) English code ('system of signals, programming code, or shared cultural/humor sensibility', from Latin codex); and (3) English chord (music). In the sense of 'electrical cord/plug', it derives from English cord.

history.form: khorde (Ancient Greek) > chorda (Latin) > corde (Old French) > cord (English)
history.meaning: catgut string > rope, twine > insulated electrical power cable
electrical power cord/plug; also programming code, humor sensibility (개그 코드), or musical chord

코드.notes: In Korean, 코드를 뽑다 ('to pull the plug / unplug the cord') uses the 'cord' sense, whereas 코드가 맞다 ('to be on the same wavelength / share a sense of humor') uses the 'code' sense.

rootFamily.gloss: shared sense of humor or comedic wavelength (gag + code)
power cord or electrical line (電源 + cord)

코딱지.etymology: Native Korean compound of 코 ('nose; nasal mucus', Middle Korean 고 ko) and 딱지 ('scab, dried crust, or flat pasted label', related to 딱 'firmly, with a snap/sticking contact'). Literally 'nose-crust', referring to dried nasal mucus.

history.meaning: dried nasal mucus, booger; metaphorically something minute and trivial

코딱지.notes: Very frequently used in the humorous colloquial simile 코딱지만 하다 ('to be the size of a booger', i.e., tiny and cramped, as of a small room or paltry salary).

rootFamily.gloss: scab over a wound, crust, or folded paper slap-tile; parking ticket
sleep crust in the corner of the eye (눈 + 꼽/딱지)

cognates.meaning: humorous drama, film, or entertainment genre

코미디.etymology: Borrowed from English comedy, which came via Old French comedie and Latin comoedia from Ancient Greek komoidia ('a comedy, humorous performance'), a compound of komos ('revel, festival procession, merrymaking') + aoidos / aoide ('singer / song').

history.meaning: revel-song; light dramatic play with a happy or humorous resolution
comedy genre in television, film, theater, or stand-up; an absurd situation in real life

코미디.notes: Colloquially used to mock an absurd or hypocritical real-life situation: '이건 완전 코미디네' ('This is a total farce/comedy!'). Note that standard Korean spells the second syllable 미 (코미디), not *메 (*코메디).

코앞.etymology: Native Korean spatial-temporal compound formed from 코 ('nose', Middle Korean 고 ko) and 앞 ('front, space directly before', Middle Korean 앏 alp). Literally 'the space directly in front of one's nose', designating extreme physical proximity or temporal imminence.

history.meaning: the nose and the front space before a person
right under one's nose (spatially); just around the corner, imminent (temporally)

코앞.notes: Used both for physical closeness (역이 바로 코앞이다, 'the station is right in front of us') and for looming deadlines or broadcasts (방송이 코앞에 닥쳤다, 'the broadcast is right upon us').

cognates.meaning: athletic trainer, private tutor, or carriage

코치.etymology: Borrowed from English coach, which originally denoted a large four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage named after the Hungarian village of Kocs (via German Kutsche and French coche). In 1830s Oxford University slang, coach came to mean a tutor who 'carries' a student through exams, and by the late 19th century an athletic or performance trainer.

history.meaning: horse-drawn carriage > academic tutor (1830s) > sports/acting instructor (1860s)
sports or acting trainer; act of giving hands-on advice, tips, or direction

코치.notes: In everyday Korean, 코치 often means the act of tipping someone off or giving behind-the-scenes advice (누가 코치해 줬어?, 'Who coached you / told you what to say?'), not just a professional sports coach.

rootFamily.gloss: to coach, train, or give pointed advice and direction

코트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English coat ('outer garment, overcoat', from Old French cote) and court ('enclosed sports playing area', from Old French cort).

history.meaning: overcoat; sports court
coat, overcoat; tennis/basketball court

코팅되다.etymology: Hybrid passive verb formed from the English loanword 코팅 (koting, from English coating) and the native Korean passive verbalizer -되다 (-doeda, 'to become, be done'). Note an important semantic specialization in Korean: when applied to paper, menus, ID cards, or signs, 코팅하다 / 코팅되다 specifically means 'to laminate / be laminated in clear plastic film' (rather than English 'laminate'), alongside its broader industrial sense of surface coating. Thus 코팅된 카드 is the natural everyday Korean phrase for a 'laminated card'.

history.meaning: protective outer layer applied to a surface
to be laminated (of paper/cards) or coated

코팅되다.notes: A great false-friend tip for learners: in Korean stationery and cafés, 'laminating a menu card' is always called 코팅 (coating).

콕.etymology: Native Korean ideophone (의태어/의성어, sound-symbolic adverb) belonging to a productive ablaut/consonant-gradational paradigm: the bright vowel ㅗ (콕) expresses a sharp, small, pinpoint poke, prick, or peck (as with a needle, beak, or fingertip), contrasting with the dark vowel ㅜ in 쿡 (a deeper, heavier jab or thrust) and the plain consonant ㄱ in 곡/국.

history.meaning: ideophone for a sharp, pinpoint prick, poke, peck, or exact selection

콕.notes: Frequently reduplicated as 콕콕 ('poking or throbbing repeatedly') or paired with 집다 in 콕 집어 말하다 ('to pinpoint and state', literally 'to pick out with a sharp poke').

rootFamily.gloss: repeatedly poking, pecking, or stinging sharply (reduplicated)
with a deeper, heavier jab or thrust (dark-vowel counterpart)
to pinpoint, single out precisely (콕 + 집다)

cognates.meaning: live musical performance before an audience

콘서트.etymology: Borrowed from English concert, from French concert and Italian concerto ('agreement, harmony, musical consort or performance'), derived from the verb concertare ('to bring into agreement, harmonize; to contend'), from Latin com- ('together') + certare ('to strive, contend').

history.meaning: harmonious agreement of voices/instruments; public musical performance
history.stage: Early Modern to Modern European (16th–19th c.)

history.meaning: live music concert or talk-concert event

콘서트.notes: In Korea, 콘서트 has also spawned the compound 토크 콘서트 ('talk concert'), a popular live event format combining onstage panel conversation with musical segments.

rootFamily.gloss: live stage event blending conversation and music (talk + concert)
solo concert by a single artist or group (單獨 + 콘서트)

cognates.meaning: things contained; creative media or information material

콘텐츠.etymology: Borrowed from English contents (the plural of content, 'that which is contained in a vessel, book, or medium', from Medieval Latin contentum, neuter past participle of Latin continere 'to hold together, enclose'), reinforced by Japanese media industry usage (コンテンツ kontentsu). In Korean, the morphologically plural form 콘텐츠 functions as a singular or uncountable noun for creative/digital media content.

history.meaning: things held within; subject matter or chapters of a work; media assets
cultural, broadcast, or digital media content and intellectual property

morphemes.meaning: that which is contained, media material (English content)
fossilized English plural suffix (-s, adapted as -츠)

콘텐츠.notes: Where English says 'digital content' or 'cultural content' in the singular, Korean always uses the plural-derived form 콘텐츠 (e.g., 한류 콘텐츠, 문화 콘텐츠).

rootFamily.gloss: cultural content, entertainment IP (文化 + 콘텐츠)
killer content, flagship hit program or media asset (killer + contents)

cognates.meaning: summons, phone call, cue, or poker bet acceptance

콜.etymology: Borrowed from English call ('to cry out, summon, telephone, or match a bet in poker'), which entered late Old English (ceallian) from Old Norse kalla ('to cry loudly, summon by name'), from Proto-Germanic *kallona ('to shout, call'). In Korean, it spans broadcasting jargon ('call time / cue'), telephone/taxi dispatch, and the colloquial slang interjection 'Deal! / I'm in!' (from poker's 'call').

history.meaning: to shout, summon > telephone call, actor's call time, or poker bet match
phone call; actor's on-set call time/cue; slang interjection meaning 'Agreed! / Count me in!'

콜.notes: When someone suggests going for food or drinks in a K-drama, replying '콜!' ('Call!') means 'I'm totally in! / Deal!'—borrowed from calling a bet in card games.

rootFamily.gloss: taxi summoned by phone or app dispatch (call + taxi)
early-morning call time for cast and crew on a shoot (早朝 + call)

cognates.meaning: carbonated soft drink originally flavored with kola nut extract

콜라.etymology: Borrowed from English cola, popularized globally by the trademark Coca-Cola (coined in 1886 by John Stith Pemberton). The element cola derives via New Latin Cola acuminata from West African languages (such as Temne an-kola and Mandinka kolo), naming the caffeine-rich kola nut indigenous to West African tropical forests.

history.meaning: caffeine-bearing nut of the West African kola tree > carbonated soft drink flavored with it
cola soft drink; metaphorically a refreshing, cathartic plot development (paired with 사이다)

콜라.notes: In Korean internet and drama slang, 답답한 고구마 ('stifling sweet potato') and 톡 쏘는 사이다/콜라 ('fizzy cider/cola') contrast frustrating vs. cathartic plot twists.

rootFamily.gloss: cider / clear lemon-lime soda paired with 콜라 in Korean snack culture

cognates.meaning: degree of excellence, grade, or distinctive attribute

퀄리티.etymology: Borrowed from English quality, which came via Old French qualite from Latin qualitas ('character, nature, property, condition'), a philosophical noun coined by Cicero from the interrogative/relative adjective qualis ('of what kind, of such a sort', from the Proto-Indo-European pronominal stem *kwo-).

history.meaning: of what sort > essential property or nature > degree of excellence or craftsmanship
production value, degree of craftsmanship, or standard of excellence in media and goods

퀄리티.notes: Frequently shortened to 퀄 and combined with Sino-Korean prefixes 고- (高, 'high') and 저- (低, 'low') to form the ubiquitous slang terms 고퀄 ('high-quality / high production value') and 저퀄 ('low-effort / low-quality').

rootFamily.gloss: high quality, high production value (高 + quality, often clipped to 고퀄)
low quality, poor craftsmanship (低 + quality, often clipped to 저퀄)

퀴노아.etymology: Borrowed from English quinoa, itself borrowed from Spanish quinoa (or quinua), which was adapted from Classical Quechua kinwa (Southern Quechua kinwa / kiwina), the indigenous Andean name for the nutrient-rich goosefoot pseudocereal Chenopodium quinoa.

history.meaning: Andean goosefoot grain plant (Chenopodium quinoa)
edible seed of the Andean quinoa plant
quinoa (often cooked with rice or served in salads as a health food)

퀴노아.notes: In South Korea, quinoa gained popularity in the 2010s as a 'superfood' grain frequently mixed into multigrain rice (잡곡밥) or health-conscious diet salads.

cognates.meaning: cue sign; hand signal to begin broadcasting
