큐사인.etymology: Compound loanword used in Korean television and radio production, formed from English cue ('stage or broadcast signal to begin action', from 16th-century theatrical abbreviation Q/qu for Latin quando 'when', or Old French queue 'tail end of a preceding line') + English sign ('gesture, visual signal', via Old French signe from Latin signum 'mark, token').

history.meaning: theatrical prompt + visual gesture or token
director's hand signal to start filming or speaking on air

morphemes.meaning: cue; prompt to begin a broadcast or performance

큐사인.notes: While English speakers simply say 'cue', Korean broadcasting jargon routinely pairs it with 사인 ('sign') as 큐사인 to refer to the floor director's physical hand gesture launching a take.

크기.etymology: Native Korean abstract noun lexicalized from the adjective stem 크- ('to be big, large', Middle Korean 크다) and the nominalizing suffix -기. Just as 밝기 ('brightness') and 길이 ('length') turn descriptive adjectives into measurable dimensions, 크기 neutralized the positive sense of 'bigness' to become the everyday Korean noun for 'size' in general.
크기.notes: Applies to objects of any size, small or large.

크다.etymology: Native Korean adjective and verb descending from Middle Korean 크다 ('to be big, large, great; to grow up').

history.meaning: to be large, great; to grow
to be big, large, loud; to grow

cognates.meaning: fatty part of milk; cosmetic ointment

크림.etymology: Borrowed from English cream, from Middle English creme, from Old French cresme (Modern French crème), a confluence of Late Latin crama ('cream of milk', likely of Gaulish origin) and Ecclesiastical Latin chrisma ('anointing oil, unguent', from Ancient Greek khrîsma 'that which is smeared', from khríō 'to rub, anoint').

history.meaning: anointing unguent + fatty milk layer
dairy cream; ointment-like emulsion
dairy cream, custard filling, or cosmetic skin cream

크림.notes: In Korean, 크림 spans both culinary dairy toppings/fillings and skincare moisturizers; fresh whipped cream used on cakes is specifically distinguished as 생크림 (生 + cream).

크림색.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from English loanword 크림 (from English cream, ultimately from Old French cresme) + Sino-Korean 색 (色, 'color, tint').

history.meaning: cream + color
cream color, off-white

큰.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) adnominal (determiner) inflection of the descriptive verb 크다 ('to be big, large, great; to grow'), formed from the stem 크- plus the adnominal modifier suffix -ㄴ. Directly attested in 15th-century Middle Korean texts (such as Yongbieocheonga, 1447) as 큰 (khun), modifying nouns in both literal spatial senses and figurative senses of importance or seniority.

history.meaning: to be large, great / big, great (adnominal)
big, large, major, eldest (in kinship compounds)

morphemes.meaning: adnominal modifier suffix for descriptive verbs

큰.notes: Beyond physical size, 큰 prefixes kinship terms to denote the eldest branch of a family—for example, 큰아버지 ('eldest paternal uncle, father's older brother') and 큰언니 ('eldest older sister').

rootFamily.gloss: to be big, large; to grow up

큰길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 큰 (adnominal form of 크다 'to be big, wide') + 길 ('road, street, way', Middle Korean 길).

history.meaning: main road, highway
main road, thoroughfare, wide street

큰돈.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean compound written without a space, uniting the adnominal modifier 큰 ('large, great', from 크다) and 돈 ('money, coin'). Listed as a single headword in standard Korean dictionaries alongside 목돈 ('lump sum') and 잔돈 ('small change'), 큰돈 idioms naturally with 들다 ('to cost a small fortune').
큰돈.notes: Contrasts with 잔돈 ('small change') and 용돈 ('pocket money').

큰일.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 큰 (adnominal form of 크다 'big, great, serious') + 일 ('work, matter, affair, event', Middle Korean 일).

history.meaning: great matter, important task
big event; serious trouble, emergency

cognates.meaning: closing segment of a broadcast or game

클로징.etymology: Borrowed from English closing (gerund/verbal noun of close, 'to shut, bring to an end'), which entered Middle English via Old French clos- (stem of clore 'to shut') from Latin clausus, past participle of claudere ('to shut, block, conclude'). In Korean broadcasting terminology, 클로징 specifically denotes the final wrap-up segment or sign-off remarks at the end of a show.

history.meaning: to shut, close, bring to an end
concluding part or act of ending
closing segment or sign-off remarks of a broadcast program

클로징.notes: In Korean TV and radio scripts, 클로징 is paired with 오프닝 ('opening') and frequently appears in the collocation 클로징 멘트 ('closing remarks/sign-off speech').

rootFamily.gloss: closing remarks at the end of a broadcast

클립.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English clip ('fastener for holding papers or hair together; video excerpt', from Old English clyppan 'to embrace, clasp').

history.meaning: paperclip, fastener; short video clip
paperclip, clip

클립보드.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English clipboard ('writing board with a hinged clip at the top; temporary software buffer'), compound of clip + board.

history.meaning: board with a spring clip; memory buffer
clipboard

큼직하다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive adjective formed from the verb/adjective root 크- ('big') plus the expressive suffix -ㅁ직하다 ('pleasantly or amply having a quality', compare 굵직하다 'thickset' and 묵직하다 'pleasantly weighty'). Rather than neutral 크다, 큼직하다 conveys a satisfying, bold, generous scale.

키.etymology: Two main sources merged under the same form: (1) native Korean 키 ('stature, height of a person; winnowing basket; helm/rudder', Middle Korean 키); (2) 20th-century loanword from English key ('metal key, keypad button, musical key').

history.meaning: bodily height; lock key, button
height, stature; key, helm

키우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 크다 ('to be big, grow', Middle Korean 크다 -> 키우다 / 틔우다) with the causative suffix -이우- / -우-.

history.meaning: to make grow, raise
to raise, bring up, cultivate, enlarge

cognates.meaning: one who kicks; unexpected twist or clincher

키커.etymology: Borrowed from English kicker, an agent noun derived from the verb kick (Middle English kiken 'to strike out with the foot', possibly from Old Norse kikna 'to bend backward at the knees') + agentive suffix -er. In Korean, it is used both literally in football for a set-piece taker and metaphorically in variety/cooking shows for a decisive 'clincher' or secret ingredient.

history.meaning: to strike with the foot > one who kicks; surprising twist
designated ball kicker in sports; decisive masterstroke or secret ingredient

키커.notes: In Korean variety television and culinary programs, 킥 (kick) or 키커 (kicker) often refers to a secret ingredient or comedic punchline that elevates the entire dish or scene.

rootFamily.gloss: kick; secret culinary or comedic twist

cognates.meaning: one who kills; something extraordinarily impressive or formidable
killer; someone irresistibly charming to a target group

킬러.etymology: Borrowed from English killer, agent noun from Middle English killen ('to strike, beat, put to death') + -er. In colloquial Korean slang, X 킬러 underwent playful semantic shift: when preceded by a food or item (e.g., 고기 킬러 'meat killer'), it means an insatiable enthusiast who 'demolishes' or devours X; when preceded by a demographic, it means a heartthrob who 'slays' them.

history.meaning: to strike dead > one who kills; formidable person or thing
assassin; someone who devours a favorite food or charms a specific group

킬러.notes: Calling someone a 빵 킬러 ('bread killer') or 치킨 킬러 ('chicken killer') in Korean is affectionate everyday slang meaning they are a huge fan who finishes every last bite of that food.

rootFamily.gloss: all-kill; sweeping every music chart or opponent
killer question; ultra-difficult exam problem designed to differentiate top scorers

킬로.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from French or English kilo, clipping of kilogramme / kilogram or kilomètre / kilometer (from Greek chilioi 'thousand').

history.meaning: thousand (unit prefix); kilogram or kilometer
kilogram, kilometer

cognates.meaning: metric unit of length equal to 1,000 meters

킬로미터.etymology: Borrowed from American English kilometer (ultimately from French kilomètre, coined in 1795 during the introduction of the metric system), combining the metric prefix kilo- (from Ancient Greek khílioi 'one thousand') and meter / mètre (from Ancient Greek métron 'measure, rule', from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- 'to measure').

history.meaning: one thousand + measure
metric unit of 1,000 meters
kilometer (often clipped to 킬로 in speech)

morphemes.meaning: meter; base metric unit of length

킬로미터.notes: In casual spoken Korean, both 킬로미터 ('kilometer') and 킬로그램 ('kilogram') are routinely shortened to 킬로, with context clarifying whether distance or weight is meant.

타다.etymology: Multiple native Korean homophonous verbs descending from distinct Middle Korean roots: (1) 타다 ('to burn, catch fire, be scorched', Middle Korean 타다); (2) 타다 ('to ride, get on a vehicle', Middle Korean 타다); (3) 타다 ('to receive a share/prize; to mix/dissolve in liquid').

history.meaning: to burn; to mount/ride; to receive
to burn; to ride/board; to blend into water; to receive

타르트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from French tarte or English tart ('open-topped pastry shell with sweet or savory filling', ultimately from Old French tarte).

history.meaning: baked pastry tart
tart (pastry)

타르트지.etymology: Hybrid culinary compound formed from 타르트 ('tart', from French tarte / English tart) + Sino-Korean 지 (地, used in culinary terminology via Japanese kiji 生地 for 'dough base, pastry crust, fabric').

history.meaning: tart + pastry dough base
tart crust, pastry shell

타보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb (syntactically spaced as 타 보다 in standard orthography, often written unspaced in scripts) formed from 타다 ('to ride, board, mount a vehicle', Middle Korean 타다 thata) + infinitive/connective suffix -아 (coalesced with stem vowel ㅏ) + auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see; to try doing and experience the result', Middle Korean 보다 pwota).

history.meaning: to ride, mount + to see, try experiencing
to try riding; to experience boarding a vehicle or attraction

morphemes.meaning: experiential auxiliary verb: to try doing, see how it is

타보다.notes: The auxiliary construction -아/어 보다 attaches to almost any action verb to express 'try V-ing' or ask about life experience ('Have you ever ridden/tried...?').

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look at; (auxiliary) to try doing
to put aboard, give a ride to (causative of 타다)

타오르다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 타다 ('to burn, catch fire, blaze', attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 타다 thata) + connective suffix -아 (coalesced) + 오르다 ('to rise, ascend, go upward', Middle Korean 오르다 woluta). Originally depicting flames leaping skyward, it extended metaphorically to intense emotions, jealousy, or competitive passion flaring up.

history.meaning: to burn + to rise, ascend
to blaze up, burst into flames; to burn with passion or ambition

타오르다.notes: Notice that Korean has two homophonous native verbs 타다 (both Middle Korean thata): one meaning 'to ride' (as in 타보다) and one meaning 'to burn' (as in 타오르다).

rootFamily.gloss: to blaze up fiercely; burn with ardor (불 'fire' + 타오르다)

타이머.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English timer ('clockwork or electronic device that measures elapsed time or triggers an action', from time + -er).

history.meaning: time-measuring or countdown device
timer

타이어.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tire / tyre ('rubber covering fitted around a wheel rim').

history.meaning: rubber wheel covering
tire

cognates.meaning: title track of an album or single

타이틀곡.etymology: Hybrid loanword and Sino-Korean compound (혼종어) combining English title (타이틀, via Old French title from Latin titulus 'inscription, label, heading') + Sino-Korean 곡 (曲, 'melody, tune, song, musical piece', originally 'bent, winding' in Old Chinese). In the South Korean music industry, 타이틀곡 shifted to mean the main promotional single of an album regardless of whether it shares the album's title.

history.meaning: inscription/title (Latin) + melody/tune (Middle Chinese)
flagship promotional song or lead single of an album

타이틀곡.notes: False friend alert: in K-pop and Korean broadcasting, 타이틀곡 does not mean 'the track named after the album', but rather the 'lead single' promoted on music shows alongside a music video (contrasted with 수록곡 'B-side/album tracks').

rootFamily.gloss: title; championship belt or lead role
名曲: masterpiece song, classic tune

타일.etymology: Modern Korean loanword borrowed from English tile, which itself descends through Old English tigel from Latin tegula ('roof tile', related to tegere 'to cover'). In Korean architecture and everyday interiors, 타일 refers primarily to flat glazed ceramic or stone wall and floor tiles, while traditional curved clay roof tiles retain the word 기와.
타일.notes: Counted with 장 (타일 네 장, 'four tiles').

타임.etymology: Modern Korean culinary loanword borrowed from English 'thyme' (from Old French thym, Latin thymus, and Ancient Greek θύμον, 'fragrant herb'). Used in Korean kitchens and herb gardens for the aromatic Mediterranean herb Thymus vulgaris, alongside its Sino-Korean botanical name 백리향 (百里香, 'scent carrying a hundred li').
타임.notes: Counted in sprigs with 줄기 (타임 줄기 두 개).

타임캡슐.etymology: Modern Korean loanword borrowed directly from English time capsule (coined in 1938 for the 1939 New York World's Fair from time + capsule, ultimately from Latin capsula 'small box or chest'). Adapted into Hangul as 타임캡슐 (taimkaepsyul), it became widely popular in South Korea during the late 20th century—notably around the 1994 Seoul 600th Anniversary Time Capsule buried at Namsan—and among school friends and families burying keepsakes in tin boxes under courtyard trees.

history.meaning: sealed container preserving mementos for a future generation
time capsule

타임캡슐.notes: Typically paired with verbs such as 묻다 ('to bury'), 숨기다 ('to hide'), or 열다 ('to open').

탁.etymology: Dual-origin form in The Producers: (1) Native Korean (고유어) mimetic/onomatopoeic adverb 탁, depicting a sharp snap, crisp tap, sudden breakthrough, or unobstructed opening (the yang-vowel ablaut counterpart of 턱); and (2) Sino-Korean surname 탁 (卓, Middle Chinese træwk 'lofty, eminent, stand tall'), borne by the drama's lead music-show producer Tak Ye-jin (탁예진).

history.meaning: lofty, eminent (Middle Chinese) / sharp snapping or popping sound (Korean)
sharply, with a snap, wide open; Korean family name Tak (卓)

탁.notes: As an ideophone, 탁 captures crisp, decisive release—such as slapping one's knee in realization (무릎을 탁 치다) or a view opening up unobstructedly (시야가 탁 트이다).

rootFamily.gloss: tapping or snapping repeatedly; briskly dusting off
with a heavy thud; abruptly (yin-vowel counterpart of 탁)
卓越하다: to be eminent, surpassing, outstanding (sharing Hanja 卓)

탁월하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 탁월 (卓越, 'standing out high above others, excellence', from 탁 卓 'tall, lofty, eminent' + 월 越 'to cross over, surpass') + native light verb 하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: lofty and surpassing -> to be outstanding, excellent
to be outstanding, excellent, superb

탁자.etymology: Sino-Korean 탁자 (卓子), compounding 탁 (卓, 'high table, stand') and diminutive/nominal suffix 자 (子, 'object, piece of furniture', from Middle/Early Mandarin 桌子 zhuōzi).

history.meaning: table, stand
table, desk

탄력.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 彈力, combining 彈 (탄알 탄 / 튕길 탄, 'to spring back, snap, pluck a bowstring') and 力 (힘 력, 'force, strength'). In physics and baking alike, 탄력 denotes the elastic power of something—such as gluten-rich bread dough—to bounce right back into shape after being pressed.
탄력.notes: Pronounced [탈력] due to liquidization of ㄴ + ㄹ to [ㄹㄹ].

탄산수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 탄산수 (炭酸水), formed from 탄산 (炭酸, 'carbonic acid', from 탄 炭 'charcoal, carbon' + 산 酸 'acid') + 수 (水, 'water').

history.meaning: carbonic acid + water
sparkling water, carbonated water

cognates.meaning: to be born, come into being

탄생하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb formed from 탄생 (誕生, 'birth, nativity, coming into existence') + native light verb 하다 ('to do'). In Classical Chinese, 誕 (탄, Middle Chinese danX) originally meant 'great, expansive, to magnify' and in the Book of Odes (詩經) came to mean 'to bring forth, give birth', paired synonymously with 生 (생, Middle Chinese sraeng, 'to bear, be born, live').

history.meaning: to bring forth life, give birth (elevated/literary)
to be born (honorific); for a new work, star, or institution to come into being

morphemes.meaning: 誕: birth, nativity, bring forth grandly
生: life, birth, come into being

탄생하다.notes: While 태어나다 is the everyday native-rooted verb for a baby being born, 탄생하다 carries a grander, more dramatic or celebratory tone—often used for the 'birth' of a hit TV show, a masterpiece, or a new star.

rootFamily.gloss: 誕生日: birthday (formal/elevated) or founding day

탄수화물.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) scientific compound 탄수화물 (炭水化物), borrowed from Meiji-era Japanese chemical nomenclature 炭水化物 (tansuikabutsu), which was coined as a direct calque of 19th-century German Kohlenhydrat / French hydrate de carbone ('hydrate of carbon'): 탄 (炭, 'charcoal, carbon') + 수 (水, 'water, hydrate') + 화 (化, 'chemically combine, transform') + 물 (物, 'substance, matter').

history.meaning: hydrate of carbon (calqued from German Kohlenhydrat)
carbohydrate; dietary carbs (rice, bread, noodles)

탄수화물.notes: In Korean fitness and dieting culture, 탄수화물 is frequently abbreviated to its first syllable 탄 in the compound 탄단지 (탄수화물·단백질·지방, 'carbs, protein, and fat'—the three macronutrients).

탄탄하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated bright-vowel mimetic root 탄탄 ('firm, solid, tightly built', vowel-harmonic counterpart of 튼튼하다) + -하다.

history.meaning: solid, compact, firmly established

탐험.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 探險, combining 探 (찾을 탐, 'to reach in and search out, investigate') with 險 (험할 험, 'uncharted, steep, adventurous'). Used literally for polar or jungle expeditions and playfully in everyday Korean for neighbourhood treasure hunts and back-alley rambles.

탓.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 탓 ('cause, reason, fault, blame').

history.meaning: reason, fault, blame
fault, blame, negative cause

cognates.meaning: Korean martial art of kicking and punching

태권도.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) neologism 태권도 (跆拳道), coined in Seoul on April 11, 1955 by a naming committee led by General Choi Hong-hi (최홍희) to unify the post-liberation Korean martial arts schools (관). It combines 태 (跆, 'to tread, trample, kick with the foot') + 권 (拳, 'fist, strike with the hand') + 도 (道, 'way, path, spiritual discipline'), chosen also for its phonetic resemblance to the traditional Korean folk kicking game 택견 (taekkyeon).

history.meaning: traditional Korean foot-fighting game / early 20th-century karate-influenced kwan names
the way of foot and fist; unified Korean martial art and Olympic sport

morphemes.meaning: 跆: to kick, stomp, tread with the foot
拳: fist, punch with the hand

태권도.notes: Because 跆拳道 was intentionally phoneticized to echo native Korean 택견 while using Sino-Korean characters, it became one of the most globally recognized Korean-coined Sino-compounds.

rootFamily.gloss: 跆拳: kicking and punching; taekwondo (clipped form)

태블릿.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th–early 21st century from English tablet ('flat slab, drawing pad, portable touchscreen computer', ultimately from Old French tablete, diminutive of Latin tabula).

history.meaning: tablet computer, graphics tablet, pill
tablet (computer)

태어나다.etymology: Lexicalized verb universally used in Modern Korean for 'to be born', formed from Sino-Korean 태 (胎, 'womb, fetus, pregnancy', Middle Chinese thoj) + verbal connective element -어 + native Korean 나다 ('to emerge, come out, sprout, happen', Middle Korean 나다 nata). Originally transparent as 'to come out from the womb (胎)', it fused into a single indivisible verb stem 태어나-.

history.meaning: womb, fetus (Sino-Korean) + to emerge, come forth (Middle Korean)
to be born, come into the world

morphemes.meaning: 胎: womb, embryo (fused into stem 태어나-)
to come out, emerge, be born

태어나다.notes: Most native speakers feel 태어나다 to be a pure native Korean word because of 나다, making its origin in the Hanja 胎 ('womb') a classic piece of hidden Korean etymology.

rootFamily.gloss: to come out, emerge, sprout, be born
母胎: mother's womb; matrix or origin (as in 모태 솔로 'single since birth')

태연하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 태연 (泰然, 'calm, composed, undisturbed', from 태 泰 'great, peaceful, tranquil' + 연 然 'manner, -ly') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: calm and self-possessed in manner
to be calm, unperturbed, nonchalant

태우다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) morphological causative of 타다 ('to ride, get on a vehicle' or homophonous 'to burn'), formed from stem 타- + causative suffix -이우- (attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 태오다 thaywota and 타이다 thayita, where ㅏ + ㅣ coalesced into the front vowel ㅐ). In the context of vehicles, it means 'to cause/let someone ride, put someone in a car, give a lift'.

history.meaning: to cause to ride, mount on a horse or vehicle; to cause to burn
to give someone a ride, put aboard; to burn or scorch

morphemes.meaning: causative suffix (coalesced with 타- to form 태우-)

태우다.notes: Because 태우다 is the causative of both homophonous verbs 타다 ('to ride' and 'to burn'), 차에 태우다 means 'to put someone in a car / give a lift', whereas 고기를 태우다 means 'to burn the meat' and 속을 태우다 means 'to worry oneself sick (burn one's insides)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to give someone a ride, offer a lift
to burn up, incinerate; devote passionately

태워오다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) serial verb compound formed from 태우다 ('to put in a vehicle, give a ride to', causative of 타다 'to ride') + connective suffix -어 (contracted with stem-final 우 into 워) + deictic motion verb 오다 ('to come toward the speaker's location', Middle Korean 오다 wota). It denotes bringing a passenger to the current location by vehicle.

history.meaning: to cause to ride + to come toward the speaker
to drive or bring someone here in a vehicle

morphemes.meaning: connective suffix (contracted with 우 to 워)
to come (deictic directional verb toward speaker)

태워오다.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes direction relative to the speaker: 태워오다 means 'drove someone here (toward where we are now)', whereas 태워가다 means 'drove someone there (away from here)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to give a ride, put in a vehicle
to drive someone all the way to their destination for them

택배.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound 택배 (宅配), borrowed in the late 20th century from Japanese 宅配 (takuhai, clipped from 宅配便 takuhaibin 'home-delivery parcel service'), composed of 택 (宅, 'house, residence, home', Middle Chinese dræk) + 배 (配, 'to distribute, allocate, deliver', Middle Chinese phwojH). Literally 'home distribution', it designates courier parcel delivery to a residence or office.

history.meaning: residence, home + distribute, apportion
door-to-door courier parcel service
parcel delivery service; a delivered package itself

택배.notes: In everyday Korean, 택배 refers both to the courier delivery system and metonymically to the physical box/package itself (e.g., 택배 왔다! 'The package arrived!'), whereas food delivery from restaurants is called 배달 (配達).

rootFamily.gloss: 配達: delivery (especially restaurant food, milk, or mail)

택시.etymology: Borrowed from English taxi, preserving both syllables as 택 (taek) + 시 (si).
택시.notes: Pairs with the native verb 타다 ('택시를 타다', 'take a taxi') and 잡다 ('hail a taxi').

cognates.meaning: taxi fare (using 代 dai instead of 費 hi)

택시비.etymology: Hybrid loanword and Sino-Korean compound (혼종어) combining English loanword 택시 (taxi, clipped from taximeter cab, from French taximètre, ultimately from Medieval Latin taxa 'tax, charge' + Greek métron 'measure') and Sino-Korean suffixoid 비 (費, 'expense, cost, fee, fare', Middle Chinese phj+jH).

history.meaning: taximeter cab (English) + expenditure, fee (Middle Chinese)
taxi fare, cab money

택시비.notes: The Sino-Korean morpheme -비 (費) productively attaches to both Sino-Korean and foreign roots to denote specific expenses, such as 택시비 ('cab fare'), 차비 ('transit fare'), and 식비 ('food expenses').

rootFamily.gloss: 車費: transportation fare, transit money
食費: food and dining expenses

택하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verb formed from the single-character root 택 (擇, 'to choose, select, pick out, distinguish', Middle Chinese dræk, Old Chinese *lˤrak) + native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Attested since Middle Korean literature, where monosyllabic Sino-Korean verbal roots regularly combined directly with -하다.

history.meaning: to select, pick out, sort
to choose, select, opt for (a path, method, or alternative)

morphemes.meaning: 擇: to choose, select, pick out

택하다.notes: While 선택하다 (選擇하다) is the everyday word for making a choice, single-character 택하다 sounds slightly more concise or literary, often used for choosing a life path, fate, or one option out of two (둘 중 하나를 택하다).

rootFamily.gloss: 採擇하다: to adopt, select (a resolution, script, or policy)
二者擇一: choosing one of two alternatives

터.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 터 / 엏 (theh, a final-h noun meaning 'ground, building site, foundation'). From the concrete spatial meaning 'the ground or position on which one stands', it grammaticalized after the prospective adnominal suffix -(으)ㄹ into a bound noun (의존 명사) expressing planned intention ('in a position to / intending to') or strong supposition ('bound to be').

history.meaning: ground, site, foundation, lot
building site, venue; situational footing or basis
site, ground; bound noun expressing intention ('intend to') or conjecture ('must be')

터.notes: In everyday speech, -(으)ㄹ 터이다 ('intend to / bound to') almost always contracts with the vowel ㅣ of the copula 이다 to produce -(으)ㄹ 테다, -(으)ㄹ 텐데, and -(으)ㄹ 테니까, though uncontracted -(으)ㄹ 터 remains common before निक्का (-(으)ㄹ 터이니) or at clause endings.

터져주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 터지다 ('to burst, pop, explode, break out', lexicalized inchoative/intransitive derivative of 트다 'to crack open, split, sprout' + -어지다) + connective -어 (contracted with 지 to 져) + benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give; to do favorably for someone', Middle Korean 주다 cwuta). In entertainment slang, 터지다 means for ratings, laughter, or a project to 'blow up / hit the jackpot', and -어 주다 frames that breakthrough as a much-needed favor to the speaker.

history.meaning: to split open > to burst open + to give/do for someone's benefit
to burst open, explode, or become a smash hit (for the speaker's sake)

morphemes.meaning: to split, crack open, break through
connective suffix (contracted with 지 to 져)
benefactive auxiliary verb: to do favorably for someone

터져주다.notes: In Korean TV production and comedy, 빵 터지다 ('to burst out laughing / be a huge hit') and 대박이 터져주다 ('for a jackpot hit to graciously happen') capture the producer's wish that audience reactions will explode.

rootFamily.gloss: to burst, explode, break out, hit the jackpot
to split open, crack, sprout, open up
to pop, detonate, cause to burst (causative)

터지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb formed from 터 (bound root related to 트다 'to burst open, crack, sprout', Middle Korean 트다) + inchoative/passive auxiliary -어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to split open, burst
to burst, pop, explode, break out

턱.etymology: Native Korean monosyllabic body-part noun 턱 ('chin, jaw'), attested in Middle Korean as ᄐᆞᆨ. From the projecting shape of the lower jaw, Korean also extended 턱 metaphorically to any raised step or sill on the ground (문턱 'door threshold', 창턱 'windowsill').
턱.notes: Common in 턱을 괴다 ('prop one's chin in one's hand') and 문턱 ('doorsill').

털다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 털다 ('to shake off dust or particles, beat out, empty out').

history.meaning: to shake off, knock dust from
to dust off, shake out, empty, rob

털보네.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) trimorphemic noun formed from 털 ('hair, beard, fur', Middle Korean 터리 theli / 털 thel) + personifying suffix -보 ('person characterized by an abundance of a trait or habit', hence 털보 'hairy or bearded fellow, Beardy') + associative/collective suffix -네 ('household, family, or shop belonging to X'). Literally 'Beardy's place/shop'.

history.meaning: hair, fur, plumage
bearded/hairy person + household/shop suffix > Beardy's family or shop

morphemes.meaning: person characterized by a notable trait or habit
family, household, home, or shop of X

털보네.notes: Traditional Korean neighborhood shops and diners are affectionately named [Nickname/Child's Name] + -네 (e.g., 털보네 'Beardy's Place', 순이네 'Suni's Shop'), evoking a warm, family-run corner store.

털어놓다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 털다 ('to shake off dust, empty a container completely by shaking or knocking it', Middle Korean 털다 thelta) + connective suffix -어 + auxiliary verb 놓다 ('to put down, set out in the open, leave in a resulting state', Middle Korean 놓다 nwohtha). From the literal image of turning a pouch upside down and shaking out every last item, it evolved metaphorically into 'to confide everything, make a clean breast of, pour out one's heart'.

history.meaning: to shake off, empty out + to put down, lay out
to empty out completely; to confide candidly, disclose everything without reserve

morphemes.meaning: to shake off, empty out completely
to put down, lay out (completive auxiliary verb)

털어놓다.notes: 털어놓다 frequently pairs with 속마음 ('inner feelings'), 고민 ('worries'), or 비밀 ('secrets') when someone finally opens up and tells the whole truth.

rootFamily.gloss: to shake off dust; to empty out a pocket or account; to rob
to put down, let go, set in place
to empty out and squander completely (털다 + -어 + 먹다)

털털하다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) descriptive verb formed from the reduplicated ideophone 털털 (evoking the brisk, uninhibited motion of shaking dust off without fuss—related to 털다 'to shake off'—or a rough, unpretentious rattling motion) + adjective-deriving light verb 하다. Used of temperament, it describes a person who is refreshingly unaffected, easygoing, and not picky about small formalities.

history.meaning: briskly shaking off / rattling without fuss + to be
easygoing, unaffected, free and easy, not finicky

morphemes.meaning: ideophone: briskly shaking off; unpretentious and unfussy

털털하다.notes: In Korean character descriptions, calling someone 성격이 털털하다 is high praise—it means they are down-to-earth, approachable, and hold no airs or grudges (as opposed to 까칠하다 'prickly/fussy').

rootFamily.gloss: to shake off, brush away without fuss
an easygoing, unpretentious person; a rattling old vehicle
to clatter, chug, rattle along noisily

텅.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/ideophonic adverb expressing the state of a large space or hollow interior being completely empty (commonly in 텅 비다 'to be completely empty').

history.meaning: hollowly, completely empty

텅텅.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) reduplicated mimetic/onomatopoeic adverb (부사) formed by doubling 텅 ('hollow, cavernously empty'). Originally echoing the deep, resonant sound of striking a hollow drum or stepping into an empty cavern (the yin-vowel ablaut counterpart of yang-vowel 탕탕), 텅텅 intensifies the sense of complete vacancy across a large space.

history.meaning: hollow resonance > cavernously, completely empty throughout

morphemes.meaning: ideophone: hollow, wide open and empty
reduplicated syllable intensifying emptiness across space

텅텅.notes: 텅 and its intensified reduplication 텅텅 almost exclusively modify the verb 비다 ('to be empty') in the idiom 텅(텅) 비다—used for an empty studio, an empty bus, or even an empty head/wallet.

rootFamily.gloss: with a hollow echo; wide and completely empty
banging, booming; wide open (yang-vowel ablaut counterpart of 텅텅)
to be completely empty, deserted (collocation 텅 비다)

테.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 테 ('hoop, rim, frame, border bound around a barrel, wheel, or eyeglasses').

history.meaning: barrel hoop, circular band
rim, frame (of glasses), hoop, border

테두리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun joining 테 ('rim, hoop, eyeglass frame') with 두리 ('surrounding perimeter', derived from the verb root 두르- 'to encircle, wrap around' + nominalizer -이). Together 테두리 names both physical rims—such as a fountain basin or tin lid—and drawn page borders.
테두리.notes: Applies equally to 3D rims (분수대 테두리) and 2D borders (그림 테두리).

테이블.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English table ('piece of furniture with a flat top supported by legs; data chart', from Old French table, Latin tabula).

history.meaning: dining or work table
table

테이프.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tape ('narrow strip of cloth, adhesive plastic, or magnetic recording ribbon', from Old English tæppe).

history.meaning: adhesive tape, ribbon, magnetic tape
tape

cognates.meaning: state of being stretched tight; mental or emotional strain
emotional excitement, energy level, high spirits (wasei-eigo sense)

텐션.etymology: Borrowed from English tension, via Old French tension from Latin tensio ('a stretching'), derived from the past participle stem tens- of tendere ('to stretch, strain, extend', from Proto-Indo-European *ten- 'to stretch'). Alongside the standard English sense of dramatic suspense or physical tautness, colloquial Korean and broadcasting slang adopted the Japanese-mediated semantic shift where 텐션 means 'emotional energy, hype, excitement level, or vibe'.

history.meaning: to stretch > a stretching > physical tautness or psychological strain
level of excitement, liveliness, or emotional energy
dramatic suspense; upbeat energy level, hype, or mood vibe

텐션.notes: False friend alert: in Korean variety shows and daily conversation, 텐션이 높다 ('tension is high') or 텐션 올리다 ('raise the tension') does NOT mean people are stressed or hostile—it means they are hyped up, energetic, and in high spirits!

rootFamily.gloss: high energy, exuberant mood, hyperactive spirits
lowered energy, subdued or tired mood
sense of dramatic tension or tautness

cognates.meaning: portable shelter of fabric stretched over poles

텐트.etymology: Borrowed from English tent, from Middle English tente, from Old French tente, from Medieval Latin tenta ('stretched cloth, pavilion'), a nominalized feminine past participle of Latin tendere ('to stretch, spread out', from Proto-Indo-European *ten- 'to stretch'—making 텐트 a direct Indo-European root-doublet of 텐션).

history.meaning: to stretch > stretched canvas shelter
portable shelter of cloth supported by poles
camping tent or outdoor canopy

텐트.notes: In Korean, 'to pitch a tent' is expressed with the verb 치다 ('to strike/set up'): 텐트를 치다 (whereas the Sino-Korean equivalent 천막을 치다 is used for large event canopies or relief tents).

rootFamily.gloss: rooftop tent mounted on a vehicle
large tent, canopy, pavilion (Sino-Korean synonym 天幕)

cognates.meaning: cultural stay program at a Korean Buddhist temple

템플스테이.etymology: South Korean English-based compound (템플 temple + 스테이 stay, modeled on 홈스테이 homestay) officially coined in 2002 by the Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism (대한불교조계종 한국불교문화사업단) during the 2002 Korea-Japan FIFA World Cup to provide foreign visitors and domestic retreats with overnight lodging and monastic life experience at traditional Korean Buddhist temples (사찰). English temple comes from Latin templum ('consecrated space'), and stay comes via Old French ester from Latin stare ('to stand, remain').

history.meaning: sanctuary/monastery + overnight lodging
cultural and meditative overnight retreat program at a Korean Buddhist monastery

morphemes.meaning: stay; overnight lodging and experiential retreat

템플스테이.notes: In Korean pop culture (including The Producers), going on a 템플스테이 is a classic trope for overworked urbanites or celebrities seeking digital detox, monastic vegetarian meals (발우공양), and 108 prostrations (108배) to clear their minds.

rootFamily.gloss: homestay; lodging with a local host family
overnight lodging in a traditional Korean house (韓屋 + stay)

cognates.meaning: powdered ink for printers; skin lotion

토너.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English toner, an agentive derivative of tone (from Old French ton, Latin tonus, and Ancient Greek tonos 'stretching, tension, pitch'). In Korean, 토너 denotes both electrostatic powdered ink used in office laser printers/copiers and liquid cosmetic skin lotion.

history.meaning: tension of a cord, vocal pitch, or shade of color
chemical agent that alters color tone, printer ink powder, or skin lotion
printer/copier toner cartridge or cosmetic skin toner

토너.notes: In office settings (such as a broadcast station newsroom or production office in The Producers), 토너 almost always refers to copier/printer ink cartridges rather than skincare lotion.

rootFamily.gloss: to tone up, brighten skin tone

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Dictionary): 토너

토마토수프.etymology: Compound loanword formed from 토마토 ('tomato', from English tomato) + 수프 ('soup', from English soup).

history.meaning: soup made from tomatoes
tomato soup

토스트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English toast ('sliced bread browned by radiant heat; toasted sandwich', from Old French toster, Latin torrere 'to parch, roast').

history.meaning: toasted bread
toast, toasted sandwich

토요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 토요일 (土曜日), combining 토 (土, 'earth / Saturn'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day').
토요일.notes: Part of the traditional East Asian seven-luminaries week cycle adopted into modern Korean calendar usage.

톡.etymology: A native Korean ideophonic (의성어/의태어) adverb depicting a sharp, light snapping, tapping, or popping sound or motion. With yang-vowel harmony (오), 톡 conveys a lighter, crisper, more decisive impact than its yin-vowel counterpart 툭 (which feels heavier and duller). In idiomatic collocations like 톡 까놓고 말하다 ('to lay it all out and speak bluntly'), it evokes snapping open a cover cleanly.

history.meaning: onomatopoeia for a crisp tap, snap, or sudden protrusion
sharply, lightly snapping; openly and bluntly (with 까놓다)

morphemes.meaning: crisp tapping, snapping, or popping ideophone

톡.notes: Notice the Korean vowel-harmony contrast: 톡 (bright vowel ㅗ) feels crisp, snappy, or stinging (톡 쏘다 'to be tangy/pungent'), whereas 툭 (dark vowel ㅜ) feels heavier or more nonchalant (툭 던지다 'to toss out casually').

rootFamily.gloss: with a heavier thud, casually, bluntly
tapping or patting lightly and repeatedly
to be tangy, pungent, or sharp-tongued

톡톡.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated ideophone (의성어/의태어) 톡톡 (toktok), formed by doubling the single-pulse root 톡 (tok, representing a light, crisp snap, tap, or pop). In Korean sound symbolism, the bright vowel ㅗ (o) combined with the aspirated alveolar stop ㅌ (t) conveys a small, light, crisp impact—such as tapping a wooden music stand with a violin bow, tapping someone's shoulder, or raindrops pattering on leaves—in contrast to heavier 툭툭 (tuktuk, with dark vowel ㅜ) or solid door-knocking 똑똑 (ttokttok, with tense ㄸ).

history.meaning: reduplicated ideophone for light, crisp tapping or popping
tap-tap, lightly and crisply tapping

morphemes.meaning: single light tap or pop (bright-vowel sound symbolic root)
reduplicated syllable indicating repeated light taps

톡톡.notes: Often modifies 두드리다 ('to tap/rap', e.g., 보면대를 톡톡 두드리다 'to tap a music stand lightly').

톱.etymology: A loanword (외래어) from English top (from Old English topp 'summit, crest, highest point'), partly mediated in journalistic and entertainment jargon via Japanese トップ (toppu). Note that Korean also possesses a homophonous native noun 톱 meaning 'saw' (attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 톱 / thwop), which is etymologically unrelated.

history.meaning: highest point, crest, tuft
highest rank, foremost position, lead story in journalism
first place, top celebrity rank, or lead headline article

morphemes.meaning: top, highest position, lead story (from English top)

톱.notes: Although standard orthography prescribes 톱 (following British/RP-based loanword transcription rules), colloquial speech and entertainment media very frequently pronounce and spell it 탑 (reflecting American English vowel quality).

톱스타.etymology: A compound loanword (외래어) formed from English top (highest rank) + star (celebrity, from Old English steorra, PIE *h₂stḗr), widely popularized in East Asian entertainment journalism alongside Japanese トップスター (toppu sutā) to designate A-list actors, singers, and entertainers who command headline billing.

history.meaning: highest-ranking or most famous performer
A-list celebrity, top-tier entertainer

톱스타.notes: In Korean entertainment industry discourse, 톱스타 specifically denotes an A-lister with nationwide recognition and top commercial/casting power, often contrasted with 신인 (rookie) or 중견 배우 (mid-career actor).

통.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and counter: (1) 통 (桶, 'tub, barrel, bucket, cylindrical container', from Middle Chinese *duwngX); (2) 통 (通, 'counter for letters, phone calls, or documents; whole/entirety').

history.meaning: wooden tub, barrel, container; counter for letters/calls
container, bin, barrel; counter for letters/calls

통계상.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound combining 통계 (統計, 'statistics', from 統 거느릴 통 'to govern, unite, gather as a whole' + 計 셈할 계 'to calculate, reckon') and the Sino-Korean bound relational suffix -상 (上, 위 상 'upon, from the standpoint of, in terms of').統計 was coined in Meiji-era Japan to translate English 'statistics' and adopted into Korean during the Enlightenment period.

history.meaning: systematic numerical calculation of collective data (statistics)
from the perspective of statistics; statistically speaking

morphemes.meaning: in terms of, from the standpoint of (上)

통계상.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -상 (上) attaches productively to nouns to mean 'in terms of X' or 'from the standpoint of X' (e.g., 이론상 'theoretically', 사실상 'virtually/in fact', 통계상 'statistically').

cognates.meaning: to circulate a notice; official bulletin

통보.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun written 通報, composed of 通 (통할 통, 'to pass through, communicate, transmit') and 報 (알릴 보 / 갚을 보, 'to report, inform, requite'). Originally attested in Classical Chinese administrative usage for circulating an official dispatch, in modern Korean it specifically denotes a unilateral notification or announcement of a decision.

history.meaning: to transmit an official report or circulate a dispatch
formal or unilateral notice, notification, or announcement

통보.notes: In everyday Korean interpersonal and workplace contexts (like firing someone or breaking up), 통보 carries a strong nuance of a one-way, unilateral announcement rather than a mutual consultation (상의): e.g., 일방적 통보 ('unilateral notice') or 이별 통보 ('dumping someone by announcing a breakup').

통보할.etymology: The prospective adnominal (관형사형) inflection of the Sino-Korean verb 통보하다 ('to notify'), composed of the Sino-Korean noun 통보 (通報: 通 통할 통 'to transmit, communicate' + 報 알릴 보 'to report, inform'), the native Korean light verb stem 하- ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá), and the prospective/irrealis adnominal ending -ㄹ ('which will / to [modify a following noun]').

history.meaning: which is to transmit a report or notify
to notify, that will notify (prospective modifier before a noun)

통보할.notes: The prospective modifier form -할 frequently combines with bound nouns to form grammatical constructions such as 통보할 때 ('when notifying'), 통보할 예정 ('scheduled to notify'), or 통보할 수 있다 ('can notify').

통신.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound written 通信, formed from 通 (통할 통, 'to pass through, connect, communicate') and 信 (믿을 신 / 소식 신, 'trust, letter, message, tidings'). In pre-modern Literary Sinitic and Joseon diplomacy (e.g., 조선통신사, the Joseon Tongsinsa diplomatic missions), it meant exchanging envoys or letters in good faith; in the modern era it came to denote telecommunications, news wire services, and colloquially an informal 'grapevine' or news channel (e.g., 매니저 통신 'the managers' grapevine').

history.meaning: to exchange letters, tidings, or diplomatic envoys in good faith
telecommunications, news wire dispatch, or informal grapevine

통신.notes: Beyond formal telecommunications (정보통신), Korean media and variety shows playfully append 통신 to a group name (like 매니저 통신 'the manager wire/grapevine') to mimic an official news agency (통신사, such as 연합뉴스) while referring to backstage gossip.

rootFamily.gloss: news agency or telecom carrier (通信社)

통지서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 통지서 (通知書), formed from 통지 (通知, 'notification, notice', from 통 通 'to communicate, pass through' + 지 知 'to know, inform') + 서 (書, 'written document').

history.meaning: notification + written document
written notice, notification form

cognates.meaning: ventilation, air circulation (通風); gout (痛風)

통풍.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun written 通風, composed of 通 (통할 통, 'to pass through, circulate freely') and 風 (바람 풍, 'wind, air current'). Literally 'letting the wind pass through', it refers to air circulation or ventilation in a room or garment. Note that it has an exact Sino-Korean homophone 통풍 (痛風, 아플 통 + 바람 풍), a traditional medical term meaning 'gout'.

history.meaning: allowing wind or air currents to pass through unobstructed
ventilation, air circulation, breathability of a space or fabric

통풍.notes: Watch out for the common homophone pair: 통풍 (通風) means 'ventilation/airiness' (통풍이 잘 되다 'to be well-ventilated'), whereas 통풍 (痛風, literally 'painful wind') is the medical condition 'gout'.

통하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 통 (通, 'to pass through, communicate, circulate, be understood') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to pass through, lead to, communicate
to go through, circulate, make oneself understood, flow

통학.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound written 通學, composed of 通 (통할 통 / 다닐 통, 'to pass through, go back and forth, commute') and 學 (배울 학, 'learning, school'). Coined in modern East Asian educational vocabulary (alongside Sino-Japanese 通学 tsūgaku) to describe traveling daily from home to school, contrasting with living in a dormitory (기숙 寄宿).

history.meaning: attending school by traveling daily from one's residence
history.stage: Meiji Sino-Japanese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: commuting to and from school

morphemes.meaning: to go back and forth, commute, pass through (通)

통학.notes: Korean distinguishes commuting by destination using the prefixal Hanja 通 (통-): 통학 (通學) is commuting to school, whereas 통근 (通勤) is commuting to work.

통화.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun written 通話, formed from 通 (통할 통, 'to pass through, connect, communicate') and 話 (말씀 화, 'speech, talk, conversation'). Literally 'connecting speech across a distance', it became the standard East Asian term for a telephone conversation. Note its Sino-Korean homophone 통화 (通貨, 'currency in circulation', where 貨 is 재물 화 'goods, money').

history.meaning: conversing with someone or speaking over a telegraph/telephone line
a telephone call or phone conversation

통화.notes: When calling someone in Korea, the standard phrase for 'the line is busy' is 통화 중이다 (literally 'currently in the middle of a phone call'). Don't confuse it with the economic homophone 통화 (通貨, 'currency').

통화하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verbal compound combining the noun 통화 (通話, from 通 통할 통 'to connect, pass through' + 話 말씀 화 'speech, talk') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do', from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá). It specifically means to hold a conversation over the telephone, as opposed to merely dialing a number.

history.meaning: to connect speech / converse across a distance
to speak on the telephone, have a phone conversation

통화하다.notes: Whereas 전화하다 (電話하다) focuses on the act of placing a phone call ('to call someone'), 통화하다 (通話하다) focuses on actually being connected and talking with the other person on the line.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a phone call (電話)

퇴근.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 퇴근 (退勤), composed of 퇴 (退, 'to step back, withdraw, leave') and 근 (勤, 'diligent labor, official duty, service'). Paired symmetrically with its antonym 출근 (出勤, 'setting out for work'), it has been the standard Korean term across government offices, workshops, and companies for finishing the workday and heading home. It combines with -하다 to form the verb 퇴근하다 ('to get off work') and with 후 ('after') in 퇴근 후에 ('after work').

history.meaning: withdrawing from official duty at the end of the workday
leaving work, clocking off for the day

rootFamily.gloss: to leave work, finish work for the day

퇴근.notes: 퇴근 후에 ('after leaving work') is one of the most frequent everyday time phrases in Korean conversation.

퇴근하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed from 퇴근 (退勤, composed of 退 물러날 퇴 'to withdraw, step back, leave' + 勤 부지런할 근 'diligent labor, official duty, office work') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá). It pairs symmetrically with its antonym 출근하다 (出勤하다, 'to go to work / clock in').

history.meaning: withdrawing from one's post after completing official duty
to leave the workplace after finishing work for the day, to clock out

퇴근하다.notes: In Korean workplace culture (and notoriously in TV broadcasting stations in The Producers, where overnight editing is routine), 퇴근하다 is one of the most emotionally charged daily words, spawning slang like 칼퇴근 ('leaving work right on the dot like a knife').

rootFamily.gloss: going to work, clocking in (出勤)
to work, be on duty (勤務)

cognates.meaning: leaving the hospital (usually 出院 in modern Mandarin)

퇴원.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun written 退院, composed of 退 (물러날 퇴, 'to withdraw, leave, depart') and 院 (집 원, 'courtyard building, public institution', here specifically clipping 병원 病院 'hospital'). Adopted across modern East Asian medical administration (alongside Japanese 退院 taiin) as the direct antonym of 입원 (入院, 'hospital admission/hospitalization').

history.meaning: withdrawing from a monastic hall, academy, or institutional building
official discharge of a patient from a hospital

morphemes.meaning: institution, hospital building (院, clipping of 病院)

퇴원.notes: Forms a neat antonymic pair with 입원 (入院, 'hospital admission'): 입원 refers to checking into the hospital as an inpatient, and 퇴원 refers to being discharged.

rootFamily.gloss: to be discharged from the hospital

cognates.meaning: to be discharged from the hospital

퇴원하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed by attaching the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá) to the Sino-Korean noun 퇴원 (退院, from 退 물러날 퇴 'to withdraw, depart' + 院 집 원 'hospital institution', a clipping of 병원 病院). It denotes completing inpatient medical treatment and leaving the hospital.

history.meaning: to depart from an institution or hospital
to leave or be discharged from the hospital after inpatient care

퇴원하다.notes: In Korean grammar, 퇴원하다 is an active intransitive verb ('the patient checks out / leaves the hospital'), whereas English usually expresses this passively ('to be discharged from the hospital'). To say a doctor discharged someone, Korean uses the causative 퇴원시키다.

rootFamily.gloss: to be hospitalized, admitted to hospital (入院)

cognates.meaning: exit from a stage, venue, or sports field (ejection)
to exit a stage, hall, or arena

퇴장.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun written 退場, composed of 退 (물러날 퇴, 'to withdraw, retreat, leave') and 場 (마당 장, 'open ground, stage, venue, arena'). Used in theater, broadcasting, ceremonies, and sports for exiting the stage or studio floor—or being sent off/ejected from a match—in direct opposition to 등장 (登場, 'entering the stage') or 입장 (入場, 'entering the venue').

history.meaning: withdrawing from an examination hall, ceremonial ground, or stage
stage exit in theater/TV, leaving a ceremony venue, or ejection in sports

퇴장.notes: In TV variety shows and drama scripts (like The Producers), 퇴장 appears constantly as a stage direction ('[Character] exits') and in variety subtitles when a cast member is eliminated from a game and must leave the set.

rootFamily.gloss: to exit the stage or venue, be sent off
appearance on stage or screen (登場)

cognates.meaning: to retire or resign from one's job
to resign or retire from office

퇴직하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed from 퇴직 (退職, composed of 退 물러날 퇴 'to withdraw, step down' + 職 직분 직 'office, post, employment') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá). It denotes stepping down from one's salaried occupation or official post, whether through age-based retirement (정년퇴직) or voluntary/involuntary departure.

history.meaning: to step down from an official post or government office
to retire or leave one's job/employment permanently

퇴직하다.notes: Unlike English 'retire' (which usually implies stopping work permanently due to age, called 은퇴하다 隱退하다 or 정년퇴직하다 in Korean), 퇴직하다 covers leaving any salaried job, which is why severance pay for any departing employee in Korea is called 퇴직금 (退職金).

투룸.etymology: A Korean-coined pseudo-anglicism (콩글리시, Konglish) compounded from English two (Old English twā) + room (Old English rūm 'space, chamber'), modeled by analogy on 원룸 ('one-room', i.e., a studio apartment, itself influenced by Japanese ワンルーム wanrūmu). In South Korean real-estate usage, 투룸 specifically denotes a compact apartment layout with two separate rooms (typically a bedroom and a living/second room) plus a kitchen/bathroom.

history.meaning: cardinal number two + chamber/room
compact apartment unit with two distinct rooms (as opposed to a studio 원룸)

투룸.notes: A classic Korean real-estate false friend: 원룸 ('one-room') means a studio apartment, and 투룸 ('two-room') usually means a one-bedroom apartment with a separate living room (or two bedrooms with a kitchenette) in a small multi-unit building (빌라/오피스텔).

cognates.meaning: camera shot framing two subjects together
camera shot or photo of two people together (often romantic)

투샷.etymology: Borrowed from English cinematography and television production jargon two-shot (from two + shot, Old English sceot 'rapid motion, discharge, range'), reinforced by Japanese broadcasting/entertainment usage ツーショット (tsūshotto). Originally a technical camera framing term showing two subjects in a single frame, it expanded in Korean media and everyday speech to mean any photo or on-screen appearance of two people together.

history.meaning: film or television camera angle framing two performers together
a camera frame or photograph capturing two people side by side

morphemes.meaning: camera shot, frame, photograph (from English shot)

투샷.notes: In broadcasting scripts and variety shows like The Producers, 투샷 is essential PD/cameraman jargon for framing two hosts or guests together on screen, and in fan culture it often implies visual chemistry between two celebrities. (Prescriptive loanword orthography writes 투숏, but 투샷 is overwhelmingly standard in actual broadcast and public usage.)

rootFamily.gloss: solo camera shot framing one person ('one-shot')
full-body or wide group camera shot ('full shot')
close-up shot or nice shot in photography/coffee

cognates.meaning: package tour, guided tour, concert tour

투어.etymology: A loanword (외래어) borrowed from English tour, which derives via Middle French tour ('a turn, circuit, journey') from Old French torn / tor and Latin tornus ('lathe, circular movement'), ultimately from Ancient Greek tornos ('carpenter's compass, lathe'). In Korean, 투어 refers to a guided visit (such as a 방송국 견학 투어 'broadcasting station viewer tour'), a travel itinerary, or a concert/sports tour.

history.meaning: lathe, tool for drawing a circle, circular turn
a circuitous journey, guided excursion, or series of performances
guided tour, package excursion, concert tour, or golf tour

morphemes.meaning: tour, guided excursion, circuit (from English tour)

투어.notes: In Korean lifestyle and media usage, 투어 is productively attached to nouns to mean 'a themed outing/crawl'—such as 맛집 투어 ('a foodie tour of famous restaurants') or 시청자 투어 ('a viewer tour of a TV network').

rootFamily.gloss: tourism, sightseeing (native Sino-Korean equivalent 觀光)

투자하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verb formed from the noun 투자 (投資, composed of 投 던질 투 'to cast, throw, put into' + 資 재물 자 'capital, resources, wealth') and the native Korean verbalizer 하다 ('to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá). Metaphorically 'throwing capital into an enterprise', it is used in modern Korean both for financial investment (in stocks, real estate, or TV/film production) and figuratively for investing time or effort.

history.meaning: putting financial capital into a business venture for profit
history.stage: Modern Sino-Japanese / Early Modern East Asian economic lexicon

history.meaning: to invest money, capital, time, or effort into something

투자하다.notes: Just like English 'invest', 투자하다 takes the particle -에 for the target of investment: 시간과 노력을 일에 투자하다 ('to invest time and effort into one's work') or 드라마 제작에 투자하다 ('to invest in drama production').

cognates.word: 投資公司 / 投资公司 (tóuzī gōngsī)

투자회사.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound noun (投資會社) combining 투자 (投資, 'investment', from 投 던질 투 'to cast, put in' + 資 재물 자 'capital, funds') and 회사 (會社, 'company, corporation', from 會 모일 회 'to gather, assemble' + 社 모임 사 'association, society'). In the Korean entertainment and broadcasting industry, 투자회사 often refers to venture capital or media investment firms that finance drama and film production.

history.meaning: capital investment + commercial association/corporation
history.stage: Early Modern Sino-Japanese / Sino-Korean economic terms

history.meaning: investment firm, capital management company

투자회사.notes: In financial and media contexts, 투자회사 is often shortened to 투자사 (投資社, 'investment firm / financier'), paralleling 제작사 (製作社, 'production company') and 방송사 (放送社, 'broadcasting network').

투철하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from 투철 (透徹, composed of 透 사무칠 투 'to penetrate, pass right through, be transparent' + 徹 통할 철 / 뚫을 철 'to pierce through, pervade to the bottom') and the native Korean suffix 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 / hòtá). Originally describing water or enlightenment that is crystal-clear all the way through, in modern Korean it characterizes a mindset, sense of duty, or spirit that is thoroughgoing, unwavering, and rock-solid.

history.meaning: penetrating all the way through; crystal-clear and unobstructed (often in Buddhist/literary prose)
to be thoroughgoing, resolute, unwavering, or rock-solid (of a sense of duty or spirit)

morphemes.meaning: to penetrate, pass through, be transparent (透)

투철하다.notes: 투철하다 has a very strong collocational preference in Korean: it almost always modifies words for mindset, spirit, or professional duty, such as 직업정신이 투철하다 ('to have a rock-solid work ethic'), 사명감이 투철하다 ('to have an unwavering sense of mission'), or 프로 의식이 투철하다 ('to be thoroughly professional').

투표.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun written 投票, composed of 投 (던질 투, 'to cast, throw, drop in') and 票 (표 표, 'slip of paper, ticket, ballot'). Literally 'casting a ballot slip into a box', it was standardized in late 19th-century East Asian constitutional and parliamentary terminology (alongside Japanese 投票 tōhyō) to translate Western 'voting / ballot' and is today used equally for political elections and TV audience popularity polls.

history.meaning: casting a written slip or ballot to select a candidate or decide a motion
voting, casting a ballot, or a poll/election vote

투표.notes: In Korean variety and audition programs (as well as workplace scenes in The Producers), 인기투표 ('popularity poll/vote') and 문자 투표 ('live SMS viewer voting') are staples of broadcast culture.

툴툴거리다.etymology: A native Korean expressive verb formed from the reduplicated ideophonic root 툴툴 (depicting muttering, grumbling, or shaking something off with discontent) and the verbal suffix -거리다 ('to repeatedly make the sound or motion of'). By Korean vowel-harmony sound symbolism, 툴툴 (with the dark/yin vowel ㅜ) expresses a heavier, sulkier, more sullen grumbling than its bright/yang counterpart 톨톨.

history.meaning: to repeatedly mutter or grumble under one's breath in displeasure
to grumble, mutter complaints, or grouse sullenly

morphemes.meaning: ideophone for sullen muttering or grumbling under one's breath
verbal suffix indicating repeated sound or action (interchangeable with -대다)

툴툴거리다.notes: Often used in K-dramas to describe the classic 'tsundere' behavior of a character who grumbles and complains (툴툴거리면서) while still doing everything asked of them. It is completely interchangeable with 툴툴대다.

rootFamily.gloss: to grumble, mutter complaints repeatedly (synonym with -대다)
to grumble in a deeper, heavier voice (투덜거리다)

퉁치다.etymology: A colloquial Korean compound verb combining 퉁 (most likely derived from the Sino-Korean root 通 통할 통, 'as a whole, in bulk, passing through together', phonologically reinforced by tensed/aspirated colloquial pronunciation [tʰuŋ], or from merchant jargon for lumping items together) with the native Korean verb 치다 ('to strike, reckon, count as', Middle Korean 티다 / thità). Literally 'to reckon in one lump', it evolved into the everyday idiom for offsetting debts, lumping obligations together, or calling things even.

history.meaning: to reckon or settle multiple items together as a single lump sum
to call it even, offset mutual debts/favors, or lump things together roughly

morphemes.meaning: lump sum, offsetting bulk (colloquial variant associated with 通)
to reckon, count as, strike (native verb 치다)

퉁치다.notes: Extremely common in casual spoken Korean when settling small debts, favors, or mistakes—for example, 점심 내가 샀으니까 이걸로 퉁치자! ('Since I bought lunch, let's call it even with this!') or combining a birthday and holiday gift into one.

rootFamily.gloss: wholesale, in bulk, as a whole (통째로)
to offset, cancel out (formal Sino-Korean equivalent 相殺하다)

튀기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 튀다 ('to spring, bounce, splatter, pop', Middle Korean 튀다) + causative suffix -기- ('to make splatter/pop; to deep-fry in hot oil').

history.meaning: to cause to bounce/splatter -> to deep-fry in oil

튀다.etymology: A native Korean verb (고유어) attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 뛰다 (ptwuyta, with initial consonant cluster ㅸ/ㅂㄷ representing a reinforced stop) alongside aspirated forms meaning 'to spring, spatter, rebound, leap'. Through semantic radiation from the core physical sense of 'springing or spattering outward suddenly', 튀다 developed three major modern senses: (1) to splatter or bounce (of sparks, oil, water, or balls), (2) to stand out conspicuously (of colors, fashion, or personality), and (3) in colloquial slang, to bolt, flee, or run away suddenly.

history.meaning: to leap, spring up, spatter, or rebound suddenly
to splatter/bounce; to stand out noticeably; (slang) to bolt, run off, flee

morphemes.meaning: to spring, splatter, bounce, stand out, bolt

튀다.notes: Context determines which of the three vivid meanings of 튀다 is active: 기름이 튀다 ('oil splatters'), 옷 색깔이 너무 튄다 ('the clothes' color really stands out/is flashy'), or 돈 안 내고 튀었다 ('bolted/ran off without paying').

rootFamily.gloss: to pop out, spring out, blurt out
to dash over, bounce up here

튀어나오다.etymology: A trimorphemic native Korean serial-verb compound (합성동사) built from 튀- (stem of 튀다 'to spring, bounce, pop'), the infinitive/connective suffix -어, 나- (stem of 나다 'to emerge, come out', Middle Korean 나다 / nàtá), and 오다 ('to come toward the speaker', Middle Korean 오다 / wòtá). Combining manner of motion (튀어 'springing') with path (나- 'out') and deictic direction (오다 'hither'), it means to pop out, protrude, or jump out suddenly toward the observer.

history.meaning: to spring forth and emerge hither
to pop out, jump out suddenly, protrude, or be blurted out (of words)

튀어나오다.notes: Besides someone physically jumping out of a room or car (갑자기 어디서 튀어나왔어? 'Where did you suddenly pop out from?'), 튀어나오다 is used for protruding body parts (입이 툭 튀어나오다 'to pout one's lips out') and involuntary speech (진심이 툭 튀어나오다 'one's true feelings slip/blurt right out').

rootFamily.gloss: to bounce, splatter, stand out, bolt
to dash out, spring out away from speaker (with 가다)

튀어오다.etymology: A native Korean directional compound verb formed from 튀- (stem of 튀다 'to spring, bounce, dash'), the connective suffix -어, and the deictic motion verb 오다 ('to come toward the speaker', Middle Korean 오다 / wòtá). Literally 'to come bouncing/springing hither', in colloquial Korean it vividly describes someone rushing, dashing, or bounding right over to the speaker's location at once (often when summoned urgently).

history.meaning: to come rebounding or springing toward the speaker
to bounce toward the speaker; (colloquial) to dash or rush right over here

튀어오다.notes: In workplace or senior-junior hierarchy scenes (like a senior PD calling a junior PD or a celebrity summoning their manager), 당장 튀어와! ('Get yourself over here right this second!') is a common, forceful colloquial command. Its opposite direction is 튀어가다 ('to dash over there').

rootFamily.gloss: to dash over there, bounce away (with 가다)
to pop out, jump out toward speaker

트럭.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from American English truck ('motor vehicle designed to carry freight').

history.meaning: freight motor vehicle, lorry
truck

cognates.meaning: athletic workout, coaching, tracksuit (トレーニングウェア)

트레이닝.etymology: A loanword (외래어) borrowed from English training, the verbal noun of train (from Middle English trainen, Old French trainer 'to draw, drag, instruct by trailing', and Vulgar Latin *traginare, extended from Latin trahere 'to pull, draw'). In South Korean usage, 트레이닝 refers specifically to systematic skill coaching (such as K-pop idol vocal/dance training or acting coaching), fitness workouts, and—often shortened from 트레이닝복—a tracksuit or sweatsuit.

history.meaning: to pull, draw along, bring up by disciplined course
systematic instruction, physical conditioning, or coaching
skill/idol coaching, athletic workout, or tracksuit (트레이닝복)

morphemes.meaning: to train, coach, condition (from English train)

트레이닝.notes: In the Korean entertainment industry (central to The Producers), 트레이닝 specifically evokes the rigorous vocal, dance, and media coaching given to agency trainees (연습생). Additionally, 트레이닝복 (colloquially slurred to 추리닝 via Japanese トレーニング) means a tracksuit/sweatsuit.

rootFamily.gloss: personal or athletic trainer (from English trainer)

트집.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound formed from the verb stem 트- (from 트다, Middle Korean 트다, 'to crack open, burst, split') and the noun 집 ('flaw, crack, scar, blemish', preserved in compounds such as 흠집). Originally referring to a physical crack or split opening in a vessel or surface, it underwent semantic extension to mean a minor flaw or pretext seized upon to pick a quarrel or criticize someone.

history.meaning: a physical crack, split, or blemish opening on a surface
a nitpicked flaw, pretext for complaint, or fault-finding

트집.notes: Almost always used in the collocation 트집을 잡다 ('to nitpick, find fault, or pick a quarrel over nothing').

특가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 특가 (特價), contracted from 특별 가격 (特別價格, 'special price') by joining 특 (特, 'special, exceptional') directly with 가 (價, 'price, value'). Widely used in Korean markets, catalogs, and shops for a promotional or bulk discount price, it takes the instrumental particle -로 in 특가로 사다 ('to buy at a bargain/special price'). Because 특 ends in the velar stop ㄱ, the initial velar stop of 가 tensifies in pronunciation to [특까] (teukkka).

history.meaning: special reduced price
bargain price, special promotional price

특가.notes: Sungmin's accidental purchase of twenty-four folding chairs at a 특가 ('special bargain price') in Season 2 pays off on opening night!

특권.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 特權, composed of 特 (특, 'special, exceptional, outstanding', originally a prized bull for sacrifice) and 權 (권, 'power, authority, right', originally a steelyard weight used to measure balance and leverage). Standardized in late 19th-century East Asian legal vocabulary (alongside Japanese 特権 tokken) to translate European concepts of legal privilege and exclusive prerogative.

history.meaning: exceptional sacrificial bull + steelyard weight / authority
exclusive legal or social privilege and prerogative

특권.notes: Frequently paired with 의식 in 특권 의식 ('sense of entitlement / elitism') when criticizing powerful figures or senior officials.

특급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 특급 (特急), shortened from 특별 급행 (特別急行, 'special express') or 特級 ('special grade').
특급.notes: Widely used on express trains and courier vans (특급 배달, 'express delivery').

특별히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb derived from the Sino-Korean noun 特別 (특별, 'special, extraordinary', from 特 특 'special, exceptional' + 別 별 'separate, distinguish, divide') combined with the native Korean deadjectival adverbial suffix -히 (from Middle Korean -히, deriving adverbs from -하다 descriptive verbs). Literally 'in a manner that stands apart from the ordinary.'

history.meaning: in a distinct or extraordinary manner
specially, particularly, extraordinarily

특별히.notes: In negative sentences (e.g., 특별히 문제없다), it translates naturally to 'nothing in particular' or 'not especially.'

특수하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb combining the Sino-Korean root 特殊 (특수, 'special, particular, distinct', from 特 특 'special, exceptional' + 殊 수 'different, unique, distinct') with the native Korean light verb and adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be'). Unlike 특별하다 (which implies positive extraordinariness), 특수하다 emphasizes technical, structural, or situational distinctiveness.

history.meaning: distinctly different from ordinary cases
to be special, specialized, or particular in nature

특수하다.notes: Used for specialized fields or circumstances (e.g., 특수 효과 'special effects', 특수 부대 'special forces') rather than personal favors.

특식.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 特食, formed from 特 (특, 'special, exceptional') and 食 (식, 'food, meal, eating'). Coined to denote a special, upgraded meal served on holidays, anniversaries, or high-stress workdays in institutional cafeterias, military barracks, or broadcasting station canteens to boost morale.

history.meaning: exceptional, standout + cooked grain, food, meal
special holiday or morale-boosting meal in an institution or household

특식.notes: Common in workplace, school, and military culture when the cafeteria serves premium dishes like galbi or samgyetang instead of regular fare.

특이하네.etymology: Inflected form of the hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb 특이하다 (from Sino-Korean 特異 특이 'peculiar, unusual, singular', composed of 特 특 'special' + 異 이 'different, strange', plus the native adjective-forming stem -하-) conjugated with the native Korean mirative/exclamatory sentence-final ending -네, which expresses immediate personal realization or mild surprise upon noticing something unexpected.

history.meaning: peculiar/unusual + mirative sentence-final marker

특이하네.notes: In polite conversation, saying '특이하네(요)' is a diplomatic way to call someone's taste or behavior 'weird' or 'eccentric' without using the blunt 이상하다 ('strange').

특이하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 特異 (특이, 'peculiar, singular, unusual', composed of 特 특 'special, exceptional' and 異 이 'different, divergent, extraordinary') combined with the native Korean adjectivalizer -하다 ('to be'). It describes traits or phenomena that diverge noticeably from standard norms.

history.meaning: standing out as markedly different from the norm
to be unique, peculiar, or unusual

특이하다.notes: Can carry either a neutral-positive nuance ('unique, distinctive') or a politely critical nuance ('quirky, odd') depending on tone of voice.

특집.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 特輯, consisting of 特 (특, 'special, exceptional') and 輯 (집, 'compile, gather together, edit', originally referring to fitting together the parts of a carriage). First used in print journalism for a specially compiled magazine or newspaper feature, it was adopted into radio and television broadcasting to denote a special holiday or thematic broadcast episode.

history.meaning: special + assembling carriage parts / compiling texts
special compiled print issue or special television/radio broadcast

특집.notes: Essential broadcasting terminology in Korean TV stations (e.g., 명절 특집 'holiday special', 납량 특집 'summer horror special').

rootFamily.gloss: special issue of a periodical (特輯號)

특집쇼.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and English loanword compound combining Sino-Korean 特輯 (특집, 'special compilation, special broadcast', from 特 특 'special' + 輯 집 'compile, edit') with the English loanword 쇼 (syo, from English show, ultimately from Old English scēawian 'to look at, inspect, display'). Refers to a large-scale special entertainment or variety broadcast.

history.meaning: special broadcast compilation + entertainment show

특집쇼.notes: Typical of year-end or anniversary television programming where a network stages a lavish one-off concert or variety spectacle.

특혜.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 特惠, composed of 特 (특, 'special, exclusive, exceptional') and 惠 (혜, 'favor, grace, benevolence, benefit'). While the characters literally mean 'special benevolence,' in contemporary Korean socio-political usage it frequently carries a critical connotation of unfair preferential treatment, cronyism, or special exemptions given to elites.

history.meaning: special, exceptional + benevolence, kindness, favor
special favor, exclusive benefit, or unfair preferential treatment

특혜.notes: Whereas 혜택 (惠澤) is a positive 'benefit' or 'perk', 특혜 (特惠) in news and workplace contexts often implies unfair favoritism (특혜 논란 'favoritism controversy').

rootFamily.gloss: grace, moral debt of kindness (恩惠)

특히.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean adverb formed directly by attaching the native Korean deadjectival adverbial suffix -히 ('-ly') to the single Sino-Korean bound root 特 (특, 'special, exceptional, standout'). It functions as a more concise, high-frequency counterpart to 특별히 ('specially, particularly').

history.meaning: in a standout or particular manner

특히.notes: Used to single out a standout example from a broader group ('especially X'), whereas 특별히 often modifies actions ('went out of one's way to do X specially').

튼튼하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated dark-vowel mimetic root 튼튼 ('sturdy, strong, robust, durable', heavy-vowel counterpart of 탄탄하다) + -하다.

history.meaning: strong, sturdy, robust, solid

틀.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 틀 (thul, 'wooden frame, mold, loom, mechanical contrivance'). Originally denoting a rigid physical frame or casting mold used by artisans (such as 베틀 'weaving loom' or 창틀 'window frame'), it developed the abstract sense of an established structural format, convention, or fixed routine.

history.meaning: physical wooden frame, casting mold, or mechanical loom
physical frame or mold; abstract format, framework, or convention

틀.notes: Central to idioms like 틀에 박히다 ('to be stuck in a mold / stereotyped, conventional') and 틀을 깨다 ('to break the mold').

틀다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 틀다 (thulta, 'to twist, wind, wring, turn'). Because early mechanical devices, water faucets, phonographs, radios, and television sets were operated by physically twisting a crank, valve, or rotary dial, the verb semantically expanded from 'to twist/turn' to 'to turn on (an appliance)' and 'to put on / play (music or a broadcast)'.

history.meaning: to twist, wind, wring, or turn physically
to twist or turn; to turn on a tap/appliance or play media/music

morphemes.meaning: to twist, turn, wind; to turn on or play media

틀다.notes: Used for playing recorded audio/video or turning on a TV/radio/fan/faucet (노래를 틀다, 티브이를 틀다), whereas 켜다 means switching on power or lights.

rootFamily.gloss: to get twisted, go awry, fall out with someone

틀리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 틀다 ('to twist, wind, turn awry', Middle Korean 틀다) + passive suffix -리-, literally 'to be twisted out of alignment' -> 'to go wrong, be incorrect, be mistaken'.

history.meaning: to twist -> to be twisted, go awry
to be wrong, incorrect, mistaken

틀림없다.etymology: Lexicalized native Korean compound adjective uniting 틀림 (substantive nominalization of 틀리다, 'to go awry, be mistaken') with 없다 ('not to exist'). Literally 'there is zero mistake', it functions after noun + 이/가 as Korean's idiomatic equivalent of 'it must certainly be X'.
틀림없다.notes: Used with subject particle 이/가 (X이/가 틀림없다 'it has to be X').

틀림없이.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized adverb formed by attaching the adverbial suffix -이 to the compound stem 틀림없- ('without error or discrepancy'). Attested across modern Korean speech and prose, 틀림없이 expresses strong speaker conviction either about an inference ('definitely') or about a future commitment ('without fail').
틀림없이.notes: Placed near the start of a clause to express confident deduction.

틈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 틈 ('crack, gap, chink, spare moment'), nominalized with -ㅁ from the verb 트다 ('to split open, crack, chap').

history.meaning: to crack open -> crack, opening, gap
gap, crack, opening, spare time

티.etymology: Loanword (외래어) formed by clipping 티셔츠 (tisyeocheu), itself borrowed from English T-shirt, an early 20th-century compound named after the capital letter T formed by the garment's body and short sleeves when laid flat. In everyday Korean speech, the clipped monosyllable 티 functions both as an independent noun ('T-shirt / casual top') and as a productive compounding head.

history.meaning: collarless short-sleeved undershirt shaped like the letter T
T-shirt, casual knit pullover or top

티.notes: In Korean fashion vocabulary, 티 has broadened beyond short-sleeved T-shirts to include long-sleeved casual tops (긴팔티) and turtlenecks (목티). Do not confuse with homophonous native Korean 티 ('speck/flaw' or 'outward sign/air', as in 티를 내다).

티모.etymology: Hybrid English-initial and Sino-Korean compound combining 티 (the Korean phonetic rendering of the English letter T, used as an anonymizing initial for a person or entity) with the Sino-Korean pronoun/determiner 某 (모, 'a certain, unnamed, so-and-so'). Patterned after traditional journalistic anonymization formulas like 김모 씨 ('a certain Mr. Kim') or A모 씨 ('a certain person A').

history.meaning: a certain unnamed person or thing (so-and-so)
a certain unnamed person or entity whose name begins with T

morphemes.meaning: the English letter T (initial of a redacted name)
a certain, unnamed person or thing (某)

티모.notes: A classic Korean media and gossip trope: reporters and variety shows use initials plus 모 (某) to hint at a celebrity's identity while technically avoiding defamation laws.
