티브이.etymology: Loanword (외래어) representing the phonetic Hangul transcription of the English initialism TV, short for television—a 20th-century hybrid coinage combining Ancient Greek têle (τῆλε, 'far off, at a distance') and Latin vīsiō ('sight, vision', from vidēre 'to see'). Because Korean lacks the labiodental fricative /v/, the English letter name V (/viː/) is normatively transcribed as two syllables, 브이 (beu-i).

history.meaning: system for transmitting moving images and sound over a distance
television set or television broadcasting medium

티브이.notes: While 티브이 is the official Standard Korean spelling prescribed by the National Institute of Korean Language, almost all speakers pronounce and informally write it as 티비 (tibi).

티켓.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English ticket, which entered Early Modern English from Middle French estiquette ('little note, label, slip of paper', modern French étiquette), from Old French estiquier ('to attach, stick, pin up'), ultimately from Frankish *stikkan ('to pierce, stick'). In Korean, it frequently coexists with the Sino-Korean synonym 표 (票) for concert, theater, and airline passes.

history.meaning: attached slip of paper or warrant granting admission or rights
admission ticket, voucher, or qualification pass

티켓.notes: Often used for entertainment, concerts, and flights (콘서트 티켓, 항공 티켓) and metaphorically for securing a spot in a competition (본선행 티켓 'ticket to the finals'). Its French doublet エ티켓 (étiquette) also exists in Korean.

rootFamily.gloss: ticketing, rushing to book concert/show tickets online
box-office draw, star's power to sell tickets

티타임.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tea time / teatime ('afternoon break for drinking tea and light refreshments', from tea + time).

history.meaning: time for afternoon tea; social break
tea time, coffee/tea break

팀.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English team, from Middle English tem, from Old English tēam ('offspring, family, set of draft animals harnessed together in a row'), from Proto-Germanic *taumaz ('that which draws or pulls, bridle, team', related to *teuhaną 'to pull, lead'). In South Korean corporate and broadcasting culture, it denotes a formal organizational unit or production crew.

history.meaning: set of draft animals yoked together; group working or playing together
sports team, corporate department unit, or television production crew

morphemes.meaning: team, crew, organizational unit (from English team)

팀.notes: Since the late 1990s corporate restructuring in Korea, traditional bureaucratic sections (과/부) were largely reorganized into 팀 ('teams'), making 팀장 ('team leader') a ubiquitous workplace title.

팀장급.etymology: Hybrid English loanword and Sino-Korean compound formed from the English loanword 팀 (from team, Old English tēam) + the Sino-Korean bound root 長 (장, 'head, chief, elder, leader') + the Sino-Korean affix -級 (-급, 'grade, rank, class, level', originally referring to the order of silk threads and later to severed enemy heads used to tally military rank in Qin China). Denotes personnel whose seniority or status is equivalent to a team leader.

history.meaning: chief/leader + rank/grade level
team-leader rank or equivalent seniority level

팀장급.notes: The suffix -급 (級) is highly productive in Korean hierarchy and slang, ranging from corporate ranks (팀장급, 부장급) to quality tiers (특급 'top-tier', 역대급 'all-time level').

파내다.etymology: Native Korean resultative compound verb combining 파다 ('to dig, hollow out earth', Middle Korean 파다) with the completive-outward verb 내다 ('to extract, bring forth'). Whereas 파다 alone can mean digging a hole, 파내다 specifically focuses on unearthing and lifting out what was buried inside.
파내다.notes: Takes source particle -에서 and object particle -을/-를.

파랗다.etymology: Native Korean color adjective descending from Middle Korean 파랗다 ('to be bright blue or vivid green'), bright-vowel harmonic counterpart of 퍼렇다, related to 풀 ('grass, vegetation') and 푸르다 ('to be blue/green').

history.meaning: to be bright blue or green
to be bright blue, azure (or pale with cold/fear)

파손하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean transitive verb combining Sino-Korean 破損 (파손, 'breakage, damage, destruction', composed of 破 파 'break, shatter, split stone' + 損 손 'diminish, injure, damage, lose') with the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Used primarily in formal, legal, or administrative contexts to report property damage or vandalism.

history.meaning: to shatter stone + to diminish or damage
to damage, break, or vandalize physical property or objects

파손하다.notes: Belongs to formal and legal register (e.g., 기물 파손 'destruction of property', 차량을 파손하다 'to damage/vandalize a vehicle'); in everyday speech, 망가뜨리다 or 부수다 is preferred.

파슬리.etymology: Modern Korean culinary loanword borrowed from English 'parsley' (ultimately from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον, 'rock celery', via Old French peresil). Widely grown in Korean kitchen herb pots and used fresh or finely chopped in soups, pasta, and bakery savouries.
파슬리.notes: Often paired with other Western herbs like 타임 ('thyme') and 로즈마리 ('rosemary').

파악.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 把握, combining two near-synonymous hand-radical (扌) characters: 把 (파, 'hold, take hold of, grip in the hand') and 握 (악, 'clasp firmly, clench in the palm'). From the concrete physical action of gripping an object tightly in one's hand, it evolved metaphorically (paralleling English 'grasp' and German 'begreifen') to mean thoroughly understanding or reading a situation.

history.meaning: to grip or clench firmly in one's hand
intellectual grasp, clear comprehension, or reading of a situation

morphemes.meaning: hold, grip, take in the hand (把)
clasp, clench, hold in the palm (握)

파악.notes: Extremely common in the workplace expression 분위기 파악 ('reading the room') and 주제 파악 ('knowing one's place / limits').

cognates.meaning: to grasp, seize, be sure of

파악하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from Sino-Korean 把握 (파악, 'grasping, comprehension', from 把 파 'hold, grip in the hand' + 握 악 'clasp tightly in the palm') and the native Korean transitive verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to take firmly in hand,' it denotes ascertaining facts, verifying statuses, or figuring out complex circumstances.

history.meaning: to grasp mentally, figure out, or verify the facts of a situation

morphemes.meaning: hold, grip, take in the hand (把)
clasp, clench, hold in the palm (握)

파악하다.notes: Unlike 이해하다 ('to understand empathetic/conceptual meaning'), 파악하다 emphasizes actively assessing, surveying, or pinned-down verification of a situation (현황을 파악하다 'to ascertain the current status').

rootFamily.gloss: to seize control of, dominate (掌握-)

파워.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English power, which came via Anglo-Norman pouer and Old French poeir ('to be able, capability, authority') from Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularizing Classical Latin posse ('to be able, have power', contraction of potis 'able, powerful' + esse 'to be'). In Korean, it commonly denotes social clout, organizational leverage, or consumer influence alongside physical force.

history.meaning: ability, strength, political or physical force
physical energy, social clout, or market leverage

파워.notes: While native 힘 covers physical strength and general power, 파워 is favored in media and business for measurable clout or star leverage (브랜드 파워, 티켓 파워, 파워 게임).

파이.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pie ('baked dish of fruit, meat, or sweet filling in a pastry crust') and from Greek/English pi (π, ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter).

history.meaning: baked pastry pie
pie

파이팅.etymology: Pseudo-anglicism (콩글리시) adapted from the English gerund/participle fighting (from fight, Old English feohtan 'to combat, contend, strive', from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną). Entering Korean through mid-20th-century boxing and sports cheers (influenced by Japanese ファイト faito 'fighting spirit!'), it underwent a complete semantic shift from physical combat to a universal cheer of encouragement and solidarity ('Go for it!', 'You've got this!').

history.meaning: engaging in combat or athletic struggle
cheer of encouragement, support, or determination ('Go for it!')

morphemes.meaning: cheer of encouragement and solidarity (from English fighting)

파이팅.notes: A quintessential Korean false friend for English speakers: shouting 'Fighting!' in Korea is a warm expression of support (often accompanied by a raised clenched fist), commonly pronounced 화이팅 (hwaiting) in casual speech.

파일럿.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English pilot (specifically elliptical for pilot program or pilot episode), which derives via Middle French pilote and Old Italian pilota ('helmsman, steersman') from Medieval Greek *pēdōtēs ('rudder-steerer'), from Ancient Greek pēdón (πηδόν, 'oar blade, rudder'). In English and subsequently Korean broadcasting, a 'pilot' guides the way as an experimental test broadcast before a show is greenlit for regular programming.

history.meaning: oar/rudder → ship's helmsman → aviator or preliminary test guide
experimental test broadcast episode (or aircraft pilot)

morphemes.meaning: pilot, test broadcast episode (from English pilot)

파일럿.notes: In Korean television industry jargon, a 파일럿 (pilot) must achieve strong ratings and buzz to survive and win 정규 편성 ('regular programming slot').

파트너.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English partner ('associate in business, dance, sports, or marriage', from Anglo-Norman parcener, altered after part).

history.meaning: colleague, companion, teammate
partner

파티.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English party ('social gathering'), which came from Middle English partie ('part, division, faction, company of people'), from Old French partie, originally the feminine past participle of partir ('to divide, share'), from Latin partīrī ('to divide, distribute'), from pars, partis ('part, portion'). Adopted into Korean in the 20th century for Western-style celebratory or social gatherings.

history.meaning: divided portion → political/military group → social gathering of guests
celebratory or social party/gathering (or gaming group)

파티.notes: Used both for social celebrations (생일 파티 'birthday party', 홈파티 'house party') and in Korean online gaming culture for a group of players teaming up for a quest (파티원 'party member').

파헤치다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed by joining the verb stem 파- (from 파다, Middle Korean 프다, 'to dig, excavate, scoop out earth') with 헤치다 (Middle Korean 헤티다, 'to scatter apart, push aside, pry open', derived from 헤다 'to scatter, disperse'). The literal image of digging into the ground and scattering the soil aside gave rise to the figurative sense of relentlessly unearthing hidden secrets, scandals, or the truth.

history.meaning: to dig into the earth and scatter or push it open
to dig up physically; to expose, delve into, or dissect a hidden matter

morphemes.meaning: to scatter apart, push aside, uncover

파헤치다.notes: A favorite verb of investigative journalism and entertainment reporting (진실을 파헤치다 'to uncover the truth', 비밀을 파헤치다 'to dig up secrets').

rootFamily.gloss: to push aside, scatter open, make one's way through

판.etymology: Sino-Korean and native Korean noun: (1) Sino-Korean 판 (板/版, 'wooden board, plank, printing block, edition'); (2) Sino-Korean/native 판 (局/場, 'scene, situation, round of a game or match', from Middle Korean 판).

history.meaning: flat board, plank, printing plate, edition
board, plate; round of a game, situation/arena

판단하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb combining Sino-Korean 判斷 (판단, 'judgment, decision, adjudication', from 判 판 'cleave in half, distinguish, judge' + 斷 단 'sever, cut off, decide') with the native Korean verbalizer -하다 ('to do'). Both Hanja characters contain blade components—判 has the knife radical (刂/刀) and 斷 has the axe radical (斤)—encoding the ancient legal metaphor of 'cutting cleanly between two sides' to render a decisive judgment.

history.meaning: to cleave in two with a knife + to sever cleanly with an axe; to adjudicate
to judge, evaluate logically, or make a decision

판단하다.notes: Focuses on rational assessment and decision-making (상황을 판단하다 'to judge a situation'), rather than moral condemnation or interpersonal criticism (which is 비판하다).

판명.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound from 判明, composed of 判 (판, 'cleave apart, distinguish, judge') and 明 (명, 'bright, clear, evident', combining sun 日 and moon 月). Literally meaning 'distinguished and made bright/clear,' it refers to a previously uncertain fact, cause, or identity being definitively established, proven, or brought to light.

history.meaning: to distinguish clearly and bring into the light
definitive proof, verification, or conclusive determination of a fact

판명.notes: Almost always used with -되다 or 나다 in formal announcements and news reports (예: 거짓으로 판명 나다 'to turn out / be proven to be false').

rootFamily.gloss: to be proven, turn out to be, be identified
to be verified, come to light conclusively

팔.etymology: Two homophonous Korean words: (1) Sino-Korean numeral 팔 (八, 'eight', from Middle Chinese *pɛt); (2) native Korean noun 팔 ('arm', Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ).

history.meaning: cardinal numeral 8; upper limb
eight (num.); arm (noun)

팔각.etymology: Sino-Korean geometric compound 八角, combining 八 (여덟 팔, 'eight') and 角 (뿔 각, 'angle, point, corner'). Famous in Korean cultural architecture through 팔각정 (八角亭, 'octagonal pavilion') and in cartography for the eight-pointed compass rose marking the four cardinal and four intercardinal winds.

팔다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ다 ('to sell, trade away').

history.meaning: to sell
to sell

팔로잉.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from the English verbal noun/gerund following, derived from follow (Old English folgian 'to accompany, go after, pursue', from Proto-Germanic *fulgōną) plus the suffix -ing. Beyond its global social media sense ('following an account'), in South Korean reality-variety television production jargon it specifically denotes 'follow-cam duty'—where a camera operator or junior PD shadows a single cast member continuously on foot to capture every reaction.

history.meaning: the act of going after or accompanying someone; a group of supporters
social media following; one-on-one shadowing camera duty in variety TV production

팔로잉.notes: In Korean variety shows like 2 Days & 1 Night or Running Man, each cast member is assigned a dedicated VJ and rookie PD for 팔로잉 ('one-on-one shadowing'), requiring intense physical stamina.

rootFamily.gloss: follow (on social media or in photography/sports)

팔리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 팔다 ('to sell', Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ다) + passive suffix -리- ('to be sold, sell well; for one's attention to be distracted').

history.meaning: to be sold
to be sold, be in demand; to be absorbed/distracted

팔불출.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 八 (팔, 'eight'), 不 (불, 'not'), and 出 (출, 'go out; emerge into society'), literally denoting 'eight [types of fools who] should not go out [into the world]' or 'one guilty of the eight follies.' Originally designating a dim-witted person lacking basic judgment, the word underwent semantic amelioration in modern colloquial Korean to denote a 'doting fool' who boasts excessively about their spouse or child.

history.meaning: a person committing eight kinds of foolishness unfit for public society
a doting fool who brags tirelessly about their spouse or children

팔불출.notes: Today used almost exclusively with affectionate teasing for someone who cannot stop bragging about their partner or kids (akin to 아들바보 or 딸바보).

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (Standard Korean Language Dictionary)

팔십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 팔십 (八十, 'eighty'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 십 (十, 'ten').

history.meaning: eight + ten
eighty

팔십삼만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral formed from 八 (팔, 'eight'), 十 (십, 'ten'), 三 (삼, 'three'), and 萬 (만, 'ten thousand; myriad'), literally 'eighty-three ten-thousands' (83 × 10,000 = 830,000). It exemplifies the East Asian myriad-based (10⁴) numerical grouping system inherited from Middle Chinese, in contrast to the thousand-based (10³) grouping of European languages.

history.meaning: eighty-three myriads (830,000)
eight hundred thirty thousand (830,000)

팔십삼만.notes: To convert large Korean numbers into English quickly, mentally shift the comma one place to the left: 83만 (팔십삼만) = 83 × 10,000 = 830,000.

팔십퍼센트.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the Sino-Korean numeral 팔십 (八十, 'eighty', from 八 'eight' + 十 'ten') with the English loanword 퍼센트 ('percent', ultimately from Modern Latin per centum 'by the hundred'). In modern Korean usage, Sino-Korean numerals are systematically paired with international scientific and statistical units like 퍼센트.

history.meaning: eighty (Sino-Korean) + by the hundred (Latin/English)
eighty percent (80%)

팔십퍼센트.notes: In casual spoken Korean, 퍼센트 is very frequently clipped to 프로 (via Japanese パーセント / プロ, though coalesced with Dutch/German Prozent), so 팔십퍼센트 is often heard as 팔십프로.

cognates.meaning: Eight Characters of birth time; horoscope; fate

팔자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 八 (팔, 'eight') and 字 (자, 'character; letter'), literally 'the eight characters.' Shortened from 사주팔자 (四柱八字, 'Four Pillars and Eight Characters') in traditional East Asian sexagenary astrology, where the year, month, day, and hour of one's birth are each represented by one Heavenly Stem (天干) and one Earthly Branch (地支), totaling eight characters believed to govern one's lifelong destiny.

history.meaning: the four pillars and eight cyclic characters of a birth chart
one's predestined fate, fortune, or lot in life

팔자.notes: Frequently heard in fatalistic exclamations like 내 팔자야! ('What a lot in life I have!') or the admiring idiom 상팔자 ('an enviable/top-tier life').

rootFamily.gloss: Four Pillars of Destiny; birth horoscope and fate
enviable lot in life; easy street

팔천.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 팔천 (八千, 'eight thousand'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 천 (千, 'thousand').

history.meaning: eight + thousand
eight thousand

팔호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 팔호실 (八號室, 'Room No. 8'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 호 (號, 'number, designation') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

history.meaning: eight + number + room
Room 8

팝콘.etymology: 20th-century loanword from American English popcorn (a compound of echoic pop 'to burst with a sharp sound' and corn 'maize, grain', from Proto-Germanic *kurną). Adopted into Korean alongside movie-theater snack culture, where the syllable-final /p/ and /n/ map cleanly onto Korean coda consonants 팝 (pap) and 콘 (kon).

history.meaning: puffed kernels of heated maize
popcorn; (slang) spectator drama

팝콘.notes: Just as in English internet culture, Korean netizens use 팝콘각 ('a popcorn angle/situation') or 팝콘 가져와 ('bring the popcorn') when watching juicy drama unfold online or in a variety show.

rootFamily.gloss: sizzling sweet corn baked with cheese (popular Korean pub dish)

cognates.meaning: burlesque song or ode sung alongside another

패러디.etymology: Borrowed from English parody, which derives via French parodie and Late Latin parōdia from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, 'burlesque poem or song'), a compound of παρά (pará, 'beside, counter to, mock') and ᾠδή (ōidḗ, 'song, ode'). Adopted into modern Korean media and literary terminology to denote satirical or comedic imitations of well-known works.

history.meaning: a song sung alongside or in mock imitation of serious poetry
humorous or satirical imitation of a work or style
parody; spoof in television, film, or internet media

패러디.notes: A staple of Korean variety shows (*예능*) and sketch comedy, where iconic scenes from hit K-dramas or commercials are recreated for comedic effect.

rootFamily.gloss: a parody work or spoof production

cognates.meaning: prevailing style of dress; manner of making

패션.etymology: Borrowed from English fashion, which comes via Anglo-Norman faciun and Old French façon ('make, shape, appearance, manner') from Latin factiōnem (accusative of factiō, 'a making or doing', derived from faciō 'to make, do'). Entered Korean in the 20th century to denote clothing design, sartorial style, and prevailing trends.

history.meaning: the act of making; physical shape or manner
prevailing custom or style of dress and adornment
fashion; clothing style and apparel trends

패션.notes: Often appears in K-pop and entertainment contexts in compounds such as 공항패션 ('airport fashion'—celebrities' styled outfits photographed at Incheon Airport) and 패션테러리스트 ('fashion terrorist'—someone with terrible outfit coordination).

cognates.meaning: bundle; cosmetic treatment applied to the skin (face pack)
facial mask treatment (clipping of face pack)

팩.etymology: Borrowed from English pack (from Middle English pakke, from Middle Dutch pak 'bundle'), specifically mediated via the Japanese cosmetic clipping パック (pakku, shortened from English face pack / mud pack). In Korean skincare and beauty usage, 팩 narrowed semantically to denote a concentrated facial mask treatment—above all a single-use sheet mask (마스크팩) or wash-off mask.

history.meaning: cosmetic paste or compress applied to the face
cosmetic facial pack or mask
facial sheet mask or skincare pack; (homonym) pack/carton or game cartridge

팩.notes: False friend alert: while 팩 can mean a 'pack' (like a milk carton or retro game cartridge), in everyday Korean conversation 팩을 하다 almost always means 'to put on a facial skincare mask' (as in the K-beauty routine 1일 1팩, 'one sheet mask a day').

cognates.meaning: inspired by a god; temple devotee; frenzied

팬.etymology: Borrowed from English fan ('enthusiastic devotee or admirer'), originally a late 19th-century American English clipping of fanatic (first popularized among baseball enthusiasts), which derives from Latin fānāticus ('inspired by a deity, frenzied, ecstatic'), from fānum ('temple, sacred place'). In contemporary Korean, 팬 is a foundational term in entertainment, sports, and K-pop culture.

history.meaning: pertaining to a temple; divinely inspired or frenzied
enthusiastic devotee of a sport, celebrity, or art
fan; admirer; supporter of a celebrity or program

팬.notes: Because native Korean lacks the labiodental fricative /f/, English /f/ is systematically adapted as aspirated bilabial /pʰ/ (ㅍ), making fan and pan homophones (팬) in Korean.

rootFamily.gloss: a fan's loving heart and devotion

팬분.etymology: Hybrid compound combining the English loanword 팬 (fan, clipped from fanatic < Latin fānāticus 'temple devotee') with the Korean honorific bound noun and classifier 분 ('esteemed person'). The honorific morpheme 분 is attested from Middle Korean onward (widely linked by philologists to Sino-Korean 分 'one's station, status, or portion') as an exalted classifier and suffix for respected individuals.

history.meaning: admirer (English) + esteemed person of standing (Korean honorific)
respected fan (polite/honorific reference used by celebrities and staff)

팬분.notes: Celebrities, idols, and broadcast producers nearly always add the honorific suffix -분 (and plural -들, forming 팬분들) when speaking publicly about their fans to show gratitude and respect.

팬층.etymology: Hybrid loan-Sino-Korean compound joining the English loanword 팬 (fan, from fanatic) with the Sino-Korean suffixal noun 층 (層, 'story of a building, geological stratum, layer, social class or demographic bracket'). Literally 'fan stratum,' it models demographic compounds (analogous to Japanese ファン層 fansō) to describe the age, gender, or size of a show's or artist's following.

history.meaning: admirer (English) + tier, layer, or social stratum (Sino-Korean)
fan base; demographic stratum of supporters

팬층.notes: Commonly collocates with adjectives of thickness or breadth in Korean media analysis: 팬층이 두텁다 ('to have a thick/solid fan base') or 팬층이 넓다 ('to have a broad fan demographic').

cognates.meaning: organized association of devotees of a celebrity or team

팬클럽.etymology: Borrowed from English fan club, a compound of fan (clipping of fanatic < Latin fānāticus 'temple devotee') and club ('voluntary association of people', an early 17th-century semantic extension of English club 'thick stick, clump, gathering', of Old Norse origin *klubba). In South Korea, formal 팬클럽 organizations became a defining institutional feature of pop culture from the 1980s onward.

history.meaning: organized society of admirers of a public figure or entertainer
official or unofficial fan club supporting a celebrity or group

팬클럽.notes: In Korean entertainment culture, official 팬클럽 memberships often have their own distinct fandom names, official colors, cheering lightsticks (응원봉), and tiered membership recruitment periods (기수).

팽이.etymology: Native Korean noun denoting a conical spinning top. Attested in Early Modern Korean as 핑이 (phingi) and in regional dialects as 팽돌이 and 뺑이, it derives from the Korean ideophonic/mimetic root 팽- / 핑- (expressing rapid whirling, spinning, or dizzying rotation) combined with the native nominalizing suffix -이 ('thing or agent that performs the action').

history.meaning: whirling toy; spinning top (from mimetic root 핑-/팽- + nominalizer -이)
spinning top; (figurative) someone spinning around busily without rest

팽이.notes: Used vividly in similes like 팽이처럼 돌다 ('to spin around like a top'), describing an overworked producer or staff member running around non-stop all day.

rootFamily.gloss: traditional Korean game of spinning tops on ice with a whip cord
spinning round and round; stretched tautly
whirling or spinning smoothly in a circle

팽팽하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated mimetic root 팽팽 ('pulled taut, stretched tight, evenly matched') + adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: taut, tight, closely contested

퍼뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive/causative verb formed from the root 퍼- (from 펴다 'to spread out, unfold' / 퍼지다 'to spread') + intensive transitive suffix -뜨리- ('to spread widely, disseminate, circulate').

history.meaning: to spread out, disseminate, circulate

퍼센트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English percent ('parts per hundred, %', from Modern Latin per centum 'by the hundred').

history.meaning: per hundred (%)
percent, percentage

퍼지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to spread out, diffuse, or circulate widely.' Attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 펴디다 (phye-tita), morphologically derived from the transitive verb stem 펴- (펴다, 'to unfold, spread out, straighten') plus the inchoative/passive auxiliary formative -디다 (modern -지다). Subsequent palatalization of -디- to -지- and vowel backing after the bilabial aspirate (펴- > 퍼-) yielded modern 퍼지다.

history.meaning: to become unfolded; to spread out (intransitive of 펴다)
to spread; to diffuse (post-palatalization)
to spread, circulate (of rumors, smells, news), or become soggy/overcooked

퍼지다.notes: Besides rumors (소문이 퍼지다) or scents spreading, 퍼지다 is also used colloquially when noodles get bloated and soggy from sitting in broth too long (라면이 불어 퍼지다) or when someone slumps exhausted on the floor.

rootFamily.gloss: to unfold; to spread out; to straighten
to unfold wide; to display or wage

펑.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic and mimetic adverb imitating a loud popping, bursting, or exploding sound, or describing a wide gap/hole opening suddenly.

history.meaning: pop! bang! with a burst

cognates.meaning: hole in a tire; act of pricking
flat tire; rupture; breakdown (clipping of puncture)

펑크.etymology: Borrowed via Japanese パンク (panku), a phonetic clipping of English puncture ('a small hole in a tire made by a sharp object', from Late Latin punctūra 'a pricking', from Latin pungō 'to prick, pierce'). In Korean, the initial vowel was reanalyzed closer to English /ʌ/ as 펑크 (peongkeu), and its sense expanded from a flat tire or torn stocking to any sudden breakdown, no-show, or last-minute cancellation in a schedule.

history.meaning: a pricking; perforation or flat tire
flat tire; rupture or sudden failure
flat tire; sudden cancellation, no-show, or unfilled hole in a broadcast/schedule

morphemes.meaning: puncture; flat tire; sudden cancellation or no-show

펑크.notes: A crucial false friend in Korean broadcasting and daily life: 펑크를 내다 ('to make a puncture') does not mean playing punk rock—it means bailing on an appointment, missing a deadline, or leaving a sudden gap in a TV shooting schedule!

rootFamily.gloss: to get a flat tire; for a plan or booking to fall through suddenly
to bail on an appointment; to cause a sudden cancellation or no-show

페달.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pedal or French pédale ('foot lever on a bicycle, car, piano, or machine', from Italian pedale, Latin pedalis 'of the foot').

history.meaning: foot-operated lever
pedal

페이지.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English page ('one side of a leaf of a book or document', from French page, Latin pagina).

history.meaning: leaf or side of a book
page

페인트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English paint ('liquid pigment coating applied to surfaces', from Old French peindre, Latin pingere).

history.meaning: liquid pigment coating
paint

페인트칠.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from English loanword 페인트 ('paint') + 칠 ('coating, varnishing, painting', from Sino-Korean 漆 'lacquer, varnish').

history.meaning: paint + coating/application
painting, applying a coat of paint

페인트칠하다.etymology: Compound verb formed from 페인트칠 ('applying paint', from English paint + 칠 漆 'coating') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to paint, apply a coat of paint

페타치즈.etymology: Compound loanword from English feta cheese. Feta comes from Modern Greek φέτα (féta, literally 'slice', referring to thick slices of curd cured in brine), borrowed in the 17th century from Italian fetta ('slice'). Cheese derives from Old English ċēse, from West Germanic *kāsijaz, an early borrowing from Latin cāseus ('cheese', from Proto-Indo-European *kwath₂- 'to ferment, sour').

history.meaning: slice (Italian > Greek) + fermented curd (Latin > English)
feta cheese (Greek brined curd cheese made from sheep's and goat's milk)

페타치즈.notes: In Korean culinary usage, foreign varietal names that stand alone in English (like 'feta', 'mozzarella', or 'cheddar') almost always retain the head noun -치즈 attached (페타치즈, 모차렐라치즈) for clarity.

펠트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English felt ('non-woven textile produced by matting and pressing wool fibers', from Old English felt).

history.meaning: matted wool fabric
felt (fabric)

펴다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 펴다 ('to unfold, spread out, straighten, open').

history.meaning: to unfold, spread out, straighten
to unfold, open, spread, straighten

편.etymology: Sino-Korean noun derived from Hanja 便 (편, originally 'ease, convenience', which developed a spatial and relational sense of 'direction, side, party, faction' in Korean usage). From the concrete sense of 'side' or 'faction' (as in 내 편 'my side'), it grammaticalized into a bound noun after adnominal verb clauses (-는/은 편이다) expressing 'tendency, inclination, or the side of doing X.' (Note: homophonous with 篇 'volume, episode, film').

history.meaning: direction; side; party in a dispute or relationship
side, faction, ally; (bound noun) general tendency or inclination (-는 편이다)

편.notes: Extremely versatile: as an independent noun it means 'ally/side' (누구 편이야? 'Whose side are you on?'), as a bound noun it softens statements into tendencies (조용한 편이다 'tends to be quiet'), and via homophonous 篇 it counts TV episodes or films!

편들다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 편 (便, 'side, party, faction') and the native Korean verb 들다 (Middle Korean 들다 tulta, 'to lift, hold up, raise' or 'to enter into'). Originally an idiomatic verb-object phrase 편을 들다 ('to hold up/enter someone's side'), it lexicalized into the single verb 편들다 meaning 'to take sides with, back up, or show partiality toward someone.'

history.meaning: to raise/support or enter into a person's side in a dispute
to take someone's side; to favor or defend partially

편들다.notes: Notice how Korean speakers use both the fused compound verb (왜 걔를 편들어?) and the separable object phrase (왜 걔 편을 들어?) interchangeably in conversation.

rootFamily.gloss: to help out; to lend a hand or chime in supportively

편성.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 編 (편, 'to weave, plait cords, arrange in sequence, compile') and 成 (성, 'to complete, accomplish, form into a whole'), literally 'weaving and arranging into a finished structure.' Used traditionally for organizing military units, it was adapted in modern East Asian broadcasting (alongside Japanese 編成 hensei) to denote television and radio program scheduling and slot allocation.

history.meaning: weaving together into a whole; organizing troops or texts into structured units
organization of a unit, budget, or broadcast program schedule/lineup

편성.notes: In Korean television production (*프로듀사* context), securing 편성 ('getting a broadcast timeslot on the network schedule') is the make-or-break hurdle for every pilot program and drama.

rootFamily.gloss: reorganization; seasonal overhaul of a TV network's lineup
director/department of broadcast programming at a network

편안하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 편안 (便安, 'comfortable and peaceful, well and at ease', from 편 便 'convenient, comfortable' + 안 安 'peaceful, tranquil') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: at ease and peaceful -> to be comfortable, peaceful
to be comfortable, relaxed, peaceful

편지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 편지 (便紙), originally meaning 'handy/convenient note paper or message sent by courier', from 편 (便, 'convenient, opportunity, messenger') + 지 (紙, 'paper'), attested in Middle Korean as 편지.

history.meaning: convenient paper note -> written letter, epistle
letter, mail

cognates.meaning: editing; compilation (written 編集 since 1946 Tōyō Kanji reform)

편집.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 編 (편, 'to bind bamboo slips with silk or leather cords; to weave, compile') and 輯 (집, 'to gather together harmoniously, assemble chariot parts, collect'). In Classical Chinese, 編輯 referred to gathering and binding written bamboo slips into a coherent book; in modern Korean media, it extended from print publishing to film, audio, and video editing.

history.meaning: binding inscribed bamboo slips and gathering writings into a compiled book
compilation and editing of publications, film, audio, or television footage

편집.notes: In Korean variety TV, 편집 refers both to creative post-production (adding witty captions and sound effects) and to cutting a cast member's boring scenes out of the broadcast.

rootFamily.gloss: cutting an entire segment or guest appearance out in editing

편집기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 편집 (編輯, 'editing, compilation', from 編 'compile' + 輯 'assemble') plus the suffixal morpheme 기 (機, 'machine, mechanism, apparatus', or 器, 'instrument, device, tool'). Originally denoting mechanical film splicers and linear tape-editing decks in broadcasting stations, it now also encompasses non-linear digital editing software and text editors.

history.meaning: mechanical film splicer or linear videotape editing console
editing machine, video editing console, or digital editing software

편집기.notes: Can refer either to physical studio hardware in a broadcast editing bay (編輯機) or to a software tool like a video/text editor (編輯器).

편집되다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean passive verb combining the Sino-Korean verbal noun 편집 (編輯, 'compilation, editing', from 編 'weave, compile' + 輯 'gather, assemble') with the native Korean passive/inchoative light verb 되다 (Middle Korean ᄃᆞ외다 towoyta, 'to become, be formed into'). In television industry parlance, it underwent semantic specialization to mean 'to be cut/edited out of the final broadcast.'

history.meaning: compilation (Sino-Korean) + to become / be made (Middle Korean)
to be edited (of a publication or video); to be cut out on the editing-room floor

morphemes.meaning: passive / inchoative light verb ('to become, be done')

편집되다.notes: When a celebrity on a Korean variety show says 내 분량이 편집됐다 ('my screen time was edited'), it means their scenes were cut out completely, not merely polished!

rootFamily.gloss: to have one's entire appearance cut from the broadcast

편집실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun uniting 편집 (編輯, 'editing, compilation', from 編 'weave, compile' + 輯 'gather, assemble') with the spatial suffix 실 (室, 'room, chamber, suite'). Originally referring to the editorial room of a newspaper or publishing house, in television broadcasting it denotes the post-production editing bay where producers spend sleepless nights cutting episodes.

history.meaning: editorial office of a newspaper or publishing house
post-production video editing room/bay in a broadcasting station; editorial room

편집실.notes: In Korean television dramas like *The Producers* (*프로듀사*), the 편집실 is the iconic cramped, dimly lit room where junior PDs practically live while racing against broadcast deadlines.

편집하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 편집 (編輯, 'compilation, editing', from 編 'bind bamboo slips, compile' + 輯 'gather together harmoniously') and the native Korean light verb 하다 (Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota, 'to do, make'). It denotes compiling and editing written works or assembling, cutting, and post-processing film and broadcast footage.

history.meaning: to compile writings + to do (Middle Korean light verb)
to edit (books, articles, audio, film, or television broadcasts); to cut out footage

편집하다.notes: Watch out for the famous Korean broadcasting idiom 악마의 편집 ('devil's editing'), which refers to producers splicing reactions and dramatic music together out of context to manufacture suspense or conflict.

rootFamily.gloss: to be edited; to be cut out of a broadcast

편집해버리다.etymology: Compound auxiliary verb construction built from 편집하다 (編輯하다, 'to edit, cut out', from Sino-Korean 編 'compile' + 輯 'assemble' + native light verb 하다 'do'), conjugated into the infinitive connective 해 (from 하- + -여), and fused with the native Korean completive auxiliary verb 버리다 (from Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다 polita, lexical verb 'to throw away, discard, abandon'). Grammaticalization of 버리다 into an aspectual auxiliary adds a vivid sense of irreversible completion—'to edit right out once and for all.'

history.meaning: to throw away, cast off, abandon (lexical verb beginning to grammaticalize as completive auxiliary)
to edit out completely and irreversibly (with relief, decisiveness, or finality)

morphemes.meaning: completive auxiliary ('completely, once and for all', from 'throw away')

편집해버리다.notes: Adding -아/어 버리다 to 편집하다 transforms a neutral technical action ('to edit') into an emotionally charged decisive act ('to ruthlessly cut/axe a scene right out').

rootFamily.gloss: to throw away; (auxiliary) to do completely/irreversibly

편하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 편 (便, 'convenient, comfortable, easy') + native adjective suffix -하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: to be comfortable, convenient, easy

편히.etymology: Derived adverb formed from Sino-Korean 편 (便, stem of 편하다 'to be comfortable, easy') + native adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: comfortably, easily, at ease

펼쳐지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb formed from 펼치다 ('to spread out, unfold, open wide') + auxiliary passive/inchoative construction -어지다 ('to become unfolded, stretch out before one's eyes').

history.meaning: to unfold, spread out, be staged

펼치다.etymology: Native Korean intensive transitive verb derived from 펴다 ('to unfold, spread out', Middle Korean 펴다) with the intensive verbal extension -ㄹ치- ('to spread wide open, unfold, display').

history.meaning: to unfold -> to spread out wide, open up
to unfold, spread out, open (a book/wings), wage/stage

평가원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 평가원 (評價員 or 評價院), formed from 평가 (評價, 'evaluation, appraisal', from 평 評 'to criticize, judge' + 가 價 'value, price') + 원 (員 'staff member, evaluator, inspector' or 院 'institute, agency').

history.meaning: evaluation + staff member / institute
evaluator, appraiser; evaluation institute

평범하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 평범 (平凡, joining 平 'level, calm, unremarkable' and 凡 'everyday, ordinary, universal') plus native 하다. In Korean it carries a neutral-to-warm tone—describing a steady normal pace or quiet everyday life—and contrasts with 특별하다 ('to be special').
평범하다.notes: Prenominal form 평범한 modifies 일상 ('everyday life'), 사람, or 보폭.

평상시.etymology: Sino-Korean trimorphemic compound from 平 (평, 'level, flat, even, ordinary'), 常 (상, 'constant, regular, unchanging, usual'), and 時 (시, 'time, season, period'). Formed by suffixing 時 ('time') to the disyllabic Sino-Korean stem 평상 (平常, 'ordinary state, normality'), it designates normal, everyday times in explicit contrast to emergencies (비상시, 非常時) or special occasions.

history.meaning: even and constant; ordinary, everyday state
normal, everyday times; usual occasions

평상시.notes: Nearly synonymous with 평소 (平素, 'usual times'), though 평상시 slightly emphasizes 'during normal, non-emergency conditions' (antonym: 비상시 'time of emergency').

cognates.meaning: all one's life; throughout one's life

평생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 平 (평, 'level, even, throughout, ordinary') and 生 (생, 'birth, life, living, lifetime'). Attested in Classical Chinese (e.g., the Analects of Confucius, 論語) as 平生 (píngshēng, 'during one's past/ordinary life; for as long as one lives'), it was borrowed into Korean both as a noun meaning 'one's entire lifetime' and as an adverb meaning 'forever, for all one's life.'

history.meaning: in one's everyday life; throughout one's life from youth onward
one's whole lifetime; (adverb) for all one's life, forever

평생.notes: Functions seamlessly as both a noun (내 평생의 소원 'the wish of my whole life') and an adverb without any particle (평생 잊지 못할 거야 'I will never forget it for the rest of my life').

rootFamily.gloss: one's whole life; from birth to death

평소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 평소 (平素), joining 평 (平, 'ordinary, level, peaceful, usual') and 소 (素, 'plain, unadorned, habitual, from the start').

history.meaning: ordinary times, everyday life
ordinary days, usual times

평수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 坪 (평, 'level ground; a pyeong, traditional East Asian unit of floor and land area equal to a 6-ja by 6-ja square, or 400/121 ≈ 3.3058 square meters / 35.58 sq ft') and 數 (수, 'number, count, figure'). Standardized across Korea during the Meiji/colonial era alongside the Japanese 坪數 (tsubosū, where 1 tsubo equals two tatami mats), 평수 remains the universal colloquial measure for apartment and house sizes.

history.meaning: number of pyeong/tsubo (6×6 shaku/ja squares ≈ 3.3 m² each) in a parcel of land or building
history.stage: Early 20th-century East Asian Real Estate & Architecture

history.meaning: floor area or unit size of a home, apartment, or office measured in pyeong

morphemes.meaning: pyeong (traditional unit of floor area ≈ 3.3058 m²) (坪)

평수.notes: Even though South Korea legally mandated square meters (제곱미터, m²) for official real estate contracts in 2007, Koreans still overwhelmingly discuss apartment sizes in 평수 in daily conversation (1 평 ≈ 3.3 m²).

rootFamily.gloss: pyeong (unit of area ≈ 3.3 m² or 35.6 sq ft)
per pyeong (used for real estate prices per unit area)

평평하다.etymology: Formed from reduplicated Sino-Korean 평평 (平平, doubling 平 'level, flat, smooth') plus native 하다. Repeating the character reinforces physical evenness across an entire surface—essential when leveling courtyard tables, laying puzzle cards edge to edge, or balancing a pocket compass.
평평하다.notes: Compare native 납작하다 ('thin and flat in profile, like a pancake or flagstone').

평화롭다.etymology: Derived adjective formed from Sino-Korean 평화 (平和, 'peace, harmony', from 평 平 'level, calm' + 화 和 'harmony, peace') + native adjectival suffix -롭다 ('characterized by').

history.meaning: peace + characterized by -> peaceful
to be peaceful, tranquil, harmonious

cognates.meaning: to discard; to scrap; to abandon

폐기하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 폐기 (廢棄, from 廢 'to abolish, abrogate, fall into ruin' + 棄 'to abandon, cast aside, discard') with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Both Hanja reinforce the sense of casting away something no longer valid or usable, yielding the meaning 'to officially discard, scrap, destroy, or annul.'

history.meaning: casting aside and abandoning what is ruined or obsolete
to discard, scrap (footage, expired food, documents), or abrogate (a treaty/plan)

폐기하다.notes: More formal and decisive than native 버리다 ('to throw away'): 폐기하다 is used for scrapping unusable broadcast footage, shredding confidential documents, disposing of expired convenience-store food (폐기), or annulling a treaty.

rootFamily.gloss: to give up; to abandon (literally 'throw away and discard')

cognates.meaning: abolition; repeal; cancellation of a service or program
to abolish; to annul; to abrogate

폐지.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 廢 (폐, 'to abolish, discontinue, cast aside, fall into disuse') and 止 (지, 'to stop, halt, cease', originally an ancient pictograph of a human foot 止 indicating coming to a standstill). Literally 'abolishing and bringing to a stop,' it denotes the formal repeal of a law or institution, and in Korean television broadcasting specifically signifies the permanent cancellation (axing) of a program.

history.meaning: abolishing and halting an established custom, law, or office
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Modern Sino-Japanese-Korean Legal Term

history.meaning: abolition of a law/system; permanent cancellation of a broadcast program

폐지.notes: In Korean TV industry jargon, 프로그램 폐지 ('program abolition/cancellation') carries a much harsher, more involuntary nuance than 종영 (終映, 'planned conclusion of a show's run'). (Also homophonous with 폐지 廢紙 'waste paper/cardboard').

rootFamily.gloss: to be abolished; for a TV show to be canceled
abolitionism; argument for canceling or repealing something

cognates.meaning: to abolish, to annul, to stop using

폐지되다.etymology: Hybrid passive verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 폐지 (廢止, "abolition, discontinuation, cancellation") with the native Korean passive-inchoative verbalizer -되다 ("to become, to be made"). The Sino-Korean stem comprises 廢 (폐, "to abolish, discard, fall into ruin", depicting a shelter 广 collapsing over發) and 止 (지, "to stop, halt", originally a pictograph of a foot). In broadcasting, it specifically denotes a television or radio program being canceled and taken off the air.

history.meaning: to abolish an institution, law, or practice; to bring to a permanent halt
to be abolished, repealed, or canceled (including a broadcast program)

morphemes.meaning: passive verbalizer (to become, to be done)

폐지되다.notes: In Korean TV industry jargon, 프로그램이 폐지되다 is the standard term for a show getting axed due to low ratings or controversy, whereas 취소되다 is used for a single event or broadcast episode being canceled.

rootFamily.gloss: closing down a business, cessation of operations

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 폐지되다

폐지설.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 폐지설 (廢止說), formed from 폐지 (廢止, "abolition, cancellation" — 廢 "abolish, discard" + 止 "stop, cease") and the productive Sino-Korean bound suffix -설 (說, "theory, view, rumor, talk"). In Classical Chinese, 說 originally meant "to explain, speak, persuade", and in modern Sino-Korean journalism and entertainment media it functions as an enclitic noun meaning "rumors of X" or "speculation about X".

history.meaning: to cease/abolish + speech, explanation, or circulating opinion
rumor or speculation regarding the cancellation/abolition of a program or policy

폐지설.notes: The suffix -설 (說) is ubiquitous in Korean entertainment news to mean "rumors of": 열애설 (dating rumors), 불화설 (feud rumors), 해체설 (disbandment rumors), and 폐지설 (show cancellation rumors).

포.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English four, which descends from Middle English fowre and Old English feower, from Proto-Germanic *fewwor, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kwetwores ("four"). Because Korean lacks the labiodental fricative /f/, the initial consonant is adapted into Korean phonology as the aspirated bilabial stop ㅍ (/pʰ/), yielding 포 (po). It is used in Korean broadcasting cues, countdowns ("원, 투, 쓰리, 포"), and compound loanwords.

history.meaning: the cardinal number four (4)
four (used in countdowns, music beats, sporting/broadcast cues, and English compounds)

포.notes: While everyday Korean uses native 넷 (net) or Sino-Korean 사 (四), English numerals 원, 투, 쓰리, 포 are standard in studio floor directing, music cues, and camera countdowns.

cognates.meaning: to abandon, to forsake, to cast aside

포기.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 포기 (抛棄), composed of 抛 (포, "to throw, cast away, fling aside", combining the hand radical 扌 with 尤/力) and 棄 (기, "to discard, abandon, forsake", originally depicting a child or basket being cast away with two hands). Historically used in Classical Chinese for physically casting something away, it acquired the modern legal and psychological sense of "renunciation of a right" or "giving up on an effort" during late 19th-century East Asian modernization alongside Japanese 抛棄/放棄 (hōki).

history.meaning: to fling away, cast aside, desert physically
giving up, abandonment of a goal, right, or endeavor

morphemes.meaning: throw away, fling aside, cast off

포기.notes: Notice the homophonous native Korean word 포기 (counter for heads of Napa cabbage, as in 배추 한 포기), which inspires the popular Korean pun "포기는 배추 셀 때나 쓰는 말이다" ("'Pogi' is a word only used when counting cabbages — never give up!").

rootFamily.gloss: desertion, abandonment (of a child or duty)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 포기 (抛棄)

포기하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 포기 (抛棄, 'throwing away, abandonment, renunciation', from 포 抛 'to fling, cast aside' + 기 棄 'to abandon, discard') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to cast aside and abandon
to give up, abandon, renounce

cognates.meaning: sharp tip, exact spot, key detail, score point

포인트.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English point, which entered Middle English via Old French point ("dot, prick, moment in time, detail") from Latin punctum ("small hole, prick, point", the neuter past participle of pungere "to prick, pierce"). In Korean, 포인트 covers a wide semantic range: the exact spot or location, the key highlight or crux of a joke/story/look, and loyalty reward points.

history.meaning: a prick made by a sharp instrument; a dot, exact spot, or salient detail
exact spot, key highlight, focal point, or reward points

포인트.notes: In Korean variety shows, drama production, and fashion, 포인트 often means the "standout highlight" or "crux" (e.g., 웃음 포인트 "the funny part/punchline", 관전 포인트 "key things to watch out for").

rootFamily.gloss: key things to watch for (in a show or match)

포장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포장 (包裝), joining 포 (包, 'wrap, bundle') and 장 (裝, 'dress, pack, outfit').
포장.notes: Also used at Korean restaurants and bakeries in 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it to go').

포장마차.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character compound 포장마차 (布帳馬車), formed from 포장 (布帳, "cloth curtain, canvas canopy, tarpaulin" — 布 "hemp/cotton cloth, canvas" + 帳 "curtain, tent, canopy") and 마차 (馬車, "horse-drawn carriage, wagon" — 馬 "horse" + 車 "wheeled cart, vehicle"). Originally referring to a covered wagon, the term was repurposed in mid-20th-century urban Korea (especially along Cheonggyecheon and Jongno in Seoul during the 1950s–1970s) for wheeled street-vendor carts enclosed by orange or clear plastic tarpaulins serving soju and late-night snacks.

history.meaning: cloth tent/canopy + horse-drawn wagon (a covered wagon)
tarpaulin-enclosed street food cart or tented outdoor drinking stall

포장마차.notes: Frequently shortened to 포차 (pocha) in casual speech and on restaurant signs (e.g., 실내포차 "indoor street-tent-style pub"); in K-dramas, the 포장마차 is the archetypal setting for candid late-night confessions over soju and udon.

rootFamily.gloss: clipped form of 포장마차; casual pub styled like a street tent

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 포장마차

포장지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포장지 (包裝紙), formed from 포장 (包裝, 'wrapping, packaging', from 포 包 'to wrap' + 장 裝 'to dress, pack') + 지 (紙, 'paper').

history.meaning: packaging + paper
wrapping paper, packing paper

cognates.meaning: impassive countenance that conceals one's thoughts or emotions

포커페이스.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from American English poker face, a compound of poker (the bluffing card game, which emerged in the American South in the early 19th century, likely influenced by French poque and German Poch) and face (from Old French face < Vulgar Latin *facia < Latin facies "appearance, visage"). First attested in American English journalism in the 1870s–1880s for a player who reveals neither excitement nor dismay at their cards, it entered Korean to describe maintaining a deadpan, unreadable expression under pressure.

history.meaning: blank, unreadable facial expression adopted by a card player to avoid giving tells
impassive, deadpan expression that conceals true feelings in social or professional situations

morphemes.meaning: the card game poker (from English poker)

포커페이스.notes: In Korean usage, keeping a poker face is commonly phrased as 포커페이스를 유지하다 ("to maintain a poker face"), whereas failing to hide one's emotions is 표정 관리가 안 되다 ("to fail at managing one's facial expression").

rootFamily.gloss: pace, speed or rhythm of progress (homophonous loanword from English pace)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 포커페이스

포크.etymology: Modern Korean culinary loanword from English fork, which goes back via Old English forca to Latin furca ('two-pronged pitchfork'). Borrowed alongside 나이프 ('knife') and 스푼 ('spoon') for Western-style dining and café pastry service, 포크 complements traditional Korean 젓가락 ('chopsticks') and 숟가락 ('spoon').
포크.notes: Counted with 개 in everyday speech.

포함.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포함 (包含), joining 포 (包, 'to wrap, encompass, enclose') and 함 (含, 'to hold in the mouth, contain, include').

history.meaning: encompassing and containing
inclusion, containment

cognates.meaning: to contain, to embody, to include

포함시키다.etymology: Hybrid causative verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 포함 (包含, "inclusion, containment") with the native Korean causative verbalizer -시키다 ("to make/cause to do"). The Sino-Korean stem consists of 包 (포, "to wrap, envelop, embrace", originally depicting a fetus inside a womb) and 含 (함, "to hold in the mouth, contain, harbor", from 今 phonetic + 口 "mouth"). The native suffix -시키다 derives from Middle Korean 시키다/식히다 ("to cause someone to do"), here functioning as a transitive/causative verbalizer ("to cause to be included; to add into").

history.meaning: to wrap up and hold within; to encompass or contain
to cause something or someone to be included in a group, list, or edit

morphemes.meaning: hold in the mouth, contain, include

포함시키다.notes: While prescribers sometimes prefer the simpler transitive verb 포함하다 ("to include"), 포함시키다 is strongly favored in spoken Korean when an agent actively adds a person, scene, or item into an existing lineup or roster.

rootFamily.gloss: wrapping, packaging, or street-stall tarp (shares 包)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 포함시키다

폭.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 폭 (幅, 'width of cloth, breadth, span; counter for hanging scrolls or paintings', from Middle Chinese *pjuwk).

history.meaning: strip of cloth, width, breadth
width, breadth, range

폭신하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the bright-vowel mimetic root 폭신 ('soft, cushiony, yielding gently under pressure', harmonic counterpart of 푹신하다) + adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to be soft, fluffy, cushiony

폭우.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭우 (暴雨), from 폭 (暴, 'violent, sudden, fierce') and 우 (雨, 'rain').
폭우.notes: Shares 폭 (暴, 'fierce') with 폭풍 (暴風, 'storm') and 폭설 (暴雪, 'heavy snowfall').

폭풍.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭풍 (暴風), combining 폭 (暴, 'fierce, violent') and 풍 (風, 'wind').
폭풍.notes: Pronounced [폭풍] with unreleased [ㄱ] before aspirated ㅍ.

cognates.meaning: ticket, ballot, bank note, slip of paper

표.etymology: Sino-Korean monomorphemic noun 표 (票), from Middle Chinese *pjiewH (票). In early Chinese texts, 票 (composed of 襾/西 above 火 "fire") denoted leaping sparks of fire or nimble lightness; during the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties, it came to designate an official bamboo tally or paper warrant issued for rapid dispatch, and then generalized to any printed slip of paper serving as a credential: a ticket, banknote, coupon, or voting ballot.

history.meaning: leaping spark of fire; rapid official warrant, paper slip, or tally
ticket, voucher, or voting ballot (and counter for votes)

morphemes.meaning: slip of paper, ticket, ballot, vote

표.notes: Do not confuse the two common Sino-Korean homophones written 표: 票 means "ticket" (기차표 "train ticket") or "vote/ballot" (한 표 "one vote"), whereas 表 means "surface, chart, table, or outward expression" (시간표 "timetable", 표현 "expression").

rootFamily.gloss: voting, casting a ballot (투 投 "throw/cast" + 표 票 "ballot")
check, bank draft, or cashier's check (수 手 "hand" + 표 票 "slip/note")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 표 (票)

표시.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 標示 (also written 表示), combining 標/表 ('emblem, surface mark, beacon') with 示 (보일 시, 'to show, point out visibly'). It covers both carved or inked symbols on maps and physical warning labels or checkmarks in a ledger, and forms 표시하다 ('to mark, indicate').
표시.notes: Collocates with 하다 ('make a mark') and 찾다 ('find a symbol').

표정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 표정 (表情), joining 표 (表, 'outer surface, to express, show') and 정 (情, 'feeling, emotion, state of mind').

history.meaning: expressing inner feeling on the surface
facial expression, look

표지.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous compounds: (1) 표지 (表紙, 'book cover', from 표 表 'outer surface' + 지 紙 'paper'); (2) 표지 (標/標識, 'sign, mark, road sign, emblem', from 표 標 'mark, sign' + 지 識 'to recognize, mark').

history.form: 表紙 (book cover) / 標識 (sign, mark)
history.meaning: outer paper cover; identifying sign or marker
cover (of a book/magazine); sign, marker

표현.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 표현 (表現), formed from 表 (표, "outer garment, surface, exterior, to show/display outwardly", originally depicting fur 毛 on the outside of a garment 衣) and 現 (현, "to appear, become visible, manifest", combining the jade/luster radical 王/玉 with 見 "to see"). While attested in Classical Chinese in the literal sense of "becoming visible on the surface", it was systematized in Meiji-era Japanese (表現, hyōgen) as the philosophical, artistic, and linguistic calque for European expression (French/English expression, German Ausdruck) and subsequently adopted into modern Korean.

history.meaning: to appear or manifest on the outer surface
linguistic phrasing, artistic representation, or outward expression of inner thought and emotion

표현.notes: 표현 (表現) refers to verbal phrasing or outward expression of feelings (애정 표현 "expression of affection"), whereas 표정 (表情, with 정 情 "emotion") specifically means "facial expression".

rootFamily.gloss: expressive power, ability to articulate or convey feelings
facial expression, look on one's face (shares 表)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 표현 (表現)

cognates.meaning: to express, to represent, to put into words
to show, to display, to express

표현하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 표현 (表現, "outward manifestation, phrasing, expression" — 表 "outer surface, display" + 現 "appear, become visible") with the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do, to make", from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota). Literally meaning "to make visible on the outside", it denotes articulating inner thoughts, emotions, or artistic ideas in words, gestures, or media.

history.meaning: Sino-Korean stem ("outward manifestation") + Middle Korean light verb ("to do")
to express, phrase, articulate, or represent thoughts and feelings outwardly

morphemes.meaning: to do, to perform (from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다)

표현하다.notes: Korean speakers often comment on whether someone is good or bad at expressing feelings with 표현을 잘하다 ("to be expressive/affectionate") vs. 표현이 서툴다 ("to be clumsy at expressing one's feelings").

rootFamily.gloss: to announce, publish, present publicly (shares 表)
to appear, to emerge in reality (shares 現)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 표현하다

푸르다.etymology: Native Korean colour adjective 푸르다 (Middle Korean 프르다), preserving traditional Korean grue semantics encompassing clear sky/sea blue, tempered blued steel, and vibrant spring foliage. Morphologically it is the classic 러-irregular stem in Korean: adding -어 produces 푸르러요 and 푸르렀어요 rather than dropping ㅡ.
푸르다.notes: Prenominal form 푸른 appears in 푸른 하늘 ('blue sky') and 푸른 숲 ('green forest').

푹.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb expressing deep immersion, sinking in softly, boiling thoroughly, or sleeping soundly (bright-vowel counterpart 폭).

history.meaning: deeply, soundly, thoroughly, sinking in

풀.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 플 (phul, "grass, herbaceous plant"), attested in the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446, "플 위 草") and Yongbieocheonga (1447). During the late 17th and 18th centuries, Early Modern Korean underwent regular labial vowel rounding (원순모음화), whereby the high central unrounded vowel ㅡ (/ɨ/) shifted to the rounded back vowel ㅜ (/u/) after bilabial consonants (ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅍ), transforming 플 (phul) into modern 풀 (pul). Within Korean, its root is etymologically linked to the color adjective 푸르다 (Middle Korean 프르다 phuluta, "to be green/blue, lush like fresh grass").

history.meaning: grass, herbaceous plant, greenery
grass, weeds, herbaceous vegetation (via labial vowel rounding ㅡ > ㅜ after ㅍ)

morphemes.meaning: grass, herb, plant (from Middle Korean 플)

풀.notes: 풀 has an important native homophone 풀 ("starch paste, glue", also from Middle Korean 플); in the common idiom 풀이 죽다 ("to feel dejected/downcast, to lose one's spirit"), the image blends wilted grass and fabric that has lost its stiff starch.

rootFamily.gloss: to be green, blue, or lush (from Middle Korean 프르다, sharing the root of 플 "grass")
blade or leaf of grass (풀 + 잎 "leaf")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 풀

풀다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) transitive verb descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 플다 (phul-ta, "to untie, unfasten, loosen, dissolve"), attested in Seokbo Sangjeol (1447) and Worin Seokbo (1459). Like the noun 풀 ("grass"), the stem vowel underwent regular labial rounding (원순모음화: ㅡ > ㅜ after the bilabial aspirated stop ㅍ) in Early Modern Korean, shifting 플다 to 풀다. From its concrete physical sense of untying a knot or unwrapping a bundle, it developed a rich metaphorical network in Korean: solving a problem (문제를 풀다), relieving fatigue (피로를 풀다), and venting or resolving pent-up anger and resentment (화를/스트레스를 풀다).

history.meaning: to untie a knot, unfasten a cord, unwrap, or dissolve
to untie, unpack, solve (a puzzle), or relieve/vent (stress, anger, resentment)

morphemes.meaning: untie, loosen, unravel, relieve (from Middle Korean 플-)

풀다.notes: 풀다 is one of Korean's most versatile polysemous verbs: 짐을 풀다 (unpack luggage), 문제를 풀다 (solve a problem), 썰을 풀다 (spin a story/spill tea), 피로를 풀다 (relieve fatigue), and 화를 풀다 (let go of anger or take out anger).

rootFamily.gloss: to come untied, be solved, or subside (passive/intransitive derivation with -리-)
solving, explanation, or unpacking the meaning of something (풀- + nominalizer -이)
putting out starch/paste, or relieving pent-up resentment (한풀이 "resolving deep resentment")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 풀다

풀리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 풀다 ('to untie, loosen, dissolve, solve', Middle Korean 플다) + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to untie -> to come untied, loosen
to come untied, be solved, thaw, subside (of anger/fatigue)

풀어놓다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 풀다 ("to untie, loosen, resolve", < Middle Korean 플다 phulta) + the infinitive/connective suffix -어 (-eo) + the auxiliary/lexical verb 놓다 ("to put down, set, leave in a resulting state", < Middle Korean 놓다 nohta). In Middle Korean, serial verb constructions with 플어 놓다 literally meant "to untie and leave loose/unfettered" (e.g., untethering livestock or unwrapping goods). In modern Korean, the auxiliary -어 놓다 adds resultative/preparatory aspect ("to do something beforehand and keep it in that state"), so 풀어놓다 means either to turn loose/spill out stories, or to smooth over and pacify someone's tense feelings in advance.

history.meaning: to untie and leave unbound; to release from a tether
to release, unpack and lay out, or smooth over/soothe someone's mood beforehand

morphemes.meaning: infinitive linker connecting main verb to auxiliary
put down, leave in a completed/prepared state (from Middle Korean 놓-)

풀어놓다.notes: When used with a person or their mood (마음을/기분을 미리 풀어놓다), the auxiliary -어 놓다 emphasizes doing the groundwork in advance — "smoothing things over beforehand" so a difficult conversation goes well.

rootFamily.gloss: to let go of, release one's grip (놓다 + 주다)
to open up and leave open (열다 + -어 놓다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 풀어놓다

풀어주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb composed of 풀다 ("to untie, loosen, relieve", < Middle Korean 플다 phulta) + connective suffix -어 (-eo) + benefactive auxiliary verb 주다 ("to give, to do for someone's benefit", < Middle Korean 주다 cwuta). Literally "to untie or loosen for someone", it is widely used in interpersonal contexts for relieving another person's anger (화를 풀어주다), easing their tension or sulking (기분을 풀어주다 "to appease, cheer up"), or letting someone off the hook.

history.meaning: to untie, unbind, or release on someone's behalf
to untie/set free for someone; to appease, soothe, or cheer up someone who is upset or tense

morphemes.meaning: give, do for someone's benefit (from Middle Korean 주-)

풀어주다.notes: In workplace and drama dialogue, 기분을 풀어주다 or 화를 풀어주다 specifically refers to coaxing, appeasing, or cheering up someone who is sulking (삐지다) or angry.

rootFamily.gloss: to come untied, to stop being angry/tense (기분이 풀리다)
to listen sympathetically to someone (듣다 + -어 주다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 풀다

품다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 품다 ('to hold in one's bosom, embrace, brood/incubate eggs, harbor a thought'), related to the noun 품 ('bosom, breast of a garment').

history.meaning: to hold in the bosom, brood over
to embrace, harbor (feelings/dreams), incubate

품위.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 품위 (品位), joining 품 (品, 'grade, quality, character, article') and 위 (位, 'rank, standing, dignity').

history.meaning: official rank and grade -> personal dignity and refinement
dignity, grace, poise

cognates.meaning: out of stock, sold out (source of the Sinographic compound)

품절되다.etymology: Hybrid passive verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 품절 (品切, "out of stock, sold out") with the native Korean passive-inchoative verbalizer -되다 ("to become"). Notably, 품절 (品切) is an orthographic borrowing (직역 차용어) from Japanese 品切れ (shinagire, a native Japanese kun-reading compound of 品 shina "goods, article, merchandise" + 切れ kire "running out, being cut off, exhaustion"), read aloud in Korean with the Sino-Korean pronunciations 품 (品) and 절 (切).

history.meaning: merchandise running out of stock in commerce
to become sold out or out of stock (read with Sino-Korean readings of 品切 + -되다)

morphemes.meaning: cut off, run out, be exhausted

품절되다.notes: Korean pop culture playfully extends 품절 ("sold out") to attractive celebrities who get married: 품절남 (品切男, "a 'sold-out' man, i.e., a taken/married heartthrob") and 품절녀 (品切女, "a 'sold-out' woman").

rootFamily.gloss: married/taken man ("sold-out man" in entertainment slang)
sold out (of tickets/seats: 매 賣 "sell" + 진 盡 "exhausted")

풍경.etymology: Sino-Korean poetic compound 風景, pairing 風 (바람 풍, 'breeze, local character') with 景 (볕 경, 'sunlight, luminous view'). Celebrated across classical East Asian painting and poetry, 풍경 captures not merely static geography (경치) but the living atmosphere of streets, trees, and people together.
풍경.notes: Note homophone 풍경 (風磬, 'bronze windbell under temple eaves').

cognates.meaning: to sweep over, dominate, captivate (an era)
to sweep across, to be all the rage, to be fashionable

풍미하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb combining the Sino-Korean literary noun 풍미 (風靡, "sweeping across, dominating, captivating") with the native Korean light verb -하다 ("to do"). In Classical Chinese, 風靡 consists of 風 (풍, "wind") and 靡 (미, "to bend down flat, fall over, yield", composed of 麻 "hemp" over 非); the compound originally depicted blades of grass and trees bending flat in unison before a powerful gust of wind (草木風靡). By metaphorical extension, it came to mean overwhelming, captivating, or defining an entire era or generation.

history.meaning: grass and plants bending flat before a sweeping wind; to overwhelm or sweep across
to captivate, sweep over, or define an era/generation (especially in cultural history)

morphemes.meaning: bend down flat, yield, sweep over
to do, to perform (from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다)

풍미하다.notes: 풍미하다 (風靡-) is almost always paired with an era as its direct object — e.g., 한 시대를 풍미하다 or 90년대를 풍미하다 ("to define/captivate the 1990s"). Do not confuse it with the homophone 풍미 (風味, "rich flavor, savor").

rootFamily.gloss: sweeping over, captivating an era; or homophonous 風味 (flavor, zest)
scenery, landscape, or cultural atmosphere (shares 風)
trend, prevailing social custom or fashion (shares 風)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 풍미하다

퓨즈.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English fuse ('electrical safety device containing a low-melting wire; cord for igniting explosives', from Italian fuso / Latin fusus).

history.meaning: electrical safety fuse
fuse

프랑스식.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from 프랑스 ('France', from French France) + Sino-Korean suffix -식 (式, 'style, manner, method').

history.meaning: French style
French-style, French manner

cognates.meaning: commercial chain license; sports league team; right to vote
franchise chain store or sports franchise

프랜차이즈.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English franchise, which entered Middle English from Old French franchise ("freedom, immunity, privilege, frankness"), derived from franc ("free, exempt", originally referring to the Franks, the ruling Germanic tribe of Gaul). In 20th-century American business English, franchise narrowed to a commercial license granting a local operator the right to run a branch under a corporate brand; in Korean, 프랜차이즈 refers primarily to large food-and-beverage chain brands (coffee shops, fried chicken chains, bakeries) as opposed to independent mom-and-pop shops.

history.meaning: legal freedom, royal privilege, or immunity (Old French) > commercial chain license (20th-c. English)
commercial chain brand or chain store (especially in food, coffee, and retail)

morphemes.meaning: franchise, chain store brand (from English franchise)

프랜차이즈.notes: In everyday Korean, 프랜차이즈 (or the Sino-Korean equivalent 가맹점 加盟店 "affiliated branch store" / 체인점 "chain store") contrasts with 개인 카페 or 동네 맛집 (independent local shops).

rootFamily.gloss: chain store (loanword hybrid of English chain + Sino-Korean 점 店 "shop")
directly managed corporate branch store (as opposed to a franchised branch)

프런트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English front ('front desk or reception area of a hotel; forward part', from Old French front, Latin frons).

history.meaning: front part; hotel reception desk
hotel front desk, reception; front

cognates.meaning: clipped form of program (プロ) or professional (プロ)

프로.etymology: Polysemous loanword clipping (외래어 약어) that entered Korean during the 20th century largely through Japanese truncation patterns (プロ puro), merging three distinct European loanwords: (1) a truncation of 프로그램 (program < English program), meaning a television or radio broadcast show; (2) a truncation of 프로페셔널 (professional < English professional), meaning a seasoned expert or professional athlete/worker; and (3) a colloquial truncation of 프로센트 (< Dutch/German Prozent via Japanese パーセント/プロ), meaning "percent (%)". In broadcasting dramas like The Producers, 프로 most frequently means either "a TV show" (예능 프로 "variety show") or "acting like a true professional".

history.meaning: truncations of English program and professional in 20th-century Japanese media and sports jargon
(1) broadcast TV/radio show; (2) professional expert; (3) percent (%) in spoken Korean

morphemes.meaning: broadcast program (< 프로그램) or professional (< 프로페셔널)

프로.notes: Context instantly disambiguates the three senses of 프로 in Korean: 예능 프로 (a variety TV show), 프로 정신 (professionalism / pro mindset), and 백 프로 (100 percent).

rootFamily.gloss: broadcast TV/radio program or computer program

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 프로

cognates.meaning: scheduled broadcast show, plan of events, software program

프로그램.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English program, which derives via Late Latin programma ("public proclamation, written notice") from Ancient Greek prógramma (πρόγραμμα, "a public written notice or agenda"), a noun of result from the verb prográphō (προγράφω, "to write forth publicly, to set forth in advance": pro- πρό "before, forth" + gráphō γράφω "to scratch, write"). In 19th-century Europe it came to denote a printed theater or concert bill, and in the 20th century expanded to radio/television broadcast shows and computer software.

history.meaning: a public written notice or edict posted in advance
scheduled broadcast show (TV/radio), event agenda, or computer software

morphemes.meaning: program, broadcast show (from English program < Greek pro- "forth" + gramma "written thing")

프로그램.notes: In Korean broadcasting, 프로그램 refers to the show as an ongoing series or format (e.g., 예능 프로그램 "variety show", 음악 프로그램 "music show"), while an individual aired installment is called 회 (回) or 방송분 (放送分).

rootFamily.gloss: clipped colloquial form of 프로그램 ("TV/radio show")
computer programmer or broadcast schedule planner
pilot program, test broadcast episode before regular scheduling

프로그램이.etymology: Inflected nominative noun phrase consisting of the English loanword 프로그램 (peurogeuraem, "broadcast program, TV show" < English program < Late Latin programma < Ancient Greek prógramma "public written notice") followed by the native Korean nominative case particle -이 (-i). In Korean morphophonology, the subject marker exhibits allomorphic alternation conditioned by syllable coda: -이 (attested in 15th-century Middle Korean as 이 i) attaches to consonant-final stems like 프로그램 (ending in ㅁ /m/), whereas -가 (-ga, which emerged in the 16th–17th centuries) attaches to vowel-final stems.

history.meaning: English loanword ("broadcast show") + native Korean postpositional nominative marker after a consonant coda

프로그램이.notes: When speaking rapidly in Korean, the final labial nasal ㅁ of 프로그램 resyllabifies smoothly across the morpheme boundary into the vowel-initial particle -이, pronounced [프로그래미 peurogeuraemi].

rootFamily.gloss: saying it is a program / just because it is a show (quotative-copular form)

프로그램이라고.etymology: Inflected quotative-copular noun form combining the English loanword 프로그램 (peurogeuraem, "TV show, broadcast program" < English program < Greek prógramma) with the native Korean copula stem -이- (-i-, "to be", retained obligatorily after consonant-final nouns) and the indirect quotative/causal ending -라고 (-rago, historically contracted from the declarative copula ending -라 + quotative verb 하고 "saying that"). Depending on clause syntax, -이라고 either marks quoted identification ("called a program / saying it is a show") or expresses an emphatic/concessive premise ("just because it is a show / calling itself a show").

history.meaning: contraction of copula declarative -이라 + quotative verb ᄒᆞ고 ("saying that it is...") in Early Modern Korean
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern Korean Grammar

history.meaning: saying that it is a show; calling it a show; (emphatic) just because it is a show

morphemes.meaning: to be (obligatory overt form after consonant-final nouns)
saying that it is / called / because it is (contracted from -라 하고)

프로그램이라고.notes: In conversational Korean, Noun + -(이)라고 often carries a slightly humbling, skeptical, or explanatory nuance: "내가 만든 프로그램이라고..." ("Calling it a show that I made... / Just because it's my show...").

프로답다.etymology: Hybrid adjective formed from 프로 ('professional', clipping of English professional) + native Korean adjectival suffix -답다 ('worthy of, like a true ...').

history.meaning: befitting a professional
to be truly professional, worthy of a pro

cognates.meaning: film, television, music, or theatrical producer
to lead forth, bring forward, bring into existence (verbal root)

프로듀서.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English producer, an agent noun formed from the verb produce + agentive suffix -er. English produce derives from Latin prōdūcere ("to lead forth, bring forward, draw out, bring into existence"), compounded from prō- ("forth, forward") and dūcere ("to lead, guide", from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- "to pull, lead"). Originally used in 19th-century English theater for the person who stages a play before the public, it expanded in 20th-century cinema, music, and television to the person overseeing creative and financial production. In Korea, its hybrid pluralized blend 프로듀사 (Producer + Sino-Korean agentive -사 士/師) is the eponymous title of the 2015 KBS drama.

history.meaning: to lead forth onto the stage (Latin) > theatrical, film, or broadcast producer (English)
television, film, or music producer (often abbreviated to PD 피디 in Korean broadcasting)

morphemes.meaning: producer (from English produce < Latin pro- "forth" + ducere "to lead" + -er)

프로듀서.notes: While 프로듀서 is the formal full loanword (used in credits, music production, and the drama title 프로듀사), Korean TV station staff almost universally say 피디 (PD) in daily workplace speech.

rootFamily.gloss: PD (Producer-Director), the standard Korean broadcasting title
production, or a production company (from English production)
producing, overseeing creative production (from English producing)

cognates.meaning: side view of a face, contour, biographical profile
outline, contour, side view of a face (ultimate Romance source)
biographical profile, side view of a face

프로필.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from French profil (and reinforced via German Profil and Japanese プロフィール purofīru), rather than directly from the English diphthongized pronunciation /ˈproʊfaɪl/.
