French profil was borrowed in the 17th century from Italian profilo ("drawn outline, contour, side view of the face"), a deverbal noun from profilare ("to draw in outline, border with a thread"), from Latin prō- ("forth, forward") + fīlum ("thread, stroke of a pen, contour line"). In Korean, 프로필 preserves both the artistic/camera sense of a "side facial view" (옆모습) and the media sense of a cast member's biographical summary or headshot (프로필 사진).

history.meaning: an outline drawn as with a thread; the side contour of a human face in portraiture
(1) side profile of a face; (2) personal biographical summary or profile picture/headshot

morphemes.meaning: side profile, contour, biographical profile (from French profil < Italian profilo)

프로필.notes: Notice the vowel in Korean 프로필 (peuropil, not *프로파일): because it entered Korean via French/German art terminology (profil / Profil) and Japanese プロフィール, it uses [i] rather than the English [aɪ], and is often clipped to 프사 (프로필 사진 "profile picture") on KakaoTalk.

rootFamily.gloss: profile picture (popular clipping of 프로필 사진 used on KakaoTalk and social media)
criminal profiler (borrowed later directly from American English profiler with [aɪ])

플러그.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English plug ('electrical connector with prongs; stopper, spark plug', from Middle Dutch plugge).

history.meaning: electrical plug, stopper
electrical plug, plug

cognates.meaning: replaying recorded audio or video footage; lip-sync track playback
playback of recorded sound or video

플레이백.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English playback, a 20th-century nominalization of the phrasal verb play back (composed of Old English plegan "to move briskly, perform, play" + Old English bæc "back"). Coined in the early sound-recording and cinema industry around the late 1920s, playback denotes immediately replaying newly recorded audio or video tape/digital footage—either on set for the director and cast to check a take (모니터링 플레이백), in an editing room for a preview screening, or playing pre-recorded music on set for performers to synchronize with.

history.meaning: the reproduction of newly recorded sound or film footage immediately after recording
playback screening or immediate replay of recorded broadcast/film footage to check a take or edit

morphemes.meaning: play, perform, reproduce media (from English play)
back, again, in return (from English back)

플레이백.notes: On a Korean television or film set, when a director calls "플레이백 해 봐" ("Run the playback"), the crew gathers around the field monitor to review the take that was just shot.

rootFamily.gloss: playlist, curated list of songs or videos (shares 플레이)
flashback scene in a drama or film (shares 백)
replay, instant replay in sports and broadcasting

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (우리말샘): 플레이백

피.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) monomorphemic noun descending unchanged in segmental shape from 15th-century Middle Korean 피 (phi, "blood"), attested in Yongbieocheonga (1447) and Worin Seokbo (1459). Even Earlier, in 12th-century Early Middle Korean (Gyerim Yusa / Jilin Leishi, 1103), it was transcribed in Chinese characters in a way suggesting an earlier bisyllabic or cluster-initial form (*pɨl or *pihi) whose syncope generated the aspirated bilabial initial ㅍ (/pʰ/). Beyond literal bodily blood, 피 carries strong metaphorical senses of biological kinship ("flesh and blood") and intense vital effort ("blood, sweat, and tears").

history.meaning: blood (of humans or animals); biological lineage or kinship
blood, vital fluid, family bloodline, or intense lifeblood effort

morphemes.meaning: blood, kinship, lifeblood (from Middle Korean 피)

피.notes: Native Korean 피 ("blood") is used in everyday speech and vivid idioms like 피 땀 눈물 ("blood, sweat, and tears") or 피가 마르다 ("one's blood runs dry [from extreme anxiety/stress]"), whereas Sino-Korean 혈 (血) appears in technical and medical compounds like 혈액형 (blood type) and 고혈압 (high blood pressure).

rootFamily.gloss: vein, blood vessel, or bloodline (피 + 줄 "cord, line", with 사이시옷 ㅅ)
complexion, color of one's face (피 + 빛 "color, light")
bruise, blood clot under the skin (피 + 멍 "bruise")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 피

피곤하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb (adjective) combining the Sino-Korean noun 피곤 (疲困, "fatigue, exhaustion, weariness") with the native Korean adjective-forming verb -하다 ("to be in the state of", < Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hota). The Sino-Korean stem consists of 疲 (피, "weary, exhausted, fatigued", composed of the sickness radical 疒 and phonetic 皮) and 困 (곤, "distressed, hemmed in, exhausted, sleepy", pictographically a tree 木 trapped inside an enclosure 囗, unable to grow). Together, 疲困 originally described being physically worn down and hemmed in by hardship, evolving into the standard everyday Korean word for feeling tired.

history.meaning: physically worn out, hemmed in by hardship, weary and sleepy
to be tired, fatigued, exhausted, or draining (of a person or situation)

morphemes.meaning: to be in a state of (adjective-forming suffix from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다)

피곤하다.notes: Beyond physical tiredness ("나는 피곤하다" = "I am tired"), describing a person's personality or behavior as 피곤하다 (e.g., 참 피곤한 스타일이다) means they are "high-maintenance, exhausting, or tiresome to deal with."

rootFamily.gloss: accumulated fatigue, exhaustion (피 疲 "weary" + 로 勞 "toil/labor")
being in a bind, awkward predicament, or trouble (shares 곤 困 "hemmed in")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 피곤하다

피다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) intransitive verb descending from 15th-century Middle Korean 피다 (phita, "to blossom, bloom, unfold, catch fire"), attested in Yongbieocheonga (1447, "곶 됴코 여름 하ᄂᆞ니" alongside 피다 in 15th-century Buddhist texts). Internally within Korean historical morphology, intransitive 피다 ("to unfold on its own, blossom") is etymologically paired with transitive 펴다 (Middle Korean 펴다 phyeta, "to spread out, unfold, flatten"): both derive from a shared root meaning "to open out from a folded or closed bud", extended to flowers blooming, embers kindling, a person's wrinkled face brightening (얼굴이 피다), or one's fortune blossoming (인생이 피다).

history.meaning: to unfold, blossom (of flowers), or kindle/spread (of fire)
to bloom, blossom, brighten (of one's complexion), or flourish (of one's life/fortune)

morphemes.meaning: bloom, blossom, open up, flourish (from Middle Korean 피-)

피다.notes: Beyond flowers blooming (꽃이 피다), Korean frequently uses 피다 metaphorically for someone looking radiant and thriving (얼굴이 활짝 피다 "one's face is glowing/blooming") or one's luck finally turning around (인생이 피다).

rootFamily.gloss: to cause to bloom, or to burn/smoke (causative derivation 피- + -우-)
to spread out, unfold, straighten out (transitive etymological doublet)
to bloom in full, open out (피다 + -어 나다 "come out")

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 피다

cognates.meaning: program director / floor director in broadcasting

피디.etymology: Broadcasting initialism (두문자어) borrowed from the English letters PD, standing for Producer-Director (or Program Director). Adopted into South Korean radio and television networks (such as KBS, MBC, and SBS) alongside Japanese broadcasting terminology in the mid-20th century, a Korean PD combines two roles that Western film/TV production typically separates: the creative/administrative producer who plans, casts, and budgets the show, and the on-set/editing director (연출자) who calls the shots in the field and editing room.

history.meaning: broadcasting executive or director overseeing radio/television programming
television or radio producer-director who both directs on set and oversees a show's production and editing

피디.notes: In Korean television stations, PDs are organized into a strict seniority hierarchy: 막내 피디 / 조연출 (junior assistant PD, or AD), 메인 피디 (main PD who directs the show), and 씨피 (CP, Chief Producer, who oversees several shows).

rootFamily.gloss: polite honorific title for a producer-director ("PD-nim")
Chief Producer (senior broadcasting executive overseeing multiple PDs and programs)
Floor Director (studio assistant managing cues on the stage floor)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language (표준국어대사전): 피디 (PD)

피디님.etymology: Hybrid occupational title combining the English broadcasting initialism 피디 (PD, "Producer-Director" or "Program Director") with the native Korean honorific suffix -님 (-nim). The suffix -님 descends from 15th-century Middle Korean 님 (nim), which functioned both as an independent noun meaning "lord, master, revered person, beloved" (surviving as modern Korean 임/님 in poetic usage) and as an honorific suffix attached to kinship and status titles (e.g., 아바님 "honored father", 스승님 "honored teacher"). In modern Korean broadcasting, 피디님 is the universal respectful form of address and reference used by cast members, writers, and junior staff for a television or radio director.

history.meaning: independent noun meaning "lord, master, esteemed person" and honorific title suffix
honorific title and vocative address for a television or radio producer-director (PD + -님)

morphemes.meaning: esteemed title marker (from Middle Korean 님 "lord, master")

피디님.notes: In Korean broadcasting culture, even veteran celebrity hosts and senior screenwriters address a young director as 피디님 (or surname + 피디님, e.g., 백승찬 피디님) on set to show professional respect for their role.

rootFamily.gloss: PD (Producer-Director), base occupational title without honorific
esteemed television/radio writer (작가 作家 "writer" + honorific -님)
esteemed director (used mainly for film/drama directors: 감독 監督 + -님)

피디라고.etymology: Inflected form of the Korean broadcasting initialism 피디 (PD, from English Producer or Program Director) combined with the quotative and identificational particle -라고, historically contracted from the copula stem 이- plus the declarative quotative ending -다 하고.

history.meaning: broadcasting producer or director
saying that (someone) is a PD; called a PD

피디라고.notes: After a vowel-final noun like 피디, the copula stem 이- drops before -라고 (unlike consonant-final nouns which take -이라고, e.g., 감독이라고).

피디수첩.etymology: Hybrid compound title combining the English-derived broadcasting initialism 피디 (PD, 'Producer/Program Director') with Sino-Korean 수첩 (手帖, 'pocket notebook, memo pad', from 手 'hand' + 帖 'written note, register'). Named after MBC's flagship investigative journalism program launched in May 1990.

history.meaning: hand-held memo book or small register
PD Notebook (investigative journalism television program)

피디수첩.notes: In Korean media culture, 피디수첩 (MBC's *PD Notebook*) is the quintessential archetype of hard-hitting investigative TV journalism, often referenced satirically in variety and drama shows when characters conduct exposés.

피아노.etymology: Borrowed from English/Italian piano (short for Italian pianoforte, 'soft-loud').
피아노.notes: Takes the native Korean verb 치다 ('피아노를 치다', 'to play the piano').

피우다.etymology: Native Korean causative/transitive verb derived from 피다 ('to bloom, blossom; for a fire to burn up', Middle Korean 피다) + causative suffix -우- ('to make bloom, kindle a fire, smoke tobacco, emit a scent').

history.meaning: to bloom, burn -> to make bloom, kindle
to blossom, light a fire, smoke, give off a scent

morphemes.meaning: to cause to bloom or burn

피하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the Hanja root 피 (避, 'to avoid, evade, flee, step aside', Middle Chinese *bjieH*) combined with the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). Attested in Middle Korean as 피ᄒᆞ다 (避ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: to withdraw from, flee, avoid
to flee from, shun, avoid
to avoid, evade, escape, dodge

morphemes.meaning: light verb deriving active verbs ('to do')

피하다.notes: Takes the accusative particle -을/-를 in Korean (e.g., 눈을 피하다 'to avoid eye contact', 비를 피하다 'to take shelter from the rain').

핀.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pin ('slender pointed metal fastener, hairpin, badge, bowling pin', from Old English pinn, Latin pinna).

history.meaning: pointed metal fastener, hairpin
pin, hairpin, clip

핀셋.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century (via Japanese pinsetto ピンセット) from Dutch pincet ('tweezers, small forceps'), itself borrowed from French pincette (diminutive of pince, from pincer 'to pinch').

history.meaning: small forceps, tweezers
tweezers, forceps

cognates.meaning: thin layer; photographic strip; motion picture

필름.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English *film* (ultimately from Old English *filmen* 'membrane, thin skin, foreskin', from Proto-Germanic *\*felminją*). With epenthetic liquid gemination (/l/ rendered as ㄹ+ㄹ across syllables) and paragogic vowel ㅡ (/ɯ/) to break the final consonant cluster /-lm/. In colloquial Korean, it underwent a metaphorical extension to mean 'conscious memory reel' during drinking.

history.meaning: thin membrane or skin
photographic cellulose strip; motion picture
photographic film; figuratively, continuity of conscious memory

필름.notes: In everyday Korean, the idiom 필름이 끊기다 (literally 'for one's film to snap/be cut off') is the standard expression for blacking out and losing memory after heavy drinking.

필연적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun derived from 필연 (必然, 'inevitability, certainty', attested in Classical Chinese such as the *Hanfeizi*, from 必 'surely, necessarily' + 然 'to be so, thus') suffixed with the adjectival/determinative marker -적 (的), which gained widespread productivity during the Meiji-era modernization of East Asian philosophical vocabulary to translate European '-ic / -ical / necessary'.

history.meaning: necessarily so; certain to happen
inevitable, necessary, bound to happen

필연적.notes: Often contrasted directly with 우연적 (偶然的, 'accidental, coincidental'); used with 이다 as a predicate (필연적이다) or with 으로 as an adverb (필연적으로 'inevitably').

필요.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 필요 (必要), joining 필 (必, 'certainly, inevitably, must') and 요 (要, 'important, essential, to demand, require').

history.meaning: indispensable requirement, necessity
need, necessity

필요하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 필요 (必要, 'necessity, requirement') + native Korean adjective suffix -하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: to be necessary, needed
to be needed, necessary, required

핏줄.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 피 ('blood', Middle Korean 피) + the genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷, continuing the Middle Korean genitive particle ㅅ) + 줄 ('line, cord, vein, streak', Middle Korean 줄). Literally 'blood-line' or 'cord of blood', signifying both anatomical blood vessels and biological kinship/bloodline.

history.meaning: blood vessel; line of kinship by blood
blood vessel; bloodline, family lineage, flesh and blood

핏줄.notes: While 혈관 (血管) is the clinical Sino-Korean term for anatomical blood vessels, 핏줄 carries warm emotional weight when referring to family ('one's own flesh and blood', e.g., 핏줄은 못 속인다 'blood will tell / you can't fool genetics') or visible veins bulging on the neck/forehead.

rootFamily.gloss: complexion; flush of blood in the face (핏기)

핑계.etymology: Nativized word ultimately derived from the Sino-Korean compound 빙자 (憑藉, historically also read 핑자, from 憑 'to lean on, rely on' + 藉 'mat, to borrow, use as a pretext'). In Early Modern Korean, 핑자 underwent phonological shift and folk remodeling via 핑조/핑계 to modern 핑계 ('excuse, pretext'), losing transparency as a Hanja compound while its doublet 빙자하다 ('to use as a pretext') survived in formal Sino-Korean register.

history.meaning: leaning upon; borrowing something as a pretext or support
excuse, pretext, alibi

핑계.notes: Commonly collocated with the verb 대다 (핑계를 대다 'to make up an excuse'); remember the famous Korean proverb 핑계 없는 무덤 없다 ('There is no grave without an excuse' — everyone has an excuse for their failures).

rootFamily.gloss: to make an excuse; use as a pretext
using as a pretext (formal doublet, 憑藉)
piece of an excuse; mere pretext

핑크.etymology: Loanword from English *pink*, which originally referred in 16th-century English to a plant of the genus *Dianthus* with frilled pale-red petals (perhaps from Dutch *pink* 'small' or from the verb *to pink* 'to pierce/scallop edges') before becoming a color term in the 17th–18th centuries. Adapted into Korean phonology as 핑크 with final paragogic vowel ㅡ.

history.meaning: garden flower with scalloped, pale-red petals
pale red color characteristic of the flower
the color pink; romantic or rosy atmosphere

핑크.notes: Coexists with the Sino-Korean term 분홍 (粉紅, 'powder red'); 핑크빛 ('pink-colored') is standard media slang for a budding romance (e.g., 핑크빛 열애설 'pink/rosy dating rumors').

하겠습니다.etymology: Inflected form of the native Korean verb 하다 ('to do, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다) + the voluntative/conjectural pre-final suffix -겠- (historically grammaticalized in Early Modern Korean from the resultativegerundive -게 + 잇- 'to exist so as to be') + the deferential formal polite declarative ending -습니다 (from Middle Korean -ᄉᆞᆸ- humble object-exalting suffix + -니- indicative + -다 declarative).

history.meaning: humbly comes to be in a state of doing; will humbly do
I will do it; allow me to do it (deferential polite)

하겠습니다.notes: In workplace and broadcasting settings, 하겠습니다 is the standard crisp, professional way to accept an instruction or announce one's immediate intention (e.g., 시작하겠습니다 'I will begin now', 열심히 하겠습니다 'I will work hard').

하기.etymology: Nominalized form of the native Korean verb stem 하- ('to do, make, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ-) combined with the deverbal nominalizer suffix -기 (Middle Korean -기). Unlike the older nominalizer -(으)ㅁ which denotes completed or abstract facts, -기 historically rose to prominence from Late Middle Korean onward to denote dynamic, ongoing, or future-oriented action processes.

history.meaning: the act or process of doing
doing; to do (action nominalization)

하기.notes: Forms the backbone of essential grammatical constructions like -기 때문에 ('because of doing'), -기 시작하다 ('to start doing'), -기로 하다 ('to decide to do'), and standalone headings on to-do lists.

rootFamily.gloss: truly, indeed (lexicalized from 하기야 'if we speak of doing/saying it')

하긴.etymology: Colloquial contraction of 하기는 ('indeed, when one thinks of it, to be sure'), formed from the nominalized stem 하기 (from 하다 'to do, say') + contrastive topic particle -는.

history.meaning: indeed, come to think of it, after all

하나.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞ나 (stem ㅎᆞ낳-, 'one, single unit').

history.meaning: one
one

하나하나.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated compound of 하나 ('one', Middle Korean ㅎᆞ나), meaning 'one by one, each and every one individually'.

history.meaning: each individual one, one by one

하는데.etymology: Inflected connective form of the native Korean verb stem 하- ('to do, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ-) + the circumstantial/contrastive suffix -는데. The suffix -는데 grammaticalized from the adnominal processive suffix -는 + the bound noun 데 ('place, circumstance, case', Middle Korean ᄃᆡ) + the locative particle -에 (literally 'in the circumstance where one does').

history.meaning: in the place or circumstance where (someone) does
does/says, and (setting background context) or but (mild contrast)

morphemes.meaning: circumstantial, background, or contrastive connective ending

하는데.notes: One of the most versatile endings in spoken Korean: used mid-sentence to set the stage before a main clause ('I'm doing X, and/but...'), or sentence-finally (often with -요 as 하는데요) to trail off politely, express surprise, or invite the listener's reaction.

rootFamily.gloss: however, by the way (lexicalized from 그런 데 'in that circumstance')

하늘.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 하〮늘〯 (stem 하늘ㅎ-, 'sky, heaven').

history.meaning: sky, heaven
sky, heavens

하니까.etymology: Inflected causal and discovery connective form of the native Korean verb stem 하- ('to do, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ-) + the connective suffix -(으)니까. The ending -니까 developed in Early Modern Korean as an emphatic Reinforcement of the older sequential/causal ending -(으)니 (Middle Korean -으니) combined with the interrogative/focus particle -가/-까.

history.meaning: as/since (someone) does; upon doing
because (someone) does/says; when (I) did, I discovered that...

morphemes.meaning: subjective causal or realization connective ending ('because; upon doing')

하니까.notes: Has two distinct uses: (1) subjective justification ('since/because one does X', whichunlike -아서/-어서 can be followed by imperatives and propositives like 하니까 가자!), and (2) discovery upon completion ('when I did X, I found out that...'). In speech, 말이야 + 하니까 or 그냥 하니까 often stresses an obvious reason.

하다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞ다 ('to do, make, say, think; to be'), the primary light verb and adjective-forming auxiliary in Korean.

history.meaning: to do, make, say
to do, make; light verb

하루.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from 15th-century Middle Korean ᄒᆞᄅᆞ ('one day'), with oblique stem ᄒᆞᆯ리- (e.g., ᄒᆞᆯ리라 'it is one day'). Probably internally related to the native Korean numeral root ᄒᆞᆫ- / ᄒᆞ나 ('one'), following the native Korean series of day-count words (ᄒᆞᄅᆞ '1 day', 이틀 '2 days', 사흘 '3 days', 나흘 '4 days'). With the loss of the vowel 아래아 (ㆍ) and vowel rounding in the second syllable, ᄒᆞᄅᆞ evolved regularly into modern 하루.

history.meaning: one day; the first day of the month
one day; a full 24-hour day; daily life

하루.notes: Refers to the span of a single day (e.g., 하루 종일 'all day long'); also appears in the idiom 하루아침에 ('overnight / in a single morning') and the proverb 하룻강아지 범 무서운 줄 모른다 ('a one-day-old puppy doesn't know to fear a tiger' — fools rush in).

rootFamily.gloss: day by day; every single day
in a single morning; overnight (하루 + 아침)

하룻밤.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 하루 ('one day', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᄅᆞ) + the genitive compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 밤 ('night', Middle Korean 밤). In Middle Korean it is attested as ᄒᆞᄅᆞᆺ밤, literally 'the night of a single day', hence 'one night, a single night'.

history.meaning: a single night; the night of one day
one night; an overnight stay

하룻밤.notes: Because both 하루 and 밤 are native Korean words and the first ends in a vowel while the second begins with a lax consonant triggering tensification ([하룯빰 / 하루빰]), Korean orthography requires writing the 사이시옷 (ㅅ) in 하룻밤.

하면.etymology: Inflected conditional/temporal form of the native Korean verb stem 하- ('to do, make, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ-) + the conditional connective suffix -(으)면 (Middle Korean -(으)면). Derived from a combination of the irrealis/prospective adnominal or nominal element -음/-을 and a topical/conditional particle in Old and Middle Korean.

history.meaning: if or when (someone) does or says
if/when (one) does; speaking of (after a noun)

하면.notes: Beyond simple 'if/when one does' (e.g., 시작하면 'once you start'), placing 하면 immediately after a noun means 'speaking of X / when it comes to X' (e.g., 예능 하면 KBS 'When you think of variety shows, you think of KBS'). Also famous in the motivational slogan 하면 된다 ('If you do it, it works / Where there's a will, there's a way').

cognates.meaning: stage right (audience left); lower seat; inferior player

하수.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 하수 (下手, literally 'lower hand', from 下 'below, lower' + 手 'hand, side, skill'). In traditional Chinese and Korean usage, 下手 meant an 'inferior player' (e.g., in Baduk/Go or martial arts) or 'subordinate position'. In modern Korean theater and television stagecraft, the sense 'stage right (house left, from the audience's perspective)' was reinforced by Meiji/Taishō-era Japanese theatrical terminology 下手 (shimote), contrasting with 상수 (上手, kamite, 'stage left / house right').

history.meaning: to put one's hand to; lower seat; inferior skill/player
stage right (audience's left side of the stage) in kabuki and modern theater
stage right (audience left) in TV/theater; low-skilled player; sewage (下水, homograph)

하수.notes: In broadcasting and stage direction (*The Producers*), 상수 (上手) and 하수 (下手) are essential floor-directing terms: viewed from the audience or camera, 상수 is the right side (stage left) and 하수 is the left side (stage right). Note that 하수 (下手) is also used in gaming/sports for a 'noob/inferior player' (opposite of 고수 高手 'master').

rootFamily.gloss: stage left (audience right); superior player (上手)

하숙집.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun combining 하숙 (下宿, 'boarding, lodging', from 下 'down, subordinate, temporary' + 宿 'to lodge, stay overnight', popularized in modern East Asia via Japanese 下宿 *geshuku* for student room-and-board lodging) with the native Korean noun 집 ('house, home', Middle Korean 집). Literally 'boarding-house'.

history.meaning: renting a room with meals provided (student/worker boarding)
boarding house providing room and daily meals

하숙집.notes: Unlike a modern studio apartment (원룸) or exam-prep dormitory (고시원), a traditional Korean 하숙집 is run by a landlady (하숙집 아줌마) who cooks home-style breakfast and dinner for the student boarders (하숙생).

하시더라고요.etymology: Complex inflected form of the native Korean verb stem 하- ('to do, say', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ-) + subject honorific suffix -시- (Middle Korean -시-) + retrospective/evidential suffix -더- (Middle Korean -더-, marking a past state or action directly witnessed by the speaker) + declarative quotative/connective element -라고 (from -다 하고, integrated into the retrospective reporting construction -더라고) + polite addressee particle -요. Expresses the speaker's polite recollection to the listener of something a respected third party did or said that the speaker personally observed.

history.meaning: (I witnessed that the esteemed person) was doing / did
I noticed/saw that (he/she, honorific) did or said...

morphemes.meaning: declarative reporting ending ('I tell you that...')

하시더라고요.notes: In conversational storytelling, -더라고요 is used when reporting something you personally saw, heard, or experienced firsthand; adding -시- (하시더라고요) shows respect toward the person whose actions or words you witnessed. Often pronounced (though non-standard in writing) as 하시드라고요.

하얗다.etymology: Native Korean color adjective descending from Middle Korean 하야〮ㅎᆞ다〮 ('to be pure, bright white'), bright-vowel harmonic counterpart of 허옇다, expanded from the root of 희다 ('to be white').

history.meaning: to be dazzlingly or pure white
to be pure white, snow-white

하우스.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English house ('building, dwelling; plastic greenhouse via 비닐하우스; club/venue'), from Old English hūs.

history.meaning: dwelling, building; vinyl greenhouse
house; vinyl greenhouse (비닐하우스)

하지만.etymology: Grammaticalized conjunction formed from 하지 (stem 하- of 하다 'to do, be so' + connective base -지) + concessive particle -만 (shortened from -마는 'even though, however'), literally 'it is so, but...'.

history.meaning: however, but, nevertheless

cognates.meaning: to get off a vehicle; to finish work/step down

하차.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 하차 (下車, literally 'descending from a vehicle', from 下 'to descend, go down' + 車 'wheeled vehicle, carriage, train'). Originally used in Classical Chinese for an official alighting from his carriage upon arriving at a post, and in modern transport for getting off a train or bus. In contemporary South Korean broadcasting and entertainment jargon, it underwent a vivid metaphorical shift: a television show or drama is conceptualized as a moving train or bus, so 'getting off the vehicle' (하차) means leaving the cast or stepping down from a program before or during its run.

history.meaning: to descend from a carriage or chariot
alighting from a train, subway, or bus
stepping down from or leaving the cast of a TV/radio program

하차.notes: A signature K-entertainment and *The Producers* keyword: when a celebrity leaves a variety show or drama cast (voluntarily or by firing), Korean headlines always call it 하차 (e.g., 자진 하차 'voluntary departure from a show', 강제 하차 'forced removal from a show'). Its transport antonym is 승차 (乘車, 'boarding a vehicle').

rootFamily.gloss: to step down from a show; to get off a vehicle (下車-)
to remove/drop someone from a show; make get off (下車-)

하차시키다.etymology: Hybrid causative verb combining the Sino-Korean noun 하차 (下車, literally 'getting off a vehicle', metaphorically 'leaving the cast of a broadcast program', from 下 'down' + 車 'vehicle') with the causative verbalizer -시키다 ('to cause to do, make someone do', historically a causative derivative of Middle Korean 시키다/식히다 'to make someone perform an action'). Literally 'to make someone get off the vehicle', hence 'to drop/remove a cast member from a show'.

history.meaning: to make a passenger disembark from a vehicle
to remove, fire, or drop a cast member from a TV/radio program

morphemes.meaning: causative light verb ('to make/cause to do')

하차시키다.notes: Central to the plot of *The Producers* (프로듀사), where variety PDs agonize over how to tell veteran cast members that the network is dropping them (하차시키다) during a seasonal program overhaul (개편).

rootFamily.gloss: leaving a show; getting off a vehicle (下車)
to leave a show; to get off a vehicle (下車-)
getting off and getting on vehicles (下乘車)

하차하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean verb formed from the noun 하차 (下車, 'alighting from a vehicle; leaving a broadcast program', from 下 'descend' + 車 'vehicle') and the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do'). While originally restricted to disembarking from trains, buses, or carriages, in modern South Korean media it is the standard verb for stepping down from a television or radio program.

history.meaning: to get off a carriage, train, or bus
to get off a vehicle; to step down from or leave a broadcast show

하차하다.notes: Takes the ablative particle -에서 for both vehicles and TV programs: 버스에서 하차하다 ('to get off the bus') and 프로그램에서 하차하다 ('to step down from the program').

rootFamily.gloss: leaving a show; getting off a vehicle (下車)
to remove someone from a show (下車-)

cognates.meaning: why must it be; there is no need to

하필.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb (also used predicatively before 이다 or with -이면) from Classical Chinese 하필 (何必, literally 'why must it necessarily be?', from 何 'what, why, how' + 必 'necessarily, must'). Famous from the opening line of *Mencius* (孟子): 王何必曰利 ('Why must Your Majesty necessarily speak of profit?'). In Korean, the rhetorical question 'Why did it have to be [this one out of all possibilities]?' evolved into an adverb expressing exasperation at ironic, unlucky, or inconvenient timing/selection ('of all things, of all times, as luck would have it').

history.meaning: why must it necessarily be...? (rhetorical question)
of all things/times/places; as bad luck would have it

하필.notes: Almost always expresses frustration at Murphy's Law or bad luck (e.g., 하필 오늘 비가 오네 'Of all days, it has to rain today!'; often expanded to 하필이면 'if it had to choose out of all options, why...').

하하.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic interjection and mimetic adverb representing open-mouthed, cheerful laughter ('haha!').

history.meaning: haha! (sound of laughing aloud)

하한가.etymology: Sino-Korean three-morpheme financial compound 하한가 (下限價, from 下 'lower, bottom' + 限 'limit, boundary' + 價 'price, value'), formed from 하한 (下限, 'lower limit, floor') + -가 (價, 'price'). Coined in modern Korean stock-market terminology for the maximum daily downward price limit (circuit-breaker floor) a stock can fall in a single trading session, and used figuratively in everyday slang to mean 'hitting rock bottom in popularity or reputation'.

history.meaning: the lowest permissible price floor in regulated trading
daily lower price limit on the stock exchange; figuratively, rock-bottom reputation/value

하한가.notes: In Korean variety and entertainment talk (including *The Producers*), saying someone's image or popularity 'hit 하한가' (하한가를 치다) means their stock/reputation has plummeted to rock bottom; its exact opposite is 상한가 (上限價, 'daily upper price limit / skyrocketing popularity').

rootFamily.gloss: daily upper price limit; peak popularity (上限價)

학교.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 학교 (學校), joining 학 (學, 'to learn, study, learning') and 교 (校, 'schoolhouse, wooden enclosure, to examine').

history.meaning: place of learning, school
school

cognates.word: 學校生活 / 学校生活 (xuéxiào shēnghuó)

학교생활.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 학교 (學校, 'school', from 學 'to learn, study' + 校 'school, enclosure, wooden stocks/building', a Classical Chinese compound attested in *Mencius* and revitalized in modern East Asia for Western-style schools) + 생활 (生活, 'life, living, daily existence', from 生 'to live, be born' + 活 'to live, be active', also attested in *Mencius*). Literally 'school life'.

history.meaning: place of learning + daily living and activity
school life; a student's daily life and conduct at school

학교생활.notes: Appears in the official Korean school transcript name 학교생활기록부 (often abbreviated 생기부, 'Student School Life Record'), and parallels compounds like 사회생활 (社會生活, 'social/workplace life') and 회사생활 (會社生活, 'office life').

학구적.etymology: Sino-Korean determiner and noun derived from 학구 (學究, 'pursuit of learning, academic inquiry; a scholar/pedant', from 學 'to study, learn' + 究 'to investigate thoroughly, examine to the bottom', originally a Tang-dynasty title for candidates studying the classics, *xuejiu*) + the adjectival/attributive suffix -적 (的). Popularized in modern Korean alongside Meiji-era Japanese 学究的 (*gakkyūteki*) to mean 'scholarly, studious, academically minded'.

history.meaning: investigation of learning; Tang-era title for a classicist or village schoolmaster
scholarly, academic, studious, bookish

학구적.notes: Often used to describe someone's personality, demeanor, or appearance (e.g., 안경을 써서 학구적으로 보인다 'Wearing glasses makes you look scholarly/studious').

rootFamily.gloss: passion for learning; academic zeal (學究熱)

한.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral ('one, a single, approximately') descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆫ, adnominal modifier form of ㅎᆞ나 ('one'). (A homophonous Sino-Korean prefix 한- 大/韓/漢 also occurs in compounds.)

history.meaning: one, a single (before nouns)
one, a single; approximately (adv.)

한가득.etymology: Native Korean emphatic adverb formed by prefixing the native intensifier 한- ('great, full, very, right in the middle', Middle Korean 한-, derived from the adnominal form of 하다 'to be great, abundant, many') to the adverb 가득 ('full, to the brim', Middle Korean 가ᄃᆞᆨ, related to the ideophonic root 가ᄃᆞᆨᄒᆞ다 'to be full'). Literally 'greatly/completely full to the brim'.

history.meaning: greatly full; filled to capacity
brimming all over; chock-full; in great abundance

morphemes.meaning: full to the brim, filled up

한가득.notes: Note that the prefix 한- here means 'big/great/completely' (from old 하다 'to be great', as in 한가운데 'right in the middle' or 한겨울 'midwinter'), NOT 'one' (하나). It gives a warm, vivid sense of overflowing abundance (e.g., 선물을 한가득 안고 'holding an armful of gifts').

rootFamily.gloss: to be full to the brim
right in the very middle (한 + 가운데)

한가운데.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from the intensive prefix 한- ('exact, right in the middle, great', Middle Korean 한-) + 가운데 ('middle, center', from Middle Korean 가온대).

history.meaning: exact middle
the very center, right in the middle

cognates.meaning: leisure, free time; quiet and unhurried

한가하다.etymology: Hybrid Sino-Korean descriptive verb (adjective) formed from the Sino-Korean noun 한가 (閑暇, 'leisure, spare time, peaceful idleness', from 閑 'barrier, quiet, idle, unoccupied' + 暇 'leisure, free time, respite') + the native Korean adjectival/verbal suffix -하다 (Middle Korean -ᄒᆞ다). Attested in Middle Korean texts as 한가ᄒᆞ다 (閑暇ᄒᆞ다).

history.meaning: unoccupied time; peaceful leisure and rest
to be at leisure, unhurried, free from duties
to be idle, free, leisurely, slow (of business)

한가하다.notes: Can describe a person having free time (오늘 한가해요? 'Are you free today?'), a peaceful scene, or a store/office being slow with few customers or tasks; also has a derived native-style adverb/adjective stem 한가롭다 ('peacefully leisurely').

한계.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 한계 (限界, from 限 'limit, threshold, restriction, boundary' + 界 'boundary, border, realm, world'). Originally denoting a physical border or jurisdictional boundary between territories, in modern East Asian usage (reinforced by Japanese 限界 *genkai* in scientific, economic, and philosophical translations) it came to denote the utmost limit of capacity, endurance, or possibility.

history.meaning: territorial boundary or line of demarcation
limit, bound, limitation of ability or endurance; marginal (in economics)

한계.notes: Commonly used in expressions like 한계에 부딪히다 ('to hit a wall / reach one's limit'), 한계를 넘다 ('to surpass one's limits'), and 인내심의 한계 ('the limit of one's patience'). In economics, 한계 translates English 'marginal' (e.g., 한계효용 'marginal utility').

한구석.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from the native determiner 한 ('one, a certain', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ, adnominal form of ᄒᆞ나 'one') + 구석 ('corner, nook, recessed spot', Middle Korean 구석). Literally 'one corner' or 'a certain secluded corner'.

history.meaning: one corner; a recessed nook
a corner, a nook; figuratively, a quiet recess of one's mind or heart

morphemes.meaning: one, a certain (native determiner ᄒᆞᆫ > 한)

한구석.notes: Frequently used both for physical spaces (방 한구석에 'in a corner of the room') and metaphorically for an unspoken feeling lingering in the back of one's mind or heart (마음 한구석이 짠하다 'a corner of my heart aches/feels touched'). Written as one word without a space when meaning 'a corner/nook'.

한꺼번에.etymology: Native Korean lexicalized adverb formed from 한 ('one, same', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ) + the bound noun 꺼번 ('time, occasion, turn at once', attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄭᅥ번 / 거번, related to 번 番 'turn, time' with an intensive prefixal element) + the locative/temporal particle -에 ('at, in'). Attested in Early Modern Korean as ᄒᆞᆫᄭᅥ번에, literally 'at one single turn/occasion', hence 'all at once, simultaneously'.

history.meaning: at one single turn or occasion; all together at the same time
all at once, simultaneously, in one go

morphemes.meaning: one, single, same (native determiner ᄒᆞᆫ > 한)
bound root meaning 'single turn/batch of occurrences' (꺼번)

한꺼번에.notes: Compare 한꺼번에 ('all at once / simultaneously in a big rush or batch', e.g., 손님이 한꺼번에 몰려왔다 'customers poured in all at once') with 단번에 (單番에, 'at a single stroke / on the first try') and 한번에 ('in one go'). The bound root 꺼번 only survives in Korean today inside 한꺼번에.

rootFamily.gloss: at one go; once (한 + 번 番 + 에)
at a single stroke; right away (單番에)
at the same time, simultaneously (同時에)

한대요.etymology: A colloquial indirect-quotative contraction of native Korean 한다고 해요 (handago haeyo, 'says that [someone] does'), combining the verb stem 하- (ha-, 'to do', from Middle Korean 하〮다〮), the present-tense declarative quotative ending -ㄴ다 (-nda) plus complementizer -고 (-go), the pro-verb 하- (ha-, 'to say'), the infinitive -어 (-eo), and the polite sentence-final particle -요 (-yo). Through regular conversational syncope of -고 하- (-go ha-), 한다고 해요 contracts to 한대요.

history.meaning: to do; to say or report (expressed analytically before modern quotative contractions)
they say that (someone) does; reportedly does or says (polite informal indirect quotation)

한대요.notes: Distinguish spelled 한대요 (indirect quotation: 'they say someone does') from 한데요 (background observation or mild contrast from descriptive stems).

rootFamily.gloss: to do; to make; to say
says that it is; is called (polite)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: Standard Korean Dictionary (하다)

한두.etymology: A native Korean compound numeral determiner formed by juxtaposed apocope of 한 (han, adnominal form of 하나 hana, 'one', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon < ᄒᆞ나〮 hona) and 두 (du, adnominal form of 둘 dul, 'two', from Middle Korean 두〮 du < 둘〯 dulh). Both numeral stems undergo regular pre-nominal final consonant drop before classifier nouns.

history.meaning: one or two (pre-nominal numeral compound)
one or two; a couple of (approximate small quantity)

한두.notes: As a pure pre-nominal determiner (관형사), 한두 must always precede a counter or noun (e.g., 한두 번 'once or twice'); the standalone nominal equivalent is 하나둘.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한두

한때.etymology: A native Korean compound noun and temporal adverbial composed of the adnominal numeral/determiner 한 (han, 'one; a certain; peak/prime', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon 'one, same' and ᄀᆞ장/한 'great') and the native noun 때 (ttae, 'time, season, occasion', from Middle Korean ㅳᅢ pstae). It denotes either a single bygone period ('at one time, once in the past') or the prime part of a span of time.

history.meaning: one time; the same time; a certain period
at one time; once (in the past); for a brief period; the prime of life

한때.notes: Frequently used adverbially without a particle to contrast a glorious or notable past state with the present ('at one time, back in the day').

rootFamily.gloss: at times; from time to time
in the middle of; right at the peak of (a time)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한때

cognates.meaning: Korean Wave; also homophonous with 'cold current' (寒流)

한류.etymology: A late-1990s Sino-Korean compound (韓流) coined in Taiwanese and mainland Chinese entertainment journalism (Mandarin Hánliú, 'Korean current/trend', punning on homophonous 寒流 Hánliú 'cold air current') and re-imported into Korean as 한류 (hallyu, with liquid assimilation /n.l/ → [ll]). It combines 韓 (한 han, 'Korea, Korean', originally the Three Han confederacies 三韓) and 流 (류/유 ryu/yu, 'stream, current, trend').

history.meaning: flow or wave of South Korean pop music and TV dramas across East Asia
the Korean Wave; global popularity of South Korean popular culture and entertainment

한류.notes: Pronounced [할류] (hallyu) due to regular nasal-liquid assimilation, and identically spelled in Korean to 한류 (寒流, 'cold ocean/air current').

한마디.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 한 ('one', adnominal of 하나) + 마디 ('joint of bamboo, node; a phrase or word of speech', Middle Korean 마디).

history.meaning: a single word, a brief remark

한밤중.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native intensifying prefix 한- ('dead centre, peak'), native 밤 ('night'), and Sino-Korean 중 (中, 'middle').
한밤중.notes: Parallel to 한낮 ('high noon') and 한겨울 ('midwinter').

한번.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 한 ('one', adnominal of 하나) + Sino-Korean 번 (番, 'turn, time, occasion'); lexicalized as a single word when meaning 'once (at some point), as a try, really'.

history.meaning: one time -> once, give it a try

한복.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound (韓服) combining 韓 (한 han, 'Korea, Korean', adopted in 1897 for the Korean Empire 大韓帝國) and 服 (복 bok, 'clothing, garment, dress'). Coined in the late 19th to early 20th century to distinguish indigenous Korean dress (formerly simply called 옷 ot or 우리 옷 'our clothes') from newly introduced Western attire (양복 洋服, yangbok).

history.meaning: clothing or garments in general prior to contrast with Western dress
traditional Korean attire (specifically jeogori, chima, and baji) contrasted with Western clothing

한복.notes: In North Korea, traditional Korean dress is instead called 조선옷 (朝鮮옷, Joseon-ot) rather than 한복.

cognates.meaning: instant; moment; blink of an eye

한순간.etymology: A hybrid native–Sino-Korean compound combining the native Korean adnominal numeral 한 (han, 'one, a single', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon) with the Sino-Korean noun 순간 (瞬間, sungan, 'blink of an eye, instant'), which itself derives from Buddhist Chinese translation terminology (rendering Sanskrit kṣaṇa 'split second') composed of 瞬 (순 sun, 'to wink, blink the eye') and 間 (간 gan, 'interval, space between').

history.meaning: the interval of a single blink of an eye; a brief moment (Buddhist temporal unit)
a single instant; a fleeting moment; in a flash

morphemes.meaning: to blink; wink of an eye (瞬)

한순간.notes: Often paired with the locative particle -에 as 한순간에 ('in a single instant, all at once') to emphasize how quickly something changes or collapses.

rootFamily.gloss: a brief moment; a little while (한동안)

한숨.etymology: A native Korean compound noun formed from the adnominal adjective 한 (han, 'great, big, deep, long', fossilized adnominal participle of Middle Korean 하〮다〮 hada 'to be great, large, much', distinct from ᄒᆞ다 hoda 'to do') and 숨 (sum, 'breath, respiration', from Middle Korean 숨〯 sum, nominalization of 쉬다 swida 'to breathe, rest'). Literally 'a great/deep breath', specialized to mean a sigh of grief, relief, or exhaustion.

history.meaning: a deep or heavy breath; a sigh
a sigh (of worry, sorrow, frustration, or relief)

morphemes.meaning: great; deep; big (from archaic 하다 'to be great')

한숨.notes: Here 한- means 'big/deep' (as in 한길 'main road' or 한겨울 'midwinter'), NOT 'one', though the phrase 한숨 자다 ('to take a nap') uses the homophonous numeral 한 ('one'). Collocates with 쉬다 (한숨을 쉬다, 'to heave a sigh') or 내쉬다.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한숨

한없이.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean derivative adverb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 한 (限, han, 'boundary, limit, restriction'), the native negative existential adjective stem 없- (eop-, 'to not exist, to be lacking', from Middle Korean 없〯다〮 eopsda), and the productive adverb-deriving suffix -이 (-i). Literally 'without limit' or 'boundlessly'.

history.meaning: without a boundary or limit; endlessly
endlessly; boundlessly; infinitely; to no end

한없이.notes: Even though 한 (限) is Sino-Korean, 한없다 and 한없이 are lexicalized as single words written without a space and often express emotional depth (e.g., 한없이 작아지다 'to feel infinitely small').

cognates.meaning: Wagyu; indigenous Japanese beef cattle (analogous Sino-compound)

한우.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound (韓牛) combining 韓 (한 han, 'Korea, Korean') and 牛 (우 u, 'cow, ox, cattle'). Originally a livestock classification term designating the indigenous yellow-brown taurine cattle breed of the Korean Peninsula (Bos taurus coreanae) as distinct from imported dairy cattle (유우 乳牛) or foreign beef cattle (육우 肉牛); by metonymy it denotes premium domestic Korean beef.

history.form: 조선우 (朝鮮牛, Joseon-u) / 한우 (韓牛, hanu)
history.meaning: native Korean draft cattle breed contrasted with foreign breeds
native Korean cattle; high-grade domestic Korean beef (prized for rich marbling)

한우.notes: In South Korean culture and TV dramas like *The Producers*, 한우 is the archetypal luxury gift or celebratory company-dinner (회식) treat, far pricier than imported beef (수입 소고기).

한자리에.etymology: A native Korean adverbial phrase lexicalized from the compound noun 한자리 (hanjari, 'one place, the same spot, a single seat/gathering') plus the locative case particle -에 (-e, 'in, at, to'). 한자리 combines the adnominal numeral 한 (han, 'one, the same', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon) and 자리 (jari, 'seat, spot, place, position', Middle Korean 자리〮 jari).

history.meaning: in one spot; on the same mat or seat
in one place; all together at a single gathering or occasion

한자리에.notes: Almost always collocates with verbs of gathering such as 모이다 (한자리에 모이다, 'to gather together in one place'). Written without a space when meaning 'at the same gathering/place'.

rootFamily.gloss: one place; the same seat; a single sitting

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한자리

한잔.etymology: A hybrid native–Sino-Korean compound noun formed from the native Korean adnominal numeral 한 (han, 'one', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon) and the Sino-Korean noun/classifier 잔 (盞, jan, 'small cup, wineglass, goblet'). While 한 잔 (spaced) literally counts 'one cup/glass', the unspaced compound 한잔 lexicalizes the social act of having a light drink (typically alcohol, tea, or coffee) together.

history.meaning: one cup or goblet of wine/liquor
a drink (especially a casual round of alcohol or beverage shared socially)

한잔.notes: Korean orthography distinguishes spaced 한 잔 ('strictly one glass in quantity') from solid 한잔 ('a casual social drink', rarely limited to just one glass!).

한잔하다.etymology: A hybrid compound verb derived from the lexicalized noun 한잔 (한盞, hanjan, 'a drink, a round of drinks', from native 한 'one' + Sino-Korean 盞 jan 'cup, wineglass') verbalized with the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do, to partake in', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ다 hoda). It underwent semantic broadening from 'to drink one cup' to 'to go out for drinks; to have a drink together'.

history.meaning: to take a cup of wine or tea
to have a drink (especially alcohol) socially; to grab a drink together

morphemes.meaning: to do; to have; to partake in

한잔하다.notes: Saying 언제 술 한잔하자 ('Let's grab a drink sometime') is a classic Korean social pleasantry akin to 'Let's get lunch sometime' in English.

rootFamily.gloss: to propose a toast; cheers (乾杯하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한잔하다

한참.etymology: Native Korean compound noun and adverb formed from 한 ('one, a full') + 참 ('stage, rest stop on a journey, interval of time', Middle Korean ㅊᆞᆷ).

history.meaning: one full stage/interval -> a good while, a long time
a long while, quite some time

한테.etymology: Native Korean colloquial dative/locative particle ('to, from, at [an animate being]'), contracted in Early Modern Korean from 한데 ('in the same place, together', from 한 'one, same' + 데 'place').

history.meaning: at the same place -> to/for (a person or animal)
to, at, from (animate dative marker)

한판.etymology: A hybrid native–Sino-Korean compound combining the native Korean adnominal numeral 한 (han, 'one, a full', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon) with 판 (板 or 局/場, pan, 'board, arena, stage, round of a game or contest'). Originally referring to a single board or round in traditional games like baduk (바둑), janggi (장기), or ssireum (씨름) wrestling ring, it broadened to mean a decisive bout, match, or all-out clash.

history.meaning: one board; one round of a board game or wrestling match
a bout; a round; a decisive match or clash; a big round of action or merriment

morphemes.meaning: board; arena; round of a match or game (板)

한판.notes: In judo and ssireum, 한판승 (한판勝) corresponds to an 'ippon' (instant full-point victory); colloquially 한판 붙다 means 'to have a showdown/fight'.

rootFamily.gloss: board; scene; situation; round of a game
decisive match; contest of victory or defeat (勝負판)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한판

한편.etymology: A hybrid native–Sino-Korean word composed of the native adnominal numeral 한 (han, 'one; the same', Middle Korean ᄒᆞᆫ hon) and the Sino-Korean noun 편 (便, pyeon, 'side, direction, party, team'). As a noun it means 'one side' or 'the same team/side'; via grammaticalization as a discourse conjunction and adverb, it means 'on the other hand; meanwhile'.

history.meaning: one side or direction; the same party or faction
meanwhile; on the other hand (conjunctive adverb); one side; the same team (noun)

한편.notes: Watch the dual meaning: as a predicate noun (우린 한편이다 'We are on the same side/team'), 한 means 'same'; as a transition word (한편... 'Meanwhile / On the other hand...'), it shifts the scene or perspective.

rootFamily.gloss: opposite side; the other side (反對便)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 한편

할머니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 할미 / 할머니, formed from 한- / 할- ('big, great, venerable', adnominal of 크다/하다 'great') + 어미 / 어머니 ('mother').

history.meaning: great-mother -> grandmother
grandmother, elderly woman

cognates.meaning: allotment; installment payment; division of shares

할부.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound (割賦) borrowed via modern Japanese commercial-legal terminology (Japanese 割賦 kappu, 'allotment, payment in installments'), combining 割 (할 hal, 'to cut, divide, apportion, cleave') and 賦 (부 bu, 'to allot, levy, distribute, pay'). It denotes dividing a lump-sum price into scheduled periodic payments.

history.meaning: allotment of taxes or divided installment payments in Meiji commercial law
installment plan; payment in monthly installments (especially on credit cards)

할부.notes: In South Korean retail and credit-card culture, clerks routinely ask 일시불이세요, 할부세요? ('Lump sum, or installments?'), with 무이자 할부 meaning 'interest-free installments'.

cognates.meaning: to allot; to pay in installments

할부하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean verbal compound (割賦하다) formed by attaching the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do') to the Sino-Korean noun 할부 (割賦, halbu, 'installment payment', composed of 割 hal 'to divide, cut' + 賦 bu 'to allot, distribute'). It means to divide a purchase price or debt into multiple scheduled payments.

history.meaning: to allot or divide a payment into scheduled portions
to pay in installments; to buy on an installment plan

할부하다.notes: Often contrasted in everyday shopping with 일시불로 계산하다 ('to pay in a single lump sum').

rootFamily.gloss: to discount; to reduce price (割引하다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 할부하다

할아버지.etymology: Native Korean kinship compound from 한-/할- ('great, big', from 하다 'to be great/many' in Middle Korean) + 아버지 ('father').

할인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 할인 (割引, first popularized via Meiji Japanese waribiki 割引), joining 할 (割, 'to cut, divide, proportion') and 인 (引, 'to pull back, deduct, draw').

history.meaning: deducting a proportion -> price discount
discount, price reduction

cognates.meaning: discount; reduction in price (native Japanese reading under the same kanji)

할인하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound verb (割引하다) formed from the Sino-Korean noun 할인 (割引, harin, 'discount') and the native verb suffix 하다 (hada, 'to do'). 할인 (割引) is an orthographic Sino-Korean reading (음독 차용) of the Japanese commercial compound 割引 (waribiki, from 割 wari 'rate, ten percent, division' + 引 hiki 'pulling back, deducting').

history.meaning: deducting a percentage (wari) from a price; price discount
to discount; to reduce a price or fare by a certain rate

morphemes.meaning: to pull back; to deduct; to draw (引)

할인하다.notes: While 할인하다 is the standard formal/commercial verb for discounting, colloquial spoken Korean very frequently uses the native verb 깎다 (kkakkda, literally 'to shave/whittle down').

함께.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆷ끠 ('together, at the same time'), formed from ㅎᆞᆫ ('one, same') + 끠 (locative/temporal noun 'time, occasion', modern 때).

history.meaning: at one and the same time, together
together, with

함께하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 함께 ('together', Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆷ끠) + 하다 ('to do, share').

history.meaning: to do together, share, accompany

함부로.etymology: A native Korean adverb traced to Early Modern Korean 함버로 / 함부로 (hambeoro / hamburo), analyzed by Korean historical linguists as deriving from an unattested or fossilized verbal/nominal base 함벌 (hambeol, 'roughness, unrestrained manner', or 한벌 'all at once without distinction') plus the instrumental adverbial particle -로 (-ro, 'by way of, with'). It denotes acting without caution, permission, or restraint.

history.meaning: without restraint or care; rashly; indiscriminately
carelessly; recklessly; lightly; without permission or due respect

morphemes.meaning: instrumental adverbial marker ('in the manner of')

함부로.notes: Carries a strong interpersonal warning in Korean when paired with speech or behavior: 함부로 말하다 means not merely 'to speak carelessly' but 'to speak out of turn, rudely, or presumptuously'.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 함부로

함정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 함정 (陷穽), joining 함 (陷, 'to sink, fall into, trap') and 정 (穽, 'pitfall, covered pit for catching wild beasts').

history.meaning: pitfall dug to trap animals
pitfall, trap, snare

cognates.meaning: to agree; to suit one's wishes (Sino-Vietnamese)

합의.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound (合意) composed of 合 (합 hap, 'to join, combine, match, unite') and 意 (의 ui, 'mind, thought, intention, will'). Literally 'joining of minds/intentions', it denotes reaching a mutual agreement, consensus, or legal settlement between two or more parties.

history.meaning: harmony or alignment of intentions and opinions
mutual agreement; consensus; out-of-court legal settlement between disputing parties

morphemes.meaning: to join; to unite; to match (合)

합의.notes: In Korean law and police dramas, 합의 보다 ('to reach a settlement') specifically refers to the victim and perpetrator agreeing on compensation so the victim drops criminal punishment wishes.

rootFamily.gloss: to reach a mutual agreement (合意하다)

cognates.meaning: settlement money (typically called 示談金 jidankin, though 合意金 gōikin is transparent)

합의금.etymology: A three-character Sino-Korean compound (合意金) combining 합의 (合意, habui, 'mutual agreement, legal settlement', from 合 hap 'to join, unite' + 意 ui 'mind, intention') with the suffixoid Sino-Korean root 금 (金, geum, 'metal, gold, money, sum of funds'). It specifically denotes financial compensation paid to settle a civil or criminal dispute out of court.

history.meaning: sum of money paid upon reaching a mutual settlement
settlement money; out-of-court compensation paid to a victim or opposing party

합의금.notes: Distinguished from 위자료 (慰藉料, 'consolation money / damages for emotional distress' in divorce or tort suits) and 벌금 (罰金, 'state-imposed criminal fine').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 합의금

합치다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean transitive/intransitive verb formed from the Sino-Korean root 합 (合, hap, 'to join, unite, combine, add together') plus the native Korean verbalizer and intensifier/causative suffix -치다 (-chida, attested from Early Modern Korean on Sino-Korean and native stems, compare 겹치다 'to overlap', 넘치다 'to overflow'). It means to combine, merge, or pool separate things into one.

history.meaning: to join together; to unite or merge into a single whole
to combine; to unite; to pool (strength, money, or numbers) together

morphemes.meaning: to join; to combine; to unite (合)

합치다.notes: Unlike many Korean verbs, 합치다 functions both transitively ('to combine X and Y', 힘을 합치다 'to join forces') and intransitively ('to merge/come together').

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 합치다

항목.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 項目, combining 項 (항목 항, originally 'nape of the neck', extended to individual sub-clauses) and 目 (눈 목, originally 'eye', extended to itemized headings in a list or catalogue). It is the standard Korean noun for numbered items on an inspection checklist, questionnaire, or official notice.
항목.notes: Pairs with ordinal numbers like 첫째 항목 ('item one') and 둘째 항목 ('item two').

항상.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb and noun 항상 (恒常), joining 항 (恒, 'constant, perpetual, lasting') and 상 (常, 'always, ordinary, unchanging').

history.meaning: constant and unchanging
always, constantly

항의.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound (抗議) composed of 抗 (항 hang, 'to resist, oppose, defy, hold up against') and 議 (의 ui, 'to discuss, deliberate, express an opinion, criticize'). In Classical Chinese (e.g., *Book of Han*), 抗議 meant 'to speak forthrightly or debate frankly against authority'; in modern East Asian usage it specialized into 'formal protest, objection, or complaint'.

history.meaning: to offer frank, unyielding counsel or remonstrance to a superior
protest; formal objection; vigorous complaint against perceived unfairness

morphemes.meaning: to resist; to oppose; to defy (抗)

항의.notes: In broadcasting (as in *The Producers*), 시청자 항의 ('viewer protests/complaints') flooded into the station message board whenever a program aired a controversial scene.

rootFamily.gloss: to protest; to lodge a complaint (抗議하다)

해.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 해〮 ('sun, sunlight, year'), from Old Korean *hɛ ('sun, year').

history.meaning: sun; year
sun, daylight; year

cognates.meaning: to be resolved; to be settled (analogous Sino-root)
to resolve; to settle; to solve

해결되다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean passive/inchoative verb (解決되다) formed from the Sino-Korean noun 해결 (解決, haegyeol, 'resolution, settlement') and the native passive/inchoative verb 되다 (doeda, 'to become, to get done', from Middle Korean 되다 / 도외〮다〮 dooida). 해결 combines 解 (해 hae, 'to untie a knot, loosen, explain, solve') and 決 (결 gyeol, 'to breach a dike, decide, settle'). Literally 'for a knot to become untied and a channel opened'.

history.meaning: untying a knot and opening a blocked water channel; resolving a difficulty
to be solved; to get resolved; to be settled (of a problem, dispute, or crisis)

morphemes.meaning: to untie; to loosen; to solve (解)
to decide; to breach/clear; to settle (決)
passive/inchoative verbalizer ('to become, to be done')

해결되다.notes: 해결되다 is the intransitive/passive counterpart ('the problem gets solved') of transitive 해결하다 ('to solve the problem'), taking the subject particle 이/가 rather than object 을/를.

rootFamily.gloss: to solve; to resolve; to settle (解決하다)

cognates.meaning: to solve; to resolve; to settle
to solve; to resolve; to settle

해결하다.etymology: A Sino-Korean transitive compound verb (解決하다) combining 해결 (解決, haegyeol, 'resolution, solution') with the native Korean light verb 하다 (hada, 'to do'). The Sino-Korean compound 解決 joins 解 (해 hae, 'to untie a horn-knot with an awl, loosen, unravel') and 決 (결 gyeol, 'to open a sluice/dike, decide decisively'), shifting metaphorically from clearing physical tangles and blockages to settling complex problems or disputes.

history.meaning: to untangle knots and clear blockages; to settle a matter decisively
history.stage: Classical Chinese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: to solve (a problem); to resolve (a conflict); to take care of or settle (an issue or bill)

morphemes.meaning: to untie; to unravel; to solve (解)
to decide; to settle; to clear (決)

해결하다.notes: Beyond solving abstract problems, 해결하다 is used colloquially for taking care of everyday needs (e.g., 점심을 라면으로 해결하다 'to take care of lunch with ramen').

rootFamily.gloss: to be solved; to get resolved (解決되다)

해내다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed by fusing 해 (hae, the irregular infinitive/connective form 하여 hayeo of 하다 hada 'to do', from Middle Korean ᄒᆞ야 hoya) with the auxiliary/main verb 내다 (naeda, 'to put forth, bring out, produce, see through to the end', from Middle Korean 내〮다〮 naeda, causative of 나다 nada 'to come out'). As a resultative compound, it means 'to do something all the way out to completion; to pull off or accomplish despite difficulty'.

history.meaning: to do and bring forth; to carry an action through to completion
to pull off; to accomplish; to achieve or manage to do successfully despite obstacles

morphemes.meaning: doing (contracted infinitive 하여 of 하다 'to do')
to bring out; to carry through to completion (from 내다)

해내다.notes: Always implies overcoming difficulty or expectations: simply finishing homework is 숙제를 하다, whereas pulling off an impossible broadcast deadline is 결국 해내다 ('to pull it off in the end').

rootFamily.gloss: to endure; to stick it out to the end (버텨내다)
to find out; to discover against odds (찾아내다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 해내다

해놓다.etymology: A native Korean serial verb construction and compound combining 해 (hae, contracted infinitive 하여 hayeo of 하다 hada 'to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ야 hoya) and the auxiliary verb 놓다 (nota, originally 'to put, place, set down, release', Middle Korean 놓〮다〮 nohta). Grammaticalized as a resultative-preparatory aspectual construction (-어 놓다), it means 'to do something and leave the resulting state in place; to get something ready beforehand'.

history.meaning: to perform an action and set/leave it in place
to do beforehand; to get ready in advance and leave in a prepared state

morphemes.meaning: doing (contracted infinitive 하여 of 하다 'to do')
to put; to leave a completed state in place (놓다)

해놓다.notes: Pronounced [해노타] (haenota) because final ㅎ of 놓- aspirates the following ㄷ; in colloquial speech, 해 놓다 often contracts further to 해 놔 (hae nwa).

rootFamily.gloss: to put; to place; to keep a state (놓다)
to do and keep for later reference (해두다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 놓다

해달다.etymology: A native Korean benefactive-quotative verbal construction combining 해 (hae, contracted infinitive 하여 hayeo of 하다 hada 'to do') with 달다 (dalda, defective quotative verb stem meaning 'to give [to me, the speaker/requester]', from Middle Korean 다〮라〮 dara, imperative used when requesting something for the speaker). Unlike 주다 (juda, 'to give in general'), 달다 is used exclusively in imperative quotations (-어 달라고 하다 'to ask someone to do X for oneself'). Literally 'to ask someone to do [it] for me/oneself'.

history.meaning: do (it) and give (the benefit) to me! (direct benefactive request)

history.form: 해 달다 / 해달다 (haedalda, in 해 달라고 / 해 달라다)
history.meaning: to ask or request (someone) to do something for the requester/subject

morphemes.meaning: doing (contracted infinitive 하여 of 하다 'to do')
to give to the requester; to do for the speaker (defective quotative stem 달-)

해달다.notes: A classic Korean grammar trap: when reporting 'She asked me to do it for her', you MUST use 해 달라고 했다 (when the requester and recipient are the same person), whereas 해 주라고 했다 means 'She told me to do it for someone else'. (Note: homophonous lexical 해달다 'to attach/hang onto' uses 달다 'to hang'.)

rootFamily.gloss: to ask for; to say 'give me' (달다, defective verb)
to do for someone; to give the favor of doing (해주다)
to ask someone to look after/watch (봐달다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 달다 (auxiliary verb)

해두다.etymology: A native Korean serial/auxiliary verb construction combining 해 (hae, contracted infinitive 하여 hayeo of 하다 hada 'to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ야 hoya) and the auxiliary verb 두다 (duda, originally 'to put, place, keep, store', from Middle Korean 두〮다〮 duda). As an aspectual construction (-어 두다), it means 'to do something and keep/preserve the result for future use or finality'. In discourse (그렇게 해 두자), it means 'let us leave it at that / let us call it that for now'.

history.meaning: to do something and keep or store the result
to do in advance and keep ready; to leave a matter settled as such ('let's call it that')

morphemes.meaning: doing (contracted infinitive 하여 of 하다 'to do')
to keep; to put and preserve for later (두다)

해두다.notes: While 해놓다 and 해두다 both mean 'to do beforehand', 해두다 more strongly emphasizes preserving or retaining the result for future benefit (or leaving a topic settled: 비밀로 해 두자 'let's keep it a secret').

rootFamily.gloss: to put; to keep; to leave in place (두다)
to do beforehand and leave in place (해놓다)
to know in advance for future reference (알아두다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 두다

해드리다.etymology: A native Korean humble/object-honorific benefactive verb construction combining 해 (hae, contracted infinitive 하여 hayeo of 하다 hada 'to do', Middle Korean ᄒᆞ야 hoya) with the humble auxiliary verb 드리다 (deurida, 'to humbly give or offer to a superior', from Middle Korean 드리〮다〮 deurida, originally causative of 들다 deulda 'to enter', i.e. 'to cause to enter into a superior's presence'). It is the deferential counterpart of 해주다 (haejuda, 'to do for someone').

history.meaning: to perform an action and humbly present/offer it to an honored person
to do (a favor, service, or arrangement) for a respected person or elder

morphemes.meaning: doing (contracted infinitive 하여 of 하다 'to do')
to humbly give/do for a superior (드리다)

해드리다.notes: Essential in Korean workplace and service etiquette: when doing something for a senior producer, client, or elder, 해주다 sounds blunt, whereas 해드리다 (e.g., 제가 예약해 드릴게요 'I will arrange the reservation for you') shows proper deference.

rootFamily.gloss: to do for someone (plain/equal register, 해주다)
to humbly tell or inform a superior (말씀드리다)

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language: 드리다

해맑다.etymology: A native Korean derivative adjective formed by prefixing 해- (hae-, intensive/expressive prefix meaning 'freshly, whitishly, brightly, purely', related to the bright-vowel colour/light root 해- in 해사하다 'fair and clean' and 하얗다/희다 'white', or folk-etymologically associated with 해 'sun') to the native adjective 맑다 (makda, 'to be clear, limpid, pure, sunny', from Middle Korean ᄆᆞᆯ다〮 / 맑다〮 malkda). It describes a complexion, smile, or spirit that is radiantly clear, pure, and guilelessly innocent.

history.meaning: clear and pure (of water or sky) → brightly clear, fair, and untainted (of a face or heart)
bright and innocent; radiantly pure and guileless (especially of a child's smile or expression)

해맑다.notes: Whereas 맑다 describes clear water, weather, or voice, 해맑다 is used almost exclusively for human expressions—especially a bright, uncorrupted, childlike smile (해맑은 미소) or naive innocence. Pronounced [해막따] before consonants and [해말근] (해맑은) before vowels.

rootFamily.gloss: clean, fair, and neat in appearance (해사하다)

해머.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English hammer ('heavy striking tool with a metal head, sledgehammer, athletic throwing hammer', from Old English hamor).

history.meaning: striking tool, sledgehammer
hammer, sledgehammer

해버리다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb formed from 해 (the infinitive stem of 하다, 'to do') and the auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to throw away, discard', from Middle Korean ᄇᆞ리다). Through grammaticalization, the lexical verb meaning 'to cast away' evolved into a completive aspectual auxiliary expressing that an action is finished completely, irrevocably, or unexpectedly, often carrying an emotional nuance of relief or regret.

history.meaning: to do and cast away; to finish doing completely
to end up doing; to finish doing completely or irrevocably

morphemes.meaning: to throw away; completive aspect marker

해버리다.notes: Though orthographically spaced as 해 버리다 in strict prescriptive norms, it is frequently written solid as 해버리다 and conveys that an action happened all the way to completion, often accidentally or to the speaker's relief or dismay.

rootFamily.gloss: to throw away, discard; completive auxiliary

해보다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 해 (the infinitive form of 하다, 'to do') with the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see, look at', from Middle Korean 보다). Following a common cross-linguistic grammaticalization pathway, the verb of visual perception ('do and see what happens') developed into a conative and experiential auxiliary meaning 'to try doing' or 'to have the experience of doing'.

history.meaning: to do and see; to test out an action
to try doing; to experience doing

morphemes.meaning: to see; conative and experiential marker

해보다.notes: Unlike 노력을 하다 ('to make a strenuous effort'), 해보다 means 'to give something a try' to see how it turns out, or in past tense (해봤다) 'to have experienced doing'.

rootFamily.gloss: to see, look; to try doing

해석하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) verbal compound formed from 해석 (解釋, 'interpretation, explanation') and the native verbalizer 하다 ('to do'). The Hanja compound pairs 해 (解, 'to untie, loosen, dissect, explain', originally depicting a knife 刀 and hands separating an ox horn 角 from an ox 牛) with 석 (釋, 'to unravel, release, elucidate'), shifting from the physical untangling of knots to the intellectual explication of texts, data, or situations.

history.meaning: to untangle, loosen, or expound a classical text
textual exegesis, explanation, interpretation
to interpret, construe, analyze, or translate

해석하다.notes: Used both for subjective interpretation of behaviour or art ('reading into a situation') and for translating or parsing sentences in foreign-language study.

해오다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb composed of 해 (the infinitive stem of 하다, 'to do') and 오다 ('to come', from Middle Korean 오다). As an auxiliary verb, deictic 오다 ('movement toward the speaker's present location/time') grammaticalized into a continuative aspectual marker indicating an action that has been carried out continuously from the past up to the present moment.

history.meaning: to do and come; to continue doing up to the present
to have been doing continuously; to do and bring

morphemes.meaning: to come; continuative aspect toward the present

해오다.notes: Contrasts directionally with 해가다: 해오다 looks from the past up to 'now' ('have been doing until now'), whereas 해가다 looks from 'now' onward into the future ('keep doing from here on').

rootFamily.gloss: to continue doing onward into the future

해외.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 해외 (海外), compounded from 해 (海, 'sea, ocean') and 외 (外, 'outside, beyond'). In Classical Chinese cosmography (such as the Shanhaijing 山海經), 海外 referred to distant lands lying beyond the Four Seas (四海) believed to encircle the central realm; in modern Korean it denotes foreign countries or anywhere 'overseas' regardless of maritime geography.

history.meaning: lands lying beyond the Four Seas surrounding the central realm
overseas, abroad, foreign countries

해외.notes: Because South Korea is geopolitically cut off by land to the north, 해외 ('overseas') functions as the standard everyday word for 'abroad' in travel, business, and broadcasting (e.g., 해외 촬영, 'overseas filming').

rootFamily.gloss: at home and abroad, domestic and international (國內外)

해장.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun altered phonetically from earlier 해정 (解酲), compounded from 해 (解, 'to untie, relieve, dispel') and 정 (酲, 'sickness from drunkenness, hangover'). Attested in Joseon-era medical and culinary texts as 해정 (as in 해정탕 解酲湯, 'hangover-relieving soup'), the second syllable shifted in popular speech from 정 to 장, later giving rise to the folk-etymological Hanja spelling 解腸 ('soothing the intestines').

history.meaning: relieving illness or stupor caused by drinking alcohol
hangover cure; eating soup or food to recover from drinking

morphemes.meaning: hangover, sickness from alcohol (from 정 酲)

해장.notes: Central to Korean drinking culture, 해장 most commonly refers to eating hot broth (해장국) or ramen the morning after drinking, while 해장술 means 'hair of the dog' (alcohol drunk to cure a hangover).

해주다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) benefactive compound verb formed from 해 (the infinitive stem of 하다, 'to do') and 주다 ('to give', from Middle Korean 주다). Through serial verb grammaticalization, the donor verb 주다 ('give') lost its literal sense of physical transfer to become a productive benefactive auxiliary indicating that an action is performed for the benefit of another person.

history.meaning: to do and give; to perform an action for someone
to do for someone; to grant the favor of doing

해주다.notes: When the beneficiary of the action is socially superior or older, 주다 must be replaced by its humble/honorific counterpart 드리다, yielding 해드리다 ('to do for an esteemed person').

해코지하다.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound verb derived from the noun 해코지 ('spiteful harm, injury') and the native verbalizer 하다 ('to do'). The noun 해코지 stems from Earlier Modern Korean 해콫다 ('to harm, injure'), built on the Sino-Korean root 해 (害, 'harm, injury, damage') combined with a native Korean verbal/nominalizing element -콫- / -코지, denoting deliberate, malicious attempts to hurt someone.

history.meaning: to inflict spiteful harm; malicious injury
to harm, hurt, or do malicious mischief to someone

morphemes.meaning: native nominalized formative expressing harmful action

해코지하다.notes: Unlike neutral words for damage (피해를 주다), 해코지하다 specifically implies personal malice, retaliation, or someone trying to physically or socially hurt a target out of spite.

cognates.meaning: favorable conclusion to a story or situation
happy ending (of a story or film)

해피엔딩.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed directly from the English phrase 'happy ending' (compounded from Middle English 'happy', from 'hap' meaning 'chance, fortune', and 'ending', the verbal noun of Old English 'endian'). Adopted into Korean film, television drama, and literary criticism in the twentieth century to denote a narrative conclusion in which the protagonists achieve a joyful resolution.

history.meaning: a fortunate or joyful conclusion to a narrative
happy ending (in television drama, cinema, or real-life events)

해피엔딩.notes: In Korean television drama (드라마) production, scripts are frequently debated as ending in a 해피엔딩 ('happy ending'), 새드엔딩 ('sad ending'), or 열린 결말 ('open ending').

rootFamily.gloss: ending, closing credits or final scene
ending fairy (close-up shot at the end of a performance)

cognates.meaning: core, kernel, heart of the matter

핵심.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 핵심 (核心), compounded from 핵 (核, 'pit or stone of a fruit, kernel, nucleus') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind, center'). Combining the hard seed-kernel at the center of a fruit with the vital heart of the body, the compound evolved metaphorically from a physical center into the indispensable crux of an argument or the central figure of a group.

history.meaning: the inner seed-kernel and heart; the innermost center
core, crux, essence, or key figure

핵심.notes: Frequently used as a pre-noun modifier (e.g., 핵심 인물 'key figure', 핵심 요약 'core summary') to highlight what is most essential.

cognates.meaning: mobile phone (in Singaporean and Malaysian English)

핸드폰.etymology: South Korean pseudo-anglicism (콩글리시, Konglish) coined in the 1990s from the English roots 'hand' (핸드) and 'phone' (폰, clipping of telephone, from Greek tele 'far' + phone 'voice'). Originally created to distinguish portable handheld cellular telephones from earlier vehicle-mounted car phones (카폰), it became the most widespread colloquial Korean word for a mobile phone.

history.meaning: English constituent nouns 'hand' and 'phone'
handheld cellular telephone, mobile phone, smartphone

핸드폰.notes: While official broadcasts and news media prefer the Sino-Korean/hybrid terms 휴대전화 (携帶電話) or 휴대폰, everyday conversation overwhelmingly uses 핸드폰 or simply 폰.

cognates.meaning: steering, handling of a vehicle or ball

핸들링.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English 'handling', the gerund-noun of 'handle' (from Old English handlian, 'to touch or manage with the hands', derived from hand). In Korean, beyond its automotive sense of steering responsiveness, it is widely used in entertainment, broadcasting, and corporate jargon to mean managing, directing, or dealing with cast members, clients, or complex operations.

history.meaning: touching with the hands; steering, managing, or controlling
vehicle steering; management or handling of people and projects

핸들링.notes: In Korean office and TV production slang, 사람을 핸들링하다 ('to handle people') refers to tactfully managing difficult celebrities, executives, or team members, whereas plain 핸들 alone usually means a car's 'steering wheel'.

cognates.meaning: ground beef patty served in a bun

햄버거.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from American English 'hamburger', which originated as a clipping of 'Hamburger steak'—minced beef prepared in the style of migrants from the German port city of Hamburg (German Hamburger, combining the toponym Hamburg with the demonymic suffix -er). Introduced to South Korea after the Korean War via U.S. military bases and popularized nationwide with fast-food chains from the late 1970s.

history.meaning: native or culinary product of the city of Hamburg
ground beef patty served inside a sliced round bun
hamburger; fast-food burger sandwich

morphemes.meaning: hamburger (from English hamburger, ultimately from Hamburg + -er)
