햄버거.notes: Just as in English, the false reanalysis of 'ham-burger' led Korean to adopt productive -버거 compounds for non-beef sandwiches such as 새우버거 ('shrimp burger') and 치킨버거 ('chicken burger').

햇볕.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 햇볕, formed from 해 ('sun') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 볕 ('warmth of the sun, sunshine').

history.meaning: warmth of the sun's rays
sunshine, warmth of the sun

햇빛.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 햇빛, formed from 해 ('sun') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 빛 ('light, radiance, color').

history.meaning: light of the sun
sunlight, sunbeams

햇살.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound joining 해 ('sun') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 살 ('rays, arrows, spokes').
햇살.notes: Evokes individual warm beams of sunlight streaming through a courtyard or window.

행간.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 행간 (行間), compounded from 행 (行, 'row, column, line of text') and 간 (間, 'interval, space between'). From its literal typographical meaning of the blank space between written lines of characters, it developed the figurative sense of unspoken subtext or implicit meaning, especially in the calqued idiom 행간을 읽다 ('to read between the lines').

history.meaning: physical space between columns or lines of text; within military ranks
line spacing; implicit subtext ('between the lines')

행간.notes: Although the Hanja 行 traditionally carries the reading 항 when meaning 'row/rank' (as in 항렬 行列), in 행간 (行間) it is always pronounced 행 and almost always used figuratively for reading hidden intentions.

행동.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) coordinate compound 행동 (行動), formed from 행 (行, 'to walk, go, act, practice') and 동 (動, 'to move, stir, act'). In Classical Chinese the pair denoted physical walking and bodily movement; during the late nineteenth-century modernization of East Asian lexicon, it was standardized to translate Western philosophical and psychological concepts of purposeful 'action' and 'behavior'.

history.meaning: to walk and move about; bodily movement
action, behavior, conduct, deed

morphemes.meaning: to walk, go, act, carry out

행동.notes: Covers both a single concrete 'action' (행동을 취하다, 'to take action') and a person's general 'behavior' or 'conduct' (행동이 바르다, 'to be well-behaved').

rootFamily.gloss: words and deeds, speech and conduct (言行)

행복하다.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) descriptive verb formed from 행복 (幸福, 'happiness, good fortune') and the native adjectivalizer 하다 ('to be'). The Hanja compound joins 행 (幸, 'good luck, fortunate favor') and 복 (福, 'blessing, prosperity'); originally denoting objective external fortune in Literary Chinese, it acquired the modern subjective sense of emotional 'happiness' in the late nineteenth century via Meiji Japanese translation of English 'happiness'.

history.meaning: auspicious fortune, divine blessing, prosperity
state of subjective happiness and well-being
to be happy, blessed, or deeply content

행복하다.notes: Expresses deep, lasting life satisfaction or emotional fulfillment ('happy, blessed'), whereas momentary cheerfulness or feeling good is expressed by 기쁘다 ('glad, joyful') or 기분이 좋다 ('in a good mood').

행사.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 행사 (行事), compounded from 행 (行, 'to carry out, perform, conduct') and 사 (事, 'affair, matter, ceremony, business'). Originally a verb-object construction in Classical Chinese meaning 'to conduct affairs or rituals', it nominalized in Korean and Japanese to denote an organized public event, ceremony, or promotional function.

history.meaning: to carry out affairs; official proceedings or ritual conduct
organized event, ceremony, or promotional appearance

행사.notes: In the Korean entertainment industry, 행사 specifically refers to paid off-air appearances (such as university festivals or corporate events) where singers or entertainers perform, distinct from its homograph 행사 (行使, 'exercising a right or power').

rootFamily.gloss: progression, hosting an event or show (進行)

행운.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 행운 (幸運), from 행 (幸, 'good fortune, blessing') and 운 (運, 'revolving fate, luck').
행운.notes: Commonly paired with native verb 빌다 in 행운을 빌어요 ('wishing you good luck').

행정.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 행정 (行政), compounded from 행 (行, 'to execute, carry out, practice') and 정 (政, 'governance, state affairs, rule'). Attested in Classical Chinese historiography (such as the Shiji 史記) as the verb-object phrase 'to exercise governance', it was repurposed in modern East Asian legal and bureaucratic terminology to mean public or institutional 'administration'.

history.meaning: to carry out governance; to administer state affairs
public or organizational administration; executive management

행정.notes: Used both for state governance (행정부, 'the executive branch') and for everyday institutional paperwork and office logistics (행정 업무, 'administrative duties').

행정반.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) compound noun 행정반 (行政班), formed by affixing 반 (班, 'squad, unit, section, class') to 행정 (行政, 'administration', from 행 行 'to execute' + 정 政 'governance'). Originating in South Korean military organization for a company-level administrative office and supply room ('orderly room'), the term is also used humorously in civilian workplaces such as broadcasting stations for an admin or supply desk.

history.meaning: administration + squad or organizational section
military company orderly room; administrative and supply desk

행정반.notes: Because almost all South Korean men serve in the military, calling an office supply desk or operations room the 행정반 immediately evokes the relatable regimentation of army barracks life.

rootFamily.gloss: chief of the administrative squad, first sergeant (行政班長)

행주.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) noun 행주 ('dishcloth, kitchen wiping rag'), attested in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Early Modern Korean glossaries (such as the Yeogeo Yuhae 譯語類解 of 1690) in the form ᄒᆡᆼ조 (haengjo), which later underwent vowel raising of final -오 to -우. Although popular folk etymology links it to the Battle of Haengju Fortress (행주산성, 1593) alongside 행주치마 ('apron'), philological evidence shows ᄒᆡᆼ조 was an independent word for a wiping cloth.

history.meaning: cloth used for wiping dishes and kitchen surfaces
dishcloth, kitchen rag for wiping tables and dishes

행주.notes: Korean strictly distinguishes between a 행주 (a clean cloth used only for kitchenware, counters, and dining tables) and a 걸레 (a rag or mop head used for floors and general dirt).

향.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 향 (向), derived from the Classical Chinese character 向, originally an oracle-bone pictograph of a ventilation window set into the wall under a roof (宀 + 口) facing a specific compass point. From 'north-facing window', the character evolved to mean 'to face toward', 'direction', and specifically in architecture and real estate, the 'exposure' or compass orientation of a building toward sunlight.

history.meaning: window in a wall; to face toward; compass orientation
direction, orientation, or sunlight exposure of a house or room

morphemes.meaning: to face toward, direction, orientation, exposure

향.notes: In Korean housing and real-estate conversations, 향 (向) refers to which way a home's main windows face for sunlight (especially 남향 南向, 'south-facing exposure'); do not confuse it with its common homophone 향 (香, 'fragrance, scent, incense').

향기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 향기 (香氣), joining 향 (香, 'fragrance, sweet smell, incense') and 기 (氣, 'air, breath, aura, vapor').

history.meaning: fragrant vapor, sweet scent
fragrance, aroma, sweet scent

향하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 향 (向, 'to face toward, head toward, direction') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to face toward, head for

향후.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) temporal noun 향후 (向後), compounded from 향 (向, 'to face toward, heading toward') and 후 (後, 'after, behind, later, future'). Literally meaning 'facing toward what comes after', it originated in Literary Chinese documentary style and functions in formal modern Korean to denote the period starting from the present and extending into the future ('henceforth, from now on').

history.meaning: facing afterward; from this time forward, hereafter
henceforth, from now on, in the upcoming future

향후.notes: Belongs to formal, journalistic, and business registers (e.g., 향후 계획, 'future plans'; 향후 5년간, 'over the next five years'), whereas everyday speech prefers 앞으로 ('from now on').

cognates.meaning: to promise, to give one's word or consent

허락.etymology: Sino-Korean (한자어) noun 허락 (許諾), compounded from 허 (許, 'to allow, permit, grant') and 락 (諾, 'to assent, say yes, approve'). In accordance with Korean historical phonology, the character 諾 (read 낙 word-initially under the South Korean initial sound rule 두음법칙) preserves its original liquid initial 락 when occurring word-internally after a vowel, yielding 허락.

history.meaning: to grant permission and give verbal assent; to promise
permission, consent, approval

허락.notes: Used for personal or interpersonal consent (e.g., 부모님의 허락, 'parents' permission'), whereas institutional or legal authorization is called 허가 (許可).

허락하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 허락 (許諾, 'permission, consent', from 허 許 'to allow, grant' + 락/낙 諾 'to assent, promise') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to grant consent, permit
to permit, allow, consent

허브.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English herb ('aromatic or medicinal plant used in cooking, tea, or perfumery', from Old French herbe, Latin herba) and hub ('central connection point').

history.meaning: aromatic culinary/medicinal plant; central hub
herb; central hub

허술하다.etymology: Hybrid Korean descriptive verb 허술하다, attested in Early Modern Korean alongside 허소하다 (虛疎-, 'empty and sparse, negligent'). Built on the Sino-Korean root 허 (虛, 'empty, hollow, unguarded') combined with a native Korean derivational formative -술 (or a phonological nativization of 소 疎 'sparse, lax' to 술) and the adjectivalizer 하다, it describes structures, plans, or people that are flimsy, loosely guarded, or full of gaps.

history.meaning: to be sparse, loosely guarded, or poorly put together
flimsy, rickety, lax, sloppy, or full of loopholes

morphemes.meaning: native derivational suffix indicating looseness or state

허술하다.notes: Applies equally to physical objects ('a rickety shed, shabby clothes'), security or plans ('lax security, a sloppy excuse'), and a person's endearing lack of sharpness ('a bit clumsy or gullible').

rootFamily.gloss: weak point, loophole, blind spot (虛點)
to be weak, hollow, or depleted (虛-)
to be shoddy, inferior, or amateurish

허전하다.etymology: Hybrid/native Korean adjective formed on Sino-Korean 허 (虛, 'empty, hollow, void') + expressive suffix -전- + -하다, describing a lonely, wistful sense of emptiness when something or someone is missing.

history.meaning: to feel empty, wistful, or missing something

헌.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner descending from Middle Korean 헌 ('old, worn-out, shabby, secondhand'), frozen past adnominal participle of 헐다 ('to wear out, become dilapidated, crumble', Middle Korean 헐다).

history.meaning: to wear out -> worn-out, old
old, worn, used, secondhand (as in 헌 옷, 헌 책)

헌책방.etymology: Warm Korean hybrid compound prefixing the native adnominal modifier 헌 ('old, pre-owned, well-worn', from the verb 헐다 'to wear thin with age', contrasting with 새 'brand-new') onto 책방 (冊房, 'book-room, cosy bookshop'). In Seoul neighbourhoods, 헌책방 evokes stone alleys lined with treasured out-of-print volumes.

헐.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) colloquial interjection 헐, which emerged in South Korean youth and internet slang in the late 1990s and 2000s. Phonologically, it is an expressive ideophonic alteration of the traditional exclamation 허 / 허어 (a sigh of disbelief or futility, related to 헐떡이다 'to gasp') with a clipped liquid coda -ㄹ that mimics one's breath catching or jaw dropping in dumbfounded speechlessness.

history.meaning: traditional sigh or exclamation of emptiness and disbelief
slang interjection of dumbfounded shock, disbelief, or awkwardness ('no way, wow, ugh')

morphemes.meaning: ideophonic interjection of breathless disbelief or shock

헐.notes: One of the most versatile informal Korean interjections: depending on intonation, 헐 can mean 'No way!', 'Are you serious?', or an awkward 'Ugh / Oh boy' when someone says something absurd.

rootFamily.gloss: sigh or exclamation of disbelief and futility

헐값.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun formed from 헐- (the stem of 헐하다, 'to be cheap, inexpensive, or easy', originally built on Sino-Korean 헐 歇 'to rest, subside, abate'), the native adnominal modifier suffix -ㄹ, and the native noun 값 ('price, value', from Middle Korean 값). Literally meaning 'a reduced or cheapened price', it lexicalized as a single noun denoting a dirt-cheap bargain price.

history.meaning: a low or abated price
dirt-cheap price, giveaway price ('for a song')

헐값.notes: Often used with the particle 에 as 헐값에 넘기다 or 헐값에 팔다 ('to sell off dirt cheap / for a song'), frequently implying that something was sold well below its true worth.

rootFamily.gloss: to be cheap, inexpensive, or easy to deal with

헐뜯다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) compound verb combining 헐- (the stem of 헐다, 'to demolish, tear down, wear away', from Middle Korean 헐다) and 뜯다 ('to pluck, tear off, rip apart', from Middle Korean ᄠᅳᆮ다). Originally describing the physical act of demolishing and ripping apart a structure, it underwent metaphorical extension to denote tearing down a person's reputation through slander, backbiting, and malicious criticism.

history.meaning: to tear down and rip apart physically
to slander, malign, disparage, or verbally tear someone down

morphemes.meaning: to tear off, pluck, rip apart

헐뜯다.notes: Evokes vivid imagery of picking someone apart piece by piece; commonly used in 남을 헐뜯다 ('to badmouth or slander others behind their backs').

rootFamily.gloss: to demolish, tear down a building or wall
to bite and tear; to attack or criticize fiercely

헛소문.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound noun formed by prefixing native Korean 헛- ('empty, vain, false, groundless', derived from the stem of 헛되다 and historically associated with Sino-Korean 허 虛 'empty') to the Sino-Korean noun 소문 (所聞, 'rumor, hearsay'). In 소문 (所聞), 소 (所, 'that which') nominalizes 문 (聞, 'to hear'), literally 'that which is heard'; adding 헛- yields 'a baseless or false rumor'.

history.meaning: groundless or empty hearsay
false rumor, baseless gossip

헛소문.notes: The native prefix 헛- is highly productive in Korean for anything done in vain or without basis, as seen in 헛수고 ('wasted effort'), 헛기침 ('a fake cough / clearing one's throat'), and 헛소문 ('false rumor').

헝겊.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 헝겁 / 헝겊 ('piece or scrap of woven cloth, rag'), likely formed from 헌 ('worn, old, scrap') + 거죽/꺼풀 ('outer skin, layer, covering').

history.meaning: scrap of cloth, rag
piece of cloth, rag, fabric patch

cognates.meaning: pair of small loudspeakers worn over the ears on a headband

헤드폰.etymology: Loanword (외래어) borrowed from English 'headphone(s)', a compound of 'head' (from Old English heafod) and '-phone' (from Greek phone, 'voice, sound', via 'telephone'). Adopted into Korean with radio broadcasting and studio recording technology in the twentieth century to denote electroacoustic transducers worn over the head.

history.meaning: pair of audio receivers held over the ears by a band worn on the head
over-ear or on-ear headphones

헤드폰.notes: In Korean, 헤드폰 refers specifically to larger over-ear or on-ear cans joined by a headband (such as those worn by radio PDs and studio engineers), whereas small in-ear buds are called 이어폰 ('earphones').

헤매다.etymology: Native Korean (고유어) verb 헤매다 ('to wander around lost, roam aimlessly, flounder'), attested in Early Modern Korean as 헤매이다 and 헤매다. Analysed philologically as built on the root 헤- (related to 헤다 / 허위다, 'to grope, flail, or part water/obstacles', also seen in 헤엄 'swimming' and 헤집다 'rummage') combined with a verbal formative -매다, originally depicting someone groping through pathless terrain or water before broadening to physical or mental disorientation.

history.meaning: to grope about and wander without finding one's way
to wander around lost; to flounder or struggle in confusion

morphemes.meaning: to grope, part obstacles, flail through
verbal formative of wandering or struggling

헤매다.notes: Used both literally for getting lost on the streets (길을 헤매다, 'to wander around lost') and figuratively for struggling with a difficult task or life phase (초반에 좀 헤매다, 'to flounder a bit at the beginning').

rootFamily.gloss: to swim (literally 'to part water and move')
to rummage through, dig around, stir up
to wander, roam about (Sino-Korean 彷徨)

헤어지다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb derived from Middle Korean 헤여지다 (heyejida), composed of the verb stem 헤- (he-, from 헤다 "to scatter, disperse, separate"), the infinitive connector -어 (-eo), and the inchoative auxiliary verb 지다 (jida, "to become"). Originally meaning "to become scattered or separated," it specialized into the interpersonal sense "to part ways" or "to break up."

history.meaning: to scatter, disperse, or separate
to become scattered or parted from one another
to part ways, separate, or break up romantically

헤어지다.notes: A homophonous verb 헤어지다 (from 헤다 "to wear out") means "to become worn out or tattered" for clothing and fabric, whereas the interpersonal sense means "to part ways or break up."

헤엄치다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the noun 헤엄 (heeom, "swimming") and the active verb 치다 (chida, "to strike, make vigorous movements"). The noun 헤엄 descends from Middle Korean 헤욤 (heyom), the substantive (-옴/-움) nominalization of the Middle Korean verb 헤다 (heda, "to swim, float, paddle through water").

history.meaning: to swim; the act of swimming or paddling through water
to swim by striking the water
to swim (general native verb)

헤엄치다.notes: While 수영하다 (水泳하다) refers to swimming as a sport or exercise, native 헤엄치다 is used broadly for humans, fish, and animals moving through water.

rootFamily.gloss: to part or push through (water, crowd)

헷갈리다.etymology: A native Korean compound verb formed from the prefix 헷- (het-, a vowel-fronted variant of 헛- meaning "in vain, amiss, awry, wrongly") and 갈리다 (gallida, "to be divided, split, or branched," the passive of 가르다 "to divide, sort"). Literally meaning "to be sorted or branched awry," it evolved to describe mental confusion when unable to tell things apart.

history.meaning: to be split or sorted awry; to become entangled
to be confused, mixed up, or unable to distinguish

morphemes.meaning: to be divided, branched (passive of 가르다)

헷갈리다.notes: Both 헷갈리다 and 헛갈리다 are recognized as standard Korean (복수 표준어), and the verb can be used both intransitively ("to feel confused") and transitively ("to confuse A with B").

rootFamily.gloss: to be confused, mixed up (standard variant)

혀.etymology: A native Korean noun descending directly from Middle Korean 혀 (hyeo, also attested as 혜 hye). Internal reconstruction and dialectal forms (such as Jeju and southern dialect 세 se / 쎼 ssye, alongside compound stems like 셑 syet) point to a Proto-Koreanic form *kjet ("tongue"), which underwent palatalization and loss of the final consonant in isolation.

history.meaning: tongue (anatomical organ)
tongue; speech
tongue; manner of speaking

혀.notes: Featured in vivid somatic idioms such as 혀를 내두르다 ("to wag one's tongue in astonishment") and 혀가 짧다 ("to have a lisp or speak overly cutesily").

rootFamily.gloss: surface or blade of the tongue

현.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous nouns and prefixes: (1) 현 (絃/弦, 'bowstring, string of a musical instrument'); (2) 현 (現, 'present, current, existing'); (3) 현 (縣, 'county, prefecture').

history.meaning: musical string; current/present; county/prefecture
instrument string; present/current; prefecture

현관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현관 (玄關), originally a Zen Buddhist term meaning 'the mysterious gateway to profound truth' (from 현 玄 'profound, dark, subtle' + 관 關 'barrier, gate'), later applied to the entrance hall of a temple and finally any home's entryway/vestibule.

history.meaning: gateway to profound mystery -> temple entrance hall
entranceway, vestibule, foyer

현관문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현관문 (玄關門), formed from 현관 (玄關, 'entranceway, foyer') + 문 (門, 'door, gate').

history.meaning: vestibule + door
front door, main entrance door

현금.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현금 (現金), joining 현 (現, 'present, on hand, ready') and 금 (金, 'gold, metal, money').

history.meaning: ready money on hand
cash, ready money

현대식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현대식 (現代式), formed from 현대 (現代, 'modern times, the present age', from 현 現 'present' + 대 代 'era, generation') + 식 (式, 'style, mode').

history.meaning: modern era + style
modern style

현명하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 현명 (賢明, 'wise and clear-sighted', from 현 賢 'worthy, virtuous, sagacious' + 명 明 'bright, clear, discerning') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: sagacious and discerning -> to be wise
to be wise, sensible, sagacious

현물.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 現物, composed of 현 (現, "present, actual, manifest, existing now") and 물 (物, "thing, object, physical commodity"). Originally used in East Asian commercial and administrative contexts to denote actual physical goods on hand as opposed to cash (현금 現金) or future contracts (선물 先物).

history.meaning: actual physical objects or goods present on site
payment in kind, physical goods, spot commodity

현물.notes: In television and radio production, 현물 협찬 refers to sponsors providing "in-kind" goods (such as clothing, food, or gift vouchers) rather than cash funding.

현실.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun from 現實, formed from 현 (現, "appear, manifest, present, actual") and 실 (實, "fruit, substance, true, real"). Popularized across East Asia during the late 19th-century Meiji translation movement (Japanese 現実 genjitsu) to render the Western philosophical and everyday concept of "reality" or "actuality" in contrast to ideal (이상 理想) or illusion.

history.meaning: actuality, philosophical reality (Meiji translation of English 'reality')
the real world, reality, actual circumstances

현실.notes: In colloquial Korean, 현실 is often used almost adverbially or attributively (e.g., 현실 웃음 "a genuine, real-life laugh" or 현실 남매 "true-to-life bickering siblings").

현실성.etymology: A Sino-Korean derivative noun from 現實性, combining 현실 (現實, "reality, actuality," from 現 "present, actual" + 實 "substance, real") with the productive abstract suffix -성 (性, "nature, quality, property"). It denotes the degree to which a plan, script, or idea is grounded in reality or feasible in practice.

history.meaning: the property of being real, authentic, or practical
realism (in media/art) or feasibility (of a plan)

현실성.notes: Frequently paired with 있다/없다 or 떨어지다: 현실성이 없다 means a proposal is "unrealistic/impractical" or a drama plot lacks "believability."

rootFamily.gloss: realism as an artistic movement (寫實主義)

cognates.meaning: scene of an event or crime

현장.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 現場, composed of 현 (現, "present, actual, appearing now") and 장 (場, "open ground, place, site, arena"). Meaning "the actual site where something is happening right now," it refers to crime scenes, construction sites, and in broadcasting/film, the live shooting location or set.

history.meaning: the actual place where an event occurs
the scene, on-site work area, or filming location/set

현장.notes: In Korean TV and film production (as in *The Producers*), 현장 almost always serves as shorthand for 촬영 현장 ("the filming set/location").

rootFamily.gloss: sense of being on the scene, liveliness (現場感)

현재.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun and adverb from 現在, composed of 현 (現, "manifest, appear, present") and 재 (在, "exist, be located at"). Originally a Chinese Buddhist translation (현재세 現在世) of Sanskrit pratyutpanna ("that which has arisen and is currently existing"), denoting the present world among the Three Ages (삼세 三世: past 과거, present 현재, future 미래), before generalizing into everyday temporal usage.

history.meaning: the present existence or cosmic age (translating Sanskrit pratyutpanna)
the present time, currently, as of now

현재.notes: Used after a time expression or statistic (e.g., 오후 5시 현재), it corresponds to English "as of [5 p.m.]."

혈압.etymology: Sino-Korean medical compound 혈압 (血壓), joining 혈 (血, 'blood') and 압 (壓, 'pressure, to press down').

history.meaning: blood + pressure
blood pressure

협박.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 脅迫, uniting 협 (脅, originally "ribs, flanks of the torso," extended to "to press by the flanks, coerce, intimidate") and 박 (迫, "to press closely, compel, urge"). The compound literally depicts pressing tightly upon someone to force compliance through fear or threat of harm.

history.meaning: to press hard upon and coerce by force or fear
intimidation, threat, blackmail, coercion

협박.notes: Stronger and more formal/legalistic than 단순한 위협 ("threat/menace"); 협박 implies frightening someone to compel action or submission.

협박죄.etymology: A Sino-Korean legal compound noun from 脅迫罪, consisting of 협박 (脅迫, "intimidation, threat," from 脅 "threaten, coerce" + 迫 "press hard, compel") and the legal suffix 죄 (罪, "crime, offense, guilt"). Under Article 283 of the South Korean Criminal Act, it designates the statutory offense of threatening a person with harm sufficient to cause fear.

history.meaning: statutory offense of criminal intimidation under modern codified penal law
crime of intimidation, criminal threat charge

협박죄.notes: Unlike 공갈죄 (恐喝罪, "extortion/blackmail"), which requires demanding property or financial gain, 협박죄 is established simply by communicating a credible threat of harm.

협박하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean verb formed by attaching the native light verb -하다 (hada, "to do") to the Sino-Korean noun 협박 (脅迫, from 脅 "ribs; to coerce, threaten" + 迫 "to press hard, compel"). It means to frighten or coerce another person by threatening them with harm.

history.meaning: to press upon and coerce through fear
to threaten, intimidate, or blackmail

협박하다.notes: Takes the accusative particle -을/를 on the victim (누구를 협박하다, "to threaten someone") and often -겠다고 to state the threatened action.

rootFamily.gloss: to menace, pose a threat (威脅하다)

협상.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 協商, composed of 협 (協, "harmony, unite, cooperate," graphically combining 十 "ten/many" with 劦 "three strengths working together") and 상 (商, "to deliberate, consult, measure, trade"). Literally "cooperative deliberation," it denotes formal or informal negotiations to reach a mutual agreement.

history.meaning: to deliberate together in harmony; diplomatic entente or consultation
history.stage: Late Imperial Chinese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: negotiation, bargaining, parley

협상.notes: Commonly used in collocations like 협상 테이블 ("negotiating table"), 협상이 결렬되다 ("negotiations break down"), and 연봉 협상 ("salary negotiation").

협찬처.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 協贊處, formed from 협찬 (協贊, "sponsorship, backing, support," from 協 "cooperate, join forces" + 贊 "assist, support, praise") and the bound noun -처 (處, "place, agency, organization, office"). In Korean television and media production, it specifically designates a corporate sponsor that provides funding, locations, or products for a program.

history.meaning: joint support, endorsement, or patronage of an event
sponsoring company, agency, or client in broadcasting and events

협찬처.notes: Essential K-drama industry jargon: producers and stylists must constantly appease their 협찬처 ("sponsors") by ensuring sponsored clothes, cafes, or cars get screen time.

형.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 형 (兄, 'elder brother', from Middle Chinese *xjwæng), thoroughly naturalized into Korean kinship terminology as 'older brother (of a male)' or 'older male friend'. (Homophonous 형 型 means 'model, type, mold'.)

history.meaning: elder brother
older brother (male speaker); type/form (型)

형광등.etymology: A Sino-Korean scientific compound noun from 螢光燈, combining 형광 (螢光, "fluorescence," literally "firefly light" from 螢 "firefly, glowworm" + 光 "light, luminescence") and 등 (燈, "lamp, lantern"). Coined in East Asia to translate Western "fluorescent lamp," referring to gas-discharge tubes coated with phosphor that glow via fluorescence.

history.meaning: firefly glow; scientific translation of 'fluorescence'
fluorescent tube lamp; (slang) a person who is slow to catch on

형광등.notes: Because older starter-type fluorescent tubes flicker for several seconds before lighting up, calling someone a 형광등 in Korean slang means they are "slow on the uptake" (reacting to a joke or hint way too late).

형님.etymology: Hybrid honorific kinship noun formed from Sino-Korean 형 (兄, 'elder brother') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: respected older brother

형제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 형제 (兄弟), joining 형 (兄, 'elder brother') and 제 (弟, 'younger brother').

history.meaning: older and younger brothers
brothers, siblings

형태.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 形態, formed from 형 (形, "shape, physical form, outline") and 태 (態, "bearing, posture, appearance, condition"). While already attested in Classical Chinese for physical appearance and bearing, it was standardized in modern East Asian academic and general vocabulary to denote structural "form," "configuration," or linguistic/biological "morphology."

history.meaning: physical shape and outward bearing
form, structure, configuration, or mode of organization

형태.notes: More abstract and analytical than 모양 ("outward shape/look"); 형태 can describe intangible structures like 가족 형태 ("family structure") or 근무 형태 ("work arrangement").

호.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun and bound counter from 號 (호 호), originally meaning "to cry out, roar" (composed of 号 "to cry out" and 虎 "tiger") and extended in Classical Chinese to "a name, title, designation, or mark." In Korean, it functions both as an independent noun for a scholar's or artist's pen name (아호 雅號) and as an ordinal suffix/classifier for room numbers, magazine issues, train cars, and alert levels.

history.meaning: to cry out; an appellation, title, or identifying mark
literary pen name; sequential number for issues, rooms, vehicles, or grades

호.notes: Placed after Sino-Korean numbers to name numbered rooms (302호 "Room 302"), subway lines (2호선 "Line 2"), magazine issues (5월호 "May issue"), or named typhoons (제1호 태풍).

rootFamily.gloss: room number in a hotel or building (號室)
title, appellation, form of address (號稱)

호감.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 好感, formed from 호 (好, "good, favorable, fond of") and 감 (感, "feeling, sensation, emotion, impression"). Literally "a good feeling," it denotes a favorable impression, fondness, or romantic/interpersonal attraction toward someone.

history.meaning: favorable sentiment or positive emotional impression
favorable impression, romantic interest, or public likability

호감.notes: In Korean broadcasting and pop culture, 호감 (and 호감형 "likable type") vs. 비호감 ("unlikable/off-putting") is the standard metric for a celebrity's public image.

rootFamily.gloss: level of public likability or affection (好感度)

호두나무.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from 호두 ('walnut', altered from Sino-Korean 호도 胡桃 'western/steppe peach', from 호 胡 'northern/western steppe peoples' + 도 桃 'peach') + native Korean 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모).

history.meaning: walnut + tree
walnut tree, walnut wood

호떡.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound noun from 胡떡, combining the Sino-Korean prefix 호- (胡, historically denoting northern/western "foreign" peoples and later Qing-dynasty China) with native Korean 떡 (tteok, from Middle Korean 뗘 "rice cake, griddle cake"). Introduced to Korea in the 1880s by Chinese merchants from Shandong following the Imo Incident, the original Chinese filled flatbread was adapted into a pan-fried sweet pancake stuffed with brown sugar, cinnamon, and nuts.

history.meaning: Chinese-style wheat flatbread introduced by Qing merchants in late Joseon Korea
sweet pan-fried yeast pancake filled with melted brown sugar and nuts

morphemes.meaning: rice cake, pastry, griddle cake (native Korean)

호떡.notes: Featured in the common Korean idiom 호떡집에 불났다 ("a fire broke out in a hotteok shop"), used when a room or office erupts into noisy, chaotic commotion.

호실.etymology: Sino-Korean bound compound 호실 (號室), joining 호 (號, 'number, designation') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber'), attached after numerals to name a specific room number.

history.meaning: number + room
room number (e.g., 302호실)

호의.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 好意, composed of 호 (好, "good, kind, favorable") and 의 (意, "mind, thought, intention, heart"). Attested in Classical Chinese and shared across East Asia, it literally means "a good or kind mind/intention" and denotes goodwill, benevolence, or a kind favor extended to another.

history.meaning: kind thoughts or favorable intentions toward someone
goodwill, kindness, favor, well-meaning gesture

호의.notes: Famous in the modern Korean movie-inspired proverb 호의가 계속되면 권리인 줄 안다 ("When goodwill continues, people mistake it for an entitlement").

호텔.etymology: Borrowed from English hotel (ultimately French hôtel).
호텔.notes: Contrasts in scale with smaller neighbourhood 게스트하우스 ('guesthouses') and traditional 한옥 숙소.

호피.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 虎皮, composed of 호 (虎, "tiger") and 피 (皮, "skin, hide, pelt, fur"). In pre-modern Korea, where both striped tigers and spotted leopards were categorized together under the overarching class of 범/호 (虎), 호피 denoted prestigious big-cat pelts; in contemporary Korean fashion (호피 무늬), it shifted to refer primarily to spotted leopard print.

history.meaning: actual tiger or leopard pelt used for ceremonial rugs, robes, and tribute
tiger skin; (in fashion) leopard print or big-cat animal print

호피.notes: Watch out for this classic Korean fashion quirk: although 호 (虎) literally means "tiger," 호피 무늬 in clothing almost always means spotted "leopard print" rather than tiger stripes!

호흡.etymology: A Sino-Korean coordinative compound noun from 呼吸, uniting 호 (呼, "to exhale, breathe out") and 흡 (吸, "to inhale, breathe in, draw in"). From the literal physiological cycle of breathing out and breathing in, both Korean and Japanese developed the figurative theatrical and interpersonal sense of "breathing in unison"—hence "chemistry," "teamwork," or "pacing."

history.meaning: exhaling and inhaling; the breath of life
physiological respiration; rhythmic synchronization and chemistry between performers or partners

호흡.notes: In Korean entertainment and sports, 호흡을 맞추다 ("to match one's breathing") means "to work together as co-stars/partners," and 호흡이 잘 맞다 means "to have great chemistry/teamwork."

혹사당하다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean passive verb from 酷使當하다, composed of 혹사 (酷使, "working someone mercilessly, overwork, abuse," from 酷 "cruel, severe, harsh" + 使 "to use, employ, drive to work"), the Sino-Korean passive/experiential stem 당- (當, "to undergo, suffer, meet with"), and the native light verb -하다 ("to do/be").

history.meaning: driving a person, body part, or tool to work with harsh severity
to be overworked, exploited, or pushed to exhaustion

혹사당하다.notes: Used both for employees being worked to the bone by superiors (e.g., junior TV producers pulling all-nighters) and for body parts like a pitcher's shoulder or a singer's vocal cords.

혹시.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb 혹시 (或是), joining 혹 (或, 'perhaps, someone, by any chance') and 시 (是, 'this, to be right/so'); used in Korean to mean 'by any chance, perhaps, in case'.

history.meaning: perhaps it is so
by any chance, perhaps, just in case

혼.etymology: A Sino-Korean noun from 魂 (넋 혼, "soul, spirit"), a phono-semantic character combining the semantic component 鬼 ("ghost, spirit") with the phonetic and conceptual component 云 ("rising clouds, ethereal vapor"). In traditional East Asian dual-soul cosmology, 혼 (魂) is the yang spiritual soul governing consciousness and intellect that ascends at death, paired with 백 (魄), the yin corporeal soul tied to the body.

history.meaning: the ethereal yang soul governing mind and consciousness in classical Chinese cosmology
soul, spirit; presence of mind or wits in everyday idioms

혼.notes: In everyday Korean idioms like 혼이 빠지다 or 혼이 나가다 ("one's soul leaves the body"), 혼 translates best as "one's wits" or "presence of mind" ("to be spaced out / beside oneself").

rootFamily.gloss: soul and body; one's entire being (魂魄)
to get scolded; to be frightened out of one's wits (魂나다)

혼나다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 혼 (魂, "soul, spirit, wits") and native Korean 나다 (nada, from Middle Korean 나다 "to come out, exit, arise"). Originally a vivid hyperbolic expression meaning "for one's soul to leave one's body" out of terror or shock, it semantically bleached into meaning "to have a rough ordeal" and most commonly "to get scolded."

history.meaning: for one's soul or wits to depart the body from extreme fright or shock
to get scolded or told off; to go through a terrible ordeal

혼나다.notes: Although learners first meet 혼나다 as "to get scolded (by a parent, teacher, or boss)," it also retains its broader sense of "having a terrible time" (e.g., 길 찾느라 혼났어 "I had a heck of a time finding the way").

rootFamily.gloss: to be frightened out of one's wits; to get severely scolded (魂쭐나다)

혼내다.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 혼 (魂, "soul, spirit, wits") and native Korean 내다 (naeda, from Middle Korean 내다, the lexical causative of 나다 "to make come out, drive out"). Literally meaning "to drive someone's soul or wits out of their body," it serves as the active counterpart to 혼나다 and means "to scold, reprimand, or teach someone a lesson."

history.meaning: to frighten someone so severely that their wits leave them; to punish
to scold, reprimand, or tell someone off

morphemes.meaning: to make come out, put forth (causative of 나다)

혼내다.notes: Often paired with the benefactive auxiliary 주다 as 혼내 주다 ("to give someone a good scolding" or playfully "to teach the bad guy a lesson").

rootFamily.gloss: to get scolded, have a hard time (魂나다)

혼란.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 混亂, composed of 혼 (混, "to mix, mingle; turbid, muddy torrents of water") and 란 (亂, "tangled silk threads; disorder, chaos, rebellion"). Combining the metaphors of muddy water and tangled threads, it denotes a state of mental confusion, social chaos, or organizational turmoil.

history.meaning: turbid mixing and disorder; breakdown of order
confusion, chaos, turmoil, disarray

혼란.notes: Forms the common descriptive adjective 혼란스럽다 ("to be chaotic / to feel confused") and phrases like 혼란에 빠지다 ("to fall into chaos/confusion").

rootFamily.gloss: confusion, mixing up two things (混同)

혼자.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 호〮오〮자〮 / 호올로 ('alone, by oneself'), derived from the numeral root ㅎᆞ올- / ㅎᆞᆫ- ('one, single, solitary').

history.meaning: by oneself, alone
alone, by oneself

홀로.etymology: A native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 호올로 (hoollo) and earlier 하올로 (haollo). It is morphologically built from the archaic Koreanic numeral root 하올 / 홀 (hol, "one, single, solitary," related to 하나 "one" and 혼자 "alone") combined with the instrumental/directional particle -로 (-ro, "by, as").

history.meaning: by oneself, singly, without companions
all alone, by oneself, solitarily (poetic/literary and standard adverb)

morphemes.meaning: one, single, solitary (from Middle Korean 호올-)

홀로.notes: More literary, poetic, and expressive than everyday 혼자 ("alone"); while 혼자 can function as both a noun and an adverb, 홀로 is strictly an adverb.

rootFamily.gloss: unmarried or solitary person, single body

홍보팀장.etymology: A three-part hybrid compound noun (弘報팀長) combining Sino-Korean 홍보 (弘報, "public relations, publicity," from 弘 "wide, broad, spread" + 報 "report, announce, inform"), the English loanword 팀 (tim, from English "team"), and the Sino-Korean title suffix -장 (長, "chief, head, leader"). It designates the manager or head of a public relations department.

history.meaning: disseminating information widely to the public; public relations (PR)
PR team leader, head of corporate or broadcast public relations

홍보팀장.notes: In Korean corporate and broadcasting hierarchies, 팀장 ("team leader") is a key mid-to-senior management title used directly as a polite form of address (홍보팀장님).

홍삼.etymology: A Sino-Korean compound noun from 紅蔘, composed of 홍 (紅, "red, crimson") and 삼 (蔘, "ginseng"). It refers to fresh Korean ginseng root (수삼 水蔘, Panax ginseng) that has been steamed and sun-dried, a preservation process recorded in Korea since the Goryeo dynasty (12th century) that caramelizes the starches and turns the root a deep reddish-brown.

history.meaning: steamed and dried ginseng root prized as a medicinal tonic and royal trade item
red ginseng (commonly consumed in extracts, pouches, and health supplements)

홍삼.notes: Squeezed pouches of 홍삼 진액 ("red ginseng extract") are a ubiquitous staple on Korean drama sets and in offices whenever characters are exhausted or overworked.

홍삼가루.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 홍삼 (紅參, 'red ginseng', steamed and dried Panax ginseng root that turns reddish-brown during processing) with native Korean 가루 ('powder, flour', from Middle Korean 가〯ᄅᆞ).

history.meaning: steamed red ginseng + ground meal or powder
powdered red ginseng taken as a health tonic

홍삼가루.notes: Red ginseng (홍삼) — whether as liquid extract pouches or powder (홍삼가루) — is a ubiquitous stamina supplement in Korean office and broadcasting culture.

홍차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 홍차 (紅茶), literally 'red tea', from 홍 (紅, 'crimson, reddish') + 차 (茶, 'tea').
홍차.notes: East Asian languages name black tea after the warm reddish-amber colour of the brewed liquid rather than the dry leaves.

홍합탕.etymology: A Sino-Korean culinary compound of 홍합 (紅蛤, 'mussel', literally 'red clam', named for the reddish-orange flesh of the female Korean mussel Mytilus unguiculatus) and 탕 (湯, 'hot water, broth, soup').

history.meaning: red-fleshed bivalve clam + hot broth or decoction
clear mussel soup seasoned with garlic and chili

홍합탕.notes: Served steaming in a clear, garlicky broth, 홍합탕 is one of Korea's classic indoor pojangmacha (tent bar) side dishes paired with soju.

화.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Hanja 火 (화, 'fire'). Under the influence of traditional East Asian humoral medicine, excess internal 'fire' (火氣, 화기) in the heart and liver was understood as the physiological seat of pent-up rage, frustration, and acute emotional heat, yielding the everyday sense 'anger, temper'.

history.meaning: fire, flame; physiological heat in traditional medicine
fire; internal emotional heat, anger, indignation

화.notes: Combines with native Korean verbs like 화가 나다 ('anger arises / to get angry'), 화를 내다 ('to vent anger'), and 화를 참다 ('to suppress anger'), and underlies the culturally recognized Korean psychosomatic syndrome 화병 (火病, 'fire-illness').

rootFamily.gloss: to get angry, lose one's temper

화끈화끈하다.etymology: A native Korean reduplicated ideophonic (의태어/의성어) adjective formed from the mimetic root 화끈 ('with a sudden flush of burning heat or spicy tingling') plus the adjective-forming verb 하다 ('to do, to be'). Its dark-vowel counterpart 후끈후끈하다 expresses deeper, heavier, stifling heat, whereas bright-vowel 화끈화끈하다 evokes a sharp, flushing, or fiery sensation on the skin or tongue.

history.meaning: flushing or burning repeatedly with sharp heat
to feel burning hot, flushed (of face/ears), or fiery spicy

morphemes.meaning: with a sudden flush of heat or fiery tingle

화끈화끈하다.notes: Used both for the sensation of one's face or ears burning from embarrassment (얼굴이 화끈화끈하다) and for the fiery burn of spicy food or bold, hold-nothing-back action (화끈하다).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel a sudden burning flush
sultry, stiflingly hot (heavy vowel harmony counterpart)

화나다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 화 (火, 'fire; fiery anger, wrath') + native Korean intransitive verb 나다 ('to arise, break out, come forth', Middle Korean 나다).

history.meaning: anger/fire + to arise
to get angry, become upset

화내다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 화 (火, 'fire; anger, temper') + native Korean transitive/causative verb 내다 ('to put forth, let out, produce', Middle Korean 내다).

history.meaning: anger/fire + to let out
to express anger, lose one's temper

화단.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from的花 (화, 'flower, blossom') and 壇 (단, 'raised earthen platform, altar, terrace'). Originally denoting a stepped brick or stone terrace built in courtyard gardens for cultivating ornamental peonies and seasonal blooms, it now refers to any bordered flowerbed around buildings or streets.

history.meaning: raised earthen or stone platform for growing flowers
flowerbed, planted garden border

화단.notes: Distinguish 화단 (花壇, 'flowerbed') from homophonous 화단 (畫壇, 'the painting/art world', where 壇 figuratively means 'arena/circle').

화면.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화면 (畫面), joining 화 (畫, 'picture, painting, image') and 면 (面, 'face, surface, plane').

history.meaning: surface of a painting
picture plane; television, monitor, or phone screen

화분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화분 (花盆), joining 화 (花, 'flower, flowering plant') and 분 (盆, 'basin, earthen pot, bowl').

history.meaning: flower basin, flowerpot
flowerpot, potted plant

화살.etymology: A native Korean compound of 활 ('bow', Middle Korean 활) and 살 ('arrow, shaft, spoke, ray', Middle Korean 살). In compounding before the coronal fricative ㅅ, the final liquid ㄹ of 활 regularly drops by Korean morphophonemic l-deletion (ㄹ 탈락: 활 + 살 > 화살), creating a disyllabic word that disambiguates 'arrow' from its homophone 살 ('flesh' or 'years of age').

history.meaning: bow-arrow, shaft shot from a bow
arrow; arrow symbol or pointer

morphemes.meaning: bow (from 활 with ㄹ-deletion before ㅅ)

화살.notes: The same l-deletion rule (ㄹ 탈락) before ㄴ, ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅈ is seen in 소나무 ('pine tree', from 솔 + 나무) and 부삽 ('fire shovel', from 불 + 삽). In figurative usage, 비난의 화살을 돌리다 means 'to deflect the arrows of blame'.

화살표.etymology: A compound of native Korean 화살 'arrow' and Sino-Korean 표 (標) 'mark, symbol'.
화살표.notes: The arrow drawn on signs, maps and plans.

화요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화요일 (火曜日, 'day of Mars / Tuesday'), formed from 화요 (火曜, 'celestial luminary of Fire, the planet Mars', from 화 火 'fire' + 요 曜 'shining celestial body') + 일 (日, 'day').

history.meaning: day of the Fire star (Mars)
Tuesday

화음.etymology: Sino-Korean 화음 (和音), compounding 화 (和, 'harmonize, blend') + 음 (音, 'sound, tone').
화음.notes: Standard musical term for two or more notes sounding simultaneously in harmony.

화이트보드.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English whiteboard ('glossy white board for non-permanent dry-erase markers', compound of white + board).

history.meaning: glossy dry-erase board
whiteboard

cognates.meaning: to put on makeup, cosmetic adornment

화장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound from 化 (화, 'to transform, change, refine') and 粧 (장, 'to adorn, dress up, apply rouge and powder', a variant of 妝 combining 米 'rice powder' with 庄). Literally meaning 'transformative adornment of the face', it denotes applying cosmetics.

history.meaning: to transform and adorn the face with powder and rouge
history.stage: Literary Chinese / Early Modern East Asian

history.meaning: cosmetic makeup, dressing the face

morphemes.meaning: to adorn, apply cosmetics or rice powder

화장.notes: Has a famous Sino-Korean homophone 화장 (火葬, 'cremation', literally 'fire-burial') — though identical in spelling, 화장 (化粧) has a short vowel while 화장 (火葬) traditionally had a long initial vowel.

화장실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound joining 화장 (化粧, 'makeup, toilet, personal grooming') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber'). Coined as a polite euphemism equivalent to English 'powder room' or 'toilet' (originally a dressing room for grooming), it displaced older terms like 변소 (便所) to become the standard everyday Korean word for 'restroom, bathroom'.

history.meaning: dressing room or powder room for applying cosmetics
restroom, bathroom, lavatory

화장실.notes: Unlike American English 'bathroom' (욕실, 浴室, which refers specifically to a room with a bath/shower), 화장실 is used universally in Korea for public restrooms and toilets.

화제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 話 (화, 'speech, talk, spoken words, conversation') and 題 (제, 'heading, forehead, subject, theme, title'). Originally 'subject of conversation', in modern media and broadcasting Korean it frequently carries the heightened sense of 'hot topic, sensation, talk of the town'.

history.meaning: theme or subject of a conversation or discourse
topic of conversation; media buzz, hot topic

화제.notes: In entertainment and TV production (*프로듀사*), 화제가 되다 ('to become a hot topic / go viral') and 화제성 ('buzzworthiness') are key metrics alongside viewer ratings (시청률). Do not confuse with 화재 (火災, 'fire disaster').

cognates.meaning: gentle and bright (of spring breeze or weather)

화창하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb combining 화창 (和暢, from 和 'harmonious, mild, gentle, warm' + 暢 'unobstructed, clear, flourishing, carefree') with the native adjective-forming suffix -하다. The compound 和暢 goes back to Wang Xizhi's celebrated 353 CE *Lantingji Xu* (蘭亭集序: 惠風和暢, 'the genial breeze is mild and exhilarating'), describing clear, balmy spring weather.

history.meaning: mild, harmonious, and pleasantly unobstructed (of spring breeze)
to be bright, balmy, clear, and sunny (of weather)

화창하다.notes: Almost exclusively collocated with 날씨 ('weather') or 봄날 ('spring day'), as in 화창한 봄날 ('a bright, balmy spring day').

화초.etymology: Sino-Korean coordinate (dvandva) compound from 花 (화, 'flower, blossom') and 草 (초, 'grass, herbaceous plant'), literally 'flowers and grasses', denoting ornamental flowering plants and herbaceous garden flora cultivated in pots or beds.

history.meaning: blossoms and grasses, flowering herbs
ornamental flowering plants, houseplants

화초.notes: Commonly used in 화초를 가꾸다 ('to tend/cultivate potted plants and flowers').

화해.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 和 (화, 'harmony, peace, reconciliation') and 解 (해, 'to untie, loosen, resolve, dissolve'). Literally 'restoring harmony and untying a knot of conflict', it refers to making up after a quarrel or reaching an amicable settlement.

history.meaning: to untie enmity and restore peaceful harmony
reconciliation, making peace after an argument or dispute

화해.notes: Notice the contrast between 화(火)를 내다 ('to get angry', with 火 'fire') and 화해(和解)하다 ('to make up / reconcile', with 和 'harmony').

화해하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 화해 (和解, 'reconciliation, making peace', from 화 和 'harmony, peace' + 해 解 'to untie, resolve, loosen') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to resolve discord in harmony
to reconcile, make up, make peace

확.etymology: A native Korean monosyllabic mimetic adverb (부사) with a bright vowel ㅏ and tense/aspirated onset ㅎ, depicting a sudden, forceful, sweeping, or flaring action — such as a gust of wind, a sudden surge of heat or emotion, or doing something in one decisive stroke. Its dark-vowel counterpart 훅 conveys a deeper, inward or heavier puff or sudden lunge.

history.meaning: with a sudden flare, gust, or decisive sweep

morphemes.meaning: suddenly, in one clean sweep, with a sudden flare or rush

확.notes: In colloquial speech, 확 is also used as a playful threat intensifier before a verb (e.g., 확 마! or 확 깨물어 버린다, 'I swear I'll just—!'), expressing an impulse to do something drastically on the spot.

rootFamily.gloss: suddenly, with a deep rush or puff (dark-vowel counterpart)
with a sudden burning flush (extended stem)

확률적.etymology: Sino-Korean derivative composed of 확률 (確率, 'probability', from 確 'certain, firm, definite' + 率 'ratio, rate, proportion', coined in Meiji-era Japan as 確率 to translate mathematical 'probability' — literally 'the ratio of certainty') plus the adnominal/determiner suffix -적 (的, '-ic, -ical, relating to').

history.meaning: relating to mathematical probability or statistical likelihood
probabilistic, statistical (often followed by 으로 'statistically')

확률적.notes: Pronounced [황뉼쩍] due to nasalization of ㄱ before ㄹ (ㄱ+ㄹ → ㅇ+ㄴ) and tensification of ㅈ after ㄹ. Almost always used with the instrumental particle as 확률적으로 ('probabilistically, statistically speaking') or before a noun as 확률적 계산.

cognates.meaning: to secure, ensure, maintain hold of

확보하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 확보 (確保, from 確 'firm, solid, certain' originally with 石 'stone' radical + 保 'to protect, keep, hold, guarantee') and the native light verb 하다 ('to do'). Literally 'to hold firmly and securely', it means to secure resources, budget, airtime, evidence, or personnel.

history.meaning: to hold firmly and guarantee possession or safety
to secure, obtain and hold onto (funds, space, talent, evidence)

확보하다.notes: In broadcasting and business Korean, 확보하다 is the standard verb for securing a budget (예산을 확보하다), casting a star, or securing broadcast slots (편성을 확보하다).

cognates.word: 確保してあげる (kakuho shite ageru)

확보해주다.etymology: A benefactive serial-verb construction built on Sino-Korean 확보하다 (確保-, 'to secure, obtain firmly', from 確 'firm, certain' + 保 'keep, hold') combined via the infinitive connector -어 (-해) with the native Korean auxiliary verb 주다 ('to give, to do for someone's benefit', Middle Korean 주다).

history.meaning: to secure and give/grant for another's benefit
to secure (time, space, seats, or resources) for someone

morphemes.meaning: do and... (infinitive form হ여 > 해 of 하다)
to give; benefactive auxiliary ('do for someone')

확보해주다.notes: In Korean orthography, auxiliary verbs like 주다 can be written either spaced (확보해 주다, principle) or attached (확보해주다, permitted and very common in subtitles). Adding -주다 turns a neutral action into a favor done for someone else.

rootFamily.gloss: to confirm or check for someone

cognates.meaning: to be firmly convinced, firm belief

확신.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 確 (확, 'firm, solid, rock-steady, certain', containing the stone radical 石) and 信 (신, 'to believe, trust, faith', depicting a person 亻 standing by their word 言). Literally 'rock-firm belief', it denotes unshakable personal conviction or subjective certainty.

history.meaning: firm, unyielding belief or conviction
conviction, firm belief, confidence in an outcome

확신.notes: While 확실성 (確實性) refers to objective certainty of a fact, 확신 (確信) refers to a person's subjective psychological conviction (확신이 서다 / 확신이 들다, 'to feel convinced').

확실하게.etymology: Productive adverbial derivation from the Sino-Korean descriptive verb 확실하다 (確實-, from 確 'firm, solid, definite' + 實 'real, true, substantial, fruit-filled' + -하다 'to be'), inflected with the native Korean adverbializer suffix -게 ('in a manner that is, so as to be').

history.meaning: in a firm, verified, and unmistakable manner
clearly, definitely, reliably, without ambiguity

morphemes.meaning: productive adverbial suffix ('-ly, in such a way')

확실하게.notes: Korean has two adverbs from 확실하다: thelexicalized Sino-Korean adverb 확실히 ('certainly, indeed' — often used as a sentence adverb) and the productive manner adverb 확실하게 ('in a clear-cut, thorough, unambiguous way', e.g., 일 처리를 확실하게 하다, 'to handle work thoroughly and decisively').

확실하다.etymology: Sino-Korean descriptive verb joining 확실 (確實, from 確 'firm, hard as stone, unmistakable' + 實 'full, substantial, true, real', originally 'a house 宀 filled with wealth 貫') with the native adjective-deriving verb 하다 ('to be'). Literally 'firm and substantial', hence 'certain, clear, beyond doubt'.

history.meaning: solid, genuine, verified as true and substantial
to be certain, clear, definite, reliable

확실하다.notes: Can describe both the epistemic certainty of information (그 소식이 확실해요?, 'Is that news for sure?') and a person's decisive, no-nonsense character or action (성격이 맺고 끊는 게 확실하다).

확실히.etymology: Derived adverb formed from Sino-Korean 확실 (確實, stem of 확실하다 'to be certain, sure, definite', from 확 確 'firm, solid, certain' + 실 實 'true, real, substantial') + native adverbial suffix -히.

history.meaning: firmly and truly -> certainly, definitely
certainly, definitely, for sure

확인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 確 (확, 'firm, solid, certain, definite') and 認 (인, 'to recognize, discern, acknowledge, verify', composed of 言 'words' and 忍 'endure/discern'). Literally 'to recognize firmly as true', it means checking, verifying, or confirming a fact or message.

history.meaning: to recognize and verify with certainty
history.stage: Early Modern Sinitic / Japanese legal-administrative coinage

history.meaning: confirmation, verification, checking (messages, facts, identity)

확인.notes: In everyday Korean, 확인하다 covers both English 'confirm' and 'check' (e.g., 문자 확인했어? means 'Did you check/see my text message?'). In chat apps, 읽씹 ('read and ignored') happens right after 확인.

확인되다.etymology: Formed from the Sino-Korean noun 확인 (確認, combining 確 'firm, certain, solid' and 認 'recognize, verify') plus the passive verb -되다. While 확인하다 means 'to check or verify something actively', 확인되다 states objectively that an item has been verified and ticked off.
확인되다.notes: In polite past speech, 확인되었어요 regularly contracts to 확인됐어요.

확인하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 확인 (確認, 'confirmation, verification', from 확 確 'firm, certain' + 인 認 'to recognize, acknowledge, verify') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to verify with certainty
to confirm, check, verify

확정하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 확정 (確定, from 確 'firm, solid, unalterable' + 定 'to fix, settle, establish, decide') plus the light verb 하다 ('to do, make'). Literally 'to fix firmly', it denotes finalizing a schedule, casting lineup, legal ruling, or decision so that it is no longer tentative.

history.meaning: to fix firmly and settle without further change
to finalize, confirm officially, settle definitely

확정하다.notes: Carefully distinguish 확인하다 (確認-, 'to check/verify whether something is true') from 확정하다 (確定-, 'to finalize/lock in a plan, cast, or schedule', e.g., 출연을 확정하다, 'to finalize one's casting appearance').

cognates.meaning: 60th birthday (completion of the sexagenary calendar cycle)
60th year of life, return to the first sexagenary year

환갑.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 還 (환, 'to return, come full circle, revolve back') and 甲 (갑, 'first of the Ten Heavenly Stems 천간, armor, shell; shorthand for 갑자 甲子, the first year of the 60-year sexagenary cycle 육십갑자'). Because the 10 Heavenly Stems and 12 Earthly Branches combine into 60 unique year names, reaching one's 60th birthday marks the 'return to the甲 (birth) year' — traditionally celebrated as completing a full cycle of life.

history.meaning: return of the sexagenary birth year after sixty years
sixtieth birthday celebration (환갑잔치)

morphemes.meaning: to return, come back around in a cycle
first Heavenly Stem (shorthand for the 60-year sexagenary cycle 甲子)

환갑.notes: Historically, living to complete all 60 years of the zodiac cycle (육십갑자) was rare enough to warrant a grand banquet (환갑잔치); in contemporary Korea, where life expectancy is much higher, families often celebrate 칠순 (70th) or 팔순 (80th) more lavishly instead. Synonymous with 회갑 (回甲) and 화갑 (華甲).

rootFamily.gloss: sixtieth birthday (returning to the first stem)
people of the same age (sharing the same zodiac year)

환경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 環 (환, 'jade ring, circle, to surround, encircle') and 境 (경, 'boundary, border, territory, region, circumstances'). Originally denoting 'the surrounding territory or borders' in Classical Chinese, it was popularized in modern East Asian usage via Japanese 環境 (kankyō) as the translation of English 'environment' and French 'milieu' (both ecological and social/workplace surroundings).

history.meaning: surrounding borders or encircling territory
natural, social, or working environment and conditions

환경.notes: Used equally for the ecological environment (자연환경, 환경 보호) and for one's working or living conditions (근무 환경, 가정 환경).

환기창.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 환기창 (換氣窓), formed from 환기 (換氣, 'ventilation, exchanging air', from 환 換 'to exchange, replace' + 기 氣 'air') + 창 (窓, 'window').

history.meaning: air ventilation + window
ventilation window, air vent

환대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 歡待, joining 歡 (기쁠 환, 'joyful, delighted') and 待 (대접할 대, 'wait upon, treat, receive a guest'). Literally 'receiving a guest with joy', 환대 expresses the heart of guesthouse hospitality—welcoming visitors warmly with hot tea and open doors rather than stiff formality.
환대.notes: Combines with -하다 to form 환대하다 ('to welcome warmly, show hospitality').

환불하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 환불 (還拂, 'returning a payment, refund', from 환 還 'to return, give back' + 불 拂 'to pay out, clear away') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to pay back / refund money
to refund, get or give a refund

환영.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 歡迎, combining 歡 (기쁠 환, 'joyful, glad') and 迎 (맞이할 영, 'go out to meet, receive an arriving guest'). Literally 'going out gladly to greet someone', 환영 is used both as a modifier before nouns (환영 간판 'welcome sign', 환영 인사말 'welcome speech') and in the verb 환영하다 ('to welcome').
환영.notes: The formal polite present 환영합니다! is printed on welcome signs and spoken to arriving guests.

환영하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 환영 (歡迎, 'joyful reception, welcome', from 환 歡 'joyous, glad' + 영 迎 'to go out to meet, greet, receive') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to greet with joy
to welcome, greet warmly

환자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 患 (환, 'affliction, worry, illness, suffering, disease', written with 串 'pierced/strung together' over 心 'heart', depicting a heart pierced with distress) and 者 (자, 'person who, one who'). Literally 'one who is afflicted with illness', it is the standard medical and everyday word for 'patient'.

history.meaning: person suffering from a disease or affliction
history.stage: Classical and Early Modern Sinitic medicine

history.meaning: medical patient; (slang) someone obsessed or acting crazy

환자.notes: Beyond its literal medical sense, colloquial Korean playfully uses 환자 (or 중증 환자) to tease someone with an incurable habit or obsession, such as 'workaholic patient' or 'love-struck patient'.

환장하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 환장 (換腸, literally 'exchanging or twisting one's intestines/bowels', from 換 'to exchange, turn over, invert' + 腸 'intestines, bowels, internal organs', traditionally conceived as the seat of deep emotion and sanity) plus 하다 ('to do, be'). From the visceral image of one's insides churning or flipping upside down, it came to mean losing one's mind with frustration, exasperation, or intense craving.

history.meaning: for one's bowels/insides to turn over; to become deranged or frantic
to go crazy (from frustration/exasperation, or from being madly obsessed with something)

morphemes.meaning: to exchange, invert, turn upside down

환장하다.notes: Has two vivid colloquial uses: (1) exasperation when someone drives you up the wall (아유, 내가 아주 환장하겠네!, 'Ugh, you're driving me crazy!'), and (2) with -에, being crazy/madly obsessed over food, money, or a hobby (고기에 환장하다, 'to go crazy for meat'). Compare 애간장이 녹다 ('one's liver and bowels melt with anxiety').

환하다.etymology: Native/Sino-Korean adjective attested in Middle Korean as 환ㅎᆞ다 ('to be bright, clear, open and wide; to be well-versed in'), traditionally linked either to a native mimetic root 환- ('bright, open') or Sino-Korean 환 (煥, 'shining, brilliant').

history.meaning: to be bright, luminous, wide open
to be bright, well-lit, radiant; to know inside out

활동.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 活 (활, 'living, lively, active, flowing', with the water radical 氵 evoking running water) and 動 (동, 'to move, stir, act', combining 重 'heavy' and 力 'strength'). Literally 'lively movement', it denotes energetic action, organized activities, or an entertainer's active promotional period.

history.meaning: lively movement, physical motion; organized social or professional activity
history.stage: Classical and Modern East Asian Sinitic

history.meaning: activity, operations; a celebrity's promotional cycle or career activity

활동.notes: In K-pop and Korean broadcasting (*프로듀사*), 활동 specifically refers to an artist's promotional cycle for an album or a celebrity's active work in the industry (e.g., 방송 활동을 시작하다, 'to begin broadcast promotions/activities').

활짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb expressing the manner of a door, window, flower, or smile opening wide, brightly, and completely (bright-vowel counterpart of 훌쩍).

history.meaning: wide open, in full bloom, beamingly

홧김.etymology: A hybrid Sino-Korean and native Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 화 (火, 'anger, fiery temper') with the native Korean bound noun 김 ('steam, vapor, breath; warm impulse, momentum, occasion of an action', from Middle Korean 김 'steam, vapor'), linked by the genitive/compounding interfix सा이시옷 (ㅅ), which marks tensification of ㄱ to [ㄲ] ([홷낌] / [확낌]). Literally 'on the rising steam/heat of anger'.

history.meaning: the rising vapor or impulse of anger
in a fit of anger, on the spur of pique (almost always 홧김에)

홧김.notes: Almost always used in the locative-causal phrase 홧김에 ('in a fit of anger / out of spite in the heat of the moment', e.g., 홧김에 사표를 냈다, 'I handed in my resignation in a fit of anger'). Compare 술김에 ('under the influence/momentum of alcohol') and 잠결에 ('half-asleep').

rootFamily.gloss: under the influence of alcohol, tipsy impulse

황금빛.etymology: Hybrid compound uniting Sino-Korean 황금 (黃金, 'yellow gold') with native Korean 빛 ('light, gleam, colour').
황금빛.notes: Korean productively attaches native 빛 to nouns to describe warm luminous hues (보랏빛, 은빛, 황금빛).

황동.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 황동 (黃銅), joining 황 (黃, 'yellow') and 동 (銅, 'copper, bronze'), literally 'yellow copper' (i.e. brass, an alloy of copper and zinc).

history.meaning: yellow copper -> brass
brass

cognates.meaning: finely sliced raw fish or meat (archaic/literary namasu)
finely sliced raw fish or meat (ancient cuisine)

회.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from Hanja 膾 (회, 'finely sliced raw fish or meat'), composed of the flesh radical 月 (肉) and 會 ('to gather, meet'). In Classical Chinese (famously in Confucius's *Analects* 10.8: 膾不厭細, 'sliced raw meat/fish cannot be cut too fine'), 膾 denoted thinly sliced raw fish or meat; while the dish largely faded in China after the Song–Ming dynasties, Korean culinary tradition preserved both the dish and the character 膾 (회) for raw sliced fish (생선회) and raw beef (육회).

history.meaning: finely sliced raw fish or meat dressed with condiments
thinly sliced raw fish (생선회), seafood, or meat (육회)

morphemes.meaning: finely sliced raw fish or meat

회.notes: Don't confuse culinary 회 (膾, 'sliced raw fish') with its frequent homophones 회 (回, 'time, episode, round', as in 드라마 1회 'Episode 1') and 회 (會, 'meeting, association', as in 회식 'company dinner'). In Korean idiom, 회를 치다 literally means 'to slice raw fish' (or figuratively to tear someone apart verbally).

rootFamily.gloss: spicy raw fish salad with vegetables over rice

회사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound of 會 (회, 'to assemble, meet, association') and 社 (사, 'tutelary altar of the soil; society, organized group, guild'). Coined in Meiji-era Japan as 会社 (kaisha) to translate Western commercial 'company, corporation, joint-stock society' and adopted into Korean during the late 19th-century Enlightenment period (개화기), it denotes both a business corporation and, in everyday speech, one's workplace/office.

history.meaning: commercial association, joint-stock company, firm
company, corporation; 'work, the office' in daily conversation

morphemes.meaning: society, organized group, company, shrine of the soil

회사.notes: In everyday Korean, Koreans say 회사에 가다 ('to go to work / the office') or 지금 회사야 ('I'm at work right now') even when working at a broadcasting station (방송사) or public institution rather than a private corporation. Notice that reversing the two characters gives 사회 (社會, 'society').

cognates.meaning: corporate life, life as an office worker

회사생활.etymology: A four-character Sino-Korean compound combining 회사 (會社, 'company, firm, workplace', from 會 'gather, association' + 社 'society, firm') and 생활 (生活, 'living, daily life, existence', from 生 'live, birth' + 活 'lively, active, survive'). It refers to the routines, hierarchy, social dynamics, and culture of life as a salaried employee.

history.meaning: life within a commercial company or modern organization
workplace life, corporate life, office life

회사생활.notes: Often written either spaced (회사 생활) or as a single conceptual unit (회사생활); synonymous with the slightly more formal 직장 생활 (職場生活, 'workplace life'), which is a central theme of Korean office dramas like *프로듀사* and *미생*.

회색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 회색 (灰色), joining 회 (灰, 'ash, ashes') and 색 (色, 'color').

history.meaning: ash color -> gray
gray, grey

회색빛.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 회색 (灰色, 'ash color, gray') + native Korean 빛 ('light, hue, tint, color', Middle Korean 빛).

history.meaning: gray + hue/light
grayish hue, gray tint

회식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 會食, composed of 會 (회, 'to meet, assemble, gather') and 食 (식, 'food, meal, to eat'). Literally meaning 'gathering to eat together', it evolved in modern Korean corporate and organizational culture into the institutionalized practice of after-hours dining and drinking with coworkers.

history.meaning: gathering together to share a meal
company dinner, team get-together over food and drinks

회식.notes: In Korean workplace culture (and constantly in *The Producers*), 회식 is more than just dinner—it is a semi-mandatory team-building ritual involving barbecue, soju, and multiple rounds (1차, 2차).

cognates.meaning: member of an organization or club

회원.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 會員, formed from 會 (회, 'association, society, club, gathering') and the personal/membership suffix 員 (원, 'member, personnel, official'). Adopted across East Asian modern lexicon to denote an enrolled member of an association, club, or service.

history.meaning: person belonging to an assembly or society
registered member of a club, organization, or website

morphemes.meaning: member, person belonging to a group (員)

회원.notes: The Sino-Korean suffix -원 (員) productively forms nouns denoting people by role, such as 사원 (company employee), 점원 (shop clerk), and 공무원 (civil servant).

회의.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 會議, combining 會 (회, 'to assemble, meet together') and 議 (의, 'to deliberate, discuss, consult'). Attested in Classical Chinese for official court deliberations and popularized in late 19th-century Meiji/East Asian institutional usage for formal meetings and conferences.

history.meaning: assembling to deliberate on affairs
formal meeting, conference, or production session

회의.notes: Beware the homophone 회의 (懷疑, 'doubt, skepticism'), which uses different Hanja; in workplace dramas like *The Producers*, 회의 almost always refers to a staff or planning meeting (기획 회의).

cognates.word: 会議室 (かいぎしつ, kaigishitsu)

회의실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 會議室, formed by suffixing 室 (실, 'room, chamber, office') to 會議 (회의, 'meeting, conference', from 會 'gather' + 議 'deliberate'). Literally 'meeting room', a transparent architectural term across modern East Asian workplaces.

history.meaning: chamber designated for deliberations and meetings
conference room, boardroom

회의실.notes: The suffix -실 (室) attaches to almost any noun to name a specialized room: 대기실 (waiting/green room), 편집실 (editing room), 사무실 (office), 화장실 (restroom).

회중.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 懷中, combining 懷 (품 회, 'bosom, inner fold of a coat') and 中 (가운데 중, 'inside'). Coined when compact European instruments arrived in East Asia that could be tucked inside one's coat breast rather than mounted on walls or ship decks, it survives chiefly in 회중시계 ('pocket watch'), 회중전등 ('flashlight'), and 회중 나침반 ('pocket compass').
회중.notes: Used attributively before portable precision items.

cognates.meaning: speaking horizontally and vertically; talking at random or eloquently
cognates.word: 橫說豎說 / 横说竖说 (héngshuōshùshuō)

횡설수설하다.etymology: Hybrid verb derived from the four-character Sino-Korean idiom 橫說竪說 (횡설수설) plus the native light verb 하다 ('to do'). Composed of 橫 (횡, 'horizontal, crosswise, sideways'), 說 (설, 'speech, to speak'), 竪 (수, 'vertical, upright'), and 說 (설, 'to speak')—literally 'speaking sideways and speaking lengthwise', hence babbling incoherently without logic or direction.

history.meaning: speaking both crosswise and lengthwise; unbridled or disjointed talk
to ramble incoherently, babble nonsense (especially when flustered or drunk)

횡설수설하다.notes: A classic four-character idiom (사자성어) used in everyday speech to describe someone rambling nonsensically due to drunkenness, panic, or sleep deprivation.

효과.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 效果, uniting 效 (본받을 효 / 효험 효, 'proven efficacy, working result') and 果 (열매 과, 'fruit, tangible outcome'). Literally 'the fruit borne by an action', 효과 is the standard Korean noun for whether a remedy, method, or protective coating actually works.
효과.notes: Commonly pairs with 있다 ('be effective, work') and 보다 ('see results').

cognates.word: 後 (ご, go / あと, ato)

후.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and bound temporal postposition from 後 (후, 'behind, rear, after, later, subsequent'). In Classical Chinese it denoted spatial rear position as well as temporal succession; in Korean it functions independently after time expressions or clauses (e.g., 10분 후 '10 minutes from now') and as a prolific prefix in Sino-Korean compounds.

history.meaning: behind in space; later in time; posterity
after, later, from now (following a time noun or -ㄴ/은 clause)

후.notes: Interchangeable in many temporal contexts with the native Korean word 뒤 ('behind, after'), e.g., 조금 후에 = 조금 뒤에 ('a little later / after a short while').

후기.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous compounds: (1) 후기 (後記, 'postscript, afterword, user/customer review written after an experience', from 후 後 'after, behind' + 기 記 'record, note'); (2) 후기 (後期, 'latter period, late phase', from 후 後 'later' + 기 期 'period').

history.form: 後記 (postscript, review) / 後期 (latter period)
history.meaning: note written afterward; second/later period
review, impression, postscript; late period

후배.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun from 後輩, combining 後 (후, 'after, later') and 輩 (배, 'generation, cohort, rank, class of people'—originally rows of carriages). Literally 'those of a later cohort', denoting someone who entered a school, profession, or organization after oneself.

history.meaning: people of a subsequent generation or later cohort
junior colleague, underclassman, younger member in a field

후배.notes: Paired with 선배 (先輩, senior) and 동기 (同期, same-year peer), 후배 defines the strict vertical hierarchy of Korean schools and broadcasting stations, often addressed affectionately or formally as 후배님.

rootFamily.gloss: peer of the same generation/age (同輩)

cognates.meaning: waiting to fill a vacancy; candidate, alternate

후보.etymology: Sino-Korean noun from 候補, composed of 候 (후, 'to wait, watch for, attend upon') and 補 (보, 'to mend, supplement, fill a vacancy'). Originally a bureaucratic term in imperial China and Joseon Korea for an official who had passed examinations and was 'waiting to fill a vacant post', it broadened in modern usage to any election candidate, award nominee, or backup contender.

history.meaning: awaiting appointment to a vacant official post
candidate, nominee, contender, reserve player

morphemes.meaning: to supplement, mend, fill a post (補)

후보.notes: Used across politics (대통령 후보 'presidential candidate'), sports (후보 선수 'bench/substitute player'), and entertainment awards or casting shortlists.

후지다.etymology: Native Korean colloquial adjective (후지- + -다). Originally a dialectal and slang term denoting something worn out, sunken, or inferior in quality, likely connected to the sound-symbolic root 후무리다 / 후줄근하다 ('limp, baggy, worn-out') or dialectal forms for hollow/inferior things. Now standard colloquial Korean for 'shabby, tacky, low-end, or outdated'.

history.meaning: dialectal/colloquial: sunken, worn-out, inferior in quality
shabby, crummy, low-end, outdated (of facilities, gear, or ideas)

후지다.notes: Very common in casual speech (often in the modifier form 후진, e.g., 후진 컴퓨터 'a crummy old computer'); avoid confusing the modifier 후진 (from 후지다) with Sino-Korean 후진 (後進, 'backward/developing' or 'reversing a car').

rootFamily.gloss: shabby, poor, run-down (modest/native-Sino blend feel) 변변찮다 synonym group

후회하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from the Sino-Korean noun 後悔 (후회, 'regret, remorse') and the native verb 하다 ('to do'). 後悔 combines 後 (후, 'afterwards, later') and 悔 (회, 'to repent, regret, feel remorse'), literally 'feeling remorse after the fact'.

history.meaning: remorse felt after an action has already been taken
to repent, regret one's past deeds
to regret, rue, feel sorry about

후회하다.notes: Unlike 아쉬워하다 (feeling wistful/sad about a missed opportunity), 후회하다 specifically expresses remorse over a choice or mistake one made.

rootFamily.gloss: free of regret, without remorse (後悔 없다) / 회한 (悔恨, bitter regret)

훅.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic/mimetic adverb (의성어·의태어). Originally imitative of a sudden strong puff of breath or gust of warm air (cf. 후 'puff of breath' + intensive final stop -ㄱ), it extended metaphorically to describe any action or sensation that rushes in, leaps forward, or passes by in a sudden flash ('whoosh, in a flash').

history.meaning: with a sudden puff of breath or burst of heat/scent
in a flash, whoosh, suddenly and intensely (coming close or passing by)

morphemes.meaning: mimetic root: sudden puff, gust, or rapid lunge

훅.notes: Frequently pairs with verbs of motion or emotion: 훅 들어오다 ('to come right into someone's personal space / catch someone off guard emotionally') and 훅 가다 ('to pass in a flash' or slang 'to be ruined/swept away instantly').

rootFamily.gloss: gently blowing a puff of breath (lighter vowel/coda counterpart)
in sudden repeated gusts or puffs; flaring up
suddenly rising heat or emotion (vowel-alternant intensive)

훈남.etymology: Early 2000s Korean internet and media blend (신조어) combining the first syllable of 훈훈하다 (from Sino-Korean 熏熏, 'warm, heartwarming, genial') with the Sino-Korean bound noun 남 (男, 'man, male'). Coined to describe a man whose appeal comes not necessarily from sculpted celebrity features (꽃미남), but from a warm, kind, and comforting aura that makes others feel good.

history.meaning: heartwarming + man (blend coined in 2000s Korean internet culture)
warm, charming, handsome guy next door

훈남.notes: Contrasts with 미남 (美男, 'classically handsome man') and 차도남 ('cold urban man'); its female counterpart is 훈녀 (훈훈한 여자).

훈훈하다.etymology: Hybrid adjective formed from the reduplicated Sino-Korean root 훈훈 (熏熏, from 熏 'warm vapor, smoke, fragrance rising, to warm gently') plus the native adjective-forming verb 하다. Originally describing mildly warm, balmy air or gentle heat, it developed a prominent figurative sense of 'heartwarming, congenial, and pleasing to look at'.

history.meaning: balmy, gently warm (of weather or rising warmth)
balmy and warm; heartwarming, genial, wholesome (of atmosphere, news, or appearance)
